trees.name: The Wild Service Tree of Moesgård
trees.age: up to about 145 years (2010 register estimate)
trees.access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
trees.transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park east of the manor buildings

best_time.label: October, when the crown turns deep crimson

trees.story:
Denmark's largest wild service tree grows in a museum park, and it is a species most Danes could not name. The national tree register holds it twice. A 2010 report called it presumably the largest wild service tree in Denmark and possibly in Europe. A second surveyor came back in 2022, measured it properly and recorded it as simply alive: 17.5 metres tall, 1.38 metres through the trunk, and 4.33 metres around when the tape is dropped to knee height, because the stem splits into two and then several more about a metre up. Both entries carry the same coordinates, so this is one tree filed twice rather than a pair.

Sorbus torminalis is scarce this far north and rarely gets near this size. Its Danish name, tarmvridrøn, and its Latin one both point at the same old use of the fruit, a remedy for gripes and colic. The berries are hard and brown and only edible once frost has softened them, and in October the whole crown turns deep crimson, which is the other reason people hunt the species out.

Danish Wikipedia's article on the species names this park as the home of the country's largest specimen, which supports the register, though the claim may trace back to the same original observation rather than a second measurement. The register rates it nationally noteworthy, its top tier, and put a maximum age of about 145 years on it in 2010.

trees.name: The Silver Fir by Moesgård's Small Cemetery
trees.access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
trees.transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park
trees.story:
Forty and a half metres of silver fir stand at the far edge of Moesgård's park, over a graveyard that belongs to a family rather than a parish. The burial ground was begun in 1870 by the Dahls, who then owned the manor, walled with a low stone fence and screened by planting. In 1926 fourteen graves were moved into it from Søndre Kirkegård in Aarhus when that cemetery was cleared. The fir stands beside them.

The height is the point. A surveyor recorded it in March 2022 at 40.5 metres, 3.91 metres round, alive and healthy. That is a serious size for Abies alba anywhere, and an unusual one in Denmark, where the species is a planted guest from the mountains of central Europe rather than a native. No source records its age. The register leaves the field empty, and so does this page.

Silver fir carries its cones upright on the upper branches, standing on the limbs like candles, and they fall apart scale by scale where they grow instead of dropping whole. You will not find one intact on the ground under this tree, however long you look. The compensation is that everything worth seeing is forty metres over your head, which is a fair excuse to stand still for a while in a quiet corner of the park.

trees.name: The Hornbeam of Moesgård
trees.access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
trees.transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park
trees.story:
The surveyor who measured this hornbeam filed a small complaint along with the numbers: a fine tree, but it stands a little in the shade of some plane trees. He recorded it in March 2022 at 19 metres tall and 2.69 metres round, alive and healthy, and rated it regionally noteworthy.

Nineteen metres is a lot of hornbeam. The species usually reads as a hedge or a clipped avenue, because that is what people do to it: it takes cutting better than almost anything and comes back denser each time. Left alone it makes a tall tree with a fluted, muscled trunk that looks poured rather than grown, and wood so hard that Europe used it for cogwheels, mill gearing and butchers' blocks until metal took the work over. The Danish name, avnbøg, files it with the beeches it is not related to.

It stands on the north side of the eastern end of Moesgård's park, the half laid out as a landscape garden with its trees set clear of one another. Only the tree register carries it, with a GPS position and a photograph, and no source anywhere gives it an age. Take the shade note as a tip: come when the sun is low and behind you, and the trunk does the work.

trees.name: The Black Locust on Moesgård's Mound
trees.access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
trees.transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story:
A dead crown is not usually a reason to walk anywhere. This black locust has one, and it stands on a mound somebody built, which between them make it the strangest thing in the park. It is 4.98 metres around and 15.5 metres tall, and when the tree register surveyed it in March 2022 the verdict was alive but weak, with a large part of the crown dead and the tree weakened by age.

Read that girth carefully. Black locust grows fast and thickens early, so five metres of trunk means far less here than the same figure would on an oak. The species is North American, brought to Europe in the early seventeenth century and named after Jean Robin, gardener to the French kings, and it arrived in Danish parks as an exotic with rot-proof timber and hanging white flowers in early summer. It also breaks. Brittle wood under a heavy crown is why old locusts end up looking like this one.

The mound is man-made, the register says, though no source names who raised it or when. And that survey is four years old now, so a tree already shedding its crown then may have shed more since. Worth knowing before you go, and worth telling us what you find when you get there.

trees.name: The Happy Pig (Den Glade Gris)
trees.access: Free, public forest (Skåde Skov / Moesgård Skov), open access
trees.transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus towards Moesgaard Museum, then a walk into Skåde Skov towards Ørnereden (roughly 1.2km north of the main Moesgård tree cluster, along forest paths)

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are gone and the twisted frame shows

trees.story:
Somebody looked at this beech and saw a pig. The name stuck: Den Glade Gris, the Happy Pig. It grows in Skåde Skov near Ørnereden, up the forest paths north of Moesgård, and the only official record of it is one register entry sent in by email in July 2020, carrying a GPS position and a description of its growth form: twisted and stunted.

That is the entire file. No height, no girth, no age, no planting date. What there is instead is a shape, and shapes like this are made rather than born. A beech browsed by animals, snapped by snow or bent by wind while it is young grows up with its trunk wandering, and once the habit is set it keeps it for the rest of a long life. Danish woods are full of straight beech grown for timber, which is exactly why the crooked ones get named.

It reads best in January and February. A beech in leaf hides its own frame, and the frame is the whole point of this one. If you find it, tell us how big it has got and what it actually looks like to you, because nobody has ever measured it and one person's pig is another person's dragon.

trees.name: The Women's Oak of Viby (Kvindeegen)
trees.access: Free, open access, public roadside space opposite Viby Church
trees.transport: Viby J station (Aarhus Letbane light rail and regional trains), short walk to Viby Church on Kirkevej

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Danish women voted for the first time in 1915. The year after, the Viby branch of Dansk Kvindesamfund planted an oak to mark it, on a patch of ground the municipality handed over opposite the entrance to the churchyard. It is still there, and still called Kvindernes Eg, the Women's Oak.

It is the youngest tree on this list and the only one planted for a reason anybody bothered to write down. Trees of this kind went in across Denmark after the constitutional change of 5 June 1915, which gave the vote to women and to servants at a stroke. This one has stood through Viby's growth from a parish outside Aarhus into a suburb inside it; the light rail now stops a short walk from the church gate.

The national tree register logged it in 2008 as alive and regionally noteworthy, then made a mess of its age. The file says 110 years, and also that the figure applies to 2008, which would put the planting in 1898, eighteen years before it happened. The planting year is the part two independent sources agree on, so count from 1916: about 110 years now, which is roughly the age at which an oak stops reading as a young tree and starts reading as a fixture.

trees.name: The Oak of Skåde
trees.access: Free, visible and reachable from the public road (Elmehøjvej); it stands at the roadside, not on private land
trees.transport: Bus lines serving Skåde/Emiliedalsvej (e.g. 18 or 100) from central Aarhus, then roughly 10-15 minute walk along Elmehøjvej

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Danish protection orders normally cover coastlines, moors and the ground around churches. In 1965 one was placed on a single oak at the side of Elmehøjvej. The national register of protected sites still carries it, with directions that end by telling you the oak stands on the left of the road.

It is not a giant by the standards of protected oaks elsewhere in Europe. A surveyor put it at 16 metres tall and 3.76 metres round in 2019, alive and in good order. Nobody has dated it. An open-grown pedunculate oak takes a long time to lay down that much trunk, which points at something between one and a half and two and a half centuries, but that is arithmetic rather than a record, and no source gives a planting year.

The protection date is the more useful number. In 1965 somebody in Skåde thought a roadside tree was worth writing into law, at a time when the suburb around it was filling in, and sixty years later it is still at the kerb. That is not how most roadside oaks end up.

Stand at the verge and look at the crown rather than the trunk. A tree grown in the open spreads sideways because nothing has ever crowded it out of the light, and this one has had all the room it wanted.

trees.name: Ficus Gabriel Miró II
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, the square between the Ayuntamiento and Parque de Canalejas
trees.access: Free, open public plaza in the city centre, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 10 minutes on foot; also served by city bus lines 2, 3, 5, 12 near Federico Soto
trees.story:
Local press calls this the largest ficus in Spain's catalogue. The canopy is what earns the claim: 40.5 metres across on the Valencian register's own figures, thrown over a city square, on a trunk 10.65 metres round and a tree 25.3 metres tall. It is the thickest of the four Moreton Bay figs on Plaza Gabriel Miró and the widest of them by some margin.

Its age is the part nobody has settled. Todoalicante puts it at about 120 years, a figure the paper ties to that measured canopy. A rounder 170 also circulates, with no measurement behind it and no particular one of these four trees attached to it, so 120 is the number this page uses.

Ficus macrophylla comes from the east coast of Australia, and at this size it stops behaving like a street tree. Aerial roots come down from the limbs, thicken where they reach soil and fuse into the base, which is why the city has fenced the root plates of the figs on this square. That, and the fact that people climb them to be photographed.

The square has had a hard recent year. In September 2025 a centenarian elm broke and came down at the San Fernando corner of it, and the city ordered a review of every monumental tree on its books.

trees.name: Ficus Gabriel Miró IV
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, the square between the Ayuntamiento and Parque de Canalejas
trees.access: Free, open public plaza in the city centre, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 10 minutes on foot
trees.story:
Twenty-six metres is tall for a fig. This is the tallest of the four Moreton Bay figs on Plaza Gabriel Miró, 26.6 metres on the Valencian register, with a trunk 10.32 metres round, and it stands on its own at the southern end of the square, about forty metres from the other three.

Nobody has dated it. What exists instead is the square. El Español puts the present layout at 1918, when the sculpture known as La Aguadora was installed, and treats that as roughly when these figs went into the ground. That is a reading of the setting rather than a record of a planting, so the honest figure is over a century, not a year.

The species is Australian, from the wet coastal forests of Queensland and New South Wales, where it germinates high in the crown of another tree and lets its roots down the host's trunk to the soil. In a Spanish square it has to start at ground level like everything else, and it compensates from above: limbs that run out horizontally, aerial roots dropping from them, props thickening into a second and third trunk.

El Español rates the Gabriel Miró group as probably the most notable ficus specimens in the country, with canopies over twenty-five metres. This one covers 31.5 metres of pavement.

trees.name: Ficus Gabriel Miró I
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, the square between the Ayuntamiento and Parque de Canalejas
trees.access: Free, open public plaza in the city centre, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 10 minutes on foot
trees.story:
The register calls this one number I, which turns out to be a filing decision rather than a ranking: of the four figs on the square it has the third-thickest trunk. Seven and a half metres round, 23 metres tall, a crown of 33 metres. In most European cities that is the biggest tree in town. Here it is the middle of the group.

No source dates it. The square took its present shape in 1918 and its figs are described together as over a century old, which is as close as the record comes to a number for this one.

What it does have is the ground under it. A mature Ficus macrophylla lifts its roots into buttresses and lets more down from the branches, so the base is a low tangle of grey props rather than a trunk with a clean edge to put a tape around. The 7.6 metres is a measurement of that tangle, taken where it is tightest.

Alicante has decided these trees are worth explaining. The city has fenced their root plates, because visitors climb them for photographs, and installed plaques beside them, making this square one of five signposted stops on a route through its monumental ficus.

trees.name: Ficus Gabriel Miró III
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, the square between the Ayuntamiento and Parque de Canalejas
trees.access: Free, open public plaza in the city centre, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 10 minutes on foot
trees.story:
The slimmest trunk on the square carries the second-widest crown on it. The Valencian register puts this fig at 6.4 metres round, the least of the four, and 19 metres tall, also the least, and then gives it a canopy 35 metres across. The other three went up. This one went sideways.

That is worth standing under. A low, wide Moreton Bay fig brings its horizontal limbs within a few metres of your head, and the aerial roots it drops from them hang in the space you are walking through. Where one reaches soil it thickens, takes weight, and in time stops being a root at all and becomes part of the trunk.

The Valencian catalogue treats each of these four figs as a monument in its own right, with its own entry and its own measurements rather than one line for the group. That reflects what a visitor actually finds on the square: four large trees of one species, none of them a copy of the others, one tall and narrow, one enormous in every direction, one middling and one that spread out at head height.

No planting date survives for this one. The four are described together as over a century old, and that is the honest range.

trees.name: Ficus del Passeig de Canalejas
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, between the Explanada de España and the sports marina
trees.access: Free, public waterfront park (Parque de Canalejas), always open, no gate found
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 12-15 minutes on foot; a few minutes' walk from the Explanada de España and the sports marina
trees.story:
Eleven and a half metres round the base, and nothing else on this walk comes close. The Ficus del Passeig de Canalejas is one of the few trees in the Valencian catalogue carrying a name of its own instead of a number, and the measurements back it up: 11.59 metres of girth, 20.8 metres of height, a crown 38.7 metres across the paseo.

The park around it was laid out in 1886 to a design by the architect González Altés, on the strip between the Explanada de España and what is now the sports marina. The Gabriel Miró square a few minutes north took its present shape in 1918; this ground was drawn thirty years earlier, and its figs have had the time to show it. Trunks that twist and fold, aerial roots let down from the limbs and grown thick enough to stand as second and third trunks, surface roots running out in slabs between the benches. One local account puts it plainly: these trees have accompanied several generations of Alicante residents.

Nobody has dated this one individually. The register measures rather than dates, and the park's Moreton Bay figs are described collectively as over a hundred years old. By El Español's count six of them stand here, alongside eleven Ficus nitida, which is reason enough to walk the paseo slowly.

trees.name: Ficus of Parque de Canalejas
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, between the Explanada de España and the sports marina
trees.access: Free, public park/plaza area, no gate found
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 10 minutes on foot
trees.story:
Seven metres of trunk holding up thirteen metres of tree. That ratio is the reason to stop here: the Valencian catalogue measures this fig at 7.05 metres round and only 13 metres tall, with a crown of 16, so from the path it reads as a wide grey mass at ground level with a fairly modest tree on top of it.

On a Moreton Bay fig the trunk is not really one stem. Aerial roots come down from the limbs, meet the soil, thicken, take load and fuse into the column, so a girth figure on this species measures the result of a process rather than a single stem that grew outwards. Seven metres of it is a lot of process.

The register lists this tree without a name, as a monumental tree of local interest, one of four standing within about twenty-five metres of each other. Nobody has dated it. What it has is the age the park has: Parque de Canalejas was laid out in 1886 and its Moreton Bay figs are described as more than a century old, which is a range rather than a birthday.

The park is free, open and a couple of minutes' walk from the four big figs on Plaza Gabriel Miró.

trees.name: Ficus of Parque de Canalejas (west)
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, between the Explanada de España and the sports marina
trees.access: Free, public park/plaza area, no gate found
trees.transport: TRAM Luceros stop (lines L1-L4), roughly 10 minutes on foot
trees.story:
Two registered figs stand about twenty metres apart here and they are visibly not the same tree. This is the taller one, 19 metres against its neighbour's 13, on the slimmer trunk, 6.35 metres round against 7.05, and it carries the wider crown at 21 metres. Same species, same park, same century, opposite habits: one built downwards into bulk, this one went up.

Both are listed in the Valencian catalogue as monumental trees of local interest, and neither is given a name there. So this one is identified the way a visitor identifies it, by where it stands and what it looks like, and no source anywhere puts a date on it. Parque de Canalejas was laid out in 1886 and its Moreton Bay figs are described as over a hundred years old, which is the range that honestly applies.

What the species offers at this size is the underside. Horizontal limbs, aerial roots hanging free of the ground with others already thick enough to carry weight, and surface roots running out across the soil in low ridges. It is an evergreen from the Australian east coast doing in a Mediterranean park what it does in a subtropical forest, minus the host tree it would normally have started in.

trees.name: The Ficus de Benalúa
trees.access: Free, in a small public garden beside the health centre's entrance, between Calle San Agatángelo and the building; no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: About 10 minutes' walk from Alicante's main railway station (Alacant Terminal); Estación-Aguilera and Mercado de Benalúa bus stops are closer
trees.story:
The oldest fig in Alicante grew from a sapling taken before 1860 from the city's Agricultural Research plot, ground that is now the Jardín Botánico. It was replanted in the garden of a private house, the Chalet de Grau, and never moved again, even as everything around it did: the chalet became a shelter for minors, the shelter closed and was demolished in 1998, and the plot sat empty for years before the city decided to build a health centre on it.

The first plans put a car park under its crown. Neighbours in Benalúa organised against it, and the city moved the twenty-four parking spaces to the far side of the building instead, folding the tree into a small garden by the entrance. It was the tree's second rescue. An earlier mayor had once proposed lifting it whole to Plaza de Navarro Rodrigo, a few streets away, a transplant residents fought off as too risky for a tree already past its first century.

The city's own figure for the trunk is a startling 23.7 metres round, measured over the fused apron of aerial roots that a Ficus macrophylla grows once it settles in for a century. The regional government's monumental tree register, which measures the clean trunk beneath the roots, gives 14.69 metres instead, still the widest on any Alicante page. Either way, at over 150 years old, it is the oldest and thickest fig the city has.

trees.name: The Fig of Plaza de Navarro Rodrigo
trees.access: Free, open public square with playground, fountain and kiosk; no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: About 10-12 minutes' walk from Alicante's main railway station (Alacant Terminal); Mercado de Benalúa bus stop is closer
trees.story:
Plaza de Navarro Rodrigo is one of Benalúa's oldest squares, laid out on land the Marqués de Benalúa donated to the city and named for the nineteenth-century politician and writer who represented Alicante in parliament. A fountain, a children's playground and a kiosk share the square with this one Indian laurel fig, its canopy wide enough, 27 metres across, that it shades most of the gardens on its own.

The tree is one of six sites across Alicante where the city has put up an information panel on its ficus population, alongside Plaza Gabriel Miró and Parque de Canalejas, warning against climbing the aerial roots or damaging the bark. Unlike the two celebrity figs a kilometre away, this one carries no recorded age at all. The Valencian government's register lists its measurements and its protected status and nothing else.

It nearly had company. A former mayor once proposed moving the giant Ficus de Benalúa here from its garden on Calle San Agatángelo, a transplant Benalúa's own residents fought off as too dangerous for a tree already past its first century. The plan died, the Benalúa fig never left its garden, and Navarro Rodrigo kept its one fig standing quietly among the flower beds instead.

trees.name: The Ficus of Avenida de Salamanca
trees.neighbourhood: Ensanche, beside Alicante's main railway station
trees.access: Free, on the public forecourt of Avenida de Salamanca outside the main entrance of Alicante's railway station, no gate or opening hours. The neighbouring Plaza de la Estrella is under redevelopment as of April 2026; this tree stands on the station forecourt itself, outside that fenced area.
trees.transport: Directly outside Alicante's main railway station, Alacant Terminal / Estacion de Renfe
trees.story: Alicante's monumental-fig register carries a category most of its other trees do not: generic protection rather than the individually named local-interest status the city centre's figs hold. Read alone that could suggest an afterthought, but three independent sources put it plainly, this fig grows on the public forecourt outside the main entrance of Alicante's principal railway station, one of six sites the city itself chose for an information panel on its monumental figs. At 6.9 metres round and 28 metres tall, it is the largest of three planted together at the station facade, thick enough that most visitors stepping off a train would notice it without knowing to look. A 2026 report on the neighbouring Plaza de la Estrella redevelopment, the future entrance to a planned 2.1 kilometre green corridor through the city, calls the fig population here century old and says the trees will be kept as the new plaza's anchor rather than removed for it. No source dates this specific tree, so that stays a fact about the intersection rather than a number for the page. It stands close enough to Benalúa's two figs to fold into the same southern outing, a few minutes further down the same stretch of the city.

trees.name: The Fig of Paseito de Ramiro
trees.neighbourhood: Sant Roc, facing the Postiguet beach
trees.access: Free, open public park (Paseito de Ramiro), no gate or opening hours; part of the city's own official 'Red de Senderos Urbanos' walking route
trees.transport: Facing Playa del Postiguet on Avenida Juan Bautista Lafora; about 15-18 minutes on foot from Plaza Gabriel Miro (the main city-centre cluster); seafront bus stops near the Postiguet/Marina are closer
trees.story:
A fig here has a crown 27 metres across, wide enough that its neighbour, growing nineteen metres away, is usually mistaken for the same tree. Alicante's regional tree register counts them as two separate Indian laurel figs, Ficus microcarpa, 2.67 and 2.85 metres round, 13 and 16 metres tall, and treats their shared plot in Paseito de Ramiro, facing Postiguet beach, as one small park rather than two addresses.

The city's own printed walking route through the old town is the only source that puts an age on them at all: about 80 years, tucked into an itinerary that also notes a 56-metre stretch of 16th-century city wall running through the same park. The ground has an older history than the figs do. It was once the medina's own souk, and in the early 20th century became one of Spain's first outdoor schools, named for the historian Rafael Altamira. Neither fact dates the trees themselves, only the plot they grew up in.

The park sits on the city's official Red de Senderos Urbanos walking route, a few minutes from the beach, free and open with no gate.

trees.name: The Lime by the Mill of Piet
trees.age: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.access: Free. Public park on the old bastions, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Alkmaar station, on the bolwerk near the Vrouwenstraat.

best_time.label: July, when the flowers scent the whole slope

trees.story:
The register says this is the thickest lime on the bastions, which is a small crown and a well-defined one, because the bastions are a closed set.

Alkmaar's walls and bastions were built in 1565, at the height of the fortification boom that preceded the revolt against Spain, and this is where the city's luck comes in: most Dutch towns pulled their earthworks down and sold the land, and Alkmaar largely did not. In 1870 Louis Paul Zocher, of the family that laid out half the parks in the country, converted the surviving works into a city park in the landscape style. Curved walks, water, planted slopes, all of it on a defensive earthwork.

The lime went in at the end of the nineteenth century, so it belongs to Zocher's park rather than to the fortress.

Bastion soil is a genuine advantage. It is deep, artificial and undisturbed, which is more than any street can offer, and that is part of why the biggest trees in this city are all standing on a rampart.

It is near the mill called the molen van Piet. In July the flowers are heavy and the whole slope smells of them.

trees.name: The Willow of the Veenbos
trees.age: roughly 175 to 225 years, from the register's wide planting band of 1800 to 1850
trees.access: Free. Stands in open polder land at Grootschermer.
trees.transport: About 10 km southeast of Alkmaar, at Grootschermer in the Schermer polder.

best_time.label: January, when the pollard shape stands out against the polder

trees.story:
A willow that reaches two centuries has almost always been cut, and cut hard, over and over.

White willow is a fast, soft, short-lived tree left to itself: it puts on height quickly, gets heavy, splits down the middle at forty or fifty years and collapses. The ones that get old are the ones that were pollarded, cut back to the same point on the trunk every three to eight years for the withies. Doing that keeps the crown light, keeps the tree from tearing itself apart, and produces the shape everybody recognises from a Dutch polder: a short fat trunk, usually hollow, with a mop of thin straight rods on top.

So the age band of 1800 to 1850 on this tree is really a record of how many times somebody came back with a saw.

It stands in the Veenbos in an old polder at Grootschermer, north of the city, in exactly the landscape the species belongs to: peat, ditches, water at the surface, and no shelter at all.

Go in winter. A pollarded willow in a flat wet polder under a low sun is one of the sights this country actually does better than anywhere else.

trees.name: The Plane of the Alkmaarderhout
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Public wood and park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km southwest of Alkmaar station, in the Alkmaarderhout.
trees.story:
The city decided to plant this wood in 1607, which makes it older than most of what Europeans think of as parks.

What followed was not peaceful. Part of the Hout was cut down again during the siege of Alkmaar in 1672, the disaster year, when the Dutch Republic was attacked from three sides at once and a besieged town needed wood far more than it needed shade. From the middle of the eighteenth century there are winding rococo lanes, which are still traceable. Most of the trees standing here now are twentieth century, from when Leonard Springer made a design for the whole wood and the deer park was built.

This plane, banded 1850 to 1860, is older than that and is now the oldest tree in the Alkmaarderhout, a position it inherited last summer. The beech that held it, nearly seven metres round, came down in the Poly storm of 2023.

It stands between the flower clock and the music garden on the Wilhelminalaan.

Bark flaking in cream and olive, big lobed leaves, and hard spiky seed balls hanging on their stalks through the winter.

trees.name: The Elm of the Munnikenbolwerk
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Public park on the old bastions, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Alkmaar station, behind De Vest.
trees.story:
Any old elm in the Netherlands is a survivor, and this one has had about a century and a half of chances to die.

Dutch elm disease is named after the Dutch scientists who identified the fungus in the 1920s, not after the country's elms, though those suffered as badly as any. The first wave killed a great many trees between the wars. The second strain, far more aggressive, arrived in the 1970s and took most of what was left, emptying avenues across the whole country in a decade. It spreads through bark beetles and through root grafts between neighbouring trees, which is why lines of elms died in sequence and isolated ones sometimes did not.

Standing alone on a bastion behind a cultural centre is, in that light, a good address.

It was planted between 1880 and 1890 on the Munnikenbolwerk, one of the 1565 works that Zocher turned into park in 1870.

The leaf tells you: distinctly lopsided at the base, one side starting lower on the stalk than the other. And elms come into leaf late and hold on late, so this is often the last green thing on the bastion in November.

trees.name: The Plane of the Clarissenbolwerk
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Public park on the old bastions, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Alkmaar station, on the Clarissenbolwerk.
trees.story:
Bastion, water, plane tree. It is a combination the Dutch nineteenth century arrived at repeatedly and it works every time.

The Clarissenbolwerk is one of the 1565 works, named for the Poor Clares whose convent stood nearby, and the moat that made it a defence is what now makes it a view. Zocher's 1870 conversion was built on exactly that logic: the water was already there and had already been shaped, so all a designer had to do was plant the banks and cut the paths.

The plane is from about 1900, a generation after the layout, and it was chosen for what a plane does by the water. The trunk is pale and mottled, so it reads clearly against dark water; the crown is broad enough to overhang; and the species does not mind a high water table, which most large trees do.

It is by the water near Zevenhuizen 23.

The reflection is the thing here. Go on a still morning early enough that the moat has not been disturbed, and look at the flaking bark twice, once up and once down.

trees.name: The Weeping Willow behind Alcmaria
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1 km northeast of Alkmaar station, in the Victoriepark on the Wagenweg.

best_time.label: March, when the bare branches turn yellow-green before leafing

trees.story:
The park is named after a victory, the monument was raised in 1876, and the tree behind it weeps. Somebody enjoyed that.

The Victoriepark dates from 1822, when the North Holland Canal was dug and the city moat between the Friesepoort and the Waterpoort was filled in. The design is probably by J. D. Zocher, of the same family as the man who reworked the bastions. The Victory monument went up in 1876, and in 1903 Leonard Springer laid out the park as it is now.

The willow is from roughly that Springer period, banded 1900 to 1910.

Weeping willow is one of the oldest ornamentals in cultivation and almost every one in Europe is a clone, propagated from cuttings for centuries, because the trees planted here are nearly all female and set no viable seed. A willow twig will root in a bucket of water, which is how a single tree became a continent's worth.

A hundred and twenty is old for the species. Go in March, when the branches turn yellow-green before the leaves come and the whole tree lights up for a fortnight.

trees.name: The Plane of the Walhuis Garden
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free from the street; the garden belongs to the museum, so opening hours apply if you want to stand under it.
trees.transport: About 12 km southeast of Alkmaar, in the old centre of De Rijp.
trees.story:
De Rijp was a whaling and herring town on an island in a lake, and it got rich enough that the merchants' warehouses still stand.

This plane grows in the garden of the museum of Jan Boon junior, the last of a family of shipowners and traders. The museum occupies the Walhuis, a former warehouse of 1725, which stands behind what was Jan Boon's house. A merchant family, a warehouse, a house, a garden, and then nobody left to inherit any of it, which is how a private house becomes a museum.

The tree is later than the buildings, banded 1880 to 1890, so it belongs to the last generation of the family rather than to the trading years.

A plane in a small town garden grows differently from one on a boulevard. There is no competition and no pruning regime, so it spreads rather than reaching, and after a century and a half it tends to be far too large for the plot, which is exactly the effect worth going for.

De Rijp itself is worth the trip regardless. Wooden houses, a seventeenth century town hall, and a street pattern that has not moved.

trees.name: The Catalpa on the City Wall
trees.age: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.access: Free. Public park on the old rampart, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km east of Amersfoort station, on the eastern edge of the old centre.

best_time.label: early July, when the whole crown is in white bells

trees.story:
It is growing on a defensive earthwork built to keep the duke of Gelre out.

Around 1388 Amersfoort put up a second city wall, and put most of the effort into the northeast, because that was the side the trouble was expected from. The wall is largely gone. The bank it stood on is not, and the Plantsoen Oost is what the city made of the remains: a narrow park along the old rampart, planted with big trees whose roots are in six centuries of packed defensive earth.

The catalpa is behind Binnen de Veste 41 and the register singles it out for its flowering, which is fair. Catalpa flowers in late June and early July, weeks after everything else has finished, in upright panicles of white bells with yellow and purple markings inside the throat, and on a mature tree there are hundreds of them at once.

Then it produces the beans. Slender pods up to forty centimetres long hang all winter on the bare tree, which is where the name Indian bean tree comes from, and why this is worth a look in January as well.

Huge heart-shaped leaves, and it comes into leaf later than anything else in the park.

trees.name: The Oak at the Hertekop
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.access: Free. Stands in the verge at a public road junction.
trees.transport: About 3 km south of Amersfoort station, at the Arnhemseweg and Dodeweg crossing.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns drop into the verge

trees.story:
Everything at this crossroads has been replaced except the tree.

It was called the Hertekop after a hunting chalet built here with deer antlers fixed to it. The chalet became an inn. The inn became one of those places everyone in a town knows, where people arranged to meet and where walks and outings started from. Then a southern ring road was laid around Amersfoort, and later joined to a new trunk road running in from Utrecht, and the place changed out of all recognition. The chalet went.

What is here now is a slip road off the A28 and a junction of the Arnhemseweg and the Dodeweg. What is also here is an oak the register bands 1750 to 1800, which was already a substantial tree when the chalet was a going concern, and which is the oldest living thing in Amersfoort.

It is not a beautiful setting and that is exactly the reason to go. Two and a half centuries of a place reorganising itself around a fixed point, and the fixed point is a tree that nobody decided to keep so much as never quite got round to removing.

Park on the Dodeweg rather than trying to stop on the Arnhemseweg.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Xaverius Church
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Free. Stands in the church grounds on 't Zand, reachable in daylight.
trees.transport: About 900 m east of Amersfoort station, on 't Zand.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns copper

trees.story:
The church went up between 1881 and 1883. The beech was already about fifty years old when the first stone was laid.

That is worth pausing on, because the natural assumption at any church with a big tree beside it is that somebody planted the tree to go with the building. Here the register is explicit that the order runs the other way: banded 1830 to 1840, the beech predates the church by half a century, and whoever chose this plot chose a plot with a mature beech on it.

The register also gives it a health note, which is the sort of thing worth passing on. It calls the tree reasonably good for its age and for its position in an urban area, which is faint praise and honest. City copper beeches have a hard time of it: shallow feeding roots under paving, salt, and no leaf litter left to rot back into the soil.

Copper beech is not a species. It is a purple-leaved mutation of the common beech that turns up occasionally in the wild and is then propagated by grafting, so almost every one you meet was chosen by somebody.

In October the purple burns through to copper, and it is the best week to come.

trees.name: The Plane of the Snouckaertlaan
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Free. Street tree on public ground.
trees.transport: About 500 m southeast of Amersfoort station, at the top of the Snouckaertlaan.
trees.story:
A plane of this age on a Dutch street corner is a tree that has survived every plan anyone has had for the ground.

The register bands it 1830 to 1840, which puts it here before the villa quarter around it, before the Utrechtseweg was the road it is now, and before almost any of the buildings it stands among. It has spent nearly two centuries on the corner of the Snouckaertlaan while the city rearranged itself.

Planes get this job because they take punishment better than anything else their size. Compacted soil, roots cut for cables, salt, exhaust, and hard pruning: a plane shrugs at all of it and regrows. The species is a hybrid, probably of the oriental plane and the American sycamore, and it first appeared in European gardens in the seventeenth century as an accident of two exotic trees being planted near each other.

The bark is the giveaway and the reason it works in a city. It sheds in irregular plates, taking whatever has settled on it with it, so the trunk is a camouflage of cream, olive and grey that never blackens.

The seed balls hang on all winter, on stalks, like small hard fruit.

trees.name: The Weeping Silver Lime of Park Schothorst
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Amersfoort station, in Park Schothorst.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers late and the scent carries through the wood

trees.story:
This tree carries two different kinds of leaf and you can find both from where you stand.

It is a grafted weeping lime. The weeping form, 'Petiolaris', cannot be grown from seed and is joined onto an ordinary lime rootstock, which means the tree is really two plants sharing a trunk. Above the graft the branches arch out and hang down, carrying leaves on unusually long stalks that let each one swing and show its white felted underside. Below the graft the rootstock keeps sending up its own shoots, and those carry plain lime leaves on short stalks. Look low on the trunk for ordinary foliage and up into the hanging branches for the long-stalked kind.

The register also notes the root flare, which is unusually pronounced and which people walk over constantly, and adds that the tree seems to be standing up to it. That is an honest way of saying it is being slowly damaged and is winning anyway.

It is at the back of Park Schothorst on the edge of the wood, banded 1830 to 1840.

Come in July. Silver limes flower late, and the scent of one this size carries a long way through a wood.

trees.name: The Copper Beech behind the Amershof
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Visible and reachable from the street at the back of the building.
trees.transport: About 700 m east of Amersfoort station, on the Burgemeester De Widtstraat.

best_time.label: April, when the new leaves open translucent red

trees.story:
It is at the back entrance of a function venue, which is a demotion, and it is the reason to look.

A copper beech planted between 1880 and 1890 was put in by somebody laying out a garden. Nobody plants a purple beech at a service door. So this tree has been through the usual sequence for a city centre: a private garden, a change of ownership, a building extended over most of the ground, and the tree left standing in the leftover space that the extension did not need, which happened to be by the back door.

It is a common story and it accounts for a striking share of the big old trees in any Dutch city centre. The ones that survive are rarely the ones that were treasured. They are the ones that were standing somewhere nobody wanted to build.

What you get is a full grown copper beech in a small hard space on the Burgemeester De Widtstraat, dark and dense and considerably too large for its surroundings, which is a good look at what the species does when nothing restrains it but paving.

Best in October and, for a different reason, in April, when the new leaves come out a translucent red before they darken.

trees.name: The Copper Beech at the Zonnehof
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Reachable on foot from the Zonnehof, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 500 m southeast of Amersfoort station, at the Zonnehof.

best_time.label: late October, at full colour

trees.story:
The Zonnehof is a piece of open ground on the edge of the old centre that the twentieth century got hold of, and this beech was standing before any of it.

Banded 1880 to 1890, it belongs to the villa gardens that lined the Utrechtseweg when this was the smart approach to the city rather than a through road. Those gardens have gone. The beech is on the northeast side of Zonnehof 2, behind the building that fronts the Utrechtseweg, which is to say in the gap between two eras of construction.

Standing under a copper beech in a city is a specific experience worth going out of your way for. The leaves are thin and the purple pigment is a filter rather than a coating, so strong light coming through a mature canopy arrives underneath as a deep wine red. Photographs never get it because a camera corrects it away. You have to be under it, and it wants a bright day.

This one is a short walk from the plane on the Snouckaertlaan and from the beech behind the Amershof, so all three fit into twenty minutes.

The fourth week of October, if you want it at full colour.

trees.name: The Heimanseik
trees.access: Paid entry, part of Artis zoo and botanical garden
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, directly adjacent

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Amsterdam's oldest tree spent its first ninety years alone. This pedunculate oak took root around 1750, nearly a century before Artis existed at all, in a patch of land that later became a zoo built around it rather than the other way round. It is the one tree in the park older than the institution itself, a genuine relic wearing a visitor wristband it never applied for. Orangutans once used its lower limbs as a climbing frame during outdoor play, before keepers decided a 275-year-old oak deserved a rest from primates swinging off its branches. It is named after Eli Heimans, the schoolteacher-naturalist who wrote about it in 1903 and helped make unglamorous urban nature a subject worth admiring in its own right. His name stuck to the tree the way ivy sticks to a wall. Two fungi now grow in its trunk, common enough in oaks this age, and arborists check it every year to judge how much longer the trunk can be trusted to stand. Summer oaks can live seven centuries, so at 275 this one is, technically, still young. Amsterdam's ground rarely lets anything get that far.

trees.name: The Leidsebosje Planes
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram 1/2/12, Leidseplein, 2 min walk
trees.story: When the city needed to widen a bridge in 1925, Amsterdam moved two fully grown plane trees rather than fell them. Residents near Leidseplein had objected loudly enough that engineers floated the two trunks on rafts and winched them several meters sideways, roots and all, to clear space for a new roundabout. A century later both trees have more than doubled their girth: each now measures over seven meters around, the thickest trunks in the city. A small wooden woodcutter figure, carved by an anonymous sculptor in 1989, sits astride one tree appearing to saw off the very branch supporting it. When that branch actually needed removing around 2020, city gardeners moved the sculpture to the other tree rather than let the joke become true. Amsterdam has since proposed the pair for national monument status, an unusual honor for something that is, after all, still just two street trees that once got in the way of traffic planning. They stand a two minute walk from Leidseplein's trams and taxis, indifferent to both.

trees.name: The Vondelpark Poplar
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: Tram 2, Emmastraat, or Tram 3/12, Van Baerlestraat, then 5-10 min walk into the park
trees.story: One of the tallest trees in Amsterdam stands on the edge of a bicycle path, not in a forest. Sources disagree on exactly when this Canadian poplar went into the ground, sometime between the park's founding around 1870 and a specifically documented 1885, but either way it has reached roughly 38.5 meters, taller than most buildings in the surrounding Oud-Zuid neighborhood. Its trunk measures 617 centimeters around, the third thickest in the city behind only the two plane trees in Leidsebosje. Poplars grow fast and die relatively young for a tree, rarely making it past 150 years, so this one is closer to the end of its run than the beginning, and unlike an oak it will not get centuries more to look forward to. Vondelpark's own written guide to its old trees singles this poplar out specifically, distinguishing it from an ash of similar age elsewhere in the park that never got nearly as large. Whether anything in the city stands taller is an open question: the elm at the Oudemanhuispoort is the usual rival and we have found no measurement of it we trust, so if you know one, tell us. Cyclists and joggers pass beneath this crown on Van Eeghenlaan every day without registering that one of the tallest trees in a city of canals and gabled houses is a poplar nobody planted to be a landmark.

trees.name: The Wertheimpark Wingnut
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, 5 min walk

best_time.label: midsummer, when the long green catkins hang down

trees.story: This tree has outlasted the park's own name twice. Wertheimpark was laid out in 1812 and named for the Jewish philanthropist Abraham Carel Wertheim in 1898, a year after his death. In August 1942 Amsterdam's Nazi-appointed mayor renamed it Parktuin to erase the connection, and the wartime name lasted until liberation restored the original in May 1945. The wingnut, a Caucasian species with broad horizontal branches that thicken into plank-like ribs to support their own weight, was already forty years old by the time any of that happened. It now spreads a canopy 24 meters across in a park barely three-quarters of a hectare in size, one of roughly fifteen trees here over a century old. Since 1993 the park has also held Gebroken Spiegels, Amsterdam's memorial to Dutch victims of the Holocaust, and the annual remembrance ceremony takes place within sight of the tree's crown. The municipality classified the wingnut as a monumental tree in 2002, a smaller but no less deliberate act of naming than the ones the park itself went through.

trees.name: The Cycad of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry, Hortus Botanicus ticket required
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, directly outside
trees.story: This plant was already growing in South Africa when Amsterdam's Hortus Botanicus bought it in 1850, and the two have been growing together ever since. It is an Eastern Cape giant cycad, estimated today at around 300 years old, kept potted under glass in the garden's Palm House for the 175 years it has lived here. Cycads as a group have barely changed in 300 million years and survived two mass extinctions that wiped out most of the plant kingdom around them, which makes one specimen's three centuries look almost brief by comparison. A younger female cycad, roughly 200 years old, grows opposite it, and Hortus staff hand-pollinate the two every year because the specific wasps and beetles that pollinate cycads in the wild do not live in an Amsterdam greenhouse. A few meters further into the same glasshouse stands a specimen of Encephalartos woodii, a cycad extinct in the wild since the early 1900s; every plant of that species alive anywhere today is a clone of a single specimen found in South Africa in 1895. The Hortus has been growing rare and difficult plants since 1638, and this cycad has now been part of that project for nearly half the garden's history.

trees.name: The Olifantsiep
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Tram 14, Zeeburgerdijk area
trees.story: One branch of this elm grows so low and so heavy that the city built it a prop, and that branch is where the tree gets its name: early residents thought it looked like an elephant's trunk reaching for the ground. Amsterdam planted this twin-stemmed elm on Zeeburgerdijk sometime between 1900 and 1915, according to conflicting municipal and conservation records. The city has tens of thousands of elms, more per capita than almost anywhere else in Europe, a legacy of planting elms along canals for their tolerance of the polluted, waterlogged soil common near open sewers a century ago. Dutch elm disease, first identified and named in the Netherlands in the 1920s, wiped out huge numbers of European elms over the following decades, and Amsterdam's collection survived largely because of an aggressive, decades-long eradication and breeding program that continues today. The Olifantsiep, girth pushing five metres, has outlived that epidemic and the severe storm of January 2018, and still leafs out every spring behind a low fence anyone can lean on.

trees.name: The Lomanstraat Cathedral of Trees
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Tram 2, Amstelveenseweg, 5-10 min walk
trees.story: Nobody designed the tunnel of trees on Lomanstraat. When the street was planted in the early 1900s as part of Plan Zuid, architect Hendrik Petrus Berlage's expansion of the city southward, the trees on both sidewalks simply did what trees flanked by tall apartment blocks do: leaned toward the middle of the street, chasing the light above the buildings. A century of that lean has interlocked their crowns into a continuous green tunnel overhead, and the street is now one of the most photographed in Amsterdam-Zuid, nicknamed the cathedral of trees by people who have walked under it. A persistent local story claims the trees survived wartime firewood shortages because a German office once stood on the street, which is the kind of detail that sounds too tidy to verify and probably is. What is verifiable is simpler: given decades and a narrow gap of open sky, ordinary street trees will find a way to close it, and nobody in Amsterdam-Zuid had to plant a cathedral on purpose. It just grew there.

photo.attribution: Alf van Beem, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Amstelkade Olive Willow
trees.species: Olive Willow, likely Russian Olive (Elaeagnus angustifolia)
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Tram 3 or 4, Amsteldijk/Rivierenbuurt area

best_time.label: May and June, when the small yellow flowers scent the whole street

trees.story: Despite the name, this tree is not a willow and has nothing to do with olives. The olijfwilg on Amstelkade is an Elaeagnus, a shrub-turned-tree genus with silvery, willow-shaped leaves and small fragrant flowers that ripen into fruit resembling tiny olives, hence a common name that misleads on both counts. Planted in 1948, three years after the Netherlands emerged from wartime occupation, it has grown along the Amstelkanaal into what the city's own tree inventory calls a specimen unique in the Netherlands for its combination of size and age. Nobody has documented a comparable one anywhere else in the country. At under 80 years old it is the youngest tree on this list by decades, included not for age but because Elaeagnus rarely gets the decades of undisturbed growth it takes to reach tree scale, most specimens staying shrub-sized in gardens rather than lining a public street. Amsterdam's official register of notable trees lists it among the city's most distinctive, a quiet distinction for a tree most passersby would assume was an ordinary willow if they noticed it at all.

trees.name: The Wingnuts of Amstelveld
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Tram 4, Prinsengracht or Frederiksplein, few min walk

best_time.label: midsummer, when the wingnuts trail their catkins

trees.story: In 2006 the city government tried to cut down 14 of these trees, and lost. The district council issued a felling permit that summer for over a dozen of the square's 46 Caucasian wingnuts, part of a resurfacing plan under an outdated tree ordinance. Two residents filed objections, then a court challenge, then finally an appeal to the Raad van State, the country's highest administrative court, after a district court sided with the city. No tree was felled while the case ran, and by 2010 the dispute ended with the square fully replanted around the surviving wingnuts rather than in place of them. To protect the three oldest, most valuable specimens from a resurfacing project's foot and cart traffic, engineers installed an underground support system to stop the soil from compacting around their roots, an unusually expensive concession for a handful of street trees. The wingnuts' surface roots still push up paving stones around the square often enough that it is a known feature of walking across Amstelveld, not a defect. The market that runs here on Mondays sets up its stalls under the same canopy the city once planned to remove.

trees.name: The Rijksmuseum Wingnut
trees.access: Free, Rijksmuseum garden, no museum ticket required
trees.transport: Tram 2, 5 or 12, Rijksmuseum/Museumplein stop, right outside

best_time.label: midsummer, for the hanging catkins

trees.story: The Rijksmuseum's own architect planted this tree in his own garden design, and it outlived every renovation the museum went through afterward. Pierre Cuypers, who designed the Rijksmuseum building itself, laid out its surrounding gardens between 1884 and 1916 in distinct historical styles, neo-Renaissance parterres beside a wild landscape garden, and planted a Caucasian wingnut near the director's villa in the southeast corner around 1907. By a 2014 survey the tree stood over 19 meters tall with a trunk more than four meters around. When the museum closed for a decade-long renovation completed in 2013, the landscape firm Copijn redesigned the gardens from scratch and could have cleared the site for something new. Instead the wingnut was kept and built around, one of the few mature trees preserved through the entire project. Wingnuts are still uncommon as full-grown specimens in the Netherlands, which puts this tree in the same small company as the ones in Wertheimpark and Amstelveld across town, three separate stands of the same species that all happened to reach old age inside Amsterdam's public gardens rather than getting cleared for something newer.

trees.name: The Turkish Hazel of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry, Hortus Botanicus ticket required
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, directly outside (same stop as the Hortus's already-published cycad)
trees.story: Bomenstichting, the Dutch tree foundation, calls this the oldest and thickest Turkish hazel in the Netherlands: planted in 1795, and three metres around today. That makes it two centuries younger than the Hortus itself, which has grown rare and difficult plants since 1638, but older than almost everything else standing in the garden. Turkish hazel is native to Asia Minor and the Balkans, a relative of the small hazel that produces the nuts, built at oak scale instead: pyramidal, broad-crowned, capable of forty metres. This one flowers in January, when its male catkins hang and shed pollen while the rest of the garden sits bare, a small performance almost nobody times a visit around. The 1795 planting date and the 300 centimetre girth both trace back to the tree's own record-keepers rather than an outside survey, so treat the figure as the Hortus's own claim rather than a courtroom fact. It grows a few minutes from the garden's giant cycad, itself pushing three centuries old, so two of Amsterdam's oldest living things now share the same corner of the Plantage. Entry costs a Hortus ticket, same as it always has: rare plants have never been free to see here.

trees.name: The Turner's Oak of the Hortus
trees.age: roughly 131 to 161 years (sources disagree on planting year)
trees.access: Paid entry, Hortus Botanicus ticket required
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, directly outside
trees.story: This oak does not drop its leaves in autumn. It holds them, dark and leathery, through the whole Dutch winter, and only lets go in spring when new growth physically pushes the old leaves off the twig. Turner's oak is a hybrid raised in an English nursery in the late eighteenth century, a cross between the evergreen holm oak of the Mediterranean and the pedunculate oak of northern Europe, and it took half its habit from each parent. It grows slowly and stops at around ten metres, which for an oak is nothing at all. The acorns hang on long stalks. The graft union is still visible about thirty centimetres above the ground, the seam where a nurseryman joined this tree to somebody else's roots. When that happened is contested. Amsterdam's register of protected trees says 1865; the Bomenstichting guide to the city's monumental trees says 1895. Thirty years apart, the same tree, and neither shows its working, so read the age as somewhere between 130 and 160 years. Either way it stood here for a century before the University of Amsterdam let go of the garden in 1987 and a private foundation took it on, which is why the register lists this tree's owner as a private party rather than the city. January is the month to come, when the rest of the garden is bare and this one is not. Entry needs a Hortus ticket.

trees.name: The Westkant Plane of Wertheimpark
trees.access: Free, public park (Wertheimpark)
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, about 5 min walk
trees.story:
Five metres of trunk in a hundred and twenty-five years is quick work. Amsterdam's register of special trees puts this plane's planting at 1900 and its girth at 500 centimetres; the Dutch Tree Foundation, surveying the same park for its own walking guide to the city's monumental trees, describes a plane here with a trunk of almost five metres. Two institutions, one measurement, no argument.

London planes grow fast when young, and this one had good ground for it. Wertheimpark was laid out in 1812 as Amsterdam's first public park, on the edge of the Plantage, a quarter the city had set aside for gardens rather than housing over a century earlier. The park has stayed small, barely three quarters of a hectare, which packs around fifteen trees over a century old into a two minute walk.

This is the west side specimen, on the Plantage Parklaan flank, a short distance from Jan Wolkers' Auschwitz memorial of 1977: broken mirrors set into the ground so the sky comes back cracked. The plane was already forty years old when the deportations that monument answers to began.

The city files it as beschermwaardige houtopstand, its settled protected class rather than the provisional tier. That guarantees nothing about a tree's health, but it does mean somebody with a clipboard comes back.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Wertheimpark
trees.access: Free, public park (Wertheimpark)
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, about 5 min walk
trees.story:
In a bad summer this plane stays green while its cousins go brown. Plane anthracnose, the leaf blight that leaves common planes blotchy and half bare by August, troubles the Oriental plane much less, which is one way to pick this tree out of the group standing along Wertheimpark's water.

Its age is a real disagreement rather than a rounding error. Amsterdam's register of special trees gives a planting year of 1900. The Dutch Tree Foundation's guide to the city's monumental trees dates what reads as the same tree to 1880 or 1890. Nobody has reconciled the two, so the honest answer is somewhere between 126 and 146 years old, and this page is not going to pick a winner for the sake of a tidy number.

The trunk measures 4.42 metres around. Platanus orientalis is the older half of the London plane's parentage, a species from the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia that European gardens have been planting since the sixteenth century, and its leaves are cut deeper, into narrower fingers, than the hybrid lining most Amsterdam streets. In a park this small you can stand under both within two minutes and see it.

It sits in a tight group of five or six registered trees along the water, including two Caucasian wingnuts of roughly its own age, which makes this corner of the park the densest thing of its kind in central Amsterdam.

trees.name: The Leopold Maple of Wertheimpark
trees.access: Free, public park (Wertheimpark)
trees.transport: Tram 14, Artis stop, about 5 min walk

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open pink and white before they green

trees.story:
The point of this tree happens in April. Acer platanoides 'Leopoldii' opens its new leaves pink and white, streaked and splashed as though someone had flicked paint at them, before they settle into a mottled green for the summer. The cultivar came out of Louis van Houtte's nursery in Ghent in the middle of the nineteenth century, one of a wave of variegated garden forms the Belgian trade sold across Europe, and it is why a fairly ordinary sized maple ended up on Amsterdam's register of special trees.

Ordinary is the right word for the rest of it. The register gives a planting year of 1920 and a girth of 262 centimetres, which for a Norway maple of that age is unremarkable, and the register is also the only document anywhere that names this individual tree. Everything else known about it is known about the cultivar in general.

What it has is position. It stands along the water in Wertheimpark with an Oriental plane eighteen metres away and two Caucasian wingnuts beside them, in a park of three quarters of a hectare holding around fifteen trees over a century old, with Artis on one side and the Hortus a few minutes down the road. Come in late April and it is the one in the group visibly doing something.

trees.name: The Oudemanhuispoort Elm
trees.access: Free. The inner courtyard of the Oudemanhuispoort passage, open in the daytime on weekdays.
trees.transport: Metro or tram to Rokin, about 5 min walk
trees.story:
The tallest tree in Amsterdam stands in a courtyard barely wider than it is tall. The Hollandse iep in the Oudemanhuispoort reaches 35 metres, higher than anything else in the city, and the enclosure is the reason. Brick buildings surround the garden on four sides, so a tree here has exactly one direction available to it, and this one took it. The register puts the planting at 1890.

The Oudemanhuispoort was built in the eighteenth century as an almshouse for the city's elderly poor. It belongs to the University of Amsterdam now, and the vaulted passage along one side has carried a second-hand book market for well over a century. Thousands of students walk past the trunk every day on the way to a lecture, which is a lot of foot traffic for a tree almost nobody has heard of.

The species is the other half of it. Dutch elm disease reached the Netherlands in the 1920s and killed elms here by the hundred thousand, and Amsterdam, an elm city by tradition, lost a great deal of its stock. This one was already about thirty years old when the disease arrived, and it is still going.

Go on a weekday, in from the Kloveniersburgwal end, and look into the southwest corner. It is not a tree that announces itself from the street, because from the street you cannot see it at all.

trees.name: The Wilhelminalinde
trees.access: Free, beside the Amsterdam Museum on the Kalverstraat.
trees.transport: Tram to Spui or Dam, about 3 min walk
trees.story:
Wilhelmina had been queen for eight years before anyone crowned her. She inherited the throne in 1890 at the age of ten, her mother governed as regent until she came of age, and the inauguration finally happened in September 1898. Amsterdam marked it by planting a lime, and the lime is still standing on the Kalverstraat.

The address is the odd part. The Kalverstraat is the busiest shopping street in the Netherlands, a canyon of chain stores that hundreds of thousands of people walk down in a week, and the coronation tree sits just off it by the Amsterdam Museum, in the complex that was the city's civic orphanage for four centuries.

Commemorative trees are usually the most forgettable objects in a city. They go in at a ceremony, the plaque weathers, and within a generation nobody remembers the occasion. This one outlived its occasion in the most literal way available: Wilhelmina reigned for fifty-eight years, through two world wars and five years of broadcasting to the occupied Netherlands from London, and abdicated in 1948. The tree was fifty. Early in 2025 it was added to Amsterdam's list of two hundred champion trees.

What it is not is old. At around 128 it is younger than half the trees on this page, and limes routinely pass three hundred. We have not established which lime it is; several species and hybrids are planted here under the same name. If you know, tell us.

trees.name: The Van Loon Copper Beech
trees.access: Paid entry, the garden of Museum Van Loon.
trees.transport: Tram 24 to Keizersgracht, about 3 min walk
trees.story:
The best evidence for this tree's age is a photograph. In Museum Van Loon's own collection sits a picture from 1923 showing the beech as a young tree, which is what puts its planting in the 1890s and makes it around 130 years old now.

It stands in one of the last intact canal-house gardens in Amsterdam. The house at Keizersgracht 672 went up in 1672, its first resident was Ferdinand Bol, who trained in Rembrandt's workshop, and the Van Loon family bought it in 1884. Behind the formal parterres stands a coach house dressed up with a classical front, and the garden between the two survived the century in which most Amsterdam back gardens were built over, subdivided or paved for cars.

A copper beech is not a wild plant in any meaningful sense. It is a colour mutation of the common beech that appears now and then in European woods and was propagated by nurseries because people liked the look of it, so every purple beech in a nineteenth-century garden is there because somebody chose it and paid for it. This one was a wealthy family's ornamental decision, taken when their house was already two hundred years old, and it is still standing exactly where they put it.

The garden opens with a museum ticket. It is small, walled and quiet, in the middle of a canal ring that is neither.

trees.name: The Rijksmuseum Poplar
trees.access: Free, the Rijksmuseum garden, open daily.
trees.transport: Tram 2 or 12 to Rijksmuseum, about 3 min walk
trees.story:
This poplar was planted as architecture. The Rijksmuseum opened in 1885 and the ground around it was laid out as an outdoor annexe of the collection, filled with fragments rescued from demolished Dutch buildings: gateways, doorframes, a pavilion. Early in the twentieth century a line of Italian poplars went in to frame one of those historic gates, and this is one of them.

The choice makes sense the moment you look at the tree. Populus nigra 'Italica' barely spreads. It grows as a narrow column, which is why it was planted in rows across Europe for two centuries to line roads, mark boundaries and give flat country a vertical. In a garden of salvaged stone doorways it does the work of a pilaster.

The register puts the planting between 1910 and 1920, so it is around 110 years old, and for this cultivar that is a considerable age. Lombardy poplars are fast, soft-wooded and short-lived by the standards of the trees on this page, and most of those planted in the same decade elsewhere in Europe are long gone. This one stood through the wartime evacuation of the museum's collection to shelters outside the city, and through the ten-year rebuild that gutted the building and reopened it in 2013, while the garden around it was redesigned more than once.

Free, with the garden. The Jan Luijkenstraat side is the quiet way in.

trees.name: The Weteringplantsoen Wych Elm
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.transport: Tram to Weteringcircuit, the stop is beside the plantsoen
trees.story:
Nobody knows when this elm was planted and the register says so outright: history unknown, planting somewhere between 1900 and 1910. What is documented is what stands in front of it. The Van Randwijk monument on the Weteringplantsoen carries the best known line in Dutch resistance writing, Henk van Randwijk's warning that a people which yields to tyrants will lose more than life and property, and then the light goes out. Van Randwijk edited the underground paper Vrij Nederland through the occupation.

The tree behind the monument is a wych elm, and that is the interesting part of the label. Ulmus glabra is usually counted as the only elm truly native to the Netherlands, and it is highly susceptible to Dutch elm disease, which arrived in the 1920s and worked through the country for the rest of the century. A mature wych elm standing in a Dutch city centre is not a common thing. This one is around 120 years old, so it was here before either world war and has stood through both.

It sits in a strip of grass and gravel between the Weteringschans and the water, the sort of triangle a city ends up with where two roads fail to meet cleanly. Free, always open, and a few minutes' walk from the Rijksmuseum. Three more trees on this list stand within two minutes of it.

trees.name: The Weteringplantsoen Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, on the public traffic island, always visible.
trees.transport: Tram to Weteringcircuit, the stop is beside the tree

best_time.label: mid November, when the fans turn gold and drop within days

trees.story:
There is a ginkgo growing on a traffic island on the Weteringschans, and it is the least likely thing on this list. The species is around 200 million years old, older than the flowering plants, and it survives in the wild in a handful of Chinese valleys. Its Dutch name, tempelboom, records how it got through: monks planted it in temple grounds and kept it going while it disappeared everywhere else. This one lives between lanes of traffic.

Amsterdam put it in somewhere between 1910 and 1920 and the register records no history for it whatsoever, which suits a tree that simply gets on with things. Ginkgo tolerates exactly the conditions that kill other street trees: compacted soil, road salt, exhaust, root space measured in single square metres. Several ginkgos within two kilometres of the Hiroshima hypocentre survived the bomb and are still growing.

Come in November. For eleven months this is a green tree with odd fan-shaped leaves that people walk past without a glance. Then over about a week the whole crown turns a flat saturated gold, and then it drops the lot, often in a day or two, leaving a gold ring on the tarmac around it. Traffic islands rarely get a moment like that.

Free, always visible, and easy to miss for most of the year. The wych elm, the leaning poplar and the plane are all a minute or two away.

trees.name: The Leaning Poplar of the Weteringschans
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.transport: Tram to Weteringcircuit, on the corner of the Weteringcircuit
trees.story:
Every year Amsterdam inspects this poplar and decides whether it can stay another one. It leans, visibly and considerably, out over the Weteringschans, and a trunk more than five metres round leaning towards a busy road is a question a city has to keep answering. So far the answer has been yes.

The reason it can be is under the pavement. A tree growing off vertical loads one side of its root plate far harder than the other and responds by laying down extra wood exactly where the pull is, thickening those roots into anchors. Leaning is not the same as unstable, and this one has had a century to engineer itself. The city prunes the heavy limbs on the road side to keep the load down, and inspects it annually.

It is a Canadapopulier, a cross between two other poplars that appeared in France around 1750 and was then planted across the continent for its speed. Speed is the point of the species and also the catch: poplars grow fast, get large and are not built for the long term, which makes a specimen of this girth at 116 to 126 years old worth stopping for.

The street it leans over was laid on Amsterdam's city ramparts after they were levelled between 1820 and 1840, and kept the name Schans until 1850. Free, always there, and impossible to confuse with the trees around it.

trees.name: The Weteringplantsoen Plane
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.transport: Tram to Weteringcircuit, about 2 min walk
trees.story:
This is the oldest tree in this group and the register has nothing to say about it. Planting: somewhere between 1880 and 1890. Reason for protection: monumental. History: unknown. That is the entire file on a London plane that has stood on the Eerste Weteringplantsoen for around 140 years.

The date is worth holding on to, because of what the ground nearby had just stopped being. The Weteringschans beside it was laid out over Amsterdam's city ramparts after they were levelled between 1820 and 1840. A plane planted here in the 1880s went in while that change was still recent and this whole edge of town was new.

London plane is the standard European city tree, and the reasons go beyond fashion. It sheds its bark in plates and takes the grime with it, which is how it stayed alive and legible through a century of coal smoke that turned other species black.
