It puts up with compacted roots, hard pruning and drought, and it is why the same tree lines streets from Barcelona to Berlin. Amsterdam has hundreds of them. This one has been at it longer than nearly all of them.

Free, at the quieter end of the plantsoen. The leaning poplar, the wych elm and the ginkgo are each within two minutes on foot, which makes this corner an unusually dense patch of old trees for the middle of a city.

trees.name: The Falckplantsoen Pagoda Tree
trees.age: roughly 116 to 136 years (the register gives two different planting bands)
trees.access: Free, on the street.
trees.transport: Tram to Frederiksplein or Weteringcircuit, about 5 min walk

best_time.label: August, when the wide crown fills with white flowers

trees.story:
In August this tree covers itself in white flowers, weeks after every lime and chestnut in the city has finished. The Japanese pagoda tree is a legume from Korea and China, with fine pinnate leaves and a crown that goes wide rather than tall, and late summer flowering is the reason people plant it.

It has the room to spread because a canal was filled in. The Falckstraat was named in 1870 after a prominent Amsterdammer and is unusually broad for the centre, because it was laid over a stretch of the Achtergracht filled in around 1869. A filled canal leaves a generous street, a generous street leaves root space, and root space is how a crown this wide ended up thriving on a corner of the Reguliersgracht.

Its age is genuinely unsettled. The register gives the planting band in two places and gives it differently, once as the 1890s and once as the 1900s, so the honest answer is somewhere between 116 and 136 years. The trunk carries a large wound on its south side, partly grown over, and the city prunes the heavy overhanging limbs on a schedule to keep the crown in balance. A second, smaller pagoda tree stands beside it.

Free, on the street corner, and worth timing. For most of the year it is a good tree with unusual foliage. In August it is the reason to be standing there.

trees.name: The Wertheimpark Sycamore
trees.access: Free, public park.
trees.transport: Tram 14 to Artis, about 3 min walk

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story:
A sycamore is the most ordinary large tree in northern Europe, which makes it worth asking why this one sits on the national register for dendrological reasons rather than for history or memorial value. The register does not say. Under history it writes: unknown. Somebody with a measuring tape decided this specimen was exceptional enough to protect and left it at that.

It stands behind the monument to Abraham Carel Wertheim, the banker and philanthropist the park was named after in 1898, a year after his death. The tree went in between 1910 and 1920, so it is around 110 years old and has spent every year of it a few metres behind that monument.

Acer pseudoplatanus is a maple that acquired the English name sycamore, which it shares with an unrelated American plane, and the confusion has never been cleared up. It seeds itself into every gap in every European city, grows anywhere, and if nothing interferes it can pass four hundred years, which makes 110 barely adulthood. The species is so common that a good specimen tends to be overlooked, which is roughly what happened here until the register caught up with it.

Free, in a park of three quarters of a hectare holding around fifteen trees over a century old. Go and see whether you can work out what the surveyor saw.

trees.name: The Last Elm of Stationsplein
trees.access: Free, on the public square in front of Amsterdam Centraal.
trees.transport: Amsterdam Centraal; the tree stands on the square in front of the station
trees.story:
Around thirty elms were planted in front of Amsterdam Centraal after the station opened in 1889. One of them is still standing.

The rest went to Dutch elm disease, which reached the Netherlands in the 1920s and then killed elms across the country by the hundred thousand. The fungus travels in bark beetles and blocks the tree's own water vessels, so a mature elm can go from healthy to dead inside one summer. Amsterdam's elm stock, one of the largest in Europe, was hit hard. This tree stood through all of it, on one of the busiest pieces of ground in the Netherlands, and surveyors still rate its condition as reasonable.

It is not resting on its history either. When it was last measured in 2022 its trunk was over three metres round, and it is recorded as adding a little more than a centimetre of girth every year, which is a tree still doing business rather than hanging on.

By that same 2022 survey the city had planted young elms on the square around it. If those take, the old view in front of the station slowly comes back and this one stops being the last of anything, which is what everybody involved would prefer.

Free, in the open, straight out of the station's main doors. Trams, bikes and the whole flow of the station pass within metres of it, and almost nobody looks up.

trees.name: The White Poplar of Broersepark
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
The register that protects this poplar says plainly that it is no longer impressive. Its own entry drops the word monumental and then keeps the tree on the list for one reason: with a planting recorded between 1860 and 1870, it is probably the oldest thing growing in the Broersepark.

The park in Amstelveen is much younger than that. It was designed in 1926 and laid out over the following years as a Wandelpark, a place made for walking, and only in 1967 took the name of Chris P. Broerse, the garden man who had worked there since the first season. On the dates in its file the poplar was already sixty years old before anyone drew a line on the plan. Nobody wrote down who put it there.

It wears the years openly. The crown has been knocked about, the trunk leans, and the root plate has lifted enough to raise a hump at the foot. In 1999 honey fungus, a wood-rotting parasite, turned up at the base, and the condition has been rated moderate ever since. What it still does as well as anything younger is the trick white poplars are named for: a gust turns the leaves over and the whole crown flickers silver.

You will find it on the south side of the park, at the edge of the pond. Only the national register describes this tree, so if you know more of its story, tell us.

trees.name: The Jakoba Mulder Tulip Tree
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: late October, when the whole crown turns clear butter-yellow

trees.story:
Jakoba Mulder helped design the Amsterdamse Bos, and then somebody planted a tree inside it in her honour. She lived another fifty years to watch it grow.

Mulder was born in Breda in 1900 and worked as an architect and town planner. The forest, originally called the Boschplan, was laid out slowly between 1934 and 1970 on polder ground southwest of the city, and the stretch this tree stands in lies in Amstelveen. The national register puts the planting at around 1938 and records that the tulip tree was reportedly her favourite of the lot. She died in Amsterdam in 1988, by which time the forest was nearly finished and the tree was half a century old.

It has grown into the specimen you would want as a memorial: whole, evenly proportioned, no lost limbs, nothing much wrong with it. Tulip trees come from the eastern American forests, and the leaf gives them away, shaped as though somebody snipped the tip off square. The flowers open high in the crown in June, greenish-orange and genuinely tulip-shaped, and most people pass underneath without once looking up. By late October the whole crown goes clear butter-yellow.

You can see it from the cycle path, south of the Bosbaanweg at the edge of the playing field. Only the register describes it in any detail, so if you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Old Lady of the Forest
trees.age: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.access: Free, on municipal land, open to the public.

best_time.label: October, when the conkers come down into the grass of the Speelweide

trees.story:
The trunk you are looking at carries on about two metres below your feet. When the Amsterdamse Bos was built the ground level here was raised, and the soil around this chestnut was banked up carefully, with rubble, rather than replaced.

She is called De Oude Dame van het Bos, the old lady of the forest, and she has the better claim to the ground than the forest does. The register records her planting in 1895; work on the Bos only began in 1928. In her first decades she stood in the Rietwijkeroordpolder, beside a farmhouse, in a landscape that no longer exists in any form. The polder went under the trees, the farm was pulled down, and the horse chestnut was left standing where it was, with its feet buried.

The years show on her. The register notes a possible bleeding canker on the heavy northwest limb and at the trunk itself, and a large torsion crack running through a damaged branch on the north side. It also notes that she comes into full leaf and is otherwise in good heart. In May the candles go up, white with a red fleck at the throat, and by October there are conkers in the grass.

Find her at the western edge of the Grote Speelweide in Amstelveen, at the treeline near the canoe hire. Only the national register describes this one, so if you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Poplar of the Eleanor Rooseveltlaan
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, a small public municipal garden.
trees.story:
Hardly anyone lets a Canadian poplar reach this age. The register puts this one's planting between 1900 and 1910, which makes it about 120, and the species is normally out of the ground long before that.

Populus x canadensis is a hybrid of an American poplar and a European one, bred for speed, and it went into the Dutch landscape in enormous numbers along roads, dykes and field edges. It makes height in a decade and shelter in two. What it does not make is old bones: the wood is soft, heavy limbs come out in a gale, and most street poplars are taken down at fifty or sixty on exactly that reasoning. This one is still standing in a strip of municipal garden on the Eleanor Rooseveltlaan in Amstelveen. Roosevelt herself was a young woman in New York when it was planted.

The register knows nothing else about it. Under the tree's own history it records a single word: unknown. Nobody wrote down who put it there, or why a fast nursery hybrid on a suburban corner was left alone long enough to end up on a national list of monumental trees. If you know that story, tell us.

Come on a windy day. Poplar leaves hang on flattened stalks that let them twist edge-on to a gust, so a crown this size does not rustle so much as pour.

trees.name: The Elm of Elsenhoeve
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, a small public municipal garden.
trees.story:
This elm is alive because somebody injects it, every year. The register's entire note on the tree is one line of Dutch saying exactly that: treated annually against elm disease.

Dutch elm disease emptied European streets of a tree that used to define them. The fungus travels from tree to tree in bark beetles and can wilt a mature elm within a season. It is named after the Netherlands not because it began here but because Dutch scientists were the ones who identified the fungus, in the 1920s, which is roughly when this tree went into the ground: the register puts its planting between 1920 and 1930. It has lived its whole life alongside the thing that kills its kind, through a century in which most of Europe's elms disappeared.

Ulmus x hollandica is a natural hybrid, wych elm crossed with field elm, and the Amsterdam region is one of the few places in Europe where elms are still an ordinary street tree rather than a rescued specimen. That took decades of felling infected wood, watching for beetles, and precisely the treatment this one gets.

It stands in front of Speelboerderij Elsenhoeve, a children's farm on the Bankrasweg in Amstelveen, so most of the people underneath it are five years old and looking at goats. The pin marks the garden rather than the trunk, and only the national register describes this tree, so if you know more of it, tell us.

trees.name: The Red Horse Chestnut of Wilhelminaplein
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.

best_time.label: May, when it carries candles of deep rose-pink instead of white

trees.story:
Half of this tree is American. The red horse chestnut is a cross between the white-flowered chestnut of every Dutch avenue and Aesculus pavia, a red-flowered species from the American southeast, and it turns up in the record in Germany around 1820 with nobody quite able to say who made it.

The result is the best-behaved chestnut on any street. In May it holds up candles of deep rose-pink rather than white, a little later than its white parent, so a street planted with both appears to flower twice. It sets very few conkers, and the husks it does set have almost no spines, which makes it a disappointing tree for anyone under twelve. In exchange it largely escapes the leaf miner moth that has been browning out Dutch horse chestnuts by August for twenty years now; the caterpillars strongly prefer the white parent, and this hybrid stays green into autumn while its neighbours look scorched.

This one stands in public planting on the Wilhelminaplein in Amstelveen, with a registered planting somewhere between 1920 and 1930, which puts it at roughly a century old. That is all anybody has written down. The national register's history field for this tree is blank, and no second source describes it at all. If you know who planted it, or what for, tell us and we will add it.

trees.name: The Beatrix Lime
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.story:
This lime went into the ground on 31 January 1938, the day Princess Beatrix was born. The register still lists it as De Beatrix linde.

Dutch towns marked royal births with trees as a matter of course, and this was a birth worth marking: Beatrix was the first child of Juliana, who was herself the only child of Queen Wilhelmina, and the line had been running on a single life for two generations. The baby the tree was planted for became queen in 1980 and stayed on the throne until 2013. The tree has stood on this corner the whole time, including the German occupation that sent the family into exile in London barely two years after the planting.

It has not aged as easily as she has. The register's inspectors record dead wood in the top and along the main limbs, and a flush of young shoots breaking out inside the crown, which is what a stressed lime does when it starts rebuilding itself lower down. They want the ground around the roots examined to turn things around. A street tree in trouble is almost always suffering from what is under it rather than what is above.

You will find it where two through-roads meet at the Veenendaalplein in Amstelveen, in full view, which the register notes with some approval. Nobody has recorded which lime species it is.

trees.name: The Catalpa of the Cleopatralaan
trees.age: roughly 70 years, from a registered planting date around 1960
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.

best_time.label: July, when it opens white orchid-shaped flowers freckled with purple

trees.story:
Every spring this tree gives its street a fright. The southern catalpa is one of the last trees in Europe to come into leaf, often not until the end of May, by which point everything around it has been green for six weeks and it is still a bare grey skeleton hung with last year's beans.

Those beans are the other thing. The flowers open in July, white and orchid-shaped, freckled with purple and striped yellow down the throat, in upright clusters that a grown tree carries by the hundred. What follows is a crop of thin brown pods up to forty centimetres long that hang on through the winter and give the species its other name, the Indian bean tree. Nothing else on a Dutch street looks remotely like it.

Catalpa bignonioides is a narrow native, from a corner of the American southeast around Georgia and Florida, and it took to European cities largely because it puts up with being boxed in by pavement.

This one grows opposite the houses on the Cleopatralaan in Amstelveen. Nobody wrote down when it was planted. The register reasons that the neighbourhood went up in the 1960s and the tree probably dates from the same work, which places it somewhere in the 1950s or 1960s, and that reasoning is the whole of the evidence. If you know better, tell us.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Sint-Willibrorduskerk
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Tram to Berchem, short walk

best_time.label: April and May, when its new leaves are brightest copper-red

trees.story: Nobody can say for certain which revolution this tree commemorates, only that it commemorates one. Standing 21 metres tall with a trunk 4.95 metres around, this copper beech dominates the small square between a rectory and the Sint-Willibrorduskerk in Berchem, and its size and position both point to it having been planted as a vrijheidsboom, a liberty tree, the European tradition of marking a political upheaval by putting a tree in the ground rather than raising a statue. The candidates are 1789, the year the Brabant Revolution briefly threw off Austrian rule, or 1830, the year Belgium itself declared independence, and heritage assessors who protected the tree as a monument in 1949 could not settle on which. It most likely began life inside the rectory's enclosed garden, sheltered there long enough to build the girth and canopy spread, some 32 metres across, that it shows today, before the garden wall came down and left it standing in the open square people see now. Whichever revolution it marks, it has now outlived both the political order it may have celebrated and the one that replaced it.

trees.name: The Summer Linden of Rivierenhof
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Rivierenhof, Deurne

best_time.label: late June and July, when its flowers scent the whole meadow

trees.story: A single linden tree earned government protection in 2010 not for its species, which is common, but for exactly where it stands: in front of Sterckshof castle, at the heart of a park whose ownership reads like a highlight reel of Antwerp history. Hof Ter Rivieren began as a modest farm in the 15th century, became the country retreat of a wealthy Antwerp merchant in the 16th, and was bought by the Jesuits in 1618 as a rural escape from the city. The linden, a summer lime rather than the more common small-leaved variety, now anchors a 30 metre protected zone around its own base, a rare individual tree designation from Flanders' heritage agency rather than a blanket park listing. Its size alone does the talking: a broad, high crown visible across the meadow it stands in, opposite the entrance to the Sterckshof manor house, forming what heritage assessors call a visual unity with the protected building beside it. The Rivierenhof became a public park a century ago, one of the largest green spaces in the Antwerp region today, and this tree predates that public opening by centuries, a private estate's ornament turned into a landmark anyone can walk up to for free.

photo.attribution: Geert Van der Linden / Flanders Immovable Heritage Agency, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Black Locust of Hertoghepark
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram to Desguinlei or Markgravelei, short walk

best_time.label: late May, when its white flower clusters hang from every branch

trees.story: The thickest black locust tree recorded anywhere in Belgium grows in a small city park hemmed in by three Antwerp streets. At 4.10 metres around, measured in 2009, this robinia holds the species' national girth record in the country's own dendrological inventory, an unglamorous but real distinction for a tree species better known for lining railway embankments than for record breaking size. Hertoghepark is a fragment of the Leikwartier, a garden district laid out from 1547 by the property speculator Gilbert Van Schoonbeke on land he bought from the Van de Werve family, meant as leafy weekend retreats for Antwerp's wealthy merchant class outside the city walls. The Hertoghe and Belpaire family gardens and the old Mertens farm were later folded together into the single park that survives today, protected since 1974 as a historic cultural landscape. Black locust is not a long lived species by tree standards, rarely making it past a century and a half in good health, so this specimen's champion status says less about extreme age and more about how much room and light it found in a private garden turned public park, growing largely undisturbed while the city grew dense around it.

trees.name: The Black Mulberry of Hertoghepark
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram to Desguinlei or Markgravelei, short walk

best_time.label: August, when the fruit drops and stains the ground

trees.story: Sharing Hertoghepark with Belgium's thickest black locust is a much smaller record holder: a black mulberry measured at 1.28 metres around in 1989, listed as the national champion of its species regardless of that modest girth. Mulberries simply do not grow thick trunks the way oaks or planes do, so a champion mulberry looks unremarkable standing next to almost anything else in the same park, its record coming from being the best example available rather than from raw size. The species has a long history in gardens like this one: black mulberry was planted across Europe for centuries wherever someone hoped, usually in vain in this climate, to raise silkworms, and even where the silk trade never took off the trees stayed for their fruit, staining hands and pavement a deep purple black every late summer. This one has stood through the same garden district history as its more imposing neighbour, part of the Leikwartier laid out from 1547 and consolidated into today's protected city park in 1974. Its precise planting date is not recorded, only that it has held its national champion title since at least the 1989 measurement that put it on record.

trees.name: The Cut-Leaved Horse Chestnut of Middelheim
trees.access: Free, public sculpture park
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Middelheim

best_time.label: May, when its candle-shaped flower spikes cover the canopy, same as any horse chestnut despite its oddly cut leaves

trees.story: Most of Middelheim's fame comes from the sculptures scattered across its lawns, but one of its most unusual residents is a tree: a cut leaved white horse chestnut, a genetic curiosity in which every leaflet emerges narrow and deeply serrated instead of the broad fan shape that makes ordinary horse chestnuts so recognisable. Measured at 1.35 metres around in 2016, it is a rare enough variant that Middelheim's own dendrological collection, built up alongside the open air sculpture museum that gives the park its international reputation, treats it as one of the grounds' notable specimens in its own right. The wider Middelheim estate combines with neighbouring Den Brandt and Vogelenzang to form the Nachtegalenpark, merged into one public green space in 1911 after the city bought up what had been a string of private pleasure estates dating back to the 13th and 14th centuries. Sculptures by artists from Rodin to contemporary names now stand under a tree canopy considerably older than the museum around them, and this misshapen horse chestnut, planted for its oddity rather than its beauty, has outlasted several generations of visitors who came only for the art.

trees.name: The Canadian Poplar of Eric Sasselaan
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kiel / Nieuw Zuid
trees.story: At 35 metres, this Canadian poplar is among the tallest trees recorded anywhere in Antwerp, its trunk clear of branches for a full 6 metres before the crown even begins, a shape that comes from growing hard and fast for light rather than from any deliberate pruning. Measured at 5.40 metres around in 2011, it stands beside a bridge on Eric Sasselaan, an ordinary stretch of the city with nothing else to recommend it as a destination, which is exactly the point: this is not a castle park or a botanic garden specimen but a street tree that simply grew bigger and faster than anyone expected a hybrid poplar to. Canadian poplar is a fast growing hybrid, not a long lived species by any measure, typically reaching its full size within decades rather than centuries, which makes its scale here more a demonstration of what the species can do under good conditions than a claim to great age. It is a reminder that not every remarkable tree in a city has a noble family or a monastery behind it. Some are simply the biggest thing of their kind that a stretch of unremarkable pavement happened to grow.

photo.attribution: Geert Van der Linden / Flanders Immovable Heritage Agency

trees.name: The Peace Tree of the Grote Markt
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Short walk from Antwerpen-Centraal station or any tram to Groenplaats

best_time.label: June and July, when its flowers scent the whole square

trees.story: The youngest tree on this list stands in the middle of the oldest square. On 3 September 1994, the city planted a small linden on the Grote Markt, ringed by the Renaissance guildhalls and the Gothic town hall that make this square one of the most photographed in Belgium, to mark exactly fifty years since Antwerp's liberation from German occupation in 1944. A bronze plaque set into four chained posts around its base spells out the anniversary in plain terms: Vrijheidsboom, 50th anniversary of the liberation of Antwerp. Unlike everything else on this list, there is nothing uncertain about this tree's age or its meaning, no disputed circumference, no folklore standing in for a missing record. It is barely three decades old, a sapling by the standard of a churchyard beech or a castle park oak, and it will not be the oldest or the largest tree in Antwerp for a very long time yet. What it offers instead is the opposite of ambiguity: a single, dated, deliberately public act of remembrance, growing in the one square in the city that every visitor already walks through.

photo.attribution: Geert Van der Linden / Flanders Immovable Heritage Agency

trees.name: The Park Trees of Den Brandt
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Middelheim / Den Brandt
trees.story: Behind a castle built in 1790 that itself replaced a medieval structure destroyed centuries earlier, Den Brandt's park holds a valuable, largely uncatalogued collection of solitary trees and tree groups around an artificial pond and open lawn, laid out in the English landscape style once fashionable among Antwerp's merchant elite. The estate is first documented in 1396, when it was likely a farmstead rather than the country residence it later became, and it stayed in private hands for centuries, passing to the della Faille de Waerloos family in 1804 and then to the Kreglinger family in 1910, who bought both the castle and 16 hectares of grounds around it. The public only gained access in 1911, and today Den Brandt forms one third of the combined Nachtegalenpark alongside Middelheim and Vogelenzang. No single tree here carries a published age or circumference record in the sources checked for this entry, so none is claimed. What survives is a planting scheme old enough that Flanders' heritage inventory rates the tree population itself as valuable, an English style landscape garden whose individual specimens have simply never been measured for public record the way the specimens at nearby Hertoghepark or Rivierenhof have.

photo.attribution: Kris Vandevorst / Flanders Immovable Heritage Agency

trees.name: The Historic Grounds of Zoo Antwerpen
trees.access: Paid zoo admission
trees.transport: Adjacent to Antwerpen-Centraal station
trees.story: Belgium's oldest zoo has spent more of its history rebuilding than expanding. Zoo Antwerpen opened on 21 July 1843, right beside what would become the city's Centraal Station, and its site and tree cover were repeatedly caught in the crossfire of a location that made strategic sense for a railway hub and none at all for a garden: German bombardment damaged the zoo badly in August 1914, and the Second World War hit it even harder, destroying the aquarium, reptile house, bird house, hippo house and winter garden in a single conflict. That the zoo's landscaped grounds, laid out and steadily replanted under head gardener Florent Blockx from around 1935 onward, survived both wars intact enough to be protected as a landscape in 1975 and recognised as a full historical monument in 1984, says as much about the tree cover's resilience as about the animals it shelters. A dedicated irrigation system installed in 1982 keeps the older plantings alive through Belgian summers. No single tree here is singled out in the historical record, so this entry stands for the grounds as a whole, a rare case of a European zoo's landscaping surviving through two world wars fought in the same city block.

trees.name: The Millennium Ginkgo of the Stadspark
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Short walk from Antwerpen-Centraal station

best_time.label: November, when its fan shaped leaves turn gold and drop within days of each other

trees.story: Antwerp's first public park has spent the last forty years quietly losing the very trees that made it worth designating in the first place. When the German landscape architect Eduard Keilig laid out the Stadspark in 1869 on the site of the city's demilitarised Spanish fortifications, he built it around mature tree cover that came with the land, a striking contrast of an irregular pond, an island reached by a suspension bridge and a steep grassy slope. Surveys by Belgium's own dendrological association in 1986 and 2005 both flagged the same problem: a historically significant tree population under real pressure from disease, storm damage and basic safety concerns, with large sections already removed by the time of the second survey. Rather than pretend nothing had changed, the city marked the turn of the millennium in the winter of 1999 to 2000 by planting a ginkgo, a species famous for outliving almost everything around it, as a deliberate long view gesture in a park whose 19th century originals were already disappearing. What remains is a park honest about its own losses, old fortification earthworks reshaped into a pond and hillside nearly forty years before Belgium's dendrologists started counting what the storms had taken.

trees.name: The Oak by the Statue of Frederick Henry
trees.age: roughly 340 years, if the register is right that it went in with the palace avenues between 1685 and 1690
trees.access: Paid. Inside Paleis Het Loo: the palace and formal gardens need a museum ticket, the surrounding Paleispark a two euro day ticket from the machines at its entrances.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Apeldoorn station, bus to Paleis Het Loo.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down

trees.story:
William III wanted somewhere to hunt, and in 1685 he built a palace on the sand north of a village nobody had heard of. In front of it he had oaks planted in avenues, the Koningslaan, because that is what you did with an approach.

The national register believes this is one of them. It gives the tree a planting band of 1600 to 1700 and then says why it leans late: probably planted at the same time as the Koningslaan oaks, which means between 1685 and 1690. That reasoning is the register's own and it is worth repeating rather than hiding, because it is the whole basis for calling this tree roughly 340 years old. Nobody has taken a core.

What is certain is that it was standing when William became King of England in 1689 and left for London, when the French occupied the palace in 1795, and when the last royal resident died in 1962.

It stands beside the statue of Frederick Henry, which is the easiest landmark on the estate. The oak is the heavy one behind it, with the low branching of a tree that grew up in the open rather than in a wood.

trees.name: The Pollarded Lime of Ugchelen
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.access: Free. Public ground behind the fire station, with a bench and a sign from the road.
trees.transport: About 5 km southwest of Apeldoorn station, in Ugchelen. Bus to Ugchelen, then a short walk to the G. P. Duringlaan.
trees.story:
Over six metres round, measured at chest height, and it stands behind a fire station.

That is the whole appeal. Apeldoorn has a royal palace full of documented trees and its thickest and one of its oldest is a lime hidden at an angle behind a municipal building in a village on the southern edge, where you would walk past it for years without knowing.

It is a leilinde, a lime that was pollarded and trained flat, which is what people did to a tree standing against a house front: you kept it low, you cut it back hard every few years, and it gave shade in summer without taking the light in winter. The register reads it the same way and supposes there was once a cottage or a small farm here, with the lime trained across its facade, planted somewhere between 1750 and 1800.

The village council thought this was worth doing something about. They put up a sign on the road pointing to it, and the town had already put a bench there years earlier, so you can sit down and look at it properly.

That is the correct response to a tree like this, and it is rarer than the tree.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Upper Garden
trees.age: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820
trees.access: Paid. Inside the formal gardens of Paleis Het Loo, covered by a museum ticket.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Apeldoorn station, bus to Paleis Het Loo.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns to copper

trees.story:
Copper beeches were a fashion, and this one arrived at the height of it.

The purple-leaved form of the common beech is a natural mutation. It turns up on its own now and then in European woods, and from the eighteenth century onward nurseries learned to graft it and sold it hard to anyone laying out a landscape garden. Between 1810 and 1820, when this one went into the back of the upper garden at Het Loo, having one was a statement about being current.

Two centuries later the fashion has aged into something better. A copper beech at this size is a dark solid mass of a tree, and in a formal garden built on symmetry and pale gravel it does the useful job of being the one heavy dark thing in the composition.

Stand under it rather than in front of it. Beech leaves are thin enough that a mature purple canopy lit from above turns the light underneath a deep red, which is the reason people planted them and the reason the photographs never work.

It is at the far end of the Boventuin, behind the formal planting.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of the Palace Garden
trees.age: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820
trees.access: Paid. Inside the formal gardens of Paleis Het Loo, covered by a museum ticket.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Apeldoorn station, bus to Paleis Het Loo.

best_time.label: June, when the green and orange flowers are up in the crown

trees.story:
It flowers in June and almost nobody notices, because the flowers are green and orange and they sit upright at the ends of branches twenty metres up.

That is the thing worth knowing about a tulip tree. It is not named for its shape. It is named for the flower, which is a real tulip-shaped bloom about six centimetres across, pale green with an orange band at the base, and on a tree this size they are held so high that most people who walk past in flowering season see nothing at all. Bring something to look through, or wait until they drop.

The leaf is the other giveaway and it works all summer: squared off at the tip, as though somebody cut the point off with scissors. There is no other tree in a Dutch garden with that leaf.

It is an eastern North American species, in European gardens since the seventeenth century, and it was planted here in the same stretch as the copper beech beside it, between 1810 and 1820.

In October it turns clear yellow, which on a tree this tall is the version of it most people actually see.

trees.name: The Copper Beech by the Pond
trees.age: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850
trees.access: Paid. Inside the formal gardens of Paleis Het Loo, covered by a museum ticket.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Apeldoorn station, bus to Paleis Het Loo.
trees.story:
A generation younger than the beech at the back of the upper garden, and planted where it would be reflected.

This is the second copper beech in these gardens and the placing is the point of it. It stands on the west side of the pond, which means the water sits between you and the tree for most of the approach, and a dark purple canopy over still water is a trick that landscape gardeners had worked out long before anyone here was planting.

The register puts it between 1840 and 1850. By then the copper beech was no longer a novelty and had settled into being a standard part of the vocabulary, the heavy dark accent you put where a composition needs weight.

What two centuries add is bulk that no design anticipated. These trees keep thickening long after they stop rising, so a mature one ends up out of scale with everything planted alongside it, and the garden quietly rearranges itself around the biggest thing in it.

Go on a still morning and look at the water rather than the tree.

trees.name: The Red Oak of the Wilhelminapark
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km northeast of Apeldoorn station, on foot.

best_time.label: October, when it goes properly red

trees.story:
This park exists to sell building plots.

The ground was the De Vlijt estate, mostly heath. In 1825 its owner Ameshof built the villa Marialust and dug the large pond that still lies in front of it. Sixty years later the company that had the land wanted to sell it off for villas, and worked out that people pay more for a plot beside a park than a plot beside a field. So in 1885 they laid out the road pattern, and made a walking park around the pond that was already there.

It worked well enough that in 1889 they offered the roads and the park to the town, which took them. In August 1890 the council asked the king for permission to name it after Princess Wilhelmina on her tenth birthday. He said yes, and from 17 August 1890 it has been the Wilhelminapark.

The register puts this red oak between 1860 and 1870, which places it before the park and inside the estate that preceded it. Red oak is an American species, planted here for its autumn colour, and in a good year it is the reddest thing in Apeldoorn.

trees.name: The Lime of Het Woldhuis
trees.age: roughly 325 to 425 years, from the register's planting band of 1600 to 1700
trees.access: Free. Recorded as visitable in the national register; the tree stands on the estate grounds at Het Woldhuis 1.
trees.transport: About 6 km east of Apeldoorn station, on the Woudhuis side.
trees.story:
The register gives this lime the same planting band as the oak at the palace, 1600 to 1700, and unlike the oak it offers no reasoning at all. That is a century of uncertainty stated plainly, and it is the honest position: somebody surveyed a very old lime on an estate east of the town and could not date it more closely than that.

So it is either the oldest tree in Apeldoorn or roughly the same age as the palace oak, and there is no way to settle it without a core.

What a band that wide does tell you is what the tree looks like. Limes of this age are rarely single clean trunks. They tend to have been cut, layered, split by their own weight and regrown, sometimes hollow, often with the ground around the base thrown up by roots that have had three or four hundred years to spread. A lime is also one of the few trees that can produce a new trunk from a fallen limb that touches soil, which is part of why they last.

If you go and can take a girth measurement at 1.30 metres, send it to us. That is the number that would settle this.

trees.name: The Pin Oak of the Oranjepark
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1 km northeast of Apeldoorn station, on foot.

best_time.label: late October, when it turns scarlet

trees.story:
A pin oak of this age is unusual in the Netherlands, because the species did not become a standard street and park tree here until well into the twentieth century. One planted between 1860 and 1870 was somebody's deliberate choice rather than a default.

It is easy to identify and hard to confuse with the pedunculate oaks around it. The leaves are cut into narrow, sharply bristled lobes with deep rounded bays between them, nothing like the soft rounded lobes of a native oak. The lower branches sweep downward toward the ground while the upper ones point up, which gives an old one a distinctive drooping-skirted outline you can read from across a lawn.

Its other habit is holding its dead leaves. Pin oaks often keep a rustling brown canopy through most of the winter and only drop it when the new buds push in spring, so this is a tree that looks occupied in January when everything around it is bare.

It stands on the west side of the Oranjepark, opposite the P. Krugerstraat. In late October it turns a deep scarlet that lasts a fortnight.

trees.name: De Poortwachters
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Gulden Bodem park, north Arnhem; about a 30 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station, or a short bus ride toward Alteveer

best_time.label: July, when the chestnuts hang cream-coloured catkins the length of a hand

trees.story: Locals call them Hans, Gretel and the Witch, and Arnhem's storytellers like to credit Karel van Egmond, the last independent Duke of Guelders, with planting these three sweet chestnuts by hand. The dates do not support it: van Egmond died in 1538, and these trees, girths of 750, 718 and 472 centimetres, are closer to 370 years old, planted around 1650 to 1700 at the gateway to Huis Zypendaal. The name that stuck anyway is De Poortwachters, the Gatekeepers, because for the better part of four centuries every visitor to the castle has had to walk between them first. The Hansel and Gretel nicknames follow the same logic: the two thickest, standing side by side, are the well fed pair, and the leaner third is the witch left behind. They survived a fire in 1945, the year Allied troops finally liberated Arnhem after the previous autumn's battle for the city, and outlast everything else the same way they always have, rooted exactly where the path forces you past them. In 2024, for Sonsbeek park's 125th anniversary, artists wired sensors into six of the park's trees for a temporary route called Arnhemse Bomen Vertellen, Arnhem's Trees Tell, translating each tree's sap flow and trunk movement into sound; the Poortwachters were its first stop.

trees.name: The Dalweg Oak
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Sonsbeek estate, north Arnhem; about a 20 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station via Park Sonsbeek

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Most oak stories are about longevity. This one is about plumbing. The Dalweg Oak has spent close to three centuries rooted on a slope where groundwater runs permanently just beneath the surface, so in the driest summer its roots still reach water, and in the wettest winter the slope drains before it can drown. That single accident of geology explains a tree with a 35 metre crown, wider than most Dutch houses are tall, and a trunk that measured roughly 6.2 metres around in 2015, thick enough to rank among the largest oaks in the country. It has not had an easy run at the top: a beech grew up beside it and a self seeded Douglas fir plantation crowded in later, both stealing light, and the oak has shed side branches in response for years. None of that has touched its vitality. Planted somewhere between 1700 and 1750, it stands above the walking path that climbs from Dalweg to Braamweg, one of the quieter corners of the Sonsbeek, Zypendaal and Gulden Bodem estate that the municipality bought whole in 1899 and never fenced off. No plaque marks it. You just have to look up while you are still catching your breath from the hill.

trees.name: The Huissensedijk Plane
trees.access: Free, public churchyard, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Elden, south Arnhem, near GelreDome stadium; reachable by bus from Arnhem Centraal station, about 25 minutes
trees.story: The thickest Oriental plane in the Netherlands stands beside the smallest, whitest church in Arnhem, and the two have shared roughly two centuries of the same ground. Sources disagree on exactly how long: the tree is usually dated to somewhere between 1725 and 1800, its circumference now around 7.1 to 7.5 metres, short stemmed with arms so thick they read as separate trunks holding up one broad crown above the dike. In the winter floods of 1926, with the surrounding polder underwater, a farmer strung a rope from his raised farmhouse to this tree and used it to pull a small boat across the flooded land so his children could still reach school and the household could still shop. During the Second World War, German troops occupying the little Bonifatiuskerk beside it made the tree a direct witness to the occupation, and when the Battle of Arnhem tore through the city in September 1944, the village of Elden and this tree both came through largely unscathed while much of Arnhem did not. Its wounds since have been more mundane: storm damage patched in 1980, its heavy crown cabled in the 1990s to keep the arms from splitting under their own weight. It still stands exactly where the dike meets the church, in a corner of the city built around a football stadium and a ring road that mostly gets driven past rather than walked to.

trees.name: The Poplar of Lauwersgrachtpark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: City centre, behind Musis Sacrum; about a 10 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station
trees.story: The Netherlands' oldest poplar grows behind a concert hall, on the last stretch of canal Arnhem never filled in. Most of the city's old defensive moat became streets generations ago; the Lauwersgracht survived by accident, and this Canadian poplar has grown alongside it since somewhere between 1750 and 1800, long enough that the Bomenstichting's national register of monumental trees lists it as the oldest of its kind in the country. It is not a pure species but a hybrid clone, one of the first crosses of Populus nigra, Europe's native black poplar, with an American parent, made in France around 1800 and planted across the continent before anyone had settled on what to call it. A postcard from around 1920 already shows a mature tree leaning over the water in almost the same spot; a photograph from 2008 shows the same reflection, barely changed. It stands today in Lauwersgrachtpark, tucked behind Musis Sacrum's concert stages just off the Eusebiusbuitensingel, the kind of tree a city walks past on the way to a show without knowing it is looking at the oldest poplar in the Netherlands.

trees.name: The Scarlet Oak of Velperplein
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Velperplein, city centre; about a 15 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station

best_time.label: October into November, when the canopy turns a deep, genuine scarlet

trees.story:
Nineteen designers entered a public competition in 1880 for what to do with a canal the city had just filled in, and Leonard Springer's plan, entered under the motto Natura, Ars et Technica, beat all of them. The park he built over the old Jansgracht became the Velperplein plantsoen, and this scarlet oak is one of its survivors, a North American species with no obvious business looking so at home in a Dutch civic square. Scarlet oak earns its planting for one trick, a canopy that turns a genuinely deep red most European oaks cannot manage, which is presumably why someone chose it here.

The municipal monumental tree register dates its planting to somewhere around 1900 to 1910, a generation or two after Springer's own scheme went in rather than part of it, though the register's own file admits an earlier date is possible too. Either way it has stood through the plein's complete rebuilding between 1995 and 2005, when new roads, cycle paths, a bus station and a parking garage entrance were dug in around it. It grows in the park's southeast corner, a few steps from Musis Sacrum's front doors, unfenced and unticketed. If you know its planting date more precisely than the council does, tell us.

trees.name: The Weeping Pagoda Tree of Musis Sacrum
trees.access: Free, public pavement, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Velperplein, city centre; about a 15 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station

best_time.label: July, when its weeping branches hang thick with honey-scented white flowers

trees.story:
Arnhem's national tree register keeps two grounds for protecting a tree, being old or being rare, and this weeping pagoda tree qualifies on the second alone. Nobody has recorded when it went into the ground; the council's own file says simply unknown. The shape gives away what it is: Styphnolobium japonicum 'Pendula', a grafted, deliberately weeping form of the Japanese pagoda tree, its branches trained to cascade rather than reach, so that in summer the white, faintly honey-scented flowers hang close enough to brush a passer-by's shoulder instead of drifting overhead.

It stands directly in front of Musis Sacrum, Arnhem's concert hall since 1847, on the roadside edge of the Velperplein rather than tucked into the park behind it, which is presumably why the register lists its setting as street rather than garden. Municipal survey work puts its planting band at 1900 to 1910, two or three generations after the concert hall itself went up. No ticket, no gate: it stands on open pavement outside a building that still hosts Arnhem's own orchestra. Nobody has published an independent account of this specific tree beyond the national register, so treat the date as the council's best estimate rather than a settled fact.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Velperplein
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Velperplein, city centre; about a 15 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station
trees.story:
Arnhem already has one Oriental plane with a claim to national fame, a giant beside a village church in Elden with a trunk over seven metres round. This is a second, smaller one, growing in the Velperplein park in the city centre, and its interest is where it grows rather than its size. Oriental plane is not the hybrid London plane that lines half of Europe's boulevards; it is the older, straight species, native from the Balkans to Iran, and this one has spent well over a century on a small, endlessly rebuilt city island rather than open ground.

The monumental tree register puts its planting around 1900 to 1910 and links it, cautiously, to Leonard Springer's prize-winning 1880 design for the park, built over a filled-in canal after the city ran a public competition for the site; the register's own dating and that 1880 connection do not quite line up, so the link is a guess rather than a documented fact, and it is told here as one. What is not in doubt is that the tree has outlasted the square around it twice, once when the park went in and again when the whole plein was rebuilt for new roads, cycle paths and a bus station between 1995 and 2005. It stands in the open, free to walk up to any day of the year.

trees.name: The Black Walnut of Velperplein
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Velperplein, city centre; about a 15 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station
trees.story:
Every few years since 2006, whoever surveys Arnhem's monumental trees has come back to this black walnut and written down bad news: a conspicuous wound low on the trunk, a crown that had visibly thinned since the 1990s, deadwood spotted in 2014. In 2024 the surveyor found something new growing in the trunk cavity, a resin-varnish fungus, though likely a young colony rather than an advanced infection. And yet the same notes say that in recent years the tree has stood full and healthy in leaf, which reads either as a genuine recovery or as a walnut simply refusing to follow its own file.

It grows in the strip of park on the northwest side of Velperplein, planted, the city's register guesses, around the same time as Leonard Springer's 1880 design for the square, though the tree's own dated band puts it a generation later, 1900 to 1910. Black walnut is an American import, grown here for its wood and its nuts rather than any native pedigree, and this one has outlived the plein's late 1990s and early 2000s rebuild, the new roads, cycle paths, bus station and a parking garage tunnel dug in around it. It still stands, free to see, on a corner of green between a 19th-century concert hall and a theatre.

trees.name: The Sessile Oak of Musispark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Musispark, city centre; about a 15 minute walk from Arnhem Centraal station
trees.story:
Sonsbeek Park's oaks get most of Arnhem's attention, but a fifteen minute walk closer to the station, in the smaller Musispark behind Musis Sacrum, a sessile oak has been standing since roughly the 1890s with nobody much noticing. The monumental tree register ties its planting to a renovation of the singel plantsoenen, Arnhem's ring of canal-side parks, carried out to Leonard Springer's design around 1890, a decade after his prize-winning Velperplein scheme across the water.

Sessile oak differs from the pedunculate oak that fills most of the Netherlands by carrying its acorns on short stalks pressed close to the twig rather than dangling on long stems, worth checking if you want to be sure which species you are standing under. This one grows about 65 metres from a Canadian poplar the national register lists as the oldest of its kind in the country, so a single stop in this park puts two record-adjacent trees within sight of each other. Both are free to reach, along Eusebiusbuitensingel near the start of Parkstraat, no gate and no ticket. The register is the only source that has written this tree down; a Gelderlander photograph or an older map naming a firmer planting date would be welcome.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Overcingel
trees.age: roughly 200 years, from a registered planting date around 1830
trees.access: Free with a walking card from Het Drentse Landschap's Assen office (Kloosterstraat 5); open without one during the crocus season in February and March.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles open right across the spread of the crown

trees.story:
Nobody is certain whether this is one tree or a bouquet of them. The register calls it a multi-stemmed white horse chestnut, which was a fashionable thing to plant in the 1820s, and then offers the other reading: that the trunk was once cut through at sixty centimetres and grew back from the stump. If that is what happened, this is the thickest single-stemmed horse chestnut in the Netherlands.

Either way it sits in the register's ereklasse, the top rank, held by 99 trees in the whole country.

It grows on Overcingel, a private estate whose manor house dates from 1777 and whose garden was reworked in 1824 by the landscape architect Lucas Pieter Roodbaard. When the chestnut itself went in is not recorded. The register's planting band is the 1820s, and its inspectors guess it arrived with that redesign because Roodbaard planted chestnuts often. A guess is what it stays.

Age is not the first thing you notice. The tree is wide, low and heavy, held together with anchors driven through trunk and crown, with a large cavity on the path side, plates of bark coming loose and bleeding canker at the foot. Its condition has been slipping for about ten years.

Only the national register describes this tree. If you know more of its history, tell us.

trees.name: The Hollow Oak of Overcingel
trees.age: roughly 230 to 280 years, from the register's planting band of 1750-1800
trees.access: Free with a walking card from Het Drentse Landschap's Assen office (Kloosterstraat 5); open without one during the crocus season in February and March.
trees.story:
A fungus usually taken as a sign a tree is dying has been working through this oak's heartwood for decades, and it is still standing. The register calls it zwavelzwam, sulfur polypore, feeding through a cavity that opens the whole north side of the trunk.

It grows a short walk from Overcingel's horse chestnut, on the same estate laid out around a manor house of 1777 and remade in the English style by Lucas Pieter Roodbaard in 1824. The register's planting band puts the oak at 1750 to 1800, decades wider than the chestnut's, which makes this the older of the estate's two register trees rather than a companion planted alongside it.

Somewhere between 1970 and 1985, tree surgeons patched the trunk with the grafts and braces of that decade's practice. Since then the crown has been cut back hard, from 27 metres to 14, what arborists call veteran pruning: reducing a failing crown to buy the trunk more years. On the south side the tree has grown a thick collar of reaction wood and pushed roots up above the soil, bracing itself against the lean the hollow has left it with.

It still leafs out on what remains of its branches. Whether it keeps doing that is a question the register itself leaves open.

trees.name: The Oak of the Hertenkamp
trees.age: roughly 180 years, from a registered planting date around 1850
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
Assen's old deer park still has its stable in it, built in 1875, and this oak grows right by it at the pond, planted, most likely, when the park itself was laid out in 1841.

It has spent the last fifteen years in visible decline, and unevenly. The whole north side of the crown is dying back, its trunk opened by wounds and cavities on the same side, while the south side is holding its own and still carries a healthy head of leaves. Which half a visitor notices first depends on which side of the pond they approach from.

The Hertenkamp itself has been open parkland since the nineteenth century, one of the pockets Assen kept green as the town grew around it. Nobody has published a firmer date for the oak than the 1840s planting band the national tree register gives it, and the register is the only source that has looked closely enough to describe its condition at all. If you have watched that north side change, or know more of this tree's history, tell us.

trees.name: The Oak of Valkenstijn
trees.age: roughly 150 years, from a registered planting date around 1880
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down across the park

trees.story:
This oak's girth runs past four metres, and it is in better shape than most trees this old get to be: a sound trunk, a clear run for its crown, and a growing spot nobody has ever crowded.

It stands in Valkenstijn, nearly ten hectares of park in what is now Assen-Oost, and the park is the shrunken core of something larger. The ground was once called Vredeveld, after a manor house founded around 1650 that stood, by the end derelict, until it was pulled down in 1966. The oak is registered to the 1870s, two centuries after that house first went up, which makes it a comparative latecomer to land that had already been landscaped for generations.

What Vredeveld's grounds became is now open to anyone: old trees, avenues, hedgerows and wide meadows, with Valkenstijn as public parkland at the centre of the district that grew up around it. The register calls the oak's planting only likely rather than certain. What it does not have to guess about is the tree itself, sound, spacious and doing well.

trees.name: The Heaviest Oak in Assen
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Visible from Beilerstraat (public street), opposite house number 5. It grows on private grounds at Nassaulaan 1 and cannot be approached directly.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down onto Beilerstraat

trees.story:
The register calls this the heaviest oak in Assen and one of the thickest in the whole of Drenthe, then adds the honest complaint: almost nobody has heard of it, next to the famous oaks of Beilen and Mensinge.

It grows on the grounds of Nassaulaan 1, a neoclassical house built around 1830 at what was then the edge of town, but it leans so far toward Beilerstraat that it reads from the street as if it belongs there. Beilerstraat itself stayed empty of houses until 1833, when the first one went up at number 2, which makes this oak roughly as old as the street having any houses on it at all.

A large limb has come down recently, and a 2022 storm tore off another, though that one missed the trunk. The crown tips show some dieback. None of it looks serious: the trunk itself is sound and unwounded, and the tree still comes into leaf well.

You cannot walk up to it. It grows on private ground. But it stands close enough to Beilerstraat, opposite house number 5, that seeing it needs nothing more than the pavement.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Huges' Garden
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
Behind a house called Nieuw Echten, reached only by a footpath squeezed between two front doors on Alteveerstraat, sits a pocket garden nobody driving past would guess exists. It carries the name of a family, Huges, who lived in the house from 1934 to 1970, decades after the garden itself had already been laid out in the English landscape style, with a pond at its centre.

The weeping beech growing there predates the Huges family by about half a century. The register puts its planting somewhere in the 1880s. A weeping beech's whole trick is gravity: instead of reaching up, its branches arch out from the trunk and fall, so a mature one reads less like a tree and more like a room, walls of foliage hanging to the ground with the trunk hidden somewhere inside.

The path in runs between numbers 59 and 61 Alteveerstraat, open to anyone who finds it. Nobody has published more about this specific tree than the national register, which is the only source we have for it. If you know the garden's own history better, tell us.

trees.name: The Broken Cypress of Overcingel
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free with a walking card from Het Drentse Landschap's Assen office (Kloosterstraat 5); open without one during the crocus season in February and March.
trees.story:
This one is included for what it might become rather than what it is. The register's own notes call it barely monumental any more, because at some point the main trunk broke off, and what stands today is largely regrowth.

It shares Overcingel's grounds with the estate's oak and horse chestnut, on land landscaped in 1824 by Lucas Pieter Roodbaard, and the register guesses all three went in around that redesign, though nothing dates the cypress itself more precisely than the 1880s. Bald cypress is an unusual choice for a Drenthe estate garden, a wetland conifer from the American South, deciduous unlike most conifers, its needles turning rust orange and dropping every autumn.

What the register is watching, and what a visitor can watch too, is whether the tree manages to rebuild a real crown from where it broke. That is an open question rather than a finished story, and it is the honest reason to include a damaged tree on this list: it is alive, it is trying, and nobody yet knows how it ends.

It stands on the same private grounds as its two Overcingel neighbours, reachable with a walking card from Het Drentse Landschap's Assen office, or without one during the February and March crocus season.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Huges' Garden
trees.age: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns copper

trees.story:
The same footpath that leads to the weeping beech behind Nieuw Echten passes a second registered tree a few steps further on: a copper beech, its leaves running dark purple-red instead of green, planted about a decade later, in the 1890s.

Both trees share the same pocket garden, laid out in the English landscape style around a pond before the Huges family gave the place its name between 1934 and 1970. Where its weeping neighbour is shaped by how it was bred, arching its branches down instead of up, this one is shaped only by where it was planted: a natural, open growing spot with room to spread, which the register credits for its condition. It is straightforwardly healthy, with nothing in the record to flag.

Copper beech turns from purple toward copper through October, the colour shift that gives the cultivar its name doubling up for a few weeks before the leaves drop. It is the more dramatic of the garden's two beeches to see at that time of year.

Reached the same way as the weeping beech, through the footpath between Alteveerstraat 59 and 61, open to anyone who finds it.

trees.name: The Oak of Port Natal
trees.age: roughly 180 years, from a registered planting date around 1850
trees.access: Free, alongside Beilerstraat on the edge of the former Wilhelmina Ziekenhuis grounds, visible from the public street.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down by the water

trees.story:
Two stone gateposts stand next to this oak with nothing left between them to mark: they are what remains of the driveway to Port Natal, a psychiatric hospital built here in 1920 and replaced in 1990 by the Wilhelmina Ziekenhuis that occupies the site today. The oak predates all of it. The register's planting band puts it in the 1840s, when this was still the edge of an estate rather than a hospital ground, and the view across an English-style landscape garden from where it stands is, the register notes, still easy to picture.

It grows at the waterside, close by Beilerstraat, with a sound, unmarked trunk and a crown the register simply calls reasonable, no drama attached. What has changed around it several times over is what the tree stands next to: a country estate, an asylum, and now a hospital, each replacing the last while the oak kept growing.

It is visible from the public street along the former hospital grounds. If you know more of Port Natal's own history, or this oak's, tell us.

trees.name: The Sacred Olive Tree of the Acropolis
trees.age: 70-110 years (current wood); mythologised lineage to 480 BC
trees.access: Paid entry, standard Acropolis of Athens ticket
trees.transport: Acropoli metro station (Line 2), 5 min walk, or Acropolis entrance on Dionysiou Areopagitou

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: The olive tree beside the Erechtheion has died and returned at least twice, and both times the same legend gets the credit. Herodotus wrote that when Xerxes' Persian army burned the Acropolis in 480 BC, the sacred olive Athena was said to have grown in her contest with Poseidon went up with it, only to sprout a new shoot a cubit high the very next day. The tree standing here now is a second resurrection: German occupying forces damaged the earlier specimen during the Second World War, and sources disagree on exactly when its replacement went in, some say 1917, before that war even started, others say 1952, after it. What both agree on is the point of the story rather than the paperwork: someone has kept an olive growing on this exact spot for as long as Athens has kept records, using cuttings from the previous tree rather than starting over with something unrelated. The Erechtheion behind it, an asymmetrical marble temple finished around 406 BC to house the Acropolis's holiest relics, has needed far more restoration than the tree ever has. Entry is included in the standard Acropolis ticket, and the olive stands walled into the Pandroseion, the small sanctuary against the temple's west side.

photo.attribution: George E. Koronaios, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Olive Tree of Pisistratus
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Agioi Anargyroi railway station (Piraeus-Platy suburban line), short walk

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: A tree in a pocket park behind a suburban church carries a claim that would make it older than the Parthenon: officially attested by the Hellenic Archaeological Society in 1919 at more than 2,500 years, and popularly billed since as the oldest living olive tree on Earth. Modern olive dating complicates that considerably. Olive trunks rot hollow from the inside as they age, taking the innermost, oldest rings with them, and radiocarbon studies of other headline-grabbing old Mediterranean olives have repeatedly found real ages closer to three or four hundred years once properly tested. No such study has been published for this specimen, so its 1919 figure rests on early 20th century measurement methods rather than anything a lab would confirm today. What isn't in dispute is the name behind it: Pisistratus, the 6th century BC tyrant of Athens, is credited with the wave of olive planting that turned Attica into the region's defining olive economy, and this suburb sits on what was once part of that grove. Part of the trunk was cut for firewood during the wartime occupation of the 1940s, and it grew back regardless. It is now a protected natural monument, free to visit, standing in a small park behind the church that gives the area its name.

trees.name: The Regrown Olive of Plato's Academy
trees.access: Free, open daily except Monday, 9am-4pm
trees.transport: Bus to Akadimia Platonos or Kolonos, or 20 min walk from Metaxourgeio metro station (Line 2)

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: A city bus ended nearly 2,400 years of continuous shade in 1976, when it struck and split the trunk of the olive tree beneath which Plato is said to have taught. The tree stood in the grove of Akademos, the suburb that gave Plato's school, and eventually the English word academy, its name, and tradition held that the sacred grove here had grown from cuttings of Athena's own tree on the Acropolis centuries before Plato ever arrived to teach beneath it. The collision didn't kill the root system, and what grows in the archaeological park today is a genuine regrowth from that same base rather than a replacement sapling brought in from a nursery, a distinction the site treats as worth preserving. It is a young tree by any measure, decades old rather than millennia, and it looks like one: slim and upright, nothing like the gnarled giants elsewhere on this list. What makes it worth the detour is what it stands on rather than what it currently looks like, the excavated foundations of the gymnasium and residence buildings where Plato, and later Aristotle as a student, actually walked. The park is free, open daily except Monday from 9am to 4pm, and considerably quieter than the Acropolis eight kilometres away.

trees.name: The Transplanted Olive of Megali tou Genous Scholis
trees.age: up to 1,500 years (Agricultural University of Athens assessment)
trees.neighbourhood: Opposite Evangelismos Hospital, near the Hilton
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Evangelismos metro station (Line 3), 2 min walk

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: In December 2015, a construction crew dug up an entire mature olive tree in the village of Elaionas, in the hills above Aigio, and drove it more than 200 kilometres to a traffic island in central Athens. The tree wasn't being rescued from age or disease. It stood inside the corridor cleared for a new railway line, and Greece's rail construction authority, ERGOSE, had committed to relocating rather than felling the older olives caught in its path, part of a program that has since moved more than 500 trees out of expropriation zones since 2013. The Agricultural University of Athens assessed this particular specimen at up to fifteen centuries old before the move, old enough to have already been ancient when the Byzantine Empire ruled from Constantinople. It survived the truck journey and a complete change of soil, climate and neighbours, and now stands on a traffic island opposite Evangelismos Hospital, a few steps from the Hilton, doing exactly what it always did: producing shade and, most years, olives. Nothing about its current setting hints at the story behind it. It is easy to walk past a well-kept municipal olive tree without a second look, which is roughly what most passersby here do. The square is unstaffed and open at all hours, a two minute walk from Evangelismos metro station.

photo.attribution: George E. Koronaios, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the National Garden
trees.access: Free, National Garden of Athens
trees.transport: Syntagma metro station (Lines 2 and 3), 5 min walk
trees.story: The largest holm oak in the National Garden of Athens is old enough to have been planted by Queen Amalia's own gardeners, and big enough that it is rarely matched by wild specimens anywhere else in Greece. Amalia, the Bavarian-born wife of Greece's first king, Otto, commissioned the garden in 1839 as the country's first Western-style landscaped park, bringing in the French landscape architect François-Louis Bareaud to lay it out and filling it with species from across the Mediterranean and beyond. The holm oak is one of the survivors of that original planting scheme, now well past 150 years old, its evergreen canopy dense enough to blacken the ground beneath it even at midday. Unlike the garden's more famous palms and the eucalyptus that arrived later from Australia, Quercus ilex is native to Greece, so this particular tree represents restraint rather than imperial botanical trophy hunting, a local species given room to reach a size it rarely gets in the wild once grazing and firewood collecting are factored in. The tree stands among the garden's quieter paths, away from the pond and the small zoo that draw most visitors. Entry to the National Garden is free, every day, year round.

trees.name: The Cypresses of the First Cemetery of Athens
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: Syngrou-Fix metro station (Line 2), 10 min walk
trees.story: Athens's grandest 19th century cemetery reads like an open-air sculpture museum, and the cypresses planted around its edges were a public health measure before they were ever a landscaping choice. When the First Cemetery was established in 1837, four years after Otto arrived as Greece's first king, municipal rules required burial grounds to sit at least 100 metres outside the city and to be screened with trees, ideally on a hillside for ventilation, a sanitary theory of the era that happened to also produce a genuinely beautiful result. Cypress, pine and olive went in from the start, and the layout was formalised in 1861 into the maze of paths visitors walk today. Cypress carries its own symbolism here beyond the practical planting brief: in Greek tradition it is the tree of mourning and the underworld, planted in cemeteries for exactly the reason it now shades this one. Some of the original trees from that 1837 to 1861 planting window are still standing, making them among the oldest deliberately planted cypresses in modern Athens, though no individual specimen here has its own published age or measurement. The cemetery holds the graves of Heinrich Schliemann and Melina Mercouri among thousands of others, is free to enter, and stays open daily.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of Zappeion
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: Syntagma metro station (Lines 2 and 3), 10 min walk
trees.story: Almost two hundred plane trees went into the ground around the Zappeion in 1857, two decades before the neoclassical hall they now surround had even been designed. The gardens predate their own centrepiece building, laid out first in a formal French geometric style and later softened into looser English-style plantings, with eucalyptus imported from Australia joining the original planes early on. The Zappeion itself, completed in 1888, went on to host fencing at the first modern Olympics in 1896 and, decades later, the signing of Greece's accession treaty to the European Communities in 1979, so its plane-lined approach has watched two very different kinds of history. Oriental plane is the tree most associated with Greek public space generally, prized for a canopy dense enough to cool a whole square and bark that flakes away in patches, shedding pollution and disease along with it. Most of the original 1857 trees have since been replaced or supplemented after a century and a half of storms and old age, so what stands today is a mixed-generation avenue rather than a single dateable planting, honestly closer to 60 to 165 years old tree by tree. The gardens are free and open daily, a short walk from Syntagma Square through the adjoining National Garden.

trees.name: The Olive Woodland of Filopappou Hill
trees.access: Free, unrestricted, open at any hour
trees.transport: Acropoli or Thissio metro station (Line 1 or 2), 10 min walk

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: Before 1954, Filopappou Hill was mostly bare, grazed down to scrub with the occasional stray olive holding on. What covers it today, a deliberately hypnotic woodland of hundreds of olive trees planted in staggered density, is not survival but design: the architect Dimitris Pikionis spent three years reshaping the hill by hand, with his students and local stonemasons paving footpaths from salvaged marble fragments and demolished building rubble rather than working from finished drawings. He replaced the site's non-native planting with species indigenous to Attica, olive chief among them, and the result is now considered one of the twentieth century's most significant works of landscape architecture, studied by architecture schools well beyond Greece. None of this makes the trees themselves ancient.
