Its counterpart down in the Parc de la Ciutadella went into the ground 35 years earlier and is the thicker tree; this one has the better spread. The city catalogued it in 1998. What both share is the fruit, a heavy green sphere the size of a grapefruit with a surface like folded brain, which drops in autumn and is eaten by nothing that currently exists. It stands a few minutes' walk from the pepper tree on Carrer Joaquim Blume.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Placa Carles Buigas
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Espanya (Metro L1/L3), 8 min walk up Avinguda Maria Cristina

best_time.label: white candles stand upright over the whole crown

trees.story: Barcelona's register of trees of local interest runs past two hundred entries and contains exactly one horse chestnut. This is it, and the date on it is 1937, which was not a good year to be planting anything in this city. The air raids on Barcelona ran through that year and the next, and the hill directly above the square held anti-aircraft positions. The tree went in anyway and now stands 20 metres tall with a trunk 1.9 metres around, a decent size for a species that does not really belong at this latitude. Aesculus hippocastanum comes from a few mountain valleys in the Balkans, wants cool damp summers, and tends to sulk in Mediterranean cities, going brown at the edges by August in a hard year. This one has managed 89 seasons of it. It shares Placa de Carles Buigas with a tipu tree that is also on the register, so the two are one stop rather than two, on the walk up from Espanya towards the Montjuic gardens. The conkers are why the tree travelled so far beyond its native range in the first place and why generations of children knew it by name: shiny, useless, and briefly the most valuable object in a schoolyard.

trees.name: The Jujube of the Jardins Joan Maragall
trees.access: Free, but the gardens open at weekends only. Check the current hours before going.
trees.transport: Espanya (Metro L1/L3), 15 min walk up Montjuic, or bus 55 to Estadi Olimpic
trees.story: This garden opens two days a week, which is most of the reason almost nobody has seen the tree in it. The Jardins Joan Maragall surround the Palauet Albeniz, a small neoclassical pavilion built for the 1929 International Exposition and kept ever since as the residence the Spanish royal family uses when it is in Barcelona. The public is let in at weekends. The jujube standing there was planted in 1958, reaches 10 metres with a 1.6 metre trunk and a crown 12 metres across, and was catalogued as a tree of local interest in 1998. Ziziphus jujuba has been cultivated in China for something like four thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest orchard trees on earth, and it reached the Mediterranean early enough that the Romans were already growing it. The fruit is the size of an olive and turns from green to a deep red brown. Fresh it tastes like a slightly floury apple; dried and wrinkled it tastes like a date, which is where the English name Chinese date came from. It is a thorny, slow, obstinate tree that will grow in poor dry ground, and it is planted here purely as an ornamental. Check the opening days: on a weekday the gate is as close as you get.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Jardins de Mossen Cinto Verdaguer
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: Paral.lel (Metro L2/L3) then the Montjuic funicular, 5 min walk

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter gold and then drops in a day or two

trees.story: The ginkgo has no living relatives. Not a rare genus inside a large family: the entire order it belongs to died out except for this one species, and fossil leaves from 200 million years ago are close enough to the modern ones that a botanist can match them by eye. It survived in a handful of Chinese temple groves and was carried out from there first by monks and then by European collectors. Barcelona's is a young example, planted in 1958 in the Jardins de Mossen Cinto Verdaguer on the Montjuic hillside, now 17 metres tall with a crown nearly as wide and a trunk 1.4 metres around. The garden it stands in is the city's bulb garden, terraced and best known for its tulips and narcissi in spring and its water lilies in summer, which leaves the ginkgo the autumn entirely to itself. That is the month worth coming for. The leaves turn from green to a flat butter yellow over about a fortnight, then drop almost all at once, often within a single still day, leaving a gold circle on the ground that is the entire point of the tree. The city catalogued it in 1998. The gardens are free and open daily.

trees.name: The Judas Tree of Placa Joanic
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Joanic (Metro L4), on the square itself
trees.story: This tree is twice as wide as it is tall. Five metres of height, a crown ten metres across and a trunk 1.8 metres around, the proportions of something that decided early to spread rather than climb. It is a Judas tree, and the Catalan name on the city register, arbre de l'amor, is a good deal kinder than the English one. The English name comes from the story that Judas hanged himself from a Cercis and its white flowers turned red with shame; the likelier explanation is that arbre de Judee, tree of Judea, got misheard somewhere along the way, Judea being a place it genuinely grows wild. What the tree does in April accounts for both names. The flowers break straight out of the bark, off the old wood of the branches and the trunk itself, before a single leaf has opened, so the whole frame of the tree turns magenta for a fortnight and then greens over as if nothing happened. This one was planted in 1956 on Placa de Joanic and catalogued in 1996. It stands about 330 metres from the holm oak on Carrer de l'Encarnacio, the oldest measured tree in Barcelona, which makes the two of them a short and unusually good walk through the middle of Gracia.

trees.name: The Black Poplar of Chante-Grillon
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc Chantegrillon, city-managed)
trees.transport: Bus stop Cite Chantecrit (lines 4/45/7), a few minutes walk; no direct tram stop
trees.story: No tree in Bordeaux's remarkable-tree register has a bigger waistline than this one: 741 centimetres around, three trunks fused near the ground into something closer to sculpture than timber. It is one of only seven trees in the city carrying the A.R.B.R.E.S. label Arbre Remarquable de France, awarded in 2012, and it holds that title in a small municipal garden on the right bank rather than in one of Bordeaux's grand parks. The two official descriptions do not agree on its dimensions. The metropole's tree register records 19 metres of height and a trunk diameter of 236 centimetres. The city's own magazine calls it the record-holder of the garden at 31 metres, with a main trunk of 320 centimetres. Both are published figures, and the gap probably comes down to where the tape went around that fused base. Neither source gives an age at all. Black poplar is a riverside species and this is a riverside city. It grows fast, splits easily in storms and rarely survives to this size in a park, which is most of the reason the register puts it at the top of its own list. Bark and leaves from the species were once boiled up in French folk medicine against rheumatism. The tree is also classified under the city's urban plan, so the ground around it cannot be built on. Go and look at the base. That is where the whole story is.

trees.name: The Pecan of the Jardin Public
trees.access: Free, public park (Jardin Public, Bordeaux's main 18th-century public garden)
trees.transport: Tram C, Jardin Public stop, at the park edge
trees.story: The tallest tree in Bordeaux's Jardin Public is an American nut tree. At 38 metres the pecan stands above everything else in the garden, and that figure is one of the rare cases where the city's register and the city's own magazine give exactly the same number instead of two measurements taken a decade apart. Pecan belongs to the river bottoms of Texas, Louisiana and the Mississippi valley, where it needs long hot summers to fill its nuts. Bordeaux, warm and Atlantic, is about as far as the species gets in a European public garden without ending up in an orchard. It is one of the seven Bordeaux trees carrying the A.R.B.R.E.S. label of 2012, which is a national association's judgement rather than a municipal one. The trunk figures wobble slightly between sources, 421 centimetres around in the register against a range of 358 to 420 on the city page, which is the ordinary drift of one tree measured twice by different people. No age has ever been published. The Jardin Public was laid out in the 1740s as a promenade for a city grown rich on wine and colonial trade, then rebuilt as an English-style park a century later. The pecan is at most as old as that second version of the garden and probably younger. It stands on the central lawn, a few paces from the ginkgo.

trees.name: The Kentucky Coffeetree of Parc Bordelais
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc Bordelais); the tree itself sits behind a safety perimeter due to trunk cavities, viewable but not approachable at the trunk
trees.transport: Tram D, Courbet stop, short walk into the park
trees.story: The French call this tree chicot, meaning stump, because its winter silhouette is so bare and so sparsely branched that people assume it has died. It has not. The city puts it at more than 130 years old and says it dates from the creation of the Parc Bordelais, which opened in 1888, making it one of the oldest things in a park built to give a fast-growing western suburb somewhere to walk. Kentucky coffeetree is a genuine rarity in France. The genus holds two species in the world, this one and a Chinese cousin, and it survives largely because people planted it. Colonial settlers in North America roasted the seeds as a coffee substitute, which is where the English name comes from and which is not a recipe worth reviving, since the raw seeds and pods are toxic. The timber went into fence posts and railway ties. You will look at this one from a short distance. Cavities in the trunk mean the city has fenced a perimeter around it and prunes it regularly to keep weight off the limbs, and the register lists its vigour as weak, which for a tree of this age under active management describes the care rather than an ending. It measures 292 centimetres around and 14 metres tall, modest next to the park's big planes. The point of this one is that it is here at all.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Place Gambetta
trees.access: Free, public square (Place Gambetta, fully reopened to pedestrians in 2021 after a renovation)
trees.transport: Tram A or B, Gambetta stop, right at the square

best_time.label: May and June, when the cream-white flowers open the size of a dinner plate

trees.story: When Bordeaux rebuilt its busiest square in 2021, the design added more than fifty new trees around the ones already standing. This magnolia is one of two named individually in the historic centre's conservation plan, the document that decides what may not be touched inside the old city. Local press and the metropole's own consultation platform both describe the square's magnolias as centenaires, a hundred years old and more. That is a description rather than a measurement, so read the age as the neighbourhood's estimate and not a ring count. What has been measured: 358 centimetres of girth and 17 metres of height, large for a southern magnolia and very large for one growing in paving. Magnolia grandiflora comes from the American southeast and reached French gardens in the 18th century, where Bordeaux's mild Atlantic winters suited it immediately. It keeps its leaves all year, thick and glossy with a rust-coloured felt underneath, and it flowers in May and June with cream-white blooms the size of a dinner plate that carry a lemon scent several metres. Place Gambetta has been traffic, then a building site, then a pedestrian square in the space of a decade. It has also been one of the most walked-through points in Bordeaux for far longer than that. The magnolia is the element that simply stood there through all of it.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Jardin Public
trees.access: Free, public park (Jardin Public)
trees.transport: Tram C, Jardin Public stop

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter gold and drops within days

trees.story: The French name for a ginkgo is the forty crown tree, after an 18th-century collector in Montpellier said to have paid forty ecus for a single sapling when the species had just reached Europe from China by way of the Netherlands and England. At that price it was less a tree than a status object. This one is now 27 metres tall with a crown 27 metres across and 405 centimetres around the trunk, which is as wide as any ginkgo in Bordeaux's register. It is protected twice over, once as a remarkable tree and once under the city's urban plan. Ginkgo biloba is the last survivor of a plant family older than the flowering plants and older than any bird. Every specimen in Europe descends from trees kept alive in Chinese temple grounds long after the species had vanished from the wild. This individual has no published age, and nobody has recorded whether it is male or female, which matters more than it sounds: female trees drop a fleshy seed that smells like something died. A Bordeaux blogger writes most autumns about the gold carpet under a ginkgo in this garden. That post gives no coordinates, so read it as the species doing what it does here rather than proof about this exact trunk. The gold is real either way, and it lasts about a week.

trees.name: The Redwood Twins of Chante-Grillon
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc Chantegrillon, city-managed, same small garden as the register-topping black poplar)
trees.transport: Bus stop Cite Chantecrit (lines 4/45/7), a few minutes walk; no direct tram stop
trees.story: Two coast redwoods stand about ten metres apart in a small garden on Bordeaux's right bank, one measuring 393 centimetres around and the other 390. The near-identical size and the spacing say they went into the ground together, almost certainly planted as a deliberate pair. The city's register lists them as two entries even though a visitor sees one thing. Sequoia sempervirens grows on a narrow strip of the Californian and southern Oregon coast where summer fog rolls in off the Pacific and does half the watering. Bordeaux is not that. The species has been planted all over Europe and mostly sulks, so a matched pair reaching this girth in an Atlantic French city is the notable part. No source gives an age for either of them. They stand in Parc Chantegrillon, the same small park that holds Bordeaux's thickest registered tree, a black poplar with a 741 centimetre base. Two of the city's strangest specimens in one municipal garden is not a coincidence: somebody chose this ground for exactly this kind of planting, and the whole site is now classified under the urban plan. Beyond the register, nobody has written about these two individually, so the city's measurements are what exists. Stand between them and look up. The bark gives the species away, soft and fibrous and deep red where the light hits it.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of Parc Bordelais
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc Bordelais, labelled a 'Jardin Remarquable' by the French Ministry of Culture in 2011)
trees.transport: Tram D, Courbet stop, short walk into the park

best_time.label: October to November: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: Bordeaux's register files this tree as the false elm of Siberia, which is wrong on the geography by about three thousand kilometres. Zelkova carpinifolia comes from the Caucasus and northern Iran, and it reached France in the late 18th century after the botanist Andre Michaux saw the species near the Caspian Sea. One tree from that introduction, planted in 1786, still stands in the Jardin des Plantes in Paris. This one grows beside the lake in the Parc Bordelais, 371 centimetres around and 23 metres tall. Caucasian elm has a shape unlike anything else in a French park: a short trunk that breaks into a dense sheaf of near-vertical branches, so the whole tree reads as a giant upturned broom. Older Bordeaux specimens were often grafted onto elm rootstock, and on some the join is still visible as a change of bark near the base, worth a look while you are down there. The register records its vigour as weak. That is worth knowing rather than worrying about, because the species shrugs off the Dutch elm disease that erased the real elms from these parks, and it can carry declining branches for decades. No newspaper has ever profiled this particular tree, so the measurements are the city's and the rest is what the species does. The park around it was named a Jardin Remarquable by the culture ministry in 2011.

trees.name: The Black Locust of Parc Bordelais
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc Bordelais)
trees.transport: Tram D, Courbet stop, short walk into the park

best_time.label: May to June, when it flowers

trees.story: The register records this black locust as 412 centimetres around and three metres tall. Read that twice. It is thicker than either of the redwoods on the other side of the city and barely taller than a first-floor window, and the two figures agree with each other internally, since the recorded trunk diameter of 131 centimetres matches the girth. That is not a slipped decimal in one field. It is the profile of a tree that has been pollarded hard, or broken by a storm, or cut back to a stump and left to resprout. Which of the three, nobody has written down. No press piece explains it and no photograph has been published that would settle it in a second, so what this entry describes is a shape rather than a canopy: a very wide, very low trunk in the middle of the Parc Bordelais, vigour recorded as weak, still officially listed among Bordeaux's remarkable trees. The species has a long French history. Robinia pseudoacacia arrived from North America in 1601 with Jean Robin, gardener to Henri IV, and the genus carries his name. The tree he planted is still alive in Paris. Black locust also regrows ferociously from cut stumps, which is exactly how a trunk this wide can outlive its own crown. Whatever happened here, the base came through it.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Parc de Bourran
trees.neighbourhood: Merignac, about 5 km west of central Bordeaux
trees.access: Free. Municipal park, open daily.
trees.transport: Merignac, about 5 km west of the centre. Tram A runs out this way from central Bordeaux, roughly twenty minutes, then a few minutes on foot to the park entrance.
trees.story:
A Californian giant sequoia with a trunk close to six metres round stands in what used to be a Bordeaux wine estate. The metropolitan register measures it at 597 centimetres and 24 metres tall, which makes it the heaviest trunk on this page after the Chante-Grillon poplar.

The ground explains the tree. Parc de Bourran was a vineyard belonging to Bordeaux parliamentary families, and in 1768 it was bought by Francois-Armand de Saige, a wine merchant rich enough to control everything from the grape to the shipment, and mayor of Bordeaux in 1791. In 1775 he had an ice house dug into the limestone here, described at the time as the largest in France, and its vaulted cellars still sit under the lawn. The park you walk through now was laid out later by the landscape architect Louis Le Breton, and the whole thing, park and chateau together, was listed as a monument historique in 1992.

Sequoiadendron only reached Europe in the 1850s, so however large this one looks it cannot be older than that, and nobody has published a planting date. The register records its size and says nothing about its age, and neither does this page.

The park belongs to the city of Merignac and is free to walk into.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Parc de Bourran
trees.neighbourhood: Merignac, about 5 km west of central Bordeaux
trees.access: Free. Municipal park, open daily.
trees.transport: Merignac, about 5 km west of the centre. Tram A runs out this way from central Bordeaux, roughly twenty minutes, then a few minutes on foot to the park entrance.
trees.story:
At 32 metres, this deodar is the tallest tree the Bordeaux register records in Parc de Bourran, and its crown spreads twenty metres across. The trunk measures 534 centimetres round.

Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, where it is a timber tree of the high valleys, and it arrived in European gardens in the 1830s. Nineteenth-century landscape designers used it exactly as it is used here: one enormous evergreen, placed where its shape can be read from a distance across open ground. The park was laid out by Louis Le Breton on the remains of a wine estate, and its planting is a catalogue of what a wealthy nineteenth-century garden could get hold of, with a giant sequoia, a coast redwood, a dawn redwood and a bald cypress standing within a few hundred metres of this cedar.

The register gives no age for it and no planting date exists, so this page does not offer one. What can be said is that the park's design and its exotic conifers belong to the same period, and the deodar is the largest of them.

Park and chateau were listed as a monument historique in 1992. The park is free and belongs to Merignac.

trees.name: The Oak of Cvetni Trg
trees.access: Free, public square, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Vračar district, Njegoševa ulica; about a 15 minute walk from Slavija Square

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Belgrade's oldest protected natural monument stands on a market square, not in a forest or a palace garden. The pedunculate oak on Cvetni trg, in the Vračar district, is what is left of the oak and ash woodland that once covered this whole part of the city before Belgrade's 19th-century expansion cleared it for streets and a marketplace; virtually everything else that grew alongside it is gone, and this one tree carries the entire ecosystem's memory alone. It stands about 25 metres tall with a trunk 4 metres around, first protected in 1980 and reconfirmed in a 2001 review, its branches now held with steel cables against the ordinary damage of two centuries. Vračar itself grew up around the tree rather than the other way round: the oak was already old when the square took shape, and the streets, the market stalls and the apartment blocks all arranged themselves at a respectful distance from a trunk that outdates every building currently standing near it. It gets no palace, no royal legend, no famous name attached, just a metal fence, a protection order first signed in 1980, and roughly two centuries of continuous growth on a spot that could easily have gone under concrete instead.

photo.attribution: BuhaM, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Great Plane of Topčider
trees.access: Free, public park, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Topčider district, Savski venac; about a 20 minute drive or bus ride from central Belgrade
trees.story: Seventeen iron posts have held up the crown of Belgrade's largest tree since 1881, propping branches that would otherwise have snapped under their own 49 metre spread a century and a half ago. The plane tree stands in front of Milošev Konak in Topčider, the hunting lodge Prince Miloš Obrenović built as Serbia was clawing its way toward autonomy from the Ottoman Empire, and a popular story credits the prince himself with planting it from a single weak seedling in an old lime kiln. The dates do not cooperate: Miloš left Topčider for exile in 1839, and the tree itself, dated to 1834 by the same municipal records that later declared it a natural monument, was most likely planted after he had already gone. What survives the legend is the tree itself, a trunk 7.35 metres around, a height of 34 metres, and a canopy that shades nearly 1,900 square metres of the park, nearly two centuries into a life that has outlasted a princedom, a kingdom, and two versions of Yugoslavia. Declared a natural monument in 1979, it remains, by most measures, the biggest single tree in the Serbian capital.

photo.attribution: Andy Mabbett (Pigsonthewing), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Two Yews of Belgrade Cathedral
trees.access: Free, public church courtyard, viewable during normal visiting hours
trees.transport: Stari Grad, Kneza Sime Markovića; a 5 minute walk from Knez Mihailova street

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Two yews flank the gate into Belgrade Cathedral's courtyard, one on each side of the entrance on Kneza Sime Markovića street, and between them they demonstrate something most visitors never think to check: yews come in two sexes, and these are one of each. The slightly taller tree, at 13.3 metres, is male; the shorter one, 11.8 metres, is female, and unlike most paired ornamental plantings nobody chose them to match on purpose, they were simply planted together around the turn of the 20th century and grew into their roles. Both were formally protected as natural monuments in 1979, valued specifically for being unusually large, healthy specimens of a species rarely found this size inside a dense city center rather than out in a forest or a rural churchyard. The Cathedral itself, built between 1837 and 1840, is one of Belgrade's most visited churches, and its courtyard sees a steady stream of visitors who walk directly between the two trees without necessarily noticing that the one on their left and the one on their right are, in the plainest botanical sense, a couple.

photo.attribution: BrankaVV, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Yews of Zemun Park
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Zemun, on the Danube waterfront; about a 25 minute bus ride from central Belgrade

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Zemun's Gradski park protects nine trees as a single natural monument, not one, an unusual designation that covers five European yews and four groups of Caucasian wingnut scattered through a park most Belgraders think of simply as Zemun's green center. All are roughly 110 years old, planted around the turn of the 20th century when Zemun was still an Austro-Hungarian town across the river from the Kingdom of Serbia rather than the Belgrade municipality it later became. Caucasian wingnut, a fast growing riverside tree from the Caucasus and northern Iran, is rare enough in Serbian parks that finding four separate stands of it in one place justified protecting the whole grouping in 1991 rather than picking out a single champion specimen. The yews do the more familiar work, dark, dense evergreen shapes among the park's roughly 1,300 other trees, old enough and large enough to count as genuine heritage rather than ordinary planting. Nothing here has a named legend attached, no prince, no botanist, no famous visitor, just a formal designation covering an entire pocket of a park that has quietly outlasted the empire it was planted under.

photo.attribution: Milica Buha (BuhaM), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: Dicke Marie
trees.access: Free, public forest, open at all times
trees.transport: 12-15 min walk from Alt-Tegel U-Bahn (U6), via the Tegel harbour bridge and lakeside path

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Berlin's oldest tree is older than the city itself. When Berlin got its first written mention in 1237, this pedunculate oak in the Tegel Forest had likely already been growing for over a century, its germination dated to around 1107. How much older it has grown since is a genuine dispute. Forestry officials have long put it at 800 to 900 years. In 2021 the German Dendrological Society's own National Heritage Tree board reassessed the same trunk and came back with a more conservative 500 to 600, arguing that internal decay makes anything more precise a guess. Both numbers can't be right, and this project would rather say so than pick the more impressive one. What isn't disputed: two teenage brothers who summered nearby at Schloss Tegel, Alexander and Wilhelm von Humboldt, are said to have named the tree after the family's cook around 1800, and the joke outlived them both. Goethe reportedly rested in its shade in 1778. The oak has grown gnarled and hollow rather than tall, topping out at just 15 to 16 metres, its bulk going into a trunk nearly six metres round instead. On 9 July 2021 it became the first forest tree in Germany named a National Heritage Tree, a small formal honor for something that was already, by any count, the oldest living thing in a city of 3.8 million people.

trees.name: The Humboldt Oak
trees.access: Free (a 1 euro donation is requested at the gate); park open daily until sunset, the palace interior open only on Mondays, May to September
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Alt-Tegel U-Bahn (U6)

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: The thickest trunk in Berlin does not belong to the city's oldest tree. It belongs to its neighbour. A few hundred metres from Dicke Marie, inside the grounds of Schloss Tegel, this pedunculate oak has swollen to 7.80 metres around, wider than Dicke Marie despite being younger by centuries: 400 to 500 years old rather than 800 or more. It takes its name from the same family who has owned Schloss Tegel since 1766 and still does today, one of the few noble German estates that never left its original bloodline. Alexander von Humboldt, the naturalist whose name later ended up on a university, an ocean current and a squid, grew up walking past this oak on his way to the lake. Berlin listed it as a natural monument in 1939, protecting a crown that now spans 18 metres, wide enough to shade a tennis court. The palace itself only opens to visitors on Mondays between May and September, but the park around it, this tree included, stays open year round until sunset, for a suggested one euro donation left at the gate. Stand under it and you are looking at more wood, by circumference, than anywhere else in the German capital, a record that has nothing to do with age at all.

trees.name: The Steinlanke Oak
trees.access: Free, public forest, open at all times
trees.transport: Bus 218 from S-Bahnhof Wannsee (toward Theodor-Heuss-Platz), then a lakeside forest walk; roughly 45-60 min on foot from Wannsee station if not using the bus

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Grunewald's oldest tree survived storms that took its own crown apart. Foresters put its age at 350 to 400 years depending on which survey is cited, a girth measurement that grew from 6.48 metres in 2018 to a commonly quoted 6.70 metres more recently, either of which means it was standing before Prussia existed as a kingdom. It grows at the Große Steinlanke, a quiet inlet of the Havel on the forest's western edge, its trunk gnarled and visibly weathered, the upper crown thinned by what local foresters describe as probable lightning strikes accumulated over centuries. A small sign near the Großes Fenster clearing, by the volunteer lifeguard station, points visitors to it, one of the few individually marked trees in a forest better known for its total size than any single specimen. Grunewald is Berlin's largest contiguous forest, threaded with lake paths popular with swimmers and joggers in summer, and this oak predates every villa and boathouse now standing near it. Reaching it takes real effort: the nearest train station, Wannsee, is nearly an hour's walk away, so most visitors take the 218 bus toward Theodor-Heuss-Platz and finish on foot along the shoreline. Nothing about it looks spectacular from a distance. Up close, the girth and the storm damage written into its upper branches tell a longer story than any plaque could.

trees.name: The Swamp Cypress of Charlottenburg
trees.access: Free, palace gardens open daily; the state rooms charge admission separately
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Sophie-Charlotte-Platz U-Bahn (U2) or Richard-Wagner-Platz U-Bahn (U7)

best_time.label: late October, when it drops its needles like a deciduous tree, the habit that confuses visitors expecting a conifer to stay green

trees.story: A swamp tree from the American South has spent two centuries in a Prussian palace garden. This bald cypress, native to the flooded river bottoms of the southeastern United States, went into the ground in Schlosspark Charlottenburg around 200 years ago, most likely during Peter Joseph Lenné's redesign of the grounds into an English-style landscape park. It has grown to five metres around and over 15 metres tall, dropping its needles every winter like a deciduous tree despite being a conifer, a habit that confuses first-time visitors expecting evergreen. Berlin protects it as a natural monument for a reason that has little to do with its size: its aging, partly hollow wood now shelters the hermit beetle, a rare, EU-protected species that depends on old, decaying timber exactly like this to survive at all. You are now more likely to help that beetle by leaving a tree standing than by planting a new one. The palace itself, the largest surviving Hohenzollern residence in Berlin, charges admission for its state rooms, but the gardens are free and open daily, the formal French parterre near the palace giving way further back to Lenné's looser, English-style paths, where this cypress stands among other 19th-century imports the royal gardeners tested against Berlin's winters. Most of them did not last two centuries. This one has.

trees.name: The Great Elm of Treptower Park
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Treptower Park S-Bahn station (S8/S9/S41/S42/S85/S46)
trees.story: The newest tree on Germany's national heritage register has its roots in a river. This European white elm, standing directly on the Spree's bank in Treptower Park, was declared a National Heritage Tree only on 25 September 2025, one of the most recent additions to a small national list that otherwise mostly honors trees for age or scale alone. This one earns its place partly through rarity: Ulmus laevis is a floodplain elm scarce enough in Germany that a healthy 250-year-old specimen counts as remarkable regardless of size. Its roots reach directly into the Spree, drawing on a water supply few park trees get, which foresters credit for a vigor unusual in a tree this old. The trunk measures 6.35 metres around and the crown rises 25 metres, making it one of the largest trees in a park better known for its Soviet war memorial than its vegetation. It stands near the Rosengarten, a short walk from the boat landing, easily found by anyone walking the riverside path instead of heading straight for the monument. Dutch elm disease wiped out most of mainland Europe's mature elms across the twentieth century, a fungus spread by bark beetles that killed trees by the millions. This species, less favored by those beetles than the more common field and Wych elms, simply kept growing while its relatives disappeared.

trees.name: The Mahlsdorf Village Lime
trees.access: Free, stands on public ground in front of the church on Hönower Straße, viewable at all times (a low fence protects the base and root area)
trees.transport: 10-12 min walk from Berlin-Mahlsdorf S-Bahn station (S5)

best_time.label: late June, when the lime blossom scents the street

trees.story: In 2021 Berlin's district register dropped two of Mahlsdorf's protected trees, a Balkan horse chestnut and a black poplar, from its list of natural monuments. A crooked, ten metre lime standing in front of the neighbourhood's oldest building was not one of them. The Mahlsdorf Village Lime, a small-leaved lime outside the old parish church on Hönower Straße, has been protected since 1993 for outright rarity rather than size, a designation it has now outlasted two neighbours to keep. Its age is put at a minimum of 300 years, with local historians tracing the planting to the 17th century. Height was never the point: centuries of storm damage bent and hollowed the crown instead of raising it, leaving a squat, mossy shape barely taller than the church roofline while its trunk swelled to a girth of 4.45 metres, wider than many trees three times its height. By 1995 the district judged the limbs unsafe to leave unsupported and spent 8,000 Deutsche Mark bracing them with steel cables and fencing the base, work that still holds the tree together today. It stands on the old village high street, beside a church that itself survived the Thirty Years' War and the 1945 bombing, two witnesses to the same stretch of road that outlasted the empire, kingdom and two republics built around them.

trees.name: The Treskow Plane
trees.access: Paid entry (Tierpark Berlin zoo ticket required)
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Tierpark U-Bahn station (U5)
trees.story: The oldest tree at Berlin's Tierpark predates the zoo around it by roughly two centuries. This London plane, its branches so intertwined that some have fused into single, oval cross-sectioned limbs, was already standing when the grounds were still the pleasure gardens of Friedrichsfelde Palace, a Hohenzollern summer residence later owned by the agricultural reformer Johann Carl Sigismund von Treskow, whose name it now carries. Lichtenberg's environmental office estimated its age at 250 years in a 2015 survey, putting its planting sometime in the mid-1700s, two centuries before the palace grounds reopened as a public zoo in 1955. It has grown a trunk 4.65 metres around and a crown 20 metres wide, tall enough at 25 metres to be visible over the enclosures near it. Reaching it requires a Tierpark Berlin ticket, since it now stands inside the zoo's grounds rather than in an open park, an unusual condition for a tree on this list but not a disqualifying one: anyone can buy a ticket at the gate. Look past the animals for a moment and you are standing under a plane tree that has outlasted a palace, survived the transition from royal garden to public zoo, and kept growing through both.

trees.name: The Kaisereiche
trees.access: Free, public street corner
trees.transport: 10 min walk from S-Bahnhof Feuerbachstraße (S1), or the Kaisereiche bus stop directly

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Someone tried to kill this oak as a political protest, and Berlin planted a replacement within weeks. The original Kaisereiche went into the ground on 22 March 1879, planted by a local publisher to mark Kaiser Wilhelm I's 82nd birthday and golden wedding anniversary, at what was then a traffic circle on the edge of the new suburb of Friedenau. In November 1883, five years after two separate assassination attempts on the Kaiser had given Chancellor Bismarck his pretext for the Anti-Socialist Laws, someone damaged the tree badly enough that it needed full replacement, an act read at the time as a protest against those same laws. The oak standing at the corner of Rheinstraße and Moselstraße today is that replacement, which makes it roughly 143 years old rather than the 147 the original planting date would suggest, a small but honest distinction most retellings skip. Berlin protects it as a natural monument, and in 2004 a Hohenzollern descendant, Franz Friedrich Prinz von Preußen, unveiled a plaque marking 125 years since the first tree went in. The intersection has no official street name of its own, but Berlin's transit map still labels the bus stop and taxi rank here Kaisereiche, a small act of memory that has outlasted the publisher, the Kaiser, and the empire both men served.

photo.attribution: Dirk Ingo Franke, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Schlosspark Britz
trees.access: Free (Gutspark); Schloss Britz's period rooms charge separate admission
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Parchimer Allee U-Bahn (U7), or bus 181 to Alt-Britz

best_time.label: late October, when every leaf turns gold and drops within days

trees.story: Berlin's oldest and tallest ginkgo survived something most of its European relatives never had to: being fashionable. Ginkgo biloba reached European gardens in the 18th century as a botanical curiosity, a living link to trees that grew alongside dinosaurs, and wealthy estates across the continent planted them as status symbols rather than for shade or timber. This one went into Gutspark Britz sometime between 1880 and 1890, when royal garden inspector Wilhelm Nahlop redesigned the grounds of a former manor estate into the landscape park still standing today. It has grown a trunk over three metres around and stands close to 20 metres tall, the largest ginkgo recorded anywhere in the German capital. Ginkgos are dioecious, meaning individual trees are strictly male or female, and this one's autumn performance is the reward for the wait: every leaf turns a uniform gold within days of each other in late October, then drops almost at once, rather than the gradual, patchy fade most trees go through. The palace itself, Schloss Britz, charges a small admission fee for its restored period rooms, but the surrounding Gutspark is free and open daily, its grounds having won a national landscape prize in 1997, decades after the ginkgo inside it had already quietly become the biggest in Berlin.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Tiergarten
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Bellevue S-Bahn station, inside the Tiergarten's Englischer Garten section
trees.story: A tree that can live 3,000 years in California has had 135 of them in central Berlin. This giant sequoia, planted in 1891 in the Englischer Garten section of the Tiergarten, arrived in Europe only decades after the species itself did: the first seeds reached the continent in 1853, imported from California just two years after the tree was formally described at all, setting off a brief craze among wealthy estate owners for what nurseries of the time marketed as Wellingtonia. Berlin's planting, in the city's largest and most central park, is modest by the standards of a species that can exceed 90 metres in its native range, but it remains one of the tallest and bulkiest conifers growing anywhere in the capital. It stands a short walk from Schloss Bellevue, the German president's official residence, in a section of the Tiergarten deliberately landscaped in the looser, informal English style rather than the geometric French gardens found elsewhere in the park. Two world wars swept through the Tiergarten in the twentieth century, and postwar Berliners felled most of the park's remaining trees for firewood during the famine winters that followed 1945. This sequoia, planted decades earlier by gardeners with no idea what the century ahead held, made it through anyway.

trees.name: The Great Oak of Pfaueninsel
trees.access: Free to walk once on the island. The island itself is car-free and reached only by a short chain ferry from the Nikolskoer Weg landing (adult single ticket 6 euros as of April 2026, family ticket 12 euros); the castle interior (separate, recently reopened after 2021-2025 restoration) is a different ticket and not needed to see this tree.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then roughly a 10-15 minute walk into the island to the Schlosswiese meadow area

best_time.label: January, when the leaves are gone and the five-limbed crown structure shows plainly

trees.story:
Pfaueninsel's oaks were already old when the island became a royal garden. In 1793, Friedrich Wilhelm II ordered the landscaping of this Havel island, and his court gardener kept the oak stand standing rather than clear it, because the trees were already a century old by then. This one, on the meadow near the Schloss, may be one of those originals: at 565 to 567 centimetres around, it was until recently the largest and most striking oak on the island, its short trunk splitting low into one main stem and five curving limbs.

Nobody has measured its age directly, so a range is the honest answer here: somewhere between 200 and 400 years, bracketed from the island's own history rather than a bore sample. What is on record is a more recent event. Surveyors who examined the tree later criticized a crown reduction carried out on it, describing the pruning as unnecessary and unprofessional work on a specimen that deserved better handling.

The island itself has stayed almost untouched since. Pfaueninsel is reachable only by a short chain ferry, has no cars, and keeps the eighteenth century pleasure-garden layout Friedrich Wilhelm II laid out around trees like this one. Peacocks still roam it, the reason for the name. Walk the meadow near the Schloss and this is the oak the Prussian court gardener chose to save.

trees.name: The Tuereiche (Door Oak) of Pfaueninsel
trees.species: Sessile Oak (Quercus petraea) per monumentaltrees.com; Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) per baumkunde.de, an unresolved species conflict
trees.access: Free to walk once on the island, reached only by the chain ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, the same crossing as the island's other oaks.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then a walk into the island near the Schloss.
trees.story:
Somebody built a working door into this oak's trunk, and it is still there. The Tuereiche, the Door Oak, stands near the Schloss on Pfaueninsel, its 5.58 metre girth measured just once, in 2017, by a tree registry that has not been back since.

Two sources agree on its size and disagree on its species. One calls it a pedunculate oak, the other a sessile oak, working from what looks like the same underlying survey rather than two independent looks at the tree. Berlin's own list of protected trees on the island names four sessile oaks and no pedunculate ones, which tips the balance without settling it outright.

Its age, about 250 years by the registry's estimate, is a guess made honestly: nobody has cored it, and the door itself, whatever its original purpose, carries no date of its own. What is certain is the island around it. Pfaueninsel became a royal retreat in 1793, and Friedrich Wilhelm II's gardeners built the new landscape around oaks that already stood there, this one very possibly among them.

Reach it by the same short ferry that serves the rest of the island's oaks, then walk toward the Schloss. Look for the door before you look for the tree. Most visitors do it the other way round and miss it entirely.

trees.name: The Pond Oak of Pfaueninsel
trees.species: Sessile Oak (Quercus petraea), per Berlin's official Naturdenkmal register
trees.age: undocumented; likely 100-300 years, inferred from the island's wider oak stand
trees.access: Free to walk once on the island, reached only by the chain ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, the same crossing as the island's other oaks.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then a longer walk to the northern part of the island near the Wasservogelteich.
trees.story:
The most precise thing known about this oak comes from a stranger's holiday photo. In May 2024 a visitor uploaded a picture of a wide-crowned oak north of the Wasservogelteich, Pfaueninsel's waterfowl pond, and the phone's own GPS placed the tree more accurately than any register description on file.

Berlin's protected-tree list already knew it existed: one of four sessile oaks on the island carrying legal Naturdenkmal status, described only by compass bearing and a rough distance from a landmark. No age is recorded anywhere, and none should be invented, though the island's oak stand generally predates the royal garden built around it from 1793.

What the photo confirms is that the tree is alive, healthy and exactly where the register said it should be: a wide, well-formed crown branching low over the path. It sits far enough from Pfaueninsel's other two documented oaks, roughly a kilometre, that it will not fit into the same five-minute stop, but the whole island is under a kilometre long, an easy single walk that takes in all three.

Same ferry, same island, further into it: past the Schloss and toward the pond, where deciduous woodland shelters some of Pfaueninsel's least visited but longest-standing residents.

photo.attribution: S.Makhin, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Ferry Landing Plane
trees.access: Free, and no ferry ticket required: this tree stands on the mainland side of the crossing, by the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel restaurant and ferry dock, unlike the island's other protected oaks, which need a paid ferry.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then under 5 minutes on foot to the ferry landing area
trees.story: Three of Pfaueninsel's protected oaks require a ferry ticket. This plane tree does not. Berlin's Naturdenkmal register lists it at Pfaueninselchaussee 100, the address of the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel, the old inn that has stood at the mainland ferry dock since long before the chain ferry became the island's only public access. The oaks across the water needed the eighteenth century royal garden that grew up around them to survive this long; this plane needed nothing more than the road leading to the crossing point, protected for its beauty and its tie to the place rather than for age or rarity, the reason the district gives on its own designation record. No planting date survives, and no second source beyond the government ordinance has turned up despite real searching, an honest gap rather than an invented history. What makes it worth including anyway is the position: anyone heading for the Pfaueninsel oaks passes directly beside it, on the free side of the water, before they have paid for anything at all. See this one on the way in, whether or not the ferry crossing that follows fits the day.

trees.name: The Cut-Leaf Oak of Pfaueninsel
trees.species: Sessile Oak, cut-leaf variety (Quercus petraea var. laciniata)
trees.access: Free to walk once on the island, reached only by the chain ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, the same crossing as the island's other oaks.
trees.transport: Bus 218 (from S-Bahnhof Wannsee or Heckeshorn) to the 'Pfaueninsel' stop, then a 5 minute walk to the ferry landing, then the ferry crossing, then roughly 10-15 minutes into the island to the area northeast of the Schloss, close to the Great Oak.
trees.story: Forty five metres from Pfaueninsel's Great Oak stands a second, stranger oak that Berlin protects for an entirely different reason. Where its famous neighbour earned Naturdenkmal status for size and disputed age, this one is registered for rarity alone: a cut-leaf sessile oak, Quercus petraea var. laciniata, a naturally occurring variety with deeply dissected, almost fern-like foliage instead of the plain oval leaf every other oak on the island carries. The two trees stand close enough that a visitor could assume the register was describing the same tree twice. It is not. The government ordinance that protects both lists them under separate numbers, at separate coordinates, for separate reasons, one for its bulk, the other purely because its leaf shape almost never occurs in the wild. No age is recorded for this one at all, since rarity rather than antiquity is the whole case for protecting it, and no source beyond the designation record itself has been found describing this specific tree. Find the Great Oak first, then look forty five metres further for its odd, deeply cut cousin, the rarer of the two despite standing in its more famous neighbour's shadow.

trees.name: The Lietzensee Plane
trees.access: Free, public park (Lietzenseepark)
trees.transport: Sophie-Charlotte-Platz or Kaiserdamm (U2), about 10-12 minutes' walk
trees.story:
This plane added 43 centimetres to its waistline in ten years. Measured at chest height it went from 6.00 metres in 2015 to 6.43 metres in 2025, which by circumference makes it the sixth thickest tree on record anywhere in Berlin. A laser measurement in 2025 put its height at 22 metres.

The date usually given for its planting is 1807, an estimate rather than a ring count. That would make it a sapling in an occupied city, the year after Napoleon's army marched through the Brandenburg Gate and took the Quadriga off the top of it to Paris. Everything around the tree arrived later. Lietzenseepark is a twentieth century arrangement of terraces and lakeside paths, laid out around trees that were already big when the surveyors turned up.

Berlin protects it as a natural monument under the number 4-26/B, which is the city saying in administrative language that nobody touches this one. It was photographed alive and in full leaf in May 2025.

The register keeps no age and no girth of its own, so both figures above come from the volunteer surveyors who have been measuring it every five years, which is also how anyone knows it is still growing. From here the shore path runs about 170 metres to a Caucasian wingnut, the other reason this lake is on the map.

trees.name: The Lietzensee Wingnut
trees.access: Free, public park (Lietzenseepark)
trees.transport: Sophie-Charlotte-Platz or Kaiserdamm (U2), about 10-12 minutes' walk

best_time.label: July and August, when half-metre chains of winged nutlets hang from every branch tip

trees.story:
Berlin has five Caucasian wingnuts on record, and this one is not yet a hundred years old. The planting date on file is 1927, which by the standards of most trees on this map is recent, and it is not why anyone stops here.

The shape is. The trunk breaks into several stems close to the ground, so the surveyors who measured it gave up on the usual chest height and put the tape around the base instead: 5.94 metres at ground level, a figure they flagged themselves as flattering, because a fork counts as girth in a way a single trunk never does. What it produces is a tree that reads as a small grove growing out of one root plate.

Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the Caucasus and northern Iran, where it grows in wet ground along rivers, which is why it has done so well on the edge of a Berlin lake and why it is a rare thing in the drier planting beds of the rest of the city. In midsummer it hangs chains of winged nutlets, half a metre long, off the tips of every branch.

Berlin protects it as natural monument 4-25/B. The most recent published photograph of it dates from June 2015 and the register listing has carried it since, so if you find it changed, tell us. The Lietzensee plane stands about 170 metres along the same shore.

trees.name: The Karpfenteich Elm
trees.access: Free, public park (Schlosspark Charlottenburg)
trees.transport: Richard-Wagner-Platz (U7) or Sophie-Charlotte-Platz (U2), about 12-15 minutes' walk
trees.story:
Nobody knows how old this elm is, and that is the honest answer rather than a gap waiting to be filled. Berlin protects it as natural monument 4-27/B at the southeastern corner of the carp pond behind Charlottenburg Palace, and neither the city register nor the surveyors who have measured it twice will put a year on it.

What is on record is size and a near standstill. Its trunk was 4.85 metres around in 2015 and 4.88 metres in 2020, roughly six millimetres of growth a year, the pace of a tree that finished the growing part of its life a long time ago. A laser put it at 21.5 metres tall in July 2020.

The species is the reason to look twice. European white elm is uncommon in city plantings, and Dutch elm disease has taken most of the big elms across the continent over the past century, so a mature one of this girth is a survivor rather than a specimen.

Its address helps. The grounds were laid out in the 1690s as the formal garden of Sophie Charlotte's summer palace and later loosened into an English landscape park, and the carp pond it stands on belongs to that second version. The swamp cypress at the other end of the same park is about a hundred metres away. The last published photographs of the elm were taken in February 2015 and July 2020.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Fraenkel Garden
trees.access: Free, the garden is open to the public with a visitor centre (restored and reopened 2016)
trees.transport: BVG ferry F10 to Alt-Kladow, or bus, then a walk to the garden on Luedickeweg
trees.story: Berlin declared this copper beech a natural monument in 1993, growing inside Landhausgarten Dr. Max Fraenkel, a garden the banker Fraenkel commissioned around 1930 on the Havel shore at Kladow, on ground that had been a brickworks. He hired Erwin Barth, then the city's director of gardens, who laid out a formal rose garden, a perennial-lined cascade and fruit and vegetable plots close to the house, then a looser landscape section further out with a waterfall, ponds and a tea pavilion. The garden changed hands and use across the rest of the century before Spandau's district authorities restored it and reopened it to the public in 2016, with a visitor centre standing where a private family once entertained guests. The beech carries the register's protection for beauty and local historical interest, but no source yet gives its age or girth, so both stay open questions for whoever measures it next. It stands somewhere within the garden's 2.97 hectares, free to walk and easy to reach from central Berlin, on the same route the BVG ferry and the weekend cyclists take out to Kladow. Its crown, dark purple against the garden's greens, is one more layer in grounds that were built up in stages across nearly a century.

trees.name: The Bald Cypresses of Parco Marenzi
trees.access: Free, public municipal park, reopened 20 April 2026 after pond restoration.
trees.transport: Central Bergamo (Citta Bassa), about a 10 to 15 minute walk from Porta Nuova.
trees.story: These two are American swamp trees, and they have been standing in a walled Bergamo garden for more than two centuries. Bald cypress evolved for the flooded bottomlands of the American South, where it pushes woody knees up out of the waterlogged ground to breathe. Both do it here, at the edge of Parco Marenzi's small artificial lake, which is about as close to Louisiana as Lombardy gets. The national register measures the pair separately, at 455 and 380 centimetres round the trunk, and lists them a third time as a single group; what a visitor gets is one destination, two enormous trunks and roughly 32 metres of tree above them. The park is a 9,000 square metre nineteenth century garden behind walls, and for years that was literal. It stayed shut while the pond and its water system were rebuilt, and reopened to the public in April 2026 after a 180,000 euro restoration. In May 2025, for Italy's national day of monumental trees, the city ran a guided forest bathing walk among them, on the reasoning that a bald cypress can live a thousand years. These two are barely a fifth of the way there. They turn rust orange and drop their needles in November, which is the only time of year a conifer this size looks dead and is not.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Parco Caprotti
trees.access: Free, public municipal park.
trees.transport: Central Bergamo (Citta Bassa), close to Via Tasso, a short walk from Parco Marenzi.
trees.story: Bergamo's own green space writers call Parco Caprotti perhaps the least known park in the lower town, which is a strange thing to say about a garden holding a 25 metre Atlas cedar, a sequoia and a ginkgo. The three arrived together. The grounds go back to the fifteenth century, but the planting is the work of Carlo Caprotti, an industrialist who gave the park its current layout around the turn of the twentieth century and stocked it the way wealthy Italians of that era stocked gardens, with conifers from other continents chosen for size. The Atlas cedar comes from dry mountain forest in Morocco and Algeria. Here it has 405 centimetres of trunk circumference and the flat, layered branching that the species only develops with age, close cousin to the cedar of Lebanon and often mistaken for it. Beyond the register entry the documentation is thin: one local green space site names it, and no newspaper or municipal page found so far does, so treat the garden's history as local knowledge rather than settled record. The tree itself is not in question, and neither is the way in. Parco Caprotti is free, open, and a short walk from Parco Marenzi, which makes the two of them half an afternoon in the lower town.

trees.name: The Strawberry Tree of Via alla Rocca
trees.access: Free, public park below the Rocca fortress in Citta Alta.
trees.transport: Citta Alta, Bergamo's upper town; reachable on foot or by the funicular from Citta Bassa, then a short walk to the Rocca grounds.
trees.story: Most strawberry trees are shrubs you can see over the top of. This one is 16 metres tall with a trunk 355 centimetres round, which for Arbutus unedo is close to the ceiling of what the species does. It grows in the public park below the Rocca, the medieval fortress crowning Bergamo's upper town, and locally it is read as a symbol of strength and resistance. That reading is not sentiment. The species carries dark green leaves, white flowers and red fruit on the same branches at the same time, and nineteenth century Italian patriots noticed the tricolour and adopted it, which makes its position under a fortress about as pointed as a planting gets. The strawberry tree is slow, hard and stubborn, native to Mediterranean scrub, and it flowers in late autumn while the previous year's fruit is still ripening, so October and November give you both colours on one branch. The fruit is edible and dull, which is what the Latin name says: unedo, eat only one. Beyond the national register, which lists it on girth and height alone, a single local source names it, so who planted it and when has not survived. The Rocca grounds are free, reached on foot or by the funicular from the lower town and then a short climb.

trees.name: The Silk Mulberries of Giardino Paul Harris
trees.access: Free, public garden in the Santa Lucia district.
trees.transport: Citta Bassa, Santa Lucia district, a short walk from central Bergamo.

best_time.label: June and July, when the pale fruit drops and stains the path

trees.story: These three trees were planted as machinery. White mulberry leaf is the only thing a silkworm will eat, and for centuries the gardens and field edges around Bergamo were planted with mulberries to supply the province's silk trade, which stripped the leaves each spring and fed them to trays of larvae in farmhouse lofts. The industry is gone. Its trees are still here, in a small public garden in the Santa Lucia district, where three old white mulberries survive as a group. The national register lists them exactly that way, as a homogeneous set rather than three separate specimens, with no individual measurements, so what you are visiting is a garden with three trunks in it rather than one named tree. That is also why the pin is approximate: the register gives the garden's centre point and nothing finer, though the garden is small enough that the trees find you. Mulberries grown for leaf were cut back hard year after year, and it shows in the species: squat trunks, heavy stubbed limbs, none of the reach of a tree left alone. Beyond the register a single local source names them and their silk connection, and their ages are unrecorded. In June and July they drop pale fruit that stains the path underfoot.

trees.name: The Giant Cedar of Pedrengo
trees.access: Free, small public urban park (Parco Frizzoni), a Fondo Ambiente Italiano (FAI) recognised site.
trees.transport: Pedrengo, a village about 5km / roughly 15 minutes by car or local bus from central Bergamo; day-trip distance, not walkable from the city centre.
trees.story: This cedar has its own lightning conductor. It stands alone in the middle of the lawn in a small public park in Pedrengo, a village about five kilometres east of Bergamo, roughly fifteen minutes by bus or car and not a walk from the city centre. Out on open grass at 32 metres by the national register, or 35 by the regional tourism board, it is the tallest thing for some distance, and somebody decided it was worth wiring rather than losing. Its root plate is fenced for the same reason. The trunk measures 683 centimetres round in the register and 720 in the tourism survey, which is measurement variance rather than a dispute, and either way it takes four adults with linked arms to close the circle. The crown spreads about 25 metres, and the leading tip droops over in the way old deodars do, a shape known as a stork's nest. It was planted at the end of the nineteenth century, which is as precise as the record gets, so somewhere around 130 years old is the honest figure. Three more large cedars of the same species stand nearby in the same park, unregistered and worth the extra two minutes. Parco Frizzoni is free, small, and recognised by FAI, Italy's heritage trust.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Villa Piccinelli
trees.access: Free, public park managed by the Comune di Seriate; the greenhouse/pavilion inside is used for occasional exhibitions, but the park grounds are municipal and open.
trees.transport: Seriate, about 4km / roughly 10 to 15 minutes by bus or car from central Bergamo; day-trip distance.
trees.story: The merchants who owned this garden brought plants back from Asia, Africa and the Americas, and built a Moroccan style greenhouse in 1860 to keep the fragile ones alive. The Himalayan cedar never needed it. It came from mountain forest that gets snow, so it took to the high bank above the Serio river without help, and is now 30 metres tall with a trunk 465 centimetres round, the largest tree in the park. Deodar is the timber cedar of the western Himalaya, cut for temples in India because the wood does not rot, and it reached European gardens only in the 1830s, which puts a hard upper limit on how old any specimen on this continent can be. The eighteenth century villa was built by the Piccinelli family on trading money; the council owns the grounds now and runs them as a free public park, with the old greenhouse still standing as a garden pavilion and used for occasional exhibitions. No age is recorded for the tree anywhere we could find, only the measurements. Parco Piccinelli is in Seriate, about four kilometres from central Bergamo and ten to fifteen minutes by bus, so this is a short trip out rather than a stop on a city walk. The grove of pagoda trees a few minutes away in the same park is the other reason to make it.

trees.name: The Pagoda Trees of Villa Piccinelli
trees.access: Free, public park managed by the Comune di Seriate, the same grounds as the Himalayan Cedar of Villa Piccinelli.
trees.transport: Seriate, about 4km / roughly 10 to 15 minutes by bus or car from central Bergamo; day-trip distance.

best_time.label: August and September, when cream flowers open and little else is in bloom

trees.story: Local press calls this the most renowned of Seriate's seven registered monumental trees, and it is not a tree. The national register lists it as a homogeneous group of pagoda trees, with trunks ranging from 265 to 455 centimetres round and heights up to 35 metres, which means the grove holds both its founders and its successors and no single specimen carries the entry. The pin is approximate for that reason: the register gives a centre point for the group rather than a position for each trunk. It sits in the same municipal park as the Villa Piccinelli cedar, a few minutes' walk away, in Seriate, about four kilometres out from central Bergamo. Despite the name the pagoda tree is Chinese rather than Japanese, planted around temples there long before European gardeners got hold of it in the eighteenth century. Its useful trick is timing. It flowers in August and September, when almost everything else in a northern Italian park has finished, hanging cream panicles over the grass and then dropping them, so the ground under these trees goes pale for a couple of weeks in late summer. Strings of seed pods follow in autumn, shaped like beads on a wire. Seriate has a second registered pagoda tree at Villa Ambiveri, on private ground, which is a different tree and not this one.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Viale delle Rimembranze
trees.neighbourhood: Torre Boldone, a comune bordering Bergamo
trees.access: Free, standing along a public street (Viale delle Rimembranze) in the village centre of Torre Boldone.
trees.transport: TEB tramline T1 (Bergamo-Albino), Torre Boldone stop, then a short walk along Viale delle Rimembranze.

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story:
Torre Boldone had two comune-protected giants until 2017, when the Cedar of Lebanon in Parco dei Sordomuti was illegally felled. This horse chestnut, standing on Viale delle Rimembranze since long before either tree was designated, became the village's last one and has had a hard decade of it since.

An agronomist checked it in 2017 and found nothing worse than ordinary decline. The comune's own crew then pollarded it without authorisation the following January, cutting its height by roughly a third, a job forestry officials confirmed had no permit and that a local environmental group formally protested. A large limb came down on its own in June 2021.

Nobody has published a sighting since. What keeps it on this list is a colder kind of evidence: Lombardy's regional register of monumental trees, most recently updated in October 2025, still lists it standing, at a girth of 391 centimetres unchanged from before the damage. A comune has to report a felling for a tree to drop off that register, and nobody has.

So this entry ships on an official record rather than a fresh photograph. If you walk Viale delle Rimembranze and the chestnut is there, or isn't, tell us. Torre Boldone has already lost one monumental tree to a saw it was not supposed to hold; this is how you find out whether it kept the other.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of Jardines de Albia
trees.access: Free, open public square in central Bilbao, accessible at all times
trees.transport: Abando metro/train station, about 5 minutes' walk
trees.story:
A photograph from the 1940s shows these plane trees already standing clear of the five-storey buildings around them. They still do. Jardines de Albia is barely 4,500 square metres, one block of green in Bilbao's Abando district, and the trees are what the Bilbao daily Deia reached for in 2023 when it called the square almost unchanged: grandes plataneros, more than a hundred years old, grown to the height of the facades that enclose them.

Stand in front of the Antonio Trueba statue, put up in 1892, and you get the whole square at once: bronze poet, gravel, crowns closing overhead. The place has been named three different things in its life, Jardines de Albia, Plaza de Trueba and Jardines de Berastegui, and people here still use all three.

What nobody has done is measure one of these trees. No source names an individual specimen, gives it a girth or records when it went in, so the age is what that 1940s photograph will carry and nothing more: over a century, not a figure anyone has taken a tape to. Read the pin the same way. The coordinates are the square's, not any one trunk's, which matters less here than usual because the square is the thing you came to stand in. If you know when Albia was planted, or which of these planes is the oldest, tell us.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of Deusto
trees.access: Free. Stands at the entrance forecourt of the University of Deusto's main (1886) building, on the public avenue facing the Guggenheim across the river; the building itself is a working university, but the entrance grounds where the tree stands are open to the public.
trees.transport: San Mames or Deusto metro/tram stop, about 10 minutes' walk; also on the riverside walkway opposite the Guggenheim Museum.

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn copper and drop and the conifer stands bare

trees.story:
A tree from the swamps of the American south stands at the front door of a Basque university, looking across the river at the Guggenheim. Bald cypress belongs in standing water in Louisiana and Florida, and this one has spent its life on a paved forecourt in rainy Bilbao, at the entrance to the 1886 main building of the Universidad de Deusto.

The Bilbao history site Absolut Bilbao puts it at nearly 25 metres tall, with a crown more than eight metres across and a trunk around three metres thick. Treat those numbers as reported rather than measured: they come from a single source, and three metres of trunk would be exceptional for the species outside its native bottomlands. Large, and roughly stated, is the honest reading.

Its party trick is seasonal. Taxodium distichum is a conifer that goes bare, turning rust and copper in November and dropping its needles while the evergreens around it stay green, which is the thing visitors argue about before somebody looks it up.

The building behind it dates from 1886 and the tree stands on its forecourt, but nothing we could reach dates the tree, and a university campus plants trees in every decade of its life. This one may be original to the building or may be decades younger. Nobody has put a number on it. If you know when it went in, or have taken a tape to that trunk, tell us.

trees.name: The Centenary Trees of Parque de la Misericordia
trees.access: Free during the day; the park is walled and gated shut at night, per bilbaovisitavirtual.eus.
trees.transport: Sabino Arana tram/metro stop, about 4 minutes' walk.
trees.story:
More than forty species of tree grow inside the walls of a Bilbao almshouse. The Santa y Real Casa de Misericordia moved to this site in Indautxu in 1872 and laid a romantic-style garden out around itself, and two sources describe what stands there now in the same terms: Spanish Wikipedia counts over forty different species and calls them arboles centenarios, and a Bilbao visitor guide says plainly that these are trees with more than a century of life behind them.

The garden is the destination here rather than any one trunk. It is walled, gated shut at night and only 16,600 square metres, so you can walk all of it in twenty minutes and see most of what it holds. A tall palm dominates the middle. Among the specimens people point to are sequoias, magnolias, lindens, a Canary Island date palm and a bald cypress.

Be clear about what is not known. No source names a single tree in this garden, dates one or measures one. The century-old claim covers the planting as a group, and the species above are what guides and visitors report rather than a survey anyone has published. The garden was laid out in 1872, which fits trees of that age and is not proof that any particular one stood here at the start. If the Misericordia keeps records of what went in when, we would like to see them.

trees.name: The Centenary Horse Chestnut of Parque de Doña Casilda
trees.access: Free, open public park, Bilbao's largest and most central, accessible at all times.
trees.transport: Indautxu or San Mames metro, about 5-10 minutes' walk; also served by several bus lines along Alameda de Recalde and Astarloa.

best_time.label: May, when the crown goes up in white candles and the tree is easy to pick out

trees.story:
In a park stocked with trees from five continents, the specimen the guides keep naming is a horse chestnut. Parque de Doña Casilda de Iturrizar is Bilbao's largest central park, 115,200 square metres of ponds, pergola and imported botany begun in 1907, and its planting runs to dozens of species from all over the world. The one that gets singled out is Aesculus hippocastanum, a Balkan tree so common on northern European streets that children in four countries grow up throwing sticks at it, and here it is always described the same way: centenario, over a hundred years old.

Worth knowing how thin that is. Two separately hosted travel pages make the claim, and they make it in almost the same words, un centenario castaño de Indias, which reads like both are repeating one municipal or tourist-board line rather than two people noticing the same tree. Take it as decent evidence that the tree is there and what species it is, and weaker evidence about its age. Nobody has measured it, and centenario is the only number anyone offers.

No source says where in the park it stands either, and 115,200 square metres is a lot of ground to sweep for one chestnut. May makes it easier. The crown goes up in white candles and there is no mistaking which tree you are looking at. If you find it, tell us where it is.

trees.name: The Ironwoods of Khlong Lot
trees.age: over 217 years (planted during King Rama I's reign, 1782-1809)
trees.access: Free, public canal-side street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from MRT Sanam Chai (Blue Line), via Atsadang Road
trees.story: Five ironwood trees standing over a Bangkok canal are, in effect, a two-century-old weapons reserve nobody ever needed to use again. King Rama I ordered Thai ironwood planted along Khlong Lot shortly after founding Bangkok in 1782, part of a hardwood stockpile meant to build warships for a kingdom still fighting Burma on a near-annual basis. Ironwood's real advantages, dense grain, genuine rot-resistance, and enough buoyancy once cut to float downriver, made it the standard timber for Siamese naval construction, and someone in the new capital planted with fleets in mind rather than gardens. The trees outlasted every war they were grown for and most of what came after: seven remained by 1998, five by 2019, worn down by two centuries of city growth rather than by axes. Thai folk belief holds that timber cut for shipbuilding carries its own protective spirit into the vessel, called Chao Mae Takian, so wood taken from here would once have gone to sea as more than lumber. In December 2021, Bangkok's environmental office joined a heritage-tree foundation, the Ministry of Defence and three professional associations to formally restore what remains, an unusually wide coalition for five trees behind a temple most visitors walk straight past on the way to something older-looking. They still stand exactly where Rama I put them, doing nothing more useful now than being two hundred years old.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree of Wat Saket
trees.neighbourhood: Pom Prap Sattru Phai, near the Golden Mount
trees.access: Free entry to temple grounds; a small fee applies only to climb the Golden Mount itself
trees.transport: 14 minute walk from MRT Sam Yot (Blue Line), or a short walk from Phanfa Leelard pier via the Khlong Saen Saep canal boat
trees.story: Two monks left Bangkok on a mission from King Rama II and came back three years later with tree cuttings instead of relics. In 1814, Phra Achan Dee and Phra Achan Thep returned from Sri Lanka after studying at Anuradhapura, the city that has kept an unbroken line of Bodhi trees since a cutting from Bodh Gaya arrived there in the third century BC.
