Of the three saplings they carried home, the king had one planted at Wat Saket in 1818, at Lan Pho directly in front of the ordination hall, where it has stood ever since below the temple's later, far more famous addition: an 80 metre artificial hill capped in gold that Rama III would not begin building for another decade. The tree predates the Golden Mount that now draws every visitor's eye upward and past it. Two centuries on, it is genuinely struggling. Competing vegetation and fungal pressure have weakened the trunk enough that the temple launched a public restoration campaign timed to Makha Bucha 2026, asking Buddhists to help nurse a 208-year-old living relic back to health rather than simply photograph the hill behind it. Free to see, no ticket required beyond the small fee charged only for the climb up the Mount itself.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree of Wat Phra Kaew
trees.access: Paid entry (Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew ticket, standard foreign-visitor rate), strict dress code, open approximately 8:30am-3:30pm daily
trees.transport: 5 minute walk from Tha Chang Pier (N9, Chao Phraya Express Boat), or about 15 minutes on foot from MRT Sanam Chai (Blue Line)
trees.story: Inside the single most photographed temple complex in Thailand grows a tree that gets photographed by almost nobody. King Rama IV had a Bodhi tree planted beside the Prasat Phra Thep Bidon in 1864, grown from a shoot cut from the tree at Bodh Gaya where the historical Buddha reached enlightenment. In 1903, fire tore through the building it shades, destroying the original gilt stupa and part of the structure; the tree, already thirty-nine years old, stood close enough to watch and kept standing while King Rama VI rebuilt what became the Royal Pantheon of the Chakri dynasty. That pantheon now holds statues of the dynasty's kings and opens to the public exactly one day a year, Chakri Memorial Day, April 6th, from eight until noon. The tree faces no such restriction. It grows in the section of Wat Phra Kaew that every visitor to the Grand Palace already walks through on the way to the Emerald Buddha, sharing ground with the complex's gilded chedis and mythological guardian statues, and drawing none of their attention. At 162 years old it is younger than most of the buildings around it, proof that even Thailand's most sacred royal compound has kept adding, burning and rebuilding since 1782, not stood frozen at its founding.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree of Wat Benchamabophit
trees.access: Paid entry (small temple fee), standard dress code, typically open daily
trees.transport: Best reached by taxi or Grab; no BTS or MRT station within comfortable walking distance
trees.story: When Thailand received its first-ever direct cutting from the actual Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya in 1891, King Chulalongkorn did not plant it right away. He sent it two hundred kilometres to Wat Asdangnimit in Si Racha to be nursed for nine years first, unwilling to risk India's most sacred sapling on an unproven transplant. Only in 1900, once it had grown strong enough to travel again, did he personally plant it at Wat Benchamabophit, on the lawn behind the ordination hall, in the temple he had built as his own before ascending the throne and where his ashes would later be interred beneath the main Buddha image. Every other Bodhi tree in Thailand before this one had arrived at one remove, propagated from Sri Lankan trees that themselves descended from a cutting planted at Anuradhapura more than two thousand years earlier. This was the first to skip that detour and come straight from the source. Unusually for a Thai temple, this Bodhi stands where a chedi would normally rise, treated as the ordination hall's spiritual counterweight rather than a subordinate planting. At 126 years old it remains younger than the marble temple around it, itself finished only in 1911, eleven years after this tree was already established.

trees.name: Lan Pho, the Bodhi Tree of Thammasat University
trees.age: at least 90 years, exact planting date undocumented
trees.access: Free, public university campus grounds, generally open during daytime hours
trees.transport: 6 minute walk from Tha Phra Chan pier (Chao Phraya Express Boat), or roughly 15-20 minutes on foot from MRT Sanam Chai (Blue Line)
trees.story: A single tree on a university lawn became the starting point for the protest that ended a Thai dictatorship. On 6 October 1973, students gathered under this Bodhi tree at Thammasat University to demand the release of activists arrested for distributing leaflets calling for a new constitution, a protest that grew within days into the mass uprising of 14 October 1973, which brought down the government of Field Marshal Thanom Kittikachorn. Three years later, the same tree stood over one of the darkest days in modern Thai history, the 6 October 1976 massacre, when paramilitary and police forces killed student protesters occupying the same grounds. The plaza around the tree, still called Lan Pho, the Bodhi Court, has carried that weight ever since, a birthplace of Thai democracy and the site of a massacre within three years of each other, under the same branches. The tree itself predates all of it. Thammasat was founded on this former Front Palace site in 1934, and the tree was already established ground the university simply inherited, mature enough that nobody has ever recorded when it was planted. At well over ninety years old, and probably far older, it is a tree that Thai political history simply happened around rather than the other way round.

trees.name: The Old Government House Fig
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
Moreton Bay figs do not so much grow as advance. This one holds a 23 metre crown on buttress roots that leave the trunk above knee height and run into the ground like low walls, with two metres of trunk standing behind them.

It sits on the path to Old Government House, the oldest public building in Queensland and now part of a university campus, so the tree is what you look at while walking between two versions of the same city. The record comes from the National Trust of Australia's significant tree database, which dates the planting to somewhere between 1864 and 1884, during the curatorship of Walter Hill. Hill was appointed the gardens' first curator in 1855 and spent decades planting the ground out. A twenty year window is as precise as the paperwork gets, and nobody has narrowed it since.

That one record is also the whole of the evidence. We have not found a second write-up dealing with this specimen rather than with the gardens' figs in general, so read the date and the age as the Trust's account rather than as a settled fact. The tree itself needs no defending. Good condition, no fence, no ticket, and buttresses you can put a flat hand against.

trees.name: The Macadamia Nut Tree
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
Nobody farmed macadamias until someone in Brisbane planted this tree. Walter Hill, first curator of the City Botanic Gardens, began trialling the nut here in 1858 from seed brought down from Gympie, and the tree those trials produced is still standing at the southern end of the rainforest section: 17 metres tall, a metre through the trunk.

The National Trust's significant tree database and the State Library of Queensland both record it as the first macadamia brought into cultivation anywhere. Popular accounts go further and call it the oldest cultivated macadamia alive and the starting point of Australia's macadamia export industry, which is now a crop grown commercially across four continents. Those accounts are not what the entry rests on, but they do not contradict it either.

The scale is the thing worth carrying home. Every macadamia in every jar of mixed nuts descends from a wild rainforest species that no one had thought to plant deliberately until a colonial gardener put some seed in the ground here and waited. The founding specimen of a global crop is usually long gone, ploughed out when an orchard was replanted or a road went through. This one ended up inside a public park in the middle of a state capital, unfenced, with a path running past it.

trees.name: The Banyan Tree of City Botanic Gardens
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
Forty-nine metres around. That is the National Trust's figure for this banyan's trunk, and it is only possible because a banyan refuses to keep to one. The tree drops aerial roots from its limbs, they thicken into props where they land, and the props fuse back into the mass. Measure the result and you are measuring something that has been walking outward since the 1870s.

It went in during Walter Hill's curatorship and now stands 29 metres tall with a crown 20 metres across. The National Trust record calls it the best known example of its species in Australia and gives it the finest aerial root structure in these gardens. The State Library of Queensland's account arrives at the same 49 metre circumference independently, which is worth knowing about a number that reads like a typing error.

Ficus benghalensis is the fig of Indian village squares, the species whose old specimens end up roofing markets and meetings rather than merely shading them. Brisbane's subtropics suit it well enough that this one has behaved exactly as it would at home. Stand under it and the height is not the interesting part. The floor is: root, prop and trunk have become genuinely hard to tell apart, which is the whole point the measurement is trying to make.

trees.name: Prince Albert's Cook Pine
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 8 minutes) or George Street bus stops nearby
trees.story:
An avenue of six Cook Pines was proposed for the ground in front of the old Parliament House in 1868. Two went in, planted by Prince Albert, Duke of Edinburgh, Queen Victoria's second son, during his visit that year. The other four were never planted, one of the two is gone, and the survivor is now the tallest tree in the gardens at roughly 45 metres.

One correction to the record, because it circulates: the State Library of Queensland's write-up calls the prince the later King Edward VII. He was not. That was his elder brother, and the Duke of Edinburgh never took the throne. The National Trust record names him correctly.

The species comes from New Caledonia and grows as a narrow column rather than a spreading conifer, which is why a single one reads as deliberate where a lone fig would read as an accident. Cook Pines also lean, and they lean consistently: a 2017 survey of the species worldwide found them tilting toward the equator, which in Brisbane means north.

Its lower branches have been removed to stop people climbing, which tells you what 45 metres of straight trunk does to the human imagination. The trunk is 0.9 metres through, narrow for the height, and from the George Street side the tree is visible well before you reach the gardens.

trees.name: The Eagle Street Fig Trees
trees.species: White Fig and Banyan Fig (Ficus virens and Ficus benghalensis)
trees.access: Free, a small public reserve (triangular traffic island / pocket park) open at all times
trees.transport: Short walk from Riverside ferry terminal (about 3 minutes) or Central Station (about 8 minutes)
trees.story:
A triangle of central Brisbane was granted in Queen Victoria's name so that wharf labourers and carriers would have somewhere shaded to sit down. Governor Sir Henry Wylie Norman signed it on 16 May 1889, and Walter Hill, first curator of the city's botanic gardens, planted the reserve with three figs: two White Figs and one Banyan.

They are still on the island where Eagle, Elizabeth and Creek Streets meet, carrying 29 metres of combined height in the middle of Brisbane's financial district. The wharves have gone. The carriers have gone. The shade does the job it was planted to do, now for office workers eating lunch on a bench instead of carters resting a horse.

Queensland added the site to its heritage register on 13 May 2004, Brisbane City Council keeps its own local citation, and the National Trust records the trees individually, which is an unusual amount of paperwork for three trees on a traffic island. Four independent records describe the same planting and none of them disagree.

It is the one stop on this list outside the gardens, about a kilometre north and an easy walk, three minutes up from the Riverside ferry terminal. One small bounded reserve, three trees, and a single obvious place to stand and look up into all of them at once.

trees.name: The Crows Ash
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
The first recorded act of gardening on this ground was a felling. In 1826 an older crows ash was cut down here to mark the spot where the Moreton Bay penal settlement would put its government garden, and the ground has been a garden ever since.

The tree standing there now is not that tree, and no record suggests any descent between them. It was planted in 1884, is 21 metres tall and a metre through the trunk, and belongs to a genus named for Matthew Flinders, who charted this coast three decades before the settlement that cleared its predecessor.

Crows ash is a rainforest hardwood, sold as Australian teak, and its seed capsules are the detail worth looking down for: woody, covered in short spines, and splitting open into five parts like a carved wooden flower. They end up on the grass under the tree, which stands between the formal flower garden and the river.

One caution about the dating. A single record carries this tree, the National Trust of Australia's significant tree database, and we found no second source naming this individual, although the gardens are separately documented as holding native Flindersia of the same era. So 1884 is the Trust's date rather than a corroborated one, and the age here is stated on one authority.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
The record for this fig traces it, cutting by cutting, back to the tree the Buddha is said to have sat under. The line runs from Bodh Gaya in India to an ancient tree in Sri Lanka grown from it, and from there to this one, planted in the early 1880s. That is what the National Trust's entry states, and it is a claim that cannot be checked at either end. No second source adds anything independent to it: the audio guides and walking tours repeat the same paragraph. Treat the pedigree as tradition rather than as documented fact.

The tree can be checked. Twenty five metres tall, three metres through the trunk, and one of the widest canopies in the gardens, which in a garden this full of figs is a real distinction. Its leaves are heart shaped with a drawn out tip and they move in air still enough to leave everything around them alone.

One piece of the story is documented and it runs the other way. In 1983 the fourteenth Dalai Lama blessed this tree, during the same visit on which he attended the planting of a cutting taken from it at the University of Queensland. Whatever the ancestry behind it, there is a verified descendant of it growing across the city.

trees.name: The Weeping Figs at Alice Street Gate
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
Walter Hill delivered his verdict on these two trees in 1872, and it is not a boast. The figs, he wrote, 'tended greatly to diminish the appearance of bareness'. They are 40 metres tall now, two metres through, standing either side of the Alice Street gate, and bareness is no longer the difficulty.

Weeping figs are the species sold by the thousand as pot plants for office lobbies. Given open ground, subtropical rain and roughly a century and a half, this is what they do instead: a matched pair holding up the main entrance the way a gatehouse would, which is how the National Trust describes them, as a landmark denoting the way in.

The dating is not clean, and the framing is not either. The National Trust puts the planting at 1868 and treats these two as a deliberate pair marking the entrance. Wikipedia's account of the gardens describes an avenue of weeping figs planted in the 1870s and does not single them out. Species and rough decade are agreed between the two; whether this pair was planted as a pair, or is what remains of a longer line, rests on the Trust's record alone, as does the earlier date.

Either way they are the first thing the gardens show you, and the last thing you walk through on the way back out to Alice Street.

trees.name: The Mahogany of Commerce
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
Nothing would grow under this tree, and that turned out to be useful. Walter Hill planted it in 1861, testing whether West Indian mahogany could take root as a colonial timber crop the way it had elsewhere in the empire. The tree took, growing into what the National Trust's significant tree database calls probably the first mahogany planted in Queensland and among the oldest of its species anywhere in Australia: 41 metres tall, its trunk two metres through.

The bare ground under its canopy shaped part of the garden decades later. A later curator, Harry Oakman, turned the empty soil beneath and around the mahogany into what became the gardens' rainforest section, so a tree brought in to test a colonial industry ended up dictating the layout of an entirely different corner of the park.

The timber trade Hill hoped for never really arrived. Mahogany stayed a curiosity in Australia rather than a crop, unlike the macadamia planted a few decades later just 35 metres away. The most recent recorded inspection, from February 2014, found the tree in good condition. What is left of the experiment is one very tall, two-metre-thick specimen and the ground it cleared for something else entirely.

trees.name: The Tamarind Tree
trees.age: not firmly documented; the register's own estimate is roughly 190 years
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
The National Trust's own record puts this tamarind older than the garden around it: 'thought to predate the formation of the Botanic Gardens', which were declared in 1855, with an estimated age near 190 years. That would set its planting in the mid-1830s, two decades before Walter Hill ever picked up a spade here. It rests on one source and reads better as an estimate than as a settled fact.

What is not in doubt is that it is a real, fruiting tamarind. A Rare Fruit Council Australia trip report from May 1994 describes visiting it two years earlier: 'a large multi-stemmed tamarind, about forty foot tall with a forty six foot spread', starting to fruit for the season. The National Trust's current entry gives it 18 metres and makes no mention of multiple stems, a gap of three decades and one that measurement alone does not resolve; the two accounts may describe the same tree at different points in its growth, or there may be more to the difference than growth explains.

It stands in the older, southern reach of the gardens, on the path toward Old Government House, still producing the sour brown pods that turn up in curries and chutneys across a tropics it was never native to. Whatever its real age, it is fruiting now, which most of Brisbane's founding-era trees no longer bother to do.

trees.name: The Silky Oak
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)

best_time.label: October and November, when the orange flower combs open

trees.story:
Most grevilleas are shrubs you can see over the top of. This one is 32 metres tall.

Silky oak is the largest of Australia's grevilleas, and it is not an oak at all. It sits in the protea family beside the banksias, and it took its name from the timber, which cuts with a fine silky figure that cabinetmakers chased for a century. This tree stands in the north east part of the City Botanic Gardens, between the pond and the Morning Star sculpture, its trunk 0.7 metres through and a little over two metres around.

In spring it does at 32 metres what the rest of the genus does at knee height: dense one sided combs of orange flower held out along the branches, until the whole crown changes colour.

The National Trust of Australia put it at roughly a hundred years old when it was measured in February 2014, an approximation rather than a ring count, which places it somewhere near 110 now. That makes it a seedling around the time of the First World War, and the gardens around it have twice gone under the river since, in 1974 and again in 2011.

One record carries this tree, the Trust's significant tree register, and its last inspection is that 2014 one, which found it in good condition. We found no second source naming it. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Hoop Pine
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
The hoops are real. Run your eye up the trunk and you find it ringed at intervals with raised bands, stacked like the hoops on a barrel, which is where the tree got its name.

It stands on raised ground just inside the George Street fence, about halfway along, where the gardens meet the QUT campus. Thirty three metres tall, its trunk a metre through and a shade over three metres around, it carries the stiff dark prickly foliage that gives every araucaria its slightly prehistoric look. That look is not a trick of the light. This is an old lineage of conifer, and its close relatives are the monkey puzzle and the Norfolk Island pine.

Araucaria cunninghamii takes its name from Allan Cunningham, the botanist who came up the Brisbane River in the 1820s while the place was still a penal settlement. The species went on to build the city he was looking at: hoop pine was the softwood Queensland's sawmills ran on for generations, and it remains the state's main plantation conifer.

The National Trust of Australia's significant tree register put its age at roughly sixty years when it was measured in January 2014, an approximation rather than a planting date, which puts it somewhere in its seventies now. The Trust went back to the listing in February 2023. That register is the only source we could find naming this particular tree.

trees.name: The Big-leaf Mahogany
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)
trees.story:
It was planted in 1869 to be looked at, and the staging still works. Walk in from Alice Street and it is there on your left, positioned so that arriving visitors would meet it, which is what Walter Hill intended when he put it in during his curatorship of the gardens.

This is big-leaf mahogany, the species behind most of what the world sells as mahogany. Across its native range in Central and South America it has been logged hard enough to sit under CITES protection. Here nobody has ever come for the timber, and 157 years have produced a tree 22 metres tall, a metre through the trunk and a little over three metres around.

Worth knowing before you go looking, because these gardens hold two mahoganies planted eight years apart. The other is Swietenia mahagoni, a different species, planted in 1861 and standing about 400 metres away in the middle of the rainforest section. This one is the Alice Street tree, the big-leaf, near the entrance rather than deep in the planting.

Queensland had been a colony in its own right for ten years when it went into the ground, and Brisbane was still a small colonial town rather than a city.

The planting date, like everything else here, comes from the National Trust of Australia's significant tree register, which recorded the tree in good condition in 2014 and is the only source we found naming it.

trees.name: The Black Bean
trees.access: Free, City Botanic Gardens is a public park open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Short walk from Central Station (about 10 minutes) or the QUT Gardens Point ferry terminal (about 5 minutes)

best_time.label: spring into early summer, when orange pea flowers open along the older branches

trees.story:
The seeds look like chestnuts and will make you seriously ill. Black bean drops heavy pods holding two or three glossy brown seeds the size of a golf ball, and people ate them anyway: Aboriginal peoples along this coast sliced, leached and roasted them over several days to strip the toxins out. That is a great deal of work for a seed, which tells you what the return was worth.

The tree stands on the northern edge of the rainforest section, 22 metres tall, its trunk a metre through and a little over three metres around. It is a legume, despite growing into a rainforest hardwood, and in spring the pea flowers open in orange and yellow racemes on the older wood rather than out at the tips.

The species has one famous piece of joinery to its name. When the Speaker's Chair in the British House of Commons was destroyed in a 1941 air raid, the replacement Australia presented in 1951 was carved from black bean timber. Not from this tree. It went into the ground around 1944 and was roughly seven years old at the time, a decent sapling and no use whatsoever to a carver.

The National Trust of Australia's significant tree register put it at about seventy years old when it was measured in February 2014, in good condition. That register is the only source we found naming this tree.

trees.name: The Talking Tree of Newstead House
trees.access: Free. Stands in the circular garden bed on the entrance driveway roundabout inside Newstead Park, a public Brisbane City Council park with no gate or fee; Newstead House itself (the museum building) is separately ticketed and open Friday to Sunday, but the tree is outside on the public drive, not inside the ticketed grounds.
trees.transport: Breakfast Creek Rd at Evelyn St bus stop (routes 227, 300), about 2 minutes' walk. Bowen Hills rail station is about 9 minutes' walk; Teneriffe CityCat ferry terminal about 16 minutes' walk.
trees.story:
A speaker hidden in the garden bed narrates Newstead House's history to whoever pauses under the giant fig growing on the driveway roundabout in front of it, which is where the tree earned its local name, the Talking Tree. The fig has the better claim to the story: Patrick Leslie built the house in 1846, and by the property's own account the fig was already a substantial tree when he did, older than everything else on the site.

It is a Cunningham's fig, Ficus virens, and it has hollowed out the way old figs do, described on Queensland's heritage register as a magnificent hollowed out Cunningham fig believed to be 200 years old, growing inside its own circular garden bed. Nobody has taped its girth, so 200 is a long-held estimate rather than a measurement, and one account puts it closer to 300.

The tree stands on the public entrance drive, open every day with no gate and no ticket. Newstead House itself, the museum building further up the drive, only opens Friday to Sunday, but the fig and its roundabout sit outside that line. If you know its real age, tell us.

trees.name: The Monumental Planes of the Montagnola
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Bologna Centrale train station
trees.story: Bologna's first public park started as a rubbish tip. The raised ground of the Montagnola had been used since medieval times to dump debris, and only became public space in 1662, planted first with orchards and mulberries before Napoleon, passing through the city in 1805, ordered it redesigned along French garden principles by the architect Giovanni Battista Martinetti. The plane trees that give the park its shaded, formal character today date from that redesign, and roughly ten of them, out of some fifty planted across the park's six hectares, still count as genuinely monumental: trunks running one to one and a half metres across, several confirmed to exceed four metres in circumference. A dramatic 1896 entrance staircase from Via Indipendenza, nicknamed the Pincio of Bologna after Rome's own hillside park, was added decades later, but the trees along the park's two concentric paths are the oldest surviving element of Martinetti's original scheme, healthy and still growing more than two centuries after Napoleonic administrators decided a rubbish heap deserved better.

trees.name: The Sequoia of the Giardini Margherita
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Bologna city centre, or bus to Viale Gozzadini
trees.story: A coast redwood is a genuine oddity in an Italian city garden, and this one has grown into one of the tallest living things in Bologna: 37.4 metres, a trunk 520cm around, standing near the artificial lake that anchors the Giardini Margherita's English-style landscape design. Sequoia sempervirens is native to a narrow strip of California and southern Oregon coastline, kept alive there by coastal fog the species depends on to survive the dry summer months, conditions nothing like Bologna's own inland climate, which makes this specimen's continued health after more than a century something closer to a curiosity than a certainty. The gardens themselves opened in 1879 on land bought from a former convent estate, laid out as Bologna's first genuinely English-style public park, complete with an Etruscan necropolis whose remains are still visible near the grounds. Among the park's other conifers, oaks and horse chestnuts, the sequoia is unmistakable purely by scale, visibly taller than everything around it long before a visitor reaches the lake it stands beside.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Piazza Minghetti
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza Maggiore
trees.story: At 39.5 metres, this plane is the tallest of any monumental tree catalogued anywhere in Bologna's province, rising directly behind the bronze statue of the 19th century statesman Marco Minghetti that gives the square its name and its own local nickname for the tree, the guardian of the piazza. Its trunk measures 455cm around, respectable but not exceptional for a plane tree this old, which makes the height the genuinely remarkable figure: two centuries of growth in a confined city square, competing for light against surrounding buildings rather than spreading wide the way an open-park specimen might. The statue it now shades, sculpted by Giulio Monteverde and unveiled in 1896, commemorates a politician who served as Italy's Prime Minister in the 1860s, a piece of civic memory considerably younger than the tree standing over it. Piazza Minghetti sits inside Bologna's Quadrilatero, the tight medieval grid of streets and market stalls just east of Piazza Maggiore, making this one of the easiest monumental trees in the city to combine with an ordinary walk through the historic centre.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Piazza Malpighi
trees.access: Free, public garden square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza Maggiore, near the Basilica di San Francesco
trees.story: This plane tree grows in a garden raised more than four metres above the surrounding piazza, a quirk of geography with a specific origin: the ground was once known as the Cavallerizza, a riding ground used from 1612 for horsemanship and public events, before the noble Rusconi family converted it into a private garden around 1825 and planted, among other trees, this Oriental plane. Two centuries on it has become, by most local accounts, the single most imposing tree standing anywhere in Bologna's historic centre, 36 metres tall with a trunk 520cm around, close by the Rusconi family's own palazzo. Its elevated setting has become something of a double-edged inheritance: the raised garden and the tall retaining wall separating it from the piazza below have almost certainly limited how far its root system can spread, yet the tree shows no clear sign of decline generations after its likely planting date. It remains one of eight trees on Italy's official monumental register within Bologna city limits, a shy giant, in the words of one local tree writer, tucked into a garden most passersby in the piazza below never think to look up into.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Rizzoli
trees.access: Free, hospital garden (check visiting hours)
trees.transport: 10 min walk uphill from Porta San Mamolo
trees.story: This cedar grows in the garden of a working orthopaedic hospital, on ground that has already been a monastery, a royal residence and a public park before it became a place of medicine. San Michele in Bosco started as an Olivetan monastery rebuilt in 1437, later served briefly as Villa Reale when King Victor Emmanuel II stayed there around Italian unification in 1860, and only became a hospital in 1896, when the Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli opened here in the presence of Italy's royal family, funded by a bequest from the surgeon Francesco Rizzoli. The cedar, planted around that same transition, has reached nearly 30 metres, its trunk 520cm around, standing in a garden landscaped specifically to frame the new medical facility when it opened. Himalayan cedar, native to high-altitude forests stretching from Afghanistan to Nepal, was a fashionable choice for grand Italian institutional gardens of the period, valued for its size and its distinctive drooping branch tips, and this specimen has had well over a century to earn its place on Italy's official monumental tree register.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Piazza Cavour
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza Maggiore

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold

trees.story: Piazza Cavour was Bologna's first deliberately designed public garden-square, laid out by the Turin architect Pietro Ceri in the years after Italian unification cut new streets through the city's medieval fabric, and this ginkgo has stood in it since roughly that original planting, around 150 years now. It is, by the official register's own measurements, the smallest of Bologna's monumental trees by height, 29.5 metres against taller planes and cedars elsewhere in the city, and its trunk runs 338cm around, but no other tree on this list turns quite the same colour: every autumn its fan-shaped leaves shift to a uniform, near-luminous yellow within days of each other, a synchronised display few other species manage. The square has a more recent claim to local affection too. Bolognese singer-songwriter Lucio Dalla lived facing Piazza Cavour for much of his life, and this ginkgo, visible from his own windows for decades, has become informally associated with him since his death in 2012, a civic tree with an unusually specific personal thread running through its more official designation.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Small entry fee, Orto Botanico ed Erbario
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza Maggiore

best_time.label: November, when its old canopy along Via Irnerio turns a single uniform gold

trees.story: Bologna's botanical garden traces its founding to 1568, when the naturalist Ulisse Aldrovandi established it as one of the earliest such gardens anywhere in Europe, decades before ginkgo itself had even reached the continent. This specimen, an old female tree with a trunk 80cm across, came later, among the first ginkgos planted anywhere in Italy after the species reached European cultivation in the 18th century, brought from a mountainous pocket of southeast China where it had survived, essentially unchanged, for some 200 million years. It now dominates the garden's front section along Via Irnerio, included on the Emilia-Romagna region's own list of protected monumental trees for its size and age within a collection built primarily around gymnosperms, cone-bearing trees, from across Europe and Asia. Ginkgo biloba is famously resistant to disease, pollution and even fire in a way few other large trees can match, a resilience this specimen shares with every ginkgo on this list without needing any specific incident to prove it.

trees.name: The Cypress of Carducci's Tomb
trees.access: Free, public cemetery
trees.transport: Bus to Certosa, or 20 min walk from Porta Saragozza
trees.story: A cypress stands directly over the granite tomb of Giosue Carducci in the Certosa di Bologna, one of the tallest and most immediately recognisable trees within a cemetery field otherwise dominated by low funerary monuments, and it has become known simply as the poet's own cypress. Carducci, who became the first Italian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1906, is buried in a section of the Certosa reserved for his memory, his surname cut into a single block of stone with no other ornament, a deliberate austerity that the cypress towering behind it makes considerably more dramatic than the monument alone would manage. The Certosa itself, a working cemetery since 1801 built on the site of a 14th century Carthusian monastery, is regarded as one of Europe's great open-air museums of funerary sculpture, some 30 hectares holding roughly 6,000 works of historic and artistic interest, and cypress plantings run throughout its oldest sections, including a double row leading to the monastery's original entrance. This particular tree earns its own name for standing over the one grave in the entire complex that draws readers rather than art historians.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Villa Ghigi
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk uphill from Porta San Mamolo
trees.story: This cedar was planted by Callisto Ghigi himself when he first acquired the hillside property that still carries his family's name, and it now dominates the meadow directly in front of the villa, tall enough that local photographers treat it as the park's single most reliable subject. Villa Ghigi sits just outside Porta San Mamolo on Bologna's southern hills, opened to the public by the city in 1974 and now spanning some 30 hectares of former agricultural land, old orchard rows of cherry, pear, apple and fig trees still legible in the landscape alongside century-old beech groves and native downy oaks. The cedar itself has been measured at 159cm in diameter and roughly 24 metres tall, and shows visible lightning-strike scarring on part of its crown, damage it has carried rather than been felled by. Its position on the open lawn in front of the villa gives visitors one of the clearest unobstructed views of any single tree on this list, framed against the hillside panorama over Bologna's historic centre that the whole park is known for.

trees.name: The Camphor of San Michele in Bosco
trees.access: Free, hospital park (check visiting hours)
trees.transport: 10 min walk uphill from Porta San Mamolo
trees.story: The garden surrounding the Rizzoli hospital splits into two distinct characters, and this camphor grows in the gentler of the two: a western section mixing old oaks, holm oaks, cypresses, lindens and horse chestnuts into something closer to an informal woodland than a designed garden, in contrast to the dense conifer forest of cedars and black pines covering the site's eastern slope. Cinnamomum camphora is native to East Asia and reached Italian institutional gardens through the same 19th century acclimatisation wave that filled Naples, Rome and other cities with newly fashionable evergreen imports, valued for the camphor oil its wood and leaves produce and for a dense, glossy canopy that holds its colour through the Bolognese winter. Its exact planting date is not recorded, folded into the general landscaping the hospital's founders carried out around 1896 rather than documented tree by tree, but it shares the same hillside history as San Michele in Bosco's Himalayan cedar: monastery ground, briefly royal, now medical, with the trees the one constant through every change of use.

trees.name: The Grey Walnut of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Small entry fee, Orto Botanico ed Erbario
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza Maggiore
trees.story:
Bologna's grey walnut is the only Juglans cinerea recorded anywhere on Italy's national register of monumental trees, one specimen among more than 4,500 entries. It grows in the university's botanical garden on Via Irnerio, close to the ginkgo at the garden's front section, and stands 32 metres tall, a serious height for a species native to the river valleys of the eastern United States and Canada rather than to Italy. The regional register measures its girth at 4.2 metres; university-cited press coverage of a 2025 conservation project puts it nearer 4.7, and neither figure has been reconciled here, so both are recorded rather than one invented winner.

That conservation project is the tree's real story right now. Professor Alberto Minelli of the university's agro-food science department began a five-year programme in February 2025 to monitor a specimen the garden's own curator, Umberto Mossetti, describes as living in an extremely delicate balance with what surrounds it: reached what the university calls an irreversible aging phase, vulnerable to parasites and disease, and under added pressure from a changing climate. Nobody has recorded when it was planted. What is on record is that the university is treating its survival as a live question rather than a settled fact, five years of advanced diagnostics and soil analysis aimed at keeping the only tree of its kind on Italy's whole register standing a while longer.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Villa delle Rose
trees.access: Free public gardens, gallery hours (Galleria d'Arte Moderna, Villa delle Rose)
trees.transport: Via Saragozza; bus 13 or a walk up from Porta Saragozza
trees.story:
Five metres forty-five around the trunk, thirty-two metres tall, and it grows in the garden of an art gallery. Villa delle Rose stands on Via Saragozza, the long road running out of the city towards the portico that climbs to San Luca, and the villa is now one of the two homes of Bologna's Galleria d'Arte Moderna. Its gardens are free to walk into, but they keep the gallery's hours rather than a park's, so this is a tree with an opening time.

The cedar is the largest thing in them. Cedrus atlantica comes from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, cold forest on thin soil above a thousand metres, where the remaining stands are shrinking and the species is now listed as endangered in its own range. In a walled Bolognese garden it has had none of that difficulty, and the size shows. It carries the flat, slightly ascending plates of foliage that a cedar only makes when it has been given room, so the crown reads as a stack of dark tiers.

Nothing dates it. The national monumental tree register carries the girth and the height and no age at all, and no second source names it, so the honest answer is that it is large enough to be protected and nobody has published a number. Bologna's two other registered cedars are both deodars, up on the hills south of the centre. This one you can reach on a bus.

trees.name: The Shaw Memorial Elms
trees.age: planted between 1772 and 1812, so roughly 214 to 254 years old
trees.access: Free, public park (Boston Common), directly on the Freedom Trail
trees.transport: Park Street MBTA station (Red/Green Line), roughly 3-5 minute walk
trees.story: Augustus Saint-Gaudens's memorial to Robert Gould Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th was built around these two elms, not the other way round. The trees came first, planted somewhere between 1772 and 1812, probably under the 1780 permission to plant elms across from John Hancock's mansion while he was governor. The bronze arrived in 1897 and sits on a vault designed to spare their roots. The Boston Globe calls them the oldest English elms in the Western Hemisphere. One caveat on the species. Two institutional sources and the memorial's own conservation record call them English elm; a single minority account describes them as American elm. The weight of evidence sits with English elm, but the disagreement is real. Their survival is not luck. In 1927 they were written off as close to dead. The arborist Henry Davis began treating them free of charge in the 1970s and the care has never stopped: bricks packed inside the hollow trunks for stability, six to eight feet taken off the crowns in 2013, inspections every fortnight. That retrenchment pruning is what gives them the blunt, cut back outline they carry through winter. Even the cramped root vault helps, densifying the wood against Dutch elm disease. Prunings have been turned into pens and sold. The two of them stand where the Freedom Trail meets Beacon and Park, shading the regiment they now outlive by more than a century.

trees.name: The Peters Hill White Oak
trees.age: roughly 195 to 220 years, core-sampled in 2018 to a germination date in the early 1800s
trees.neighbourhood: Peters Hill, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line) roughly 15-20 minute walk, or bus to the Arborway/Peters Hill Gate entrance
trees.story: Harvard's Arnold Arboretum has been cataloguing plants since 1872 and did not get round to this one until 2010. It shows up on an 1894 city survey of Peters Hill, already growing wild on ground the Arboretum later absorbed, so when it was finally accessioned it went into the books as found growing in place rather than planted. It may be the oldest tree in the entire landscape. In 2018 a core taken from the southwest stem gave 142 countable rings, with perhaps 60 more lost in a hollow centre, putting germination in the early 1800s. It is double leadered, two stems fused near the base with the seam still visible, roughly 17 metres tall and spreading 28 metres over the crabapple collection below it. A 1927 bird's eye map of the Arboretum drew it as a lone shepherd guarding an endless flock, the flock at the time being hawthorns that have since been replaced. Two honest notes. Everything known about this tree comes from the Arboretum itself, rigorous work with published ring counts, but we found nothing independent of the institution. And no coordinates are published, so the pin is the northeast slope of Peters Hill above the crabapples rather than the trunk. Walk up the slope and look for the widest crown on the hill. At that spread it is not a difficult hunt.

trees.name: The Franklin Tree of the Explorers Garden
trees.age: roughly 121 years (accessioned as a rooted cutting in 1905)
trees.neighbourhood: Bussey Hill, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line) roughly 15-20 minute walk, or bus to the Arborway entrance near Bussey Hill

best_time.label: September, when the cream flowers open while the leaves are already turning red

trees.story: There is no wild Franklinia anywhere on earth and there has not been for about two hundred years. John Bartram found the species growing on a few acres beside the Altamaha River in Georgia in 1765, his son William collected seed around 1776, and within roughly fifty years the wild population was gone and never seen again. Every Franklin tree alive today, in every garden in the world, descends from that one collection. This is one of the oldest of them. The Arnold Arboretum took it in as a rooted cutting in 1905 from a Pennsylvania nursery, on a line traceable back to material from 1884. The International Dendrology Society, which has no stake in Harvard's reputation, calls it the largest and oldest known example of the species anywhere, and photographed it standing in October 2025. It is a small tree in the tea family and the only member of its genus, and it flowers on an odd schedule. Large cream white flowers with a boss of yellow stamens open late in the season, so the last of them are still out while the leaves around them are turning red. Seeing both at once on the same branch is the reason to come. It grows in the Explorers Garden on Bussey Hill. No coordinates are published for the individual plant, so the pin is the garden and the labels there take you the rest of the way.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood of the Public Garden
trees.access: Free, public park, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Arlington MBTA station (Green Line), roughly 2-3 minute walk

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn foxy orange and fall

trees.story: Until 1944 this species was known only from fossils and assumed to have been extinct for millions of years. Then living Metasequoia turned up in Sichuan, and in early 1948 the first seeds to leave China arrived at Harvard's Arnold Arboretum in Jamaica Plain, a few miles from where this tree stands, just ahead of the door closing on scientific exchange with China for decades. The Arboretum raised seedlings and sent them around the world. This one was planted in the Public Garden in 1963, one of four here. It is not old, and it is not pretending to be. At about 63 it earns its place on what it is rather than how long it has stood. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer, which most people meet for the first time in autumn, when a tree that plainly looks like a redwood turns foxy orange and drops every needle it has. The trunk is fluted and deeply hollowed under each branch, another oddity of the species, and a younger 'Gold Rush' cultivar stands across the path for comparison. One note on sourcing: the 1963 planting date and the exact placement come from the Friends of the Public Garden, whose own people care for the tree, and we found no record of this specimen independent of them.

trees.name: The Original Dawn Redwood of the Arboretum
trees.age: roughly 77 years, grown from seed collected in Hubei, China in 1948
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 20 minute walk to the Arborway Gate and Hunnewell Visitor Center, or the 39 bus to the Arborway stop

best_time.label: late October into November, when a conifer this size turns rust orange and drops every needle it has

trees.story:
This tree grew from the seed shipment that put a fossil back into the ground. In 1948 the Arnold Arboretum took delivery of seed collected in Hubei, China, from a species that had been known to science only from fossils until living trees turned up in the interior a few years earlier. The seed was raised here, and the Arboretum's own account of what came up is worth quoting: the first of its kind to grow in North America in over two million years. The accession number is 524-48. From that lot and its siblings, dawn redwoods went out to gardens across the world, which is how a tree that was a rumour inside living memory became an ordinary sight on ordinary streets.

It stands near the Hunnewell Visitor Center, opposite the Arborway Gate, so it is the first thing worth walking to once you are through. It is also fifteen years older than the dawn redwood in the Public Garden across town, and its senior in the plainest sense: same species, same 1948 seed, one generation up.

One honest note on the record. A separately numbered 1948 accession is described elsewhere as the Arboretum's oldest dawn redwood, out along Conifer Path, and we could not establish whether that is this tree under a second label or a sibling raised from the same seed. Both came off the same shipment.

trees.name: The Wilson Paperbark Maple
trees.age: roughly 119 years (collected as a wild seedling in 1907)
trees.neighbourhood: Meadow Road, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 10-12 minute walk via the Forest Hills Gate and Meadow Road

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and low winter sun catches the peeling cinnamon bark

trees.story:
Almost every paperbark maple in America descends from two seedlings one man dug out of a Chinese wood in the autumn of 1907. The plant collector Ernest Henry Wilson found them in forest north of Yichang, in Hubei, lifted them and shipped them to the Arnold Arboretum. Both survived. This is one of the two, accession 12488, and by the Arboretum's record the pair are the first and the oldest paperbark maples on the continent and the genetic source of most of the ones planted in the country since.

The species has gone the other way at home. Acer griseum is now endangered in the wild in China, its remaining stands small and scattered, which makes a specimen tree in Jamaica Plain a piece of conservation as much as a piece of horticulture.

Come in winter. The bark is what the tree is named for and it is the reason to make the walk: it lifts off the trunk in thin cinnamon and copper curls that stay attached rather than falling, and with the leaves gone and low sun on it the trunk is the whole show.

One note on the record. All of the above traces back to the Arboretum, including a published feature written out of its own history, so this is one institution's account, thorough and public, but not independently corroborated. No coordinates exist for the individual tree. The pin is the maple collection off Meadow Road, about ten minutes up from the Forest Hills gate.

trees.name: The Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress
trees.neighbourhood: Dana Greenhouses, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain
trees.access: Free, public arboretum. The bonsai itself is on view only mid-April through late October at the Bonsai and Penjing Pavilion, and staff rotate roughly 30 trees through the display every two to three weeks, so this specific specimen is not guaranteed to be out on any given visit; the pavilion posts what is currently on view.
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 10 minute walk to the Centre Street Gate, then a further 5 minute walk to the Dana Greenhouses
trees.story: This tree is 289 years old and it fits on a table. It was started in 1737, when Boston was still a colonial port, and it has spent every one of those years in a pot, watered and pruned by somebody, without a gap. Larz Anderson, a Harvard graduate and American ambassador to Japan, bought it from the Yokohama Nursery Company around 1913 with roughly 39 other bonsai and shipped the lot home to his estate in Brookline, where it stood on his terraces for 24 years. After he and his wife Isabel died, the collection passed to the Arnold Arboretum, which eventually built a pavilion to house it. A cutting taken in 2017 is displayed beside it, the same tree at nine years old and at 289. Two things to know before you go. The 1737 date comes from Anderson's own records rather than from any independent dating, so it is one careful line of evidence repeated by everyone since, not two. And the pavilion rotates around 30 trees through its display every two or three weeks from mid April to late October, so this particular one is not guaranteed to be out on the day you arrive; the pavilion posts what is currently on view. It is ten minutes on foot from Forest Hills, and the Arboretum around it is worth the trip whatever is in the display that week.

trees.name: The Sapporo Katsuras
trees.neighbourhood: Meadow Road, Arnold Arboretum, Jamaica Plain
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Forest Hills MBTA station (Orange Line), roughly 15-20 minute walk via the Forest Hills Gate to Meadow Road, or the Arborway entrance

best_time.label: October, when the falling leaves turn apricot gold and smell of burnt sugar

trees.story: These two trees began as seed in a packet posted from Sapporo. William S. Clark, president of Massachusetts Agricultural College and the man who left his Japanese students the parting line "Boys, be ambitious", went to Hokkaido in 1876 to help found what is now Hokkaido University. He collected katsura seed there and sent a share to his friend Charles Sprague Sargent, the Arnold Arboretum's first director. It arrived in 1878, six years after the Arboretum itself existed at all, and the two multi stemmed trees on Meadow Road are what grew from it. They are the oldest katsuras in a collection of 35 and among the oldest documented anywhere in North America. Come in October. Katsura leaves turn apricot and gold, and as they fall and dry they give off a smell most people read as burnt sugar or candy floss; you often catch it before you find the tree. Winter is worth a different look, the silvery grey bark peeling away in narrow rectangular sheets and curved seed follicles hanging on into the cold before the wind takes the seed. Sargent went to Hokkaido himself in 1892 and wrote about katsura as a defining tree of the island's wet lowland woods. One note on sourcing: both accounts here are the Arboretum's own, a plant record and an Arnoldia article rather than two unconnected institutions, though the article's author visited and describes both trees alive and in health.

trees.name: The Longfellow Linden
trees.neighbourhood: Cambridge (within the day-trip boundary of Boston, roughly 20-25 minutes via Red Line to Harvard Square then a short walk)
trees.access: Free; National Historic Site grounds are open to the public daily during daylight hours (house tours are separately ticketed but the East Lawn where the tree stands is publicly accessible)
trees.transport: MBTA Red Line to Harvard Square, then about 8-10 minutes on foot down Brattle Street

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the whole East Lawn smells of it

trees.story: In the summer of 1844 Henry Wadsworth Longfellow came home to find that workmen had "lopped away the long low branches of my Linden tree, misunderstanding my directions", and he wrote it up in his journal as a small catastrophe. The tree outlived him. It went into the ground around 1800 to 1810, planted by Andrew Craigie, who owned the Brattle Street estate before the poet came to it in 1843, and it stands on the East Lawn of a house that had served as George Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston a generation before the linden existed. Fanny Longfellow wrote in 1843 of wanting "a linden avenue in which my poet intends to pace in his old age". This is the only tree of that avenue still standing. By 1846 he was describing her reading Heine underneath it. The National Park Service puts it at 82 feet, against roughly 60 for the species, with a trunk 84 inches through, and rates its condition fair to poor: the trunk cavity is filled, cables carry the branches, heavy pruning comes round every five years. Since the early 2000s the park has been growing a genetically identical cutting against the day it goes. The grounds are free and open in daylight; only the house tours are ticketed.

trees.name: The Houghton Beech
trees.neighbourhood: Cambridge, Mid-Cambridge/University Park (within the day-trip boundary; on the Red Line corridor)
trees.access: Free; stands beside a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue, fully visible and reachable at any time
trees.transport: MBTA Red Line to Central Square, then about 8 minutes on foot along Mass Ave toward Harvard Square

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken to purple-black

trees.story: This is Cambridge's only living Historic Landmark, and it was made one in 1985 to stop a building. A developer's plans for the site would have taken a third of the copper beech's crown and finished it off, so about thirty neighbours formed a group called the Friends of the Beech Tree and petitioned the city; the Historical Commission designated the tree itself, the legal instrument normally reserved for buildings. The Harvard Crimson, reporting from the October 1985 hearing, called it 203 years old, which puts its planting around 1782 and makes it roughly 240 now. That figure carries more weight than the biography printed around it in the same article, which has Henry O. Houghton serving as mayor decades before he founded the Riverside Press. A 2018 local survey of Cambridge trees offers a looser "planted 150+ years ago", a lower bound rather than a contradiction. Houghton planted three beeches on his family estate here. This is the one left. MIT bought the property in the 1970s and took down the buildings, and the tree stayed, which is how a private estate specimen ended up standing on a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue between Central and Harvard. Most of Boston's notable trees sit inside curated collections. This one you walk past on the way to the bus.

trees.name: The Mulberries of Nieuwe Veste
trees.access: Free, public library and cultural centre, open during opening hours
trees.transport: Central Breda, Molenstraat; 10 minute walk from Breda railway station

best_time.label: August into September, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: A library was built around these trees rather than the other way round. Three black mulberries have grown in this small courtyard since around 1780, when it was still the garden of Huize Ocrum, a manor house owned at the time by Gerrit Willem Motman, steward of the Dutch princely domains. The house came down over the following two centuries as the site changed hands and purpose, but the mulberries stayed, and when architect Herman Hertzberger designed De Nieuwe Veste, Breda's combined library, music school and cultural centre, in the mid-1990s, he folded the new building's plan around the courtyard rather than clear it. The trees now shape the layout of a public building constructed more than two hundred years after they were planted, an unusually literal case of architecture yielding to something already there. At roughly 245 years old they are, as far as any documented planting date in Breda goes, the city's oldest living trees, though the courtyard they stand in is modest and the trees themselves are not large by monumental-tree standards elsewhere in the country. Free to visit during the library's opening hours, they are also one of the few entries on this list a visitor can reach without ever stepping outside.

trees.name: The Trumpet Tree of Wilhelminapark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Zandberg neighbourhood, Breda; 15 minute walk from Breda railway station

best_time.label: July, when the catalpa's white flower spikes open

trees.story: This catalpa grew sideways instead of up, and Breda decided to help it keep doing so. It leans out over the pond in Wilhelminapark, a park laid out in 1894 by landscape architect Leonard A. Springer, far enough over the water that the municipality now props its lowest limbs on columns rather than let them snap or drag. Local tradition credits Queen Wilhelmina herself, the park's namesake, with intervening at some point to see the tree preserved rather than felled for convenience, though the story's exact origin is harder to pin down than the tree's current, very visible lean. Catalpas are not native to the Netherlands, brought from the southeastern United States as an ornamental species prized for its huge heart-shaped leaves and its white, purple-throated flower spikes in midsummer, and this one has had well over a century in Dutch soil to develop the sprawling, horizontal habit the species is capable of when nothing stops it. No exact planting record survives, so its age is inferred from the park's own founding date rather than documented outright. Wilhelminapark itself has lost several of its other historic trees in recent years to disease and storm damage, which makes this one's continued, actively supported survival more notable rather than less.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Valkenberg
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Central Breda, beside Breda Castle; 10 minute walk from Breda railway station

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.story: A tree from the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas has been growing in Breda's oldest park for close to two centuries. This Caucasian wingnut, planted around 1830 in Valkenberg beside Breda Castle and the Grote Kerk, was measured in September 2020 at 5.82 metres around, a size that reflects how fast and wide the species spreads once established rather than any particular rarity of specimen. Wingnuts were a genuine curiosity in 19th-century Dutch parks, planted by landscape designers testing what exotic species could handle the local climate, and this one has clearly handled it: its suckering roots have likely spread new stems around the original trunk over the decades, the species' usual habit when left alone in open ground. Valkenberg itself predates the tree by centuries, laid out on the grounds beside Breda Castle, once the seat of the House of Nassau and now a military academy, with the Grote Kerk's tower visible over the park's mature tree canopy. The wingnut is one of several genuinely old trees in the park, including planes and horse chestnuts pushing a century themselves, but its size and unusual leaf, long pinnate fronds rather than a single broad leaf, make it the one visitors actually stop under.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Laurenspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Ginneken, Breda; bus from Breda railway station or a 25 minute walk
trees.story: Despite its name, Ulvenhoutselaan runs inside Breda, not the separate village of Ulvenhout the street is named after, and this giant sequoia stands well within city limits along it, in the Ginneken district in the south of town. Planted in 1885, measured at 25 metres tall and 5.70 metres around, it belongs to the wave of Californian conifers that spread through Dutch estates and parks in the second half of the 19th century, after the species was first introduced to Europe in the 1850s and became, briefly, a fashionable statement for anyone with land to plant on. At 140 years old it has had time to become a genuinely large tree by Dutch standards without coming close to challenging its own species' natural lifespan, which can run past two thousand years in California's Sierra Nevada. Ginneken itself was a separate village until it merged into Breda in the 20th century, which makes the sequoia's setting a small irony of its own: a street named for a village that is not this tree's home, in a neighbourhood that used to be a different one. Free to see, in a quiet residential park rather than a tourist destination, it rewards anyone who already knows where to look.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Biscainhos
trees.access: Free. The Biscainhos museum garden is open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00-12:30 and 14:00-17:30 (closed Mondays and some holidays); garden entry is free, just ask at reception. The palace's indoor exhibit is a separate paid ticket (EUR 2), not needed to see the tree.
trees.transport: Central Braga, an easy walk from the historic centre / cathedral.

best_time.label: September to October: clear yellow, one of the most reliable autumn trees

trees.story:
Portugal shortlisted this tree for its Tree of the Year in 2026, one of ten finalists nationally. It is a tulip tree, Liriodendron tulipifera, native to the eastern United States, and the coverage of that shortlist calls it the largest of its kind in the country.

The measurements depend on who took them. Portugal's register of trees of public interest recorded 6.5 metres round the trunk, 27.4 metres tall and a crown of 18 metres when it classified the tree in 2010. The 2026 reporting gives 30 metres and 19. Both are plausible for a tree that has kept growing, and neither is picked here as the winner.

Age is firmer. The register put it at 270 years at that 2010 measurement, which makes it roughly 285 now, and the newspaper coverage places the planting in the reign of Joao V, who died in 1750. It went into the baroque garden of the Palacio dos Biscainhos, a hectare of formal beds, orchard and kitchen garden behind a Braga townhouse that is now the city's museum.

It was planted as one of a symmetrical pair. The other tulip tree lasted until the late 1970s; a replacement went in nearby in 1997 and is still an obviously young tree. The gap between the two is the clearest thing on the site for understanding what 285 years actually does.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of Santa Tecla
trees.access: Free. Stands in Largo de Santa Tecla, a public square used as a neighbourhood gathering space, open at all times.
trees.transport: About 1.5km from central Braga; a 20-25 minute walk, or a short bus/taxi ride.
trees.story:
The parish spent about six years asking before this cork oak was protected. When the classification came through they marked it on 21 March 2012, World Forest Day, with fourth-year pupils from the primary school up the road, who were handed the job of guarding it.

The national register gives the trunk 3.5 metres round, the tree 15 metres tall, and the crown 21 metres across, which is wider than the tree is high. That shape is the point of it. Largo de Santa Tecla is a square people actually use, and what a crown like that produces on a Minho summer afternoon is shade. The register dated the tree to 150 years at the 2011 measurement, so about 165 now.

Quercus suber is the tree the cork industry is built on, and Portugal produces more cork than any other country. The bark is the reason: thick, spongy, fire-resistant, and it grows back after stripping, which almost no other tree manages. A cork oak standing in a public square is generally left unharvested and keeps that bark, deeply furrowed and pale, a surface that looks several sizes too big for the trunk underneath.

Three oaks classified in the same act stand about sixty metres away, so the whole stop takes a minute.

trees.name: The Three Oaks of Santa Tecla
trees.access: Free. Same public square as the Cork Oak of Santa Tecla, open at all times.
trees.transport: About 1.5km from central Braga; a 20-25 minute walk, or a short bus/taxi ride.

best_time.label: August to September: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Three oaks, one entry. Portugal's register of trees of public interest classifies these as a conjunto arboreo, a single grouped listing, and gives one set of figures for all three: 2.7 metres round, 16.7 metres tall, and 85 years old when they were measured in 2011, so around a century now. It does not say which of the three the tape went round, or whether the number is an average.

They stand in the same square as the cork oak, sixty metres off, and were protected in the same act, celebrated at the same ceremony on World Forest Day in March 2012. The local paper covering it described the oaks as one of the main attractions of Largo de Santa Tecla, valued for shade in summer and for the space underneath them, which the neighbourhood uses as its own.

Quercus robur is the common oak of northern Europe, and northern Portugal is near the warm edge of where it grows well. The name comes from the acorns: they hang on long stalks, peduncles, while the leaves sit almost directly on the twig, which is the reverse of the arrangement on a sessile oak and the quickest way to tell the two apart in autumn.

trees.name: The Trees of the Embrace
trees.species: Pedunculate Oak and London Plane (Quercus robur, Platanus x acerifolia)
trees.access: Free. Standing at the funicular (Elevador do Bom Jesus) station, a public spot at the base of the Bom Jesus do Monte sanctuary hill, open at all times; the funicular itself is a separate paid ride up the hill and not needed to see the trees.
trees.transport: About 5km east of central Braga; city bus to Bom Jesus do Monte, then a short walk to the funicular station.
trees.story:
An oak and a plane standing twenty metres apart at the foot of the Bom Jesus funicular are registered under the same name: arvore do Abraco, the tree of the embrace. That is not a nickname picked up from a guidebook. It is written into each tree's own entry in Portugal's register of trees of public interest, and both were classified on the same day in July 2010.

What nobody has written down is why. No source we have found explains the name: whether the two crowns once met over the path, whether it belongs to a story attached to the sanctuary on the hill above, or whether it is simply what people in Tenoes have always called them. If you know where the name comes from, tell us and it goes on the page.

Both trees were put at 100 years old when they were measured in 2010, which makes them around 115 now. The oak is the heavier of the two, 3.7 metres round with a crown almost 25 metres across; the plane is slimmer at 2.55 metres and marginally the taller at 26.

They stand at the station of the Elevador do Bom Jesus, the water-counterbalanced funicular that has hauled pilgrims up to the sanctuary since 1882. Looking at the trees costs nothing. The ride is a separate ticket.

trees.name: The Domesday Oak
trees.access: Free, open access, Ashton Court Estate (daily from 8am, closing time varies by season)
trees.transport: Bus or short drive from central Bristol; no on-site rail

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Ashton Court appears in the Domesday Book, the survey William the Conqueror ordered of his new kingdom in 1086, and one oak in the estate's parkland is thought to have already been growing around that time, which is where its name comes from. At an estimated 700 years old, it may be the oldest living tree in greater Bristol. Its condition tells the story as plainly as its age: the trunk has split and partially collapsed, one section settling almost horizontally toward the ground while the rest hangs on, now held upright by timber struts and steel wire rather than its own strength. Visitors who knew the tree decades ago recall climbing inside a fuller, healthier trunk; today's crown is thinner and the bark flaking with decay. In 2002, the Tree Council named it one of 50 Great British Trees to mark the Queen's golden jubilee, official recognition for a specimen that has no sign or marker pointing casual visitors to it today, easy to walk past in a park that holds more than a hundred other ancient pollard oaks, the largest such cluster in Britain outside Windsor Great Park.

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of Ashton Park
trees.access: Free, open access, Ashton Court Estate (daily from 8am, closing time varies by season)
trees.transport: Bus or short drive from central Bristol; no on-site rail

best_time.label: October, when the spiny husks split and the nuts fall

trees.story: Sweet Chestnuts spiral as they age, their bark twisting around the trunk in a pattern that gets more pronounced with every passing century, and Ashton Park's oldest is a dramatic example: an estimated 600 years old, with a girth of over eight metres, according to the Bristol Tree Forum's own survey of the city's veteran trees. Sweet Chestnut is not native to Britain, introduced by the Romans and long favoured by estate owners for timber and for the nuts it produces, and a tree of this size and age likely dates to well before Ashton Court passed through its various private owners into Bristol City Council's hands in 1959. It shares its parkland with the Domesday Oak and more than a hundred other ancient pollard oaks, together forming the largest concentration of veteran trees anywhere in Britain outside Windsor Great Park, a legacy of centuries spent as private deer park rather than farmed or built over.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Blaise Castle
trees.access: Free, open access, Blaise Castle Estate (daily, dawn to dusk)
trees.transport: Bus from central Bristol; no on-site rail

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: John Scandrett Harford, a wealthy Bristol banker, bought Blaise Castle Estate in 1789 and hired the two biggest names in English landscape design of the era, Humphry Repton and later John Nash, to remake it into a Picturesque parkland. Repton's method favoured framing views with carefully placed specimen trees rather than dense planting, and the Cedars of Lebanon he set out near Blaise Castle House are some of the estate's oldest surviving evidence of that design still growing where he placed it. Cedar of Lebanon was still a relatively novel import to English gardens at the time, prized for its wide, flat-tiered canopy and biblical associations, and a tree planted in Repton's era has now had well over two centuries to develop the broad, layered crown the species is known for. Bristol Corporation bought the estate in 1926, turning Harford's private grounds into a free public park, and the cedar has stood through that entire transition from private landscape statement to a tree thousands of Bristol families walk past on the way to the children's playground nearby.

trees.name: The Oak of Kings Weston
trees.access: Free, open access, Kings Weston Estate (daily, dawn to dusk)
trees.transport: Bus from central Bristol; no on-site rail

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Sir John Vanbrugh, the architect behind Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard, designed Kings Weston House for the politician Edward Southwell between 1712 and 1719, one of the grandest early 18th-century houses in the Bristol area. An oak growing in the estate's parkland predates that whole building project by well over a century, already an old, established tree when Vanbrugh's workmen were still laying foundations. At an estimated 450 years, it is the oldest tree recorded on the entire estate, a living link to the land before Southwell's family ever owned it. Kings Weston's grounds also hold a lime avenue planted alongside the house's construction around 1720, the oldest of its kind in the city, but the oak stands apart from that formal design, a survivor from an entirely different era of the landscape's history rather than a planned garden feature.
