Wikipedia's account of the forest names a stand of oak among the survivors of that original cover, which is exactly what this is: not an import chosen for a garden, but a tree the friars found already growing when they built the convent and its wayside chapels. This one stands by the chapel of Sao Pedro on the Via Sacra, four metres ninety around the trunk and twenty-four metres tall, with a crown that reaches almost twenty-one metres across, comfortably the widest native canopy in the collection. The state's 2016 measurement put it at three hundred years, tied with the cypress at the first Via Sacra station for the second oldest tree in the register after the Cedro de Sao Jose, though no source beyond the register dates this individual tree. It is easy to walk past it looking for the exotic specimen and miss the one tree here that was never planted for effect.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of the Lago Grande
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: South slope above the Lago Grande, about 900 m from the Largo do Mosteiro
trees.story: Portugal's national tree gets one entry in a forest built to show off everything else. Quercus suber, the cork oak, is the species the country names much of its rural economy after: cork bark is stripped from living trunks every nine years or so without killing the tree, and most of the world's supply still comes from Portuguese hillsides. Here, on the south slope above the Lago Grande, it stands quietly among cypresses from Mexico, redwoods from California and a eucalyptus that ranks among the tallest trees in Europe, four metres and a quarter around the trunk and seventeen and a half metres tall, its thick, deeply fissured bark visibly different from every conifer around it. The register gives no age, which for a cork oak is not unusual: old specimens can run past three centuries and nobody has cored this one to count the rings. What identifies it beyond the bare register entry is the species itself: Wikipedia's account of the forest's surviving native cover names oak among its few original inhabitants, the same corroboration the pedunculate oak by the Capela de Sao Pedro carries. Stand here and you are looking at the one tree in this collection that needed no ship to arrive.

trees.name: The Redwood of the Fonte de Santa Teresa
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: On the Trilho da Agua, about 300m south-west of the Largo do Mosteiro
trees.story:
Bucaco's third redwood stop stands on a slope above what locals reckon the best spring water in the whole forest, the Fonte de Santa Teresa, named for the sixteenth century Carmelite reformer Teresa of Avila. The register measured it in 2016 at 5.58 metres round and 45 metres tall, about 150 years old at the time, which puts it in the ground within a few decades of the forest's other sequoias, planted when the fashion for collecting the world's conifers was at its height.

The fountain it grows beside is one stop on the Trilho da Agua, a walking trail built around Bucaco's historic water sources, Fonte Fria and Fonte do Carregal among them, that the forest describes as contemplative rather than athletic. A redwood needing fog and damp air to thrive has, by accident or design, ended up on the one trail in the forest built around water.

Coast redwoods drink through their needles as much as their roots, drawing a real share of their water straight from the sea mist Bucaco's hillside catches off the Atlantic, which is the reason this species does as well here as it does anywhere outside its native California fog belt. This one has had a century and a half to put that trick to use.

photo.license: Provided by the Fundacao Mata do Bucaco, all rights reserved

trees.name: The Dudul din Batiștei (White Mulberry of Batiștei)
trees.access: Free, public church courtyard, viewable during normal visiting hours
trees.transport: Sector 2, near Piața Universității; about a 10 minute walk from University Square metro station

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: According to a story carved onto a plaque in its own church porch, a boy named Manciu once told Prince Constantin Brâncoveanu that the mulberry tree he had just been scolded for climbing would outlive the prince himself. It did, by a very wide margin. Brâncoveanu was executed by the Ottomans in 1714, and the white mulberry in the courtyard of Batiștei Church is still standing, now generally reckoned Bucharest's oldest living tree, though estimates for exactly how old split between a documented 200-plus years and a traditional claim, tied to the Brâncoveanu legend, of over 300. Either figure makes it older than the church building around it in its current form, and older than the surrounding streets, which grew up around the tree rather than the other way round, back when this stretch of the city was a mahala, a merchants' and craftsmen's quarter where local children apparently used the tree as a climbing frame long before anyone thought to protect it. It carries official status as an arbore ocrotit, a protected tree, one of a small number in the capital with that designation and a documented legend to go with it rather than just a girth measurement.

trees.name: The Secular Plane of Cișmigiu
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Central Bucharest, main entrance on Bulevardul Regina Elisabeta; a 5 minute walk from Izvor or Universitate metro stations
trees.story: In 2018 a municipal crew digging a trench for park lighting cut through two of the main support roots of Cișmigiu's oldest tree, and within two years a full quarter of its crown had dried out and died. The plane tree is reckoned at around 200 years old by one account and closer to 170 by another that ties its planting more directly to the park's own founding, when Viennese-trained landscape architect Wilhelm Meyer turned a drained swamp into Bucharest's first public garden between 1847 and its 1854 opening. Either figure makes it one of the very few survivors of that original planting scheme still standing. Popular legend has occasionally stretched its age to 300 or even 500 years, a claim the park's own history rules out immediately: nothing could have been growing here before the marsh itself was drained in 1830. What is true is dramatic enough without embellishment. The tree has outlived a kingdom, two world wars, and decades of the regime that followed, only to lose a quarter of its living crown to a lighting cable trench nobody has since gone back to properly repair. It is still standing, still shading part of the park it has occupied for close to two centuries, its damage visible to anyone who looks up rather than hidden away.

trees.name: The Turkish Hazel of Cișmigiu
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Central Bucharest, main entrance on Bulevardul Regina Elisabeta; a 5 minute walk from Izvor or Universitate metro stations

best_time.label: September into October, when the nuts ripen and split open

trees.story: Romania has only two officially protected specimens of Corylus colurna, the Turkish hazel, and one of them grows inside Cișmigiu, Bucharest's oldest and most visited public park. Most of the species' native range lies far to the southeast, in the Balkans, Anatolia and the Caucasus, which makes a mature, healthy specimen this far north and west of its usual territory a genuine rarity rather than an ordinary park planting. Cișmigiu itself began as a swamp: the site was drained in 1830 on the order of General Pavel Kiseleff, then redesigned from 1847 by the Viennese-trained landscape architect Wilhelm Meyer, who filled the new grounds with imported and unusual species before the garden's official opening in 1854. No record fixes an exact planting date for this particular hazel, but its inclusion among Meyer's original plantings would put it among the oldest trees the park has, and its formal protection recognizes the tree for a fact simpler than age: outside a handful of botanical collections, there is nowhere else in the country to see one like it.

trees.name: The Ginkgos of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Paid entry, University of Bucharest Botanical Garden, standard visiting hours
trees.transport: Cotroceni district, Șoseaua Cotroceni 32; about a 10 minute walk from Eroilor metro station

best_time.label: November: the whole crown turns butter gold, then drops in a day or two

trees.story: Bucharest's Botanical Garden protects four ginkgo trees as a group, 200 metres inside its main entrance, under the local nickname arborii pagodelor, the pagoda trees, a label more commonly attached to an entirely different species, the Japanese pagoda tree. Ginkgo biloba earned the borrowed name anyway, probably because its fan-shaped leaves and East Asian origin read as pagoda-adjacent to whoever named it first, and the name stuck regardless of the mismatch. The garden itself dates to 1860, moving to its current site on the edge of the Cotroceni district in 1884, and functions as the University of Bucharest's living plant collection rather than a public park in the ordinary sense, which is part of why these four trees have survived largely undisturbed while so many of the capital's older street and park trees have not. No record gives an exact planting date for the group, but ginkgo has been standard in serious botanical collections since the 18th century, and a garden built to university academic standards from the 1880s onward is exactly the kind of institution that would have planted one of the world's oldest surviving tree lineages among its founding specimens rather than adding it later as decoration.

trees.name: The Tree of Science
trees.access: Free, open access, Margaret Island (public park, open daily)
trees.transport: Bus 26 (the island's only bus route, from Nyugati ter) or tram 4/6 to Margit hid, budai hidfo, then a walk onto the island
trees.story: Archduke Joseph, Palatine of Hungary, planted this plane tree with his own hands in 1823 on what was then his private island retreat, two years before Count Istvan Szechenyi founded the Hungarian Academy of Sciences a short walk away across the water. The near-coincidence in dates gave the tree its modern title: the city and the Academy jointly named it the Tree of Science, a formal honour for a plane that has quietly outlasted both the Habsburg court that planted it and the war that nearly took its neighbours. Its statistics explain the reputation on their own: a trunk 6.64 metres around, a crown 55 metres wide, and a canopy foresters have estimated at 30 to 50 tonnes of leaf and wood, among the most admired plane crowns anywhere in Europe. It has stood through two world wars, the 1956 revolution, and repeated redesigns of the island around it, rooted between the ruined Dominican convent where Saint Margaret of Hungary once lived and the Art Nouveau water tower built in 1911. Archduke Joseph is the reason Margaret Island has any ancient trees at all: he turned a semi-wild royal hunting ground into a private garden in the 1810s and 1820s, planting exotic specimens with no way of knowing they would still be standing two centuries later, at nearly double the height of the buildings around them.

trees.name: The Pagoda Tree of Buda Castle
trees.access: Free, open access, Buda Castle South Gardens (terraces open daily)
trees.transport: Buda Castle Funicular from Clark Adam ter, or the free public elevator at the Castle Garden Bazaar; bus 16 from Deak Ferenc ter

best_time.label: cream flowers in late summer, when almost nothing else flowers

trees.story: By the time Franz Joseph became emperor, this tree had already outlived the reason anyone remembered planting it. Antal Tost, gardener to Palatine Joseph, chose a Japanese pagoda tree for the slope beside Buda Castle's great southern rondella around 1790, when the species itself was still a botanical novelty in Europe, imported from China only a few decades earlier despite its misleading name. By 1862, an academic lecture was already calling it the largest tree in the castle garden. It survived the 1848-49 revolution, when fighting tore through the district around it, and came close to losing a very different fight decades later: when the castle's gardens were redesigned at the end of the 19th century, the plan called for the tree's removal, until head gardener Karoly Mraz personally persuaded Franz Joseph to spare it. It survived the Second World War too, through fighting that flattened much of the district above it. Today it stands roughly 230 to 250 years old by the estimates on record, Budapest's oldest documented tree, on ground that is free to walk through the South Gardens' terraces. Locals nicknamed it simply the Nagy Fa, the Big Tree, long before anyone thought to give it a more official name.

trees.name: The Old Acacia of Erzsebet Square
trees.access: Free, open access, Erzsebet ter (public square, open at all times)
trees.transport: Deak Ferenc ter (metro lines M1/M2/M3, adjacent square), short walk

best_time.label: hanging white pea flowers, strongly scented

trees.story: A 1960s survey by Budapest's own parks department already described this black locust as over a hundred years old, which places its planting somewhere in the 1860s, not long after Erzsebet Square itself was laid out on the site of a demolished monastery cemetery. It has stood at the corner toward Jozsef Attila utca through everything the square went through since: the aftermath of the square's namesake, Empress Elisabeth's assassination in 1898, the arrival of the city's first long-distance bus station on the same ground in the 20th century, and the underground shopping centre and park redesign that replaced the bus station later still. Black locusts are not typically long-lived or especially prized trees; 19th-century Hungary planted them mainly to bind the sandy soil of the Great Plain rather than for their looks, which makes this one's survival at the dead centre of the capital more a matter of civic accident than deliberate preservation. It has not gone entirely unscathed: its upper branch dried out sometime in the 1980s, and it has leaned slowly ever since, now propped at two points by the city's own parks maintenance company rather than left to fall on its own schedule. Nobody planted it to be remembered. It simply refused to be removed for a century and a half while the square around it was rebuilt three times over.

trees.name: The Taban Mulberry
trees.access: Free, open access, Taban Botanical Trail (public hillside, open at all times)
trees.transport: Tram 19 or 41 along the Danube to Varkert Bazar, then a walk uphill into Taban

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: Popular legend says Ottoman occupiers planted this mulberry during their century and a half ruling Buda, which would make it well over 400 years old; the more carefully sourced version, and the one this project follows, credits Empress Maria Theresa's 18th-century push to build a domestic silk industry, which put mulberry orchards across Taban specifically to feed silkworms, with a 1771 report confirming mulberries already growing in the district by then. Either story would make it one of the oldest trees in Budapest; historians settle on 200 to 250 years as the defensible range, though some push it as high as 300. It once grew inside the yard of a house whose fence has long since vanished, its canopy spilling toward what was then the top of the Komuves lepcso, a stone staircase since rebuilt slightly further along the hillside than its original route. By 2021 the tree was in poor enough condition that Budapest's parks authority began active conservation work to save it, propping and pruning rather than letting a specimen this rare simply fail. A sign on today's Taban Botanical Trail warns visitors not to climb its branches, a small, practical reminder that a centuries-old story is still standing on a genuinely fragile trunk.

trees.name: The Seven Chieftains Plane
trees.access: Free, open access, Margaret Island (public park, open daily; Palatinus Strand itself is a paid bathing complex, but the tree stands outside it on open parkland)
trees.transport: Bus 26 (the island's only bus route, from Nyugati ter), stop near Palatinus Strand
trees.story: This tree is not the one its name first belonged to. Palatine Joseph's original favourite plane on Margaret Island, split into seven trunks after an 1838 flood snapped it as a sapling, was struck by lightning and finally died around 1935; Hungarians called it the Het Testver, the Seven Brothers. A different plane growing 265 metres north, opposite what is now the Palatinus Strand, took catastrophic damage of its own during the fighting that swept the island in January 1945. Rather than remove it, head gardener Antal Kunsch cut the wrecked trunk back hard, and the tree responded by resprouting into seven new limbs of its own, an accident of pruning that echoed the older tree closely enough that Budapest's parks authority renamed it in tribute: the Hetvezer, the Seven Chieftains. Eight decades later it casts roughly 300 square metres of shade, nearly 30 metres tall, its bark peeling in the mottled patches typical of old planes, on ground that thousands of sunbathers walk past every summer on their way to the baths without necessarily knowing they are looking at a war wound that became one of the island's best-loved trees.

trees.name: The Old St Lucie Cherry of the Fuveszkert
trees.access: Paid entry, ELTE Fuveszkert botanical garden. Adult ticket 2200 Ft (2026 pricing), open daily 9:00-17:00 in main season (ticket office closes 16:30); hours vary by season, check before visiting
trees.transport: M3 metro to Nagyvarad ter, then roughly 5-10 minute walk through Orczy-kert to the garden entrance on Illes utca

best_time.label: April into May, when the whole crown flowers white and fragrant

trees.story:
The St Lucie cherry is usually a shrub. Six metres is a good one. This tree is 11.2 metres tall, with a trunk 339 centimetres around and a crown twelve metres wide, which is extraordinary for a species that normally grows out of a dry limestone slope at the edge of a wood. Hungarians call it sajmeggy. Nobody expects one to reach the size of an oak.

It also got here first. ELTE's Fuveszkert is Hungary's oldest botanical garden, founded in 1771, but it only reached this ground in 1847, when the university bought the ten hectare Festetics castle garden with the backing of Palatine Archduke Joseph. Before the Festetics family took the property in 1798 it belonged to Marton Szeleczky, an imperial loyalist, and the cherry was already standing on his private estate. The garden was laid out around it rather than planted with it. At roughly 250 years old it has watched a nobleman's grounds turn into a scientific collection and then into a place anyone can buy a ticket to, without ever moving.

It stands alone beside the main path, about eighty metres in from the Illes utca gate, on level ground you can reach with a pushchair or a wheelchair. Our pin is the garden rather than the tree, so look for the solitary one with the wide low crown.

trees.name: The Count's Mulberry of Karolyi Garden
trees.access: Free, open access, Karolyi kert (public park in central Budapest), opens 8:00 daily, closes at sunset (seasonal)
trees.transport: Ferenciek tere metro (M3), roughly 7 minute walk; also close to Astoria (M2) and Kalvin ter (M3/M4)

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen and drop

trees.story:
It takes two adults with their arms spread to get around this trunk, and nobody knows who planted it. The two candidates sit half a century apart. Count Antal Karolyi bought the palace next door in 1768 and rebuilt the garden in the baroque manner soon after, which would make the mulberry a tree of the late 1700s. A later Karolyi, Gyorgy, modernised the same garden in the 1830s. Both sources that describe it say plainly that the planting date is unknown and neither picks a side, so somewhere between 230 and 250 years is the working figure rather than a fact.

What it stood through is better documented. In 1795 the palace held its reception for the newly installed Palatine Joseph, and in 1800 a name day ball for Alexandra Pavlovna, both of them spilling out into this garden. In 1838 the Danube came into Pest and the palace took in hundreds of families whose houses had dissolved in the water. After the 1848 revolution failed, General Haynau ran his headquarters from the same building, and the garden outside went on being a garden.

It is probably the oldest white mulberry in Hungary. Safety pruning has left it blunter than it was, which is the price of keeping a heavy old tree standing in a park full of children. Look along the perimeter wall near the Ferenczy Istvan utca gate. In June and July the fruit drops and stains the path.

trees.name: The Old Acacia of Szechenyi Square
trees.age: documented as 227 years (planted 1789), though disputed; possibly considerably younger
trees.access: Free, open access, but stands on a traffic island on Szechenyi Istvan ter surrounded by roads; reached on foot via pedestrian crossings only, not a park setting
trees.transport: Close to Deak Ferenc ter and the Buda-side approach to the Chain Bridge; several city bus and tram routes serve Szechenyi Istvan ter directly

best_time.label: hanging white pea flowers, strongly scented

trees.story:
This tree is celebrated for being 227 years old, and a historian has taken that number apart with photographs. The popular account, carried by Az Ev Faja when the tree was nominated in 2015, has it planted in 1789, the year the Bastille fell, as the last survivor of a Danube side avenue laid out in the 1780s. That would make it older than the Chain Bridge beside it, older than the Academy of Sciences and older than the Gresham Palace.

Then Zsofia Viczian went through the pictures. Photographs and postcards of the square from before 1867 show no tree at this spot, only the mound of earth raised for a coronation. Gyorgy Klosz photographed the place in 1875 and cart drivers are standing where the trunk was supposedly already growing. The tree first appears as a substantial thing in a postcard from the 1930s, which would put it nearer 120 or 150 years. Both accounts are in print and neither has given way.

Whatever its age, it is a wreck kept upright by attention. The trunk leans hard, about four metres around and only six metres tall, propped since the 1980s on wooden supports set on iron beams, cushioned where they meet the bark. A large branch died in that decade and took its counterweight with it. It came through the war and nine renamings of the square. It stands on a paved traffic island, so you cross a road to reach it.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Dobrentei Square
trees.access: Free, standing in a public square
trees.transport: Dobrentei ter tram stop (lines 19/41) or a 5 minute walk from Rudas Gyogyfurdo, on foot
trees.story: Everything else on this square went. Twentieth-century clearance took Tabán's palaces, its cafes and its Serbian Orthodox church, and the oldest thing left standing on Döbrentei tér is a plane tree of about 115 years. Photographs from the 1900s and 1910s catch it as a young tree, which is how a Budapest history publication dated it, and FŐKERT, the city's parks company, carries it on its own register of notable trees. The trunk is over four metres around and the crown reaches about twenty metres, higher than the roofs beside it, and visibly lopsided, because the tree has never been able to spread toward the building at its back. It came through the fighting around Buda Castle in the 1940s that flattened much of this neighbourhood, and then through the rebuilding of the Elizabeth Bridge, when trees at the bridgehead were candidates for removal. District I gave it local protection in 2011 and fixed a plaque to the trunk. The beer garden at its foot took the name Platán from it, and generations have used the tables in its shade as a meeting point. A second plane stands nearby by the Rudas baths; this entry is the Döbrentei tér tree, the documented and protected one. The pagoda tree at Buda Castle is 350 metres uphill, the Tabán mulberry about 600.

trees.name: The Black Walnut of the Franciscan Ruins
trees.access: Free, standing in public parkland
trees.transport: Margaret Island, roughly 10-12 minute walk north from the Margaret Bridge entrance, or the island's internal bus (26) to the nearest stop

best_time.label: late September into October, when the green-husked walnuts drop and stain everything they touch

trees.story: Budapest's biggest black walnut is also the frailest tree on this list, and both facts come from the same survey. FŐKERT, the city's parks company, dated it to around 213 years in its 2020 dendrological study of Margaret Island, which makes it roughly 219 now, and measured its trunk as the thickest black walnut on the island by a wide margin: the runner-up was 119 centimetres smaller around. A national database ranked it second in Hungary for trunk girth. It was probably one of the first trees planted here, in the early 1800s under head gardener Károly Tost, beside the palatine's summer residence. A 1907 newspaper piece describes a walnut in a meadow at the island's centre, 3.5 metres around and 25 metres tall, almost certainly this one. The same 2020 assessment found it hollow and rotting at the trunk and root collar, its crown cut hard back after storm damage and a safety pruning in 2016, and estimated it had about a decade left. That window closes around 2030. It was standing at the last assessment and it is very likely standing now, but the newest evidence here is six years old, so go with your eyes open. It stands by the Franciscan ruins, a hundred metres from the island's oldest yew and 350 from its oldest oak.

trees.name: The Island's Oldest Pedunculate Oak
trees.access: Free, standing in public parkland
trees.transport: Margaret Island, roughly 12-15 minute walk north from the Margaret Bridge entrance, near the Rose Garden

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This oak is older than the park it stands in. Margaret Island was redeveloped as a landscape park under Archduke Joseph in the 19th century, and a handful of trees on the higher, better-drained eastern strip predate that work as remnants of the oak, ash and elm floodplain forest that covered the ground before anybody designed anything. This pedunculate oak is the island's largest and one of its oldest: FŐKERT's 2020 survey dates it to around 203 years then, so roughly 209 now, and a 1988 measurement put it at 28 to 30 metres tall with a trunk 345 centimetres around. Little of that old forest is left. Around a hundred oaks over ninety years old remain on the island's public land, most of the losses coming from the 2010 flood and the storms of that decade. Its shape records a life spent in a crowd. The crown is asymmetric from growing hemmed in by neighbours, structural limbs were cut back decades ago, and the cavities left by removed branches have recently been treated. Nothing in the record suggests decline, though the most recent condition assessment is the 2020 one. It stands in the Upper Rose Garden beside Zielinszky Szilárd sétány, about 350 metres from the Tree of Science, the Seven Chieftains Plane and the island's black walnut, which together make a loop of under two kilometres.

trees.name: The Island's Oldest Yew
trees.access: Free, standing in public parkland
trees.transport: Margaret Island, roughly 10-12 minute walk north from the Margaret Bridge entrance, near the Franciscan ruins

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Two old yews stand near the Franciscan ruins on Margaret Island, and only one of them still reads as a tree. This is the larger. The other was cut back radically decades ago for reasons nobody wrote down, and now sits at 4.5 metres tall under a crown 7 to 8 metres wide, so anyone comparing the two is not looking at damage from the same event but at one tree that was left alone and one that was not. FŐKERT's 2020 survey of the island calls this the largest and oldest yew there, with nothing comparable anywhere else on the island, and dates it to around 203 years at the time, so roughly 209 now. A former head gardener put it in the 1800s independently. A 1967 survey recorded four old shrub-form yews on the island, two of them standing on their own by the Franciscan ruins; this is one of that pair. For a yew, 209 years is nothing. The species runs to millennia, and English churchyards hold specimens ten times this age, which makes the island's oldest yew a young tree with old damage: rot at the root collar and trunk, bark loss, a major limb long gone leaving the crown truncated, lower branches clipped since a 2012 tidy-up. The most recent assessment is 2020. The black walnut is a hundred metres away.

trees.name: The Ficus of Alameda Apodaca
trees.access: Free, public seafront garden
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cadiz train station
trees.story: Four fig saplings carried from India by missionary nuns are the origin story behind this tree and its three siblings scattered across Cadiz. One of the nuns died during the voyage and was nursed in her final days at the city's Hospital de Mora; the surviving sisters planted the saplings as a memorial, two here on the seafront Alameda and two more near the old hospital site. Planted in 1903, more than two decades before Juan Talavera y Heredia's regionalist redesign gave the Alameda its current look, the tree has since grown into something closer to a small grove than a single trunk, its lower branches sending down aerial roots that thicken into extra trunks over the flat marble terrace where it stands. Locals sometimes call the pair the Ficus Gemelos, the twin figs, though decades of divergent growth have left one visibly larger than the other. Cadiz's Atlantic wind is hard on a tree built this wide and this exposed, and its wood is known locally as brittle, prone to losing a branch when a storm comes through the bay. None has come down yet. The promenade it shades looks straight across the bay toward the mainland, a public garden with no entry fee and no fence around the roots.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of Parque Genoves
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Cadiz train station, entrance on Avenida Doctor Gomez Ulla
trees.story: Cadiz used to have two famous dragon trees, then a storm took the roof off the wrong one. The Drago del Tinte, growing in a former arts and crafts school elsewhere in the city, collapsed in April 2013, leaving this specimen in Parque Genoves as the last dragon tree of any age left standing in Cadiz. Estimates for how old it actually is vary widely: the city's own parks department calls it simply centenario, over a hundred, while local guides put it as high as two hundred, and no planting record settles the question either way. What is certain is the shape, a squat grey trunk that branches only once it flowers, which for Dracaena draco can take decades, giving this specimen the umbrella silhouette that takes most dragon trees a lifetime to earn. It grows near the park's north entrance, in a garden laid out in the 19th century specifically to show off exotic imports from across the old Spanish trading network. The species itself is native to the Canary Islands and Macaronesia, not Cadiz, its sap once bottled and sold across Europe as sangre de drago, dragon's blood, a dye and a wound treatment.

trees.name: The Pohutukawa of Parque Genoves
trees.age: reported as over a century, exact planting date undocumented
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Cadiz train station, entrance on Avenida Doctor Gomez Ulla

best_time.label: May and June, when it blooms crimson

trees.story: A tree from the opposite side of the planet turns part of Cadiz crimson every early summer. This Metrosideros excelsa, a pohutukawa native to New Zealand's coastline, blooms in May and June with a mass of red flowers so consistent that New Zealanders call the species their Christmas tree, seven months out of sync with the Southern Hemisphere's own December summer. Spanish and international sources both describe it as the oldest documented pohutukawa anywhere in Europe, over a century old, a parent to cuttings that have gone on to seed the species in gardens across the continent. City arborists took no chances after it lost a branch in a winter storm: the parks department brought in a specialist firm to run a resistograph test and sound tomography on the trunk, then fitted a support structure, and Cadiz's own planning rules now protect it as a specimen of heritage value. It grows multi-trunked from the base, a shape more shrub than tree at first glance until the size of the individual limbs corrects that impression. Parque Genoves, the 19th century garden built to display exactly this kind of imported curiosity, gives it company: a dragon tree, an ombu, and a floss silk tree share the same grounds, each from a different continent, none native to Spain.

trees.name: The Ombu of Parque Genoves
trees.age: undated, cannot be aged by growth rings
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Cadiz train station, entrance on Avenida Doctor Gomez Ulla
trees.story: This tree cannot be aged the normal way, because it does not grow the annual rings that make dating a trunk possible. Phytolacca dioica, the ombu, is technically an herbaceous plant that behaves like a tree, its trunk swollen not with wood but with water storing tissue soft enough that, unlike almost everything else in this park, it cannot be milled for lumber or dated by a cross section. What Cadiz's parks department can say is that it has stood in Parque Genoves long enough to reach a circumference of about five and a half metres and a height of nearly fifteen, a spongy grey mass of trunk that looks poured rather than grown. Native to the pampas of Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil, the ombu became a fixture of Spanish gardens the way palms and eucalyptus did elsewhere, brought back by a trading city that spent centuries filling its public spaces with whatever grew well in a similar climate somewhere else in the Spanish world. Its own bulk does the work other trees do with age or history: nobody needs telling this one is old, only shown its trunk. Free to see, alongside a dragon tree, a pohutukawa and a floss silk tree in the same 19th century garden.

trees.name: The Floss Silk Tree of Parque Genoves
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Cadiz train station, entrance on Avenida Doctor Gomez Ulla
trees.story: Its name translates as the drunken stick, and one look at the trunk explains why. Ceiba speciosa, a floss silk tree from Argentina, Paraguay and southern Brazil, swells its bottle shaped trunk up to two metres across, studded with the conical thorns that in the wild deter animals from climbing it for water during the dry season. Cadiz's specimen grows in Parque Genoves, tucked behind the park's cafe near its fountain statue, a South American oddity planted alongside a dragon tree, a pohutukawa and an ombu in a 19th century garden built specifically to show off exactly this kind of imported curiosity. Like its neighbours, no planting record survives to date it precisely, only the trunk's own girth as evidence of age. When it flowers, usually toward autumn, the blooms come in shades of pink through white, briefly the showiest thing in a park that otherwise reads as a study in strange bark and stranger silhouettes. Free to visit, no ticket required, in a city whose 19th century merchants filled its public gardens with specimens from every port they traded through rather than sticking to anything native.

trees.name: The Twin Figs of Giardini Pubblici
trees.neighbourhood: Giardini Pubblici, between Castello and La Vega
trees.access: Free entry, public park, open daily dawn to dusk (Comune di Cagliari, Sardinia's oldest public park)
trees.transport: Bus lines 6 and 7 to the Via Regina Elena stop; roughly 10 minutes' walk from Piazza Yenne
trees.story:
The national register does not measure these two figs separately. It files them as an insieme omogeneo, a homogeneous group, which is how they read from the path: two Moreton Bay figs of much the same size and age, standing together on the avenue near the main entrance of the Giardini Pubblici.

They are the quieter half of Cagliari's fig story. The park opened between 1866 and 1873 on ground the city had used for its bastion and its lazzaretto, which makes it the oldest public park in Sardinia, and these two went in early enough that published estimates of their age start at 140 years and run as far as 195. Nobody has narrowed that. The city's own pages and the local press cite different figures and neither has been withdrawn.

In November 2021 the council put three of the park's trees onto the Sardinian regional list of monumental trees: this pair and the honey locust a short walk away. Regional money followed, earmarked for maintenance on the park's protected trees. What that buys is time. A Ficus macrophylla at this size carries limbs longer than most trees are tall, drops aerial roots from them and thickens the ones that reach soil into props, and keeping that structure standing over a public path is the whole job.

trees.name: The Spino di Giuda of Giardini Pubblici
trees.neighbourhood: Giardini Pubblici, between Castello and La Vega
trees.access: Free entry, public park, open daily dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Bus lines 6 and 7 to the Via Regina Elena stop; roughly 10 minutes' walk from Piazza Yenne
trees.story:
Italians call this species spino di Giuda, Judas's thorn, and the local name for this particular tree sometimes adds inerme: thornless. That is the joke of it. A wild Gleditsia triacanthos defends itself with branched spines that grow in bunches straight out of the trunk, long enough to go through a boot. The form planted in parks has had them bred out.

It is the third of the three Giardini Pubblici trees Cagliari's council put onto the Sardinian regional list of monumental trees in November 2021, alongside the pair of Moreton Bay figs a short walk away, and by some distance the least obvious of them. The national register measured its trunk at 2.94 metres round in 2020 and nobody has taped it since. No source gives it a documented age; the figures that circulate for the park's protected trees put it somewhere over a century, and that is as close as the record comes.

Honey locust is a tree of central North America and it does not look like the figs at all. The leaves are pinnate and small enough to read as ferns from underneath, they come late and go early, and the seed pods are long, dark and twisted, hanging in the crown well after the leaves have gone.

trees.name: The Jacaranda of Giardini Pubblici
trees.neighbourhood: Giardini Pubblici, between Castello and La Vega
trees.access: Free entry, public park, open daily dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Bus lines 6 and 7 to the Via Regina Elena stop; roughly 10 minutes' walk from Piazza Yenne

best_time.label: May, when the whole crown turns violet-blue

trees.story:
For a few weeks each May this tree stops being green. Jacaranda mimosifolia flowers in violet-blue trumpets across the entire crown, and what falls carpets the ground beneath it in the same colour, which is why the species has been planted in warm cities from Pretoria to Lisbon to Sydney.

It is the odd one out among the Giardini Pubblici's protected trees, and much the smallest: Italy's national register of monumental trees gives it 1.74 metres round and 16 metres tall, against figs that go to twelve. Its record is also the thinnest here. That register is the only source that has measured this tree on its own, and when regional funding for maintenance of the park's monumental trees came round in 2025 the coverage named the jacaranda without adding an age or a condition report specific to it. So the century or more given on this page is an estimate in line with the trees standing around it, not a dated figure, and it should be read that way.

The species comes from the dry forests of northwestern Argentina and Bolivia. It flowers on bare or barely-leafed branches, which is what produces the effect: no green to dilute it, just the whole shape of the tree in one colour for a fortnight.

trees.name: The Ficus of Piazza Matteotti
trees.neighbourhood: Marina, opposite the port and central station
trees.access: Free, public square; a temporary precautionary fence currently rings the ground beneath the canopy (branch-drop risk), so visitors can see and stand near the tree but not walk directly under the crown
trees.transport: Directly outside Cagliari's central railway station (Stazione di Cagliari); city buses converge on the piazza
trees.story:
Twelve metres around the trunk. That is the largest girth Italy's national register of monumental trees records for any tree in Cagliari, and it belongs to a fig from the far side of the world standing on the square outside the central railway station.

Ficus macrophylla comes from the coastal forests of eastern Australia, and at this size it stops behaving like a street tree. Aerial roots come down from the limbs, thicken where they meet the ground and fuse into a base with no clean edge to put a tape around. Local reporting puts the tree at 140 to 150 years old.

The fence is the first thing a visitor notices. The city ringed the ground under the canopy in November 2025 as a precaution against branch drop, so you can stand beside the tree but not walk under it. It is not a sign of decline. A University of Sassari team assessed the trunk in January 2025 with a dendrodensimeter, an instrument that reads the density of the wood as it drills, and reported no risk of structural collapse and no damage from the building works going on in the piazza. In April 2026 the councillor responsible for the city's green spaces said the same thing plainly: the tree is healthy, and has been under continuous technical management since 2019.

trees.name: The Ficus of Piazza Ingrao
trees.access: Free, public square on the Via Roma waterfront
trees.transport: 5-10 minutes' walk from Piazza Matteotti / the central railway station, along Via Roma
trees.story:
Local press calls this the fig that survived the bombs. Cagliari was hit hard from the air in 1943 and the Moreton Bay fig on the corner where Via Roma meets Via Regina Margherita came through it, which is a large part of why the city is fond of it.

CagliariNews dates the planting to about 1883, when the harbour front was being laid out as the Parterre della Darsena, so the tree is over 140 years old. Italy's national register of monumental trees measures the trunk at 9.8 metres round, second in the city only to the fig outside the railway station, five minutes west along the same waterfront.

Sardinia added it to the regional list of monumental trees on 21 January 2025, on the same day as the cypress in the Pirri cemetery. The case local reporting made for it was not only age. A canopy this size over one of Cagliari's busiest junctions cools the air under it, takes in what the traffic puts out, and holds resident and migrating birds through the year. It is a working tree in a place that badly needs one, and the fact that it is Australian, like every other big fig in this city, has stopped being remarkable to anybody who lives here.

trees.name: The Cypress of Pirri Cemetery
trees.access: Free, public municipal cemetery; open during standard cemetery visiting hours
trees.transport: Roughly 4 km from the historic centre; CTM city bus lines serve Pirri directly
trees.story:
The cemetery came second. Pirri's burial ground was consecrated on 8 November 1913 and this cypress was already standing on the site, more than two hundred years old by the reckoning of the Sardinian press that covered its protection in 2025.

That makes it, on the published figures, the oldest tree on this page. It is also improbably heavy for its species. Italy's national register of monumental trees puts the trunk at 6.3 metres round, where a Mediterranean cypress normally goes up as a narrow dark column and stays that way for centuries.

Cupressus sempervirens has been the tree of Mediterranean burial grounds since long before this one was planted: evergreen, so it never looks dead, and slow enough to outlast everyone buried beneath it. The unusual part here is the order of events. This tree did not arrive to mark the graves, the graves arrived around the tree, and generations of Pirri residents have used it as a landmark rather than a monument.

Sardinia added it to the regional list of monumental trees on 21 January 2025, the same day as the fig on Via Roma. Pirri is a district about four kilometres out from the old centre, on a city bus route, and this is a working cemetery rather than a garden: visiting hours, quiet, and people there with a reason.

trees.name: The Tintitaco
trees.access: Free, public park (Parco della Rimembranza / Parco delle Rimembranze), open daily
trees.transport: Roughly 15-20 minutes' walk from the city centre, or a short bus ride to Via Sonnino
trees.story:
This tree has no English name. Sardinians call it the tintitaco, the Italian tree registry that keeps the fullest record of it translates that as the Admiral's Tree, and Prosopis torquata, a thorny mesquite from the dry country of northwestern Argentina, is otherwise close to unknown in European parks.

The name points at the story local sources tell. An English naval commander, a ship that put into Cagliari to sit out a storm with a cargo of exotic plants, and this one left behind as a gift to the city. It is repeated in several places and documented in none, so read it as the city's own account rather than as a record.

The measurements come with the same caution. The national register lists the trunk at 3 metres round; the Italian tree registry gives 5.7 metres, taken at ground level because the trunk divides low, at about 1.3 metres. Both are right at the height they were measured. Age splits the same way: roughly 166 years on the registry's most recent update, around 200 in local reporting, and no figure at all on the national sheet.

The state of it is not in dispute. One heavy limb rests on scaffolding and a metal cage holds the trunk on one side. It is alive, protected under Sardinian law, and very obviously being kept that way.

trees.name: Newton's Apple Tree
trees.access: Free, visible from Trinity Street outside the college gate at any time
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Cambridge railway station

best_time.label: September, when the historic 'Flower of Kent' apples ripen

trees.story:
This is not Newton's apple tree, and it is genetically the same tree. The one he described stood at his family home, Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, and the falling-apple story comes from accounts he gave late in life rather than from anything in Cambridge. That original died around 1815 to 1820. Before it did, cuttings and grafts were taken and propagated onward as a genetically identical line, and in 1954 Trinity College planted one of them outside its main gate, directly below the room Newton lived in as a student.

So the tree in front of you is 72 years old and its tissue traces back, graft by graft, to the actual tree behind one of science's most famous stories. That is the whole reason to stop.

It is a 'Flower of Kent', an old English cooking variety, which means the fruit is edible and unremarkable: tart, disease-prone, nobody's choice for flavour. Newton would have known it as a kitchen apple rather than anything special.

It stands fenced for protection on Trinity Street, visible from the pavement outside the gate at any hour, and it is a five-minute walk from the older tree on this list, the Milton Mulberry at Christ's College, which was already grown when Newton arrived.

trees.name: The Milton Mulberry
trees.access: Christ's College Fellows' Garden, limited public visiting hours (check college website)
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Cambridge railway station

best_time.label: August into September, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: James I wanted England to have a silk industry to rival France and Italy, and in the early 1600s ordered mulberry trees planted nationwide to feed silkworms. Christ's College planted one in its Fellows' Garden in 1608 or 1609, the year after the poet John Milton was born; by the time Milton arrived as a student in 1625, the tree was already established, and college tradition holds he spent time beneath it, though no contemporary record proves it directly. The silk scheme collapsed everywhere in England, partly because James's advisors specified the wrong species for silkworms to thrive on, but the mulberry outlived the industry it was planted for by well over a century. In 1795 a storm uprooted it completely. Rather than replace it with a sapling, the college's gardeners let it regrow from its own root system, and what stands today, propped on wooden posts, low and sprawling with trunks and branches poking out at odd angles from a raised mound, has been growing continuously from that same root for well over two centuries since. It still produces a real crop of mulberries each summer, which the college's gardeners harvest and turn into jam for the kitchens.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Jesus College
trees.access: Jesus College Fellows' Garden, limited public visiting hours (check college website)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cambridge railway station
trees.story: Edward Daniel Clarke, a Jesus College fellow and later Cambridge's first professor of mineralogy, spent the years around 1800 travelling through Greece, Egypt and the Ottoman Empire, a journey that eventually filled six published volumes and made him one of the era's best-known explorer-scholars. In 1802, at Thermopylae, the narrow pass where three hundred Spartans and their allies held off the Persian army in 480 BC, Clarke collected seed from the plane trees growing there. He brought it home to Jesus College and had it raised into seedlings; one of them was planted in the Fellows' Garden the same year. Oriental Planes are long-lived, broad-crowned trees native across the eastern Mediterranean, and this one has had well over two centuries in an English college garden to put on size, now standing more than 25 metres tall. It is a genuinely unusual case among Cambridge's collected trees: not a symbolic gift or a scientific graft, but a seed one traveller happened to pick up at one of the most storied battle sites in Western history and carry home in his luggage.

trees.name: The Giant Redwood of the Botanic Garden
trees.access: Paid admission (modest fee, free for University of Cambridge students, staff and members), daily except Christmas Day and Boxing Day
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Cambridge railway station
trees.story: In 1852, the Cornish plant collector William Lobb reached Calaveras Grove in California and became one of the first Europeans to see Giant Redwoods growing wild, trees already thousands of years old and taller than anything in Britain. Recognising what he had found, he cut his expedition short and raced seed back to England for the Veitch nursery in Exeter, which was selling seedlings within a year, an unusually fast turnaround for a tree nobody in Europe had grown before. Cambridge University Botanic Garden was among the very first customers, planting out its own seedlings around 1855. Two of that original planting still stand on opposite sides of the garden's Main Walk near the fountain, and a third, at the junction with Henslow Walk, has grown into the tallest tree in the entire garden at just over 30 metres. Redwoods take centuries to reach the scale they are famous for in California, so at under two hundred years old this specimen is, by the standards of its own species, still young, a fast-growing adolescent rather than anything close to the giants Lobb originally found.

trees.name: The Cambridge Oak
trees.access: Paid admission (modest fee, free for University of Cambridge students, staff and members), daily except Christmas Day and Boxing Day
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Cambridge railway station
trees.story: Most oaks on this site are one of a small handful of well-known species. The Cambridge Oak is not: it is a hybrid, most likely a cross between the evergreen Quercus rugosa, native to Mexico and the southwestern United States, and Britain's own native Pedunculate Oak, a pairing that should not naturally occur an ocean apart and that appears to exist, in this precise combination, only here. It came from the Worcester nursery of Messrs Smith sometime between 1873 and 1875 and was planted in Cambridge University Botanic Garden soon after. By 1910, the tree had already earned a place in Elwes and Henry's authoritative survey The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland, which singled it out as the finest specimen of its kind in the entire country, a claim about a tree that may have been, functionally, one of a kind to begin with. It has grown considerably since, from under 12 metres tall in 1910 to nearly 17 metres with a 19.5 metre crown spread by a 2005 measurement, though a butt-decaying fungus now regularly fruits on its trunk each autumn, a visible sign of age and decline rather than imminent death. The garden has already grafted a younger replacement, planted near the Terrace Garden in 1991, as insurance for whenever the original eventually goes.

trees.name: The Cedar of the Palco
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.

best_time.label: August to October: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Seven and three quarter metres around the trunk, and sixteen metres tall. That ratio is the whole story of this cedar: it has spent its life spreading rather than climbing, and no thicker trunk appears anywhere in the national register's entries for Caserta. It stands in the flat southern end of the English Garden, the stretch the royal gardeners called the Palco, which holds more oversized trees per hectare than the rest of the park put together. Cedar of Lebanon reached western Europe in the seventeenth century as a curiosity out of the mountains of Lebanon and Syria, where the species is now down to scattered protected groves after three thousand years of cutting for temples, palaces and ships. In a Campanian garden fed by the Carolino aqueduct it grows faster and wider than it ever would at home, which is what you are looking at. The garden around it was laid out from 1786 by John Andrew Graefer, an English gardener sent over on the recommendation of the Royal Society, for a queen who wanted something less geometric than the rest of the park. Both registers put the tree at over 150 years without being more precise, so it belongs somewhere between the first planting and the Victorian expansion.

trees.name: The Plane That Grew Sideways
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the interlaced branches show

trees.story: This tree is too small to qualify and the register listed it anyway. Campania asks a plane for four metres of trunk before it counts as monumental; this one has two metres sixty and stands nine metres tall, and it got in on the strength of a crown twenty-five metres across. The regional record calls it among the most beautiful and most photographed plants in the English Garden, which is an unusual thing for a government form to say about anything. The branching is what makes it. Instead of one trunk driving upward, the limbs leave low and travel outward in long sinuous curves that cross and interlace, so the tree reads as a wide low room rather than a column, and visitors come to it on purpose. The old royal gardeners knew it as the Indian plane, which it is not: Platanus x acerifolia is a seventeenth-century hybrid of the Oriental and American planes, and its bark flakes off in fine plates to leave the grey, cream and brown patchwork the species is known for. Come in January or February. With the leaves off, the whole tangle of branches is visible, and that is the only time of year you can see what the shape is actually doing.

trees.name: The Yew of the Bath of Venus
trees.age: the register says 150 years, its own note implies 250 or more
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis, then to the far end of the English Garden. An electric shuttle runs the axis.

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: This yew was already a grown tree when it was carried into the garden, which makes it older than the garden. The Campania register is explicit: the specimen was mature when it was set in place at the creation of the English Garden in the 1790s, and it calls the tree one of the patriarchs of the whole design. That is also why the age field on the same record, which says 150 years, cannot be right, and it is stated here as the disagreement it is. Nearly four metres round the trunk and twenty metres tall, it stands at the Bath of Venus, the grotto at the top of the garden where a Carrara marble Venus by Tommaso Solari, carved in 1762 and installed here around 1840, crouches on a rock above a pool. The Reggia's own description of the place records that the water surrounding the statue rises from the base of a monumental yew. That is this tree. Yew is the slowest-growing timber tree in Europe and among the longest-lived, which is exactly why an eighteenth-century designer would move a mature one rather than plant a sapling and wait. The boulders, the ferns and the ruined cryptoporticus behind it were all built to look accidental. The yew is the only part that is not.

trees.name: The Douglas Fir of the English Garden
trees.age: the register says about 200 years, which is the outer edge of possible
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story: At forty metres, only one other tree in Caserta's register stands as tall, and this one's stated age does not quite work. The Campania register gives it about two hundred years, which would mean a planting around 1826. David Douglas did not send the first seed of the species back from the Pacific Northwest until 1827, and it spread through European gardens over the decades that followed, so two hundred is the outer edge of what is possible and is more likely a round number than a measurement. The tree itself is not in doubt. Five metres eighty around the trunk, forty metres of it, with the thick corky grey bark split into broad plates, which is armour: in its native range the species survives ground fire that kills its neighbours because that bark insulates the trunk. Douglas fir is the timber tree of the American west, the one that built ships, bridges and most of Oregon, and nineteenth-century Europe planted it hard for exactly that reason. Here it does no work at all. It stands in the middle of a landscape garden designed to look wild and engineered to the last stone, alongside a cedar, a cork oak and a plane from three other continents, all of them collected for a queen who wanted a botanical garden and got one.

trees.name: The Sweet Osmanthus of the Winding Path
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.

best_time.label: late September and October, when flowers you have to look for fill the path with apricot

trees.story: The national register credits this tree with six and a half metres of trunk. The regional one adds the detail that makes sense of it: that figure is every stem added together, not one trunk, because Osmanthus fragrans grows as a bundle rather than a column. It is ten metres tall, which is large for the species, and the register calls it a rarity in this climate. The reason to walk to it is the smell. For a few weeks in autumn a sweet osmanthus in flower puts out one of the strongest scents any hardy tree makes, apricot and ripe peach, carried well past the tree itself, and it comes from flowers so small you have to hunt for them: clusters of cream stars a few millimetres across, tucked into the leaf axils. In China, where the species comes from, those flowers are picked for tea, for wine and for sweets, and the city of Guilin takes its name from them. Graefer and the botanists who followed him were buying novelty from the far side of the world for a queen who wanted her garden to beat the other royal gardens of Europe. This is one of the few things they planted that a visitor notices without being told what it is.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of the Palco
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story: Thirty-eight metres is a strange height for a camphor tree. In Japan and southern China, where the species is native and where it is planted at shrines, it usually spreads wide and low. A camphor drawn up to thirty-eight metres has been competing for light its whole life, and this one stands in the most crowded corner of the English Garden, the low meadow the gardeners called the Palco, on the south-eastern side towards Puccianiello. The register puts it at about two hundred years, which places it with the first generation of the garden. Camphor is a laurel, and the whole tree smells. Crush a leaf and you get the entire medicine cabinet, because the wood and foliage are the historic source of camphor itself, distilled for centuries for embalming, moth-proofing, liniment and, for a few decades, smokeless gunpowder. The chemistry is a defence, which is why camphor timber resists insects and why it was cut in enormous quantity in Taiwan and Japan until synthetic camphor arrived and the trade collapsed. This one was never cut. Its bark is fissured in long vertical lines, its new leaves flush bronze before turning glossy, and it is not alone: the Reggia has more camphors elsewhere in the park, including a row of eight nearer the palace.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of the Palco
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story: This is the one tree on the walk you can put a hand on and be surprised. Cork oak grows an outer bark up to thirty centimetres thick, spongy and slightly warm to the touch, and it is the only European tree whose bark regenerates completely after being stripped, which is why Portugal and Spain harvest it on a nine-year cycle for wine corks and floor tiles. Four metres twenty around the trunk and twenty-eight metres tall, this one has never been harvested. A stripped cork oak carries a smooth ochre trunk for years afterwards, so the deep fissured layer here is the mark of a tree left alone since it was planted. The register adds something worth knowing: several smaller cork oaks stand scattered around it in no pattern at all, which is what happens when an old tree in an irrigated garden is left long enough to seed itself. The bark is also why the species survives fire across the Iberian dehesa. It insulates the trunk well enough that the tree comes back from a burn that kills everything around it, a useful thing to have evolved in a landscape people have been burning for grazing for four thousand years. In a garden of imported curiosities, this one is a Mediterranean native doing what it does at home.

trees.name: The Coast Redwood of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story: Redwoods do not usually reach four and a half metres of trunk this fast. On the fog-fed Pacific coast where Sequoia sempervirens is native, that girth marks a tree several centuries old; this one did it in about a hundred and fifty years, on the far side of the planet from northern California. The Campania forestry register does not date it by ring count. It reasons the age instead: past 4.69 metres around the trunk the species already clears the regional threshold for monumental status, and the tree went into the ground with the rest of the English Garden's plantings, so a century and a half follows from the garden's own history rather than a direct measurement. Twenty-six metres up, little about the tree reads as Mediterranean. The bark is the giveaway: deep, spongy, fissured red-brown, built to shrug off fire in a climate this garden has never had to test it against. Coast redwood is one of the tallest living things on the planet and one of the newer arrivals in this eighteenth-century garden, added long after the original 1786 layout that John Graefer designed for Queen Maria Carolina. It shares no relation with anything else on this list, which is exactly the point of a garden built to hold one of everything.

trees.name: The Chilgoza Pine of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story: Two trees in Caserta's monumental register share the title of tallest, and this pine is one of them: forty metres, tied with the Douglas fir a short walk away. Pinus gerardiana is a strange choice for a European garden. It grows wild only in the dry inner valleys of the north-west Himalaya, across Pakistan, Afghanistan and northern India, where its seeds, chilgoza pine nuts, are a real harvested crop rather than a curiosity, sold by weight in markets from Kabul to Delhi. Almost nothing else in cultivated Europe reaches this size; most specimens outside the species' native range stay ornamental and modest. This one has a girth of three metres ten, respectable rather than remarkable next to the garden's giant cedars and redwoods, and the height is the whole story: whoever planted it, sometime in the century and a half the register credits it with, gave it the room and the time to do something the species rarely gets to do this far from the mountains it comes from. The needles grow in bundles of three, unusually long, and the cones take two full years to ripen the seeds inside them. Nobody has recorded checking whether it still fruits this far from home, but if it does, autumn is when to look.

trees.name: The Second Plane of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story: Caserta's monumental register credits only one tree in the entire city with a wider trunk than this one, the cedar of Lebanon at the far end of the same garden. This plane measures seven metres twenty around, which makes it the widest broadleaf tree the register has found anywhere in Caserta, plane, oak or otherwise. Platanus x acerifolia lines half of Europe's boulevards as a pollarded street tree kept small on purpose; nothing gets this wide doing that job. This one has had the opposite treatment since the English Garden's layout went in for Queen Maria Carolina in 1786: room, undisturbed roots, and nobody ever cutting it back. Twenty-five metres tall, in the lower stretch of the garden closest to the palace, the section finished first and given the longest run of any part of the grounds to grow into itself. It carries none of the low, sinuous branching that makes its garden-mate near the entrance famous for its shape. This one went straight up and simply kept getting wider, plain in form and enormous in scale, a different argument for the same species.

trees.name: The Third Plane of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story:
Caserta's monumental register now credits this garden with three London planes, and this one is the third thickest tree in the whole city register regardless of species, five metres sixty around and thirty metres tall. Only the cedar of Lebanon by the Palco and the garden's other giant plane, near the entrance, beat it.

The English Garden was laid out for Queen Maria Carolina starting in 1786, one of the first landscape gardens of its kind on the European continent, informal and winding where the rest of the Reggia's grounds run in strict Baroque lines. Three planes surviving from roughly the same planting era says something about the site more than about any one tree: deep soil, an unbroken water supply from the garden's own network of streams and pools, and two and a half centuries without the hard pruning street planes usually get. Left alone, Platanus x acerifolia does not stay a tidy shape, it becomes what stands here, a straight trunk carrying a huge, high canopy.

The register puts its age at roughly 150 years, later than the garden's founding but still older than the unification of Italy. Free to see once inside; the garden itself is a paid section of the wider Reggia grounds.

trees.name: The Araucaria of Piazza Vanvitelli
trees.access: Free, public square (Piazza Vanvitelli), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk east of the Reggia di Caserta, close to Caserta railway station
trees.story:
Every other tree on this page stands behind a ticket gate. This one grows in the middle of Caserta's own civic square, free for anyone to walk up to, a Chilean monkey puzzle 330 centimetres around and 25 metres tall with the palace itself visible over its crown.

Piazza Vanvitelli used to be the town's market square before it became a public garden in the late 1800s, planted in two phases and then reworked again in 1995 to recover the original specimens. Campania's own monumental register ties this tree's age directly to that first planting, putting it at over 200 years, among the oldest trees this city protects and one of the very few outside the Reggia's grounds.

Araucaria araucana is native to the volcanic slopes of Chile and Argentina, its stiff, spiralled, spine-tipped leaves an adaptation against browsing dinosaurs that vanished tens of millions of years before anyone planted one in a European market square. It shares this square with a casuarina and a yew, both also on the region's monumental list, all three within fifty metres of each other on ground that costs nothing to visit.

trees.name: The Casuarina of Piazza Vanvitelli
trees.access: Free, public square (Piazza Vanvitelli), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk east of the Reggia di Caserta, close to Caserta railway station
trees.story:
Casuarina equisetifolia looks like a conifer and is not one. The drooping, needle-like growths that give it a pine's silhouette are jointed green stems; the actual leaves are reduced to tiny scales at each joint, an adaptation from its native coastlines of Australia and the Pacific islands, where the species holds sand dunes together in wind that would strip a broadleaf tree bare. In the centre of Piazza Vanvitelli, Caserta's town square, it just looks like an unusually feathery pine.

Campania's monumental register measures its trunk at 270 centimetres, close to the minimum three metre threshold the region sets for the species and, together with its 15 metre height and its age, enough to earn it protected status. Like its two square-mates, the araucaria and the yew nearby, its planting is tied to the square's own history: laid out in phases from the late nineteenth century, on ground that had been Caserta's market square before that.

A casuarina this size, this far from a coastline, is a small oddity in its own right. It costs nothing to see, stands in the open square rather than behind any gate, and shares its fifty metres of ground with two other protected trees.

trees.name: The Yew of Piazza Vanvitelli
trees.access: Free, public square (Piazza Vanvitelli), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk east of the Reggia di Caserta, close to Caserta railway station

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story:
A European yew in a flower bed on Piazza Vanvitelli is easy to miss next to its two showier square-mates, the monkey puzzle and the feathery casuarina a few steps away. It is no less protected: Campania's monumental register measures its trunk at 270 centimetres, well past the 250 centimetre minimum the region sets for the species, on a tree only 12 metres tall.

That gap between girth and height is normal for a yew. The species grows slowly and thickens for centuries after most trees would have stopped, which is exactly why an unremarkable-looking specimen can carry an old trunk. The register ties this one's age to the square's own history rather than giving a number, the same reasoning it gives the araucaria and casuarina nearby: planted when Piazza Vanvitelli was first laid out as a garden, on what had been the town's market square before.

Free, outdoors, and in a civic square rather than behind the Reggia's paid gate, this yew and its two neighbours are the only entries on this page that cost nothing to see.

trees.name: The Bottle Tree of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story:
An Australian bottle tree, also called a kurrajong at home, stands thirty-five metres tall in a Bourbon queen's garden, roughly twice the height the species usually reaches. Brachychiton populneus grows across the dry eastern half of Australia, where most specimens top out somewhere between fifteen and twenty metres. The register puts this one at thirty-five, with three metres sixty around the trunk, which makes it an exceptional tree for the species by a wide margin.

Kurrajong belongs to the mallow family, alongside cotton, cacao and the baobab, and it shares the baobab's habit of storing water in a swollen trunk. Australian graziers cut the branches to feed stock through drought, the fibrous bark was worked into cord, and the seeds are edible once roasted. None of that has ever been asked of this one. It stands in the English Garden at the top of the Reggia's grounds, the informal twenty-three hectares laid out from 1786 for a queen who wanted a botanical collection rather than another parterre, and it has spent its whole life being watered by an aqueduct and looked at.

The Campania register credits it with about a hundred and fifty years. That figure is the register's own estimate rather than a ring count, and the national list carries the same trunk, the same height and no age at all.

trees.name: The Himalayan Chir Pine of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story:
The chir pine is tapped for resin on Himalayan foothills from Pakistan to Nepal, and one of them grows in the garden of a Bourbon palace outside Naples. Pinus roxburghii is a tree of dry slopes between roughly 500 and 2,000 metres, where whole local economies run on it: resin for turpentine and rosin, timber for building, and needles swept up in quantity for fodder, fuel and bedding. Those needles are among the longest of any pine, up to thirty centimetres, carried in drooping bundles of three, so the crown reads looser and shaggier than any European pine standing near it.

This one is twenty-five metres tall with three metres fifty around the trunk. A Himalayan pine is not garden decoration, it is a collector's tree, and the English Garden spent much of the nineteenth century working as a botanical collection under Giovanni Gussone and later Nicola Terracciano, who filled it with species nobody in Campania had grown before. The queen it was built for in 1786 wanted a garden that would beat the other royal gardens of Europe, and the botanists who came after her kept buying.

The register puts the pine at about a hundred and fifty years and marks the number as an estimate. Nothing in this garden has been dated by counting rings, so read it as a period rather than a date.

trees.name: The Turkey Oak of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
