trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story:
In a garden collected out of Australia, the Himalaya and California, this oak grows wild in the hills a few kilometres away. Quercus cerris is native across southern Europe and Asia Minor, and grand gardens of the nineteenth century planted it anyway, because it grows faster than almost any other oak and reaches size while the owner is still alive to see it. This one is thirty-five metres tall with three metres forty-five around the trunk.

It is easy to identify once you look down. The acorn cups are covered in long whiskery scales, shaggy as a thistle head, and the acorns take two seasons to ripen instead of one. The leaves are rough to the touch, deeply and irregularly cut, and many of them hang on brown into the winter.

What the tree has watched from this spot is the end of a dynasty. The English Garden was Bourbon royal property for its first seventy years, laid out from 1786 and stocked with imports for a queen. In 1860 the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies fell, and the palace and its grounds passed to the House of Savoy and then to the Italian state, which is who charges for the ticket today. The register's hundred and fifty years is an estimate rather than a measurement, so this oak may have arrived just before that change of ownership or just after it.

trees.name: The Southern Magnolia of Piazza Carlo di Borbone
trees.access: Free. On the palace grounds at Piazza Carlo di Borbone, in front of the Reggia; open as part of the public square, no ticket needed to see it from the piazza.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace directly across the piazza.

best_time.label: May to July, when the white flowers open, up to thirty centimetres across and smelling of lemon

trees.story:
Four metres forty around the trunk is a great deal of magnolia, and this one asks nobody for a ticket. It grows on Piazza Carlo di Borbone, the elliptical square in front of the Reggia, rather than behind the wall of the English Garden up the hill, twenty-five metres tall and open to anyone at any hour.

Magnolia grandiflora comes from the warm southeastern United States and has been planted as a specimen tree across Europe since the middle of the eighteenth century, for two reasons. The leaves stay on all year, dark and leathery on top with a rust-coloured felt underneath that is worth turning one over to see. And the flowers are enormous, cream white, up to thirty centimetres across and scented of lemon, opening a few at a time through the summer rather than all at once, so the tree is never covered in them and never quite out of them either.

The building behind it has had a stranger life than the tree. By 1944 the palace was Allied headquarters in the Mediterranean, and on 29 April 1945 the surrender of German forces in Italy was signed inside it. The magnolia was well grown by then: the Campania register credits it with about a hundred and fifty years, an estimate rather than a recorded planting date, which would have made it roughly eighty years old on the morning of the signing.

trees.name: The Upright Osage Orange of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.

best_time.label: September and October, when grapefruit-sized green fruit thump down and lie where they land

trees.story:
The best bow wood in North America grows in a royal garden outside Naples. Maclura pomifera takes its English name from the Osage nation, whose bows were traded far beyond their own country, and the wood behind that reputation is heavy, springy and so rot-resistant that a fence post cut from it outlasts the fence. Before barbed wire, American farmers planted the tree in thorny hedgerows across thousands of miles of the Midwest.

The fruit is the reason to come in autumn. Each one is the size of a grapefruit, green, wrinkled like a brain, heavy enough to be worth not parking under, full of sticky white latex and eaten by almost nothing alive. One well-argued theory holds that its dispersers were the mastodons and giant ground sloths that disappeared from North America some thirteen thousand years ago, which would make every fruit dropped here an offer to a customer who no longer exists. They come down through September and October and lie where they land.

Two Osage oranges in this garden hold monumental status, and the register describes this one as the upright specimen: two metres sixty around the trunk, twenty-five metres tall, and about two hundred years old by the register's estimate. Taken at face value that puts it within thirty years of the garden's creation in 1786, which would make it one of the older residents of a collection built almost entirely out of foreigners.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the English Garden
trees.access: Paid. Inside the English Garden of the Reggia di Caserta, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket (9 euro, plus 1 euro if booked online). Closed Tuesdays.
trees.transport: Caserta station faces the palace. From the park gate it is about 2.5 km up the main axis to the English Garden, or take the electric shuttle.
trees.story:
Ancient writers put this tree forward as the lotus that made Odysseus's crew forget the way home. Celtis australis carries small dark fruit on long stalks, sweet and vaguely date-like when ripe, which is enough to keep the identification alive; a thorny North African shrub, Ziziphus lotus, has an equally old claim on the same story, and nobody has settled it.

The wood is not in dispute. Hackberry is hard and flexible in a way few Mediterranean broadleaves are, and Italian workshops turned it for centuries into tool handles, walking sticks, whip stocks and the long forks used for turning hay. It is also one of the standard shade trees of the Italian piazza, planted for a wide canopy and for roots that put up with being paved over.

This one has been asked to do neither job. Three metres fifty around the trunk and twenty-five metres tall, it stands in the English Garden among kurrajongs, redwoods and Himalayan pines, which is an odd room for a species most Italians walk past without looking up. The trees around it were shipped in from four continents for a queen who wanted a collection. The hackberry needed no shipping at all: the species grows wild across Italy and through the Mediterranean basin. The register gives it about two hundred years, an estimate rather than a count, which makes it one of the longer-standing things in a garden laid out from 1786.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Villa Bellini
trees.access: Free, Villa Bellini is Catania's main public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Central Catania on Via Etnea; about a 10-15 minute walk from Catania Centrale station or Piazza Stesicoro.
trees.story:
Fourteen metres around the trunk, and a crown that reaches forty-three metres across. On the figures published by Italy's tree registers, only one Moreton Bay fig in Sicily is bigger, the giant in Palermo's botanical garden. What stops people in Villa Bellini, though, is at ground level. A Ficus macrophylla drops aerial roots from its branches and thickens them into buttresses once they reach soil, and this one has thrown a long, coiling sprawl of them out across the ground, the kind of shape that has people reaching for octopus tentacles to describe it.

Its age is genuinely unsettled. One contributor account gives a planting date of 1860, which would make it about 165 years old and would have put it in the ground the year before Italy became a single country. The Italian registry that measured it most recently states an age of around 146. The two do not reconcile, neither has been withdrawn, so both are here.

The recent record is firmer. A 2026 assessment rates its health as adequate rather than good, and the bark carries graffiti and paint from visitors who could not keep their hands off it. Walk under it, walk around it, leave it alone. It stands in Catania's main public park on Via Etnea, free and open daily.

trees.name: The Larger Bunya Pine of Villa Bellini
trees.access: Free, Villa Bellini is Catania's main public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Central Catania on Via Etnea; about a 10-15 minute walk from Catania Centrale station or Piazza Stesicoro.
trees.story:
Italy's national register of monumental trees records this bunya pine at 45 metres tall. That figure does not hold up. A second registry measured the same specimen at about 22 metres, and 45 would be remarkable for an Araucaria bidwillii growing anywhere outside its native forest. The trunk measurements agree far better, 3.40 metres around on the national sheet against 3.33 on the other, and that is the more useful number anyway.

The species grows wild in a few pockets of southeast Queensland and nowhere else on earth. It builds a dark, symmetrical dome on a straight column of a trunk, carries stiff glossy leaves in spirals along the branches, and drops cones weighing several kilograms from the top of the crown, which is why Australian parks sign the ground underneath them.

Villa Bellini holds a whole collection of araucarias, the Norfolk Island pine, the Cook pine and the hoop pine among them, but only two are individually listed as monumental: this one and its neighbour, twenty to thirty metres away across the garden. From the path they read as a pair, and there is no reason to see them as anything else. No source records an age for either. Nobody wrote the planting down, and the two registries that took the trunks in hand did not attempt a figure.

trees.name: The Smaller Bunya Pine of Villa Bellini
trees.access: Free, Villa Bellini is Catania's main public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Central Catania on Via Etnea; about a 10-15 minute walk from Catania Centrale station or Piazza Stesicoro.
trees.story:
Forty centimetres of trunk is the whole difference between this bunya pine and the one standing twenty to thirty metres away. Italy's national register lists them as two separate monuments, at 3.00 and 3.40 metres around, and a second registry re-measured them at 3.05 and 3.33. On height the difference more or less vanishes and may even run the other way: this one comes out at roughly 22.5 metres against its neighbour's 22, a gap nobody would pick out from the path. The national register puts this tree at 40 metres, which the independent measurement does not support and which reads as an error on the sheet, the same kind that inflates its neighbour to 45.

Araucaria bidwillii is native to a small stretch of southeast Queensland, and in a Sicilian garden it does what it does at home: a straight bare column carrying a dark tiered crown, with leaves stiff and sharp enough to be worth not grabbing.

Neither tree has a documented age. No planting record survives and neither register carries a figure, so what a visitor gets is size rather than years. The two stand close enough that they are one stop on a walk through Villa Bellini, which is the honest way to see them: side by side, forty centimetres apart in the paperwork and near enough identical in person.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico (University of Catania botanical garden): EUR3 full price, EUR2 reduced. Open Mon-Fri 9:00-19:00 (last entry 18:00), Sat 9:00-14:00 (last entry 13:00), closed Sundays and public holidays.
trees.transport: On Via Etnea in central Catania, about a 15-20 minute walk from Catania Centrale station, close to Villa Bellini.
trees.story:
Two dragon trees flank the marble staircase of the botanical garden's neoclassical building. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists one of them, two metres round, and does not say which. Both are visible from the foot of the steps, so the question settles itself in person.

Dracaena draco is endemic to the Canary Islands and native nowhere near Sicily, and it looks the part: a pale grey trunk that forks, then forks again, into a flat crown of rosettes, each one a burst of stiff blue-green blades. The forking is how it grows. The stem divides only after it flowers, and it flowers at intervals of many years, which is also the reason nobody can tell you how old this tree is. A dragon tree lays down no annual rings, so the usual method simply does not apply, and no source has published an age for the Catania specimen.

The name is not decoration. Cut the bark and the sap oxidises dark red, sold across Europe for centuries as dragon's blood and used in varnish, dye and medicine.

Unlike the two Villa Bellini trees a few minutes down Via Etnea, this one sits behind a ticket desk in the University of Catania's botanical garden: three euros, two reduced, weekdays until seven and Saturday mornings, closed Sundays.

trees.name: The Olive of the Orange Courtyard
trees.access: Free, the Patio de los Naranjos is open daily 08:30 to 19:00 (the prayer hall is ticketed separately)
trees.transport: In the historic centre, a few minutes on foot from anywhere in the old town

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: This tree is on a map drawn in 1741, which is a rarer thing than being old. Most claims about an ancient tree's age come from tradition; this one comes from an inventory of the courtyard that counted, alongside the olive, ninety-five orange trees, six cypresses, ten palms and a chinaberry. Two and a half centuries later roughly half its trunk is gone. It hollowed through the twentieth century, decayed badly from the 1980s, and what leans toward the fountain now is a shell that still manages about sixty kilos of olives a year. The cathedral chapter has conserved what remains and planted a young olive nearby to take over eventually. In 2018 researchers took leaf and fruit samples without harming it and found a cultivar barely recorded anywhere else, which they have proposed naming after the city. The fountain beside it is officially the Fuente de Santa Maria, finished in December 1741, but everyone calls its spout the Cano del Olivo, after the tree. Suitors were once told to drink from it for luck in love.

trees.name: The Orange Courtyard of the Mezquita
trees.age: a grove documented since 1512, replanted tree by tree
trees.access: Free, open daily 08:30 to 19:00
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot

best_time.label: late March into April, when the whole courtyard flowers and the scent carries into the streets

trees.story: Ninety-eight bitter orange trees stand here in rows that line up with the columns of the prayer hall next door, so the courtyard reads as the building continuing outdoors into the light. It may be the oldest surviving garden in Europe: the enclosure goes back to the mosque founded in 784, orange trees are recorded in it from at least 1512, and the shallow channels that link the tree pits still carry the water that feeds them. In 2001 workers found a tenth-century cistern twelve metres beneath the paving, built to hold twelve hundred cubic metres so that washing and irrigation would never stop. Be honest about the trees themselves: they are ordinary Seville oranges, replaced one by one as they fail, so the grid is old and the individuals are not. What is worth timing a trip for is the last days of March, when the whole courtyard flowers at once and the scent of azahar carries out into the surrounding streets. Since 2026 the chapter has turned the bitter harvest, previously thrown away, into vinegar.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the Viana Palace
trees.age: said by the palace to be over 400 years
trees.access: Paid entry to the Palacio de Viana museum; closed Mondays, shorter hours in July and August
trees.transport: About 15 min walk northeast of the Mezquita
trees.story: Twelve courtyards, eighteen noble families, five centuries of owners, and the oldest inhabitant of the house is a tree. The palace calls this holm oak four hundred years old, which would make it older than most of the building around it, and at over twenty-five metres it rises clear above the roofline, so you see it from the street before you have paid to go in. It stands in the middle of a garden that only became a garden in 1814, when the seventh Marquis of Villaseca bought the land and laid it out in the French manner with sixteen box parterres that are themselves two centuries old now. Against the walls grow espaliered lemon, lime, mandarin, orange and grapefruit, the oldest plants in the palace after the oak itself. A holm oak is an evergreen, so there is no season to catch it in: the leaves are small, dark and leathery, closer to an olive's than to the lobed oak leaf on an English pub sign, and they stay all year. Worth knowing before you go: the four-century figure rests on the palace's own account, with no forestry survey behind it.

trees.name: The Jacaranda of the Orive Garden
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden
trees.transport: About 12 min walk northeast of the Mezquita

best_time.label: May, when it turns violet before the new leaves arrive

trees.story: For four hundred years nobody outside could see this tree. It grew in a walled orchard belonging first to a Dominican convent, on ground granted in 1241, and then to a Renaissance palace built in 1560 by the architect Hernan Ruiz II, and the gate was only opened to the public in 2004. It has come close to dying twice since. Naturalists recording it note that it barely survived the freeze of 2003, when Cordoba hit nine degrees below zero, and the municipal catalogue records the winters of 2010 and 2011 killing jacarandas across the city while this one held on. What stands there now is three trunks grown together into what looks like one tree, spreading a crown twenty metres across at nearly nineteen metres tall, probably the largest of its kind in the city. For most of the year it is a fine green canopy over a quiet square. For a couple of weeks in May it turns violet, flowering largely before the new leaves arrive, which is the whole reason jacarandas were planted across southern Spain in the first place.

trees.name: The Giant Plane of the Agriculture Gardens
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: About 16 min walk northwest of the Mezquita
trees.story: At thirty-seven metres this is the tallest tree in Cordoba's own catalogue of singular trees, and it stands in the city's oldest public garden, opened on the first of March 1811 by a mayor who had spent years travelling the Islamic world disguised as a Syrian prince. The trunk measures nearly four metres around and widens to over five at the base, which is what a plane does when nothing has hurried it. Cordobans do not call this place the Agriculture Gardens. They call it Los Patos, after the duck pond, and they have done so for generations. The tree rings a small central plaza together with several other big planes, so the one to look for is the tallest, the one whose crown disappears above the others when you stand underneath. The gardens were reorganised in 1864 and bought outright by the council in 1866, so the ground has been public for a hundred and sixty years, which in a city that keeps its best trees behind walls is worth something. A plane's autumn in Andalusia is a dull brown, so come for the size, not the season.

trees.name: The Split Plane of the Alpargate
trees.age: one of the oldest planes in the city
trees.access: Free, open square
trees.transport: About 22 min walk northeast of the Mezquita
trees.story: A cyclone tore this tree in half and it is still twenty-four metres tall. What stands over the Plaza del Cristo de Gracia today is the surviving portion of something that was once roughly twice the size, and the municipal catalogue rates it as very probably one of the oldest planes in Cordoba. Its crown occupies twenty of those twenty-four metres, so from beneath it there is essentially nothing else to see. It shades a Baroque fountain that the city paid for with the proceeds of three bullfights held in 1747, and which was moved to this square from the Puerta Nueva in 1950. During Holy Week the brotherhood of the Padres de Gracia carries its floats in and out beneath the branches, which is the one week of the year the tree has to make room for something. The catalogue's own photograph records a small indignity worth mentioning, because it says a lot about how cities treat their big trees: someone has bolted an electrical box to the trunk.

trees.name: The Judas Tree of the San Rafael Cemetery
trees.age: undated, the largest of its species in the province
trees.access: Free, cemetery open from 08:30, closing 18:00 to 20:00 depending on season
trees.transport: About 20 min walk east of the Mezquita

best_time.label: March and April, when magenta flowers push straight out of the bare bark

trees.story: A tree that flowers straight out of its own bark, standing at the gate of a cemetery. Judas trees do not put their blossom on new shoots the way most trees do; the magenta flowers push directly through the old wood of the trunk and the heavy limbs, before any leaves appear, so for two or three weeks in early spring the whole frame of the tree is coloured rather than covered. Botanists recording Cordoba's remarkable trees name this one the largest specimen of its species in the province: two and three quarter metres around, though only ten metres tall, splitting into three arms below head height. It shares the entrance with a Mexican fan palm, two big red river gums and an uncommon jujube, in a cemetery that thousands of people walk through in the last days of October. Which is the wrong time to see it. Come in March instead, when the gate is quiet and the tree is doing the one thing it is famous for.

trees.name: The Cypress of the Alcazar Entrance
trees.access: Free, outside the Alcazar's ticket gate
trees.transport: Centro Historico, next to the Alcazar; short walk from the Mezquita-Catedral
trees.story:
Twenty-six and a half metres tall on a crown three and a half metres wide. That is a proportion closer to a lamp post than a tree, and it is what a Mediterranean cypress does when it is left to grow the way it wants: straight up, in one dark column, branches held so tight to the trunk that the whole thing reads as a single line.

It stands outside the ticket gate of the Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, which means it costs nothing to see. Everything else here is behind the wall and behind a turnstile: the long pools, the clipped hedges, the fortress Alfonso XI built in 1328, where Ferdinand and Isabella later held court and where the Inquisition ran its tribunal for three centuries. The cypress is the one thing the city left on the outside.

It is also young. Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees put it at about seventy-seven years when it was surveyed, and a register age is always the age on the day somebody wrote it down, so add whatever has passed since. That catalogue is the only source describing this tree at all. Cypresses run to several centuries, which makes this one barely started, and it is on the list anyway because of the shape rather than the years. Stand at the base and look up the column: there is almost nothing between you and the top of it.

trees.name: The Siberian Elm of the Alcazar
trees.access: Paid entry (Alcazar gardens); free on summer mornings
trees.transport: Centro Historico, inside the Alcazar gardens; short walk from the Mezquita-Catedral
trees.story:
A Siberian elm is not supposed to reach twenty-seven metres. The species rarely passes fifteen, which is part of why it was planted across Spain in such numbers during the twentieth century: fast, cheap, indifferent to drought and poor soil, resistant to the Dutch elm disease that was destroying the country's field elms, and modest enough not to become a problem later. This one ignored the brief.

It grows inside the gardens of the Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, among the long water channels and clipped hedges laid out below the fortress, where nearly everything else is kept to a shape. The elm was allowed to run. Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees records its height and its species and nothing about its age, and no other source names it, so how it got here and when is simply not documented.

Reaching it costs money for most of the year, since the Alcazar charges admission, though on summer mornings the gardens are free. That is a real difference from the cypress standing outside the same gate, and worth knowing before you plan the walk.

Ulmus pumila comes from the steppe of northern China, Mongolia and eastern Siberia, ground where trees stay short because the wind and the drought keep them there. Give it Andalusian irrigation and a garden that never let it go without, and it turns into this.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Plaza del Cardenal Toledo
trees.access: Free, on a public square
trees.transport: Centro Historico; short walk north of the Mezquita-Catedral
trees.story:
The square was arranged around the tree. Plaza del Cardenal Toledo got its garden in 1945, and this deodar was already standing, so the paths and the benches went where the cedar allowed them. It remains effectively the only tree on the square, twenty-two and a half metres of it, which on a small plaza north of the Mezquita means it is also the roof.

Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees put it at about a hundred and two years old at survey, which is a floor rather than a figure, since it has gone on growing since somebody wrote that down. The catalogue is also the only source that says anything about this tree. Nothing else names it, which is ordinary for a square cedar and worth saying plainly rather than dressing up.

Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through Kashmir into Nepal, where it is a timber tree of high mountain forest and where the Sanskrit name means the wood of the gods. In Andalusia it is an ornamental, planted through the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries into gardens and new squares, and it does well as long as it is watered. The habit gives it away from a distance: a straight leader, branches sweeping down and out, every shoot tip drooping, so the whole tree looks like it is leaning slightly towards you.

trees.name: The Chinaberry of the Puerta de Almodóvar
trees.neighbourhood: Centro Histórico, beside the Alcázar walls
trees.access: Free, in the public gardens that surround the Puerta de Almodóvar city gate
trees.transport: Historic centre, a few minutes on foot from the Alcázar and the Mezquita
trees.story:
Four hundred square metres of shade, thrown by a species most cities plant as a modest street tree. Chinaberries usually stop somewhere around ten metres. This one is twenty-four and a half, which makes it less a tree in the gardens at the Puerta de Almodovar than the ceiling over them, and the reason people look up before they look at the gate.

Cordoba's own catalogue of singular trees measured it at about seventy-two years old, and a register age is the age on the day somebody wrote it down, so add what has passed since. That catalogue is the only source that has dated it. Local guides to the gate describe a giant cinamomo standing here, using the Spanish name for the species, which confirms the tree and what it is without confirming its years, so read the age as the city's estimate rather than a settled fact.

The gate beside it has six centuries on it either way. What stands today is a fourteenth-century Christian rebuild on the line of an older Arab gate, and the wall running from it towards the Alcazar is the one the tree grows against.

Melia azedarach came out of southern Asia and spread through Mediterranean cities for the shade and the lilac blossom, and its hard seed stones were strung as rosary beads, which is how the species picked up its other name of bead tree.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Agriculture Gardens
trees.access: Free, public garden, popularly called the Jardín de los Patos
trees.transport: Historic centre / Ciudad Jardín, walking distance from Ronda de los Tejares

best_time.label: late November into early December, when the whole crown turns gold and drops within days

trees.story:
Every other tree in this garden has living relatives. This one has none. Ginkgo biloba is the only surviving species of an entire order of plants, and the fan-shaped leaf you pick up under it is the same shape found pressed into rock from two hundred million years ago.

Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees calls this the oldest ginkgo in the city's public gardens and put it at about seventy-two years when it was surveyed, a figure no independent source has ever checked. What other sources do confirm is which tree is meant: the garden's local history pages name it, and a geocache placed at its foot carries its name and is still listed as active, which is a small modern receipt that it is still standing.

The Jardines de la Agricultura opened in 1811 and nobody in Cordoba calls them that. They are Los Patos, after the duck pond. A ginkgo of seventy is barely started by the standards of a species that routinely passes a thousand years in China and Japan, so this is an early chapter rather than a veteran.

Come in late autumn. Ginkgo leaves turn a uniform gold and then release almost in unison, so the tree goes from lit to bare in a few days, and on the best of those days the gold is on the branches and on the ground at the same time.

trees.name: The Casuarinas of the Plaza de Jerónimo Páez
trees.neighbourhood: San Salvador y La Compañía, Centro Histórico
trees.access: Free, open public plaza in the historic centre
trees.transport: Five minutes on foot from the Mezquita-Catedral
trees.story:
Three trees that read as pines from across the square and are not related to pines at all. What hangs off a casuarina in fine green threads is jointed twig, not needle; the leaves are reduced to rings of scales at each joint, the tree flowers, and the resemblance to a conifer is coincidence. In wind they hiss rather than rustle, which is why the species travels under the name whistling pine in half the countries that grow it.

The city's catalogue of singular trees registers three of them on this small plaza in front of the Archaeological Museum and puts the tallest above thirty metres. It gives no age, and no other source supplies one. An independent description of the square mentions its large casuarinas without measuring anything, which is as far as corroboration goes here, and the plaza was remodelled and refenced in stages that only finished in January 2011, so how much of what stands predates that work is genuinely open.

The ground under them is better dated than they are. The plaza takes its name from the Palacio de los Paez de Castillejo, now the Archaeological Museum, and beneath it lies a Roman theatre that an earthquake brought down in the third century.

The three grow close together against the museum wall, which makes them one sight with one place to stand rather than three separate errands.

trees.name: The River Red Gum of the Celia Méndez Garden
trees.neighbourhood: Distrito Sureste, roughly 3km east of the historic centre
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours not confirmed)
trees.transport: Distrito Sureste, roughly 3km east of the historic centre; not within the existing 2.3km walk
trees.story:
The thickest trunk in Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees belongs to an Australian. This river red gum measures 4.86 metres around and stands 34.8 metres tall in a public park three kilometres east of the Mezquita, well outside the ring of old trees the city puts on its maps.

It is there because the ground used to be huertas, the irrigated market gardens that fed Cordoba along the Guadalquivir before the city grew east across them. The catalogue calls this tree a relict of those gardens. Eucalyptus camaldulensis follows watercourses in its own country and was planted across Spain in the twentieth century for that exact habit, cheap timber on wet ground, and this one outlived the reason it was put in.

One caution, plainly. The municipal catalogue is the only source that records this tree at all. Searching for it turns up a different and better-known Cordoba eucalyptus several kilometres away, so anyone checking online will most likely end up reading about the wrong one. The girth and the height are the city's own measurements and nobody has published a second set.

No age is on file, and none should be guessed. Red gums put on bulk fast where there is water, so five metres of trunk here does not imply centuries, and nothing in the record claims them.

trees.name: The Ash of Santa Marina
trees.age: argued to be over a century, not precisely dated
trees.access: Free, standing beside a public church on a public plaza
trees.transport: Historic centre, walking distance
trees.story:
Somebody cut the top off this tree and it is still the largest ash in Cordoba. What stands on the north side of the church of Santa Marina is a heavy old trunk carrying thin, sparse regrowth and not much leaf, about nine and a half metres of it in total. By trunk perimeter it has been recorded as the biggest of its species in the city twice: in a 1984 book on Cordoba's trees, and again in the 2002 provincial inventory of singular trees.

The age is argued rather than documented. Rafa Tamajon, the local botanist who has written most about these trees, reads it as centenarian from its growth pattern and the history of the site, but there is no ring count and no planting record, so somewhere between one and one and a half centuries is as precise as anyone can honestly be. The trunk carries visible decay and the tree is described as declining. That is worth knowing, because it is the argument for going now rather than eventually.

Ash wants damp ground and Cordoba is not damp country, which is part of why one of this size got written down here at all.

A practical note: the sources place it on the plaza and on the church's north side, and that is as close as the pin goes. Walk the north wall and look for the big trunk under the small crown.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Santa Maria de Trassierra
trees.neighbourhood: Santa Maria de Trassierra, Sierra de Cordoba
trees.access: Standing in the small village of Santa Maria de Trassierra, in the Sierra de Cordoba above the city. Included in the municipality's own singular-tree catalogue, which generally covers accessible specimens, but this pass could not independently confirm the exact street-level setting (square, street or institutional grounds) beyond the catalogue's coordinate, so treat the setting as likely public but not individually verified.
trees.transport: Reachable by Aucorsa bus line L-T from central Cordoba in about 19 minutes, but the line runs only about five services a day, which strains the day-trip boundary; check the timetable before planning a visit around it.
trees.story:
Santa Maria de Trassierra is a village in the hills above Cordoba, and this stone pine is one of the specimens the city's own catalogue of singular trees reaches out beyond the city walls to include. Three metres twenty six round, twenty five metres tall, and estimated at about ninety years old, it is younger than most trees on this list but old enough, and large enough, to have earned its own entry in an official register that mostly protects far older specimens.

Pinus pinea is the pine that shapes half of Mediterranean Spain's skyline, its flat, umbrella-shaped crown grown for shade and for the pine nuts inside its cones, both of which took centuries of selective planting to produce the tree people now picture as wild. A tree this size at this age has grown fast even by the species' own standards, likely helped by open ground and full sun in a small village rather than competition in a planted stand.

Reaching it from central Cordoba means the Aucorsa L-T bus, about nineteen minutes, but the line runs only a handful of times a day, so check the timetable before building a trip around it. Nobody has published a closer account of exactly where in the village it stands. If you have seen it, tell us.

trees.name: The Bur Oak on the Midway
trees.access: Free, public park path along the Midway Plaisance
trees.transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from Millennium Station downtown, then a short walk to Ellis Ave and the Midway
trees.story: When the Midway Plaisance was cleared and regraded for the 1893 World's Fair, one tree was left standing, and this is it. By then it was already substantial enough that the ecologist Henry Cowles used it in his 1901 textbook as the example of its kind. Accounts of the fair place it behind the Sitting Bull's Cabin exhibit and the ostrich farm concession, neither of which lasted the year. Sources disagree on how it got here, and it is worth stating both. The University of Chicago Magazine quotes a campus environment official describing it as ostensibly planted as part of a Native American exhibit during the fair itself. The better supported account, from the Hyde Park historian Gary Ossewaarde, from Cowles in 1901 and from a local history record of a 2024 trunk measurement, has it standing long before 1893 and deliberately spared. That measurement reportedly ran past the largest bur oak on the Morton Arboretum's own growth reference chart, which would push it beyond the 250 or so years usually quoted. Bur oak is the tree of the prairie edge in this part of Illinois, corky barked enough to survive the fires that kept the grassland open. This one is the last of that landscape left on the Midway. It stands near Ellis Avenue, in front of the university hospital, on a pin that is close rather than surveyed.

trees.name: The Bur Oak Grove of Wooded Island
trees.age: the grove's oldest survivors are roughly 200 to 300 years
trees.access: Free, public park, Chicago Park District (Wooded Island / Osaka Garden)
trees.transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from downtown, then roughly a 15 to 20 minute walk east across Jackson Park to Wooded Island; or CTA bus to the Museum of Science and Industry and cross the Clarence Darrow Bridge

best_time.label: September and October, when the big fringed bur oak acorns come down

trees.story: One of these oaks blew down around 2016, and its rings were counted back to roughly 1730. It had been standing for nearly three centuries when it fell. The ones still up are of the same generation: DNAinfo reported 250 year old bur oaks across the island, with a red oak of about 150 among them. Wooded Island is the part of the 1893 World's Fair that was deliberately left alone. Frederick Law Olmsted kept buildings off it entirely while the Court of Honor went up in white plaster to the south, and fair era painters kept turning their backs on the architecture to paint these oaks instead. The island sits on an undisturbed sand ridge, which is why the soil under the trees was never scraped and rebuilt the way the rest of Jackson Park was. In 2016 the Army Corps of Engineers spent 8.1 million dollars restoring the habitat here and wrote the old bur oaks into the plan, along with roughly 120 bur oak saplings that had seeded themselves around their parents. An oak stand actually reproducing inside a city is a rare thing to stand in. The place to stand is the path just south of the Osaka Garden, looking into the south end of the island, where the grove reads as one thing rather than as scattered trees.

trees.name: The Bur Oak Savanna of Union Ridge Cemetery
trees.age: the oldest estimated at 325 to 375 years, based on trunk size
trees.access: Free, cemetery grounds open to visitors during posted hours
trees.transport: Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line to Norwood Park station, about 22 minutes from Ogilvie Transportation Center downtown, then a short walk
trees.story: The oldest oak in this grove has been estimated at 325 to 375 years, which would make it roughly two centuries older than the city around it. It was already a mature prairie tree when Chicago was a portage and a fort. The figure comes from Scott Carlini, quoted in a 2016 hunt for the city's oldest tree, and it is based on trunk diameter rather than a ring core, so treat it as directional. We found no second independent estimate, which is why this entry stays flagged. What is solid is the setting. Union Ridge took its first burial in 1841 and is described by the Norwood Park Historical Society as the oldest continuously operating cemetery in Chicago. The ground was open prairie before it was platted, and what stands here is a genuine relict bur oak savanna: widely spaced, heavy limbed trees with daylight between them, which is what oaks look like when they grow up in grassland rather than in forest. Bur oak's thick corky bark let it survive the fires that kept that prairie open, and the graves that arrived in 1841 put an end to both the fires and the plough. It is a working cemetery, so come during posted visiting hours and behave like a guest. The pin is the entrance; the old section and its oaks are inside the grounds.

trees.name: The Champion Boxelder of Edgebrook
trees.access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter trail was not confirmed
trees.transport: Metra Milwaukee District North Line to Edgebrook station, the last stop still inside Chicago city limits, roughly 30 minutes from Chicago Union Station, then about a 15 to 20 minute walk east on Devon/Central Ave to the golf course entrance
trees.story: Boxelder is the tree nobody wants. It seeds itself into alleys and back lots, drops limbs, hosts the boxelder bugs that get into houses in autumn, and is generally written off as a weed that never lives long enough to get big. This one is the biggest known in Illinois. The state's Big Tree Register, run by University of Illinois Extension, ranks it champion of its species: just over nine feet around the trunk, 55 feet tall, a crown spreading 35 feet, and 172.3 points on the register's scoring formula, ahead of the runner up down in Shawnee National Forest at the far southern end of the state. It was measured and listed in 2026 with a dated photograph, so it is standing now. One honesty note, and it is the reason this entry is flagged: the register is the only source we could find on it. The Sun-Times feature on the state's big trees, the Extension's own announcement and the Forest Preserves champion list all fail to mention it, most likely because the title is very new. No Illinois register carries an age field either, so nobody has dated this tree and we are not going to guess at it. Visiting is a golf question. It stands on Edgebrook Golf Course, a public course run by the Forest Preserves of Cook County, which normally means a green fee to walk the fairways, and whether it can be seen from the perimeter is unconfirmed.

trees.name: The Champion Red Pine of Indian Boundary
trees.access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter path was not confirmed
trees.transport: Metra Milwaukee District West Line to River Grove or Elmwood Park, roughly 20 minutes from Chicago Union Station; or CTA/Pace bus along Forest Preserve Dr/Cumberland Ave. Exact walk time from the nearest stop to the tree was not verified.
trees.story: This is the state champion red pine of Illinois, and it holds the title partly for want of competition. The Illinois Big Tree Register lists exactly one red pine anywhere in the state, and this is the one, standing on the Indian Boundary golf course on Chicago's northwest side. Its 153.52 points come from a trunk 6.8 feet around, a height of 64 feet and a crown spreading 31.5 feet, measured and listed in 2026, which doubles as the freshest evidence that it is alive and thriving. Nobody has dated it. Red pine is a northern species, well outside its natural range down here, so this is a planted tree rather than a relic of anything, and the register carries no age field for any entry. Any figure attached to this tree is worked backwards from its trunk rather than measured, and should be read that way. What is documented is the size, and for Pinus resinosa the giveaway is the needles: paired, three to six inches long, snapping cleanly in half when you bend one. Access is the honest problem. Indian Boundary is a public 18 hole course run by the Forest Preserves of Cook County, so walking the fairways generally means paying a green fee, and whether the tree can be seen or reached from outside the course was not established. Ask at the clubhouse before planning the trip.

trees.name: The Kenilworth Witness Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Oak Park (day trip from Chicago, not within city limits)
trees.access: Free, public parkway tree (the strip of village-owned land between sidewalk and street), viewable from the public right of way; it fronts a private residence so stay on the parkway/sidewalk
trees.transport: CTA Green Line to Oak Park Ave station, roughly 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop, then about a 10 minute walk north; alternatively Metra Union Pacific West Line to Oak Park station
trees.story: Local history holds that this bur oak was a witness tree, a landmark the Potawatomi used to find the route back to the Des Plaines River after a hunt. Oak Park's own paper, the Wednesday Journal, reported that reading in 2014 along with the claim that it is the oldest parkway tree in the village. Its age depends on which article you open. The 2014 survey puts it at about 230 years. A 2011 piece in the same paper, written when Openlands and the Morton Arboretum gathered its acorns for a historic oak propagation project, calls it three centuries old. That is a gap of seventy years, nobody has resolved it, and both figures stand here rather than one being quietly chosen. There is a harder caveat. No source has confirmed this tree alive since that 2014 article. In October 2025 another Oak Park heritage bur oak of the same generation, over on Forest Avenue, was removed after disease took it. That was a different tree at a different address, but the cohort is visibly failing, so go expecting an oak and not a guarantee. It stands on the parkway, the village-owned strip between sidewalk and street, in front of a private house on North Kenilworth Avenue in the Hemingway district. Public ground, so stay on the pavement. Oak Park is not Chicago but the suburb immediately west, 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop on the Green Line.

trees.name: The Cedar of Villa Olmo
trees.access: Free, public park (Comune di Como), open daily during park hours
trees.transport: Como Nord Lago station, then roughly 25-30 min on foot north along the Via Borgovico lakefront promenade, or a local bus toward Villa Olmo

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Lombardy held a public vote for its tree of the year in 2024, and this cedar won it. The Comune di Como announced the result that November, crediting not the measurements but the setting, the history and the number of people with a memory attached to it. The measurements are worth having anyway. The trunk runs to roughly eight metres around, the thickest in Como's monumental list, and the tree stands twenty five metres high, with several heavy limbs forking low from the base rather than rising as one clean stem. Three registers put its age near two hundred years and agree closely: the national monumental register, the Italian tree register RAMI at about 197 years, and a provincial survey at roughly 200. It has not had an easy decade. Storms broke major branches in 2016 and again the following year. As of the summer of 2026 it stands inside a ring of protective stakes with a wrap around the bark, which is what a city does for a tree it has decided to keep. The park behind Villa Olmo is Como's main public green space, five hectares and some 780 trees, free and open daily. Generations of Como children have played in this cedar's shade, and the lakefront walk north to Villa del Grumello and Villa Geno starts here.

photo.attribution: Daniela Manili Pessina, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Villa Geno
trees.access: Free, public park and lakeside promenade; the Comune di Como has owned Villa Geno's villa, park and walk since 1911
trees.transport: roughly 15 min on foot from Como Nord Lago station, north along the Viale Geno lakefront promenade
trees.story: The Italian tree register lists this one as Il Maggiore, the greater one, because there are two of them and somebody had to rank them. A pair of Himalayan cedars closes the end of Viale Geno, the lakeside promenade Como walks in the evening, and Lombardy's tourism office gives their girths as 5.80 and 4.30 metres. The national register records this tree at 5.60, near enough to make it the larger of the two. They stand over a clearing beside a lakeside fountain that throws its jet more than forty metres into the air, which means most people meeting these cedars are looking the other way when they arrive. Villa Geno began as an eighteenth century estate. The Cornaggia family bought it in 1850 and had the architect James Tazzini rebuild the house, and in 1911 the whole property, villa, park and the promenade leading to it, passed to the city of Como. The cedars have therefore spent most of their lives in public ownership, shading a walk that is free at any hour and about fifteen minutes on foot from the station. Deodars droop at the tips of every branch, which at this size reads as a very large tree hanging its head, and they hold that shape all year. No age has been published for either of the pair.

trees.name: The Sycamore of Villa Geno
trees.access: Free, public park and lakeside promenade (Comune di Como)
trees.transport: roughly 15 min on foot from Como Nord Lago station, north along the Viale Geno lakefront promenade
trees.story: At thirty three metres this is the tallest tree on Como's lakefront walk, and the only American on it. Platanus occidentalis is the sycamore of the eastern United States, a species Europe mostly grows as one parent of the hybrid London plane rather than in its own right, and a full grown one in an Italian park is unusual. Its trunk measures five and a half metres around. That figure comes from the national monumental register and is matched to within a few centimetres by a survey of the province's trees run by A Scuola dagli Alberi. Those two records are the only ones we have found for this tree, so read the numbers as well corroborated and the biography as absent: nobody has published an age, a planting date, or the name of whoever put it here. It stands a few dozen metres from the two Himalayan cedars and the ginkgo in the same clearing at the end of Viale Geno, where the promenade runs out at the water. Bark is the giveaway if you are unsure which tree you are looking at. Sycamores shed theirs in plates and leave the trunk mottled cream and olive, brighter and flakier than the plane trees in the squares behind you. Free, open, and a fifteen minute walk from the station.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Villa Geno
trees.access: Free, public park and lakeside promenade (Comune di Como)
trees.transport: roughly 15 min on foot from Como Nord Lago station, north along the Viale Geno lakefront promenade

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter gold and drops within days

trees.story: This ginkgo is male, which in this species is a decision rather than an accident. Female trees drop a fleshy seed that smells like something died in the flowerbed, so parks that want the autumn colour without the complaints plant males, and the nursery trade has propagated them from cuttings for over a century. The colour is the reason to come. Ginkgo leaves hold their green late, then go to a flat butter gold across the whole crown at once, usually in November here, and drop within a day or two of each other. Twenty metres of that standing over a lakeside clearing justifies the walk out along Viale Geno. The tree is roughly a hundred years old according to the provincial survey that recorded it, which puts its planting in the villa's first decades as public property. Como took over Villa Geno, its park and its promenade in 1911. On girth the sources do not quite agree: the national monumental register has 312 centimetres, the provincial survey about three metres flat, close but not the same measurement, and we have flagged that rather than pick one. The species has been around long enough not to care. Ginkgo biloba is the last surviving member of an order of plants that predates flowering trees entirely.

trees.name: The Cedar of Villa del Grumello
trees.neighbourhood: Villa del Grumello, lakefront (between Villa Olmo and Villa Geno)
trees.access: Free entry Sundays 10:00-19:00 (plus an evening aperitivo slot to 21:00); from April 2026 also open Monday-Friday 9:00-17:00 and Sunday 9:00-18:00, closed Saturdays. Part of the 'Kilometer of Knowledge' pedestrian path linking Villa Olmo, Villa del Grumello and Villa Sucota.
trees.transport: roughly 20 min on foot from Como Nord Lago station along Via Borgovico, between Villa Olmo and Villa Geno

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Six metres of trunk, standing directly in front of the house, in a park that grows a botanical collection dedicated to Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist Como claims as its own. The cedar came a great deal later than Pliny. The Italian tree register dates it to about 156 years, putting it in the ground around 1870, and the national register's girth of 595 centimetres matches the provincial survey's rough six metres almost exactly. Both rate it of national importance. Cedars of Lebanon do their growing outward. A tree of this age is young by the species' standards, and what it has already built is the flat tiered crown that makes a cedar readable from across a park, layer above layer, each one nearly horizontal. The four hectare grounds hold more than this one tree: pines, redwoods, and a camphor leaning at an angle that looks temporary and is not. The villa sits on the lakefront between Villa Olmo and Villa Geno and forms the middle stretch of Como's Kilometro della Conoscenza, the pedestrian path linking the three estates. One thing to plan around. The Grumello park does not keep ordinary park hours. Entry is free, it opens on Sundays and on weekdays, it shuts in the late afternoon rather than at dusk, and on Saturdays it does not open at all.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Villa del Grumello
trees.access: Same schedule as the Villa del Grumello cedar: free Sundays 10:00-19:00, and Mon-Fri 9:00-17:00 plus Sun 9:00-18:00 from April 2026, closed Saturdays
trees.transport: roughly 20 min on foot from Como Nord Lago station along Via Borgovico, between Villa Olmo and Villa Geno

best_time.label: November, when the ginkgo goes gold beside the greenhouses

trees.story: This ginkgo and the cedar a short walk away were almost certainly planted by the same person in the same decade. The Italian tree register dates the ginkgo at roughly 146 years and the cedar at roughly 156, which for ages estimated rather than counted is the same answer twice. Somebody was landscaping the Grumello grounds in the 1870s and buying the fashionable things. Ginkgo was exactly that. Europe had only had the tree since the 1730s, when seed reached Dutch collectors from Japanese temple gardens, and by the mid nineteenth century no serious villa garden was without one. This one went in beside the greenhouses, where the estate kept the plants that needed help surviving the winter. The ginkgo needed none. It is among the toughest trees in cultivation, which is how a species that had spent millions of years in the fossil record ended up in every second European park. Its trunk is now around four metres in circumference: 390 centimetres in the national register, roughly four metres in the provincial survey. In November the whole crown goes gold and then drops, often inside a couple of days. Access is the catch. The park is free but opens on Sundays and weekdays only, on a set schedule that ends in the late afternoon, and never on Saturdays.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Villa del Grumello
trees.access: Same schedule as the Villa del Grumello cedar: free Sundays 10:00-19:00, and Mon-Fri 9:00-17:00 plus Sun 9:00-18:00 from April 2026, closed Saturdays
trees.transport: roughly 20 min on foot from Como Nord Lago station along Via Borgovico, between Villa Olmo and Villa Geno

best_time.label: May to June, when it flowers

trees.story: The villa's own website lists magnolias among the centuries-old trees of its park, and that is as precise as anyone has been about this one. The national monumental register records a trunk of 330 centimetres, and the Italian tree register knows it as the Magnolia di Villa Grumello. Neither publishes an age, and no independent measurement exists to check the girth against, so this entry rests on thinner ground than the cedar and the ginkgo in the same grounds. It is on the register, it is where the register says it is, and beyond that the honest answer is that nobody has written the tree up. What you get is the plant itself, which needs no biography. Magnolia grandiflora came out of the American southeast in the eighteenth century and became the status tree of European villa gardens: evergreen, glossy, dark, and through May and June covered in heavily scented white flowers up to thirty centimetres across, visible from the far end of a lawn. It keeps its leaves through winter, so it looks much the same in January as in August, which is odd company for the deciduous giants around it. Entry is free, in a park that opens on Sundays and weekdays to a set schedule and stays shut on Saturdays.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Piazza Camerlata
trees.access: Free, standing in a public square (Piazzale Camerlata), open at all times
trees.transport: Como San Giovanni station, then roughly 20-25 min on foot or a short bus ride south to Piazzale Camerlata
trees.story: Piazzale Camerlata is where Como's traffic converges, and a plane tree with a trunk four and a third metres around stands in the middle of it. Two registers agree on that figure almost to the centimetre: the national monumental list records 430 centimetres and the Italian tree register 4.30 metres. They part company only on the Latin name, one calling it Platanus x acerifolia and the other Platanus hispanica, which are two names for the same hybrid rather than two different trees. Neither publishes an age. A search of the local press turned up a good deal about the square and nothing at all about the tree, so how much of the junction's history it has actually stood through is anybody's guess. The square has plenty of it. Camerlata was a commercial crossroads on the old Via Regina by the fifteenth century, took its present shape in 1879 and now centres on a monumental fountain by Cesare Cattaneo and Mario Radice. The Italian register surveyed the plane in September 2025 and rated its condition good, which is the most recent evidence that it is thriving rather than merely standing. It is a separate errand from the lakefront villas, about 2.9 kilometres south of them, twenty minutes on foot from Como San Giovanni or a short ride by bus. Free, at any hour, in the way a public square is free.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Quarcino
trees.access: Free, in the churchyard of the small 10th-century Romanesque parish church of Santi Filippo e Giacomo in Quarcino (also called Sagnino); no source found stating restricted hours or closure, treated as an ordinarily open Italian parish churchyard per project default (CLAUDE.md's churchyard rule) since no evidence of enclosure or restriction turned up despite a targeted search
trees.transport: roughly 4km from Como centre in the Quarcino/Sagnino hill neighbourhood; reachable by local bus or a ~15 min drive/taxi, no direct rail stop

best_time.label: May, when the whole crown goes up in white candles beside the church

trees.story: The church beside it is a thousand years old, and the tree cannot be, because the species had not arrived yet. Horse chestnut comes from the mountains of the Balkans and only spread through western European gardens from the sixteenth century, so every one in Italy was planted by somebody on a date somebody chose. Nobody wrote this one down. The national monumental register gives a trunk of 335 centimetres and no age, and the Italian tree register adds a health rating of good and no age either. What the tree does have is an unusually well pinned position. A photographer entered it in Wiki Loves Monuments in September 2018, filed under veteran trees of Como, and the coordinates on that image land within a metre or so of the register's own point, which is better location evidence than most undated trees get. The church is Santi Filippo e Giacomo, Romanesque, tenth century in its earliest phase and rebuilt twice since, standing in the hill neighbourhood of Quarcino, also called Sagnino, four kilometres above the lake. Locals have put it forward for FAI's Luoghi del Cuore, the heritage fund's public list of places people care about, which is a fair description of what is here: a small parish church, a big tree next to it, no crowd. No source records opening hours for the churchyard. In May the whole crown goes up in white candles.

trees.name: The Mulberry of Proviantgarden
trees.access: Free, open access, public courtyard on Slotsholmen
trees.transport: Christianshavn metro station or Copenhagen Central Station, short walk across Slotsholmen

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen and drop

trees.story: King Christian IV tried to build a Danish silk industry the way his contemporaries elsewhere in Europe were doing it, by planting mulberry trees to feed silkworms, and this is the one tree from that entire royal venture that anyone can still point to. It stands today at Proviantgarden, part of the naval arsenal Christian IV built on Slotsholmen from 1603 to supply his warships, on ground that once fronted a working harbor basin where vessels docked to be provisioned and armed. Tradition credits a sailor who brought it home from Asia rather than a court gardener, and it has stood long enough to have watched those same tall ships come and go for provisions centuries before Slotsholmen became the seat of Denmark's parliament and courts. The Danish silk venture itself mostly failed; Copenhagen's climate never suited silkworms the way Christian IV hoped, and the street name Silkegade nearby is now the closest most Copenhageners get to the story. This tree is the exception, a specimen one detailed historical account describes as having remarkable vitality, still leafing out every spring in a courtyard surrounded by 17th-century naval buildings that have long since changed jobs, now government offices rather than stores for rope and ships' biscuit.

trees.name: The Ancient Cycad of the Palm House
trees.access: Paid entry to Palmehuset (the outdoor Botanical Garden itself is free)
trees.transport: Norreport railway and metro station, short walk
trees.story: In 1842, the Danish botanist Frederik Liebmann sailed to Mexico and came home with, among other specimens, a small cycad that looked more like a stunted pineapple than anything resembling a tree. It has spent nearly two centuries since then growing at its own unhurried pace in Copenhagen's Botanical Garden, first at the garden's earlier city-centre site and then, from 1874, in the Palm House built specifically to keep tropical and subtropical plants alive through Danish winters. Cycads are not actually related to palms or ferns despite resembling both; they are among the oldest living groups of seed plants on Earth, largely unchanged since long before flowering plants existed, which makes a 184-year-old specimen barely middle-aged by the standards of its own family. Liebmann died in 1856 at just 43, only 14 years after bringing the plant home, but his cycad has outlived him by more than a century and a half and remains, by the garden's own account, its oldest living specimen and one of its genuine star attractions, a slow-growing plant that has simply outlasted everyone who ever went looking for one.

trees.name: Thorvaldsen's Robinia
trees.access: Free, open access, public ground beside Thorvaldsens Museum
trees.transport: Christianshavn metro station or Copenhagen Central Station, short walk across Slotsholmen

best_time.label: May, when it flowers in heavy white clusters

trees.story: Bertel Thorvaldsen spent more than 40 years in Rome becoming Europe's most celebrated Neoclassical sculptor before returning home to Copenhagen in 1838 to a hero's welcome, and this multi-stemmed black locust growing beside the museum built to house his life's work is said to have come home with him, grown from seed he carried back from Italy. Denmark's dendrological society surveyed the tree in 1995 and recorded a trunk over three metres around, splitting into several stems rather than one, and estimated its age at up to 155 years at that time, consistent with a planting soon after Thorvaldsen's actual return. That would put the tree, and not just the museum, among the direct physical legacies of a sculptor whose bronze and marble work now sits in collections from the Vatican to Warsaw. Black locust is not a species anyone would plant deliberately for its connection to fine art. It is a hardy, fast-growing tree valued more for binding loose soil and producing useful timber than for looking distinguished, which makes its adoption into Thorvaldsen's own story feel almost like an accident that stuck, a workmanlike species growing beside one of Europe's grandest personal museums, surveyed precisely enough by Danish tree recorders in 2008 to give this project one of its few confirmed coordinates.

trees.name: The Husalle Lindens
trees.access: Free, open access, Kongens Have (public park, open daily)
trees.transport: Norreport railway and metro station, short walk

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: Kongens Have is Copenhagen's oldest public park, laid out from 1606 for King Christian IV beside his new Rosenborg Castle, and its formal linden avenues were planted soon after: Kavalergangen and Damegangen, the two clipped alleys nearest the castle, date to around 1664 and 1700. Almost none of those original trees survive; both avenues have been replanted more than once in the four centuries since. Husalle, a third avenue running parallel to the garden's main axis a little further north, has fared differently: its lindens are described by garden historians as among the oldest living trees in Denmark, having escaped the repeated replacements that emptied the more formal avenues nearer the castle of their original planting. The garden itself has survived far more than ordinary wear. It has hosted royal pleasure grounds, public promenades, and, in recent years, a summer sound installation that lets speakers hidden in ten of its trees tell stories to anyone who walks close enough to trigger them, a very modern use for trees old enough to have shaded Danish kings centuries before recorded sound existed. Husalle's lindens do their storytelling the old way, simply by having outlasted almost everything planted around them.

trees.name: The Temple Tree of Landbohøjskolens Have
trees.access: Free, open to the public sunrise to sunset (university garden, protected since 1965)
trees.transport: Frederiksberg metro station, roughly 5-8 minute walk

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns gold and drops the whole crown within a week

trees.story:
This ginkgo is male, and the female it pollinates lives on the other side of the street. The two trees have never touched. The university library, writing up the garden's own history, calls it the largest ginkgo in the collection and gives 1883 as its planting year, which would make it about 143. That date comes from that one source and nowhere else, so read it as the garden's account rather than a measured fact.

It is planted in the middle of a large stone mound, which is a strange thing to do to a tree and suits this one. Ginkgo biloba is the last surviving member of a lineage older than flowering plants, and the Danish name for it, tempeltræet, points at the temple courtyards in China and Japan where the final populations were kept alive by monks while the wild ones disappeared. The garden around it was laid out in 1858 for the Royal Veterinary and Agricultural College and has been legally protected since 1965.

Protection is not immortality. The blood beech planted the year the garden opened, which the official heritage listing still describes as the thickest tree here, was felled in 2018. Nothing suggests the ginkgo has gone the same way and the species is famously hard to kill, but the newest dated confirmation we could find of this one is not recent. The garden is free and open from sunrise to sunset.

trees.name: The Handkerchief Tree of Assistens
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 5-7 minute walk; the station sits at the cemetery's northeastern corner, close to this tree

best_time.label: May, when the bracts open and the Danish name for it, dove tree, makes sense

trees.story:
What looks like flowers on this tree are leaves. For roughly two weeks in May the handkerchief tree hangs hundreds of paired white bracts through its crown, each pair a modified leaf wrapped around a small dark ball of actual flower, and Danish names it better than English does: duetræ, the dove tree. Davidia involucrata grows wild in the mountains of western China and reached Western cultivation only in 1904, through the plant hunter Ernest Wilson. It is still an uncommon thing to find in Denmark, and this one is multi-stemmed, so in May the bracts come at you from several directions at once.

Nobody wrote down when it was planted. The Danish Dendrological Society surveyed Assistens in November 2019, put a GPS point on this tree, measured 1.4 metres around its stems and recorded it alive and healthy. That is the honest limit of what is known here: a girth, not an age. The range on this page is inferred from that measurement and from how recently the species arrived in Danish gardens, not read off any record.

It stands in section A of a cemetery Copenhagen treats as a park. People run, read and eat their lunch here, a few hundred metres from the graves of Hans Christian Andersen and Søren Kierkegaard.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Assistens
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen) or the Kapelvej main entrance, roughly 5-10 minute walk
trees.story:
Every weeping beech is a graft, and on this one the join is in plain sight. About a metre up the trunk there is a visible union where a cutting of the pendulous form was fixed onto ordinary beech rootstock, and the surveyor who measured the tree in November 2019 noted that the grafted top is now putting on wood faster than the stock beneath it, so the trunk steps outward where the two meet. Look for that step before you look at the curtain.

The same survey recorded something less comfortable: a large wound at the base of the trunk. The tree was logged as alive, 3.29 metres round and 15 metres tall, but it is a healthy crown standing over an open injury, which is worth knowing rather than glossing over.

Weeping beech became a Danish cemetery fashion in the nineteenth century under the name sørgebøg, mourning beech, planted to hang over a grave the way a mourner leans over it. No planting date survives for this one. The 80 to 150 years on this page is worked back from the girth, not counted.

It stands in section B, just right of the Kapelvej entrance, which makes it the first serious tree most visitors to Assistens Kirkegård walk straight past.

trees.name: The Great Maple of Assistens
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 10 minute walk

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story:
The thickest tree at Assistens is also the least exotic species in it. At 4.19 metres round, this sycamore out-measures every tree the Danish Dendrological Society registered inside these walls, including the rarities people actually come to see, and it does it as a common European maple that seeds itself into any gap it can find. Twenty-two and a half metres tall, one trunk to about two metres up and then a fork into two, alive and healthy at the November 2019 survey, rated regionally noteworthy.

Assistens was not built for strolling. It opened in 1757 outside the city ramparts as an overflow burial ground, taking the dead that Copenhagen's crowded parish churchyards could no longer hold, and the famous names arrived later. The city then grew out past it, Nørrebro packed in around it, and the place slowly turned into what it is now: a walled park with graves in it, where on a warm afternoon the living comfortably outnumber the mourners.

No planting date exists for this maple, and the 100 to 180 years given here is inferred from its girth rather than counted. What is certain is the measurement, taken with GPS in the field, and that nothing else registered in this cemetery is thicker. Section C, a little southwest of the section's centre.

trees.name: The Beech by the Boat Trip
trees.access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
trees.transport: Frederiksberg Allé metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-12 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance

best_time.label: late October, when the copper leaves come down onto the canal below it

trees.story:
This beech is registered under the name of a boat trip. Danish dendrologists filed it as Bøgen ved Bådfarten, the beech by the boat trip, which makes it the easiest tree on this list to find: walk to the jetty in Frederiksberg Have where the flat-bottomed boats set off around the canals, and the tree is the big one standing over you. Its trunk is 4.68 metres round and 1.49 metres across, measured in October 2016 and recorded alive.

The water it stands beside is the reason the garden looks the way it does. Frederiksberg Have began around 1700 as a Baroque layout of straight lines below the royal palace, then was redrawn between 1798 and 1804 into a romantic landscape of winding canals, islands and staged views, which is the fashion this beech grew up inside. The garden is protected under Danish conservation law and free to walk into.

Its age is not documented anywhere. The 120 to 220 years here comes from girth alone, and the garden's own heritage listing is careful on the point: the trees it names as three centuries old are the lindens on Mathildehøj, not this beech. Only one other tree in Frederiksberg Have carries a thicker trunk, and it is a short walk away in the same garden.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Frederiksberg Have
trees.access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
trees.transport: Frederiksberg Alle metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-15 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
This oak has no recorded birthday, but the garden gives it a ceiling. Frederiksberg Have was laid out as royal ground around 1700 and rebuilt between 1798 and 1804 into the romantic landscape park it still is, so whatever the tree's exact age, it cannot be older than the garden that had to exist before anyone planted in it. What was measured rather than guessed: 4.95 metres round, 28.8 metres tall, 1.58 metres through, surveyed by the Danish Dendrological Society in October 2016 and rated municipally noteworthy. That is the thickest trunk of any tree on this list standing inside the city itself; the oaks out in the deer park north of town are thicker again.

The 130 to 250 years on this page is arithmetic on that girth against how fast a parkland oak puts on wood, not a date from any record, and it should be read as the wide guess it is. A pedunculate oak growing in the open with room on every side thickens faster than one shut into a wood, which is exactly the situation here, and one reason the upper end of that range is probably generous.

The garden around it is public, protected and busy: lawns, canals, the palace up on its hill, boats in summer. The oak has watched the whole thing turn from a royal retreat into the city's back garden.

trees.name: The Honey Locust of Assistens
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 10 minute walk

best_time.label: October, when the small leaflets turn clear yellow and come down almost at once

trees.story:
Someone has been keeping notes on this tree since 1941. That year a Danish gardening magazine ran a feature on beautiful trees and included a honey locust in section E of Assistens cemetery. In 1949 Jens Østergaard came to measure it for a nationwide survey of Gleditsia triacanthos in Danish gardens, published in the Dendrological Society's 1952 yearbook: twelve metres tall, standing on what the surveyor recorded as former rampart ground, clay loam, listed as site number six of only thirty-five in the whole country. In November 2019 the Society came back with a GPS and a tape. Sixteen metres, 1.18 metres round, alive and healthy.

Four metres of growth in seventy years is exactly what this species should manage, which is what makes the paper trail worth more than a plaque. The same tree, in the same spot, written up three times across eighty years by people with no reason to exaggerate.

The thorns are what to look for, and you will have to look up. Honey locust usually arms its trunk with branched spikes at chest height. This one carries only a few, sitting two and a half to three metres up, out of reach and easy to walk straight past.

Assistens opened in 1760 as a burial ground for the poor, on ground outside the city ramparts, and Hans Christian Andersen lies a few minutes' walk from here. The honey locust was rare enough in Denmark to be worth cataloguing nationally. It still is.

trees.name: The Pacifier Tree
trees.access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
