trees.transport: Frederiksberg Alle metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-12 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance
trees.story:
Every November this hornbeam gets harvested. Since 2004 parents in Frederiksberg have brought toddlers here to tie up the pacifier they have agreed to give up, and once a year the whole crop comes down so the tree can start again. Danish dendrologists list it on their national register under the name everyone else uses: Suttetræet, the pacifier tree.

That register entry is unusual for what it leaves out. Every other tree recorded in Frederiksberg Have carries a height, a girth, often a planting year. This one carries none of them. Nobody has measured it and nobody has dated it, so read any age attached to this tree as a guess rather than a measurement. It is a mature garden hornbeam. That is the whole of what is known.

Which is rather the point. Carpinus betulus is the workhorse of formal European gardens, planted by the thousand for its density and its patience under the shears, and Frederiksberg Have has been royal ground since about 1700 and a romantic landscape park since its rebuilding between 1798 and 1804. The garden's history is documented down to the decade. The tree's is not. What it has instead is twenty-two years of small plastic objects and a steady supply of three-year-olds making a decision.

Come in autumn if you want to see it fully loaded. The November harvest clears it back to bare branches.

trees.name: The Sky-Reacher of Assistens
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 5-7 minute walk
trees.story:
Skyrækker, the Danish name for this species, means sky-reacher. At 15.5 metres this one does not out-top the big beeches and maples around it, but at 4.01 metres round it is the largest exotic tree the Danish Dendrological Society registered inside these cemetery walls, and the only Ailanthus they found here at all.

It also comes with an open question. The surveyors who measured it in November 2019 logged its condition as levende, svag: alive, but weak. They noted severe bark scraping low on the western side of the trunk, the kind of injury that interrupts the traffic between roots and crown. Nothing found since updates that note, so what stands behind this entry is one careful observation now about seven years old. If you go and find it changed, tell us.

No source gives its age either. Somewhere between sixty and a hundred and twenty years is an inference from girth alone, not a record.

Ailanthus altissima reached Europe from China in the eighteenth century as a fashionable exotic and is now better known for pushing up through railway ballast and cracked concrete anywhere it can get a root down. This one was planted on purpose, in a cemetery that collected rarities, and the handkerchief tree and the ginkgo a few paths away come from the same appetite. Assistens works as a public park as much as a burial ground, and that collection is a large part of why.

trees.name: Skovfogedegen
trees.access: Free, no ticket. Stands on public ground beside the road Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), opposite Bellevue Strand. Open at all times.
trees.transport: Klampenborg is roughly 10.9 km north of central Copenhagen. S-train line C (Kystbanen) from Copenhagen Central to Klampenborg station, about 16-20 minutes, then about 8 minutes on foot north along Strandvejen to the tree.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the hollow trunk and low crooked frame read clearly

trees.story:
Ten metres and 42 centimetres around, and empty in the middle. Skovfogedegen has lost its entire heartwood to rot, which an oak can survive: water and sugars travel in the thin growing layer just under the bark, so a hollow trunk is a shell that still works. Three dated Danish sources put the tree here since around the year 1200: the national encyclopedia, the historical-sites database Historisk Atlas, and a 2025 feature in the newspaper Kristeligt Dagblad. That makes it roughly 800 years old, and by a wide margin the oldest and thickest tree on this list. One untraced web page gives 500 years instead. Nothing stands behind it, and the three that agree are dated and named.

The hollow has been put to use. Johan Georg Weissler, a Catholic forest ranger who died in 1854, used the cavity as a private prayer chamber in the early 1800s, and skovfoged, forest ranger, is where the tree's name comes from. At other times the hole held peat.

The Danish Dendrological Society measured it at 12.9 metres tall and logged it living but weak in 2010. A photograph taken in March 2025 shows the same hollow trunk still standing. It is not a city tree: it grows beside the road Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, 11 km north of Copenhagen, opposite Bellevue Strand.

trees.name: Klopstocks Eg
trees.access: Free, no ticket. Stands right beside Prinsessestien, a public path through Lyngby Aamose along Molleaadalen. Legally protected (fredet) since 1956, with a memorial plaque added in 1984, so a public authority has long treated it as open ground for visitors.
trees.transport: Kongens Lyngby is roughly 11.9 km northwest of central Copenhagen. S-train to Sorgenfri station (about 22-24 minutes from Copenhagen H), then about 15 minutes on foot west along Prinsessestien through Lyngby Aamose to the tree.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Denmark protected this oak by law in 1956 and still cannot date it within four centuries. The Danish Dendrological Society's register gives 800 years as a maximum rather than an estimate, which is a different kind of number: the most the tree could be, not the best guess at what it is. So the range here runs from 400 to 800 years, and nobody has narrowed it.

What has been measured: 6.05 metres round, 1.93 metres through, alive at the last field report. A storm in 2013 broke off a large branch and the tree carried on without further loss.

The name belongs to Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock, the German poet who came to Denmark in 1751 at the invitation of Frederik V, stayed twenty years, and spent his summers at Gramlille on Lyngby Hovedgade, a short walk from here. Nothing is recorded about what he did under this particular tree. It carries his name the way a street does, by association with the neighbourhood he lived in. It has also been called Monrads Eg, after D.G. Monrad. A memorial plaque went up in 1984.

The oak stands right beside Prinsessestien, a public path through Lyngby Aamose in the Molleaadalen valley, about 12 km northwest of Copenhagen and a quarter of an hour on foot from Sorgenfri station.

trees.name: Englaenderegen
trees.access: Free, no ticket, and marked wheelchair-accessible on the Nature Agency's own listing. Stands in the open deer park of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, a public UNESCO-listed royal hunting landscape with no gates or opening hours beyond dusk closing for cars.
trees.transport: Central Copenhagen to Dyrehaven's edge is roughly 12.6 km. S-train line C to Klampenborg station (about 16-20 minutes from Copenhagen Central), then a walk of roughly 35-40 minutes through the deer park, past Eremitageslottet, to reach Magasindammen; this tree sits deeper into the park than the entrance, so the walk-in is the honest, longer part of the trip.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
This oak was dying, and treasure hunters saved it by accident. Generations of digging around its roots broke up the packed soil and let air back in, which is what the Danish Dendrological Society's register credits with its recovery. Nobody was trying to help the tree. They were looking for a chest of money.

The name, Englaenderegen, the Englishman's oak, comes from the British siege of Copenhagen in 1807. Two soldiers, tired of service, are said to have stolen their regiment's pay chest and buried it beside a freestanding oak northeast of the Hermitage. Neither came back for it, and one confessed on his deathbed to a priest. Searches followed for over a hundred years, including one made at the request of Queen Victoria, and nothing has ever been found. The chest is legend. The holes were real, and they are the part that mattered.

The register measures the trunk at 5.46 metres round and 1.74 metres through, and dates it at 240 to 360 years using a growth formula applied to 1995 measurements, which puts it at roughly 270 to 390 now. It stands by the pond Magasindammen in Jaegersborg Dyrehave, the royal deer park north of Copenhagen, and the Nature Agency marks the site wheelchair accessible. Getting there is the long part: 35 to 40 minutes on foot from Klampenborg station, past Eremitageslottet.

trees.name: The Witch's Yew
trees.access: Paid entry (Blarney Castle & Gardens ticket)
trees.transport: Bus 215 from Cork bus station to Blarney, about 30 min, then a short walk

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: In 2019 the Irish public voted this yew the country's Tree of the Year, and the next spring 11,372 Europeans backed it for the European title. What they were voting for is a tree growing where no tree should: straight out of the top of a limestone outcrop in the Rock Close, the strangest corner of the Blarney Castle gardens. Experts put it at more than 600 years, older than the designed landscape around it and roughly contemporary with the 1446 castle keep that most visitors climb without noticing it. When the Jeffreyes family laid out the Rock Close in the 1750s they built a folly called the Witch's Kitchen directly beneath the yew, treating a tree already centuries old as ready-made scenery. Legend houses the Blarney Witch here: she is said to have been the first to tell mortals what kissing the Blarney Stone actually does, and to be locked inside the nearby Witch Stone by day, free only after dark. Entry to the gardens is paid, but the one ticket covers the stone, the castle and this tree, and only the tree was alive in the Middle Ages.

trees.name: The Great Western Red Cedar of Blarney
trees.access: Paid entry (Blarney Castle & Gardens ticket)
trees.transport: Bus 215 from Cork bus station to Blarney, about 30 min, then a short walk
trees.story: The estate calls this the most photographed tree in its gardens, which is a serious claim on grounds that also hold a medieval yew and the Blarney Stone. The reason is the shape. The trunk divides low and its limbs run out sideways, each one thicker than most full-grown trees, so the whole plant reads less like a conifer than a wooden octopus caught mid-stride. Children understand it instantly; the low wooden fence around it exists because everyone's first instinct is to climb. In its native Pacific Northwest a Western Red Cedar grows as a straight sixty-metre rainforest column, and the totem poles and canoes of the coastal First Nations were carved from its trunks. Planted here in the early 1900s by the estate's own record, this one chose width over height, and a century of soft Irish rain has clearly agreed with it. The estate has put a small species board at its base, a landowner explicitly inviting visitors to come and stand under it, which is exactly what you should do: the view from inside the canopy, surrounded by rising limbs, is the best in the gardens.

photo.attribution: Marathon, via geograph.org.uk and Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Boole Library Redwoods
trees.access: Free, open campus
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Grand Parade; buses along Western Road
trees.story: The tallest trees on University College Cork's campus were paid for with beer. William Crawford of the Beamish & Crawford brewery, one of the young college's great benefactors, donated the pair of Giant Redwoods that now stand 27 and 29 metres above the Boole Library, and at roughly 150 years old they have barely started: in California's Sierra Nevada the species passes 2,000 years and 80 metres. They are the obvious landmarks of a campus that is quietly one of Ireland's best tree collections, planted continuously since the college opened in 1849 and accredited as an arboretum by the international ArbNet programme in 2020, around 2,500 trees of some 120 species. The library beneath them is named for George Boole, the college's first professor of mathematics, whose two-value algebra now runs inside every computer on the desks inside. Students cram under trees that will outlive everything they are studying, and the university runs public tours of the campus trees led by its own plant scientists. Free, open to any walker, and fifteen minutes on foot from Grand Parade.

trees.name: The Monterey Pine at the Gates
trees.access: Free, open campus
trees.transport: Buses along Western Road; 15 min walk from Grand Parade
trees.story: Every graduation procession through University College Cork's ceremonial Western Road gates since 1929 has walked beneath this pine, which makes it the most photobombed tree in Cork: it stands in the background of a century of family photographs without ever being the subject. The species has one of the strangest stories in forestry. In the wild the Monterey Pine survives on a few kilometres of Californian coast and two Mexican islands, and is formally listed as endangered there, yet planted forestry made it one of the most cultivated trees on earth, the backbone of timber industries from New Zealand to Chile and a fair share of Ireland's own plantations. So the endangered Californian at the front gates is also a quiet joke about globalisation, thriving further from home than almost any tree on campus. UCC's arboretum staff list it among their top ten campus trees for the way its dark, wind-shaped crown frames the entrance. It is free to see at any hour, on the main bus corridor into the city, and the gates beside it are the best-looking way to enter the campus arboretum anyway.

trees.name: The 1870 Magnolia of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk

best_time.label: late February into March, when huge pink cups open on bare branches

trees.story: For about ten days in late winter this tree does something almost nothing else in Ireland can: it covers itself in rose-pink flowers the size of dinner plates while its branches are still completely bare. Campbell's Magnolia flowers before it leafs, and it needs decades of growth before it starts, which is why the great specimens are all in old gardens. Fota's was grown from seed collected near Darjeeling in the Himalayan foothills and planted in 1870, six years before the celebrated tree at Kilmacurragh in Wicklow that usually gets the attention. It stands in an arboretum the Smith-Barry family built across three generations, starting in the 1820s, on an island in Cork Harbour whose frost-free air let them grow things the rest of Ireland could not; the collection around the magnolia runs from Chilean conifers to Japanese cedars. The Office of Public Works keeps the arboretum free to enter, and the train from Cork's Kent Station reaches Fota in thirteen minutes. Time the trip for the flowers if you can. An 1870 magnolia in full February bloom is worth rearranging a week around.

trees.name: The Cappadocian Maple of Blarney
trees.access: Paid entry (Blarney Castle & Gardens ticket)
trees.transport: Bus 215 from Cork bus station to Blarney, about 30 min, then a short walk

best_time.label: October, when it turns a pure, saturated gold

trees.story:
This maple comes from the mountains around Cappadocia in central Turkey and the Caucasus beyond it, a long way from the limestone and yew of the Blarney gardens it has spent a century in. The National Biodiversity Data Centre's 2009 heritage tree survey lists it among the estate's exceptional specimens, aged to somewhere between one and one and a half centuries, without recording who planted it or why.

The species is a close relative of the Norway maple, and the giveaway is the same: snap a leaf stalk and the sap that beads up is milky white rather than clear. Its autumn colour is the real reason gardeners plant it far from home. Where a sugar maple goes red, Acer cappadocicum turns a pure, saturated gold, holding the colour for weeks longer than most maples before it drops.

It shares the wider Blarney grounds with the Witch's Yew and the Great Western Red Cedar, both already well documented; this maple has had no such attention. The heritage tree register is the only source that has looked at it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

trees.name: The Beech of Blarney
trees.access: Paid entry (Blarney Castle & Gardens ticket)
trees.transport: Bus 215 from Cork bus station to Blarney, about 30 min, then a short walk
trees.story:
The national heritage tree survey rates this beech among Blarney's exceptional specimens, alongside the more famous yew and cedar, and puts it at somewhere between 150 and 200 years old, which would make it a near contemporary of the Rock Close's Witch's Kitchen folly rather than of the medieval castle itself.

A beech left alone for that long builds a dome-shaped crown wide enough to shade the ground beneath it into permanent twilight, which is why almost nothing grows under a mature beech but the beech's own fallen leaves, slow to rot and thick enough to smother competitors. Its bark stays smooth its whole life, grey and almost elephantine, unlike the cracked and plated bark most trees this old develop, and generations of visitors carving initials into it are why old beeches so often carry scars that never grow over.

What sets this one apart from the estate's other specimens has not been written down anywhere the register can point to. It stands somewhere in the wider Blarney gardens, and the heritage register is the only source describing it. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk
trees.story:
Crush a leaf from this tree and it releases the smell the whole species is named for: camphor, the same compound once distilled from it for mothballs, chest rubs and embalming. It is a subtropical evergreen from southern China, Taiwan and Japan, and it has no business surviving outdoors in Ireland at all. It survives here because Fota Island sits in Cork Harbour with a frost-free microclimate that the Smith-Barry family exploited for three generations, from the 1820s onward, planting things nowhere else in the country could keep alive.

The national heritage tree survey bands its age to 50 to 100 years, decades younger than the arboretum around it, and lists nothing more about how it got here. Every part of the tree, bark, wood, leaf and root, carries the same aromatic oil, which is also why camphor trees resist insects and rot better than almost anything else in a temperate garden that was never built to hold them.

The register is the only source that has described this specific tree. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

trees.name: The Spiral Cedar of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk
trees.story:
Every needle on this conifer grows in a tight curl instead of lying flat, a Victorian nursery mutation known in the trade as Granny's Ringlets long before anyone wrote down which nursery found it first. The whole tree reads from a distance as an ordinary Japanese cedar wearing a bad perm, and up close each curled needle turns out to be a single leaf twisted almost into a full loop.

The national heritage tree survey classes it among the estate's arboricultural curiosities rather than its exceptional specimens, which is the register's own way of saying it is here to be strange rather than to be huge, and bands its age to 100 to 150 years, planted around the time Fota's collection was at its Victorian height.

Ordinary Cryptomeria japonica is Japan's national tree, planted by the million as timber and temple avenue trees across the country; this cultivar exists purely as a curiosity, propagated by cutting because a seed would not reliably grow the twist back into the next generation. The register is the only source describing this specimen. If you know its planting date, tell us.

trees.name: The Canary Palm of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk
trees.story:
A palm tree growing outdoors on an island in Cork Harbour, at the same latitude as Newfoundland, is the clearest single demonstration of what the Gulf Stream does for this stretch of Irish coast. Phoenix canariensis comes from the Canary Islands, off the coast of Morocco, and it tolerates an occasional light frost but nothing like an ordinary Irish winter further from the sea. Fota's frost-free microclimate, the same one that let the Smith-Barry family plant camphor trees and holm oaks here across three generations from the 1820s, is the only reason this specimen has a trunk at all rather than having died back to the roots decades ago.

The national heritage tree survey bands it to 100 to 150 years old, which for a palm growing this far outside its comfort zone is a genuinely long survival. A mature specimen carries a crown of stiff, grey-green fronds up to six metres long, and the trunk thickens with a diamond pattern of old leaf-base scars that never smooths out.

The register is the only source describing it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

trees.name: The Celery Pine of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk
trees.story:
This conifer has no true leaves. What looks like foliage is flattened stem tissue, called a cladode, doing photosynthesis in place of leaves the plant never bothers to grow, and in this species the cladodes are notched and lobed enough to look uncannily like celery leaves, which is where the English name comes from. The Maori name, tanekaha, belongs to the same tree in its native New Zealand, where its reddish bark was once stripped for a red-brown dye and its timber prized for being straight-grained and durable.

The national heritage tree survey classes it, fairly, among the estate's arboricultural curiosities, and bands its age to 50 to 100 years. It is one of the odder choices in a collection the Smith-Barry family built across three generations from the 1820s onward, expressly to grow plants nothing else in Ireland could support, and a New Zealand conifer that photosynthesises without leaves fits that brief exactly.

The register is the only source describing this specimen. If you know more about it, tell us.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk
trees.story:
This is the oldest tree the national heritage survey found at Fota, banded to 200 to 300 years, which would put its planting close to when the arboretum's grounds were still ordinary farmland, decades before the Smith-Barry family began building their tree collection here in the 1820s.

Holm oak is a Mediterranean evergreen, dark and dense-leaved, holly-like enough at a glance that its name and the English word holly share the same root. It tolerates salt spray and coastal wind better than almost any other oak, which is exactly the pressure Fota Island sits under in Cork Harbour, and that tolerance is likely the plain reason it has outlasted collection trees planted a century after it.

The survey also noted fungal growth on this specimen, unremarkable in itself: a two or three hundred year old tree carries decades of dead wood inside it, and fungi feeding on that wood are part of how a veteran tree ages rather than a sign it is failing. The register is the only source that has looked at it closely. If you know its actual planting date, tell us.

trees.name: The Coast Redwood of Fota
trees.access: Free (paid parking); Apr-Oct 9:00-18:00, Nov-Mar 9:00-17:00
trees.transport: Train from Cork Kent to Fota, 13 min, then a 10 min walk
trees.story:
In its native range along the California and Oregon coast, Sequoia sempervirens is the tallest tree species on earth, and specimens there run past a hundred metres and two thousand years old. Fota's, banded by the national heritage tree survey to 150 to 200 years, is a child by comparison, planted not long after the species reached European gardens through Victorian plant collecting in the 1840s and 50s.

The species does well in Ireland's wet, mild climate for the same reason it does well on the fog-soaked Pacific coast: a coast redwood pulls a large share of its water straight out of humid air through its needles rather than relying on roots alone, which is part of why it can grow so fast and so tall. Fota's frost-free microclimate, the one the Smith-Barry family built their whole collection around from the 1820s, is generous even by Irish standards, and this tree has had a century and a half of it.

The register is the only source describing this specimen, distinct from University College Cork's own pair of giant sequoias in the city. If you know when it went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Olive Tree of Vouves
trees.age: contested: at least 2,000 years, possibly up to 4,000
trees.neighbourhood: Ano Vouves village, next to the Olive Tree Museum of Vouves
trees.access: Paid entry through the small Olive Tree Museum of Vouves beside the tree, historically a nominal fee of a euro or two, though some recent visitors report no charge. Museum open daily 10:00-19:00 from April to October, by appointment from November to March. Signposted, and no permission is needed.
trees.transport: No public transport nearby. A car is the realistic way: roughly 25 minutes from Kolymvari and about 40 minutes from Chania.

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story:
Two sets of scientists have dated this olive and their answers differ by two thousand years. Ring analysis by Oliver Rackham and Jennifer Moody, published in 1996, established a floor and no more: at least 2,000 years old. Scientists at the University of Crete have since put it at 4,000, a figure now repeated from the Greek press to Forbes, and one that would make it the oldest living olive known anywhere. Neither number can be checked. The tree's heartwood rotted away centuries ago, which is what happens to ancient olives rather than a fault in this one, and it removes the material any dating method needs. English Wikipedia's summary is blunt: the exact age cannot be determined, and there is no agreed scientific method for dating olive trees at all.

The trunk is not in dispute. It measures 12.5 metres around and 4.6 metres across, hollowed into a twisting shell with the grain running in curves. The tree still fruits, grafted with the Tsounati cultivar, and the Region of Crete declared it a protected natural monument in 1997. Branches from it were woven into victory wreaths at the Athens Olympics in 2004 and Beijing in 2008. Two Geometric-period cemeteries were found nearby, which tells you people were here three thousand years ago and nothing whatsoever about the tree.

trees.name: The Olive Tree of Azoria (Kavousi)
trees.access: Free, publicly signposted ('Old Olive Tree' / palia elia signs from the east entrance of Kavousi). It stands beside a public road next to the Azoria archaeological site, and no permission is needed.
trees.transport: No public transport. A car is the realistic way: about 1 km south of Kavousi village, roughly 20 minutes from Ierapetra and about an hour from Agios Nikolaos.

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story:
Somebody grafted this tree in the Bronze Age and it is still carrying the join. The crown you look at is a mouratoelia, a local eating cultivar, growing on a wild olive rootstock underneath, and Greek and international sources describe it as the oldest known example of olive grafting anywhere in the world. That claim is repeated everywhere and traced to no single paper, so take it as the consensus rather than a citation.

The age is firmer than that, and firmer than Crete's more famous olive in the west. Ring analysis reported by the municipality of Ierapetra dates the planting to between 1350 and 1100 BCE, putting the tree somewhere around 3,000 to 3,400 years old, and the press has settled on about 3,250. One method, one range, and the sources agree with each other, which is not something the olive at Vouves can offer.

It stands about a kilometre south of Kavousi on the road toward Avgos, beside the excavated settlement of Azoria that gives it its name, signposted from the eastern entrance of the village as the old olive. The trunk runs 14.2 metres around and 4.9 metres across. It still bears fruit. Branches from it made the winner's wreath for the women's marathon at the Athens Olympics in 2004, and Greece has declared it a protected monument of nature.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Krasi
trees.neighbourhood: the village square, beside the stone spring-fountain
trees.access: Free. It stands in the open village square at Krasi, about 600 m above sea level, beside the stone fountain that still runs all year. Tavernas sit under the canopy, so the square is in daily use rather than fenced off.
trees.transport: Krasi is roughly 12 km inland from Malia on the Heraklion coast, up the road towards the Lasithi plateau. A car is the realistic way; the tree is in the village square and cannot be missed.
trees.story:
The trunk measures roughly 24 metres around, which is among the largest recorded for a plane tree in Europe. Local practice turns that number straight into an age: each metre of perimeter is said to stand for a century, so the village puts the tree at 2,400 years. That is arithmetic performed on a tape measure rather than evidence about the tree, and it is worth saying why the sum is unsafe here in particular. Oriental planes regenerate from the root. A stool this size can be many centuries of renewal rather than one stem that has lived continuously since antiquity, so a vast perimeter is not the same thing as a vast age. Nobody has dated this one. If you know of a study that has, tell us.

What the tree unarguably is: the centre of Krasi, a village 600 metres up on the road from Malia toward the Lasithi plateau. It grows in the Megali Vrisi square beside a stone fountain that still runs all year, and the tavernas put their tables under the canopy, so the square works as a room with a roof rather than a monument behind a rope. Sources report it as a proclaimed monument of nature; the declaring instrument itself was not traced. In a Cretan July, the shade is the whole argument.

trees.name: The Evergreen Plane of Gortyn
trees.neighbourhood: at the back of the archaeological site, near the Odeon and the Law Code
trees.access: Paid entry to the Gortyn archaeological site, open daylight hours. The tree stands at the back of the enclosure, near the Odeon and the Law Code, rather than by the entrance, so plan on buying a ticket.
trees.transport: Gortyn lies beside the old national road at Agioi Deka, about 45 km south of Heraklion in the Messara plain. A car, or the Heraklion to Mires bus; the site entrance is on the main road.
trees.story:
Every other oriental plane on Crete is bare in January. This one is not. The tree at Gortyn is Platanus orientalis var. cretica, an evergreen form of a deciduous species, reported from perhaps fifty places on the island and from almost nowhere else, and it holds its leaves straight through the winter. That is the reason to walk to the back of the archaeological site, and it is a better reason than the one the guidebooks give.

The guidebook reason is Europa. Gortyn is where Zeus, in the shape of a bull, is said to have carried her, and their union under a plane tree is stamped on the city's own ancient coins. That story belongs to the place and not to this trunk, and nothing connects the two. Read the coins as evidence of how long people here have associated the site with a plane tree, which is genuinely interesting, and not as a birth certificate for the one growing there now.

Nobody has dated it, and there is a botanical reason why nobody easily could. Planes regenerate from the root, so what looks eternal can be a succession of new stems on an old base, and the sources describing this one note that in its present form it is relatively small. It is protected, it is evergreen, and its age is an open question. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Sacred Oak of Theoskepasti
trees.access: Free. Stands in the open yard beside a public chapel next to the UNESCO-listed monastery complex; no permission needed, open in daylight.
trees.transport: No public transport reaches Kalopanagiotis usefully; by car roughly 50 km / 60-70 minutes from Nicosia via the Troodos foothill roads.
trees.story: The chapel next door is named after what this tree is said to have done. Panagia Theoskepasti means God-covered, and the account told in Kalopanagiotis is that the oak's branches spread far enough over the small 12th century chapel to hide it from raiders passing through the Marathasa valley. Tradition rather than record, but it has carried the name for a long time. The tree is a prinos, the Cypriot word for kermes oak, though one account of the site calls it a holm oak instead, a related but different species, and nobody has settled which it is. If you can tell the two apart on sight, tell us. Local tradition puts the oak at roughly 700 years. Every source repeats that figure and none of them measured it, so read it as a claim rather than a count. What is on record is that the Cyprus Department of Forests holds the tree under protection. It stands in the open yard beside the chapel, a few steps from the Agios Ioannis Lampadistis Monastery, which UNESCO listed in 1985 among the Painted Churches of the Troodos Region. Kalopanagiotis sits on the northern flank of Troodos, about an hour of mountain road from Nicosia, and the oak asks nothing of a visitor: no gate, no ticket, daylight hours.

trees.name: The Old Olive Tree of Xyliatos
trees.access: Free, standing in the open in the Potima area of the village; no permission needed.
trees.transport: No useful public transport; by car roughly 25 km / 35-40 minutes from Nicosia, in the Troodos foothills near the Xyliatos dam and forest.

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: This olive is wider around than it is tall. Thirteen metres of trunk circumference against a height of about six, which is roughly what an olive does when it is given enough centuries: the trunk splits, hollows and fuses back on itself while the crown stays low and hard. It is held to be the largest-girth olive on Cyprus, and the oldest. How old is exactly the argument. The Xyliatos Community Council, which campaigned to have the tree protected, says about 1,700 years. A Cypriot tourism site says 800. Neither shows any working, no ring count and no growth-rate calculation, and olives are close to impossible to date anyway, because the old heartwood rots out and leaves nothing continuous to read. Both figures are received, so the honest answer is the range. What is documented is 2004, the year the Department of Forests placed the tree under protection after the council pressed for it. On the council's figure the olive was already old under Byzantine rule and would have stood through Richard the Lionheart's sale of the island in 1191, the Lusignan and Venetian centuries and three hundred years of Ottoman administration. On the tourism figure it starts around that same 1191. It grows in the open at Potima, a named spot in the village, in the foothills near the Xyliatos dam.

trees.name: The Ancient Laurel of Apostle Philip
trees.age: roughly 1,000 years by one source, only 'a few centuries' by another
trees.access: Free, standing beside a small rural chapel in the open countryside; no permission needed. Reached by an unpaved/minor road about 3 km west of Omodos village; no gate or restriction mentioned by either source.
trees.transport: No public transport; by car about 3 km from Omodos village (itself roughly 55 km / 60-75 minutes from Limassol), on rural roads.
trees.story: Bay laurel is the herb in the kitchen cupboard, usually a shrub and rarely a tree of any size. This one is eight metres around. It stands at Pente Litharia, Five Rocks, about three kilometres west of Omodos down a minor road, beside the oldest of that village's country churches, the Chapel of Apostle Philip. How old the laurel is depends on who is asked, and the two answers are far apart. A Limassol heritage site calls it roughly 1,000 years. Omodos's own village site will say only that it is a few centuries. Neither counts rings, so the vaguer figure stays vague here rather than being sharpened into the flattering one. Local tradition holds that the site was a shrine to Apollo before it was Christianised, and points at the laurel as what survived the change, laurel being the tree sacred to Apollo in Greek myth. Both accounts repeat that story and neither is archaeology. What is dated is the building: the chapel was renovated in 1773. Height is given as 17 metres on one page and 10 metres on another from the same source, so take the crown as tall rather than measured. It stands in open country with no gate, no ticket and nobody to ask, which is roughly how it has been since somebody first decided this spot was worth a chapel.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Ayia Mavri
trees.age: roughly 800 years by two sources, 1,200 by a third
trees.neighbourhood: Between Koilani and Pera Pedi, Krasochoria wine region
trees.access: Free, standing in the open beside a small rural riverside chapel; no permission needed. Reached by the road connecting Koilani and Pera Pedi villages.
trees.transport: No public transport; by car about 30 km / 40-45 minutes from Limassol, in the Krasochoria wine-village region of the Troodos foothills.
trees.story: Cyprus put this tree on a postage stamp. The national post office's Centennial Trees of Cyprus series records the Oriental plane at Ayia Mavri as about 800 years old, with a trunk 8.20 metres round and a crown reaching 38 metres, and notes that it was formally designated for protection in 2004. A Limassol heritage survey, working from its own measurements, gives the same age and close to the same figures, 8 metres and 36. A third Cypriot site says 1,200 years instead and offers no measurements at all, so the age sits between two sources that agree and one that does not. Planes want their feet wet, which explains the address: the bank of the Kryos river, beside the small Ayia Mavri chapel, on the road linking Koilani to Pera Pedi through the Krasochoria, the wine villages of the southern Troodos. Platanus orientalis is the eastern Mediterranean's own plane, the species that shades village squares from Greece to Anatolia and one parent of the London plane that later took over northern European cities. On the lower estimate this tree was already growing when the Lusignan kings ruled Cyprus, and it has stood through the Venetian, Ottoman and British administrations since. Free, open, and about forty minutes of hill road from Limassol.

trees.name: The Line-of-Sight Oak
trees.access: Free, a public city park (Dealey Plaza), open at all times
trees.transport: DART West End station, about 5-8 minute walk
trees.story:
The shots fired at President Kennedy on 22 November 1963 passed through this canopy. The limousine came out from behind the tree on Elm Street, and the live oak has stood over that spot ever since. It is the most photographed patch of ground in America and hardly anyone looks at the trees.

The Texas Historic Tree Coalition named this one the line-of-sight tree when it declared the Dealey Plaza grove historic on 6 November 1999, and measured it the same day: 30 feet tall, a crown spreading 60 feet, a trunk 97 inches round. The grove went in with the plaza itself in the late 1930s, which puts these oaks a little short of ninety years, young for this list and full grown by 1963. Ten wide, low-branched live oaks stood in the plaza on the day, and live oaks stand there now.

Dealey Plaza was made a National Historic Landmark District in 1993. The trees got a designation of their own six years later, which is rare: historic sites usually protect the buildings and leave the planting to take its chances. No source publishes a coordinate for the tree, so the pin marks the pergola end of the plaza rather than the trunk. The plaza is small enough that this costs you nothing.

trees.name: The Grassy Knoll Oak
trees.access: Free, a public city park (Dealey Plaza), open at all times
trees.transport: DART West End station, about 5-8 minute walk
trees.story:
The grassy knoll is a slope with oaks on it, which is the part the photographs never quite show. This is the largest of them, and the largest of the three trees measured by name when the Texas Historic Tree Coalition declared the Dealey Plaza grove historic on 6 November 1999: 40 feet tall, a crown spreading 96 feet, a trunk 125 inches round.

The knoll is the low rise on the north side of Elm Street, and it is one of the most argued-over pieces of ground in the country. Some witnesses to the shooting of 22 November 1963 believed a shot came from behind the picket fence at the top of it. Police who went up there found no gunman. The oak was already a broad tree by then, planted with the rest of the grove in the late 1930s when the plaza was laid out.

What you get standing here is the geometry that every account of that afternoon argues about, at ground level, in the shade of a tree that was in the frame. The line-of-sight oak is a minute away across Elm Street. No tree-level coordinate exists, so the pin marks the knoll itself, which is a compact and unmistakable landform: walk up the slope to the fence and you are there.

trees.name: The W.W. Glover Cemetery Post Oak
trees.access: Free, a public pioneer cemetery on a one-acre plot at 6650 Military Parkway; volunteer-maintained and generally visitable, guided tours can be arranged via cemetery@dallascounty.org
trees.transport: No nearby DART rail station; nearest is a car or rideshare, roughly 15 minutes from downtown Dallas
trees.story:
The biggest post oak in Dallas County stands in a one-acre pioneer cemetery on Military Parkway, and nobody has dated it. The Texas Big Tree Registry put a tape around it on 10 September 2020 and recorded 166 inches of circumference, 50 feet of height and a 49 foot spread, which makes it the county champion of its species.

It shares the plot with more than seventy graves from the settlement era. George W. Glover acquired the land in 1844 and deeded it to his son William Wald Glover in 1872. The first burial was in 1857, a five year old called Sarah Beeman. The last was in 1951, after which the place went quiet and the oak carried on. Volunteers maintain it now, and a Texas historical marker stands at the gate.

Post oaks are slow growers with hard, dense wood, which is why they turn up as the oldest thing left standing on ground that has been farmed, grazed and built over. This one is thicker than any other recorded in the county, and no source gives it a year. If you know when it went in, or you have a tape measure and half an hour, tell us and we will put a number on this page. The register's own coordinate places the tree, so the pin is good.

trees.name: The Bur Oak at Big Spring
trees.neighbourhood: Pleasant Grove / Pemberton Hill, Great Trinity Forest
trees.access: Free, a public city-owned nature preserve in the Great Trinity Forest; park near the Texas Horse Park entrance, 811 Pemberton Hill Road
trees.transport: No nearby DART rail; nearest is a car or rideshare, roughly 15-20 minutes from downtown Dallas
trees.story:
Sam Houston camped at this spring in the summer of 1843 with his Indian treaty delegation, and by the account of the arborists who later dated it, the bur oak beside the water was already about sixty years old. That was two years before Texas joined the union and while Dallas was a cabin and a ferry crossing.

The Texas Historic Tree Coalition made it an Official Historic Tree on 29 March 2014 and gathered its figures the same day: over 235 years old, 60 feet tall, a 65 foot crown, a trunk 47 inches through, so roughly twelve feet round. Add the decade since and it is closing on 250.

Big Spring is a natural spring in the Great Trinity Forest and one of the first places in the area that European settlers claimed, taken in 1842 by John Beeman, whose daughter Margaret married the founder of Dallas the following year. The city bought the spring and its bottomlands in 2003 and in 2016 made the surrounding fifteen acres a historic overlay district, the first time Dallas used that protection for a piece of ground rather than a building.

Park at the Texas Horse Park entrance on Pemberton Hill Road. The pin marks the preserve rather than the trunk, so expect to walk and look.

trees.name: The Centennial Tree
trees.access: Free, a public city park (Reverchon Park), open daily
trees.transport: DART Cityplace/Uptown or Katy Trail area; roughly 10-15 minute walk from the nearest DART rail stop, easier by bike or car
trees.story:
This bur oak was already a mature tree when John Neely Bryan turned up in 1841 and founded the city. The estimate is over 250 years, which puts its start in the 1770s, when the nearest thing to Dallas was a Caddo trail. It stands about 70 feet tall with a trunk roughly sixteen feet round.

It got its name in 1936, when a celebration for the centennial of Texan independence from Mexico was held at the tree rather than at any building, and it has been the Centennial Tree ever since. In 2015 the city gave it formal protection under its historic tree programme, so the oak now outranks most of what is built around it in Reverchon Park.

The age is worth reading carefully. It comes from one arborists' assessment rather than a ring count, and nobody has cored it. A bur oak with a sixteen foot waist is entirely consistent with two and a half centuries, and this species routinely gets there, but treat the number as a good estimate and not a measurement.

Reverchon Park runs down a slope off Maple Avenue near the Katy Trail. The pin marks the park rather than the trunk, so allow a few minutes of looking once you are inside the gates.

trees.name: The West Dallas Gateway Pecan
trees.access: Free, standing on public right-of-way/parkland at a city street intersection, visible and reachable at all times
trees.transport: No nearby DART rail station; nearest is a car, bike or rideshare, roughly 10 minutes from downtown Dallas across the Commerce Street bridge
trees.story:
This pecan was standing at the Trinity crossing before anyone built a bridge over it. The first one went up in 1855, and the Texas Historic Tree Coalition dates the tree to more than 175 years, roughly the age of Dallas itself.

From that corner it watched the last bison herds and the men who shot them, then the cattle drives north on the Shawnee Trail, then a century of traffic that ended with a six-lane intersection at its feet. It sat in the Trinity floodplain through the floods of 1866, 1871, 1890 and 1908. In 2009 the city planned to redesign the intersection and the tree was in the way; a neighbour, Katherine Homan, ran a campaign that saved it. It has since lost three major limbs and been hit by vehicles more than once, and it is still in leaf. In 2023 it got a permanent designation plaque, which is a modest reward for surviving everything else.

Nobody has published a girth for it. If you get a tape around that trunk, send us the number.

The pin sits at the Beckley Avenue end of the Commerce Street bridge, on the south side of the junction, which is where the tree stands. Come by bike or car; there is no rail stop nearby.

trees.name: The Ferris Plaza Live Oaks
trees.access: Free, a small public plaza (0.9 acres) in downtown Dallas, open at all times
trees.transport: DART Union Station / West End station, about 2-3 minute walk (Ferris Plaza sits directly across from Union Station)
trees.story:
In 1998 the city and the corporation across the street proposed removing 21 mature live oaks from this plaza, by most accounts to move a roost of grackles along with them. Arborists, the Texas Historic Tree Coalition and the mayor stopped it. Nineteen of the oaks are still here and the plan is not.

This is a grove rather than one tree: nineteen live oaks ringing a single fountain in a plaza of nine tenths of an acre. The fountain is the place to stand, and it puts several of them over your head at once. The largest trunk in the group runs to about eleven feet round; across the grove the trunks average roughly 30 inches through, from 21 up to 36. They reach about 50 feet. The tree coalition dates the present grove to a replanting in 1949 and 1950, which period photographs of the plaza confirm, so call them 75 years old.

Ferris Plaza itself is older and was the front door of Dallas, laid out under George Kessler's city plan directly opposite Union Station, a decade before Dealey Plaza existed two blocks away. It is named for Royal A. Ferris, who paid for the fountain. In 1965 more than 2,000 people assembled under these trees for a march led by the NAACP in support of the voting rights protests at Selma.

trees.name: The Moore Park Big Tree Grove
trees.access: Free, a public city park (Moore Park), open at all times
trees.transport: No nearby DART rail station; nearest is a car, bike or rideshare, roughly 10 minutes from downtown Dallas

best_time.label: October and November, when the pecans come down

trees.story:
Moore Park was created in 1938 as one of only five parks Dallas set aside for its Black residents, and renamed two years later, at a Juneteenth ceremony, for the civil rights leader Will Moore. The trees on the creek bank were there before either date.

About sixteen old trees stand on the south bank of Cedar Creek near its confluence with the Trinity, less than two miles from downtown. Mostly pecans, with a bur oak and a bois d'arc among them, though the sources disagree on the exact count and the mix. They disagree on the age too. The tree coalition's record from the designation day in November 2023 gives 155 to 190 years; its own text elsewhere on the same page says at least 150; a Texas conservation news site covering the same event reports at least 125 and possibly older. The honest span is roughly 125 to 190. The older end of that puts the grove here before John McClannahan Crockett, the second mayor of Dallas, bought the ground in 1869. The younger end does not.

The biggest trunk is given as somewhere between ten and fifteen and a half feet round, and the trees run 70 to 80 feet tall with crowns over 100 feet across. Walk in from East 8th Street and follow the creek; the pin marks the park, not a trunk.

trees.name: The Weichselboom of Parklaan
trees.access: Free, visible from the public street
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
trees.story: The St Lucie Cherry growing against Den Bosch's old city wall on Parklaan is a species most Dutch gardeners have never planted on purpose. Prunus mahaleb is usually grown as rootstock for other cherries, not as a specimen tree in its own right, which is part of why this one, roughly a century old and large enough to be nominated for the Dutch national Bomen Top 50 in 2022, stands out on the municipality's own monumental-tree register. Its Dutch name, Weichselboom, comes from the Weichsel river region further east, where the species is more commonly used for the sour Morello-style cherries that give it its alternative name. Rooted directly against the medieval city wall, the tree has spent its whole life with one side of its root system pressed into centuries-old masonry rather than open soil, a growing condition few trees this size are ever asked to tolerate. The wall itself predates the tree by roughly four centuries, part of the fortifications that once ringed the entire old town before most of it was leveled to regulation height after 1874. Parklaan today is a quiet residential street, and the tree is visible from the pavement without needing to enter anyone's garden.

trees.name: The Norway Maple of Bastion Oranje
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 15-minute walk

best_time.label: October to November: clear yellow, sometimes red

trees.story: This Norway maple grows on top of two-metre-thick fortress walls built in 1634, the year the Dutch States Army needed a new bastion to close a gap in Den Bosch's defences after capturing the city five years earlier. A windmill stood on the bastion for most of its working life; when it came down between 1880 and 1890, landscape architect J.M. Marechal was already laying out the site as one of several former bastions turned into public parks, following the 1874 law that stripped the city's walls of their military status. The municipal tree register puts this maple at roughly 120 years old, the oldest individually measured tree on the bastion today, with a girth over four metres. A second, slightly younger Norway maple grows nearby on the same earthwork, which is likely why older records disagree about which species belongs to which tree here. What both maples share is the ground under them: the earthen rampart that once absorbed cannon fire now just needs mowing, and the Bastionder, an underground exhibition on the city's fortifications, sits below the park the trees grow in.

trees.name: The Plane, Lime and Silver Maple of Bastion Vught
trees.species: London Plane, Large-leaved Lime and Silver Maple (Platanus x hispanica, Tilia platyphyllos, Acer saccharinum)
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
trees.story: Three monumental trees, a plane, a lime and a silver maple, stand within forty metres of each other at Bastion Vught, one of only three bastions to survive from Den Bosch's ring of 17th-century fortifications largely intact. Dutch States Army troops breached this exact stretch of wall during the 1629 siege that ended Spanish control of the city, and the site kept its military role for another two and a half centuries before the 1874 law that downgraded fortifications nationwide reduced the walls and freed the ground for parkland, the same shift that turned Bastion Oranje into a park across town. The three trees now anchor that park. The plane is the largest by trunk girth at just over four metres, the lime is the tallest-claiming of the three by canopy spread, and the silver maple, a species chosen for fast growth rather than longevity, has still reached a comparable size in the same roughly one hundred years. All three are sourced to the municipality's own monumental-tree register rather than a second independent account, honestly flagged here, though the register's coordinates place them precisely on the bastion itself.

trees.name: The Poplar of Zuiderpark
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 20-minute walk or short bus ride
trees.story: At 33 metres, the balsam poplar in Zuiderpark is one of the tallest individually recorded trees in the municipal register covering all of Den Bosch, taller than most of the city's church spires. It predates the park around it by decades: Zuiderpark itself only opened in 1958, and gained a deliberately planted circle of ornamental poplars during a 1993-1999 redesign, but this specific tree, at roughly 90 years old on the register's own count, was already growing here before either the park or its poplar circle existed, a survivor from whatever stood on the site before, rather than a member of the later planting. Balsam poplar is grown more for its resin-scented spring buds than for ornament, the smell carrying across a park on a warm day before anyone spots the tree responsible. No second source beyond the register documents this specific poplar's history, an honest gap rather than a missing footnote, but its height and girth are themselves a verifiable record, not a claim resting on memory or estimate.

trees.name: The Plane of Sint Janskerkhof
trees.access: Free, public square beside the Sint-Jan cathedral
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 14-minute walk
trees.story: Six metres and twelve centimetres around the trunk, and no other tree on this page comes within a metre of it. The plane grows on a square that spent most of its history as a graveyard. Sint Janskerkhof is exactly what the name says, the churchyard of the Sint-Jan cathedral, and the dead of Den Bosch were buried here until the ground was cleared from 1860 onward. The municipal register puts this London plane at roughly 170 years, which places its planting within a decade or so of that clearance: the burials stopped, the square was laid out, and somebody put a plane at the corner with Choorstraat. Since then it has watched the cathedral beside it spend more of its life under scaffolding than not, restoration on the Sint-Jan having run in campaigns from the 19th century to the present. The register grades its vitality as reduced, the middle category rather than the worst, so it is holding rather than thriving. One caution about the evidence: the register is the only source that names this individual tree. A 1996 survey of the city's oldest trees names planes among the species that make this quarter old without picking out this one. The Casinotuin trees are a few minutes' walk south.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Casinotuin
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
trees.story: The city register gives this beech an age of zero. That is a blank field rather than a fact, because the trunk measures 4.33 metres round and the crown stands 24 metres up, which no seedling manages. Nobody has dated it, so this page does not either. What has been measured is size, and by that measure it is the thickest tree the register records in the Casinotuin. Copper beech is a purple-leaved form of the common beech, propagated from chance mutations found in the wild and planted through the 19th century for exactly the effect it still has, a mass of dark red over a park where everything else is green. This one grows on the old inner-city water in a garden that a 1996 survey of Den Bosch's oldest trees singled out for its beeches, along with the ramparts across town. A smaller weeping beech stands about 13 metres off, drooping like a closed umbrella, and the two are impossible to mix up once you have seen them side by side. Vitality here reads as normal, the best grade the register awards, which for a tree with no recorded age is the more useful number anyway. What it does not tell you is when somebody planted it, and on current evidence nobody knows.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Casinotuin
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 16-minute walk

best_time.label: May, when all five chestnuts put up white candles at once

trees.story: Five horse chestnuts stand within sixty metres of each other along this stretch of the Casinotuin, and this is the thickest by a clear margin: four metres round against roughly three and a half for the next in line. That is the field mark and also its limit. With five similar trees in one short walk, expect to compare trunks rather than to spot it from the path. The group is a survivor set rather than a fixed avenue, because the park has already lost one of its monumental chestnuts, which went over at the Nachtegaalslaantje corner. The register puts this one at about a century and 24 metres tall, with vitality marked as reduced. That is common in older Dutch horse chestnuts: the species has spent two decades under bleeding canker and leaf miner, and one that reaches four metres round with neither finishing it off has done well. No source other than the municipal register names this individual tree, which is why it is flagged here rather than presented as documented. For a fortnight in May the whole group flowers at once, white candles standing upright over every crown, and the question of which trunk is thickest stops mattering entirely.

trees.name: The Plane of Hekellaan
trees.access: Free, at a public park entrance
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 17-minute walk
trees.story: Boom en Bosch, the local tree-protection group, calls this the largest and perhaps the most beautiful plane tree in the city. They are right about the second half and out by a few hundred metres on the first, because a thicker plane stands at Sint Janskerkhof and the register's tape says so. The two sources also disagree about its age. Boom en Bosch estimates around 150 years, the municipality records 120, neither has a ring count behind it, so the entry here carries the whole range instead of picking a winner. What nobody disputes is the trunk: 4.8 metres round, at the park entrance on Hekellaan along the southern edge of the old fortifications. Plane was the standard 19th-century choice for exactly this position, tolerant of compacted soil, city air and roots being dug through, which is why Dutch park gates are full of them and why the oldest ones tend to stand where a bastion was flattened. The register grades its vitality as normal, the best it gives. It is the only plane at this entrance and unmistakably the heaviest trunk here; the nearest tree of comparable bulk is a horse chestnut some forty metres off, a different species with a different bark entirely.

trees.name: The Silver Maple by the Oude Dieze
trees.access: Free, public park along the old moat
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
trees.story: Silver maple is a nursery tree, planted for speed rather than for length of life. It grows fast, splits at the fork in a storm and is usually gone before it turns a hundred. This one is on the municipal monument list at roughly 110 years, 25 metres tall, with a trunk close to four metres round, standing along the Oude Dieze where the old inner-city water runs through the Casinotuin. The species comes from the river bottoms of the eastern United States, and a canal bank in Den Bosch is about as close as a Dutch park gets to that. The leaves give it away: deeply cut, pale and nearly white underneath, so the whole crown turns over silver whenever a wind comes up the water. No other maple of its species grows within sight, so there is nothing here to confuse it with; the purple-leaved copper beech about 40 metres away across the same stretch of park is a different tree altogether. Vitality reads as reduced, and the register is the only source that names this individual tree, the 1996 survey of the city's old trees having named maples in this quarter without identifying which. Bastion Oranje and its pair of Norway maples are about six minutes west.

trees.name: The Oak of Pettelaarse Schans
trees.access: Free, continuously open heritage site (a restaurant operates on part of the grounds with its own separate hours)
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 30-minute walk, or a shorter ride on a bus toward Zuid/Paleiskwartier

best_time.label: late September and October, when acorns cover the fort mound

trees.story: The earthwork under this oak is younger than the oak. Pettelaarse Schans was rebuilt into the star shape visitors walk today in 1959, during the works that made the Zuiderplas lake, and the register puts this pedunculate oak at about 120 years, which means it was planted around 1906 and was already full-grown when the diggers arrived. The site is far older than either. A fort stood here in the 17th century and was demolished in 1672, so the ring of trees on the mound traces a plan that has been dug, flattened and dug again. Then the caveat, because it decides whether you find the right trunk: three oaks stand within about fifty metres of each other up here. This is the thickest at 4.21 metres round, but its neighbour fourteen metres away runs to 3.52 and a third, forty-eight metres off, to 3.92, and telling them apart by eye is genuinely hard. The dependable anchor is the plane tree twelve metres away, a different species with pale flaking bark that nobody mistakes for an oak. Only the register names this individual tree. The fort's history is well documented; this particular oak's is not, and in late September the ground under all three is deep in acorns anyway.

trees.name: The Poplar of Pettelaarse Schans
trees.access: Free, continuously open heritage site (a restaurant operates on part of the grounds with its own separate hours)
trees.transport: 's-Hertogenbosch railway station, then about a 30-minute walk, or a shorter ride on a bus toward Zuid/Paleiskwartier
trees.story: If the register's count holds, this poplar was planted around 1941, which puts it in the ground under German occupation and makes it a young tree when the fighting for the city came through in the autumn of 1944. Which planting phase it belongs to has not been written down anywhere we could find, and that stays a gap here rather than getting filled in: the fort was demolished in 1672 and reshaped into its present star in 1959, and this tree predates the second date by nearly twenty years. At 28 metres it is the tallest thing standing on the mound, with a trunk 4.18 metres round. Canadian poplar is a hybrid of the European black poplar and the American cottonwood, bred for timber and shelter belts rather than for parks, which is why it puts on height like this and why one left alone to grow old is rarer than the species' sheer commonness suggests. A second Canadian poplar stands seven metres away and is visibly slimmer, just over three metres round, so the pair separate without a tape measure. The register lists this one's vitality as reduced. The three oaks are a short way west along the same mound, which makes the Schans a walk rather than a single stop.

trees.name: The Black Mulberry of Hofje van Pauw
trees.access: Free, public courtyard accessible via the gatehouse during the day; the surrounding houses are private residences, please respect residents' privacy
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 10-minute walk

best_time.label: July to August: dark fruit that stains everything under the tree

trees.story: The black mulberry in the courtyard of Hofje van Pauw has been fruiting since before the Dutch East India Company's Delft chamber was a century old. Tree specialist Jorn Copijn identified it in 2023 as Morus nigra subsp. multicaulus, a subspecies not officially recorded in Europe until 1821, more than a century after this specimen was already growing here. The likely explanation involves no botanist at all: the VOC had traded out of India, where the subspecies originates, since 1700, and Delft kept its own VOC chamber from 1602, so a sea captain or merchant returning home is the more probable route than any recorded introduction. At 319 years old it ranks among the oldest fruit trees documented in the Netherlands. The hofje itself, an almshouse Elisabeth Pauw endowed by testament in 1707 for women who had fallen on hard times, still houses residents today, now adults with intellectual disabilities, and the tree has outlived every one of them. Its courtyard gate on Paardenmarkt stays unlocked during the day. Visitors are asked to keep to the garden and skip the windows, since the houses ringing the tree are still lived in, not a museum.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnuts of Sint Agathaplein
trees.species: Horse Chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum and Aesculus x carnea)
trees.access: Sint Agathaplein is a free public square; an active construction site next door (the Prinsenhof renovation, underway to 2027) may temporarily affect the immediate surroundings
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 10-minute walk

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story: Five horse chestnuts on Sint Agathaplein, three white-flowered and two red, have stood outside the building where William of Orange was shot dead since 1920, planted as part of a coordinated square-wide planting rather than growing in on their own. The address carries more history than the trees themselves: Museum Prinsenhof occupies the former convent where William, leader of the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule, was assassinated on the staircase in 1584, and the bullet holes are still in the wall inside. De Boominspecteurs, commissioned by the municipality to assess the square's trees ahead of a major renovation, confirmed the chestnuts as part of the site's protected planting. The renovation itself started in 2025 and is due to finish in 2027, with the museum closed for the duration, and the municipality has stated the square's monumental trees are being kept in the new design even where other, younger planting is not. What that means for a visitor right now is straightforward caution rather than a locked gate: Sint Agathaplein is a public square, but a live building site sits next to it, so the usual free, unrestricted access may be temporarily altered until the work finishes.

trees.name: The Willemslinde of the Prinsentuin
trees.access: Museum Prinsenhof and its garden are mid-renovation (started 2025, due to reopen 2027-2028); the municipality has confirmed the garden's historic trees are being kept, but the Prinsentuin itself may not be openly walkable until the work finishes, check current status before visiting
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 10-minute walk

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: This winter linden did not grow from a seed that fell nearby. It grew from a twig cut from the Wilhelmslinde in Dillenburg, Germany, the tree under which William of Orange spent his childhood before he became the reluctant leader of the Dutch revolt and was assassinated in Delft in 1584. Supporters of the House of Orange took cuttings from the Dillenburg original and planted them at sites tied to William's life, and this one went into the Prinsentuin, the garden beside Museum Prinsenhof, in 1956. It is by a wide margin the youngest tree on this list, not even a century old against the mulberry's three, but it carries the most direct physical link to the man Delft is built around commemorating. The museum grounds are mid-renovation as of 2026, work that started in 2025 and runs to 2027, and the municipality has said the garden's historic trees are being kept rather than cleared for the new design. Until the museum reopens, treat the Prinsentuin as a garden worth checking on rather than one guaranteed open on any given day.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwoods of TU Delft's Botanic Garden
trees.age: age undocumented, among the first of the species grown in Europe after its 1944 rediscovery
trees.access: Paid entry, standard botanic garden admission
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 15-minute walk, or tram/bus to TU Noord
trees.story: Every dawn redwood alive today, anywhere in the world, descends from a single discovery: a species known only from 150-million-year-old fossils, presumed extinct, until a forester found a living stand of it in a remote Chinese valley in 1944. An international seed-collecting expedition followed in 1947, and botanical gardens across Europe, including several in the Netherlands, raised their first Metasequoia glyptostroboides from that single haul. Two of them now dominate the middle section of TU Delft's Botanic Garden, tall enough to be the garden's own reference point long before a visitor reaches the rarer specimens around them. Nobody recorded the exact planting year for these two, so no source gives a precise age, only the certainty that they belong to the first generation of the species ever grown outside China since its rediscovery, making them roughly seventy to eighty years old by extension rather than by record. The garden charges standard admission and sits a short walk from Delft's main station, a working research collection rather than a park, with the redwoods' feathery, deciduous foliage turning copper in autumn before it drops, unusual for a conifer and part of what first convinced botanists this was something genuinely new.

trees.name: De Kozakkenlinde
trees.age: roughly 325 to 425 years, and the register suggests a planting in 1614
trees.access: Free. Stands on a public country road at Diepenveen.
trees.transport: About 5 km north of Deventer station, on the Kozakkenweg at Diepenveen.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers and the whole tree hums

trees.story:
There was a holy oak on this spot and when it died they replaced it with a lime.

That is the register's reading, planting in 1614, following the death of the Hijligen eik that had stood here. Sacred trees were real fixtures of the Dutch countryside, marking a boundary, a court, a crossing or a spot where something had happened, and when one died the community's instinct was often to put another tree in its place rather than let the place go unmarked. That instinct is why the road is called what it is and why this tree exists.

The name it carries now comes from two centuries later. In 1813, during the French occupation of Deventer, the lime is said to have served as a lookout tree for Cossacks fighting against the French. Russian irregular cavalry had followed Napoleon's retreat west across Europe and reached the Netherlands that winter, and a big lime on a rise with a view is exactly what a scout wants.

Both stories are tradition rather than record. The tree is not: it is an enormous old lime on a country road, standing where somebody in 1614 decided a tree should stand.

Go in July, when it flowers and hums.

trees.name: De Reus van De Worp
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, supported by a 1917 photograph showing it still small
trees.access: Free. Open floodplain land across the river from the town.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Deventer station, across the IJssel by the foot ferry to De Worp.
trees.story:
The giant of De Worp is called that because of its size, and its size is what nearly got its age wrong.

A poplar this big looks old. The register says it is not especially, and it makes the argument with a photograph. An image of the Lange Laan in the Ossenwaarde taken in 1917 shows this tree standing small and distant, clearly a young and relatively slight thing. That rules out the older datings the girth would suggest and supports a planting somewhere between 1900 and 1910.

Which means a bit over a century has produced a tree people call a giant. That is what Canadian poplar does. It is a hybrid grown for speed, capable of several feet a year on wet ground, and this ground is as wet as it gets: the floodplain of the IJssel, flooded regularly, deep silt, and a water table close to the surface.

The trade-off is that poplars go brittle and are usually removed before they reach this stage.

Stand at the base and look up, then remember that everybody who ever posed under it in a photograph is gone and the tree is younger than most of them were.

trees.name: The Black Walnut of the Worpplantsoen
trees.age: roughly 205 years, from a replanting the register dates to 1820 to 1822
trees.access: Free. Public park in the floodplain; the tree stands on the campsite ground.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Deventer station, across the IJssel to the Worpplantsoen.

best_time.label: September, when the heavy green nuts come down

trees.story:
This tree exists because of ice.

The park across the river was replanted in 1816 and the young trees were damaged by ijsgang, the drifting ice that comes down the IJssel when a frozen river breaks up and shoves plates of ice over the banks. It is a serious force and it does not care about a six-year-old sapling. So the planting was done again in 1820 to 1822, and the register dates this walnut to that second attempt.

Black walnut is North American and was an unusual choice for a Dutch public park, then and now. It is grown mostly for its timber, which is among the most valuable in the world, and a two-hundred-year-old one standing in a park rather than a sawmill is a piece of luck.

It is easy to identify once you know where to look. Large compound leaves with fifteen or more leaflets, coming into leaf very late and dropping early. In autumn it produces heavy green fruit the size of tennis balls that fall hard and stain everything they touch a deep brown.

September, then, and mind your head.

trees.name: The Oak by the Bandstand
trees.age: roughly 205 years, from the park's documented replanting of 1822
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Deventer station, across the IJssel by the foot ferry.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down across the park

trees.story:
The French cut down the trees here and the city planted them again.

The Worpplantsoen lies in the floodplain of the IJssel directly opposite Deventer, and it is one of the oldest city parks in the Netherlands. During the French occupation the existing stock was destroyed, which was not vandalism but supply: an occupying garrison needs fuel and timber and a park across the river is the easiest source there is. In 1822, with the French gone, Deventer replanted, and a large share of the oaks, beeches and planes standing there now are from that year.

So the park is roughly the age of the peace that followed Napoleon, and it was made as a deliberate act of repair.

This oak is one of them, just north of the bandstand. At around two centuries it is at half its likely life, and the trees around it are its exact contemporaries, which is unusual: most parks are a mixture of ages, and this one has a cohort.

Come across on the foot ferry rather than driving round. It is the correct approach, the town behind you and the trees ahead.

trees.name: The Copper Beech at the Bandstand
trees.age: roughly 205 years, from the park's documented replanting of 1822
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Deventer station, across the IJssel by the foot ferry.

best_time.label: late October, when the purple burns through to copper

trees.story:
A copper beech planted in 1822 was an early one, and in a public park it was very early indeed.

The purple form of the common beech was still a rarity at that date. It occurs naturally as an occasional mutation and had been propagated by grafting in European nurseries for perhaps sixty years, mostly for private estates and botanic collections. Putting one at the centre of a municipal park in the IJssel floodplain, in a replanting made to repair the damage of an occupation, was a choice with some ambition in it.
