It sits centrally, near the bandstand, which is exactly where a designer would place the darkest tree available: the focal point of the composition, seen from every path.

Two hundred years on it is doing the job at a scale nobody planned. A mature copper beech is a solid dark mass, and this one anchors the middle of a park that is otherwise green, open and flat.

The last week of October, when the purple burns through to copper and the whole park briefly reorganises itself around it. Failing that, April, for the translucent red of the new leaves.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Diepenveenseweg Cemetery
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Free. Public cemetery, open in daylight. Visit quietly.
trees.transport: About 2 km north of Deventer station, on the Diepenveenseweg.
trees.story:
A weeping beech in a nineteenth century cemetery is not a coincidence, it is a convention.

The form was fashionable exactly when these grounds were laid out, and the reading was obvious enough that nobody had to explain it: a tree whose branches fall to the ground rather than reaching up. Cemeteries across northern Europe filled with weeping beeches, weeping willows and weeping ashes in the same few decades, and this one, banded 1830 to 1840, is from the beginning of that.

The register calls this burial ground historically and ecologically very valuable, in the old ring of the city, and it is looked after by a foundation for Deventer's old cemeteries.

What makes the tree worth the walk is that a mature weeping beech is hollow. The branches arch out and hang to the grass all round, so you can push through the skirt and stand inside a green room with a trunk in the middle. Doing that in a cemetery feels like trespass and is not.

One to see in leaf, so any time from May to October. In winter it is a bare cage, which is its own thing but less startling.

trees.name: The Oak of Landgoed Frieswijk
trees.age: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820
trees.access: Estate land recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 7 km northeast of Deventer station, off the Raalterweg at Schalkhaar.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns are down

trees.story:
The register is honest about this one in a way that is worth quoting: the planting history is not known, and the oak was probably put in during the first half of the nineteenth century.

That is the ordinary state of most old trees. No document, no planting record, nobody who wrote it down, and a dating arrived at by looking at the tree and at what was happening on the estate around it. It is worth seeing that stated plainly, because the confident specific ages attached to famous trees usually rest on no more than this and simply do not admit it.

What can be said is that Frieswijk is an estate northeast of Deventer, that the oak stands about 125 metres south of the Raalterweg, and that a pedunculate oak of two centuries in this country is at roughly half its span.

Oak on this ground is the default rather than the exception, which is part of why it goes unrecorded. Somebody planted it because you planted oak, and then two hundred years passed.

It is a walk out of town and the best reason to go is the walk. Come in October for the acorns.

trees.name: The Black Locust of Park Merwestein
trees.age: 300 to 325 years, established by municipal research in September 2020
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1 km northeast of Dordrecht station, near the S. van Hoogstratensingel entrance.

best_time.label: early June, when it hangs with white pea flowers and smells of honey

trees.story:
Somebody actually checked. In September 2020 the municipality investigated this tree and put it at 300 to 325 years old, which is a far better answer than almost any tree on this site can offer, and it agrees with the national register's independent band of 1700 to 1750.

What makes the number remarkable is the species. Black locust is North American, from the Appalachians, and it reached Europe at the start of the seventeenth century, named after Jean Robin, the French royal gardener who is credited with planting the first one in Paris. A specimen planted in Dordrecht around 1700 belonged to the first wave of them in this country, when the tree was still an expensive curiosity rather than the roadside coloniser it later became.

It has aged the way black locusts do, which is dramatically. The bark on an old one turns into deep, twisting, rope-like ridges, the trunk usually leans or forks, and the wood is so rot-resistant that the tree keeps standing in a state that would have finished anything else.

In late May and early June it hangs with white pea flowers that smell strongly of honey. Three hundred years and it still does that every year.

trees.name: The Plane of the Arend Maartenshof
trees.age: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820
trees.access: Free. Open almshouse courtyard; people live here, so visit quietly and in daylight.
trees.transport: About 800 m north of Dordrecht station, in the old centre.
trees.story:
This courtyard was built by a man with a reputation problem.

Arend Maartenszoon was known in Dordrecht as a money-grubber. In 1625 he put up 38 dwellings for the poor of the city and attached his name to them, which is the oldest form of reputation management there is and, four hundred years later, has worked: the Arend Maartenshof is still standing, still housing, and still called after him.

The plane came much later, banded 1810 to 1820, so it went in when the court was already nearly two centuries old. That is the usual pattern for an almshouse yard. The buildings come first, the tree arrives when somebody decides the middle of the square ought to have something in it, and then it grows to be the thing everyone actually remembers.

A hofje with a big tree in it is one of the best small spaces the Netherlands produces: low houses on four sides, a gate off a busy street, and a sudden drop in noise. This one is a working example rather than a museum, so go quietly.

The bark flakes in cream and olive plates, and the seed balls hang through the winter.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Weizigtpark
trees.age: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 500 m west of Dordrecht station.

best_time.label: March, when it flowers on bare twigs before anything else stirs

trees.story:
It was standing in a field for half a century before anyone made a park around it.

The Weizigtpark grew out of the country estate of the same name, but the corner this maple occupies was not part of the designed grounds at all. It was grazing land, and it was only laid out as park in about 1947. The register bands the tree 1890 to 1900, which puts it in the meadow, decades ahead of the paths and the planting.

That explains its shape if you look. A tree that grows up in open ground with nothing crowding it spreads low and wide and keeps its bottom branches, while a tree grown in a plantation is drawn up tall with a narrow crown and a clean trunk. The old meadow trees in a Dutch park are usually the broad ones.

Silver maple is worth knowing for two things. The leaf is cut into five narrow lobes and is bright white underneath, so the whole crown flickers pale in wind. And it flowers in March, before any leaf, in small red and yellow tufts directly on the bare twigs, weeks before anything else in the park does anything at all.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Varkenmarkt
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Inner courtyard off the Varkenmarkt, reachable in daylight.
trees.transport: About 1 km northwest of Dordrecht station, in the old centre.

best_time.label: April, when the new leaves open translucent red

trees.story:
The name of the square says what happened here: a pig market, and a lively livestock trade for a long time. Near this tree there was also a synagogue, which was pulled down in 1965.

So the beech is standing in a piece of Dordrecht that has been comprehensively emptied of its old uses. The animals went, the congregation's building went, and the courtyard by number 70 is now a quiet interior space with a very large purple tree in it.

The register makes a point about this one that it rarely makes: it is growing in a natural rooting position, and its trunk base and the ground around it are unrestricted. That is close to unheard of for a mature beech in a city centre. Almost every urban beech is slowly strangled by paving over the root plate, so a big one with open soil around its flare is a tree that has had what it needed, and it shows in the size.

Worth seeing in April as much as in October. Copper beech opens its leaves a translucent red that darkens to purple within a fortnight, and in an enclosed courtyard the light through them is extraordinary.

trees.name: The Plane at Sorghvliet
trees.age: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850
trees.access: Private estate south of Dordrecht, recorded as visitable in the national register. Check before setting out.
trees.transport: About 3 km south of Dordrecht station, at Landgoed Dordwijk.
trees.story:
The estate was laid out around 1635 and was then called the Torensteedje. At the entrance there is still a castle farm, part of which dates from that founding period, which is close to four hundred years of the same buildings being used for the same purpose.

The plane is nothing like that old. Banded 1840 to 1850, it belongs to the second half of the estate's life, when Dordwijk was being reworked the way most Dutch country places were in the nineteenth century: the formal geometry of the seventeenth century replaced with lawns, clumps and winding approaches, and single specimen trees planted where they would be seen from the house.

That is what this tree is. Not part of an avenue and not part of a wood, but a chosen thing placed in a view, near the house called Sorghvliet.

Planes were the fashionable choice for exactly that role: fast, huge, and with bark that keeps a pale flaking pattern all year, which makes one visible from a long way off across grass in any season.

The register records the estate as visitable, but it is private ground south of the city, so it is worth checking access before you go.

trees.name: The Tree of Heaven of the Botgensstraat
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Reachable via the small street behind the Botgensstraat.
trees.transport: About 1 km northwest of Dordrecht station, in the old centre.

best_time.label: August, when the winged seed bunches turn rusty red

trees.story:
Nobody plants these on purpose any more, which is why the oldest one in Dordrecht is worth going to look at.

Tree of heaven came from China, arrived in Europe in the eighteenth century as an ornamental, and was planted hard in cities because it grows faster than anything else and does not care about bad soil, drought or fumes. Then it turned out that it seeds prolifically, suckers aggressively through paving and cellars, and poisons the ground against competitors with a chemical in its roots. It is now one of the most unwanted plants in Europe.

This one predates all of that argument. Banded 1900 to 1910, it is the oldest of its kind in the city, and the register makes a point of saying it holds up well in its very stony surroundings, which is the whole nature of the species in one sentence.

You reach it through a small street behind the Botgensstraat, which is exactly the sort of leftover urban gap it thrives in.

Enormous compound leaves up to a metre long, and in late summer dense bunches of papery winged seeds that often turn a rusty red. Crush a leaf and it smells unpleasant. That is diagnostic.

trees.name: The Large-Leaved Lime of Louter Bloemen
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Small public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 4 km west of Dordrecht station, at Louter Bloemen.

best_time.label: late June, when it flowers and the park hums

trees.story:
This small park is all that is left of a country place, and it reads like one the moment you walk in: dominated by tall beeches, with the light already gone by the time it reaches the ground.

The lime is one of two standing close together. This one is a large-leaved lime and beside it is a big small-leaved lime, which is a useful accident, because those two species are the parents of the common lime planted everywhere in this country and are far less often seen themselves.

The difference is easy in the hand. Large-leaved lime has bigger, softer leaves with fine hairs on the underside and on the stalk, and it flowers first, in June. Small-leaved lime has smaller, hairless, bluish-backed leaves with rusty tufts in the vein angles, and flowers two to three weeks later. Standing between the two of them is the cheapest botany lesson in Dordrecht.

Both are banded to the middle of the nineteenth century, which puts them in the estate planting rather than in anything the city did later.

Go in late June, when the large-leaved one is out and the whole park smells of it and hums.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of Trsteno
trees.access: Free, open access, public village square in Trsteno (outside the paid arboretum gate)
trees.transport: Local bus from Dubrovnik's Pile Gate toward Trsteno/Orasac, or a car via the D8 coast road, roughly 20km northwest of the old town
trees.story: Around 500 years ago, a sea captain remembered as Florio Jakob Antunov sailed home to Trsteno from Constantinople with five young plane tree saplings and planted them beside a spring on the village's main square. Three did not survive; two did, and they have spent the five centuries since growing into what botanists call unique specimens of their kind anywhere in continental Europe, trunks five metres across and canopies rising as high as 50 to 60 metres over the village road. They have outlasted the Republic of Dubrovnik that existed when they were planted, survived the 1991 war that reached this coastline, came through a 2000 forest fire that swept the surrounding hills, and, in February 2020, caught fire themselves when nearby weed-burning sent a spark into a rotten branch; firefighters put it out with foam before serious damage was done. Croatia nominated the pair for European Tree of the Year in 2018, official recognition for two trees that have needed no institutional protection to survive this long, only the water from the spring they were planted beside and, evidently, considerable luck. They stand on public ground, not inside the paid arboretum next door, free for anyone driving the coast road through Trsteno to stop and stand beneath.

trees.name: Trsteno's Ginkgo
trees.access: Paid entry, Trsteno Arboretum (open daily, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: Local bus from Dubrovnik's Pile Gate toward Trsteno/Orasac, or a car via the D8 coast road

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn brilliant yellow

trees.story: A botanical survey of Trsteno Arboretum identifies eight trees as the collection's oldest documented specimens, each with a planting date recorded to the year rather than estimated from growth rings, and this ginkgo, planted in 1858, is one of two of its kind on that list. Ginkgo biloba is sometimes called a living fossil, a species whose basic form has barely changed across more than 200 million years of fossil record, old enough to have grown alongside dinosaurs, which makes a specimen planted only in the 19th century a relative newcomer by the standards of its own genealogy even as it becomes one of the oldest trees on these particular grounds. It was planted a few decades after Trsteno's own arboretum had already been developing for more than three centuries, part of a wave of exotic introductions to the garden's collection during the 19th century that also brought a second ginkgo in 1861, an American linden the same year as this one, and the yew and persimmon still growing nearby. Ginkgos are famously resistant to disease, pests and pollution, and unlike many of the collection's more delicate Mediterranean and subtropical specimens, this one has needed comparatively little intervention to reach the arboretum's list of oldest survivors.

trees.name: Trsteno's Cedar of Lebanon
trees.access: Paid entry, Trsteno Arboretum (open daily, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: Local bus from Dubrovnik's Pile Gate toward Trsteno/Orasac, or a car via the D8 coast road

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Planted in 1871, this cedar is the youngest of the eight trees Trsteno's own dendrological survey names as the arboretum's oldest documented specimens, and even at roughly 155 years old it already qualifies as a mature, textbook example of a species famous for taking its time. Cedar of Lebanon grows slowly by the standards of most garden trees, developing the wide, flat-tiered canopy visitors associate with the species only after many decades, which means this specimen has spent most of its life still visibly maturing into its now-characteristic shape. It arrived at Trsteno during the same 19th-century wave of exotic plantings that brought the arboretum's ginkgos and other now-venerable specimens, decades after the two famous 500-year-old plane trees outside the gate were already ancient by any measure. The cedar's own native range runs through the mountains of Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, forests logged for construction timber since the biblical era and now surviving only in fragments, which makes botanical gardens like Trsteno part of the species' effective range as much as its wild mountains are. Visitors touring the arboretum's grounds, a paid ticket beyond the free plane trees at the village gate, pass this cedar as part of the same 19th-century collecting era that shaped most of what grows here today.

trees.name: Trsteno's Yew
trees.access: Paid entry, Trsteno Arboretum (open daily, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: Local bus from Dubrovnik's Pile Gate toward Trsteno/Orasac, or a car via the D8 coast road

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Yews are Europe's slowest-aging trees by reputation, individual specimens in churchyards across the continent routinely claimed to be a thousand years old or more, sometimes credibly. Trsteno's own yew makes no such claim: its planting is recorded precisely, 1859, part of the same run of 19th-century plantings that gave the arboretum its ginkgos and cedar, and at around 167 years it is a comparative youngster next to its species' most famous specimens. What it demonstrates instead is how the arboretum itself has worked for nearly six centuries: founded in the 1490s by the Gucetic-Gozze family as a Renaissance summer garden, expanded across generations with whatever species each era's owners could get their hands on, from Mediterranean natives to exotic imports arriving by ship. The yew belongs to the second big wave of that expansion, the 19th-century collecting push that also planted the arboretum's ginkgos and its Lebanon cedar within a few years of each other. It stands as a quieter, darker counterpoint to Trsteno's famous sunlit plane trees at the village gate outside, evergreen where they turn deciduous, patient where they grew fast, part of the same six centuries of continuous cultivation on one stretch of Adriatic coastline.

trees.name: The Hungry Tree
trees.access: Free, open grounds, daylight hours
trees.transport: 15 min walk from O'Connell Street, or bus routes along Church Street / North King Street
trees.story: A cast iron bench has been disappearing into this tree for decades, and the tree is winning. Planted a little over a century ago inside the south gate of King's Inns, Ireland's school of law since 1541, the plane grew directly against a Victorian bench and simply kept going. Bark now spills over the seat's arms and back like dough left to rise. Nobody planned it as art: an early photographer noticed the effect and gave it a name that stuck. It has since appeared on guidebook covers and in Robert Ballagh's 1981 book Dublin, turning what the Tree Council of Ireland itself calls an otherwise unremarkable specimen into one of the city's most photographed trees. The tree is younger than almost everything around it. King's Inns has trained Irish barristers since the reign of Henry VIII, while the plane itself was likely seeded sometime between 1900 and 1940. The grounds are free and open during daylight hours, reached through an archway from Henrietta Street. Resist the urge to sit on what remains of the bench.

photo.attribution: Declan Maher, via Geograph Britain and Ireland / Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: Queen Victoria's Sequoia
trees.access: Free, but by guided tour only: house tours Saturdays year round, garden tours June to October, tickets on the day from Phoenix Park Visitor Centre
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Ashtown rail station, then a walk through the park; also bus routes 37, 38, 39
trees.story: A California redwood has been growing on Irish presidential land since a queen put it there. During her 1861 visit to Dublin, Queen Victoria planted a young giant sequoia in the grounds of what was then the Viceregal Lodge, now Áras an Uachtaráin, home to the President of Ireland. The tree is still alive. Seed of the species had only reached Britain from California in 1853, which makes this one of the earliest giant sequoias planted anywhere in Europe. It started a habit rather than a one-off gesture: visiting heads of state since, including Charles de Gaulle, John F Kennedy, Pope John Paul II, Queen Elizabeth II and Barack Obama, have each planted their own tree in the grounds, so Victoria's sequoia now stands among a small forest of political arrivals rather than alone. In its native Sierra Nevada the species can live three thousand years. At around a hundred and sixty five, hers has barely started. The gardens run free guided tours from June to October, and the house itself on Saturdays year round, tickets issued on the day from the Phoenix Park Visitor Centre.

trees.name: Dean's Tree
trees.access: Free, but open to the public only on Section 482 open days: May (all month), June (all month), and mid-August (15th-23rd), 10am-2pm
trees.transport: Car recommended; Dublin Bus route 68 serves Newcastle village

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Local tradition puts this yew at over seven hundred years old. A more cautious estimate, based on girth alone, still lands at over five hundred. Either figure makes it older than the house whose garden it now shares, built in 1710, and very likely the oldest living thing in County Dublin. Jonathan Swift, Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, is said to have sat beneath it while writing and while courting Esther Vanhomrigh, the Vanessa of his poems, who lived nearby in Celbridge. Nobody can confirm the story, and old trees near famous writers tend to collect this kind of legend whether or not it happened, so take the Swift connection as folklore worth repeating rather than a documented fact. What is certain is the tree itself: a girth of five metres, split with age, still green, standing in a corner of a garden ringed with benches for visitors to sit exactly where Swift supposedly did. The Old Glebe is a private home and only opens to the public on set dates each year, under Ireland's Section 482 scheme for historic houses: all of May, all of June, and nine days in mid-August, 10am to 2pm. Check the dates before making the trip.

trees.name: Addison's Walk
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: A double row of yews in Ireland's national botanic garden may predate the garden itself by roughly sixty years. Thomas Tickell, a minor poet and friend of the essayist Joseph Addison, lived on this land from 1736 until his death in 1740, and is said to have planted this avenue in Addison's memory. The Dublin Society did not acquire the site to found the gardens until 1795, more than fifty years after Tickell died, a gap none of the surviving accounts explain, so treat the 1730s planting date as informed tradition rather than settled fact. What survives is real regardless of who is right: a dark, formal walk of clipped yew running through a garden otherwise built for scientific display rather than sentiment, doing exactly what a memorial avenue is supposed to do, nearly three centuries on. Whether Joseph Addison ever actually visited Glasnevin is a question the garden's own historians admit they cannot answer, but his name has outlasted the argument regardless. The National Botanic Gardens are free to enter and open every day of the year except Christmas Day.

trees.name: The Provost's Plane
trees.access: Free, campus grounds generally open to visitors during daylight hours
trees.transport: Luas Green Line to Trinity, or Pearse Street DART station, both a short walk
trees.story: Trinity College's own estates team cannot quite agree on how old their most impressive tree is. One internal account points to an image of it from 1760; another puts its planting in the early 1800s, documented on the college's 1892 tree map, and its age at around two hundred years. Either way, it has been rooted at the corner of Grafton and Nassau Street since before Dublin had trams, and that turned out to matter. When the city's first tram line opened along Nassau Street in 1872, and again a century later when the Luas arrived, the plane needed pruning on a schedule built around a transport timetable, including nighttime work between midnight and half past three so services would not be disrupted. It now stands 31 metres tall with a canopy spreading nearly 30 metres, and a girth of 4.64 metres that took two centuries to grow. It shades a corner of the Provost's private garden behind a high wall, and most of the shoppers on Grafton Street a few metres away have no idea it is there.

trees.name: The Champion Planes of New Square
trees.access: Free, campus grounds generally open to visitors during daylight hours
trees.transport: Luas Green Line to Trinity, or Pearse Street DART station, both a short walk
trees.story: Two plane trees in New Square have outgrown almost everything else on Trinity's campus, and both went in around 1834, when the college was rebuilding this quadrangle. The larger of the pair has a girth over five metres, the widest trunk of any tree on college grounds by Trinity's own count. Students eating lunch on the grass beneath them are sitting under trees planted when Daniel O'Connell was a sitting MP at Westminster, decades before the Easter Rising and a full century before the Irish Free State existed. Trinity's own tree survey lists this pair among the oldest specimens left on the main campus, most of the older generation having since died or been felled, including a celebrated pair of Oregon maples in Library Square that came down in 2018, one collapsing overnight in June and the other felled weeks later once the same fungal decay was found in it. New Square sits behind the Museum Building, a short walk from the queue for the Book of Kells, and unlike that queue, it costs nothing and never has one.

trees.name: The Many-Trunked Holm Oak of St Anne's Park
trees.access: Free, public park, open at all hours
trees.transport: DART to Raheny or Harmonstown station, then a short walk
trees.story: Most of St Anne's Park's holm oaks do exactly what Lord Ardilaun planted them to do: stand in a straight, uniform line and block the wind coming off Dublin Bay. This one refused to cooperate. A 2009 field survey for the Heritage Trees of Ireland project singled it out from the surrounding avenue as a genuine arboricultural curiosity, a holm oak that grew several trunks from a single base instead of the clean single stem its neighbours all share, most likely the result of being cut back hard while young and responding by throwing up multiple new leaders rather than one. Evergreen and Mediterranean, like the rest of the avenue Ardilaun planted from the 1870s onward to shelter his estate from the coast's easterly winds, it has had a full century or more for its odd shape to settle into something closer to sculpture than accident, gnarled and dense where its neighbours are straight and orderly. It stands near the park's northeast corner, not far from the carved cypress trunk that draws most of the attention in this part of the grounds. Unlike that piece of dead wood turned into art, this one is still doing what a tree does every spring: pushing out new leaves from several trunks instead of one.

trees.name: The Holm Oak Avenue
trees.access: Free, public park, open at all hours
trees.transport: DART to Raheny or Harmonstown station, then a short walk
trees.story: Lord Ardilaun planted a windbreak in the 1870s that is still doing its job a century and a half later. Sixty seven holm oaks, evergreen and Mediterranean, line the main avenue and old estate boundaries of St Anne's Park, chosen because Dublin Bay's cold easterly winds off Bull Island would otherwise strip anything deciduous bare for half the year. Arthur Guinness, first Baron Ardilaun, inherited the estate in 1868 and spent much of his fortune turning it into a private demesne with formal gardens and grand tree-lined approaches, only for Dublin Corporation to buy the whole estate from his family in 1939 and open it to everyone. The oaks never got the memo that they were meant to shelter a private house: they shelter dog walkers, parkrunners and a Saturday market instead. Unlike most street trees, a holm oak keeps its dark, leathery leaves through the Irish winter, so the avenue looks essentially the same in January as it does in July, a rare piece of consistency in a park that changes with every season around it.

trees.name: The Great Sycamore of Farmleigh
trees.access: Free, grounds open daily 10am-6pm, last entry 5pm
trees.transport: Dublin Bus route 37 to Castleknock Gate

best_time.label: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story: The oldest tree on the Farmleigh estate predates the Guinness family who made the place famous by about a century. This sycamore, standing at the edge of what is still called the donkey field, is estimated at over 220 years old, meaning it was already mature when Edward Cecil Guinness bought Farmleigh in 1873 and began rebuilding the house around it. Everything else here, the cedars, the sequoias, the Thuja avenue Guinness planted along the main approach, arrived later as part of his deliberate planting scheme. The sycamore did not: it was simply already there, a survivor of whatever farmland stood on this ground before Farmleigh existed as a name. Today the house serves as the Irish state's official guesthouse for visiting dignitaries, but the 78 acres of grounds around it are free to the public every day, a rare arrangement for a working state property. Farmleigh's own visitor material points to this tree specifically as the oldest thing growing on the estate. No independent survey has verified that figure beyond the estate's own long-standing estimate, so it is presented here as tradition rather than a laboratory result.

trees.name: The Oak Avenue of Corkagh
trees.access: Free, public park, open at all hours
trees.transport: Dublin Bus routes 13, 68, 69 or 151, or a longer walk from the Red Cow Luas stop

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: An avenue of oaks in Corkagh Park once led somewhere: to a country house that no longer exists. Oak Avenue was the main approach to Corkagh House, seat of the Finlay and Colley families from the 18th century until the last of the estate's two big houses burned down in the late 1970s. Some of the oaks that lined that approach are still standing, over two hundred years old, planted long before the fire and long before Dublin City Council opened the wider 300 acre demesne to the public in 1986. New oaks have been planted alongside the survivors since, close enough in age that telling the two generations apart takes a trained eye rather than a glance. Archaeologists working on the park's masterplan turned up the foundations of a medieval castle and a moated site here in 2023, a reminder that people have been building and rebuilding on this ground since at least 1326, when Corkagh first appears in the records as part of the Archbishop of Dublin's manor. The oaks are the one part of that long history still doing the job they always did: marking a way in.

trees.name: The Last Elm of College Park
trees.access: Free, campus grounds generally open to visitors during daylight hours; College Park is Trinity's cricket/sports ground, walkable around the perimeter
trees.transport: Luas Green Line to Trinity, or Pearse Street DART station, both a short walk
trees.story: Trinity College once had around sixty elms scattered across its grounds, and Dutch elm disease is the obvious explanation for why almost none of them are left. Trinity's own botanists checked and found no trace of the fungus in college specimens, and now suspect something duller: soil conditions doing slowly what the disease usually does fast. Whatever the cause, this wych elm in College Park is the survivor, the last of a population that once shaded most of the campus and that mostly vanished across Ireland and Britain from the 1970s onward. Nobody at Trinity has put a number on its age. It was already established enough by the 1970s to be counted among the trees dying around it, which sets a floor under its age rather than a figure: call it at least eighty years, probably more. College Park is Trinity's cricket ground rather than a garden, so the elm shares its patch of grass with match days and net practice, a five minute walk from the queue for the Book of Kells and entirely ignored by it. It is easy to miss for the same reason it survived: nobody was watching this one closely enough to notice it was different, until one day it was the only elm left standing.

trees.name: The Glasnevin Atlas Cedar
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough
trees.story: The Atlas Mountains cedar growing in Glasnevin is safer here than at home. Cedrus atlantica is native to a narrow band of mountains in Morocco and Algeria, and the IUCN now lists the species as Endangered in the wild, squeezed by drought, logging and a warming climate its native range cannot easily outrun. This specimen in the National Botanic Gardens has none of those problems, recorded by the Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey among the garden's Exceptional Specimen Trees, likely somewhere between 120 and 165 years old by now. No second source describes this individual tree, so treat the age as a register estimate rather than a measured fact, honest as far as it goes. What the survey does record is form: a maiden tree, grown straight from seed rather than grafted, its blue green needles held in dense, upswept clusters along near-horizontal branches, the shape that made this species and its blue foliage varieties a favourite of formal Victorian planting schemes across Europe. Somewhere on a mountainside a few thousand kilometres south, its wild relatives are losing ground season by season. This one, planted decades before anyone worried about that, just keeps growing. It stands close to the Botanic Gardens' yew avenue, Addison's Walk, on the same afternoon's walk.

trees.name: The Glasnevin Dawn Redwood
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough
trees.story: Until 1941, botanists knew the dawn redwood only from fossils, certain a conifer that shed its needles every winter had gone extinct millions of years earlier. Then living trees turned up in a valley in Sichuan, China, and seed from the first Western collecting expeditions went out to major botanic gardens worldwide by the late 1940s, ending the species' presumed extinction in real time rather than in a museum case. Glasnevin's specimen sits in that plausible window: the Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey puts it at 50 to 100 years old then, which works out to roughly 65 to 115 now, consistent with descent from that original wave of seed, though no source confirms this exact tree's planting date or lineage. Metasequoia glyptostroboides is deciduous, unlike almost every other conifer, its feathery needles turning a rusty bronze each autumn before dropping, a habit that startles visitors expecting a fir or a pine to stay green all winter. It is a single-source find, register only, an honest gap rather than a padded one. Find it in the National Botanic Gardens, a short walk from Addison's Walk's yew avenue and this cluster's other exceptional specimens, one of the closest things botany has to a resurrection story growing quietly in a Dublin garden bed.

trees.name: The Glasnevin Caucasian Elm
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough

best_time.label: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: A nurseryman in County Offaly once took cuttings from this exact tree and started selling clones of it. Zelkova carpinifolia 'Glasnevin' is a named cultivar, propagated by Jan Ravensberg from material taken off this specific specimen in the National Botanic Gardens, one of the more unusual honours a single tree in Dublin has received: not just admired, but copied and put into commercial circulation under its own place name. The species itself, the Caucasian elm, comes from the mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian, and grows into a distinctive multi-stemmed, upright vase shape rather than the single trunk most elms produce, its bark smooth grey brown until age begins to plate it. Unlike Ireland's native elms, decimated by Dutch elm disease through the twentieth century, Zelkova carpinifolia carries strong natural resistance to the fungus, part of why old specimens like this one still stand where true elms mostly do not. The Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey puts it at 150 to 200 years old then, roughly 165 to 215 now, the oldest of the garden's newly catalogued specimens, though no source gives a firm planting date. Autumn turns it a rich copper before the leaves drop. It stands 200 metres from Addison's Walk, well within the same visit.

trees.name: The Glasnevin Swamp Cypress
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough
trees.story: A tree built for Louisiana swampland grows in a Dublin botanic garden, and it still remembers where it came from. Taxodium distichum, the swamp or bald cypress, is native to the flooded river bottoms of the southeastern United States, and where its roots sit in standing water it grows knobby woody projections called pneumatophores, or knees, that rise above the waterline, thought to help the tree breathe in waterlogged ground. Whether this particular Glasnevin specimen stands wet enough to show them is not confirmed by any source found, an honest gap rather than an invented detail. What the Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey does confirm is the tree itself: one of the garden's Exceptional Specimen Trees, in the 100 to 150 year age band then, roughly 120 to 165 now. Like the dawn redwood elsewhere in this same cluster, it is a conifer that behaves like a deciduous tree, dropping its feathery needles each winter rather than holding them evergreen, a trait that confuses visitors twice in the same afternoon if they walk both trees back to back. No second source names this specific tree, so the age stands as a register estimate rather than a settled fact. It shares this corner of the National Botanic Gardens with the Atlas Cedar and Addison's Walk, all reachable on the same short walk.

trees.name: Ireland's Largest Tree of Heaven
trees.age: disputed: register says 120-165 years, species norms suggest closer to 70-100
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough
trees.story: The largest Ailanthus altissima in Ireland stands framed between two Victorian glasshouses in Dublin, and nobody agrees on how old it actually is. Trees and Shrubs Online, the standard international dendrology reference, records it plainly as the country's largest specimen of the species, 17 metres tall with a trunk over a metre thick, shaped well enough that one garden writer has called it among the most elegant of its kind anywhere in Ireland or Britain. The disagreement is about age. The Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey bands it at 100 to 150 years, which would put it past 160 now, but Ailanthus altissima is naturally short lived and fast growing, a species where seventy years already counts as a good age in the wild. Both figures are given here rather than one being quietly dropped: either a sheltered, cared-for botanic garden specimen has simply outlived what the species usually manages on a roadside or waste ground, which is plausible, or the register's band runs generous. What is not disputed is the position, framing the view toward the Palm House and Curvilinear Range, the garden's twin 19th century glasshouses, and the species itself, native to China, notorious elsewhere as an aggressive street weed but planted here deliberately, long before anyone thought of it that way.

trees.name: The Glasnevin Hybrid Strawberry Tree
trees.access: Free, open daily except 25 December
trees.transport: Bus routes 9 and 140 from the city centre, or a 20 min walk from Phibsborough
trees.story: Peel back the bark on this tree and you find a second colour underneath. Arbutus x andrachnoides is a naturally occurring hybrid from the Mediterranean, a cross between the familiar strawberry tree and the smooth-barked Greek and Cypriot Arbutus andrachne, and it inherits the more dramatic parent's habit: chestnut brown outer bark that peels away in curling strips to reveal a glossy, copper red layer beneath, a colour show that has nothing to do with flowers or leaves. The Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey lists a specimen of this hybrid among the National Botanic Gardens' Exceptional Specimen Trees, aged 100 to 150 years then, roughly 120 to 165 now. A dendrology reference, Trees and Shrubs Online, independently photographed a specimen of the same species at Glasnevin in 2017, evidence the hybrid grows and was recently alive in these gardens, though it cannot be fully confirmed that the photographed tree and the register's tree are one and the same rather than two separate plantings nearby. Treat the connection as likely, not certain. Either way, this is the weaker-evidenced tree in this corner of the gardens, worth visiting for the bark alone: run a hand along the trunk in late summer, after the old layer has started to curl, and the colour underneath is the reason to stop.

trees.name: The Great Oak Stool
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years as a stool, from the register's band of 1750 to 1800; the stems on it are far younger
trees.access: Free. Woodland with public paths, east of the Apeldoornseweg.
trees.transport: About 6 km northeast of Ede-Wageningen station, off the Apeldoornseweg near the Immenweg.

best_time.label: January, when the bare stems show the shape of the old stool

trees.story:
This is not a trunk. It is a base, broad and low, with a ring of stems standing up out of it, and it is the oldest living thing in Ede.

Coppicing is what people did with oak on poor sandy ground for a thousand years, because it turns a slow tree into a repeating crop. Cut an oak to the ground and it does not die; it sends up a dense ring of new shoots from the stump, which are harvested again a decade or two later for firewood, fencing, charcoal and tan bark. Repeat that for centuries and the stump widens into a low circular platform of old wood, sometimes two or three metres across, with a hollow middle where the original stem rotted out.

So the age is on the base. The stems you see are young. The thing they are standing on has been cut and has regrown perhaps twenty times.

This wood shows on topographic maps from 1830 to 1850. In the 1920s and 1930s it was planted through with conifers, and on some plots and along some paths the old oak stools were spared. This is the largest of them, in a row along a path.

Come in winter, when you can see the shape of the base.

trees.name: The Pampel Oak
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Paid. Inside Nationaal Park De Hoge Veluwe, which charges an entrance fee.
trees.transport: About 15 km northeast of Ede-Wageningen station. Nearest park entrance Otterlo.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down and the boar arrive for them

trees.story:
It stands inside a fenced national park where you have to pay to walk, and both of those facts are the reason it is in good condition.

De Hoge Veluwe is 55 square kilometres of sand, heath, drift dunes and planted wood, bought up in the 1910s by Anton and Helene Kroller-Muller and later given to the state. It is enclosed, it is managed, and it is one of the few landscapes in the Netherlands where you can walk for an hour without leaving it. The Pampel is a spot in the northwest of it, off the Houtkampweg.

The oak is banded 1850 to 1860, which puts it well before the Kroller-Mullers and inside whatever estate or farm woodland was here first. On the Veluwe that usually means it grew up on land that was heath within living memory, since much of this sand was open and drifting into the nineteenth century and was only planted up afterwards.

An oak that establishes itself on poor sand grows slowly and puts on dense timber, so the girth understates the age.

Go in October, and let the acorns be the reason. Wild boar and deer here live off them.

trees.name: The Oak beside Kasteel Hoekelum
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Castle grounds on the Edeseweg, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 3 km southwest of Ede-Wageningen station, on the Edeseweg toward Bennekom.
trees.story:
There are two oaks here of the same age and they are worth seeing together, because between them they show what open ground does to a tree.

This is the one standing beside the house. It grew up close to buildings, with structures and other planting on at least one side, so it has done what a hemmed tree does: gone up rather than out, kept a narrower crown, and lost its lower branches early. The other one, out in the meadow in front, had nothing near it at all and spread instead.

Same species, same planting band of 1830 to 1840, almost certainly the same original scheme. Different shapes entirely, and the only variable is how much room each one had.

That is a more useful thing to notice than it sounds, because it is how you read any old tree. A wide low crown with heavy horizontal limbs means the tree grew in the open, even if a wood has since grown up around it. A tall clean trunk means competition.

Kasteel Hoekelum is on the Edeseweg between Ede and Bennekom, and the grounds are recorded as visitable in the national register.

trees.name: The Oak in the Hoekelum Meadow
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Castle grounds on the Edeseweg, recorded as visitable in the national register. The tree is visible from the road.
trees.transport: About 3 km southwest of Ede-Wageningen station, on the Edeseweg toward Bennekom.

best_time.label: January, when the bare frame shows against the field

trees.story:
A single oak standing alone in a field is one of the most reliable pleasures this country offers, and it is almost always deliberate.

Solitary field trees were left or planted for reasons that had nothing to do with looks. Shade for livestock, a marker on a boundary, a fixed point in a landscape without many. What they produce is a shape no woodland tree ever gets: heavy limbs leaving the trunk low down and running out horizontally as far as the wood will bear, a crown far wider than the tree is tall, and clear ground beneath.

This one has had that room since about 1830 to 1840, in the meadow in front of Kasteel Hoekelum, with its twin standing close to the house and looking completely different for it.

A free-standing oak of nearly two hundred years is also a small ecosystem on its own. Old oaks carry more dependent species than any other tree in northern Europe, several hundred of them, most in the dead wood and the crevices, so the value is in the parts that look neglected.

Go in low winter sun, when the whole frame of it is visible from the road.

trees.name: Beuk Marjan
trees.age: roughly 195 to 205 years, from the register's planting band of 1820 to 1830
trees.access: Free. Public woodland with paths.
trees.transport: About 4 km northeast of Ede-Wageningen station, in the Edese bos north of the N224.

best_time.label: October, when it turns copper against the dark conifers

trees.story:
Somebody called this tree Marjan and the name went into the national register.

That is a small thing and it is not nothing. Almost every entry in that register is a species and an address. A handful carry a name, and a name means a person: somebody local knew this beech well enough to call it something, used the name often enough that other people used it too, and it eventually turned up on an official form.

The tree itself is a beech of about two hundred years in the Edese bos, north of the N224, and its age is the interesting part in this landscape. Two hundred years ago much of the Veluwe was open drifting sand, and the woods around Ede are largely a nineteenth and twentieth century creation, planted to fix the ground and grow timber. A beech from the 1820s is from the very beginning of that effort.

Beech is also the wrong tree for this soil on paper. It wants moisture and does badly on dry sand, so a big old one out here has found itself a better pocket of ground than its neighbours.

Bring your hand. That bark is the smoothest thing in the wood.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Fire Station
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Public square, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km north of Ede-Wageningen station, on the Burgemeester van Dijkeplein.
trees.story:
A tree from the Sierra Nevada, planted in a Gelderland village in the 1880s, now standing next to a fire station.

The sequoia was the status tree of its moment. Introduced to Europe in 1853, still expensive thirty years later, and unmistakably foreign in a landscape of oak and pine, which was the entire attraction. Whoever put this one in was making a point about the ground it stood on, and that ground was not a municipal square at the time.

Everything around it has since been replaced. The tree stayed, because a sequoia in the 1880s becomes a sequoia you cannot casually remove by the 1950s, and now it is the oldest thing on the Burgemeester van Dijkeplein by a wide margin.

Go and push the bark. That is the single best thing about the species and almost nobody does it. It is thick, soft and fibrous, and your fist sinks into it, which is an adaptation to forest fire: the outer layer chars and insulates while the living tissue underneath survives. Nothing else you can touch in a Dutch town centre behaves like that.

It will still be here in a thousand years if we leave it alone.

trees.name: The Oak on the Dorpstraat
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Street tree in the village, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 8 km northwest of Ede-Wageningen station, in Lunteren.
trees.story:
A village street with an oak on it that is older than most of the houses.

Lunteren is a Veluwe village a few kilometres northwest of Ede, and this oak has been on the Dorpstraat since somewhere between 1860 and 1870. That places it before the railway came through, before the tourist trade, and before most of the building that turned a farming settlement into a commuter village.

An oak on a village street lives a harder life than an oak in a wood, and it usually looks it: pruned back from the road and the wires, roots under paving, and a lopsided crown leaning toward whatever open space there is. That is not damage so much as negotiation, carried out over a century and a half, one branch at a time.

It is also the sort of tree a village argues about. Every generation there is a reason to take it out, and so far every generation has decided not to.

Stand across the road rather than under it. From the far pavement you can see the whole shape and read where the street has pushed it about, which is the interesting part.

trees.name: The Craigmillar Castle Yews
trees.access: Paid entry, Historic Environment Scotland site
trees.transport: Bus from city centre to Craigmillar Castle Road, short walk to entrance

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Two yew trees have guarded the courtyard entrance to Craigmillar Castle since before anyone thought to write down when they were planted. Historic Environment Scotland dates them to at least 300 years, but the popular story pushes them back further: local tradition holds they were planted to honour Mary, Queen of Scots during her stay here in 1566, recovering after the birth of her son James VI. That would make them over 450 years old, a gap of a century and a half between the cautious estimate and the romantic one that no ring count can settle, since living yews rot from the inside and take their birth certificate with them. What is certain is the castle itself: a five-hundred-year-old ruin of vaulted halls and spiral stairs, seat of the Preston family and, for three weeks in 1566, the site of the Craigmillar Bond, the meeting where Mary's advisors first discussed getting rid of her troublesome husband Lord Darnley. The yews watched that plotting happen, whichever decade they were planted in. They still stand exactly where the castle's builders put them, framing the entrance the same way they have for centuries, evergreen through every season Craigmillar has seen since.

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of the Botanics
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street

best_time.label: October, when the chestnuts drop and its leaves turn gold

trees.story: The oldest tree in Edinburgh's Royal Botanic Garden was already growing here before the garden was. When the Botanics relocated to Inverleith in 1820, this sweet chestnut, now on the Pond Lawn, was already a mature tree, meaning it predates the 200 year old institution that grew up around it. No one recorded its planting date, so the garden's own arborists can only say it is over two centuries old, likely closer to three. Sweet chestnut was introduced to Britain by the Romans and spread through monastery gardens before becoming a favourite of 18th and 19th century landscapers, prized for timber that could be coppiced and split for fencing. This one was never harvested that way. It has spent recent years in decline, and RBGE's arboretum team has reduced its crown and cut back the larger failing branches to keep it alive for another generation, an unusually candid admission from an institution that measures its collection in centuries rather than seasons. Entry to the garden itself costs nothing. Find it on the Pond Lawn, one of the quieter corners of a collection that includes some of the best documented trees in Scotland, and one very old one nobody bothered to document at all.

photo.attribution: M J Richardson, via Geograph Britain and Ireland / Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Cammo Ash
trees.access: Free, Edinburgh Council nature reserve
trees.transport: Bus to Cammo Road or Cammo Walk, Edinburgh
trees.story: One of the oldest ash trees in Edinburgh grows in a park with no house left standing in it. Cammo Estate was laid out from 1710 by Sir John Clerk of Penicuik, a lawyer, composer and self-taught landscape designer who spent the following years building what may have been Scotland's first true landscape garden around Cammo House. The house is a shell now, roofless and fenced off after decades of fire and vandalism following its abandonment in the 1970s, but the plantings Clerk commissioned outlived the family that made them: beech, horse chestnut, sycamore, and this ash, its trunk over a metre and a half across, which the Woodland Trust names among the oldest ash trees in the city. Edinburgh Council now manages the grounds as a wilderness nature reserve, deliberately left less manicured than a typical park, and the ash stands among yews, rhododendron and pine planted through the 18th and 19th centuries. No one has given this specific tree a documented planting date, so its age here is an estimate built from the estate's own timeline rather than a ring count, honestly short of certainty but long on plausibility. It costs nothing to visit, and the walk in passes the ruined tower and a Pictish standing stone on the way.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at the Botanics
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: This cedar has a birth certificate few trees in Scotland can match: 1826, recorded by the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh's own staff as one of the first trees they planted after the garden moved to its current Inverleith site. That makes it two hundred years old this year, a tidy figure for a species that in the wild can live past a thousand. Cedar of Lebanon was a fashionable statement tree for early 19th century institutions wanting to signal permanence, and RBGE's planting near the Glasshouses did exactly that: broad, flat tiered branches spreading further every decade since Waterloo was recent history. The species appears throughout the Bible as a byword for strength, cut for Solomon's Temple in the older stories, though this particular specimen's only scripture is a planting record in a Scottish institution's own archive. It has outlasted the Palm House built in 1834, watched the garden expand from its original grounds into the wider collection it is today, and will likely outlast whoever is reading this. Entry to the garden grounds is free year round. The Glasshouses nearby are shut for restoration until 2027, but the cedar needs no roof.

trees.name: The Monkey Puzzles of Lauriston Castle
trees.access: Free grounds; castle interior tours paid
trees.transport: Bus to Cramond Road South, Davidson's Mains
trees.story: Five monkey puzzle trees stand near the rose garden at Lauriston Castle, planted close to the exact year the species became fashionable enough for anyone outside a botanic garden to own one. Araucaria araucana arrived in Britain in 1795, brought back by the naturalist Archibald Menzies, but stayed a rare curiosity until 1843, when the nurseryman James Veitch sent the plant collector William Lobb to Chile specifically to gather seed for commercial sale. That single expedition is why Victorian Britain filled its gardens with monkey puzzles almost overnight, and Lauriston's five, planted around that same pivotal year, are plausibly among the first large scale plantings of the species anywhere in the country, though no dated planting record for this specific garden survives to confirm it outright. Chilean by origin and built for volcanic slopes and heavy snow, they are unmistakable even from a distance: rigid, spiralling branches armoured in sharp scale like leaves, a shape nothing else in a Scottish garden shares. The castle itself, an Edwardian time capsule left almost untouched since its last owners donated it to the city in 1926, sits behind them. The grounds are free to walk. Only the castle's furnished rooms require a ticket, and the trees do not care either way.

trees.name: The Wentworth Elms of Holyroodhouse
trees.access: Paid entry, Palace of Holyroodhouse (garden included with palace ticket, April to September)
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Edinburgh Waverley station, at the foot of the Royal Mile
trees.story: Two trees growing in the King's garden in Edinburgh were thought extinct in Britain for twenty years before anyone noticed they were still alive. The Wentworth elm is a weeping cultivar that never caught on widely, and when the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh's own specimen died of Dutch elm disease in 1996, and the German nursery that first supplied the variety confirmed it had none left either, botanists assumed the tree was gone from the country entirely. It was not. A 2016 survey of the gardens at the Palace of Holyroodhouse, prompted by nothing more than routine record keeping, turned up two mature Wentworth elms that had been standing in plain sight the whole time, tall enough and photographed often enough that no one had thought to ask what species they actually were. Records show three arrived from a Berlin nursery in 1902, and ring counts from a third tree felled in 2008 dated it to around 1905, which makes the surviving two roughly 120 years old. Their identity gave itself away through a distinctive weeping habit and glossy, oversized leaves, first flagged by Dr Max Coleman of RBGE. The garden is included with a standard Palace of Holyroodhouse ticket, open April to September.

trees.name: The Camperdown Elm of St Cuthbert's
trees.access: Free, open churchyard
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Princes Street, at the west end of Princes Street Gardens
trees.story: A tree with no straight branches grows by the main door of St Cuthbert's Church, one of the oldest parish sites in Edinburgh even though the current building only dates to 1894. The Camperdown elm is a weeping cultivar discovered by accident around 1835 in the forest at Camperdown House near Dundee, when the Earl's head forester found a young elm growing contorted and low to the ground rather than upright. Every Camperdown elm alive today, including this one, is a graft from that single original tree, since the variety cannot grow from seed and only survives by cutting, making each specimen a genetic clone traceable to one 19th century Scottish forest. This one has been measured at 63cm in diameter at breast height, a girth some local sources call a contender for the largest of its kind in Scotland, though no national tree register confirms that specific claim and it is offered here with that caveat attached. What is not in doubt is the shape: branches that arch downward and knot into themselves instead of reaching up, giving the tree a low, tangled canopy unlike anything else in the churchyard around it. It stands free to view, steps from Princes Street Gardens.

trees.name: The Rockface Sycamore of Cramond
trees.access: Free, public walkway
trees.transport: Bus to Cramond village, then short walk along the River Almond Walkway

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story: At the start of the River Almond Walkway in Cramond, a sycamore grows sideways out of solid rock instead of up from soil, its roots gripping a ledge on the riverbank and its trunk reaching out over the water before turning back skyward. No record gives this tree's age or planting date. What draws people to it is simply the improbability of the thing: a substantial, clearly mature tree that appears to be growing from bare stone, a trick of root systems finding cracks and pockets of soil invisible to a passerby rather than any actual defiance of biology. Cramond itself is one of the oldest inhabited spots in Scotland, settled since Mesolithic times and later the site of a Roman fort at the mouth of the River Almond, and the walkway leading past this tree follows the river past the ruins of iron and paper mills from the Industrial Revolution before reaching the Firth of Forth. The sycamore is a footnote to that longer history rather than a documented part of it, honestly flagged here as a single source, undated curiosity rather than a verified ancient specimen. It costs nothing to see and sits directly on a public path used daily by dog walkers and cyclists.

trees.name: The Tall Trees of the Hermitage of Braid
trees.access: Free, public nature reserve
trees.transport: Bus to Braid Road or Comiston Road, Morningside

best_time.label: late October, when the beech turn copper

trees.story: The valley floor of the Hermitage of Braid holds some of the tallest trees in Edinburgh, beech and sycamore that clear 130 feet in a steep sided gorge between the Braid Hills and Blackford Hill. Some date to the early 19th century, though no formal survey has dated any single specimen precisely, and the claim rests on the reserve's own management history rather than a ring count. What makes the height plausible is the terrain itself: a sheltered river valley along the Braid Burn, protected from wind on both sides, exactly the kind of site where trees reliably outgrow their exposed neighbours on Edinburgh's open hills. The walk beneath them passes an 18th century doocot with nearly two thousand nest holes and the remains of old mills that once used the burn's power, and enough tree cover that the Hermitage feels closed in and green in a way most of Edinburgh, built on volcanic rock and open to the wind, does not. It is free to walk, all year, and the entrance off Braid Road is a short bus ride from the city centre.

photo.attribution: Callum Black, via Geograph Britain and Ireland / Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Corstorphine Sycamore
trees.access: Free, open churchyard
trees.transport: Bus to Corstorphine High Street, 2 min walk

best_time.label: April and May, when the new leaves emerge bright gold

trees.story: The tree standing in Corstorphine Kirk's churchyard today is not the tree its story is about. The original Corstorphine sycamore, reputedly planted around 1600, grew a distinctive golden foliage found nowhere else and became famous locally after 1679, when Christian Nimmo murdered her lover James, Lord Forrester, beneath its branches with his own sword. Her ghost, known as the White Lady of Corstorphine, is said to haunt the spot still. The original tree does not, since it was badly damaged in a storm in 1998 and died in 2005, ending a run of roughly four centuries. Because the variety cannot grow from seed, only from cuttings, the tree in the churchyard now is a direct clone of the original, propagated after its death and planted to keep the golden leaved variety alive at the place that gave it its name. It carries the same genetics and, given time, the same striking spring colour, but it is a young tree standing in for a very old one, honestly labelled here as such rather than passed off as the historic original. The churchyard is open and free. What you are visiting is a memory of a murder and a continuity of genetics rather than four centuries of standing wood.

trees.name: The John Muir Grove
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street
trees.story:
A ring of Californian redwoods grows in Edinburgh, named for the Scot who helped save the Californian ones. John Muir was born in Dunbar, thirty miles down the East Lothian coast, emigrated as a boy, and spent his life arguing that America should keep its wild country rather than cut it down, work that ended in the national park system. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh put his name on this grove in 1990, seventy years after the trees themselves went in.

They were planted in the 1920s in the Upper Woodland Garden and now stand over 24 metres, which for a giant sequoia is early adolescence: the species runs past 80 metres and 3,000 years on its home ground in the Sierra Nevada. What the planting got right was the arrangement. The trees form a circle, so the space they enclose is the destination rather than any single trunk, and the garden's own word for the effect, cathedral-like, is fair. Walk into the middle and stop. That is the spot, and the garden hires it out for ceremonies for exactly that reason.

The pin here is set to the Upper Woodland Garden rather than the ring itself, because no source gives coordinates for the circle. At 24 metres and rising, it is not a difficult thing to find once you are in that part of the Botanics.

trees.name: The Catacol Whitebeams of the East Gate
trees.age: planted after the species' 2006 scientific description, at least a decade old
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street; enter at the East Gate on Inverleith Row rather than the West Gate
trees.story:
Until September 2020, the Catacol whitebeam was one of the rarest trees on earth: a single wild specimen, in one ravine on the Isle of Arran, tied with Wood's cycad for the title. Then a second wild tree was found. Before that, nearly everything standing between the species and extinction was a handful of grafts, and several of them grow here, beside the coffee shop at the Botanics' East Gate.

The tree was only described as new to science in 2006. Seed germination has had limited success, so the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh propagates it by grafting cuttings onto ordinary rowan rootstock, and one of the garden's own staff records collecting berries from the East Gate tree in autumn 2014. That date is also the honest limit of what is known about these particular specimens. No source gives them a planting date or an age. They were grafted at some point after 2006 and were established by 2014, and beyond that they are undated.

This is a planting rather than one heroic tree, with other Arran-only Sorbus species standing alongside it. Small trees, easy to walk straight past. The reason to stop is that the wild population, in a Glen Catacol ravine, could be taken out by a single winter flood, which RBGE staff say in plain words. These grafts are the insurance policy.

trees.name: The Handkerchief Tree by Caledonian Hall
trees.age: roughly 95 years, accessioned by RBGE in 1928
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street

best_time.label: May, when the white bracts open and the whole tree looks hung with handkerchiefs

trees.story:
The white handkerchiefs are not flowers. Davidia involucrata produces a small, dark, unremarkable flower head and wraps it in two large white bracts, modified leaves that hang and turn in any breeze. In May a mature tree carries hundreds of them at once, which is how it collected the names handkerchief tree, dove tree and ghost tree.

This one stands in the Caledonian Hall area of the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, filed in the garden's living collection database under accession number 19280013. RBGE accession numbers open with the year the plant came in, so that reads as 1928 and puts the tree at roughly 95 to 98 years old. Treat it as a strong estimate rather than a certificate: an accession year records when the garden took a plant onto its books, not the day it went into the ground, and the two can sit a season or several years apart.

The species is native to south west China and was among the most fought-over introductions of the early 20th century, when European nurseries were sending collectors across China specifically to bring it home. RBGE holds several Davidia accessions around the garden; this is the Caledonian Hall one, the oldest-accessioned of them and the nearest to the rest of this walk. Its pin comes from the building's position on the visitor map rather than a measured point.

trees.name: The 1948 Dawn Redwood of the Chinese Hillside
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street
trees.story: Until 1944, the dawn redwood was known only as a fossil, a conifer botanists assumed had died out millions of years ago. Then a Chinese forestry official spotted an unfamiliar deciduous conifer growing near a village in central China, and by 1948 the find had become one of the great botanical events of the century: the Arnold Arboretum in Boston organised a seed-collecting expedition to the same valley and mailed packets of Metasequoia glyptostroboides seed to institutions worldwide, ending a species' presumed extinction in a single shipment. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh was among the recipients, and five specimens grown from that original 1948 consignment still stand scattered through the garden today, sharing one accession number and one origin story. This is the one on the Chinese Hillside, a short walk from the garden's other Inverleith trees. A dawn redwood grows fast for a conifer, which is why this one is barely 75 years old and already substantial, deciduous unlike almost every relative it has, its needles turning rust orange before dropping each autumn. It is not RBGE's oldest tree by a long way. It is one of the closest things botany has to a resurrection story, planted the decade the species seemed impossible.

trees.name: The Champion Whitebeam of the Botanics
trees.access: Free, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (garden free, glasshouses paid and currently closed for restoration)
trees.transport: Bus to Inverleith Row, or 25 min walk from Princes Street
trees.story: Sorbus hemsleyi is a whitebeam from central China, rare enough in cultivation that the Tree Register of the British Isles lists a single UK and Ireland champion for the species by trunk girth, and it grows here, a few paces from the garden's other rare whitebeam, the Catacol whitebeam saved from extinction by grafting cuttings onto rowan rootstock. This tree came from seed collected under accession SABE 1317 and went into the ground in 1981, a young tree by the Botanics' standards, not yet fifty, in a collection that includes trees planted two centuries earlier. What it lacks in age it makes up in rarity: whitebeams hybridise and speciate readily, throwing up dozens of narrow endemics found on a single hillside or gorge, and Sorbus hemsleyi's presence here, thriving enough in an August 2023 photograph to still hold its champion title, belongs to the same conservation instinct behind the garden's Catacol grafts a short walk away. It carries white flowers in spring and orange red berries by autumn, ordinary whitebeam fare, but the specific tree, its girth on record with Britain's tree registry, is what makes it worth finding. Free to see, in the same eastern corner of the garden as the John Muir Grove and the Handkerchief Tree.

trees.name: The Philips Tree
trees.age: about 117 years, from a documented planting in 1909
trees.access: Free. Public square outside the stadium, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: Eindhoven Centraal, then about 15 minutes on foot west, or bus to Philips Stadion.

best_time.label: May, when the candles are up

trees.story:
It has 470 square metres of ground reserved for its roots, in a city centre, next to a football stadium. That is the detail worth knowing: somebody drew a line on a map and decided nothing would ever be built inside it.

Anton Philips had the chestnut planted in 1909 in Philipsdorp, the neighbourhood his company was about to build for its workers. The reasoning was not sentimental. Philips believed staff performed better with something green around them, and the tree went in a year before the first houses did.

So it is older than the district, older than the stadium beside it, and older than the club that plays there, which the company founded in 1913. The houses went up around it, the ground was cleared for the ground, the stands grew, and the chestnut kept its square.

On a match day forty thousand people walk past it and most of them do not look up. Gate 11 is the one to aim for. It is the tree standing in its own patch of open ground while everything else is paving.

Horse chestnuts flower in candles in May and drop conkers in September, which in this spot means several thousand people kicking them across a car park.

trees.name: De Gevlekte Zuiderling
trees.age: roughly 200 years by the national register, closer to 265 by the foundation that named it
trees.access: Free. Public park at Groendomein Wasven, open daily.
trees.transport: About 4 km east of Eindhoven Centraal. Bus to Tongelre, then a short walk into the Wasven grounds.
trees.story:
On the night of 28 July 2022 three teenagers set this tree on fire. The brigade put it out, the bark and the base of the trunk were charred through, and arborists put its chances of surviving at thirty percent. What they could not tell was whether the heat had cooked the sap flow, and the answer would not be visible until the spring of 2024.

It came back. Thirty strong shoots pushed up from the ground around the trunk, and rather than clear them a specialist began weaving them together, using an American technique, into a living scaffold that will hold the old trunk up as it rots over the next thirty years. A crowdfunder raised eleven thousand euro. The burnt platform around the base was cut away by hand so the roots were not disturbed.

It stands 28 metres tall with a trunk eight metres round at the base, in the park of a castle that was demolished in 1872. In October 2009 it became the first Wereldboom in the Netherlands.

Its age is disputed. The foundation that named it says planted around 1760; the national register says the 1820s. Nobody has cored it.

Go and look at the black trunk and the young growth climbing it.

trees.name: The Oak of De Wielewaal
trees.age: roughly 170 to 180 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Public since 27 September 2025. No mountain bikes or motor vehicles.
trees.transport: About 5 km northwest of Eindhoven Centraal. Entrances at Elburglaan 2 and 12 and Oirschotsedijk 3.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down along the avenue

trees.story:
For a hundred years you could not come here. This was the private estate of Frits Philips, who built the house in 1934 and lived in it until he died in 2005, on land his father Anton had bought in 1912 when it was a farm called Het Zwarte Huis.
