The city bought the whole thing in 2022 for twenty nine million euro and opened it to the public on 27 September 2025.

It is 144 hectares, three times the size of the Vondelpark, and entry is free.

This oak was already standing when Anton Philips arrived. In 1850 the ground here was open heath; it was planted up over the second half of the century, and by 1897 the map showed pine wood cut through by avenues of oak. This is one of those avenue trees, which is why it is a good deal older than most of what surrounds it.

The estate is large enough that the pin marks the surveyed position rather than a spot you can stand on and be certain. Come in from Oirschotsedijk and follow the old avenue lines; they are still legible in the way the wood is laid out, and the oaks along them are the thick ones.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Wielewaal Pinetum
trees.age: roughly 105 to 115 years, from the register's planting band of 1910 to 1920
trees.access: Free. Public since 27 September 2025.
trees.transport: About 5 km northwest of Eindhoven Centraal. Nearest entrance Oirschotsedijk 3.
trees.story:
In 1912 Anton Philips bought a farm on the heath and immediately started collecting conifers. He laid out a pinetum, a star wood with paths radiating from a single point, a maze and a rockery, which tells you what kind of man he was about land: it was to be arranged.

This is one of the trees from that planting, a giant sequoia, a species from the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada that had been in European gardens for about sixty years when it went in here. In California they are the largest living things on earth. In a Brabant pinetum a hundred-year-old one is a tall, red-brown column with bark you can push your fist into, soft and fibrous and thick enough to have evolved against forest fire.

It has a long way to go. Sequoias run to three thousand years and this one is barely out of its first century, which is the pleasant thing about standing under it: on its own timescale, the entire Philips story happened this morning.

The pinetum is signposted from the Oirschotsedijk entrance. Look for the conifer that is obviously wider than everything around it.

trees.name: The Oak by the Wilhelmina Monument
trees.age: roughly 170 to 180 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Public city park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 4 km northwest of Eindhoven Centraal, off the Bezuidenhoutseweg.
trees.story:
In 1920 Anton Philips and his wife Anna de Jongh gave twenty five hectares of wood to the people of Eindhoven. They had bought it as pine plantation in 1912, turned it into something you could walk in, and handed it over after the neighbouring municipality of Strijp was absorbed into the city. The garden architect D. F. Tersteeg laid it out in the English landscape manner, grass opening into stands of trees, and it opened as a park in 1924.

This oak was there before any of that. The register puts it in the 1850s, which makes it sixty years older than the purchase and a survivor of whatever stood here when the ground was still being planted up from heath.

That is worth holding in mind while you look at it. The park is a designed thing, made by a company for its workers and then given away. The oak is not part of the design. It was simply already standing where somebody later decided to put a path.

It stands to the left of the path running to the Wilhelmina monument. The park was fully renovated in 2009, so the surroundings are tidier than the tree.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Glorieuxpark
trees.age: roughly 275 to 325 years, from the register's planting band of 1700 to 1750
trees.access: Free. Park owned by a religious order, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal, on the Geldropseweg.

best_time.label: October, when the purple burns through to copper

trees.story:
This is the oldest thing standing in Eindhoven, by a wide margin and by the register's own dating: a planting band of 1700 to 1750, so somewhere between about 275 and 325 years. Everything else on this page is a Philips tree. This one was full grown before the family arrived.

The ground has changed hands and purpose repeatedly around it. It was the Eikenburg estate; in 1894 the Brothers of Charity bought it and opened a boys' boarding school, adding pavilions over the decades; the boarding school closed in 1996 for lack of pupils, and care and education organisations moved into the buildings. The main house, the old school, the chapel and a mounted statue of Saint George are all listed national monuments. A religious order still owns the park, and the register records it as visitable.

One honest note. This park also held the thickest beech in the whole of North Brabant, and it is gone: a large part of its crown came down on its own in September 2013 and the remaining trunk was taken out. That was a different tree, a green beech, and the register recorded this one eleven years afterwards. If you go and find this one has followed it, tell us.

trees.name: De Lichtjesboom
trees.age: roughly 100 to 110 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.access: Free. Street tree in a public planting strip.
trees.transport: About 5 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal, in the Gijzenrooi district.
trees.story:
Every December the neighbourhood covers this oak in fairy lights, and keeps them on through January. It is not a municipal display and nobody is paid to do it. That is why the street knows it as the lichtjesboom, the little lights tree, rather than by anything the register calls it.

The rest of the year it is a good ordinary oak of about a century, standing clear of the houses in the strip of planting along the Diepmeerven, well enough placed that you see the whole shape of it from the pavement. The street name probably points at the Diepe Meerven, a small heath pool a way off toward Heeze, which is what this whole district was before it was a district.

It is the smallest tree on this page and the only one on it because of what people do with it. Eindhoven is a city that thinks about light more than most, having spent a century making it, and the version that matters here is a hundred bulbs strung through an oak by people who live on the street.

Go in December. In August you will see an oak.

trees.name: The Lime of the Noordeind
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, and the register suggests a planting around 1790
trees.access: Free. Stands on the public street opposite number 9.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Emmen centre, on the Noordeind.

best_time.label: July, when the blossom carries down the whole street

trees.story:
The oldest part of Emmen is a street, and this is the tree on it.

Emmen began as an esdorp on the southeastern shoulder of the Hondsrug, the long sand ridge that runs across Drenthe. An esdorp is a village organised around a shared arable field, the es, built up over centuries with sods and manure until the soil was deep enough to farm on ground that was otherwise heath. The Noordeind was where it started, lined with the characteristic Drenthe farmhouses, most of which have gone.

The lime stayed, planted, the register suggests, around 1790.

A village lime in this part of the country was never ornamental. It was the meeting point: shade in summer, a place to stand and settle things, sometimes the spot where local justice was spoken, and always the thing you gave directions by. That is why so many of them are older than the houses. Nobody removes the tree everyone arranges to meet at.

Go in July, when it flowers. Lime blossom on a still evening is heavy and sweet and carries the length of a village street, and it is one of the few sensory experiences here that has not changed since 1790.

trees.name: The Oak in Hunebed D42
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Open ground at the hunebed, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 3 km northwest of Emmen centre, off the Schietbaanweg.

best_time.label: October, when acorns collect between the stones

trees.story:
The oak is standing in the middle of the tomb.

Hunebed D42 is one of the larger megalithic chambers in Drenthe and one of the less visited, which is part of why this happened. Five thousand years ago people here dragged glacial boulders into a chamber and covered it with earth. Somewhere around 1880 an acorn got into the middle of it and nobody took the seedling out.

The register describes the result plainly: an enormous oak in the middle of the hunebed, which it calls a striking sight, and says the whole picture makes it worth a visit. That is unusually enthusiastic for an official survey and it is right.

What you get is two kinds of permanence in one frame. The stones have been there since before writing, before the wheel reached this part of Europe, before bronze. The oak has been there for a century and a half and is, in tree terms, not old. Standing between them rearranges your sense of both.

An oak's roots in a chamber tomb are not neutral, and that tension is part of what you are looking at.

It is off the Schietbaanweg, northwest of Emmen.

trees.name: The Oak at the Long Grave
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Open ground at the hunebed, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km northeast of Emmen centre, along the Odoornerstraat.
trees.story:
There is only one long grave in the Netherlands and this oak is standing next to it.

Hunebed D43 is a langgraf: instead of a single chamber under a round mound, it has a covering mound forty metres long with two separate burial chambers set into it, the whole thing ringed by a kerb of stones. Fifty two of them survive, and the ring has been restored so that it reads almost completely. Nothing else of this form exists in the country.

The oak went in some four and a half thousand years later, between 1860 and 1870.

What makes this pair better than the tomb alone is scale. A forty metre mound is hard to see as a shape; from a distance it is a rise in the ground. A big oak beside it gives you something to measure against, and the length of the thing suddenly registers.

Oaks and burial sites go together across northern Europe, and not by chance: burial mounds were left unploughed for centuries, so they became the one place in a farmed landscape where a tree could reach two hundred years.

Walk the full length of the kerb. It takes longer than you expect.

trees.name: The Tiger Oak of the Rensenpark
trees.age: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820
trees.access: Free. Public park in the centre of Emmen.
trees.transport: In the centre of Emmen, on the Hoofdstraat.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down

trees.story:
The register calls this one the tijgereik, the tiger oak, which is a nickname earned by geography rather than by anything about the tree.

The Rensenpark is a park in the middle of Emmen and it is built on the site of the old Dierenpark Emmen, the zoo that stood here for most of the twentieth century before moving to a new site. The animals are gone and the park is public, but the layout remembers them, and so does this oak, which spent decades standing beside an enclosure.

It was planted between 1810 and 1820, so it is a good deal older than the zoo and predates the town centre growing out to reach it.

A two hundred year old oak in a former zoo is a peculiar object to stand in front of. The ground around it was, within living memory, a place people came to look at animals from other continents, and now it is grass. The tree is the only exhibit still in position.

Acorns on long stalks, leaves seated almost directly on the twig. In October there will be a great many of them, and no tigers.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Nieuw-Schoonebeek
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.access: Grounds of the parish centre, recorded as visitable in the national register. Not a public park, so look from where you are welcome to stand.
trees.transport: About 20 km south of Emmen, at Nieuw-Schoonebeek on the Europaweg.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns copper

trees.story:
The church is gone and only the tower is left. The presbytery has been rebuilt out of recognition. The park is still there, and so is this beech.

A fine park was laid out at the old presbytery of the Catholic church of St Bonifatius in Nieuw-Schoonebeek at the beginning of the twentieth century. The beech, banded 1750 to 1800, is far older than that and was standing long before anyone laid out anything, which is the same pattern as almost every other church tree in this country: the ground was already planted and the institution arrived to join it.

If the band is right, this is as old as the lime at the Noordeind and one of the oldest trees in the municipality.

A copper beech at two and a half centuries in a Drenthe village is also slightly improbable. The purple form was a scarce nursery product in the eighteenth century, largely confined to estates and botanic collections, so somebody with money and connections put it here.

October, when it burns through to copper against a medieval tower stump.

trees.name: The Plane of the Bonifatius Park
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Grounds of the parish centre, recorded as visitable in the national register. Not a public park.
trees.transport: About 20 km south of Emmen, at Nieuw-Schoonebeek on the Europaweg.
trees.story:
A London plane in a Drenthe village is a stranger, and that is the interesting part.

The species is the definitive city tree of northern Europe, planted by the hundred thousand along boulevards from London to Vienna because it survives paving, pollution, root damage and hard pruning better than anything of its size. What it is not is a village tree. Out here, in a small park behind a parish centre on the German border, there is nothing for it to tolerate.

So it has simply grown, in good soil, unpruned, with room. That produces a shape most people never see on a plane: broad rather than columnar, low branching, and far wider than a street specimen of the same age.

It is banded 1860 to 1870, and it stands with the copper beech in the park laid out at the old presbytery, of whose church only the tower survives.

The bark is the giveaway from any distance, flaking away in irregular plates to leave a mottle of cream, olive and grey. On an unpolluted country tree the pale patches stay paler, so it is a brighter thing here than in any city.

trees.name: The Oak of Erica
trees.age: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
trees.access: Stands in a front garden on the canal side, recorded as visitable in the national register. Look from the public road.
trees.transport: About 10 km southwest of Emmen, at Erica on the Verlengde Vaart Zuidzijde.
trees.story:
This village was made by digging peat, and the oak is about as old as the village.

Erica began around 1863 as a buckwheat colony on the higher sandy ground, the kind of marginal settlement people started where nothing better was available. It became a proper peat colony when the Hoogeveense Vaart, the canal, was completed in the same period, and the centre of the place shifted to sit on the water. The address of this tree still says it: Verlengde Vaart Zuidzijde, the south side of the extended canal.

Peat colonies were built to strip the ground. Men cut the bog, dried it, and sent it out by barge, and when the peat was gone what was left was thin sand and a grid of canals. Almost nothing planted in that first generation survived, because there was no reason to keep it.

This oak was planted between 1870 and 1880 in a front garden, which is exactly why it did. A tree in somebody's own garden had a defender.

It is a private front garden on a canal bank. Look from the road.

trees.name: The Wellingtonia of the Ledeboerpark
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, and the register cites an 1865 invoice for a Wellingtonia planted here
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 2 km northwest of Enschede station, on the Hengelosestraat.
trees.story:
Somebody wrote down what this tree cost.

The register cites a document in the archive of the Twente textile families: in 1866 the mill owner H. J. van Heek and the garden architect D. Wattez corresponded about the price of a Wellingtonia, itemised on an invoice for the planting around 't Wageler in 1865. Wellingtonia was the trade name the British gave the giant sequoia after the Duke of Wellington, and in the 1860s it was the most fashionable and most expensive thing you could put in a garden in Europe. The species had only been introduced to Britain in 1853. Buying one was a way of saying what you were worth.

The park is what became of that estate. Wattez laid it out in the second half of the nineteenth century, the city absorbed it, and the Ledeboerpark on the Hengelosestraat is now open to anyone.

So you can go and stand under an object of Victorian conspicuous consumption that has quietly outlived the mills, the family's fortune and the argument about the price.

It is unmistakable: the thick red-brown trunk with soft fibrous bark, and a straight conical top.

trees.name: De Eik op 't Zeggelt
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.access: Free. Public planting in a residential district, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Enschede station, in the Lasonder-Zeggelt district.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns are down

trees.story:
The oldest tree in Enschede is not on anybody's estate. It stands in ordinary public planting in a residential district and it has a name anyway, which is usually a sign that people have been walking past it long enough to need one.

The register bands it 1750 to 1800, which makes it two to two and a half centuries and puts its first decades in a Twente of farms and hand looms, before the mills, before the railway, and long before the town around it. Enschede burned almost entirely to the ground in 1862, when a fire took the whole centre in a few hours. This oak was standing well outside it and is one of the few living things in the city that predates that day.

The register gives its position to six decimal places, which is the tell that somebody stood at the trunk with a satellite receiver rather than pointing at a street. That is unusual in this dataset and it means the pin is as good as pins get.

Pedunculate oak, so acorns on long stalks and leaves that sit almost directly on the twig. In October there will be a great many of them underfoot.

trees.name: The Beech of Landgoed Wageler
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Free. On the estate grounds, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km northwest of Enschede station, near the Ledeboerpark.

best_time.label: October, when the whole crown goes copper

trees.story:
This beech was on the estate before the estate was designed.

't Wageler is the ground that Wattez planted for the Van Heeks in the 1860s and that partly became the Ledeboerpark. The register bands this tree 1830 to 1840, thirty years earlier, which means it was a mature tree of some size when the landscape architect arrived with his plans and his invoices.

That is the ordinary way a Dutch estate garden was actually made. You did not clear ground and start over. You looked at what was standing, kept whatever was good, and arranged the new planting to make the most of it, which is why the oldest tree in a nineteenth century park is so often older than the park.

It stands along the Es, the old open arable field that these Twente farms were organised around. An es is a very specific thing here: a slightly raised field built up over centuries by carting in sods and manure, so the soil under it can be a metre deeper than the heath beside it. Good ground, and part of why a beech here grew as it did.

Smooth grey bark, deep shade, bare litter beneath.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Het Bouwhuis
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. The register records the grounds as open to the public.
trees.transport: About 5 km northeast of Enschede station, at Lonneker.
trees.story:
The farm this tree stands on was first written down in 1536.

In that year Jan van Borne, steward of the chapter of St Peter in Utrecht, reported on two holdings in the hamlet of Lonneker: Het Bouwhuis and Het Amelink. The Amelink then belonged to the Jonker van Steinfurt, which is to say the count of Bentheim. So the ground has an unbroken paper trail running back close to five centuries, into a landscape of church chapters and minor German nobility, which is roughly four hundred years before anyone here had heard of a sequoia.

The tree is the newcomer, planted somewhere between 1900 and 1910, when a giant sequoia had gone from a spectacular novelty to the standard way of announcing that a country house had grounds.

The register notes that Het Bouwhuis is open to the public and that a good many striking trees stand there, which makes this one of the easier estates on this page to simply walk into.

A hundred and twenty years is nothing for the species. In California this would be a sapling among trees three thousand years old. Here it is already the biggest thing in the field.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech by the Pond
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. The register records the grounds as open to the public.
trees.transport: About 5 km northeast of Enschede station, at Lonneker.
trees.story:
Go inside it. That is the point of a weeping beech and almost nobody does it.

The branches of a mature one arch out and then fall straight to the ground all the way round, so what you have is a green tent perhaps fifteen metres across with a bare floor and a trunk in the middle. Children work this out immediately. Adults walk past.

Weeping beech is a cultivar, not a species: a mutant form propagated by grafting, so every one is a clone of an original found in Europe in the eighteenth century. The graft union is usually visible as a swelling low on the trunk. It grows the same way a normal beech does except that it cannot hold its branches up, and left alone it will layer, meaning a branch resting on soil roots and becomes a new trunk, so an old one can slowly walk outward across a lawn.

This one stands on the northeast side of the pond at Het Bouwhuis, planted between 1900 and 1910, on ground documented since 1536.

Duck under the skirt on the pond side and look back out at the water through the leaves.

trees.name: The Sessile Oak of the Blijdensteinpark
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 2 km east of Enschede station, on the Boulevard 1945.
trees.story:
A dual carriageway runs through this park, and the tree is by a filling station. Both facts are worth stating first, because they are what this place is now.

It began as an estate. In 1855 H. G. Blijdenstein and his wife Ebeling built a villa on the Helweg, the road that later became the Gronausestraat, and laid out grounds around it. Their daughter Johanna Ida Beltman-Blijdenstein was the last person to live there. The Blijdensteins were one of the Twente textile dynasties, and like the Van Heeks and the Ledeboers what they left the city was ground with trees on it.

What happened afterwards is what happens to green space near a growing city. The Boulevard 1945 was driven straight through the park, cutting it in two, and the eastern edge now holds a petrol station.

The oak has been there since around 1900 to 1910 and has watched the arrangement change around it. It is a sessile oak, so the acorns sit tight against the twig and the leaves have a clear stalk, the reverse of the commoner pedunculate oak.

Go on a Sunday, when the road is quiet.

trees.name: The Plane of 't Zwik
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Street tree on public ground.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Enschede station, on the Cort van der Lindelaan.
trees.story:
There was a country house here called 't Zwik and there is a street pattern instead.

The city bought the place in 1917 to expand into, and built over it through the 1920s and 1930s, which was the ordinary fate of the smaller estates on the edge of a town whose population was climbing with every new mill. The house went. What survived is planting: this plane, and, sixty to a hundred metres to the west, an oak and a beech that the register also identifies as remnants of the same grounds.

That is a useful thing to know while standing here. Three trees at three points along a street are not a coincidence, they are the last legible trace of a garden, and if you draw a line between them you are walking somebody's approach.

The plane is the easiest of the three to spot: flaking bark in cream, olive and grey, big maple-shaped leaves, and the bristly round seed balls that hang on through the winter.

Planes are the great survivors of city building. They tolerate compacted soil, root disturbance, pollution and hard pruning better than anything else of their size, which is exactly why this one is still here and the house is not.

trees.name: The Gray Poplar of Palazzo dei Diamanti
trees.access: Free, in the palace garden, generally open with the palace's own hours; check before visiting
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north-west of Ferrara railway station
trees.story:
This gray poplar has grown in the garden of one of the Italian Renaissance's most recognisable buildings for more than a century and a half, long enough to have watched the palace's stone facade go from a private noble residence to a public gallery. Palazzo dei Diamanti, faced with 8,500 pointed marble blocks cut to look like diamonds, gives its name to the whole Renaissance addition to the city Duke Ercole I d'Este ordered in 1492, a planned extension that later helped earn Ferrara its UNESCO World Heritage listing.

The tree itself, 4.44 metres round and 24 metres tall, is a hybrid of white poplar and European aspen, identifiable by bark that starts pale gray with diamond-shaped fissures echoing the palace's own facade and darkens to brown with age. It was named to Italy's first official list of monumental trees under the 2013 protection law, recognised for both its age and its size.

A 2023 restoration of the garden finally opened the space properly to visitors, so a tree that had spent most of its life screening a private courtyard now grows in ground anyone can walk into.

trees.name: The Bagolaro of Parco Massari
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north-east of Ferrara railway station
trees.story:
Parco Massari has changed hands three times since architect Luigi Bertelli laid it out in 1780 for the Marchese Camillo Bevilacqua: to the Massari counts in the mid-19th century, who remade it as an English-style landscape park, and in 1936 to the city of Ferrara, which still owns it. This hackberry, about 150 years old, was already growing when that last transfer happened.

Its trunk runs 3.76 metres round, straight and fluted under gray bark, holding up a dense, rounded crown on branches wide enough in diameter to have earned it individual protection on Italy's first monumental tree list alongside the park's three cedars of Lebanon. Celtis australis takes its Italian name, bagolaro, from a Lombard word for a tool handle, a nod to timber once prized for exactly that; a second nickname, spaccasassi, rock-breaker, describes its willingness to root in poor, stony ground where softer species fail.

The species can live 600 years by some accounts, which makes a century and a half look like the opening chapter rather than the whole story.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Parco Massari
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north-east of Ferrara railway station

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn a uniform hard gold

trees.story:
Parco Massari's plant list runs long, planes, paulownias, horse chestnuts, magnolias, birches, limes, firs, pines, acacias, but the ginkgo is the one tree in it whose lineage predates the flowering plants surrounding it by tens of millions of years. This specimen, 3.80 metres round and 25 metres tall, grows among the park's other monumental trees, the three cedars of Lebanon and the bagolaro that made Italy's first official protected-tree list together.

Ginkgo biloba is the last living species of an order that once grew across the northern hemisphere and had been reduced, by the time European botanists took an interest, to a handful of cultivated groves in China. It survives poor soil, pollution and pests that would finish off almost anything else, and it turns a hard, uniform gold in autumn rather than the mixed colours most deciduous trees show.

The park itself was laid out in 1780 for a marchese, remade as an English landscape garden by the Massari family in the 19th century, and sold to the city of Ferrara in 1936, so this tree has spent at least part of its life under each of those owners.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Biblioteca Ariostea
trees.access: Free, in the library's public courtyard garden, open during library hours
trees.transport: About a 10 minute walk south of Ferrara Castello Estense

best_time.label: late November into early December, when the canopy turns gold and draws crowds to photograph it

trees.story:
The first written record of this tree dates to 1890, and it did not start out in a library garden. It is a survivor of the University of Ferrara's old botanical garden, once kept in the courtyard of Palazzo Paradiso, the building that now houses the Biblioteca Ariostea, the city's historic public library. When the university's collection moved on, this ginkgo did not go with it.

At 4.65 metres round and about 20 metres tall, with a canopy wide enough to fill the courtyard it stands in, it is a male tree, which means it never produces the strong-smelling fruit that gives female ginkgos their bad reputation, only the fan-shaped leaves that turn a uniform gold every autumn and draw crowds specifically to photograph it. Local papers cover the display most years, treating a single tree changing colour as news, which is a fair measure of how much the city has come to value it.

Ginkgo biloba's lineage runs back some 250 million years, effectively unchanged, a genuine living fossil rather than a marketing phrase. A specimen first recorded in a 19th century university garden and still standing in the 21st is, by the standards of its own family tree, barely middle-aged.

trees.name: The Plane of Viale Po
trees.access: Free, on the public street, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: About a 20 minute walk north-west of Ferrara railway station
trees.story:
The thickest trunk on this page belongs to a street tree rather than to anything growing in a park or a palace garden. This London plane on Viale Po measures 5.40 metres round, on a tree 20 metres tall, and the city has nominated it, along with a short list of other exceptional specimens across Ferrara, for protection under the Emilia-Romagna region's safeguarding measures for flora of particular merit.

London planes were planted along avenues across European cities from the 18th century onward for the same practical reasons that still apply on Viale Po: fast growth, tolerance of compacted soil and pollution, and a canopy wide enough to shade a whole street. What sets this one apart from the species doing the same job on a thousand other avenues is simply scale, a girth most street planes never come close to reaching before they are pruned back or replaced.

No individual planting date survives for it, which is ordinary for a street tree rather than a garden specimen with its own record. The register measures it; nobody has dated it.

trees.name: The Micheli Yew
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Florence's oldest verified tree grows behind a ticket gate, in a garden older than the city's most famous museums by two centuries. Pier Antonio Micheli planted this yew in 1720, while running the Orto Botanico for Cosimo III de' Medici, and it has now outlived the Grand Duchy that employed him by more than 150 years. At around 306 years old it is Florence's most precisely dated living thing: unlike the ring-count guesswork behind most ancient trees, its planting is on record because Micheli, one of Europe's first professional botanists, kept the garden's books himself. The trunk has thickened to nearly four metres around, and its dark, dense crown still throws the kind of deep shade yews are prized and feared for; every part of the tree except the red flesh around the seed is poisonous, a fact eighteenth century physicians studying it would have known well. The Giardino dei Semplici itself opened in 1545 to grow medicinal plants for the Medici, making it one of the oldest university botanical gardens anywhere in the world, and this yew has stood in it for nearly two thirds of that entire history. It survived the catastrophic 1966 Arno flood that drowned much of central Florence a few streets away, and it is still growing, still dropping the small red arils that birds strip clean every autumn.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of the Giardino dei Semplici
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
trees.story: Every commercial cork oak in Portugal and Spain gets stripped bare every nine years or so, its bark peeled for wine corks and flooring while the tree survives underneath, scarred orange until it heals. Florence's cork oak, planted in 1805 by Ottaviano Targioni Tozzetti in the same botanical garden that grew Micheli's yew, has never once been stripped. Two centuries of undisturbed growth have thickened its bark into a spongy, deeply fissured armour more than four metres around, exactly the texture and thickness that would make a cork harvester elsewhere in the Mediterranean take notice. Left alone for research and teaching rather than product, it has instead grown one of the widest, most theatrical crowns in the Giardino dei Semplici, spreading over 400 square metres of canopy from a single trunk. Targioni Tozzetti directed the garden in the early 1800s, the third generation of a Tuscan dynasty of naturalists, and this tree was one of his additions to a collection built around teaching pharmacy students to recognise plants by sight rather than from a drawing. It stands a short walk from the yew, in a garden that has quietly kept some of the oldest documented specimens of both species in Italy, without either one ever having to earn its keep.

trees.name: The Montezuma Cypress
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
trees.story: Nothing else in Florence comes from Mexico, has a trunk seven metres around, and survived being struck by lightning barely a decade ago. This Montezuma cypress, a cousin of the American bald cypress native to riverbanks around Mexico City, went into the ground at the Giardino dei Semplici in the 1880s, brought north as one of the many botanical trophies nineteenth century gardens competed to acquire. It grew for over a century without much incident, reaching a girth few trees on this list can match, before a September 2014 storm hit it directly, splitting and reshaping its crown in a single afternoon. The tree survived, though its silhouette now carries the asymmetry of that strike rather than the tidy pyramid shape the species usually holds. In its native range this cypress can live for a thousand years or more, most famously as the Arbol del Tule near Oaxaca, one of the stoutest trees on Earth; Florence's specimen is a comparative youngster, but it is already the widest girthed tree in this entire list. Visitors touring the botanical garden for its more famous residents, the Medici era yew and the cork oak nearby, often walk straight past it without registering that they have just passed something that does not grow naturally anywhere within four thousand kilometres of Tuscany.

trees.name: The Farnia of the Ippodromo
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 20 min walk from the Cascine tram stop (T1), through the park to the former Ippodromo delle Mulina

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: The tallest tree in Florence's largest park stands where racehorses used to run. This pedunculate oak, rising 29 metres above the western meadows of the Parco delle Cascine, grows on the site of the old Ippodromo delle Mulina, a trotting racecourse that operated from 1891 until Florence's city council reclaimed the disused land in recent years. The oak predates the racecourse by generations. It is one of only six trees the City of Florence has formally recognised as monumental in its own right, a status granted well before the municipality's recent push to catalogue dozens more candidates across the Cascine and its historic villas, a list that has grown from a dozen entries in 2020 to 29 by 2026. Its trunk measures close to four and a half metres around, wide enough that arborists estimate its age at well over a century without ever finding a planting record to confirm it. What is certain is its size: nothing else standing in the Cascine's 130 hectares, a park with its own dark history (Nazi occupying forces used it for a mass execution in July 1944, still marked today by a memorial stone), comes close to this oak's height. It grows at the park's western edge, past the horse chestnuts and the poplars, far from the joggers and market stalls nearer the city, exactly where a tree left alone for a century tends to end up.

trees.name: The Leccio of the Cascine
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Cascine tram stop (T1), along the Arno-side path
trees.story: This holm oak has spent its whole life fighting for balance, and it shows. Growing beside the Arno-facing path through the Parco delle Cascine, not far from the market that sets up every Tuesday along the river, the tree has developed unusually large buttress roots and long exposed root sections that flare out from its base like something built rather than grown. Arborists who surveyed it in 2022 and again in 2025 recorded a trunk holding steady at just over four metres around and a canopy reaching nearly 19 metres high, and rated its health excellent both times, buttresses and all. Holm oaks are evergreen, native across the Mediterranean, and built to survive exactly the kind of periodic flooding the Arno has delivered to this park for centuries; the exposed, muscular root system is very likely the tree's own answer to wet, shifting soil rather than a defect. No documented planting date survives for it, which is typical for a park this old and this large, but its girth puts it easily past its first century. It stands in a stretch of the Cascine most tourists never reach, well past the old horse track, in the quieter western half of a park that has been public land since Napoleon's own sister, Elisa Baciocchi, opened the former Medici hunting grounds to ordinary Florentines during her rule as Grand Duchess of Tuscany.

trees.name: The Honey Locust of Salviatino
trees.access: Free, public street corner
trees.transport: Bus line 11 to the Salviatino terminus, then a short walk down Via Lungo l'Affrico
trees.story: Florence has two trees popularly linked to Judas, and this is the one people picture wrong. The tree usually called Albero di Giuda in Italian is Cercis siliquastrum, the small pink flowered species tied to the legend that Judas hanged himself from one; this is Spino di Giuda, a completely different tree, honey locust, native to North America and named instead for its genuinely vicious thorns, some once over ten centimetres long, that grew along its trunk and branches before cultivated varieties bred them softer. Florence's specimen, standing alone at a residential intersection in Salviatino on the city's northeastern edge, has never been bred for anything. Its trunk has thickened to five and a half metres around, among the largest recorded for the species anywhere, and Italy's own monumental tree registry gives it national level significance, a rating few other Florentine trees share. No planting record survives, which is common for a tree standing on what was once open agricultural land before Salviatino urbanised around it. It offers little shade in winter and no flowers to speak of, and most residents of the surrounding apartment blocks likely have no idea their street corner holds a genuine botanical record holder.

trees.name: The Cedar of the Bobolino
trees.age: age undocumented, garden dates from the 1860s-70s
trees.access: Free, public garden, always open
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Porta Romana, along Viale Machiavelli

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Most of Florence's grand hillside gardens exist because the city briefly ran the whole of Italy. When Florence served as the young kingdom's capital between 1865 and 1871, architect Giuseppe Poggi was given the job of modernising it, and alongside demolishing the old city walls for wide boulevards he laid out a string of new parks on the hills above the Arno, of which the Bobolino, a modest wedge of public garden near Porta Romana, is one of the smallest and least visited. Its centrepiece is this cedar of Lebanon, now with a trunk over four and a half metres around and a crown just past 22 metres tall, standing roughly where Poggi's plan put it a century and a half ago. Italy's regional registry lists this cedar among Tuscany's officially recognised monumental trees, one entry in the growing tally of Florence specimens that has expanded from a dozen in 2020 to 29 candidates by 2026 as the municipality works through a backlog of overlooked trees across its parks. Unlike its more famous neighbour Boboli a few hundred metres away, the Bobolino charges nothing and never closes its gates, which makes this cedar one of the few genuinely monumental trees in Florence that anyone can walk up to at any hour of the day or night.

trees.name: The Cedar Above Pegasus
trees.access: Paid entry (Boboli Gardens ticket)
trees.transport: 15 min walk uphill from the Palazzo Pitti entrance to the Giardino del Cavaliere terrace
trees.story: Florence's public symbol has stood next to this cedar since 1865, and almost nobody visiting climbs high enough in the Boboli Gardens to notice either one. The Giardino del Cavaliere, a walled terrace at the garden's highest point, holds a winged horse statue that the Tuscany region has since adopted as its own official emblem, sculpted by Aristodemo Costoli the same year Florence became capital of the newly unified Kingdom of Italy. Growing beside it is a deodar cedar, a Himalayan species that had only reached European gardens a few decades earlier, after British and French plant hunters brought seed back from the mountains of Kashmir and Nepal in the 1830s and 40s. Boboli's specimen has grown a trunk nearly four and three quarter metres around, evergreen and untouched by the seasonal crowds that mob the garden's lower amphitheatre for weddings and photographs. No planting record for this particular tree has surfaced, so its age can only be bounded by the species' own arrival in Europe and the terrace's known history, putting it somewhere in its second century at most. It stands quietly above one of the most visited gardens in Italy, on a terrace most day trippers skip because it means one more flight of steps after the main lawns.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Piazzale Michelangelo
trees.access: Free, public piazza, always open
trees.transport: 20 min walk uphill from Ponte Vecchio, or bus lines 12/13 to Piazzale Michelangelo

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold and drop within days

trees.story: Millions of people photograph the view from Piazzale Michelangelo every year, and almost none of them photograph the tree they are standing under to do it. This ginkgo grows at the edge of the piazzale that architect Giuseppe Poggi built in 1875 as the grand viewing terrace for his newly reshaped city, planted among the dozens of ornamental species Poggi and his gardener Attilio Pucci chose to line the new hillside boulevards. Ginkgo biloba is often called a living fossil, the sole surviving member of a family of trees that flourished alongside dinosaurs and has barely changed since; this specimen, with a trunk three metres around, is a comparative newcomer at well under 150 years old, but it belongs to the oldest tree lineage on this entire list by a margin of tens of millions of years. Every November its fan shaped leaves turn a uniform gold and drop within days, all at once, rather than fading gradually the way most autumn colour does, briefly carpeting the ground in a colour that photographs even better than the skyline behind it. No exact planting date has been documented for this individual tree, only its presence in the same landscaping scheme as the piazzale itself.

trees.name: The Pine of Villa Vogel
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Bus toward Isolotto-Legnaia (lines 6 or 9) to Via delle Torri, then a few minutes' walk into the park
trees.story: Florence's Renaissance gardens get all the attention; this pine grows in a very different kind of park. The Parco di Villa Vogel sits in Isolotto-Legnaia, a residential district southwest of the historic centre with none of the tour groups that fill Boboli or the queues outside the Uffizi, in a villa the Vogel family donated to the city in the 1980s so their grounds could become a public playground, skating rink and picnic area for the neighbourhood. This stone pine stands in what surveyors describe as the oldest surviving section of that original garden, in an isolated spot still ringed by centuries-old cypresses that predate the villa's donation by generations. Its trunk measures a modest three and a third metres around, smaller than the show-garden specimens across town, but it has outlived whatever family occasion or landscaping fashion first put it there, and it now shades children's play equipment instead of a private lawn. No record of its planting survives, consistent with a garden built for a family rather than catalogued for visitors. It is a reminder that Florence's old trees are not only in ticketed gardens and postcard piazzas: some of them just ended up in the park nearest to where ordinary Florentines happen to live.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm That Was Cut Back to Save It
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)

best_time.label: October to November: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: In the 1980s this tree lost roughly two thirds of its height in a single operation, and it is still on the national register. The garden planted a Caucasian elm here in 1827 and it grew the way the species does, slowly, into a trunk now close to six metres around. Then a fungal outbreak arrived, named in one register as Dutch elm disease, and the answer was surgery rather than a saw at the base. The branches came off hard, and what stands today is a fluted grey column carrying a crown regrown out of the cuts. The national register still lists this tree at thirty metres tall. The 2021 field survey measured ten. Both numbers are honest, they simply belong to different decades, and the difference between them is the operation. Zelkova carpinifolia is not an elm, whatever everyone calls it. It is a close cousin from a small range in the Caucasus and along the southern shore of the Caspian, and it is planted across Europe precisely because it shrugs off the disease that emptied the continent of its elms, which is worth thinking about while standing in front of one that needed cutting back anyway. The trunk is the thing to look at: buttressed, silver, and wildly out of proportion to everything above it.

trees.name: The Zelkova Somebody Keeps Measuring
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)

best_time.label: October and November, when the leaves turn orange and rust

trees.story: Somebody has put a tape around this trunk three times in forty years: 3.30 metres in 1980, 3.89 in 2001, 4.40 in 2021. Very few trees anywhere carry that kind of paper trail, and it means you can watch this one grow at roughly two and a half centimetres of girth a year without waiting around for it. The garden planted it in 1891 and credits it with the widest crown in the whole collection, which in a place this old is a real claim. Zelkova serrata comes from Japan, Korea and eastern China, where it is the keyaki, the timber used for temple pillars and the bodies of taiko drums, and it is the species most often trained as a broom-form bonsai because the branching is naturally so even. At full size the same habit produces a vase: a short trunk dividing into a fan of near-equal limbs. The bark is the detail to look for. It flakes off in small rounded plates and leaves orange patches underneath, so the trunk reads as a mosaic rather than a texture, and it is the fastest way to pick this tree out from the path. In autumn the leaves turn orange and rust before they drop.

trees.name: The Flag-Crowned Pine
trees.age: over 130 years, in the garden since the late 1800s
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
trees.story: The garden keeps this pine under constant watch, and says so in print, because its crown has grown into a flag. Almost all the weight sits on one side of a long bare trunk thirty-three metres up, which is what happens when a tree spends a century reaching for the only gap in a crowded collection, and it is also the shape most likely to fail in a storm. Publishing that about a tree you are proud of is unusually frank. The pine has been in the collection since the late 1800s and took up its present position in 1922. It is the Turkish pine, though Italian sources call it pino bruzio after Calabria, and botanists have argued for a century over whether it is a species in its own right or a subspecies of the Aleppo pine; the national register still files it under Pinus halepensis. It comes from the eastern Mediterranean, from Turkey and Cyprus and the Levant, where it is the pine that colonises burnt ground first and where resin was tapped from it for centuries. Its needles are longer and darker than the Aleppo pine's, and its cones sit almost stalkless against the branch, pointing forwards. Stand back towards the garden wall to take in the whole of it.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Semplici
trees.age: at least 146 years, on the garden's books from 1880
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
trees.story: The Himalayan cedar only reached Europe in 1822, and this one was on the garden's books by 1880, which makes it an early adopter of a tree that half the continent would go on to plant in every park it built. It has had at least 146 years to make the case: four and a fifth metres round, twenty-eight metres up, with the drooping branch tips that separate a deodar from the stiffer cedars of Lebanon and the Atlas. The leading shoot nods over instead of standing straight and the outer branches hang in soft grey-green curtains, which is the quickest way to tell the three cedars apart from thirty metres off, and worth knowing here because a cedar of Lebanon grows across the river at the Bobolino. In its own range, from Afghanistan through Kashmir to western Nepal, this species reaches sixty metres on mountainsides at two thousand metres, and its wood resists rot well enough that Himalayan temples were built from it. Deodar comes from devadaru, the Sanskrit for timber of the gods. The garden acquired it during the decades when European collections competed for Himalayan and Mexican material, the same appetite that brought the Montezuma cypress here four years later. It is evergreen, so it looks much the same whenever you come, which is a reason to go rather than a reason to wait.

trees.name: The Tree of the Newlyweds
trees.access: Free, public garden, always open
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Porta Romana, along Viale Machiavelli
trees.story: Two enormous branches rise parallel to the trunk like a pair of horns, and Florence has been making the obvious joke for generations: locals know this tree as l'albero dei cornuti, the tree of the cuckolds. Newlyweds pose in front of it anyway, in such numbers that it picked up a politer second name, l'albero degli sposi, and both names are still in use. It is an incense cedar, native to the mountains of Oregon and California, and its trunk is five and a half metres around at chest height, which for the species in Europe is close to extraordinary. It stands to the left of the central flowerbed in the Giardino del Bobolino, the middle section of the English-style garden Giuseppe Poggi built along the Viale dei Colli between 1865 and 1877, when Florence was briefly the capital of Italy and Poggi was rebuilding its hillsides. Crush a fallen leaf spray and it smells sharply resinous, which is where the name comes from. A severe storm in the winter of 1985 damaged the trunk badly and it recovered. The city gave it formal protection in 2020. The cedar of Lebanon on this page stands a few steps away, so the two are one stop, not two.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of the Bobolino
trees.story:
Stone pines are known for their width, not their height. This one is 31.5 metres tall.

The umbrella pine gives the Italian skyline its flat-topped silhouette, and it usually does that from a bare trunk of ten or fifteen metres. The Bobolino pine has gone up as well as out, with a trunk of 412 centimetres around, standing on the Oltrarno hillside among the villas and small parks that cover the slope south of the river. Two other protected trees stand within fifty metres of it, so getting to all three costs nothing more than turning around.

One caution about those numbers. The national register of monumental trees is the only source that records this pine, and the city's own list and the local press coverage both trace back to that same designation, so the measurements are one reading repeated rather than three that agree. No age has ever been published for it.

A stone pine carries cones that take three years to ripen, which means the ground beneath it holds cones at every stage at once, green and closed, grey and opening, and spent. The nuts inside are pinoli, the ones that go into pesto, and prising them out of the shell is why they cost what they cost.

trees.name: The Monterey Cypress of the Giardino Simone Weil
trees.story:
In the wild this species grows on two small headlands in California and nowhere else on earth. There is one of it on a Florentine hillside.

Cupressus macrocarpa survives naturally at Cypress Point and Point Lobos near Monterey, a couple of miles of wind-flattened trees on the Pacific coast. Move it away from that coast and it behaves like a different plant: it grows fast, spreads wide and reaches sizes it never manages at home, which is how it ended up in gardens from New Zealand to Tuscany. This one has a trunk of 388 centimetres and stands 18.5 metres, dark and broad-crowned, in a free public garden a hundred metres or so from the Bobolino trees.

What is not known about it is the interesting part. The national register of monumental trees carries the species, the girth and the height, and nothing else. No age, no planting date, no record of who put it there, and no independent source was found to corroborate any of it. A Monterey cypress of this size in Italy is most likely a nineteenth-century garden planting, from the decades when the species had just reached Europe and every serious garden wanted one. That is inference rather than evidence, and it is worth knowing which of the two you are being handed.

trees.name: The Cypress of the Monte alle Croci Steps
trees.story:
This cypress grows beside a staircase, on the pilgrim climb from the river up to San Miniato al Monte.

The Via del Monte alle Croci is the stepped route that leaves Piazza Poggi and works up the hill to the basilica, which has held the highest ground in Florence since the eleventh century. Mediterranean cypress lines approaches like that all over Tuscany, planted for its narrow dark column and for a habit of outliving whoever planted it. This one is 21.5 metres tall with a trunk of 346 centimetres, which is heavy for a species that usually stays slim, and it stands about 250 metres from Piazzale Michelangelo, so the walk between the two takes no detour at all.

Nobody has published an age for it. The national register of monumental trees lists it and the comune republishes that listing, which is one source rather than two, and neither carries a date. What can be said is that a cypress puts on girth slowly, and that a trunk this size is not the work of a few decades.

Cupressus sempervirens means always green, and it is. The tree looks in January exactly as it looks in July, which is part of why this hillside reads the same in every season and why the climb is as good in winter.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of Via Giramondino
trees.story:
An Aleppo pine keeps its cones sealed on the branch for years and opens them with heat, so the fire that kills the tree sows the next generation.

That is a strategy built for a hot, dry, fire-prone coast, and it is why Pinus halepensis covers so much of the western Mediterranean while barely appearing in the Syrian city it was named after. In Florence it is a planted tree rather than a wild one. This one stands on Viale Galileo, part of the ring of hillside boulevards Giuseppe Poggi cut in the 1860s, when Florence was briefly the capital of Italy and rebuilt itself for the job. Its trunk measures 323 centimetres and it reaches 22.5 metres, the slightest of the protected trees on this stretch, though it is also the one you walk past whether you meant to or not: it sits roughly midway between the Bobolino and Piazzale Michelangelo.

The evidence behind it is thin and worth saying so. Only the national register of monumental trees records it, with the comune reprinting that entry, so there is one source and no age.

To tell it from the stone pines on the same walk, look at the bark high up, where an Aleppo pine goes pale grey with orange showing in the fissures, and at the needles, which are finer and a lighter green.

trees.name: The Strawberry Tree of the Giardino dell'Iris
trees.story:
The strawberry tree flowers and ripens fruit at the same time, so in autumn it hangs white bells and red fruit on the same branch.

Arbutus unedo is usually a shrub you can see over the top of. This one is eight metres tall and grows in the iris garden beside Piazzale Michelangelo. Its entry on the national register of monumental trees records that height and leaves the girth column empty, and no age has been published anywhere, so what is known about it is a species, a spot and eight metres. Pliny gave it the second half of its name, unedo, from unum edo, I eat only one, which remains a fair review. The fruit looks like a lychee crossed with a raspberry and tastes of very little.

Timing matters more here than for most trees on this list, and not in the tree's favour. The garden opens for only a few weeks each spring, around the iris flowering it was made for, so the autumn moment when the arbutus does its trick usually falls when the gate is shut. Go for the irises, find the strawberry tree while you are inside, and take the fruit on trust.

Its record rests on one register entry that the comune republishes, which is one source rather than two.

trees.name: The Chilean Wine Palm of Villa di Rusciano
trees.story:
This palm was very nearly harvested out of existence for its sap, which was boiled down into a honey. Getting the sap meant felling the tree.

Jubaea chilensis carries one of the thickest trunks in the palm family, a grey column more than a metre across, and it grows slowly enough that a tapped tree meant a century of growth spent on a single harvest of palm honey. Chile's wild population collapsed under that trade and now survives in a few protected valleys. The species is also among the hardiest palms there is, which is how it reached Italian villa gardens in the nineteenth century: a palm that could take a frost was worth a great deal to anyone laying out an exotic garden in a climate that kills most of them.

This one measures 349 centimetres around and stands 15.5 metres, in the park of a municipal villa east of the centre. Its record is a single line, the national listing of monumental trees with the city republishing the same entry, and it carries no age and no planting date.

It sits well east of the hillside trees and makes its own errand rather than joining a walk. Whether that is worth an afternoon depends on how many palms with a trunk like a stone column you have stood next to.

trees.name: The Cypress of Villa della Petraia
trees.story:
Only one trunk on Florence's register of monumental trees is thicker than this cypress, and it belongs to a Montezuma cypress.

At 580 centimetres around, this is not the slim dark exclamation mark that Mediterranean cypress usually makes in a Tuscan view. It is a heavy old tree, and it stands in the garden of Villa della Petraia, a Medici villa about five kilometres north of the centre, open to visitors and listed by UNESCO with the other Medici villas and gardens. The Medici bought the estate in the sixteenth century and rebuilt it, and the terraced garden the cypress grows in came out of that work.

The evidence is one entry deep. The national register carries the species and the girth, the comune reprints it, and neither publishes an age, so a tree of obvious antiquity has no date attached to it at all. It has the trunk of something that has been standing a very long time, and nobody has written down how long.

Cypress wood barely rots, which is why it was used for chests, doors and coffins, and why old cypresses tend to stay structurally sound long after other species have hollowed out. That is the quiet advantage behind most of the very old cypresses in Italy, this one included.

trees.name: The Cypress of the Boboli Gardens
trees.access: Paid entry (Boboli Gardens ticket, part of the Pitti Palace / Uffizi Galleries museum complex)
trees.transport: About 7 min walk from Ponte Vecchio; C3 bus stops at Pitti Palace
trees.story:
Boboli's most famous cypresses are the double row lining the Viottolone, the avenue that runs straight down the hill from the amphitheatre. This one stands apart from that avenue, its own listed specimen in Italy's monumental tree register, closer to the Pitti Palace end of the garden than to the avenue's cypress ranks.

At 357 centimetres round and up to 30 metres tall, it is unremarkable in a garden that specialises in exactly this species and exactly this kind of size. What sets it apart is the paperwork: the Tuscan tree register calculates its age at roughly 375 years from what it calls a registered birth year, a documentary basis this page has not been able to independently verify, so take the figure as a considered estimate rather than a fact carved in stone. If it holds, the tree predates the Boboli that most visitors recognise, laid out under later Medici dukes through the seventeenth century, though nothing ties this specific trunk to any one phase of that construction.

The Boboli Gardens began in 1549 as the Medici's private garden and only opened to the public in 1766. Entry now runs on the same combined ticket as the Uffizi and Pitti Palace, so this cypress is one of the easier stops on the whole Florence page to actually reach: a short walk from the Ponte Vecchio, inside a garden that gets crowded with or without a 375-year-old tree to look for.

trees.name: The Eschersheimer Linde
trees.access: Free, standing directly on the public street (Eschersheimer Landstraße), always visible
trees.transport: Lindenbaum U-Bahn station (U1/U2/U3/U8) right beside it; the subway curves around the tree

best_time.label: June, when it flowers and the pavement under it smells of lime

trees.story:
Frankfurt bent a subway line rather than lose this lime. The U-Bahn under Eschersheimer Landstrasse curves slightly where the tree stands, the station beside it is called Lindenbaum, and so is the street. That is a lot of infrastructure named after one large-leaved lime.

It went in at the end of the 17th century as a landmark on what was then an open road out of the city, and it was the smaller of a pair. Locals called it the Kleine Linde, because a bigger Grosse Linde stood nearby until a storm brought that one down in 1923. Around five metres round and some 25 metres tall, it has been a protected natural monument since 1937.

Being a landmark on a road that turned into a city has cost it. The street was paved, the ground around it sealed, and the roots began to suffocate. It got tree surgery in 1955 and again in 1974, drainage in 1968, and by 1984 the city was pumping water and air into the soil around it to keep it alive. Frankfurt has now spent seventy years on life support for a tree it could have removed in an afternoon.

It stands directly on the public street, so there is nothing to pay and nothing to enter. Get off at Lindenbaum station and it is right there, which is the whole point of the name.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free entry to the Botanical Garden (Botanischer Garten Frankfurt, next to the Palmengarten), open during garden hours
trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte U-Bahn/tram hub, about 10 minute walk; or Westend tram stops closer to the garden entrance

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn rust orange and fall, which is not what a conifer is supposed to do

trees.story:
Until 1943 this species was known only from fossils. Metasequoia had been described from stone and written off as long extinct, and then living trees turned up in central China and seed went round the world's botanical gardens within a few years. Which means every large dawn redwood in Europe can be dated to within a human lifetime, and this one is among the first of them: it was planted in the Frankfurt Botanical Garden around 1950, as a cutting.

Seventy-five years later its trunk measures 5.72 metres round at chest height, which the German Dendrological Society ranks as the second thickest recorded specimen of its species in the country. It is a conifer that behaves like a broadleaf, putting out soft feathery needles in spring and dropping every one of them in autumn once they have turned rust orange.

It stands in the East Asia section, opposite the flat-roofed building and to the right of the bee house, which is precise enough to walk to. Entry to the Botanical Garden is free. The Palmengarten and its two protected beeches are next door, so the two gardens make a single afternoon, and the city added this tree to its register of natural monuments in 2025.

The odd thing to hold in your head under it: this tree is younger than the news of its own species, and it is already one of the biggest in Germany.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Palmengarten
trees.access: Paid entry to the Palmengarten (botanical garden with an admission ticket)
trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte or Westend U-Bahn stations, short walk to the Palmengarten entrance

best_time.label: late October and November, when the hall of leaves under it turns copper before it comes down

trees.story:
This beech has been quietly making more of itself. Where its drooping branches reached the ground they took root, and what began as one tree is now a hall of leaves you can walk into. From outside it reads as a single heavy green dome. From underneath it is a room, held up by the parent trunk and by branch tips that grew themselves legs.

Frankfurt's own tree cadastre dates the planting to 1845. It stands just over four metres round and about 16 metres tall, and a tree surveyor who measured it in June 2023 recorded it as vital with some branch breakage, which is what happens to a weeping beech carrying that much weight sideways. The city put it on its register of natural monuments in 2025.

Weeping beeches are not a wild form. Every one is propagated from a mutant that hangs instead of reaches, so a garden that planted one in 1845 was buying a curiosity, and this is what a curiosity looks like after 180 years of being left alone.

It is in the western part of the Palmengarten by the Gesellschaftshaus, a short walk from the Palmenhaus and from the copper beech that is three decades older again. The Palmengarten charges admission, so this is the one tree in Frankfurt on this list you pay to stand under. Or inside, which is the better way to do it.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Palmengarten
trees.access: Paid entry to the Palmengarten (botanical garden with an admission ticket)
trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte or Westend U-Bahn stations, short walk to the Palmengarten entrance

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken

trees.story:
The Palmengarten opened in 1871. This beech was already 56 years old. Frankfurt's tree cadastre dates its planting to 1815, the year of Waterloo, which makes it older than the garden that now charges people to come and look at it.

It is a grafted copper beech, which is how nearly all of them are made. The purple-leaved form does not come reliably true from seed, so a shoot of it is joined onto ordinary green beech rootstock, and on an old specimen you can often still find the join low on the trunk. A surveyor measured it at four and a half metres round in August 2022 and recorded its condition as vital. The city listed it as a natural monument in 2025, under the heading of beauty and rarity, which is an unusually frank thing for a register to write down.

It stands out on the meadow in the middle section of the park with room around it, so the whole low, wide crown is readable at once rather than in pieces through other trees.

Come in late April or May rather than in August. The new leaves open translucent red and only darken through the summer, and by high season the tree has gone almost black-purple and lost half of what makes the walk worth it.

trees.name: The Eight-Stemmed Linden of Grüneburgpark
trees.access: Free, public park (Grüneburgpark), open at all times
trees.transport: Miquel-/Adickesallee or Holzhausenstraße bus/tram stops; about 10-15 minute walk from Bockenheimer Warte U-Bahn
trees.story:
Eight trunks come out of the ground here in one tight ring, and they are a single tree. This is a Bündelpflanzung, a bundle planting: several young limes set into one hole so that they grow up together and merge into a single crown. It is deliberate, not an accident of self-seeding, and it is rare enough that Frankfurt made this one a protected natural monument in 2025.

It stands at a path crossing in the middle of the Grüneburgpark, beside the small children's playground, which puts it on everyone's route and almost nobody's list. Walk in among the stems and you are standing inside the tree rather than in front of it, with eight columns around you and one canopy overhead.

Nobody has established how old it is. No published record we can find carries a planting date, and the designation does not give one either, so this page does not guess. The same goes for which lime it is: small-leaved, large-leaved and the hybrid between them are close enough that neither source commits, and we are not going to commit for them.

If you know either answer, from a park archive, an old photograph or a plaque we have missed, tell us and it goes on the page. Meanwhile the park is free, open at all hours, and the tree is unmistakable once you are looking for eight of anything.

trees.name: The Plane Tree at the Nebbiensches Gartenhaus
trees.access: Free, public park (Bockenheimer Anlage), unrestricted access confirmed by an October 2025 independent tree survey
trees.transport: Alte Oper or Bockenheimer Warte U-Bahn stations, a few minutes walk through the Anlagenring park
trees.story:
Seven metres and thirteen centimetres around the trunk, measured in October 2025. That is a plane tree you could not reach a tenth of the way around, standing in a strip of park a few minutes from Frankfurt's opera house. An independent big-tree survey recorded 713 centimetres last autumn; another surveyor measured 704 in 2022. Two measurements three years apart agreeing that closely is the kind of number worth trusting.

It was planted in 1820, ten years after the neoclassical pavilion it stands behind, the Nebbiensches Gartenhaus. Both sit in the Bockenheimer Anlage, part of the ring of parkland Frankfurt laid out on the ground where its city walls had stood, which is why the green in this part of town runs in a curve instead of a grid. The tree is around 35 metres tall with a crown some 26 metres across, and it carries entry 028 on the city's register of natural monuments.

Two centuries is not particularly old for a plane. It is old for this address, where a garden pavilion from 1810 now sits in sight of the banking towers.

Access is free and unrestricted at any hour, which is worth saying because two of the protected trees on this list stand behind an admission desk. This one is simply in a public park, and you can put your hand on it.

trees.name: The Ayasugi of Kashii Shrine
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: JR Kashii-jingu-mae Station, about 5 to 9 min walk
trees.story: Legend says this cedar started as a twig. Empress Jingu, returning from a campaign on the Korean peninsula in the third century, is said to have buried a sword, a spear and a staff on this spot, then pushed a cedar branch from her own armor sleeve into the ground beside them with a vow that it should guard Japan forever. The branch took. Its leaves grow in an alternating, woven pattern that gave the tree its name, Ayasugi, patterned cedar, and for centuries cuttings from it have been sent to the Imperial court as a token from one of Japan's most ceremonially important shrines. Kashii Shrine is a chokusaisha, one of the few shrines that still receives a personal envoy from the Emperor, and its unusual kashii-zukuri roofline is a National Important Cultural Property in its own right. The tree made its way into classical poetry too: a verse in the Shin Kokin Wakashu, compiled around 1205, already treats the Ayasugi as an old and storied thing. Today it stands 21.5 metres tall with a trunk 4.9 metres around, a dense green pyramid beside the shrine's main hall, still doing, by tradition, the exact job it was planted for eighteen centuries ago.

photo.attribution: そらみみ, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Kushida Shrine
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: Nakasu-Kawabata Station (subway), about 5 min walk

best_time.label: late November, when the whole crown turns gold within about a week

trees.story: A 1913 stone monument at the foot of this ginkgo already declared it over a thousand years old, and the monument itself is now old enough to be doubted along with the tree. A later measurement of its trunk put the real figure closer to 600 years, which barely dents the point: this is Hakata's most sung-about tree, its own line in the centuries-old Hakata Iwai Uta, the toast still performed at weddings and shop openings across the district. It stands beside the starting point of the Gion Yamakasa festival, so its crown has watched every decorated float lurch past below it every July for generations. Age has not been gentle underneath the show: the lower trunk is hollow and decayed, several major limbs have been cut back hard, and metal rings and props now hold up what canopy remains. None of that stops it turning, every November, into a single dense cone of butter-gold leaves that the whole neighbourhood times its photographs around. A female tree, it drops fruit by the bagful onto the shrine's stone paving each autumn, pollinated by male ginkgoes it cannot see from streets away.

trees.name: The Flying Plum of Dazaifu Tenmangu
trees.neighbourhood: Saifu, Dazaifu (day trip from central Fukuoka)
trees.access: Free to enter the shrine grounds; some inner buildings and treasure halls charge admission
trees.transport: Nishitetsu Dazaifu Station, 5 min walk to the shrine; about 29 min by direct express train from Nishitetsu Fukuoka (Tenjin) Station, longer with a transfer on some weekday services

best_time.label: late January into February, when it opens first among the shrine's thousands of plum trees

trees.story: When the courtier Sugawara no Michizane was exiled from Kyoto in 901, legend says three trees in his garden reacted differently: the cherry withered from grief, the pine tried to follow him and only made it as far as modern Kobe before giving up, and the plum flew the whole distance overnight to take root in front of him at Dazaifu. Michizane had written it a farewell poem asking it to keep sending its scent east even with its master gone, and the plum, so the story goes, closed the distance itself instead. Whatever actually happened, this tree has been called Tobiume, the Flying Plum, ever since, and it blooms earliest of the roughly six thousand plum trees planted across these grounds, usually from late January. Its base splits into three separate stems, evidence of centuries dying back and regrowing from the root rather than one continuous trunk, and it originally stood at a different shrine on the site of Michizane's actual residence before being moved here when Dazaifu Tenmangu was built around him. Michizane became the god of scholarship after his death, and this is the tree students touch for luck before an exam season most of them will not personally remember choosing. Dazaifu sits a short train ride from central Fukuoka, roughly thirty minutes on the direct express from Tenjin.

photo.attribution: そらみみ, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Camphor of Kego Shrine
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open 6:00-18:00
trees.transport: Nishitetsu Fukuoka (Tenjin) Station, adjacent; Tenjin-Minami subway station, about 1 min walk
trees.story: Fukuoka's busiest shopping street runs past a camphor tree older than the district's name.
