Tenjin was built up around Kego Shrine, not the other way around, and the shrine's own record puts this camphor at over three hundred years, older than the 1608 rebuilding ordered by Kuroda Nagamasa, the daimyo who also built Fukuoka Castle. The shrine traces its founding much further back, to a guardian deity said to have protected Empress Jingu's fleet during a third-century campaign, but the tree standing today is a comparatively recent arrival by that math, planted or self-seeded sometime after the shrine's Edo-period move to this exact spot. What makes it worth a detour is the contrast: department stores, a covered shopping arcade and some of the highest rents in Kyushu surround a small shrine precinct where a single camphor still throws real shade over the forecourt. Kego Park borders the grounds to the north, giving the tree a second, quieter side to be seen from. Independent measurements of its exact girth or height are hard to come by, which is unusual for a tree this central. What is not in doubt is its address: closer to a train platform than any other tree on this list.

trees.name: The Great Camphor of Tajima Hachiman Shrine
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: No direct train or subway; Nishitetsu bus route 12 from Tenjin toward Tajima, then a short walk across the Hii River
trees.story: Wrap a tape measure around this camphor and you will need eleven metres of it, roughly the wingspan of a small aircraft. It is the largest of twelve trees on these grounds that Fukuoka City has individually designated as preserved trees, a small grove of camphors and ginkgoes several hundred years old crowded into a quiet residential shrine across the Hii River from the city centre. Unlike Fukuoka's grander, more visited shrines, Tajima Hachiman keeps its own calendar: Tajima Kagura, a masked sacred dance handed down through the neighbourhood for generations, is still performed on these grounds rather than staged for tourists elsewhere. The camphor stands close to the main hall, a single column of dense evergreen crown that has outgrown its own trunk's proportions, the kind of tree whose base takes several adults holding hands to encircle. Camphor wood was prized across East Asia for shipbuilding and for warding off insects, both of which likely helped trees like this one survive centuries that felled less useful species nearby. It carries no legend as old as Fukuoka's imperial-founded shrines, and that is part of its appeal: a genuinely enormous tree, growing where people actually live, with no admission gate and no crowd between you and its trunk.

trees.name: The Great Camphor of Dazaifu
trees.access: Free, open shrine grounds
trees.transport: Nishitetsu from Tenjin via Futsukaichi, about 35 min and 400 yen, then 10 min walk
trees.story: The official sign under this camphor hedges, and it has been hedging since 1924. Erected by the education ministry and still standing, it says the age is said to be a thousand years, or perhaps fifteen hundred. That is unusually careful language for a monument, and it is the honest position: one giant-tree survey puts the tree at only three hundred and something, oral tradition stretches to two thousand, and nobody has ever cored it. What is measured is the size. Twenty-eight and a half metres tall and eleven point seven metres around, it is the largest of several camphors protected together as a national natural monument on the eighth of March 1922, the same day as the two giants at Umi a few stations north. The trunk is deeply fluted and hollow at the base, which is normal at this size rather than a sign of decline. Dazaifu Tenmangu is the head shrine of the deity of learning, so in exam season the grounds fill with students, and this tree stands to the west of all of them in front of the Seishinkan.

trees.name: Yubuta no Mori, the Bathing Camphor
trees.neighbourhood: Umi town, about 45 min from Hakata
trees.access: Free, open shrine precinct
trees.transport: About 45 min from Hakata: JR to Kashii, then the Kashii line to Umi terminus, then 9 min walk
trees.story: Its name means the bathing lid, and the legend explains the shape. Empress Jingu is said to have given birth to the future Emperor Ojin at this spot and to have bathed the newborn beneath this camphor, whose branches closed over the bath like a cover. The shrine that grew up around the story is now the principal shrine in Japan for safe childbirth, and expectant mothers travel from across the country to it. The tree is a single organism despite the word forest in its name, roughly fifteen metres around and reaching thirty metres, protected as a national natural monument since the eighth of March 1922. Sources put it at either a thousand years or two thousand, with no way to choose between them, so both stand here. What is not in doubt is its health: photographed in September 2024 it carries a full, dense, unbroken crown, which is more than can be said for several famous camphors nearer the city. Its equally protected companion stands about a hundred metres away and was designated on the same day.

trees.name: Kinukake no Mori, the Robe Camphor
trees.neighbourhood: Umi town, about 45 min from Hakata
trees.access: Free, open shrine precinct
trees.transport: About 45 min from Hakata: JR to Kashii, then the Kashii line to Umi terminus, then 9 min walk
trees.story: Twenty metres around. That is nearly double the largest tree in the city of Fukuoka, and it makes this camphor one of the great trees of Japan by measurement alone, whatever anyone decides about its age. The estimates for that run from three hundred years to two thousand, a disagreement so wide it is really an admission that nobody knows. The name means the hanging of the robe: Empress Jingu, having given birth beside its neighbour a hundred metres away, is said to have hung the birth robe on this tree. A custom still runs on it. Expectant women take one of the smooth stones kept at the shrine home with them, and after a safe birth they bring back two, so the pile grows with every delivery. The tree carries its centuries openly, the upper trunk gone and a large rough cavity opening in the side, and it was still in full leaf when photographed in September 2024. Both it and its neighbour became national natural monuments on the same day in March 1922.

trees.name: The Broad-leaf Ehretia of Dazaifu
trees.access: Free, open shrine grounds
trees.transport: Nishitetsu from Tenjin via Futsukaichi, about 35 min, then 10 min walk
trees.story: This is the largest of its species in Japan, and almost nobody visiting the shrine knows it is there. Ehretia macrophylla belongs to the borage family, the same group as forget-me-nots, and it is not a plant anyone expects at monumental size; this one is fifteen metres tall and six and a half metres around, which earned it a national natural monument designation of its own in June 1935, thirteen years after the camphors nearby. Lightning struck it in 1914 and snapped off the upper trunk, and the remaining stem is hollow to a height of about ten metres, so what stands there is a survivor rather than a specimen. It sits west of the main buildings, on the far side from the crowds heading for the exam charms. Look for a broad-leaved tree with a heavy scarred trunk and a crown that stops abruptly where the lightning ended it, then check the sign, because there is no way to tell a record-breaking ehretia from an ordinary broadleaf without one.

trees.name: The Married Ginkgos of Kushida
trees.access: Free, open shrine precinct
trees.transport: Nanakuma Line to Kushida-jinjamae, 2 min walk

best_time.label: 5 October, when priests shake the nuts down with bamboo poles

trees.story: On the fifth of October, seven priests climb in with bamboo poles and shake this tree until the nuts come down. Shrine maidens gather them with chopsticks, because ginkgo flesh smells strongly enough that nobody wants it on their hands, and the nuts are dried and kept until March, when they are given out at the Ginan Festival as charms for a harmonious marriage and for children. That is the whole reason these trees carry their name. They stand opposite the main hall, three large ginkgos of over three hundred years treated as a single married pair, and the one at the front is the female that actually fruits. They are a few steps from the far more famous ginkgo on the other side of the same precinct, the one that is older, taller and sung about in the festival song, which most visitors photograph without noticing these at all. The city lists them among its preserved trees. Come on the fifth of October for the only tree ritual in Fukuoka that involves men with poles in a shrine courtyard.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree of Kaidan-in
trees.access: Free precinct; the ordination hall itself charges a small fee
trees.transport: Nishitetsu to Gojo station, then about 10 min walk; roughly 35 min from Tenjin

best_time.label: June, when the pale yellow flowers open and the whole tree smells of them

trees.story: The bodhi tree of Japanese temples is not the bodhi tree. The Buddha's own species will not survive a Japanese winter, so temples here plant a lime, Tilia miqueliana, and call it by the same name, which is why this modest tree at Kaidan-in carries a title far larger than its six metres. It is protected all the same, designated a Dazaifu city natural monument in September 2013, and its age has an unusually firm floor: a gazetteer of the province compiled in 1814 records a single bodhi tree standing at Kaidan-in, so this one, or its immediate predecessor on the same ground, was already worth listing two centuries ago. Tradition connects the planting to Ganjin, the blind Chinese monk who crossed to Japan on his sixth attempt and founded the ordination platform this temple is built around. That is tradition only, and the arithmetic says so, because Ganjin died in 763 and the tree is two hundred years old. In June it flowers, pale yellow and heavily scented, which is the one week it stops being a small tree with a big name.

trees.name: The Great Yamamomo of Kanatake
trees.access: Privately owned but open to the public (the ward government's own page says so explicitly); visitors are asked to be careful, since foot traffic compacting the soil over the roots is named as a real risk to the tree's vigour, not a formality.
trees.transport: No train station is within walking distance (Hashimoto or Jiromaru stations are both roughly 2.7km, about 33-34 minutes on foot). Nishitetsu Bus routes 1 or 2 run to the 'Kanatake' stop from Meinohama Station's south exit, Hashimoto Station, Hakata Station bus terminal or Tenjin; the tree stands in the neighbourhood around that stop.
trees.story:
An owl sometimes nests in the hollow of this tree's trunk, which Fukuoka's own ward government mentions on its page about the specimen without treating it as remarkable, just one more fact about a tree old enough to have grown a cavity worth nesting in. Estimated at three to four hundred years old, it is the larger of only two Myrica rubra the prefecture has designated a natural monument, its root spread alone measuring eight metres across.

Red bayberry is more commonly a large shrub than a proper tree, grown across East Asia for a tart, dark red summer fruit that stains fingers and pavement alike; reaching four metres round at chest height and standing fourteen metres tall, this one has outgrown the category by any measure. The ward's own page and an independent survey of Japan's giant trees disagree on the exact girth by thirty centimetres, a gap almost certainly explained by different measurement dates rather than a mistake either way.

The tree stands on private land whose owner has kept it open to the public, and the same page that welcomes visitors also asks them to tread carefully: foot traffic compacting the soil over its roots is named as a real threat to its health, not a formality. No train station sits within walking distance; a bus from Meinohama, Hashimoto or central Fukuoka runs to the Kanatake stop nearby.

trees.name: The Married Camphor and Great Ginkgo of Torikai Hachimangu
trees.species: Camphor Tree (Cinnamomum camphora) and Ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba)
trees.access: Free. Both trees stand in the open approach/precinct of Torikai Hachimangu, a public Shinto shrine, immediately flanking the torii; no gate or restriction beyond ordinary shrine visiting hours.
trees.transport: Fukuoka City Subway Airport Line: Tojinmachi Station, about 6 minutes on foot, or Nishijin Station, about 7 minutes. Also reachable by Nishitetsu bus to the Jigyo or Imagawa-nishimachi-koen-mae stops, a couple of minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Despite the name, the Married Camphor is one tree, not two. Its trunk forks into a pair from a single base low to the ground, which is exactly why visitors to Torikai Hachimangu read it as a couple rather than a single specimen, and why a shrine built around relationships adopted it as a symbol for exactly that. Cords get tied to its shimenawa rope by people hoping their own pairing holds as well as the tree's two trunks have.

Twelve metres away, flanking the shrine's torii from the other side, stands the Great Ginkgo, called locally the Ibuki Ginkgo. The shrine's own account puts its age at five to six hundred years, a figure with no independent source found to confirm it, so treat it as tradition rather than a documented fact, the same caution this page applies to a wartime survival story attached to the tree elsewhere online, which nothing beyond the shrine's own telling supports.

Both trees stand in the open shrine forecourt, free to visit at any hour a Shinto shrine keeps its grounds open, reachable on foot from either Tojinmachi or Nishijin subway station. Camphor on the left of the torii, ginkgo on the right, both close enough to touch from the same few steps.

trees.name: The Willow of Kupaly-Subislawa
trees.access: Free, public green space, open daily
trees.transport: Oliwa district, near the Kupaly-Subislawa pond; about a 15 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station

best_time.label: April, when the catkins open, the clearest sign each spring that the fire-scarred crown is still alive

trees.story: Seven months ago this willow was still whole. On 29 December 2025, someone or something, fireworks testing has not been ruled out, set fire to the trunk of this 140-year-old white willow beside a pond in Oliwa, and the blaze burned out its core before neighbours spotted the flames and called the fire brigade. Firefighters put it out in time to save the tree next to it, a second protected willow believed to be around 165 years old, growing close enough that the fire could easily have spread. What was left standing had been hollowed out from the inside, its trunk statically unsafe, so the city's ecology department made the call foresters dread: cutting roughly four metres off the crown of a tree that had carried official protection since 2000, girth 495 centimetres, height 22 metres, just to keep it upright. The city filed a police report and the case remains open. What happens next genuinely is not settled. Botanists monitoring the tree say it may sprout new growth this season, though never at its old height again, and if it does not survive at all, Gdansk plans to leave the trunk standing anyway as deadwood habitat rather than remove it. For now it is alive, recovering by inches at a pond most of Oliwa walks past without knowing what stands there.

trees.name: The Ash of the Royal Rifle Factory
trees.access: Free, public courtyard, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Dolne Miasto, south of the city centre; about a 15 minute walk from Gdansk Glowny railway station
trees.story: This ash tree is older than the gun factory that grew up around it. The Prussian state's Royal Rifle Factory moved onto this stretch of Lakowa street in 1839, converted from an earlier sugar refinery, and expanded through the 19th century into a complex that at its 1918 wartime peak turned out 2,500 rifles a day with 6,500 workers on the payroll, before closing for good in 1921 when the newly independent Free City of Danzig demilitarised. The ash predates all of it, estimated at around 280 years old, which puts its own roots down sometime in the early 18th century, decades before anyone here was making weapons. It stands 26 metres tall with a trunk 523 centimetres around, in what is now a quiet courtyard inside the old factory walls. Its protected status is recent and came from an unusual source: since April 2017, Gdansk has run a programme letting any resident nominate a tree for legal protection, and this ash, tucked away where most passersby would never look for it, was one of the results. A factory that armed a kingdom rose and fell around it in under a century. The tree just kept growing.

trees.name: The Oak of Wzgorze Luizy
trees.access: Free, public street verge, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Lostowice district, near the Niepolomicka/Kampinoska junction; reachable by tram or bus from central Gdansk, about 25 minutes

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: At the foot of a hill named for a dead queen's role in defeating Napoleon grows Lostowice's oldest documented tree. Wzgorze Luizy, a 68 metre moraine hill, was named in 1810 for Louise of Prussia, credited with brokering the Prussian-Russian alliance that helped bring Napoleon down five years later; in 1813 Prussian Landwehr troops clashed with Napoleonic forces on this exact hill, and in 1817 an iron cross went up on the summit naming nine officers who died in it. This pedunculate oak, protected as a natural monument since the late 1980s and estimated at around 250 years old, was already mature when that battle happened, growing quietly at the base of the slope while history took place above it. It has outlasted the monument's own turbulent afterlife: the hill was informally renamed for a local landowner after the Second World War, and only recently got an official viewpoint restoring some of its original prominence. Two younger trees, an oak and a beech, grow near the summit closer to the iron cross itself, added to the protected list decades after this one. Of the three, this is the tree that was already old when the story the hill is named for happened.

trees.name: The Beech of Ludolfino
trees.access: Free, park grounds on a public university campus, open daily
trees.transport: Oliwa district, near the AWFiS campus; about a 15 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.story: An opera singer's wife gave her name to this park, and this beech has outgrown every owner who has held it since. Ludolfino takes its name from Dorothea Ludolphine Bachmann-Ackermann, wife of the singer who first carved this estate out of the neighbouring Stawowie grounds in the late 18th century; the property shows up on city maps as early as 1822. It changed hands repeatedly after that, the Braune family from 1877, a private owner named Robert von Kolkow from 1922, an Evangelical religious order that ran it as a deaconess house from 1933, and the Polish state from 1957, before landing with Gdansk's physical education academy, AWFiS, which now uses the old manor as its main library. This common beech has been protected as a natural monument since 1988, its trunk 470 centimetres around and its crown 24 metres tall, growing on ground that has technically never once belonged to the tree itself. Students studying inside the converted manor now walk past it without necessarily knowing they are passing something that predates every institution that has ever owned the land beneath it.

trees.name: The Official Chestnut Tree
trees.access: Free, open promenade at any time
trees.transport: Central Vieille-Ville, walkable from anywhere in the old town

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story: Geneva has kept an unbroken written record of a chestnut tree's first spring leaf since 1818, one of the oldest continuous phenology datasets anywhere, third-oldest in the world by the canton's own claim. Every year the sautier, the secretary of Geneva's cantonal parliament, walks to a designated tree on the Promenade de la Treille, checks for the season's first open leaf, and reports the date to the press, a civic tradition treated with the same seriousness as a budget vote. The tree doing the job today is the fourth in the role. The first died young; the second lasted from 1905 to 1929; the third served for 86 years before a root fungus called armillaria killed it from the inside, its final recorded observation logged on 13 March 2015. Its replacement was chosen that September for one quality above all others: standing conveniently opposite Tour Baudet, the tower housing the cantonal government, so the sautier's walk stays short. This is the youngest tree on this list by a wide margin, but the record it now carries is the oldest thing about it, two centuries of Geneva watching the same small square for the first sign spring has actually arrived.

trees.name: The Cedars of Parc Beaulieu
trees.access: Free, open park at any time, partially wheelchair accessible
trees.transport: Short walk from Gare Cornavin (main train station)

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: A French naturalist smuggled cedar seeds out of a garden in England, sowed them at the Jardin des Plantes in Paris, and a handful of the resulting saplings ended up gifted to a Genevan baron in 1735. Bernard de Jussieu's seed run is the same one behind the celebrated Cedar of Jussieu still standing in Paris today, a rare case of two cities' oldest cedars sharing one 18th-century courier. Baron Jean-Francois de Sellon planted his share at his lakeside estate, now Parc Beaulieu, and two of the resulting trees still stand there, close enough together to read as one destination rather than two. Geneva's own tree register calls them the oldest cedars of Lebanon in Switzerland, and possibly in Europe, a claim this entry repeats as the city's own rather than an independently verified fact. Lightning has since taken several metres off the tallest, now 27 metres instead of the 30-plus it once reached, and its trunk has grown past 6 metres around, canopy spread 34 metres, numbers that make the loss of a treetop look almost incidental. Napoleon is said to have visited the estate in 1800, back when the cedars were already mature enough to be worth the detour.

trees.name: The Grange Cedar
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus or tram to Eaux-Vives, then a short walk, roughly 15 minutes from the centre

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: This cedar is a direct descendant of the Beaulieu cedars across town, grown from their seed once the Lullin family decided their own lakeside estate needed the same fashionable tree everyone else was planting. Cedars of Lebanon became the must-have addition to Geneva's English-style landscaped parks from around 1800 onward, and the Grange estate, later the city's largest park, got its own sometime in that same window, though no source pins the planting to an exact year. Two centuries on, the tree has outgrown its parent generation: 7.62 metres around the trunk and just over 25 metres tall by a 2019 measurement, a girth that would take four or five adults joining hands to encircle. Parc La Grange has a literary footnote worth knowing: Franz Liszt and Marie d'Agoult stayed at the estate in the 1830s, and their daughter Cosima, later Richard Wagner's wife, was born nearby during that same visit. The cedar would already have been a substantial young tree by then, decades into growing toward the giant it is now. It stands near the park's main house, an easy stop on a walk through Geneva's rose garden and lakeside paths.

trees.name: The Botanical Garden Plane Trees
trees.access: Free, open garden at any time
trees.transport: Tram to Nations, then a short walk, roughly 20 minutes from the centre
trees.story: Five plane trees in Geneva's botanical garden were already mature enough to appear on a cantonal cadastral map in 1728, nearly two centuries before the garden itself moved onto the land they stand on. The Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques relocated here from Parc des Bastions in 1905, onto the former Ariana estate that property heir Gustave Revilliod had left to the city, and inherited these five trees as a ready-made avenue rather than planting anything itself. City gardeners since have deliberately left them alone: unlike Geneva's street plane trees, pruned hard every winter into tight pollarded shapes, the botanical garden's five were allowed to spread their branches naturally, the difference between a tree kept small for a pavement and one left to become what a 300-year-old plane actually looks like. Botanists have reclassified them more than once; they currently go by Platanus x hispanica, having previously been labelled Platanus x acerifolia, the taxonomy shifting even as the trees themselves have not changed in decades. The central avenue they form is still the garden's spine, a shaded walk near the entrance from chemin de l'Impératrice, in the Nations district a short tram ride from the city centre.

trees.name: The Sequoia Grove of Parc Barton
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Geneva, roughly 15 minutes, or local bus
trees.story: About thirty giant sequoias grow in one Geneva park because a British diplomat's family fell for a California fashion, and because his daughter later made sure nobody could ever cut them down. Robert Peel, son of the British prime minister and Britain's own representative to Switzerland, bought the Barton estate in 1858, right as giant sequoia seedlings from the American west were becoming the trophy planting for European estate owners with money and an English-style park to fill. He planted a grove instead of a single specimen, and it grew into what the city now calls a cathédrale végétale, a vegetative cathedral, dense enough to change the light underneath it. His daughter, Alexandra Barton Peel, inherited the estate and grew as attached to its trees as her father had been. When she bequeathed the property to the Swiss Confederation in 1935, she attached one condition, that it never be divided and that the trees growing there never be felled. The estate came close to a very different fate: League of Nations planners considered Barton as a site for their new headquarters after 1919, and only Barton Peel's refusal to sell kept the grove intact for what it is today, a public park a short walk from the lakefront.

trees.name: The Place du Cirque Plane
trees.access: Free, open public square at any time
trees.transport: Central Plainpalais, walkable from the old town, roughly 10 minutes
trees.story: The largest plane tree in downtown Geneva grows in the middle of one of its busiest intersections, and the reason it got that big is buried under the pavement. Place du Cirque sits on the former bed of the Arve river, rerouted decades before the tree was planted around 1900, and the water table left behind still runs close enough to the surface for the tree's roots to draw on it freely. The result, after roughly a century and a quarter: 35 metres tall, a trunk 4.25 metres around, one and a half metres in diameter, dimensions that would be remarkable in a forest and are startling in the middle of a traffic circle. Thousands of pedestrians pass directly under its canopy every day without necessarily registering that they are walking beneath one of the biggest trees in the canton, let alone the largest one standing in the city centre itself. The square takes its name from the travelling circuses that once pitched their tents on this stretch of the Plainpalais plain. The tree arrived after most of that history, but has since outlasted every circus that has come and gone since.

trees.name: The Venerable Oak of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, open garden during opening hours
trees.transport: Tram to Nations or the botanical garden stop, then a short walk

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
The city has drawn a quiet zone around this oak to keep visitors' feet off its roots. The périmètre de tranquillité exists because soil compaction is what kills old trees in busy gardens long before age does. Geneva's cantonal inventory rates this one's vitality as poor and its stage as senescent, which is less a death notice than the reason the perimeter is there at all.

It has earned the trouble. The City of Geneva's own museum trail names this exact tree and cites an inventory number that matches the register's, digit for digit, which is about as close to a positive identification as a tree gets. The trail dates it to 1719. That makes it roughly three centuries old, the elder of the botanical garden's living collection, and 710 centimetres round the trunk.

The same account says it once stood beside a Roman road that crossed this ground long before anything botanical did. The Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques only moved here in 1905, so the oak had been growing for 186 years before the garden arrived around it, and it is still the oldest thing inside the fence.

The 1719 date comes from that trail article rather than from a ring count or an archive entry, so treat it as a good estimate rather than a birth certificate. The Avenue de la Paix gate is the nearest way in.

trees.name: The Naville Cedar
trees.access: Free, stands at the roadside, visible and reachable at any time
trees.transport: Bus to Frontenex or a 15-20 minute walk from the centre

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story:
A mayor planted this cedar in the summer of 1820 because his son had just been born. Jean-Edouard Naville was mayor of Eaux-Vives, then still a commune in its own right rather than a district of Geneva, and he put the tree into the ground on his Montchoisy estate to mark the arrival of Emile. Two centuries later the boy is long gone and the tree is 722 centimetres round.

Where it ended up is the other half of the story. The Route de Frontenex now runs past it, the address is simply opposite number 53, and the ground around it is road and building rather than lawn. Tribune de Genève, surveying the trees that tell Geneva's history, found it holding up well in the middle of all that concrete, and the cantonal register agrees: vitality good, development stage senescent, an old tree still doing its job rather than a failing one.

The 1820 date is unusually solid for a tree this age. Registers here often record a planting as the first of January, which is a filing habit rather than a record, but this one is backed by a named man, a named son and a stated season. It is a birthday present that outlived everyone at the party, standing at a kerb on a busy road out of town.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of Parc des Eaux-Vives
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus or a 15-20 minute walk from the centre along the lakefront

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn rust and fall, leaving the one bare conifer on Geneva's lakeside walk

trees.story:
Geneva's own lakeside walking guide files this tree under arbres insolites, unusual trees, and it earns the label every November by doing what no conifer is supposed to do. The bald cypress drops its needles. They go rust and copper first, the whole tree turning the colour of a beech, and then the branches stand bare all winter while the cedars around them stay green.

Taxodium distichum comes from the swamp forests of the American southeast, where it grows with its feet in standing water and pushes woody knees up through the mud around the trunk. This one has drier ground and the lake a few metres off, a trunk 330 centimetres round, and a vitality rating of excellent, the top grade the register hands out.

Nobody has dated it. The register carries a planting year of 1912, but that date falls on the first of January along with 21 other entries in the same file, which makes it an administrative default rather than a record. Judged on girth alone the tree is somewhere between one and one and a half centuries old, and that band is as tight as the evidence honestly allows.

It stands on the city's signposted route between Parc La Grange and Parc des Eaux-Vives, which strings this and twenty other named trees into a single walk along the water.

trees.name: The Great Cedar of Port-Noir
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus or a 15-20 minute walk from the centre along the lakefront

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story:
This cedar's age was worked out by measuring a different cedar. Nobody wrote down when it was planted, the cantonal register's date of 1850 falls on a first of January and is therefore a filing convention rather than a record, and no article or archive found so far names the tree at all. So the estimate borrows from the Naville Cedar on the Route de Frontenex, about a kilometre away: same species, same lake, same climate, and a documented planting in 1820. That tree has put on 722 centimetres of girth in 206 years, roughly three and a half centimetres a year. Apply the rate here, to 743 centimetres, and you get about two centuries, which is why the range on this page runs from 180 to 230 years instead of landing on a date.

The tree itself needs no arithmetic to be worth the walk. Forty metres tall, more than seven metres round, in good health, standing at the Port-Noir end of Parc des Eaux-Vives where the park runs out towards the water. A second, slightly smaller cedar stands about fifty metres off through the trees, near enough to see from here and far enough to be a different stop.

One register entry, one line of measurements and a growth rate borrowed from a neighbour. A reader with a tape measure, or an archive card with a date on it, would improve on all of it.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Parc de l'Impératrice
trees.access: Free, public park. The city bought the estate in 1983 and the grounds are public; the chateau at the top is private, now Italy's mission to the UN. Geneva publishes no opening hours for the park itself.
trees.transport: Bus toward Chambésy/Pregny, or roughly 25 minutes on foot from the botanical garden

best_time.label: late October and November, when the crown goes butter yellow at the head of the terrace lawn

trees.story:
The château at the top of this lawn is Italy's mission to the United Nations. The lawn is not: Geneva bought the estate in 1983 and kept the grounds public, so the terrace, the long view down it and the tulip tree standing at its head belong to anyone who walks up.

The city's own description of the park puts the tulipier de Virginie and a giant sequoia together at the top of that slope, and the tulip tree is the one worth the climb. Five metres and six centimetres round the trunk, a metre and a half through, grown in open ground with nothing crowding it, which is why it has the shape a Liriodendron is supposed to have and rarely gets in a city. The species is North American and takes its name from the greenish orange flowers it opens in June, high in the crown and easy to walk under without noticing. The leaves give it away instead, cut off square at the tip as though someone had trimmed them with scissors.

Its age is a girth estimate rather than a date. The register's planting year for this entry is one of the file's placeholders, so the honest reading is somewhere between one and one and a half centuries, on a species that grows fast when it is given room. Geneva's own page calls the park's trees centenarian and leaves it there too.

trees.name: The Sécheron Plane
trees.access: Free, register situation field records it as standing in a park/square/green space, open at any time
trees.transport: Short walk from Gare Cornavin or the Sécheron rail stop
trees.story:
Thirty-eight metres of plane tree stands in a green space off the Avenue de France, and the harder question is which green space. The avenue borders several in Sécheron, Mon Repos and the Perle du Lac among them, and nothing found so far names the ground this trunk actually stands on. The coordinates are exact. Only the name of the park is missing.

The tree is not in doubt. The cantonal register gives it 636 centimetres of girth, 38 metres of height and a crown spreading 33 metres, in good health. For scale, the plane in the middle of Place du Cirque, the largest in the city centre, measures 425 centimetres. This one is half as thick again and taller, and almost nobody writes about it.

Nor does anyone date it. The register's planting field is simply empty, so the age here comes from comparing girths with that Place du Cirque tree, which is about 120 years old and the same species on the same soil. That puts this one somewhere between 150 and 200 years, a band wide enough to be honest and narrow enough to be useful.

It sits a short walk from Gare Cornavin and the Sécheron rail stop, which makes it the easiest of Geneva's giants to reach without planning anything at all.

trees.name: The Service Tree of Chambésy
trees.access: Free, standing on the roadside at Route de Pregny in a public green space, per the register's own situation field.
trees.transport: Bus toward Chambésy/Pregny, or roughly 25 minutes on foot from the botanical garden
trees.story:
Sorbus domestica is rare enough in Switzerland that a healthy one beside a road counts as a find. The service tree is the overlooked member of a familiar family, a relative of the rowan that grows into a proper timber tree and carries small brown fruit shaped like miniature apples or pears. Those fruits are why anybody ever planted it. Hard and sour straight off the branch, they were left to go soft and brown before eating, and went into cider and perry across southern Europe to sharpen them.

This one went into the ground in April 1966 on the Route de Pregny, which makes it about sixty years old, young for a tree on this list. The date is worth trusting for an unglamorous reason: the register records a real month for it, where its uncertain entries all default to the first of January. It measures 247 centimetres round and is in good health, and it is here for what it is rather than for how big it is.

The register is also the only source that mentions it, which is thin for a species this easy to mistake for a rowan or a wild service tree. If you know this tree, or know who put it there, tell us. It is a five-minute walk from the tulip tree in Parc de l'Impératrice, which makes the two of them one stop rather than two.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Parc des Eaux-Vives
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus or a 15-20 minute walk from the centre along the lakefront
trees.story:
A Mediterranean umbrella pine has no obvious business on Lake Geneva, and this one is thriving. Pinus pinea is the tree of the Roman roadside and the Italian coast, a bare trunk running up to a flat parasol of a crown, and the silhouette reads as out of place among the cedars and planes of the Eaux-Vives parks. It stands 19 metres tall with a crown 17 metres across and a trunk 280 centimetres round, and the cantonal register rates its vitality as excellent.

The species is the source of pine nuts, which take three years to ripen inside cones heavy enough to be worth watching out for underneath. Whether this tree bothers producing them this far north is a fair question, and not one the register answers.

Nobody has dated it. The planting field for this entry is empty, not even carrying the placeholder January date that fills so much of the file, and no growth figure for stone pines in this climate turned up that would support an honest estimate. So the age here is blank rather than guessed. If you know when it went in, or know somebody at the parks department who does, tell us and it goes on the page.

It stands about 65 metres from the bald cypress, which makes the two of them a single short detour off the lakeside path.

trees.name: The Plane of the University Garden
trees.access: Free, open public promenade at any time, the same park as the Official Chestnut Tree.
trees.transport: Central Vieille-Ville/Plainpalais, a few minutes' walk from Bel-Air or Plainpalais tram stops
trees.story:
This plane did not grow here. A plaque at its foot records that it was transplanted from the Place des Alpes to the Promenade des Bastions in 1878, and a tree big enough to be worth moving was already a tree when it made the trip. So 1878 is a floor for its age rather than a birthday. How much older it is, nobody has established, and the canton's register carries no planting date at all.

What it moved into was the best address in Geneva for a specimen tree. The Bastions served as the city's botanical garden from 1817 until 1904, so a plane arriving in 1878 was being placed by people whose profession was placing plants. The collection later left for the lakeside. The tree stayed, and has outgrown everything the garden left behind.

It now measures 5.38 metres around and 31 metres tall, under a crown 38 metres across, wider than the tree is high, which is what a plane does when nothing crowds it for a century and a half. The canton's inventory files its development stage as senescent. It stands alone facing the entrance on the university garden side, inside a ring of barriers whose purpose is to stop students chaining bicycles to it, and Geneva's city arborist describes it as looking rather like the king of the courtyard.

trees.name: The Hackberries of Place de l'Université
trees.access: Free, open public square at any time
trees.transport: Central Vieille-Ville/Plainpalais, a few minutes' walk from Bel-Air or Plainpalais tram stops
trees.story:
A fungus is eating these three from the inside, and the city said so itself. In 2020 Geneva's arborist told the Tribune de Genève that the micocouliers de Provence on the Place de l'Université are being hollowed out and risk coming down, which is a candid thing for a municipality to volunteer about trees it has listed as remarkable. The canton's inventory then recorded good vitality at its last field visit in 2024. Both readings can be true of a hollowing tree, which is why these are watched rather than felled.

There are three of them, standing together facing the entrance of Uni Bastions, close enough to read as one destination and collected here as one; the pin marks the group rather than a particular trunk. At this spot the register measures 3.3 metres of girth and 18 metres of height. They went in during the early 20th century, and the exact year is not recoverable from the record.

Mediterranean hackberry is a southern species living at the cool edge of its range in Geneva, which is part of why a set of them at this size is worth the canton's attention. In Provence its wood was the standard material for pitchforks, whip handles and walking sticks, chosen because it bends a long way before it breaks. These three have shaded a century of students crossing the square, and are now being tested from the inside instead.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Domaine de Penthes
trees.access: Free, public garden maintained by the City of Geneva's botanical garden service; the château itself housed the Museum of the Swiss Abroad, which closed in 2022 after the foundation's bankruptcy, but the grounds remain open to the public. Exact daily hours not confirmed in.
trees.transport: Bus toward Chambesy/Pregny, or roughly 25 minutes on foot from the botanical garden, the same road as the Tulip Tree of Parc de l'Imperatrice and the Service Tree of Chambesy.
trees.story:
Geneva has plane trees along half its streets and almost none of the tree they came from. The London plane that lines European cities is a hybrid, and this is the parent that gave it its name and most of its looks: Platanus orientalis, which the city's arborist calls a rare specimen on Genevan soil. It is also the tree the Tribune de Genève picked to open its walking tour of the canton's remarkable trees, which tells you where the professionals would start.

It stands in the garden of the Château de Penthes above the lake, 5.59 metres around and 20 metres tall, carrying a crown 25 metres wide. The canton's inventory rates its vitality excellent, which is not a given at that size. An arborist puts it at around 120 years and thinks the château's owners planted it, but that is his estimate rather than a record, he gave it in 2020, and no document naming the planting has turned up.

The grounds are nine hectares, free to walk, and kept by the gardeners of the city's botanical garden. The museum inside the château closed in 2022 when its foundation went bankrupt, and the garden simply carried on without it. Elsewhere on the lawn stands the stump of a giant sequoia that lightning finished in 1993, another of the estate's imported trophies. The plane has had better luck.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Cimetière des Rois
trees.access: Free, public cemetery grounds, open during standard cemetery daylight hours
trees.transport: Plainpalais tram stop (lines 12/15), short walk
trees.story:
This oak is nearly twice as wide as it is tall. Twelve metres of height, a crown twenty metres across, a trunk 2.64 metres round, and it sits at the main entrance of the Cimetière des Rois, the plot Geneva keeps for the people it wants to remember. Everyone going in or coming out passes under it.

Holm oak is a Mediterranean evergreen and has no obvious business this far north, yet the canton lists two of them as remarkable trees, this one and another in Parc Geisendorf, and the city's arborist rates the pair as equals. Being evergreen it looks the same in February as in July, which at a cemetery gate is closer to a job than a habit.

Behind it lies Jorge Luis Borges, who chose Geneva over Buenos Aires for the end and got a headstone carved with Old English, and somewhere behind it lies John Calvin, who asked in 1564 to be buried without a marker and was obeyed so completely that the stone bearing his initials marks a guess at the spot rather than the spot. A cemetery full of certainties about who is there and vagueness about exactly where.

The canton's last recorded field visit, in 2012, put the tree in good condition. Its planting is filed only as mid twentieth century, no closer. Which makes this a young tree keeping very old company.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Parc Mon Repos
trees.access: Free, park green space open at any time
trees.transport: Short walk from Gare Cornavin or the Secheron rail stop
trees.story:
A second giant grows a stone's throw from the Secheron Plane, and this one is a conifer rather than a plane: a Himalayan cedar, native to the high valleys of Kashmir and Nepal, brought to Europe's parks in the nineteenth century as one of the era's fashionable new conifers. Geneva's cantonal register puts it at 4.18 metres round the trunk, 28 metres tall and a crown spanning 23 metres, and rates its health good on a 2024 field visit, the freshest survey of any tree on this list.

Like its neighbour the plane, this cedar's exact park is not pinned down by any source found so far. The coordinates are precise, the green space off Avenue de France is not named with certainty (Secheron, Mon Repos and the Perle du Lac all border the same avenue), and the two trees stand close enough, about ninety metres apart, that a single stop covers both without walking anywhere else. The register carries no planting date, so this cedar's age is simply unknown rather than estimated. What is measured is measured well: a girth that would take three adults to encircle, on a species that can live for centuries in the right conditions. The nearest way in is the same one that reaches the plane, a short walk from Gare Cornavin or the Secheron rail stop.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, open garden during opening hours
trees.transport: Tram to Nations or the botanical garden stop, then a short walk
trees.story:
This cedar's growth and the garden's own site are almost exactly the same age. The Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques moved to its present Avenue de la Paix grounds in 1904 under director John Briquet, with the winter garden and surrounding landscaping built out over the following years; the cantonal register separately dates this Himalayan cedar's planting to 1912, a genuine recorded year rather than a placeholder, squarely inside that same building-out window.

It has grown into one of the garden's largest specimens: five metres round the trunk, 34 metres tall, a crown spreading 25 metres, most recently surveyed in August 2025 in good health. That makes it roughly a century old, younger than the garden's own oak nearby, which predates the garden itself by close to two centuries, but old enough to have stood through both world wars and the whole of the garden's modern development.

A second, slightly smaller Himalayan cedar from the same 1912 planting stands about two hundred metres away, last surveyed over a decade ago; this is the fresher and larger of the pair. Enter from Avenue de la Paix and the tree stands a short walk from the gate.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Parc La Grange
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus or tram to Eaux-Vives, then a short walk, roughly 15 minutes from the centre
trees.story:
Parc La Grange keeps two enormous cedars from two different mountain ranges. One, near the main house, is a Cedar of Lebanon descended from seed gifted in 1735. The other, over five and a half metres round the trunk, is an Atlas cedar, native not to the Levant but to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, and Geneva's cantonal register rates it in good health with a canopy 23 metres across and a height of 29 metres.

Cedar of Lebanon and Atlas cedar look similar enough at a glance, both broad and flat topped with the same grey green needles, that telling them apart takes a second look at the cones rather than a first glance at the silhouette. This one has no documented planting date, and the register's last field visit was in 2014, over a decade old now, the oldest confirmed sighting of any tree on this list. It is still a genuinely large specimen in a park built around genuinely large trees, worth remembering as a second cedar rather than a repeat of the one most visitors are pointed toward. This one stands elsewhere in the same grounds, near Avenue Alice-et-William-Favre, roughly fifteen minutes from the city centre by bus or tram.

trees.name: The Darnley Sycamore
trees.access: Free, open access, fenced but publicly visible year-round
trees.transport: Priesthill & Darnley railway station, then a walk through the housing estate; local buses run along Nitshill Road

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story: For an oak or a yew, 450 years would be middle age. For a sycamore, a fast-growing species that rarely lives past 400, the Darnley Sycamore is already exceptional, and Glasgow has nearly lost it more than once. Local legend holds that in 1565 Mary, Queen of Scots sat beneath its branches nursing her new husband, Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, through an illness, a story specific enough that the tree still carries his name four and a half centuries later. In 1969, a Barrhead schoolteacher marched 28 primary pupils out with placards reading 'Save the Sycamore' when council engineers proposed routing a new dual carriageway straight through it; newspaper coverage of the protest changed the road's course instead. Decades later came a stranger threat: Storm Eowyn's hurricane-force winds in January 2025, which tore away roughly half its crown and left neighbours fearing the worst. Glasgow City Council sent an arborist up on a hoist rather than write the tree off from the ground, and found the trunk sounder than photographs of the wreckage suggested. Officials now expect decades more from it, with unsafe limbs removed and the rest left to regrow. What remains today stands fenced and plaqued on a housing estate that grew up entirely around it, the only visible trace of the countryside Darnley once was.

trees.name: The Suffragette Oak
trees.access: Free, open access, Kelvingrove Park (open daily)
trees.transport: Kelvinhall or Kelvinbridge subway station, short walk through the park
trees.story: Not every remarkable tree here began as a sapling nobody thought twice about. This one was planted as a protest made permanent: on 20 April 1918, days after the Representation of the People Act gave some British women the vote for the first time, suffrage campaigner Louisa Lumsden planted a Hungarian oak in Kelvingrove Park on behalf of the Glasgow Society of Women's Suffrage, the Scottish Universities Suffrage Union, the Women's Freedom League and the United Suffragists, groups that had spent years disagreeing on tactics and, for one afternoon, planted a tree together instead. The Women's Committee of Glasgow City Council added a plaque in 1995 on International Women's Day, and in 2015 the Glasgow Women's Library campaigned it to a public vote as Scotland's Tree of the Year, beating five other historic finalists. Storm Ophelia found it in October 2017, stripping around a third of its canopy and tearing its trunk; council arborists reduced its height and rebalanced the crown to save it rather than remove it, and the timber that came down was carved into earrings, coasters and trinket boxes sold by the Women's Library. Now well over a century old and visibly reshaped by that storm, it stands a short walk from Glasgow University, one of the few trees in Britain planted specifically to mark a fight for the vote rather than a coronation or a laird's coming of age.

trees.name: The King's Park Yews
trees.access: Free, open access, King's Park (Glasgow City Council park, open daily)
trees.transport: King's Park railway station (Cathcart Circle Line), short walk

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Most of the ancient-looking yews scattered through Britain's churchyards got there because someone wanted shade over graves. These 88 got here because a Glasgow merchant who had made his fortune in the West Indies trade wanted his new estate to look established. When architect David Hamilton laid out the grounds of Aikenhead House for its owner, John Gordon, in the early 1800s, he planted a formal grove of yews on rising ground east of the mansion, then a second, larger avenue of them a little later in imitation of the first. A specialist survey of the site in 2021 confirmed what the difference in trunk girth already suggested: the smaller eastern grove of 22 trees is measurably older and larger than the 66 planted afterward, some girthed at over four metres. The mansion the yews were planted to flatter had itself replaced an even older house on the same spot, one built for a 17th-century Lord Provost of Glasgow that burned down long before. Aikenhead House passed out of private hands in 1930, when developer Sir John MacTaggart gave the house and its 68 acres of parkland to the city as King's Park. The yews needed no care to survive that change of ownership: they simply kept growing, dark and unhurried, while the mansion around them changed hands, uses, and eventually postcodes.

trees.name: Holmwood's Giant Redwoods
trees.access: Free, grounds open to walk daily; the house itself charges admission (National Trust for Scotland, members free)
trees.transport: Cathcart railway station, short walk
trees.story: Alexander 'Greek' Thomson's Holmwood is famous for its architecture, a villa modelled so closely on classical Greek temples that its own guidebooks call it his masterpiece, and for years little attention went to what was actually growing in its garden. That changed when the National Trust for Scotland's PLANTS project, a survey set up to catalogue what its properties' grounds actually contain rather than assume the historical record already covers it, worked through Holmwood's parkland and found two Giant Redwoods the trust's own records had barely registered, plus a Himalayan deodar cedar keeping them company. At around a century old, both sequoias are younger than the villa itself, planted well after paper magnate James Couper commissioned the house in 1857, and younger still than California's oldest specimens of the same species, some of which are pushing 3,000 years and eighty metres tall. Glasgow's pair share the same silhouette in miniature: a straight, buttressed trunk and soft, rope-like bark that a curious visitor can press a thumb into without hurting the tree. Whoever planted them was following a very Victorian fashion; seed brought back from California's Sierra Nevada groves after 1853 turned half of aspirational Britain's gardens into pocket-sized redwood forests, and Holmwood's pair survived to become, by complete accident of record-keeping, one of the last things about the estate anybody thought to write down.

trees.name: The Fernleaf Beech of Palazzo Doria-Tursi
trees.age: roughly 100-180 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)
trees.neighbourhood: Via Garibaldi / Strada Nuova, historic centre
trees.access: Free. Stands in the courtyard of Palazzo Doria-Tursi, a Rolli palace (UNESCO) that now houses Genoa's city hall and the Strada Nuova Museums; the main courtyard and staircase are generally open to the public without a ticket during opening hours, per general sourcing on the palace. Not personally confirmed the tree itself is unobstructed from the courtyard.
trees.transport: In the pedestrianised heart of Via Garibaldi, a few minutes' walk from Genova De Ferrari / San Giorgio

best_time.label: late October into November, when the cut leaves go copper against the stone

trees.story: Genoa's city hall has a beech in its courtyard, and its leaves are wrong. This is Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia', a cut-leaved sport of the ordinary European beech whose foliage comes out narrow and deeply slashed, closer to a fern frond than to the broad oval leaf the species is known for. The national monumental tree register records it at 230 centimetres round and 21 metres tall, which puts its crown level with the palace's upper windows. Palazzo Doria-Tursi was built in 1565 for the banker Niccolo Grimaldi, passed to the Doria family in 1596, was later bought by the Republic of Genoa, and has been the seat of the city's government since 1848. The tree is far younger than the walls around it. Nobody has dated it: no source gives a planting year, and the 100 to 180 year range here is worked back from the trunk alone, so read it as an order of magnitude rather than a number. A courtyard planting from the municipal era would fit the size, but that is inference, not record. It stands inside one of the Rolli palaces on Via Garibaldi, the UNESCO-listed street of Genoese banking houses, in a courtyard that now also serves the Strada Nuova Museums. Turn off the street and it is there between the arcades, a lace-leaved tree in a stone box.

trees.name: The Poet's Holm Oak of Montesignano
trees.age: roughly 150-300 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)
trees.neighbourhood: Montesignano / San Desiderio, eastern hills of Genoa
trees.access: not confirmed. Via Mogadiscio is a residential street in the Montesignano district; independent geocoding places it at roughly the same coordinates as the register (44.4389, 8.9665), and the Liguria regional listing ties the tree to the church of San Michele Arcangelo rather than a private garden, which is a good sign, but I did not find a source stating the tree stands on public ground or is visible from the street. A local civic-tech initiative is literally named 'Il Leccio di via Mogadiscio' after it (Genova Digitale ran information sessions there), which suggests it functions as a known local landmark rather than a hidden private specimen, but that is not the same as confirmed public access.
trees.transport: AMT bus lines 480/482, stop 'Mogadiscio 6/Giacalone', about 1 minute's walk from the stop; total time from the city centre not independently timed, likely 20-30 minutes by bus
trees.story: The civic group that runs computer lessons in this corner of Genoa named itself after a tree: Il Leccio di via Mogadiscio, the holm oak of Via Mogadiscio. That is what a neighbourhood landmark looks like when it appears on no tourist map. The oak stands in Montesignano in the eastern hills, near the church of San Michele Arcangelo, and both the national register and Liguria's separate regional list carry it, which is rarer than it sounds. They agree on 257 centimetres of girth and 15 metres of height, and the region records the reason for protection as historical, cultural and religious value rather than size. Genoese sources connect the tree to Camillo Sbarbaro, the poet of Pianissimo who spent his other working life as one of Italy's serious amateur lichenologists, collecting the lichens that grow on exactly this kind of old bark. We have not found the line or the poem, so treat the literary link as a local attribution rather than a quotable fact. Its age is unrecorded too. Italy's national register carries no age field for any entry anywhere in the country, so the 150 to 300 year span comes off the trunk and nothing else. Holm oak is evergreen, dark and hard-leaved, which means it looks much the same in January as in July, and it drops acorns sweeter than most oaks in autumn.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of San Pantaleo
trees.age: roughly 200-350 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)
trees.access: not established. No second source found describing what stands at this address or whether the tree is visible/accessible from the street.
trees.transport: Historic centre, within walking distance of Genova Piazza Principe / Via Balbi
trees.story: This is the thickest registered oak in Genoa's old town and the least documented tree on this list. The national monumental tree register gives it 305 centimetres of girth and 12 metres of height at an address on Via di San Pantaleo, in the dense Pre quarter behind Via Balbi, and that single sheet is the whole of what is known. No newspaper piece names it, no park authority claims it, no photograph turned up. Searching the street name mostly returns the deconsecrated church of San Pantaleo over by Staglieno cemetery, which is a different building in a different part of the city. So the pin here is marked approximate on purpose. We have the register's coordinates, but nothing confirms whether the tree stands where a passer-by can see it or behind a courtyard wall at that number, and this quarter is built almost entirely of walls. The age, roughly 200 to 350 years, is read off the girth, because the register records no ages. A holm oak that thick in streets this tight would have been growing before the surrounding blocks took their present shape, evergreen through every one of those winters. If you go and find it, tell us what is actually there. That is the fastest way this entry gets better.

trees.name: The Great Camphor Tree of Via Romolo Gessi
trees.age: roughly 150-250 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)
trees.access: not established.
trees.transport: Medio Ponente district, west of the centre; nearest stations around Genova Sampierdarena / Cornigliano on the Genova-Ventimiglia line
trees.story: One number makes this tree interesting, and the same number is the reason to be careful about it. The national monumental tree register lists a Nepal camphor tree on Via Romolo Gessi in Cornigliano with a trunk 734 centimetres round, about 2.3 metres through, and 24 metres tall. For comparison, the other specimens of Cinnamomum glanduliferum turned up around Genoa measure 487 centimetres at Villa Tigullio in Rapallo and between 350 and 392 at Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli. This one is half as thick again as the next largest, which makes it either a genuinely extraordinary tree or a digit that slipped in a spreadsheet. Only the register carries it. No photograph, no second measurement, no local article, which is why no superlative is claimed for it here. Nepal camphor comes from the Himalaya and southwest China, and it reached Genoese gardens in the nineteenth century, when shipping money was buying exotics by the crate and the western districts of Cornigliano and Sampierdarena still had the villa grounds to put them in, long before heavy industry took that shoreline. The age, roughly 150 to 250 years, is estimated from the trunk. The pin is approximate. Go and look, and if the trunk really is that wide, we would like to hear it.

trees.name: The Coast Redwood of Villa Serra
trees.age: roughly 120-170 years (girth-based estimate consistent with the park's founding era, no dated source for this individual)
trees.neighbourhood: Comago, Sant'Olcese (Val Polcevera, Genoa metropolitan area, NOT within the comune of Genova)
trees.access: Paid/managed historic park (Consorzio Villa Serra). Opening hours: Jan-Feb 10:00-17:00, Mar-Apr 10:00-18:00, May-Aug 09:00-20:00, Sep 09:00-19:00, Oct 10:00-18:00, Nov-Dec 10:00-17:00, Monday mornings closed.
trees.transport: NOT in Genoa proper. Sant'Olcese/Comago is a separate comune in the Polcevera valley, roughly 9km north of Genoa's centre by road. Reachable by AMT bus lines 7, 735, 737, 738 (stop 'Comago/Scuola', 10-min walk, or 'L. Secca/Manesseno', 4-min walk), typically via a first leg to Genova Bolzaneto (train or bus) then a connecting local bus into the valley. I could not pin an exact door-to-door time ; it is plausibly close to or over the 30-minute day-trip threshold and should be timed properly, and labelled honestly as Sant'Olcese/Comago rather than presented as inside Genoa, per the day-trip boundary rule.
trees.story: A Californian redwood 38 and a half metres tall grows in a valley north of Genoa, and it is not even the tallest tree in its own park. Villa Serra stands in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, up the Polcevera valley and outside the city boundary, roughly nine kilometres from the centre and reached by a bus or a train and a connecting bus. What the journey buys is the tightest group of monumental trees anywhere around Genoa: this sequoia and three others stand within about sixty metres of one another in nine hectares of English-style park. Coast redwood belongs to the fog belt of northern California, where the species grows taller than anything in Europe, and it arrived in Italian gardens in the middle of the nineteenth century as the fashionable import of the moment, which is also when this garden was laid out. That timing is where the age estimate comes from: roughly 120 to 170 years, reasoned from the founding of the park and from the trunk, with no planting record for this individual and no age field in the national register to consult. Its bark is the thing to put a hand on, soft, fibrous and deep enough to shrug off fire in its home range. The park was restored and reopened in 1992. It charges admission and closes on Monday mornings.

trees.name: The Turkey Oak of Villa Serra
trees.age: roughly 120-170 years (girth-based estimate consistent with the park's founding era, no dated source for this individual)
trees.neighbourhood: Comago, Sant'Olcese (Val Polcevera, Genoa metropolitan area, NOT within the comune of Genova)
trees.access: Same park as the Coast Redwood of Villa Serra; see that entry for hours.
trees.transport: As for the Coast Redwood of Villa Serra.
trees.story: At 41 metres this is the tallest of Villa Serra's four monumental trees, taller than the Californian redwood standing sixty metres away, which is not what anyone expects from an oak. Quercus cerris is fast and tall by European standards, native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, but it usually tops out around thirty metres. Getting past forty takes shelter, water and a long undisturbed run, and a valley-floor park in Val Polcevera supplies all three. The register puts its girth at 378 centimetres. You can tell it from the pedunculate oak a few paces away without knowing anything about oaks: the leaves are stiffer and more deeply cut, the buds sit inside thin whiskery scales, and the acorn cups look mossy, wrapped in the same curled filaments. Villa Serra is in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, up the valley from Genoa rather than in it, and its English-style grounds date from the middle of the nineteenth century. The tree's age follows from that, roughly 120 to 170 years, an estimate drawn from the planting era and the trunk rather than a dated record. No source gives it a year, and Italy's national register has no age column at all.

trees.name: The European Hop-hornbeam of Villa Serra
trees.neighbourhood: Comago, Sant'Olcese (Val Polcevera, Genoa metropolitan area, NOT within the comune of Genova)
trees.access: Same park as the Coast Redwood of Villa Serra; see that entry for hours.
trees.transport: As for the Coast Redwood of Villa Serra.

best_time.label: late summer, when the pale hop-like fruit clusters hang all over the crown

trees.story: This is the only tree on this list whose age somebody actually wrote down. Italy's national monumental tree register has no age column, anywhere, for any entry, which is why nearly every date on this page is reasoned back from a trunk measurement. Liguria runs its own regional register and that one does carry the field, and for this hop-hornbeam it reads approximately 160 to 170 years. It is a modest tree to be the best documented of the set. Ostrya carpinifolia is a small, unshowy relative of the birches that rarely makes a specimen tree at all, and park competition has drawn this one up to somewhere between 22 and 32 metres, depending on which register you believe. The two agree on the 256 centimetre trunk and disagree on the height, so both figures stand here rather than one. In late summer it makes the fruit that named it, hanging clusters of papery pale bladders that look like hops on a vine, each holding a single seed. Ligurian woodsmen cut this species for tool handles, cartwheel spokes and vine stakes, because the wood is heavy, hard and will not split. It stands with three larger trees inside sixty metres at Villa Serra, in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, up the Polcevera valley from the city.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Villa Serra
trees.age: roughly 120-170 years (girth-based estimate consistent with the park's founding era, no dated source for this individual)
trees.neighbourhood: Comago, Sant'Olcese (Val Polcevera, Genoa metropolitan area, NOT within the comune of Genova)
trees.access: Same park as the Coast Redwood of Villa Serra; see that entry for hours.
trees.transport: As for the Coast Redwood of Villa Serra.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: The park's own notes point out that a pedunculate oak can live five hundred years, which makes this one, at somewhere around 120 to 170, a tree with most of its life still in front of it. It is already 39 and a half metres tall with a trunk 296 centimetres round. Quercus robur is the common oak of northern Europe and the timber that built its navies, and in a sheltered park it grows straighter and faster than it ever does in open country. That is what has happened here: this is a tall forest-shaped oak rather than the wide-limbed field version most people picture when they hear the name. The age is an estimate and not a record. It follows from the founding of Villa Serra's English-style park in the middle of the nineteenth century and from the girth, and no source gives this individual a planting year. It completes the group of four monumental trees standing within sixty metres of each other, alongside a coast redwood, a Turkey oak and a hop-hornbeam, which is more variety than sixty metres of Liguria usually offers. The park is in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, in the Polcevera valley north of Genoa and outside the city. It is a managed historic park with an admission charge, closed on Monday mornings.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini
trees.age: roughly 100-180 years (girth-based estimate, consistent with the park's mid-19th-century creation, no dated source for this individual)
trees.access: Paid entry, roughly 9-13 EUR depending on day/residency. Open Tue-Fri 09:30-17:00, Sat-Sun 10:00-17:00, closed Mondays (seasonal variation likely; check villadurazzopallavicini.it before publishing). Roughly 3km of paths, 2.5 hours for the full circuit.
trees.transport: Pegli railway station on the Genova-Ventimiglia line, about 15 minutes by regional train from Genova Piazza Principe, short walk to the park entrance. Comfortably within Genoa and within the day-trip boundary.
trees.story: Crush a leaf from this tree and your fingers smell of a medicine cabinet. Cinnamomum camphora is the source of camphor, distilled from its wood and leaves for centuries as a medicine, a moth repellent and the plasticiser that made celluloid film possible, and this specimen has reached 36 metres with a trunk 538 centimetres round. It grows at the edge of the lake in the park of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli, which is not an ordinary garden. It was laid out in the middle of the nineteenth century by Michele Canzio, a set designer from Genoa's opera house, as a theatrical route in acts and scenes, complete with a Gothic ruin, a Chinese pagoda and an artificial lake you cross by boat to reach a temple. The camphor and the Cedar of Lebanon beside it are named together in the Ministry of Culture's own description of the park, which is a lot of official attention for two trees. The age is not documented for this individual: roughly 100 to 180 years is an estimate that fits both the trunk and the making of the garden, nothing firmer. Pegli is about fifteen minutes by regional train from Genova Piazza Principe. The park charges entry, closes on Mondays, and the full circuit runs to some three kilometres of path.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini
trees.age: roughly 100-180 years (girth-based estimate, consistent with the park's mid-19th-century creation, no dated source for this individual)
trees.access: Same park as the Camphor Tree of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini; see that entry for hours and pricing.
trees.transport: As for the Camphor Tree of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini.

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Two trees from opposite ends of the old trading world stand together at this lake: an East Asian camphor and this Cedar of Lebanon, and the Ministry of Culture names both in its description of the park. The cedar is the smaller of the pair at 25 metres, with a trunk 320 centimetres round, and it is the one with the longer history behind it. Cedrus libani is the tree of the Phoenician shipwrights and of the Bible's building accounts, cut out of the mountains of Lebanon for three thousand years until little more than remnant groves were left, then replanted across European estates in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as the grandest thing a landowner could stand on a lawn. That is roughly what happened here. Villa Durazzo Pallavicini's park in Pegli was built in the middle of the nineteenth century as a designed walk in acts and scenes, and a cedar at the water's edge is exactly the set piece such a garden reaches for. No planting record survives for this tree, so the 100 to 180 year estimate rests on the trunk and on the age of the garden around it. One caution for anyone searching: a different and larger Cedar of Lebanon grows at a Villa Pallavicini in Arenzano, twenty kilometres further west. This is not that tree.

trees.name: The Bunya Pine of Villa Groppallo
trees.access: Free entry. Stands in the gardens of Villa Groppallo inside the Parchi di Nervi, Genoa's public seafront park complex (owned by the Comune di Genova since the villas were converted to museums/galleries); the park grounds are open to the public year round, though the villas' own gallery interiors (GAM, Wolfsoniana, Raccolte Frugone) charge separate admission.
trees.transport: Genova Nervi railway station (regional trains from Genova Brignole, about 15 minutes), then roughly a 5 minute walk into the park.
trees.story:
A register once mislabelled this tree's girth as its diameter, which would have made the trunk over six metres wide rather than six metres round, a mistake plausible enough that nobody caught it until an independent citizen-science registry went out and measured the tree itself. Corrected, it still measures 6.36 metres around, among the largest bunya pines recorded in Europe.

Araucaria bidwillii comes from the subtropical rainforests of Queensland, where its cones grow to five or seven kilograms and drop hard enough that parks close the ground beneath fruiting trees during the season. This one has stood in the formal gardens of Villa Groppallo, part of Genoa's seafront Parchi di Nervi, long enough that nobody agrees on exactly how long: the official monumental register gives a floor of 75 years from its original designation, while the citizen-science count that corrected the girth estimates closer to 115. Both figures come from the same kind of measurement read differently, so the honest range spans both.

The Parchi di Nervi are Genoa's largest public park, free and open year round, though the villas converted to galleries inside it charge their own admission. The bunya pine needs no ticket, just a walk into the gardens from Nervi's own railway station.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Acquasanta
trees.access: Free, publicly accessible. Stands in the open piazza in front of the Santuario di Nostra Signora dell'Acquasanta, a working church square in the Acquasanta hamlet of Genoa (part of the Voltri district); no gate or ticket.
trees.transport: Genova Voltri railway station (regional trains from Genova centre, roughly 30 minutes), then AMT bus line 101 to the 'Acquasanta/Santuario' stop directly at the piazza (about 11-13 minutes; roughly hourly service, reduced on Sundays). This is a genuine outer neighbourhood of Genoa itself, not a separate town, but the honest one-way trip from the centre runs 40-50 minutes door to door; say so plainly rather than presenting it as a short walk from downtown.
trees.story:
Genoa's monumental tree register does not give ages, only measurements, so this cedar of Lebanon comes with a girth, four metres sixty one round, and nothing else: no planting date, no story attached to who put it here or when. It stands in the open square in front of the Santuario di Nostra Signora dell'Acquasanta, a working church in Acquasanta, a hillside hamlet inside Genoa's Voltri district.

Cedrus libani takes its name from the mountains of Lebanon, where centuries of shipbuilding and temple construction stripped most of the ancient forests that once covered them; the species survives in Europe mainly because 18th and 19th century estates and church grounds planted it as an ornamental long before conservation became a reason to care. This one shares its piazza with a second, taller monumental tree the same register protects nearby, a coast redwood, though that one has not yet been individually verified for this page.
