Acquasanta sits a genuine 40 to 50 minutes from central Genoa door to door, by train to Voltri and then a bus that runs roughly hourly. The piazza itself is open and free, no gate or ticket, the cedar visible from the church steps.

trees.name: The Cypress of San Juan de la Cruz
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 15 min walk from the city centre, near the Manuel de Falla Auditorium
trees.story: This cypress is not native to Spain, or even to the continent it is usually associated with. Hesperocyparis lusitanica, despite its name, comes from Mexico and Central America, and reached Europe through Carmelite missionaries who brought it first to Portugal, then into Spain's own monastery gardens. One of those Carmelites was San Juan de la Cruz, the mystic and poet, who served as prior of the Convent of the Martyrs here between 1582 and 1588, by his own order's account the calmest and most productive years of his life. Tradition holds he planted this tree himself, using his prior's staff, choosing the species as a personal symbol for reaching heaven. It was here that he shaped the poems he had first composed from memory in a Toledo prison, including the verses that became Dark Night of the Soul. Roughly two decades ago lightning tore away a significant part of the crown, and the tree still shows the damage today, new growth sprouting from the truncated stump rather than a single unbroken trunk. It survives regardless, in a free public garden that still keeps much of the convent's original layout, lake and orchard included.

trees.name: The Sequoias of the Generalife's Upper Gardens
trees.access: Paid entry, Alhambra and Generalife (timed ticket required)
trees.transport: Alhambra bus (C30/C32) or 25 min walk uphill from the city centre
trees.story: Coast redwoods reached Europe in 1843, and Granada planted some of the continent's first within little more than a decade, sequoias going into the Generalife's Upper Gardens between 1854 and 1856, while the gardens were still privately owned ground. Sequoia sempervirens can live three thousand years and grow past 100 metres in its native California; these specimens, still comparatively young, have nonetheless become some of the tallest living things inside the Alhambra complex. Granada's connection to the species runs oddly deeper than that planting date suggests. In 1926 an American botanist examining a separate, older redwood elsewhere on the grounds calculated it was roughly 120 years old, old enough to have been planted before European science had formally identified the coast redwood at all, a puzzle eventually attributed to Thaddaeus Haenke, a naturalist on the 1791 Malaspina expedition who is thought to have carried seed back from California decades before the species reached botanical record books. That original mystery tree died sometime before 2002. The sequoias standing in the Upper Gardens today are the later, better-documented planting, reachable only with a paid, timed Alhambra and Generalife ticket.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, open on university working days
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta Real, city centre

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold

trees.story: This was the first ginkgo Granada ever grew, planted in 1889 in a garden that had itself only existed since 1840, on ground that used to be the vegetable orchard of a Jesuit college before the University of Granada's Faculty of Law took over the site. Ginkgo biloba is the last living member of a plant order that once grew across the entire planet during the age of dinosaurs, a lineage so isolated botanists sometimes call it a living fossil, and this specimen's fan-shaped leaves, turning a uniform gold each November, still look almost identical to fossil ginkgo leaves more than 200 million years old. The species is famous for a harder kind of survival too: six ginkgos within roughly a mile of Hiroshima's atomic bomb epicentre lived through the blast and are still growing today, a fact this specimen's own garden plaque, next to a poem written for the tree by the Granada poet Elena Martin Vivaldi, does not fail to mention. The garden is open to the public on university working days, free of charge, tucked behind the Faculty of Law's own building in the city centre.

trees.name: The Palms of the Archbishop's Palace
trees.access: Free, public square; the palms stand inside the Diocesan Curia's own garden and are viewed from the plaza, not entered
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Cathedral
trees.story: Four Mexican fan palms tower over Plaza de Gracia, planted in 1923 the year construction finished on the Palacio de los Yanguas, the building bordering the square behind a garden wall on Calle Gracia. Architect Fernando Wilhelmi built it between 1920 and 1925 for the family of the Marquis of Casablanca; it later became the seat of Granada's Diocesan Curia, the archdiocese's administrative offices, which is why it is still known locally as the Archbishop's palace even though it was never built as one. Washingtonia robusta grows faster and taller than almost any other palm cultivated in southern Spain, capable of clearing 30 metres given a century, and this quartet has had almost exactly that long: over 100 years of growth, planted deliberately rather than surviving by accident, the way many of the city's oldest trees have. The species takes its genus name from Washington and its specific name from its robust trunk, an American import that became fashionable across southern European cities in the early 20th century for exactly the effect it produces here, four columns of green rising well above the surrounding rooftops. Visible from across the square is as close as most visitors get, since the palace's own garden is not open to the public.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of the Fountain of Battles
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Puerta Real
trees.story: Four enormous plane trees give Plaza del Campillo its identity, ringing a baroque stone fountain whose own history is less certain than the trees that shade it. The fountain, known as the Fuente de las Batallas for the medieval army musters once held on this ground outside the city's old walls, may originally have belonged to a 17th century convent before arriving at its current spot only in 1950. The planes around it are considerably younger than that origin story but still large enough that their trunks run past five metres around and their crowns reach roughly 30 metres, tall enough to be visible over the surrounding rooftops of the Realejo district. No individual planting date survives for these specific trees, honestly left undated rather than guessed, but their scale alone has made the square one of central Granada's most consistently used gathering spots, host to concerts during the city's spring singer-songwriter festival and its annual book fair.

trees.name: The Robinia of Cuarto Real de Santo Domingo
trees.access: Free, standing in the public entrance square (the Cuarto Real monument itself charges separate admission)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta Real

best_time.label: May, when its white flower clusters hang from every branch

trees.story: This robinia has become famous enough in Granada to appear on a national lottery ticket. In 2023 the Spanish blind people's organisation ONCE printed the tree on five million tickets as part of a series celebrating Spain's most emblematic urban trees, alongside the Granada city council's own logo, a considerable amount of public recognition for a species usually valued for fence posts rather than beauty. What makes this specimen worth printing is its trunk: barely 7.5 metres tall, modest for the species, but swollen to roughly 4.6 metres in girth, thick and deeply weathered enough that it reads as far older than its estimated two centuries. It grows directly outside the entrance to the Cuarto Real de Santo Domingo, the best-preserved surviving palace pavilion from Granada's Almohad and early Nazarid period, standing in the small public square in front of the monument rather than requiring the monument's own separate admission fee. Each May its branches fill with hanging clusters of white flowers, drawing a very different kind of attention than its trunk does the rest of the year.

trees.name: The Twin Cypresses of the Parador
trees.access: Free via the public cafe/restaurant terrace (Parador hotel grounds)
trees.transport: Alhambra bus (C30/C32) or 25 min walk uphill from the city centre
trees.story: Two centenarian cypresses flank what was once the entrance to a set of royal tombs, inside a garden that has spent the last five centuries as a Franciscan convent, then a hotel. The Parador de Granada occupies the former Convento de San Francisco, built in the 15th century within the Alhambra's own walls, on ground the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella briefly chose as their own burial place before their remains moved to the Royal Chapel in the city below. The garden that grew up around the convent later became a botanical showcase laid out with identifying labels for each species, mixing Mediterranean natives, lavender, thyme, rosemary, with the pines, figs and cypresses planted for height and structure, these two flanking the site's most historically loaded doorway. The Parador remains a working hotel, and its garden sits technically on private grounds, but the café and restaurant terrace opens directly onto it, meaning any visitor willing to buy a coffee can walk the same paths past the same trees that once shaded a monarch's intended tomb.

trees.name: The Sophora of the Parador Garden
trees.access: Free via the public cafe/restaurant terrace (Parador hotel grounds)
trees.transport: Alhambra bus (C30/C32) or 25 min walk uphill from the city centre

best_time.label: July and August, when its white flower clusters open

trees.story: Sophora japonica flowers late enough in the year to be useful: most ornamental trees in Granada's gardens finish blooming well before the height of summer, but this species holds its show for July and August, when its branches fill with hanging clusters of small white flowers, a genuine rarity in a Mediterranean garden calendar otherwise built around spring. Despite the name, the species is native to China rather than Japan, spread west along trade routes centuries before European botanists sorted out its origin, and this specimen has stood in the garden of what is now the Parador de Granada for close to two centuries, part of the same former Franciscan convent grounds that also hold the Parador's two flanking cypresses. Sharing a garden with cypresses planted for structure and pines for height, this sophora earns its place on scale and unusual timing alone, one of relatively few large deciduous flowering trees in a garden otherwise built around evergreens.

trees.name: The Cedars of Carmen de la Victoria
trees.access: Free, by prior appointment (University of Granada residence gardens)
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Plaza Nueva, uphill into the Albaicin
trees.story: Two Atlas cedars rise well above the great white perimeter wall of Carmen de la Victoria, tall enough to be one of the first things a visitor sees climbing the Cuesta del Chapiz toward the Albaicin, long before the garden gate itself comes into view. The carmen, a traditional Granada house-and-garden type built around a walled orchard, dates its oldest section, the cypress walk, to well before the University of Granada bought the property in 1944 to use as a student residence and guest house, one of the few carmenes in the neighbourhood that remained in some form of institutional rather than private ownership. Alongside the cedars grow equally old cypresses left deliberately unpruned, and a Judas tree (arbol del amor) now so aged it needs a support post to keep standing, the whole ensemble reading as a garden that has been allowed to grow rather than one kept formally trimmed. Entry is free, but the university requires visitors to book an appointment in advance, one of the few remaining Albaicin carmenes still open to the public at all.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnuts of the Alhambra Forest
trees.access: Free, public forest walk (no ticket required)
trees.transport: Entrance at Puerta de las Granadas, 10 min walk from Plaza Nueva

best_time.label: late April and early May, when the forest's chestnut blossom peaks

trees.story: The wooded hillside visitors climb to reach the Alhambra did not exist when the fortress was still in Muslim hands. Under the Nazarid rulers this slope was a cemetery, reportedly the burial ground of Muhammad I, the dynasty's founder, and his descendants, and the forest only began taking shape after Charles V arrived in the 16th century, later filled out under Ferdinand VII in the early 19th century with species including horse chestnut, plane, acacia and hackberry. The chestnuts have adapted well enough to compete for light against the forest's taller species that some individuals reach 20 metres, and each spring, generally late April into May, they put on the display that has made them the Bosque's best-known trees, dense white flower spikes covering the crown for a few weeks before giving way to spiny, inedible fruit that only superficially resembles a true chestnut. Unlike the paid monuments the forest surrounds, this walk itself, entered through the monumental Puerta de las Granadas, costs nothing and requires no ticket.

trees.name: The Linden of De Rollen
trees.access: Visible from the public road (Noorddijkerweg); De Rollen is a private working farm, not open to visitors
trees.transport: About 5km northeast of Groningen city centre; a 20-minute bike ride or bus toward Noorddijk/Ruischerbrug, then a short walk along Noorddijkerweg

best_time.label: July, when the lime flowers turn the dooryard into a hum of bees

trees.story: Groningen's oldest tree grows exactly where the national heritage register says it should: in front of the farmhouse at De Rollen, a moated farm complex on the city's northeastern edge, planted in 1684. That makes this Common Lime roughly 340 years old, standing decades before Groningen had a Noorderplantsoen or a Sterrebos to compete with. The Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed's own listing calls it plainly the oldest tree in the province, a claim the municipality's 2018 tree policy document repeats for the city specifically. De Rollen itself dates to the 17th century in its original form, rebuilt as a working farmstead in the first half of the 19th century, moat, gateposts and wooden bridge intact, and the linden predates most of what stands around it today, including the farmhouse's own current front door. Twenty-two more lindens and nine ash trees ring the property's edges, a documented perimeter planting, but none come close to this one's age. The farm still works the land, so the tree is not something to walk up to and touch. It stands in a private dooryard, visible from Noorddijkerweg itself, quietly outlasting three centuries of Groningen's growth from a fortified town into a university city, without ever once needing to move.

trees.name: The Star Point Oaks of Sterrebos
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk or short bus ride from Groningen Centraal station

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Storm Henk answered a question nobody had thought to ask properly. When the January 2024 storm toppled one of the old summer oaks planted along Sterrebos's original 18th-century layout, the city's heritage department counted its rings rather than simply clearing the wood, and found a germination year of around 1758, nearly 130 years earlier than the estimate on file. Sterrebos itself was laid out in 1765 by city gardener Jan Godfried Becker as a literal star, eight paths radiating from one central point through a plantation of oaks; this tree had evidently been planted a few years before the park's official founding date, likely an existing woodlot the design was built around rather than a fresh planting. The surviving oaks nearest the fallen one, still standing along the same southern boundary line, are now assumed to share its birth year rather than the younger estimate used before. That correction matters beyond bookkeeping: it means Groningen's civic parks are not simply Victorian additions to a medieval city, they carry at least one working generation of trees from the mid-18th century, quietly older than the park built to showcase them. Storm Henk's felled oak is gone. Its neighbours, grown from the same original planting, are not, and nobody had properly counted their age until one of them fell.

trees.name: The Winter Oak of Zuiderplantsoen
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk or short bus ride from Groningen Centraal station
trees.story: In the summer of 2025, a paving contractor's permit nearly ended this tree's life over a wheelchair-accessible path. The winter oak growing beside a footpath in Groningen's Zuiderplantsoen, part of the old Sterrebos, is a genuine rarity: over 95 percent of the Netherlands' native oaks are summer oaks, and this is one of the remaining few sessile, or winter, oaks, distinguishable by its straighter trunk and stalkless acorns. When the municipality applied to fell eight trees to widen accessibility through the reopened park, the campaign group Bomenridders objected specifically to this one, arguing a narrower path could save it. Seven of the eight felling permits were refused outright; the eighth, for this oak, went unused after the breeding season closed the window, and the alderman announced in June 2025 that accessibility around it was good enough without cutting it down. The story has not stayed tidy since. By April 2026, residents were counting roughly nine dead branches on the tree, still bare while everything around it leafed out, and blaming the thick paving laid close to its trunk for choking its roots and shedding rainwater away instead of into the soil. The tree survived the saw. Whether it survives the path built to spare it is still being decided, one growing season at a time.

trees.name: The Duck's Foot Tree of Noorderplantsoen
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station, in the city centre

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold and drop almost overnight

trees.story: The oldest tree in Noorderplantsoen is not a native Dutch species at all. Somewhere along the park's paths grows a ginkgo more than 140 years old, planted not long after the park itself was laid out over Groningen's demolished 17th-century fortifications, following an 1874 law that finally let the city expand past its old walls. Locals call it the eendenpootboom, the duck's foot tree, for the shape of its fan-like leaves, and the nickname is more accurate botany than most: ginkgo is the last surviving member of an entire plant family that predates most of the trees around it by tens of millions of years, a genuine living fossil rather than a figure of speech. In several Asian countries the species carries religious weight, planted at temples and eaten for its seeds, though the seeds are mildly toxic and best left alone here. Noorderplantsoen itself holds more than fifty labelled tree species along a marked route, the kind of park where a stroller with fifteen minutes to spare can read the name of nearly everything overhead, and this ginkgo is the one specimen old enough to have watched the entire park grow up around it, fortress moat turned ornamental pond and all.

trees.name: The Groenestein Plane
trees.access: Free, open park at any time; the villa itself remains a private residence
trees.transport: 15-20 minute walk or short bike ride from Groningen city centre, in Helpman
trees.story: South of a 19th-century country villa in Groningen's smallest urban forest grows the tree that gives Park Groenestein its scale: a plane tree large enough to anchor an entire estate's landscaping around it. The villa itself, called Groenestein, was rebuilt in 1871 over the footprint of a 1685 house, in the sober, understated style favoured by the Groningen merchant families who commissioned these southern estates, and the park around it took its current form in the same period. No source records exactly when this particular plane was planted, only that its size points toward the same 19th-century landscaping campaign that shaped the rest of the grounds, putting it somewhere around a century and a half old rather than a documented number. The municipality's own 2018 tree inventory lists it among the city's monumental specimens on that basis, size and context standing in for a missing planting record. Groenestein, known locally as the owl wood for its resident owls alongside bats, hedgehogs and squirrels, has been a national monument since 1971, but unlike several of Groningen's other historic estates its grounds stay open to anyone who wants to walk them, no appointment and no entry fee, just a short walk along the Helperzoom to a garden that has quietly outgrown the house it was built to flatter.

trees.name: The Siberian Balsam Poplar of Engelenpoortje
trees.access: Free, public alley, open at any time
trees.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
trees.story:
This poplar is not a species anyone would find growing wild anywhere. Populus x berolinensis was bred in 1865 in Berlin's botanical garden, a deliberate cross between a Siberian laurel-leaf poplar and the tall, narrow Lombardy poplar, made for exactly the trait it shows here, height with a narrow enough crown to survive in a gap between buildings barely wider than the tree itself.

It grows at the Engelenpoortje, a seventeenth-century gated alley named for a long-vanished inn, De Blauwe Engel, that once stood on the corner. The alley has not had a settled recent history: redevelopment around Groningen's Grote Markt closed it to the public in 2012, and it stayed shut for eight years before reopening at the end of 2020. Whether this poplar, which the register dates to the 1930s, stood through that closure without anyone walking past it is not recorded, though a cross this vigorous would have lost little from eight quiet years. It stands today between the shops and houses the alley threads between, free to walk past on the way from Poelestraat to the Nieuwe Markt, exactly as the seventeenth-century gate always intended.

trees.name: The Oak of Martinikerkhof
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
trees.story:
For decades in the twentieth century, Groningen parked cars on top of this oak's roots. Martinikerkhof, one of the city's three great squares, spent the years up to the 1970s as a parking lot before the city cleared the cars and let it become what it is today, a quiet, largely car-free green space in the shadow of the Martini Tower. The oak stood through all of it, in the middle of the square, and the municipality's own 2021 survey rates its condition as moderate to poor, noting plainly that the tree appears to be declining in recent years even though the ground around it is now far better than the parking lot it endured for decades. Whatever damage was done may simply have come too late to reverse.

Planted sometime around 1910 to 1920, the oak is old enough to have watched the square through both its worst years and its recovery, and its trunk base is described as intact even as its crown has thinned. It stands in the open, free, at the centre of Martinikerkhof, a short walk from the tower whose bells have marked Groningen's hours for centuries. If its condition improves or worsens, this page should be updated to match; tell us if you have seen it recently.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Prinsentuin
trees.access: Free, public walled garden, open daily until sunset
trees.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
trees.story:
The Prinsentuin has been walled off from the rest of Groningen since 1626, when it was laid out as a private pleasure garden for the region's stadholders, and the wall is still what makes it feel like a secret in the middle of a busy city centre. Visitors reach it through a gate on the Turfsingel topped with a working sundial from 1731, accurate enough to mark day length and sunrise and sunset as well as the hour, or through a smaller door on Kattenhage. Entry is free and has been for as long as records go back.

This horse chestnut, which the tree register dates to around 1850 to 1860, is not part of the garden's original seventeenth-century planting, arriving roughly two centuries after the walls went up, but it has still had well over 150 years inside them. Horse chestnut is not native to the Netherlands, imported from the Balkans as an ornamental tree from the sixteenth century onward, and this one has grown up sheltered from wind and street salt by walls built for a stadholder's roses rather than for any tree. It stands in the open garden, free, daily until sunset, a short walk from Martinikerkhof.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Akerkhof
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 12 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
trees.story:
When Groningen redeveloped the Akerkhof a few years ago to fix a square that had gone dark, dry and unloved, the plan called for cutting three trees and clearing scrub around the church to let light back in. This horse chestnut was not one of them. The municipality's own account of the project says its monumental chestnut and linden trees deliberately kept their place and gained more room as the work went on, while three new trees were planted along the redesigned Brugstraat to make up for what came down.

Akerkhof was a real cemetery from the twelfth century until burials inside the city walls were banned on hygiene grounds and the ground was cleared in 1828, which is most of why an open square with old trees exists here at all. This chestnut, dated by the register to around 1880 to 1890, is younger than that clearance but has still stood through the square's dark spell and its recent recovery. It grows in the open around the Akerk church, free to walk past any time, on a square the city now treats as worth protecting rather than merely tolerating.

trees.name: The Maple of Guyotplein
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
trees.story:
This sycamore grows on a square named for a man most Dutch schoolchildren have never heard of, Henri Daniel Guyot, a Walloon minister who founded the country's first school for deaf children in Groningen in 1790. The square itself started as the planted west side of the Ossenmarkt, given trees in 1754, and only took Guyot's name in 1890, on the centenary of his institute, by which point this specific tree, dated by the register to around 1890 to 1900, was likely just going into the ground.

A monument to Guyot has stood on the square since 1829, decades before it carried his name, and the deaf institute itself operated here for generations before the building later became Groningen's courthouse. The sycamore has outlasted the institute's departure and watched the square's slow shift from an educational address to a judicial one. Sycamore sheds bark in flaking plates as it ages, closer to a plane tree's trunk than to most other maples, worth a look on this one after more than a century of growth. It stands in the open square, free, a short walk from the city's other historic squares.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Oude Hortus
trees.access: Free, in the publicly accessible Oude Hortus garden (open during garden hours in the Hortusbuurt)
trees.transport: Groningen Centraal station, about 18 minute walk
trees.story:
A glass wall exists in Groningen because of this tree. When the university rebuilt the Muntinggebouw beside the Oude Hortus, the architects set a window into the new facade specifically so this weeping beech would still be visible from Nieuwe Kijk in 't Jatstraat outside, rather than being hidden behind a solid wall the way ordinary landscaping usually loses to construction. The garden's own visitor folder calls it "het pronkjuweel van de Oude Hortus," the showpiece of the Old Hortus, and its cascading, overhanging crown is the reason: Fagus sylvatica "Pendula" grows its branches down and outward rather than up, forming a green curtain rather than a canopy.

The garden's folder dates the planting to 1876; the Dutch national monumental tree register instead gives a broader 1880s band, so treat the age, around a hundred and fifty years, as bracketed between two sources rather than pinned to one. Construction work by the university in 1996 threatened its roots, and the tree was given formal protection at that point, a decision the glass wall later echoed.

The Oude Hortus itself began in 1626 as the university's working botanical garden, moved its living collection to Hortus Haren in 1967, and stayed open afterward as public parkland. Free, roughly twenty minutes from Centraal by foot.

trees.name: The London Plane of the Oude Hortus
trees.access: Free, in the publicly accessible Oude Hortus garden (open during garden hours in the Hortusbuurt)
trees.transport: Groningen Centraal station, about 18 minute walk
trees.story:
This plane and the weeping beech nearby went into the ground the same year, 1876, on the same patch of former university botanical garden, and one of them has grown into one of the tallest trees in the Oude Hortus. The Dutch national monumental tree register measures it at 29 metres with a trunk just over four metres round, in good health on what the register calls a favourable site, a corner plot beside the garden's newer university building.

London plane is the hybrid workhorse of European city planting, bred from American sycamore and Oriental plane and prized for tolerating compacted soil and polluted air better than almost anything else that grows this large, which is most of why it lines so many European streets and squares. This one, though, grows in a garden rather than along a road, part of a collection that began as a teaching ground for medicinal and useful plants in 1626 under the apothecary Henricus Munting.

The Oude Hortus kept its historic site as public parkland after the university moved its living plant collection to Hortus Haren in 1967, so the garden today is walkable rather than a research facility. Free entry, about twenty minutes on foot from Groningen Centraal.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Oude Hortus
trees.access: Free, in the publicly accessible Oude Hortus garden (open during garden hours in the Hortusbuurt)
trees.transport: Groningen Centraal station, about 18 minute walk
trees.story:
Woodpeckers have worked this ginkgo's upper crown for years, and the Dutch national monumental tree register still calls its trunk sound underneath the damage: a three-stemmed specimen planted in 1896 close to the facade of what was then the university's Botanical Laboratory, since replaced by a newer building. The register rates it the thickest ginkgo growing anywhere in the city of Groningen.

Ginkgo biloba is a living fossil in the least metaphorical sense available, the last surviving species of a plant family that predates most of the trees around it by tens of millions of years, easy to spot by fan-shaped leaves unlike any other tree's. This one stands roughly a hundred and thirty years old, planted twenty years after the plane and the weeping beech elsewhere in the same garden, during the Oude Hortus's working life as the university's botanical teaching collection.

The garden itself dates to 1626, founded by the apothecary Henricus Munting, and kept functioning as a research and teaching ground until 1967, when the university's living plant collection moved out to Hortus Haren and left this walled plot as the public garden it remains today. Free, roughly twenty minutes on foot from Centraal station.

trees.name: The Green Beeches of the Nieuwe Kerkhof
trees.access: Free, on the open public square (Nieuwe Kerkhof) beside the Nieuwe Kerk
trees.transport: Groningen Centraal station, about 18 minute walk
trees.story:
A parked lawn beside a seventeenth century church holds one of Groningen's largest stands of old beeches, roughly thirty of them by some counts, and the Dutch national monumental tree register singles out two as genuinely exceptional: one standing in front of the Nieuwe Kerk with a long-healed wound in its trunk, the other beside the church carrying an old broken-limb scar that woodpeckers have since hollowed out and that a self-seeded oak has taken root beside.

The Nieuwe Kerk itself, a protected national monument, was completed in 1660, and the register dates these beeches to the 1860s, roughly two centuries younger than the building they stand beside but old enough to have shaded the square through most of its life as a public space. European beech left unclipped and given room, as these two were, grows a dense, smooth-barked canopy that can live for centuries longer still.

Because the register records this pair as one entry rather than two separately pinned trunks, the coordinates here mark the general spot on the church lawn rather than one exact tree; both stand within easy sight of each other. Free, open square, a short walk from the city centre.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of Noorderplantsoen
trees.access: Free, in the public Noorderplantsoen park
trees.transport: Groningen Centraal station, about 15 minute walk
trees.story:
Noorderplantsoen used to be a fortress moat. The park was laid out in 1880 over Groningen's demolished seventeenth century city walls, in the informal English landscape style cities across the Netherlands favoured once their old defences stopped being useful, and it has carried national monument protection since 1971. Along its paths grow more than fifty labelled tree species, among them this pair of London planes, planted close to the park's own opening date and now well past a century old.

The Dutch national monumental tree register records the pair without individual measurements, situating them near Werfstraat on the park's western side. London plane, a hybrid bred in seventeenth century Europe from American sycamore and Oriental plane, tolerates compacted city soil and hard pruning better than almost any other large tree, which is why it anchors so much of Europe's oldest parkland alongside species chosen purely for looks.

Because the register treats this as one paired entry rather than two individually pinned trunks, the coordinates mark the general spot rather than one exact tree; the pair stands close enough together to find both without wandering. Free, public parkland, about a fifteen minute walk from Centraal station.

trees.name: The Mespilifolia Oak of Noorderplantsoen
trees.access: Free, in the public Noorderplantsoen park
trees.transport: Groningen Centraal station, about 16 minute walk
trees.story:
Most oaks in Noorderplantsoen are the ordinary native kind, but this one carries a cultivar name, Mespilifolia, medlar-leaved, for foliage that reads narrower and more textured than a typical sessile oak's. It grows on the park's eastern edge, clearly visible from the residential street the park backs onto, which is exactly why the Dutch national monumental tree register singles it out from the small group it was registered alongside as the specimen worth calling monumental.

Quercus petraea "Mespilifolia" grows a broad, loose crown with branches that droop slightly at the tips, and old specimens like this one develop a shallow-grooved bark distinct from the deeper furrows of a standard sessile oak. The register dates the planting to the 1880s, putting it close in age to the park's own founding in 1880, when the city converted its demolished city-wall moat into the landscaped park that still carries national monument protection today.

One of more than fifty tree species planted along Noorderplantsoen's paths, this oak is the kind of tree a visitor might walk past without a second look from the street side and stop for once they know the cultivar name to look for. Free, public parkland, roughly a fifteen minute walk from Centraal station.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Poortershoes
trees.access: Free, stands along the public Oosterweg street in front of the Poortershoes, now a busy neighbourhood community centre; open at any time
trees.transport: About a 20-25 minute walk or short bus ride from Groningen Centraal station, in the Oosterpoort neighbourhood
trees.story:
This plane is older than the building it fronts. The Poortershoes at Oosterweg 13 went up in 1881 as a school for the children of Groningen's bargemen, but the city's own archive dates the tree in front of it to 1846, thirty five years earlier, which makes it a monument in its own right rather than a landscaping choice that came with the building.

It has had the last laugh since. The school closed long ago and the building is now a neighbourhood community centre for Oosterpoort, while the plane keeps growing against it: the register notes the tree leans slightly from competing with the facade for light, and its roots have started pushing against the wall hard enough to crack the masonry. Nobody has cut it back for that.

At roughly 180 years old it is healthy and in good structure by the city's own assessment, standing right on the public street rather than behind any gate, in front of a building that has already outlived one purpose and is well into its second.

trees.name: The ANWB Linden of Wilhelminakade
trees.access: Free, public street corner, open at any time
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station, west of Noorderplantsoen
trees.story:
The organisation this tree was planted for was not yet fifty years old when it got its own tree, whatever the sign says. Groningen planted a line of lindens along the Wilhelminakade in 1928 to honour the ANWB, then still a cyclists' union rather than the roadside-assistance name it later became, and the register calls it the union's fiftieth anniversary. The ANWB itself dates its founding to 1883, which makes 1928 the forty fifth year, not the fiftieth. Nobody has explained the gap, and this page will not invent one.

The tree itself is plainer than its arithmetic problem. It is a common lime on a street corner, healthy apart from one dead branch, its base ringed with dozens of small knobbly regrowth points where the city has repeatedly cut back suckering growth over the better part of a century. That kind of pollarding scar is usually the surest sign of a genuinely old street tree: a young one has not been cut back often enough to show it.

Free to see, on the public corner of Wilhelminakade and Oranjesingel, no gate involved.

trees.name: The Wedding Lime of Herewegbuurt
trees.species: Lime (Tilia sp., recorded by the register as "zwarte linde"/black lime)
trees.access: Free, small public park/playground on a street corner, open at any time
trees.transport: About a 20 minute walk or short bus ride from Groningen Centraal station, in the Herewegbuurt south of the centre
trees.story:
This lime was planted for a wedding that took place five hundred kilometres away. On 7 January 1937 Princess Juliana married Prince Bernhard in The Hague, and Dutch municipalities across the country marked the occasion the way they had for royal weddings for a century before smartphones existed: by planting a tree. Groningen put this one on a small playground at the corner of three streets in Herewegbuurt, one black lime among what Wikipedia's own record of the tradition shows were dozens planted the same year in towns from Beekbergen to Bodegraven.

Ninety years on, the city rates its condition as reasonable rather than excellent, and its trunk has thickened by about fifty centimetres of girth over the last twenty years of measurement alone. A bench now circles the base, which is either a sign of respect or the easiest way to stop anyone parking a bike against the trunk.

Free, public and unfenced, sharing a corner with a children's playground. Nobody has pinned down the tree's exact cultivar, so if you know limes, the page could use your eye.

trees.name: The Schlossberg Field Maple
trees.access: Free, in the public Schlossberg hill park, open at all times
trees.transport: Tram 3 or 5 to the Schlossbergbahn stop, then a short walk up the hill (a paid funicular also runs)
trees.story: Graz keeps a live public register of its protected trees, and this field maple has held a place on it since the year 2000, growing on the wooded hill above the old town where a fortress once stood and a bell tower still does. Field maples rarely get singled out anywhere: they are the hedgerow tree, the one that fills gaps between grander species rather than anchoring a park on its own. This one earned protection anyway, on a hill whose beech, hornbeam and ash have been managed as a landscape park for centuries around the ruins at its summit. Austria's official record and Graz's own city register agree on the exact spot to within three metres, though neither has ever measured its girth or put a number on its age, an honest gap on an otherwise well documented tree. The Schlossberg itself needs no introduction to anyone who has visited Graz, its clock tower visible across the whole city, and the climb up past this maple is free at any hour, on foot or by the paid funicular that saves the legs.

trees.name: The Volksgarten Oak
trees.access: Free, public park (4.6 ha), open on all sides, no entry fee
trees.transport: Short walk from Graz Hauptbahnhof (about 1km)

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Three of Graz's officially protected trees stand inside one small park, and this oak is the first of them, rooted near the Muhlgasse side of the Volksgarten. The park's own history records a planted row of oaks running roughly north to south through its centre, seventy to a hundred years old, but no source confirms this particular designated tree is part of that row rather than a separate planting nearby, so the two facts stay separate here rather than joined into a tidier story that nobody actually stated. What both the city's live tree register and Wikipedia's independent list agree on is the spot itself, within two metres of each other, and the protection: this pedunculate oak has held Naturdenkmal status since May 2000. The Volksgarten covers four and a half hectares open on every side, no gate and no fee, a five minute walk from Graz's main station. Two more protected planes grow within a hundred and seventy metres of this oak, making the park itself worth the whole visit rather than a single stop.

trees.name: The Volksgarten Plane of Muhlgasse
trees.access: Free, public park, open on all sides
trees.transport: Short walk from Graz Hauptbahnhof (about 1km)
trees.story: A dated photograph on Wikimedia Commons, filed under this exact tree's own protection number, shows this plane still standing in the Volksgarten years after its formal designation, one of the small proofs this project prefers over a bare database record. It is a London Plane, the hybrid city planners across Europe reach for when they want a tree that shrugs off pollution and poor soil, and this one has done the job here since the year 2000. It grows a few paces from a protected oak and a second protected plane, the three of them forming Graz's tightest cluster of designated trees, all reachable inside one small public park. Neither source gives an age or a trunk measurement, an honest gap on a tree old enough to have earned legal protection on its own merits. The Volksgarten opens on every side with no fee and no closing time, a five minute walk from Graz's main railway station.

trees.name: The Volksgarten Plane of Volksgartenstrasse
trees.access: Free, public park, open on all sides
trees.transport: Short walk from Graz Hauptbahnhof (about 1km), enter via the Volksgartenstrasse side
trees.story: Registers occasionally list the same tree twice under two addresses, a real problem elsewhere on this site, and this plane is a genuine check against exactly that mistake: it stands on a separate legal plot from the park's other two designated trees, a hundred and seventy metres away, protected four months later in a separate 2000 decision. Not a duplicate, a third tree completing the Volksgarten's own small collection of protected specimens. It grows near the Volksgartenstrasse entrance rather than the Muhlgasse side where its two neighbours stand, which means a visitor can enter the park from either street and find a protected tree within a few steps. Graz's city register and Wikipedia's independent list place it within three metres of each other. As with its neighbours, nobody has published an age or a trunk measurement, which any reader with a tape measure could fix in the time it takes to walk the park end to end.

trees.name: The Augarten Field Maple
trees.neighbourhood: Jakomini, at the eastern edge of the Augarten park
trees.access: Free to view; stands at the edge of the public Augarten park beside a heritage building (Museum der Wahrnehmung). Not confirmed on the ground whether the tree itself sits on the museum's footprint or the adjoining park land.
trees.transport: Walkable from Graz Hauptbahnhof or the city centre; tram/bus toward Elisabethstrasse/Jakominiplatz, then a short walk to the Augarten
trees.story: This field maple carries an unusually solid floor under its age. Its formal Naturdenkmal designation dates to 1979, but Wikipedia's own record cites an earlier source, a 1956 survey of Graz's planted broadleaf trees by F. Hanselmayer, which already listed this exact maple as a tree worth protecting, decades before the legal designation caught up. That gives a hard floor of at least seventy years old as of today, derived from a dated citation rather than a guess, with no upper bound stated because nothing sources one. It grows at the eastern edge of the Augarten, a public park in Jakomini, beside a heritage bathhouse building that now houses the Museum der Wahrnehmung. Whether the tree's exact footing sits on the museum's own grounds or on the adjoining public park land was not confirmed by any source read this pass, which is why this entry is flagged rather than stated with full confidence, an honest narrow gap on an otherwise well anchored tree.

trees.name: The Schillerplatz Plane
trees.access: Free, on Schillerplatz, a public city square, open at all times
trees.transport: Tram or bus to the Schillerplatz stop, directly on the square
trees.story: A photograph taken on the second of May, 2014, and filed on Wikimedia Commons under this tree's own protection number, is the kind of small dated proof this project values: it shows the tree alive and identifiable twelve years ago, a data point independent of both the city's live register and Wikipedia's own list, which agree with each other on the exact spot to within two metres. The plane has held its Naturdenkmal status since September 1990, growing on Schillerplatz, an ordinary public square in the St. Leonhard district rather than a landscaped park, the kind of protected tree that people cross without a second glance because nothing marks it out from the street furniture around it. No age or trunk measurement has ever been published for it, which is true of most of Graz's protected trees and no reason to hold this one back: it stands on open public ground, reachable by tram or bus directly to the square, free at any hour.

trees.name: The Panoramagasse Oak (No. 54)
trees.access: Free, on public ground opposite the house number given
trees.transport: Bus toward Ruckerlberggurtel/Geidorf, then a walk up Panoramagasse

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Two pedunculate oaks stand forty metres apart on the same hillside street, protected on the exact same day in July 1979, and this is the smaller of the pair: a trunk measured at 2.80 metres round in a 2015 field survey, against 4.90 metres for its neighbour up the road. No published growth-rate figure for this species was found and verified this pass, so that girth is not converted into an age here rather than turned into a guess dressed up as a calculation. The register lists the tree opposite house number 54 on Panoramagasse, a steep street on the Ruckerlberg hillside in Geidorf that earns its name honestly, climbing above the city with views back over the rooftops. 'Gegenuber', opposite, is the register's own word for the tree's position: on the public verge across from the house, not inside anyone's private garden. Reachable by bus toward Ruckerlberggurtel and a walk up the hill, with its larger neighbour barely a minute further on.

trees.name: The Panoramagasse Oak (No. 56)
trees.access: Free, on public ground opposite the house number given
trees.transport: Bus toward Ruckerlberggurtel/Geidorf, then a walk up Panoramagasse; about a minute from the Panoramagasse Oak (No. 54).

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This oak and its neighbour forty metres down the hill were protected on the same day in July 1979, near-identical paperwork for two trees that turned out nothing alike: a 2015 field survey measured this one at 4.90 metres round, nearly double its neighbour's 2.80 metres, despite an address and a protection date that otherwise read like a matched pair. Nothing in either source explains the gap, whether one was planted decades before the other or simply grew faster on better ground, so this page states the measurement rather than guessing at a reason. It stands opposite house number 56 on Panoramagasse, a hillside street in Geidorf on the Ruckerlberg slope, on the public verge rather than inside any private plot, per the register's own wording. No published age exists for it and none is invented here; a girth this size on an oak usually means real age, but converting one into the other needs a cited growth-rate figure this pass did not have in hand, so the number stays a girth rather than becoming a guess.

trees.name: The Eggenberg Weymouth Pine
trees.neighbourhood: Eggenberg (Schlosspark Eggenberg, within the palace grounds)
trees.access: Paid entry: stands inside Schlosspark Eggenberg, the grounds of Schloss Eggenberg (UNESCO World Heritage palace), run by Universalmuseum Joanneum. Check the museum's current prices page for the park-only ticket.
trees.transport: Graz public transport toward the Eggenberg district; Eggenberger Allee 90 is the palace's signposted main entrance
trees.story: A field measurement from October 2016, cited by Wikipedia's own list of Graz's protected trees, gives this Eastern White Pine a trunk 3.70 metres round and a height of about 27 metres, figures the city's live register independently confirms exist at the same spot within three metres. It is one of ten designated trees planted together at the entrance to Schlosspark Eggenberg, five plane trees and four more Weymouth pines among them, but this is the only one with its own measurement on record, which is why it stands here alone rather than as part of a group entry: the rest read as one avenue rather than nine separate things worth stopping at individually. Pinus strobus is native to eastern North America, and this specimen has grown large enough on Austrian soil to earn legal protection in its own right, cited in 1979. Schloss Eggenberg is a UNESCO World Heritage palace on the western edge of the city, its park entered on a paid ticket rather than freely, the one exception on this page to Graz's otherwise open-access trees. A copper beech, also protected, grows fifty seven metres away in the same park, making the walk from the gate worth two trees rather than one.

trees.name: The Eggenberg Copper Beech
trees.neighbourhood: Eggenberg (Schlosspark Eggenberg, within the palace grounds)
trees.access: Paid entry: stands inside Schlosspark Eggenberg, the grounds of Schloss Eggenberg (UNESCO World Heritage palace), about 57 metres from the Eggenberg Weymouth Pine.
trees.transport: Graz public transport toward the Eggenberg district; Eggenberger Allee 90 is the palace's signposted main entrance
trees.story: Wikipedia's list places this copper beech at Eggenberger Allee 90 with a set of coordinates that match, to six decimal places, the GPS tag on a photograph taken here in June 2014 and filed on Wikimedia Commons under the tree's own protection number. Two facts agreeing that precisely is about as solid as a location gets on this page, even though the tree carries a smaller shadow of documentation than most of its neighbours: it sits in Austria's national monument register rather than the City of Graz's own separately maintained list, which does not carry it at all, and nobody has photographed or measured it since that one 2014 image. Fagus sylvatica 'Purpurea' is a cultivar bred for its dark red foliage rather than a wild variant, planted widely across European parks precisely for that colour, and this one earned formal protection in 1979 regardless of the missing girth and age figures. It grows inside Schlosspark Eggenberg, the grounds of a UNESCO World Heritage palace on the city's western edge, fifty seven metres from a protected Weymouth pine that shares its address and its 1979 designation date, reachable on the same paid ticket into the park.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of the Paco dos Duques
trees.access: Free, exterior lawn below the palace walls, outside the paid museum entrance
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot
trees.story: Most of what you see is younger than what grows beneath it. Building work on the Paco dos Duques began in 1420 for Afonso, illegitimate son of King Joao I and soon to be the first Duke of Braganza, and it was never finished. The palace slid into ruin after 1616, when Guimaraes itself was handed to a Spanish nobleman, and by the nineteenth century what was left housed an infantry barracks. The building tourists photograph today, with its steep slate roofs and half-timbered galleries, is largely a 1937 to 1959 reconstruction: the regime of the Estado Novo added two full floors to the front wing and a third to the sides, remaking a shell into the national monument it wanted Guimaraes, self-styled cradle of Portugal, to have. These two plane trees on the grassy slope below the walls predate that rebuild by decades. Measured at 150 years in 2011, they were already thick-trunked when the scaffolding went up. The larger, four and a half metres round, rises twenty-nine metres; its partner a few strides away is a size smaller, twenty-two metres tall. Stand between them and look up at the palace: the trees are the only part of the view that nobody had to reconstruct.

trees.name: The Olive Tree of Nossa Senhora da Oliveira
trees.age: unknown, the register recorded no figure at its 2021 measurement
trees.access: Paid, 1 euro cloister add-on to the Museu de Alberto Sampaio ticket, Tuesday to Sunday 10:00-18:00
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: This tree gave the city its second name. According to the legend still told here, a merchant named Pero Esteves brought a crucifix back from Normandy in 1342 and set it beside an olive tree that stood dead in the square, its trunk long dried out. Three days later, so the story goes, the olive turned green again. Guimaraes called the miracle Our Lady's, and the collegiate church behind the square has been Nossa Senhora da Oliveira, Our Lady of the Olive Tree, ever since, with an olive branch worked into the city's own coat of arms. An older layer of the same legend pushes the planting back further still, to the Visigothic king Wamba and a cutting supposedly carried from the Garden of Olives in Jerusalem. What can be said honestly is narrower: the tree growing today in the church's Romanesque cloister, two metres ninety around the trunk, is not documented as that specific plant, and Portugal's tree register, which measured it last in 2021, recorded no age at all. Whatever its years, it stands exactly where the story says it should, in the cloister that once belonged to a monastery founded by Countess Mumadona Dias in 949, on the square that gave the church, and so this whole quarter of the city, its name.

trees.name: The Camellias of Palacio Vila Flor
trees.access: Free, public garden, Monday to Saturday 09:00-13:00 and 14:30-20:00, Sunday 10:00-13:00 and 15:00-19:00
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from the historic centre, on Av. D. Afonso Henriques

best_time.label: January to March, when the camellias flower and little else in the garden does

trees.story: Eighteen camellias planted across two garden terraces here have outlived the building's most fashionable era by more than a century. The register puts them at around 195 years, planted in the 1830s, decades before the palace itself was extended into the grand house whose halls now show contemporary art. Camellia japonica arrived in Europe from East Asia in the eighteenth century as a hothouse curiosity for the wealthy; by the time these were planted it had become the flower a family used to say a garden mattered. Guimaraes and the wider Minho region took to it harder than most of Portugal, which is why the area still markets itself, without much exaggeration, along a Camellia Route. The eighteen trees here split into two groups on the lower and upper parterres of a three-terrace baroque garden, laid out with box hedges, stone fountains and a view back over the city; the garden won a national landscape architecture award in 2006. Camellias flower through the coldest months, January into March, when almost nothing else in a Portuguese garden is doing anything at all, which is presumably part of why a family planted eighteen of them and not one.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedars of Atouguia Cemetery
trees.age: about 115 years (one of the three dated; see notes)
trees.access: Free, public municipal cemetery, open during daytime visiting hours
trees.transport: About 20-25 min walk from the historic centre, or a short bus ride
trees.story: Three Himalayan cedars stand at the gates of Guimaraes' municipal cemetery, tall enough that they read as a landmark from the road below rather than as cemetery planting. Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through to Nepal, where it can live past a thousand years and grow to twice the height these have reached; introduced to European parks in the nineteenth century, it became one of the standard conifers for an avenue meant to impress. One of the three, in the cemetery car park, was measured at 100 years old in 2011 and classified that June, with a trunk four metres seventeen around. Its two companions at the main entrance, girths of 4.10 and 4.47 metres, were added to the classification later and were never separately dated, though their size suggests the same generation rather than a younger planting. A cedar planted at a cemetery gate a century ago was a statement about permanence, evergreen and famously long-lived, standing over a place built for the opposite. It has mostly kept the promise: all three are alive and, unlike the graves around them, still growing.

trees.name: The Oak of Santa Marinha da Costa
trees.access: Free. The gardens belong to the Pousada Mosteiro de Guimaraes, the hotel inside the former monastery, and the pousada describes its park as open to guests and visitors. No opening hours are published, so expect to walk in past a working hotel.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km east of the historic centre and uphill on the Costa slope, roughly 25 minutes on foot, or a short taxi ride

best_time.label: August to September: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Nobody has put a number on this oak, and the official one is no help. Portugal's register classified the trees of Santa Marinha da Costa as a single group in 1940 and gives that group 290 years as measured in 2006, but the group is six species and one of them is a eucalyptus, a tree that did not reach Portugal until the nineteenth century. The figure describes a collection, not this trunk. The pousada's own botanical guide says only that the oak is several centuries old. That is as far as anyone has gone, so it is as far as this page goes. If you know better, tell us.

What it stands over is easier to state. A circular granite tank of the baroque period, ringed with stone seating and fed by a small watercourse, sits in the walled enclosure of a monastery that Augustinian canons held for some three hundred and fifty years before the Hieronymites took it in 1528 and ran a college there; by 1541 its degrees counted equal to Coimbra's. A fire in 1951 took the tiled panels along the friars' cells and the stone stair to the chapter room. The state bought the ruin in 1972, and Fernando Tavora spent the following decade turning it into a hotel, work that won Portugal's National Architecture Prize in 1987.

The oak is older than the hotel and older than the fire, and it puts the whole tank in shade. Beyond that, nobody has said.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Silvares
trees.access: Free, on a public roundabout, open at all hours
trees.transport: About 4.5 km west of the historic centre; Guimaraes city bus line 082, the Silvares to Pevidem circular, serves the village
trees.story:
This pine is as wide as it is tall and it stands in the middle of a roundabout. Portugal's register measures it at 26 metres high with a crown 26.4 metres across, on a trunk 3.8 metres round, held over a road junction on the old ER 206 in Silvares. It was 100 years old when the register measured it in 2011, which makes it about 115 now, and it was classified of public interest in June that year. Guimaraes municipality has exactly three stone pines with that status and this was the first.

Pinus pinea is the umbrella pine, the silhouette on every postcard of the Portuguese coast, and the shape is not decoration. It sheds its lower branches as it goes up and pushes everything sideways into a flat parasol on a bare column, a design for catching light above competitors rather than beside them. In a plantation it does this modestly. With light on every side, as here, it does it to the limit, which is how a tree ends up with a crown wider than it is tall.

It also drops pinhoes, the pine nuts that go into Portuguese Christmas cooking. The cones take three years on the branch before they open, which is a long wait for one afternoon of gathering.

There is no gate and no ticket here. There is a roundabout, and a hundred-year-old parasol standing in the middle of it.

trees.name: The Lodewijk Napoleon Beech
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 15-20 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station, or tram/bus

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.story: A lonely, exiled king passed the time by carving his own royal monogram into a beech tree, and two centuries later almost nothing is left to see of it. Lodewijk Napoleon, installed by his brother as the first King of Holland in 1806, spent time at the government estate now known as Paviljoen Welgelegen, a short walk from this stretch of the Haarlemmerhout, and sometime between 1808 and 1810 carved a crowned letter R into the beech's bark, R for Roi, the French word for king. He was not a popular monarch by Dutch standards, remembered mostly for resisting his brother's harsher demands on the Dutch economy before Napoleon deposed him outright in 1810 and annexed the kingdom directly into France. The carving outlasted the reign by two centuries, slowly closing over as the tree's bark grew and healed around the old wound, the way any scar eventually fades on a tree that keeps living. By 2025, arborists inspecting it reported there was virtually nothing left to make out, the crown and the letter both swallowed by growth. The beech stands in the Haarlemmerhout, the oldest public park in the Netherlands, itself burned to nothing during the 1572-73 Spanish siege of Haarlem and replanted from 1584, meaning this specific tree is a second or third generation of forest on ground that has been fought over more than once.

trees.name: The Provinciehuis Plane
trees.access: Free, open garden at any time; the Provinciehuis building itself only opens for exhibitions, public sessions, or Open Monumentendag
trees.transport: 15-20 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station, or tram/bus
trees.story: Haarlem's thickest tree grows in the garden of the province's own seat of government, a plane tree with a trunk six metres around, measured at chest height, which takes several adults linking hands to properly encircle. It stands in the grounds of Paviljoen Welgelegen, a country house built for a wealthy Haarlem merchant in the 1780s that later became the government building of the province of Noord-Holland, its garden known as the Griffietuin. No source pins down exactly when the tree was planted, though a plane tree reaching this girth in the Dutch climate typically implies a century and a half or more of steady growth, placing its likely origin somewhere in the 19th century, around the same era the estate itself changed from private pleasure garden to civic seat. Renovation work on the Griffietuin in recent years has deliberately reconnected it with the neighbouring Frederikspark, restoring a stretch of green that visitors can walk through freely even when the government building itself is closed to the public. The building only opens fully for exhibitions, public council sessions, or the national Open Monumentendag, but the garden and its giant plane require no appointment at all, a rare case of the tree being easier to visit than the institution that happens to house it.

trees.name: The Kleverlaan Yew
trees.age: not documented, described as genuinely old
trees.access: Free, open cemetery during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kleverpark, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Haarlem

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Haarlem's oldest general cemetery is also one of the best places in the city to see what a 19th-century idea of a peaceful afterlife looked like in tree form. Zocher, the same landscape architecture family responsible for much of Haarlem's parkland, laid out Begraafplaats Kleverlaan in 1828 on the site of a former farm, choosing the English landscape style over the rigid formal rows more typical of cemetery design at the time: winding paths, ponds, gentle slopes, and specimen trees planted for their individual character rather than uniform rows of identical species. An old yew stands among the results, a species chosen deliberately and repeatedly across European cemeteries for centuries because of its association with mourning and, less morbidly, because yews simply live longer than almost anything else planted beside them, capable in the right conditions of outlasting the cemetery itself. Alongside it grow water and swamp cypresses, an Atlas cedar and a ginkgo, part of the same original planting scheme, though no source gives the yew's precise age beyond describing it as genuinely old rather than merely mature. The cemetery remains open to visitors during normal hours, free of charge, a working burial ground that also functions, almost incidentally, as one of Haarlem's better tree collections.

trees.name: The Kenaupark Red Beech
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story: This copper beech stands in front of a 19th-century villa with the kind of theatrical, deep purple-red canopy that looks almost too deliberately composed to be real, the sort of tree that would not look out of place backing a formal portrait, if the painters of Haarlem's Golden Age had lived to see Kenaupark built. The park itself dates from 1865, designed by the father-and-son landscape architects Zocher, the same family behind Haarlemmerhout's redesign a century earlier and the Kleverlaan cemetery, laid out on the site of the old city fortifications after Haarlem's walls came down and the ground beneath them needed a new purpose. Kenaupark takes its name from Kenau Simonsdochter Hasselaer, a Haarlem woman celebrated, with some historical exaggeration, for helping defend the city during the 1572-73 Spanish siege, one of the few Dutch women from that era whose name survived into a public square's naming. The beech itself has no precise recorded planting date, though its size and the park's own founding year point toward roughly a century and a half of growth. It shares the park with monumental planes, a cypress grove, oaks, a walnut and a stand of chestnuts, all part of the same original planting a Haarlem council chose to make graceful rather than merely functional out of a demolished fortress line.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Prinsenhof
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
Prinsenhof has been a garden for longer than Haarlem has had a monarchy to name a park after: a monastery garden from before 1477, when the monastery's own graveyard took over the ground, then in 1721 the city's official herb garden, the stadskruidentuin, moved in and stayed. What visitors walk through today is a municipal plantsoen that still keeps a working herb collection alongside a monumental weeping beech planted in the early twentieth century, threading a line from convent medicine to civic parkland that most Dutch cities cannot draw so cleanly on one plot.

Weeping beech is not a wild form but a cultivated one, Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula', its branches trained downward rather than reaching for light, giving it the look of a tree perpetually caught mid-collapse even in full health. The garden sits within a few dozen metres of a chestnut and, a short walk further, an oak in the neighbouring Wijngaardtuin, both from the same run of Haarlem gardens built on old monastic ground. It stands in the open, free, on land that has been under cultivation of one kind or another for well over five centuries even if this particular tree has only seen a small fraction of that.

trees.name: The Oak of Wijngaardtuin
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
The Wijngaardtuin, the vineyard garden, takes its name from a monastery vineyard planted here in the sixteenth century, land that stayed under religious cultivation for generations before the city took it over as public parkland. At the end of the nineteenth century the garden was redesigned, probably by L.P. Zocher, of the same landscape architecture dynasty that reshaped Haarlemmerhout and laid out Kenaupark within a few decades of the same commission. This pedunculate oak dates from that redesign, planted somewhere around 1870 to 1880.

It stands near a statue called Ontmoeting, Meeting, one of the more recent additions to a garden whose actual history runs back roughly five centuries to vines rather than oaks. A short walk away, in the neighbouring Prinsenhof, a weeping beech from the same general period grows on ground with an even older monastic pedigree; together the two gardens form a small, walkable stretch of what used to be entirely religious land, given over to public use only after the buildings that once justified the walls came down. The oak grows in the open, free to walk up to at any time, no different from any other city park tree except for what the ground beneath it used to grow instead.

trees.name: The Bald Cypresses of Kenaupark
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 5 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn rust orange before dropping

trees.story:
Six bald cypresses grow together on the lowest, wettest ground in Kenaupark, and that placement is not an accident. Taxodium distichum is one of the few conifers that tolerates standing water, native to swamps across the southeastern United States, and whoever planted this group at the end of the nineteenth century clearly knew the species well enough to put it exactly where an ordinary tree would struggle. Grouping conifers this way was a habit of the Zocher family, the father-and-son landscape architects who designed Kenaupark in 1865 on the site of Haarlem's demolished fortifications, with the villas around the park going up in the years immediately after.

The register lists the six as a single monumental entry rather than six separate trees, treating the grove as the thing worth protecting rather than any one trunk within it, the same logic behind the Kenaupark plane group and copper beech nearby. Bald cypress sheds its needles every autumn despite being a conifer, one of the few in temperate gardens that does, so the low ground it occupies goes from green to rust orange for a few weeks before going bare. It stands in the open park, free, a few steps from the existing Kenaupark copper beech and its neighbouring plane grove.

trees.name: The Planes of Kenaupark
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 5 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
Three London planes stand together near the start of Kenaupark, planted in the opening years after the Zocher family laid the park out in 1865 over the demolished line of Haarlem's old city fortifications. The villas that now ring the park went up in the years right after, so these planes are older than almost every building that faces them, among the first plantings to go into ground that had been earthworks and moat a few years before.

London plane is itself a hybrid, a cross between the American sycamore and the Oriental plane first bred in seventeenth-century Europe, prized for tolerating exactly the compacted, disturbed soil a newly filled-in fortification would offer. The register treats the three trees as one monumental entry rather than three individual ones, the group rather than any single trunk being the thing judged worth protecting, matching how the park's bald cypress grove a few dozen metres away is registered. They stand in the open on public parkland, free to walk past any day, close enough to Kenaupark's copper beech and lime that a single stop here takes in four of the park's oldest plantings at once.

trees.name: The Common Lime of Kenaupark
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 5 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
This common lime is the youngest of Kenaupark's protected trees, planted in the early twentieth century, decades after the Zocher family's 1865 design had already matured into the park visitors walk today. Most of Kenaupark's oldest plantings, its plane trees and bald cypress grove, went in during the park's first years; this lime is a later addition to an already-established landscape, close enough to the original design that the register still lists it as part of the same historic planting scheme rather than treating it as a later intrusion.

Common lime is itself a hybrid rather than a distinct wild species, a natural cross between the small-leaved and large-leaved lime that was the default street and park tree across Dutch cities for centuries, valued for tolerating pruning and city conditions better than most trees its size. This one grows within a hundred metres of Kenaupark's copper beech, its plane group and its bald cypresses, on ground that was open fortification earthworks within living memory of the people who first planted here. It stands in the open park, free, a few minutes' walk from Haarlem Centraal station.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Bolwerken
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 10-12 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
De Bolwerken is Haarlem's older green ring, laid out from 1828 by JD Zocher when the city's fortifications came down and needed a public use, decades before his son helped design Kenaupark a couple of hundred metres east. Most of the park's planting is contemporary with that 1828 design. This ginkgo is not: the register dates it to the 1910s, arriving on the lawn at the foot of a low rise nearly a century after Zocher laid the paths around it, a later addition to an already-mature landscape rather than part of the original planting.

Ginkgo biloba is one of the oldest tree lineages alive, unrelated to any other living tree family, which is part of why parks of this period liked to add one: a curiosity that had outlived the dinosaurs long before anyone thought to plant it in a Dutch park. Standing alone on open lawn rather than grouped like the beeches and oaks nearby, it has had space and light a crowded planting would not have given it.

It sits between the Noorderbrug and the Kruisweg crossing, a free, open stretch of park about ten minutes from Haarlem Centraal, and a natural extension of a walk that already takes in the Kenaupark cluster a short distance away.

trees.name: The Oak Pair of Statenbolwerk
trees.species: Oak (Quercus robur or Quercus petraea; the register does not specify which)
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 10-12 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
Two oaks flank the start of a footpath on the west side of Statenbolwerk, planted in the 1850s to mark the entrance the way a gate would, a decade or so before the villas that now line the park went up. Haarlem's register keeps them as one entry rather than two, the pairing itself being the point: an oak either side of a path reads as an entrance in a way one oak standing alone never would.

The register does not say which oak. Quercus robur (pedunculate) and Quercus petraea (sessile) both grow in Dutch parks of this age, and neither the register nor anything else found this pass narrows it further, so this page states the pair honestly as oak, species undetermined, until someone with a closer eye at the leaf and acorn tells us which. That gap does nothing to the trees themselves: at around 170 years old they are exactly contemporary with Statenbolwerk's own villas, planted in the same decade the walking park matured from Zocher's original 1828 design into the residential quarter that still surrounds it.

They stand free and open on public parkland, a few minutes from three more Statenbolwerk trees on this page and from Kenaupark's own cluster a few hundred metres further on, part of the same green ring that replaced Haarlem's demolished city walls.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Statenbolwerk
trees.access: Visible from the public Statenbolwerk footpath; the tree stands within the grounds of Staten Bolwerk 1, a private villa (owner_category 'particulier' in the register), so the trunk itself is not something a visitor can walk up to. The register itself marks it visitable/visible ('ja'/'ja').
trees.transport: 10-12 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
