This Caucasian wingnut grows in the garden of a private villa at Statenbolwerk 1, and the honest way to see it is from the footpath outside rather than at the trunk: the Dutch national monumental-tree register lists it as visible from public ground even though the ground it stands on is not. Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from forests around the Caucasus and the southern shore of the Caspian, a relative of walnut grown for its long hanging chains of winged seeds rather than for timber, and it took root here in the first decade of the twentieth century, once Statenbolwerk's grand villas had already gone up along the old fortification walk Zocher laid out in 1828.

At around 120 years old it is one of the younger trees on this page, but wingnuts grow fast and wide, and this one has had a private garden's room to do it without a park's usual crowding. What a visitor gets is a view rather than a walk-up: stand on the Statenbolwerk path and the crown shows above the villa's hedge, part of the same short stretch of park that already holds two more of this page's newest trees, the oak pair and the beech ensemble, both properly on public ground a few dozen metres away.

trees.name: The Beech Ensemble of Statenbolwerk
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 10-12 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal station
trees.story:
Four beeches grow together along the Statenbolwerk footpath near house number 26, planted in the 1850s as part of the same wave of planting that gave the walking park its villas a decade later. The Dutch monumental-tree register counts the four as a single entry, the row rather than any one trunk being what earned protection, the way Kenaupark's plane and cypress groups are registered a few hundred metres away.

A relative did not survive. A single copper beech about 200 metres from this group, at Statenbolwerk 2, was reportedly around 222 years old when storm Eunice tore it down in February 2022; local coverage of the felling reported its wood was later turned into cutting boards and knives rather than left to rot. This ensemble is a different, ordinary green beech, a different register entry and a different age bracket, but the loss is a reminder that a storm does not check a tree's paperwork before it falls.

The four stand in the open on public parkland, free to walk past at any time, a short stretch from the oak pair, the wingnut and the Kenaupark cluster that make this corner of Haarlem's old fortification ring one of the densest on the whole page.

trees.name: The Ash of Kleverlaan
trees.access: Free, public cemetery (Algemene Begraafplaats Kleverlaan), open during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kleverpark, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Haarlem (same stop as the already-published Kleverlaan Yew, haa_003)
trees.story: The general cemetery on the Kleverlaan is where Haarlem keeps its best trees, and this ash is one of the reasons guided tree walks stop here at all. It stands in the oldest section, on the south side, at a bend in the path with graves gathered close around its roots. The national register of monumental trees puts its planting somewhere between 1870 and 1880, so it is roughly 140 to 155 years old, and that band is as precise as the record allows. Ash rarely gets to be the tree people notice. It has no autumn colour worth the name, the bark stays grey and quiet, and the leaves drop early and more or less all at once. What it has instead is height and a light, open crown that lets the grass grow right up to the trunk, and after a century and a half over the same graves this one has plenty of both. The register is the only source that names this particular tree, which is why it is listed here with its dates attributed rather than asserted; the cemetery's beeches, cedar, walnut and yew are far better documented than its ash. If you know when it went in, or who planted it, tell us. It stands about a hundred metres from the Kleverlaan yew, so the two make one stop rather than two.

trees.name: The American Oak of Kleverlaan
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kleverpark, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Haarlem

best_time.label: late October and November, when the leaves turn deep red before they let go

trees.story: Come in through the Kleverlaan gate and the first thing you meet is an avenue of wingnuts. This American oak stands one connecting path to the left of it, which is exactly where the register tells you to look. Quercus rubra is not a Dutch tree. It came from the eastern seaboard of North America and Dutch parks and cemeteries planted it widely from the nineteenth century onward, largely for what it does in autumn. Native oaks go brown and hang on to the leaf half the winter. This one goes deep red in late October and lets go. The register dates its planting to between 1900 and 1910, making it roughly 115 to 125 years old, which is young for a monumental tree and respectable for a red oak in a Dutch cemetery. It has stood beside the gate for more than a century of funerals. The cemetery is one of three stops on the Bomenstichting's monumental tree walk through Haarlem, and this oak is one of the reasons the route comes here, though the national register is still the only source that records the tree itself. Take the dates as the register's rather than as a measurement. Its leaves are the easy check: broad, with shallow lobes ending in fine bristle points, and far bigger than anything a native oak produces.

trees.name: The Black Locust of Kleverlaan
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kleverpark, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Haarlem

best_time.label: late May and early June, when the white flower chains open and the scent carries down the path

trees.story: This black locust has its feet in a hedge. The register puts it in the first plot on the left as you come through the entrance, along the path, with the base of the trunk standing in clipped greenery, which is an odd berth for a tree of nearly a century. Robinia pseudoacacia arrived in Europe from the Appalachians in the early seventeenth century and carries the name of Jean Robin, gardener to the French kings. It spread across the continent as a street and park tree because it grows fast, tolerates poor thin soil, and smells extraordinary for about two weeks a year. In late May and early June it hangs white pea flowers in chains and the scent carries a long way down a quiet path. The rest of the year it is a scruffier proposition: deeply furrowed bark like twisted rope, a crown that looks half assembled, limbs that snap in storms. The register dates the planting to between 1920 and 1930, so roughly 95 to 105 years, and it is the only record we have found of this particular tree. No second source names it, so read the age as the register's estimate. It stands within a hundred metres of the red oak and the silver lime, which makes all three one short loop just inside the gate.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of Kleverlaan
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kleverpark, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Haarlem

best_time.label: July, when it flowers weeks after every other lime in the city

trees.story: Dead bumblebees turn up under silver limes every summer, and botanists have argued about why for a century. The old explanation was that the nectar of Tilia tomentosa is mildly toxic to bees. The current one is duller and sadder: the tree flowers when almost nothing else does, so late season bumblebees with nothing left to visit work it until they run out. Either way, this is a tree that draws insects after the rest of the city has finished flowering. It stands in the oldest part of the Kleverlaan cemetery, on a path beside the water. The national register puts its planting between 1840 and 1850, which makes it roughly 175 to 185 years old and one of the oldest things growing on this ground. Turn a leaf over and the underside is white with felt, which is where the name comes from and why the whole crown flickers pale when wind moves through it. It is also why the species survives city dirt so well: the felt sheds it. The register is the only source we have located for this tree. Nobody has published a girth or a measured age, so the band above is the register's estimate rather than anyone's tape. If you have measured it, we would like the number.

trees.name: The Zocher Beeches
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Kleverpark, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Haarlem

best_time.label: November, when three crowns go copper at once and the light under them turns orange

trees.story: The two men who laid out this cemetery are buried in it, and three beeches carry their name. Father and son Zocher were the landscape architects of the Kleverlaan grounds, and two cemetery records place their graves on the east side, near Schoterweg. The register lists three European beeches standing together at that spot under a single entry: Zocherbeuk, the Zocher beech. Whether the trees were planted at the graves or the graves placed among beeches already growing is not something any source we could reach states plainly, so we are not going to pretend otherwise. The register gives a planting band of 1800 to 1850, which is roughly 175 to 225 years, a range wide enough to allow either version. What is not in question is what they do to the ground. Mature beech keeps its lowest limbs low and sweeps them out sideways, and three of them together make one dark room with a floor of husks and nothing growing in it. That is the tree working: beech leaves cast the deepest shade of any European broadleaf, and very little survives underneath. In November the crowns go copper together. In February, bare, the grey trunks are the best thing on the path. A figure of four metres round circulates for this group, and we have not been able to confirm it.

trees.name: The Plane of Frederikspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: About 20-25 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal Station, or a short bus ride to Houtplein
trees.story: Five and a half metres around the trunk and twenty four metres up, on a scrap of green between a busy junction and the Houtplein bus stops. A professional tree care firm measured this plane at 175 centimetres of stem diameter, which is where that girth figure comes from, and the national register dates the planting to between 1860 and 1870, so roughly 155 to 165 years. It was here long before the traffic was. London plane is the tree cities keep when they keep nothing else, and this one shows why. It takes exhaust, compacted soil, hard pruning and root damage and carries on. Rather than trying to breathe through a century of grime it sheds its bark in plates, which is why the trunk is mottled cream, olive and grey instead of uniformly filthy. The species is a hybrid, an accident between the American and the oriental plane that turned up in Europe in the seventeenth century and turned out to be tougher than either parent. Stand under it in winter and the frame reads clearly: a short heavy bole, then limbs going out almost horizontally before they turn up, with bobbled seed balls hanging on long strings until spring. Two independent sources agree on this tree, which makes it the best documented entry in the Frederikspark and the easiest one to find.

trees.name: The Oak Pair of Frederikspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: About 20-25 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal Station, or a short bus ride to Houtplein
trees.story: Two pedunculate oaks stand together on the west side of the Frederikspark, and on the register's own dating they are the oldest things in it. The planting band is 1840 to 1850, so roughly 180 to 190 years, a couple of decades ahead of the big plane at the Houtplein end. Old oaks are scarce in Dutch cities for an unromantic reason: Quercus robur was the timber tree of the Republic, worth more felled than standing, and anything straight enough went into ships, locks and sluice gates. These two were left alone long enough to stop being timber and start being furniture for a park. A pair planted close grows into a single argument about light. Each crown leans away from the other and the branches on the facing sides stay short, so from a distance the two read as one lopsided tree and only resolve into two when you walk round them. In a good mast year the grass beneath is covered in acorns by October. The national register is the only source we have found for either tree, so the age is its estimate rather than a measured figure, and nobody has published a girth for them. If you get a tape around a trunk here, we would like to hear the number.

trees.name: The Pin Oak of Frederikspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: About 20-25 minute walk from Haarlem Centraal Station, or a short bus ride to Houtplein

best_time.label: late October into November, when it goes scarlet and holds it for weeks

trees.story: Pin oak reached European gardens at the start of the nineteenth century, which means this one, if the register's dating holds, belongs to the first generation planted here. The band is 1840 to 1850, so roughly 180 to 190 years old, and it stands along the path in the middle of the north side of the Frederikspark. Quercus palustris is easy once you have seen one. The lower branches sweep down toward the ground instead of reaching for the light, the leaves are cut into deep narrow lobes with bristle tips, and the crown keeps a tidy conical outline far longer than any native oak manages. Then in late October it turns scarlet and holds the colour for weeks after the limes and the ashes have given up. The name has nothing to do with the leaves. It comes from the short hard pin-like stubs of dead branchlets left along the trunk and the inner limbs, a habit the species has and most oaks do not. The tree is a swamp oak by origin, from the wet bottomlands of the American Midwest, which is one reason it has done so well in a country built on waterlogged ground. The national register is the only source we have found for it, so read the age band as its estimate. No girth has been published.

trees.name: The Juttepeer of Heilige Geesthofje
trees.access: Restricted: guided Buitenmuseum tours, by appointment, or during Open Monumentendag. Not open to casual walk-in visitors
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal or Hollands Spoor station

best_time.label: September into October, when the residents pick the pears for jelly

trees.story: Elderly women living in this almshouse have been making jelly from this pear tree's fruit since at least the 17th century, and the tree they are picking from is very likely the same one their predecessors used four centuries ago. Planted in 1638 in the inner courtyard of the Heilige Geesthofje, founded in 1616 to house women of unblemished character, the tree is widely considered the oldest pear tree in the Netherlands, a juttepeer, a small, hard, old Dutch variety better suited to cooking and preserving than eating straight off the branch. The courtyard itself functioned as a working kitchen garden for residents for most of its history, vegetables and fruit grown for the household rather than for show, and the pear outlasted whatever else was once planted alongside it. It still bears fruit every year, harvested and turned into jelly by the almshouse's current residents in a tradition nobody has needed to formally revive because it never actually stopped. The courtyard is not casually open to passersby; the almshouse still functions as a residence, and visiting means booking a guided tour through the Buitenmuseum, arranging an appointment, or timing a visit to the national Open Monumentendag, a small price for standing beside something planted six years before Rembrandt painted the Night Watch.

trees.name: The Koekamp Oak
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Adjacent to Den Haag Centraal station, 5-10 minute walk

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: William of Orange personally guaranteed this oak's forest would survive forever, four and a half centuries before anyone thought to count the tree's actual rings. In 1576, with the Eighty Years' War against Spain already underway, Orange signed a deed on behalf of the States of Holland promising that the Haagse Bos and the Koekamp within it would never be sold or logged for timber, a rare 16th-century conservation guarantee that has, remarkably, held. This oak, standing roughly 300 years old inside the Koekamp's fenced deer enclosure, is a direct beneficiary: too young to have existed when Orange made his promise, but growing on land that promise had already protected for well over a century by the time this acorn took root. Red and fallow deer still graze around its base today, the same enclosure function the Koekamp has served for centuries, a working piece of countryside preserved inside a European capital rather than a themed park built to imitate one. The forest's luck ran out only once, briefly: during the German occupation, half of it was felled for military purposes, a rare interruption in an otherwise unbroken run of protection stretching back to a promise a Dutch prince made before his own war was won.

trees.name: The Veteran Linden of Clingendael
trees.access: Free, open estate park at any time
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Haagse Hout, then a short walk, roughly 20-25 minutes from central Den Haag

best_time.label: heavily scented cream flowers, audible with bees from metres away

trees.story: This linden is the last member standing of a row that stopped existing as a row sometime in the last three centuries. An 18th-century drawing of Clingendael's formal gardens, laid out around 1730, shows several trained lindens planted in a disciplined line, pruned and trellised into the geometric shapes fashionable in Dutch garden design of the period. Every other tree in that row is gone; this one alone survived, and without the regular pruning that once kept it in formation, it has spent three centuries growing into a gnarled, irregular shape that looks nothing like the tidy row it escaped from. That accidental wildness turned out to matter. In 2019, Den Haag became the first Dutch municipality to formally create a veteran tree designation, a status imported from England that protects a tree's final life stage with dedicated fencing and minimal-intervention care rather than the routine pruning applied to younger specimens, and this linden was the first tree in the country to receive it. The designation recognizes exactly what makes the tree valuable now: not tidiness, but the accumulated evidence of three centuries alone, still standing on an estate that has otherwise been rebuilt and replanted around it more than once.

trees.name: The Postzegelboom
trees.access: Free, public street at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal station

best_time.label: September and October, when the conkers ripen and fall

trees.story: Up to a hundred stamp collectors at a time used to crowd around this horse chestnut on Wednesday and Saturday afternoons, trading and selling postage stamps under its branches for decades before the practice finally faded. The tree earned its name, the Postzegelboom, the stamp tree, from that informal open-air market rather than from anything botanical, and the trade continued through the years before the Second World War, when philatelists first started meeting under its leaves opposite the royal Noordeinde Palace. The tree itself predates that market by decades: it was already growing as a small tree in a private garden when King Willem II ordered every building opposite his palace demolished in the mid-19th century to make way for a Gothic Revival gallery. Those buildings themselves fell into disrepair and came down for good in 1883, but the chestnut, tucked into what had been someone's garden, was spared both rounds of demolition and left standing behind the new gallery. The Dutch postal service PTT thought enough of the connection to fund a full restoration by a tree surgeon in 1990, keeping alive both a monumental tree and the memory of the market that made it famous.

trees.name: The Kabouterboom
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Haagse Hout, then a short walk, roughly 20 minutes from central Den Haag

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: A hollow in this oak's trunk has been furnished like a dollhouse for as long as anyone in the neighbourhood can remember, complete with tiny notes left for gnomes nobody has ever claimed to see. At only about 94 years old, the Kabouterboom, the gnome tree, is by far the youngest entry on this list, included for a different reason than the others: generations of children from the surrounding Bosjes van Zanen neighbourhood have treated this specific oak as a shared piece of make-believe, tucking dolls, notes and small gifts into its hollow and low branches, a tradition adults have kept alive rather than outgrown. Nobody organizes it and no sign explains it; parents simply pass the game to their children the way they might pass down any local custom, and the tree accumulates a rotating cast of tiny residents as a result. It sits at the edge of the Clingendael estate, an easy detour from the veteran linden a short walk away, proof that a tree earns a place on a list like this one for reasons that have nothing to do with circumference or century, and everything to do with what a neighbourhood decided to make of it.

trees.name: The Bezuidenhoutseweg Oak
trees.age: 225 to 275 years, planted somewhere between 1750 and 1800
trees.access: Free, open parkland on the Koekamp, at any time
trees.transport: Four minute walk north from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Four minutes north of the platforms at Den Haag Centraal, on the old deer meadow called the Koekamp, stands an oak the national register dates to somewhere between 1750 and 1800. That is a fifty year shrug rather than a date, and it still makes the tree at least 225 years old, possibly closer to 275. The Koekamp is why it is here. This strip beside the Haagse Bos has been grazing meadow for centuries, cattle first and deer later, land that was never built on and never laid out as a garden, so the trees on it were left to get old rather than pruned into a design. Not all of them got the chance. During the German occupation a great many trees around the Koekamp went into stoves as firewood or were cut down to clear the line of a tank ditch dug across this side of the city. This oak stayed standing through both. It has no name, no plaque and no recorded history, it belongs to the state forestry service, and it is one of the easiest old trees in the Netherlands to reach: out of the station, over the road, and there it is. If you know who planted it, we would like to hear.

trees.name: The Westvlietweg Plane
trees.age: 225 to 275 years, planted somewhere between 1750 and 1800
trees.access: Free, on the public verge of the Westvlietweg in Leidschendam
trees.transport: Bus from Den Haag Centraal towards Leidschendam and a short walk, roughly 25 to 30 minutes
trees.story: Rich families from The Hague and Delft spent the 17th and 18th centuries building country houses along the Vliet, and this plane went into the ground while that fashion was still running. The register dates it to between 1750 and 1800, which makes it somewhere between 225 and 275 years old, standing in front of Zeerust, one of the estates strung along the Westvlietweg. The road is half the reason to come. The Vliet is a canal the Romans dug and the Dutch never stopped using, the Westvlietweg runs alongside it, and the strip is lined with the gates and coach houses of buitenplaatsen, the summer estates merchants built to get out of the city in August. Almost all the planting from that era has been replaced twice over since. This tree has not. It is a London Plane, the hybrid that would go on to become the default street tree of half of Europe, put in here long before anyone knew that is what it would become. The province owns it and the verge is public, so you can stand under it without asking anyone. Be honest with yourself about the trip, though: it is outside the city and it stands alone, so this one is a detour rather than a walk.

trees.name: The Koeweide Oak of Ockenburgh
trees.access: Free, the municipal estate park of Ockenburgh, open at any time
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Loosduinen and a walk into the estate, roughly 35 to 40 minutes from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Someone wrote a book length poem about this estate a century and a half before the oak was planted. Jacob Westerbaen, a Hague physician who turned poet, built Ockenburgh in the dunes behind Loosduinen in 1654 and then published thousands of lines describing his own grounds, walk by walk, tree by tree. The oak came much later. The register puts it in the 1810s, which makes it a little over two centuries old, growing on the north side of the Koeweide, the old cow pasture beside the country house. What it has watched is the estate's slow public turn. Ockenburgh went from private pleasure ground to a camping site to a municipal park, and the house itself stood derelict for years before it was restored. The dunes behind it were fortified during the German occupation, when the Atlantic Wall ran along this coast and large pieces of the landscape here were cleared for it. The oak kept its place on the pasture edge through all of it. The city owns the estate now and the gates and paths are free, which makes this one of the few two hundred year old trees in the country you can walk up to at any hour of any day.

trees.name: The Van Soutelandelaan Oak
trees.access: Free, public green behind the Van Soutelandelaan
trees.transport: Bus or tram to Mariahoeve, about 20 minutes from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This oak is roughly a century and a half older than every building around it. It stands in the green behind the Van Soutelandelaan, in Mariahoeve, a district that did not exist until the late 1950s, when The Hague ran out of room inside itself and put a whole neighbourhood of flats and low blocks on the estate land north east of the Haagse Bos. The register dates the oak to between 1810 and 1820, so it is somewhere past its 205th year and probably not much past its 215th. It was already a substantial tree when the ground here was still pasture and country house. Planners of that generation usually levelled a site and started from nothing; here the wood was built around instead, and a handful of trees from the estate era still stand between the blocks. A beech of nearly the same age grows about two hundred metres away, which turns this into a short walk with two old trees in it rather than a single stop. Nobody wrote down who planted the oak or why. If you grew up in this corner of Mariahoeve and know the story, tell us.

trees.name: The Grandbos Beech
trees.access: Free, public wood at the Van Soutelandelaan and Van Mojalenlaan junction
trees.transport: Bus or tram to Mariahoeve, about 20 minutes from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: late October into November, when the beech turns copper and keeps it for weeks

trees.story: Nothing about the corner of the Van Soutelandelaan and the Van Mojalenlaan announces a two hundred year old tree. The beech stands in a strip of wood called Le Grandbos, a leftover of the estate landscape that was here before Mariahoeve was built over it, and the register dates the tree to the 1820s. Beech does two things worth the walk. Its bark stays smooth and grey for its whole life, so an old trunk reads more like a column than a tree, without the deep furrows that give an oak of the same age away. And it holds autumn better than almost anything else growing in a Dutch street, going copper in late October and keeping it into November, with the fallen leaves staying orange on the ground for weeks afterwards. Underneath it, very little grows. A mature beech takes so much of the light that the ground under the crown stays bare, which is the easiest way to pick one out of a mixed wood from a distance. An oak of nearly the same vintage stands about two hundred metres off, on the other side of the Van Soutelandelaan, so this is a ten minute detour with two trees in it.

trees.name: The Malieveld Elm
trees.access: Free, the open Malieveld, at any time
trees.transport: Ten minute walk from Den Haag Centraal
trees.story: An elm from the 1830s has outlived two epidemics that killed almost everything of its kind. Dutch elm disease takes its name from the country that first identified it, in the years after the First World War, and a second, far more aggressive strain arrived in the 1970s and finished most of what the first had left. Between them they emptied Dutch streets of the tree that had defined them for centuries. This one went into the ground somewhere between 1830 and 1840 and is still standing, on the field where the country goes to be heard. The Malieveld began as a court for pall mall, the ball and mallet game the 17th century was mad about, and became the open ground in the middle of The Hague where farmers park their tractors, unions bring their whistles and hundreds of thousands of people have gathered for one cause or another. Between demonstrations it takes funfairs and circus tents. The elm has stood at the edge of all of it for close to two centuries, a short walk from the parliament buildings everybody comes here to shout at, and almost nobody in those crowds has ever looked up at it.

trees.name: De Koekampkastanje
trees.access: Free, on the Koekamp beside the Malieveld, at any time
trees.transport: Ten minute walk from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: early May, when the white candles open across the whole crown

trees.story: In March 1997 this horse chestnut was dragged eighty metres across the Koekamp on steel plates, with a hundred tonnes of soil still around its roots, and the operation went into the Guinness Book of Records. It got there by being loved. Many of the trees on this side of the city vanished during the German occupation, burned in stoves for want of coal or felled to clear the line of a tank ditch, and this chestnut came through both. Fifty years later a road nearly did what the war had not. The plan for the Koningstunnel, drawn up in 1995, ran through the chestnut and through a monumental linden standing beside it. The city expected paperwork and got an argument: people were attached to these two trees in a way nobody had budgeted for. The tunnel route was shifted sideways to spare the linden. For the chestnut, engineers asked a stranger question, whether a tree that size could simply be moved, and the answer turned out to be yes. Steel plates went under the root ball and the whole thing was hauled slowly towards the Malieveld. It recovered. The crown is full again and a small sign at the foot of the trunk records what happened, ten minutes from Den Haag Centraal.

trees.name: The Mesdag Garden Oak
trees.access: In the garden of De Mesdag Collectie at Laan van Meerdervoort 7, reached through the museum during its opening hours
trees.transport: Tram along the Laan van Meerdervoort, or a 25 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Hendrik Willem Mesdag painted the largest painting in the Netherlands, and this oak was already forty or fifty years old when he did it. The Panorama Mesdag, finished in 1881, is a cylindrical view of the Scheveningen beach fourteen metres high and a hundred and twenty round, and Mesdag lived a short walk from it, at Laan van Meerdervoort 7, in the house that is now a museum of the collection he built. The garden came with the house. The register dates this oak to the 1830s, which puts it a little under two centuries old, and notes a second oak of exactly the same age standing next to it, two trees side by side. Mesdag bought paintings the way other people buy furniture, filling the house with Barbizon and Hague School canvases until it needed a purpose built gallery bolted onto the back to hold them. The oaks were the view from all of it, and they were here before the collection, before the panorama and before the street reached this far. You reach them through De Mesdag Collectie in his old house. It is the only tree on this list that comes with a room full of Corots.

trees.name: The Oud Eik en Duin Chestnut
trees.access: Free, Oud Eik en Duin cemetery, open in daylight hours
trees.transport: Tram to the Laan van Eik en Duinen, about 25 minutes from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story: A ruined medieval chapel stands a few steps from this chestnut and is six centuries older than anything else growing on the site. Oud Eik en Duin opened as a cemetery in 1830, after a royal decree ended the practice of burying the dead inside Dutch churches and pushed new burial grounds out past the edge of town. The ground it took was already old. The chapel of Eik en Duinen, founded in the 13th century and a pilgrimage spot for centuries after, sits roofless in the middle of it, wrecked in the wars of the 16th century and left standing as a ruin ever since. The register dates this horse chestnut to the 1830s, the same decade the cemetery opened, though nobody recorded whether it belongs to the first planting or arrived some years later. Either way it has spent close to two centuries doing what cemetery trees do, growing undisturbed on land nobody is permitted to develop, which is the best thing that can happen to a tree in a city. Oud Eik en Duin is one of the largest and oldest burial grounds in The Hague, it is free, and it is open to walk through in daylight.

trees.name: The Van Hogenhoucklaan Beech
trees.age: about 190 years, and the register's own note puts it loosely in the first half of the 19th century
trees.access: Free, in the public green strip on the Van Hogenhoucklaan
trees.transport: Bus to Benoordenhout, about 15 minutes from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.story: This beech has added about a centimetre of girth a year for the last three decades, and that number is the reason anyone looked twice at it. The Van Hogenhoucklaan was laid out with its houses around 1930, and the beeches along it, mixed with American limes and a few oaks, look like they went in with the street. This one does not. It is noticeably thicker than its neighbours, and a tree growing at a centimetre a year is not one that got fat quickly; it is one that has been at it a great deal longer. The register's own surveyor lands on the first half of the 19th century, which would make it roughly a century older than the road it lines. That is an estimate rather than a date, and it is the honest kind: a measured trunk, a measured growth rate, and a conclusion stated as a probability instead of a year. Beech keeps smooth grey bark for life, so age never shows in the surface the way it does on an oak. It shows in the diameter, which is exactly what caught the surveyor's eye. Stand at the end of the green strip and look down the row. The odd one out is not hard to find.

trees.name: The Oak of the Scheveningseweg Jewish Cemetery
trees.access: In the Jewish cemetery on the Scheveningseweg, an enclosed burial ground that is not open every day; check the opening hours before travelling
trees.transport: Tram along the Scheveningseweg, about 15 minutes from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This oak was planted in a burial ground that had already been in use for a century and a half. The Jewish cemeteries on the Scheveningseweg date from the 1690s, opened outside the built up city because that was where the Jewish community of The Hague was permitted to bury its dead, on ground either side of the straight road Constantijn Huygens had laid out three decades earlier to link the city with the sea. The register dates the oak to the 1840s, which puts it a little under two centuries old. Jewish burial custom leaves a cemetery undisturbed once the graves are in place, so ground like this is often the least altered land in an old European city, and trees on it grow up without the pruning, digging and replanting that shapes a park. What came later is not the tree's story, but it is the ground's. The Jewish population of The Hague numbered around seventeen thousand before the war and most of them did not come back. The cemeteries survived. The oak stands inside the wall, in a quiet place that is not open every day, so check the hours before you make the trip.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of Paleistuin
trees.access: Free, public garden, open sunrise to sunset; occasionally closed for state visits
trees.transport: Centrum, central Den Haag; about a 15 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal station

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn rust orange before dropping

trees.story:
This bald cypress grows on a lawn in the garden behind Paleis Noordeinde, the working palace where the King of the Netherlands keeps his office, on ground first laid out as a private garden in the early 17th century by Frederik Hendrik, son of William of Orange, for his mother, and known for centuries afterward as the Prinsessentuin. What was once strictly royal property has been open to the public for generations now, a fact many visitors to the palace's public face on the street never realise extends to the grounds behind it.

The register dates the tree's planting to the 1890s, part of what it calls the garden's older planting scheme, well after Frederik Hendrik's original 17th-century design but still well over a century ago. Taxodium distichum is native to swamps across the southeastern United States and, unusually for a conifer, drops its needles every autumn, so it goes from green to rust orange before standing bare through winter alongside the garden's ponds and statues. The garden is free, open from sunrise to sunset, closed only on the occasional day a state visit requires it.

trees.name: The Chestnuts of Vijverberg
trees.access: Free, public street, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Den Haag; about a 10 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal station
trees.story:
The Vijverberg exists because of a hole in the ground. When the Hofvijver, the rectangular pond that still sits beside the Binnenhof and reflects the seat of Dutch government in postcards by the thousand, was enlarged centuries ago, the excavated sand was piled up along one side, raising the ground into the low ridge that gives this street its name, hill by the pond. Rich families built townhouses along it from the 17th century on, most with gardens facing the water.

This row of seven horse chestnuts, planted around the 1830s, lines that same historic ground today, tall enough now to shade the water they were planted to look out over. Horse chestnut is not native to the Netherlands, imported as an ornamental from the Balkans, but it became the default tree for exactly this kind of grand civic promenade across Dutch cities for two centuries running. The trees stand in the open, free, on one of the most photographed short stretches of pavement in the country, a few minutes' walk from the Binnenhof itself.

trees.name: The Planes of the Grote Kerk
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Den Haag; about a 12 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal station
trees.story:
These two London planes grow on what used to be a graveyard, the register's own note for the site reading simply planted on the former churchyard, a detail that explains why open lawn survives at all around a church this central. The Grote Kerk, Den Haag's largest and oldest church, has stood on this ground since the 15th century, and burials around it continued for centuries after, until the practice was banned inside growing Dutch cities on public health grounds and this plot became open space instead.

The two planes date from around the 1890s, late arrivals relative to the church itself but still well over a century old, standing on the Riviervismarkt square that wraps around the building. London plane, a hybrid of the American sycamore and the Oriental plane, tolerates compacted urban soil better than almost any other large tree, which is likely why it was the obvious choice once the ground stopped being used for its original purpose. The trees grow in the open, free, on a square that still draws markets and events the way the site has for centuries, just without the graves.

trees.name: The Planes of Huijgenspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: Stationsbuurt, Den Haag; about a 10 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal station
trees.story:
Huijgenspark carried an uglier name for most of its early life, Bogt van Guinea, until a murder in the neighbourhood in 1873 gave the city reason to rename it after Constantijn Huygens, the Hague-born diplomat, poet and composer whose son would go on to discover Saturn's rings. Before the park existed at all, this stretch was the busy road out toward Delft, lined with inns and wagon-hire businesses for travellers leaving the walled city, one of the few built-up areas outside The Hague's old canal ring.

These London planes went into the newly laid-out park around the 1870s, not long after it was first established in 1860 on the ground between Huijgensstraat and the old Bogt. The park was renovated in 2002, its planting refreshed and its paths repaved, but the planes from the original layout survived that work intact. They stand in the open today, free, in a park whose own name change still quietly marks a crime nobody living remembers the details of.

trees.name: The Hungarian Oaks of Huijgenspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at any time
trees.transport: Stationsbuurt, Den Haag; about a 10 minute walk from Den Haag Centraal station
trees.story:
Hungarian oak is a species most Dutch park visitors walk past without recognising, a large-leaved Balkan and southeast European oak that reaches the Netherlands only through deliberate 19th and early 20th-century planting rather than any natural range of its own. This group of three, dated by the register to around 1900 to 1910, grows on the west side of Huijgenspark, a generation younger than the park's own planes but from the same era of civic tree planting that filled Dutch municipal parks with species collected from across the continent.

The park itself replaced a busy coaching-inn district on the old road to Delft, renamed in 1873 for the polymath Constantijn Huygens after having carried the considerably less flattering name Bogt van Guinea for its first two centuries. Hungarian oak's leaves are larger and more deeply lobed than the native pedunculate oak's, worth a close look for anyone wanting to tell the two apart on sight. The trees stand in the open, free, a short walk from the park's older plane grove on the opposite side of the same green space.

trees.name: The Plane of Park Hoekenburg
trees.age: roughly 280 to 330 years, from the register's planting band of 1700-1750
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 15-minute walk.
trees.story:
One of the finds pulled out of the ground in this corner of Voorburg was a wooden post cut from an oak felled in the year 212, a date read off its rings. The excavation that produced it, in 2008, was digging up Forum Hadriani, the Roman port town raised on an older settlement of the Cananefates. The Dutch monumental tree register does not give the plane growing on that ground a nickname. It files it as the plane on the Roman foundation, and notes that it is the thickest plane in South Holland.

The age comes from the same register and stays a band: planted somewhere between 1700 and 1750, which puts the tree at roughly 280 to 330 years. Nothing in the record narrows that, and a single confident figure would be precision the surveyor never claimed. The band is wide enough to be certain of one thing, which is that this plane was rooted here well before the Netherlands became a kingdom. When the park was later renovated, the tree was carefully protected.

Planes shed their bark in plates all year round, so no month is the wrong one, and the trunk is the reason to come. Know before you set out that this is Voorburg, in the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg, a few kilometres east of central The Hague. It is a ride out of the city rather than a walk across it.

trees.name: The Copper Beech East of the Arentsburg Pond
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 13-minute walk.
trees.story:
A copper beech is an ordinary beech with a fault in it. The purple comes from a mutation that floods the leaf with red pigment until the green underneath stops showing, and because the fault only sometimes passes to the seedlings, nurserymen have spent two centuries grafting it onto ordinary beech roots instead. Nineteenth century estate owners bought the result by the thousand, which is how a tree that began as an accident in a wild wood ended up standing over a pond in Voorburg.

This one holds the east bank in Park Arentsburg. The national register puts its planting between 1830 and 1840, so call it about 190 years, and note that this is a planting estimate rather than a count of rings. Nobody has taken a core from it. The band is what the record will carry.

A second copper beech of much the same vintage stands across the water on the west side, so settle which bank you are on before you argue about which tree you are looking at. Beech keeps smooth grey bark for its whole life, so neither of them shows age in the way an oak does; it goes into girth instead. Park Arentsburg lies in Leidschendam-Voorburg, east of The Hague rather than in it, on the ground where the Roman town of Forum Hadriani once stood.

trees.name: The Copper Beech North of the Vreugd en Rust Koepel
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about an 8-minute walk.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves open thin enough for the light to come through and the crown turns translucent red

trees.story:
The register gives this tree no street address. It files it as the copper beech on the north side of koepel number one, which tells you what sort of park you are walking into. Vreugd en Rust is an old country estate turned public ground, joy and rest in Dutch, and a koepel is one of its domed garden houses.

Two copper beeches stand at that pavilion, one north of it and one south, entered separately in the national monumental tree register and both dated to a planting somewhere between 1830 and 1840. That puts them at roughly 190 years, from an estimate rather than a count of rings, and they are close enough in age and bulk that on paper the compass point is the only thing separating them. This is the northern one.

Purple beech leaves are at their oddest in May. They open thin enough for the light to pass through, so the whole crown burns translucent red for a fortnight before the pigment thickens and the tree settles into something closer to black by August. Anyone who has only seen a copper beech in high summer has seen the dull half of it. The park is in Voorburg, in the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg, which is a trip out from The Hague rather than a corner of it.

trees.name: The Copper Beech South of the Vreugd en Rust Koepel
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about an 8-minute walk.
trees.story:
Nearly all of a mature beech's roots sit in the top half metre of soil, spread about as wide as the crown reaches. Stand under this one and you are standing on it. That shallow plate is why old beeches in well used parks tend to die of nothing more dramatic than feet: the ground packs down, air stops reaching the roots, and a tree that has held on for nearly two centuries loses to a shortcut worn across the grass. Anyone looking after a park beech worries about the soil long before the branches.

This is the southern of the two copper beeches at koepel number one in Park Vreugd en Rust. The national register gives it a planting date somewhere between 1830 and 1840, so roughly 190 years, and that band is an estimate of when it went in rather than a count of rings. The register is the only source that puts any number on it.

Come in a mast year and you will hear the tree before you look at it. Beech drops its nuts in irregular gluts rather than evenly, and after a heavy one the spiky husks lie thick enough underfoot to crunch. The park is in Voorburg, part of Leidschendam-Voorburg, a short ride east of The Hague rather than a walk within it.

trees.name: The Den Burghstraat Beech of Park Arentsburg
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 13-minute walk.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the green crown turns copper beside the purple ones

trees.story:
The copper beeches across this park are this tree in fancy dress. Same species, Fagus sylvatica, one colour mutation apart, and this is the plain original, standing at the Den Burghstraat side of Park Arentsburg. The national register dates the planting to between 1830 and 1840, which makes it about 190 years old, and that band is an estimate of when it went in rather than a count of rings. Its first summers were the years the Netherlands spent losing Belgium.

Bark is why you walk up to a beech instead of photographing it from the path. It stays smooth and grey for the whole of the tree's life and it stretches as the trunk thickens rather than flaking away, so anything cut into it survives for decades. A carving stays at exactly the height it was made and grows wider and blunter year by year, which is how old park beeches end up wearing initials at head height that nobody now alive remembers cutting.

In summer it is the plain green one among the purple crowns, oval leaves where the chestnut along the path holds a hand of five. In the last days of October it turns copper and holds the colour well into November, which is the fortnight worth choosing for the walk. Park Arentsburg lies in Voorburg, in the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg, east of The Hague and not inside it.

trees.name: The Copper Beech West of the Arentsburg Pond
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 13-minute walk.
trees.story:
Landscape gardeners put copper beeches beside water deliberately. A purple crown reads nearly black against a pond, doubles itself in the reflection and does the job of a monument in a garden that has none, which is why nineteenth century Dutch parks are full of them standing precisely where this one stands. It holds the west bank of the pond in Park Arentsburg, and a second copper beech of the same era holds the east.

The national register puts the planting between 1830 and 1840, so roughly 190 years, from an estimate of when it went in rather than a count of rings. That register is the only source that dates the tree at all, which is worth knowing before anyone repeats the number as a fact.

Beech is the species Dutch tree officers now worry about most. The roots are shallow, the tree evolved for summers with reliable rain, and the dry ones of the past decade have thinned crowns and killed limbs in parks across the country. A tree with a pond within reach of its root plate is better placed than most to keep going.

Park Arentsburg lies in Voorburg, in the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg. That is east of The Hague and outside it, so treat this as a short trip out rather than a city walk.

trees.name: The Copper Beech at the Voorburg Cemetery Gate
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 6-minute walk.
trees.story:
Trees last longest on ground nobody will ever build on. A cemetery is about the safest address a tree can hold in a Dutch town: no redevelopment, no road widening, no new drains cut through the root plate, and a keeper whose job has always included the planting. This copper beech has had that arrangement at the entrance of Voorburg's Algemene Begraafplaats, on the Parkweg, for something like a century and a half.

The national register dates the planting to somewhere between 1860 and 1870, so roughly 160 years, and says nothing about who chose it. The choice looks deliberate rather than accidental. A copper beech is dark, slow, heavy and effectively permanent, and this one was set at the gate, where it is the first thing anyone passes going in and the last thing on the way out.

Beech does its ageing in girth rather than in its bark, which stays smooth and grey to the end. That makes a 160 year old beech easy to walk past and hard to walk past twice, because the scale only registers once you are close enough to think about getting your arms around it.

The ground is open daily and it is a working cemetery, so keep the visit quiet. Voorburg is part of Leidschendam-Voorburg, east of The Hague rather than in it.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Park Arentsburg
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 13-minute walk.

best_time.label: early May, when the white flower spikes stand up over the whole crown

trees.story:
When a Dutch horse chestnut looks scorched in August, the summer is not to blame. A moth called the horse chestnut leaf miner reached the country around the turn of the century, its caterpillars tunnel between the layers of every leaf, and whole crowns go brown months early. Add bleeding canker, which has killed chestnuts across the Netherlands since the 2000s, and an old one is less common than it used to be. The national register dates this tree's planting to between 1860 and 1870, so roughly 160 years, standing near the Den Burgstraat edge of Park Arentsburg.

The species is not Dutch and never was. It comes from a few mountain valleys in the Balkans, arrived in western Europe as a curiosity in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and went on to become the tree of avenues, school yards and city squares. The best known one in this country, the chestnut Anne Frank could see from the back annexe in Amsterdam, came down in a storm in 2010.

The week to come is in early May, when the flowers go up across the whole crown in white spikes and the tree turns briefly ridiculous. Late September brings conkers instead. Park Arentsburg is in Voorburg, part of the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg, east of The Hague rather than inside it.

trees.name: The Stone Bench Beech of Juliana en Bernardpark
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 10-minute walk.
trees.story:
A beech that grows alone is a different shape of tree from a beech that grows in a wood. In a forest it races its neighbours upward and ends as a long clean column with the crown somewhere overhead. Given open ground it keeps its low limbs, spreads sideways and often finishes wider than it is tall. This one has had open ground in the Juliana en Bernardpark for about 160 years, and the outline shows which life it got.

The national register puts the planting between 1860 and 1870 and locates the tree by the stone bench rather than by any house number, which is still the best direction anyone can give. So: roughly 160 years, from an estimate of the planting rather than a count of rings. Nobody has cored it, and the register is the only source that dates it at all.

That span covers the turning of Voorburg from a village of country estates into a suburb of The Hague, and the occupation, and every winter storm in between. None of it shows on the tree. Beech holds smooth grey bark to the end, which is why the only honest measure of one is its girth.

Voorburg belongs to the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg, east of The Hague and outside the city, so this is a ride out rather than a stroll.

trees.name: The Kalopa Koa
trees.access: Free day-use state park, open 7am-8pm daily, no entrance fee. Reached via the marked 0.7-mile Kalopa Nature Trail loop that starts at the parking lot near the park office.
trees.transport: No public transit. By car via Kalopa Road, about 5 miles (10 minutes) inland from Honokaa off Mamalahoa Highway (Hwy 19); free parking at the park office near the trailhead.
trees.story:
Almost none of Hawaii's native lowland forest is still standing. This koa grows in about a hundred acres of it that survived, one of the last old growth stands of native Hawaiian rainforest on the Big Island.

Koa grows nowhere else on earth. Hawaiians cut it for ocean-going canoes and surfboards, furniture makers have wanted it ever since, and that is a fair part of why so little old koa survives anywhere. This one carries a trunk 3.66 metres round, it is listed by name in the state's register of exceptional trees, and it was rated in good health when surveyors last looked at it.

It stands on the 0.7 mile nature trail that loops out from the park office. The Hamakua coast below spent a century under sugar cane and is now pasture and timber plantation. This pocket kept its own species instead, roughly twenty-five natives along the trail, several of them present as a single individual.

Nobody has dated it. The girth is on the record and the years are not, so if you know of a ring count or a survey, tell us and it goes on the page.

The park is free and open from seven in the morning until eight at night. The loop takes half an hour if you walk it without stopping, which you will not.

trees.name: The Kalopa Hame
trees.access: Free day-use state park, open 7am-8pm daily, no entrance fee. On the marked 0.7-mile Kalopa Nature Trail loop.
trees.transport: No public transit. By car via Kalopa Road, about 5 miles (10 minutes) inland from Honokaa off Mamalahoa Highway (Hwy 19); free parking at the park office near the trailhead.
trees.story:
Hame is a small tree. The botanical references give it four to ten metres, fifteen at the very outside, and it spends its whole life under somebody else's canopy. This one has a trunk 2.16 metres round, which is wider than your arms will reach and which no field guide would predict.

That is the likeliest reason Hawaii singled it out for protection under its exceptional tree law, which lists individual trees rather than whole habitats. Antidesma platyphyllum grows nowhere but these islands, and nobody travels to see one. It is a filler species, the kind of plant that quietly occupies the middle storey of a native rainforest under the koa and the ohi'a.

The Kalopa nature trail passes roughly twenty-five native species in 0.7 miles, several of them present as a single individual, and this hame is very likely one of those singles. That is the case for walking the loop slowly. A hame of this size is not something you come across on an ordinary hillside, because ordinary hillsides on this coast were cleared long ago.

Only the state register names this tree by itself, so the girth is their figure and we have not found a second measurement of it. Its age is unrecorded and we would rather leave the field empty than invent one. If you know of a count, tell us.

trees.name: The Smaller Kalopa Kopiko 'ula
trees.access: Free day-use state park, open 7am-8pm daily, no entrance fee. On the marked 0.7-mile Kalopa Nature Trail loop.
trees.transport: No public transit. By car via Kalopa Road, about 5 miles (10 minutes) inland from Honokaa off Mamalahoa Highway (Hwy 19); free parking at the park office near the trailhead.
trees.story:
This tree stands about 13 metres, which is as tall as its species has ever been documented to grow, and it does it on a trunk 82 centimetres round. You can put both arms around it comfortably.

Kopiko 'ula belongs to the coffee family and grows only in Hawaii, usually as a slim understory tree that never gets to decide how much light it receives. Height is the whole of this one's claim: the state's record puts it at 42 feet, and the species tops out at about 45.

There are two kopiko 'ula on the Kalopa nature trail and they are nothing alike. The other one, further round the same 0.7 mile loop, is over three metres round and nowhere near as tall. Between them they cover most of the range this species is capable of, which is not something you can usually see in a single afternoon.

Surveyors rated this one's condition fair rather than good, so go expecting a record holder rather than a showpiece. Its age has never been established, and the state register carries measurements without dates. If you know of a count for a Hawaiian understory tree of this size, tell us and we will add it.

The forest around it is protected native rainforest, roughly a hundred acres of it, which is why a tree of this kind survived long enough to reach its ceiling.

trees.name: The Larger Kalopa Kopiko 'ula
trees.access: Free day-use state park, open 7am-8pm daily, no entrance fee. On the marked 0.7-mile Kalopa Nature Trail loop.
trees.transport: No public transit. By car via Kalopa Road, about 5 miles (10 minutes) inland from Honokaa off Mamalahoa Highway (Hwy 19); free parking at the park office near the trailhead.
trees.story:
A kopiko 'ula is a slender thing, a coffee relative that rarely clears 13 metres and almost never gets thick. This one has a trunk 3.26 metres round. We have not found a larger one recorded anywhere, and the species grows nowhere outside Hawaii.

Trees like this are what an old forest produces when nobody interferes with it for long enough. Kalopa protects roughly a hundred acres of native Hawaiian rainforest above the Hamakua coast, most of the rest of which went to cane and then to pasture, and inside that fence an understory species that normally stays modest has run to something close to a record.

The state rates its condition fair rather than good, which is worth knowing before you walk out to it: this one is a heavyweight, not a portrait. It sits on the same 0.7 mile loop as its much slimmer and much taller counterpart, and the pair of them are the best argument the trail makes for how variable a single Hawaiian species can be.

The state register is the only source that names this tree individually. The park's own trail notes describe the forest rather than its members, so the measurement rests on one authority instead of two.

Its age is blank, as it is for everything here, because Hawaii's register records trunks and does not date them. If anyone has counted the rings of a kopiko 'ula, tell us.

trees.name: The Larger Kalopa Ohi'a Lehua
trees.access: Free day-use state park, open 7am-8pm daily, no entrance fee. On the marked 0.7-mile Kalopa Nature Trail loop, which the DLNR itself describes as passing beneath 'large, old growth ohi'a trees' forming the upper canopy.
trees.transport: No public transit. By car via Kalopa Road, about 5 miles (10 minutes) inland from Honokaa off Mamalahoa Highway (Hwy 19); free parking at the park office near the trailhead.
trees.story:
This is the largest tree on the loop: 4.39 metres round, about 26 metres tall, and rated in excellent health when the state last measured it. Ohi'a lehua is also the tree that colonises bare lava, the first green thing to appear on new ground on this island, and it goes on to hold the canopy over almost every wet native forest Hawaii has left.

The state parks department describes this trail as running beneath large old growth ohi'a, and this is the biggest of them on record. The species reaches roughly 30 metres in the wettest forest, so this one is near its ceiling. Ohi'a is a famously slow grower, which means a trunk 1.4 metres thick represents a great deal of time. Nobody has attached a number to it. If you know of a count, tell us and it goes on the page.

One honest note on finding it. The register entry carries the measurements and no address at all, so this tree is placed at Kalopa because its coordinates match the other five listed here and because the park's own account of its canopy fits what is recorded. The pin is park-level in any case. Walk the 0.7 mile loop, look up, and take the crown that everything else on the trail is standing under.

trees.name: The Smaller Kalopa Ohi'a Lehua
trees.access: Free day-use state park, open 7am-8pm daily, no entrance fee. On the marked 0.7-mile Kalopa Nature Trail loop.
trees.transport: No public transit. By car via Kalopa Road, about 5 miles (10 minutes) inland from Honokaa off Mamalahoa Highway (Hwy 19); free parking at the park office near the trailhead.
trees.story:
Pick a lehua blossom, the saying goes, and it will rain before you get home, because the flower and the tree that carries it were lovers the volcano goddess parted. The tree is the ohi'a. The red brush of a flower is the lehua.

This is the second of the two large ohi'a on the Kalopa loop: 3.84 metres round, about 22 metres tall, in excellent condition by the state's reckoning, and a little smaller than its neighbour in every direction. Between them they are the reason the trail looks the way it does. Ohi'a builds the canopy of Hawaiian wet forest and its flowers are the main food of the native honeycreepers, so an old stand of it is not only a roof, it is what keeps birds in the air above you.

Kalopa holds about a hundred acres of that forest and roughly twenty-five native species along 0.7 miles of path, several of them down to a single plant.

This tree's register entry, like its neighbour's, gives measurements and no address, so it sits here on coordinates that match the rest of the park's listed trees. Its age is unrecorded, as it is for all six. Ohi'a thickens slowly and this trunk has plainly had time, but nobody has counted, and if you have, we will take the correction.

trees.name: The Kalakaua Park Banyan
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; central downtown Hilo, an easy walk from the bayfront and most Hilo accommodation
trees.story:
Two men are credited with planting this banyan and they cannot both be right. Wikipedia and a Hilo guide both say Sheriff Luther Severance put it in at the west end of Kalakaua Park in 1882, which makes it about 144 years old. A newspaper account from 1964 credits King Kalakaua himself. Neither source settles it and this page does not pick.

What is not in dispute is the size. The exceptional-tree register puts 18.6 metres around it, and that figure is not a trunk: Ficus benghalensis drops aerial roots that thicken into props, and the measurement runs around the whole buttressed mass. Standing under one is less like meeting a tree than walking into a room with a ceiling.

It had a twin. When Waianuenue Avenue was widened, Sheriff George Williams had the other original moved about five miles up to Kaumana, which in 1882 terms is a remarkable thing to attempt and in any terms is a remarkable thing to survive.

Hawaii protects individual trees by law, under Act 105 of 1975, and the designation attaches to the specimen rather than to the ground it stands on. This one is in the middle of downtown Hilo with a lawn under it and two more protected trees in the same small park.

trees.name: The Haili Street Kamani
trees.access: Free, on a public street corner outside Haili Congregational Church
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; downtown Hilo, an easy walk from Kalakaua Park and the bayfront
trees.story:
The register calls it a False Kamani and the newspaper that loves it does not. In 2014 the Hawaii Tribune-Herald ran a piece on the treasured kamani tree at the corner of Haili and Ululani, gave its age as 194 years, and left the qualifier off, which is the usual local shorthand. Botanically the two are unrelated: true kamani is Calophyllum inophyllum, and this is Terminalia catappa, the tropical almond, whose leaves turn red and drop in a place where almost nothing else changes colour.

Take the newspaper's figure forward and the tree is about 206 years old now, which puts it here before the church it stands beside, before Hilo was a town of any size, and before anyone thought to write down what was growing on this corner.

The register records 12.2 metres around it and rates its condition good. Terminalia catappa grows in tiers, with branches thrown out in flat horizontal whorls that stack up the trunk, so from across the street it reads as a series of green plates rather than a dome.

It stands on the pavement outside Haili Congregational Church, which means you can walk up to it at any hour without asking anyone.

trees.name: The Rainbow Falls Banyan
trees.access: Free, within Wailuku River State Park, generally open sunrise to sunset. A dedicated parking area serves the falls; no public bus stop at the trailhead.
trees.transport: A short drive or taxi ride from downtown Hilo; the tree stands past the upper viewing platform along the park trail, an easy walk from the parking area.
trees.story:
The register designates this tree and then records nothing about it. No girth, no height, no condition: just an Indian banyan at Rainbow Falls, protected under Act 105 like the rest, with every measurement column left blank.

So what stands here is described rather than measured. It grows along the trail that continues past the upper viewing platform above the falls, away from the crowd that stops at the railing, and it is the sprawling aerial-root kind of banyan rather than a single trunk: props coming down from the limbs and rooting where they land, which is how one of these walks slowly sideways over a century.

Nobody has published an age for it either, and that is the honest state of it rather than a gap we intend to fill with arithmetic. Banyans cannot be aged from girth anyway, because the figure would be a measurement of the whole colony rather than of one stem.

Wailuku River State Park is free and open from sunrise to sunset, and the falls themselves are the reason most people come. The tree is the thing you find by walking two minutes further than they do. If you know when it went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Divi-Divi of Kalakaua Park
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; central downtown Hilo, an easy walk from the bayfront and most Hilo accommodation
trees.story:
A divi-divi is a strange thing to find protected in a Hawaiian town square. Caesalpinia coriaria comes from the dry forests of the Caribbean and Central America, it is the national tree of Curacao, and its seed pods were harvested for the tannin that turned hides into leather. Nothing about that story runs through Hilo, which gets more than three metres of rain a year.

It is here anyway, at 3.3 metres round, in good condition, one of three protected trees in Kalakaua Park along with the 1882 banyan and an endangered native palm. Hilo's own downtown walking tour includes the park's trees and describes them as more than a century old as a group, which is corroboration for the park and not a date for this tree, so no age is claimed here.

The species is worth looking at properly once you find it. Divi-divi grow slowly and hold their branches in a lopsided, wind-combed way even where there is no wind, and the pods curl into tight brown spirals that look more like something that fell off an animal than off a tree.

The park is small, open daily and free, and it sits in the middle of downtown, which makes all three of its trees one short stop rather than three.

trees.name: The Loulu Palm of Kalakaua Park
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; central downtown Hilo, an easy walk from the bayfront and most Hilo accommodation
trees.story:
This palm is endangered in the wild and it is growing in a public park. Pritchardia beccariana is one of roughly two dozen loulu species found nowhere on earth but Hawaii, all of them threatened, and this one is native to the Big Island specifically. Rats eat the seeds, which is most of why they are disappearing.

Hawaii's exceptional-tree register lists it at 26 feet tall and rates its condition fair, which is an honest reading rather than a reassuring one. No girth is recorded, and none would help: a palm is not a tree in the way the ageing arithmetic assumes, with no annual rings and no secondary thickening, so nobody can put a number on how long it has stood here.

Loulu once covered lowland Hawaii in forests dense enough that early accounts describe them as impassable. What is left is scattered specimens and small protected stands, which makes a healthy one in the middle of Hilo something closer to a museum piece than a park planting.

It shares Kalakaua Park with the banyan and the divi-divi, so all three are one stop, and it is the only one of them that belongs here.

trees.name: The Oak of Imstenrade
trees.age: roughly 180 to 230 years, from the register's planting band of 1800-1850
trees.access: Free, public woodland, open daily.
trees.story:
This oak grows in woodland that a nature conservation body now manages, on the north edge of ground once part of Imstenrade, one of the country estates that ring Heerlen's old core. The national tree register bands its planting to 1800-1850, which makes it somewhere between 180 and 230 years old, wide enough that neither end of the range can be ruled out.

What the register does not give is any history of the tree itself, only the place: managed woodland, publicly walkable, no plaque, no story attached. That is common for oaks that grew up inside a private estate's boundary rather than beside a house or a church, where someone was more likely to notice and remember a planting.

A pedunculate oak of this age has usually stopped growing upward and started growing outward, its lower limbs thickening into the wide, layered crown that reads as unmistakably old even to someone who could not guess a year. Two centuries in one spot also means it has outlasted whatever the estate itself was doing during that time, from working farmland to protected woodland today.

The register is the only source that has looked at this tree. If you know more about it, tell us.

trees.name: The Oak of Nieuw Eyckholt
trees.age: roughly 170 years, from a registered planting date around 1860
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.story:
A second oak from the same wider stretch of woodland as its neighbour at Imstenrade, this one growing at the edge of the trees on the north side of Nieuw Eyckholt. The register bands its planting to 1850-1860, putting it at roughly 170 years, a generation or two younger than the Imstenrade oak and considerably more precisely dated.

Eyckholt takes its name from the ruined medieval castle whose stronghold still stands nearby, first built around 1300 on the wooded slope above the Geleen valley. By the 1850s the ground around it had long since settled into ordinary estate woodland, and an oak planted at a forest edge in that decade would have grown up with room on one side and competition from other trees on the other, a lopsided crown often being the visible result.

Nothing beyond the register describes this tree specifically: no plaque, no local story, just a species, a decade and a place. That is not unusual for a woodland-edge planting rather than one that stood beside a house or a road where people were more likely to notice it and remember why it went in.

If you know more about this oak, tell us.

trees.name: The Oak of the Neighbourhood
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, on the public square.
trees.story:
The register's own name for this tree translates as simply "the oak of the neighbourhood", and its own note is almost as plain: almost certainly planted when the neighbourhood itself was built. Eikenderveld, the district it stands in, was laid out in the 1920s between the railway and the green grounds of Terworm, and this oak on the little square where Markiesstraat meets Schoutstraat, Jonkerstraat and Stadhouderstraat is registered to that decade, roughly a century old.

A street tree planted with a new neighbourhood is a different kind of veteran from an estate oak grown up in woodland: it has spent its whole life with pavement and front doors around it rather than other trees, which usually means more light, faster early growth and a more rounded, open crown. A hundred years is young by oak standards, well short of when an oak this size typically starts slowing down, so this is a tree with most of its life still ahead of it.

Eikenderveld's own name, meaning oak field, suggests the district was named for trees like this one rather than the other way round. The register is the only source describing it specifically. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Lime of Eikendermolenweg
trees.age: roughly 330 to 430 years, from the register's planting band of 1600-1700
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public land, always visible.
trees.story:
The register bands this lime to the 1600s, which would make it three to four centuries old, decades older than the plane tree across the road that already carries Heerlen's own claim to the city's oldest tree. Unlike that plane, this lime has no local nickname, no information board and no history recorded anywhere the register could point to: only a species, a rough century and an address on the other side of Eikendermolenweg from Kasteel Eyckholt's grounds.
