A lime left standing for three or four hundred years usually shows it in the trunk rather than the crown: a common lime develops burrs and epicormic shoots low down as it ages, sometimes thickening into a skirt of new growth around an old, split or hollowing base, while the crown above can go on looking healthy for centuries past what the trunk alone would suggest. Whether this one shows any of that has not been recorded.

The register survey this age comes from is recent, and nothing in it suggests the tree is gone, but a lime this old with no other source describing it is exactly the kind of gap a reader can close in one visit. If you have stood at this spot, tell us what you saw.

trees.name: The Plane of Terworm
trees.age: roughly 230 to 280 years, from the register's planting band of 1750-1800
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public land, always visible.
trees.story:
Everyone in Heerlen calls this tree the Eik van Terworm, the Oak of Terworm, and it is not an oak. It is a plane, and the name has stuck regardless, attached to a tree the register bands to 1750-1800 and local sources call the oldest in the city at around 280 years.

The register's own note gives a specific occasion: probably planted in 1749, to mark the birth of the heir to Terworm, the estate whose grounds still surround the castle a short walk away. An information board at the tree repeats the story. Planting a tree for a birth was ordinary practice on estates like this one, meant to grow alongside the child it marked and to outlast them both, which this one has done by nearly two hundred years already.

It stands alone at a junction near the Eikendermolenweg, the kind of solitary position that let it build the wide, low crown a plane develops when nothing crowds it. Locals treat it as a boundary marker between what were once separate estates, though nobody has confirmed that was the original intent rather than a story that grew up around an old tree at a crossroads, the way stories do.

Go looking for an oak and you will walk straight past it.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Meezenbroek
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
This tulip tree grows in the park built around the Meezenbroek ponds before the Second World War, in a district that started life in the 1920s as De Voorzorg, a colony of housing built for the miners working Heerlen's coal seams. The register bands its planting to 1930-1940, putting it at roughly 90 years, a near contemporary of the park itself.

Liriodendron tulipifera is North American, not European, and its name undersells the spectacle: the flowers it produces from early summer are cup-shaped, greenish yellow with an orange band inside, more like a stylised magnolia than a tulip, and easy to miss from below because they open high in the crown facing upward. The leaves are the more reliable giveaway, four-lobed and squared off at the tip as if cut with scissors, turning a clean butter yellow in autumn.

A former mining colony with a purpose-built park is not the setting most people imagine for an American forest tree, and that mismatch is most of what makes it worth a detour. The register is the only source that has described it. If you know more about when or why it was planted, tell us.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Terworm
trees.age: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1920
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public land, always visible.
trees.story:
This ginkgo grows along the drive to Kasteel Terworm, in good health as of a 2026 survey, standing where anyone walking up to the castle's front door can see it. The register bands its planting to 1910-1920, roughly a century, and offers two guesses rather than one: either it went in during an 1890s renovation under Baron de Loë, or during the few years around 1902 to 1907 when the estate was let to a mining baron named Wenckenbach, whose industry was reshaping the whole Heerlen region at the time.

Terworm's own history runs back to around 1400 and a family named Van der Worm, through at least six rebuildings to the house that stands today, a period as an open-air swimming pool in its lower pond during the 1930s, and a near miss with becoming a theme park that Heerlen's own residents blocked. It is a hotel now, and the wooded estate around it belongs to Natuurmonumenten, a conservation organisation, which is why the grounds stay open to walkers rather than becoming private again.

A ginkgo this size beside an old yew planting makes the drive up to the castle one of the more photogenic approaches in the register. If you know which decade it actually went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Catalpa at the Town Hall
trees.age: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1920
trees.access: Free, on the public square.

best_time.label: July, when the orchid-like flowers open in loose clusters across the crown

trees.story:
This catalpa stands outside Heerlen's town hall, built from the local Kunrade limestone in a style locals still call Roman, and the register bands its planting to 1910-1920, putting it at around 110 years, roughly as old as the building's neighbourhood setting. A 2021 note in the register records that the tree has since been given a bench built around its base and steel props holding up a swing hung from one of its limbs, a small piece of civic care that most trees on this list have not had recorded for them.

Southern catalpa is an American tree, grown for its broad heart-shaped leaves and, in midsummer, loose clusters of white, orchid-like flowers spotted purple and yellow inside each throat. Long bean-like seed pods follow in autumn and can hang on through winter, which is where the tree's other common name, Indian bean, comes from, misleadingly, since it has no connection to India at all.

A public bench built around a tree is usually a sign a town has decided that tree matters to keep. The register is the only source describing this one specifically. If you know its planting story, tell us.

trees.name: The King's Oak
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus 560 to the Kappatie stop, then a short walk; roughly 30 minutes from central Helsinki

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: A Swedish king is said to have knelt in the mud here and planted an acorn himself. Tradition holds that Gustav III set this oak in the ground during a visit in the late 1700s, and the district that grew up around it centuries later, Kuninkaantammi, took the tree's name rather than the other way around: king's oak first, neighbourhood second. Whether the royal hand ever touched the sapling is impossible to check now, since no contemporary record survives, only the story passed down through the area's own residents. What is measurable is the tree itself: 404 centimetres around the trunk and 20 metres tall by the city's own 2003 survey, protected as a natural monument since 1956, one of 31 such trees and formations across Helsinki. It stands where the Vantaanjoki river narrows into the Pitkäkoski rapids, on the edge of the long green corridor of Helsinki's Central Park, a spot a king or anyone else might reasonably choose to stop and admire the water. Two and a half centuries on, the oak has outlasted the kingdom that supposedly planted it: Finland left Swedish rule in 1809, a few decades after the tree, if the story holds, first broke the ground.

trees.name: The Kirjanpuisto Willow
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 15-20 minute walk from Senate Square, central Helsinki
trees.story: Twenty children once fit inside this willow at the same time, according to local lore, tucked into a hollow trunk that has been slowly swallowing itself for over a century. At 8.4 metres around, it is the thickest tree standing anywhere in Helsinki, a title with real competition from the city's oaks and limes but no serious challenger among willows. The tree was already remarkable enough by 1907 to be documented and photographed, and the city protected it as a natural monument in 1924, decades before Helsinki had any broader system for saving trees at all. Officially it is a crack willow, though residents of Kruununhaka know it by the Finnish name isoriippasalava, the big weeping willow, a name that describes its shape better than its species does. A wooden crutch now props up one of its heaviest limbs, an old-fashioned fix for an old tree that has stopped being able to hold all of itself up. The park around it, Kirjanpuisto, is barely bigger than a city block, wedged between apartment buildings a fifteen-minute walk from Senate Square, easy to miss unless you already know a tree this size is hiding there.

trees.name: The Tali Manor Oak
trees.access: Free, but within Helsinki Golf Club's grounds; use the estate's public paths rather than crossing the fairways
trees.transport: Short walk or local bus from Pitäjänmäki railway station, roughly 15 minutes

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Finland's second-thickest oak grows behind a golf clubhouse, which is either an odd place for a national record or exactly where you would expect one, since golf courses are where old estate trees survive by accident. The oak's girth has been measured twice, 56 years apart: 440 centimetres in 1957, 616 by 2013, a growth rate that on its own suggests an age reaching back to the 1600s or 1700s, before the manor whose grounds it stands on took its current shape. Talin kartano, Tali Manor, gave its land to golf in 1932, when Helsinki Golf Club built Finland's oldest course here, and the oak simply stayed put through nine decades of fairways being routed and rerouted around it. It has never been core-sampled, so its age is inference from thickness rather than a counted ring, and this entry treats it that way rather than pretending to more precision than anyone actually has. The tree stands close to the clubhouse rather than out on the playing holes, reachable on the estate's public paths without crossing a fairway, though checking in at the clubhouse first is the considerate way to go looking for it.

trees.name: The Tullisaari Lime
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Bus from central Helsinki across the Laajasalo bridge, then a 20 minute walk

best_time.label: July to August, when it flowers

trees.story: Finland's thickest park lime grows on an island in Helsinki's own harbour, in a manor garden most visitors reach by accident on the way to somewhere else. Tuurholma, now usually called Tullisaari, was a shipping family's private park until the city took it over, and the trees planted for one household's private pleasure well over a century ago have been growing for the public ever since. The lime's trunk has been measured at up to 450 centimetres around, officially protected since 1956 alongside a scatter of equally outsized specimens across the same small park, including a black alder Finland lists among its thickest, and an oak that stood as a natural monument for six decades before a 2020 storm finally brought it down. The lime alone survived that storm standing, its trunk long since hollowed by age into a shape you can see clean through, held together as much by bark as by wood. Reaching it means crossing the Laajasalo bridge from central Helsinki, a bus ride and a walk of about twenty minutes through what feels less like a city park than a private estate nobody bothered to close the gate on.

trees.name: The Herttoniemi Pear Tree
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Herttoniemi metro station

best_time.label: early May, when the pear blossoms

trees.story: The last fruit tree standing in a manor garden that once grew many is also, by several accounts, the oldest and tallest pear tree in Finland. Herttoniemi Manor kept a working orchard through the 1800s, part of the estate's kitchen garden alongside berries and other fruit, and every other tree from that planting has since died, been felled, or simply vanished from the record. This one pear held on: a trunk 277 centimetres around, a height over 15 metres, well beyond what a garden pear usually reaches before age or disease takes it down. It has lost one of its original three main limbs over the decades, the kind of damage that would finish a smaller specimen, and kept fruiting anyway, sour pears nobody plants pear trees for anymore but the tree makes regardless. Herttoniemi's manor grounds passed from private to public hands during the 20th century, the same pattern behind several of Helsinki's oldest trees, and today the pear stands in an open park a short walk from Herttoniemi metro station, no ticket or appointment required, just a tree quietly outliving the garden built around it.

trees.name: The Meilahti Ancient Pine
trees.access: Free, open shoreline park at any time
trees.transport: Tram 4 or 10 to the Meilahden sairaala stop, then a short walk
trees.story: Helsinki's oldest confirmed tree grows next to a grave older than the city itself, a Bronze Age burial cairn built around 2000 BC on a rocky shore in Meilahti. Core sampling and ring counting put the pine's age at roughly 340 years, meaning it took root sometime in the late 1600s, more than a century before Helsinki became Finland's capital and long before Meilahti was anything but rock and shoreline forest. It has grown slowly and stayed short for a pine, barely 10 metres tall, stunted the way trees often are when they spend three centuries rooted in thin soil over bare granite rather than easy farmland. That slow growth is very likely what kept it alive this long: a faster-growing tree on the same ground would have run out of room, or been worth cutting for timber, decades before this one reached its second century. The pine and the grave beside it now share the same small patch of shoreline park, reachable by tram to Meilahti hospital and a short walk toward the water, both quietly older than almost everything else in the neighbourhood around them.

trees.name: The North Haaga Snake-branch Spruce
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Local bus or train to Pohjois-Haaga, then a short walk, roughly 20-25 minutes from central Helsinki
trees.story: Most snake-branch spruces stay under 15 metres for their entire lives, a natural size limit built into the mutation that gives the variety its name, unbranched whip-like limbs that hang rather than spread. The specimen in this Pohjois-Haaga park broke that ceiling by a wide margin, reaching past 25 metres, taller than almost anything else planted in the form anywhere. Picea abies f. virgata is a genuine oddity of Norway spruce, a natural mutant first identified in the 19th century and prized ever since for looking almost nothing like a normal spruce: instead of the usual dense pyramid of branches, its limbs run long, bare and snakelike straight off the trunk, drooping rather than climbing. Helsinki protected this one as a natural monument in 1956, and by the city's own 2003 measurements its trunk had reached 164 centimetres around, respectable for the form though its real distinction is height rather than girth. It stands in an ordinary residential park between two streets, easy to walk straight past if you do not already know that an otherwise normal spruce silhouette should not, on closer look, have branches quite this strange.

trees.name: The Eira Sea Buckthorn
trees.access: Free, open waterfront path at any time
trees.transport: Tram 3 to the Eiran sairaala stop, then a short walk to the shore

best_time.label: late September, when the berries turn bright orange

trees.story: Sea buckthorn is a shrub by nature, the kind of scrubby, thorny plant that clings to Baltic sand dunes and rarely reaches head height. The one growing on Eira's shoreline forgot to read its own species description: over seven metres tall, a trunk more than a metre around, grown into something closer to a small tree than anything botanists expect from Hippophae rhamnoides. It stands on the Merisatama waterfront path directly across from the small island of Sirpalesaari, close enough to the Baltic that salt spray probably explains part of why it took root here in the first place. As a female plant it fruits every autumn, small orange berries packed with vitamin C that Finns have long picked for juice and jam, though this specimen has grown tall enough that harvesting from it would take a ladder rather than the usual bent-over shrub-picking. Nobody has dated it, since sea buckthorn does not get studied the way old oaks do, but its size alone earned it official protection as a natural monument in 1999. A short walk from the Eiran sairaala tram stop puts you right on the waterfront path beside it, no detour required if you are already out walking Eira's shore.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Landgoed Bantam
trees.age: roughly 150 years, from a registered planting date around 1880
trees.access: Free, the estate is managed by a nature conservation organisation and open to visitors.
trees.story: Left to itself in open ground an oriental plane spreads sideways rather than upward, and this one has had a meadow to do it in for about a century and a half. It stands free on the east side of the pond at Landgoed Bantam, an estate laid out as a landscape garden in the late 1870s and nicknamed Klein Zwitserland for its artificial hills. The hills and the ponds are still there, and so are the straight beech and oak avenues from the same period. The national register dates this plane to the estate's first years, giving a band that puts it at roughly 150 years old. That is a band rather than a measurement, and the register is the only source we have found for the tree, so treat the age as its estimate. Platanus orientalis is the eastern parent of the London plane that lines half the streets in Europe, and the difference shows in the leaf: cut far deeper, into five narrow fingers, closer to a maple than to its own offspring. The bark flakes in the same olive and cream plates. Individual trees of this species in Greece and Turkey are credibly reckoned at many centuries, so at 150 years this one is barely into middle age. The estate is managed as a nature reserve and open to walkers.

trees.name: The Coronation Lime of the Spanderslaan
trees.age: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.access: Free, public woodland, open daily.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when the flowers open and the crown hums

trees.story: Wilhelmina was eighteen when she was crowned in 1898, and the country marked it by planting limes. The register records this as one of them, standing at the crossing of the Spanderslaan and the Oude Meentweg with a wrought iron fence still around it, which is the giveaway: an ordinary woodland lime does not get railings. The register dates the tree to the 1890s, so roughly 130 years, and it is the only source we have located for it. Wilhelmina went on to reign for fifty eight years, through two world wars and an exile in London, and the tree has outlasted her by decades without any sign of stopping. Tilia x europaea is a hybrid Dutch towns planted by the thousand: heart shaped leaves that go butter yellow in autumn, a permanent thicket of shoots around the base of the trunk that comes back however often it is cut, and small yellow-green flowers in late June that smell of honey and pull in every bee for streets around. Look for the mushroom shaped path marker at the junction, number 24591. The tree is beside it, in public woodland that is open all day. If you know whether the fence around it is the original one from 1898, we would like to hear.

trees.name: The Bernhard Chestnut of the Hilvertsweg
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles stand up all over the crown

trees.story: At the fork of the Hilvertsweg and the Bosdrift stand two trees and two boulders, and the inscriptions on the boulders have worn down to almost nothing. The register explains them: a horse chestnut and a lime, planted in 1937 for the marriage of Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard. This is the chestnut, the Bernhard tree, roughly 90 years old on the register's dating, and the register is the only record we have found of it. Horse chestnut was an odd choice for a royal wedding if anyone was thinking long term. It is a Balkan mountain tree, spectacular for two weeks and structurally unserious for the rest of the year: soft wood, shallow roots, limbs that fail without much warning, and since the 1990s a leaf miner moth that turns the foliage brown by August across northern Europe. What it does have is May. The flowers stand up in white candles all over the crown, thousands of them, each with a yellow blotch that turns red once the flower has been pollinated so that bees stop wasting visits on it. Then in September the conkers come down and the children take them. Bernhard died in 2004. The tree has outlived him by two decades and is still holding the corner.

trees.name: The Juliana Lime of the Hilvertsweg
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when the scent crosses the road before you see the tree

trees.story: A lime was the safe choice, and that is the point of it. Dutch villages have planted limes at crossroads and in front of churches for centuries, the tree you hold a market under or hang a lantern in, and this one stands at the fork of the Hilvertsweg and the Bosdrift next to a horse chestnut, with worn inscribed stones at the foot of both. The register records the pair as planted in 1937 for the wedding of Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard, and dates this one to the 1930s, so roughly 90 years. It is the only source we have located for the tree. Juliana was twenty eight at the wedding, became queen in 1948 and abdicated in 1980 in favour of her daughter, which for a Dutch monarch is the ordinary way to leave the job. Tilia x europaea forgives almost anything done to it. Cut one to a stump and it comes back from the base, which is why so many survive road widening that finished off everything else at a junction. In late June the flowers open, pale and not much to look at, and the scent reaches you across the road. Stand under it then and the noise overhead is bees rather than traffic.

trees.name: The Cedar of Pinetum Blijdenstein
trees.age: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story: When the house came down in 1928 the land was parcelled up and sold, all of it except the walled garden, which the owner's will required to be kept. That garden is the Pinetum Blijdenstein, and this western red cedar has stood in its southeast corner since close to the beginning. Benjamin Willem Blijdenstein was an Amsterdam banker who bought six hectares here in 1880, had a villa built, and in 1898 turned the estate's walled fruit and vegetable garden into a collection of conifers. He worked on it until he died in 1914. The register dates this tree to that first period, a band that puts it at roughly 130 years old, and it names a giant sequoia from the same years standing nearby. The register is the only source we have found for it. Thuja plicata comes from the Pacific Northwest, where the coastal peoples built canoes, longhouses and totem poles out of it and where the species can pass a thousand years. Crush a spray of the flat green foliage and it smells of pineapple. The bark peels away in long fibrous strips, and the branch tips droop before turning up at the end, which is how you tell it from the cypresses around it. The paths Hendrik Copijn drew in 1909 are still broadly the ones you walk on.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of the Soestdijkerstraatweg
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public land, always visible.
trees.story: In 1990 the street was repaved and the cedar nearly died of it. Pipes went in between the trunk and the front gardens, straight across the root plate. By 1994 the municipality was digging test pits and rebuilding the soil underneath; by the summer of 1996 the tree had recovered reasonably; in May 2005 the register's own inspector recorded it as doing only moderately, with dead and broken branches. It has been pruned hard since and stands a little out of balance because of it. All of which is what a 140 year old Atlas cedar looks like when you set it in paving on a through road. The register dates the tree to the 1880s and notes that the houses along here went up around 1900, so the cedar was standing before the street was. Cedrus atlantica comes from the Atlas mountains of Morocco and Algeria, where it grows on dry limestone at altitude and is now threatened in its own range. On the Soestdijkerstraatweg it gets the opposite of everything it evolved for: wet feet, compacted ground, road salt and services under the roots. It has managed 140 years anyway. The needles sit in tight blue-grey rosettes on short spurs and the branches leave the trunk in flat horizontal tiers you can read from across the road. The register is the only source we have found for it.

trees.name: The King Banyan of Kowloon Park
trees.age: about 400 years (recognised as Hong Kong's largest urban tree in 1997)
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui station, via Haiphong Road entrance
trees.story: A third of this banyan's trunk came down in a 2007 typhoon, and what remains is still recognised as Hong Kong's largest urban tree by trunk girth, a title the government's own tree register gave it in 1997 when arborists put its age at around four hundred years. Indian laurel figs are common street trees across the city, planted by the thousand along roads and in parks, but almost none of them are left to grow old and wide the way this one has, standing above the spectator stand of Kowloon Park's mini soccer pitch since long before the park existed. The ground beneath it was British military land from the 1890s until 1967, part of the former Whitfield Barracks, three years before the Urban Council turned the site into a public park. The tree is old enough to have shaded soldiers on parade before it ever shaded families with strollers. It is now fighting a slower fight than the typhoon: brown root rot, a fungal disease that has spread through several of Hong Kong's oldest trees, has been detected in its roots, and the government has kept it under continuous monitoring and treatment rather than felling it, a decision conservation groups pushed hard for when the disease was first found. The crown still spreads wide enough over the pitch to be unmistakable, cracked trunk and all.

trees.name: The Stone Wall Trees of Forbes Street
trees.age: wall dates to the 1890s; several trees individually over 100 years
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: At Exit C of MTR Kennedy Town station (Island Line)
trees.story: When engineers first drew up plans to extend the MTR through Kennedy Town, a wall of nearly thirty banyan trees stood directly in the way, and after a 2005 flash-mob campaign by the Conservancy Association, the MTR rerouted the station underneath the old Kennedy Town Swimming Pool instead and built an exit specifically to leave the wall alone. Twenty-seven Chinese banyans and figs grow straight out of three stone masonry retaining walls along Forbes Street, roots fused into brickwork some records date to the 1890s, when the street was first laid out near the American Forbes family's Hong Kong Rope Works. It is the largest tree wall of its kind in the city, out of roughly 1,200 masonry wall trees recorded across Hong Kong, and several of its oldest specimens are individually listed on the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register. Stone wall trees grow the way this dense, hillside city forced them to: a seed lands in a crack, roots spread through mortar instead of soil, and given enough decades the tree and the wall become one structure, impossible to remove one without damaging the other. That, as much as the 2005 campaign, is what actually saved this one. It stands on an ordinary residential street a few minutes from the tram terminus, walls and trees together, exactly where the fight to keep them left them.

trees.name: The Kam Tin Tree House
trees.age: the banyan is over 100 years old; the stone ruin it engulfs is late Ming dynasty
trees.access: Free, public playground
trees.transport: By minibus from Yuen Long or Kam Sheung Road MTR station towards Kam Tin, short walk from Shui Mei Village
trees.story: Nobody agrees on what this stone house was originally for, a temple, a study hall, a family residence, but everybody agrees on why it stands empty: in 1661, the new Qing dynasty ordered Hong Kong's coastline evacuated to cut off supplies reaching Ming loyalist rebels, and the Tang clan family who owned this house in Kam Tin left with everyone else. Villagers were kept from the coast for eight years, and by the time the order lifted, whoever had lived here never came back. The building sat abandoned long enough that, at some point in the following centuries, a Chinese banyan took root in it, and it has spent more than a hundred years since growing directly through the structure rather than around it, trunk and roots forcing themselves through gaps in the brickwork until tree and ruin became a single object. What is left today reads less like a house with a tree beside it than a tree that happens to have kept a house's walls as part of its own shape, roof long gone, window openings now just holes the trunk grows past. It stands in a public playground in Shui Mei Village, a short trip by minibus from Yuen Long or Kam Sheung Road, one of the more unusual things a seventeenth-century eviction order has ever produced.

trees.name: The Camphor of She Shan Tsuen
trees.age: estimated 300-500 years, most often cited as about 400
trees.access: Free, reachable via a footpath behind the village; part of a protected Site of Special Scientific Interest, please keep to the path
trees.transport: By minibus or car to Lam Tsuen off Lam Kam Road, then a short walk to She Shan village
trees.story: Ten adults linking arms cannot fully encircle this camphor's trunk, and the tree they would be hugging predates every building in the village it half-hides. She Shan Tsuen's feng shui woodland, 5.7 hectares the government protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest in 1975, exists because villages across Hong Kong's New Territories deliberately left a strip of hillside forest standing behind their houses, believing an intact wood at a settlement's back shielded it from bad fortune and worse weather. Camphor trees anchor most of these feng shui woods, chosen centuries ago for their size and longevity rather than planted at random, and She Shan's has grown into one of the largest examples in the New Territories: a 32 metre crown, seven storeys of glossy waxy leaves, and an age historical references put between three and five centuries, most often cited at around four hundred years. Government inspectors have logged a severe cavity and dead branches in recent surveys, the ordinary wear of a tree old enough that nobody alive remembers it being young, and it remains under continuous monitoring and pruning rather than removal. It stands on the wooded slope directly behind the village, a short walk off Lam Kam Road, still doing the job it was left standing there to do.

trees.name: The King Camphor of Sha Lo Wan
trees.age: undated; local and official tourism material claims over 1,000 years but no scientific dating exists
trees.access: Free, public village land
trees.transport: By kaido ferry from Tung Chung to Sha Lo Wan, or via the Lantau coastal footpath
trees.story: Japanese soldiers cut down most of Lantau Island's large trees for fuel during the wartime occupation, and by local account, they stopped short of this one because they believed a guardian spirit haunted it and would frighten off anyone who tried. Whether the spirit or something more practical spared it, the camphor beside Sha Lo Wan's old village school survived a period when little large timber on the island did, and villagers still call it Sha Lo Wan's King Camphor. Hong Kong's own tourism authority repeats the village's claim that it is over a thousand years old, a figure with no scientific dating behind it and best treated as local tradition rather than a measured fact, though camphors are long-lived enough that a large old specimen reaching many centuries is far from implausible. What is certain is its role: Sha Lo Wan, a fishing village on Lantau's quiet north-west coast reachable by a coastal footpath or a rural kaido ferry from Tung Chung, has treated this tree as a feng shui guardian for generations, the kind of tree a village builds its sense of protection around rather than fells for a hard winter. It still stands on the government-registered slope beside the school, watched over rather than the other way around now.

trees.name: The Five-Finger Camphor of Lai Chi Wo
trees.age: undocumented; a mature specimen already large enough to be targeted during the WWII occupation
trees.neighbourhood: Lai Chi Wo, Sha Tau Kok
trees.access: Free, within an active countryside conservation and rural revival area
trees.transport: By ferry from Ma Liu Shui (weekends and public holidays) or a hike from Wu Kau Tang
trees.story: Only one of this camphor's original five trunks is missing, and the reason it lost that one and not the rest is the whole story: during the Japanese occupation, soldiers came to cut the tree for fuel, and Lai Chi Wo's villagers physically stood between them and the trunk. They lost the argument over a single branch. Four still remain, splayed from a shared base wide enough that the tree is simply known as the Five-Finger Camphor, and it has stood in the feng shui woodland behind this Hakka village since before anyone alive can date it. Hakka settlers built Lai Chi Wo in the 16th century, grew it to more than two hundred houses and over a thousand residents by laying the village out on strict geomantic lines, and then watched it empty through the 1960s and 70s as families left for the city and abroad. The camphor stayed, along with the rest of the feng shui wood's more than a hundred native plant species, and it has become the emblem of a rural revival effort that has slowly repopulated and restored the village since the 2010s. Reaching it means a ferry from Ma Liu Shui or a hike in from Wu Kau Tang, through one of the last intact Hakka settlements left in Hong Kong's New Territories, to stand under four fingers where there used to be five.

trees.name: The Stonewall Fig of Ka Wai Man Road
trees.access: Free, public garden, viewable at any time
trees.transport: Short walk from MTR Kennedy Town station Exit C, one street over from the Forbes Street stone wall trees
trees.story: Hong Kong's government files this tree under two categories at once, and the second is the interesting half. The Old and Valuable Trees register lists it as OVT and SWT together, Old and Valuable Tree and Stonewall Tree, and the department responsible for it is not the one that runs the city's parks. It is the Architectural Services Department, which looks after government masonry. The whole story sits in that administrative detail: this fig is maintained by the people who maintain walls, because a wall is what it grows out of. The measurements are serious. A trunk 1.8 metres through, seventeen metres tall, a crown spreading twenty-four metres, and an inspection record noting three separate leans, one growing toward the light, one a response to load, and one the tree corrected by itself, which is what decades of pushing out of vertical stonework and rebalancing looks like written down. No age has ever been published for it. It sits above Ka Wai Man Road in Kennedy Town, a hundred metres from the Forbes Street wall, so it extends that walk rather than repeating it. One caveat to carry along. This corner of Kennedy Town has been an active redevelopment site since late 2022, and although the register inspected the tree in March 2023, after the work started, check the garden is open before making the trip for this tree alone.

trees.name: The Banyan of King George V Park
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Short walk from MTR Jordan station, or from the northern end of Kowloon Park via Canton Road
trees.story: This park opened in June 1941 and was a rubbish dump by Christmas. King George V Memorial Park in Jordan was finished late, its opening on 11 June delayed because the governor was ill, and six months later Hong Kong fell to the Japanese and the new park was put to other use for the duration. The Urban Council rebuilt it after the war, added three Chinese-styled kiosks and reopened it on 21 March 1954, then extended it westward in the 1970s when Canton Road was realigned, and redesigned it again in the 1990s after the airport programme reclaimed the land beyond it. Through four versions of the park, this fig has stayed put. The government's tree register gives it a trunk 1.8 metres through, thirteen metres tall, an eighteen metre crown and normal vigour at its last inspection in November 2022. It gives no age, and no other source names the tree individually, so its years are undocumented. One thing to get right before setting off: Hong Kong has two parks named after King George V. This is the Kowloon one, on Canton Road in Jordan, a couple of minutes further on from the King Banyan of Kowloon Park. The other is across the harbour in Sai Ying Pun, with its own trees and its own history.

trees.name: The Camphor of Kowloon Park Drive
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui station, within Kowloon Park via Kowloon Park Drive, at the southern end of the park from the King Banyan
trees.story: The three camphors already on this page stand behind villages, kept for centuries as feng shui trees. This one stands beside a children's playground, and it is thicker than any of them. Two metres of trunk diameter, sixteen metres tall, a twenty metre crown and normal vigour at its last inspection in October 2022, at the southern end of Kowloon Park near the aviary, which puts it a ten minute walk from the King Banyan at the far end of the same park. Camphor was an industrial commodity long before it was a park tree. The wood and leaves are distilled for camphor itself, and before synthetics took over, that substance was the essential plasticiser for celluloid, which meant photographic film, and a stabiliser for smokeless powder, which meant ammunition. The two together made camphor a strategic material worth controlling, most of the world's supply came out of Taiwan and Japan under state monopoly, and the trees were felled to get it. So a large old camphor is not a neutral object in this part of the world. It is a tree that was worth more cut down than standing and did not get cut. No age is recorded for this one, and a second, smaller camphor stands in the same playground. Crush a fallen leaf and the smell settles the identification instantly.

trees.name: The Banyan of Nathan Road
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: A few minutes' walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui station Exit A1, on Nathan Road's Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard stretch
trees.story: The government's inspection of this tree reads like a description of the street it is on. Compacted soil. Cable and brace support fitted. More than seventy-five percent of the ground under its crown built over or paved. Overall risk moderate, vigour normal, which together describe a large healthy tree living in conditions no tree would choose. It stands on the Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard stretch of Nathan Road, the Golden Mile, with a trunk 2.07 metres through, nineteen metres tall and a crown spreading twenty-two metres over one of Hong Kong's busiest shopping streets. Directly opposite is St Andrew's Church, built between 1904 and 1906 in Victorian Gothic on a small rise above the road, Kowloon's oldest Anglican church and a gift to the community from Paul Chater, the Armenian-born businessman who co-founded Hong Kong Land and paid for a good deal of what the colony became. So the view is a banyan against English stonework, on a street that now sells watches and phones. The register gives no age for the tree, and no independent source names it, so what is documented is its size and its condition. It is a six or seven minute walk from the King Banyan in Kowloon Park, which makes it the easy last stop of that walk rather than a trip of its own.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Castle Park
trees.age: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.

best_time.label: March, when it flowers on bare twigs before anything else

trees.story:
This tree is a fragment of something much larger that no longer exists.

Kasteel Helmond has been standing in the middle of this town for nearly seven hundred years, a moated brick castle that is now the town hall and museum. Until the middle of the twentieth century it sat inside a big landscape park, the kind that a private owner maintains and a town cannot. In 1921 the last private owner sold the castle, and most of the park went in the decades that followed, built over or reorganised into something smaller.

The silver maple, planted between 1890 and 1900, belongs to that vanished park. So do three other trees on this page. Together they are the best physical evidence of what used to be here.

Silver maple is North American and was planted for speed and for its leaf, which is cut into five narrow lobes and is bright silver-white on the underside, so the crown flashes pale whenever there is wind.

It does one more thing worth timing a visit for. It flowers in March, in small red and yellow tufts directly on the bare twigs, weeks before anything around it moves.

trees.name: The Old Oak of Farmer Peeters
trees.age: roughly 195 to 205 years, from the register's planting band of 1820 to 1830
trees.access: Free. Public planting on the Rijnlaan.
trees.transport: About 4 km southeast of Helmond centre, at Brouwhuis.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down

trees.story:
Somebody wrote a book about the trees of this town, and because of it we know what this oak is called.

The national register does not usually explain its own names. Here it does: the tree is listed as de oude eik van boer Peeters, and the register says the name comes from 'Grote en kleine geschiedenissen rond bomen in Helmond en omgeving' by Maria van de Looverbosch, a collection of large and small histories of the trees in and around Helmond.

That chain is worth appreciating. A local writer went round asking about trees, wrote down what people called them, published it, and a national government survey later read the book and used the name. Farmer Peeters himself has vanished entirely.

The oak is banded 1820 to 1830, so it is about two centuries old and stands at Brouwhuis on the Rijnlaan, in what is now a housing district on what was farmland when it was planted.

That is the fate of most old farm oaks that survive: the fields go, the buildings arrive, and the tree ends up in a green strip with a street name around it and a farmer's name attached.

trees.name: The Oak at the Old Tower
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Open ground at the tower, reachable in daylight.
trees.transport: About 4 km northwest of Helmond centre, at Stiphout.

best_time.label: January, when the bare frame reads against the brick

trees.story:
The tower dates from about 1400 and the oak from about 1855, which is a gap of four and a half centuries between two things standing side by side.

The Oude Toren at Stiphout is a church tower without its church, which is a common enough sight in this country and always means the same thing: the nave was replaced or demolished and the tower, being solid and expensive to remove and usually owned separately, stayed. What is left is a tall brick object standing alone with a graveyard around it.

The oak came far later. It is banded 1850 to 1860 and at roughly 170 years it is at about a third of its likely span, which means that if it is left alone it will eventually catch up on the tower in a way nothing else here will.

That is the reason to come, and it is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up. Two hundred years from now a visitor will find a tower from 1400 and an oak from 1855, and the difference between them will look far smaller than it does today.

Go in winter, when the bare frame reads against the brick.

trees.name: The Beech of the Hunting Wood
trees.age: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
trees.access: Free. Public park wood at Horst.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Helmond centre, at Horst.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns copper

trees.story:
The wood this beech stands in is a leftover piece of the hunting ground of the lords of Helmont, and the register knows what the farmhands used to eat in it.

The pool here is called the spekstreuvelvenneke and it has always been there. The name comes from what happened around it: farm workers took their midday meal at this spot, and what they ate was spekstruif, a bacon pancake. That is the level of detail a national tree register does not usually carry, and it survives because somebody local made sure it did.

The wood shows on a map of 1890. It is a relict, a fragment of a much older hunting landscape that the farming and building around it never quite absorbed.

The beech, banded 1870 to 1880, is a purple one, which in a fragment of old hunting wood is an incomer: somebody planted it deliberately in a place that had otherwise simply been left.

Go in October, when it turns copper, and find the pool. The pancake is not provided.

trees.name: The Oak of the Castle Park
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down across the grounds

trees.story:
The oldest of the four survivors in the castle grounds, and the one most likely to outlast the rest by centuries.

It was planted between 1880 and 1890, when Kasteel Helmond was still a private house sitting in a large landscape park, four decades before the sale that led to most of that park disappearing. A native oak in a nineteenth century park was not the fashionable choice; the fashion was for silver maples, copper beeches and conifers from other continents, all of which are also on this page. Oak was the sober option, planted by somebody thinking further ahead than their own lifetime.

That turned out to be the right call. Pedunculate oak routinely reaches four hundred years in this country. The silver maple beside it will be lucky to see two hundred.

A castle that has stood for nearly seven centuries with an oak that might manage half of that is a decent pairing, and it is the sort of arithmetic that only becomes visible when you know the numbers.

Acorns on long stalks in October, and a great many of them on a tree with this much room.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Castle Park
trees.age: roughly 95 to 105 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.

best_time.label: July, when the scent fills the castle grounds

trees.story:
This one was planted just after the castle changed hands, which makes it the last generation of the old park rather than a survivor of it.

The sale came in 1921 and the landscape park largely went in the decades after. A silver lime banded 1920 to 1930 is therefore standing on the hinge: planted around the moment the private estate ended and the public use began, into grounds that were about to stop being anybody's private garden.

Silver lime is the best of the limes to meet in person, for a reason you can see from across the grounds. Every leaf is covered underneath in a fine white felt, so in the slightest wind the crown turns over and flickers between deep green and pale silver. Nothing else this size does it.

It has a darker habit too. It flowers late, in July, and its nectar is hard on bumblebees, so under a big one in high summer you will sometimes find them on the ground. The reasons are argued over and the current reading is more about a starving late-season insect finding a huge low-value food source than about poison.

July, then, for the scent.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Castle Park
trees.age: roughly 95 to 105 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.

best_time.label: September, when the conkers split out of their cases

trees.story:
A horse chestnut in a castle park is a tree planted for children, whether or not anyone admitted it at the time.

The conkers are the point. They ripen in September, the spiny green cases split on the ground, and what falls out is the glossiest object in northern European botany, a deep mahogany brown that fades within days of being picked up. Every generation discovers this independently at about the age of six.

This one is banded 1920 to 1930, so it went in just after the castle was sold in 1921 and the private landscape park began to break up. Planting a chestnut at that moment, in grounds that were becoming public, reads like somebody thinking about the town rather than about a garden.

The species is having a hard century. Bleeding canker has killed many mature trees since the 1990s, and the leaf miner moth, here since about 2002, browns the foliage of nearly every horse chestnut in the country from July onward.

So come in early May for the white candles, before the miner starts, or in September for the conkers. Not August.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Baobab
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
Honolulu calls this one the Dead Rat Tree. The nickname is the seed pods: grey, furred, hanging on long stalks all around the crown, and once you have seen them you cannot unsee them. Under the pods is an African baobab, planted in Foster Botanical Garden in the 1930s and already carrying a trunk close to thirteen metres around. Ninety-odd years for that waistline is quick work, even for a species that grows a trunk largely to store water in it. The city's Exceptional Trees register gives its height as about twenty metres and rates its condition good.

Baobabs belong to dry African savanna, where they stand bare for months and flower at night for bats. This one has spent its whole life on fourteen acres of downtown Honolulu at the edge of Chinatown, on ground that was a private botanical collection long before the city took it over. It sat out a 1.26 million dollar renovation that closed the garden completely, and was still standing when the gates reopened in August 2023.

About twenty five of Oahu's hundred or so protected Exceptional Trees grow inside these same fourteen acres. That is the argument for the entrance fee: nowhere else on the island puts this many designated trees within a five minute walk of each other.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Bodhi Tree
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The tree the Buddha is said to have sat under has descendants, and one of them grows in downtown Honolulu. This sacred fig was raised from a cutting of the Bodh Gaya lineage in India and arrived as a sapling in 1913, a gift to Mary Foster from Anagarika Dharmapala, the Sri Lankan reformer who spent his life campaigning to return that Indian temple to Buddhist hands. Foster planted it in her garden and went on to become a major patron of Buddhism in Hawaii, paying for the islands' first Buddhist temple.

The tree is about 113 years old now, roughly fifteen metres tall, with a trunk over seven metres around, and the city's Exceptional Trees register rates its condition excellent. Sacred figs are easy to identify once someone shows you the leaf: heart-shaped, drawn out into a long thin tail, hung so loosely on its stalk that the whole crown moves in air you cannot feel on your own skin. A tree that moves on a still day is the sort of thing people build religions around.

It is one of the few trees in this garden whose value has nothing to do with its size. There are bigger and far stranger specimens within a hundred metres of it. This is the one with a paper trail back to India and a woman who knew exactly what she had been given.

trees.name: The Hillebrand Kapok
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The oldest tree in Foster Botanical Garden is older than the garden, because the man who planted it lived here first. William Hillebrand, the German physician and botanist who made this ground his homestead, put a kapok in at around 1851. That gives it roughly 175 years. It was already a mature tree when the Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown in 1893, and a very large one when Pearl Harbor was bombed.

Its height is not in doubt. Honolulu Magazine and the city's Exceptional Trees register both give 88 and a half feet, about 27 metres, which is also how we know the two are describing the same trunk. The trunk itself they disagree on, and not by a little. The magazine reports 151 inches around, a shade under four metres. The register records 6.98 metres. The two have never been reconciled, so both stand here rather than one being quietly chosen. Some of the gap is probably method: a kapok throws out buttress roots like thin walls, and the answer changes depending on the height at which you measure.

Standing at the base, the buttresses are the point anyway. They rise past head height and divide the ground around the trunk into separate rooms, which is what a rainforest giant does when it has to hold itself up in shallow soil.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Cannonball Tree
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
The garden has put up a sign beside this tree warning visitors about falling cannonballs, and it is not a joke. Couroupita guianensis grows its fruit straight out of the trunk rather than from the branches, woody spheres somewhere between a grapefruit and a shot put, hanging on thick stalks that push out of the bark itself. Botanists call the habit cauliflory. Gravity calls it a hazard. A ripe one comes down from height and splits open with a smell that carries.

The flowers work the same way and are the reason to come: waxy, orange and pink, each one a shell-shaped hood over a dense spray of stamens, opening in ropes down the trunk at eye level while the crown sails on 29 metres above. It is a South American tree, from the Amazon and the Guianas, soft-wooded and fast, and the city's Exceptional Trees register rates this specimen's condition excellent. It is the most straightforwardly strange thing in a garden that is not short of competition.

One thing about it is missing: nobody has recorded when it went into the ground. If you know the planting date, or know someone at the garden who does, tell us and it goes on the page.

trees.name: The Foster Garden Quipo
trees.access: Paid entry: $1-5 general admission, $3 for Hawaii residents, $25 annual family pass. Open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas and New Year's Day.
trees.transport: On N. Vineyard Blvd in downtown Honolulu, on the edge of Chinatown; several TheBus routes run along Vineyard Blvd past the garden entrance.
trees.story:
This trunk is soft enough to cut with a knife. The quipo comes from the forests of Panama and Colombia, where it grows wood about as dense as balsa and gets felled for rafts and dugout canoes rather than for anything expected to hold weight. The tree wears that wood in a shape to match: smooth, greenish-grey, swollen low down and tapering upward, closer to a water tank than to anything with bark on it. Honolulu Botanical Gardens' own record puts the planting at 1930, which makes this one about 96 years old.

It has reached roughly 26 metres. That figure comes from the city's Exceptional Trees register alone and has not been checked against a second measurement, so treat it as the best number available rather than a settled one. Its seedpods are the other reason to look up: large, papery and winged, built to spin on the way down. The register rates the tree's condition excellent.

It stands near the centre of the garden, which is about right, because it is the specimen most visitors cannot name and cannot walk past either. Nothing else on these fourteen acres looks less like a tree, and that includes a baobab.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of St David's Cathedral
trees.access: Free, public street corner outside the cathedral, always visible
trees.transport: Central Hobart CBD, walkable from anywhere in the city centre
trees.story: Hobart has been raising this oak's replacements from its own acorns since 2020, which tells you how the original is doing. It stands on the corner of Murray and Macquarie Streets outside St David's Cathedral, at what the National Trust calls the finest colonial intersection in Australia: four corners of nineteenth-century sandstone, and one evergreen oak holding down the fourth. The City of Hobart's significant tree register lists it twice over, once for outstanding aesthetic significance and once for outstanding dimensions. When the National Trust measured it in March 2014 it was 16 metres tall with a two-metre girth and a condition rating of Good. By September 2023 the city's own arborists reported that it had been in decline for some years despite everything maintenance could do. Photographs from that month show it standing and in leaf, with one seedling of its own germinated in 2020 growing on beside it and several more saplings raised from its acorns. Its age is the part nobody can prove. The story people tell in Hobart is that it grew from an acorn brought back from Gallipoli after 1915 and planted for the men who did not come back, which would put it a little over a century old. No document supports that. The size fits, the tradition is real, the paperwork is missing, and the propagation programme is the city covering itself either way.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwoods of Elizabeth Street
trees.access: Free, public road reserve/footpath, always visible
trees.transport: Central Hobart CBD, on Elizabeth Street near the Elizabeth/Collins Street corner
trees.story: Until 1941 this species was known only from fossils. Botanists had described Metasequoia from imprints in stone and filed it under extinct, and then living trees turned up in a valley in Hubei province, China. Every dawn redwood outside that valley descends from seed collected there in 1947 and posted around the world, which makes the three on the road reserve outside 81 Elizabeth Street the great-grandchildren of a botanical resurrection. There are three of them, within about twenty metres of each other in front of the former Commonwealth Bank building, and the City of Hobart's significant tree register treats them as a single record rather than three, because the group is the point. Its reasoning is unusually direct: the trees together provide a striking aesthetic in a sparsely vegetated part of the city, and they are locally very recognisable. Stand at the kerb and you get all three at once. That register is also all there is. No other source names these trees, and no planting date is recorded anywhere, so their age is genuinely unknown, with one hard ceiling: nobody outside China could have planted one before 1947. Dawn redwood is one of the few conifers that sheds its needles, so the trio go coppery and then bare through a Tasmanian winter and come back feathery green in spring, which for a fossil is a reasonable annual performance.

trees.name: The Norfolk Island Pine of Ingle Hall
trees.access: Free, public street corner, always visible
trees.transport: Central Hobart CBD, corner of Macquarie and Argyle Streets
trees.story: Asked in 2025 to name his favourite tree in Hobart, the owner of the New Town Station Nursery picked this one, and his reason was that it never changes much. Norfolk Island pines grow slowly and hold their shape, a stack of horizontal branch tiers running up a near-perfect vertical, and this one has kept its corner of Macquarie and Argyle Streets while the buildings around it got taller. The City of Hobart's register singles out its trunk: it forks into two co-dominant leaders, which on most conifers reads as a fault and on this one reads as character. It stands outside Ingle Hall, one of the oldest Georgian buildings in the city, now part of the University of Tasmania's Conservatorium of Music, so on a good day the tree comes with a soundtrack. The species is native to one small island in the Pacific, 1,400 km off the Australian east coast. Cook's crew, arriving there in 1774, looked at those dead-straight trunks and saw masts for the Royal Navy; the timber turned out to be too brittle for the job. As ornamental trees for windy southern ports they have done considerably better, and Hobart is about as far south as a port gets. No planting date was ever recorded, so nobody can tell you how old it is.

trees.name: The Bhutan Cypress of Brisbane Street
trees.access: Free, public streetscape
trees.transport: Central Hobart CBD, on Brisbane Street
trees.story: This tree is on Hobart's significant tree register for one stated reason: its loss would be detrimental to the community. Not size, not age, not rarity. The Bhutan cypress at 67 Brisbane Street earned its place as a shape, a dark green cone running straight up out of the footpath, holding a vertical line on a street that otherwise runs horizontal. It is a long way from home. Cupressus torulosa grows wild in the dry inner valleys of the Himalaya, through northern India, Nepal and Bhutan, at altitudes that hand it thin air, hard sun and freezing nights, and across that range it is the tree planted around temples and monasteries. It is uncommon as a street tree in Australia, so the reason to walk past is simply that you are unlikely to meet another one on the way. The register carries no age for it and no measurements, and no other source names it at all. What you get is the council's judgement and your own eyes, which is honest ground for a tree whose whole case rests on how it looks from the pavement. It makes the smallest claim of any tree on this list and the claim holds: a Himalayan conifer, on an ordinary Hobart street, that a city looked at and decided it would rather not lose.

trees.name: The Douglas Fir of the Botanical Gardens
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
trees.transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
trees.story: This tree is older than Australia. It went into the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens in 1894, seven years before the colonies federated into a country, and it has been growing on the same ground ever since. The National Trust measured it in March 2014 at 30 metres tall with a trunk a metre through, and rated its condition Excellent, which for a North American conifer half a world from the Pacific Northwest is a good result. It stands in the Gardens' conifer collection, laid out mostly in the nineteenth century and described by the Gardens themselves as one of the most significant of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere. The Gardens were founded in 1818 and are the second oldest in Australia, and the planting logic of the period is still legible on the ground: rows of northern timber trees brought south to find out whether they would take. This one took. Douglas fir is the great timber tree of the American west, the species that framed most of the twentieth century's houses there, and it is normally met in a plantation, packed tight and pruned by its neighbours. Here it is a specimen with room around it, lower branches kept, the whole shape visible from the path. Entry is free, and the gates are open daily from 8am, closing at 5pm between April and September and at 6.30pm from October to March.

trees.name: The Queensland Kauri of the Botanical Gardens
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
trees.transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
trees.story: This tree is listed under four separate headings on Hobart's significant tree register: aesthetic significance, outstanding dimensions, venerable age, and rarity. Every other tree on this list carries one or two. The Queensland kauri stands 39 metres in the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, measured by the National Trust in March 2014 and rated Excellent, and it has been on the Trust's books since December 1994. The oddity is where it is. Agathis robusta is a rainforest tree from coastal Queensland and the Atherton Tableland, warm and wet by temperament, and Hobart sits at 42 degrees south with frost, wind off the Southern Ocean and a winter Queensland has never heard of. It ought to be sulking. Instead it is one of the tallest things in the garden. Kauri are among the longest-lived conifers on earth, and they grow a clean columnar trunk that runs branchless for a long way before the crown starts, which is precisely why the timber was cut out of Australian and New Zealand forests so quickly in the nineteenth century: a kauri log is almost all usable wood. Nobody recorded when this one was planted. The register calls it venerable and gives no number, and neither does the National Trust. The Gardens charge nothing to enter, opening at 8am daily and closing at 5pm from April to September, 6.30pm through the warmer half of the year.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoias of the Botanical Gardens
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
trees.transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
trees.story: There are two of them, they went in together in 1879, and they still mark the entrance drive of the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens. The National Trust measured the pair in March 2014 at 36 metres tall with trunks two metres through and rated them Excellent. At 147 years old they are barely started: giant sequoias routinely pass 2,000 years, and the largest living one in California is reckoned at over two millennia. Hobart's register still lists them under a nineteenth-century name, Big Tree or Wellingtonia, which is a fossil of an old argument. When seed first reached Britain in 1853 the species was named Wellingtonia gigantea after the recently dead Duke of Wellington. American botanists objected and countered with Washingtonia. The fight was not settled until 1939, when the tree finally got the neutral name it carries now, and seed had reached Tasmania well before that, which is roughly when these two went into the ground. They are the first trees you pass coming through the gates, which is the standard Victorian use for a species that gardeners of the period regarded as the largest living thing anyone had heard of. They have another eighteen centuries to make good on it. There is no admission charge; the gates open at 8am daily and close at 5pm from April to September, 6.30pm from October to March.

trees.name: The Chir Pine of the Botanical Gardens
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
trees.transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
trees.story: Hobart's register calls this the Longleaved Indian Pine, and the name is the best short description of it. Chir pine carries needles up to thirty centimetres long in bundles of three, and they droop, so a mature tree looks nothing like the stiff dark cone most people picture when they hear the word pine. It looks loose and shaggy, closer to a green waterfall. The species comes from the outer Himalaya, the dry foothill belt running from Pakistan through northern India into Nepal, where it is the resin pine, tapped for turpentine and rosin, and where its own fallen needles are flammable enough to be a recognised cause of the region's forest fires. In the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens it is doing none of that. It grows in the pinetum, the conifer collection laid out mostly in the nineteenth century, which the Gardens describe as one of the most significant of its kind in the southern hemisphere, planted when foresters were systematically testing which northern timber trees would take to a Tasmanian climate. The City of Hobart lists it for its appearance, its dimensions and its age, and records no number for any of the three. Its second page is an aerial photograph with an arrow on it, which is the city saying that finding this tree matters more than measuring it.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of the Botanical Gardens
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
trees.transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates

best_time.label: March to April: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This oak is not on Hobart's significant tree register for being large or old. It is listed for how it looks, for being part of a historic garden, and for standing where the landscape would miss it, and the register gives no height, no girth and no age at all. That is an unusual case to make for a tree and it is the honest one here. Hobart's register calls the species English Oak; this page uses Pedunculate Oak, the neutral name for Quercus robur, the same tree under a less proprietary label. It is the oak the British planted wherever they settled, and Tasmania suited it better than most of Australia did: cool, wet and far enough south that an oak can behave the way it does at home instead of merely surviving. In the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens it grows near the main house and glasshouse complex, in a garden founded in 1818 and the second oldest in the country. The Gardens hold more than one English oak, which is worth knowing if you go looking; this is the one the city registered, marked with an arrow on the register's own aerial photograph. Nobody has published a planting date for it, so how old it is remains genuinely open. Entry is free and the gates open at 8am daily.

trees.name: The Spotted Gum of the Botanical Gardens
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
trees.transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
trees.story: Every other tree on this page came from somewhere else. A Douglas fir out of Oregon, a kauri from the Queensland rainforest, two sequoias from California, a Himalayan cypress, a Norfolk Island pine, three dawn redwoods descended from one Chinese valley. This one is Australian, which on a list of Hobart's remarkable trees turns out to be the exception rather than the rule. Be precise about it, though. Corymbia maculata grows wild along the coast of New South Wales and into southern Queensland and does not occur naturally in Tasmania, so it is native to the country and not to the island, and it was planted here for the same reason as all the rest: a nineteenth century botanical garden collecting specimens from everywhere it could reach. The bark is why to walk over. Spotted gums shed theirs in irregular patches through the warmer months, leaving a smooth trunk mottled in grey, cream, olive and pink that shifts as the year goes on, and no two trees carry the same pattern. The City of Hobart lists it for its appearance, its dimensions and its place in a historic garden, and as with every Gardens entry on that register it records no measurements and no planting date, so its age is unknown. Free to enter, gates open from 8am daily.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Oosterpoortsgracht
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves come out translucent red before they darken

trees.story: Every copper beech in Europe descends from a handful of freak trees found growing purple in ordinary green forests, most famously in Germany in the seventeenth century. The colour is a mutation that overproduces red pigment, useless to the tree and irresistible to gardeners, and it has been propagated by grafting ever since. This one stands at the water's edge of the Oosterpoortsgracht in Hoorn, beside the Oosterpoort, the fifteenth century gate that is the only one of the town's medieval gates left standing. The national register dates the planting to between 1860 and 1870, roughly 160 years, and lists the tree on the municipal monument list and on the town's own tree route. Through the nineteenth century, as the walls and towers came down, the emptied defences were remade as a walking park, which is the ground this tree grew up in and the reason it has had room. Come in May rather than autumn. New copper beech leaves open translucent, lit red from behind like stained glass, and darken to near black-purple within weeks. By August the crown is a hole in the light. The register is the only source we have found that records this tree individually, so read the age as its estimate rather than a measurement.

trees.name: The Plane of the Pakhuisstraat
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story: Four metres of trunk and nowhere to put it. This plane stands on the Pakhuisstraat by the aviary in the Oosterplantsoen, and the register, which otherwise calls it a perfect specimen, notes that the base is being squeezed by the pavement along the street. That is the standard fate of a big plane in a Dutch town: the tree keeps widening at the foot and the kerb does not move. The register dates the planting to between 1860 and 1870, so roughly 160 years, and it is the only source we have found that records this tree on its own. London plane came out of a seventeenth century accident, a cross between the American and the oriental plane that nobody planned and everybody planted afterwards, and it turned out to handle coal smoke, hard soil and heavy pruning better than either parent. Hoorn was a Dutch East India Company town whose walls were coming down through the century this tree went in, and the emptied ground became the walking park it now stands in. Look at the trunk rather than the crown. The bark comes away in irregular plates and leaves a camouflage of cream, olive and grey, and at four metres round there is a lot of it to look at from close up.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Veliusbrug
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story: There were two of these by the Veliusbrug and now there is one. The other stood on the south side of the path, developed bark necrosis, went partly hollow and was taken down as a limb-drop risk. The survivor carries a serious fungal infection of its own and, in the register's assessment, is still growing reasonably. It is close to five metres round. Silver maple is the fastest growing maple there is and pays for the speed with brittle wood, which is why big old ones so often stand alone next to the place where their neighbour used to be. Acer saccharinum comes from the river bottoms of eastern North America, and everything about it suits a wet Dutch park: it tolerates flooding, roots hard into soft ground and grows a metre a year while it is young. The register dates the planting to between 1860 and 1870, so roughly 160 years, and it is the only source we have found for this tree. The name is in the leaf. Deeply cut, almost skeletal, green above and chalk white beneath, so that any wind turns the whole crown silver and back again. It flowers absurdly early, in February or March, before anything else here has thought about it, in small red clusters most people walk under without noticing.

trees.name: The Plane of Number 37
trees.age: roughly 150 years, from a registered planting date around 1880
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story: The register gives this one a planting year rather than a band: 1871, at the waterside of the Oosterpoortsgracht in the Oosterplantsoen. What it does not give is a species. It is a plane, and the entry goes no further than that, so we have not either. The two candidates are the London plane, which is most of what got planted in Dutch towns after 1850, and the oriental plane, which is its parent and turns up in nineteenth century parks more often than people expect. The leaves settle it: five deep narrow lobes cut most of the way to the middle means oriental, three to five shallower lobes on a broader blade means London. If you are standing under it and you know which one you are looking at, tell us and we will put your answer on this page. What the register does say is that the tree has grown a full, even crown, which is unusual for a plane of that age in a town, where most of them have been cut back off a building or a road at some point.
