This one has had the water on one side and the old walking park on the other, and about 150 years to use the room.

trees.name: The Elm of the Oosterpoort
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story: Dutch elm disease is named after the Dutch scientists who identified the fungus in the 1920s, not after the country's elms, but it took those too. Two waves of it, the second from the 1960s, removed the elm from most of the Netherlands as a street tree. This one has come through both. It stands on the east side of the Oosterpoort, the fifteenth century gate that is the last of Hoorn's medieval gates, at the water's edge, and the register dates it to between 1880 and 1890, so roughly 140 years. Having survived the beetle, it lost its top to a storm, probably the summer storm of 2023, and carries other wind damage besides. The register still calls the trunk impressive, and notes how well it greens up in spring. That is fair. Ulmus x hollandica leafs out in a hard, glossy green that the limes and planes around it cannot match, the leaves rough as sandpaper on top and lopsided at the base, which is the elm giveaway. Before the leaves come, in February, the whole crown turns dull red with tufted flowers. The national register is the only source we have found for this tree, so read the age as its estimate. If you know when the top came out, we would like to hear it.

trees.name: The Plane behind the Aviary
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story: This plane stands behind the aviary in the Oosterplantsoen, out of the way of the street, and it has grown accordingly: a trunk of over four metres round and, in the register's words, a perfect tree. Its neighbour a couple of hundred metres away on the Pakhuisstraat is the same species and two decades older, and has spent its life fighting the kerb. The difference between the two is simply where somebody put them. The register dates this one to between 1880 and 1890, so roughly 140 years, and it is the only source we have found that records it. Planes are the reason nineteenth century park designers could plan at all. They grow fast, take any soil, survive being moved as large trees and can be cut back to knuckles and come again, which made them the safe bet on new public ground like this, laid out where Hoorn's walls and towers had been. The catch arrives in June, when the undersides of the young leaves shed fine hairs that get into throats, and again in autumn when the seed balls break up and do the same. Neither is a reason to skip it. Stand close to the bole and look up through the mottled bark and horizontal limbs, and give it the time it takes to register how much tree is above you.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Oosterplantsoen
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers after every other lime has finished

trees.story: Silver lime is the last of the limes to flower, and in a park full of trees that have already finished it can be the only thing working in July. This one stands near the Veliusbrug in the Oosterplantsoen with a trunk of over four metres round, which the register credits to about 140 years of undisturbed growth: it dates the planting to between 1880 and 1890 and is the only source we have found that records the tree. Tilia tomentosa came from southeastern Europe and Asia Minor and Dutch towns adopted it late, largely because it holds up in dirty air better than the common lime and does not drip the same sticky rain of aphid honeydew onto whatever is parked beneath. The tomentosa in the name means felted. Every leaf is dark green above and white with fine hairs below, so the crown changes colour with the wind and, on a bright day, looks lit from underneath. In leaf it is one of the densest shade trees in this park. It also gets called out for the bumblebees found dead under it in late summer, once blamed on the nectar and now more often put down to the tree flowering when starving bees have nothing else left to visit.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Number 37
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: late September and October, when the conkers split open on the path

trees.story: The register gives this chestnut an actual planting year, 1901, which is rarer than it sounds: most trees on this list carry a ten year band and nothing better. It stands at the water's edge of the Oosterpoortsgracht opposite number 37, on the municipal monument list and on the town's tree route, and the register describes a full crown that storms have since knocked about without slowing the tree down. Aesculus hippocastanum is a Balkan tree that reached western Europe in the sixteenth century and was planted everywhere on the strength of two weeks in May. The rest of its case is autumn. Late September the spiny green cases start splitting on the path and the conker inside comes out mahogany brown and polished, the single most collectible object a European tree produces, and worthless the moment it dries out. The species name hippocastanum means horse chestnut, from an old belief that the seeds cured coughing in horses; for people they are simply poisonous. The national register is the only source we have found for this tree, so read the date as its record rather than an independent one. Come with a pocket in October and you will not leave with it empty.

trees.name: The John Knox Live Oak
trees.access: Free. Church grounds, open. The tree stands on the front lawn, visible from Gessner Road.
trees.transport: About 18 km west of downtown Houston. Drive; there is parking on site.
trees.story:
The crown is the thing. Forty metres across, on a trunk 625 centimetres round and a tree only twenty three metres tall, which is the live oak habit taken to its conclusion: this species does not race upward, it spreads until the branches come back down to meet you. The Texas A&M Forest Service measured it in March 2026, so those are current numbers rather than remembered ones.

It stands on the front lawn of a Presbyterian church on Gessner Road, in a part of Spring Branch that was farmland when the congregation broke ground in 1961. The church's own history mentions picnics held under the big trees at the front of the property, which is roughly what a tree this shape is for.

No age has been published. Live oaks are difficult to date without coring and nobody appears to have done it. What can be said is that a live oak reaching six metres of girth in a climate like this one has had a long time and a lot of water, and that it was clearly here before the church was.

The grounds are open, and a churchyard has never been a bad place to stand and look up.

trees.name: The Old Pecan Tree
trees.access: Free. Public hiking trail, open daylight hours.
trees.transport: About 32 km southwest of downtown Houston, in Sugar Land. Drive.

best_time.label: October, when the nuts come down

trees.story:
There is a footpath in Sugar Land called Old Pecan Tree Trail, and it is named after exactly what you would hope. The tree is a pecan of 467 centimetres round and twenty eight metres tall, with a crown spreading twenty five metres, measured by the Texas A&M Forest Service in March 2026. Trail guides rank it among the twenty five largest trees in Texas, which is scored on trunk, height and crown together.

Pecan is the state tree, and it is one of the few state trees anywhere chosen for something other than looks: it feeds people. A tree this size drops a serious crop, and in a good year the ground beneath it is worth walking slowly across in October.

The trail is short, well under a kilometre, and the tree is the reason it exists. That is the useful thing about a path named for a tree: nobody has to explain where to go.

No age has been recorded. Pecans of this girth in the Brazos bottomlands are generally reckoned in centuries rather than decades, but nobody has counted the rings and this page is not going to guess.

trees.name: The Kissing Tree
trees.age: already the settlement's meeting tree in 1848
trees.access: Free. Public access, on open ground behind a filling station.
trees.transport: About 33 km north of downtown Houston, at Klein. Drive.
trees.story:
Herman Strack landed at Galveston in 1848, a blacksmith out of Prussia and the first of five brothers to settle north Harris County. Family records put his homestead and forge at this tree. It got its name from what happened under it afterwards: couples met here, and a good number of proposals were made in its shade.

Everything else the Stracks built is gone. When the family restaurant closed in 2014 a developer bought the land for a Circle K, and the tree stood where the forecourt entrance needed to be. That was very nearly the end of it. Students at Klein Oaks High School ran a letter-writing campaign, Circle K eventually pledged to keep the tree, and three years later the Texas A&M Forest Service made it a Famous Tree of Texas.

So it is a live oak hung with Spanish moss on a patch of grass behind a filling station, and it is the last physical trace of a settlement that gave the whole district its name. Nobody has dated it. It was already the tree everyone met at in 1848, which puts a floor under the number if not a ceiling.

trees.name: The Spring Creek Winged Elm
trees.access: Free. Public county greenway trail, open daylight hours.
trees.transport: About 31 km north of downtown Houston. Drive to a greenway trailhead.
trees.story:
This is the largest winged elm recorded in Texas, and it is not a large tree. The trunk is 279 centimetres round, which for the species is remarkable and for this page is modest. Champion status is scored on trunk, height and crown added together, and where this tree wins is height: thirty metres, which is tall for an elm that usually tops out well short of that, with a twenty four metre crown above it.

Winged elm gets its name from the corky ridges that run down either side of the younger twigs, wide enough to look deliberate. On a tree this old you will find them out at the ends of the branches rather than on the trunk, so it is worth picking up a fallen twig.

It stands on the Spring Creek Greenway, a long ribbon of bottomland forest that Harris County has been stitching together along the creek for years, and which is one of the largest urban forested corridors in the country. The Forest Service measured the tree in December 2025.

No age is recorded. Winged elm is not a long-lived species, so this one is old for its kind rather than old in the way an oak is old.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Waterwolf
trees.age: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1920
trees.access: Free, alongside a public road through farmland, always visible.

best_time.label: May, when a field-grown chestnut carries its white candles right down to head height

trees.story:
There is a lake under this tree. Until 1852 the Haarlemmermeer covered everything you can see from here, wide enough to frighten Amsterdam and hungry enough at the edges to have earned the name Waterwolf. Three steam pumping engines emptied it over three years, and the lake floor they laid bare sits roughly four metres below sea level.

That is the ground this horse chestnut is rooted in. The register puts its planting between 1910 and 1920, which makes it about 110 years old, and out here that counts as old: no tree anywhere in the polder can predate the drainage, so the oldest possible tree in the Haarlemmermeer is younger than most of the houses in Haarlem. Aircraft climb out of the same lake bed a few kilometres north.

It stands on the west side of the Hoofdweg, the road that runs the length of the Hoofdvaart, the canal cut dead straight through the middle of the drained lake. This stretch is still farmland, and the tree has the shape a chestnut gets when nothing has ever crowded it: low, wide, branching almost from the ground, the candles in May starting at head height.

Nobody wrote down who planted it. The register's history field for this tree is blank, and it is the only source that describes it at all. If it once belonged to a farm along this road, tell us.

trees.name: The Surviving Ash of the Hoofdweg
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, alongside a public road through farmland, always visible.
trees.story:
Most Dutch ash trees of this age are dead or going. Ash dieback reached the Netherlands around 2010, a fungus out of east Asia that the European ash has no answer to, and it has worked through the country's ash population ever since, killing the crown downward from the twigs. A small fraction of trees turn out to be genetically tolerant, and those few matter enormously, because they are the parents of whatever ash the Netherlands still has in fifty years.

This one is still standing on the Hoofdweg. The register puts its planting between 1920 and 1930, which makes it about a century old, on ground that had only been dry land for about seventy years when it went in.

Ash is the tree everything used to be made of: cart shafts, tool handles, ladders, oars, early aircraft frames. It bends a long way before it gives and it gives without splintering, so it went into anything that had to absorb a shock. It is also the last tree in a Dutch hedgerow to come into leaf and among the first to drop, which leaves it bare for more than half the year. Winter is when it is easiest to name from the road: the buds are matt black and shaped like small hooves, and nothing else here has them.

The chestnut a few doors up is the older of the two. The register is the only source for either.

trees.name: The Maple of the Nieuw-Vennep Church
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, in the grounds of the church, open in daylight.

best_time.label: April, before the leaves open, when clusters of yellow-green flowers cover the crown

trees.story:
The sap of a Norway maple is milky white. That one fact separates it from the sycamore it otherwise closely resembles, and it means a broken twig on this tree bleeds like a dandelion stem instead of running clear.

It grows in the grounds of the Hervormde church on the Hoofdweg in Nieuw-Vennep, a village that exists at all because the Haarlemmermeer was pumped dry in 1852 and somebody then had to farm the lake bed. The register puts the maple's planting between 1930 and 1940, so it is about ninety years old, and it has spent every one of those years on ground nobody has ever had a reason to dig up.

Norway maple is the tree that gets the Dutch spring started. It flowers in April, before its own leaves are out, in dense clusters of a sharp yellow-green that read from a hundred metres off and can fool you into thinking the crown has leafed a month early. Bees work them hard, because almost nothing else is open yet. The leaves that follow are broad and thin with long drawn-out points, and by late October they turn clear yellow.

Churchyards are where old trees tend to survive, for the plain reason that nobody redevelops one. Nobody recorded who planted this maple, and the national register is the only source that describes it. If you know, tell us.

trees.name: The Wingnut of the Hoofddorp Market
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1935
trees.access: Free, on the Markt in front of the market hall, always visible.

best_time.label: midsummer, when strings of winged nutlets half a metre long hang from every branch

trees.story:
When Hoofddorp built a new shopping centre around its market square, the municipality made saving this tree a condition of the plan. That is on the record as the reason it is still there, planted, the register says, around 1935, in front of what is now the market hall.

Caucasian wingnut is not a tree many Dutch town squares grow. It comes from wet valley floors in the Caucasus and northern Iran, suckers readily from its own roots, and in midsummer it hangs strings of winged nutlets half a metre long from every branch tip, for a few weeks looking like a tree decked out for a parade nobody announced.

Being kept during redevelopment is not the same as being cared for since, and the register does not say anything about its condition today. What it records is a species and a rough decade, and nothing else has been published about this particular tree.

It stands in the middle of Hoofddorp, free to walk up to any day of the week. If you know more about why the council insisted on keeping it, tell us.

trees.name: The Jubilee Lime of Vijfhuizen
trees.age: roughly 115 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, alongside a public road, always visible.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers and the scent carries across the Spieringweg

trees.story:
In 1923 the Netherlands marked twenty five years of Queen Wilhelmina on the throne, and this lime went into the ground in Vijfhuizen to mark it, one of many jubilee trees planted across the country that year. The register keeps the reason on file even though almost nothing else about the tree has been written down.

It stands on the Spieringweg opposite a spot known locally as the Fortwachter, in what the register calls a plantsoen: an ordinary municipal planting strip rather than a park. A common lime grown out in the open like this builds a dense, rounded crown down to head height, and in July it does what limes do everywhere: small pale flowers open in hanging clusters, the tree hums with bees for a couple of weeks, and the scent carries across the road.

A century is not old for a lime, which can run to several, but it is old for anything standing in the Haarlemmermeer, ground that was still open water until 1852. The register is the only source that has looked at this specific tree. If you know more about the planting or the jubilee it marked, tell us.

trees.name: The London Plane of Hoofddorp
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1885
trees.access: Free, on municipal ground in front of a notary's office, visible from the Hoofdweg.
trees.story:
Locals use this plane tree to navigate by. The register's whole reasoning for designating it monumental is two words: remarkable form, landmark, and that is the sum of what has been written about it.

It grows on municipal ground in front of a notary's office at the corner of the Hoofdweg and the Manegelaan, planted, the register estimates, somewhere in the 1880s, which would make it Hoofddorp's oldest registered tree by a wide margin over almost everything else on this page. London plane is a hybrid that barely exists in the wild, first bred in seventeenth century Europe by crossing an American and an Oriental species, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, pollution and hard pruning better than almost anything else available, which is why it lines so many European streets and squares. Its bark flakes away in patches instead of splitting, so the trunk carries a camouflage pattern of grey, green and cream that keeps changing as old plates drop off.

At around 140 years old it predates the notary's office, the Manegelaan and most of what stands near it now. The register is the only source that has looked at it. If you know when it actually went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Ring Road
trees.age: roughly 115 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, on a public road corner, always visible.
trees.story:
The register's own 2024 inspection ends on an unusually candid note: the tree, it says, is not doing well these days. That is close to an editorial opinion for a database this dry.

The weeping beech stands with a handful of ordinary beeches on a corner where the Hoofdvaart, the canal cut straight through the drained lake to the old pumping station, meets the ring road that now circles Hoofddorp. The register's own guess is that before the ring road existed, this corner might have been a small park; if so, the road took most of it, and what is left reads as a traffic island with trees on it rather than the parkland setting the tree wants. Planted, the register estimates, between 1900 and 1910, it is around a century old.

A weeping beech is not a natural form. Every one alive descends by graft or cutting from a single tree found wild in Germany around 1680, propagated ever since because its branches fall instead of rising, so a mature specimen makes a tent of foliage with the trunk hidden somewhere inside. Squeezed onto a traffic corner and hemmed in by road, this one has never had the room to do that properly, which may be exactly what the register means.

The register is the only source. If you know this tree, tell us how it is doing now.

trees.name: The Roadside Maple of Badhoevedorp
trees.age: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1915, though the register's own note suggests 1895
trees.access: Visible from the Nieuwemeerdijk; the tree grows in a private front garden and cannot be approached.
trees.story:
This maple stands in the front garden of a house on the Nieuwemeerdijk built in 1915, and the register cannot quite agree with itself about which of the two is older. Its structured record bands the planting to 1910-1920. Its own descriptive note gives 1895 instead, and adds that if that figure is right, the tree was already growing on this dike before the house went up beside it. Both cannot be true, and we have not been able to resolve which the register meant.

The species is recorded no more precisely than maple, Acer species, without a name for which one. If you can put a name to it from a photograph, tell us that too.

None of the uncertainty affects what a passerby can see: a full, healthy crown that the register itself calls the single most striking thing about this stretch of the Nieuwemeerdijk, visible the whole way along the road. The tree grows in the garden of a house that is still lived in, so this is a look rather than a visit. There is no gate to try and no reason to open one, just a wide view from the roadside.

The register is the only source that has looked at this tree, and on its own evidence it has not entirely made up its mind.

trees.name: The Oldest Plane of Bahçeköy
trees.access: Free; the tree stands inside a university forestry research station reachable via public Belgrad Forest walking trails from Bahçeköy
trees.transport: No direct metro; bus from Sarıyer, or a taxi from Hacıosman station (M2 line)
trees.story: Istanbul's oldest living thing predates the city's Ottoman name by seven centuries. Inside a university forestry research station in Bahçeköy stands an Oriental plane that foresters estimate at somewhere between 1,300 and 1,400 years old, a trunk 4.5 metres across and hollowed out enough that, as Istanbul University academic Süleyman Çoban has put it, the wood actually feeding the tree is the thin outer cambium layer, not the vast dead core inside it. The tree has effectively been growing on a shell for longer than most European cities have existed. It stood here through the final two centuries of Byzantine rule, the 1453 conquest, and every Ottoman sultan who followed, unnoticed by any of them because it happened to sit in a patch of forest nobody built on. It only became a public fact recently, when Istanbul University foresters surveying their own research grounds realised they were standing next to the oldest tree in the city. Two more officially protected monumental trees share the same forest: an octopus-shaped plane a short walk away, and a double-trunked plane roughly half its age. None of them have a plaque you would notice from the forest road.

trees.name: The Ahtapot Çınar
trees.access: Free; reachable via public Belgrad Forest walking trails from Bahçeköy
trees.transport: No direct metro; bus from Sarıyer, or a taxi from Hacıosman station (M2 line)
trees.story: Seven trunks that are actually one tree share a single root system at this bend in the Bahçeköy forest. Its lowest branches touched the ground centuries ago and thickened into limbs that now radiate outward like separate trunks, which is how a plane tree ends up nicknamed the Octopus. Turkish foresters put its age at up to 580 years, old enough that a local claim ties its early growth to the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent in the 1500s, though a more conservative reading of the trunk puts it closer to 400. Either figure makes it one of the oldest individually named trees in the city, and unlike most ancient planes, which grow as a single vertical column, this one spread sideways instead, its lowest limbs thick enough to sit on. At over 40 metres tall and more than 3 metres across at the base, it dominates a bend on the old road between Çayırbaşı and Bahçeköy, a stop on the hiking routes that cross Belgrad Forest today. Locals photograph it for the shape. Foresters study it for what centuries of horizontal growth actually does to a trunk that size.

trees.name: The Hüseyin Avni Dede Plane
trees.access: Free, open bazaar entrance
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Beyazıt-Kapalıçarşı tram stop (T1 line)
trees.story: A tree in Istanbul has had the same downstairs neighbour for 58 years. Hüseyin Avni Dede came to sell books and antiques under this 375-year-old plane at the entrance to the Sahaflar Çarşısı, Istanbul's old book bazaar, in 1964, when he was ten years old and working alongside his poet father. He never really left, aside from a three-month gap in 1968. In 2022 Istanbul's Metropolitan Municipality made it official and renamed the tree after him, the Hüseyin Avni Dede Çınarı. The tree's own history runs darker. For generations Istanbulites remembered it as the Cellat Çınarı, the Executioner's Plane, because condemned prisoners were hanged from its branches into the 1960s and 70s, a detail that sits oddly beside a poet who has spent a lifetime selling verse under the same wood. Planted sometime in the mid-1600s, the tree has outlived the executions, the sultans, and most of the original Sahaflar booksellers who once worked around it. Dede is still there most days, technically a tenant of a plane tree older than the country it now stands in.

trees.name: The Taşlı Çınar
trees.access: Free, public street corner
trees.transport: 1 min walk from Gülhane tram stop (T1 line)
trees.story: A stone was lodged inside this tree's bark for roughly three centuries, and until about ten years ago you could still see it. According to the story attached to the tree, Sultan Ahmed I rode past on his white horse sometime between 1590 and 1617 while the Alemdar gate and fountain to what is now Gülhane Park were being built, and a stone kicked loose from a horseshoe struck the sapling and stayed there as it grew, sealed a few metres up the trunk like a fossil. Whether or not the horse is real, the tree is: Istanbul's own monumental tree registry lists it at roughly 446 years old, 26 metres tall, with a trunk 328 centimetres around, the thickest Oriental plane in the district. The embedded stone was removed during conservation work about a decade ago, leaving a visible cavity where it used to sit. What remains is a tree that has watched the road outside Gülhane Park go from Ottoman thoroughfare to tram line, still standing exactly where a legend says a sultan's horse put it there.

trees.name: The Çengelköy Plane
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Steps from Çengelköy ferry pier (Şehir Hatları)
trees.story: This tree spent a night on the ground and got back up. For around 180 years the plane tree at Çengelköy's ferry pier square was the neighbourhood's defining landmark, a canopy wide enough to shade the waterfront tea garden now named Çınaraltı after it. In July 2017 a storm that felled more than 2,000 trees across Istanbul tore this one out of the ground, root ball and all. City crews arrived the next morning and, rather than clear it away, tried something rarer: they propped the trunk back into position, wrapped the exposed roots in felt to stop them drying out, pruned back the crown to reduce the load, and waited. Nothing visible happened for a year. Then new shoots appeared, then small leaves, then, over successive seasons, branches thick enough to look like a tree again rather than a patient. It has not fully recovered the shape it had before the storm, but locals who watched it get carried out for dead now watch it get greener every spring, sitting exactly where it always did at the edge of the Bosphorus.

trees.name: The Cypresses of Karacaahmet
trees.access: Free, cemetery open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from Üsküdar main square, or a short bus ride toward Selimiye
trees.story: Nine cypresses inside Turkey's largest cemetery carry official Monument Tree status, and the tradition that put them there is older than any single trunk still standing. In 1582 Nurbanu Sultan, mother of the reigning sultan Murad III, donated 124 dönüms of her own land to expand Karacaahmet into a proper cemetery and had cypresses planted across it deliberately, assigning guards specifically to protect the trees. Cypresses became the default marker of an Ottoman grave from then on, dark green columns meant to stand for centuries the way a headstone stands for one lifetime. Whether any of the nine protected specimens here today are the actual seventeenth century plantings or later replacements grown from the same rootstock and tradition is not something any source pins down, which is honest: a cemetery replaces its cypresses the way it replaces its headstones, continuously, without announcing it. What is certain is that the practice has not stopped in over 440 years, and that walking Karacaahmet today, through roughly 750,000 square metres of graves under a cypress canopy older than most of the empire's other surviving buildings, is the closest thing Istanbul has to walking through an Ottoman forest.

trees.name: The Ata Fıstık Çamı
trees.access: Free, park open 24 hours; food stalls open 09:00-23:00
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Kısıklı station (M5 metro line)
trees.story: The tree that gave a hill its name is not originally from this hill. Küçük Çamlıca, Istanbul's best known viewpoint on the Asian side, takes its name from the stone pines (çam) covering it, but foresters say the grove's own symbol tree, the Ata Fıstık Çamı, was brought here from the Aegean region generations ago and adapted to Bosphorus soil rather than growing here naturally. At roughly 397 years old, with a trunk 145 centimetres across and a crown reaching 25 metres, it predates the name Çamlıca itself, which only stuck once Sultan Abdülaziz began favouring the grove in the nineteenth century. Stone pines are usually grown for their edible pine nuts, and this one has produced them for longer than Istanbul has had streetlights, trams, or bridges across the Bosphorus. Istanbul's official monument tree registry lists it, and half a dozen younger pines around it, as individually protected, each with its own name and measured age, a small forest of transplants that outlived the reason anyone brought them here in the first place. The view from the hill gets the visitors. The tree that named the hill mostly gets ignored.

trees.name: The Florya Mastic Tree
trees.access: Free, public forest, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Florya Marmaray station
trees.story: Most mastic trees stay shrub sized, a couple of metres of scrubby Mediterranean green grown for their resin, not their timber. The mastic tree inside Florya's Atatürk Forest did not get that memo. Estimated at around 500 years old, its trunk has thickened to roughly 2 metres across, the thickest mastic tree recorded anywhere in Istanbul by a wide margin, a shrub species behaving like an oak. Nobody taps it for resin the way Chios islanders have farmed the same species for a thousand years; this one grows purely as a curiosity inside a public forest planted from 1936 on reclaimed coastal land that used to be marsh. Walk the forest paths near the shore and you pass pines and cedars planted deliberately as part of a young republic's afforestation project, all of them younger than the mastic tree they grew up around, a five-century holdout that was already old when the rest of Florya was still open water.

trees.name: The Ehrami Servi of Büyükada
trees.access: Free, public street; reachable only by ferry (no bridges to the Princes' Islands)
trees.transport: Ferry to Büyükada from Kabataş or Bostancı, then a short walk or bicycle ride into Nizam
trees.story: The only tree on this list that requires a ferry to reach stands on a residential street on Büyükada, the largest of Istanbul's car-free Princes' Islands. Istanbul's official monument tree registry lists this Mediterranean cypress, grown into the tall narrow pyramidal form the species is known for, at approximately 244 years old, 18 metres tall, with a trunk 75 centimetres across. It predates the island's Belle Epoque mansions, the Greek Orthodox monastery on the hill above it, and the horse-drawn carriages that until recently were the island's only form of wheeled transport. The registry protects it under three separate criteria at once, historical importance, age, and trunk diameter, a bureaucratic way of saying there was no single reason to save it, there were three. Büyükada's own history runs through Byzantine exile, this is where empresses and princes were once banished, and through White Russian refugees fleeing the 1917 revolution, none of which this cypress witnessed directly from its residential street, but which shaped an island growing quietly taller around it for two and a half centuries.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of Beykoz Çayırı
trees.access: Free, open meadow
trees.transport: Bus or dolmuş from Beykoz pier; no metro access
trees.story: Ottoman sultans hunted on this exact meadow, which is why locals still sometimes call it Hünkar Çayırı, the Sultan's Meadow, instead of its official name. A handful of plane trees standing on Beykoz Çayırı today, three or four individually protected as monumental, date to the era when Mehmed II built a hunting lodge near what is now Tokatköy after the 1453 conquest, and Istanbul University foresters estimate their average age at somewhere between 400 and 500 years, old enough that at least some may already have been standing before the lodge itself went up. Unlike a single named specimen with one clean story, these trees are witnesses in the plural: hunting parties under the Conqueror and his successors, then the meadow's slower afterlife as Beykoz shifted from imperial hunting ground to Bosphorus village. What they lack in individual fame they make up for in setting. This is one of the few spots on this list where you can stand under a centuries-old plane tree and see the Bosphorus doing exactly what it was doing when the tree was a sapling.

trees.name: The Topkapı Palace Courtyard Plane
trees.access: Paid entry: this tree stands inside Topkapı Palace's ticketed grounds (past Orta Kapu), so a museum ticket is required to reach it
trees.transport: 5-10 min walk from Gülhane or Sultanahmet tram stops (T1 line)
trees.story: Istanbul's most famous plane tree has been dead for about a century. The Janissaries' plane in Topkapı's First Courtyard, the one said to have witnessed the conquest of 1453, dried out somewhere between 1900 and 1930, and the story outlived the tree by a long way. This is not that tree. This is a different oriental plane, further inside the palace, and it is still alive. It stands past the Orta Kapu on the Second Courtyard side, on the ground where the Imperial Council sat for four centuries. Turkey's national monumental tree registry records it at 778 years in one reading and 783 in another, a snapshot difference rather than a real disagreement, which would put its germination in the 1240s, two hundred years before Mehmed II took the city. Take that number carefully, and here is why. The registry's free text entry for this tree is boilerplate palace history that cites a page about a yew, and its web page lists the tree as standing in Gölbaşı, a district of Ankara. The underlying data has the species, the coordinates and the district right; the narrative wrapped around it does not. So the age is the registry's claim, and no independent source confirms a figure for this individual tree. It sits inside the ticketed palace grounds, so reaching it costs a museum entry, and the pin is courtyard level rather than exact.

trees.name: The Gülhane London Plane
trees.access: Free, inside Gulhane Park (open daily, standard park hours, no ticket)
trees.transport: Gulhane tram stop (T1 line) at the park's Sarayburnu-side gate, immediate walk
trees.story: A London plane cannot be much older than about 350 years, because the hybrid did not exist before roughly 1670. This one, at about 285, comfortably fits, which is not true of every tree the Turkish registry files under that name. Two of Istanbul's own registered giants carry the same label at ages that would make the hybrid older than itself; here the arithmetic works, and the identification is plausible rather than proven. Turkey's national monumental tree registry records it at 33 metres tall with a trunk 170 centimetres across and an age of 277 years. Istanbul's metropolitan municipality publishes its own page for this exact tree, with identical measurements, saying it has stood in Gülhane Park since 1741. The two numbers add up to 2018, so both trace to one survey rather than two independent measurements. Two official bodies, one field visit, worth knowing. For most of its life nobody could walk past it. Gülhane was the outer garden of Topkapı Palace, court ground rather than public space, until it opened in 1912 as Istanbul's first public park. The tree was already 170 years old by then. It stands about 40 metres from a registered nettle tree of similar age, 350 metres from the Topkapı courtyard plane and 550 metres from the Taşlı Çınar, which makes this the densest walking cluster in the city.

trees.name: The Gülhane Nettle Tree
trees.access: Free, inside Gulhane Park (open daily, standard park hours, no ticket)
trees.transport: Gulhane tram stop (T1 line) at the park's Sarayburnu-side gate, short walk within the park
trees.story: Istanbul protects this tree by name, which is unusual for a species most cities treat as background. The Mediterranean hackberry, çitlembik in Turkish, normally gets planted for shade and forgotten. This one is 23 metres tall with a trunk 145 centimetres across, and it holds a place on Turkey's national monumental tree registry at an age of 259 years, with the city's own municipal tree project publishing a page for it saying it has stood in Gülhane Park since 1759. Those two figures resolve to the same year, 2018, so the national register and the city are reporting one survey between them rather than two separate measurements. That is worth stating. What makes the number credible anyway is the species: Celtis australis is a tough, long-lived tree in Anatolian conditions, so 265 years is physically ordinary for it, which is more than can be said for some of the plane ages in the same register. It stands roughly 40 metres from the registered London plane in the same park, and the pair are the reason to come. Gülhane was Topkapı's outer palace garden and stayed closed to the public until 1912, so this tree spent its first century and a half inside a court garden and its last hundred years among people eating simit under it. The Topkapı courtyard plane is 300 metres away.

trees.name: The Topkapı Palace Yew
trees.access: Paid entry (Topkapi Palace Museum ticket covers the inner courtyards, including the 4th courtyard/Tulip Garden area)
trees.transport: Gulhane tram stop (T1 line), then roughly 10-15 minute walk through the palace grounds to the 4th courtyard

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: For a yew, three centuries is early middle age. This one, in the Fourth Courtyard of Topkapı Palace, is registered at 314 years, 13 metres tall with a trunk 103 centimetres across and a crown 12 metres wide, which by the standards of a species that can run to millennia makes it a young adult with a long career ahead. The government record has quirks worth naming. Two views of the same database give the age as 314 and 310, a four-year drift, and one of them files the tree under a district hundreds of kilometres away in Ankara province while its own description talks about Topkapı, which is a clerical slip rather than a doubt about where the tree is. Separately, an independent field survey measured three yews in this courtyard, two of them 3.26 and 3.09 metres around, and photographed them in December 2014. That is the freshest direct evidence of them standing that this entry rests on, and it is now twelve years old. Unlike the other trees on this list, it costs money. The Fourth Courtyard was the sultan's private terrace garden, above the Golden Horn beside the Baghdad Kiosk that Murad IV built in 1639, and reaching it needs a Topkapı Palace museum ticket. The free trees of Gülhane Park are 550 metres downhill.

trees.name: The Jagiellonian Oak
trees.access: Paid entry, Jagiellonian University Botanical Garden (open seasonally, check hours)
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk (garden is close to the Old Town's eastern edge)

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: For generations, guides at Poland's oldest botanical garden told visitors this oak was 500 years old, older than the university faculty that planted the garden around it. A dendrochronological study eventually corrected the number to roughly 230, a reminder that even a garden built by scientists can carry a folk legend for two centuries before anyone tests it properly. The real number is less dramatic but not much less impressive: the tree is very nearly as old as the garden itself, founded in 1783 when the Commission of National Education bought monastic land from the Jesuits to give the Krakow Academy's chemistry and natural history faculty somewhere to grow a teaching collection. Sitting at the heart of that collection ever since, the Jagiellonian Oak has outlived the partitions of Poland, two world wars, and the garden's own repeated redesigns. Its species is the single most common one Krakow protects today, a pedunculate oak among 121 individual specimens registered across the city as of 2023, but this particular tree is the one the garden itself calls its most impressive, trunk now six metres around. It stands for anyone who buys the garden's modest entry ticket, its crown wide enough to shade a good stretch of the main path, still growing quietly while its age keeps getting revised downward by better science.

trees.name: The Henryk Oak
trees.access: Free, open access, roadside on public ground in Borek Falecki
trees.transport: Borek Falecki tram loop (Zakopianska), short walk

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This oak is named after the man who spent decades making sure it did not get cut down, not after anyone who planted it. Henryk Bartyzel, who lived beside the tree from 1923 until his death in 2010, is the reason it survived a felling order from wartime occupation authorities and decades of routine maintenance on what became one of Krakow's busiest streets. The oak itself predates him by more than a century: it is the last survivor of the pine-and-oak forest that once covered the former village of Borek, the same wood that gave the village its name, bor being an old Polish word for pine forest, and it became a roadside tree almost by accident in 1790, when Austrian authorities cut the Vienna-to-Lwow highway straight through the ancient stand shortly after Poland's first partition. Everything else that forest once held is gone; only this oak, now around 240 to 250 years past that road-building, is left standing at its edge. In 2010, a civic council formally named it Henryk in Bartyzel's honour, and in 2017 a community restoration project reopened its surroundings after more than 90 volunteers cleared and replanted the ground around its base. It competed, as Krakow's first entrant, in Poland's national Tree of the Year contest in 2018.

trees.name: Poland's Oldest Black Locust
trees.access: Paid entry, Jagiellonian University Botanical Garden (open seasonally, check hours)
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk

best_time.label: May, when it flowers in heavy white clusters

trees.story: Black locusts are not supposed to be rare in Poland. The species arrived from North America in the 18th century and spread so successfully across Central Europe's sandy soils that it now grows practically everywhere, valued for holding loose ground rather than for looking distinguished. Which is what makes the specimen standing in front of Collegium Sniadeckiego, on the Kopernika Street side of the Jagiellonian University's Botanical Garden, worth singling out: at 239 years old by a 2022 measurement, with a trunk 475cm around and a height of 27 metres, it is the oldest confirmed black locust anywhere in Poland. Its age lines up almost exactly with the garden's own founding in 1783, meaning whoever first planted it did so within a few years of the garden's earliest plantings, one of the collection's original survivors rather than a later addition. May brings the reward for anyone who times a visit right: a black locust in full bloom carries heavy clusters of white flowers that draw bees from across the garden, the same nectar that makes the species one of Europe's most productive honey trees. It shares this stretch of path with a run of other exceptionally old specimens dating to the same founding decades, giving one corner of the garden a disproportionate share of Poland's oldest confirmed trees.

trees.name: The Sniadecki Dogwoods
trees.access: Paid entry, Jagiellonian University Botanical Garden (open seasonally, check hours)
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk

best_time.label: February and March, when it flowers before its leaves appear

trees.story: Jan Sniadecki was one of the Enlightenment's great Polish polymaths, an astronomer and mathematician who reformed how Krakow's university taught science, and tradition credits him with personally planting these cornelian cherries along the Botanical Garden's main path around 1790, while he was directing the observatory next door. Cornelian cherry is usually grown as a large shrub rather than what most people picture as a tree, which is part of why these specimens stand out: at roughly 230 years old, they are among the oldest cultivated cornelian cherries recorded in Poland, multi-stemmed and gnarled in a way that reads more like an old apple tree than the tidy hedge shrub gardeners plant today. They flower before almost anything else in the garden wakes up, small clusters of yellow blossom opening as early as February while frost is still a real possibility, followed by tart red fruit in late summer that Polish households have turned into preserves and liqueur for centuries. Sniadecki's connection to the garden runs deeper than one planting: the university's astronomical observatory, which he helped establish, still stands in the Collegium building the garden surrounds, and the dogwoods are the closest thing to a living monument to the man himself, unlabelled and easy to walk past without knowing what they are.

trees.name: The Filharmonia Plane
trees.age: estimated 150 to 270 years, from its girth
trees.access: Free, public park (Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station or Filharmonia tram/bus stops, short walk through Planty
trees.story:
Krakow protects ten London planes on the Planty ring, and this is the one that dwarfs the other nine. Its trunk measures 520 centimetres around, comfortably the largest girth in that group, which is what earned it a place on the city's natural monument register in 1997. Nobody has dated it. What exists is the girth, and running that figure through a published growth-factor method puts the tree somewhere between 150 and 270 years old. The band is deliberately wide. The calculation borrows its growth rate from a related American species because no factor for the London plane was found, and a tree standing in a city grows at a speed no formula can know. Read the number as an estimate taken off the trunk rather than a birth year.

The park underneath is better documented than the tree in it. Planty was laid out in the 1820s, after Krakow pulled down its medieval walls and ringed the Old Town with gardens instead. Nothing records when this plane went into that ground. Nor is the register any guarantee of survival: two other protected trees in the same part of the city, a red beech by the Archaeological Museum and a horse chestnut on ul. Podzamcze, were brought down by storms in February 2022 and July 2021.

trees.name: The Straszewskiego Ash
trees.age: estimated 150 to 220 years, from its girth
trees.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto (Planty ring, west side near Wawel)
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Straszewskiego, bordering Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Wawel tram/bus stops or Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk
trees.story:
European ash is one of the commonest trees in Poland and a thick one is not common at all. This specimen stands on the pavement of ul. Straszewskiego, on the western edge of Planty a few minutes below Wawel, and measures 375 centimetres around. That is what earned it a place on the city's natural monument register in 1987.

Its age is arithmetic rather than record. The girth works out at roughly 119 centimetres of diameter, and a published growth factor returns something near 190 years from that. Two things keep it a range instead of a number. The factor is borrowed from green ash, the closest documented relative that has one, and no tape measure can see what two centuries of drought years, good years and street rebuilding did inside the trunk. Call it 150 to 220 years and leave it there. Only a core sample would settle it.

The species itself has had a hard three decades. A fungal dieback spreading west since the 1990s has thinned ash across Europe, killing young and old trees alike and making veterans of this size less ordinary every year than they used to be. This one is still standing, on a public pavement, free to walk up to at any hour.

trees.name: The Krowoderska Lime
trees.age: estimated 130 to 175 years, from its girth
trees.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto / Krowodrza border, north of the Old Town
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Krowoderska), open at all hours
trees.transport: Nowy Kleparz or Basztowa tram stops, short walk

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story:
Four of the ages on this walk come off a tape measure rather than out of any record, and this is the only one where the arithmetic gets to use the tree's own species. The published growth factor for small-leaved lime is an exact match for what stands at ul. Krowoderska 16: a trunk 402 centimetres round, which converts to about 128 centimetres of diameter and returns roughly 150 years. Even then the honest form is a range, 130 to 175, because a growth factor describes an average lime rather than this one, and this one has spent its whole life in a street.

Poles have a longer relationship with the species than most. Lipa is the Polish name for it, and lipiec, the word for July, comes from the same root, because July is when the lime flowers and the tree fills with bees loud enough to hear from the pavement. Villages planted them at churches and crossroads for centuries.

This one has been protected since 1987 and is a city tree by contrast, on a working street north of the Old Town rather than in the park ring. It marks the far end of the Planty loop, about 1.2 kilometres from the ash on ul. Straszewskiego at the other extreme.

trees.name: The Garncarska Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Garncarska, bordering Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Teatr Bagatela tram stop or Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk

best_time.label: November, when the crown turns butter gold and drops almost all at once

trees.story:
Three trunks rise from a single base on ul. Garncarska, and the number the register carries, 275 centimetres, belongs to the largest of them rather than to one trunk. The other two measure 203 and 175. Krakow listed the tree as a natural monument in 1968, decades earlier than most of the entries around it, which suggests somebody thought it unusual long before the modern register caught up.

How old is it? Nobody knows, and here guessing would be worse than saying so. The girth-to-age arithmetic that dates the oaks and limes on this walk needs a growth factor calibrated to the species, and no reliable one exists for ginkgo: the tree thickens at wildly different rates depending on cultivar, site and how much room its roots were given. So the age field stays empty on purpose. If you have seen a planting record for this stretch of Garncarska, or a photograph old enough to help, tell us.

What it does reliably deliver is November. Ginkgo leaves turn from green to a flat butter gold and then let go almost all at once, often within a couple of days, which on a three-stemmed tree of this size means a great deal of gold hitting the pavement in one go.

trees.name: The Bartoszewski Square Oak
trees.age: estimated 140 to 210 years, from its girth
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all hours
trees.transport: Poczta Glowna or Dworzec Glowny tram stops, short walk
trees.story:
The oak was on the register ten years before the square had a name. Krakow protected it in 2008. The city council voted on 10 October 2018 to name the ground around it after Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, a Home Army member who survived Auschwitz, was honoured as Righteous Among the Nations and later served as Poland's foreign minister. It is his square, not his oak. Nothing in the record links the tree to the man beyond the address, and the dates rule out the tidier story.

It is an odd oak in its own right. This is a columnar cultivar of the pedunculate oak, which grows narrow and upright instead of spreading, closer in outline to a poplar than to the wide-crowned oaks most people picture when they hear the word. The trunk is 288 centimetres around, standing where four streets meet at the northern edge of Planty.

Its age is calculated, not recorded. That girth gives about 92 centimetres of diameter, and the published factor for the white oak group returns roughly 180 years. Take the range, 140 to 210, and take it loosely: nobody has documented how fast a columnar cultivar thickens compared with an ordinary oak, which is uncertainty stacked on top of uncertainty.

trees.name: The Basztowa Turkish Hazel
trees.access: Free, public park (Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Dworzec Glowny (Krakow Glowny) tram/bus stops, short walk through Planty
trees.story:
Turkish hazel is not the shrub its name suggests. Corylus colurna is a proper forest tree, native to southeast Europe and Asia Minor, capable of 25 metres and a neat conical crown, which is why cities plant it along streets when they want something tough and tidy. Krakow's protected list runs heavily to oaks, limes and planes, so a hazel on it is an oddity, and this one stands in Planty itself beside ul. Basztowa, close to the main station.

It grows as two stems from one base, 165 and 120 centimetres round. The 165 is the larger stem rather than a single trunk, which is worth stating plainly: the two figures do not add together, and a two-stemmed tree reads as bulkier than either measurement on its own. The city registered it in 2008.

Its age is not known. The growth-factor arithmetic used on the oaks and limes nearby needs a divisor matched to the species, and the only hazel figure in the standard tables is calibrated to common hazel, a multi-stemmed shrub with nothing like this tree's habit. Applying it would produce a number, not an estimate. If anyone holds a planting date for this corner of Planty, we would like to hear it.

trees.name: The Studencka Plane
trees.age: estimated 90 to 165 years, from its girth
trees.neighbourhood: Piasek, west of the Planty ring (Stare Miasto)
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Studencka), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.story:
Krakow's biggest registered plane, on the Planty by the Philharmonic, measures 520 centimetres round. The one outside ul. Studencka 25 is a third smaller, 315 centimetres, and still made the city's natural monument register in 1997 on its own merits, a full street away from the Planty ring in the old Piasek district.

Its age is arithmetic rather than record. Working the girth through the growth factor already used for its bigger relative on the Planty, borrowed from American sycamore since no rate has been published for London plane itself, puts it somewhere between 90 and 165 years old. That is a wide bracket on purpose. Nobody has cored the trunk, and a tree growing between a road and a row of nineteenth century apartment blocks answers to the paving and pipes around it as much as to its own species.

London planes were planted through Krakow by the hundreds a century or more ago because almost nothing kills them: not compacted soil, not exhaust, not a hard prune. This one has outlasted whatever stood on Studencka before it, on a street that has changed its own name four times since 1893 while the tree kept growing. Free to walk up to, any hour.

trees.name: The Kossaka Square Ash
trees.age: estimated 130 to 190 years, from its girth
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (Plac Kossaka), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.story:
Plac Kossaka today is better known for parked cars and a kebab stand than for its trees, which is what makes the ash at number 4 easy to miss. It measures 321 centimetres around, entered onto Krakow's natural monument register in 1997, and stands a few streets from the city's other protected ash on ul. Straszewskiego, itself 375 centimetres and estimated at 150 to 220 years old by the same method.

Scaling this tree's girth against that already-published estimate, using the same borrowed growth factor (European ash has none of its own published, so the figure comes from green ash, its closest documented relative), puts the Kossaka tree at roughly 130 to 190 years. Narrower trunk, younger tree, same square kilometre of the city.

European ash is one of the commonest species in Poland, which is exactly why a trunk this thick stands out. The species has also had a hard three decades: a fungal dieback moving west since the 1990s has thinned ash populations across the continent, killing young and old trees indiscriminately. A veteran ash surviving that, on a square used mostly for parking, is a small piece of luck rather than a guarantee. Free and open to the street at any hour.

trees.name: The Batorego Oak and Ginkgo
trees.species: Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) and Ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba)
trees.access: Free, roadside trees on public ground (ul. Batorego), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Two protected trees stand two doors apart on ul. Batorego, a pedunculate oak at number 14 and a ginkgo at number 12, both entered onto Krakow's natural monument register on the same day in 1997. The oak is the thicker of the two, 336 centimetres around; the ginkgo measures 305.

Neither has a documented age, and this is one case where guessing off the girth would mislead rather than help. Oak and ginkgo do not share a growth pattern with the ash and plane already published nearby, and no reliable published growth factor for either species in this climate was found this pass. What is verified is simpler and enough on its own: two long-lived species, planted close enough together to have been a deliberate pairing rather than a coincidence, both still standing on an ordinary residential street.

Ginkgo is the more unusual of the two. Native to China and unrelated to any other tree alive today, the species survived the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs, and six ginkgos close to the 1945 blast at Hiroshima resprouted from scorched trunks and still stand there. This one has had an easier life, on a Krakow pavement, free to see at any hour.

trees.name: The Sikorskiego Square Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Piasek, west of the Old Town
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (Plac Sikorskiego), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Plac Sikorskiego's oak is the youngest addition to Krakow's register among the trees on this page, protected in 2007 rather than in the 1997 batch that covers most of the others. Its girth, 263 centimetres, is also the smallest of the pedunculate oaks the city protects near its centre, behind both the columnar oak on Skwer Bartoszewskiego and the Jagiellonian and Henryk oaks published elsewhere on this walk.

No age has been published for it, and running an ordinary pedunculate oak's girth through a growth factor table is a riskier bet than for species like ash or plane on this list. A standard-form oak's growth rate varies more with soil, light and pruning history than almost anything else here, and no comparably grown oak from the same register gives a safe baseline to scale from. Better to leave the number out than guess at one.

What is certain is the trunk itself, thick enough at 263 centimetres to be a genuine veteran by any reasonable account, standing on a square named for the Polish general and prime minister in exile Wladyslaw Sikorski, who died in a plane crash off Gibraltar in 1943. Free to see at any hour.

trees.name: The Tarlowska Lime
trees.age: estimated 85 to 115 years, from its girth
trees.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto, near the Planty ring
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Tarlowska), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story:
Krakow already protects one small-leaved lime on this page, a 402 centimetre trunk on ul. Krowoderska whose age comes out at 130 to 175 years by the species' own published growth factor, an unusually exact match between the tape measure and the science. The lime on ul. Tarlowska is the smaller of the city's two, 259 centimetres round, entered onto the register in 2004, seventeen years after most of the trees on this walk.

Running the same growth factor against this thinner trunk gives a range of roughly 85 to 115 years, which would put its planting somewhere in the interwar years or just after, plausible for a street lime on a residential road rebuilt more than once since. As with its bigger relative, the number is arithmetic rather than record: nobody has cored it, and the bracket stays wide on purpose.

Small-leaved lime was the tree cities across Central Europe reached for through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, tolerant of pollution, easy to pollard, long-lived enough to still be standing when the street around it has changed shape several times over. This one is free to walk up to on ul. Tarlowska at any hour.

trees.name: The Sw. Jana Tree of Heaven
trees.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto (Old Town core, between the Main Square and the Planty)
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Swietego Jana), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Main Square, Stare Miasto
trees.story:
Ulica Swietego Jana runs from the Main Square to the Planty, one of the most walked streets in the Old Town, and the tree registered at number 30 is a species most European cities spend money trying to remove. Ailanthus altissima, tree of heaven, seeds into any crack in the pavement, sends up suckers under paving stones and shades out whatever grew there first, fast enough to reach a serious size within a single lifetime. Krakow protects this one anyway, entered onto the natural monument register in 1997 for a trunk 292 centimetres around.

That speed is exactly why no age is published here. A growth factor that works for an oak or a lime tells you nothing about a tree that can add a metre of height in a good year. Dublin's own registered tree of heaven carries an official estimate of 120 to 165 years that the species' own growth pattern argues should be closer to 70 or 100. Rather than repeat that kind of guess, this page states the girth and leaves the age open.

What is not in doubt is the tree itself, standing on one of Krakow's busiest historic streets, growing well before anyone thought to protect it.

trees.name: The Franciszkanska Ginkgo
trees.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto (Old Town), beside the Franciscan church
trees.access: Free. Stands on ul. Franciszkańska in the Old Town, beside the Church of the Franciscans (kościół oo. Franciszkanów); publicly visible and reachable from the street at all times.
trees.transport: Filharmonia tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Nobody has measured this ginkgo's age, but its trunk gives away that it is old enough to fruit, a milestone the species does not reach for about forty years. It grows on ul. Franciszkanska beside the Church of the Franciscans in the Old Town, a two hundred and fifty eight centimetre trunk standing where monks have kept a garden for centuries.

Poland's national register of natural monuments lists the tree's protection as dating from 1998; the city's own official list, reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, gives 1997 for this tree and several others nearby, a discrepancy that most likely traces to a province-wide reconfirmation regulation rather than a disagreement about the tree itself. Both dates are recorded here rather than picked between.

Ginkgo biloba survived in cultivation around temple grounds in East Asia for centuries before European gardens took it up, and it tends to end up beside old religious buildings for the same reason it did here: nobody with authority over sacred ground had reason to cut down something that was simply doing well. No age has been established for this specimen. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Powroznicza Red Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Podgórze, in the garden of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (district public library)
trees.access: Free. Stands in the grounds of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (Podgórze District Public Library) at ul. Powroźnicza 2, a public institution housed in a late-19th-century villa; reachable during the library's opening hours.
trees.transport: In Podgórze, roughly a 10-minute walk from Rynek Podgórski; bus routes serving nearby ul. Kalwaryjska and Rynek Podgórski are the closest public transport.
trees.story:
Krakow's monumental trees are almost all native oaks and limes, which makes this one an outlier twice over: a Northern Red Oak, a North American species, growing in the garden of a public library. The building itself has its own history worth knowing before the tree. Built as a villa in the late 1880s and once purchased for the painter Jan Matejko's daughter Beata, it has served as Podgorze district's public library since 1988, which is what keeps its garden open rather than walled off as someone's private grounds.

The oak's trunk measures three metres fourteen around, big enough that Poland's national register protects it as a natural monument, though the register itself carries no age. Its protection date is recorded two ways, 1987 in the national database and 1997 in the city's own list, likely the gap between an original designation and a later province-wide reconfirmation rather than a real dispute.

A honey locust stands twelve metres away in the same garden, registered alongside it under the same library grounds. No age has been established for either, and an introduced ornamental species like this one has no reliable local growth rate to estimate from. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Powroznicza Honey Locust
trees.neighbourhood: Podgórze, in the garden of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (district public library)
trees.access: Free. Stands in the grounds of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (Podgórze District Public Library) at ul. Powroźnicza 2, a public institution housed in a late-19th-century villa; reachable during the library's opening hours.
trees.transport: In Podgórze, roughly a 10-minute walk from Rynek Podgórski; bus routes serving nearby ul. Kalwaryjska and Rynek Podgórski are the closest public transport.
trees.story:
Twelve metres from the library's red oak stands its quieter neighbour, a honey locust with a trunk two metres twenty three around, one of relatively few of its species protected anywhere in Krakow as a natural monument. Both trees share the same garden, the grounds of the Podgorze district public library, a villa built in the 1880s that has kept its grounds open to the public since it became a library in 1988.

Gleditsia triacanthos is a North American species, armed in the wild with vicious branching thorns that cultivated street and garden specimens are usually bred without, and it took to European ornamental planting in the nineteenth century the way its oak neighbour did. Poland's national register protects it on species and location alone, with no girth or age recorded there; the city's own official list adds the measurement.

The two protection dates disagree by a decade, 1987 nationally against 1997 in the city record, in the same pattern as its neighbour and several other Krakow trees this pass checked, most likely a province wide reconfirmation rather than two different true dates. No age has been established. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Kosciuszki Silver Lime
trees.access: Free. Stands on ul. Kościuszki in Krowodrza, visible and reachable from the public street.
trees.transport: Bus routes 134 and 502 run along ul. Kościuszki.
trees.story:
Krakow already has one small leaved lime on this list whose age comes from an unusually exact match between a tape measure and the published science: the Krowoderska Lime, four hundred and two centimetres round, dated to 130 to 175 years by the species' own documented growth rate. This tree, on the same street, is a different species entirely, a silver lime, and its own trunk has grown even thicker: four hundred and twenty four centimetres.

No document records when it was planted, so its age here is derived rather than measured: applying the growth rate this city's own lime data already established, widened to allow for the difference between species, puts it at roughly 130 to 190 years old. That is an estimate from girth, not a planting record, and the wide band is the honest shape of that kind of arithmetic.

Poland's national register dates its protection to 1975; the city's own list gives 1997, the same reconfirmation-year pattern seen elsewhere on this page. It stands on ul. Kosciuszki in Krowodrza, visible from the public street, served by two city bus routes.

trees.name: The Daszynskiego Lime
trees.access: Free. Stands on Aleja Ignacego Daszyńskiego, a public avenue in Śródmieście; visible and reachable from the street at all times.
trees.transport: Tram lines 1, 10, 20, 24, 50 and 52 run along Aleja Daszyńskiego; the tree is a short walk from house number 13.
trees.story:
This lime is the youngest of three different Tilia species this page now protects, and the arithmetic that ages it borrows from the other two. Krakow's own small leaved limes gave a documented growth rate for this climate; applied to this tree's two hundred and eighty four centimetre trunk, with room left for the uncertainty of crossing species, it comes out at roughly 85 to 130 years. That is an estimate built from girth, not a planting date, and the width of the range is the honest price of that method.

Unlike its neighbours on this page, this large leaved lime carries an exact and recent paper trail: Krakow's city council protected it by name in a resolution dated 16 December 2015, entered into the national register three weeks later. No thirty year gap between two dates here, just the ordinary lag between a vote and its paperwork.

It grows on Aleja Daszynskiego in Srodmiescie, a wide tram lined avenue rather than a park, doing the quiet work street trees do: six tram lines run past it, and Wikimedia Commons already has a photograph of it standing there among the traffic.

trees.name: The Reclining Dragon Pine
trees.access: Paid entry to Yoshimine-dera (500 yen adult)
trees.transport: Hankyu Bus to Yoshiminedera stop, 8 min walk uphill
trees.story: This pine grows sideways, not up. Standing above the stone steps between Yoshimine-dera's main hall and its pagoda, the tree's trunk runs almost flat along a terrace rather than climbing skyward the way pines usually do, a five-needle pine trained or simply left to sprawl for over six centuries. A 19th century official, Hanayama's former minister Ieatsu, named it in 1857: Yuryu, the playing dragon, for the way its horizontal length resembles a dragon lounging on the ground. It once reached 50 metres end to end, long enough to rank as one of the longest documented pine specimens in Japan, until pine bark beetles infested it in 1994 and roughly 15 metres had to be cut away to save what remained. At its current 37 metres it is still one of the three trees Kyoto traditionally names as its most celebrated pines, and it remains a nationally designated natural monument, protected status Japan reserves for a small number of trees each century.

trees.name: The Land Boat Pine
trees.access: Paid entry to Kinkaku-ji
trees.transport: Kyoto City Bus 101/205 to Kinkakuji-michi, 3 min walk
trees.story: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the shogun who built the Golden Pavilion, once kept this tree as a bonsai in a pot. Sometime after Yoshimitsu's death in 1408, his potted pine was planted in the ground beside Kinkaku-ji's Kyoko-chi pond and trained into the shape of a sailing ship, its trunk and branches clipped over generations to suggest a hull, a mast and a bow pointed deliberately west, toward the Buddhist Pure Land. The result, Rikushu-no-matsu, land boat pine, has been maintained in that same nautical silhouette for roughly six centuries, making it one of the longest continuously shaped ornamental pines in Japan and one of the three trees Kyoto names among its most celebrated. Nineteenth century photographs from the 1870s and 1880s already show it in recognizably the same boat form it holds today, meaning the shape itself, not just the tree, has outlasted the Meiji Restoration, two world wars and the reconstruction of the pavilion after a 1950 arson fire.

trees.name: The Five-Needle Pine of Hosen-in
trees.access: Paid entry to Hosen-in (includes matcha service)
trees.transport: Kyoto Bus to Ohara, 12 min walk
trees.story: Visitors to this small temple in the Ohara valley sit on red felt cushions in a wooden hall and look at the garden through the frame of a doorway, a deliberate composition called a gakubuchi teien, or picture-frame garden. The subject of that living picture is this pine, trained over roughly seven centuries into a shape said to echo Mount Mikami, a solitary peak southeast of the city sometimes nicknamed Omi Fuji for its cone shape. The tree holds Kyoto City natural monument status and is one of the temple's central attractions alongside a ceiling made from the floorboards of Fushimi Castle, preserved with bloodstains from a 1600 samurai last stand. By 2021 the pine showed signs of strain from age and drought, prompting visible care from the temple's gardeners; recent visitor accounts describe it recovering vigor since. Ohara sits in the hills north of central Kyoto, quieter than the city's headline temples, and the pine rewards the trip out with a garden built around one tree's silhouette rather than a wide landscape.

photo.attribution: Maechan0360, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Inverted Ginkgo of Nishi Honganji
trees.access: Free, Nishi Honganji precinct open daily
trees.transport: Kyoto Station, 15 min walk, or bus to Nishihonganji-mae

best_time.label: late November, one of Kyoto's more dependable autumn colour displays

trees.story: This ginkgo grows low and wide rather than tall, its heaviest branches spreading outward close to the ground before the trunk narrows above them, an arrangement that from certain angles makes the whole tree look planted upside down, roots reaching for the sky. That resemblance earned it the name Sakasa Icho, inverted ginkgo, sometime after it went into the ground in front of Nishi Honganji's Goeido Hall in 1636. A second nickname, Mizufuki Icho, water-spouting ginkgo, comes from a temple legend that the tree spouted water to help extinguish fires that threatened the complex in 1788 and again in 1864, both real, documented blazes in Kyoto's history even if the tree's firefighting role is legend rather than record. Ginkgos are famously fire-resistant compared to other species, their trunks holding unusual water content, which may be where the story got its foothold. The tree is a designated Kyoto City natural monument and turns gold most reliably in late November, one of the more dependable autumn color displays in a city that plans its calendar around them.

trees.name: The Weeping Cherry of Gion
trees.age: 75-90 years (second-generation tree; sources disagree on the exact figure)
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Gion-Shijo (Keihan) or Higashiyama (Tozai Line), 10 min walk

best_time.label: late March into early April, when its cascading blossoms draw crowds for night illumination

trees.story: The tree everyone photographs at Maruyama Park is not the tree that made the spot famous. The original weeping cherry, a single white higan variety with a trunk 4 metres around, stood here for more than 200 years and earned natural monument status in 1938, only to die in 1947 in the difficult years after the war. Sano Toemon XV, a cherry tree keeper from a family that has tended Kyoto's most important specimens for generations, had collected seeds from the dying original in 1928 and grew a successor, which he donated and planted on the same spot in 1949. That second tree is the one visitors see today, floodlit most nights during bloom season into a canopy of pale pink against the dark, one of the most photographed single trees in Japan. Sources differ on exactly how old to call it, some counting from the 1949 planting and others from the 1928 seed collection, a small discrepancy left honest here rather than resolved into a false precision. Either way, the tree standing in Maruyama Park today has been growing for the better part of a century, not the two hundred years its predecessor reached.

trees.name: The Camphor of Munakata Shrine
trees.access: Free, Kyoto Gyoen open daily
trees.transport: Marutamachi (Karasuma Line) or Karasuma-Marutamachi bus stop, 5 min walk
