trees.story: Kyoto Gyoen, the wooded park that surrounds the old Imperial Palace, holds more than 200 trees old and large enough to be called giants by the environment ministry that manages the grounds today. This camphor, growing at Munakata Shrine in the park's southwest corner, is generally named as the single oldest and largest of them, though sources disagree on the tree's exact age by as much as two centuries, a spread wide enough that it is stated here as a range rather than a false certainty. The shrine itself dates to 795, founded when Emperor Kanmu had a protective deity brought from the original Munakata Shrine in what is now Fukuoka Prefecture to watch over the new capital at Heian-kyo, and this camphor has grown at the site for a large fraction of the park's history since. Kyoto Gyoen has been public parkland since the Meiji era moved the imperial residence to Tokyo, and its giant trees, ginkgos, zelkovas, hackberries and camphors among them, now shade a park most Kyoto residents walk through rather than one they think to visit specifically.

trees.name: The Emperor's Camphor of Imakumano
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: Keihan Bus to Sennyuji-michi, 2 min walk
trees.story: This tree has a birth year most ancient trees can only guess at: 1160, the year the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa founded Imakumano Shrine as a branch of the Kumano sanctuaries on the Kii Peninsula, reportedly bringing this camphor north from the original site to plant at the new one. Camphor trees are native to warmer coastal Japan, not inland Kyoto, which fits the transplant story better than it would if the species were simply local. Nearly nine centuries later the tree stands 21.9 metres tall with a trunk 6.58 metres around and a canopy spreading 23.5 metres east to west, thick enough that it functions as the shrine's unofficial landmark, visible before the shrine buildings themselves from the surrounding streets. Imakumano Shrine carries another distinction unrelated to the tree: it is traditionally named as a birthplace of Noh theatre, where a young performer called Zeami is said to have caught the attention of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu at a 14th century performance, the encounter that launched Noh toward becoming a shogunal art form. The camphor was already two centuries old when that performance happened.

trees.name: The Taiko Weeping Cherry of Daigo-ji
trees.age: about 150-170 years (not the tree Hideyoshi saw)
trees.access: Paid entry to Sanboin
trees.transport: Daigo (Tozai Line), 12 min walk

best_time.label: late March into early April, when its blossoms recreate the display Hideyoshi once staged here

trees.story: In the spring of 1598, months before his death, the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi staged one of the most extravagant cherry blossom parties in Japanese history at Daigo-ji, inviting hundreds of guests and reportedly having some 700 cherry trees transplanted to the temple grounds for the occasion. The weeping cherry now growing in the Sanboin sub-temple's garden carries his name, Taiko Shidarezakura, and his story, but it is not that tree: at roughly 150 to 170 years old it was planted in the 19th century, long after Hideyoshi's party and his own death the same year. What survives is the site and the association, strong enough that the painter Okumura Togyu made this specific tree the subject of a celebrated work simply titled Daigo, after which the tree picked up a second nickname, Togyu's cherry. Sanboin's garden itself was largely designed by Hideyoshi in the last months of his life, which means the cherry, even at a fraction of his party's age, blooms inside a landscape he did lay out himself.

trees.name: The Heian Cedar of Katanami
trees.access: Restricted, requires prior arrangement with Kyoto City and an accompanying nature guide
trees.transport: JR Bus to Shukuzan, then Keihoku community bus toward Haiya; the visitor center is close to the stop
trees.story: Deep in the forested headwaters of the Katanami River, in Kyoto's rural northern hills, stands a cedar said to have been alive when the Heian-kyo palace it is named for was first built. This forest was imperial timber land for centuries, called Goshomigoyo, and historical records describe it supplying construction material for both Heian-kyo and the earlier short-lived capital of Nagaoka-kyo, as well as replacement timber whenever the imperial palace burned, which happened more than once. The Heian Cedar and its neighbours in this grove are a distinctive local type called fuseki-dai sugi, layering cedars, a growth habit suited to heavy snow: a trunk pushed down and pinned to the ground by winter snowfall can root at the point of contact and rise again as a new, genetically identical trunk, letting a single tree effectively propagate itself sideways across a hillside over centuries. The site is not casually accessible. Kyoto City restricts entry to protect the grove, and visiting requires prior arrangement with the city and an accompanying nature guide, a real constraint on the goal of walking up to see it, stated here plainly rather than glossed over.

trees.name: The Emperor's Gift Cherry of Kamigamo
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: Kyoto City Bus to Kamigamo Jinja-mae, at the shrine gate

best_time.label: late March into early April, among the first of the shrine's cherries to bloom

trees.story: This weeping cherry began its life somewhere inside the Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds before Emperor Komei, who reigned from 1846 to 1867 and was the father of the Meiji Emperor, had it given to Kamigamo Shrine. That gift is the source of its name, Gosho-zakura, palace cherry, and the reason a cherry tree with no natural connection to Kamigamo's centuries-old shrine complex has stood on the approach path between its first and second torii gates for roughly a century and a half regardless. It blooms alongside a second named cherry, Saio-zakura, whose deep red flowers offer a contrast to Gosho-zakura's white, so that visitors walking the approach in late March or early April see two named, individually storied trees rather than an anonymous cherry avenue. Kamigamo Shrine itself, formally Kamowakeikazuchi Shrine, is one of Kyoto's oldest religious sites and a UNESCO World Heritage component, its grounds predating this cherry by many centuries; the tree is a relatively recent addition to a very old place, and its imperial provenance is what earns it a place among the shrine's named, individually recognized trees rather than the roughly 200 unnamed cherries also growing on the grounds.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Demizu-guchi
trees.access: Free. Kyoto Gyoen National Garden (the public park surrounding the Imperial Palace) is open to the public year-round, dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Marutamachi Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 10 minute walk
trees.story:
The crown of this tree is ten metres wider than the tree is tall. Kamigyo Ward's register of what it calls its pride trees measures the hackberry at the Demizu gate at 22.5 metres high, with a trunk 4.98 metres around and branches reaching 32.9 metres across, one of the largest hackberries the ward has on record. What nobody has recorded is its age. The register measures trees, it does not date them, and no other source puts a number on this one, so its size is the honest thing to say about it and its years are not.

Kyoto Gyoen took its present shape in 1877, after the emperor's court left for Tokyo and the aristocratic quarter that filled this ground was cleared into open parkland. The environment ministry that manages the park today counts more than 200 trees on it big enough to call giants: hackberries, zelkovas, camphors and ginkgos, growing on ground that was private for most of its history and public for the last century and a half. This one stands beside Demizu-guchi, a pedestrian gate in the west wall, a short walk from the camphor at Munakata Shrine in the same southwest corner of the park. Between them they anchor a corner where several remarkable trees stand within a few minutes of each other, which is rare in a city that keeps most of its best ones an hour apart by bus.

trees.name: The Zelkova of Ishiyakushi Gate
trees.access: Free. Kyoto Gyoen National Garden is open to the public year-round, dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Imadegawa Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 12 minute walk
trees.story:
Keyaki, the Japanese name for this species, is the timber temple carpenters and drum makers reach for first, which is one reason very large ones are not common. This one was left standing. Kamigyo Ward's register measures it at 22 metres tall, with a trunk 4.29 metres around and a crown spreading 29.6 metres, which puts it among the largest zelkovas the ward has catalogued. Its age is a blank. The register records dimensions and nothing else, and no other source names this tree at all, so the measurements are what can be stated and the years are not.

It grows just inside Ishiyakushi-gomon, one of nine gates in the walls that still mark out the old palace enclosure, on the Teramachi-dori side. The ground behind those walls was a district of court nobles' mansions until 1869, when the emperor moved to Tokyo and the households followed him; the plots were cleared and replanted from 1877, which is why a park in the middle of a capital city now holds trees this size at all. The zelkova sits at the opposite end of that park from the hackberry at the Demizu gate, about 1.1 kilometres away, close enough that the two mark the ends of the same walk.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Nashinoki Shrine
trees.neighbourhood: Teramachi, Kamigyo-ku (immediately east of Kyoto Gyoen)
trees.access: Free to enter the shrine precinct.
trees.transport: Keihan Jingu-Marutamachi Station, roughly 8 minute walk
trees.story:
One document describes this tree, and it is a list of measurements. Kamigyo Ward records the hackberry at Nashinoki Shrine as 21 metres tall, with a trunk 3.72 metres around and a canopy spreading 19.4 metres, and designates it one of the ward's pride trees. No source gives it an age, and nothing else written about the shrine mentions it.

Worth knowing before you arrive: the tree Nashinoki is locally known for is a different one, a katsura that carries a nickname and a following of its own. The hackberry has neither. What it has is size and a position, on Teramachi-dori directly against Kyoto Gyoen's east wall, about 850 metres from the camphor at Munakata Shrine, which costs a visitor almost nothing to add to a loop of the park.

The shrine is young by Kyoto standards. It was founded in 1885 for Sanjo Sanetomi, the court noble who fled the capital with six others in 1863 on the losing side of a factional purge, spent years in exile in Choshu, and came back to serve as chancellor of the Meiji state. The precinct that went up for him is small, walled and quiet, which is a plausible explanation for how a tree of this size has been left alone a few metres from the traffic on Teramachi-dori.

trees.name: The Grand Ginkgo of Goo Shrine
trees.neighbourhood: Karasuma, Kamigyo-ku (immediately west of Kyoto Gyoen)
trees.access: Free to enter the shrine precinct.
trees.transport: Marutamachi Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 5 minute walk

best_time.label: late November, when the whole crown goes gold at once and drops within a week

trees.story:
The guardians at this shrine gate are wild boars rather than the usual stone lion-dogs, and the tree behind them is the tallest thing on the grounds. Kamigyo Ward measures the ginkgo standing north of the main hall at 25 metres, with a trunk 3.18 metres around, the largest of six sizeable ginkgos in the precinct. A Kyoto travel description puts the shrine's big ginkgos at several hundred years old. That is an estimate rather than a measured figure and nobody has narrowed it since, so several hundred years is as close as anyone can honestly get.

The boars are for Wake no Kiyomaro, the eighth century official the shrine honours. In 769 he blocked the monk Dokyo's attempt to have himself made emperor, and was exiled and, by the shrine's telling, crippled for it; a herd of wild boars is said to have escorted him to safety, after which his legs recovered. That is why people come here to pray for their legs and feet rather than for exam results, and why boars sit where lion-dogs usually do.

In the last days of November the ginkgo turns, the whole crown going gold at once and then dropping most of it inside a week. The shrine faces Kyoto Gyoen's west wall on Karasuma-dori, five minutes from Marutamachi station.

trees.name: The Carriage-Turning Cherry of Kyoto Gyoen
trees.species: Cherry, mixed single and double flowering on one tree (Prunus sp.)
trees.neighbourhood: Southwest of Seisho-mon gate, Kyoto Gyoen, Kamigyo-ku
trees.access: Free. Kyoto Gyoen National Garden is open to the public year-round, dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Marutamachi Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 15 minute walk

best_time.label: early April, when single and double blossom open together on one crown

trees.story:
The tree that stopped an emperor's carriage is not the tree standing here now. Kurumagaeshi-zakura means the carriage turned back, and the name comes from a tradition that Emperor Go-Mizunoo, who reigned from 1611 to 1629, had already passed this cherry when he ordered his carriage brought round for a second look. That is a story told about the tree rather than anything recorded in his reign, and it is worth saying which of the two it is.

The cherry standing southwest of Seisho-mon gate today is not that tree either. The original went, and after the war the Kyoto nurseryman Sano Toujiro raised its replacement from shoots cut off it, so what grows here is roughly eighty years old and genetically the same cherry, in the same place, on its second run.

Go in April and the reason to stop has nothing to do with emperors. Single and double flowers open together on the same crown, the flat five petals of a wild cherry beside the crowded rosettes of a cultivated one, all on one tree. Kyoto Gyoen has been public ground since 1877, eight years after the court followed the emperor to Tokyo, and this corner of it puts the cherry within a kilometre of the hackberry at Demizu-guchi and the camphor at Munakata Shrine.

trees.name: Chinkapin oak (Sudajii) of Omiya Gate, Kyoto Gyoen
trees.neighbourhood: Near Omiya-gomon, south side of Kyoto Gyoen, Kamigyo-ku
trees.access: Free. Kyoto Gyoen National Garden is open to the public year-round, dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Marutamachi Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 3 minute walk
trees.story:
Before there was a city here, this was the tree that covered the ground. Sudajii, the Japanese chinkapin, was the dominant canopy of the evergreen broadleaf forest that ran across lowland western Japan until it was cleared for rice, timber and capitals, which makes a full-grown one inside Kyoto a leftover of the landscape the city replaced. This one stands at the Omiya gate on the south side of Kyoto Gyoen. Kamigyo Ward added it to its register of pride trees in October 2008 and measured it at 14.6 metres tall, with a trunk 2.78 metres around.

Nobody has dated it, and that ward register is the only document that mentions it at all, so the measurements are the whole of what anyone can offer.

Its acorns are the ones worth bending down for. Most oak acorns are too bitter to eat without leaching first; chinkapin acorns are sweet enough raw and better roasted, which is why generations of Japanese children knew them by taste rather than from a book. They come down in autumn onto the gravel.

The Omiya gate opens onto the same short circuit as the camphor at Munakata Shrine and the hackberry at Demizu-guchi, close enough together that all three fit inside one slow hour.

trees.name: Camphor of Shimodachiuri Gate, Kyoto Gyoen
trees.neighbourhood: Near Shimodachiuri-gomon, west side of Kyoto Gyoen, Kamigyo-ku
trees.access: Free. Kyoto Gyoen National Garden is open to the public year-round, dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Marutamachi Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 5 minute walk
trees.story:
Early cinema ran on this species. Camphor crystals, steam-distilled from the wood and leaves of Cinnamomum camphora, were what made celluloid film stock and photographic plates flexible enough to use, and for decades Japan and its colonies supplied most of the world's camphor, until the chemical industry worked out how to make it from turpentine instead. The trees that fed that trade came down by the forest. This one did not.

It grows just inside Shimodachiuri-gomon, a gate in the west wall of Kyoto Gyoen, and Kamigyo Ward lists it among its pride trees at 12.3 metres tall with a trunk 2.76 metres around. Its age appears nowhere. That ward register is the only document naming this tree, and it records dimensions rather than years.

Camphors are evergreen, so this is the same tree in February as in July: dense, dark, heavily leaved, and smelling of a medicine cabinet if you crush a leaf between your fingers. It is not the biggest camphor in this park. The one at Munakata Shrine, a short walk away, is far larger and several centuries older, and this is the tree most people go straight past on their way to it. Which is a decent argument for looking up on the way.

trees.name: Ginkgo of Inui Gate, Kyoto Gyoen
trees.neighbourhood: Near Inui-gomon, northwest corner of Kyoto Gyoen, Kamigyo-ku
trees.access: Free. Kyoto Gyoen National Garden is open to the public year-round, dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Imadegawa Station (Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line), roughly 3 minute walk

best_time.label: the second half of November, when it goes gold and then drops the lot within days

trees.story:
The gate this ginkgo stands at is named after a dog and a boar. Inui is the old word for northwest, written with the two zodiac animals that sat in that quarter of the compass, and Inui-gomon is the northwest corner gate of Kyoto Gyoen. The tree beside it runs to 19.5 metres, with a trunk 3.15 metres around, measured by Kamigyo Ward for its register of pride trees. That register gives no age, and no other source mentions this ginkgo, so how long it has been growing there is not known.

It is the far end of the park. The camphor at Munakata Shrine and the hackberry at Demizu-guchi are down in the southwest corner, and getting here means about a kilometre and a half north on gravel, twenty minutes if nothing distracts you, past a fair share of the two hundred trees the environment ministry counts as giants on these grounds. None of that ground is old. Aristocratic households filled this rectangle until they broke up and followed their emperor east, and what went in from 1877 was deliberate parkland, which is the only reason a walled rectangle in the middle of a city carries trees on this scale.

Come in the second half of November. Ginkgos go gold all at once, hold it for a matter of days, and then put the entire crown on the ground.

trees.name: The Miramar Moreton Bay Fig
trees.access: Free. Stands in the Fairmont Miramar Hotel entrance courtyard on Ocean Avenue, open to the public to walk up and view; it is a working hotel entrance rather than a park, so behave accordingly.
trees.transport: Santa Monica; Expo Line (E Line) to Downtown Santa Monica station, then about a 10 minute walk west to Ocean Avenue.
trees.story:
The hotel arrived second. This fig was planted around 1889 in the rose garden of the Jones mansion by Georgina Jones, whose husband, Senator John Percival Jones, had founded Santa Monica a decade and a half earlier. The mansion is long gone. The tree went on growing and the Fairmont Miramar was built around it, which is why a five star hotel now has a Moreton Bay fig standing in its front courtyard like a doorman.

It is over 80 feet tall with a canopy about 120 feet across, one of the largest of its kind in California. Moreton Bay figs come from the Australian east coast and were planted all over southern California in the 1880s by people who wanted shade quickly and got rather more than they bargained for; this is the specimen that shows why. Santa Monica made it a city landmark on 17 August 1976, among its first, citing both the tree and its link to the family that started the town.

Nobody has published a girth for it, so if you get a tape around the trunk we would like the number.

You can walk straight up to it from Ocean Avenue, free and at any hour, but this is a working hotel entrance rather than a park, so read the room.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig at St. Johns Presbyterian Church
trees.access: Free. Stands on the grounds of St. Johns Presbyterian Church and is visible from the public sidewalk at National Blvd and Military Ave; the church itself is open Tue-Fri 9am-3:30pm and Sun 9am-2pm for a closer look.
trees.transport: Palms neighbourhood, west LA; nearest Expo Line (E Line) stop is Palms station, then about a 10-15 minute walk.
trees.story:
Los Angeles has protected this fig as Historic-Cultural Monument No. 19 since 1963, which makes it older on the city's list than most of the buildings on it. The tree is older still. It was planted in 1875 by the Smith family to shade their cottage on the La Ballona ranch, by one account in honour of their first son, and it stood alone in farmland for close to ninety years before the Presbyterian church complex went up around it in 1962.

That makes it one of the two oldest documented tree plantings in the city, level with the figs at the old Plaza downtown and older than every other Moreton Bay fig on this list.

Its modern history is a slow argument with the power company, which has cut into the crown repeatedly over the years to keep the overhead lines clear. The tree has absorbed it and kept spreading over the corner of National Boulevard and Military Avenue.

You can see it from the public sidewalk at any time. For a closer look the church grounds are open on weekday mornings and Sunday. No girth or height figure has been published for it, which for a tree this size is a gap worth closing: if you measure it, tell us. The pin marks the church corner rather than the trunk.

trees.name: The Plaza Fig Trees
trees.access: Free. Stand in the open plaza around the gazebo at El Pueblo de Los Angeles / Olvera Street, open to the public at all times as a city park and historic monument.
trees.transport: Downtown LA; Union Station (Metro Rail B/D/L lines, Metrolink, Amtrak) is directly across Alameda St, about a 5 minute walk.
trees.story:
On 2 March 2019 one of these figs came down during a Chinese lantern festival in the plaza. It was 144 years old. Nobody was hurt, which given the crowd and the size of the tree was a considerable piece of luck. Three of the original four are still standing.

All of them were planted in 1875 by the horticulturist Elijah Hook Workman around the old Plaza, the square the pueblo of Los Angeles was laid out from and the closest thing the city has to a founding address. That makes them among the oldest documented plantings in Los Angeles, level with the fig at St John's church in Palms and older than the figs of Beverly Hills and Figueroa Street by a generation.

This is one entry for the group rather than three. The gazebo at the centre of the plaza is the place to stand, with the survivors around it and Olvera Street a few steps north.

After the collapse the city inspected the remaining trees and found no risk to the public, and El Pueblo began a process to decide what should be planted in the gap. That is the last dated word we have on their condition, from 2019. If you have walked through the plaza lately, tell us how the three of them look.

trees.name: The Oldest Palm Tree in Los Angeles
trees.age: documented in Los Angeles since the 1850s, at least 170 years, likely older since it was already a mature palm when first transplanted
trees.access: Free. Stands beside Exposition Park Drive at the Figueroa St entrance, a public city/state park, open daily.
trees.transport: Expo Line (E Line) Expo Park/USC station is directly adjacent, about a 2-5 minute walk.
trees.story:
The oldest palm in Los Angeles has been dug up and moved three times, and it is still going. It was taken out of a desert oasis and planted on San Pedro Street in the 1850s. In 1889 it was hauled across town to shade the entrance of the Southern Pacific Railroad's Arcade Depot on Alameda Street. On 5 September 1914, when the depot closed, someone decided it was worth saving again and moved it to Exposition Park, where it stands beside the drive at the Figueroa Street entrance. A plaque at its base records that last journey.

It is around 100 feet tall now. Its documented life in the city runs to at least 170 years, and the real figure is higher, because it was already a mature palm when it was first dug up and nobody wrote down how long it had been standing in the desert before that.

Washingtonia filifera is the only palm native to California, which is the quiet joke of the Los Angeles skyline: almost every palm you can see was shipped in, and the oldest one was already here. A dent partway up the trunk is old damage of some kind. Crews now use cherry pickers rather than climbing spikes to take the dead fronds down, so it collects no new scars.

The Expo Line stops two minutes away.

photo.attribution: Clyde Charles Brown, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Arboretum Coast Live Oak
trees.access: Paid entry to the Los Angeles County Arboretum & Botanic Garden (around general admission as of a 2024/2025 visitor report; check current pricing). Open daily during garden hours; easy parking on site.
trees.transport: Arcadia; Metro Gold/A Line Arcadia station, then roughly a 15-20 minute walk, or local bus/rideshare.
trees.story:
This oak was already a big tree when the Tongva village of Aleupkigna, the place of many waters, still stood on this ground and before the people who lived there were pushed off it. The Arboretum puts it at over 200 years, which means it also predates by a century the Baldwin ranch era of the 1880s that the gardens around it were built from.

Coast live oaks are the tree southern California had before anyone planted anything: evergreen, wide rather than tall, holding their leaves through the dry season on a root system that goes looking for water. This one is stop 2 on the Arboretum's own walking tour, uphill and north of the entrance rotunda, near the Celebration Garden.

Two things to know before you go. The age comes from the Arboretum's own signage and tour notes rather than from an independent measurement, so read it as a careful institutional estimate. And the tree has been under treatment for a fungal disease, with visitors asked to keep out from under the branches while it is being worked on. Look from the edge of the canopy rather than standing beneath it, and check at the gate for the current advice.

The Arboretum charges admission and is open daily, with parking on site.

trees.name: The Beverly Hills Moreton Bay Fig
trees.access: Free. Stands in Beverly Gardens Park, a public linear park running along Santa Monica Blvd, open at all times.
trees.transport: Beverly Hills; Metro D (Purple) Line Wilshire/Rodeo station is about a 10 minute walk south.
trees.story:
Everyone in Beverly Hills tells the same story about this fig and nobody has produced the paperwork. The story is that Burton Green planted it: the oil man who founded the city in 1906, laid out Beverly Gardens Park and hired Wilbur D. Cook to design it. The park's history is documented and the tree's is not, so treat the planting as local tradition rather than record.

The tree itself needs no defending. It is over a century old, it gets described as one of the largest Moreton Bay figs in the country, and it stands beside the Electric Fountain at Santa Monica and Wilshire, the 1931 fountain given to the city by the family of the silent film comedian Harold Lloyd. The fountain gets the photographs. The fig is the older object and by some distance the stranger one, a low wide dome of a tree with limbs that run out almost horizontally before they think about going up.

Beverly Gardens Park is a long thin public park running for blocks along Santa Monica Boulevard, open at all hours and free. The pin marks the fountain rather than the trunk, and the tree stands beside it.

No girth and no planting year have been published. If you know either, we would like to hear it.

trees.name: The Auto Club Moreton Bay Fig
trees.access: Free to view from the Figueroa St sidewalk, where the tree guards the entrance to the Auto Club headquarters courtyard; the building is a working AAA member service branch, open to the public during business hours for a closer look, and the tree is decorated and publicly celebrated each December with a holiday tree-lighting event.
trees.transport: Just south of Downtown LA near USC; Expo Line (E Line) Expo Park/USC or Jefferson/USC stations, then about a 10-15 minute walk.
trees.story:
Charles C. Chapman planted this fig outside his own house on Figueroa Street in 1894. The house is gone. The tree is not, and when the Automobile Club of Southern California came to build its headquarters on the site it built around the fig instead of felling it, opening the Spanish Colonial Revival building by Sumner Hunt and Silas Burns on 27 January 1923.

A century of undisturbed growth shows. The branches spread over 100 feet, and the aerial roots that Moreton Bay figs drop from their limbs have reached the ground and hardened into buttresses, so that the tree now appears to be standing on several trunks at once.

The Auto Club has treated it as a member of staff ever since. It threw the fig a hundredth birthday party in 1994, and every December it decorates the tree and holds a public lighting event under it, which is a fine time to come and about the only occasion in Los Angeles when people gather to look at a fig.

You can see it from the Figueroa Street sidewalk at any hour; the building is a working AAA branch and open to the public during business hours if you want to stand under the canopy. The pin comes from the street address, so aim for the corner of Figueroa and Adams.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Prinsentuin
trees.age: roughly 195 to 205 years, from the register's planting band of 1820 to 1830
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles are up across the whole crown

trees.story:
This tree is almost exactly as old as the idea of a public park in this country.

Between 1822 and 1824 the city had a new garden laid out on the northern fortifications, in the existing grounds, by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the Frisian garden architect who spent his career converting Dutch formality into the romantic English manner: curved paths, water, planned views, no straight lines. It has been open to the public ever since, which makes the Prinsentuin one of the first public walking parks in the Netherlands and this chestnut one of the original plantings.

Two hundred years of people walking under a tree is not neutral. Horse chestnuts suffer badly from compacted ground and this one has had two centuries of feet. It is also the species now under attack across Europe from the leaf miner moth, which browns the foliage from July onward and makes a mature chestnut look half dead by August without actually killing it.

So come in May, when it is at its unarguable best: white candles held upright all over the crown, in a park laid out by a man who would have chosen it for exactly that.

It stands beside the Historisch Centrum, on the Groeneweg side.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Westerkerk
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.access: Free. Stands on the street by the church, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 800 m north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.story:
The national register does not usually tell you a tree is going to die. About this one it does.

In the 1990s the ground it roots in was compacted, which for a beech is close to the worst thing that can be done to it: the fine feeding roots sit in the top half metre of soil and they need air in it. The tree took a blow it never came back from. The ground has since been improved and its condition has not recovered, and the register states plainly that it will in time have to be felled.

It is the oldest tree in Leeuwarden, banded 1750 to 1800, standing by a church whose history runs back to the fifteenth century and which has been reworked repeatedly for the different uses it has been put to.

There is nothing tragic to look at. A declining old beech is still an enormous dark thing on a city street, and the decline is mostly visible in what is missing: thinner cover at the top of the crown, more light coming through than there should be, dead ends on the upper branches.

This is the only tree on this site we would tell you to see sooner rather than later.

trees.name: The Beech at the Pier Pander Temple
trees.age: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.story:
There is a small classical temple in this park, built in 1924 to hold the work of one sculptor.

Pier Pander was born in Friesland in 1864, the son of a rag merchant, and got out through talent and patronage: Rome, a career in marble, and an early death in 1919. The temple was raised to his own plans five years later, a domed round building in a public park, to house his sculpture. There are not many Dutch artists with a temple.

The beech stands beside it. Its date is not certain: the register bands it 1840 to 1850 and notes that trees here could equally have gone in when the temple was built, but photographs from the 1930s argue for the earlier reading. This is the Noorderplantage, laid out in 1843 on the former Noorderdwinger bastion and joined to the Prinsentuin at its eastern end, and the register's general conclusion is that the oldest trees in it date from between 1830 and 1880.

A beech beside a domed white building is a deliberate effect: smooth grey bark against smooth stone, and in summer a canopy dense enough to put the whole temple in shade.

trees.name: The Plane of the Old City Cemetery
trees.age: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850
trees.access: Free. Open ground, no longer in use as a cemetery.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Leeuwarden station, on the Jelsummerstraat.

best_time.label: March, bare, with the heron colony visible in the crowns

trees.story:
Grey herons nest in the tops of these trees.

That is the first thing to know about the old city cemetery, and in February and March it is loud. Herons are colonial breeders, they choose tall trees near water, they start early in the year, and a heronry is not a quiet place: a large ragged nest per fork, birds arriving with sticks, and a noise like an argument in a shed. From below you mostly see the undersides and hear the rest.

The ground was laid out in 1833 to a design by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the same architect as the Prinsentuin, which is why a cemetery here reads like a landscape garden with graves in it. It went out of use long ago and is now a national monument. Ivy has taken many of the trunks.

The plane is on the path between sections two and three, banded 1840 to 1850, so from the earliest planting. London plane is the classic city tree because it sheds its bark in plates and with it the soot, which is why the trunk is a camouflage of cream, olive and grey.

Go in early spring, before the leaves, when you can see the birds.

trees.name: The Beech behind Tresoar
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.

best_time.label: October, when it turns copper and the litter goes orange

trees.story:
It stands next to the building where Friesland keeps its memory.

Tresoar is the Frisian historical and literary centre, the archive of a language with its own literature and its own long argument about being a language. The beech is directly behind it, in the Prinsentuin, on the line of the old northern fortifications that the park was built on and that have been a national monument since 1967.

The register bands it 1860 to 1870, which places it a generation after Roodbaard's layout rather than in it, planted into a park that already existed.

Beech is the tree that makes a Dutch park feel like a wood. It casts the heaviest shade of any large tree here, dense enough that almost nothing grows under a mature one, so the ground beneath is bare orange leaf litter and roots. That is not neglect, it is the tree winning.

Run your hand over the trunk. Beech bark stays smooth and thin its whole life, which is why people carve it, and why an old one in a public park usually carries a century of initials that have stretched and blurred as the trunk widened.

trees.name: The Ash by the Tea House
trees.age: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.story:
The register calls this a very impressive specimen of the species and then adds, in the same breath, that its crown has developed one-sidedly because of the park trees standing next to it.

Both are true and the second explains the first. A tree that grows up hemmed in on one side puts everything it has into the open side, so you end up with an asymmetric crown reaching out over the path or the water, which reads as dramatic rather than damaged. Roodbaard's successors planted a park; the trees then negotiated among themselves.

It stands on the bank by the Theekoepel, the tea house, in the Noorderplantage end of the grounds, and the register bands it 1870 to 1880.

An ash of that age is worth stopping for now more than it was twenty years ago. Ash dieback, a fungal disease that arrived in the Netherlands in 2010, has killed a large share of the country's ash in the years since, and a tolerant mature tree is no longer an ordinary thing. A minority resist it, apparently on genetics rather than luck, and every big healthy one left is a candidate.

Black buds in winter, in opposite pairs. Nothing else here has them.

trees.name: The Marilandica Poplar
trees.age: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
trees.access: Free. Open public park.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.story:
The trunk is the reason to come. It is deeply grooved and covered in burrs, hard woody swellings the size of fists and heads, which on a poplar of this age turn the bole into something closer to rock than bark.

Burrs are the tree's response to damage or infection: a knot of dormant buds that keeps growing without ever making a shoot, laying down wildly disordered grain. Woodturners prize the timber for exactly that and pay serious money for a burr this size. Standing on a public park bank by a city canal is the safest place it could be.

Marilandica is a named clone of the Canadian poplar, the hybrid of European black poplar and American cottonwood, selected and propagated by cuttings, which means every Marilandica anywhere is genetically the same tree. This one has been growing since the 1870s at the centre of the Prinsentuin by the Noorder Stadsgracht.

Poplars are planted for speed and taken out early because they get brittle. This one has been left, and a century and a half of being left is what produced the trunk.

Go and put your hands on it. That is the whole visit.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Boerhaave
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station

best_time.label: October to November: clear yellow, one of the most reliable autumn trees

trees.story: This tree exists because a London apothecary put a Virginia seed in the post. On 1 October 1716, botanist Isaac Rand shipped seed of an American species barely known in Europe to Leiden; eleven days later, on 12 October 1716, the Hortus Botanicus's own professor Herman Boerhaave sowed it in the garden that still bears the tree today. Boerhaave was not primarily a botanist. He is remembered as one of the founders of modern clinical medicine, teaching physicians from across Europe to examine patients at the bedside rather than argue from old texts, and the same instinct for direct observation over inherited authority shows up in his own tidy planting record for this tree, the reason its age is unusually certain for something three centuries old. The Hortus calls it the oldest tulip tree on the European continent, the species having only reached English cultivation in 1663 and taken decades more to spread further. Its yellow-green, cup-shaped flowers only appear once a tree reaches real maturity, easy to miss on a young specimen and unmistakable on one this size. It stands near the garden's entrance, a short walk from the Rapenburg canal, three centuries into a life that started as cargo.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold before dropping almost overnight

trees.story: Planted in 1785, this ginkgo spent a century and a half as what botanists call, without much romance, a male specimen, producing only the small catkins that never make seed. In 1935, gardeners grafted several female twigs onto its branches, cut from a ginkgo at Huis ten Donck, a country estate near Rotterdam. Only one graft took. It still lives today, a single genetically female branch grown into an otherwise male tree, and every autumn that one branch alone produces the species' distinctive plum-like seeds, whose fleshy coating gives off a smell closer to rancid butter than to fruit, an insect lure rather than a flaw. Ginkgo biloba is the sole surviving member of an entire plant order, its lineage traceable in the fossil record to roughly 270 million years ago, long before flowering plants existed at all, which makes this specific tree's mid-1930s surgery a strange collision of eras: a living fossil, tinkered with using the grafting techniques of a 20th-century orchard. The Hortus built its greenhouse complex around the tree in 1938, close enough that the ginkgo effectively anchors the entire glasshouse wing rather than sitting apart from it.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: An Englishman gave this tree its first paper trail. George Loddiges, a London nurseryman whose own family ran one of Europe's great commercial gardens, documented it in 1836, and the Hortus dates the tree itself to around 1840, making it a weeping beech, a cultivar with heavy main branches held almost horizontal and side branches that trail down to the ground, grafted onto ordinary beech rootstock since the weeping form does not come true from seed. It grows directly beside the garden's pond next to an equally old fernleaf beech, the two forming one of the Hortus's most photographed corners, dense green tents a visitor can walk directly beneath rather than merely past. Age has not been kind to the original tree lately; its condition has been declining for some years, enough that the Hortus planted a younger weeping beech beside it in 1982, a gift after the sapling appeared at Amsterdam's Floriade garden show that year, deliberately positioned as an eventual successor rather than a separate attraction. Nothing here pretends the older tree will stand forever. It has already outlived the nurseryman who first wrote it down by more than a century, and for now it is still the one worth walking to.

trees.name: The Golden Chain of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station

best_time.label: late May and June, when its yellow flower chains hang from the branches

trees.story: For decades this tree was sold on a story its own garden no longer believes. A popular account claimed it dated to 1601, planted during the tenure of the great botanist Carolus Clusius, and the myth gained a kind of proof in 1931 when a caretaker named Veendorp found several fused trunks with a great many growth rings inside and read that as confirmation. The Hortus's own later archival research concluded otherwise: the fused-trunk trick inflated the ring count, and the documented evidence instead points to the 1720s, sown by Herman Boerhaave, the same professor responsible for the garden's tulip tree a few years earlier. Roughly 300 years old rather than 400, it remains modest in size for its age, a small, unshowy tree next to the tulip tree and ginkgo it shares the garden with, its bright yellow, pea-family flower clusters in late spring the only real hint of anything remarkable underneath the plain trunk. What makes the story worth telling is not the tree's stature but the correction itself: an institution with every incentive to keep the more romantic number instead published the less impressive, better-supported one.

trees.name: The Beets Beech of the Burcht
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: This tree is named after a student who wrote one of the Netherlands' best-loved books while it was still young. Nicolaas Beets studied theology in Leiden through the 1830s and, in 1839, the same year this copper beech was planted on the slope of the city's medieval fortress mound, published Camera Obscura under the pseudonym Hildebrand, a collection still assigned in Dutch schools today. Beets spent much of his student life around the Burcht, an 11th-century shell keep the municipality bought in 1651 and turned into a public park, and in 1989 the city formally named the tree in his honour, unveiling a bench beside it the same day. At 4.72 metres in circumference it is the thickest tree on the mound, one of a handful of veterans that survived the winter of 1945, when nearly every other tree in Leiden was felled for fuel during the Hunger Winter but the Burcht's older specimens were deliberately spared. That survival is now in question again, from a different direction: a root-rot fungus has been quietly turning the tree's root system to pulp, and as of the most recent inspection the municipality was investigating whether anything could extend its life rather than simply waiting for it to fall.

trees.name: The Groenesteeg Beech
trees.age: about 200 years, likely planted around the cemetery's 1813 founding
trees.access: Free, cemetery open to visitors during daylight hours year-round
trees.transport: 20 minute walk, or a short bike ride, from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: Two beech varieties grafted together, growing at different rates for two centuries, is why this one looks nothing like a normal beech. A copper beech was grafted low onto a common green beech rootstock, standard practice since copper beech does not breed true from seed, but the mismatched growth rates produced an unusually broad, gnarled base, branches starting barely two metres up, topping out into a comparatively slender 15-metre crown that still spreads 24 metres wide. Groenesteeg cemetery was laid out in 1813 over one of Leiden's demolished city fortifications, and the tree was likely planted around that founding date, making it roughly 200 years old, a genuine rarity since few beeches live that long anywhere. Measured at 6.5 metres in circumference, it is officially the thickest beech in the Netherlands and the thickest tree in the entire province of South Holland, wide enough that calling it merely large undersells the effect of walking up to the trunk itself. In October 2025 it placed fourth in the national Boom van het Jaar (Tree of the Year) public vote, drawing over a thousand votes on its own oddity and scale alone, beaten only by a giant sequoia in Enschede and two other regional finalists. Like its neighbour on the Burcht mound, it is fighting a root fungus, though here the cemetery's caretakers are actively treating it, with annual nutrient injections and a policy of leaving fallen leaves in place to feed the soil around its base.

trees.name: The Date-plum of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: Children call this one the Halloween tree, and the holes in its trunk have a stranger history than the nickname suggests. Late in the 19th century a maple seeded itself inside the trunk of the date-plum and grew there. Nobody took it out for roughly forty years, until 1931, and the cavities it left behind were then packed with concrete. Another forty years passed before the tree surgeons at Copijn removed that concrete again, which is how the openings you can see today came to exist. Iron pins were fitted inside what was left of the trunk to hold it together, and they are still doing that work. The national monumental tree register dates the tree to 1740, which would make it the second oldest in the Hortus Botanicus after the tulip tree Herman Boerhaave sowed in 1716. Its recorded planting band is wider, 1700 to 1750, so read the age as somewhere between 275 and 325 years in the same bed. Date-plums are either male or female, and this is a male, so it never fruits. The blue-black fruit the species is named for hangs on a younger female specimen the garden keeps in the fern garden instead. This tree offers a hollow trunk held up by ironmongery and a nickname it earned honestly.

trees.name: The Old Plane of the Plantsoen
trees.access: Free, public city park, open at any time
trees.transport: 20 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: This plane tree was already standing before the park around it existed. The Plantsoen was laid out between 1835 and 1842 as a job-creation scheme, an English landscape park built over Leiden's demolished bolwerken, the earthworks that had defended the city until they stopped being useful. Salomon van der Paauw designed it, which is why there are no straight paths, why the sightlines keep opening onto the water of the Singel, and why there has been an aviary here since 1867. The register dates this plane to the 1820s and calls it the oldest tree in the park, older than the layout it stands in. Its formal planting band is wider, 1800 to 1850, so its age is somewhere between 175 and 225 years. Planes became the workhorse of European city parks because they put up with compacted soil, air that would finish off a beech, and hard pruning, which is why so many survive from exactly this period of municipal park building. Most of them went into new ground as young stock. This one, by the register's dating, was already a tree when the diggers arrived. Stand at Plantsoen number 1 and look up the trunk: the flaking bark gives the species away, and above it sits a crown that has had two centuries to fill out.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Witte Singel
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station

best_time.label: May, when the white flower candles stand up over the water

trees.story: At 5.8 metres round, this is the thickest horse chestnut in the Netherlands by the national monumental tree register's own measurement. It stands at the edge of the Hortus Botanicus with its roots almost in the water of the Witte Singel, and the register's note dates it to 1841, inside a recorded planting band of 1800 to 1850. There is a hollow in the trunk on the water side, fitted with iron pins to stop the remaining wood pulling itself apart, which is the standard treatment for a veteran that has outgrown its own structural margin. It has a problem every horse chestnut in northern Europe now shares. The horse chestnut leaf miner, a moth whose larvae eat the tissue between the two surfaces of a leaf, reached the Netherlands in the late 1990s and browns the foliage from midsummer onward. It disfigures without usually killing, so a chestnut in August looks considerably worse than it is. Come in May instead, when the flower candles are up and none of that has started. Horse chestnuts went into Dutch cities by the thousand in exactly this period, mostly along avenues and canal banks, and almost none of them reached this girth. Conkers drop here in September, onto a bank where the water does half the collecting for you.

trees.name: The Siebold Zelkova
trees.age: the register's band says 1800-1850 while its own note says 1858, so between 165 and 225 years
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: These are the first zelkovas that ever left Japan. Philipp Franz von Siebold, the physician who spent the 1820s on the Dutch trading post at Deshima and sent home more Japanese plants than any European before him, brought zelkovas out with him in 1830. Two of them ended up here. One grew as a single trunk and stands at the centre of the Japanese garden; this one came up with five stems, so the register measures its girth on the thickest of them, about two metres, which undersells the mass of the thing considerably. The dating needs stating plainly, because the register disagrees with itself. Its planting band puts the tree between 1800 and 1850, while its own note says the two Leiden zelkovas went into the ground in 1858 and 1860. Take the age as somewhere between 165 and 225 years, and if you know which is right, tell us. Zelkova serrata is a relative of the elm that turned out to be largely resistant to Dutch elm disease, which is a good part of why it appeared on European planting lists after the 1970s, when the elms were dying in every city on the continent. This tree predates that fashion by more than a century, and it got here because one man wanted Japan in a Dutch garden.

trees.name: The Leaning Catalpa of the Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry to Hortus Botanicus Leiden (around 14 euros for adults)
trees.transport: 15 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station

best_time.label: late June and July, when the white flower trusses open

trees.story: This catalpa is kept out of the canal by cables tied to another tree on this list. It stands right on the edge of the singel behind the glasshouse, and at some point it leaned far enough that it was going to end up in the water. The answer was anchors, run across to the zelkova in the Japanese garden, and that arrangement is what still holds it upright. Two monumental trees, one carrying the other. The register dates it to 1820, inside a recorded band of 1820 to 1830, and counts it among the five thickest catalpas in the Netherlands. The catalpas planted across Europe came mostly from the American south and arrived in the 18th century for exactly the reason people still plant them: outsized heart-shaped leaves that come late and drop early, upright trusses of white flowers marked purple and yellow in the throat, then long thin seed pods that hang on all winter like forgotten string. It is a soft-wooded, brittle tree, never built for two centuries of Dutch wind on an exposed bank, which makes the cabling less an indignity than the reason there is still anything here to look at. Walk behind the glasshouse and follow the line of the water until you find the one that is not standing straight.

trees.name: The Plane at Plantsoen 11
trees.access: Free, public city park, open at any time
trees.transport: 20 minute walk from Leiden Centraal station
trees.story: The London plane is a hybrid nobody set out to make. Somewhere in the 17th century an oriental plane from the eastern Mediterranean crossed with an American one, probably in a nursery, and the accident grew faster than either parent, shrugged off coal smoke and put up with having its roots under paving. Europe then planted it in every city it had. This one went into the Plantsoen in the 1850s, on the stretch of the park at number 11, more than a decade after the park itself was finished in 1842. The Plantsoen was Leiden's first proper public park, cut into the line of the old defensive bolwerken between 1835 and 1842 as work for the unemployed, to a design by Salomon van der Paauw, and it is now part of the Singelpark, the green ring the city has been stitching back together around its historic centre. The register notes that no other part of that ring carries as many different old trees. Bark is the thing to look at here. Planes shed theirs in irregular plates, one reason they cope with dirty city air, and it leaves an old trunk looking like military camouflage in cream, olive and grey. This one has had roughly 170 years of shedding, and it stands on the water, which is the view the whole park was drawn around.

trees.name: The Olive Trees of Santo Amaro
trees.access: Free, open access, public garden around the chapel
trees.transport: 11 min walk from Alcântara-Terra station (Linha de Cascais), or tram 15E to Calvário then 9 min walk

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: Four olive trees outside a small round chapel in Alcântara have outlived every Portuguese king since before the Braganza dynasty existed. By the city's own classification records they are about 457 years old, the oldest documented trees in Lisbon, planted well before the Capela de Santo Amaro beside them took its current circular form in 1549. The chapel has been rebuilt and restored more than once since; the olives outside it have simply kept growing. None of the four is tall, barely six metres at most, but their trunks have hollowed and twisted with age into shapes closer to driftwood than farmland olive stock. City foresters classified them for their cultural, pedagogical and landscape interest, bureaucratic language for what amounts to old age handled well. Olive trees usually mark farmland, not clifftop chapels with river views, and these four have quietly ignored the fact that a working port and, eventually, a 25 de Abril Bridge grew up around them. The hilltop they share is one of the better free viewpoints over the Tagus, and on a typical afternoon the view gets most of the attention, while four of the oldest living things in the city stand a few steps away, propped, gnarled, and largely unbothered.

trees.name: The Ajuda Dragon Tree
trees.access: Paid entry to Jardim Botânico da Ajuda (about 1 euro; free Sunday mornings 10:00-13:00)
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Belém station (Linha de Cascais); tram 18E stops nearby
trees.story: Cut into its bark and this tree bleeds red. The resin of Dracaena draco oxidizes into a dark crimson sap once prized across Europe as dragon's blood, used in medieval varnish, dye and folk medicine. This specimen was already a mature adult when the Italian botanist Domingos Vandelli transplanted it into Lisbon's first botanical garden in 1768, which makes it at least 258 years old and possibly closer to 400, since dragon trees carry no annual rings and nobody recorded its birth. Its crown once spread nearly 23 metres across, among the largest of its kind in the country, until a rot infection took hold around 2006 and cost it roughly half its size. A steel frame now holds up what remains. The garden, built on the grounds of the royal Ajuda Palace for King José I, treats the tree as its emblem, and cuttings from its offshoots have been propagated into a small nursery of younger dragon trees nearby. Dragon trees grow slowly and can live for centuries once established, so this one, missing half its canopy and still standing, may yet be young for its kind.

trees.name: The Cypress of Príncipe Real
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Short walk from Rato station (Metro Yellow Line)
trees.story: Lisbon's first legally protected tree is not a cedar at all. Everyone calls it the cedro-do-Buçaco, but the tree presiding over Príncipe Real garden is Cupressus lusitanica, a cypress from the mountains of Mexico and Guatemala with a Portuguese name it never earned. In 1940 it became the first tree in the country classified as being of public interest, decades before Portugal had a formal national registry for such things. Its canopy, once a vast gazebo-like dome some 30 metres across, has thinned with age and storms down to about seven metres of visible height, though the trunk still measures four metres around at the base. Portuguese heritage records put it at roughly 150 years old, predating most of the surrounding 19th century garden. One international tree registry claims it instead dates to around 1740, nearly twice that age, a gap nobody has resolved. Locals shelter under its remaining canopy on Saturday organic market mornings, largely unaware they are standing under a tree whose paperwork outranks almost every building in view, and whose exact age is still an open question among the people paid to know it.

trees.name: The Ombú of Largo do Limoeiro
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Portas do Sol tram stop (12E/28E)
trees.story: The square is named after a lemon tree that is long gone. What replaced it as the local landmark is an ombú, a South American species with a swollen, fluted trunk that can measure some seventeen metres around at the base, wider than most house facades on the street. It grows against the outer wall of the old Limoeiro prison, a building that held political prisoners for much of the 20th century and now trains judges. Municipal archive photographs show it already a substantial adult tree by 1910, which would put its real age closer to 115 years than the 100 usually quoted. Ombú wood is famously soft and fire resistant, of no real use to carpenters, which may be exactly why this one survived when more useful trees nearby did not. It stands a few steps from the Portas do Sol viewpoint, one of the finest views over the Alfama rooftops to the river, though most visitors walk straight past its swollen trunk toward the railing. True to its local nickname, bela-sombra, beautiful shade, it still throws excellent cover over an otherwise unremarkable stretch of pavement.

trees.name: The Tipu of Jardim de São Bento
trees.access: Free, public garden beside the Assembleia da República
trees.transport: 2 min walk from São Bento train station (Linha de Sintra)

best_time.label: late winter into spring, when the garden turns a startling shade of orange

trees.story: Portugal's parliament keeps a South American tree on its doorstep. This tipu, planted around ninety years ago in the small triangular garden beside the Palácio de São Bento, blooms with orange flowers marked by a brownish red spot at the base of each petal, a native of Bolivia and Argentina with no historical connection to the 16th century Benedictine monastery the palace used to be. The monastery became the seat of the Portuguese parliament in 1834 after the religious orders were dissolved, and the garden beside it has since watched ministers, protesters and the occasional political crisis unfold a few dozen metres from its canopy. The tree is one of Lisbon's officially classified trees of public interest, a status shared by barely two dozen specimens across the entire city. Its timber, tipa, is prized in South America for furniture, though nobody here has any plans to cut this one down for a table. Late winter and spring bring its flowering season, when the garden's modest third of a hectare turns a startling shade of orange directly across the street from where the country's laws get written.

trees.name: The Coral Trees of Jardim da Luz
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 1 min walk from Colégio Militar/Luz station (Metro Blue Line)

best_time.label: June, when both trees erupt in flowers shaped like a rooster's crest

trees.story: Despite the name, this tree has never been near India. Portuguese sailors called the genus Erythrina a coral tree of the Indies after landing in Brazil convinced they had reached Asia, a five century old geography mistake baked permanently into the common name. Two specimens grow on the south side of Jardim da Luz in Carnide, both classified as trees of public interest since 1996 and both about a century old, standing twelve and fifteen metres tall. Each June they erupt in bright red flowers shaped unmistakably like a rooster's crest, the detail behind the species name crista-galli. The garden's formal name, Jardim Teixeira Rebelo, honours the founding director of the nearby Military College, though most locals still call it simply Jardim da Luz after the Baroque church across the square. A metro station sits so close to the garden gate that riders on the Blue Line surface almost directly beneath the coral trees' canopy without noticing. For two South American transplants misnamed after the wrong continent, they have settled into suburban Lisbon without complaint, flowering every summer regardless of what anyone calls them.

trees.name: The Nettle Tree of Avenida de Berlim
trees.access: Free, public street/traffic island
trees.transport: Roughly 15 min walk from Bela Vista station (Metro Red Line), or bus to Avenida de Berlim
trees.story: One tree remembers the farms that used to be here. Before Lisbon's eastward expansion in the 1940s and 1950s paved over the quintas of Olivais with apartment blocks, this stretch of land was countryside, and a single European nettle tree from that era survived the building work, still standing at what is now the junction of Avenida de Berlim and Avenida Francisco Luís Gomes. Portugal's national registry of public-interest trees measured it in 2015 at 75 years old and 15.7 metres tall, younger than the round century once claimed for it but still older than the apartment blocks around it, with a broad symmetrical canopy that looks deliberately planted rather than accidentally spared, though it was almost certainly the latter. The species produces small sweet fruit that gives it a folk nickname referencing the birds that come to eat it, and its wood was historically valued for tool handles and whip stocks for its flexibility. Officially classified as a tree of public interest under process KNJ1/405, it now stands beside a bronze sculpture called Homem Sucata, Scrap Man, welded from actual car parts in 1993, an odd pairing of the area's rural past and its industrial present sharing the same traffic island. Commuters on the surrounding avenues have an older neighbour than the surrounding tower blocks suggest.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Praça Paiva Couceiro
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Roughly 10 min walk from Arroios station (Metro Red Line)

best_time.label: November, when its leaves turn uniform bright yellow and drop almost simultaneously

trees.story: Ginkgo biloba is often called a living fossil, a species virtually unchanged for over 200 million years and one of the very few plants known to have resprouted near ground zero at Hiroshima, a resilience the species carries in its reputation rather than this particular tree's own biography. Lisbon's specimen in Praça Paiva Couceiro, in the working class Penha de França neighbourhood, is a comparatively young member of an ancient lineage: over a century old and classified as a tree of public interest, though nobody has pinned down its exact planting date. Its fan shaped leaves turn a uniform bright yellow every November before dropping almost simultaneously, a spectacle unrelated to anything else on this list and one that draws a small annual crowd of photographers to an otherwise unremarkable square. Ginkgos are dioecious, male or female, and only female trees produce the notoriously foul smelling fruit; whether this one has simply spared the neighbourhood that autumn hazard, or its sex was never recorded, nobody seems to know. Either way, it is Penha de França's one living link to a genus older than most of the world's mountain ranges.

trees.name: The Paineira of Jardim Alfredo Keil
trees.neighbourhood: Praça da Alegria, Avenida da Liberdade
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 6 min walk from Restauradores station (Metro Blue Line)

best_time.label: October, when the tree turns the garden pink

trees.story: Every October this tree turns a small garden pink. The silk floss tree in Jardim Alfredo Keil is one of six individually classified specimens within a nine tree ensemble that the city declared collectively of public interest in 2017, a South American species whose thorny green trunk and cotton candy coloured blooms have become an unofficial marker of autumn across Lisbon in recent years. The garden itself, laid out in 1882 on the former site of the Feira da Ladra flea market before that market moved to Alfama, is barely large enough to contain the tree's crown, and a bust of the composer Alfredo Keil, who wrote the melody that became Portugal's national anthem, watches from one corner. No source isolates exactly how old this particular paineira is, since the 2017 classification covers the whole collection of trees rather than dating each specimen individually. The fruit that follows the flowers splits open to release seeds wrapped in a silky white floss, once used to stuff pillows and life jackets, a soft, practical footnote to a tree that spends every autumn putting on the loudest show in the neighbourhood.

trees.name: The Giant Rubber Tree of Mouraria
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Short walk from Martim Moniz station (Metro Green Line)
trees.story: Nobody knows how this tree got here, and that is most of its appeal. A rubber fig now towers some six metres over a narrow street in Mouraria, its roots having escaped a cracked pot years ago and driven straight into the ground below, its trunk and branches now filling the gap between two building facades on Rua de São Cristóvão as though it had been planted there on purpose. It was not. Plant researchers who have examined it, including the botanist André Mota, can confirm the species and describe its improvised growth, but not its origin story. Unlike the classified trees of public interest elsewhere on this list, this one carries no official age, no protected status and no municipal plaque, just several hundred enthusiastic online reviews and a café that opened next door in 2022 partly because of the foot traffic the tree now draws. It is the youngest and least official entry here, almost certainly under 40 years old, included not for its age but for the fact that a potted houseplant broke loose and quietly became one of the most photographed trees in the neighbourhood.

trees.name: The Fig of the Estrela Garden
trees.access: Free, open daily 07:00 to midnight
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Estrela (Basílica), then about 2 min walk
trees.story: Lisbon has bolted a metal plate to this trunk, and where the age should be it says one word: unknown. That is unusually honest for a municipality, and it is also the most interesting thing about the tree. The garden around it opened in April 1852 after ten years of stop-start construction, so the fig cannot be much more than a century and three quarters old, which for something this bulky is the surprise. Moreton Bay figs grow at a speed that makes ordinary trees look idle. The plate arrived in 2020, when Lisbon gave 27,610 of its trees an identity card and hung QR codes on around 750 of them. Look up and you see why this species unsettles people: aerial roots hang from the limbs like rope, and where they reach soil they thicken into new trunks, so the tree slowly becomes a colony of itself. It is not alone here either. At least five mature figs stand in these five hectares, and the one at the pond's edge, roots spilling over the kerb toward the ducks, is the one everybody photographs.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of the Estrela Garden
trees.age: unknown, planted after the garden opened in 1852
trees.access: Free, open daily 07:00 to midnight
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Estrela (Basílica), then about 2 min walk
trees.story: Nobody can tell you how old this tree is, and that is a property of the species rather than a gap in the paperwork. A dragon tree is not a tree in the ordinary sense: it lays down no annual rings, so the one method that reliably ages an oak or a beech simply does not apply. Botanists count branch generations instead, because the crown forks only after each flowering, which happens at intervals of a decade or more. What that produces is this shape, a trunk splitting into a tight umbrella of stiff blue-green blades that looks less grown than engineered. Cut the bark and the sap runs red, which is where the name comes from and why the resin was traded across medieval Europe as dragon's blood, used for varnish, medicine and dye. The species belongs to the Canary Islands and Madeira, where it is now scarce in the wild. This one has stood among the palms and benches near the centre of the garden since some point after 1852, quietly outliving every gardener who has worked around it, and Lisbon has a second on our map in the botanical garden at Ajuda.

trees.name: The Strangler Fig of Príncipe Real
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all times
trees.transport: Metro Rato (yellow line), about 6 min walk uphill, or tram 24E to Praça do Príncipe Real
trees.story: Everyone in this square looks at the cypress. It sits under a metal frame like a green table, it was the first tree in Lisbon given legal protection, in 1940, and it takes all the photographs. Three Australian figs stand around it and almost nobody registers them, which is odd, because they are the reason the square feels roofed. This one carries the thickest trunk of the three, just over six metres around, and holds its crown twenty one metres up. Ficus macrophylla does not start life as a tree in Australia. It germinates in the fork of another one, drops roots down the host's trunk and thickens them until the host is enclosed and dies, which is why the species is called a strangler. Here it had nothing to strangle, so the aerial roots simply hang, reach the gravel and stiffen into props. Underneath all of this is water. The Patriarcal reservoir was finished in 1864, an octagonal chamber on thirty one pillars holding 880 cubic metres for the city, and the garden is its lid. On Saturday mornings a producers' market sets up between the trunks.

trees.name: The Yew of Campo Santana
trees.access: Free, municipal garden, open daily
trees.transport: Metro Intendente (green line), about 8 min walk, or Metro Avenida (blue line), about 10 min

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: A European yew has no business growing here. The species belongs to damp northern churchyards and mountain shade, and Lisbon offers neither, yet this one has put on close to four metres of girth and fourteen metres of height on a hill above the Avenida. Portugal classified it in May 1968, which makes it one of the earliest protected trees in the city, and the national register now puts it a little past 130 years old. The ground under it has a harder history than the lawns suggest. This field held a slaughterhouse and then a bullring, and in 1817 the men condemned with Gomes Freire de Andrade were hanged on it, which is how Campo de Santana became Campo dos Mártires da Pátria. The garden came afterwards, laid out around a lake with exotic birds wandering the paths, and the medical school and the Hospital de São José still crowd its edges. At the top of the same field stands the statue of Sousa Martins, a physician who died in 1897, its plinth buried under marble plaques left by people who believe he still answers. Every part of a yew is poisonous except the red flesh around the seed.

trees.name: The Weeping Fig of Campo Santana
trees.access: Free, municipal garden, open daily
trees.transport: Metro Intendente (green line), about 8 min walk, or Metro Avenida (blue line), about 10 min
trees.story: Ficus benjamina is the tree most people know as a pot plant, the glossy thing sulking in an office corner and shedding leaves whenever somebody moves it. Fifty paces from the yew, on the same slope, one of them has a trunk five metres around and a crown twenty metres up. Portugal classified it on exactly the same day as the yew, 21 May 1968, and the national register still files it under a second name that says what the species does when nothing stops it: matapalo, tree killer. Like its Moreton Bay relatives it can begin high in another tree and work downward, and even planted honestly in soil it keeps the habit of letting fine roots down from the limbs. One useful correction before you go. The register maps a single specimen here. Portuguese sources describing the garden count two of them, classified together under the same 1968 diploma. That gap between a national list and what a city actually holds is completely normal, so expect a pair and stand at the bigger one. The garden around them runs to twenty eight tree species, a Himalayan cedar and a paper mulberry among them, so the fig is not the only import that outgrew its label.

trees.name: The Taxodium of the Jardim da Parada
trees.age: unknown, not recorded in the national register
trees.access: Free, public garden. A metro construction site takes part of the block until at least the end of 2026 and paths move around it; the classified trees sit inside a protected radius away from the works
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Campo de Ourique, then about 5 min walk
trees.story: Six and a half metres around the trunk and twenty six metres up, this is the largest tree in a garden that fills one whole city block, and for four years it has been at the centre of an argument about a railway. Lisbon is building a metro station under Campo de Ourique. The worksite takes a slice of the garden, residents formed a movement to stop it, and in 2024 they tied coloured ribbons through the branches: black for a tree to be felled, red for high risk of dying, yellow for at risk. The metro company's public answer was a twenty metre radius around the garden's three classified trees with no work inside it and continuing health checks, with six unclassified hackberries taken out instead, four of them replanted in the same holes. The tree carries a small taxonomic dispute of its own. The national register lists it as Taxodium mucronatum, the Montezuma cypress of Mexican riverbanks, the species that produced the widest trunk ever measured on a tree. The parish council and the Portuguese encyclopedia both call it a bald cypress. Nobody has published a resolution. The garden was the parade ground of the Campo de Ourique barracks, which is why nobody calls it by the president's name.

trees.name: The Pohutukawa of the Jardim da Parada
trees.age: unknown, not recorded in the national register
