trees.access: Free, public garden. A metro construction site takes part of the block until at least the end of 2026 and paths move around it; the classified trees sit inside a protected radius away from the works
trees.transport: Tram 25E or 28E to Campo de Ourique, then about 5 min walk

best_time.label: May and June, when the crown fills with crimson stamens

trees.story: Two of them stand ten metres apart at the edge of this garden and the register protects them as separate trees, which is fair enough: one measures 4.55 metres around the trunk, the other 4.9. From underneath they read as a single thing, a low tangle of grey limbs running almost horizontally out over the pavement with curtains of aerial root hanging off them, more like a tree that fell and carried on than one that stood up straight. Metrosideros excelsa comes from the coast of New Zealand's North Island, where it grips volcanic cliffs with exactly those roots. In Campo de Ourique it grips a kerb. Flowering lands in May and June here, half a year away from the December bloom that made it a Christmas tree at home, and it is not a subtle event: the crown fills with crimson stamens and almost no petal worth the name, and the pavement underneath goes red as they drop. Both trees were classified in September 2018, late for something this size, and both now sit inside the twenty metre no-work radius the metro company promised around the garden's classified trees.

trees.name: The Tipuana of the Ninth of April Garden
trees.access: Free, municipal garden with permanent public access. This is not the museum's own garden next door and no ticket is needed
trees.transport: Bus 727 or 713 stops on Rua das Janelas Verdes at the Museu de Arte Antiga, 1 min walk; from Santos station it is about 8 min uphill
trees.story: This garden is named after a defeat. On 9 April 1918 the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps was overrun at La Lys in Flanders in the course of one morning, and Lisbon put the date on a small terrace above the river. The tipuana shades most of it: twenty two metres tall, three and a fifth metres round the trunk, classified in 2001 along with two neighbours, and by the national register's arithmetic somewhere near 145 years old now. Tipuana tipu is Bolivian and Argentine, a legume that behaves like a plane tree in Mediterranean cities and gets planted everywhere for it, along whole Lisbon avenues. What it does that plane trees do not is drip. In warm months the canopy releases a fine sticky rain, honeydew from the sap-feeding insects living in it, and anyone who has parked a car under one does not do it twice. The ground itself was the walled garden of the Albertas, a Carmelite convent, before the city took it over. Two older names for the place survive in daily use because of that, Jardim das Albertas and Jardim da Rocha do Conde de Óbidos. Walk to the parapet and the Tagus opens up, container cranes and all.

trees.name: The Date Palm of the Ninth of April Garden
trees.access: Free, municipal garden with permanent public access. This is not the museum's own garden next door and no ticket is needed
trees.transport: Bus 727 or 713 stops on Rua das Janelas Verdes at the Museu de Arte Antiga, 1 min walk; from Santos station it is about 8 min uphill
trees.story: Lisbon's city hall calls this the tallest tree in the city and puts it at 38 metres, four metres over the triumphal arch at the bottom of the Baixa. The national register measured it in 2015 and wrote down 26.7. Both figures are published, neither has been reconciled, and standing at the foot of it you will not settle the question either, because a date palm gives the eye nothing to measure against: no branches, no taper, just a grey column of old leaf bases and then a burst of fronds a long way up. Phoenix dactylifera is a desert crop from Mesopotamia and North Africa, grown for its fruit for at least five thousand years and almost never allowed to get this tall, because an orchard keeps its palms low enough to climb and harvest. Nobody was harvesting this one. It was classified in 2001 along with the tipuana and the flame tree beside it, and the register's clock puts it near 145 years. The trunk is barely one and a half metres around. It has held all that up for a century and a half, on the lip of a terrace above the Tagus that flatters the height even further.

trees.name: The Tipuana of Jardim Roque Gameiro
trees.access: Free, public garden beside Cais do Sodré station
trees.transport: Cais do Sodré station (Metro Green Line, train and ferry hub), 2 minute walk, the garden is directly adjacent

best_time.label: February to May, when the canopy turns burnt orange above the bus terminal

trees.story: This tree stands in the middle of a bus terminal, and that is the honest story rather than something to smooth over. The garden, popularly called Jardim do Cais do Sodre, sits exactly where the Sintra and Cascais railway lines, the Green Line metro and the Cacilhas ferry all converge, one of the first patches of green a visitor arriving into Lisbon by train or boat actually walks past. For years Carris buses ate most of the available space; a renovation under the city's 'A Square in Each Neighbourhood' programme has been handing some of it back. Through all of it, a single Tipuana tipu has kept growing at the centre, classified a Tree of Public Interest since 2001 and now roughly 115 years old, a South American species that reached Lisbon long before anyone built a transit hub around it. Its trunk runs just under three metres round. Nearby stands a bronze sculpture called Homem do Leme, the Helmsman, and an old kiosk once used as a ticket office, both easier to notice than the tree that predates them. Come between February and May and the argument for stopping gets easier: the canopy turns a burnt orange with clustered flowers, briefly outshining the buses idling underneath it.

trees.name: The Tipuana of Praça São João Bosco
trees.access: Free, public garden and traffic circle, open at all hours
trees.transport: Tram 25E to Campo de Ourique / Prazeres, then about a 5 minute walk
trees.story: A tree with a thirty four metre crown grows in the middle of a traffic circle, and by 2018 that crown had become the problem. City arborists and technicians from Portugal's nature institute came out that March to relieve the load: selective limb removal, canopy thinning, cuts meant to let wind pass through rather than push against it, the kind of surgery a tree this size needs to keep standing over a road. The garden that holds it, seven thousand square metres wrapped around a statue of Don Bosco raised in 1988, forms the roundabout that carries traffic between Campo de Ourique and the Prazeres district, directly across from Lisbon's second largest cemetery. The national register measured the tipu's trunk at 100 years old back in 2010, putting it past its first century now, a South American import from the subtropical lowlands of Bolivia and Argentina. It earned legal protection as a tree of public interest in January 2019, one of a few dozen trees in Lisbon to hold that status. Its trunk runs 3.4 metres round, modest next to the spread it throws overhead. Late spring dusts the roundabout's lawns orange when it flowers. Cars circle it a thousand times a day; almost none of the drivers know what they are driving around.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Parque Bensaúde
trees.access: Free, public municipal park
trees.transport: About 15 minutes' walk from Colegio Militar/Luz station (Metro Blue Line)
trees.story:
Four trees in Parque Bensaúde carry a national protection order, and the one the neighbourhood is proudest of is not among them. That is the cork oak, reckoned the oldest in Lisbon, standing elsewhere in the same park. The official list runs differently: two holm oaks, a red-flowering gum and a field maple.

This is the heavier of the two oaks. Its companion, about 50 metres away, is a tree you can get your arms around. This one is not: 3.12 metres of trunk, 21 metres of height, and the low dense crown of small hard leaves that holm oaks keep through winter.

The ground was private for most of that time. It began as the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas, a 17th century estate on the road out to Luz, and later carried the name of the Bensaúde family who owned it. Only in recent decades has anyone been free to walk under this tree.

All four were classified together in 2004. The register recorded this oak at 100 years old when it was measured in 2017, which puts it near 110 now. That is a surveyor's estimate rather than a count of rings, and holm oaks grow slowly enough that it could be out by a decade in either direction.

trees.name: The Second Holm Oak of Parque Bensaúde
trees.access: Free, public municipal park
trees.transport: About 15 minutes' walk from Colegio Militar/Luz station (Metro Blue Line)
trees.story:
Two holm oaks in Parque Bensaúde were classified on the same day and recorded at the same age. One measures 3.12 metres round the trunk. This one measures 1.72.

They stand about 50 metres apart in the same soil, which is a useful reminder that girth and age are only loosely related. Light, water and whatever the roots hit underground do most of the deciding. This is also the shorter of the pair at 17 metres, and it is the one you can actually put your arms around, which is the quickest way to know you have found the right tree.

Holm oak is the evergreen workhorse of the Iberian countryside, dark and dense, holding its small leathery leaves right through winter. There is no bare season here and no autumn colour, so the tree looks much the same in January as in July.

The park around it was the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas, a 17th century estate later held by the Bensaúde family and opened to the public as a municipal park off the Estrada da Luz. Both oaks were classified in 2004, alongside a red-flowering gum and an unusually thick field maple a short walk west.

The register logged 100 years at its 2017 measurement, so roughly 110 today, on a surveyor's estimate rather than a dated planting.

trees.name: The Red-Flowering Eucalyptus of Parque Bensaúde
trees.access: Free, public municipal park
trees.transport: About 15 minutes' walk from Colegio Militar/Luz station (Metro Blue Line)

best_time.label: high summer, when the whole crown turns scarlet

trees.story:
This is the smallest of the four protected trees in Parque Bensaúde and the only one on the list for what it does rather than what it is. At 7 metres tall and 1.45 metres round it is beaten on every measurement by its neighbours. Then high summer arrives and the whole crown goes scarlet.

Corymbia ficifolia comes from a narrow strip of coast in southwest Western Australia, a natural range small enough to drive across in an afternoon, and it has been planted around the mild parts of the world for exactly this: dense clusters of red flowers held above the leaves, lasting weeks and dropping a carpet underneath.

No age is recorded for it anywhere. It was classified in 2004 for its flowers and for being uncommon in the city rather than for any claim to antiquity, and nobody has dated it since.

It stands about 40 metres west of the larger holm oak, close to the field maple, so the park's four classified trees make one loop of a few minutes. Parque Bensaúde was the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas before the council opened it, which is how a private planting of an Australian ornamental ended up on a public list. Somebody wanted red flowers in their own garden, and a century later the garden became everybody's.

trees.name: The Field Maple of Parque Bensaúde
trees.access: Free, public municipal park
trees.transport: About 15 minutes' walk from Colegio Militar/Luz station (Metro Blue Line)
trees.story:
A field maple with a 3.5 metre waist is an oddity. This is the modest one of the European maples, a hedgerow and woodland-edge tree that usually tops out around 15 metres and rarely gets thick, and this one has a trunk wider than either of the classified holm oaks standing a few dozen metres east of it.

It reaches 13.5 metres at the western end of Parque Bensaúde, the fourth of the four trees the state singled out here in 2004. No age is recorded for it. Field maples are hard to date without cutting into them and this one has never been surveyed for age, so the honest answer is that it is old enough to have grown far beyond the usual size, and no more precise than that.

Look at the leaves to be sure you have the right tree. Field maple carries small five-lobed leaves with blunt rounded tips, quite unlike the sharp-pointed maples of parks and streets, and older twigs often develop corky ridges you can feel with a thumb. In autumn it turns clear yellow, briefly, before Lisbon's mild weather takes the leaves off.

The park was the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas, a 17th century estate, which explains how a northern European maple got here at all. Somebody planted it in a private garden and let it get on with it.

trees.name: The Paperbark of Jardim Constantino
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Short walk from Arroios or Anjos station (Metro Green Line)
trees.story:
Lisbon has one prickly paperbark, and this is it. The Portuguese record of Jardim Constantino calls the tree unique in the city, which is a strong claim for a garden of a quarter of a hectare to hold.

Melaleuca styphelioides is an Australian tree grown for its bark: white, spongy, laid down in papery layers you can press a thumb into, peeling in sheets around a trunk 1.58 metres round. The leaves are small, stiff and sharp-tipped, which is the prickly half of the name. At 18 metres with an 11 metre crown it is the tall thin one in this garden. The fig a few steps away is the wide one.

The garden opened in 1889 and takes its name from Constantino José Marques de Sampaio e Melo, a florist. It runs to a lake, a playground and a statue of Prometheus, and it sits in Arroios two streets off the metro, so this tree has spent its whole life in a city square rather than a park.

It was classified in 1996, half a century after its neighbour. The register recorded 107 years when it was measured in 2017, so roughly 115 now, which would put it in the ground around 1910, a generation after the garden itself.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Jardim Constantino
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Short walk from Arroios or Anjos station (Metro Green Line)
trees.story:
A garden of a quarter of a hectare in Arroios holds a fig with a 26 metre crown, which accounts for most of the shade in the place. Jardim Constantino is small: a lake, a playground, a statue of Prometheus and two protected trees. This is the wide one.

Ficus macrophylla comes from the east coast of Australia and was planted across Lisbon in the late 19th and early 20th centuries for exactly this reason. It grows fast, throws a dense crown, and drops the buttressing roots that make a mature specimen look like it is holding the ground down. At 24 metres tall on a trunk 2.33 metres round, this one has done the job.

It has been protected since 1947, which is early. The paperbark standing a few metres away had to wait until 1996 for the same status. The register recorded 107 years when the tree was measured in 2017, so roughly 115 today.

Lisbon has better known Moreton Bay figs, at Príncipe Real and in the Estrela garden, both of them on their own city-centre stages with a crowd in front of them. This one has a neighbourhood square, a bench underneath and no queue.

trees.name: The Belas-Sombras of Jardim António Feijó
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Short walk from Arroios or Anjos station (Metro Green Line)
trees.story:
The two fattest trunks in this garden are not really wood. Phytolacca dioica, the bela-sombra, is a giant herb rather than a tree, and the swollen base that makes it look ancient is soft, water-storing tissue you could dent with a thumbnail. It grows fast, it produces no timber worth the name, and it falls apart earlier than its bulk suggests.

There are two of them here, and they came out almost identical: 10.45 and 10.4 metres round, 17.6 and 16.4 metres tall. They stand about 30 metres apart, one at the southeast corner of the garden and one at the top of it, so the visit is both or neither.

The garden wraps around the Igreja de Nossa Senhora dos Anjos, inaugurated in 1911, and the pair went in at roughly the time the church was finished. They were classified in 1947, among the earliest protection orders in Lisbon, and reclassified in 2018.

The register recorded them at 105 years when they were measured in 2015, so roughly 115 now. With a bela-sombra that figure is softer than usual. The trunk does not lay down the tidy annual rings you could count in an oak, so any age for one is worked back from size and from whatever the planting records say.

trees.name: The Bela-Sombra of Praça António Sardinha
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Short walk from Arroios station (Metro Green Line) or Penha de Franca bus routes
trees.story:
The roots of this one come out of the ground looking like more trunks. The parish council's own account of Praça António Sardinha describes a century-old bela-sombra whose roots resemble trunks converging into one, which is a fair description of what a big Phytolacca dioica does. The base spreads into buttresses and folds until it is hard to say where the tree stops and the ground starts.

At 10.9 metres round it is thicker than either of the pair 600 metres away in Jardim António Feijó. Its crown reaches nearly 21 metres across on a tree only 16.2 metres tall, so it is wider than it is high.

None of that is wood. The bela-sombra is a giant herb from the South American pampas, all soft water-holding tissue, which is why it swells so quickly and why a careless machine can damage it in a way an oak would shrug off.

It stands beside a primary school, and when the square was rebuilt in 2023 the works were laid out around it. It was classified in 2000. The register recorded 105 years at the 2015 measurement, so roughly 115 now, an estimate from size rather than a dated planting.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of Quinta Conde dos Arcos
trees.access: Free, public urban park (three gates, open roughly 6:30am to 8-10pm depending on season)
trees.transport: In Olivais; nearest metro is Encarnacao or Bela Vista (Red Line), roughly 15-20 minutes' walk
trees.story:
This dragon tree is more than twice as wide as it is tall: 6.2 metres of height under a crown almost 14 metres across, on a trunk 4.75 metres round. Dracaena draco grows that way on purpose. It puts up a stem, flowers, then forks, over and over, until an old one looks like an umbrella made of umbrellas.

Nobody can date it properly. Dragon trees lay down no annual rings, so every age published for one is worked back from the branching or from records. The register recorded 200 years when it was measured in 2010, which makes it roughly 215 now, and that is about as precise as this species allows.

It grows in the Quinta Conde dos Arcos, a private estate the Lisbon council expropriated in 1940 and later opened as a nine-hectare park in Olivais. The old palace holds the municipal gardening school. The parish council names this dragon tree as the one tree of public interest among the 28 species growing there, and runs free guided walks on set dates through the year.

The sap runs red where the bark is cut, which is where the name comes from. Dragon's blood was shipped out of the Canaries and Madeira as a dye and a medicine for centuries before anyone thought to plant one of these in Lisbon.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Hospital Pulido Valente
trees.access: Free, grounds of a public NHS hospital (Hospital Pulido Valente, part of ULS Santa Maria); the tree stands in the open forecourt of Edificio D. Carlos, visible without entering clinical areas, but visitors should behave as hospital guests
trees.transport: Near Hospital Pulido Valente / Lumiar (Metro Yellow Line, short walk)
trees.story:
The national register puts this plane tree at 364 years old. If that is right, it was standing here before the hospital, before the road and before most of Lumiar.

Treat the number carefully. It comes from the classification file opened in 1945 and has been repeated since, including in the book Árvores da Cidade, which gives the same 364 years and near-identical height and crown figures. Two sources, one origin, and nobody has ever dated the wood. Add the years since that survey and the register's own figure would make it about 375 today.

What has actually been measured is impressive enough on its own: 5.85 metres round the trunk, 28 metres tall, and a crown 37 metres across, nine metres wider than the tree is high. It fills the forecourt of the Edifício D. Carlos at Hospital Pulido Valente, and the hospital holds its anniversary events underneath it.

This is not a park. It is a working public hospital, and the tree stands in the open forecourt where you can see it without going near a clinical area, so go as you would go into someone's front garden and stay out of the way.

The London plane is the tree Lisbon planted everywhere in the 19th century for shade. This one, if the file is right, was already old when that fashion started.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Travessa do Arco da Torre
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Short walk from Belem or Restelo, served by tram 15E and several bus routes along Avenida da India
trees.story:
Two minutes from the queue at the Torre de Belém, on a back lane most visitors never turn into, stands a plane tree 29 metres tall. Travessa do Arco da Torre runs parallel to Avenida da Torre de Belém, near Largo da Princesa, and this is the tree that overtops the rooflines along it.

The trunk is 3.75 metres round and the crown spreads to nearly 27.5 metres, close to park dimensions for something growing out of a public street with no garden around it. Street planes are usually cut back hard for the wires and the windows. This one has been left to spread.

The register recorded 150 years when it was measured in 2010, so roughly 165 now, and the independent coverage of Lisbon's classified trees gives it about the same. It was classified in 2000.

That age puts its planting in the 1860s, when Belém was still being stitched into the city and long before the waterfront acquired its monuments, its museums and its crowds. Everything that now draws several million people a year arrived within sight of this tree, and it has watched the lot from one street back, over the roofs, with a couple of parked cars underneath it.

trees.name: The Monterey Cypress of Parque do Caramão da Ajuda
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: In Belem/Ajuda, reachable by bus along Calcada da Ajuda; no metro station nearby
trees.story:
Monterey cypress has one of the smallest natural ranges of any conifer: two headlands on the California coast near Monterey, a few kilometres of cliff, and nothing else in the wild. It also grows happily almost anywhere mild and coastal, which is how one ended up roughly 9,000 kilometres away with a 3.9 metre trunk in a park above Belém.

At 18.5 metres tall with a 17 metre crown, this is a heavy, wide, dark tree, the shape Monterey cypresses take once the wind has had a few decades at them: horizontal limbs, flattened top, foliage in dense sprays that smell of lemon when crushed.

It stands in the Parque do Caramão da Ajuda, which is a public park and not the Tapada da Ajuda next door. That distinction is worth getting right before setting out, because the two are neighbours and only one of them has this tree.

Beyond the state register, nobody appears to have written it up. The register classified it in 2000 and recorded 85 years when it was measured in 2015, which puts it around 95 now, and those are the only figures anyone has published. It is a solid enough record as far as it goes, and it is the whole of what is known about this cypress.

trees.name: The Furmanska Lipa (Carter's Linden)
trees.access: Free, public square, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Ljubljana city centre, Borstnikov trg; about a 10 minute walk from Preseren Square

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: Carters bound between Vienna and Trieste used to stop under this linden to buy hay for their horses, and the trade gave the tree its name, Furmanska lipa, the Carter's Linden. It went into the ground in 1626, on what is now Borstnikov trg, and by the time Florijancic drew his map of Ljubljana in 1744 the tree was already old enough, at roughly 118, to be worth marking. In 2026 it turns 400, the oldest documented tree in the city by a wide margin. Its shade did more than shelter horse traders. France Preseren, Slovenia's national poet, wrote under it alongside his closest friend Matija Cop and the writer Andrej Smole, all three now central figures in the country's literary canon; later the architect Joze Plecnik and the priest-writer Fran Saleski Finzgar sat under the same crown. The square itself sits on ground that was once Roman Emona, the road running past it still called Rimska cesta, Roman Road, so the tree has spent four centuries growing on a spot that was already old when it was planted. The inn it still fronts, Gostilna Pod lipo, under the linden, takes its own name directly from the tree. Four hundred years on, both are still standing.

trees.name: The Marmontova Lipa
trees.access: Public botanical garden, free entry, open daily in the growing season
trees.transport: Rudnik district, southeast of Ljubljana Castle, beside the Gruberjev kanal; about a 15 minute walk or short bus ride from the city centre

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: This linden and the garden around it were planted the same year, and both were named for the same brief, foreign occupation. In July 1810, with Ljubljana serving as capital of Napoleon's short-lived Illyrian Provinces, botanist Franc Hladnik founded what is now the oldest continuously operating botanical garden in southeastern Europe, and among its first plantings went in a linden later named for Auguste de Marmont, the French marshal who governed the province. The Illyrian Provinces lasted only four years before Austria took the region back, but Marmontova lipa outlived the empire that named it by two centuries and counting. It remains the garden's single mightiest tree, still shading the same paths Hladnik laid out, in a garden that has run without interruption since a French general's brief and largely forgotten administration. Ljubljana's Botanical Garden was declared a cultural monument of national importance in 2008, two centuries after Marmont's name first got attached to a sapling, by which point the marshal himself was a footnote and the tree had become the point.

trees.name: The Elder Plane of Streliska
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Ljubljana city centre, Streliska ulica; about a 15 minute walk from Preseren Square
trees.story: Two trees are all that is left of an avenue that once ran from the foot of Ljubljana Castle to the start of the road toward Dolenjska, a double row of planes planted along what was then the edge of the old city. Florijancic's 1744 map of Ljubljana shows the avenue already in place; today only two of its trees survive, both on Streliska ulica, both individually protected as natural values of national importance, a designation held by almost nothing else in the city's narrow historic centre. This one is the thicker of the pair, its trunk 596 centimetres around and its crown reaching 33 metres, making it one of the largest trees of its species anywhere in Slovenia. It has outlived the old fortifications it once grew beside by more than two centuries; Ljubljana's city walls came down long ago, but the avenue's last survivors kept growing regardless, witnesses to a street plan nobody alive remembers walking.

trees.name: The Corner Plane of Streliska and Strossmayerjeva
trees.access: Free, public street corner, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Ljubljana city centre, corner of Streliska and Strossmayerjeva; about a 15 minute walk from Preseren Square
trees.story: A short walk from its twin on Streliska ulica stands the second survivor of Ljubljana's vanished plane-tree avenue, rooted exactly at the corner where Streliska meets Strossmayerjeva. The two trees are the only physical evidence left of a double row that once ran the length of the street, visible on the city's 1744 map and gone everywhere else since. This one carries its own separate listing in both of Slovenia's national heritage registers, the Register of Natural Values and the Register of Immovable Cultural Heritage, protected not for any single record-breaking measurement but for being one half of a pair whose surviving presence is the whole point: two trees, planted together, are what is left of a street plan otherwise erased. The streets around it have been repaved and renamed since the avenue first went in, most recently Strossmayerjeva itself, renovated in recent years without disturbing the tree on the corner. It has no plaque and needs none. It is simply still there, half of the last two.

trees.name: The Totteridge Yew
trees.access: Free, open access, churchyard
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Totteridge & Whetstone station (Northern Line)

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: The oldest living thing in London stands in a churchyard most people drive straight past. This yew was already ancient when the Romans built Londinium two thousand years ago, and the church beside it is the newcomer: St Andrew's dates only to the 13th century, a good thousand years younger than the tree growing at its edge. A 2008 survey by the Conservation Foundation, the Ancient Yew Group and Barnet Council named it possibly the oldest tree in the city, though ring counting is useless here. Yew heartwood rots away long before it can be counted, which is why the estimate spans a thousand years, 1,000 to 2,000, rather than a single number. What survives is a hollow, propped trunk with a girth of nearly eight metres, kept alive the way most ancient yews are kept alive: repeated pollarding, cutting the tree back hard and often enough to reset its own clock rather than let it grow toward collapse. Totteridge was a village long before London reached it, and its Hundred Court, the local medieval assembly that settled disputes and collected dues, once met in the yew's shade, using the tree as a landmark centuries before anyone thought to measure its age.

trees.name: The Royal Oak
trees.access: Free, open access, national park
trees.transport: Bus or car to Richmond Park, then on foot near Pen Ponds

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: The wall came second: this oak was already centuries old when Charles I enclosed Richmond Park around it in 1637, walling off common land for his own deer rather than planting anything new. It has lived behind royal fences ever since. The tree is a massive hollow pollard now, its trunk split and gnarled into a shape wide enough to shelter a small football team, kept alive by the same repeated cutting-back that saves most ancient oaks from their own weight. Richmond Park holds one of the largest collections of ancient oaks in Europe, and the Royal Oak is treated as its figurehead: Sir David Attenborough chose it as the symbol of a conservation campaign for the park's veteran trees, and it carries its own entry in the Woodland Trust's national Ancient Tree Inventory, a formally surveyed and registered specimen rather than a folk legend. Fallow deer, descendants of the herd Charles I first enclosed the park to hunt, still graze in its shadow, close enough on a quiet afternoon that the oak and the animals read as one scene rather than two separate facts.

trees.name: The Cheapside Plane
trees.access: Free, public square, City of London
trees.transport: 2 min walk from St Paul's tube station
trees.story: The only Great Tree of London still standing inside the Square Mile grows out of a churchyard that no longer has a church. St Peter Cheap burned down in the Great Fire of 1666 and was never rebuilt, and the plane tree that replaced its congregation is old enough that nobody can say exactly when it was planted. By 1853 a cab company was advertising its rank simply as 'Under the tree, Cheapside,' proof the tree was already a fixed point on the map before street numbering caught up with London's growth. In 1901 the press went further and called it the most valuable tree in the world, a claim about the land beneath it as much as the tree itself. It has survived since through the Blitz, through the City's total postwar rebuilding, and through a peculiarity of property law: the leases on the buildings flanking it forbid construction above two storeys on that side, an accident of contract law that has kept its canopy open to the sky for longer than most buildings nearby have existed. William Wordsworth is thought to have had this exact tree in mind writing his 1800 poem Poor Susan, in which a countrywoman hears a thrush singing from a tree on Cheapside and briefly mistakes the City for home.

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Berkeley Square Plane
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Green Park or Bond Street tube
trees.story: In 2008 a valuer put a price on one of the plane trees in Berkeley Square: 750,000 pounds, briefly the most valuable tree in Britain, a number that says more about Mayfair real estate than about the tree itself. The square's planes went into the ground in 1789, planted by the MP Edward Bouverie, who lived at number 13, and they now rank among the oldest London planes anywhere in the city. There are more than thirty of them, planted as a single scheme rather than one famous specimen, which is why this entry marks the square itself rather than a single trunk. The nightingale of the song 'A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square' almost certainly never existed as a literal bird here, nightingales do not really sing over central London traffic, but if one had, these are the branches it would have used. The planes were named among the original 41 Great Trees of London, and the Grade II listed garden they shade has kept the same rectangular shape since the square was laid out, a fixed green rectangle while Mayfair rebuilt itself around it for over two centuries.

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of Greenwich Park
trees.access: Free, open parkland, Greenwich Park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Maze Hill station, into Greenwich Park

best_time.label: October, when its spiny nut cases carpet the ground beneath it

trees.story: Charles II wanted Versailles and settled for Greenwich instead. After taking the throne in 1660, he ordered grand formal avenues cut through the old royal hunting park, hundreds of sweet chestnuts marched up the hill toward the future Royal Observatory in straight French rows. Most of that planting is gone, lost to storms, disease and three and a half centuries of ordinary attrition. This chestnut is one of roughly fifty survivors, and the one the Great Trees of London list points to in the Flower Garden. Its trunk has thickened into something closer to architecture than plant, and it has been pollarded more than once, a pruning technique that resets a tree's internal clock and is a large part of why it is still standing while so many of its neighbours from the same planting are not. Its slowly rotting heartwood, hollow in places, now shelters beetles and fungi that need old deadwood and nowhere else. Every October it drops a carpet of spiny green cases across the grass, food for the park's squirrels and for anyone willing to peel one open. It has stood through the Restoration, two world wars and the digging of anti-aircraft gun pits nearby. Unlike the oak that once stood a short walk from here, it has never stopped growing.

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Mulberry of Charlton House
trees.access: Free, open grounds of Charlton House community centre
trees.transport: Charlton rail station, 5 min walk

best_time.label: August, when it still fruits every summer despite four centuries of leaning

trees.story: James I wanted Britain to grow its own silk, and in 1608 he ordered mulberry trees planted across the country to feed the silkworms that would spin it. The plan collapsed almost immediately over a basic mistake: silkworms eat white mulberry leaves and mostly refuse black ones, and the trees planted nationwide, including this one, were black mulberries. Charlton House got one of them, and unlike England's silk industry, the tree itself survived the error by four hundred years and counting. It now leans so far from vertical that its lower branches nearly touch the ground, propped up by a scaffold of wooden supports rather than left to collapse under its own spread, and it still fruits every August, small dark berries falling onto grass that has replaced whatever formal garden once surrounded it. The tree predates the surrounding community centre by roughly three centuries. Charlton House itself, a Jacobean mansion finished the same decade this mulberry went into the ground, has changed use many times since, while the tree in its garden has simply kept growing, propped a little more with each passing century.

photo.attribution: Ethan Doyle White, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Fulham Palace Oak
trees.access: Free, Fulham Palace Gardens open daily
trees.transport: Putney Bridge tube, 10 min walk
trees.story: This oak survived five centuries partly because people kept attacking it. It was coppiced long ago, cut back hard to its base, a brutal-looking practice that paradoxically resets a tree's age clock and can add centuries to its life rather than shorten it. What grew back is a Holm Oak, an evergreen Mediterranean species that has no business thriving this far north, and quite possibly the oldest specimen of its kind anywhere in Britain. It grows in the grounds of Fulham Palace, for centuries the working home of the Bishop of London rather than a royal estate, and the two bishops most often credited with planting it, Edmund Grindal and John Aylmer, both lived here in the second half of the 16th century, among the first people in England to try growing the species at all. The oak was named among the original 41 trees given Great Tree status in 1988, and a later record corrected an old misidentification of the tree as a common Pedunculate Oak rather than the rarer Mediterranean evergreen it actually is. Fulham Palace Gardens are free to enter daily, which means reaching London's likely oldest holm oak costs nothing but the walk from Putney Bridge station.

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: Barney the Plane
trees.access: Public access, Barnes area
trees.transport: Barnes station or bus
trees.story: The biggest London plane in the city is a tree most Londoners have never heard of. Nicknamed Barney, it stands at Barn Elms in the riverside suburb of Barnes, tucked at the edge of the land next to the London Wetland Centre, and it is old enough, over 300 years, that it is treated locally as potentially the single oldest London plane anywhere in the capital. The species is the city's signature tree for a reason: it tolerates soot, survives brutal pruning, and outlives almost everything planted around it, and Barney is the patriarch of them all in Barnes. Its own Great Trees of London plaque states the claim plainly, calling it simply the oldest in London, though the tree's coordinates only firmed up in 2026, when a photographer's geotagged shot of Barney was checked against the plaque's own recorded position and the two turned out to sit within nine metres of each other, close enough to count as the same tree rather than two separate estimates. Most visitors to Barn Elms come for the birdwatching at the Wetland Centre next door and walk straight past the small plaque without noticing it, which is itself part of Barney's story: London's biggest plane tree stands anonymously beside one of the city's most visited nature reserves.

trees.name: The Old Lions of Kew
trees.access: Paid entry to Kew Gardens
trees.transport: Kew Gardens tube station (District Line), 5 min walk

best_time.label: August to September, when it flowers

trees.story: John Smith, Kew Gardens' first curator, gave five of its oldest trees a nickname that stuck: the Old Lions, veterans that have outlasted every curator, director and fashion in planting since the garden began. The group spans the site rather than clustering in one corner: an oriental plane near the Orangery, an elm, a locust, and the most storied of the five, a Japanese pagoda tree planted in 1762 that ranks among the oldest of its species growing anywhere in Europe outside its native range. All five predate Kew's formal existence as a public institution. They were already growing when Princess Augusta laid out the first pleasure garden here in the 1750s, decades before Kew merged with the neighbouring Richmond estate and grew into the botanic garden it is today. Seeing all five in one visit means crossing a meaningful stretch of the grounds, since Smith grouped them by age and survival rather than by location, but each carries its own small marker naming it as one of the Lions. Entry to Kew requires a paid ticket, unlike most of London's ancient trees, but the garden built its reputation partly on outliving its own founders, and these five are the proof of it.

trees.name: The Evelyn Mulberry
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Deptford or Deptford Bridge station, 5 min walk

best_time.label: August, when the fruit ripens, one of the few parts of Sayes Court's story that still repeats every year

trees.story: John Evelyn's garden at Sayes Court was one of the most celebrated in 17th century England, laid out by a writer and diarist who helped define English ideas about forestry and planting, and it lasted less than four decades before a tenant wrecked it for sport. Tsar Peter the Great of Russia rented the house in 1698 while studying shipbuilding nearby, and legend holds that he spent his evenings being wheeled through Evelyn's prized holly hedges in a wheelbarrow, flattening years of careful topiary for entertainment. Historians doubt Peter planted anything here himself, and this mulberry's own age is uncertain enough that the honest claim is only that it may have survived the same visit that ruined everything around it, not that it predates the destruction with certainty. What remains today is a fenced, propped tree standing in an unremarkable public park where almost nothing else of Evelyn's garden survives, plus a stone marker at its base that tells visitors the wheelbarrow story rather than leaving them to wonder why one old mulberry gets special treatment. It still fruits every August, one of the few parts of Sayes Court's story that still repeats on schedule rather than existing only in an old diary.

photo.attribution: Robin Webster, via Geograph Britain and Ireland / Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The St Paul's Churchyard Planes
trees.access: Free, open access, public churchyard garden on the north side of St Paul's Cathedral (no ticket needed for the garden, only for the cathedral interior)
trees.transport: 2 min walk from St Paul's station (Central Line)
trees.story:
Four planes stood on the north side of St Paul's churchyard until the Great Storm of 1987 took one of them down. The three that remain are, according to one detailed local history of the cathedral, over 250 years old, which would put their planting in the middle of the 18th century, when Wren's dome was still the newest thing on the skyline and the ground beneath them was a working burial place. That age comes from a single account. The London Parks and Gardens Trust inventory for the churchyard agrees only that these are among the oldest plane trees in the City, without giving a number or a date, so read 250 years as the best figure anyone has published rather than a measured one.

What they lived through is less disputed. On the night of 29 December 1940 incendiary bombs set the streets around the cathedral alight and burned out much of the City. The dome held, and so did the planes. Londoners later planted this species everywhere precisely because it shrugs off soot and smoke; these three were in the ground a century before that fashion started.

This is an ensemble rather than one specimen: three unnamed trees, none of them individually catalogued or given coordinates by any source. Stand on the paved path along the north side and all three are in one view. The pin marks that garden, not a particular trunk.

trees.name: The Amwell Street Fig
trees.access: Free, open access, standing against a street frontage on public pavement
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Angel station (Northern Line) or Farringdon station

best_time.label: late summer, when the figs ripen against the old school wall

trees.story:
This fig may have been planted as a teaching aid. It sprawls across the front of the former Clerkenwell Parochial Schools on Amwell Street, several stems rising from one rootstock and propped where the limbs have outgrown their own strength. Paul Wood, who has spent years cataloguing London's street trees, reckons it has stood here since the schools opened, put in deliberately at the front of the building and perhaps partly so that Bible lessons had something living to point at. Figs run all through scripture, and a fig outside the classroom window is an illustration nobody can lose.

The dates want care. The Amwell Society dates the school building to 1830, while other accounts say 1827. And the planting claim rests on that one specialist reading rather than on two independent records, so roughly 195 years is a careful estimate, not a birth certificate.

Clerkenwell changed around it more than most of London did: watchmakers, radical printers, the New River head a few streets north still delivering water into the city, charity schoolchildren giving way to board schools and then to flats. The building stopped being a school. The fig stayed, and Islington still counts it among the borough's notable street trees.

It is a working fruit tree on a public pavement in central London, which is the part that stops people. Come in late summer and the figs are there, at eye level, on the street.

trees.name: The Dorchester Plane
trees.access: Free, stands in The Dorchester Hotel's open forecourt directly on Park Lane, clearly visible and reachable from the public pavement without entering the hotel
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Hyde Park Corner station (Piccadilly Line)
trees.story:
One of the Great Trees of London stands at the front door of a hotel where a night costs more than most people's monthly rent, and you can walk up to it for nothing. The London Tree Forum and the Countryside Commission put this plane on their 1997 list of the capital's great trees, which was generous of them: the Great Trees map dates its planting to the early 1930s, making it younger than almost every other tree on this page by a century or more.

The arithmetic is suggestive rather than proven. The Dorchester opened in 1931, and a plane put into a brand new Park Lane forecourt in the early 1930s fits that opening neatly, but no source actually joins the two facts, and the planting date itself comes from that one specialist record.

What the tree unquestionably has is roots. Its root plate has risen clear of the ground and spread across the forecourt in ridges, the sort of thing a city normally paves over and here has been designed around instead: the hotel's recent refit tucked its garden underneath the tree rather than the other way round.

It has stood through the Blitz, when the hotel's reinforced concrete frame earned a reputation for being bomb-proof and politicians and generals moved in for the duration, and through ninety years of Park Lane traffic since. You see it from the pavement. No need to go inside.

trees.name: The Marylebone Elm
trees.access: Free, stands on the open public pavement directly outside the small Garden of Rest, no restriction
trees.transport: 6 min walk from Baker Street station (Bakerloo, Circle, District, Hammersmith & City, Jubilee, Metropolitan Lines)
trees.story:
Dutch elm disease killed around 25 million British elms from the 1960s on, roughly three quarters of the country's population. This one was missed. It stands on the pavement of Marylebone High Street, more than 100 feet of it by the Great Trees of London map, the last elm of its kind in Westminster to have escaped the beetle that carried the fungus through every hedgerow around it.

Specialist tree writers identify it as a Huntingdon Elm, a hybrid of wych and field elm. A recent account of the street calls it simply a wych elm, so the exact cultivar is not universally agreed. Nor is the age: writers through the 2010s consistently put it at about 150 years, which makes it roughly 160 now, a figure carried forward rather than measured.

It has outlived a church. The small garden beside it, the Memorial Garden of Rest, was laid out in 1951 on the site of the old St Marylebone parish church, which was bombed in the war and then demolished. The building is gone. The tree that grew outside it is still there, leaning out over the pavement as though it means to cross the road.

A naturalist photographed it in bud and healthy in 2017, and someone walking the High Street described it still standing there in April 2026.

trees.name: The Embankment Plane
trees.access: Free, stands on the public pavement/verge at the Horse Guards Avenue and Victoria Embankment junction, fully open access, no restriction
trees.transport: 7 min walk from Westminster station (Circle, District, Jubilee Lines)
trees.story:
The tree that helped make London a city of planes is not a London Plane. It is an Oriental Plane, one of the two species crossed to produce the hybrid now growing down half the streets in the capital, and it stands where Horse Guards Avenue meets the Victoria Embankment, on ground that was river water until Bazalgette's engineers pushed the Thames back in the 1860s.

The Great Trees of London map dates it to 1870 and gives the species. Both of those rest on that one specialist record. General histories of the Embankment agree that planes went in along the new road from about 1870, the first scheme in the city to plant a thoroughfare with trees systematically, but none of them names this individual tree. So it is a survivor of that first planting on the evidence available, rather than a documented one.

It has had a good view. Cleopatra's Needle was raised a few hundred metres along the same Embankment in 1878, trams came and went, the Ministry of Defence rose behind it in the 1950s, and Whitehall traffic has run past its trunk for a century and a half.

It gets called one of the tallest planes in Britain, a claim nobody appears to have checked. Easier to say what it plainly is: a very large tree on one of the busiest corners in Westminster that almost nobody stops for.

trees.name: The Great Plane of Brunswick Square
trees.access: Free, open public garden square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Russell Square station (Piccadilly Line)
trees.story: This plane was planted for orphans. Brunswick Square Gardens was laid out in 1796 as green space for the children of the Foundling Hospital, and this tree is reckoned to date from that laying out, which makes it around 230 years old. Only the planes of Berkeley Square, put in seven years earlier, are commonly held to be older among the planes of central London. It has stood through everything Bloomsbury became: the Hospital selling up and moving out of London in the 1920s, its buildings coming down, the square rebuilt around the gap, the Blitz, and the concrete decks of the Brunswick Centre arriving to the west in the 1970s. The institution it was planted to shade is gone. The tree is not. In 2008 it was named one of the ten Great Trees of London, and it has since been given its own information board in the square, which is a quiet way of saying the neighbourhood knows what it has. Photographs taken in spring 2026 show it in full health. Neither source that agrees on the 1796 planting records a girth or a height, so there are no measurements to quote here, only the thing itself: a very large plane in a small square five minutes from Russell Square station, free and open, with the Foundling Museum on the far side telling the rest of the story.

trees.name: The Valence Park Holm Oak
trees.access: Free, public park; the moat enclosure immediately beside the oak was closed for restoration works stated (2026) to complete by spring 2026, so current accessibility right up to the trunk is unconfirmed as of, though the wider park stays open
trees.transport: Becontree station (District Line) then bus 62 to Becontree Avenue/Valence Avenue, or Chadwell Heath rail station, roughly 20-25 min walk or a short bus ride either way
trees.story: The October 1987 storm brought down some 15 million trees across southern England and left this one untouched. Its low, heavily buttressed frame is credited for that: a holm oak that grows outward rather than upward gives the wind nothing to lean on. Roughly ten years later it was added to the Great Trees of London list. How old it is depends on which source you take, and the two do not agree. The Barking and Dagenham Post, quoting the borough's own heritage education officer, credits the Mertinn family, German immigrants who had made their money in jewellery and bought the estate in the early 1700s, with planting it to make their grounds look grander. That would put it close to 350 years. The London Gardens Trust's survey record for the site is more clinical and dates the grounds' holm oak and yew only to the nineteenth century, which would make it under 225. Both agree on what stands there: one of the most impressive holm oaks in London, beside the moat of Valence House, a medieval manor that is now the borough's museum. One practical note. The moat enclosure immediately beside the tree was closed for restoration work due to finish in spring 2026, so whether you can currently get right up to the trunk is unconfirmed. The park around it stays open, and the pin here is park level rather than surveyed.

trees.name: The Ravenscourt Park Baobab Plane
trees.species: London Plane, Baobab Group (Platanus x hispanica)
trees.age: roughly 100 to 200 years, exact age unknown
trees.access: Free, open public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Ravenscourt Park station (District Line)
trees.story: A virus is the best explanation anyone has for the shape of this tree. It carries a swollen, knobbled trunk under a crown far too small for it, the signature of the rare Baobab group of London plane, a form believed to come from viral infection rather than ordinary growth. Few are known; the closest comparable specimens grow in Canterbury. Nobody can say how old it is, and the sources sit far apart. A specialist plane blog puts its planting somewhere in the nineteenth century, so 150 to 225 years. A local tree firm reckons closer to 100, while allowing it might date to 1812, when the park was the private estate of George Scott. The same firm repeats a story that a wartime bomb damaged the tree and that the regrowth explains its shape; no other source carries it, so treat that as local legend until one does. What is documented is stranger. The arborist Richard Moore took cuttings from this exact tree. Two of six rooted and now grow at a sculpture park in Dorset, still far too young to show whether the swelling travels with the cutting or belongs only to the parent. It is one of two Great Trees of London inside Ravenscourt Park, standing south of the lower grassy area near the elm avenue, five minutes from the District Line station, and it is unmistakable once you are in front of it.

trees.name: The Fountain Court Mulberries
trees.neighbourhood: Temple, City of London / Westminster border
trees.access: Genuinely public but restricted hours: Middle Temple's garden and Fountain Court are open to the public on weekdays roughly 12:30-3pm, excluding bank holidays, entered via the Garden Room off Middle Temple Lane; occasionally closed for high winds or private functions
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Temple station (Circle, District Lines)

best_time.label: August, when the black mulberries ripen and drop

trees.story: Two black mulberries lean on wooden crutches either side of a fountain that has been running since 1681. They were planted for a queen's jubilee and the sources cannot agree which one. Middle Temple's own archive dates them to 1897 and Victoria's Diamond Jubilee. An independent mulberry history gives 20 June 1887, her Golden Jubilee, and adds that the planting was marked with a dinner in Middle Temple Hall. Ten years apart, both plausible, neither picked here: call the trees roughly 130 to 140 years old. Four went in together and only these two are left, the other pair removed in the 1970s. Black mulberry ages like this, going crooked and heavy limbed early, propping itself on whatever it is given, and fruiting hard regardless. Fountain Court is a small enclosed square between Middle Temple Hall and the gardens that run down toward the river, a working courtyard of the legal quarter rather than a park, and one of the quietest corners in the City. Access is real but narrow. The court and garden open to the public on weekdays, roughly 12:30 to 3pm, not on bank holidays, entered through the Garden Room off Middle Temple Lane, and they close in high winds or for private functions. Turn up inside that window and both trees are there, one on each side of the water.

trees.name: The Inner Temple Mulberry
trees.access: Public, open weekdays 12:30pm-3:00pm only (not full daily access)
trees.transport: Temple station, 4 minute walk

best_time.label: August, when the mulberries ripen and stain whatever is underneath them

trees.story: The Inner Temple's garden opens to the public for two and a half hours on weekday afternoons, and this tree is a fair reason to time the visit. A black mulberry stands by the railings of Benchers' Walk, outside Paper Buildings, its trunk about a metre and a half around and ten metres of crown above it. The Inner Temple's own history of the garden names it as one of the survivors of an old orchard, alongside a large-fruiting walnut and a quince, which is the institution itself calling this inherited planting rather than decoration. What no source will say is how old it is. There is no planting date anywhere, and black mulberries are among the hardest trees to age: they rot hollow early, lean until they need propping, and root wherever a low branch touches soil, so the trunk stops being a record of anything. This entry carries no age for that reason rather than a guess. The ground is famous for a scene that never happened here. Shakespeare set the plucking of the red and white roses, and with it the start of the Wars of the Roses, in the Temple garden; the tree is centuries younger than the fiction. Two hundred and fifty metres across the lane, Middle Temple's mulberries at Fountain Court at least have a disputed planting date to argue over. This one does not even have that.

trees.name: The Finsbury Circus Pagoda Tree
trees.access: Free, public garden, standard park hours
trees.transport: Moorgate station, 3 minute walk; Liverpool Street station, 6 minute walk

best_time.label: August, when it flowers cream-white and almost nothing else in London does

trees.story: This is the only Japanese pagoda tree in the City of London, on the City of London's own account of its gardens, and a City business paper's tour of Finsbury Circus says the same. The species comes from China and flowers cream in August, when almost nothing else does, which is a useful habit in a garden ringed by offices where lunch happens outdoors. Both sources tie the tree to the garden's original 1815 layout by George Dance the Younger, and neither produces a planting record, so the age here is circumstantial: roughly two centuries, inferred from the design rather than read off a document. Treat it as a range rather than a birthday. It has come through the most disruptive stretch of its life. Finsbury Circus lost most of its surface to Crossrail works for over a decade, then closed in 2023 for the first full renovation of the gardens in more than a hundred years and reopened in May 2025. The gardens are small, 2.2 hectares, so finding it takes a minute. Half a kilometre south, the Cheapside Plane is the only Great Tree of London still standing inside the Square Mile, and Kew's Old Lions include pagoda trees of roughly the same generation in a botanical collection. This one has spent its two hundred years in the middle of the banking district instead.

trees.name: The Quaker Garden Planes
trees.access: Free, public recreation ground (laid out 1965 within the GLC Banner Street estate), entered from Banner Street or Chequer Street
trees.transport: Old Street station, 6 minute walk
trees.story: George Fox, who founded the Quakers, was buried on this ground in 1691, and the plane trees standing over it are nowhere near old enough to have seen it. The burial ground took Quaker dead from 1661 until 1855, and the space became a public recreation ground in 1965, laid out inside the Banner Street estate with the trees left in place. Their age is genuinely disputed. Bunhill Fields Quaker Meeting's own account of the garden says the mature London planes here were planted about 1880, which makes them roughly 145 years old. A local record drawing on the London Gardens Trust inventory describes three notable planes, two of which may date from the 18th century, which would make them a century older and among the oldest planes in London. The two claims have not been reconciled, and this page follows the Meeting's own figure because it is the institution's own history, while saying plainly that the bigger claim is out there. It is worth not confusing this with the celebrated burial ground next door. Bunhill Fields holds Blake, Defoe and Bunyan and gets the visitors; the Quaker ground is a separate, quieter square of grass and trees between Banner Street and Chequer Street, six minutes from Old Street. The Amwell Street Fig is about 1.4 kilometres west if you want to make an afternoon of it.

trees.name: The Ravenscourt Park Tree of Heaven
trees.access: Free, open public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Ravenscourt Park station (District Line)
trees.story: Tree of heaven is the species councils spend money removing. This one has a plaque. The circular green plaque at its foot calls it one of the largest examples of the species in the country and one of the Great Trees of London, and the Tree Register's champion database carries it too, with at least one account calling it the tallest of its kind in Britain. Nobody gives it an age, and that absence is the interesting part. Ailanthus altissima arrived in Britain from China in the 18th century, spreads by seed and suckers, and is usually treated as short-lived, rarely making it much past fifty years. Something this size therefore breaks the pattern for its own species, and since no source anywhere offers a planting date, this entry gives no age rather than inventing one. It qualifies on size and status, not on years. It is also the cheapest addition to a walk on this whole list. The Ravenscourt Park Baobab Plane, with its swollen virus-knobbled trunk, stands about 150 metres away in the same park, which means Hammersmith now offers two Great Trees of London within a two minute walk of each other, near the sports area and the playground, five minutes from Ravenscourt Park station. The coordinates here come from the Great Trees map and are tree-level, so the pin lands on the trunk.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico di Lucca
trees.transport: About 15 min walk from Lucca station, in the southeast corner inside the walls

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: This tree is two years younger than the garden around it. Maria Luisa di Borbone, Duchess of Lucca, founded the Orto Botanico in 1820 as a teaching collection for the city's medical school, and in 1822 the first director, Paolo Volpi, put a young cedar in the ground with Count Bernardino Orsetti. The seedling came from the botanical garden at Pisa. Two centuries later it is six and a half metres round the trunk, about twenty metres tall, and it holds its foliage in the flat horizontal plates that only an old Lebanon cedar makes, so the whole crown reads as a series of dark tiers rather than a dome. The garden calls it the patriarch and uses it as its symbol. The species itself comes from the mountains of Lebanon, Syria and southern Turkey, where the Phoenicians cut it for ships and the same forests supplied Solomon's temple, and where very little of it is left standing. Almost every specimen in Europe descends from a handful of eighteenth and nineteenth century plantings like this one. Stand at the trunk and the visitor beside you is roughly one tenth of its girth.

trees.name: The Redwood of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico di Lucca
trees.transport: About 15 min walk from Lucca station, in the southeast corner inside the walls
trees.story: The tallest living thing inside Lucca's walls is Californian. At thirty-five metres this redwood clears every tower in the old town except the two you can climb, and it was planted around 1850, which is the detail worth pausing on. Western botanists had only described the coast redwood in 1847, and the first seed reached Europe a few years before that. A garden in a walled Tuscan city was therefore growing one within a decade of the species existing on paper. It is now five and three quarter metres round. Coast redwood is the tallest tree species on earth, and the record specimens in northern California pass a hundred and fifteen metres, so this one is a child by the standards of its own kind and will very likely still be growing in three hundred years. Put a hand on the trunk: the bark is soft, dry and fibrous, thirty centimetres deep on old trees, and it is what lets a redwood survive fires that kill everything around it. A second registered redwood stands forty metres away, a little smaller, and the garden counts a third among its nineteenth century plantings.

trees.name: The Three-Trunked Ginkgo
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico di Lucca
trees.transport: About 15 min walk from Lucca station, in the southeast corner inside the walls

best_time.label: mid-November, when it turns hard yellow and drops it all at once

trees.story: Lightning took this tree down after the war and it came back as three. The ginkgo planted here in 1862 was struck in the post-war years and thrown into regrowth, and the garden let three of the resulting shoots run. They are now three full trunks of one tree, twenty-six metres tall, which is why the national register, which lists a trunk girth for almost everything it protects, leaves the figure blank for this one. There is no single trunk to measure. Ginkgo biloba is the last species of an entire order of plants, with no living relative closer than the conifers, and fossils of nearly identical leaves come out of rock two hundred million years old. It survives what other trees do not: it was among the first things to grow back near the epicentre at Hiroshima, and the trick on display here, rebuilding itself from a wrecked base, is the same trait. Come in the middle of November. The garden treats the turn as one of its events of the year, when the leaves go from green to a hard uniform yellow and then drop, often most of them within a day or two, leaving a gold floor and a bare tree above it.

trees.name: The Monterey Cypress on the San Regolo Bastion
trees.access: Free, on the public walk along the city walls
trees.transport: On the walls at the San Regolo bastion, directly above the botanical garden
trees.story: In the wild this species grows in two small groves on a single stretch of Californian coast near Monterey and nowhere else on earth. This one is twenty-eight metres tall and stands on the roof of a gun platform built between 1600 and 1605 by Piero Vignarelli, on walls that were designed to stop artillery and never had to. That is the joke of Lucca's fortifications: four and a half kilometres of state of the art sixteenth century defences that were never attacked, and which the city therefore turned into a park. Maria Luisa di Borbone laid out the promenade along the top in the 1820s, and from 1860 Cesare Bicchi, who ran the botanical garden immediately below the bastion, used the walls as an extension of his collection and planted exotic conifers where cannon had stood. This cypress is his, and at three and a half metres round it is one of only three trees on the whole circuit that the national register protects. It is evergreen, so it looks the same in February as in August, and it is free to visit at any hour, which the garden below it is not.

trees.name: The Holm Oaks on the Torre Guinigi
trees.age: not dated, the living oaks are replantings
trees.access: Paid entry to the Torre Guinigi, 8 euro, 230 steps and no lift
trees.transport: In the middle of the old town, at Via Sant'Andrea and Via Guinigi
trees.story: Seven oaks grow forty-four metres above the street, in a brick box of earth on the roof of a medieval tower, and they are the emblem of the city. The Guinigi were Lucca's ruling family in the early fifteenth century, when Paolo Guinigi held the city as its lord, and a tower crowned with trees already appears in Giovanni Sercambi's illustrated chronicle from that period. So the idea is six hundred years old. The trees are not. Holm oaks in a container do not live like holm oaks in the ground, and the seven up there have been replaced more than once without anyone recording when, which is why this entry gives no age. What the box does is keep them small: an ordinary Quercus ilex reaches twenty metres and these are shrubs by comparison, dense, dark, evergreen, with the small hard leaves that let the species hold a Mediterranean summer. Getting there costs 8 euro and 230 steps up the inside of the tower. You come out under the canopy, with the roofs of Lucca below and the Apuan Alps behind, which is a better arrival than most trees on this site can offer.

trees.name: The Cedar of the Righteous at Villa Bottini
trees.age: undated, and no older than the 1840s
trees.access: Free, public garden of Villa Bottini, open during garden hours
trees.transport: Just inside Porta San Gervasio on Via Elisa, about 5 min walk from the botanical garden
trees.story: On 25 April 2021 this cedar was given a name. Lucca's Garden of the Righteous, in the grounds of Villa Bottini, dedicates trees to people who sheltered others during the war, and this one carries don Renzo Tambellini, an Oblate priest of the Holy Face who from the middle of 1943 turned his community's house into the hub of a network that hid Jews and partisans, and who was later given the gold medal for civil merit. Two more trees went to two more priests the same morning, an incense cedar for don Guido Staderini and a plane for don Sirio Niccolai. The tree itself is the largest registered trunk in the whole municipality: seven metres round and thirty metres tall, in the garden of a villa finished in 1581 for Bernardino Buonvisi, a silk merchant who built it to receive delegations rather than to live in. Nothing dates the cedar, though the species only reached European gardens from the Atlas mountains of Morocco and Algeria around 1840, which puts a hard ceiling on it. The garden is municipal and free, and it is 300 metres from the botanical garden gate.

trees.name: The Corsican Pine of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry, Orto Botanico di Lucca
trees.transport: Inside the city walls, Centro Storico; walking distance from Piazza Napoleone
trees.story:
The garden has two oldest trees and only one of them is famous. Lucca's Orto Botanico put its Cedar of Lebanon in the ground in 1822 and this Corsican pine in the same season, two years after Maria Luisa di Borbone founded the place as a teaching collection, which makes them joint founders. The cedar became the garden's symbol and its patriarch. The pine just grew: thirty and a half metres now, two metres eighty-two round the trunk.

Pinus nigra subsp. laricio is the Corsican and Calabrian form of the black pine, and it is the tall, straight one. It sends up a single clean stem with the branches in loose whorls, and it was cut for ships' masts for exactly that reason, under Genoese rule and then French. In a walled garden in Tuscany it has had no wind to fight and no neighbours to race, and it has gone straight up anyway, because that is what the tree does.

Two sources carry the 1822 date, the national monumental tree register and the local paper's 2024 survey of the thirty-six monumental trees in the comune, which is more than most of the trees on this page can claim. It is inside the garden, which charges admission, and it is a two-minute walk from the cedar, the redwood and the three-trunked ginkgo. Most visitors walk past it to photograph the cedar.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Via dell'Orto Botanico
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: Inside the city walls, Centro Storico; walking distance from Piazza Napoleone, just outside the botanical garden

best_time.label: May and June, when the flowers open up to thirty centimetres across and the street smells of lemon

trees.story:
Three metres twenty-three round the trunk and twenty-four metres tall, which is a great deal of magnolia. Magnolia grandiflora usually settles for half that in a European garden and does much of its growing sideways. This one stands on the street outside the botanical garden's wall, so unlike almost everything else on this walk it costs nothing and is never shut.

It appears on the national monumental tree register and nowhere else. No planting date, no plaque, no local article: one line in a register, and the tree. The garden a few metres away dates its own founding trees precisely, to 1820 and 1822, which makes the silence about a magnolia this size just outside its wall a small mystery. Inventing a year for it would not solve that.

The species comes from the American southeast, Florida up through the Carolinas, and reached European gardens in the eighteenth century, where it became the choice for anyone who wanted evergreen leaves the size of a hand. They are dark, stiff and polished on top and rust-brown and felted underneath, so the whole crown changes colour when wind gets into it.

Then in May and June it flowers, cream-white and up to thirty centimetres across, a few at a time over several weeks rather than all at once, and on a still evening the street smells of lemon.

trees.name: The Plane of Via del Fosso
trees.neighbourhood: Centro Storico, Via del Fosso canal street
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: Inside the city walls, Centro Storico; on the canal street between the Orto Botanico and Villa Bottini
trees.story:
Via del Fosso has a canal running down the middle of it, open to the sky, and this plane grows on the bank. That is most of the explanation for a trunk three metres sixty round and a crown thirty metres up. A London plane with permanent water at its roots and a straight open corridor of light above the channel has nothing to compete for.

The fosso is a working watercourse, not an ornament. It was cut to bring water into Lucca for mills and workshops, it runs down the eastern side of the walled city on the line of an older moat, which is what the name means, and it still runs. The street it makes is one of the quietest inside the walls and it is the natural route between the botanical garden at one end and Villa Bottini at the other, so this tree is on the walk whether or not you went looking for it.

The national monumental tree register lists it and gives the measurements. It does not give an age, and nothing else published names this individual tree. Planes are hard to read by eye in any case: put one somewhere it likes, as this one plainly is, and it will build a trunk several times faster than an oak on the same street would.

trees.name: The Nepal Camphor of Via Barsanti e Matteucci
trees.neighbourhood: San Marco, outside the city walls
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: San Marco district, north of the walls; roughly 900m walk from the Orto Botanico cluster
trees.story:
A Himalayan tree on a street named after an engine. Eugenio Barsanti and Felice Matteucci patented their internal combustion engine in 1854, working between Lucca and Florence, and the city gave them this road. The largest thing standing on it is a Cinnamomum glanduliferum from the forests of Nepal, northern India and southern China: three metres eighty-four round the trunk, twenty-four metres tall.

It is the bigger of the two in the city. The other grows inside the Orto Botanico, planted in 1888 and recorded as such. This one, out in San Marco north of the walls, has a girth a third larger and nothing behind it but a line in the national monumental tree register. No planting date, no owner, no article. That is the usual fate of a big tree on an ordinary street.

The leaves carry camphor oils, which is where both names come from; the species is a close relative of the true camphor tree and the wood was used the same way. It is evergreen, so February looks much like July, and the leaves have a pale, almost blue-grey underside that flickers when the wind turns them over.

It is a nine hundred metre walk from the botanical garden cluster, and it is outside the walls, which is the whole reason it is not better known.

trees.name: The Plane of Porta San Donato
trees.access: Free, always open. The tree stands on the public ramparts of Lucca's Renaissance walls (Passeggiata delle Mura), a pedestrian and cycle path that rings the whole old town with no gate or ticket.
trees.transport: On foot, about 1.2 km (15-20 minutes) west of the Orto Botanico cluster, reachable directly by walking the wall-top path from any of the city gates; no vehicle access onto the walls themselves.
trees.story:
Lucca's Renaissance walls are planted almost entirely as a single ring of trees, but the register singles out only three individuals along the whole circuit, and this plane, growing on the ramparts near Porta San Donato, is the thickest of the three: 4.88 metres round and 30 metres tall, the largest plane tree in the city by that measurement.

Porta San Donato itself dates to 1629, one of the six gates built when Lucca reinforced its walls against a siege that never came; the fortifications outlasted every threat they were built for and became, instead, the tree-lined promenade that rings the old town today. Nobody has dated the tree specifically, only the gate beside it.
