The wall-top path, the Passeggiata delle Mura, is public, paved and open around the clock, wide enough for the joggers and cyclists who use it as Lucca's ring road for people rather than cars. This plane stands about a kilometre and a half west of the Orto Botanico cluster, an anchor for the far side of a wall walk rather than an extension of it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress Twins of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico (the botanical garden charges a standard admission ticket); open during the garden's published hours.
trees.transport: Inside the Orto Botanico, on the same visit as the garden's other published trees (Cedar of Lebanon, Redwood, Three-Trunked Ginkgo, Corsican Pine).

best_time.label: late October and November, when the needles turn rust orange before they drop

trees.story:
Two bald cypresses stand fifteen metres apart at the pond in Lucca's botanical garden, buttressed at the base and throwing up the woody knees that let the species breathe in waterlogged ground, a trick it brought from the swamps of the American south. Both are registered as individually monumental, 3.15 and 2.80 metres round.

They are the only conifer in the garden that behaves like a deciduous tree, turning rust orange and dropping its needles each autumn, which in a collection built mostly around evergreens makes the pond the one spot in the Orto Botanico with a real November moment. Nobody has recorded when either tree was planted.

The garden charges standard admission and keeps published hours, unlike most of what stands on this page. Once inside, the cypresses sit a short walk from the cedar of Lebanon, redwood and three-trunked ginkgo already on this list, all reachable on one visit.

trees.name: The Balearic Box of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico (standard admission ticket); open during the garden's published hours.
trees.transport: Inside the Orto Botanico, a short walk from the bald cypresses by the pond and the garden's other published trees.
trees.story:
Box is usually a hedge plant, clipped into shapes barely taller than a person. This one is seven metres tall, a Balearic box growing to the size of an actual tree, which the species rarely does anywhere it is not native. Its natural range is the Balearic Islands and a sliver of the southwest Mediterranean coast; everywhere else it stays a shrub, including, almost everywhere, in this garden's own country.

The Orto Botanico's own account, not independently re-checked this pass, puts the planting at around 1880, which would make it roughly a century and a half old, modest in girth (88 cm) but old for how slowly box grows. Italy's monumental tree register designates it in its own right, a second signal beyond the measurements that this is not just an old hedge left to run wild.

It stands inside the garden's paid grounds, a short walk from the bald cypresses at the pond. If you know its planting date for certain, tell us.

trees.name: The Silver Lime and Fastigiate Yew of the Orto Botanico
trees.species: Silver Lime (Tilia tomentosa) and Fastigiate Yew (Taxus baccata var. fastigiata)
trees.age: the lime about 126 years, planted around 1900
trees.access: Paid entry to the Orto Botanico (standard admission ticket); open during the garden's published hours.
trees.transport: Inside the Orto Botanico, a short walk from the garden's other published trees.
trees.story:
The youngest tree the register protects in Lucca's botanical garden stands sixty metres from one of its slowest growing: a silver lime planted around 1900, its leaves silvery on the underside and turning up in wind, next to a fastigiate yew whose narrow, upright habit is not what makes it interesting. What makes it interesting is the girth. Yew adds wood at a crawl, and a columnar yew this thick, 2.60 metres round, has been doing it for a very long time even though nobody has put a number on how long.

The lime is easier to date, if only just: the garden's own account, not independently re-checked this pass, gives around 1900, putting it at roughly 126 years old and the youngest specimen the monumental register lists here. Its own girth, 3.60 metres, is already considerable for a tree that young, a sign of how much room and light the garden gives its plantings.

Neither tree carries much recorded history beyond its own measurements. They stand a short walk apart inside the Orto Botanico's paid grounds, on the same visit as the garden's older, better documented trees.

trees.name: The Heritage Oak of Grant Hall
trees.access: Free. Public university campus, open grounds, walkable any time the campus is open.
trees.transport: On the UNLV campus; nearest RTC bus stops serve Maryland Parkway, short walk in.
trees.story:
Nevada's champion live oak is a campus shade tree. Quercus virginiana belongs to the humid American South, the wide dark thing you see hung with Spanish moss; this one grows in the Mojave, on the Academic Mall at UNLV, and the Nevada Big Tree Register makes it the largest of its kind recorded in the state.

It is a Heritage oak, a cross bred for the height of one oak and the width of another, and the university's own arborists describe it in exactly those terms. The register measured it in 2015 at 46 inches around, 56 feet tall and 41 feet across. UNLV put it at roughly 60 feet in November 2025, which is a decade of growth rather than a disagreement between sources.

None of that makes it old, and this page does not pretend otherwise. Nobody has published a planting date, and girth alone will not date a hybrid for which no growth rate exists. If you know when it went in, tell us.

What it is instead is the front door of an accidental arboretum. A university in a desert planted a collection, watered it, and now holds state records for species from four continents, most of them within a fifteen minute walk of this oak.

The pin marks Grant Hall rather than the trunk, because neither source gives coordinates. Walk to the building and look for the widest crown on the mall.

trees.name: The Kissing Tree of Carlson Hill
trees.access: Free. Public university campus, open grounds, walkable any time the campus is open.
trees.transport: On the UNLV campus; nearest RTC bus stops serve Maryland Parkway, short walk in.
trees.story:
The state champion weeping mulberry has its own fan account on Instagram. Students at UNLV call it the kissing tree, they photograph it, they meet under it, and on Take Your Child to Work Day the children go inside it, because a weeping mulberry is essentially a tent: the branches come off the top of the trunk and hang to the ground on every side, leaving a hollow in the middle.

The Nevada Big Tree Register measured it in 2015 at 68 inches around, 18 feet tall and 31 feet across, the largest recorded Morus alba 'Pendula' in the state. In November 2025 the university described it at about 20 feet tall and 30 feet wide, still on the grassy hill outside the Carlson Education Building, which is how we know it is alive.

Its age is unknown. No planting date has been published, and a grafted weeping cultivar is not something a girth measurement can date honestly. If you know, tell us.

Start here if you are only walking part of the campus. Seven more state champions stand within a few minutes of it, but this is the one people actually use, which is a fair test of a tree. The pin marks the Carlson building rather than the trunk; the hill is right outside, and you will recognise the shape immediately.

trees.name: The Chir Pine of the Geoscience Building
trees.access: Free. Public university campus, open grounds, walkable any time the campus is open.
trees.transport: On the UNLV campus; nearest RTC bus stops serve Maryland Parkway, short walk in.
trees.story:
A Himalayan pine is the largest of its species in Nevada, and it happens to stand outside the geoscience building. Pinus roxburghii grows on the dry outer foothills of the Himalaya, from Pakistan across to Bhutan, in country that takes a monsoon and then goes months with nothing. That is exactly the trick required in southern Nevada, which is why it is planted across the Southwest and why this one reaches 52 feet in the Mojave.

The Nevada Big Tree Register recorded it in 2015 at 48 inches around, 52 feet tall and 25 feet across, at the Lilly Fong Geoscience Building on the UNLV campus. The university named the same tree at the same height in November 2025, which is the evidence that it is still standing.

The needles give it away. They come in threes, hang in loose tassels and can reach a foot long, so the whole tree looks softer and shaggier than the short-needled pines used in landscaping around it. Stand under it in a wind and it sounds different too.

Neither source gives a planting date, so no age is claimed here. Nobody in the state has a bigger one on record, which is a different kind of distinction and the only one we can back.

The pin is the building rather than the trunk; the tree is the obvious one out front.

trees.name: The Sissoo of Barrick Museum
trees.access: Free. Public university campus, open grounds (a parking lot tree, but freely walkable), walkable any time the campus is open.
trees.transport: On the UNLV campus; nearest RTC bus stops serve Maryland Parkway, short walk in.
trees.story:
The largest Indian rosewood in Nevada shades a museum car park. Dalbergia sissoo is the tree that furniture and instrument makers in northern India have cut for centuries, and it is uncommon in Las Vegas for a practical reason: it grows fast and takes almost anything, which sounds ideal until a city has to maintain a street full of them, so many municipalities in the valley leave it off the planting list. This one was left alone in the Barrick Museum lot at UNLV and became the state champion.

The Nevada Big Tree Register measured it in 2015 at 58 inches around, 48 feet tall and 29 feet across. The university named the same tree in November 2025 and made the point that matters on an asphalt lot in a desert city, which is that it throws real shade over parked cars in July.

There is no age for it. Neither source gives a planting date, and sissoo grows quickly enough that a guess from girth would flatter it badly. If a campus grounds record has the year, we will take it.

This is the least scenic setting on the list and one of the better arguments in it. Nobody designed this tree into a landscape. It went into a car park, nobody removed it, and the state now has no larger example of its species.

The pin marks the parking lot, not the trunk.

trees.name: The Desert Willow of the Research Administration Building
trees.access: Free. Public university campus, open grounds, walkable any time the campus is open.
trees.transport: On the UNLV campus; nearest RTC bus stops serve Maryland Parkway, short walk in.

best_time.label: late spring into high summer, when it carries pink trumpet flowers through the heat

trees.story:
Everything else on this campus was brought here. The desert willow was already living in this landscape when the city arrived. Chilopsis linearis grows wild in the washes out at Red Rock Canyon, half an hour west, where flash floods do the pruning; the state champion is this one at UNLV, pruned instead by grounds staff into something taller and tidier than any wild plant gets.

The Nevada Big Tree Register measured it in 2015 at 60 inches around, 42 feet tall and 34 feet across, by the Research Administration Building. The university named the same 42 feet in November 2025.

It is not a willow. The long narrow leaves are the reason for the name, but it sits with catalpas and jacarandas, and it flowers like them: pink trumpets in loose clusters from late spring through the worst of the summer heat, worked over by hummingbirds. That is the reason to time a visit.

Two honest notes. Its age is not recorded anywhere we could find and cannot be derived. And this pin is the roughest on the page: we could not place the Research Administration Building on a current campus map, so the coordinates fall on the campus generally rather than on a building. Ask at a campus desk, or send us the spot and we will fix it.

trees.name: The Coolibah Eucalyptus of Winchester Park
trees.access: Free. Clark County-run public park, open during park hours.
trees.transport: Winchester Park, near Desert Inn Road and McLeod Drive, central Las Vegas valley; RTC bus routes serve Desert Inn Road.
trees.story:
This is the tree from Waltzing Matilda, growing beside a county cultural centre in Las Vegas. Eucalyptus microtheca is the coolibah of inland Australia, the shade over dry riverbeds and flood plains a long way from anywhere, and the largest one recorded in Nevada stands in Winchester Park off Desert Inn Road.

The Nevada Big Tree Register measured it in 2015: 80 inches around, 70 feet tall, 47 feet across. Two more state champions grow in the same park, which is a strange concentration for a small county park and the reason to come out here rather than only walking the university campus.

Now the part we cannot dress up. Those measurements are a decade old. The most recent independent mention we can find is a 2016 newspaper piece reporting three champions at this park without naming their species. And a windstorm in July 2025 brought down mature trees across the valley. We have no evidence this one was among them and no evidence it was not, so it is on the map with that said out loud, because a reader standing in the park can settle in ten seconds what we cannot settle from a desk.

The three Winchester trees share a single pin at the park, not at any trunk. Go in and look for the eucalyptus with the broad low crown. Then tell us what you found.

trees.name: The Lemon Eucalyptus of Winchester Park
trees.access: Free. Clark County-run public park, open during park hours.
trees.transport: Winchester Park, near Desert Inn Road and McLeod Drive, central Las Vegas valley; RTC bus routes serve Desert Inn Road.
trees.story:
Crush a leaf of this one and your hands smell of citronella for the rest of the afternoon. The lemon-scented gum of Queensland, listed by the state register as Eucalyptus citriodora and by most botanists now as Corymbia citriodora, is the biggest tree on this whole Las Vegas list by every figure that was taken: 92 inches around, 84 feet tall and 64 feet across when the Nevada Big Tree Register recorded it in 2015.

Eighty-four feet is a serious tree in any city. In a valley where almost all the shade is engineered, a smooth pale trunk going up that far behind Desert Inn Road is not what anyone expects from a county park.

The same caution applies as to its two neighbours. The figures are eleven years old, the last independent reference we have found is a 2016 article counting three champions at this park without naming them, and the July 2025 windstorm cost the valley a lot of mature trees. We publish it because it should be there and because one local visit answers the question we cannot.

No age is recorded. Eucalypts grow fast enough that a guess from girth would be worse than an empty field, so the field stays empty. The pin is the park, shared with the coolibah and the xylosma.

trees.name: The Shiny Xylosma of Winchester Park
trees.access: Free. Clark County-run public park, open during park hours.
trees.transport: Winchester Park, near Desert Inn Road and McLeod Drive, central Las Vegas valley; RTC bus routes serve Desert Inn Road.
trees.story:
Nevada's champion xylosma is a hedge nobody cut. Xylosma congestum is sold all over the Southwest as a clipped evergreen screen, kept at chest height along car parks and front walls for decades at a time. Left alone it becomes a small tree, and the largest one on record in this state is 24 feet tall on a 55-inch trunk, in Winchester Park.

That is the quiet appeal of a big-tree register. Champions are recorded species by species, so the list ends up documenting what ordinary landscaping plants do when somebody forgets to prune them. A 24-foot xylosma is a stranger sight than a 70-foot eucalyptus, and there is one of each in this park.

The caveats are the same as for its two neighbours. The measurements are the register's 2015 figures, the most recent independent reference we found is a 2016 article naming three champions here without listing their species, and a windstorm in July 2025 took down mature trees across the Las Vegas valley. Nobody has told us this one is gone. Nobody has confirmed it is standing either.

No age is recorded for it. The pin is the park rather than the tree, shared with the other two. If you go out and find it, or find a gap where it was, tell us and the page changes that day.

trees.name: The Pin de Bunge, or Pin de Napoléon
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)
trees.story: This pine's bark peels in patches of grey, green and cream as it ages, a trait so distinctive that the species barely needs its Latin name to identify it. Pinus bungeana is native to central China, first documented for Western science by the Russian botanist Alexander von Bunge in 1831 at a temple garden in Beijing, and this specimen was probably planted in 1856, the year construction began on the Parc de la Tête d'Or itself, making it one of the park's original plantings rather than a later addition. The International Dendrology Society's own reference site names it directly as the oldest cultivated Pinus bungeana in Europe, calling it a national treasure of the Lyon botanical garden, a specific claim rather than a vague superlative, and one this project treats as credible given the source. Locally it carries the nickname Pin de Napoléon, though no source connects the name to any specific historical event rather than general period association, so that link is not claimed here as fact. Nearly 170 years on, its trunk has developed the pale, almost white patchwork bark that only develops with real age, the single feature that makes this pine worth seeking out among the arboretum's thousands of other specimens.

trees.name: The Osage Orange of the Tête d'Or
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)
trees.story: This tree's American ancestors were weapons before they were shade. Maclura pomifera is named for the Osage nation of the central United States, who prized its wood, dense, springy and rot-resistant, for war bows and arrows above almost any other timber available to them. The species reached Europe in 1823, and French growers in the south of the country initially planted it not for its odd, wrinkled, inedible fruit but as living fencing and, briefly, as a food source for silkworms before mulberry proved more practical. This specimen in the Tête d'Or's arboretum has grown into something closer to a specimen tree than a hedge: a dendrologist's survey put its girth at 3.70 metres a metre above the ground, with a trunk described as ridged and hollowed over some two metres of its height, reasonably read as the marks of a genuinely old, over-a-century specimen rather than a fast-growing recent planting. Osage orange also spreads by layering, sending down roots wherever a low branch touches soil, so what looks like one tree in a dense stand may in places be a single genetic individual repeating itself.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of the Tête d'Or
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)

best_time.label: November, when its needles turn copper and drop, the one month it truly looks like the Louisiana wetlands it comes from

trees.story: This tree grows as though it remembers the Louisiana wetlands its species comes from, even landlocked in a Lyon park more than eight thousand kilometres away. Taxodium distichum is one of the few conifers that sheds its needles every autumn, and where it grows in standing water, it sends up woody knees, called pneumatophores, that poke above the surface to bring oxygen to submerged roots, a trait this specimen displays even without the flooded ground its Gulf Coast relatives depend on. A dendrological survey recorded its girth at 5.45 metres a metre above ground and its height at just over 30 metres, among the largest measured trees anywhere in the park's arboretum, with a deeply fluted, buttressed trunk in excellent health. No source gives it a specific planting date, so its age is estimated here from the park's own founding in the 1850s rather than documented directly, but a tree of this size, in a species not known for exceptionally fast growth, is a serious candidate for one of the arboretum's oldest original plantings.

trees.name: The Giant Chestnut of Parc de la Garde
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Bus to Parc de la Garde stop, or 15 min walk from Gorge de Loup station

best_time.label: May, when its candle-shaped flower spikes cover the canopy

trees.story: Most visitors to this park come for the wildness rather than any single tree, but the chestnut at its centre is the reason locals bother naming the place at all. Parc de la Garde keeps a half-forested character unusual for a Lyon city park: its lower half is genuinely wooded, criss-crossed by informal paths, and holds a small stone bridge that once carried the old Vaugneray tramway line through the woods before the route was abandoned. The horse chestnut standing among these trees has been formally recognised with France's national Arbre Remarquable label, described locally simply as an enormous trunk carrying multiple large branches, a scale that marks it out even among the park's other mature trees. No source gives the tree an individual age or measured girth beyond that general description, so any figure here is an estimate rather than a documented record. The label itself, rather than any dramatic history, is what distinguishes this specimen from the thousands of ordinary horse chestnuts planted across French parks in the 19th and 20th centuries.

trees.name: The Japanese Pagoda Tree of Parc de Gerland
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Stade de Gerland tram stop (T1)

best_time.label: August, when it flowers later than almost anything else still blooming in the park

trees.story: Gerland is one of Lyon's newer large parks by name, built out on former industrial and marshland south of the city centre and reworked repeatedly through the 20th century, so a tree old enough to carry a national remarkable-tree label stands out by contrast with almost everything else growing around it. In 2024 the A.R.B.R.E.S. association added this Japanese pagoda tree to its national list, formally measuring it at 16 metres tall with an 18 metre crown spread and a trunk 302 centimetres around at chest height, figures precise enough to track any future growth or decline against. Despite the common name, the species is native to China rather than Japan, introduced to Europe in the 18th century and prized since for flowering late in summer when few other large trees are still blooming, a trait that makes it valuable to bees and other pollinators after the main spring flush has finished. No individual planting date is documented, so the tree's age is estimated here from its measured size rather than a verified record, but the label recognition alone marks it as one of the more significant individual trees in a 40 hectare park built mainly for sport and recreation rather than horticulture.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Parc de la Chapelle
trees.age: locally claimed at 500 years, botanically disputed
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Gorge de Loup station
trees.story: This cedar is effectively the reason the park around it exists in its current shape: much of Parc de la Chapelle is built around a single enormous specimen, with the site's open lawn and paths arranged to give the tree room rather than the other way around. Measured at 28 metres tall with a 32 metre crown spread and a trunk 6.35 metres around, it received France's national Arbre Remarquable label on 16 October 2024, and city sources describe it as multi-centenary, some putting a figure of around 500 years on it directly. That number sits awkwardly against the species' own history: Cedrus atlantica, native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, was not introduced into French cultivation until the 1840s, which would make a genuinely 500-year-old specimen growing in a Lyon park difficult to reconcile with any documented planting. The claim is stated here as what it is, a locally repeated figure rather than a settled fact, alongside the tree's real, independently confirmed scale and its 2024 national label. Whatever its true age, it is locally described as possibly the largest Atlas cedar in Lyon, and its branches shelter birds and squirrels in a quiet residential corner of the 9th arrondissement.

trees.name: The Oak Collection of Parc de la Cerisaie
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Croix-Rousse metro station (Line C)
trees.story: This park takes its name from a cherry orchard that no longer exists, replaced just before the First World War by a very different planting scheme. Landscape architect René-Edouard André, son of the more famous Édouard André whose formal garden style shaped parks across France and beyond, designed Parc de la Cerisaie in 1913 on the Croix-Rousse hillside, centring the roughly 1,200-tree planting on a significant oak collection alongside birches, yews and beeches. That timing puts the park's founding trees at just over a century old today, planted the year before the war that would go on to reshape the neighbourhood and the city around them. No individual tree in the collection carries a separately documented age or measurement, so the range given here describes the park's own founding date rather than any single named specimen, consistent with how this project treats other undated group plantings. What survives is less a single monumental tree than a coherent, deliberately designed early 20th century woodland, unusually intact for a century-old civic planting scheme.

trees.name: The Garden Trees of Jardin des Chartreux
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 15 min walk (uphill) from Vaise or Croix-Rousse metro stations
trees.story: This garden sits on the steep slope between the Croix-Rousse plateau and the Saône, on ground once attached to a Carthusian monastery that gave the neighbourhood its name and that disappeared, like most French religious houses of its kind, during the Revolution. What remains today is a public garden of broad lawns and mature trees, magnolia, cedar and horse chestnut among the species named in descriptions of the site, arranged to take advantage of a genuinely striking view over the Saône quays and the hills of Fourvière on the opposite bank. No individual tree here has a documented planting date or measurement, and no single specimen is singled out by name the way the labelled trees elsewhere on this list are, so this entry describes the garden's mature tree cover as a group rather than claiming one named champion. The steep terrain that makes the view worthwhile also keeps the garden genuinely quiet, a local rather than a tourist destination, reached by a climb up from the river that most visitors to Lyon never make.

trees.name: The Cappadocian Maple of the Tête d'Or
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)

best_time.label: October into November, when its leaves turn a rich butter yellow

trees.story: This maple comes from a stretch of the world most visitors to a French municipal park have never had reason to think about: the mountain forests running from the Caucasus through northern Iran and on toward the Himalayas, where Acer cappadocicum grows wild among beech and oak. Lyon's botanical garden, folded into the Tête d'Or since 1857, was built to hold exactly this kind of geographic range, species chosen for scientific and educational value as much as for looks. A dendrological survey of the park recorded this specimen's girth at 3.20 metres a metre above ground and its height at 26 metres, respectable rather than record-breaking figures next to the arboretum's largest specimens, but enough to mark it as a genuinely mature, long-established tree rather than a recent planting. No individual planting date is documented, so its age is estimated here from its measured size and the arboretum's own founding period rather than a verified record. In autumn its leaves turn a clean, even yellow, a display Cappadocian maples are specifically valued for in cultivation, though no source dates this specimen's colour peak precisely enough to state a reliable calendar window here.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Rue Viret
trees.neighbourhood: Villeurbanne (Les Poulettes, adjoining Gratte-Ciel), roughly 1.4 km east of Parc de la Tete d'Or
trees.access: Free, public street corner in a residential neighbourhood, no restriction
trees.transport: Charpennes Charles Hernu metro station (Line A/B), about 7 min walk; Le Tonkin tram stop about 4 min walk

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Villeurbanne's official tree register calls this pedunculate oak rare, and it means it plainly: street plantings here run to plane and lime, so a full-grown Quercus robur on a residential corner stands out as an exception the city itself has flagged. The 2017 survey that logged it recorded good health and real size and nothing else, no planting date, no measured age, just a note that this one was worth watching. An investigative piece on Lyon's remarkable trees found it again in 2025, still standing at the same corner of Rue Viret and Rue Francis de Pressense, eight years on from that first record. It grows a fifteen minute walk from the Art Deco tower blocks of Gratte-Ciel, Villeurbanne's landmark 1930s housing project, in the quieter grid of streets just west of it. Nobody has measured its trunk or dated its rings, so this page will not guess a number rather than invent one. What two independent records agree on is simpler: an oak grown too large and too old to belong on an ordinary street, still there, still worth the detour from the park at the Tete d'Or.

trees.name: The Anne Frank Chestnut
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all times
trees.transport: Short walk from Place Guichard - Bourse du Travail metro station (Line B), same street (rue Moncey)

best_time.label: May, when white candles stand upright over the whole crown

trees.story:
This chestnut is not old. It is barely twelve, planted at the centre of Place Marc-Aron in December 2014 to replace a statue called Renaissance that the square's renovation had removed. What makes it worth a stop is where it comes from: it is a cutting from the horse chestnut Anne Frank could see through the attic window of her hiding place in Amsterdam, the tree she described in her diary as one of the only things connecting her to the outside world.

That original tree fell in a storm on 23 August 2010. Before it went, the Anne Frank Foundation had already taken roughly 150 cuttings and sent saplings to institutions and public spaces worldwide, Washington DC, Jerusalem and Paris among them, so the tree from the diary kept growing in dozens of places after the original one did not. Lyon's arrived on rue Moncey in a public ceremony and now stands in a small square two minutes' walk from Place Guichard metro station, marked by nothing more than its own planting.

It will not be Lyon's oldest or largest tree for a very long time, maybe not ever. It is here because of what it descends from rather than what it has personally witnessed, the one entry on this list whose whole story predates its own roots.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Place Antoine-Rivoire
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all times
trees.transport: About 5 min walk from Cordeliers metro station (Line A)
trees.story:
Lyon's street-tree database holds over 100,000 records, and barely more than half of them carry a planting date at all. Of the ones that do, this plane is the oldest: put in the ground in 1894, at the centre of a square barely bigger than a tennis court in the heart of the Presqu'ile. A city forestry official is on record saying plainly that none of Lyon's plane trees reach the three or four centuries some regional specimens do, so call this the oldest dated tree in the city's records rather than its oldest tree outright.

The square itself has buried more history than its tree has years. From the 16th century until the French Revolution it was the parish cemetery of Saint-Nizier, the church that still stands two streets over. The Revolution cleared the cemetery, and the square that replaced it was called Place de la Fromagerie until 1934, when it was renamed for Antoine Rivoire, a founder of Lyon's trade fair and tourism board.

The plane tree stands alone at the centre of it now, at the junction of four small streets, on ground that spent three centuries as a burial ground before anyone planted anything there at all.

trees.name: The Cedar of Square Gabrielle Dupond-Ebrard
trees.access: Free, public municipal square, open street-level access, no gate or entry restriction found.
trees.transport: Point du Jour neighbourhood, Lyon 5th arrondissement; served by TCL buses in the area.

best_time.label: autumn, when upright barrel cones sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story:
The square's namesake hid people from the Gestapo two streets from here. Gabrielle Dupond-Ebrard lived at 13 avenue du Point du Jour until 1985, working with the Combat resistance network under Pierre Guillain de Benouville, and her house served as a secretariat and shelter for refugees during the German occupation. Lyon later named this small square after her, and the cedar growing in it now outranks almost everything else about the place: a local streets guide calls it simply the square's main feature.

Nobody has measured it. The city's own register of remarkable trees lists it only as a very large specimen, with no planting year and no girth on file, unusual for a species normally easy to date from its own architecture. Cedar of Lebanon grows a tiered, almost horizontal branch structure as it ages, each level wider than the one above it, so the size the register does record is at least visible rather than guessed.

The square sits about 450 metres from the giant chestnut of Parc de la Garde, already on this list, so the two make an easy pair on the same walk through Point du Jour. If you know how old this cedar is, or can get a tape around the trunk, tell us.

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of Molenweg
trees.access: On private farmland, visible from the public access road
trees.transport: About 4km northeast of Maastricht centre, in Amby; reachable by bus or a 15-minute bike ride

best_time.label: October, when the spiny husks split and the nuts fall

trees.story: Nobody can say exactly when this tree was planted, and the people who study it are refreshingly honest about that. Standing beside the entrance gate of the Prickaerts family farm in Amby, this sweet chestnut has a trunk 25 metres tall and, as of a 2021 measurement, just over six metres around, up from 5.25 metres when first recorded in 1986. The national tree register estimates it was planted between 1750 and 1800; a 2022 assessment by Monumental Trees suggested 1800, plus or minus 40 years. A persistent local story credits Russian Cossack troops with planting it during the 1814 blockade of Maastricht, but researchers who looked into Cossack military behaviour during that campaign found the tale, in their own words, highly unrealistic, and no supporting evidence has ever surfaced. Only a dendrochronological core sample would settle the question with any precision, and none had been taken as of the most recent published research, part of an ongoing joint study between the Bomenstichting and Wageningen University sampling several of Maastricht's oldest trees. Until that happens, this chestnut carries its age the same way it carries its twisted, weather-beaten trunk: honestly, and without pretending to a certainty nobody has actually earned.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoias of Tongerseweg
trees.access: Free, cemetery open to visitors during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: 15-20 minute walk or short bus ride from Maastricht centre
trees.story: Some of the honour squares in Maastricht's oldest surviving cemetery were planted not with the usual yews or cypresses but with giant sequoias, a species native to a single mountain range in California and almost never found in a 19th-century Dutch burial ground. The cemetery itself has taken Maastricht's dead since 1812, making it one of the oldest municipal cemeteries in the Netherlands, and its brick chapel and the towering sequoias are what most visitors remember. The largest measures 6.85 metres around and 36.6 metres tall, roughly 150 years old, among the thickest specimens of its kind recorded anywhere in the country, though no longer the tallest: other Dutch sequoias have since overtaken it in height while it kept adding girth instead. Planting a species built to eventually reach 90 metres and outlive the Roman Empire in a graveyard designed for individual human memory is its own quiet statement, whether or not the 19th-century planners intended it that way. The cemetery, now a national heritage monument holding more than a thousand trees in total, remains open to visitors during normal hours, sequoias included.

trees.name: The 1700 Oaks of Cannerbos
trees.access: Free, open public woodland at any time
trees.transport: 20-25 minute bus ride from Maastricht centre, or a longer bike ride

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: A baron's coat of arms is the reason this forest has straight lines running through it at all. Around 1700, Baron Daniel Wolfgang van Dopff, who had just built Kasteel Neercanne into the hillside beside it, laid out the slope forest above his new estate as a sterrenbos, a half-star pattern of radiating paths that echoed the half-star on his own family crest, complete with a belvedere, a tea house and a temple of love at the centre where the paths converged. Oaks, elms, beeches and alders went into the ground as part of that original planting scheme. The formal star layout did not survive the 19th century, when neglect let the forest grow back into something closer to ordinary woodland, but a number of oaks along and around the forest's edge are still standing from that first planting, roughly 300 years old today, the clearest physical trace left of Van Dopff's geometric ambition. Kasteel Neercanne itself, built into an old marl quarry, still stands beside the forest and today operates as a restaurant and hotel, while the wooded slope above it remains open, publicly accessible walking terrain.

trees.name: The Three Oldest Beeches of Stadspark
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Maastricht centre

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.story: Stadspark's own marked walking route names these three beeches, standing together partway along the Jeker, as the oldest trees in a park that otherwise holds more than 1,400 of them. At around 160 years, they date to the park's main 19th-century expansion rather than to its far older origins: Stadspark traces its beginnings to a linden planting in 1648 and a formal walking path laid out from 1706, but none of those 17th and early 18th-century originals are known to have survived into the present, so these beeches, planted as the various sub-parks along the Jeker were laid out through the 1800s, are as far back as anyone can point with confidence today. The park itself is one of the oldest continuous city parks in the Netherlands, a 10-hectare green belt running along the Jeker and the old fortification walls, now home to roughly 800 trees across some 160 species from across the world, including a ginkgo, a tulip tree, silver limes and an American yellowwood elsewhere on the same route. The three beeches remain the route's own answer to the obvious question a visitor would ask first: which of all this is the oldest.

trees.name: The Tallest Plane Tree in the Netherlands
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Maastricht centre
trees.story: Three plane trees grow in a row beside Van Heylerhofflaan on Stadspark's edge, planted together around 1870, and one of the three has since measured 39 metres tall, the tallest plane tree ever recorded in the Netherlands. Its two companions are barely shorter, at 37.5 and 36.5 metres, which makes the whole trio a small, accidental grove of national height records rather than a single freak specimen. None of the three is the thickest tree in Stadspark, a title that belongs to a separate, unrelated plane elsewhere in the park, a reminder that height and girth are different competitions and a tree can win one without the other. Planted during the same 19th-century wave of park-building that gave Stadspark most of its current character, this row has had roughly a century and a half of steady, undisturbed growth along a riverside strip of ground with nothing overhead to compete with for light, which is likely the plainest explanation for why it, rather than an older or more storied plane elsewhere in the country, holds the record today.

trees.name: The Juliana Birth Linden
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Maastricht; about a 10 minute walk from Maastricht station
trees.story:
This lime was planted on Keizer Karelplein to mark the birth of Princess Juliana in April 1909, the future queen who would go on to reign over the Netherlands for 32 years, and the tree still carries a small royal fence around its base. What that fence does not carry is any mention of Juliana at all: the register notes, with some evident amusement, that the ironwork skips the commemoration entirely and instead repeats a single instruction six times over, no bicycles.

The tree stands at Keizer Karelplein, one of three squares that ring the Basilica of Saint Servaas, Maastricht's oldest surviving church and the burial place of the city's first bishop. Juliana herself never had any particular connection to Maastricht beyond the timing of her birth, which was enough in 1909 for a municipality to plant a tree and forget, or simply never get around to, actually saying why. It stands in the open square today, free to see, a two minute walk from a second monumental linden on the neighbouring Vrijthof.

trees.name: The Linden of Vrijthof
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Maastricht; about a 10 minute walk from Maastricht station
trees.story:
Vrijthof takes its name from the churchyard it once was, the free forecourt of the Basilica of Saint Servaas that doubled as a burial ground through the Middle Ages, before it became the wide public square that now hosts Maastricht's Christmas market and biggest outdoor terraces. Archaeological digs beneath the paving have turned up Roman infrastructure and early medieval graves, so the square's actual history runs back roughly two thousand years even though almost nothing visible on it does.

This common lime, dated by the register to around 1880 to 1890, is one of the square's more recent arrivals by that measure, standing beside what was once the rijkswacht building at the square's edge. Common lime is itself a hybrid, a natural cross between the small-leaved and large-leaved lime that was the default civic tree across Dutch and Belgian cities for centuries. It grows in the open square, free, a two minute walk from a second commemorative linden on the neighbouring Keizer Karelplein, both sharing the same historic church complex without either predating it by more than a fraction.

trees.name: The Black Walnuts of Nolenspark
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Maastricht centre
trees.story:
Maastricht's Stadspark grew westward in 1886, absorbing the ground that became Monseigneur Nolenspark and Henri Hermanspark, under the design of Lievin Rosseels, son of the Leuven landscape architect Egidius Rosseels who had laid out the park's earlier southward expansion in the 1860s. This group of black walnuts, an American species grown here for its wood and its nuts rather than any native pedigree, most likely went into the ground during that same 1886 westward push, though no record fixes the planting to a specific year.

The walnuts share the park with a run of other trees from the same expansion, weeping silver limes along the water, a pair of tulip trees, and the row of planes further along Van Heylerhofflaan that includes the tallest recorded plane in the Netherlands, all part of one coordinated late-19th-century planting scheme rather than separate additions over time. They stand in the open park, free, on ground that was still farmland or open country before Rosseels arrived to make it a park.

trees.name: The Weeping Silver Limes of Haet ende Nijt
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Maastricht centre
trees.story:
Haet ende Nijt, Hate and Envy, is the pointedly named moated monument at the heart of Stadspark's western reach, and when Lievin Rosseels redesigned this stretch of the park in 1886 he deliberately removed the five-sided earthen bank that had partly enclosed it, so that the monument would sit fully surrounded by water and read more clearly from the paths around it. This group of weeping silver limes grows along that same bank, planted a little earlier, the register dates them to the 1860s, during the park's first southward expansion rather than the later westward one.

Weeping silver lime is a cultivated, downward-branching form of the ordinary silver lime, its leaves silvery on the underside and prone to catching wind in a way that makes the whole canopy shimmer, a trait 19th-century park designers prized enough to plant it beside water on purpose. The trees stand in the open along the bank, free, one stop among several from the same era, the black walnuts and tulip trees a short walk further into the same park.

trees.name: The Tulip Trees of Nolenspark
trees.access: Free, open public park at any time
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Maastricht centre

best_time.label: June, when the tulip-shaped flowers open high in the canopy

trees.story:
These two tulip trees likely went into Monseigneur Nolenspark during the same 1886 westward expansion of Maastricht's Stadspark that brought in the park's black walnuts and its weeping silver limes along the Haet ende Nijt bank, all under Lievin Rosseels' design. Nobody recorded the exact planting year for this pair specifically, so the register places them in the same general period as the rest of the expansion rather than on a dated line of its own.

Tulip tree is not related to the tulip at all, named only for flowers shaped like the bulb, and it is one of the tallest-growing hardwoods in eastern North America, capable of well over 50 metres in its native range even if Dutch specimens rarely approach that. Its leaves have a distinctive squared-off tip, unlike almost any other tree grown in Europe, which makes it one of the easiest species in this park to identify at a glance even without a label. The pair stands in the open near Van Heylerhofflaan, free, close enough to Stadspark's record-holding plane row and the park's other 1880s plantings to make one stop worth several.

trees.name: The Ahuehuete of the Parterre
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Retiro (Metro L2) or Puerta de Alcala, 5 min walk
trees.story: This tree carries two stories about its own birth that cannot both be true. The popular version, repeated in guidebooks and on the sign at its base, says it was planted in 1633 when the Count-Duke of Olivares opened the grounds that became Retiro Park, which would make it nearly 400 years old and Madrid's unrivalled oldest tree. Madrid's own municipal arborists are skeptical: the Parterre garden around it was completely replanted in 1714, and some specialists place the tree's actual origin after 1814, closer to two centuries old rather than four. Called Ahuehuete, from the Nahuatl for old man of the water, or simply El Abuelo, the grandfather, it is a Montezuma cypress, a species native to Mexican wetlands where individual specimens are known to live for millennia and reach trunk diameters wider than a house. In arid, landlocked Madrid it has thrived regardless of which age is correct, its buttressed trunk and feathery foliage looking more at home beside a Mexican river than beside a formal Spanish parterre.

photo.attribution: UAM Biblioteca y Archivo, Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Crystal Palace
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Ibiza (Metro L9) or Retiro (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.story: This cedar stands directly in front of the pond at the Palacio de Cristal, a 19th century glass and iron pavilion built in 1887 to exhibit plants and animals brought back from the Philippines, and it has spent most of the pavilion's history as part of the same postcard view: the glass palace reflected in the water, framed by the cedar's dark, tiered branches. Deodar cedars come from the western Himalayas, where the name deodar derives from a Sanskrit phrase meaning timber of the gods, and the species reached European ornamental gardens in the early 19th century as one of many exotic conifers collectors raced to introduce. Madrid's climate, hot and dry in summer rather than the Himalayan cedar's native monsoon-fed mountains, has suited this specimen well enough that it now ranks among Retiro's six officially singular trees, protected under the same regional catalogue as its more famous neighbour, the disputed-age Ahuehuete a short walk away.

trees.name: The Three-Trunked Yew of the Velazquez Palace
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Ibiza (Metro L9), 10 min walk

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Rather than one trunk, this yew splits into three, each thick enough to measure separately: 142, 120 and 140 centimetres around, fused into a single crown 18 metres wide standing beside the eastern wall of the Palacio de Velazquez, a red-brick exhibition hall built in 1883. European yews are famously slow growing and long lived, capable of reaching ages in the thousands of years in the right conditions, and famously toxic in almost every part except the flesh around the seed, a combination that has made the species a fixture of European churchyards for centuries, planted as much for its poison as its evergreen symbolism. At only 12 metres tall despite its age, this specimen shows the yew's characteristic patience: slow vertical growth traded for density and longevity. A wooden fence now rings the tree for its protection, a modest concession for one of only six trees in the whole of Retiro Park to hold official singular tree status from the Community of Madrid.

trees.name: The Bald Cypresses of the Crystal Palace Pond
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Ibiza (Metro L9) or Retiro (Metro L2), 8 min walk

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn copper and drop, doubled in the pond the trees grow from

trees.story: Several bald cypresses grow directly out of the pond in front of the Palacio de Cristal, their trunks and lower roots permanently submerged, a planting scheme that only works because this particular conifer, unlike almost every other cone-bearing tree, tolerates and even prefers standing water. Bald cypresses develop distinctive above-water root growths called pneumatophores, sometimes called cypress knees, that let the roots breathe oxygen the flooded soil cannot supply, an adaptation evolved in the swamps of the southeastern United States rather than anywhere near Madrid. Planted around 1918, roughly three decades after the glass pavilion itself went up in 1887, the grove has grown into one of the more unusual sights in a park otherwise dominated by conventional planting: full-grown conifers standing calf-deep in a reflecting pool, doubling their own image in the water they grow from. One specimen among the group carries the Community of Madrid's singular tree designation, protecting a planting choice that was, by the standards of 1918 Spanish gardening, a genuine experiment.

trees.name: The Cypress of the Royal Botanic Garden
trees.access: Paid entry to the Royal Botanic Garden
trees.transport: Atocha (Metro L1) or Banco de Espana (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.story: This cypress has stood on the Plano de la Flor terrace since before the Royal Botanic Garden moved to its current site. King Carlos III relocated the garden here in 1781, transplanting an existing scientific collection to sit beside his new Prado promenade, and this cypress, already growing or planted around that time, has outlasted every institutional change since: French occupation during the Peninsular War, a 19th century closure and near-abandonment, and a 20th century restoration that returned the garden to something close to its original Enlightenment-era design. At 32 metres it is both the oldest and the tallest tree in a garden that exists specifically to hold record specimens, and its trunk, a metre and a half across, has grown thick enough that the tree is now folded into the Paisaje de la Luz, Landscape of Light, the cultural corridor linking the Prado, the botanic garden and the Retiro that UNESCO named a World Heritage Site in 2021.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of the Botanic Garden
trees.access: Paid entry to the Royal Botanic Garden
trees.transport: Atocha (Metro L1) or Banco de Espana (Metro L2), 8 min walk

best_time.label: September to October: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: Nobody can agree how tall this tree is. It reaches over 30 metres in the garden's north zone along the Paseo de Mutis, and garden staff and visiting botanists put the exact figure several metres apart depending on the method, which is the ordinary fate of a tree measured from the ground by eye rather than climbed with a tape. The species itself, Zelkova carpinifolia, comes from mountain forests spanning Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkey and Iran, and only reached European gardens in the 18th century, part of the same wave of scientific plant collecting that filled Madrid's garden with foreign specimens under royal sponsorship. It is a relative of the elms without being one, which is how it has come through a century of Dutch elm disease that emptied streets across Europe of the real thing. This particular tree is roughly two centuries old, which for a species this fast-growing means it reached close to its full height early and has held it ever since. It carries singular tree designation number 260 in the Community of Madrid's regional catalogue, one number among 280 protected specimens across the wider region.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the Trillo Roundabout
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Casa de Campo (Metro L5/L10), 20 min walk or park shuttle
trees.story: Roads converge on this tree rather than around it. The Glorieta del Trillo, where the Carretera de Somosaguas, the Paseo de los Castanos and the Camino de Rodajos all meet inside Casa de Campo, is named for the holm oak growing at its centre, a roughly 300 year old specimen with a crown 18.5 metres across and a trunk 4.6 metres around. Casa de Campo itself was a royal hunting estate from the 16th century until 1931, when the Second Republic opened it to the public, which means this oak spent roughly two centuries of its life on private land reserved for the Spanish crown's deer and boar hunts rather than growing in anything resembling a public park. Holm oaks are Iberia's signature evergreen, slow growing and built to survive exactly the hot, dry summers and cold winters Madrid delivers, and this one has outlasted the hunting estate, the monarchy that owned it, and the Republic that opened the gates, still marking the same road junction today.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of Campo del Moro
trees.access: Free, public garden (closed Mondays)
trees.transport: Principe Pio (Metro L6/L10/R), 10 min walk
trees.story: This pine grows in the gardens spread beneath the Royal Palace's western facade, a formal landscape that took its current shape only in the 1890s even though the land had belonged to the crown for centuries before that, used variously as a hunting ground, a military exercise field and, briefly, a source of building stone. At 30 metres tall with a trunk 2.55 metres around, the pine ranks among six officially singular trees inside Campo del Moro's twenty hectares, sharing that status with a stone pine, an oak, a coast redwood and a pair of yews scattered through the same grounds. Aleppo pines are a Mediterranean basin native, drought tolerant and comfortable in Madrid's dry summers in a way many of the garden's more exotic imports are not, which may explain why this specimen has reached such size in only a century and a half, a fraction of the multi-century ages claimed for some of the city's other singular trees.

trees.name: The Grandfather Cedar of Parque del Oeste
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Moncloa (Metro L3/L6), 10 min walk
trees.story: Known locally as El Abuelo, the grandfather, this Atlas cedar grows near the Fuente de la Salud and the artificial stream that cuts through the northern part of Parque del Oeste, a park built on former rubbish dumps and quarry land at the turn of the 20th century and rebuilt again after Civil War fighting damaged it in the 1930s. Atlas cedars are native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria and reached European gardens as an ornamental import around 1840, which sets an outer limit on how old any specimen in Madrid could plausibly be; the species itself is capable of living centuries, some specialists say close to a thousand years under ideal conditions, though this individual tree's precise age has not been established by any source found. What is established is its status: one of the Community of Madrid's officially catalogued singular trees, numbered and registered like the 279 other specimens across the region, marking it as protected regardless of whether its exact birth year is ever pinned down.

photo.attribution: Luis Fernandez Garcia, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Stone Pine of the Priest's House
trees.access: Free, but visitor numbers are limited and advance booking is recommended; closed Mondays and Tuesdays
trees.transport: Canillejas (Metro L5), 15 min walk, or El Capricho (Metro L5), 5 min walk
trees.story: This stone pine grows half hidden among shrubs near a small hermitage called the Casa del Cura, the priest's house, in a park built for a duchess rather than a king. Maria Josefa Pimentel, Duchess of Osuna, commissioned El Capricho in 1784, hiring French landscape designers Jean-Baptiste Mulot and Pierre Provost to lay out French, English and Italian style gardens across fourteen hectares in what was then open countryside east of Madrid, now the Barajas district near the airport that shares its name. The pine likely dates from that same late 18th century construction period, making it a contemporary of the duchess's original vision rather than a later addition. Unlike Madrid's grander royal gardens, El Capricho suffered decades of neglect and, during the Spanish Civil War, served as a military command post, before the city restored it and reopened it to visitors in the 1990s. The pine survived all of it, one of the park's few catalogued singular trees and among the oldest living witnesses to the duchess's original 18th century design.

trees.name: The Strawberry Tree of the Plaza de la Lealtad
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Banco de Espana (Metro L2), 3 min walk

best_time.label: November and December, when it flowers and ripens last year's fruit at once

trees.story: Madrid's coat of arms shows a bear reaching up into a strawberry tree, and this is the closest thing the city has to the original. It stands in the southern corner of the Plaza de la Lealtad, opposite the Ritz, propped on iron crutches installed when its own limbs grew heavy enough to threaten pulling it over. Strawberry trees are usually shrubs, three or four metres of Mediterranean scrub. This one has been allowed to grow into an actual tree for more than a century, which is why the props are needed at all. It is also why the Comunidad de Madrid added it to the singular-tree catalogue in 2015 for cultural rather than botanical significance: the emblem, made real. Historians are fairly sure the heraldic tree of 1222 was never a madrono in the first place and that the bear on the crest was reaching for something else entirely, but the city has committed. The fruit is the payoff. Through November and December it carries white bell flowers and the previous year's fruit at the same time, red warty spheres that look like lychees and taste of very little. The Latin unedo means eat only one.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at the Prado
trees.access: Free, public garden on the Paseo del Prado
trees.transport: Banco de Espana (Metro L2) or Estacion del Arte (Metro L1), 5 min walk

best_time.label: August to October: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Nobody agrees how old this cedar is, and the gap is a century. The regional catalogue and the city's tree literature give roughly 120 years. The guides to the Paseo del Prado put it at 232, which would date the planting to within a generation of Juan de Villanueva's museum building. A third account, more plausible than either, ties it to 1871, when the garden on the museum's western slope was laid out around the Velazquez statue. What is not in dispute is the shape: 26 metres tall, a crown 22 metres across and a trunk four and a half metres around, so the tree is nearly as wide as it is high, its upper branches held out in the flat horizontal plates that only old Lebanon cedars make. It stands a few steps from the museum's busiest door, and most of the several million people who pass it every year are looking at the queue. Cedrus libani is the tree of the Phoenician fleets and of Solomon's temple, reduced in its Lebanese homeland to a handful of protected groves. Madrid keeps one on the Paseo del Prado, inside the stretch of city that UNESCO inscribed in 2021.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Plaza de Murillo
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Estacion del Arte (Metro L1), 4 min walk
trees.story: The Plaza de Murillo, the small formal square between the Prado's south door and the gate of the Royal Botanic Garden, holds four catalogued conifers and one broadleaf that outgrew every one of them. This hackberry stands 25 metres tall, close to the recorded ceiling for the species, and is about 140 years old, which puts its planting in the decade the square took its present shape. Celtis australis is the almez, a southern European tree with a smooth grey trunk that looks poured rather than grown, and fruit the size of a pea that turns from orange to near black. Spanish villages once coppiced it for the handles of hayforks, because the young wood bends a long way before it snaps, and whole valleys in Aragon lived off that trade. It is also, unglamorously, one of the toughest street trees in existence, indifferent to drought, wind and exhaust, which is exactly why a specimen this size is still standing on an island of pavement in central Madrid. Look for its flowers in April and you will not find them; they are green and smaller than a grain of rice. Stand under it in July, when the stone outside the Prado is at forty degrees, and the reason the square was planted this way needs no explaining.

trees.name: The Himalayan Spruce of the Plaza de Murillo
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Estacion del Arte (Metro L1), 4 min walk
trees.story: Of the four conifers catalogued in the Plaza de Murillo, this is the one nobody can name. Picea smithiana grows wild between two and nearly four thousand metres up, in Afghanistan, Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and reached Europe in 1818 when seed arrived in Scotland. It has the longest needles of any spruce and the most extreme weeping habit in the genus: the side branches hang almost vertically off the limbs, so a mature tree looks like it is slowly melting. This one is 22 metres tall with a trunk 1.85 metres around. Its age is honestly unsettled. The city's guides say 140 years; the botanical account attached to the square claims a planting around 1790, which would make it older than the Botanic Garden's present layout and older than nearly anything else rooted along the Paseo del Prado. The species honours Sir James Edward Smith, who founded the Linnean Society and bought Linnaeus's entire collection at twenty-four. Its other name, morinda, is a Himalayan word for flower honey and refers to the resin that beads on the young cones. A high-altitude spruce is the wrong tree for a Madrid summer by every measure that matters, which is what makes it worth standing under.

trees.name: The Four-Trunked Silver Maple of Cecilio Rodriguez
trees.access: Free, public park. The Cecilio Rodriguez gardens keep shorter hours than the rest of the Retiro and close at dusk
trees.transport: Ibiza (Metro L9), 5 min walk
trees.story: This maple gave up on having one trunk early. It divides at about head height into four main stems, each carrying its share of a crown 15 metres across and 20 metres tall, a form silver maples fall into readily and gardeners usually correct. Nobody corrected this one. It stands inside the Jardines de Cecilio Rodriguez, the walled Andalusian-style garden in the south-east corner of the Retiro, laid out in the 1940s on ground first set aside in 1929 for an extension to the park's zoo. The peacocks that patrol the hedges are what came of that plan instead. Acer saccharinum is North American, a tree of the river bottoms of the eastern United States, and it takes its name from the underside of the leaf rather than from sap: turn one over and it is pale silver white, so a breeze through the crown changes the colour of the entire tree at once. It flowers before it leafs, in tight red clusters in late February, weeks before anything else in the park has woken up. The garden shuts at dusk and is one of the quietest corners of the Retiro, which for a park this busy is worth knowing about.

trees.name: The Tall Cedar of the Avenida del Peru
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Retiro (Metro L2), 10 min walk into the park, or O'Donnell (Metro L6), 8 min

best_time.label: August to October: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: At 33 metres this is the tallest tree on the Retiro's catalogued list, and it does not look it, because it stands at a junction of wide avenues where nothing nearby gives the eye anything to measure against. Walk up to the trunk, 3.3 metres around, and the height arrives all at once. It is a Cedar of Lebanon of about 120 years, at the meeting of the Avenida del Peru and the Plaza de Guatemala in the park's north-east, a few paces from the equestrian monument to General Martinez Campos. That statue was unveiled in 1907, when the cedar was already a young tree of perhaps twenty, watching masons set the plinth. Lebanon cedars grow through three clearly different shapes. Young ones are narrow cones, middle-aged ones broaden, and only the old ones flatten into the tiered, table-topped silhouette that ended up on the Lebanese flag. This one is midway through the second stage, still conical at the top and already spreading below. Its crown spans 11 metres against the 22 of the older cedar down at the Prado. The two of them, twenty minutes apart on foot, are the same species caught at two points in a life that can run past a thousand years.

trees.name: The Blue Gum North of the Estanque
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Retiro (Metro L2), 8 min walk
trees.story: In February 2015 the Comunidad de Madrid revised its register of singular trees and published two lists side by side. One added 69 trees. The other struck 43 off, for the blunt reason that they were dead or gone, and among them was the Eucalipto del Parque del Retiro. On the same page, a different eucalyptus a few hundred metres away was written into the catalogue in its place, listed for historical significance. This is the replacement. It stands north of the Estanque Grande, near the Paseo de Coches, over 20 metres tall with a crown about as wide and a trunk you cannot get your arms halfway round. Eucalyptus globulus is Tasmanian, brought to Spain in the 1860s on the theory that it drained marshes and drove off malaria, and planted so enthusiastically across the north-west that it has become a management problem there. In a Madrid park it is simply a giant, its bark peeling away in long ribbons and its leaves smelling of a cough sweet when you crush one. The trunk carries a century of carved initials, which is why the tree writers who have followed it since the 2000s keep asking the park for a sign and a low rail.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Paid entry, EUR 7.50 adult, open daily 09:00-18:00 (last admission 30 min before close)
trees.transport: Bus 29, 30, 31 or 31A from central Funchal (about 10 minutes), or the Teleférico do Jardim Botânico cable car from Monte. No car needed for this one.

best_time.label: November, when the crown turns gold and drops it in a few days

trees.story:
Madeira's official register of monumental trees records this ginkgo for exactly one reason, size, and where the age should go it says sem referencia, no reference. Nobody has dated it. What the surveyors did measure is 18 metres of height and a trunk 1.62 metres round, which is a substantial specimen of a tree that has no obvious business thriving at this latitude and manages it anyway.

Ginkgo biloba is the last species left of an entire lineage, with no close living relative anywhere, and it reached European gardens only in the eighteenth century. This one grows in the Jardim Botanico da Madeira on the slope above Funchal, among roughly 3,000 species pulled in from every continent the garden could reach, ten minutes out of the city by bus or a cable car ride down from Monte.

The garden opened to the public in 1960, which dates the garden and not the tree. Nobody has recorded when this ginkgo went in. If you have a planting record, or a girth measured more recently than the survey, send it to us.

And then in November the crown turns butter gold and drops the lot inside a few days, which is the week to be standing under it.

trees.name: The Cypress of Quinta Magnolia
trees.access: Free entry, open daily 08:00-20:00
trees.transport: Central Funchal park, walkable from the Lido seafront area or a short bus or taxi ride from the city centre. No car needed for this one.
trees.story:
Madeirans call this species cedro-das-barracas, the shed cedar, because the young leading shoot was traditionally cut off so the crown would thicken outward into a roof of shade. Nobody did that to this one. It went up instead: 29.5 metres tall on a trunk 6.06 metres around, more than a metre of solid diameter, which the island's register singles out as exceptional for a Cupressus lusitanica and enough to make it one of the largest of its kind on Madeira.

The species is not Portuguese, whatever the name says. It comes from Mexico and Central America, and it took its Latin name from trees already growing in Portugal rather than from anywhere near its actual origin.

Its age is not recorded. The register gives its condition as bom, good, and notes that it is under permanent technical monitoring, which is what the island does with trees it has no intention of losing. Nobody has dated it, and if you know when it was planted, tell us.

It stands in Quinta Magnolia, a public park of some 40,000 square metres in the middle of Funchal, free and open from eight in the morning until eight at night, which makes this the easiest tree on the list to go and see.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Emperor's Garden
trees.access: Paid entry, around EUR 1 (often free on Sundays), open weekdays 09:30-17:30, Sundays and holidays 10:30-17:30
trees.transport: Monte parish, reachable by the Monte cable car from Funchal plus a short walk, or by bus toward Monte. No car needed for this one.
trees.story:
The last Emperor of Austria died in this garden. Karl I, deposed in 1918 and exiled to Madeira, spent his final months at what was then Quinta do Monte and died there in 1922, which is why the estate is now the Jardins do Imperador, the Emperor's Garden.

The tree that dominates it is a copper beech, 36 metres tall on a trunk 3.52 metres round. That is an odd thing to find here. Fagus sylvatica is a northern European forest tree and this is a subtropical island in the Atlantic; what makes it possible is Monte itself, high on the slope above Funchal in the belt of cloud that the trade winds push up against the mountain. The parish is permanently damp and several degrees cooler than the seafront, and the beech behaves accordingly.

Madeira's monumental tree register lists it for size, records its condition as good, and gives its age as sem referencia, no reference. Nobody has dated it, and the estate's own history does not settle it. If you know when this beech was planted, tell us.

Entry costs around a euro, often nothing on Sundays, and the Monte cable car from Funchal stops a short walk away.

trees.name: The Douglas Fir of Queimadas
trees.access: Free, public forest park
trees.transport: By car from Funchal via Santana, roughly 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes of driving; there is no practical public transport to the park, so a car is the realistic way.
trees.story:
A Douglas fir has no business in a laurel forest, and this one is 39 metres tall. It is the tallest tree on this list, a North American conifer planted inside Parque Florestal das Queimadas, which sits in the laurisilva that UNESCO listed as World Heritage: the largest surviving remnant of the laurel forest that once covered much of southern Europe. Madeira's register lists it for size at 3.61 metres round, condition good, age no reference.

Worth being straight about what it is. Nothing here is native, and it is on this page because it is a genuinely large specimen at a place people already come to, not because it belongs to the forest around it.

That place is the trailhead for PR9, the Levada do Caldeirao Verde, one of the walks that brings people to Madeira in the first place, and the register calls Queimadas one of the most visited sites on the island. The park is free and open, with the levada path running off into the laurel.

Nobody has dated the fir, and there is a reason not to guess from its height: Douglas firs grow fast, so a big one need not be an old one. If you find a planting record, send it.

trees.name: The Witch Tree of Fanal
trees.access: Free, public land inside the Madeira Natural Park, rated 'muito facil' (very easy) by the register; a short walk from the Fanal parking area, but there is no on-site signage naming or pointing to this specific tree
trees.transport: By car only; roughly 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes from Funchal via the ER209, and well over an hour back, because Paul da Serra is mountain plateau driving rather than a suburban hop.
trees.story:
The grove these trees belong to was already standing when the Portuguese found Madeira uninhabited in 1419. Fanal is a protected 20-hectare nucleus of til, Ocotea foetens, on the Paul da Serra plateau inside the UNESCO laurel forest, and the island's register dates it only as centenas de anos, hundreds of years, referencing a stand that predates settlement. The eight trunks the surveyors measured run from 0.68 to 2.28 metres round.

One tree in it has become the one everybody photographs. Travel and photography sources call it the Witch Tree, arvore da bruxa, for a trunk that twists hard and limbs that read as outstretched arms under a coat of moss. Tourist literature puts it at 500 or 600 years; the register will say no more than hundreds, and neither figure rests on a measurement, so this page does not sharpen it.

Nothing on the ground names it. There is no sign, no arrow and no path to the trunk, and visitors regularly report hunting around the grove before they find it, which is why our pin marks the area rather than the tree. Come in the morning fog if you can. That is when Fanal looks the way it does in the photographs, and when the tis stop reading as trees.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree Grove of Neves
trees.access: Free entry, public garden with an information centre open Monday-Friday 09:00-12:30 and 14:00-17:30; guided visits available by contacting the centre
trees.transport: About 5 km from central Funchal by road; no direct public transport noted, so a taxi or car is the realistic way.
trees.story:
The Regional Government of Madeira bought this piece of land for one reason: the trees standing on it. The Nucleo dos Dragoeiros das Neves is a small purpose-built garden in Sao Goncalo, five kilometres out of central Funchal, laid out around what the island's register calls a notable group of centenary dragon trees. It has an information centre, opening hours, a phone number and guided visits available on request, which is remarkable treatment for a garden you can cross in a minute, and it tells you how little of Madeira's original dragon tree population is left.

Dracaena draco is native here and to the Canaries and almost nowhere else, and it grows slowly enough to make the register's word centenarios mean something: roughly ten years to reach two or three metres. The thickest trunk in the group measures 4.77 metres around and the stand reaches 13 metres. The register gives no age beyond centenary, and this page invents none.

Cut the bark and the sap runs red. That is dragon's blood, imported into Europe for centuries as a dye, a varnish and a medicine, and the trees were tapped hard for it. Entry is free, the information centre keeps weekday hours, and the whole visit takes twenty minutes.

photo.attribution: Paulo SP/ Wikimedia, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Finer Holm Oak of Edinburgh Gardens
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park, 24 hectares, unrestricted access per the National Trust record.
trees.transport: Rushall railway station (Mernda line) is about a 3 minute walk from the gardens; tram route 11/112 runs along nearby St Georges Road.
trees.story: Edinburgh Gardens has two holm oaks, and the National Trust of Australia has a view about which one to look at. Its Significant Tree Register calls this the finer of the two examples of the species in the gardens, and it is certainly the heavier: the City of Yarra records 177 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is about 5.56 metres of girth, since that 177 is a width across the trunk and not a measurement around it.
