That is the thickest trunk here and a record nowhere else: the Trust's own significance statement points to a tree at Talindert, near Camperdown in western Victoria, as the biggest of its kind in Victoria. This one is about 20 metres tall and stands near the bowling club. The same Trust survey, in 2011, recorded its condition as poor and noted that it is overcrowded by nearby elms. Those elms are worth knowing about. Dutch elm disease never reached Australia, and Edinburgh Gardens holds one of the most significant stands of mature elms left in the world, trees of a size Britain and Europe stopped having half a century ago. The oak has been growing up inside all of that. Its age is the register's band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey, with no planting year on record.

trees.name: The Remnant River Red Gum of Edinburgh Gardens
trees.age: over 100 years, possibly a remnant predating the park
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park.
trees.transport: Rushall railway station (Mernda line) is about a 3 minute walk from the gardens; tram route 11/112 runs along nearby St Georges Road.
trees.story: Queen Victoria granted this ground to the people of Fitzroy in 1862. The river red gum may have been standing here already. The City of Yarra's register classes it as remnant, the category it uses for indigenous vegetation that was left rather than planted, and tags the same entry outstanding size, particularly old and significant habitat value. What the register does not give is a year. Its age band is the coarse one, over a hundred years at the survey in August 2012, and no independent source names this individual tree, so how much of this site's history it actually saw is an open question. If you know of a heritage citation or an old photograph that dates it, we would like to see it. The measurements are firmer: 28 metres tall, and 138 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which works out at roughly 4.33 metres of girth, since Yarra publishes the width across a trunk rather than the way round it. Eucalyptus camaldulensis is the most widely spread eucalypt in Australia, the tree of inland rivers and creek beds, and it has a habit of shedding heavy limbs in still weather, which is part of what makes an old one in a public park unusual. Most of what grows in these 24 hectares was brought in and planted. This one may not have been.

trees.name: The English Elm of Darling Gardens
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park (also used as an off-leash dog area, does not restrict general access).
trees.transport: Clifton Hill railway station (Hurstbridge/Mernda lines) is about a 6 minute walk; tram route 86 on Queens Parade is about a 6 minute walk (24-Gold St/Queens Pde stop).

best_time.label: April and May, when the elm turns yellow

trees.story: The English elm barely exists as a mature tree in England any more. Melbourne kept its. Dutch elm disease killed elms across Britain and Europe by the tens of millions from the 1960s on and never reached Australia, which left this city holding elm plantings of an age and size Europe lost. The National Trust of Australia dated this one at about 120 years in February 2011, so roughly 135 now, and calls it an outstanding example of the species. It stands 28 metres tall at the Gold Street end of Darling Gardens, and the City of Yarra's register gives it 154 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is 4.84 metres of girth: the register's figure is a diameter, so every girth on this page is a conversion from one. The two registers disagree about the name. Yarra records it as Ulmus minor 'Atinia'; the Trust's entry says Ulmus procera. Both mean English elm, and botanists have spent decades arguing over whether they are one tree or two. Darling Gardens was permanently reserved in 1866 and laid out with elms and oaks in the 1890s. The Trust's dating puts this tree's planting in that same decade, which is arithmetic rather than a record: nothing ties this trunk to that scheme by name.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Darling Gardens
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park.
trees.transport: Clifton Hill railway station (Hurstbridge/Mernda lines) is about a 6 minute walk; tram route 86 on Queens Parade is about a 6 minute walk (24-Gold St/Queens Pde stop).
trees.story: Darling Gardens has two trees on the National Trust's register. This is the other one. The Trust names a holm oak of regional significance alongside the elm, and it is much the smaller of the pair: 84 centimetres of diameter at breast height in the City of Yarra's survey, roughly 2.64 metres of girth once converted from the width across the trunk that the register publishes, against the elm's 4.84. It stands 16 metres tall about ninety metres from the elm, nearer the middle of the park than the Gold Street corner. Size is plainly not why it is listed. Quercus ilex is the evergreen oak of the Mediterranean, dark, leathery and dense enough that little grows under it, and it holds its canopy through the entire year. In a Melbourne February that is the difference between shade and no shade, and in July, when the elms around it are bare, it is still in full leaf. Spain and Portugal have grazed pigs on the acorns of this species for centuries, which is the other reason it travelled as far as it did. The age on file is the register's blunt band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey, with no year and no independent date behind it. If you know when Darling Gardens' oak went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Curtain Square
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park (also used as an off-leash dog area).
trees.transport: Curtain Square/Rathdowne St bus stop is directly outside; tram route 96 on Nicholson Street is roughly a 5-10 minute walk.
trees.story: This park was a hole in the ground, and prisoners dug it. Between 1853 and 1866 the block was a bluestone quarry worked by men from the Collingwood Stockade, and bluestone is the rock Melbourne's kerbs and laneways are still made of. The pit was filled, levelled and planted, and Curtain Square became a square. This fig went in somewhere after that. It is a Moreton Bay fig, Ficus macrophylla, an Australian tree but not a Melbourne one: its home range runs up the east coast around Moreton Bay in Queensland, roughly 1,400 kilometres north, and Victorian gardeners planted it down here anyway for the shade and the ropey buttress roots. It stands 25 metres tall with a trunk of about 4.77 metres round, converted from the 152 centimetres of diameter at breast height the City of Yarra's register publishes, because the register measures across the trunk rather than around it. Local accounts describe a surviving avenue of Moreton Bay figs at the Canning Street entrance, which is where this tree stands. Whether this particular trunk belongs to that avenue is not something anyone has written down. Its age is the register's own band, over a hundred years at the survey in August 2012, and there is no planting date on record. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The London Plane of Curtain Square
trees.access: Free, always open. Public City of Yarra park.
trees.transport: Curtain Square/Rathdowne St bus stop is directly outside; tram route 96 on Nicholson Street is roughly a 5-10 minute walk.
trees.story: The most recent evidence that this tree is standing is from 2012. The City of Yarra's arborists surveyed Curtain Square in August of that year and recorded a London plane on the Rathdowne Street side of the park: 24 metres tall, 170 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to roughly 5.34 metres of girth, since the register publishes the width across a trunk rather than the measure around it. Only one trunk on this page is heavier, the holm oak in Edinburgh Gardens. The age band on the record is 81 to 100 years, putting the planting somewhere in the decade after the First World War and the tree at roughly a century now. Nothing newer than that survey turned up. Squares here do lose trees: in 2017 Curtain Square's avenue of elms, some of them about a hundred years old, was cut down on safety grounds and replaced with scarlet oaks. That was a different avenue and a different species, and nothing suggests this plane was touched. Still, if you walk through, look and tell us what is there. London plane is a hybrid of an American and an oriental parent, crossed in the seventeenth century, and it turned out to shrug off soot, drought and butchered roots better than anything else, which is why it lines streets on five continents including this one.

trees.name: The Osage Orange of Yarra Boulevard
trees.access: Free, always open. Public parkland along Yarra Boulevard, part of Yarra Bend Park / the Boulevard Parklands, a well-used shared walking and cycling corridor along the Yarra River.
trees.transport: No tram or train stop immediately adjacent. Reachable via the Yarra River shared path or Yarra Boulevard itself; the nearest railway stations (Burnley, Victoria Park, or East Richmond) are roughly 2km away by path.
trees.story: Yarra Boulevard was built to give men work during the Depression. The tree beside it was already seventy years old. The Victorian Heritage Database's citation for the Boulevard Parklands records an Osage orange north-east of the point where the road meets Swan Street and dates it to the 1860s, which makes it around 160 now. Nothing else here has been dated that far back. The City of Yarra's register lists one at that spot too: 27 metres tall, 169 centimetres of diameter at breast height, about 5.31 metres of girth once converted, since the register gives the width across a trunk rather than the distance around it. Nobody has matched the two records trunk to trunk, but Osage orange is rare enough here that they almost certainly describe the same tree. The height is the odd part. Maclura pomifera is a thorny, low, awkward thing in its native Red River country of Texas and Oklahoma, and it rarely gets far past 20 metres anywhere. This one reached 27 on a river flat in Melbourne. Its wood is so dense and rot-resistant that Osage fence posts routinely outlast the wire stapled to them, which is part of why a tree from a small corner of America ended up on four continents. The road, by comparison, is barely ninety.

trees.name: The River Red Gum of Yarra Boulevard
trees.access: Free, always open. Public parkland along Yarra Boulevard, part of Yarra Bend Park / the Boulevard Parklands.
trees.transport: No tram or train stop immediately adjacent. Reachable via the Yarra River shared path or Yarra Boulevard itself; the nearest railway stations (Burnley, Victoria Park, or East Richmond) are roughly 2km away by path.
trees.story: This one was probably never planted. The City of Yarra's register tags it remnant, its word for indigenous vegetation left standing rather than put in, and records 22 metres of height and 152 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to about 4.77 metres of girth, since the register publishes the width across a trunk rather than the way round it. Its age is the standard band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey. The Victorian Heritage Database's citation for these parklands says the remnant indigenous vegetation through the park is mostly river red gums, but it names no individual trees, so for this particular trunk the claim rests on the city's register alone. It stands about 1.4 kilometres along the Boulevard from the Osage orange and marks the far end of the second walk on this page, which begins in Burnley Gardens; the northern parks sit six or seven kilometres away. Eucalyptus camaldulensis is the tree of Australian watercourses, the species that held the banks of the Yarra before there was a Melbourne on them, and the Boulevard is a shared walking and cycling corridor along the river rather than a park you cut across. Come for the river as much as for the tree.

trees.name: The Bhutan Cypress of Burnley Gardens
trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
In the Himalaya this species passes 30 metres. Here it stands at 13. Cupressus torulosa, the Bhutan cypress, is a mountain conifer, and the one in Burnley Gardens has had an easier life than its relatives on a Himalayan slope: open ground, no competition for light, and a botanic garden looking after it. The City of Yarra's arborists recorded it on 4 October 2012 at 103 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to about 3.24 metres of girth, because the register publishes the width across a trunk rather than the distance around it. They tagged it rare or localised, and particularly old.

Burnley Gardens is nine hectares holding close to a thousand plant species, run by the University of Melbourne and free to walk into, and some of the oldest trees in the city are in it. This cypress is the sort of thing a register exists for: an unusual species, grown large, in a garden where somebody planted it deliberately and then nobody wrote down when.

That is the honest limit here. Nothing beyond the city's register names this individual tree, and its age is the register's blunt band, over a hundred years at the 2012 survey, with no planting year attached. If you know when the Burnley cypress went in, tell us.

trees.name: The River Red Gum of Burnley Gardens
trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
The city register gives this tree a hundred years. A local account of the same garden gives one of its red gums four hundred.

The register is the firmer of the two. The City of Yarra surveyed Burnley Gardens on 4 October 2012 and recorded a river red gum of 17 metres and 92 centimetres of diameter at breast height, about 2.89 metres of girth once converted, since the register measures across a trunk rather than around it. It tagged the entry remnant, which is its word for indigenous vegetation left standing rather than planted, alongside outstanding size, particularly old and significant habitat value. The age field is the coarse one: over a hundred years, no year attached.

The other figure comes from a 2015 account of Burnley's Native Garden, which describes a river red gum in the south-west corner believed to exceed 400 years and to predate the European settlement of this ground. Nobody has tied that description to a particular trunk, and the Native Garden may hold more than one old red gum, so both numbers stand here and we pick neither. If you know which tree that account means, we would like to hear it.

What is not in doubt is the setting. The tree stands on a bend of the Yarra, on the sort of ground where Eucalyptus camaldulensis was growing long before anyone laid a garden over it.

trees.name: The Sugar Gum of Burnley Gardens
trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
Burnley Gardens' best known sugar gum is a table. The heritage-listed specimen on the entrance drive, dated to about 1887, dropped limbs once too often and came down in 2008; its timber was carved and the table unveiled in 2013. This is a different tree, and this one is alive.

It stands further into the grounds, and the City of Yarra recorded it on 4 October 2012, four years after that removal: 22 metres tall, 144 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which works out at roughly 4.52 metres of girth. That 144 is a width measured across the trunk, not a tape run around it. Particularly old, outstanding size, location of landscape context, in the register's own words. The age is the band and nothing more, over a hundred years, with no year behind it.

What says it is still standing is an iNaturalist record from September 2025, research grade, of a living Eucalyptus cladocalyx within about 25 metres of the register's point. Whether that photograph and that survey are the same trunk is inference rather than record, though nothing planted since 2008 could be this thick.

Sugar gums have a local reputation for shedding branches, which University of Melbourne researchers restated as recently as 2024. It is part of why an old one still upright in a public garden is worth the walk.

trees.name: The Yate of Burnley Gardens
trees.access: Free, open to the public. Burnley Gardens is a botanic garden on the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus: no gate charge and no ticket, though it is a working university campus as well as a garden.
trees.transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
trees.story:
Yate grows wild on a strip of coast in the far south-west of Western Australia and almost nowhere else. This one is 18 metres tall and about four metres round, on the other side of the continent.

Eucalyptus cornuta takes its name from its buds, which taper to a long horn before the flowers open. A tree of this size well outside its range is the kind of thing a university's botanic garden accumulates: Burnley Gardens holds close to a thousand plant species across nine hectares, free to walk into, and the City of Yarra's register lists this one for its outstanding size and its place in the landscape.

Most of the trees on this page carry the register's blanket band of over a hundred years. This one got a narrower reading, 81 to 100 years at the survey on 4 October 2012, which puts the planting somewhere between roughly 1926 and 1945. Somebody looked and made a closer call, which is worth saying, because almost nowhere else on this page did they.

The measurements: 127 centimetres of diameter at breast height, so a girth of about 3.99 metres, converted from a diameter, which is what the register publishes rather than a circumference. Nothing outside that register names this tree. If you can date the Burnley yate, or have watched it flower here, tell us.

trees.name: El Sabino de San Juan
trees.access: Free, standing in a public plazuela (small plaza) in the barrio of San Juan, open at all times.
trees.transport: In central Xochimilico, within walking distance (roughly 1-1.5 km) of the Xochimilico historic centre and the Tren Ligero Xochimilico terminus; exact walk time not independently confirmed.
trees.story: Eighteen and a half metres around. That is the circumference the city's environment department recorded for this ahuehuete when it wrote the tree into the new register of heritage trees in 2025, and it makes El Sabino the thickest of the twelve trees Mexico City has so far declared. Local tradition, set down by the chronicler Rodolfo Cordero Lopez, holds that Cuauhtemoc planted it in 1521 in thanks to the Xochimilca people. Nobody has ever tested that. No ring count or growth study has been published, so the round 500 years is a story the barrio tells rather than a number anyone has measured. What is documented is harder to read. In September 2018 the tree broke apart in high winds, a year after specialists from the Universidad de Chapingo had warned that it was not being properly maintained. What stands in the plazuela today is the surviving part, recorded at 24.5 metres tall and formally protected seven years after that night. The city has form here. El Sargento, the giant ahuehuete of Chapultepec that generations of Mexicans were taken to see, dried out in 1969 and is a relic now. This one is not. It stands in a small plaza in Barrio San Juan with the neighbourhood around it, which is roughly how it has survived everything else.

trees.name: El Viejo del Agua (Ahuehuete de Santa Catarina)
trees.age: roughly 700 years (city's own estimate, basis not published)
trees.access: Free, standing beside the Santa Catarina Martir parish/plaza in the historic barrio; publicly visible year round.
trees.transport: In the Barrio de Santa Catarina, Azcapotzalco; nearest Metro is Camarones (Linea 7) or El Rosario area, roughly 2 km away. Exact walk time not independently confirmed.
trees.story: The first tree Mexico City ever declared natural heritage stands behind a primary school. In June 2025 the head of government came to Barrio de Santa Catarina in Azcapotzalco, gave this ahuehuete the name El Viejo del Agua and made it the opening entry in a register of protected trees that did not exist the week before. The timing was deliberate: 2025 marked seven centuries since the founding of Tenochtitlan, and the city put the tree's age at 700 years to match. Take that figure carefully. Every outlet repeated it and none of them published how it was reached, with no ring count and no growth-rate calculation on record, so the honest range is somewhere between five and seven hundred years. The trunk is not in doubt. The city's own measurement is 13.8 metres of circumference, under a crown that reaches about 27 metres. Ahuehuete is Nahuatl for old one of the water, which is a species name rather than a claim about this specimen: Taxodium mucronatum grows where the water table is high, and Mexico City is built over a drained lake. What is certain is the company it keeps. It stands beside the parish church of Santa Catarina Martir, in the barrio that argued for its protection and got it before any other tree in the city.

trees.name: Laureano
trees.age: disputed: sources give 35 years and separately 100-115 years
trees.access: Free, stands on the public sidewalk at the street corner; visible and reachable at any time.
trees.transport: In Colonia Tlacoquemecatl del Valle, Benito Juarez, roughly 1.5 km from Metro Division del Norte (Linea 3); walk time not independently confirmed.
trees.story: A property developer wanted this tree gone, and the street would not have it. The laurel fig on the corner of Miguel Laurent and Fresas was in the way of a building project in Tlacoquemecatl del Valle, and instead of losing it the neighbours took the argument to the borough of Benito Juarez and to the city's environment department. In June 2025 the tree was declared protected, and the neighbours had already given it a name: Laureano. How old it is depends on which article you read. El Universal has published both 35 years and more than a hundred, calling it centenario in the second piece, and nobody has resolved the gap. We are not going to pick one for you. What can be measured has been: 2.8 metres of trunk circumference, 23 metres tall, and a crown close to 20 metres across, which for a street tree on a residential corner is a considerable amount of shade to be standing under. That crown is the point. It is why people who walk under it every day noticed when it was threatened, and why a fig that may not even be a century old now carries the same legal protection as ahuehuetes said to be seven hundred. Protection here followed attachment, not age.

trees.name: Ahuehuete de Parque Espana
trees.access: Free, standing inside the public Parque Espana, open daily during park hours.
trees.transport: In Roma Norte; roughly 900 m from Metro Insurgentes (Linea 1) or Metrobus Alvaro Obregon, about a 10-12 minute walk.
trees.story: This tree has a birthday, which on this page is rare. It went into the ground on 21 September 1921, the day Parque Espana was inaugurated for the centenary of Mexican independence, and it has been growing in the same spot in Roma Norte ever since. Almost every other protected tree in Mexico City is dated by legend, by estimate or not at all. This one has a date somebody wrote down. A century of city has happened around it. The Roma was still a young neighbourhood of new houses when the park opened; the 1985 earthquake brought several of them down within a few streets of here; the district emptied and refilled and became the part of town everyone now has an opinion about. The ahuehuete has been the constant. When Excelsior went to the park for its hundredth birthday in 2021, the tree was described as full of life and among the tallest standing there. The city's own measurements make it 28 metres tall with a trunk just over 5 metres around, which for a tree with a documented start is a useful reference point: this is what a century of growth looks like in this soil, in a species whose older relatives elsewhere in the city run to three and four times that girth.

trees.name: Ahuehuete del Jardin de San Fernando
trees.access: Free, standing inside the small public Jardin de San Fernando, open daily; the adjoining Panteon de San Fernando (a separate, ticketed historic cemetery where Benito Juarez is buried) is not the tree's location.
trees.transport: In the Guerrero neighbourhood; roughly 600-800 m from Metro Hidalgo (Lineas 2 and 3), a short walk.
trees.story: Mexico City had protected no trees by name at all until 2025, and this was one of the first two it named. The ahuehuete in the Jardin de San Fernando went into the register at the opening of the programme, alongside a tree in Azcapotzalco, in a decree that recorded it at about 25 metres tall with a trunk 158 centimetres across. The environment department's own field sheet, from a separate visit, gives a thicker trunk and a height nearer 28 metres, with a circumference of 5.5 metres and a crown 22 metres wide. Two measuring passes, two sets of numbers, both official, and the difference tells you roughly how much precision to expect from any figure on a tree this size. It stands in a small public garden in Colonia Guerrero, off Avenida Hidalgo, a few minutes' walk from Metro Hidalgo and free to walk into. Do not confuse it with the Panteon de San Fernando next door, the historic cemetery where Benito Juarez is buried, which is a separate site with its own entrance. Nobody has put an age to this tree. There is no planting date in any source we can find and no measured estimate, so it goes on the map undated. If you have seen a figure in print, or an old photograph of this square, send it over.

trees.name: Ahuehuete de Tacuba
trees.access: Free, standing on the public sidewalk (banqueta) at the street corner, visible and reachable at any time.
trees.transport: In the historic Tacuba neighbourhood (site of the Noche Triste/Noche Victoriosa retreat route); roughly 900 m-1 km from Metro Tacuba (Linea 2 and 7 interchange).
trees.story: The famous tree of Tacuba is a ruin, and this is the one still growing. A few streets from here, in Popotla, stands what remains of the Arbol de la Noche Triste, the ahuehuete under which Hernan Cortes is said to have wept during his retreat from Tenochtitlan in 1520. The city's own venue page for the site describes the remains as exactly that, remains. There is nothing left to walk to. Meanwhile, on a pavement corner where Marina Nacional meets Golfo de Bengala, a living ahuehuete has quietly reached a circumference of just over 10 metres. Ten metres of trunk on a street corner, with a crown 18 metres wide and 22 metres of height above it, and until June 2025 it carried no protection of any kind. It was declared an Arbol Patrimonial that month, in the same decree as the ahuehuete in Parque Espana. Nobody has dated it. The city's file records the trunk, the crown and the height and leaves the age column blank, and a girth alone is not an age without a growth rate for this species in this soil. If you know of a source that puts a number on it, we would like to see it. What can be said without hedging is that in a district known for a dead tree, this is the large old one that survived.

trees.name: Ahuehuete de San Diego Churubusco
trees.access: Free, standing in the public plaza/park around the former convent (which today houses the Museo Nacional de las Intervenciones); open during park hours.
trees.transport: In Coyoacan, roughly 500-700 m from Metro General Anaya (Linea 2).
trees.story: This ahuehuete may or may not have been standing when the United States army took the convent behind it. The Battle of Churubusco was fought here on 20 August 1847, and the building the Mexican garrison defended is now the Museo Nacional de las Intervenciones, a museum of every foreign invasion the country has faced, on the site of one of them. Whether the tree saw any of it is genuinely unknown. No age has been recorded for it by the city or anyone else, and we would rather leave the field empty than invent a number that suits the setting. Tell us if you find one. What was measured is odd enough on its own. The city's file lists two trunks under this single entry, 154 and 161 centimetres across, with circumferences of 4.8 and 5.1 metres, which means either one tree forked low into two great stems or two trees standing close enough that the surveyor registered them as one. Both are worth the walk, and they are not the same thing, so if you get there before we do, say which it is. It reaches 20 metres under a crown 16 metres wide, in the public park that wraps the old convent walls. Metro General Anaya is under ten minutes away on foot and the park costs nothing.

trees.name: Ahuehuete de Rio Magdalena (Callejon del Rio)
trees.access: Free, standing on a public median (camellon) along the historic Callejon del Rio, following the course of the Rio Magdalena; open at all times.
trees.transport: In the Barrio de Santa Catarina, Coyoacan, an easy walk (roughly 700-900 m) from the Jardin Centenario / Coyoacan historic centre; nearest Metrobus is Av. Miguel Angel de Quevedo, about 1 km away.
trees.story: The river this tree is named after is not there any more. Callejon del Rio in Coyoacan follows the old course of the Rio Magdalena, one of the last rivers in Mexico City to run in the open, and the ahuehuete now stands on the median strip left behind, 5.65 metres around and 26 metres tall. Ahuehuetes are water trees. This one is left holding the line of a watercourse that has been culverted underneath it, which is as good a summary of what happened to this city's hydrology as any plaque could manage. It was declared an Arbol Patrimonial in 2025 in a pair with the ahuehuete at San Diego Churubusco. One caution about the name: the press called it the Rio Magdalena ahuehuete, the city's register lists it by its street address on Callejon del Rio in Barrio Santa Catarina, and no single document states outright that the two refer to the same trunk, though the address puts it on that river's line. No age has been recorded. This is one of the two trees on this page that make a real walk: the fresno on Avenida Francisco Sosa is about 700 metres away through the same barrio, with Coyoacan's historic centre and the Viveros a short distance further on.

trees.name: Fresno de Santa Catarina (Avenida Francisco Sosa)
trees.access: Free, standing on the public sidewalk (banqueta) of the property at number 202, visible and reachable at any time.
trees.transport: In the Barrio de Santa Catarina, Coyoacan, on the historic Avenida Francisco Sosa, an easy walk (roughly 700-900 m) from the Jardin Centenario / Coyoacan historic centre.
trees.story: Its crown is as wide as the tree is tall: 26 metres across, 26.5 metres high, on a pavement outside a house on Avenida Francisco Sosa. That is a lot of tree to fit on one of the most photographed colonial streets in Mexico City, and it took until 2025 for anyone to protect it. The fresno at number 202 was the twelfth and final tree in the city's first batch of declared Arboles Patrimoniales, and the only ash among a list otherwise dominated by ahuehuetes. The trunk measures 6.1 metres around, which for a shamel ash is exceptional; the species is planted everywhere in this city and almost never left standing long enough to reach that. Francisco Sosa runs from the Jardin Centenario out towards San Angel, past walled houses that were country estates when Coyoacan was a village outside the capital, and the tree has the scale of that older street rather than the modern one. Nobody has dated it. There is no planting record in the city's file or in the press coverage of its protection, so the age stays blank until somebody produces one. Walk on and the Rio Magdalena ahuehuete is about 700 metres away in the same barrio, which makes these two the one genuine pair on this page.

trees.name: Il Sacerdote
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Porta Venezia (M1)

best_time.label: October into November, when its needles turn rust orange before falling

trees.story: For years, gardeners in Porta Venezia's park called this tree a metasequoia and had the genus wrong before anyone checked properly. It is in fact a bald cypress, one of the first ever planted in Milan, native to the swamps of the American South rather than to any part of Italy, and one of very few conifers anywhere that drops its needles for winter, the trait that gives the whole species its English name. Standing roughly 35 metres tall with a trunk 6.2 metres around, it grows at the edge of the artificial lake inside the Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Milan's oldest public park, opened in 1784 on land a Habsburg duke gave up for prisoners to landscape. Other cypresses share its stretch of water, but this is the tallest and widest of the whole stand, the reason the Milanese writer and forest scholar Tiziano Fratus nicknamed it Il Sacerdote, the priest, for the way its bare winter branches spread like a robe. Its roots, like those of every bald cypress in wet ground, throw up woody knees above the waterline to breathe, a feature visitors often mistake for stumps. At around 156 years old it predates the park's nineteenth century English-garden makeover and has outlasted the zoo that once shared these grounds, dismantled in 1992.

trees.name: Platano di Indro
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.story: The largest plane tree in Milan does not grow tall so much as it grows sideways, in every direction at once. Named for Indro Montanelli, the journalist the park was rededicated to in 2002, it stands about 50 metres from his statue with a trunk 8.36 metres around, the widest of any plane in the city, rising from a short, irregular, deeply fluted base that splits almost at ground level into at least five major limbs, each thick enough to be a trunk of its own. The effect, according to arborists who have surveyed it, is closer to a vase held open than to the single straight column most plane trees grow into. No planting record survives, ordinary for a park redesigned twice since 1784 and never catalogued tree by tree until recently, so its age can only be guessed at from girth: somewhere in its second century, possibly its third. What is documented is who lives in it. Ring-necked parakeets, an escaped-pet species now breeding wild across Milan, nest in cavities high in the crown, adding flashes of tropical green to a tree already too disorderly to look properly manicured. Visitors chasing the statue for a photograph rarely look up at what is standing over it.

trees.name: Bagolaro dei Giardini Montanelli
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.story: Milan calls this species spaccasassi, the stone-splitter, for roots strong enough to crack paving, and this hackberry has had over a century and a half to test the claim against the paths of the city's oldest public park. Standing 27 metres tall with a trunk 4.24 metres around, it is one of seven trees the city has formally recognised as monumental within the Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, sharing that status with the plane and the cypress a short walk away. Celtis australis is native across the Mediterranean and was planted widely in nineteenth century Milan for the same reason it thrives today: almost nothing bothers it, not soot, not drought, not the compacted soil under a park crossed by tens of thousands of people a week. Its small, dark, cherry-like fruit ripens in autumn and draws blackbirds rather than people, who mostly walk past a tree with none of the visible drama of its more contorted neighbours. Italy's monumental tree registry puts its age at 164 years, calculated from growth data rather than any surviving planting record, the only figure any source gives; treated here as an estimate rather than a settled fact.

trees.name: Il Ginkgo dell'Orto Botanico di Brera
trees.access: Free entry, Orto Botanico di Brera (Mon-Sat, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Lanza (M2) or Montenapoleone (M3)

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn uniform gold and drop within days

trees.story: Behind Palazzo Brera's courtyard grows a pair of trees older than the idea of Italy itself: a male and a female ginkgo, planted together in 1775 when Empress Maria Theresa's new botanical garden was barely a year old, grown from seed carried directly from China less than two decades after the species had reached Europe at all. Ginkgo biloba is often called a living fossil, essentially unchanged for over 200 million years and the sole survivor of a family that once grew alongside dinosaurs; this pair is a comparative sapling by that measure, but at somewhere between 235 and 251 years old, depending on whether growth-ring calculation or the garden's own planting record is trusted, they are the oldest documented trees in Milan by a wide margin. In March 2026 the university marked their joint 250th anniversary with a public conference built entirely around the two trees. Every November their fan-shaped leaves turn a uniform gold and drop within days rather than fading gradually, briefly carpeting the beds around them. Entry to the garden is free, a rarity among Milan's oldest sites, down a courtyard most visitors to the Pinacoteca next door never think to enter.

trees.name: La Catalpa della Guastalla
trees.access: Free, public garden (gated, roughly 7:00-21:00, hours vary seasonally)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Crocetta (M3)

best_time.label: June, when its white, orchid-like flowers cover the crown

trees.story: Milan's oldest public garden, laid out in 1555 for a countess who did not live to see it finished, keeps its strangest tree behind a baroque fish pond nobody expects to find in the middle of the city. This catalpa, a North American species imported to Europe for ornamental foliage rather than any practical use, has spent roughly 136 years twisting instead of growing straight, until arborists describe its 3.5-metre trunk as closer to a piece of vegetal sculpture than an ordinary shade tree. Every June its crown fills with white, orchid-patterned flowers in dense upright clusters, followed by the long, thin seed pods that earned the species its American nickname, the cigar tree. The Giardini della Guastalla itself predates almost everything else on this list: founded by Ludovica Torelli, Countess of Guastalla, as a garden for the girls' college she funded, it became one of Milan's first public parks open to all, four centuries after her death. At just over 12,000 square metres it is one of the smallest gardens on this list and one of the easiest to walk past, a few streets from the university hospital rather than fronting any grand piazza.

trees.name: La Quercia Rossa di Piazza XXIV Maggio
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Porta Genova (M2), or tram 3/9/15 to Porta Ticinese

best_time.label: October and November, when its leaves turn a deep, oxidised red

trees.story: This oak was already growing in an American nursery when Milan was still deciding what to do with the site of one of its six historic gates. Giunio Capè had the sapling brought to Piazza XXIV Maggio at the end of the First World War and planted it in 1924 in memory of his son Giuseppe, an Alpine soldier who survived the war, and of the Alpini who did not. A century later the oak stands nearly 20 metres tall with a trunk just under 5 metres around, held up since 2019 by a discreet steel exoskeleton a Bergamo carpentry firm built to support a crown that had begun to outgrow its own structure. Quercus rubra is native to eastern North America and turns a deep, almost oxidised red in October and November, the colour that gives the species its name and, briefly each autumn, the only real red in a square better known for the nineteenth century customs arches of the old Porta Ticinese behind it. Milanese press sometimes calls it the oldest tree in the city; it is not, several trees on this list are older, but it may be the only one whose exact planting date and reason for standing there are both on record.

trees.name: La Quercia Rossa del Trotter
trees.access: Free, public park, open outside school hours (times vary by season)
trees.transport: Bus or tram toward Loreto/Turro, then a short walk to Via Giacosa

best_time.label: October and November, when its canopy turns red above the old racetrack

trees.story: This oak grows on a horse-racing track that stopped racing a century ago and became a school instead. Parco Trotter takes its name from the Società del Trotter, which ran harness races here from the 1800s until the track moved to San Siro in 1924; when the sporting company folded, Milan's city council bought the abandoned oval and turned it, starting in 1919, into Casa del Sole, a 128,000 square metre open-air school for children with tuberculosis and other chronic illness, built on the belief that fresh air and space were themselves a treatment. The ring shape of the old racetrack still defines the park's paths today, cut across by a single straight avenue of plane trees. This red oak, planted not long after the school opened, now stands about 40 metres tall, taller than any other tree on this list, with a trunk 4.3 metres around, growing beside Via Giacosa near the park's old chapel. The school never fully closed. Children still attend classes on these grounds, which is why the park keeps unusual hours, open to the public only outside school time, free every day it opens rather than at any point in between.

trees.name: La Paulownia di Via Madonnina
trees.access: Free, visible from the street (small municipally-owned lot rather than a walk-in garden)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Lanza (M2)

best_time.label: April, when its lilac flowers cover the bare branches before the leaves appear

trees.story: Milan's most photographed tree grows on a triangular scrap of land where a building once stood, until Allied bombs brought it down during the Second World War. Nothing was rebuilt on the corner of Via Madonnina and Via San Carpoforo, and sometime in the decades after the war a paulownia took root in the cleared gap, on land nobody had any particular plan for. By the 2010s the plot had become something else entirely: probably the most photographed tree in the city according to local press, its lilac flowers a fixture of every spring guide to the Brera district. That popularity is the only reason it still stands. A developer held rights to build a small residential block on the triangular lot, and only a sustained campaign by Brera residents, who formed a committee specifically to save the tree, persuaded Milan's city council to acquire the 155 square metre plot in 2016 in exchange for a larger site elsewhere in the city. The paulownia survived a violent storm in July 2023 that uprooted an old fig tree growing beside it. No scientific study has ever aged it precisely; residents describe it as over 65 years old, grown entirely on its own rather than planted by anyone with a plan.

trees.name: La Pianta di Affori
trees.age: 187 years by dendrochronological analysis; local tradition claims over 250
trees.access: Free, public street corner
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Affori Centro (M3)
trees.story: Every Milanese from Affori knows this tree simply as la Pianta, the Plant, as if there were no other, and local legend insists Napoleon is the reason it stands where it does: supposedly planted to honour a Milanese noblewoman he had fallen for during his Italian campaign, sometime around 1800. Core samples taken in 2013, when a restoration crew drilled into the trunk to check its health, tell a more modest story: growth rings put the tree at about 187 years old at the time, closer to the 1820s than the Napoleonic Wars. This page gives both figures, since neither can be disproved outright and the drilled sample is the harder evidence. What is not in dispute is the tree itself: a plane 20 metres tall with a trunk over 2 metres in diameter, standing at the corner of Viale Affori and Via Astesani since before the surrounding neighbourhood existed as anything but farmland. An owl once nested in a cavity on its western side; the memory is marked today by a small wooden owl sculpture at the base of the trunk. A metal bracket further up the trunk, once used to string electrical cable through the branches, is a rare surviving trace of how Milan wired its outer suburbs before anyone thought to protect the tree carrying the load.

trees.name: Il Noce del Caucaso di Parco Sempione
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cadorna (M1/M2) or Cairoli (M1)

best_time.label: October and November, when its foliage turns gold above the pond

trees.story: This walnut grows almost horizontally over the water, its lower limbs bending so far toward the pond in Parco Sempione that locals joke it is trying to drink from it. Pterocarya fraxinifolia is native to the Caucasus and northern Iran, a wetland species that thrives on constantly moist soil, exactly the condition it gets growing at the edge of the artificial lake beside the Ponte delle Sirenette, a footbridge moved here in 1930 when the canal it originally crossed elsewhere in Milan was filled in. Its trunk measures 4.35 metres around and 18 metres high, and Italy's monumental tree registry lists it, along with a second specimen 1.6 kilometres away in the Giardini Montanelli, as the oldest Caucasian walnut in the city, though no source gives either tree an exact age or planting date. Compound leaves, similar in shape to an ash tree's, turn a warm gold in October and November alongside the marsh cypresses planted at the same waterline, briefly making the pond's edge the best autumn colour anywhere in the park. Visitors headed for the Castello Sforzesco or the Triennale rarely detour the extra hundred metres to the water's edge where it grows.

trees.name: Il Noce del Caucaso dell'Orto Botanico di Brera
trees.access: Free entry, Orto Botanico di Brera (Mon-Sat, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Lanza (M2) or Montenapoleone (M3)

best_time.label: June and July, when half-metre chains of winged seeds hang from every branch

trees.story: The famous trees in this garden are the two ginkgos of 1775, and neither of them is the one the state decided to protect. That honour went to a Caucasian wingnut at the back of the arboretum, declared a monumental tree of Italy on 11 February 2025, the first tree in the Orto Botanico di Brera ever to carry the designation, granted in the year the garden turned 250. Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the forests between the Black Sea and northern Iran, where it grows in ground too wet for most hardwoods, and it behaves in Milan the way it behaves at home: instead of one clean column it throws its limbs sideways into a low green dome, with a root system spreading as wide as the crown. The national register measures the trunk at 4.7 metres around and the tree at 29 metres, which makes it the tallest of the three wingnuts standing in central Milan and the only one on university ground. Its age has never been established by ring count or planting record; the university says over eighty years, which is a floor rather than a figure. In summer it hangs chains of winged green seeds half a metre long from every branch, the detail that gives the genus its name, from the Greek for wing and nut.

trees.name: Il Platano della Biodiversita
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Palestro (M1) or Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.story: Milan picked one plane tree in this park and started counting what lives on it. The city's monumental tree file calls it simply Platano VTA 43474, and it was entered into a research cycle measuring how much biodiversity a single urban tree carries in its crown and on its bark: the beetles, lichens, mosses, spiders and birds that treat 30 metres of plane tree as an address. The answer, in a city of 170,000 street and park trees, turns out to be a lot, which is why a tree with no legend attached to it now has a municipal page of its own. It stands about 30 metres tall on a trunk 1.6 metres thick, and its roots do something planes often do in compacted parkland: instead of diving, they spread flat across the surface of the root plate like poured wax. The city built a low wooden fence around the base purely to keep service vehicles off them. Its main limbs join the trunk at weak, narrow angles, so rather than shorten them, arborists tied them back to the trunk with anchoring cables. Almost nobody walking the path notices either the fence or the cables, which is the point of both.

trees.name: Il Noce del Caucaso dei Giardini Montanelli
trees.age: age undocumented, among the oldest of its species in Milan
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Turati (M3) or Palestro (M1)

best_time.label: late October, when the long compound leaves turn butter yellow

trees.story: Milan has three Caucasian wingnuts worth crossing town for, and this is the widest of them: 5.5 metres around, against 4.7 in the Brera botanical garden and 4.35 for the better-known specimen leaning over the pond in Parco Sempione. The city's own arborists pair this tree with the Sempione one as the two oldest of their species in Milan, which is as close to a date as anyone has put on either. It is a squat, wide, low tree rather than a tall one, 20 metres at most, because Pterocarya fraxinifolia spends its growth on width and on suckers: left alone it throws up new shoots from the base until a single tree reads as a thicket. Ash-like compound leaves, sometimes 60 centimetres long, turn butter yellow in late October. The species arrived in European gardens from the Caucasus and northern Iran in the early 1780s, brought back by a French botanist who found it growing in the wet forests south of the Caspian, and Milan planted it in parks for the same reason it planted bald cypress: land near ornamental water needed trees that would not sulk with wet feet. Walk the gardens' western edge toward Via Manin and it is the broad, many-stemmed one nobody photographs.

trees.name: Il Platano del Giardino Bazlen
trees.access: Free, public garden with a playground
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Crocetta (M3), or tram 16 along Corso di Porta Romana
trees.story: The garden is named after the two men who invented Adelphi, and the tree is the only thing in it older than the publishing house. Roberto Bazlen and Luciano Foa founded Adelphi Edizioni in Milan in 1962; the small green square off Corso di Porta Romana that carries their names is mostly a children's playground now, and this plane is the last big tree left standing in it. Its top was cut out at some point, which took metres off its height and left it stockier than it should be, but the trunk is still 1.95 metres thick, wide enough that the whole playground arranges itself around the base. The city is blunt about what happens next. Wood-decaying fungi have colonised the trunk and cannot be removed, so the tree is inspected at the collar and at every branch join, and the municipal page states plainly that it will be kept for as long as its presence does not create a safety problem over the play area beneath it. That is an unusually honest sentence to publish about a monument, and it is the reason to go now rather than eventually. Planes tolerate Milan's air better than almost anything else, which is how this one outlasted every other large tree on its own block.

trees.name: Il Platano Siamese di Villa Litta
trees.age: age undocumented, planted with the villa's 18th-century park
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Affori FN (M3) or Affori Centro (M3)

best_time.label: January, when the leaves are off and the two fused trunks and their cables are fully visible

trees.story: Two plane trees grew close enough together here that they stopped being two. Their roots fused, then part of their trunks, then their crowns interlaced, and the result is catalogued by the city as one tree, Platano VTA 9595, nicknamed the Siamese. It reaches 34 metres, and the reason the city protects it has less to do with size than with occupancy. Colonies of ring-necked parakeets and starlings nest in its cavities, crows keep a nest in the crown, and until a few years ago the large hollow on the north trunk held a Great Grey Owl, a bird whose natural range is the boreal forest of Lapland and Siberia. Woodpeckers drill the trunk for the insect larvae that come with rotting heartwood, and those holes are also the clearest sign of what is happening inside: the city writes that the tree is at the end of its biological cycle, its internal decay advanced, its stability worse than it was, the heavy steel cables binding the two trunks together recently replaced. It stands 300 metres from the Pianta of Affori, in a park the Litta family laid out in the second half of the 1700s, and a visit is worth making sooner rather than later.

trees.name: Il Platano di Piazza Sant'Ambrogio
trees.access: Free, public square outside the Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Sant'Ambrogio (M2)
trees.story:
This plane tree joined Italy's national register of monumental trees in November 2025, which makes it one of the newest protected trees in the country and one of the taller ones in Milan. It stands 34 metres on a trunk 4.2 metres around, in the square in front of the Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio. Regione Lombardia announced it in a batch of 48 new entries that took the region's total to 476 recognised specimens.

Its age has never been published. Italy's national register carries girth and height and no field for years, and no city document or newspaper survey has filled the gap, so the only honest handle is size. A London Plane of this girth in Milan is usually somewhere in its second century, and the range given here is exactly that: an estimate read off a tape measure, not a record.

What it stands over is dated to the year. The basilica behind it was founded in 379 by Ambrose himself, and the low brick building with two unequal towers that you see today is the eleventh and twelfth-century replacement. Against that clock the tree is a newcomer. Against any other it is old.

It is also the tree most often photographed by accident in this city, sitting in the background of everybody's picture of the church, while being the reason the square has any shade at all.

trees.name: Il Platano di Viale Cervantes
trees.access: Free, public park (Parco Sempione, opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Cadorna (M1/M2) or Arco della Pace tram stop
trees.story:
Parco Sempione is the most walked park in Milan, and this tree only entered the national register of monumental trees in November 2025. It stands on Viale Cervantes at 33 metres, on a trunk 3.9 metres around, one of 48 Lombard trees designated in a single announcement that took the region past 476 protected specimens.

Its age is not on record. Italy's register lists girth and height and leaves the years blank, and no local survey has ever dated this one, so the two numbers on the tape are the only figures that describe it honestly: 390 centimetres around, 33 metres up. Everything past that is inference from size, and inference is the right word for it.

Where it stands is more interesting than what it measures. Viale Cervantes runs through the park between the Castello Sforzesco at one end and the Arco della Pace at the other, which makes it a route rather than a destination, and almost everyone on it is going somewhere else. The same avenue carries the Caucasian Wingnut that bends out low over the park's pond, close enough that the two are a single short walk. Between them they make this stretch the part of Sempione worth slowing down for, which is not how most people use it. It is 33 metres of reason to stop.

trees.name: Il Platano dei 34 Metri ai Giardini Montanelli
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Palestro (M1) or Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.story:
Depending on which document you trust, this is either one of the two tallest trees in Milan or simply one of the taller ones. Il Giorno's survey of the city's monumental trees calls 34 metres the greatest height reached by any plant in Milan and names two plane trees that get there, one at Villa Litta and this one, off via Palestro. Italy's national register separately lists a Villa Litta plane at 43 metres. The title is contested, and that is worth saying rather than picking a side.

The measurement of this tree is not contested: 475 centimetres around the trunk, 34 metres tall. Its age is blank. The national register has no field for years and no newspaper or municipal file has dated it, so girth and height are the only honest numbers here.

It is also not the famous tree in these gardens. That is the plane with the 8.36-metre trunk, dated to 239 years, which grew outwards into five limbs instead of upwards. This one did the opposite. It has a second registered plane nearby at 32 metres, plus a bald cypress, a Mediterranean hackberry and a Caucasian wingnut: six register-listed monumental trees inside one set of railings, in a park first laid out in 1784.

Nobody stops for this one, because in company like that, being the tallest is not conspicuous. Look up rather than at the trunk.

trees.name: The Archdevil of Villa Marietti Radice Fossati
trees.access: Free. The villa buildings are a lived-in community and the park around them is not: the Comune di Milano, which owns the villa, states on its own page for this tree that with the discretion due to an inhabited place you may pass through the gate and visit the park.
trees.transport: Short walk from Milano Villapizzone railway station
trees.story:
The comune's own page for this hackberry calls it arcidiavolo, the archdevil, after a folk tale that blamed its hooked leaves on Lucifer, said to have carried the species down from heaven clutched in his claws. The city's monumental-tree list is usually a good deal drier than that.

The tree stands in the park of Villa Marietti Radice Fossati, in Villapizzone, northwest of the centre. The villa was given its rural character by the Radice Fossati family, fell into disrepair through the 1970s, and was pulled back out of it by a small experimental community of Jesuit fathers. The Comune di Milano took ownership in 1993 and confirmed the community's loan of the buildings, which have been residential ever since. So the buildings are somebody's home and the park around them is not, and the city says plainly that with the discretion due to an inhabited place you may pass through the gate and visit the park.

The trunk measures 4.2 metres round and the crown spreads more than 20 metres, throwing shade over roughly 200 square metres by the comune's reckoning. Its roots, structure and vegetative state are all recorded as good, and nothing on record says the tree has ever needed work. Nobody has published an age for it, only that girth, among the largest for the species anywhere in Milan.

trees.name: Il Platano di Viale Montesanto
trees.access: Free. A street tree on the public pavement, reachable at any hour
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Repubblica (M3), or about 12 min from Porta Garibaldi FS (M2, M5)
trees.story:
A newspaper survey of Milan's monumental trees once put the city's ceiling at 34 metres. Italy's national register disagrees in several places, and this plane is one of them: 38 metres, growing at a street number rather than in a park.

It stands outside Viale Montesanto 4 to 6, on the ring of boulevards that traces the line of Milan's sixteenth-century Spanish walls, on the stretch between Porta Garibaldi and the Giardini Montanelli. The register gives the trunk at 5.25 metres round. The city's celebrated plane, the Platano di Indro in the Giardini Montanelli, carries 8.36 metres and spent it going sideways into five limbs. This one had a pavement, a road and a row of facades, so it went up.

Nobody has published an age for it. The national register carries girth and height and keeps no field for years, and no municipal file or local survey has filled the gap for this particular tree, so the tape measure is the only evidence there is. If you know when this stretch of the viale was planted, tell us and we will say so.

There is no gate and no opening time. You walk the pavement to number 4 and look up until the crown closes over the road.

trees.name: Il Platano di Piazzale Libia
trees.access: Free. A public street tree on the square, reachable at any hour
trees.transport: About 8 min walk east from Porta Romana (M3), or 12 min north from Lodi T.I.B.B. (M3)
trees.story:
Milan's best known plane trees stop at 34 metres. This one is 35, and it is standing in the middle of a traffic square.

Piazzale Libia lies about a kilometre out from Porta Romana in the south-east of the city, a junction broad enough to have kept room in the middle of it for a tree this size. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists the plane there at 35 metres on a trunk 4 metres round. That is taller than the register's own entry for the plane in front of the Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio and taller than the one in the Giardini Montanelli that a local survey named among the tallest plants in Milan.

Street planes almost never get the chance. Across Italy they are cut back on a cycle to clear the wires and the balconies, and a plane that has been topped does not come back to a height like this. Whatever else was done to this tree, nobody took its crown out.

Its age is not recorded anywhere. The national register measures girth and height and stops there, and no other document names this tree at all, so the years are simply missing. Anyone who knows when the square was planted can close that gap for us.

Nothing to pay and nothing to open. Cross at the lights, stand under it, and work out how much of the sky it is holding up.

trees.name: The Plane of Viale Vittorio Veneto 3
trees.access: Free, street tree on the public boulevard (Bastioni) near Porta Venezia.
trees.transport: About 300 m northeast of the Giardini Indro Montanelli cluster, on foot.
trees.story:
A story went round Milan in 2018 that the big plane on Viale Vittorio Veneto, growing in the old tram-line median near Porta Venezia, had dried out and been cut down. It probably wasn't this one. That felled tree measured about three metres round; this one, still standing at the same address, measures 5.70 metres, nearly double, too large a gap to be the same trunk misremembered. The register lists this plane as one of the largest in the city by girth, 36 metres tall.

Viale Vittorio Veneto runs along the Bastioni, the boulevard laid over Milan's old Spanish city walls after they came down, three hundred metres from the plane trees and monuments of the Giardini Indro Montanelli. No source beyond the register names this specific tree, so its age and any history particular to it stay unrecorded.

It grows as a street tree on the public boulevard, free to see at any hour, no gate and no ticket. If you know anything about its planting, or about the tree that really was felled here in 2018, tell us.

trees.name: The Transplanted Olive of La Concepcion
trees.access: Paid entry, Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion
trees.transport: Bus from city centre to the garden entrance on Camino del Jardin Botanico

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: This olive did not grow where it now stands. It was dug up whole in Velez-Malaga, a town roughly 40km east along the coast, and moved into the Mediterranean plant collection of the Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion, where it has continued growing as if nothing happened. The garden itself began in 1855, built by the Marquises of Casa Loring on a former farm estate, and later expanded by the Echevarria-Echevarrieta family before its 1943 declaration as a historic garden, but this olive predates all of that by centuries: the garden's own estimate puts it at roughly 400 years old, a trunk perimeter of 3.30 metres marking the slow accumulation of growth rings no one has counted directly, since felling a living tree to check would defeat the point. Olives resist precise dating the way most ancient trees do, hollowing and regrowing from their own base over centuries, which makes any figure an estimate rather than a measurement. What is certain is the transplant itself, a considerable feat of tree-moving for a specimen this size, undertaken to bring one of the region's oldest surviving olives into a collection built specifically to house trees too remarkable to leave where they were found.

trees.name: The Ficus Avenue of the Alameda Principal
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Malaga Centro-Alameda tram/metro station, or 5 min walk from Plaza de la Marina
trees.story: Malaga's central promenade has had three different trees in its 240-year history, and the ones standing today were themselves meant to be temporary. The Alameda was laid out in 1783 with white poplars, which gave the street its name (alameda meaning poplar grove), later replaced with orange trees and oleanders. Those in turn came out in 1876, when architect Joaquin Rucoba's renovation brought in large-format ficus from India, Ficus microcarpa, known locally as laurel de indias. Nobody expected the imports to become the defining feature of the street, but 150 years on, their broad, wind-flattened canopies form a continuous green roof over the traffic below, dense enough that Malaguenos still call the shade underneath one of the coolest places in the city centre in August. Twenty-three of the original mature specimens survive today alongside younger replacements, and when Malaga built a metro line beneath the Alameda in 2018 and 2019, the works were designed specifically to protect their roots, removing traffic lanes rather than digging near the trunks. It remains one of the few 19th century streetscapes in Spain where the accidental choice, not the planned one, is the thing everyone remembers.

trees.name: El Barrilito
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Plaza de la Marina

best_time.label: February into May, when the barrel-shaped trunk sits beneath a canopy of cream-white flowers

trees.story: Everyone in Malaga who has walked past this tree calls it by its nickname rather than its species: El Barrilito, the little barrel, for a trunk so swollen it looks less like wood than like something inflated. Ceiba chodatii stores water in that trunk to survive its native South American dry season, and this specimen has taken the adaptation further than most, measured in April 2022 at 5.86 metres around at chest height, a girth that local tree enthusiasts consider possibly the thickest of its kind anywhere in Spain or continental Europe, a claim no national register has settled outright. It grows in the Jardines de Alfonso Canales, a small formal garden between Calle Vendeja and Plaza de la Marina named for the Malaga-born poet, where a bronze bust of Canales was installed beside the tree in 2007. For a period the tree stood behind a protective fence, removed in 2009, and it now shares its plaza with a set of bright red benches from a public art project, an odd but fitting pairing for a tree whose entire appeal is how strange it looks. In 2022 the city tagged it as one of ten singular trees under a European urban-tree awareness campaign, one of six on this list to carry that same designation.

trees.name: The Floss Silk Tree of Cortina del Muelle
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Malaga Cathedral

best_time.label: October into November, when it drops its leaves and flowers pink at the same time

trees.story: This tree survived a construction project by becoming part of the construction. When the streets around Malaga Cathedral were remodelled roughly a decade ago, most of what stood in the way came out. This Ceiba speciosa, a South American species closely related to the Barrilito across town but distinguished by its spinier bark and paler, pink-tinged flowers, did not: engineers built an elevated planter bed around its base instead, integrating a 23-metre tree into the finished streetscape rather than removing it. The result is a strange piece of urban furniture, a raised stone ring on a historic pedestrian street with a substantial tropical tree growing straight out of the middle of it, steps from the cathedral that gives Cortina del Muelle its foot traffic. Malaga tagged it in 2022 as one of ten singular trees under the city's TreeTags scheme, citing its height and its unusually deliberate preservation as the reasons for the designation. No individual age or planting date survives for this specimen, honestly left as an estimate rather than guessed.

trees.name: The Fig of the Picasso Gardens
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Malaga Centro-Alameda station
trees.story: This fig predates the garden built around it by decades. The Jardines de Picasso opened in 1981, laid out in a symmetrical petal pattern to mark the centenary of Picasso's birth in the city, but its two oldest Ficus macrophylla were already mature trees when the ground beneath them was formally landscaped, their aerial roots by then thick enough to rise nearly a metre clear of the soil. The city's own tagging scheme describes the pair as centenarian and among the largest of their kind found anywhere in Europe, a claim offered here with the same caution this site applies to any superlative no national register has independently confirmed. Between the two trees stands Siextasis, a sculpture by Malaga-born artist Miguel Ortiz Berrocal, better known for puzzle-like bronzes that separate into dozens of interlocking pieces, placed there as the garden's own tribute to Picasso. The pairing gives Jardines de Picasso an odd distinction: a public garden where the trees are older than the art dedicated to the city's most famous painter, and both were already there before the garden had a name.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Cypress Cottage
trees.access: Paid entry, Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion
trees.transport: Bus from city centre to the garden entrance on Camino del Jardin Botanico
trees.story: Hackberry wood was cheap and ordinary enough that for centuries nobody thought to plant it for looks: it went into barrel staves, walking sticks, fishing rods and farm tools, and children used its small dark berries as ammunition for peashooters, the kind of tree valued for use rather than admired for size. This one at La Concepcion grew past all of that. Standing beside a building the garden calls the Casita de los Cipreses (Cypress Cottage), it now measures roughly 24 metres tall with a trunk 3.72 metres around, dimensions the garden's own record and an independent tree-history blog both describe as probably the largest and best-preserved hackberry anywhere in Malaga province. Celtis australis can live to six hundred years in the right conditions, which makes this specimen, at an estimated two centuries old, still comfortably short of its own species' ceiling. It grows within a botanical collection assembled since 1855 specifically to bring together trees too large or too rare to encounter anywhere else nearby, and next to the garden's showier imports, palms and figs from three continents, this unglamorous, useful species holds its own purely on scale.

trees.name: The Tallest Araucaria in the Province
trees.access: Paid entry, Jardin Botanico-Historico La Concepcion
trees.transport: Bus from city centre to the garden entrance on Camino del Jardin Botanico
trees.story: Araucaria heterophylla has been growing on earth since the Triassic, more than 200 million years, long enough to have shared the planet with the first dinosaurs, though the specimen standing beside La Concepcion's waterfall is a considerably more recent arrival. Native to a single small Pacific island roughly 1,600km east of Australia, the species became a fashionable planting in Malaga's gardens in the mid-19th century, when ship traffic and colonial-era plant collecting made previously unreachable species suddenly available to anyone with land and money. This one has been growing for close to two centuries since, long enough to reach 46 metres, the tallest confirmed araucaria anywhere in Malaga province according to the garden's own record. Its form is the reason the species was ever fashionable in the first place: branches arranged in perfectly regular tiers around a single straight trunk, giving young and old specimens alike a symmetry that looks almost designed rather than grown. Ships once used the trunks of related araucaria species for their main masts, a practical use this ornamental specimen, standing landlocked beside a garden waterfall, will never see.

trees.name: The Native Oak of Malaga Park
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Plaza de la Marina
trees.story: Almost everything remarkable in Malaga's tree canon arrived from somewhere else: Australia, South America, India, the Himalayas. This holm oak did not. Quercus ilex is the tree of the native Andalusian forest, the species that would dominate this coastline's hills if centuries of farming, grazing and building had not cleared most of it away, and its presence in Parque de Malaga reads less as a planting choice than as a reminder of what stood here before the park did. The park itself only exists because 19th century Malaga reclaimed land from the sea, built on a stretch of shoreline formerly occupied by a fortress esplanade, and filled with species from five continents once the 1896 development law inspired by Canovas del Castillo cleared the way. Amid that deliberately exotic collection, palms, dragon trees, ficus, jacarandas, this encina stands out for being ordinary in the best sense: 19 metres tall, 0.9 metres in trunk diameter, unremarkable anywhere else in Andalusia and quietly notable here for being the one tree in the city's own 2022 singular-trees list that actually belongs to this coastline.

trees.name: The Rare Cassia of Malaga Park
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Plaza de la Marina
trees.story: Parque de Malaga holds roughly 300 different tree species across its 3.3 hectares, a density built deliberately when the park was landscaped on reclaimed harbour ground at the turn of the 20th century, and Peltophorum dubium is one of its genuine rarities, a South American species uncommon enough in Spanish cultivation that the city's own 2022 tagging campaign singled it out specifically for being unusual rather than for size or age. In its native Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, the species is known as cana fistula, valued for durable timber and for the sprays of small yellow flowers it produces along the humid riverbanks it prefers. Malaga's specimen has adapted to considerably drier conditions than its home range, growing to 13 metres with a trunk half a metre across, modest dimensions next to some of the park's giant ficus and araucarias but enough to have earned its own identifying plaque under the same European urban-tree scheme that tagged the Barrilito and the Cortina del Muelle ceiba. It stands as one small proof of the park's original ambition: not simply a green space, but a working plant collection assembled from five continents and still, more than a century later, capable of surprising a visitor who thinks they know what a Spanish city park should look like.

trees.name: The Avocado of Ciudad de Jaen School
trees.access: Restricted: working school grounds, visits by prior appointment only
trees.transport: Bus to Churriana, Calle Torremolinos
trees.story: Malaga and neighbouring Granada now grow nine of every ten avocados sold in Spain, an industry whose roots trace back to Churriana, a district in the city's southwest better known today for hosting the airport than for starting a national crop. Early avocado trees reached this coastline in the mid-19th century, brought back by travellers with ties to Cuba and the Americas and planted first as curiosities on private estates rather than as a business. This tree, growing in the courtyard of a working primary school, is one of the survivors from that early period, tagged by the city in 2022 as one of ten singular trees and described in that designation as among the first avocado specimens brought to Malaga, more than 150 years old and still standing roughly 11 metres tall inside a low protective wall. The school's parents' association has taken its name directly from the tree, calling itself AMPA Aguacate, and generations of Churriana schoolchildren have grown up eating lunch in its shade decades before avocado became the crop that now defines the region's agriculture. It is not freely open to the public: visiting means contacting the school directly and arranging a time, an honest limitation for a tree that otherwise has one of the best stories on this list.

trees.name: The McGill Law Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, on open McGill University campus grounds; the law faculty's outdoor grounds are publicly walkable
trees.transport: McGill or Peel metro station, roughly 10-15 minute walk uphill

best_time.label: late October, when the whole crown turns gold and drops within days

trees.story:
Asked to name the most remarkable tree in Montreal, a botanist who has spent twenty-five years looking for them picked this one, standing on a lawn beside the McGill law faculty.

Suzanne Hardy's case for it is partly the tree and partly who put it there. She believes it is likely the first ginkgo of its kind planted in Montreal, and that it went in about 120 years ago at the hands of the Olmsted family. Frederick Law Olmsted laid out Mont-Royal Park, the hill this ginkgo sits at the foot of, so the tree and the mountain above it come from the same drawing office. Six of the seven trees on this page are up on that hill. This one waits at the bottom of it.

The age is her estimate rather than a measurement. Nobody has published a girth, there is no plaque, and the pin marks the corner of Peel Street and Doctor Penfield Avenue rather than the trunk itself; the Chancellor Day Hall grounds are open to walk through and it is not a large lawn.
