Legend credits the original planting to Saint Benedict of Norcia in the 5th or 6th century, using land donated for the monastery, and whether or not that founding story is literal, a plane tree of real age genuinely dominated this cloister for centuries, reaching a documented 8.45 metres in trunk circumference before termite damage forced its removal in 1959. Rather than replant from scratch, the monastery let the stump regrow from its own root system, so the tree visible today, now well past six decades old itself, is a direct continuation of the original rather than an unrelated replacement, a distinction this site is careful to draw clearly. The cloister itself, the oldest part of the complex, dates to the 10th century and carries a cycle of early 16th century frescoes depicting Saint Benedict's life on two of its four walls. The complex now houses Naples's State Archive, and the cloister remains publicly accessible during archive opening hours.

trees.name: The Pine of Posillipo
trees.access: Free, public hillside street
trees.transport: Bus C31 to Posillipo, or 20 min walk from Mergellina
trees.story: For roughly a century, one pine tree on a hillside above Mergellina was arguably the single most photographed tree on earth, framed against the Bay of Naples and Vesuvius in postcards, oil paintings and tourist snapshots from the late 19th century clear through the 1970s, an image so ubiquitous it became visual shorthand for the entire city. That original stone pine, which grew tall enough to be visible from the water sometime after 1855, was felled in 1984 after a terminal disease left no realistic option to save it, ending a run of well over a century as Naples's most recognisable living landmark. The hillside did not stay bare. In 1995 the environmental group Legambiente planted a new stone pine on the same spot near the church of Sant'Antonio a Posillipo, an act the organisation still marks the anniversary of every year, treating the replanting itself as worth remembering rather than something to quietly gloss over. The tree visible today is that younger pine, honestly labelled here as a replacement rather than the storied original, standing on a hillside that still frames one of the most photographed views in Italy.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of the Villa Comunale
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza del Plebiscito or the Chiaia seafront
trees.story: Naples's seafront garden holds five of the twenty-six trees the Campania region has catalogued as monumental across the whole city, and this Oriental plane, standing beside the Fontana dei Leoni near the garden's street boundary, is among the most substantial: 18 metres tall with a trunk 428cm across. The Villa Comunale itself dates to the years of French rule in the early 19th century, when Naples answered to Joseph Bonaparte and then Joachim Murat, and its planting scheme, planes alongside weeping willows, citrus and acacias, followed instructions traceable to that Bonapartist administration rather than to the Bourbon court that had governed the city before and would again after. The garden runs along the Chiaia waterfront between the sea and the city's grand 19th century apartment blocks, and this plane is one of three catalogued specimens of its species growing within it, alongside one monumental eucalyptus and a single giant palm that share the same official protected status.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Sant'Andrea delle Dame
trees.access: Free, university building courtyard (check faculty opening hours)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Napoli Museo metro
trees.story: Four 16th century Neapolitan noblewomen, sisters who took religious vows together, founded the convent whose cloister now holds this holm oak, one of two trees the site is best known for alongside a camphor said to have been planted by Joachim Murat during his brief reign as King of Naples. At 24 metres, the oak is the taller of the pair and the more anonymously documented, no individual planting date or attributed founder the way the camphor has, simply a long-established presence in a cloister garden enclosed by piperno stone arcades and rows of Washingtonia palms locally reckoned the tallest in the city. The convent the sisters founded in 1580 has since become the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli, and the cloister, once a place of enclosed religious life, now sits inside a working university building, its centuries-old wooded garden intact around students and staff rather than nuns. Quercus ilex is Mediterranean by origin, evergreen year round, and slow enough growing that a specimen this size represents a very long, very undocumented stretch of the site's history.

trees.name: The Cretan Palm That Came Back From a War
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily from 7am
trees.transport: Bus C63 or 178 to Capodimonte, then in through the Porta Grande
trees.story: This palm arrived in Naples as a war souvenir. Campania's regional register records it as a ricordo di guerra, brought back during Italy's military campaigns in the eastern Mediterranean in the early 1900s, which is how a tree endemic to Crete and a handful of Aegean islands came to stand a few steps inside the main gate of a Bourbon hunting park. Phoenix theophrasti is one of only two palms native to Europe, the other being the dwarf fan palm of the western Mediterranean. It is named for Theophrastus, the Greek who wrote the first surviving books on plants around 300 BC, and in the wild it clings on in a few dozen ravines and beaches on Crete and the Turkish coast. This one does something its species is not supposed to do. The trunk divides low down into several stems, which the register calls atypical for the genus and which is how you pick it out from every other palm in the park. It stands sixteen metres and measures 3.8 metres round, a figure the national and regional registers give identically. The register put its age at 100 years when the record was compiled, so read it as a little over a century now.

trees.name: The Paperbark of the Garden of the Princes
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily from 7am. The Garden of the Princes reopened to visitors in June 2025 after restoration
trees.transport: Bus C63 or 178 to Capodimonte, or a 20 minute uphill walk from Museo metro station
trees.story: At 75 centimetres round, this is the slenderest tree Italy's monumental register lists anywhere in Naples, and it is on the list for what it is rather than for how big it got. The museum calls it a true rarity and says it grows in the Bourbon royal sites of Naples and effectively nowhere else in the country, planted here in the middle of the nineteenth century. Melaleuca styphelioides comes from the east coast of Australia, and the whole point of it is the bark. It builds in hundreds of thin papery layers, cream and pale brown, soft enough to press a thumb into, and it lifts off in sheets you could write on. Aboriginal Australians used exactly that: as bandaging, as roofing, as a wrapping for food cooked in ground ovens. The leaves are small and sharp, which is where the name prickly paperbark comes from, and in summer the tree carries short cream flowers like a bottlebrush. It stands nine metres, which for the species is respectable. Do not walk up looking for something monumental in the usual sense. This one asks you to come close and put a hand on the trunk.

trees.name: The False Kapok of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, no booking. Open weekdays only: Mon, Wed, Fri 9:00-14:00, Tue and Thu 9:00-16:00, closed Saturday and Sunday
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cavour or Museo metro, or bus along Via Foria

best_time.label: October and November, when the bare crown fills with pink flowers

trees.story:
Naples has 53 entries on Italy's national monumental register and this one has the widest trunk of the lot. What you actually walk up to is not the single swollen bottle the species is famous for. It is four or five enormous stems rising together out of one fused base, smooth and grey-green, leaning gently apart like a hand opening. The 880 centimetres the national register records is a measurement taken around the whole of that base; Campania's regional register says 800. Either figure wins.

Ceiba speciosa comes from Brazil, Peru and Argentina, a relative of the kapok whose pods split open into silky white floss. Young trees arm themselves with fat conical spines and shed most of them as the bark stretches, which is why this one is smooth everywhere you can reach. The leaves repay a look as well: five to seven pointed leaflets spreading from one stalk like fingers.

Come in October or November. The crown fills with big five-petalled flowers, pink at the tips and streaked yellow towards the throat, and since the leaves are going at roughly the same time the flowers end up sitting on bare wood. They drop in quantity, so the grass underneath turns pink well before the tree above has finished.

It has stood here more than a century, through the years the Allies used this garden as a barracks, a car park and a football pitch.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, no booking. Open weekdays only: Mon, Wed, Fri 9:00-14:00, Tue and Thu 9:00-16:00, closed Saturday and Sunday
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cavour or Museo metro, or bus along Via Foria

best_time.label: late November, when the fans turn flat gold and drop almost together

trees.story:
Every other tree on this walk came to Naples as a novelty from somewhere far away. This one is a survivor from somewhere far back. Ginkgo biloba is the last living member of a lineage that covered the planet before flowering plants existed, and it now grows wild in two small pockets of eastern China and nowhere else on earth. Everything else its family ever produced is a fossil, which is why the garden's own notes call it a living one.

The specimen here is three metres round and sixteen tall, and the national and regional registers agree on both figures exactly. Its age is recorded as more than a hundred years and nothing tighter, because nobody planted it with a note.

Come in the second half of November. Ginkgo leaves are small stiff fans, split down the middle, held on long stalks, and they do not fade through brown the way most leaves do. They go from green to a flat saturated yellow, hold it for roughly a fortnight, and then let go, often most of the tree inside a day or two after the first hard night. What is left is a gold circle on the ground the exact width of the crown, which is worth the walk on its own. The garden singles the leaves out as its reason to visit in winter.

trees.name: The Crenate Oak of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, no booking. Open weekdays only: Mon, Wed, Fri 9:00-14:00, Tue and Thu 9:00-16:00, closed Saturday and Sunday
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cavour or Museo metro, or bus along Via Foria
trees.story:
This oak is two species at once. Quercus crenata is the natural hybrid of the Turkey oak and the cork oak, and Italian calls it cerro-sughera after both parents in turn. It appears wherever the two grow within pollen range of each other, it is never common, and it does not breed true, so most specimens are one-offs rather than a population.

You can read the parentage off the tree. The bark thickens and cracks into something approaching the cork oak's spongy layer, never quite as deep, but soft enough to press a thumb into. The leaves settle the question: shallow rounded teeth all around the margin, which is what crenata describes, and a habit of hanging on through the winter instead of dropping cleanly, so from December to March the tree is half evergreen and looks undecided about it.

At 440 centimetres round and 18 metres it is one of the widest trunks the registers record inside this garden. Both of them list it and neither can agree what to call it. The national register writes Quercus crenata, the regional one writes Quercus hispanica, which is the older umbrella name for crosses between the same two parents. An argument about what to call a hybrid is roughly the argument a hybrid deserves.

trees.name: The Blue Gum of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, no booking. Open weekdays only: Mon, Wed, Fri 9:00-14:00, Tue and Thu 9:00-16:00, closed Saturday and Sunday
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cavour or Museo metro, or bus along Via Foria
trees.story:
Thirty metres, which makes this the tallest tree the registers record inside the garden, and the reason it stands here at all is a nineteenth century medical theory that turned out to be wrong.

Eucalyptus globulus was planted across southern Europe from the 1860s onward because it grows fast, drinks enormously, and was believed to dry marshy ground and so drive out malaria. Some authorities went further and credited the aromatic oil in its leaves with cleaning the air. The drinking part was real. The rest was not, since malaria is carried by mosquitoes rather than by bad air, which is what the word literally means. By the time that was settled the tree had been planted from Portugal to the Caucasus, and it is now the most widely grown eucalyptus on the planet.

This one measures 440 centimetres round. Look for two completely different leaves on the same tree. Young shoots carry rounded stalkless pairs clasped around the stem, coated in a waxy bloom that reads as pale blue, which is where the name comes from. The mature crown carries long dark sickles that hang edge-on to the sun, so a tree this size throws almost no shade. Crush one between your fingers and the smell arrives instantly, sharp and medicinal, the oil the nineteenth century was banking on.

trees.name: The Chilean Wine Palm of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, no booking. Open weekdays only: Mon, Wed, Fri 9:00-14:00, Tue and Thu 9:00-16:00, closed Saturday and Sunday
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cavour or Museo metro, or bus along Via Foria
trees.story:
This palm was very nearly drunk out of existence. Jubaea chilensis carries one of the thickest trunks of any palm on earth, and that trunk is full of sweet sap. Chilean producers spent the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries felling mature wild palms in order to tap them, boiling the sap down into a syrup sold as palm honey and taking the crop of small coconuts as a bonus. A tapped palm never recovers, because a palm has exactly one growing point and it sits at the top. Groves that once ran to millions of trees were cut back to a few thousand hectares, and the species is now protected at home and listed as threatened.

It is also one of the slowest palms there is. A seedling can spend a decade doing nothing visible before it starts building a trunk at all, which is how this one is only four metres tall after more than a century, while measuring 250 centimetres around. The garden calls it a splendid specimen and grows younger ones near it.

Stand close and look at the trunk rather than up at the crown. It is smooth, grey and straight-sided, marked all over with the diamond scars of fronds that dropped a very long time ago.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of the Principessa Jolanda Gardens
trees.access: Free, inside the Real Bosco di Capodimonte's outdoor grounds, in the Giardini della Principessa Jolanda section reached by the monumental staircase off Salita di Capodimonte
trees.transport: Bus C63/178 to Capodimonte, or 20 min uphill walk from Museo Nazionale metro

best_time.label: August to October: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story:
A monumental plane on this same staircase was destroyed by a storm in 2022. The cedar of Lebanon beside it is still standing, and confirming that was most of the work of getting it onto this page.

It grows in the Giardini della Principessa Jolanda, a corner of the Real Bosco di Capodimonte laid out in the 1830s on the hill above the city. Both registers that carry it, the national one and Campania's own card, agree on the measurements to the centimetre: 4.18 metres round, 18 metres tall. Neither gives an age, and the garden's own layout date is not the tree's, so the years stay blank rather than borrowed.

What settled it was the museum's own page about the garden, written after the 2025 restoration reopened it, which names a splendid cedro del Libano among the specimens standing in the grounds today. Present tense, current document, which is exactly the evidence an old register entry cannot give you.

Cedars of Lebanon were the status tree of nineteenth-century European estate planting, imported for the flat tiered silhouette that reads as ancient long before the tree is. This one has had nearly two centuries of Neapolitan sun to grow into that shape, and it is a short walk from the palace itself if you are coming for the Caravaggio.

trees.name: The Podocarpus of Piazza Cavour
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Museo or Cavour metro station, 2 min walk
trees.story:
There are two of these in Piazza Cavour and one of them is lying down. The register carries the upright one, 25 metres tall with a trunk 2.42 metres round; the other, nicknamed il Podocarpo sdraiato, the reclining podocarpus, toppled and went on living horizontally, and was struck off the regional register for it.

So identifying this tree matters more than usual, and the identification is solid: a photograph on Wikimedia Commons from 2018 carries coordinates a few metres from the register's point and shows a single tall upright trunk under a full crown, which is the standing tree and not its fallen neighbour.

Podocarpus macrophyllus is not a pine despite its English name. It is a southern conifer from China and Japan, with long strap-shaped leaves rather than needles, and it carries its seeds on a swollen fleshy stalk that turns purple and is the only part of the plant that is not toxic. Birds take them; the seed itself they leave.

Neither register gives it an age. It stands in a working square above the Museo metro station, two minutes from the National Archaeological Museum, which makes it the easiest tree on this page to add to a day you were already having.

trees.name: The Eucalyptus of the Villa Comunale
trees.access: Free, public park (Villa Comunale), open 07:00-22:00 daily, last entry half an hour before closing
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza del Plebiscito or the Chiaia seafront, near the Piazza Vittoria end of the park
trees.story:
Six metres seventy-six round the trunk, which makes this the thickest tree on Naples' own register. It stands in the Villa Comunale, the long public garden on the seafront at Chiaia, against the fence on the right as you come in from the Riviera di Chiaia gate.

Both registers agree on it exactly, the national list and Campania's own card: 6.76 metres of girth, 25 metres of height. A river red gum, Eucalyptus camaldulensis, which in Australia grows along seasonal watercourses and is the most widely planted eucalypt on earth, chosen everywhere in the nineteenth century for the speed at which it turns wet ground into timber.

A claim follows this tree around the tourism sites, that it was the first eucalyptus planted in Europe, in 1805. It may well be, and none of those pages says where the date comes from, so it is not on this page as a fact. If you can point at a source, we would like it. Neither register carries an age at all.

The garden itself was laid out in 1697 as a royal promenade and opened to the public in the nineteenth century, and it still runs a kilometre along the bay with the aquarium in the middle of it. The park closes at ten.

trees.name: The Gnarled Lime of Hallerwiese
trees.access: Free, public city park (Hallerwiese, St. Johannis district)
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified
trees.story: Lightning has struck this lime and a storm has taken pieces off it, and it is still putting on growth. Nuremberg's own survey of the city's oldest trees describes it as a gnarled linden of roughly three hundred and fifty years at the southern end of the Hallerwiese, damaged and healthy at the same time, which is a fair summary of what that many centuries do to something that cannot move. It is protected as ND-5 on the city's 2020 natural monument ordinance. What nobody has settled is which lime it is. German parks of this period were planted with three of them almost interchangeably, summer lime, winter lime and the hybrid between the two, and no source identifies this one, so it stays a lime and goes no further. Three hundred and fifty years covers most of what happened to Nuremberg. The tree was already mature while the city was still a free imperial city answering to nobody but the emperor, and it was well over a century old when that ended in 1806 and Nuremberg was handed to Bavaria, bankrupt and stripped of its independence. Two large planes stand on the green immediately behind it, planted at close to the same time. The meadow is free and open, roughly fifteen minutes on foot from the Hauptmarkt.

trees.name: The First Plane of Hallerwiese
trees.access: Free, public city park (Hallerwiese, St. Johannis district)
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified
trees.story: The London plane is not much older than this tree. The hybrid turned up in European gardens some time in the seventeenth century, a cross between an American and an Oriental plane that nobody set out to make, and Nuremberg's survey of its oldest trees puts this one and its neighbour at over three hundred years, which places the pair within a couple of generations of the hybrid's own beginning. Both stand on the green behind the old gnarled lime, planted at close to the same moment, and both carry their own entry on the city's 2020 natural monument ordinance, this one as ND-4. The register lists them separately. The newspaper survey describes them as a pair and does not tell them apart, which is why this page does not pretend to either. What is not in question is the size. Planes put on girth faster than limes and then hold it, and three centuries on the Hallerwiese have given these two the heavy trunks that make the species recognisable from the far end of a park, bark flaking off in jigsaw plates to leave a camouflage of cream, olive and grey underneath. It is the one large tree that looks different every year in the same way. Free and open, about fifteen minutes on foot from the Hauptmarkt.

trees.name: The Second Plane of Hallerwiese
trees.access: Free, public city park (Hallerwiese, St. Johannis district)
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified
trees.story: City foresters plant planes because they are difficult to kill, and this one has had the chance to prove it. It is the second of the two large planes on the Hallerwiese, protected as ND-3, standing about forty metres from its twin and, by the city's own reckoning, over three hundred years old. Planes tolerate compacted soil, road salt, drought and smoke better than almost any other large broadleaf, which is why they line boulevards across Europe, and why this pair was still standing after the night of 2 January 1945, when an RAF raid destroyed roughly nine tenths of Nuremberg's old town on the far side of the Pegnitz. The medieval centre was rebuilt over the following decades from photographs and salvaged stone. The trees needed nothing. Nuremberg's own survey of its oldest trees treats the two planes as a pair and never separates them, while the ordinance gives each its own number, so this page keeps them as two entries while admitting they are one sight. Walk to the gnarled lime first, which is the oldest thing on the meadow, and the planes stand on the green immediately behind it. All three are within a minute of each other, free and open, about fifteen minutes on foot from the Hauptmarkt.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Kontumazgarten
trees.access: Free, public city park (Kontumazgarten, Kleinweidenmühle district), has a playground
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified

best_time.label: May, when it puts up hundreds of white candles over the playground

trees.story: This park was a quarantine station. Kontumaz is the old German word for it, and the ground here is where Nuremberg held arriving travellers and goods until the city was satisfied they carried nothing worse than themselves. It is a lawn and a playground now, and this chestnut is protected on it as ND-6 under the city's 2020 natural monument ordinance. The ordinance calls it Kastanie and leaves it there, chestnut, without saying which kind. In a planted German municipal park an unqualified Kastanie is almost always the horse chestnut rather than the sweet chestnut, so that is what this page records, on inference rather than on anyone's botanical word. No source gives it an age either. What the register does confirm is that in 2020 the city still counted it worth protecting by name, which is the most recent thing anyone has published about this tree. Come in May. Horse chestnuts flower by putting up hundreds of white candles at once, upright over the entire crown, and a mature one doing that above a children's playground is the best ten days this park has all year. By late September it is dropping conkers in spiny green cases that split open on the ground, which is the other reason children have always known this species better than adults do.

trees.name: The Founders' Plane of Kontumazgarten
trees.access: Free, public city park (Kontumazgarten, Kleinweidenmühle district), has a playground
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified
trees.story: Six individually protected trees stand on 1.7 hectares here, which is a great deal of legal attention for one small park. Kontumazgarten is a lawn, a playground and some old trees, and the city's 2020 natural monument ordinance lists ND-6 through ND-11 inside it: a chestnut, two beeches and three planes, each with its own number and its own protection. This is the first of the planes, ND-7. A Naturdenkmal is not a plaque. It is a legal designation under German conservation law that attaches to a single named object rather than to an area, and it makes cutting, damaging or altering the tree an offence, which is why a municipal park gets redesigned around a tree rather than through it. The ordinance is also the only source. It gives the species and the position and stops: no age, no girth, no description, and no article or survey names this plane on its own. So what is documented is the city's own judgement, repeated six times over in one small green, that this particular set of trees was worth writing into law. The six sit within about a hundred and fifty metres of each other, which makes the park a single stop rather than six errands. Free, open, with a playground, about fifteen minutes from the old town.

trees.name: The First Beech of Kontumazgarten
trees.access: Free, public city park (Kontumazgarten, Kleinweidenmühle district), has a playground
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified

best_time.label: late October and November, when it turns copper and holds it

trees.story: Almost nothing grows under a beech, and the tree is doing that on purpose. European beech holds its leaves in dense overlapping layers that let very little light reach the ground, so the soil beneath a mature one is usually bare and brown, which is why beech woods feel like rooms rather than thickets. This is the first of two beeches protected inside the Kontumazgarten, listed as ND-8 on Nuremberg's 2020 natural monument ordinance. The city recorded it and stopped there. No age, no measurements, no description, and no independent source names it, so the honest position is that it is old enough for a city to protect by name and nobody has published a number. The bark is the way to read a beech: it keeps a smooth grey skin for its whole life, so unlike an oak it hides nothing, and every scar, carving and old wound stays legible for decades. Come in late October or November. Beech is the best autumn tree in central Europe by some margin, turning through yellow into copper and russet and holding the colour for weeks, and young beeches keep their dead leaves right through winter instead of dropping them. The park is free, open and has a playground, about fifteen minutes on foot from Nuremberg's old town.

trees.name: The Close Plane of Kontumazgarten
trees.access: Free, public city park (Kontumazgarten, Kleinweidenmühle district), has a playground
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified
trees.story: These two planes stand five metres apart and the law counts them as separate monuments. ND-9 and ND-10 on Nuremberg's 2020 natural monument ordinance each have their own register number, their own coordinate and their own protection, and anyone walking into the Kontumazgarten will see one pair of trees. That gap between how a register sees a park and how a person sees it is worth knowing before you go hunting for ten separate trees in this city. This is ND-9, the closer of the two to the lawn. Neither has an age on record, neither has been measured in any published source, and no article names either of them individually, so what exists is the city's designation and the trees themselves. Planes grown this close do something worth looking up at: instead of two round crowns they build one shared canopy, each leaning away from the other's shade until the pair spreads wider than either would have alone, while the trunks stay straight because neither has room to lean into the gap. The join is directly overhead if you stand between them. Treat the two as one stop rather than two. Free, open, with a playground beside them, about fifteen minutes on foot from the old town.

trees.name: The Paired Plane of Kontumazgarten
trees.access: Free, public city park (Kontumazgarten, Kleinweidenmühle district), has a playground
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified
trees.story: Germany protects individual trees the way other countries protect buildings. A Naturdenkmal is a legal designation that attaches to one named object rather than to a landscape, and Nuremberg's 2020 ordinance runs to dozens of them, each with a number, a location and a species. This plane is ND-10. It stands about five metres from ND-9, its near neighbour, the two of them effectively one sight carrying two entries in law. The ordinance is also the only thing ever written about it. No age, no girth, no height, nothing beyond the species and a point on the map, and no survey or article names it on its own. That is thin, and it is better said than dressed up: the reason to walk over here is the park as a whole, six protected trees in one small green, not this individual plane's biography. What a plane does give you is scale without the wait. The species grows faster than almost any other large broadleaf that also lives a long time, which is exactly why nineteenth century park designers reached for it so often, and why three of the six protected trees in this park are planes rather than anything slower. Free and open, with a playground, about fifteen minutes on foot from the old town.

trees.name: The Second Beech of Kontumazgarten
trees.access: Free, public city park (Kontumazgarten, Kleinweidenmühle district), has a playground
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 15-20 min) from Nuremberg Altstadt/Hauptmarkt; specific tram/bus stop not verified

best_time.label: late October and November, when the mast drops and the crown turns russet

trees.story: Two trees in this park would be here without anyone's help, and both of them are beeches. European beech is the natural dominant of central Germany: left alone, most of Franconia would return to beech forest within a couple of centuries, shading out nearly everything else. The horse chestnut in this park came from the Balkans and the three planes are a garden hybrid that did not exist before the seventeenth century, which leaves this beech and its neighbour as the locals. It is ND-11 on Nuremberg's 2020 natural monument ordinance, the last of the six protected trees in the Kontumazgarten. As with the rest of them the register is the entire file: species, position, protection, and no age, measurement or description anywhere. Beech also suffers in cities, which is the other half of why an old one in a small urban park earns a listing. It has shallow roots, thin bark that scalds in full sun, and little tolerance for compacted ground or drought, all of which a public lawn supplies in quantity. Late October and November is the time to come, when it turns copper and holds it, and the ground underneath fills with beech mast, small triangular nuts in prickly husks that were fed to pigs for centuries before anyone thought of a park.

trees.name: The Old Lime of Stadtpark
trees.access: Free, public city park (Stadtpark)
trees.transport: 'Stadtpark' bus stop (line N1); roughly 15-20 min walk from Nuremberg Hauptbahnhof
trees.story: The sign at the foot of this tree and the botanists who have looked at its leaves do not agree on what it is. The sign says Winterlinde, small-leaved lime. An independent German tree register assessed the leaf hairiness and concluded large-leaved lime, which is what this page records, with the disagreement left standing rather than quietly resolved. Everything else about it is settled and considerable. Nuremberg's own survey of its oldest trees calls this one of the strongest and oldest in the city, roughly four hundred years old with a trunk about eight metres around, growing in the Stadtpark just south of the Schiller monument and northeast of the pond. It is the best documented old tree in Nuremberg: two independent sources plus the 2020 natural monument ordinance, where it sits as ND-38. Four hundred years puts its first decades inside the Thirty Years War, which emptied and impoverished Franconia and cost Nuremberg a large part of its population to famine and plague while the armies moved around it. It was a sapling then, on ground that was not yet a park. The park was laid out around it much later. The N1 bus stops at Stadtpark, and the walk from the Hauptbahnhof takes about fifteen minutes.

trees.name: The Olive Grove of the Cimiez Monastery Garden
trees.age: undated, some individually estimated over 400 years
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: Bus lines 15, 17, 20, 22 to Monastère de Cimiez stop

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: Franciscan monks reached this hilltop above Nice in 1546 and laid out a grid-patterned vegetable and orchard garden following the monastic planting rules of Albert the Great, a layout that, unusually, has not changed since. What grows there today, thousands of olive trees spread across the monastery garden and the adjoining Jardin des Arènes, includes specimens local sources place at more than four hundred years old, though no individual tree has ever had its own age separately measured or recorded, so the figure describes the grove rather than one named tree. The garden sits directly beside the ruins of a first century Roman amphitheatre, meaning visitors can stand among trees planted under the Ancien Régime while looking at stonework that predates them by a millennium and a half. Entry has always been free, and the grove today is as much a public living room as a historic garden: people picnic, paint and do yoga under trees that were already old when the Franciscans who planted their ancestors were still tending the hill.

trees.name: Matisse's Olive Tree
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: Bus lines 15, 17, 20, 22 to Monastère de Cimiez stop

best_time.label: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: Henri Matisse spent the last years of his life a short walk from this hill and asked to be buried on it, under a tree rather than inside a mausoleum. He was laid to rest in 1954 on land adjoining the Cimetière du Monastère de Cimiez, the formal cemetery where painter Raoul Dufy and Nobel laureate Roger Martin du Gard are also buried, but on ground that had been part of his own property, beneath an olive tree that visitors consistently describe as old rather than newly planted for the occasion. No source gives the tree an individual age, so any figure here is a rough estimate rather than a documented fact, but its presence fits the wider Cimiez hillside, where centuries-old olives are the norm rather than the exception. The grave itself is famously plain, a pale stone slab for Matisse and his wife, a deliberate contrast to the ornate 19th and early 20th century monuments filling the cemetery just beside it. It remains freely visitable, reached on the same path as the cemetery and the Musée Matisse a few minutes further on.

trees.name: The Founding Trees of Jardin Albert 1er
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Masséna tram stop
trees.story: This garden began as a swamp with a name that admitted it: Prato de la Fous, roughly the meadow of the mad, marshy ground at the mouth of the Paillon river that nobody had found a use for. A drainage and landscaping project started in 1829 gave the site its first real shape, and in 1851 the city drew up a specific planting list, 70 horse chestnuts, 60 elms, 40 lindens, 30 acacias and 24 mimosas among them, before levelling and planting the ground in 1852. The garden has changed names as often as it has changed fashion since, Jardin Paradis, Jardin des Plantes, Jardin des Palmiers, before settling on its current name in 1914 in tribute to the Belgian king's resistance to Germany. Ten plane trees stand among the garden's mix today, alongside descendants of that original 1851 species list, though no individual tree here carries its own measured age, so any figure is an estimate based on the garden's founding rather than a documented record. It remains one of Nice's oldest continuously maintained public gardens, a short walk from where the Paillon once flowed uncovered.

trees.name: The Olive and Pine Grove of Colline du Château
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk (or free lift) from Old Nice / Place Garibaldi
trees.story: For most of Nice's history this hill was a fortress rather than a garden. A citadel stood here from the 11th century, guarding the bay, until the troops of Louis XIV demolished it in 1706 rather than let it fall back into Savoyard hands. The ruins sat mostly untouched for over a century before the city began turning the hilltop into a public park in 1822, planting stone pines, olives, carob trees, cypresses, evergreen oaks, hackberries and mastic trees across what is now a 19.3 hectare Mediterranean garden with more than three kilometres of paths. Centuries-old olive trees are among the oldest individual specimens now growing there, alongside stands of Aleppo pine, though no source gives any single tree in the park a documented age, so any figure is an estimate from the park's own founding date rather than a measured record. The climb rewards itself regardless of the trees: the summit is the highest point in central Nice, with the bay, the old town and the Paillon valley all visible from the same viewpoint the citadel's own defenders once used.

trees.name: The Cypresses of the Cimetière du Château
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk (or free lift) from Old Nice / Place Garibaldi
trees.story: This cemetery exists because the King of Sardinia decided in 1783 that burying the dead inside church chapels was a public health risk, and ordered the practice stopped across his kingdom, which then included Nice. The city chose the ruined citadel grounds on the hill above the old town, terracing the site into the stepped, orderly plots still visible today. When Nice was annexed by France in 1860, the cemetery was enlarged and reorganised, work that involved cutting back or replanting the site's cypress cover along with new paths and retaining walls, so most of the cypresses standing today likely date from that period rather than the cemetery's 1783 founding, though no individual tree has a documented planting record. What survives is a genuinely striking setting: 2,800 graves on terraces overlooking the bay and the port, shaded by cypress trees that give the whole hillside its dark, vertical silhouette from the sea. The cemetery remains free and open to visitors alongside the surrounding Colline du Château park.

trees.name: The Palms of the Promenade des Anglais
trees.access: Free, public promenade
trees.transport: Adjacent to Jardin Albert 1er / Masséna tram stop
trees.story: The promenade that gave Nice its postcard image was planted for practical reasons before it became a symbol. By February 1862, city planners were already putting palms, evergreen oaks, carob trees and maritime pines into the ground along the seafront, a revision of an earlier plan that had called only for oaks or pines spaced ten metres apart; officials added the faster-growing palms and shrubs specifically because pedestrians needed shade sooner than slow-growing oaks could provide it. By 1868 a further row of larger palms had gone in along the promenade's northern side, and palm plantings spread rapidly through Nice's public and private gardens between 1867 and 1878, a fashion the city is still identified with today. No individual palm from that original planting is documented as still standing, and Nice's palms since have faced repeated disease pressure, so any specific tree's age here is an estimate rather than a verified record tied to a named specimen. The promenade itself, though widened and rebuilt many times since, still runs the same shoreline these first plantings were meant to shade.

trees.name: The Washingtonia Palms of Villa Masséna
trees.age: undated, garden opened to the public in 1921
trees.access: Free, public garden (the museum inside charges separate admission)
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Promenade des Anglais / Masséna tram stop
trees.story: A Belle Époque prince's winter garden became one of Nice's most formal public spaces almost by accident of inheritance. Prince Victor d'Essling, descendant of Napoleon's Marshal Masséna, had his seafront villa built from 1898 in a neoclassical style modelled on the Villa Rothschild in Cannes, with a garden laid out by the noted French landscape architect Édouard André. When Victor's son ceded the property to the city in 1919, he attached one condition: a museum inside, and the garden opened to the public outside. That happened in 1921, and André's design, structured around three formal flowerbeds on its eastern side with Washingtonia filifera palms rising at each corner, has since been restored to match his original plan after later alterations blurred it. No individual palm here carries a documented planting date, so any age given is an estimate tied to the garden's known 1898-1921 development window rather than a measured record, but the specimens are substantial enough to frame the formal garden exactly as André intended over a century ago.

trees.name: The First Canary Island Date Palm of France
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Port area, or bus to Cyrnos stop
trees.story: Every Phoenix canariensis lining a promenade or a hotel driveway anywhere in France arguably traces back to one estate on Nice's eastern port. Baron Georges Vigier bought a Venetian-style villa here in 1863 and hired Jean-Pierre Barillet-Deschamps, the head gardener of Paris's own parks department, to landscape 30,000 square metres of grounds with tropical plants, tree ferns, bamboo, orange and olive groves and vineyards. In 1864, according to the garden's own preservation society, Vigier acclimatised the Canary Island date palm here for the first time in France, a claim resting on a single detailed source rather than independent corroboration, though the species did subsequently spread through Riviera gardens over the following decades in exactly the pattern that origin story implies. Vigier went on to breed a hybrid palm of his own, named the Vigieris after him. The estate itself shrank drastically after his era, down to a single hectare when the modern Parc Vigier opened to the public in 1971, but palms including rare Livistona australis specimens still stand among its collection today.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine Forest of Mont Boron
trees.access: Free, open daily
trees.transport: Bus line 14 to Mont Boron, or 30 min walk from Nice Port
trees.story: This entire forest exists because a 19th century engineer refused to give up on bare rock. When Nice became French in 1860, the summit of Mont Boron was heathland, stripped of tree cover by centuries of grazing and cutting. Forester Prosper Demontzey, who later became one of France's most influential figures in mountain reforestation, took on the hillside in 1862 and tried sowing Aleppo pine seed directly into the exposed ground first. It failed repeatedly. What worked was planting young pines into deep, prepared holes instead, a labour-intensive method that eventually caught, and the pine cover that established itself went on to shelter the return of olive and carob trees beneath it as the canopy matured. The forest today covers 57 hectares with eleven kilometres of marked trails, wrapping around the villas that Second Empire figures like Baron Haussmann built on the hill once it was fashionable and shaded again. No individual tree from Demontzey's original planting is identified as still standing, so any age given describes the reforestation campaign rather than a specific measured pine.

trees.name: The Strawberry Tree of Château de Crémat
trees.access: Guided tours Monday-Saturday 10:00-17:30, booking required via the estate's website
trees.transport: Car recommended; Bellet hills, north-west Nice

best_time.label: October into December, when it flowers and ripens last year's strawberry-red fruit at the same time

trees.story: This tree grows on a wine estate whose owners kept rebuilding the same hillside into ever grander versions of itself. Antoine Mari bought the land on the hill of Crémat in 1906 and built a medieval-style château with a machicolated tower, part of the Bellet appellation that has grown grapes on Nice's inland hills since Roman times. Irène Bretz, a wealthy American who took over the estate in 1923, added neo-Tuscan flourishes and built out the surrounding gardens further, the setting in which this Arbutus unedo, listed with precise coordinates on the regional remarkable-trees registry for the Alpes-Maritimes, now stands. The species carries both flowers and red, strawberry-like fruit on its branches at the same time in autumn, an unusual trait for a Mediterranean evergreen, and no individual age is documented for this specimen beyond its listing as a notable specimen. The estate still produces organically farmed Bellet wine today and takes visitors on booked tours through its gardens, art collection and cellars, one of the few trees on this list that comes with a tasting afterward.

trees.name: The Sycamore of Valkhofpark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Central Nijmegen, on the Valkhof hill; 10 minute walk from Nijmegen railway station

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story: Nijmegen's most recent Tree of the Year grows on ground that has been fought over since the Romans. Valkhofpark sits on the Valkhof hill, site of a Roman legionary camp and later Charlemagne's imperial palace, and in 2021 neighbourhood residents voted this sycamore, planted around 1880, the year's outstanding tree. It stands roughly 23 metres tall with a trunk just under four metres around, respectable rather than record-breaking, in a park whose ruins date back two thousand years. What makes it the park's chosen tree is not age relative to the site, since the Roman camp beneath it long predates any living thing above ground, but presence: it is the sycamore visitors actually notice among the park's mix of younger plantings and older ruins, singled out for a vote most Dutch neighbourhoods hold every year for a genuinely ordinary species elevated by a genuinely extraordinary setting. Valkhofpark itself is a national monument, one of the oldest continuously used defensive and residential sites in the country, its two surviving medieval structures, the Barbarossa ruin and the Nicholas Chapel, predating the tree by roughly seven centuries. Free to enter and in the middle of the city, it turns a Roman hilltop into an ordinary place to sit under a tree.

trees.name: The Mother Ginkgo of Kronenburgerpark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Central Nijmegen; 10 minute walk from Nijmegen railway station

best_time.label: November, when the ginkgo turns gold

trees.story: One ginkgo in a Nijmegen park quietly created a plant variety now sold across Europe. Sometime around 1930 a tree took root in Kronenburgerpark, laid out in 1881 and 1882 just outside the old city walls, and decades later a nurseryman noticed one of its branches growing in a strange, compact, witch's-broom tangle unlike the rest of the tree. Grafted, propagated and registered in 1995, that mutation became Ginkgo biloba 'Mariken', a dwarf ornamental cultivar now sold by nurseries well beyond the Netherlands and later awarded the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, named after Mariken van Nieumeghen, the 16th-century Dutch morality play about a Nijmegen woman who makes a pact with the devil. The original tree that produced it is still standing in the park today, roughly 95 years old and about 2.85 metres around, ordinary in form itself even as its genetic accident spread to gardens it will never see. Ginkgo is a living fossil, a lineage that predates flowering plants by tens of millions of years and survived almost unchanged, which makes this park's real contribution almost funny: not the tree's age, but one freak branch that turned into a garden-centre product. Kronenburgerpark is free, central and a national monument in its own right, landscaped around what had recently been the city's demolished fortifications.

trees.name: The Beech Circle of Sterrenbos
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: South Nijmegen, Brakkenstein; near Radboud University and Radboudumc, reachable by bus along Heyendaalseweg

best_time.label: October and November, when the beech leaves turn copper before they fall

trees.story: Nijmegen's oldest tree does not stand on a battlefield or beside a museum. It stands in a star. Sterrenbos, a star-shaped pattern of radiating forest avenues laid out on the Brakkenstein estate in the 18th century, still survives inside what is now Park Brakkenstein, and a circle of beeches planted as part of that original scheme is, according to local historians, the oldest living tree stock inside city limits, estimated at 250 to 300 years old. Not every original beech has made it this far. Some in the ring have died of old age over the past three centuries and the surviving trees now stand with visible gaps between them, which is itself part of the honest story: this is a living remnant of a planting scheme, not a complete, restored set. The star pattern of avenues around the circle predates the park as a public space by roughly two centuries, laid out when Brakkenstein was still a private country estate first documented in 1654, decades before the beeches themselves went in. What remains today is free and open, part of a park wedged between Radboud University's campus and a rail line in the south of the city, and it is the closest thing this city has to a tree that watched its own park being invented around it.

trees.name: The Julianaboom
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Nijmegen-Oost, Altrade neighbourhood; 20 minute walk or short bus ride from the city centre

best_time.label: September and October, when the conkers ripen and fall

trees.story: This chestnut has a birthday on record: 4 September 1948, the day Juliana became Queen of the Netherlands after her mother Wilhelmina's abdication. Nijmegen marked the occasion by planting a white horse chestnut in what is now Julianapark, a former cemetery ground in the Altrade neighbourhood turned public park and named for the new queen. It is an ordinary species grown into an unusually well-documented individual, its planting date tied to a specific historical event rather than estimated from growth rings or a park's founding year, the kind of precision most trees on this list do not have. Horse chestnuts are not native to the Netherlands, brought west from the Balkans in the 16th century and adopted so thoroughly into Dutch parks and streets that most residents assume they always belonged. This one has outlived the queen it was planted for by more than two decades, and the country it grew up in has changed monarchs twice since. Julianapark itself is small, free and largely residential in character, a quiet green space east of the city centre with none of Valkhofpark's Roman weight or Kronenburgerpark's fortress history, just one dated tree doing what a planted anniversary tree is supposed to do: mark a date and keep growing past it.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Krayenhoffpark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Biezen neighbourhood, Nijmegen; short walk from Nijmegen railway station via Voorstadslaan
trees.story: A Californian giant grows in one of Nijmegen's smallest parks, in a neighbourhood built for railway employees. Krayenhoffpark, in the Biezen district near the city's rail yards, holds a giant sequoia measured in September 2020 at just under four metres around and about 25 metres tall, likely planted sometime in the 1920s though no source gives an exact date, an inference from size rather than a documented planting. That gap in the record is honest rather than a failure of research: this is a neighbourhood park, not an estate or a botanical garden with its own archive, and the tree's presence here at all says more about the era than about any specific person who planted it. Giant sequoias reached Europe from California's Sierra Nevada in the 1850s and became a genuine planting fashion among estate owners and, eventually, municipal parks departments for the next three quarters of a century, moving a tree that can live past 2,000 years into gardens designed to last decades. In its native range this specimen would be barely into adolescence; in a small Dutch park surrounded by early 20th-century housing, it is already the tallest living thing most residents will see on a walk to the shops. Free, small and unglamorous by the standards of Nijmegen's grander parks, it rewards anyone who actually looks up.

trees.name: The Hornbeam of Krayenhoffpark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Biezen neighbourhood, Nijmegen; short walk from Nijmegen railway station via Voorstadslaan
trees.story:
This hornbeam stands close enough to Krayenhoffpark's giant sequoia to be mistaken for an afterthought planted in the famous tree's shadow, but it is roughly the same age and belongs to a species the Dutch have grown for a very different reason. Where the sequoia was an imported curiosity, hornbeam is a native workhorse, historically clipped into hedges and avenues across the Low Countries because it tolerates hard pruning and holds its dead brown leaves through winter, giving a bare hedge some cover even in the coldest months.

The register dates this one to somewhere around 1900 to 1910, planted while the Biezen neighbourhood around it was still going up to house railway workers from the nearby yards. Left to grow naturally rather than clipped, as this one has been, hornbeam reaches a modest, broad-crowned shape closer to a beech than to the tight hedge most people picture. It grows a few metres from the park's sequoia, free, in the same small green space that gives an otherwise unremarkable railway district its one patch of shade older than most of the houses around it.

trees.name: The Black Locust of Krayenhoffpark
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Biezen neighbourhood, Nijmegen; short walk from Nijmegen railway station via Voorstadslaan
trees.story:
The Dutch name for this tree translates literally as false Christ's-thorn, a reference to the sharp paired spines that line its young branches, thorns sharp enough that European folklore once linked the species to the biblical crown of thorns despite the tree being a North American import that no one in the region had ever seen before the 17th century. This specimen, dated by the register to around 1880 to 1890, predates its own park: Krayenhoffpark and the railway workers' housing around it were built in the early 20th century, decades after this tree first went into what was then open ground on the edge of the city.

Black locust fixes nitrogen in the soil through bacteria living on its roots, the same trick clover and beans use, which is part of why it was planted so widely across poor European soils long before anyone understood the chemistry behind why it thrived where other trees struggled. It stands a few steps from the park's hornbeam and its better-known giant sequoia, free, the oldest of the three despite being the least conspicuous.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Begraafplaats Daalseweg
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open during normal daytime hours
trees.transport: Altrade neighbourhood, Nijmegen; about a 20 minute walk from Nijmegen railway station
trees.story:
Four Catholic parishes petitioned Nijmegen's city council in 1884 for permission to open a shared cemetery on the Daalseweg, and the bishop of 's-Hertogenbosch consecrated it the following June. The city architect Jan Jacob Weve designed the grounds around two broad paths crossing at right angles, lined with copper beeches he is himself buried among, and this sweet chestnut grows on the cemetery's west side from roughly the same founding decade. The cemetery closed to new burials in 1948 when a replacement opened elsewhere, and many graves were later cleared for housing, but the grounds survived intact enough to be named a national heritage site in 2002.

The cemetery holds a harder history than most: 300 victims of the February 1944 bombing of Nijmegen, a raid that killed roughly 800 people in a single afternoon, were buried here. Sweet chestnut is not native this far north, introduced originally by the Romans for its edible nuts, and this one has stood through the cemetery's whole active life and its decades since as a protected historic ground rather than a working one. It grows in the open, free to visit during normal cemetery hours, a short walk from Julianapark's own commemorative chestnut.

trees.name: The Kabouterboom
trees.age: 300 to 400 years, and by some accounts 450
trees.access: Free. Woodland on the Heerlijkheid Beek estate, open to walkers.
trees.transport: About 4.5 km east of Nijmegen centre. Bus 5 or 8 towards Beek, then a walk up into the Kastanjedal.
trees.story:
Children in Beek have been told for generations that gnomes live inside this tree, which is how a sweet chestnut came to be called the Gnome Tree. It is an easy story to believe. The trunk is hollow, at least eight and a half metres around, and the openings in it are the size of doorways.

That girth makes it the thickest tree in the Netherlands, and the hollowness is why nobody can say how old it is: there is no core left to count. Estimates run from three hundred years to four hundred and fifty. The register that lists it puts the planting between 1600 and 1700 and notes that chestnuts have probably been grown around Nijmegen since the Romans, who liked the crop and liked this ridge.

In January 2005 children set it on fire. It burned inside, which a hollow tree does readily, and everyone assumed that was the end of four centuries. It leafed out again that spring and has gone on since.

It stands in the Kastanjedal, a valley of old chestnuts in the Heerlijkheid Beek estate, which Het Geldersch Landschap keeps open to walkers.

trees.name: The Limes of the Kopse Hof
trees.access: Free. Public open ground on the Kops Plateau, reached by the lime avenue.
trees.transport: About 2.6 km east of the centre, a half-hour walk out along the Berg en Dalseweg.
trees.story:
The Romans picked this spot in about 12 BC and built a fort on it, because from sixty four metres up you can see the Waal, the Ooijpolder, the Betuwe and most of the way to Arnhem. Eighteen centuries later somebody planted limes for the same view.

The group stands on the hilltop at the end of a lime avenue, and the two were almost certainly planted together, the avenue as the way up to the hill. The register dates both between 1750 and 1800 and can show its working: the hill is on the Tranchot map of 1803, and both the avenue and the hill are drawn on the cadastral map of 1811.

It lists the hilltop group under a category that has nothing to do with size. They are recorded as a kruisboom, a cross tree, which is what the Dutch register calls a tree planted for a religious purpose. The note says only that they may have served one, which is the honest version: nobody now knows what was meant to happen here.

The register counts three at the viewpoint. Locally they are called the four apostles, which suggests there were once four, and that is the kind of arithmetic old trees usually lose.

trees.name: The Yew of the Bartholomeuskerkje
trees.access: Free. Open churchyard.
trees.transport: About 4.7 km east of Nijmegen centre, on the Rijksstraatweg at Beek. Bus 5 or 8.
trees.story:
A charter of 1286 is the first mention of the little church this tree stands beside, and the churchyard around it has been in use ever since. The building had a hard nineteenth century: shared between Catholics and Protestants from 1796, neglected by both, closed in 1824 as unsafe, and only saved when King William I put money towards its repair.

The yew was there through all of it. The register records a painting by Barend Cornelis Koekkoek from about 1830 showing the church with this tree beside it, already looking like it had been standing a long while, and concludes the tree is probably older than two hundred years. That is one source making a careful argument rather than a measurement, so treat the age as an argument too.

What is not in doubt is what a yew does with time. It grows slowly, hollows early, and then keeps going for centuries after the point where any other tree would have finished, which is why yews and graveyards have kept each other company across northern Europe for a thousand years.

The churchyard is open, small, and quiet, and the foundation that looks after it describes it as park-like. That is fair.

trees.name: The Wilhelminaboom of Hertogplein
trees.access: Free, a public square in the city centre, open at all times
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk from Nijmegen Centraal station
trees.story:
Nijmegen crowned a queen with a tree. On 1 September 1898, five days before Wilhelmina's coronation, the city planted a lime on Hertogplein and ringed it with a wrought iron fence topped with small crowns, designed by the architect Derk Semmelink. The fence survived the German occupation. Its crowns did not: soldiers stripped them during the war, and the fence stood bare until 24 July 1948, when students at Nijmegen's trade school forged replacements and the city held a public ceremony to fit them back on.

Whether the tree itself survived that long is less certain. Dutch Wikipedia's own account of the square says the original lime has since made way for another, without saying when. A 2025 local history piece describes the tree standing today and does not mention any replacement at all. The national tree register dates this spot to the 1880s, a decade before the coronation planting both other sources describe. Nobody has reconciled the three, so this page will not pretend to: what stands on Hertogplein now is a lime, ringed by a fence built for a different one, and its true age is unknown.

The fence, at least, is certain. It has outlived at least one tree already.

trees.name: The Beverboom of Park Leeuwenstein
trees.species: Magnolia (Magnolia sp., exact species not confirmed)
trees.access: Free, public municipal park, open at all times
trees.transport: About 2.9 km from Nijmegen city centre, Nijmegen-West
trees.story:
Park Leeuwenstein is what is left of a demolished mansion's garden, and this magnolia is what is left of its exotic specimen trees. Villa Leeuwenstein went up in the mid-1800s and came down in 1958, too dilapidated to save, but the trees its owners planted around it kept growing after the house did not. A storm on 18 January 2018 took the park's giant sequoia and a swamp cypress in one night, leaving this tree, the beverboom, as the park's oldest surviving specimen.

Beverboom is old Dutch for magnolia, specifically for Magnolia virginiana, though the exact species growing here has not been confirmed. A 2023 local survey of the park still listed a cucumber magnolia, Magnolia acuminata, among its special trees, and it may be the same tree the national register pins here by coordinate rather than by name. Acuminata flowers greenish yellow after its leaves open in late spring; virginiana flowers cream white and fragrant in early summer. A photograph at flowering time would settle it.

Whichever it is, the register dates the planting to the 1880s, roughly 140 years, a specimen tree that has already outlived the house it was planted beside and two of its own neighbours.

trees.name: The Pastorie Chestnut of Lent
trees.access: Free, on the public square in front of the parish church, open at all times
trees.transport: About an 8 minute walk from Nijmegen Lent railway station
trees.story:
A parish square in Lent doubles as a chestnut's front garden. The Onze Lieve Vrouw Geboorte church went up between 1877 and 1879, designed by the architect G. te Riele Wzn, and the register dates the chestnut on its forecourt to the following decade, planted around the time the church's own rectory rose beside it. The national heritage register's listing for the site still describes it today: an old chestnut tree stands on the square in front of the church, the rectory on its north side.

Lent itself has changed more than the tree has. It was a village on the Waal's north bank until Nijmegen annexed it in 1998, and since 2016 an artificial island and a new bridge have turned its riverside fields into the city's newest district. The square with the chestnut sits a few streets back from all of that, beside the road into what is still, for now, a village centre with its own parish rather than a suburb of one.

The tree is roughly 130 years old and stands in the open, free to see at any hour, a short walk from Lent's own railway station.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Begraafplaats Daalseweg
trees.age: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890-1900
trees.access: Free, public cemetery grounds, open during daylight hours. Please be respectful, it is a working cemetery.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km northwest of Nijmegen railway station, roughly 20 minutes on foot or a short bus ride.
trees.story:
A weeping beech droops on purpose. Every ordinary beech reaches up for its share of light; this one carries a mutation that pulls its branches down instead, so its crown pours toward the ground rather than spreading for the sky. It stands to the right of the entrance gate at Begraafplaats Daalseweg, the first tree a visitor meets.

The cemetery itself is a protected national monument, not for any single tree but for its whole design: two paths cross the grounds, both lined with beeches, meeting at a crucifix at the centre. The weeping beech at the gate breaks that planned rhythm on purpose, an ornamental flourish set apart from the disciplined rows behind it.

The Dutch national register of monumental trees dates the planting to between 1890 and 1900, putting it at roughly 125 to 135 years old, and lists it as the cemetery's own protected specimen. It is the only source found for this particular tree: local histories of the cemetery describe the beech-lined paths and the crucifix at length but none names this one specifically, so the age comes from the register alone.

The grounds belong to a working Catholic cemetery and stay open during daylight hours, free to enter. Go quietly.

trees.name: The Plane of the Petruskerk
trees.age: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870-1880
trees.access: Free, public church square, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 3.5 km west of Nijmegen railway station, reachable by bus toward Hees, roughly 10 minutes' walk from the nearest stop.
trees.story:
London planes shed their bark instead of quietly laying down new rings underneath it, sloughing off patches through the year to show paler wood beneath, which is why an old plane looks mottled and half-flayed rather than simply weathered. This one stands on the small square beside the Petruskerk in Hees, a Nijmegen district that was its own village before the city grew out to meet it.

The Dutch national monumental tree register dates the planting to between 1870 and 1880, making the tree roughly 145 to 155 years old, and lists it as protected. That register is the only source found naming this specific tree: histories of the square and the church describe the setting in detail but not this plane by name, so the age rests on the register's word alone.

The square sits on church grounds and reads as ordinary open public space, a small plaza in front of a working parish rather than an enclosed courtyard, and the register itself records it as visitable. Nothing else about this particular tree has surfaced yet. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Antonius Abtkerk
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750-1800
trees.access: Free, church grounds visible and open to visitors.
trees.transport: About 4 km west of Nijmegen railway station, reachable by bus toward Hees.
trees.story:
This copper beech is older than the church beside it. The current Sint Antonius Abtkerk on Dennenstraat, a red-brick building by the architect Pieter Cuypers, went up in 1879 and 1880. The national register places the beech at the boundary of the church and its rectory somewhere between 1750 and 1800, roughly a century older than the bricks next to it.

That is not as strange as it sounds. The parish itself predates Cuypers by centuries: an older church stood on this ground before his, a barn chapel was rebuilt here in 1826, and parish history traces the site back to a sixteenth century predecessor. A beech planted in the late 1700s would have grown up beside whatever building stood here then, and simply outlasted it, the way old trees on church land tend to.

Copper beeches carry a mutation that floods their leaves with red pigment, so from a distance this one reads almost black against the brick. The Dutch national monumental tree register is the only source found for this specific tree, roughly 225 to 275 years old by its planting estimate; local parish and heritage histories confirm the site's long religious use but do not mention the beech itself, so the age stands on the register alone.

The grounds are recorded as visitable and visible from outside, ordinary church land in the Hees district rather than a closed private garden.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of Sumatraplein
trees.access: Free. Public street tree on municipal ground (owner_category 'gemeente' in the register), visible and accessible at all times.
trees.transport: About 1.3 km southeast of Nijmegen railway station, in the Nijmegen-Oost neighbourhood; roughly 15-20 minutes on foot or a short bus ride.
trees.story:
Most of Nijmegen's protected trees carry the register's full monumental status. This one carries a lower rank, 'potentieel', a candidate rather than a confirmed monument, which changes nothing about standing in front of it: a silver maple planted somewhere between 1900 and 1910 on a residential street in Nijmegen-Oost, now past its first century.

Acer saccharinum grows fast and splits easily, which is why American cities stopped planting it as a street tree decades before European ones did; the trees that survive from an early planting wave tend to be the ones nobody got around to replacing. This one has made it past 120 years on a municipal verge, owned and maintained by the city rather than a private garden, which is also why it can carry a public register entry at all.

No independent source beyond the national tree register names this specific tree, and no girth has been recorded, so treat the age band as the register's own estimate rather than a measurement. It stands in the open on Sumatraplein, free to see at any hour, about twenty minutes on foot from the station.

trees.name: The McDonogh Oak
trees.age: 700 to 800 years, and by some accounts up to 900
trees.access: Free. Public city park, open daily.
trees.transport: City Park, about 6 km north of the French Quarter. Canal Streetcar to City Park / Museum, then a walk west along the grove.
trees.story:
The branches are too heavy for the tree now, so they rest on wooden crutches. That is the first thing you notice and the whole story in one image: a crown about forty six metres across on a trunk of eight metres, held up because nobody is willing to cut it back.

City Park reckons it at seven to eight hundred years, which puts its first century somewhere around the time the Choctaw were the only people here and five hundred years before the French arrived. It lost a major limb in 1981, which is why there is a cement patch as well as the props.

The reason it is still standing is geological rather than lucky. The Old Grove sits on the strip between City Park Avenue and Bayou Metairie, and the bayou spent centuries overflowing and dropping silt, which raised this ground about a metre above the rest of the park. When the levees failed in 2005 and most of City Park went under, the Old Grove stayed dry.

There is a plaque at the foot of the trunk. It is a considerable understatement.

trees.name: The Anseman Oak
trees.access: Free. Public city park, open daily.
trees.transport: City Park, about 6 km north of the French Quarter. Enter from City Park Avenue at the Anseman Avenue entrance.
trees.story:
Victor Anseman was a florist who retired and then gave the last fifteen years of his life to a park. In 1891 he pulled together the business and political people of the city into the City Park Improvement Association, which is the reason there is a park here at all rather than a subdivision. He died in 1904 and they named this oak after him.

It is a good choice of monument. The tree is given the same range as the McDonogh Oak, five hundred to nine hundred years, and some accounts make it the older of the two. Neither has been cored, so the order between them is a matter of who is doing the estimating.

It stands at the western end of the same high strip of ground, just inside the entrance that also carries his name. The pin here marks the entrance rather than the trunk, because the grove holds hundreds of old oaks and pretending to know which metre is the one would be a promise this page cannot keep. Walk in from City Park Avenue opposite North Alexander and look for the biggest thing standing.

trees.name: The Dueling Oak
trees.access: Free. Public city park, open daily.
trees.transport: City Park, beside the New Orleans Museum of Art. Canal Streetcar to City Park / Museum.
trees.story:
Between 1834 and 1844 there were stretches when scarcely a day passed without a duel being fought under these trees. Creole New Orleans settled its arguments here with swords and pistols, over insults, politics, cards and women, and the oaks were the address everyone understood without being told.

There were two. A hurricane took one in 1949 and the other is still standing, roughly three hundred years old, twenty one metres tall on a trunk seven and a half metres round.

What makes it worth the walk now is the contrast rather than the gore. The tree stands where Dueling Oaks Drive meets Dreyfous Drive, which puts it a few steps from the Besthoff Sculpture Garden and the art museum. So the spot where men shot each other over remarks at dinner is now the quietest corner of the park, full of people looking at bronze.

The pin marks the junction rather than the trunk. You will not need it: there is only one oak there with a story attached.

trees.name: The Tree of Life
trees.age: about 285 years, from a planting date of around 1740
trees.access: Free. Public park, outside the zoo fence, no ticket needed.
trees.transport: Audubon Park, about 8 km upriver from the French Quarter. St Charles Streetcar to Audubon Park, then walk toward the river.
trees.story:
Eleven metres round, eighteen tall, and a crown reaching close to fifty metres across, which means the limbs left the trunk, ran horizontally as far as they could, and then came back down to the grass. That is why this is the most climbed and most photographed tree in Louisiana: it invites you up without asking you to be able to climb.

The sign by it gives a planting date of around 1740. A better story says Etienne de Bore, the first mayor of New Orleans and the man who worked out how to granulate sugar commercially, planted it in 1771 as a wedding present for his wife. That version is tradition rather than record, and it has the wrong decade, but it has stuck hard enough that the tree carries his name as often as its other one.

In 1934 it became one of the forty three founding members of the Live Oak Society, an organisation whose members are all trees and whose only human is a secretary who keeps the roll.

It stands outside the zoo fence, so you do not need a ticket. The giraffes are on the other side.

trees.name: The Giant Camphor of Naratsuhiko Shrine
trees.access: Free, grounds open 09:00 to 17:00
trees.transport: Bus from JR or Kintetsu Nara toward Aoyama Jutaku, about 15 min, alight at Narazaka
trees.story: Twelve point eight metres around at the ground, and it holds a rope. This camphor stands behind the main hall of a shrine on Narazaka, the pass road that carried travellers into Japan's first permanent capital from the north, which means anyone walking into Nara from Kyoto in the eighth century passed beneath it. It rises about thirty metres and forks into two great limbs some seven metres up, each of which forks again, so from below the crown reads less like a tree than like several trees agreeing to share a base. The prefecture designated it a natural monument in 1951. What makes it worth the bus ride rather than merely worth reading about is the eighth of October. On that evening the shrine performs the Okina-mai, a masked dance recognised as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property and one of the oldest surviving ancestors of Noh theatre, and it is danced here, under this tree, as it has been for centuries. Be honest about the thousand years: like almost every great camphor in Japan, the figure is traditional rather than measured. The girth supports it.
