trees.name: The Great Cedar of Kasuga Taisha
trees.access: Kasuga Taisha precinct, open 06:00 to 18:00; the outer grounds are free, and it is unclear whether this tree stands inside the paid inner area, so check on arrival
trees.transport: About 25 to 30 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden
trees.story: There is a picture scroll, donated to this shrine in 1309, in which this cedar appears as a sapling. Seven centuries later it is roughly eight metres around and twenty-five tall, standing beside the hall where offerings are shared after the rituals, and the sapling in the painting is the same organism. Almost no ancient tree anywhere can be checked against its own portrait as a young plant. The better story is what grows out of its base. A second tree, a shinpaku, took root there and grew toward the neighbouring hall, and rather than cut it back somebody cut a hole in the roof and let it through. The hall still has the hole. Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768 for the deity of the Fujiwara clan and rebuilt every twenty years for centuries, so the buildings around this cedar are younger than the cedar, repeatedly. One practical note before you go: sources place the tree beside the Naoraiden near the inner gate, and it is not clear from the shrine's own pages whether that spot falls inside the free outer precinct or the paid inner one.

trees.name: The Five-Colour Camellia of Byakugo-ji
trees.access: Paid, 500 yen for adults, open 09:00 to 17:00; over 100 stone steps from the road, not step-free
trees.transport: Bus from Nara station toward Takabatake, then about 10 min walk and the steps

best_time.label: late March into mid-April, when one tree opens red, white and pink at once

trees.story: One tree, five colours, and it does not drop its flowers the way a camellia is supposed to. This four hundred year old camellia opens red, white and peach blossoms on the same plant, along with striped and variegated ones, which is how it earned its name and its place among the three famous camellias of Nara. Most camellias shed the whole flower head at once, which is why the Japanese associated them with beheading and why samurai were said to dislike them; this one is a chiri-tsubaki, shedding petal by petal instead, so the ground beneath it in April is a scatter of loose colour rather than a row of fallen heads. It is only about five metres tall. The prefecture designated it a natural monument in 1957. Byakugo-ji itself sits on a hillside at the southeastern edge of the city with the whole Nara basin spread out below, which is the compensation for the climb: over a hundred stone steps stand between the bus stop and the tree, and there is no way around them.

trees.name: The Soapberry with a Bamboo Through It
trees.access: Free, open parkland at all hours
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, beside the Nara National Museum

best_time.label: October and November, when the translucent amber fruit ripens

trees.story: The trunk is hollow, and a bamboo has grown up inside it and out through the top. Bamboo from the tea house grove behind found the cavity in this soapberry, went up through it and emerged from the crown, so what stands on the bend of the Kasuga approach is one tree wearing another. The shrine's own guide describes the effect as a mother holding a child. At four and a half metres around and over fifteen tall it is claimed as the largest soapberry in Nara Prefecture, and nobody has published an age for it, which is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a number. Its black seeds had two jobs. Strung, they became prayer beads. Loose, they were the weights inside the shuttlecocks of hanetsuki, the New Year battledore game, which is why the tree turns up in old accounts of the season. The pulp around them lathers in water, and that is where the English name comes from: this is the tree people washed with before soap was cheap.

trees.name: The Camphors of Tobihino
trees.access: Free, open meadow at all hours
trees.transport: About 15 min walk from Kintetsu Nara
trees.story: Three trees planted in 1908 have grown into one cloud. They stand in a ring fence in the middle of the Tobihino meadow, marking the spot where Emperor Meiji sat to watch army manoeuvres, and in a little over a century they have closed into a single dome so complete that most people photograph them believing they are looking at one enormous tree. The largest trunk is nearly five metres around and the crown reaches twenty-six metres. What makes the spot rather than the tree is everything else in the frame: open grass, morning mist off the hills behind, and the deer of Nara Park grazing right up to the fence, because Tobihino is where they gather. This is the youngest tree on this page by several centuries and it earns its place on presence alone. Come early. The meadow faces east, the light comes in under the crown, and the deer are out before the buses are.

trees.name: The Great Nagi of Kasuga Taisha
trees.access: Kasuga Taisha precinct; outer grounds free, check on arrival which zone this tree falls in
trees.transport: About 25 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, or bus to Kasuga Taisha Honden
trees.story: This tree should not be here at all. Nagi grows wild in Kyushu and Taiwan, far to the south, and the nine hectares of it on this hillside are the northernmost stand of its kind, a national natural monument since 1923. Nara City's own record is blunt about why: the grove is not natural. Trees were offered to the shrine during the Nara period and the descendants of those offerings spread across the slope, so what looks like ancient woodland is the result of twelve centuries of donation. This individual is the largest of them, three and a third metres around and thirteen metres tall, which for a species this slow is why estimates run to five centuries and beyond. It is a conifer that has forgotten how to look like one: the leaves are broad, leathery ovals with parallel veins running end to end and no midrib at all, so people who know their trees stop, look again, and go and read the sign. The city protected the tree itself in 1997, along with a twenty metre square of ground around it.

trees.name: The First Cherry of Nara
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: Bus to Himuro Jinja / Kokuritsu Hakubutsukan, which stops at the gate, or about 15 min walk from Nara station

best_time.label: late March, when it opens before every other cherry in Nara

trees.story: Nara's spring officially starts at this tree. The weeping cherry standing beside the approach to Himuro Shrine opens before any other cherry in the city, which earned it the name Nara ichiban zakura, first cherry of Nara, and turns a quiet shrine into a queue for about ten days in late March. It leans over the pond in front of the gate, so the flowers arrive twice, once above you and once in the water. The shrine underneath it is stranger than the tree. It stands on the site of a Nara period ice house and enshrines the deity of ice: blocks were cut in winter, packed into a pit insulated with straw and kept through the summer for the imperial court, and ice merchants still come here to pray for their trade. Every year at the end of May the shrine holds a festival where offerings are made in ice, including whole fish frozen inside blocks. The tree is young by the standards of this page, and its hundred years rests on a single source, so treat the number lightly and the timing seriously.

trees.name: The Chinaberry of the East Pagoda Ruins
trees.access: Free, open parkland at all hours
trees.transport: About 20 min walk from Kintetsu Nara, in the grounds between Todai-ji and the park

best_time.label: mid-May, when it covers itself in pale purple sprays

trees.story: It stands on ground that once held one of the tallest buildings in Japan. Todai-ji's east pagoda rose seven storeys and is reported at around a hundred metres, burned, was rebuilt, burned again and was never rebuilt a third time, so all that remains is a raised platform in the grass with a chinaberry beside it four and a half metres around and twenty metres tall. Nobody has published its age. What is recorded is the reason its species turns up in places like this: chinaberry was believed to drive off evil spirits and was traditionally planted in graveyards and at sites where the dead were remembered, which is exactly what a burned pagoda platform became. For most of the year it is an unremarkable spreading tree that visitors walk past on their way to the Great Buddha. For two weeks in the middle of May it covers itself in loose sprays of pale purple flowers, and the official guide to Nara Park's giant trees singles that fortnight out as the reason to come.

trees.name: The Thickest Black Pine of Nara Park
trees.access: Free, open parkland at all hours
trees.transport: About 5 min walk from Kintetsu Nara
trees.story: Black pines were planted through Nara Park for centuries for no reason except that they looked right, and this is the fattest survivor of that long habit: three and a half metres around, twenty-eight metres tall, and roughly two hundred and fifty years old, which puts its planting in the middle of the Edo period. It is also the easiest tree on this page to reach, about five minutes from the station, standing at the corner of the block that holds Kofuku-ji's National Treasure Hall. Look at the ground under it before you look up. Flying squirrels live in the park and strip the cones for their seeds, leaving the gnawed cores scattered beneath the tree in a shape the locals compare to fried prawns, so a handful of little stripped spindles on the path is the sign that something was in the crown overnight. The official guide to the park's giant trees ends its entry on this tree by remarking that the Edo period gardeners who put it here would be pleased with how it turned out, which is a fair summary of the whole park.

trees.name: The Roben-sugi of Nigatsu-do
trees.age: current tree roughly 60 years old, replanted after 1961
trees.access: Free, part of Todai-ji's outer precinct (Nigatsu-do itself has no admission fee)
trees.transport: City loop bus from Kintetsu Nara Station to Daibutsuden Kasuga Taisha-mae, then about 15 min walk uphill
trees.story:
An eagle carried off a baby and left it in a cedar on this slope, and the baby grew up to found Todai-ji. That is the legend of the Roben-sugi. The infant was Roben, later the temple's first abbot, found and raised by a monk, and the tree on the spot has carried his name ever since. A stone monument beside it records the story.

This is not that cedar, and nobody here pretends it is. The original lived roughly six hundred years and reached 21.2 metres before the Second Muroto Typhoon came through Nara on 16 September 1961 with winds recorded at 75 metres a second. What happened afterwards is where the accounts part. One says the replacement failed to take and the tree standing today went in on 16 March 1967, raised from the one that died. Another calls this the fourth generation rather than the third. They disagree about how many attempts it took, not about whether this one has held.

So it is roughly sixty years old, which makes it the youngest tree on this page. Nara is a good place to be relaxed about that. The address is the relic here, not the timber.

It stands below the slope Nigatsu-do occupies, immediately north of the small Kojo Shrine, and the pin follows that description rather than a surveyed trunk. Free, part of Todai-ji's outer precinct, and the climb up is short.

trees.name: The Hangman's Elm
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: West 4th Street (Metro A/B/C/D/E/F/M), 3 min walk
trees.story: This elm is one of the oldest living things on Manhattan Island, and almost everything colorful ever said about it is unproven. Its nickname comes from a folk legend that traitors and criminals were hanged from its branches during and after the American Revolution, a story with no supporting court or newspaper record; the earliest known references to it as a hanging tree only appear in print in the late 19th century, generations after the events they describe. What is documented is its age: the New York City Parks Department measured it at 310 years old in 1989, later revising that to a more cautious more than 300 years, with some accounts pushing the figure to 346. It stands at the northwest corner of Washington Square, a plot of land that served as a potter's field and public execution ground in the early 1800s, close enough to the tree that a real 1820 hanging nearby, of Rose Butler for arson, may be the seed of fact the legend grew from. The tree survived a 2012 park renovation that construction crews came close to damaging.

trees.name: The Black Tupelo of the Ramble
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 81st Street-Museum of Natural History (Metro B/C), 8 min walk

best_time.label: late September into October, often the first tree in the Ramble to turn, in brilliant scarlet

trees.story: Central Park has two competing claimants for its oldest tree, and this one has the better paperwork. A London plane near the Reservoir might date to 1862, when the Reservoir itself was excavated, but this black tupelo in the Ramble, the deliberately wild, maze-like woodland Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux designed into the park's plan, has documentation placing its planting at 1858, four years earlier, during the park's original construction. Black tupelos are native to eastern North American wetlands and swamps, not the schist bedrock Central Park sits on, which makes this a planted specimen rather than a survivor of the farmland and settlements the park displaced. The species is prized by ecologists for its brilliant, early scarlet fall color and by foresters for its resistance to rot, qualities that have let this tree outlast most of the park's original 1850s plantings. It stands in one of the Ramble's quieter, less trafficked paths, a 19th century engineering project that has spent a century and a half looking convincingly unplanned.

trees.name: The Camperdown Elm
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Prospect Park (Metro B/Q/S), 10 min walk
trees.story: Every Camperdown elm on Earth is a clone, and this one is among the oldest. The cultivar began in the 1830s when a gardener for the Earl of Camperdown found a single mutant elm branch, contorted and weeping instead of growing upright, on the Camperdown House estate near Dundee, Scotland. Because the mutation cannot be grown from seed, every specimen since has been propagated by grafting a cutting onto a straight-trunked host, which makes each Camperdown elm in the world a genetic twin of that one Scottish branch. This graft was planted near Prospect Park's Boathouse in 1872, a gift to the young park, and by the 1960s had declined badly enough that Brooklyn nearly lost it, until the poet Marianne Moore, a devoted Prospect Park visitor, wrote publicly in its defense and helped rally the conservation campaign that saved it. She later called it Brooklyn's crowning curio. Its low, twisted canopy, propped and cabled for support, still spreads wide enough that visitors duck to walk beneath it, a shape no other tree in the park shares by nature.

trees.name: The Sassafras of Green-Wood
trees.access: Free, cemetery open daily (check seasonal hours)
trees.transport: 25th Street (Metro R), at the cemetery gate

best_time.label: October, when its leaves turn a mix of yellow, orange and purple, sometimes all on the same branch

trees.story: Green-Wood Cemetery has counted this as its oldest tree, possibly older than the cemetery itself, which was founded in 1838 on rolling glacial hills chosen specifically because the terrain already supported mature, established woodland. Sassafras trees rarely reach the size or age this specimen has, since the species usually grows as a smaller understory tree that spreads through root suckers rather than living to great individual age; this one, or rather these two, since it appears as a pair of trunks a few feet apart, may be the last survivors of a larger colonial root system that once covered more ground. Nobody has cored the tree to confirm an exact age, and Green-Wood's own arborists are candid that the favorable growing conditions inside a manicured 478 acre cemetery likely inflate its size relative to a wild sassafras of the same age, making size an unreliable proxy for years here. What is certain is that it predates most of the 600,000 people buried around it, a rare case of a cemetery's oldest resident having no grave at all.

trees.name: The Queens Giant
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Douglaston (LIRR Port Washington line), 10 min walk

best_time.label: October, when its canopy turns a luminous golden yellow

trees.story: This tree was already centuries old when New Amsterdam was still a Dutch trading post, and unlike almost everything else on this list, nobody planted it. At 133.8 feet the Queens Giant is the tallest carefully measured tree in New York City, a tulip poplar growing wild in a stretch of Alley Pond Park's forest that has never been cleared, and the New York City Parks Department dates it to at least 368 years old, with other estimates ranging as wide as 350 to 450. Tulip trees can live 600 years and reach over 150 feet under ideal conditions, and this specimen's height alone marks it as one of the oldest living things in the entire New York metropolitan region, likely older than any building, monument or institution in the five boroughs. Some local histories connect the surrounding land to 17th century transactions between the Dutch West India Company and the Matinecock people who lived here before European settlement, though no source confirms this specific tree witnessed any documented exchange. It has simply kept growing, in a park most of the city drives past on the Long Island Expressway without knowing it is there.

trees.name: The Manchurian Linden of Kissena Park
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Kissena Park, Queens Q17/Q25/Q34 bus, 5 min walk
trees.story: This linden is a leftover from a 19th century nursery business rather than a park planting, standing 75 feet north of a restroom next to Kissena Park's tennis courts on land that was once part of Samuel Bowne Parsons's commercial tree nursery. Parsons, whose family also planted Manhattan's Hangman's Elm-era Washington Square trees and much of Central Park's original stock, ran one of the era's most important import operations from this site starting in the 1870s, bringing Japanese maples to America for the first time and propagating rhododendrons at commercial scale. After Parsons died in 1906, the city absorbed part of his former grove into what became Kissena Park, and this Manchurian linden, a species native to forests spanning China, Korea and Russia's far east, is one of more than 100 imported tree varieties that trace back to the original nursery grounds still growing in the park today. It carries Great Tree status as a living fragment of Flushing's forgotten reputation as America's premier 19th century horticultural center, a history most visitors to the tennis courts beside it have no reason to suspect.

trees.name: The Clove Lakes Colossus
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Staten Island Railway to Clove Road area, or S61/S62 bus, 10 min walk

best_time.label: October, when its canopy turns golden yellow

trees.story: Staten Island's tallest tree stands 119 feet, more than 14 feet shorter than Queens' record-holding tulip tree, but old enough on its own terms to anchor the north end of Clove Lakes Park, easily found along a paved path where its trunk, 21.4 feet around, dwarfs everything nearby. Tulip trees like this one are among the tallest native hardwoods in eastern North America, capable of shooting straight up through a forest canopy in search of light rather than spreading wide the way an open-grown oak would, which is part of why the species so often produces the height records claimed on lists like this one. Clove Lakes Park itself preserves one of Staten Island's last stretches of the mixed hardwood forest that once covered most of the borough before 20th century development, and the Colossus, reported at well over 300 years old, would have been an established mature tree when the surrounding land was still farmland rather than parkland. It remains one of Staten Island's contributions to New York City's official Great Trees registry, one of ten entries from the least visited of the five boroughs.

trees.name: The Yew of Hero Park
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: S61/S62 bus to Victory Boulevard, at the park

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: This yew is one of 144 evergreens planted in 1920 around a glacial boulder called Sugar Loaf Rock, each tree standing as a living memorial to a Staten Island resident killed in the First World War. A plaque at the boulder names every soldier the grove commemorates, making Hero Park one of the more literal war memorials in New York City: not statues or a wall of names alone, but a planted forest where each individual tree corresponds to an individual death, a practice with a documented precedent in similar WWI memorial tree plantings elsewhere in the country around the same period. European yews are exceptionally long lived and slow growing, a species choice that all but guaranteed this planting would still be standing a century later, evergreen through every winter since 1920 the way the soldiers it honors never got to see. At just over a century old it is younger than most other trees on this list, but its age is not really the point; the grove was planted to hold a specific memory in place, and a century on, it still does.

trees.name: The Red Oak of the Thain Family Forest
trees.access: Paid entry to the New York Botanical Garden
trees.transport: Metro-North Harlem Line to Botanical Garden station, at the Mosholu entrance

best_time.label: late October, when its leaves turn the deep oxidised red the species is named for, inside forest that predates the city around it

trees.story: This oak grows in the middle of the Spicebush Trail inside the Thain Family Forest, a 50 acre stretch of the New York Botanical Garden that has never been logged and represents the largest surviving remnant of the woodland that once covered most of New York City before European colonization. The Botanical Garden was deliberately sited here in 1895 specifically because this forest already existed, a decision that preserved a functioning fragment of pre-colonial Lenapehoking rather than planting a garden from scratch. At a trunk diameter over five feet, this red oak, designated a Great Tree in 2024, ranks among the largest and most accessible specimens in a forest that also holds tulip trees, sweetgums, hemlocks and beeches estimated at up to 300 years old in less visited sections. Red oaks support more moth and butterfly species as larval hosts than almost any other tree genus in the northeastern United States, more than 400 by some counts, making this single oak a small ecosystem of its own even before accounting for its age or size.

trees.name: The Red Horse Chestnut of Van Cortlandt House
trees.access: Free to view from the park; paid entry to enter the Van Cortlandt House Museum itself
trees.transport: Van Cortlandt Park-242nd Street (Metro 1), 10 min walk

best_time.label: May, when its pink flower spikes stand out against the ordinary white-flowering chestnuts nearby

trees.story: This tree grows on the east lawn of the Van Cortlandt House, built in 1748 and the oldest building still standing in the Bronx, and local tradition holds that a member of the Van Cortlandt family planted it themselves, though no source confirms exactly when. Red horse chestnuts are themselves a hybrid, a cross between the European horse chestnut and a red-flowered American buckeye species, bred for ornamental gardens rather than found in the wild, which means whoever planted this one chose it deliberately for its spring flowers rather than letting it seed in naturally. At nearly 88 feet tall with a trunk over three feet across, it has grown large enough to be one of three horse chestnuts at the house included in the NYC Parks Great Trees registry, all three now part of a Great Tree Clone Program in which cuttings are propagated and planted at new sites around the city, extending the genetic line of trees like this one even as the originals eventually age out. Van Cortlandt House operated as a Revolutionary War-era headquarters at times for both American and British forces, meaning this tree, whatever its precise age, grows on ground that has seen the city's founding conflict up close.

trees.name: The Great Elm of Central Park West
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 81st Street-Museum of Natural History (Metro B/C), 4 min walk
trees.story:
Central Park once had roughly 500 American elms along its western edge. By 1985, a New York Times survey counted 23 left, and this is one of them. It stands right at the park's edge on Central Park West and 77th Street, directly across from the American Museum of Natural History, wider than it is tall: NYC Parks measures it at just under 51 feet high with a 55 foot canopy.

Dutch elm disease reached New York in the 1930s and worked through the city for decades, killing elms faster than anyone could replant them. This one kept standing while its neighbours came down one by one, close enough to the street that passersby now call it, without much competition, the most beautiful tree on the block.

Nobody has dated it precisely. What is documented is its survival: officially designated one of the city's Great Trees, standing beside a statue of Alexander von Humboldt, who spent his career cataloguing exactly this kind of specimen. No planting record narrows the guess further than a century or more, so that wide range is what the story states rather than a false precise number.

Walk in from the Museum of Natural History subway stop and it is the first tree inside the park, an entrance marker planted long before anyone thought to protect it.

trees.name: The Elms on the Rocks
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 72nd Street (Metro B/C), 8 min walk
trees.story:
Two American elms grow straight out of exposed bedrock east of Central Park's Mall, their roots spread flat across the rock like something poured rather than planted. NYC Parks designates them as two separate Great Trees, ids 38 and 39, but they stand close enough on the same outcrop that almost nobody visits one without the other.

The rock underneath predates both trees by a margin that makes their own age beside the point. This is Manhattan schist, some of it dated by geologists at over a billion years old, exposed here by the same nineteenth century landscaping that shaped the rest of the park. The trees carry no planting record of their own, each roughly 78 feet tall, trunks gnarled from decades of finding purchase where there is barely any soil to root in.

What they prove is less about age than persistence. An elm in open parkland can be felled by disease or storm in a season. One growing out of solid rock has already solved a harder problem, and its awkward, rock gripping shape is the visible record of that fight.

They sit a few hundred metres from the Mall's elm allee and about 600 metres from the Ramble, an easy stop on the same walk through the park's oldest plantings.

trees.name: The Elm Allee of Literary Walk
trees.age: about 100 years (planted in the 1920s, the third planting on this site)
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 72nd Street (Metro B/C), 8 min walk
trees.story:
Central Park's most photographed avenue of trees is not the original one. The Mall, also called Literary Walk, has been replanted with American elms twice before the row standing today: the first two plantings failed when foot traffic compacted the soil around the roots, and the elms there now went in during the 1920s, the third attempt, protected from the start by low fencing along the path.

That makes these trees roughly a century old, not the century and a half some press coverage implies by counting from the park's 1858 design. NYC Parks lists the grove as an official Great Tree, and it is often called the largest grove of American elms in the world, a claim the park's own conservancy states more carefully: one of the largest remaining plantations of a species that Dutch elm disease has been cutting down, city-wide, since the 1930s. Central Park still holds about 1,600 elms, several hundred on a rotating fungicide programme, and still loses 15 to 30 a year to the same disease that ended the first two plantings here by other means.

Walk the Mall in full leaf and it reads as a cathedral aisle, two unbroken rows meeting overhead. Every one of them is a replacement, and every one of them is still, by the numbers, worth the trip.

trees.name: The Second Camperdown Elm of Green-Wood
trees.age: believed 19th or early 20th century planting, exact date unconfirmed
trees.access: Free, cemetery open daily (check seasonal hours)
trees.transport: 25th Street (Metro R), at the cemetery gate
trees.story:
Brooklyn has two Camperdown elms, and genetically they are the same tree. Every Camperdown elm alive is a graft from one contorted branch found on a Scottish estate near Dundee in the 1830s, a mutation that cannot be grown from seed, so each specimen is a cutting of a cutting of that single original. The famous one stands behind the Boathouse in Prospect Park, planted in 1872. This one grows two miles south, inside Green-Wood, where Garden Path meets Pink Avenue.

Nobody wrote down when it went in. New York's Great Trees register named it in 1985 and recorded the species and the corner, not a date, and no later source has supplied one. What the sources do agree on is the order: this is the younger of the two, and old enough to be counted among Green-Wood's landmark trees. A precise year would have to be invented, so there is none here.

The shape carries it anyway. Camperdowns arch their limbs downward and tangle them into one another instead of reaching up, which makes a low dome you duck into rather than stand under, dark inside even at midday. Victorian day-trippers came out to this cemetery in numbers that helped make the public case for Brooklyn's parks, and they came for exactly this: a landscape with curiosities in it. Green-Wood is free and open daily, and the R train stops at the gate.

trees.name: The Kansas Hawthorn of the Lily Pool
trees.access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden
trees.transport: Franklin Ave-Botanic Garden (Metro 2/3/4/5) or Prospect Park (B/Q/S), 5-10 min walk

best_time.label: October, when the leaves turn scarlet and the branches hang with dark crimson haws

trees.story:
The largest Kansas hawthorn in the United States grows in Brooklyn, and the species normally gives up at around twenty feet. This one reached 35, on a 20 inch trunk under a 28 foot crown, and in 1985 the American Forestry Association named it a national champion. New York State has carried it on its Big Tree Register since 2009 as one of only two champion trees in the five boroughs. None of that was the plan. Rochester's parks department sent it down as a gift in 1912, and it was planted across from the Lily Pool at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, which had opened to the public only a year or so before. It has stood there through everything the garden has become since.

Crataegus coccinioides is a hawthorn of the American Midwest, a thorny, unfashionable small tree that most visitors walk past for eleven months of the year. October is the exception, when the leaves go scarlet and orange and the branches hang with dark crimson haws.

Entry to the Garden is paid. The pin here sits at the Washington Avenue gate rather than at the tree, because no survey has recorded its coordinates: walk to the Lily Pool by the conservatory and look for the small tree carrying an unreasonable amount of fruit.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of the Rock Garden
trees.access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden
trees.transport: Franklin Ave-Botanic Garden (Metro 2/3/4/5) or Prospect Park (B/Q/S), 5-10 min walk

best_time.label: July and August, when foot-and-a-half chains of winged nutlets hang from every branch tip

trees.story:
This tree came from Rome in 1922, and one of its limbs now rests on a crutch. The Caucasian wingnut on the Flatbush Avenue side of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, just north of the Rock Garden, has grown heavy enough that the garden props and cables its lower branches to stop them tearing out of the trunk. That trunk is the argument: the Garden calls it nearly nine feet through, the city's Great Trees register measures ten, and the two figures have never been reconciled. It stands about 60 feet tall and close to as wide, with roots surfacing in long ridged patterns that run out from the base across the ground.

Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the wet forests between the Black Sea and northern Iran and reached European gardens in 1782, which is how an Italian nursery came to have one to send. The name is literal. In midsummer the tree hangs chains of small winged nutlets a foot and a half long from its branch tips, green ropes that stay up, browning, into autumn, and nothing else in the garden does anything like it. A clone of it went in near the Herb Garden in 1978, and the difference in size between the two makes the case for coming to see this one.

Entry to the Garden is paid, and the pin sits at the main gate: the tree is a walk away, along the Flatbush Avenue boundary.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon Grove near Conservatory Water
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Q train to 72nd Street (Second Avenue), about 10 minute walk west into the park via the 72nd Street/Fifth Avenue entrance

best_time.label: September to November, when upright cones sit on the branches like rows of eggs

trees.story: Central Park's own Conservancy calls this a single cedar of Lebanon. A blogger who found the same spot in 2016 counted several, growing together as a small grove, both describing the identical trees just inside the park's 72nd Street entrance, behind the information kiosk near Conservatory Water. Nobody has resolved the discrepancy, and this project would rather say so than guess. What both sources agree on is the plaque at the base, dedicating the planting for grandchildren, a gift from patrons Linda and Mort Janklow, and the species itself: Cedrus libani, the tree on Lebanon's flag and, in the older stories, the timber said to have built Solomon's Temple. It is evergreen where almost everything else in this part of Central Park is not, a pyramidal, blue green shape that holds its form across every season rather than only one. Its cones grow upright on the branch instead of hanging, ripening through autumn into rows that look, from a distance, like eggs balanced along each limb. No planting date survives for this grove; a 2016 estimate guesses a few decades old for Central Park's cedars generally, honest but not a measurement of this specific planting. Conservatory Water sits a five minute walk from three of this walk's other trees, the closest addition this cluster has had.

trees.name: The American Elm at the East 97th Street Entrance
trees.access: Free, public park, right at a park entrance path
trees.transport: 4/5/6 train to 96th Street/Lexington Avenue, about 10-12 minute walk east and north to the East 97th Street entrance
trees.story: Most of New York's elms are gone. Dutch elm disease arrived in the 1930s and by the postwar decades had killed the overwhelming majority of the American elms that once shaded nearly every street in the city, a loss so total that Central Park's surviving giants now register as minor miracles rather than ordinary trees. This one stands at the park's East 97th Street entrance, its northernmost officially designated Great Tree, an eighty foot canopy spread wide enough to be one of the broadest in the entire register, and a trunk the tree guides describe, not unkindly, as looking like an old witch, its serpentine branches twisting rather than reaching straight up. Nobody recorded when it was planted; city records only say the 1800s, a stretch of a century or more that leaves its exact age an open question. What is documented is what it survived: the fungus that erased its species from most of the city, and, per the park's own account, the storms that have since taken out other Central Park trees around it. New York designated it a Great Tree in 1985, one of the original class, decades before the citywide relaunch that added scores more in 2024. Walk in from Fifth Avenue at 97th Street and it is the first thing waiting.

trees.name: The London Plane of the Reservoir
trees.access: Free, public park, beside the Reservoir's public running/bridle path
trees.transport: 6 train to 96th Street, about 10 minute walk west into the park to the Reservoir's Bridle Path
trees.story: A tree with more than one trunk is hard to age by the usual rule of thumb, and that uncertainty is most of this one's story. The London plane on the Bridle Path near East 96th Street rises just over ninety six feet from a base that splits into multiple trunks fused so thoroughly that its combined diameter tops five feet, bark mottled in patches of green, tan and grey that one NYC Parks writer compared to an impressionist canvas. The claim attached to it, that it was planted around 1862 when the Reservoir beside it was first excavated, comes from one nature writer's educated guess rather than any planting record, which makes 'possibly the oldest tree in Central Park' a title worth repeating with the word possibly intact. A rival candidate exists across the park: a black tupelo in the Ramble that one book on the city's great trees dates to 1858, four years earlier, an argument nobody has settled because neither tree came with a receipt. What is not in dispute is the setting. The Reservoir's running path carries thousands of people past this trunk every week, most looking at the water and the skyline reflected in it rather than down at the multi-trunked plane that has, by the most generous reading, watched the water since before the Civil War.

trees.name: The Yoshino Cherries of the Reservoir
trees.age: not documented; the planting traces to a 1912 gift from Japan
trees.access: Free, public park, beside the Reservoir's public running path
trees.transport: 4/5/6 train to 86th Street, about 10-12 minute walk west into the park to the Reservoir's east side

best_time.label: mid-April, usually a week or two before the Reservoir's Kwanzan cherries across the water

trees.story: Everyone knows Washington's cherry trees came from Japan in 1912. Fewer know New York got a gift the same year: a planting of Yoshino cherries along the Reservoir's east side, sent alongside the 3,020 trees that went to the Tidal Basin and somehow left out of the story that made the capital famous for its blossoms. Thirty five trees stand there today, city designated as a single Great Tree entry rather than thirty five separate ones, which is the honest way to register a planting nobody experiences tree by tree. They bloom white shading to pale pink each April, usually a week or two before the Reservoir's showier Kwanzan cherries on the opposite bank, and the flowers carry a faint almond scent the plum colored Kwanzans do not. Here is the part no one advertises: Yoshino cherries rarely live past sixty years even with good care, and nothing in the historical record says whether the trees blooming today grew from the original 1912 shipment or replaced it at some point since, the way Washington's own planting has been replanted in stages for a century. So the honest claim is not that these particular trunks are old. It is that this exact stretch of path has carried the same seasonal show, on the same imported species, since Woodrow Wilson's first year in the White House.

trees.name: The Thousand-Year Camphor of Nankunsha
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Sumiyoshitaisha Station (Nankai Main Line); Sumiyoshi-Torii-mae tram stop (Hankai Line) is right at the gate
trees.story: Once a month, on the shrine calendar's first day of the earthly-branch cycle, pilgrims climb the steps to Nankunsha and buy a small ceramic cat. Miss a month and a four-year cycle called hattatsu-mairi starts over: 48 cats, one paw raised for household safety, the other for business luck, collected at the foot of this camphor tree until a full set earns a trade-up to a bigger cat. The custom has made Nankunsha, a small shrine tucked behind Sumiyoshi Taisha's main hall, one of the most visited corners of Osaka's oldest and most revered shrine complex, even though the tree itself predates the ritual by centuries. The Sennen-kusu, literally the Thousand-Year Camphor, has a trunk measuring nearly ten metres around and stands roughly as old as its name claims, a start somewhere around the late Heian period. Osaka City has designated it a preserved tree. Sumiyoshi Taisha's own founding legend reaches back roughly 1,800 years, to Empress Jingu's return from a campaign on the Korean peninsula, and this camphor is one of the oldest living things still standing on ground that has hosted continuous worship since. Visitors rarely come for the tree alone. They come for the cats, then notice, almost as an afterthought, what has been growing over their heads the whole time.

trees.name: The Married Camphor of Nankunsha
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Sumiyoshitaisha Station (Nankai Main Line); Sumiyoshi-Torii-mae tram stop (Hankai Line) is right at the gate
trees.story: At ground level this camphor splits cleanly into two trunks rising from one root, and that accident of growth turned it into a wedding-day landmark. The Meoto-kusu, literally the Married Couple Camphor, stands at the gate of Nankunsha inside Sumiyoshi Taisha, roughly 800 years old and nearly eight metres around at its widest trunk. Couples visiting the shrine for a ceremony, or hoping to arrange one, stop here before anywhere else, and the tree shows up on more Sumiyoshi Taisha souvenirs than any of the shrine's own buildings. It shares its small precinct with an older, single-trunked neighbour, the Sennen-kusu, and the two are usually mentioned in the same breath, though sources agree they are separate trees with distinct measurements and roughly two centuries between their ages. Like its neighbour, the Meoto-kusu carries an Osaka City preserved-tree designation. Both grow on ground that has hosted Shinto worship since Sumiyoshi Taisha's legendary third-century founding, the kind of continuously used shrine land that let a tree like this get old in the first place, never cleared for redevelopment the way so much of the rest of the city has been. What the couples actually want is simpler than any of that history: a photograph beside the split trunk, and whatever luck a shrine can offer on the way to the altar.

trees.name: The Achihayao Shrine Camphor
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Hanaten Station (JR Gakken Toshi Line / Osaka Metro Imazatosuji Line)
trees.story: Lightning found this camphor sometime during the Taisho era, between 1912 and 1926, and burned out most of its main trunk. What survived was roughly a third of the original tree, its supporting limbs still living beneath a long dead spar from the original trunk, enough that a tree doctor could eventually nurse it back into something recognisably whole. What stands today at Achihayao Shrine is that survivor: about six metres around, sixteen metres tall, and by tradition close to 1,000 years old. Osaka Prefecture designated it a natural monument in 1970 under the plain name the Camphor of Achihayao Shrine, one of the few individually protected trees left in Tsurumi Ward. The shrine itself appears in the Engishiki, the 10th-century register of officially recognised shrines, which places worship on this exact spot at least a thousand years back, roughly matching the tree's own traditional age. Unlike Sumiyoshi Taisha's better-known camphors across the city, Achihayao draws a quieter crowd: local families and anyone who has read that this is one of the only trees in Osaka that visibly carries its own near-death on its trunk. Most ancient trees hide their age. This one wears it as a scar, three minutes from a suburban train station most visitors to Osaka never have a reason to use.

trees.name: The Namba Shrine Camphor
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Shinsaibashi Station (Osaka Metro Midosuji Line)
trees.story: In 1811 a theatre manager named Uemura Bunrakuken opened a puppet theatre in Namba Shrine's courtyard, and the venue's nickname eventually gave its name to an entire art form: Bunraku, Japan's classical puppet theatre, is named for the man who staged it here, under this camphor's shade. The tree itself predates that history by two centuries or more, close to 400 years old today, and it holds a distinction unrelated to puppetry: it was the first tree ever named to Osaka City's official preserved-tree register. Shrine buildings around it did not fare as well. Namba Shrine burned completely in the March 1945 Osaka air raids and was not rebuilt until 1974. The four-hundred-year age given to this camphor today only works if it is the same tree that came through that fire still standing, on a plot that briefly had nothing else left. It grows a five-minute walk from Shinsaibashi, one of central Osaka's busiest shopping streets, largely unnoticed by a crowd with somewhere else to be. The shrine's own history reaches back further still, to a legendary founding under the fifth-century Emperor Hanzei, though the current site dates only to a 1597 relocation. Whatever the exact count, this camphor has outlasted every structure that has ever stood beside it.

trees.name: Munch-eika
trees.access: Free, open access, Montebello (residential area, tree visible from public streets)
trees.transport: Montebello railway/metro station, short walk

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Oslo's own city-planning office names this oak the city's oldest tree, roughly 500 to 600 years old with a trunk about eight metres around, growing in the Montebello area on the city's west side. Its name almost certainly points to Edvard Munch, whose home and studio at nearby Ekely stood a short walk from here for the last decades of his life, though the exact naming story is not documented anywhere this project could confirm, only the coincidence of the painter's name and the neighbourhood. What is documented is the oak's remarkable persistence: a tree with this trunk girth would have already been mature when Christiania, as Oslo was then called, was still a modest fortified trading town centuries away from the industrial and cultural boom that eventually brought artists like Munch to its western suburbs. Oslo's municipal magazine on street trees uses the Munch-eika as its lead example of what the city stands to lose when old trees go untended, a reminder that a tree with five centuries behind it can still be brought down by root damage, soil compaction or simple neglect in a matter of years rather than centuries. It survives today as one of very few individual trees in Oslo old enough to predate the city's written records of its own tree population.

trees.name: The Linden Alley of Dronningparken
trees.access: Free, open access, Dronningparken/Slottsparken (public park, open at all times)
trees.transport: National Theatre railway and metro station, short walk

best_time.label: July to August, when it flowers

trees.story: Before Oslo's Royal Palace existed, this stretch of ground was Sommerro, a meadow the mayor Christian Henrik Stoedt turned into a small rococo garden in 1751. When the merchant Bernt Anker took over the property in 1778, he kept the formal garden but planted a linden avenue through the surrounding land he was reshaping into a more naturalistic park, the alley that still opens today toward Henrik Ibsens gate. The Royal Palace itself would not be built for another half-century, going up between 1823 and 1849 around and beside the park Anker had already shaped; when it was finished, his linden alley became part of the grounds of a building that did not exist when the trees were planted. Not everything from that planting survives: when a new entrance to the National Theatre metro station opened in the park's southwest corner in 1998, the oldest lindens in that stretch were removed to make way for it. The alley that remains is Oslo's clearest surviving link to the city's pre-royal, merchant-era parkland, predating the palace it now appears to belong to by nearly half a century.

trees.name: The Birches of Birkelunden
trees.access: Free, open access, Birkelunden (public park, open at all times)
trees.transport: Tram to Birkelunden or Olaf Ryes plass, adjacent
trees.story: A cavalry officer named Thorvald Meyer laid out this park in the 1860s as he subdivided the farmland around it into what became Grunerlokka, one of Oslo's first planned working-class districts, and lined its edges with birch trees, the species that gave the park its name, bjork being Norwegian for birch. Meyer gave the park to the city for free in 1882, and between 1916 and 1920 much of its internal planting was rearranged into a practical playground for the neighbourhood's children, though the perimeter birches from Meyer's original layout mostly stayed in place. In 2006, Birkelunden and the streets and apartment blocks around it became the first protected urban cultural environment in Norway, a designation covering 116 hectares, 139 buildings, the neighbourhood's Paulus Church and its school, with the park's own birch trees, now around 160 years old, standing at the centre of what the protection order is meant to preserve. Grunerlokka has since become one of Oslo's most fashionable neighbourhoods, its industrial-era apartment blocks converted into some of the city's most sought-after addresses, but the birches ringing the square are the one feature that connects today's cafes and boutiques back to Meyer's 1860s farmland subdivision without needing a plaque to explain it.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Botanisk Hage
trees.access: Free, open access, Botanisk hage (public garden, open at all times; glasshouses may charge separately)
trees.transport: Toyen metro station, short walk

best_time.label: October, when its fan-shaped leaves turn brilliant yellow

trees.story: Norway's oldest botanical garden, founded in 1814 on land the newly created University of Oslo assigned to its first botany professor, Christen Smith, holds what its own museum believes to be the oldest ginkgo tree anywhere in Northern Europe. It was planted in 1870 behind what would become the Victoria House, a tropical glasshouse built six years later specifically to grow and display the enormous Victoria water lily, and the ginkgo has spent the century and a half since then growing into the garden's largest specimen of its kind. Ginkgo biloba survived essentially unchanged for over 200 million years in the fossil record before nearly disappearing everywhere except a few pockets of China, which is why Europeans often call it a living fossil or, in Norwegian, a temple tree, a name reflecting the species' long cultivation around Buddhist and Confucian temple grounds in East Asia. The Victoria House itself marked its 150th anniversary in 2026, a reminder that even the garden's celebrated glasshouse is younger than the tree growing quietly behind it. Ginkgos are famously resistant to pollution, pests and disease, among the reasons this one has outlasted several rebuilding phases of the garden around it since 1870.

trees.name: The Lime of Macharen Church
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, on the public square.
trees.story:
This lime stands by Macharen's Sint-Petrus-Bandenkerk, on the village square, banded by the national tree register to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old. Macharen is one of the small riverside villages folded into the municipality of Oss, and a lime on the church square was the ordinary choice for a Dutch village centre for centuries: shade for the market, a meeting point, and a tree nobody had much reason to remove once the buildings around it had grown up to match its age.

Common lime, the hybrid the Dutch planted almost everywhere for this purpose, tolerates hard pruning and pollarding better than most trees, which is why so many village limes were kept small and dense for generations before eventually being let go, and a lime this age has usually been through both phases of its life.

The register gives no history beyond the species and the decade, which is typical for a tree whose interest is where it stands rather than any single event attached to it. If you know more about this lime, or when the church itself dates from, tell us.

trees.name: The Lime of the Old School
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public land, always visible.
trees.story:
A second lime in Macharen, on the Hoogstraat by what the register calls Basisschool De Linde, a primary school apparently named for this very tree. It is banded to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old, a generation younger than its counterpart at the church square a few streets over.

A lime that gives a school its name is a small but telling sign of how central a village tree can become: not just scenery but a landmark children are taught by its presence, generation after generation, whether or not anyone still remembers who planted it. Common lime tolerates the compacted soil and foot traffic around a schoolyard better than most species, part of why it became the default village tree across the Netherlands for so long.

The register carries no further history for this tree, only the species and the decade. If you know anything about the school's own naming, or the tree's history before the register recorded it, tell us.

trees.name: The Sycamore of Kloosterstraat
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, on the public square.
trees.story:
This sycamore in Megen was planted in 1928, one of the few trees on this list whose year the register states outright rather than banding into a decade. That puts it at just under a century old, younger than most of Oss's other registered trees but dated with unusual precision.

Megen is a small walled town on the river Maas, and Kloosterstraat, the street this tree stands on, takes its name from the Franciscan monastery still active there, one of the reasons the town's historic core survived largely intact. A sycamore maple planted on a town street in the 1920s would have grown up fast by the standards of its longer-lived neighbours on this list, sycamore being one of the quicker-growing trees the Dutch planted for shade rather than for centuries of standing.

The register gives no further history: a firm planting year, but nothing about who planted it or why. If you know the story behind it, tell us.

trees.name: The Beech of Sint-Lambertuskerk
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, public cemetery grounds, open in daylight.
trees.story:
This beech grows in the churchyard of Sint-Lambertuskerk in Haren, another of the small villages gathered into the municipality of Oss, banded by the national register to a planting around 1890, roughly 140 years old. A churchyard beech of this age has usually had an easier life than a street tree of the same vintage: less pruning, less soil compaction, and the kind of undisturbed ground that lets a beech build the wide, low, dome-shaped crown the species is known for when nothing crowds it.

A beech that old also carries the smooth grey bark the species keeps its whole life, unlike most other large trees, which is part of why old beeches so often bear generations of carved initials that never grow over or fade.

The register describes the site, a working cemetery still in use, but nothing about the tree's own history beyond species and decade. Churchyards are consistently where this project finds its oldest small-village trees, for the plain reason that nobody redevelops a cemetery. If you know more about this one, tell us.

trees.name: The Lulboom of Megen
trees.age: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1940
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.

best_time.label: July, when the silver lime flowers and the whole spot smells of it

trees.story:
Locals call this pair of silver limes the Lulboom, and the register itself repeats the nickname rather than softening it. It marks the town's coronation tree: in 1937, when Princess Juliana, later queen, married Prince Bernhard, Megen planted a royal lime at a prominent spot just outside its historic core to mark the occasion, banded now by the national register to 1930-1940, roughly 90 years old.

What has grown up around the planting since is the real story. A bench sits beside it, and generations of Megen residents have used the spot as an informal meeting point, sitting, talking, watching the view over the Maasdijk, which is how a formal royal planting acquired an entirely unroyal nickname somewhere along the way. Two cannon from 1809 and 1811 stand under the tree, unconnected to the planting itself but folded into the same small monument over time.

The register records the silver lime twice, as two adjoining registrations metres apart, which this page treats as one entry rather than two, since a visitor sees a single planting rather than a pair. If you know more of the Lulboom's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Klaphekkenstraat
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, on the public square.

best_time.label: May, when the white candle-shaped flower spikes cover the crown

trees.story:
This horse chestnut stands on the public square where Klaphekkenstraat meets Goudmijnstraat in Oss itself, banded by the national register to a planting around 1930, roughly a century old. Oss grew fast through the twentieth century on the back of its meat-processing and margarine industries, Unilever's roots running straight through the town, and a tree this age on an ordinary residential square is a small, quiet survivor of the neighbourhood's early expansion.

A horse chestnut of a century's growth is close to its prime: full canopy, an established root system, and every May a full display of the white candle-shaped flower spikes the species is planted for everywhere from parks to school playgrounds. Chestnuts of this age are also the ones most often lost to bleeding canker and leaf miner damage in the Netherlands, so a healthy century-old specimen is worth noting for that reason alone, though the register records no condition detail for this one.

The register is the only source describing it. If you know when it was planted, or anything of the square's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Response Linden
trees.access: Free, open public square, no barrier
trees.transport: Rideau Station (O-Train Confederation Line) approx 3 min walk
trees.story:
The memorial this linden stands beside was built for one war and unveiled three months before the next one began. King George VI pulled the cover off it in May 1939, in front of a crowd of 100,000. The monument has a formal name, The Response, and it shows twenty-two bronze figures hauling a field gun and its team through a granite arch, soldiers and nurses and airmen pressed together in the gap. In 2000 the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier was set into the ground in front of it, holding a Canadian recovered from a cemetery near Vimy Ridge whose name was never established.

The tree is the quiet part of all that. It stands at the memorial end of Confederation Square, a small-leaved lime with the dense rounded crown the species makes when nobody interferes with it, and it is the only thing in that square that changes with the season while the bronze does not. Every 11 November the national ceremony fills the ground beneath it. For the rest of the year it shades office workers eating lunch on the steps of the busiest traffic island in the country.

When it was planted, nobody wrote down. The capital's register of remarkable trees names the tree and gives it no date, and no other source has anything to say about this particular one. If you know its age, tell us.

trees.name: The Vitifolia Linden (west of the pair)
trees.access: Free, open public park, no barrier
trees.transport: Rideau Station (O-Train Confederation Line) approx 6-8 min walk
trees.story:
Look up and the leaves look wrong for a lime. This is the Vitifolia cultivar of the large-leaved lime, selected for foliage that is broad, blunt-toothed and lobed enough to pass for a grapevine, which is what the name means. Two of them stand in Major's Hill Park about thirty-five metres apart, and they are the only ones the capital's register of remarkable trees lists anywhere in Ottawa. This is the western tree of the pair.

By the register's account both were held in the Central Experimental Farm nursery around 1897 and put in the ground here in or around 1900, which makes them roughly 125 years old. The hedging is the register's own and it stays: that one document is the only thing dating either tree. The man behind the planting is not in doubt. William Saunders ran the Dominion Experimental Farms from 1886 to 1911 out of the farm across town, and the nursery he built there supplied the stock that turned a working river port into somewhere a government could plausibly sit.

Major's Hill Park has been public ground since the 1870s, on the bluff where the Rideau Canal drops through its locks to the Ottawa River. The lime has stood through the whole modern life of the park, and from underneath it you look straight across the cut at Parliament Hill.

trees.name: The Vitifolia Linden (east of the pair)
trees.access: Free, open public park, no barrier
trees.transport: Rideau Station (O-Train Confederation Line) approx 6-8 min walk
trees.story:
Ottawa's register of remarkable trees lists exactly two vine-leaved limes in the city, and this is the eastern one. Its twin stands thirty-five metres away across the grass. The cultivar carries the name Vitifolia because the leaves are cut like a grape's, big and coarse and nothing like the neat heart-shaped leaf most people picture on a lime. In the last week of June the crown hums: limes flower late, the scent carries, and every bee in the park works the tree at once.

The dating comes from a single source, the National Capital Commission's register, which says both trees were likely raised in the Central Experimental Farm nursery around 1897 and planted here in or around 1900. Roughly 125 years, then, with the register's own likely and its in-or-around left in place, because no second document names either tree.

What that decade explains is why they are here at all. Ottawa spent the years around 1900 deliberately rebuilding its own appearance, and ornamental stock from the government farm was the cheapest way to do it. Major's Hill Park sits on the bluff above the canal locks with Parliament Hill directly opposite, which made it the first place the effort showed. Stand between the two limes and you are standing in the result.

trees.name: The Yellow-wood of Major's Hill Park
trees.access: Free, open public park, no barrier
trees.transport: Rideau Station (O-Train Confederation Line) approx 6-8 min walk

best_time.label: early June, in the years it flowers, when the crown hangs with white chains

trees.story:
The wild range of this species is a scatter of hillsides in Kentucky, Tennessee and the western Carolinas, and even there it is one of the rarest native trees in eastern North America. This one grows well over a thousand kilometres north of all of it, on the edge of a downtown park in Ottawa.

American yellowwood, Cladrastis kentukea, which older labels and the capital's own register still call Cladrastis lutea. The name is literal. The heartwood is bright yellow and was once boiled down for dye. The bark is smooth and pale grey, closer to a beech than to anything else growing near it, and the tree forks low and spreads wide, so it is one to walk under rather than past. Every few years, and pointedly not every year, it hangs the whole crown with drooping chains of white flowers that smell like wisteria, which is the family it belongs to. In the years it skips, it just makes leaves.

It shares this end of Major's Hill Park with the two vine-leaved limes, and unlike them it arrived without paperwork. The register names the tree and gives no planting date, and nothing else we can find mentions this specimen at all. Somebody in the parks service probably knows the year. If that is you, we would like it.

trees.name: The Serbian Spruce Trio
trees.access: Free, open public park, no barrier
trees.transport: Elgin/Laurier, short walk from Rideau Station or Parliament, approx 5-8 min
trees.story:
In the wild, Serbian spruce survives in one place on earth: a handful of limestone gorges along the Drina, in the mountains between Serbia and Bosnia, where it hangs on as a leftover from a colder world. Three of them stand together in Confederation Park, close enough that they read as one tree with three trunks, a short walk from the city's South African War Memorial.

They are easy to pick out once you know what to look for. A Serbian spruce is absurdly narrow for its height, a spire rather than a cone, with short branches that sweep down and then turn up at the tips. The needles are flat, dark green on top and marked underneath with two chalk-white bands, so on a windy day the whole group flickers between green and silver. That narrow build is also why the species is planted here at all: it sheds the better part of two metres of snow a winter without losing its limbs.

Confederation Park itself opened in 1967, laid out for Canada's centennial on two and a half hectares between Elgin Street and the canal. When the three spruces went in is not recorded anywhere we can find, and the register that lists them gives no date. If you have a photograph of this corner from before they were there, that would settle it.

trees.name: The Mackenzie King Pear
trees.access: Free, open public park, no barrier
trees.transport: Elgin/Laurier, short walk from Rideau Station or Parliament, approx 5-8 min

best_time.label: early May, when the whole crown goes white before most of the park has leaves

trees.story:
A prime minister used to live where this pear is standing. Until 1923 William Lyon Mackenzie King rented at the Roxborough Apartments on Elgin Street, the grandest block in the city when it opened in 1910, and his diary is openly sentimental about the day he left it for Laurier House. The Roxborough came down in 1966 and Confederation Park was laid out over the site, so the smartest address in Ottawa is now lawn, memorials and one Ussurian pear.

The species comes from the Russian Far East and northern China and is about as cold-hardy as pears get, which is why it is here and why most orchard pears are not. In early May it flowers hard, the whole crown white, ahead of nearly everything else in the park. Whether anything follows is a point the sources argue about: the capital's register says a stand-alone Ussurian pear sets no fruit because it depends on cross-pollination, while growers of the species describe it as at least partly self-fertile, with a second tree improving the crop rather than making it possible. Go for the blossom, and treat any small hard pears in autumn as a bonus.

Its own age is unrecorded. The register names the tree, ties it to King's old address and stops there, which leaves the planting year open. Somebody watched it go in. If that was you, we would like the date.

trees.name: The Ottawa Improvement Commission Horse Chestnut
trees.access: Free, open public grounds, no barrier
trees.transport: Rideau Station (O-Train Confederation Line) approx 6-8 min walk

best_time.label: late May, when the crown fills with white candles

trees.story:
The body that planted this tree was called the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and it was handed sixty thousand dollars a year to make a lumber town look like a capital. It was created in 1899 and it is the ancestor of today's National Capital Commission. Its early planting leaned on the Central Experimental Farm across town, whose arboretum had gone from 200 trees in 1889 to 3,000 by 1899 and could supply stock by the wagonload. The capital's tree register puts this horse chestnut in those first years, likely planted circa 1900. Likely and circa are the register's own words and they stay: no second source names this particular tree. Call it roughly 125 years old and treat the year as approximate.

It is not a chestnut and it is not from anywhere near here. Aesculus hippocastanum grows wild in a few mountain valleys in the Balkans and was carried across Europe and then North America purely as an avenue tree, for the reason that shows in late May, when the crown fills with upright white flower spikes standing on the branches like candles. The nuts that drop in September are the ones children fight with and nothing eats.

It stands at the Sussex Drive end of the Major's Hill Park slope, a few minutes uphill from the two vine-leaved limes.

trees.name: The Tulip Season Willow
trees.access: Free, open public park, no barrier
trees.transport: Rideau Station (O-Train Confederation Line) approx 6-8 min walk
trees.story:
The crack willow is named for the noise, and the noise is the strategy. Its twigs snap off cleanly at the base in wind, float away down the water and root wherever they wash up, which is how one willow turns into a riverbank full of them. This one grows below Major's Hill Park on the slope toward the Ottawa River, with the National Gallery of Canada on one side and the twin spires of Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica on the other. There are few better places in the city to stand under a tree.

Mid-May is when the ground around it is worth the walk on its own account. The park is planted out for the Canadian Tulip Festival, which began with a gift of bulbs from the Dutch royal family after the Second World War, and the beds run right up to the willow while the crowds work their way along them. The tree's own contribution to spring is a couple of weeks of small green catkins in April that nobody has ever crossed town for.

Willows grow fast, hollow early and are almost always younger than they look, which makes guessing at this one pointless. The register names it and records no age, no girth and no planting date. If anyone has put a tape around it, we would take the number.

trees.name: The Iffley Yew
trees.access: Free, open access, churchyard
trees.transport: 45 min walk or short bus ride from central Oxford

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: St Mary the Virgin in Iffley is one of the most complete unaltered Norman churches left in England, built around 1170 by the local lord of the manor and his wife. Against its southeast wall grows a yew so large that its canopy shades several gravestones beneath it, its trunk hollow, rust-red and furrowed with age, still producing dense evergreen foliage and berries every year. An 1892 account in Chambers Journal put its age at over 1,600 years, which would mean druids could plausibly have gathered beneath it a thousand years before the church's Norman builders laid a single stone, since pre-Christian communities across Britain regarded yew groves as sacred sites long before churches were built on top of them. Later, more cautious assessments back away from that figure and describe the tree only as a strong candidate for being contemporary with the Norman church itself, still a respectable 850 years or so. Either estimate makes it one of the oldest living things in Oxfordshire. Charles Dodgson, better known as Lewis Carroll, spent most of his life as an Oxford academic and is thought to have visited Iffley's church often; local tradition credits this yew as the inspiration for one of his early illustrations of the tree in Alice's Adventures Underground, the manuscript that became Alice in Wonderland.

trees.name: The Bobart Yew
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, opposite Christ Church Meadow
trees.access: Paid admission (modest fee, free for University of Oxford students, staff and members), daily except Christmas Day and Boxing Day
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Oxford railway station

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Oxford Botanic Garden is Britain's oldest botanic garden, founded in 1621 as a physic garden for teaching medicinal plants to university students. Jacob Bobart the Elder, a German-born gardener who became the garden's first curator, planted a yew in the Walled Garden in 1645, according to his own handwritten planting notes, one of a pair he set at the site. Herbalists of the time dismissed yew as having no medicinal use worth the space, but Bobart planted it anyway, alongside an avenue of others, and it has outlasted every argument about its usefulness by nearly four centuries. Only one of the original pair survives today. In February 2020, Storm Ciara tore off a large section of its upper canopy, scattering branches across the Walled Garden and leaving the tree looking badly maimed. The garden's own staff were unworried: yews regenerate from collapsed and layered branches in a way few other trees can, regrowing new stems from wood that would kill most species, and the tree was expected to recover fully rather than decline. It remains the oldest documented plant in the garden's entire collection, its exact planting year more precisely known than almost any other tree on this list, thanks to one meticulous 17th-century gardener's own notebook.

trees.name: The White Mulberry of the Botanic Garden
trees.neighbourhood: City centre, opposite Christ Church Meadow
trees.access: Paid admission (modest fee, free for University of Oxford students, staff and members), daily except Christmas Day and Boxing Day
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Oxford railway station

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: White Mulberry is not a tree Britain's climate treats kindly. It was imported by the thousand in the 17th and 18th centuries in a failed attempt to build a domestic silk industry, since it is the preferred food of silkworms, and most of those plantings died out or were grubbed up once the silk scheme collapsed. Oxford Botanic Garden's specimen survived because it was never planted for industry. It dates to the late 1790s, when the garden's keeper John Sibthorp rearranged the grounds and its planting scheme, and it is now thought to be the oldest White Mulberry still growing anywhere in Britain, a claim made by Morus Londinium, the mulberry research project that tracks the species' surviving specimens nationwide. Two and a bit centuries on, the tree has the low, wide, gnarled habit White Mulberries take on with age rather than the upright form of a young specimen, its bark deeply fissured. It stands as one of the oldest plants in a garden already 400 years old, a survivor twice over: first of an industry that failed around it, then of two more centuries most of its own species in Britain never reached.

trees.name: The Pococke Plane
trees.access: Paid admission to Christ Church (Pococke Garden viewable as part of the college visit)
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Oxford railway station
trees.story: Edward Pococke spent years in Aleppo and Constantinople as an Oxford scholar sent to master Arabic manuscripts, and returned in 1636 to become the university's first Regius Professor of Hebrew and Laudian Professor of Arabic. Tradition holds that he brought back more than languages: a seed of Oriental Plane, a species barely known in England at the time, which he planted in what is now Christ Church's Pococke Garden. The tree that stands there today has a girth approaching nine metres, by most measures the thickest and, by extension, oldest Oriental Plane recorded in Britain. Its own growth pattern complicates the story it is credited with, though: the shape and growth rate documented since the early 1900s suggest the visible tree may actually be a rooted layer, a branch that touched the ground, took root, and grew into what looks like a separate trunk, dating from around the mid-18th century rather than being Pococke's original 1636 planting itself. Whether it is the original tree or its own regrown descendant standing in the same spot, it has anchored the same corner of the garden for at least two and a half centuries. Lewis Carroll, an Oxford mathematics don for most of his career, is thought to have drawn on it for the Tumtum tree in his poem Jabberwocky, the one the Jabberwock supposedly rests beneath.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of North Walk
trees.access: Free, open access, University Parks (daily, 7:45am to dusk)
trees.transport: 20 min walk from Oxford railway station

best_time.label: October to November: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: Oxford's University Parks hold nine trees recognised as national champions, the tallest or largest recorded example of their species anywhere in Britain, and the Caucasian Elm on North Walk is the one that towers over the rest of the list. At around 33 metres it is the tallest Caucasian Elm recorded in the country, its crown spreading some 14 metres wide, dense and many-stemmed in the way the species characteristically grows once mature. Zelkova carpinifolia looks enough like a true elm to share the common name, but it belongs to a separate genus entirely, which is precisely why specimens like this one across Britain survived the Dutch Elm disease epidemic that devastated the country's actual elms from the 1970s onward. The Parks themselves opened to the public in 1864, laid out on former university-owned farmland along the River Cherwell, and have been adding notable specimen trees to their collection ever since. This one has had over a century to put on height in the open, undisturbed ground along North Walk, uncompeted for light in a way few urban trees ever get to be, which is likely a large part of how it became a national record holder rather than merely an old tree.

trees.name: The Goethe Palm
trees.species: European Fan Palm / Saint Peter's Palm (Chamaerops humilis)
trees.neighbourhood: Orto Botanico (UNESCO World Heritage botanical garden, founded 1545)
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required; exact current price not verified )
trees.transport: ~1.9 km / roughly 25-30 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified
trees.story: Goethe walked through this garden in 1786, stopped at a palm, and left with the beginnings of a theory.
