He was working towards his essay on the metamorphosis of plants, the argument that every organ of a plant is a modified leaf, and this dwarf fan palm, whose fronds change shape as they climb the stem, is the specimen credited with helping the idea along. It has been in the ground since 1585, one of the first plants set out after the Orto Botanico was founded in 1545, which makes it roughly 440 years old. Chamaerops humilis is a Mediterranean plant with no patience for Veneto frost, so the garden built a glass house around it, an octagonal greenhouse raised to fit one shrub. Up close it is not a single trunk but a clump of about 25 stems, each roughly half a metre round, 4.5 metres of girth in total. The Italian register rates its health as good, last checked in July 2026, and files it under a second name, the Palm of Saint Peter, which is what Padua called it long before a German poet turned up. A panel beside the glass tells the visitor the rest. It is the least imposing tree on this list and the only one that ended up in a book about how plants are put together.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required)
trees.transport: ~1.9 km / roughly 25-30 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified
trees.story: Lightning opened this plane from the base upward and it kept going. The trunk is hollow, a shell you can see into, and the tree still leafs out every spring, because the tissue that carries water sits in the outer wood rather than the core. It went into the ground in 1680 according to the garden's own visitor leaflet, which puts it at about 345 years, and it has been measured at 6.2 metres round and nearly 25 metres tall. Worth being precise about the species: this is Platanus orientalis, the eastern plane, native in Italy only in a few pockets of Calabria and Sicily. Almost every tree called a plane in a European city, including two others on this list, is the hybrid that came later. The date rests on that leaflet and on Italian garden-history sources agreeing on the same two details, the 1680 planting and the lightning strike, rather than on a second register entry, so read it as well corroborated rather than documented twice. What the tree's first century looked like from here: Venice still ruled Padua and had another hundred years of republic left, and the botanical garden around it was already 135 years old and busy cataloguing plants arriving from the Americas. The register rates its condition as good.

trees.name: The Grafted Ginkgo of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required)
trees.transport: ~1.9 km / roughly 25-30 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified

best_time.label: November, when it turns hard yellow and then drops the whole canopy in a matter of days

trees.story: Somebody grafted a female branch onto this male ginkgo in the middle of the 19th century, so one tree here sheds pollen in spring and drops fruit in autumn from the same trunk. Ginkgos are normally one sex or the other, and the female fruit is famous for smelling like something died, so the graft was either a teaching exercise or a practical joke that has outlived everyone involved. The tree was planted in 1750, among the first of its kind brought to Italy. The garden's register goes further and says it may have been the first in the country and the second in Europe, after a tree planted in Utrecht in 1727; treat that as the register's claim rather than a settled fact. It stands 17 to 20 metres tall on a trunk four metres round. The species is the last survivor of an order of plants that was widespread before the dinosaurs and had been reduced to a few cultivated Chinese groves by the time European collectors found it, a biography nothing else in this garden can match. The register rates its condition as adequate rather than good, last checked in July 2026, so this is not a tree without problems. Come in November anyway.

trees.name: The 1786 Magnolia of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required)
trees.transport: ~1.9 km / roughly 25-30 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified

best_time.label: June and July, when the lemon-scented flowers open a few at a time, each the size of a dinner plate

trees.story: This magnolia was planted in 1786, the same year Goethe came through the gate. It is one of the first Magnolia grandiflora set out in Italy, reportedly among the oldest still standing anywhere in Europe, and it has been in this arboretum for 240 years, spreading a crown about 13 metres across. The species had reached Europe from the American southeast only a few decades earlier, and a botanical garden's job in the 1780s was exactly this: get the new plant into the ground and find out whether it survives the winter. It did. Its girth is a small lesson in reading registers. One file gives 2.22 metres, from a document the register itself flags as needing an update, while a 2026 remeasurement gives 2.54 metres. Trees do not shrink, so the older figure is the one to distrust. Southern magnolia is evergreen, dark and leathery the whole year, which makes the flowering the event: cream-white, lemon-scented, the size of a dinner plate, opening a few at a time so the tree is never covered at once and never quite finished either. Padua's other famous magnolia, 300 metres away in a cloister at the Basilica, is a different tree planted a generation later. The two get confused constantly, including by sources that should know better.

trees.name: The Magnolia of the Saint
trees.neighbourhood: Piazza del Santo, adjoining the Basilica di Sant'Antonio
trees.access: The cloister sits inside the Basilica's museum complex, reached on the combined museum-sites ticket (per santantonio.org: Tue-Sun 09:00-13:00 and 14:00-18:00, closed Mondays; full-price ticket quoted at EUR 10 / reduced EUR 7 as of the 2026-08-06 search, not independently re-verified at the ticket office)
trees.transport: ~1.7 km / roughly 25 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified

best_time.label: June and July, when the low branches put the flowers at eye level in the cloister

trees.story: The cloister is named after the tree. The Chiostro della Magnolia is the first courtyard of the Basilica di Sant'Antonio, the 13th-century pilgrimage church that has drawn visitors to Padua for 800 years, and the magnolia at its centre was planted in 1810 according to the Basilica's own account. That makes it about 215 years old, 25 metres tall and 4.4 metres round, listed on Italy's national register of monumental trees under its own code. What makes it worth the ticket is the habit. The branches leave the trunk low and several of them rest on the ground, so instead of a column with a crown on top you get a green room with walls, filling most of the courtyard. The tree went in while northern Italy was still being fought over by France and Austria, and it has grown in the same enclosed square of air ever since, sheltered on four sides by stone, which is roughly why a magnolia from Georgia and Florida has done so well this far north. Do not confuse it with the 1786 magnolia in the Orto Botanico, 300 metres south. Padua has three well-known magnolias carrying three different dates and the sources muddle them regularly. This is the one inside the Basilica's museum complex, reached on the combined ticket, and closed on Mondays.

trees.name: The Great Plane of Parco Treves
trees.neighbourhood: Parco Treves de' Bonfili, on Padua's 16th-century Venetian walls
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: ~1.6 km / roughly 24 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified
trees.story: Forty-eight metres. That is what put this plane on Italy's national register of monumental trees, not its age, which at roughly 155 years is fairly ordinary for the species. It stands in Parco Treves de' Bonfili, a small park built on Padua's 16th-century Venetian walls, and its trunk was measured at 6.37 metres round in 2022. The park is the reason it grew that way. Giuseppe Jappelli laid the ground out between 1829 and 1835 for the Treves de' Bonfili brothers as the first designed garden in Padua, part private botanical collection and part romantic landscape, planted for effect and for the long term by people who expected to be dead before it worked. Almost none of the built work survives: a neoclassical temple, the gardener's house and a small caryatid shrine, and that is the lot. The trees outlasted the architecture. The register rates this one's condition as adequate rather than good, which at 48 metres and nearly two centuries is not a surprise, and is worth knowing before you stand under it in a wind. Two more registered trees stand within 60 metres of it, a second plane and a leaning hackberry, which makes this the shortest worthwhile tree walk in the city: three protected trees, about ten minutes, no ticket.

trees.name: The Second Plane of Parco Treves
trees.age: roughly 150 years (undated by the register; estimated from its companion tree)
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: ~1.6 km / roughly 25 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified
trees.story: Nobody has dated this tree. It stands about 60 metres from the great plane of Parco Treves, carries its own code on the same national register of monumental trees, was measured at 5.05 metres round in 2022, and the age field on its record is simply empty. The 150 years given here is an inference from its neighbour, which stands in the same park and was almost certainly planted with it, and should be read as an estimate rather than a fact. Everything else is confirmed twice over: species, position, protected status. It is the second largest of the park's planes and, unlike the largest, the register rates its condition as good, so the smaller tree is the healthier one. Both grew up inside a garden Giuseppe Jappelli designed in the 1830s to look like landscape rather than a park, and both lived through the century in which Padua's ramparts stopped being defences and became somewhere to walk the dog. The pair are worth seeing together for the comparison alone: same species, same soil, same start, five metres of trunk against six and a half. Trees that begin together rarely finish the same size, and standing between these two is the clearest way to see how much of a tree's life is decided by where it happened to land.

trees.name: The Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves
trees.age: not established by the register; mature/monumental by form rather than measured age
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: ~1.7 km / roughly 26 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the whole leaning frame reads at a glance

trees.story: This tree is on Italy's national register for being the wrong shape. The bagolaro sdraiato, the reclining hackberry of Parco Treves, measures 1.6 metres round, which the register itself calls unremarkable for the species; it was designated for habit, form and landscape value instead of size. Rather than rising it leans, throwing its limbs out sideways and low over the grass. How it came to grow that way is not recorded. A local story about a storm circulates, but the register says nothing of it and we could not confirm it from any second source, so it stays a story until somebody proves otherwise. What is on file: no age at all, a condition rated adequate, and a national monumental code of its own, the fourth issued inside this one small park. Celtis occidentalis is a North American tree, common enough in Italian parks as a tough shade and street species, which makes the designation both stranger and better. Somebody in an office decided that a middling hackberry growing at an odd angle in a Jappelli garden deserved the same legal protection as trees ten times its size, and they were right. It is also the easiest of the park's three protected trees to walk straight past, which would be a waste of the detour.

trees.name: The Sophoras of Piazza Capitaniato
trees.neighbourhood: Piazza Capitaniato, the University of Padua's historic Palazzo del Capitanio square
trees.access: Free, open public square
trees.transport: ~1.1 km / roughly 17 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified

best_time.label: August, when it flowers over the paving and nothing else in the square is doing anything

trees.story: These two trees were planted in 1861, when Padua was still Austrian. Five years later Veneto voted itself into the new kingdom of Italy, and the pagoda trees of Piazza Capitaniato have stood through everything since, in a square that was already six centuries into its second career. It began as the courtyard of the Carrara family's 14th-century palace and belongs to the University of Padua now, fronted by the Palazzo del Capitanio, open on all sides and free to walk into at any hour. The register counts two trees. A visitor counts one planting. They stand about 20 metres apart on the square's axis, the larger 4.6 metres round and dated to that 1861 campaign, the second undated on the register and in better condition than its neighbour, which is why they are described here as one entry. Local history sources give the same planting year independently, and the arithmetic agrees. Styphnolobium japonicum reached Europe from China by way of Jesuit collectors, despite the name, and its trick is timing: it flowers in August, when almost nothing else in a city square is doing anything at all, dropping small cream flowers over the paving for weeks. Padua's students have walked through them on the way to lectures since before Italy existed.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required)
trees.transport: About 1.9km, 25-30 minutes on foot, from Padova railway station
trees.story:
The species reached Europe in 1822, and six years later this specimen went into the ground here, the first Cedrus deodara cultivated anywhere in Italy. The garden's own account places it between the Montagnola, an artificial hill built in the 1700s, and the Fontana delle Quattro Stagioni, and every subsequent deodar cedar planted anywhere in the country traces back to trees like this one.

A deodar cedar in its native Himalaya grows at 1,200 to 3,500 metres, on mountainsides far colder in winter than the Veneto plain, which is part of why it took to cultivation here so readily. Two centuries on, it stands about four and a half metres round, one of the older conifers in an arboretum that also holds Atlas cedars and cedars of Lebanon for comparison, a planted lesson in how the genus Cedrus split across three separate mountain ranges.

The honest note: Italy's monumental tree register rates this specimen's current health as poor, the kind of assessment that means paying attention rather than staying away. Nearly two hundred years old and first of its kind in the country is a lot of biography for one tree to carry, and it is carrying it into old age rather than out of it.

trees.name: The Cryptomeria of the Orto Botanico
trees.neighbourhood: Orto Botanico (near the entrance path to the ticket office)
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required)
trees.transport: ~1.9 km / roughly 25-30 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified
trees.story:
A slim trunk for its reported age: this Japanese cedar is said to have gone into Padua's botanical garden in 1850, which would make it around 175 years old, and eighty three centimetres of girth is a modest showing for a tree that has had that long. The register that records it hedges its own date with 'sarebbe', reportedly, rather than stating it as fact, and a local tree blog independently places the same aged specimen on the path leading to the garden's ticket office without adding a firmer date of its own.

Cryptomeria japonica is Japan's national tree, valued there for straight-grained timber and planted from temple groves to reforested hillsides; in a European botanical garden it usually arrived as a curiosity from the same wave of 19th-century plant collecting that filled Padua's grounds with a magnolia from 1786 and a grafted ginkgo said to date to 1750. This one stands within a few dozen metres of both, plus an oriental plane, part of the same cluster near the garden's main path.

The garden charges standard admission, the oldest botanical garden of its kind still on its original site anywhere in the world. If the 1850 date is more than a working guess, tell us.

trees.name: The Second Ginkgo of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico admission ticket required)
trees.transport: ~1.9 km / roughly 25-30 min walk from Padova railway station; nearest bus/tram stop not verified
trees.story:
Padua's botanical garden has two ginkgos worth stopping for, and both carry the same odd trick: a female branch grafted onto a male tree, so a single trunk produces the messy, foul-smelling fruit that an all-male ginkgo never would. The more famous of the pair is dated to 1750. This is the second, the register's own 'Ginko dell'Orto Botanico n. 2', a separate three-metre-round tree with no planting date of its own on record.

Ginkgo biloba is dioecious, meaning a tree is born strictly male or strictly female, and European gardens have grafted female branches onto male specimens since at least the 18th century, partly out of curiosity and partly because male trees were what nurseries could reliably supply. Both of Padua's ginkgos wear the graft, which makes this garden an unusually direct place to see the trick performed twice.

Seventeen metres tall on a three-metre girth, it stands within a stone's throw of the garden's better-known ginkgo, inside grounds that require standard admission. Nobody has recorded when it went in. If you know, say so.

trees.name: The Ficus of Piazza Marina
trees.access: Free, public square (Piazza Marina / Giardino Garibaldi)
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Palermo Centrale station, near the historic harbour
trees.story: Half of Palermo's most famous tree is dying. A fungal infection has spread through roughly half the plant since 2016, drying out aerial roots and dropping branches in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and the city is still working out whether it can be saved. None of that undoes what is already there: a Ficus macrophylla planted around 1863 or 1864 in a garden laid out on the site of Inquisition executions, 188 people burned or garrotted in the same square over two centuries. The mayor who had it planted, the Marchese di Rudini, was marking the end of Bourbon rule after Garibaldi's arrival, and the tree later earned a second civic title, Tree of the 150 Years of Italian Unity, in 2011. Its trunk system has spread into a thicket of secondary trunks and aerial roots so dense that sources disagree on the real measurement, some citing a 20 metre circumference and others 36, depending on whether they are measuring the original trunk or the whole colonnaded mass it has since become. That confusion is itself the point: a fig this size stops being one trunk and starts being a small forest sharing one root system. Palermo's arborists are now doing what any city does for an ageing landmark, propping, monitoring and hoping the fungus loses before the tree does.

trees.name: The Falcone Tree
trees.access: Free, a street tree visible from the public sidewalk at all times
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Piazza Politeama, in the Libertà district
trees.story: This fig has been Palermo's memorial wall for over three decades. On 23 May 1992 a mafia car bomb killed judge Giovanni Falcone, his wife Francesca Morvillo, and three bodyguards on the motorway into the city. Within days strangers began taping messages, photographs and poems to the trunk of the Ficus macrophylla outside his apartment building, and they have never really stopped. Palermitans call it l'Albero della Speranza, the Tree of Hope. The building itself is an unremarkable 1960s apartment block on a residential street, which is part of what makes the tree's transformation so complete: nobody would look twice at Via Notarbartolo without it. The city has since listed it as a protected cultural asset, and in 2023 a local council motion proposed a flowerbed specifically to stabilise its roots after arborists flagged structural risk, work that has continued with pruning and monitoring since. Every 23 May the covering paper and messages are renewed for the anniversary. The tree itself is roughly 90 years old, planted decades before anyone could have guessed what it would come to hold, which makes it older than the massacre it now stands for by about half a century.

trees.name: The Ficus of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry, Orto Botanico di Palermo (standard ticket, around 6 euros)
trees.transport: 20 min walk from Palermo Centrale station, or bus to Via Lincoln
trees.story: The most famous fig tree in Palermo is not the one in Piazza Marina, it is that tree's parent. Planted in the Orto Botanico in 1845, this Ficus macrophylla has spent 180 years building a canopy now measured at roughly 3,000 square metres, reportedly the largest crown of any tree in Europe, spread across 44 secondary trunks that grow down from the branches as aerial roots and thicken into full columns once they reach the ground. In 2023 it placed fourth in the European Tree of the Year contest after winning Italy's own national vote first, on the strength of more than 10,000 European votes. The garden's own records tie it directly to its more famous relative across town: the Piazza Marina fig was grown from a cutting taken off this one. Visiting means paying the botanical garden's standard entry fee, unlike its free offspring in the public square, but it buys a walk underneath a structure that no longer reads as a single tree so much as a roofed courtyard built from one root system. The species, native to Australia's Lord Howe Island and the Queensland coast, has now been growing on this one plot for longer than Italy has existed as a unified country.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of Villa Malfitano
trees.access: Free garden access; the villa's interior requires a paid guided tour
trees.transport: 20 min walk from Piazza Politeama, entrance on Via Dante
trees.story: This tree bleeds, or its close relatives do: cut into a dragon tree's bark and the sap that runs out is dark red, sold for centuries across Europe as sangue di drago, dragon's blood, a dye and wound treatment. Palermo's own specimen, a Dracaena draco with a trunk just under six metres around, grows in the private botanical garden the Whitaker family built around their villa in the 1880s. The Whitakers had made their fortune in Marsala wine, the fortified wine Joseph Whitaker's grandfather helped turn into a British staple, and Joseph spent part of it hiring the botanist Emilio Kunzmann to fill the grounds with plants gathered from Tunisia, Sumatra and Australia rather than the classical statuary a Sicilian villa garden usually got. The dragon tree, native to the Canary Islands and Macaronesia rather than anywhere the family's ships actually sailed, was one specimen among that collection, assembled for curiosity rather than status. Its crown has since branched into the tiered, umbrella-like shape the species only reaches after decades of growth, each segment ending in a burst of stiff blue green leaves. No record survives of the exact planting date, only that it arrived with the rest of Kunzmann's garden. The park is free to walk; only the villa's interior charges for a guided tour.

photo.attribution: FrankAdamo, via Wikimedia Commons (Wiki Loves Monuments)

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of the Palazzina Cinese
trees.access: Free, Parco della Favorita, open daily
trees.transport: Bus from central Palermo toward Piazza Leoni; not a walkable distance from the historic centre
trees.story: A Bourbon king built a Chinese pavilion in Sicily, and the dragon tree standing in front of it has outlasted every reason he had for doing so. Ferdinand III commissioned the Palazzina Cinese in 1799 from architect Venanzio Marvuglia as a retreat inside what became Parco della Favorita, part of a broader taste for chinoiserie that swept European royal courts with no particular logic attached to Sicily specifically. This Dracaena draco, about 136 years old, is the largest of several dragon trees planted around the building, its trunk now measuring six metres around and its condition tracked as good in Italy's own national tree register. The palazzina itself has been restored and reopened to the public after long closures, and the tree stands in the section of the Favorita that has always stayed open regardless, a royal hunting park turned public one generations ago. Joggers and tourists pass it daily without necessarily clocking that it predates the pavilion's current public opening by over a century, and that dragon trees like this one only flower, then branch, after decades of growth, which means this specimen's entire visible shape is a record of exactly how long it has already stood here.

trees.name: The Ficus of Villa Trabia
trees.age: undated, likely planted in the late 19th century
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Piazza Politeama, in the Libertà district
trees.story: A single 1910 inventory of Villa Trabia's grounds recorded 2,790 plant species on one aristocratic estate, and one of the Ficus macrophylla planted for that collection is still standing, its trunk now nearly five metres around. The villa belonged to the Lucchesi Palli family, princes of Campofranco, who built it in the 18th century and spent the following hundred years turning the grounds into one of Palermo's most serious private botanical collections before the city eventually took the park over as public land. Roughly twenty other fig trees share the grounds today, descendants and companions from the same planting era, but this one's circumference sets it apart from the rest. The villa building itself now houses a municipal office and a public library, an unglamorous second act for grounds a prince once filled with rarities gathered from across the world for no reason beyond having them. The park was renamed in 2024 for Ninni Cassara, a police officer killed by the mafia in 1985, giving Villa Trabia the same layered history as Palermo's Falcone tree across town: a garden built for private pleasure now doubling as memorial ground. Open daily, free, no ticket required to stand beneath it.

trees.name: The Date Palm of Villa Bonanno
trees.access: Free, open access, unfenced, no closing hours
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Palermo Cathedral
trees.story: Underneath this palm garden's soil sits a Roman house with a mosaic of Alexander the Great hunting a lion, uncovered by accident in the 19th century and left exactly where it was found. Villa Bonanno, laid out in 1905 in front of the Norman Palace that still seats Sicily's regional parliament, was built specifically to show off both: the archaeology below and roughly 400 date palms imported directly from Tunisia to fill the ground above it, reportedly the largest concentrated planting of Phoenix dactylifera anywhere in Europe. This specimen, measured at up to 2.5 metres around, stands among the mature survivors of that original planting, in a square that has spent 900 years as the political centre of Sicily under Normans, Spanish viceroys and now the regional government. The garden's designer, Giuseppe Damiani Almeyda, also built a small caretaker's house on site in the same period, one of the few original 1905 structures that survived a 2013 EU funded renovation covering three of Palermo's historic squares. The garden stays open around the clock, unfenced, a rare case of a European capital's most politically important square doubling as an all hours public park rather than a monument viewed from behind railings.

trees.name: The Palm Avenue of Villa Giulia
trees.age: undated, planted in a 19th century garden expansion
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Palermo Centrale station
trees.story: Villa Giulia opened in 1778, which makes it, by most accounts, Italy's first public garden, decades before Rome, Florence or Milan opened anything comparable to ordinary citizens rather than nobility. Goethe visited in 1787 and called it the most stupendous place in the world, high praise from a man who had just finished touring the rest of the country. The garden's original 18th century layout, designed by Nicolo Palma with sculptures by Ignazio Marabitti, predates the entrance avenue most visitors actually remember: a colonnade of Washingtonia robusta, Mexican fan palms, planted along Via Lincoln when the garden expanded in the 19th century, tall enough now that walking the avenue means walking in dappled shade for its entire length regardless of the hour. The species is native to the Sonoran Desert, about as far from Sicily's climate zone as Mexico's coast, and it has thrived here since being introduced across southern Europe as an ornamental import. At the garden's centre, a marble sundial built to a 1784 design by the mathematician Lorenzo Federici still stands beside a fountain sculpted by Marabitti, both older than the palms that now frame the walk toward them. Free, open daily, still doing the job it was built for in 1778.

trees.name: The Fig of Villa Malfitano
trees.access: Free garden access; the villa's interior requires a paid guided tour
trees.transport: 20 min walk from Piazza Politeama, entrance on Via Dante
trees.story: When Delia Whitaker was buried, her funeral carriage was asked to stop under this tree. She was the last of the family to live at Villa Malfitano, and she had spent her life pausing beneath this fig, a daily habit the household knew well enough to build into the day she left the house for the last time. The tree was planted in 1888 by her father, Joseph Whitaker, known in the family as Pip, in the years he was stocking the grounds with plants gathered from well outside Sicily. It is the specimen closest to the house, and it grows the way the species does when nothing crowds it, long horizontal branches running out parallel to the ground rather than climbing, until the tree reads as a low green ceiling instead of a column. Italy's national register of monumental trees measures its trunk system at twenty-one metres around. The Italian gardens association, which keeps its own record of this place, describes it as second in size only to the famous specimen in Palermo's botanical garden, a comparison worth reporting as theirs rather than repeating as ours, since the city's big figs are measured by different people using different methods. The garden is free to walk. Only the villa's interior charges, and only for a guided tour.

trees.name: The Fig of Villa Tasca
trees.age: not documented, likely dating to the garden's Romantic-era expansion from 1855
trees.access: Paid entry, Parco di Villa Tasca (day ticket around 4 euros per grandigiardini.it 2026 pricing; an annual pass is also sold). Sources disagree on hours: the park's own listed general hours run Tuesday-Sunday from mid-afternoon into the evening, while a garden feature (grey-panthers.it) describes the historic Romantic garden itself as visited Tuesday-Sunday by reservation/group booking. Confirm current opening hours and whether the fig's part of the grounds needs a booked visit before publishing a specific time.
trees.transport: On Viale Regione Siciliana, the ring road toward Monreale; not walkable from the historic centre, reachable by bus or car
trees.story: Italy's national register of monumental trees puts this fig's trunk system at twenty-seven metres around and the tree itself at thirty metres tall. Resist doing anything with that number. Palermo's big figs are measured in different ways by different people, some on the original trunk and some on the whole colonnade of secondary trunks and aerial roots that a Ficus macrophylla eventually becomes, and the botanical garden's giant is usually described by the area of its canopy rather than by any girth at all. So the defensible statement is the register's own measurement, not a ranking. What the tree does in the garden is easier to describe. It stands over the Lago dei Cigni, the swan lake in the grounds of Villa Tasca, and one Italian garden survey puts it plainly: the sprawling fig dominates half the lake with its permanent shade. Nobody has published a planting date. The garden was remade in the Romantic style from 1855 by Lucio Tasca and extended again from 1870 with English landscape additions, which is the period this tree most plausibly belongs to, and that is as far as the evidence runs. The grounds reopened to the public as the Parco di Villa Tasca in 2020. Entry is ticketed, it sits out on the ring road toward Monreale rather than in the historic centre, and the hours are worth confirming before you go.

trees.name: The Queensland Pine of Villa Trabia
trees.access: Free, public garden (Villa Trabia). Open Monday to Friday, 9:00 to 14:00, per APGI.
trees.transport: Same neighbourhood as the already-published Ficus of Villa Trabia, roughly 130m away within the same grounds
trees.story:
A bunya pine drops cones that weigh as much as a bowling ball. Araucaria bidwillii comes from Queensland, where the fruiting season is fenced off for exactly that reason, and Palermo planted one anyway in the garden of Villa Trabia.

The garden is the story around it. Between 1886 and 1903 the head gardener Vincenzo Ostinelli turned the grounds into a giardino romantico stuffed with exotics: araucarias, palms, conifers, ornamental figs. An inventory he compiled in 1910 counted 2,790 plant species in the park. Roughly 150 of them are still there. Nobody recorded which year this pine went in, so it may or may not date from that planting, and the register does not say either.

What is measured is the trunk, 2.22 metres round, which for this species is a mature tree rather than an old one. The bunya's shape is the reason to look up: a straight column with the branches gathered into distinct tiers and turned up at the ends, like a candelabra that has been left out in the weather.

The garden opens weekday mornings only, which is worth checking before the walk, and it tightens the loop with the trees already on this page rather than adding another distant stop.

trees.name: The Silk-Cotton Tree of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico di Palermo ticket).
trees.transport: Same garden as the already-published Ficus of the Orto Botanico, a few hundred metres away
trees.story:
Palermo calls this one the drunken tree, and the trunk explains it. Ceiba speciosa swells into a green bottle shape and covers itself in conical spines, which is a defence against animals that do not exist on this continent, and it stands on the botanical garden's avenue of chorisias with several others of its kind.

It flowers when almost nothing else does. Big hibiscus-shaped blooms open through the autumn and into December, cream then pink then violet on the same tree, and the seed pods that follow split to release the silky floss the species is named for, once used to stuff life jackets.

The garden brought the species from Brazil around 1896, and the botanist Michele Lojacono Pojero recorded the first one growing in a Palermo garden in 1910. Neither date belongs to this particular tree, and no source gives it one, so its age is left open rather than borrowed from the species' arrival. Its trunk measures 3.8 metres round.

The Orto Botanico charges entry, which buys you one of the great nineteenth-century acclimatisation gardens of the Mediterranean, and this is among the odder things growing in it.

trees.name: The Yucca of Villa Malfitano
trees.access: Paid entry (Villa Malfitano Whitaker, run by the Whitaker Foundation).
trees.transport: Same grounds as the already-published Dragon Tree of Villa Malfitano and Fig of Villa Malfitano
trees.story:
This is a yucca with a trunk five and a half metres round. Yuccas are the spiky things in pots by a doorway, and this one has gone woody and enormous in the garden of Villa Malfitano, which is what a Palermo climate and a hundred-odd undisturbed years will do to a plant that is technically not a tree at all.

Botanically it is a monocot, closer kin to a grass or an agave than to an oak, and it has no annual rings, which is one reason nobody has put an age on it. The site already collects two dragon trees and several palms on the same logic: what matters is whether the thing is worth standing in front of.

Its name is unsettled. The register files it as Yucca gigantea and the city's own description calls it Yucca australis, which are names that have been swapped back and forth for the same plant. If you know which is right, tell us.

Villa Malfitano was built for the Whitakers, the English wine family who made Marsala and then spent the profits on Sicily, and the foundation that runs it charges entry to the house and garden both.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree of Vivai Lo Porto
trees.access: Vivai Lo Porto is a working plant nursery and garden centre, not a park: open to anyone who walks in during business hours (Mon-Sat 7:30-18:00, Sun 7:30-13:30 per public listings), no ticket or purchase required to view the grounds. It is genuinely public-facing (a nursery counter, not a gate to ask through) but the honest caveat for the page is that it reads as a business, not a garden attraction.
trees.transport: Corso Calatafimi, southwest Palermo, roughly 2.3km from the city-centre cluster (Villa Trabia/Villa Malfitano); its own small cluster with the register's Sterculia acerifolia 'Albero del fuoco' (girth 450cm) about 65m away, a candidate not researched
trees.story:
Palermo's largest dragon tree stands in a garden centre. Seven metres round the trunk, which is half a metre more than either of the two already on this page, and it grows behind the counter of Vivai Lo Porto on Corso Calatafimi rather than in a park.

The nursery is the recent part. The ground it sits on was an eighteenth-century estate built for Monsignor Salvatore Ventimiglia di Belmonte, the last Inquisitor of Sicily, and a nineteenth-century garden of acclimatisation was laid out there long before the Lo Porto family started selling plants from it in 1960. The tree predates the business by a century at least.

How long before that, nobody has written down. One source describes the neighbouring horse chestnut as three hundred years old and the Sterculia as over 150, and says nothing about this one. Dracaena draco grows very slowly and lives a very long time, so seven metres of girth means several hundred years, and that band is as tight as the evidence allows. If you have seen a figure for it, we would like the source.

You walk in during business hours and nobody stops you, but it reads as a working nursery rather than a garden to visit, which is worth knowing before you go.

trees.name: The Fig of the Giardino Inglese
trees.access: Free public park (Giardino Inglese / Piersanti Mattarella Park), open daylight hours, no ticket.
trees.transport: Via della Libertà area, roughly 1.1km from the Villa Trabia cluster already on the page; walkable extension of that cluster.
trees.story: Eight metres round the trunk and eleven metres tall: this is a fig that spent its growth going sideways. It stands in the Giardino Inglese, the long public park Giovan Battista Filippo Basile laid out from 1851 as Palermo pushed north out of its old walls along Via della Libertà, and of the several big Moreton Bay Figs growing there it is the one Sicily's register of monumental trees actually measured, at 820 centimetres of girth and 11 metres of height. The park's figs trace back to stock raised at the Orto Botanico across town, which is where most of this city's Australian giants began. Ficus macrophylla behaves the same way wherever it is comfortable: branches send roots down, the roots reach soil and thicken into trunks of their own, and a single stem slowly turns into a colonnade. The garden around it has changed names along with the century. It carries Piersanti Mattarella's name now, after the president of Sicily shot dead in Palermo in 1980, and on a warm afternoon it is full of people treating it as a park rather than a memorial. Nobody has published an age for this tree. The Italian register has no age column, and no one appears to have dated this specimen. If you have seen a figure for it, send it over and we will add it.

trees.name: The Embracing Fig of the Giardini Reali
trees.access: Inside the Giardini Reali of Palazzo dei Normanni (seat of the Sicilian Regional Assembly). Paid entry to the gardens (a few euros per search results, not independently verified on a fetched pricing page); opening days are limited and vary, apparently closed some weekdays for parliamentary business. State the caveat plainly and tell readers to check current hours before visiting rather than quoting an unverified schedule.
trees.transport: Piazza del Parlamento entrance; roughly 1.1km from the Orto Botanico cluster (etc) and an easy walk from Palazzo Bonanno.
trees.story:
A stone pine in the Royal Gardens is slowly disappearing into a fig. Over the decades this Ficus macrophylla has grown around a large Pinus pinea beside it and taken part of it inside itself. The Sicilian Regional Assembly, which occupies the Palazzo dei Normanni above the garden, describes the fig as embracing the pine. An Italian nature writer, less diplomatically, called it a deadly embrace. Both are looking at the same thing.

It is the largest of the three Moreton Bay Figs in the Giardini Reali, ten metres round and twenty metres tall, and the register that recorded it rates its health as excellent. Its age is a dendrological estimate rather than a documented planting: roughly 135 years, which in honest terms means somewhere between about 115 and 155. That leaves it younger and far smaller than the fig in Piazza Marina, which is the one holding Palermo's records.

What it grows on is the other half of the story. The Giardini Reali are a terraced garden on top of the walls of the Palazzo dei Normanni, the palace the Norman kings raised over the old city and which now houses the island's parliament. Against that the fig is a newcomer, and it is still the thing people stop for.

That is also the catch for a visitor. The gardens open on limited days around parliamentary business and charge an entry fee, so check the current hours before you cross town for this one.

trees.name: The Pecan of the Orto Botanico
trees.access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico di Palermo ticket, around 6 euros), the same ticket as the garden's ficus and silk-cotton tree.
trees.transport: Same garden as the Ficus and the Silk-Cotton Tree of the Orto Botanico, a short walk from both; 20 min walk from Palermo Centrale station.
trees.story:
The vine wound around this trunk is a houseplant. Monstera deliciosa is the thing sold in pots at knee height across northern Europe, and in the Orto Botanico it has been left to do what it does in the wild, climbing a pecan the way ivy climbs a wall.

The tree underneath is worth the look on its own. Thirty metres tall and 5.6 metres round, it is one of the giants in a garden full of them, and it belongs on another continent entirely. Carya illinoinensis is the pecan of the American South, a river-bottom hickory from the Mississippi basin, and it has put on full American height in a walled garden a few streets from the Sicilian coast. That is the point of the place. Palermo's botanical garden has spent two centuries working out which foreign species will take to this heat and this soil, and the answer here was emphatic.

It is easy to walk past, which is the usual fate of a tall straight tree standing among Australian figs that grow sideways and drop columns from their branches. Look up instead, and then look at what is climbing it.

Nobody has published an age for it. The Italian register carries girth and height and has no age column at all, and the local writing about the garden's giants describes this tree without dating it. If you know when it went in, tell us and it goes on the page.

trees.name: The Flame Tree of Vivai Lo Porto
trees.access: Vivai Lo Porto is a working plant nursery and garden centre, not a park: open to anyone who walks in during business hours (Mon-Sat 7:30-18:00, Sun 7:30-13:30 per public listings, same as already stated for), no ticket or purchase required to view the grounds. Reads as a business, not a garden attraction; say so.
trees.transport: Corso Calatafimi, roughly 85m from the already-published (Dragon Tree of Vivai Lo Porto): the two form a two-tree stop at one address, not a duplicate of each other.

best_time.label: May and June, when it flowers scarlet on bare branches

trees.story:
Sicily's register of monumental trees files this one as the Albero del fuoco, the tree of fire, and the name is literal. Brachychiton acerifolius sheds its leaves before it flowers, then covers the bare branches in small scarlet bells, so a big one in bloom carries down the whole length of the street. It does not do it in full every year, which is normal for the species and is part of why people remember the years it does.

This is a big one: 4.5 metres round, 20 metres tall, and described by Italian Botanical Heritage as over one hundred and fifty years old and one of the most important trees in Palermo. That is exactly as precise as the dating gets, and it stays there.

It grows in a plant nursery. Corso Calatafimi 262 was an eighteenth century estate belonging to the last Inquisitor of Sicily, then a nineteenth century garden of acclimatisation, and the Lo Porto family have been selling plants from the ground since 1960. The tree was standing here long before the tills were.

Eighty-five metres away is Palermo's largest dragon tree, also on this page, so one address gets you both. You walk in during opening hours and nobody stops you, but it is worth knowing that this is a working nursery rather than a garden arranged for visitors.

trees.name: The London Plane of Villa Tasca
trees.access: Paid entry, Parco di Villa Tasca (same grounds and ticket as the already-published Fig of Villa Tasca, ; sources disagree on exact hours, confirm before publishing a specific time)
trees.transport: On Viale Regione Siciliana, the ring road toward Monreale; not walkable from the historic centre, reachable by bus or car
trees.story:
Italy has exactly one nationally registered monumental plane tree in Sicily, and it stands in the private grounds of Villa Tasca on the ring road toward Monreale, not in the historic centre most visitors see. The trunk is four metres sixty-five around, thirty metres tall, and a foundation that tracks Italy's giant trees puts its age at around two centuries, without publishing how they arrived at the number, so treat that as their estimate rather than a measured fact.

The tree stands 184 metres from Villa Tasca's other headline specimen, the sprawling Moreton Bay fig that shades half the garden's swan lake, on the far side of the water. Where the fig grows outward into a colonnade of secondary trunks that makes its true size a matter of definition, this plane keeps to one recognisable trunk and crown, plain columnar bulk rather than a spreading thicket.

London planes are hybrids, first bred in seventeenth century Europe by crossing an American species with an Oriental one, and they became the default street tree of nineteenth century cities because almost nothing kills them, not compacted soil, not pollution, not routine pruning. What makes this one worth the ticket price is rarer: on a whole island covered in ornamental gardens built by the same wealthy families who imported half the trees on this list, nobody registered a second one.

trees.name: The Cook Pine of Villa Tasca
trees.access: Paid entry, Parco di Villa Tasca, the same grounds and ticket as the other Villa Tasca trees.
trees.transport: On Viale Regione Siciliana, the ring road toward Monreale; not walkable from the historic centre, reachable by bus or car
trees.story:
Villa Tasca's swan lake has a fig tree spreading permanent shade over one shore and a very different tree standing on the other: a Cook pine, thirty-eight metres tall by the national register's own measurement, growing in the narrow, leaning column that gives the species its slightly off-kilter look in photographs.

Araucaria columnaris comes from a single small stretch of the Pacific, New Caledonia's Isle of Pines, where eighteenth century European sailors mistook whole hillsides of the tree for a colonnade of stone columns and gave the island its name because of it. Palermo's specimen has travelled a long way from that coastline to end up leaning over a Sicilian swan lake instead.

Nobody has published an age for this tree, and no story about it should invent one. What is documented is the girth, three metres seventy, and the company it keeps: a Norfolk Island pine stands 35 metres away, a different species entirely despite the family resemblance, and the two of them frame the same lake that the garden's famous fig dominates from the opposite bank.

trees.name: The Norfolk Island Pine of Villa Tasca
trees.access: Paid entry, Parco di Villa Tasca, the same grounds and ticket as the other Villa Tasca trees.
trees.transport: On Viale Regione Siciliana, the ring road toward Monreale; not walkable from the historic centre, reachable by bus or car
trees.story:
Thirty-five metres from Villa Tasca's Cook pine stands a second, easily confused conifer: a Norfolk Island pine, four metres eighty around, growing in the same lakeside garden. Both belong to the genus Araucaria and both come from small Pacific islands charted by the same eighteenth century voyage, but they hold their branches differently. The Norfolk pine keeps a symmetrical, tiered crown, layer stacked evenly on layer, while its neighbour grows in a narrower, leaning column. Once you know to look, the two are easy to tell apart from any distance.

It shares its garden with a menagerie of large ornamental cycads and the two other headline trees already on this page, the sprawling fig and the Cook pine, part of a Romantic era garden expanded through the second half of the nineteenth century by the Tasca family. No age has been published for this individual and none is claimed here.

Norfolk Island pines are a familiar houseplant everywhere in miniature, sold small and potted as an indoor Christmas tree substitute. Almost nobody who buys one sees what it becomes given an actual island climate and a century or two of room to grow: a genuine forest giant, capable of passing sixty metres in the wild, though nothing like that height here.

trees.name: The Robinier of Square Rene-Viviani
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily
trees.transport: Saint-Michel Notre-Dame (RER B/C, Metro 4), 3 min walk

best_time.label: late May, when it still flowers despite the concrete props holding up its heaviest branches

trees.story: The oldest tree in Paris was planted in 1601, before the Mayflower sailed. Jean Robin, herbalist to King Henri IV, raised it from seed sent from the Appalachians by the English naturalist John Tradescant. The entire genus Robinia was later named after him. The tree stands in a small square facing Notre-Dame, which had already stood for centuries when the sapling went into the ground. It has since lived through the Commune, lost its crown to a German shell in the First World War, and watched the cathedral burn in 2019. Concrete props now hold up its heaviest branches and ivy hides much of the trunk, but it still flowers every spring. Parisians walk past it daily without a glance. It is protected by a low fence and a plaque that undersells it considerably. In 2021 National Geographic profiled it as a lesson in urban resilience, four centuries of city life absorbed by one imported American tree.

trees.name: The Cedar of Jussieu
trees.access: Free, Jardin des Plantes open daily
trees.transport: Jussieu (Metro 7/10) or Gare d'Austerlitz, 5 min walk

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Legend says this cedar crossed the Channel in a hat. In 1734 the botanist Bernard de Jussieu carried two seedlings from England to Paris, and when the pot broke on the journey he is said to have finished the trip with a tree cradled in his tricorne. The story is probably embellished, which the Museum's own historians admit, but the tree is real enough: the oldest cedar of Lebanon in France, planted on the slope of the labyrinth in the royal medicinal garden that became the Jardin des Plantes. It was a sapling when Louis XV ruled, stood through the Revolution while the garden's aristocratic patrons lost their heads, and watched the menagerie fill with animals confiscated from Versailles. Nearly three centuries on, its trunk is a metre and a half thick and its flat crown is visible across the garden. A plaque at its base records the planting date for anyone who thinks to look up from the path.

trees.name: The Second Robinier
trees.access: Free, Jardin des Plantes open daily
trees.transport: Jussieu (Metro 7/10), 5 min walk

best_time.label: late May, when it flowers in step with its father tree two kilometres away at Square Rene-Viviani

trees.story: Paris's second oldest tree is the son of its oldest. In 1636 Vespasien Robin, botanist to the king and son of Jean Robin, took a cutting from his father's black locust and planted it in the brand new royal medicinal garden. The father tree still stands two kilometres away at Square Rene-Viviani. The son has now been growing for close to four centuries in what became the Jardin des Plantes, making the pair almost certainly the oldest parent and child trees in any European city. It was already a mature tree when Buffon ran the garden in the 1700s and when the Museum of Natural History was founded during the Revolution. Like its father it is propped, scarred and still flowering. Botanists still take cuttings from both trees, which means the Robin family line, brought from America as a handful of seeds, keeps spreading four hundred years on. Few of the garden's seven million yearly visitors realize the unassuming acacia is nearly the oldest thing in it.

trees.name: The Buffon Plane
trees.access: Free, Jardin des Plantes open daily
trees.transport: Gare d'Austerlitz (Metro 5/10, RER C), 4 min walk
trees.story: In 1785, four years before the Revolution, the naturalist Buffon planted three oriental planes in the garden he had run for half a century. This is the survivor. Buffon was then the most famous scientist in Europe, author of a 36 volume natural history that scandalized the Church by suggesting the Earth was far older than Genesis allowed. He died in 1788 and missed the Terror by five years; his son went to the guillotine. The tree his gardeners set in the ground kept growing through all of it. Oriental planes were admired in antiquity, and the Romans planted them across their empire for shade. This one received the national Remarkable Tree label in 2001. It stands near the garden's plane alley, wide trunked and mottled, old enough that the institution around it has changed its name three times while the tree kept its place. Its two siblings from the 1785 planting are gone, which makes the survivor the last living tree Buffon is known to have planted.

trees.name: The Great Plane of Parc Monceau
trees.access: Free, park open daily
trees.transport: Monceau (Metro 2), at the park gates
trees.story: The thickest tree in Paris has a waistline of six and a half metres. Planted in 1814, the year Napoleon abdicated and the allied armies camped in the city, this oriental plane grew up in what was then the private pleasure garden of the Orleans family. Parc Monceau had been laid out as an aristocratic fantasy of ruins and follies, and the plane outgrew all of them. It is now 31 metres tall with a crown to match, the largest of its species in the city. The park around it became public under Haussmann in 1861, and the tree has since shaded Proust, who walked here as a boy, and several generations of the best dressed joggers in Paris. Its bark peels in grey and cream patches and its lower branches are thicker than most full grown street trees. The city lists it among its officially remarkable trees. Stand at the trunk and look up: the first branch is higher than the surrounding lampposts.

trees.name: The Sequoia of Buttes-Chaumont
trees.access: Free, park open daily
trees.transport: Botzaris or Buttes-Chaumont (Metro 7bis)
trees.story: A Californian giant grows on a former gypsum quarry in working class Paris. When Napoleon III opened the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont in 1867, his engineers had just finished transforming a scarred industrial pit into a romantic landscape of cliffs, waterfalls and a temple on a crag. Among the plantings was a sequoia from the Sierra Nevada, a species that had only been described by Western botanists fifteen years earlier and was the horticultural sensation of the age. It is now the tallest tree in Paris at over 35 metres, with a trunk approaching five metres around. In its native range such a tree would be a juvenile; sequoias live for three thousand years, which means this one could still be standing when every building visible from the park has been replaced. The species name honours Sequoyah, the inventor of the Cherokee writing system. The park's chief gardeners have called it the crown of their collection.

trees.name: The Elm of Saint-Gervais
trees.age: 90 years (site planted since the Middle Ages)
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Hotel de Ville (Metro 1/11), 3 min walk
trees.story: This elm is not particularly old. The address is: one has stood on this exact spot in front of the Saint-Gervais church since the Middle Ages, and for centuries it was where the neighbourhood settled its affairs. Debts were repaid under the elm on agreed days, judges heard disputes in its shade, and the phrase attendez-moi sous l'orme, wait for me under the elm, entered French as a way of saying you might be waiting a while. The medieval tree's successors appear in old engravings and even in the wrought iron balconies of the surrounding buildings, where the elm motif was worked into the metal in the 1730s. The Revolution felled the tree then standing, allegedly for cannon carriages. The current elm was planted in 1935, a young stand-in occupying one of the longest continuously treed spots in Europe. The building behind it has hosted a church since the 4th century.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of Avenue Foch
trees.access: Free, public avenue side lawns
trees.transport: Porte Dauphine (Metro 2), 2 min walk

best_time.label: October to November: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: The grandest avenue in Paris keeps its most interesting tree off the main carriageway. Avenue Foch, 120 metres wide and lined with the most expensive apartments in the city, was laid out in the 1850s as the Avenue de l'Imperatrice, the ceremonial route from the Arc de Triomphe to the Bois de Boulogne. Its lower stretch served as a tree nursery, and a Caucasian elm planted there in 1852 simply never left. The species comes from the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas and is rare in western Europe. This specimen is now 30 metres tall with a fluted, muscular trunk nearly four metres around, one of the finest of its kind in France. It has watched the avenue change from imperial parade ground to Belle Epoque promenade to the discreet fortress of embassies and old money it is today. The city has classified it among its officially remarkable trees.

trees.name: The Plane of Parc Montsouris
trees.access: Free, park open daily
trees.transport: Cite Universitaire (RER B), 2 min walk
trees.story: This plane tree is older than the park around it. Planted in 1840, it was barely twenty when Napoleon III's engineers began carving Parc Montsouris out of old quarries and windmill land in the 1860s, and they built the park around trees like this one. It is now the heavyweight of the 14th arrondissement: six metres around the trunk and 30 metres tall, officially classified as remarkable by the city. Parc Montsouris became the southern anchor of Haussmann's plan to give every quarter of Paris an English style landscape park, and students from the nearby Cite Universitaire have been reading under this tree for a century. The RER line runs in a cutting through the park, which means several million commuters a year pass within metres of one of the oldest planted trees in southern Paris without knowing it is there. The city classified it formally among its remarkable trees, one of only a handful in the south of Paris.

trees.name: The Sophora by the Lake
trees.access: Free, park open daily
trees.transport: Buttes-Chaumont (Metro 7bis), 5 min walk

best_time.label: August, when it flowers late in the season, still leaning further over the lake with every year

trees.story: Some trees earn their place through size, this one through posture. The Japanese pagoda tree at the edge of the Buttes-Chaumont lake was planted in 1873, six years after the park opened, and has spent 150 years leaning slowly toward the water. It is short for a remarkable tree, ten metres, but its trunk is nearly four metres around and its low, twisting silhouette against the lake and the artificial cliff behind it has made it one of the most photographed trees in the park. Pagoda trees reached Europe from China in the 1740s via a Jesuit missionary's seeds, and Paris planted them enthusiastically in its new parks. This one grew up alongside the Third Republic, survived both sieges of Paris in 1870 and 1871 while the park was barely three years old, and now shades rowers and picnickers on the same bank. The city lists it among its officially classified remarkable trees.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of Square Samuel Paty
trees.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, opposite the Sorbonne, 5th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, open public square, no closure found
trees.transport: Cluny-La Sorbonne (Metro 10) or Maubert-Mutualite (Metro 10), 3-4 min walk

best_time.label: October to November: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: Paris lost most of its elms to a fungus, and this one survived by not quite being an elm. Zelkova carpinifolia is a Caucasian cousin of the true elms, native to the mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian, and it is far less susceptible to the Dutch elm disease that emptied streets across Europe. That is the reason a tree of this size still stands in the middle of the Latin Quarter. The city register gives it a girth of 267 centimetres and a height of 20 metres, and gives no age at all. Nor does any other source. The species first reached Paris in 1782, but that is a date about the species, not about this trunk, and nothing documents when this one was planted. It stands in the small square facing the Sorbonne across Place Paul Painleve, with the Musee de Cluny and the Roman baths under it a minute away, on ground students have crossed on their way to lectures for as long as the tree has been there. In 2021 the Paris Council renamed the square for Samuel Paty, the history and geography teacher murdered in 2020. The tree kept its address and lost the old name, which is the sort of thing a long-lived tree tends to do more than once.

trees.name: The Oriental Planes of Square Michel-Foucault
trees.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, opposite the College de France, 5th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, open public square, no closure found
trees.transport: Maubert-Mutualite (Metro 10) or Cluny-La Sorbonne, 3-5 min walk
trees.story: Two oriental planes stand a few metres apart here, one measuring 470 centimetres around the trunk and the other 415. That is nearly nine metres of girth between them in a pocket garden of roughly 2,000 square metres, which is why they are listed here as one entry rather than two: you stand in a single spot and look up at both. Neither has a documented age. The city register records their girth and nothing more, no source gives a planting date, and large and old is as far as the evidence honestly goes. For scale, the thickest plane in Paris, in Parc Monceau, measures 645 centimetres around and was planted in 1814, and the Parc Montsouris plane reaches 605 centimetres and dates from 1840. These two sit below those and above almost everything else in the city. The garden faces the College de France across Rue des Ecoles and takes its name from Michel Foucault, who lectured in the building opposite. It was renamed for him in 2005, long after these trunks were full grown. A bronze Dante by Jean-Paul Aube stands beneath them, and the two planes shade a steady traffic of students, visitors walking up to the Musee de Cluny and people eating lunch on the slope.

trees.name: The Plane of Quai Saint-Bernard
trees.neighbourhood: Left Bank of the Seine, near the Jardin des Plantes, 5th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, open riverside quay and sculpture garden (Jardin Tino-Rossi), no closure found
trees.transport: Gare d'Austerlitz (Metro 5/10, RER C) or Jussieu (Metro 7/10), 5-8 min walk along the river
trees.story: The sculptures are the newcomers. The Jardin Tino-Rossi was laid out along the Seine in 1980 as an open-air museum of modern sculpture, and it was built around plane trees that were already standing: the garden's own record notes old planes on the site before the garden existed. One of them is on the city's register of remarkable trees, on Quai Saint-Bernard, with a girth of 380 centimetres. Which of them, precisely, is where this entry has to be careful. The register lists a plane of that size at this point on the quay and gives a position for it. A second source confirms that old planes genuinely stand here, but nothing beyond the register singles out this trunk from the others along the same walk. By that listing it is the registered tree; by any other evidence available it is one large plane among several, and no planting date is documented for any of them. That is still a good reason to walk this stretch. The quay runs below the Jardin des Plantes towards the Institut du Monde Arabe, the river on one side and bronze and stone works standing free in the grass on the other. The planes are the oldest things in the garden and the only part of it nobody designed.

trees.name: The Twisted Beech of Square des Arenes de Lutece
trees.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, next to the Roman arena, 5th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily (closes in the evening per standard Paris square hours)
trees.transport: Jussieu (Metro 7/10) or Place Monge (Metro 7), 4-5 min walk

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are gone and the twisted, spiralling branches are the whole point

trees.story:
Every wild tree of this kind on earth grows in one wood near Reims. The hetre tortillard, or fau, is a twisted-branch form of the common European beech, and its only natural population is the Faux de Verzy, roughly a thousand specimens in the Champagne hills. Why they grow that way has never been settled. This one did not arrive by accident: it is a grafted specimen, planted here around 1905, a deliberate piece of botanical strangeness dropped into the Latin Quarter.

The result is a tree that reads as two different trees depending on the month. From May to October it is a low dome of dense leaf, easy to walk straight past, closer to a large shrub than to a beech. In winter the leaves go and the architecture shows: a short trunk turning back on itself, branches spiralling and bending down, some of them trailing to the ground. The city register puts its girth at 110 centimetres, modest for its age, because this form spends its growth going sideways rather than up.

Its address is far better known than it is. The square was laid out around the excavated Roman arena of Lutetia, a first-century amphitheatre built for some 15,000 spectators, found again during nineteenth-century roadworks and saved in part by a campaign Victor Hugo lent his name to. The beech arrived long after that argument had been won.

trees.name: The Anne Frank Chestnut
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily (standard Paris square hours)
trees.transport: Rambuteau (Metro 11) or Chatelet-Les Halles, 4-5 min walk

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story:
The tree this one was cut from no longer exists. On 20 June 2007 a young horse chestnut went into the ground in a small garden off Impasse Berthaud, grown as a graft from the chestnut behind the Secret Annex in Amsterdam, the one Anne Frank could see from the attic window and wrote about in her diary. That original was already failing when the graft was taken, hollowed by fungus and moth damage and propped up with a steel frame. In August 2010 a storm brought it down. The Paris tree had been growing for three years by then.

The Ville de Paris classes it an arbre remarquable, a register otherwise filled with giants and centenarians. This one is on it for what it stands for rather than what it measures, which the classification explicitly allows. The measurements are modest and do not entirely agree: the register records 100 centimetres around the trunk, an earlier account gives 72, and the gap is roughly what a vigorous young chestnut puts on in a decade.

Mayor Bertrand Delanoe planted it alongside Hans Westra, then director of the Anne Frank House. The garden opened the same year, on the grounds of the seventeenth-century Hotel de Saint-Aignan, and at its entrance are inscribed the names of the 11,000 Jewish children deported from France. Nineteen years in, it is still a slim tree with a long job ahead of it.

trees.name: The Fig Tree of Square Georges Cain
trees.age: over a century (no exact planting date documented)
trees.neighbourhood: Le Marais, next to the Musee Carnavalet, 3rd arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily (standard Paris square hours)
trees.transport: Saint-Paul (Metro 1) or Chemin Vert (Metro 8), 4-6 min walk
trees.story:
A fig has no business standing ten metres tall in the open in Paris. Ficus carica is a Mediterranean species, knocked back by hard winters and usually trained flat against a warm wall this far north, and this one carries a trunk 145 centimetres around with nothing but sky above it. That size at that exposure is most of the reason the city lists it as a remarkable tree at all.

Nobody wrote down when it was planted. Every account of it repeats the same undated phrase, over a hundred years old, and the register designates it without naming a year, so the honest position is that it is old and that no one recorded how old.

The ground is better documented than the tree standing on it. Square Georges Cain was laid out in 1923 as an open-air store for the Musee Carnavalet next door, and pediments, columns, carved fragments and statues pulled from demolished Paris buildings sit among the planting, including a bronze by Aristide Maillol. Before any of that, these blocks were market garden, part of the culture Sainte-Catherine that fed the medieval city.

Figs are shorter-lived than almost everything else on this list and considerably less patient with frost. This one has spent decades winning that argument inside a walled square that runs warmer than the street outside, which is the quiet trick of the place and probably the reason it is still here.

trees.name: The Sequoia of the Champs-Élysées Gardens
trees.access: Free, public garden (Jardins des Champs-Élysées), open daily
trees.transport: Champs-Élysées - Clemenceau (M1, M13), about 5 min walk
trees.story: Europe had barely met this species when the tree went into the ground. Giant sequoias reached European gardens from California in the 1850s, and the fullest account of this one dates it to 1850, which would put it among the first ever planted in Paris. That is also why the city register lists it: the designation is for its age, not its size. At 19 metres it is a sapling next to the Californian originals, where General Sherman stands over 80 metres tall. The sources do not agree on the trunk. Paris measures it at 3.6 metres around; the independent account calls it a little over three metres in diameter, which is roughly three times thicker and is almost certainly circumference mislabelled. Take the register's figure. Age is loose in the same way, given as about 165 years around 2015 by one source and about 140 by a passing mention elsewhere, so somewhere between 165 and 180 years is as far as the evidence goes. It grows in the Jardins des Champs-Elysees, the ornamental gardens laid out below the avenue, a short walk from the allee Marcel Proust. It was already a mature tree for the 1900 Exposition Universelle and for every parade that has gone up the avenue since. Its southeast side, the one facing Place de la Concorde, has begun to show signs of weakness.

trees.name: The Twin Planes of Avenue Winston Churchill
trees.access: Free, public garden (Jardins des Champs-Élysées), open daily
trees.transport: Champs-Élysées - Clemenceau (M1, M13), about 4 min walk
trees.story: A trunk five and a half metres around is a great deal of plane tree for a Paris street. Two of them stand about eleven metres apart on Avenue Winston Churchill, on the axis between the Grand Palais and the Petit Palais, and the city registers them separately: one at 5.05 metres around and 28 metres tall, the other at 5.55 metres and 30 metres. From the pavement they read as a single pair, which is how they are treated here. Neither has a planting date. The register carries none and no archive found so far supplies one, so their age is inferred from girth alone and the range stays deliberately wide: certainly more than a century, possibly close to twice that. What is datable is the ground under them. Alphand laid out these gardens for Haussmann in the 1860s, and the avenue and its two palaces were built for the Exposition Universelle of 1900. The trees either predate that construction or went in with the replanting that followed it, and no source says which. London planes take city air better than almost anything else, shedding their bark in plates rather than letting soot build up on it, which is why Paris has hundreds of thousands of them. Reaching this girth still takes a long time and a spot nobody widened a road through. These two got both.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Square d'Ajaccio
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily
trees.transport: Invalides (M8, M13, RER C), about 8 min walk; Varenne (M13) about 5 min walk

best_time.label: June and July, when the cream flowers open and scent the whole square

trees.story: This tree comes from the warm swamp forests of the American southeast, and it has grown to twelve metres in a small square off the Rue de Grenelle. Southern magnolia keeps its leaves all year, thick and glossy with a rust-coloured felt underneath, and in early summer it opens cream-white flowers the width of a dinner plate, lemon-scented and gone within a couple of days. Paris put this one on its remarkable tree register at 163 centimetres around, a figure the one independent account of the square repeats exactly. Nobody has recorded its age. The square supplies the only chronological anchor: Square d'Ajaccio, formerly Square des Invalides, was laid out by Adolphe Alphand, the engineer behind most of Haussmann's parks, in the wave of small green squares cut into Paris between the 1860s and the 1880s. Whether the magnolia went in with the square or a lifetime later, no record says, which is why the estimate here is a broad one. It shares its enclosure with a plane tree forty-five metres away that is also on the register, so this is a two-tree garden and ten minutes is enough for both. Magnolia grandiflora is planted across Paris but rarely gets to stand up like this: the species is tender here, and most specimens spend their lives flattened against a warm wall.

trees.name: The Plane of Square d'Ajaccio
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily
trees.transport: Invalides (M8, M13, RER C), about 8 min walk; Varenne (M13) about 5 min walk
trees.story: Four metres ninety of trunk, in a square you can cross in twenty paces. The register gives this plane 490 centimetres around and 25 metres tall, and the one independent survey of Square d'Ajaccio quotes exactly the same 490, which is the kind of agreement that makes a measurement worth trusting. The two sources part company on the species. The city types it as Platanus x hispanica, the London plane, the hybrid Europe planted by the million from the eighteenth century onward. The visitor guide calls the square's planes oriental planes, which is one of that hybrid's two parents and a genuinely different tree. The city's own inventory wins here, but the disagreement is real and it is the sort of thing you can stand at the trunk and argue about. Its age is documented nowhere. The same guide calls the square's planes century-old, and the square dates from Alphand's programme of the 1860s to 1880s, so a hundred years is a floor rather than a figure. The tree has therefore watched the Rue de Grenelle become a street of ministries and embassies, with the dome of the Invalides two blocks east, while doing what old planes do: dropping bark in camouflage plates every summer and putting on another centimetre of belt. It stands forty-five metres from a southern magnolia that is also on the register, two designated trees inside one small enclosure.

trees.name: The Turkish Hazel of Square du Temple
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily (closes at night per standard Paris square hours)
trees.transport: Temple (M3), about 3 min walk; République (M3/5/8/9/11), about 6 min walk
trees.story: Most people picture a hazel as a shrub they can see over. This one is sixteen metres tall with a trunk 235 centimetres around. Corylus colurna, the Turkish hazel, is the outsized relative of the nut-bearing hedge hazel, native to the Balkans, Anatolia and the Caucasus, and it grows as a single straight trunk under a tidy cone of a crown. Nineteenth-century park designers liked it for the shape, and cities still plant it because it shrugs off heat, compacted soil and bad air. Nobody wrote down when this one was planted. Paris has other Turkish hazels of similar or greater girth that do carry dates, including one in Square Maurice-Gardette recorded as 1882, so comparison puts this tree somewhere between eighty and a hundred and fifty years old, and that is as precise as the evidence gets. The ground has a heavier history than the garden suggests. This is the old Temple enclosure, the Paris headquarters of the Knights Templar, and later the prison where Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were held before their executions. The tower came down in 1808 and the garden that replaced it dates from the 1850s. It now holds 71 trees and 191 varieties of plant, a good share of them foreign: a ginkgo, a Japanese pagoda tree, a Caucasian wingnut, a golden rain tree and a Chinese quince, all within a few minutes of the hazel.

trees.name: The Old Hazel of Square Maurice-Gardette
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily
