trees.transport: Saint-Ambroise (M9), about 5 min walk; Voltaire (M9), about 8 min walk

best_time.label: September into October, when the nuts drop and the neighbourhood collects them

trees.story: French regional television once ran a news piece written in this tree's own voice, headlined "I am 145, stop cracking my hazelnuts and let me age in peace". The grievance is real enough. Turkish hazel nuts are edible, they drop in quantity in early autumn, and people in Square Maurice-Gardette gather them. The two sources differ on when it started. The city register records a planting year of 1882; the broadcast piece says 1879. Three years apart, which makes it roughly 145 years old either way and, more usefully, one of the few Turkish hazels in Paris with any planting date at all. Its trunk measures 265 centimetres around and it stands twenty metres, tall enough to end the argument about hazels being shrubs. Check the bark. This species sheds it once a year in pale corky strips, closer to a birch than to anything you would expect on a nut tree, and on a trunk this size the effect is hard to miss. It shares the square with an olive, a ginkgo and a horse chestnut, none of which crowds it. One caveat on the superlative that follows this tree around. The same broadcaster has called a different Paris hazel, the one in Square Jean-XXIII behind Notre-Dame, the oldest in the city. Both claims cannot be right and nothing settles it, so this one is left as what it demonstrably is: dated, measured and unusually large.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Square d'Estienne d'Orves
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily
trees.transport: Trinité - d'Estienne d'Orves (M12), about 2 min walk, the square sits right beside the station

best_time.label: July and August, when the long seed chains hang low enough to read from the pavement

trees.story: Come up the steps from the Trinite metro and it is right there, twenty-six metres of it, reported to be the oldest living Caucasian wingnut in France. Two independent sources give a planting date of 1862 and a trunk 3.8 metres around, and they match the city register to the centimetre, which is rarer than it should be. The claim about being the oldest in the country belongs to those sources rather than to us: no ring count has been published, and a tree dated 1862 makes it plausible without proving it. Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the Caucasus and northern Iran, a wetland species happy in ground too wet for most hardwoods. It gives itself away in high summer, when chains of winged green nutlets up to half a metre long hang from the branch tips, and its ash-like compound leaves can run to sixty centimetres. Left alone the species suckers from the root plate until one tree becomes a thicket of itself, which is what makes a clean single trunk of this size worth the stop. Paris gave it the Remarkable Tree label on 1 April 2017. It stands in the small square in front of the church of La Trinite, in a quarter rebuilt during Haussmann's works, so the tree and the streets around it went up together and it has been growing beside the station entrance since before the Metro existed.

trees.name: The Chinaberry of Square Boucicaut
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily, facing the Bon Marché department store
trees.transport: Sèvres-Babylone (M10, M12), about 4 min walk

best_time.label: December and January, when the pale yellow berries hang on after the leaves have gone

trees.story: Here is a subtropical tree holding its fruit through a Paris winter. Melia azedarach, the chinaberry, belongs to the warm belt running from India to China and is normally a Mediterranean planting; the French call it lilas de Perse, Persian lilac, for the loose sprays of small mauve star-shaped flowers it opens in summer. What happens next is the reason to note the address. Those flowers become hard pale yellow berries that stay on the bare twigs long after the leaves have gone, so the tree is at its most conspicuous in December. The berries are poisonous to people, which is worth knowing if there is a child with you. The register gives it 155 centimetres around and ten metres tall, and the independent survey of the seventh arrondissement's nine remarkable trees repeats that same 155. Neither carries a planting date, and the square's own literature says only that many of its hundred-odd trees pass a century, which is a claim about the square rather than about this tree, so its age stays open. Square Boucicaut opened in 1870 as the square du Bon-Marche, named for Aristide and Marguerite Boucicaut, whose department store still faces it: fixed prices, goods you could handle before buying, and the oldest such shop in Paris. Their garden still collects oddities, Chilean araucarias and a very rare Cunninghamia lanceolata among them. The chinaberry is the one that fruits in the cold.

trees.name: The Amur Cork Tree of Square Michel-Foucault
trees.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, opposite the Collège de France, 5th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public square, open daily (24/24 in the checked period), dogs permitted on leash
trees.transport: Maubert-Mutualité (M10) or Cluny-La Sorbonne (M10), 3-5 min walk
trees.story: Paris classifies this Amur cork tree as one of its remarkable trees, and it carries proof of a rough century outdoors: a lightning scar runs down the trunk. It shares its small pocket garden, opposite the Collège de France in the Latin Quarter, with the two Oriental planes already listed here, though almost nobody looks past those two to notice it. Phellodendron amurense is a startling find in a French square, native to the river valleys of northeastern China and the Russian Far East, grown there and studied for a thick, corky, deeply furrowed bark long before anyone planted it for how it looks. This one went into the ground in 1925, and the city's own record has it at 14 metres tall with a trunk 1.8 metres round as of 2011, a girth built less by height than by branching low and wide, so the trunk balls up beneath the crown instead of running straight. Compound leaves shaped like an ash tree's turn a hard yellow every autumn. The measurement is now fifteen years old and the tree has kept growing since, and this pass found only the city's own account of it, so the numbers are given as recorded rather than confirmed twice over. Still worth the two extra steps past the planes: not every French square holds a tree from the Amur river valley with a lightning strike already behind it.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Square Louise Michel
trees.neighbourhood: Square Louise Michel, below the Sacre-Coeur, 18th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden (Square Louise Michel), open standard Paris park hours and closed at night
trees.transport: Anvers (Metro 2) or Abbesses (Metro 12), 5-8 min walk up the Butte Montmartre
trees.story:
Millions of people climb past this tree every year on their way to something else. Square Louise Michel is the terraced garden below the Sacre-Coeur, the one with the long staircase up the Butte Montmartre, and three of the city's registered remarkable trees stand within 150 metres of each other inside it. This oriental plane is the oldest and the largest of the three.

It was planted in 1857, which puts it 70 years ahead of the garden around it: the square itself was only laid out in 1927. The city register and the square's own published description agree to the centimetre, 520 centimetres round and 28 metres tall, which is a rarer kind of agreement than it ought to be.

One caveat on the paperwork. A local survey of the 18th arrondissement describes an oriental plane of 470 centimetres planted in 1840, close enough to invite confusion and different enough on both figures that it is probably a different tree somewhere else in the district. The numbers given here are the register's and the square's, not that survey's.

Everyone on the steps is looking up at the basilica. The plane is off to the side, doing nothing in particular, and has been doing it since before there was a basilica to look at.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Square Louise Michel
trees.neighbourhood: Square Louise Michel, below the Sacre-Coeur, 18th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden (Square Louise Michel), open standard Paris park hours and closed at night
trees.transport: Anvers (Metro 2) or Abbesses (Metro 12), 5-8 min walk up the Butte Montmartre

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.story:
There are two Caucasian wingnuts in this square and only one of them has a birthday. The register lists both, sixty metres apart, at 371 and 416 centimetres round. The published account of the garden describes a wingnut of 3.60 metres planted in 1899, which fits the smaller of the two closely and the larger one not at all, so the date sits here, on this tree, and the bigger one keeps no age rather than borrow one.

The heights do not line up as neatly. That same account gives its wingnut 20 metres; the register now measures this one at 26. Years of growth would explain the gap, and so would the account having described the other tree all along, and nothing available settles it.

What is not in dispute is what happens in high summer. Chains of pale green winged seeds hang straight down from the branch tips, long, narrow and unlike anything else growing on this hillside, and on a crown this size there are hundreds of them at once. Come in February and you would walk past it without a second look.

It went into the ground in 1899, the year before the funicular started hauling visitors up the slope beside it, and it has spent every summer since dangling seed chains over people too busy climbing to look sideways.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Square Louise Michel
trees.neighbourhood: Square Louise Michel, below the Sacre-Coeur, 18th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden (Square Louise Michel), open standard Paris park hours and closed at night
trees.transport: Anvers (Metro 2) or Abbesses (Metro 12), 5-8 min walk up the Butte Montmartre

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story:
The best-known figure for this chestnut is forty centimetres out of date. Two published accounts of the garden give it a trunk of 330 centimetres; the city register now measures 370. Nothing has gone wrong. The tree kept growing while the paperwork stood still, which is the most cheerful sort of disagreement between sources.

It was planted in 1902, and the register and both accounts agree on that, which makes it one of the better-dated trees on this page. In 1902 the basilica above it was a building site: work on the Sacre-Coeur ran from 1875 to 1914, so the chestnut spent its first dozen years growing under scaffolding and cranes. The garden itself arrived later still, laid out in 1927.

Horse chestnuts are the most familiar tree on this list and the most taken for granted. This one is 21 metres tall under a broad even crown, and it does the two things the species is loved for on schedule: white flower spikes standing upright all over it in May, conkers split out of their green cases on the path in September.

One correction to the name Paris gives it. The marronnier d'Inde is not from India and not from here either. It came out of the mountains of the Balkans in the sixteenth century, and Europe has been planting it in squares ever since.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Square Rene-Le Gall
trees.neighbourhood: Square Rene-Le Gall (Jardin des Gobelins), Croulebarbe, 13th arrondissement
trees.access: Free, public municipal square (Square Rene-Le Gall, also known as Jardin des Gobelins), open standard Paris park hours and closed at night
trees.transport: Corvisart or Les Gobelins (Metro 6/7), 8-10 min walk

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.story:
There is a river under this garden. The Bievre ran through the Gobelins quarter in the open until the city buried the last stretches of it, fouled by the tanners and dyers who had worked its banks for centuries, and Square Rene-Le Gall was laid out in the 1930s across the ground it used to flow over. This horse chestnut was planted in 1893 or 1894, while the water was still above ground.

It stands near the garden's obelisk, at one of the entrances, and its measurements are a small lesson in how slowly a mature tree changes. A 2011 survey recorded 18 metres tall and 360 centimetres round. The city register now gives 17 metres and 369. Nine centimetres of belt in well over a decade, and a metre of height that is measurement noise rather than a tree shrinking.

The square around it is a listed historic monument, protected since 1997, though the protection is for the 1930s design rather than for anything growing in it: rock gardens, a long sunken lawn, brick pavilions and that obelisk, laid out on a scale most Paris squares never get.

The chestnut is one of the few things here older than the design. It was already a grown tree when the diggers arrived, and it is the only part of the garden nobody drew.

trees.name: The Plane of Square Montholon
trees.access: Free, public municipal square (Square Montholon), open 9:30-21:30 weekdays and 9:00-21:30 weekends (hours vary by season per paris.fr) and closed at night
trees.transport: Cadet or Poissonniere (Metro 7), 5-7 min walk
trees.story:
Square Montholon has two enormous plane trees and the city has written down the history of only one of them. This may be that one. The official description of the square records a plane planted in 1872, standing 32 metres tall with a trunk 432 centimetres round. The register of remarkable trees lists a single plane here, at this exact spot, at 470 centimetres and 27 metres. Those are not the same numbers.

Either this trunk has put on 38 centimetres since that record was made, which is entirely ordinary, or the register has pinned the other tree of the pair, which is also entirely ordinary. Nothing available decides it, so the age given here stays broad, well over a century and probably a good deal more, rather than claiming 1872 for a tree that may not have earned it.

What is not ambiguous is the trunk in front of you. Four metres seventy puts it among the larger planes anywhere in Paris, in a garden small enough to cross in a minute.

The square opened in 1863, one of the small public gardens cut into the city while Haussmann was rebuilding it, and was redesigned in 1981. It sits off the Rue La Fayette in the 9th, gates open in the morning and shut at night, with the pair of planes doing most of the work of making it feel older than the rest of it is.

trees.name: Gija Jumulu
trees.access: Free, Kings Park is open daily
trees.transport: Kings Park, walkable from Perth CBD (~2-3 km) or via CAT bus/Kings Park shuttle

best_time.label: June to August, when it drops its leaves and the whole tree is that trunk

trees.story:
This boab did not grow where it stands. It is reckoned to be over 750 years old and it spent almost all of that beside Telegraph Creek near Warmun in the Kimberley, until 2008, when it was lifted out of the ground to clear the way for a road bridge on the Great Northern Highway. Eighteen metres tall and 37 tonnes, it then travelled 3,200 kilometres south on a truck, the longest known road journey by a living tree of that size, and was replanted in Kings Park on 20 July 2008. The Gija people, traditional owners of the country it came from, held a farewell ceremony for it six days before it left and gave it the name Gija Jumulu. Jumulu is their word for boab.

It arrived with superficial damage to its bark and was assessed as healthy in 2016. Boabs are built to absorb that sort of insult. They drop their leaves through the dry-season winter and keep photosynthesising through the bark itself, which is why the bare months show the tree at its best rather than its worst: a swollen grey bottle of a trunk above the Two Rivers Lookout, with nothing to distract from the shape. New growth usually starts again in December.

On the estimates it has another twelve centuries ahead of it, all of which it will now spend 3,200 kilometres from where it started.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig Tree, Royal Perth Hospital
trees.access: Free, visible from the Murray Street footpath in front of Kirkman House
trees.transport: Perth CBD, walkable, ~1 km from the Perth train station / Elizabeth Quay
trees.story:
The trunk measures 9.4 metres around, which is a startling thing to meet on a city footpath. The National Trust of Western Australia measured it in November 2018 and recorded three metres of diameter, 36 metres of height and a condition of good. It stands on Murray Street in front of Kirkman House at Royal Perth Hospital, and it has been the spot where staff and visitors arrange to meet each other for as long as anyone there remembers. The state heritage inventory calls it a dominant element in the streetscape and unique in form and character in the city centre, which for a heritage inventory counts as enthusiasm.

Nobody wrote down who planted it, or when. The inventory says early 1900s and stops there. The National Trust register put it at about 130 years when it took its measurements, which makes it somewhere near 138 now, and that figure is an estimate by people who assess figs for a living rather than a planting record. It could be out by a decade in either direction. If you know the date, tell us.

The paperwork behind it is considerable: National Trust classification in 1975, the interim Register of the National Estate in 1978, the state heritage list in 1985. The tree's own argument is simpler. It is enormous, it is in the middle of a working hospital forecourt, and you can walk up and put a hand on it.

trees.name: Port Jackson Fig, The Cloisters
trees.access: Free, stands in the forecourt of Mt Newman House / The Cloisters office complex, visible from St Georges Terrace
trees.transport: Perth CBD, walkable, ~1 km from Perth train station
trees.story:
In 1971 an office tower was built around this fig rather than over it. Mt Newman House went up on the site of The Cloisters on St Georges Terrace, and the architects designed the development to keep the tree where it was. The state heritage inventory files the result as a successful attempt to rehabilitate a mature existing tree and integrate it into a major city development, which is bureaucratic language for a decision most Australian cities were not making in 1971. It survived a later redevelopment of the site as well.

Its age is a matter of record rather than of estimate, which is rare. A tenant of The Cloisters planted it as a small tree in 1887, and the heritage inventory and the building's own history agree on that, so the tree is 139 years old this year.

It has grown into the space it was spared. Eighteen metres tall, a trunk 3.9 metres round, a canopy spreading roughly 15 by 18 metres, condition assessed as very good. Port Jackson figs branch low and wide, so it fills the forecourt between the tower and The Cloisters' old brickwork and turns a piece of hard city frontage into shade.

It is a minute's walk off the main run of St Georges Terrace, free, and visible from the street at any hour, and it asks nothing of you but a look upwards.

trees.name: The Proclamation Tree
trees.access: Free, public park (Mayor's Park / traffic island)
trees.transport: Fremantle town centre; Fremantle train station approx. 700m walk. Fremantle is within the day-trip boundary, roughly 30 minutes by train from Perth CBD
trees.story:
The fig has grown over the monument it shares its corner with. Under the canopy stands the William Marmion Memorial, a Celtic cross unveiled in 1902, now partly hidden by a tree that was already twelve years in the ground when it arrived.

The planting is dated to the afternoon. On 21 October 1890 Governor Sir William Robinson put this Moreton Bay fig in to mark the granting of self-government to the Colony of Western Australia, and both the state heritage record and Fremantle's own local history give the same date, which makes the tree 136 years old and one of the few on this map whose birthday is known. It went in at the corner of Adelaide, Parry and Queen Victoria Streets, the point where everyone entering Fremantle's main streets passed by, and it has held that corner ever since. The corner is now a small park hemmed in by three roads.

It sits on the state Register of Heritage Places, was classified by the National Trust in 1980 and is on the City of Fremantle's heritage list. What nobody has published is a girth figure, and a fig of this age tends to have an interesting one. If you take a tape to it, tell us the number.

Fremantle is roughly half an hour by train from central Perth, and the tree is a 700 metre walk from the station.

trees.name: The Old Jarrah Tree
trees.access: Free and outdoors, beside the public carpark on the site of the former Armadale Primary School, which the tree served from 1904 until 1987. We have not confirmed whether the ground immediately around the trunk is fenced, so treat it as a tree you can certainly see and may not be able to walk up to.
trees.transport: Armadale, on the Armadale train line, roughly 35-40 minutes by train from Perth station plus a short walk; a day trip beyond the strict 30-minute boundary but close and a single direct line
trees.story:
In 1997 vandals ringbarked this jarrah, a cut that should have finished it. Three quarters of its canopy is dead or gone and earlier lopping had already taken roughly half its height, but it answered the ringbarking with epicormic shoots along its northern side and it is still assessed as stable. Alive, in other words, and visibly not unharmed.

What happened next is the part worth knowing. 1,147 people wrote to the state government asking for the tree to be protected. A conservation order followed on 14 November 1997, a heritage agreement in 2002, and in 2003 it went onto the State Heritage Register, one of only three trees or groups of trees listed in all of Western Australia.

The register estimates it at 400 to 800 years old. That is a wide band because nobody has dated it more closely than the bulk and growth form of an old-growth jarrah allow, and we would rather give you the band than a tidy number. From 1904 until 1987 it stood beside Armadale Primary School and generations of children played under it. The school has gone. The tree and the ground are still there, now beside a public carpark.

Two things to know before you go. Our pin marks the cross-street rather than the trunk, so expect to look around. And we have not confirmed whether the ground right around the tree is fenced, so count on seeing it and not on reaching it.

trees.name: The Fraser Avenue Red Flowering Gum
trees.access: Free, Kings Park is open daily; stands near the main Fraser Avenue entrance
trees.transport: Kings Park, walkable from Perth CBD (~2-3 km) or via CAT bus/Kings Park shuttle

best_time.label: January and February, when the crown fills with scarlet flower heads

trees.story:
A hundred scarlet-flowering gums went into Fraser Avenue on 29 September 1929. This is the only one left.

They were planted for Western Australia's centenary by the Centenary Committee, the Kings Park Board and assorted dignitaries, led by A. Lovekin MLA, and every planter was handed an inscribed silver trowel for the occasion. Then patch canker went through the avenue in the 1930s and took most of them, along with much of the original 1898 planting made for Queen Victoria's jubilee. By 1938 the gaps had been filled with lemon-scented gums, which are the tall pale trunks that give Fraser Avenue its look today.

The survivor stands near the main entrance and does not announce itself: 11 metres tall, two metres through the trunk, in excellent condition when the National Trust measured it in 2014. Ninety-seven years old, from a documented planting date rather than a guess.

In high summer it does the thing its species is named for and covers itself in scarlet flower heads, which is when a modest tree becomes the reason people stop walking.

The register places it north-east of the main Fraser Avenue entrance rather than at a fixed point, so our pin is good to the area and not to the trunk. Come in January or February and you will not need the pin.

trees.name: The Palazzo Murena Cedar
trees.access: Free, inside the cloister of Palazzo Murena, seat of the University of Perugia's Rectorate; the cloister is open to the public during normal building hours.
trees.transport: Central Perugia, on Piazza dell'Universita just off Corso Vannucci; reachable on foot from Piazza IV Novembre in about 5 minutes, or via the Minimetro to Pincetto/Fontivegge then a short walk.
trees.story: In 2020 a trumpeter and an accordionist played a concert twelve metres up in this tree. Paolo Fresu and Daniele di Bonaventura performed a set titled Two for Tree from the crown of the Atlas cedar in the cloister of Palazzo Murena, the rectorate of the University of Perugia, with the audience listening from the courtyard below. The tree could take it. It was planted just after Italian unification, around 1861, in the eclectic garden taste of that moment, and is somewhere between 150 and 185 years old depending on which source you ask. The national register gives 485 centimetres of girth and 25 metres of height; La Nazione measured it in 2021 at five metres round, 30 metres tall and 35 metres across the crown. Take either. It is the largest thing inside the cloister by a wide margin, and the walls it grew up between have kept it out of the wind for its whole life. Lightning found it anyway at some point, and left scars still visible on the trunk. Climbing arborists went up in October 2010 to prune it and consolidate the crown, and it was pronounced in excellent health in 2020, the year of the concert. The cloister is free and open during normal building hours, five minutes from Piazza IV Novembre, which makes this the easiest monumental tree in Perugia to reach and the least likely to be spotted from the street.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Piazza Italia
trees.access: Free, public city square and gardens in the historic centre.
trees.transport: Central Perugia, at the top of Corso Vannucci; a 2 to 3 minute walk from Piazza IV Novembre.
trees.story: This cedar is rooted in the site of a fortress Perugia demolished out of spite. The Rocca Paolina was a papal stronghold built over the houses of the families who opposed the pope, and when the city came out from under papal rule in 1860 it tore the fortress down and laid Piazza Italia over the ground, a square whose entire argument was that the Rocca no longer stood there. The flowerbeds went in with it, and the Atlas cedar in them is one of the survivors of that planting, alongside a red fir of similar age. Local sources call it a century old specimen without fixing a year, so over a century is the honest figure rather than a precise one; the register adds 390 centimetres of girth and 23 metres of height. What makes it worth the two minute walk up from Piazza IV Novembre is where it stands, at the top of Corso Vannucci on the edge of the terrace that looks out over the Umbrian valley. The fortress is still down there under your feet, its lower streets preserved and walkable, which is how most people now arrive at the square, riding escalators up through the ruins of the thing the cedar replaced.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Porta Pesa
trees.access: Free, standing on the public square of Largo di Porta Pesa.
trees.transport: Centro Storico, Porta Pesa area (Perugia's historic 'Chinatown' district), a 5 to 10 minute walk from Piazza IV Novembre.

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: A cedar of Lebanon this thick should be twice as tall. This one measures 410 centimetres round the trunk and 12.5 metres to the top, squat to the point of oddity for the species, and it now carries elastic guy wires and fixed bracing holding its main limbs together. The city installed those over February and March 2025, along with pruning, deadwood removal and a rebalancing of the crown, work done under a care programme run with Umbria's regional forestry service for Perugia's monumental trees. Read cabling as good news. A tree gets braced when somebody has decided it is worth keeping. It grows on the open square at Largo di Porta Pesa, directly in front of the Ciabatti Montessori elementary school, so several generations of Perugian children have had it as the thing outside the window, and the comune calls it century old without naming a year. Cedar of Lebanon reached Italian gardens from the mountains of the Levant, where the surviving old groves are now fenced and counted individually. A low, wide, heavily limbed specimen like this one is what the species does when it grows in the open with nothing competing for light, which is also why it needs the hardware: those limbs are long, horizontal and heavy. Porta Pesa is five to ten minutes on foot from Piazza IV Novembre.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Croce Rossa
trees.access: Free, standing on the public square of Largo della Croce Rossa.
trees.transport: Centro Storico, a short walk from Piazza Italia and Palazzo Murena.

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: The national register knows how tall this cedar is and not how wide. Its sheet records 18 metres of height and leaves the girth field blank, a gap in the paperwork rather than a lost measurement, and nobody has filled it in since. So the honest description of Perugia's second cedar of Lebanon is this: 18 metres, standing on a public square, and you can judge the trunk yourself when you get there. It grows at Largo della Croce Rossa on Via Masi, a short walk downhill from Piazza Italia and Palazzo Murena, and La Nazione named it specifically in a survey of the city's monumental trees under municipal care, which is how we know it is being looked after rather than merely listed. No age is recorded anywhere. Cedar of Lebanon was planted all over nineteenth century Italy as a status tree, the conifer of the Bible and of Lebanon's flag, which is why a city this size ends up with two of them ten minutes apart and no particular reason for either. Between the pair, this is the taller by a clear margin, 18 metres against the 12.5 of the Porta Pesa cedar, which is roughly what the species does when it has been left to run up rather than out.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Via Fiume
trees.access: Free, standing on the public street of Via Fiume in the historic centre.
trees.transport: Centro Storico, a short walk from Piazza Italia.
trees.story: Italians call this species spaccasassi, the rock splitter, because its roots get into stone and open it. They plant it in city streets anyway, because little else gives that much shade on that little water. This one has been on Via Fiume long enough to reach 445 centimetres round the trunk and 21 metres tall, a serious size for a hackberry and a very serious size for a tree growing out of a street in a hill town rather than a garden with soil to spare. Perugia's centre is built along a ridge with its streets cut into the slope, so a tree of this age here has spent its whole life finding water under paving. La Nazione named it alongside the city's two cedars of Lebanon in a survey of the monumental trees the comune maintains, and the same programme covers it: inspection, pruning, and the working assumption that it stays. Its age is not on record and no source estimates one. Mediterranean hackberry leafs out late, drops small dark fruit in autumn that the birds clear before most people notice it, and keeps smooth grey bark like a beech into old age, which is the quickest way to tell it from anything else on the street. It is a few minutes' walk from Piazza Italia.

trees.name: The Holm Oaks of Giardini del Frontone
trees.access: Free, public municipal gardens.
trees.transport: Borgo XX Giugno, about a 15 to 20 minute walk south of the centro storico, or a short bus ride.
trees.story: On 20 June 1859 papal Swiss Guards and the Antibes Legion came up the hill and sacked Perugia, and these oaks were already old. A local history piece in 2025 put the question directly, asking what the secular holm oaks of the Frontone saw that day, the last serious violence in the city before Italian unification. The gardens are older still. They were laid out from 1707 for the Accademia degli Arcadi, a literary society that wanted somewhere to hold its summer gatherings, on ground used for military drill since the 1400s and, long before that, as an Etruscan necropolis. The avenues of holm oak went in with the garden and were finished through the 1800s, along with the pool, the statues and the Arco del Frontone of 1791. Two of the oaks are individually listed in the national register, at 350 and 342 centimetres round and 15.5 and 21.5 metres tall, standing about 70 metres apart along the same avenues. The pin marks the gardens rather than one trunk, because the walk under the oaks is the thing here, not a single tree. Holm oak holds its leaves all year, so the avenues are dark and cool in August, which is exactly what the Arcadians wanted them for. The gardens are free, opposite the Abbey of San Pietro, fifteen to twenty minutes south of the centro storico on foot.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Cimitero Monumentale
trees.access: Free, inside the public monumental cemetery; open daily, 7:00-17:30 (winter) or 7:00-18:30 (summer).
trees.transport: Monteluce district, a short bus ride or a roughly 20 minute walk from the centro storico.
trees.story: Perugia's monumental cemetery opens at seven every morning, costs nothing, and holds a Himalayan cedar with a trunk 496 centimetres round and 23.5 metres of tree above it. Italian monumental cemeteries are built to be walked in. Milan's and Genoa's draw visitors for their sculpture and their planting as much as for the graves, and this one, out on Via Enrico dal Pozzo in the Monteluce district, is the same kind of place: gravel avenues, cypresses, and this cedar over the top of them. The Templar church of San Bevignate, with its thirteenth century frescoes, stands next door. What the tree does not have is a story of its own. No newspaper, history page or municipal notice found so far names it; the register measures it and the comune's page confirms the cemetery and its hours, and that is the whole documentary record, which means its age is unknown rather than approximate. Deodar was a standard cemetery planting across nineteenth century Italy, an evergreen brought down from the Himalaya and chosen for the obvious associations, so a nineteenth century date is likely and unproven. Opening runs to half past five in winter and half past six in summer. It is a twenty minute walk from the centro storico, or a short bus ride.

trees.name: The Cypress of Parco della Cuparella
trees.access: Free, public municipal park along Perugia's historic walls.
trees.transport: Centro Storico, the closest register tree to the city centre (0.25km); a few minutes' walk from Piazza Italia and Piazza Universita.
trees.story: The park this cypress stands in used to be where people dumped things. Perugians called the slope Il Campaccio, roughly the bad field, a steep and disused strip against the medieval walls, and in the 1950s the comune handed it to the Tuscan landscape architect Pietro Porcinai, who turned it into a public garden. The nickname stuck anyway. The Mediterranean cypress here measures 293 centimetres round and 21 metres tall, and it is the closest monumental tree to the centre of Perugia, a couple of hundred metres from Piazza Italia and Piazza dell'Universita, which makes it the one to start or finish a walk on. Cypress is the least surprising tree in Umbria and the most useful. It takes thin, fast draining soil, exactly the conditions on a slope like this one, and its narrow column is the reason Italian hillsides look the way they do in every painting of them. Whether this tree predates Porcinai's redesign or went in as part of it is not recorded, and neither the register nor FAI's heritage listing for the park says. Nobody has published an age. What is on record is the site: free, open, built along the city walls, with the valley below it and the old town directly above.

trees.name: The North Oak of Strada del Gioco
trees.access: Free, roadside on Strada del Gioco; no gate and no hours.
trees.transport: About 3 km southwest of the centro storico, roughly a 40 minute walk downhill or a short bus ride.
trees.story:
Downy oak is the tree Umbrian hillsides are made of, and hardly any of them get this big. Quercus pubescens takes the dry limestone slopes that better oaks refuse, usually as a modest, crooked, hard-used tree of field edges and scrub. This one is 430 centimetres around and 21 metres tall, which put it on Italy's national monumental register on size alone. It is not even alone: a second oak within eight centimetres of the same girth stands 150 metres down the lane.

Strada del Gioco runs through Prepo, on the slope roughly three kilometres southwest of the walled centre. Perugia's other monumental trees are a nineteenth century story, cedars planted as the city laid out gardens over the ground where the papal fortress had stood. These two are the older landscape showing through: field oaks left where they were while the land around them changed use, which is how a good many large roverelle in central Italy came to survive.

The species is worth knowing in winter. Downy oak is marcescent, tending to hold its dead leaves on the lower branches through the cold months instead of dropping them, so the crown keeps a rustling copper brown long after the rest of the hillside has gone bare.

Italy's register is the only source that names this tree, and it gives a girth, a height and a position and no age, so the numbers here are the register's own and the pin is marked approximate.

trees.name: The South Oak of Strada del Gioco
trees.access: Free, roadside on Strada del Gioco; no gate and no hours.
trees.transport: About 3 km southwest of the centro storico, roughly a 40 minute walk downhill or a short bus ride.
trees.story:
The two oaks of Strada del Gioco differ by eight centimetres of girth and one metre of height, and they stand 150 metres apart. This is the thinner and taller of the pair: 422 centimetres around, 22 metres up, and nothing at all on record about its age.

Part of what a downy oak is worth in Umbria is what grows under it. Quercus pubescens is one of central Italy's classic truffle hosts, the fungus forming on oak roots in exactly the limestone soils these trees favour, and a productive oak is a tree with an argument for being left standing when a hillside gets cleared. Whether that is this particular tree's biography, nobody has written down.

Prepo is a working edge of Perugia rather than a monument to it, about three kilometres southwest of the centre and 370 metres up. There is no garden here, no plaque and no gate, just two very large oaks on a lane, which is a different sort of pleasure from the cedars that hold the city's squares. Come in winter for the second one: downy oak hangs onto its dead leaves through the cold months, and a copper crown on a bare slope carries a long way.

Nobody has dated either oak. Italy's register has no age column and no second source names them, so what exists is a girth, a height and a point on a map, and the point is good to within a lane rather than a trunk.

trees.name: S'Olivera de Cort
trees.access: Free, on the open public square in front of Palma's town hall, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: In the old town, about 10 minutes' walk from Plaça d'Espanya (Metro de Mallorca and the main EMT bus hub)

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story:
This olive is older than the square it stands in, and it has only been standing there since 1989. It grew for centuries at Pedruixella Petit, an estate near Pollenca with about two thousand olive trees, until a city gardener and the head of public works came to its owner, the hotelier Jaime Batle, and asked to buy it for the town hall square. Batle refused to sell. When he learned where it would go, he gave it away instead.

On 3 May 1989 the tree was lifted whole and replanted in Placa de Cort, directly opposite Palma's Ajuntament. Its trunk measures about seven metres round and two and a half tall before the first of four thick primary branches, on a tree only six metres high in total, the classic shape of an olive that has spent five or six centuries getting wider rather than taller.

The city promised Batle a plaque with his name on it. Four mayors came and went before it was finally installed, thirty years after the gift. By then the tree needed no introduction: it had become one of the most photographed things in Palma, a six-hundred-year-old symbol of peace and rootedness parked in front of the seat of city government, exactly where a gardener once thought it belonged.

trees.name: The Ficus de la Misericòrdia
trees.access: Free, in the garden of a public cultural centre (Consell de Mallorca); the exhibition hall keeps limited Saturday hours but the courtyards and garden are open more broadly, worth checking ahead
trees.transport: In the old town, about a 10 minute walk from Plaça d'Espanya (Metro de Mallorca and the main EMT bus hub)
trees.story:
Local naturalist writers call this without qualification the biggest tree in Palma, and the numbers back the claim: a trunk over two metres across, more than twenty metres tall, and a crown reported at around thirty five metres, planted around 1827 when the old General Hospital laid out a botanical garden here. The building it grows beside, the Casa de la Misericordia, took in Palma's poor from 1565 onward; it is a cultural centre run by the Consell de Mallorca now, with free entry to its two courtyards and this garden.

The tree has outgrown its bed in more than one direction. When the city dug up the nearby Rambla for works, it found the fig's roots running under the street, well beyond the garden wall that was supposed to contain them. At the base, a ring of decorative stones from the original nineteenth century planter still survives, now half swallowed by the trunk that has spent two centuries thickening around it.

Along with a second giant fig in Palma's municipal cemetery, planted at roughly the same time, this is one of the two largest Ficus macrophylla in the Balearic Islands, and by most measurements the larger of the pair.

trees.name: The Lagunària de la Llotja
trees.access: Free, on the open public seafront promenade, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: In the old town, about a 12 minute walk from Plaça d'Espanya (Metro de Mallorca and the main EMT bus hub)
trees.story:
Locals call it pica-pica, and the name is a warning rather than an insult. Lagunaria patersonii comes from a single small island in the Tasman Sea, Norfolk Island, and packs its seed pods with fine glass-like hairs that itch for hours if the pod is opened carelessly. English speakers call the species the itchy bomb tree for the same reason. In summer it flowers in pale pink cups that pass for a small hibiscus, which is where the polite half of its name comes from.

This specimen grows on the Passeig de Sagrera, the seafront promenade, directly in front of La Llotja, the fifteenth century Gothic merchants' exchange that is one of Palma's best known medieval buildings. At 2.6 metres round and 18 metres tall it is a substantial specimen of a species usually kept smaller as a street or garden tree, catalogued by the Balearic government among the island's singular trees for exactly that reason.

It is the most street level and sociable entry on this page: no garden wall, no ticket, just a big tree doing its work of shade and ornament on a promenade full of people, across from a building that has been central to Mallorcan trade since before Columbus sailed.

trees.name: The Ficus del Cementeri
trees.access: Free, inside the Cementiri Municipal de Palma; open daily 8:30am to 7:30pm
trees.transport: EMT city bus toward Cami de Jesus; roughly 2km, 25 minutes on foot, from the old town
trees.story:
Palma's other giant fig, planted around the same decades as the one at the Misericordia garden, grows inside the city's municipal cemetery, where it has had a century and a half to spread five massive branches out from a neck seven metres and ten centimetres round, measured at chest height in 2011. It is not as tall as its cousin across town, about fifteen metres against twenty, but what it lacks in height it makes up in reach: surface roots run out from the trunk in every direction, thick enough to break paving and shoulder headstones aside.

A cemetery might seem an odd place to send someone looking for a remarkable tree, but Palma's is landscaped rather than merely functional, and this fig is one of two enormous Ficus macrophylla shading its older section, giving what could be a bleak place genuine, peaceful shade. Together with the Misericordia fig, it ranks among the largest specimens of its kind anywhere in the Balearic Islands.

The cemetery is open to visitors daily, no ticket required, and asks only the ordinary courtesy any burial ground does.

trees.name: The Mata de Bellver
trees.access: Free, in the public Parc Forestal de Bellver surrounding the castle; the castle interior itself is ticketed but the forest park is not
trees.transport: EMT bus lines 4, 20 or 46 to Plaça Gomila, then a signposted walk (or stairway) up to the park; roughly 35-40 minutes on foot from the old town
trees.story:
Pistacia lentiscus is a shrub almost everywhere it grows, a low, dense presence in Mediterranean scrubland that most walkers step past without a glance. Left alone for a century, on the right ground, it can do something else entirely: this specimen, growing just south of the outer wall of Castell de Bellver, has pushed up four vertical trunks and taken on the size and shape of a proper tree, which is exactly why the Balearic government catalogued it among the islands' singular specimens.

It stands in the Parc Forestal de Bellver, the pine forest that wraps around the fourteenth century circular castle on its hill above the city. The castle itself keeps a ticket booth and opening hours; the forest around it, waymarked with walking trails, does not, so the mata is free to visit whether or not you go inside the walls.

There is nothing dramatic in its numbers, no record height or girth. Its interest is entirely in the exception it represents: the ordinary Mediterranean shrub that had the ground and the time to become something else.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Casa Tait
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

best_time.label: clear yellow, one of the most reliable autumn trees

trees.story: This American tulip tree became one of Portugal's first individually protected trees in 1950, a legal status most of the country's current laws postdate. It grows beside Casa Tait, a 19th-century mansion inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal that once belonged to a British port wine family, and at more than 250 years old it predates both the mansion and the palace gardens built around it by a century or more. Liriodendron tulipifera is native to the eastern United States, named for the yellow-green, cup-shaped flowers it produces each late spring, blooms that only appear once a tree reaches real maturity and can go unnoticed entirely on a younger specimen. A second tulip tree grows nearby in the same grounds, over 40 metres tall, though it lacks this one's formal protection status and shouldn't be confused with it. Porto's oldest tulip tree survived the transformation of its surrounding grounds more than once: the Palácio de Cristal itself, the glass-and-iron exhibition hall that gave the gardens their name, was demolished in 1951 and replaced by the domed sports arena still standing today, a change that came one year after this tree's own protection was made permanent. Whatever else has come and gone around it, the tulip tree has stayed exactly where it was planted.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Casa Tait
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

best_time.label: August, for the season's last flush of lemon-scented white blooms

trees.story: The base of this southern magnolia measures more than six metres around, thick enough that it would take several adults linking arms to circle it. It grows in the same grounds as Casa Tait's protected tulip tree, inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, and like its neighbour it was formally classified a tree of public interest on 21 May 2021, a status that turns deliberate damage to it into a legal offence rather than simply bad manners. Magnolia grandiflora is native to the southeastern United States, prized in European gardens since the 18th century for its glossy, leathery leaves and dinner-plate-sized white flowers, which release a lemon-and-vanilla scent strong enough to notice from several metres away. Late summer is when this specimen puts on its best show, its last flush of blooms opening just as most of the garden's spring flowering has finished elsewhere. Casa Tait's grounds, now folded into the wider Palácio de Cristal park, once belonged to the Tait family, British port wine merchants whose 19th-century money planted much of what still grows here. The magnolia, like the tulip tree beside it, has outlasted the family's ownership by generations.

trees.name: The Metrosidero of the Library
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

best_time.label: May into July, when it blazes with red flowers, six months off from the New Zealand Christmas the tree is named for

trees.story: New Zealand's Christmas tree has adapted well to a country that celebrates the holiday in December for entirely unrelated reasons. This metrosideros, a species Māori communities call pōhutukawa and prize for the blaze of red flowers it produces each southern summer, stands near the Biblioteca Almeida Garrett inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, and was formally classified a tree of public interest on 15 March 2019. In its native New Zealand the species flowers in December, coinciding with the Southern Hemisphere summer, which is how it earned its English common name; transplanted to Porto's Northern Hemisphere climate, its flowering calendar shifts to match local seasons instead. It shares this corner of the garden with a Washingtonia palm and a scattering of camellias, part of the eclectic plant collection assembled here since the gardens were laid out in the 1860s by German landscape architect Émile David. The library beside it, built decades after the original planting, inherited the metrosideros as an established feature of the grounds rather than the other way around. Most visitors walking to the library's entrance pass directly under its canopy without knowing they're standing beneath one of the southern hemisphere's most photographed flowering trees.

trees.name: The Plane of Quinta da Macieirinha
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (Museu Romântico interior charges separate admission)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops
trees.story: A house dedicated to a dead king's exile keeps its own protected tree in the garden outside. The London plane at Quinta da Macieirinha, a manor house inside the Palácio de Cristal park grounds now serving as Porto's Museu Romântico, is under formal review for protection as a tree of public interest alongside the palace's more famous specimens across the park. The museum inside commemorates Charles Albert of Sardinia, the abdicated King of Sardinia-Piedmont who spent the final months of his life at this house in 1849, having lost his throne after a failed war against Austria. The plane tree predates that story by decades, part of the working quinta's original planting before its owners ever imagined a deposed Italian monarch would die inside. London planes were a standard choice for 19th-century Portuguese gardens, valued for fast growth, tolerance of hard pruning, and mottled, flaking bark that sheds pollution along with old skin, part of why the species still lines so many European boulevards today. This one has grown alongside the house through its transformation from private residence to royal deathbed to public museum, three very different identities for the same modest patch of ground.

trees.name: The Camellias of Casa Tait
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops

best_time.label: January into February, near peak camellia bloom

trees.story: Porto calls itself the City of Camellias, and the oldest proof of that claim is a set of hedges, not a single tree. More than sixty camellia specimens grow around Casa Tait inside the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, several over a century old, planted as living, blooming partitions that section off parts of the garden the way a wall or fence would elsewhere. Camellias arrived in Portugal from China and Japan in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the country's mild, humid north proved so well suited to the plant that Portuguese growers eventually exported specimens back to camellia breeders across the rest of Europe, an unusual reversal of the typical colonial plant trade. Porto in particular leaned into the association hard enough that camellia season, roughly November through March depending on variety, now anchors a genuine tourism calendar, with garden openings and flower shows timed around peak bloom. Casa Tait's own hedges do the quieter version of that job every year: structuring the garden's paths, screening one glorieta from the next, doing exactly what a well-placed camellia has done in Portuguese gardens for two centuries. Nobody photographs a hedge the way they photograph a single dramatic tree, which may be exactly why this one has survived so many changes of garden fashion intact.

trees.name: The Bischofia Trio of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.story: Three of the oldest members of a common tropical street tree species anywhere in Portugal grow together in one Porto garden. These Bischofia javanica, a fast-growing evergreen more often planted along Asian avenues than kept in botanical collections, are estimated at 120 to 150 years old, among the oldest specimens of the species documented in the country, and Porto's city council has classified all three jointly as trees of public interest. They stand in the Jardim Botânico do Porto, the former grounds of the Campo Alegre estate before the University of Porto absorbed the property and turned its greenhouses and formal beds into a research and teaching collection now run by the university's Natural History and Science Museum. Bischofia javanica, native to South and Southeast Asia, produces small dark fruit that stains heavily when crushed, a trait that makes it common as a shade tree along tropical roads and rare as a deliberate botanical specimen in European gardens, part of why this trio's protected status matters: there are very few comparably documented examples anywhere in the country to measure them against. The garden around them holds more than 1,100 plant species across roughly four hectares, but these three, ordinary elsewhere and unusual here, are the ones with their own legal protection order.

trees.name: The Texas Madrone of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.story: A tree named for Texas and Mexico has found an unlikely second home in a university garden in northern Portugal. This Arbutus xalapensis, commonly called the Texas madrone across its native range in the Trans-Pecos region and northeastern Mexico, is currently under formal review for protection as a tree of public interest at the Jardim Botânico do Porto. The species is a close relative of the strawberry tree that grows wild across Portugal's own hillsides, sharing the same reddish, peeling bark and small urn-shaped flowers, which may be exactly why it settled into this collection more easily than most of the garden's other exotic imports. Specimens of this size are rare outside their native range, since the species is notoriously difficult to cultivate away from the dry, well-drained limestone soils it evolved for, and few botanical gardens outside Texas and northern Mexico maintain a documented example at all. The Jardim Botânico do Porto occupies the former Campo Alegre estate, absorbed by the University of Porto in the 20th century and now run as a teaching and research collection alongside its role as a free public garden. This madrone is one of the collection's quieter successes: no dramatic size record, no royal history, just a temperamental species that, against the odds, has been thriving in the wrong hemisphere for years.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Palácio de Cristal
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Câmara de Massarelos or Casa da Música metro/bus stops
trees.story: At around 24 metres tall, this Himalayan cedar is one of the largest of its species growing anywhere in Porto, a claim made cautiously since more than one Porto garden has a candidate for the title and no citywide survey has settled the question. It grows in the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, high enough on the hillside that its crown clears the rooftops below and looks out over the Douro valley, and its size alone marks it out in a garden better known for camellias and formal beds than for conifers this large. Cedrus deodara is native to the western Himalayas, where it is the national tree of Pakistan and grows at altitudes most other cedars can't tolerate, and it reached European gardens in the 19th century as one of several Himalayan conifers collectors raced to introduce once British expansion into the region made seed collection possible. Its drooping, slightly weeping branch tips distinguish it at a glance from the stiffer, more horizontal cedars of Lebanon and Atlas that grow in other Porto gardens. No precise planting date has surfaced for this specimen, only its approximate current height, so its age here is an estimate rather than a documented fact. What isn't in question is the view: few other trees in the garden let you see this much of the city at once.

trees.name: The Coast Redwood of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.story: The tallest tree species on Earth has a foothold in a four-hectare university garden in Porto, and it's already one of the biggest specimens the city has. This coast redwood, native to a narrow fog belt along the California and southern Oregon coastline where mature wild trees exceed 100 metres, is nowhere near that scale here, but the Jardim Botânico do Porto's own description lists it among the largest sequoias documented in the city. Coast redwoods reached European botanical collections in the mid-19th century, decades after their first scientific description, and gardens across Britain, France and the Iberian Peninsula planted them as living proof of the New World's most extreme trees, with no clear sense yet of how they'd perform in a climate so different from California's summer fog. This one has thrived well enough that its crown is now a genuine landmark within the garden's skyline, visible above the surrounding conifer collection from most approaches. The species can reproduce from stump sprouts as well as seed, meaning a felled coast redwood can regrow from its own base, a trait almost no other conifer shares. Porto's specimen has needed no such resilience yet. It has simply grown, steadily, since whichever year in the garden's history someone planted a California seedling in Portuguese soil and hoped for the best.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Casa da Música metro station (Line D)
trees.story: Of the three cedar species growing in this collection, the Atlas cedar is the one a local garden writer singled out as the most beautiful, an unusually direct piece of praise to volunteer about one specimen rather than a whole species. This particular Cedrus atlantica grows in the Jardim Botânico do Porto's conifer collection, native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, a range it shares with no natural competition from either of its more famous cedar relatives, the cedar of Lebanon and the Himalayan cedar, both planted nearby in the same garden. All three species look similar enough at a distance, distinguished mainly by branch angle and needle colour, that telling them apart requires standing close enough to compare bark and cone shape directly, a small identification puzzle the garden's layout seems to invite by planting the three so near each other. Atlas cedars were introduced to European gardens in the 1840s, later than Lebanon cedars but earlier than the Himalayan species, part of a decades-long sequence of cedar introductions that let 19th-century botanists compare three ecologically similar trees from three unconnected mountain ranges within a single afternoon's walk. No individual age or measurement has surfaced for this tree beyond its standing as a mature, well-formed specimen. Its reputation here rests entirely on how it looks, which, by every account gathered, is exactly the point.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of FAUP
trees.access: Free. Stands on the FAUP campus (Faculty of Architecture, University of Porto), a working academic campus rather than a public park; the Álvaro Siza-designed buildings here are a recognised architecture pilgrimage site and the grounds are walkable during campus hours.
trees.transport: STCP bus to Rua de Entre-Quintas / Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso, then a short walk onto the FAUP campus.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before darkening

trees.story: Architects travel to this campus for the buildings. The tree was here first. This copper beech grows in the gardens of the Quinta do Gólgota, the old estate that became the Faculty of Architecture of the University of Porto, a short walk from the Casa Cor-de-Rosa and the Pavilhão Carlos Ramos. Álvaro Siza began remodelling the site in 1984, and what he built here is one of the addresses the Escola do Porto is known by, visited by architecture students from all over. The beech was already more than sixty years old when the first drawings were made. It measures 4.85 metres around at chest height, stands 23 metres tall and carries a crown 20 metres across, all measured in 2020, the year Portugal's forest institute classified it a tree of public interest on the city council's proposal and with the University's agreement as owner. Copper beech is the purple-leaved form of the common European beech, planted through the 19th century by estate owners who wanted something on the lawn that was not green. This one has outlived the fashion, the estate and the family that paid for both, and it now spends its days being photographed by accident, in the background of somebody's shot of a Siza wall. Campus hours, no ticket.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of Via Panorâmica
trees.access: Free to view from the public road. The tree itself stands on a privately owned plot beside Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso (a public scenic road along the Douro bluff, next to the FAUP campus); the municipal source notes the plot has development potential, so view it from the pavement rather than entering the land.
trees.transport: STCP bus to Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso / Rua de Entre-Quintas, then a short walk along the road.
trees.story: The road came second. This camphor is very probably one of the original plantings of the Quinta do Gólgota, the 19th-century estate that Via Panorâmica Edgar Cardoso was later cut through, which makes it the survivor of a garden that has otherwise gone. Porto's city council says as much on its own record for the tree. Camphor is an East Asian evergreen, grown for the aromatic crystals distilled from its wood, and it reached Porto with the estate owners who collected the world's trees the way other people collected porcelain. This one measures around four metres in circumference at chest height and six at the base, stands 21 metres tall and spreads a crown roughly 20 metres wide. There is a healed wound low on the trunk, the kind a tree closes over decades, and the council records it as stable. Everything else around it has changed: the estate broken up, a scenic road driven along the Douro bluff, the Faculty of Architecture built next door, and the plot the tree stands on now in private hands with development potential on the municipal record. That last fact decides the visit. The land is not open and there is no way up to the trunk. You look at this tree from the pavement of the public road, and that is the whole of it. At that size it is enough, because from the roadside a camphor of four metres reads as a green wall.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Quinta Primo Madeira
trees.access: Free during university hours. Casa Primo Madeira is Pólo 3 of the University of Porto, a late-19th-century palacete restored 1986-88 by architect Fernando Távora with its garden remodelled by landscape architect Francisco Caldeira Cabral; it is an academic building on a walkable campus, and opened its doors to the public for Open House Porto in 2019.
trees.transport: STCP bus along Rua do Campo Alegre; a 10-15 minute walk from the Jardim Botânico do Porto entrance.
trees.story: Three named architects have worked on this small garden, and the trees outlasted every plan. Casa Primo Madeira is a late 19th-century palacete on Rua do Campo Alegre, built for the textile industrialist Primo Monteiro Madeira, altered for him by José Marques da Silva, then bought by the University of Porto and restored between 1986 and 1988 by Fernando Távora, with the garden itself remodelled by the landscape architect Francisco Caldeira Cabral. Through all of it the Atlas cedar stayed exactly where it was. On 30 November 2004 Portugal's official gazette classified it a tree of public interest together with two neighbours on the same lawn, a tulip tree and a plane, which is a high concentration of protected trees for a garden this size. The cedar measures 4.05 metres around at chest height and stands about 20 metres tall, with a crown roughly as wide as it is high. Cedrus atlantica comes from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, where it is now classed as endangered in the wild while growing untroubled in park after European park, an inversion that says more about grazing and logging at home than about the tree. The house is Pólo 3 of the University today. Walk in during university hours, stand on the lawn, and all three protected trees are in sight at once.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Quinta Primo Madeira
trees.access: Free during university hours, same site as (Casa Primo Madeira, Pólo 3 of the University of Porto).
trees.transport: STCP bus along Rua do Campo Alegre; a 10-15 minute walk from the Jardim Botânico do Porto entrance.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the whole crown turns clear yellow at once

trees.story: The crown of this tulip tree is wider than the tree is tall: 23.5 metres across against 21 metres of height. That shape only happens when a tree spends a century with nothing crowding it, which is precisely what the garden of Casa Primo Madeira has given it. Its trunk measures 4.35 metres around, and it was classified a tree of public interest on 30 November 2004, in the same gazette notice as the Atlas cedar and the plane standing a few paces away. Porto has more than one enormous Liriodendron tulipifera, which regularly confuses people. The famous one grows at Casa Tait in the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, protected since 1950 and considerably older. This is a different tree in a different garden about 750 metres away, planted during the same 19th-century wave of estate collecting that filled this hillside with species from other continents. Tulip trees are the tallest hardwoods of the eastern American forests and among the earliest of them to reach European gardens. The flowers, greenish with an orange band and genuinely tulip-shaped, open in June high in the crown where most visitors never spot them. The moment that carries across the whole garden comes later in the year, when a canopy that wide turns clear yellow all at once and then lets it go.

trees.name: The London Plane of Quinta Primo Madeira
trees.access: Free during university hours, same site as / (Casa Primo Madeira, Pólo 3 of the University of Porto).
trees.transport: STCP bus along Rua do Campo Alegre; a 10-15 minute walk from the Jardim Botânico do Porto entrance.
trees.story: At 6.4 metres around, this plane carries one of the thickest trunks measured anywhere in Porto. It is also the shortest of the three protected trees in the garden of Casa Primo Madeira, 17 metres tall against a crown 25 metres wide, which is the profile of a tree that never had to compete for light and put its growth sideways instead. Planes are the standard street tree of half of Europe and get treated accordingly: pollarded back to knuckles every few winters, cut clear of tram wires, kept to whatever size a pavement can hold. This one was left alone behind a wall for a century, and that difference is the reason to go and look at it. Portugal's official gazette classified it a tree of public interest on 30 November 2004, in one notice with the Atlas cedar and the tulip tree on the same lawn. The house behind it was built for the textile industrialist Primo Monteiro Madeira, acquired by the University of Porto, restored by Fernando Távora in the late 1980s, and now serves as Pólo 3, an academic building on a walkable campus that opened its doors to the public for Open House Porto in 2019. Come during university hours. The three trees stand within a minute of one another.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Palacete Burmester
trees.access: Free/low-cost. Palacete Burmester ('Casa dos Livros') is a University of Porto cultural centre within the Faculty of Sciences' green campus, reached on the same walk through the Campo Alegre botanical grounds as the already-published Jardim Botânico do Porto cluster (/007/009/010), a few hundred metres east.
trees.transport: STCP bus to Rua do Campo Alegre; entrance beside the Jardim Botânico do Porto.

best_time.label: September and October, when the conkers ripen and drop onto the lawn

trees.story: Every conker in Europe descends from a handful of mountain ravines in Greece and Albania, the only places the horse chestnut still grows wild, and where the species is now classed as vulnerable. Everywhere else it is a planted tree, and this is one of Porto's. It stands in the garden of the Palacete Burmester, the house the University of Porto runs as the Casa dos Livros on the Faculty of Sciences campus, and in 2020 it was classified a tree of public interest along with three neighbours on the same lawn: a Himalayan cedar, a tulip tree and a yew. Four protected trees in one small garden is somebody's collection rather than an accident. How old this one is, nobody has written down. Neither Portugal's forest register nor the city council gives it a date. The register holds a single measurement, a trunk 3.15 metres around in 2020, which on this species means well over a century and stops being useful after that. So the honest version is a tree that is protected, mature and undated, and anyone quoting a year for it is guessing. The garden sits a few hundred metres from the Jardim Botânico do Porto, close enough that its redwood, its bischofias and its cedars belong on the same afternoon.

trees.name: The Yew of Palacete Burmester
trees.age: unknown, mature (large girth for the species)
trees.access: Free/low-cost, same garden as (Palacete Burmester, FCUP campus, beside the Jardim Botânico do Porto).
trees.transport: STCP bus to Rua do Campo Alegre; entrance beside the Jardim Botânico do Porto.

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: A yew with a trunk 5.8 metres around normally comes with a documented history. This one has none. Portugal's forest register took the measurement in 2020, classified the tree, and left the age column empty; the city council's announcement lists the yew among four protected specimens in the garden of the Palacete Burmester and gives no date either. That gap is better left open than filled in. Taxus baccata thickens slowly enough that trees of this girth elsewhere in Europe are routinely dated in the several hundreds of years, so it is reasonable to think this one is old. It is not honest to print a number. Yews also make their own dating difficult by hollowing at the centre as they age, taking with them exactly the rings anyone would want to count. What can be said plainly is this: the tree stands in a small garden on the Faculty of Sciences campus of the University of Porto, beside the Casa dos Livros and a few hundred metres from the Jardim Botânico do Porto, and the species is scarce in Portugal outside the northern mountains, which makes a specimen this size in a city garden unusual. Every part of it is poisonous except the red flesh around the seed. It is evergreen, so February looks much like August, which at least settles the question of when to come.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Jardim das Virtudes
trees.access: Free. The Jardim das Virtudes is a public garden, open daily.
trees.transport: Sao Bento station, roughly a 10 minute walk

best_time.label: the first week of December, when it goes gold and drops within the week

trees.story:
Portugal's tree register lists this ginkgo at 35.5 metres, which makes it taller than almost anything else growing in central Porto, and the people who have watched it longest call it the Rainha das Virtudes, the Queen of the Virtudes. It stands in the Jardim das Virtudes, on the terraced slope above the Douro, where the ground falls away steeply enough that you see the whole crown at once from below rather than craning up through it. The register put its age at roughly 200 years when it was measured in 2004, and recorded a trunk 4.3 metres around and a crown spreading 17 metres. It was formally declared a tree of public interest in January 2005.

Ginkgo biloba is the last surviving member of an order of plants that was widespread when dinosaurs were, and it survives in cultivation largely because temple gardeners in China and Japan kept planting it long after it had all but vanished in the wild. What that lineage does in Porto is turn, hard, in the first week of December. Portuguese tree-watchers have documented it going gold in the same few days two years running, and the display lasts about a week before the leaves drop more or less at once. Come in late November or early December, or come another time and see a very large tree.

trees.name: The Bunya-Bunya of Jardim da Cordoaria
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden, open daily
trees.transport: Central Porto, adjacent to the Faculty of Law; roughly 10 minutes on foot from São Bento station, several STCP bus routes stop at Cordoaria
trees.story:
The tallest thing in the Jardim da Cordoaria is Australian. The bunya pine here runs to roughly 40 metres, a dark dome standing clear above the plane trees, on a straight trunk 3.6 metres round.

Araucaria bidwillii grows naturally in a few pockets of southeast Queensland and nowhere else. The leaves are stiff, glossy and sharp enough to draw blood, arranged in spirals along the branch, and the tree has a habit that made it famous at home. It drops cones the size of a football weighing several kilograms, which is why bunya groves were gathering places and why nobody sensible parks under one in season.

Local tree histories put this one in the ground between 1867 and 1869, when the garden was laid out. The register, measuring in 2004, recorded 130 years, which works out at roughly 150 today. The planting dates would make it a few years older still. Two independent routes to the same decade is about as good as tree dating gets.

It was classified in 2005, in the same decree as the avenue of plane trees a few steps away, so this small garden gives you two protected entries in one stop. Stand in the plane tunnel and look up at the far end: the araucaria is the thing breaking the roofline.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Casa Allen
trees.access: Free, public building and gardens run by the Direção Regional de Cultura do Norte; guided garden visits offered alongside the exhibition spaces
trees.transport: In the Massarelos district, walking distance from Palácio de Cristal and the Marquês metro/tram area

best_time.label: clear yellow, one of the most reliable autumn trees

trees.story:
Two official documents give this tree's waist as 5.24 metres and 7.75 metres. The register measured 5.24 at chest height in 2015. The 2021 news coverage of its classification gives 7.75 as the perimeter at the base. Both agree exactly on everything else, 31 metres tall with a 29 metre crown, so the gap is almost certainly about where the tape went rather than a disagreement about the tree.

Either way it is a big tulip tree. Liriodendron tulipifera comes from the eastern United States, where it is the tallest hardwood of the Appalachian forest, and 31 metres is a serious height for one in Europe. The leaf is the giveaway from below: four lobes with the tip cut off square, as though someone had gone at it with scissors.

No age has ever been recorded for it, by the register or by anyone else.

It grows in the garden of Casa Allen, a 1920s house by the architect José Marques da Silva, now Casa das Artes and run by the Direção Regional de Cultura do Norte. The garden is genuinely open, with guided visits alongside the exhibition rooms, but it keeps the building's hours, which on most days do not begin until half past two in the afternoon. Turning up at eleven gets you a locked gate.

trees.name: The Magnolia Ring of Jardim de São Lázaro
trees.neighbourhood: Cedofeita, Santo Ildefonso, Sé, Miragaia, São Nicolau e Vitória
trees.access: Free, public garden, Porto's oldest (opened 1834)
trees.transport: Central Porto, close to Praça da Batalha and the Bolhão/São Bento area, well served by STCP buses

best_time.label: June and July, when all twelve open lemon-scented white flowers around the lake

trees.story:
Twelve southern magnolias stand in a ring around the lake in the oldest public garden in Porto. The Jardim de São Lázaro opened in 1834, the city's first, and the magnolias came later. The register recorded them at 100 years when it measured in 2004, which puts them near 120 now and means they were planted into a garden that was already the best part of a century old.

Magnolia grandiflora is from the American southeast and is built for this job.
