The leaves are thick, dark and permanently glossy, with a rust-coloured felt on the underside that shows when the wind lifts them. In early summer the flowers open the size of a dinner plate, cream white, and carry the length of the lake on a still evening.

Each of the twelve has a trunk about 2.6 metres round and stands close to 16 metres tall. They were classified as a single group in 2005, which is the right way to read them: one lake, one loop of path, all twelve in view as you walk it, rather than twelve separate trees to hunt down.

Porto has other notable magnolias, including one classified only recently. This is the set arranged around water, in the garden the city opened first.

trees.name: The Camellias of Largo da Igreja de Paranhos
trees.access: Free, public church square (largo), open at all times
trees.transport: Paranhos, near the Faculty of Science campus; served by Porto metro Line D/Combatentes area buses

best_time.label: January and February, when both are in full flower against the church wall

trees.story:
Most people picture a camellia as a shrub in a pot. These two are six and a half metres tall with crowns ten metres across, and the state has had them under protection since 1992.

They stand a few metres apart in the largo in front of the Igreja de São Veríssimo de Paranhos, a working parish church with an open square, so there are no gates and no hours. The trunks are modest, 1.15 and 1.25 metres round, because a camellia puts its growth into a dense mass of branches rather than one stem. From the far side of the largo the pair reads as a single green wall with a church behind it.

Porto has traded on camellias since the 19th century, when the varieties came in through the port and the city's gardens filled with them. The register recorded these two at 200 years old when it measured in 2006, which puts them near 220 now. If that holds, they were growing here before the fashion arrived.

Beyond the register itself they have gone unwritten about. No article, no local history, no photograph that names them. For a city that calls itself the city of camellias that is an odd gap, and it is worth saying plainly that the age and the species here rest on the state's record alone.

trees.name: The Metrosideros of Passeio Alegre
trees.neighbourhood: Aldoar, Foz do Douro e Nevogilde
trees.access: Free, public riverside garden in Foz do Douro
trees.transport: Foz do Douro, near the Douro river mouth; served by tram line 1 and STCP buses along Rua do Passeio Alegre

best_time.label: late spring, when both crowns turn red with stamens above the river mouth

trees.story:
Two of these stand eleven metres apart on the grass at Passeio Alegre, and neither is much taller than a house. Seven metres of height, trunks 3.15 and 2.62 metres round, crowns averaging nearly 13 metres. They are wider than they are tall, and that shape is the whole point.

Metrosideros excelsa grows on sea cliffs at home in New Zealand, anchored in rock and salt wind, and the mouth of the Douro is the closest thing Porto has to that. Aerial roots hang off the older limbs. The bark is grey and fibrous. Nothing about the tree says ornamental until late spring, when the crowns go red with stamens rather than petals, thousands at once.

The two were classified together in 2005 as isolated specimens, which is exactly how they stand: out on the open lawn rather than in the promenade's tree lines. The register recorded both at 70 years when it measured in 2004, so roughly 90 now, and the city's own environment service puts them at over 80, which agrees.

Passeio Alegre is the long formal garden at the Foz end of the waterfront, laid out in the 19th century as the place Porto came to walk on a Sunday. It is still doing that job, and these two have watched every version of it.

trees.name: The Seven Fan Palms of Palácio de Cristal
trees.access: Free, public garden, one of Porto's most visited green spaces
trees.transport: Central Porto; several STCP bus routes and a short walk from Casa da Música metro station
trees.story:
The building these palms were planted for was demolished in 1951. The palms are still standing.

Seven Mexican fan palms line the Avenida das Tílias in the gardens of the Palácio de Cristal, and they date to the planting that went in around the international exhibition of 1865, the event the crystal palace itself was built for. That building came down after eighty-six years and was replaced by the domed pavilion sitting there now. The palms carried on and reach almost 25 metres.

Washingtonia robusta is from northwest Mexico and puts up a slender grey trunk far faster than most palms, topped with a crown of stiff fan-shaped leaves that clatter in wind. Seven of them in a line, all the same age, is an unusual survival. Palms at that height tend to go in storms or in redevelopment, and these have sat through both.

They were classified in 2019. The register carries the classification and an age of 150 years at its 2015 measurement, roughly 160 now, which matches the exhibition-era planting. It carries no measurements at all for this entry, so the heights here come from an independent account of the gardens rather than from the state.

The gardens are free and busy, and the peacocks have the run of them.

trees.name: The Magnolias of Jardim de Arca d'Água
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden with playground, lake and bandstand
trees.transport: Paranhos, close to the Asprela / hospital and university cluster; served by Porto metro Line D and STCP buses

best_time.label: huge fragrant white blooms, up to 30cm across, open through May and June

trees.story:
This garden holds 96 plane trees, 57 camellias and 13 southern magnolias, and only the magnolias are protected. The set was classified in 2021, which means the state looked at everything growing in the Jardim de Arca d'Água and singled out the smallest group in it.

Finding them takes a minute of looking. The garden covers 22,000 square metres and the register gives one coordinate standing in for all thirteen, so the pin here points at the garden rather than at the trees. They are not hard to pick out once you are inside. Magnolia grandiflora has thick dark leaves with a rust-brown felt on the underside, quite unlike the planes and the camellias around them, and in early summer the flowers are the size of a plate.

No age is recorded for them. The register gives one representative trunk at 2.43 metres round and leaves the rest blank, so the honest answer is that nobody has dated these trees.

The garden opened in 1928 in Paranhos, on ground named for its arca de água, the stone chamber where a spring is captured and held. The springs here supplied Porto with water for centuries before anyone thought to lay a bandstand and a playground over them.

trees.name: The Alameda dos Plátanos of Jardim da Cordoaria
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden, open daily
trees.transport: Central Porto, adjacent to the Faculty of Law; roughly 10 minutes on foot from São Bento station
trees.story:
The state protected this one as a tunnel rather than as thirty-seven trees. The Alameda dos Plátanos runs through the Jardim da Cordoaria in central Porto, its plane trees trained until the crowns closed overhead, and the classification of 2005 treats the whole avenue as one thing of public interest.

That is the right reading. Walked separately these are ordinary London planes, 19 metres tall, carrying the flaking camouflage bark the species is known for. Walked together they make a green corridor with the light coming through in patches, which is why the avenue turns up in photographs of Porto far more often than any single tree in the garden.

The register measured in 2004 and recorded 140 years, putting the avenue near 160 now. An independent survey of Porto's classified trees calls it more than 150 years old and gives the same 19 metre height, so the two figures agree.

The garden was a rope walk before it was a garden, a long open strip where cordage was laid out and twisted, which is where the name Cordoaria comes from and why the space still runs in long lines. Stand in the tunnel and look up at the far end. The dark dome breaking the roofline is the bunya pine, classified in the same decree on the same day.

trees.name: The Tulip Trees of Praça Pedro Nunes
trees.neighbourhood: Cedofeita, Santo Ildefonso, Sé, Miragaia, São Nicolau e Vitória
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Central Porto, near the Faculty of Engineering / Rivoli area, walkable from Trindade and Bolhão metro stations

best_time.label: clear yellow, one of the most reliable autumn trees

trees.story:
Praça Pedro Nunes is small enough to cross in twenty seconds and holds four tulip trees, each about 22 metres tall. They were classified together as one group in 2005, standing beside the former Liceu D. Manuel II, and generations of pupils came out of that building into their shade.

Liriodendron tulipifera is worth identifying from the pavement. The leaf looks as though someone cut the tip off with scissors, four lobes and a flat top, unlike anything else growing on a Porto square. The flowers are genuinely tulip-shaped, greenish yellow with an orange band, and genuinely hard to see, because they open high in the crown in early summer and face upward.

The register measured in 2004: trunks 3.6 metres round, 22 metres tall, crowns 17 metres across, and an age of 80, which puts the group near 100 now.

One thing to know before going. The register and a 2005 survey of Porto's classified trees are the only records of this group, and no recent article or dated photograph confirms that all four are still there. Four large trees in a central square are unlikely to have gone quietly, but the last written confirmation is twenty years old, and anyone standing in the square can settle it faster than any archive.

trees.name: The Elephant's-Foot Plane Avenue of the Cordoaria
trees.age: about 160 years, planted around 1866 when the garden was laid out
trees.access: Free, public garden (Jardim da Cordoaria, also called Jardim de Joao Chagas), triangular and unfenced, open at all hours.
trees.transport: Central Porto, about a 5-10 minute walk from Sao Bento railway station.
trees.story:
Thirty-seven plane trees line one avenue in the Jardim da Cordoaria, and every one of them has the same strange deformity: a disease swelled their bases into something that looks, unmistakably, like an elephant's foot. The trees are perfectly healthy. Portugal's monumental tree register classifies the whole avenue as one entry, the Alameda dos Platanos, rather than splitting it into 37 separate trunks, because that is how a visitor actually experiences it: one long, uniform, oddly-footed colonnade.

The garden itself predates the plane trees by centuries in name only. Rope-makers worked this ground for two hundred years, which is where Cordoaria comes from, until the council cleared them out in the 1860s and hired the landscape architect Emile David, who also laid out the gardens of the nearby Palacio de Cristal, to build a proper garden in their place. The planes went in around 1866. A cyclone tore through in 1941 and reshaped the garden's canopy, but the avenue survived it and was formally classified a tree of public interest in 2005.

The garden is triangular, unfenced and free, a short walk from Sao Bento station. Walk the length of the avenue once and every trunk repeats the same swollen, elephantine base.

trees.name: The Bunya-Bunya of the Cordoaria
trees.access: Free, public garden (Jardim da Cordoaria, also called Jardim de Joao Chagas), triangular and unfenced, open at all hours.
trees.transport: Central Porto, about a 5-10 minute walk from Sao Bento railway station.
trees.story:
At 40 metres this bunya pine is the tallest tree in the Jardim da Cordoaria and one of the tallest anywhere in Porto, a conifer from Queensland's rainforests standing beside a Cedar of Lebanon and a Cedar of Atlas at the garden's lake, close enough together that a local tree-walking group uses the three of them to teach visitors how to tell the different conifers apart.

Araucaria bidwillii belongs to a genus that once grew across the ancient supercontinent Gondwana and now survives as a handful of species scattered from Australia to South America, most of them, like this one, planted deliberately as curiosities far from where they evolved. Portugal's monumental tree register measured this specimen at 3.6 metres round, 40 metres tall with a 12-metre crown, and classified it a tree of public interest in the same 2005 notice that protects the garden's plane tree avenue nearby.

It has stood in this triangular, unfenced garden for roughly a century and a half, since not long after the ground stopped being a rope-makers' yard and became a public park. Free to see at any hour, a short walk from Sao Bento station.

trees.name: The Linden of Park Jagdschloss Glienicke
trees.neighbourhood: Schlosspark Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge
trees.access: Free, open to the public year-round. Stands in Park Jagdschloss Glienicke, the open parkland around the hunting lodge, not the fenced institute garden behind the building itself
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then a short walk into the park

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: Two hundred metres from this lime tree is the bridge where the Cold War traded people. Glienicker Brücke carried the spy exchanges between the Americans and the Soviets, and the border ran down the middle of the water beneath it. The tree stands on the eastern bank, which is to say in Berlin, though it is a twelve-minute tram ride from Potsdam's main station and a long way from anything a Berliner thinks of as the city. It is a small-leaved lime, a Winter-Linde, protected by the Land of Berlin as a natural monument under the number 6-99/B, standing in the open parkland of Park Jagdschloss Glienicke around the old hunting lodge. What that protection does not come with is information. The register gives a species, a parcel number and a place, and records no age, no girth and no note on the tree's condition, because it is a legal instrument rather than a survey. So this entry is thinner than most here, and it says so. One official source names the tree and nothing else we could find does. What that source does establish is the thing worth walking for: somebody looked at this particular lime, among all the trees in a large park, and decided it was not to be cut down.

trees.name: The King's Linden
trees.neighbourhood: Schlosspark Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge
trees.access: Free, open to the public year-round, no gate, no hours and no admission. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then a short walk into the Schlossgarten

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime blossom opens and the scent carries across the lawn

trees.story: People took tea under this lime, and the floor they did it on is still there. A mosaic pavement near the Lions Fountain in the Schlossgarten marks the spot where visitors to Prince Carl of Prussia's estate sat beneath the tree, and the park's own account calls it one of the most impressive solitary trees on the estate. Berlin's register of natural monuments agrees in its own dry way. It gives the tree a number, 6-100/B, and a name, Königslinde, the King's Linden, which is unusual in a document that mostly records species and parcel numbers and then stops. The garden around it was laid out from 1816 by Peter Joseph Lenné for Prince Carl, an English landscape of long sightlines on a Prussian riverbank, and it is now part of the UNESCO World Heritage site covering the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin. It is open, free, and has no gate. Neither the register nor the park's history gives this lime an age or a girth, so it gets neither here. It stands on Königstraße opposite the Wiesenteich pond, on the Berlin side of the Glienicke bridge, twelve minutes from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof on the 93 tram, and it is the tree on this walk that people actually sat under.

trees.name: The Schlosspark Glienicke Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Schlosspark Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge
trees.access: Free, open to the public year-round, the same parkland as the two limes, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then a walk of a few minutes further into the park than the lime trees

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Berlin protects this oak by law and almost nothing else about it is on record. It appears in the Land of Berlin's register of natural monuments as 6-105/B, a Stiel-Eiche, a Pedunculate Oak, standing about 150 metres north of Königstraße 35C in Schlosspark Glienicke. That entry gives a species, a parcel and a position, and there it ends: no age, no girth, no word on the tree's condition, because the register exists to say what may not be felled rather than to describe what is there. So this is a tree you go and read for yourself. It grows in the landscape garden Peter Joseph Lenné began laying out in 1816 for Prince Carl of Prussia, a park of engineered views designed to look accidental, now inside the UNESCO World Heritage site that covers the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin. Oaks are the long-lived furniture of gardens like this one, and often older than the design around them. The one fact the register does carry says something a tape measure would not: out of the thousands of trees standing in this parkland, somebody walked up to this one and wrote it down. It is a few minutes further into the park than the two protected limes. If you get a tape round it, we would like the number.

trees.name: The Jägerhof Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Volkspark Klein-Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge
trees.access: Free, open to the public. Volkspark Klein-Glienicke was opened to the public in the 1930s when Berlin acquired the estate; the Jägerhof and the ground around it are publicly accessible, high above the Havel-side path near the Krughorn
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then roughly a 15-20 minute walk south along the park path to the Jägerhof

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are down and the whole frame of the old crown shows

trees.story: The oak was here first. The Jägerhof in Volkspark Klein-Glienicke went up some time before 1830, and by the reckoning of the German veteran-tree archive that measured this tree, it was already more than a hundred years old when the builders arrived. That puts its beginning before roughly 1730, which makes 300 years a fair estimate and not a precise one. Nobody has cored it, and Berlin's register of natural monuments, which protects it as 6-73/B, has no age field to put a figure in. The girth is firmer: 566 centimetres at chest height, taped in 2023. Nearly six metres of trunk, and by a wide margin the heaviest tree on this walk. It stands high above the Havel path near the Krughorn headland, south along the park from the Glienicke bridge and about fifteen to twenty minutes on foot from the other three trees here. Berlin bought the estate in the 1930s and opened it to the public, so the ground under this oak has been walkable for the better part of a century. Before that it was hunting country, which is what a Jägerhof is for. The lodge was built for the sport. The oak was simply standing in the way of it, and outlived the whole arrangement.

trees.name: The Hejnowicz Plane
trees.access: Free, on the open public square at all hours
trees.transport: Fredry tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk
trees.story: Before Poznan gave these four planes legal protection, it listened to them. The city's climate and environment department commissioned a dendrological survey that included acoustic tomography, sound pushed through the trunk to map solid wood from rot, and all four came back in good to very good condition with a low risk of dropping limbs. On 16 May 2023 the council made them pomniki przyrody, natural monuments, at the request of the Stare Miasto district council, and gave each one a name instead of a number. This is the Hejnowicz Plane, for Professor Alina Hejnowicz. It stands at the eastern end of the group, roughly thirty metres from its nearest neighbour, and belongs to a set measured at between twenty and twenty-three and a half metres tall. They went into the ground at the start of the twentieth century, which puts their planting close to the moment the square itself changed identity: Prussian Wilhelmsplatz until 1918, Plac Wolnosci, Freedom Square, ever since. Neither the national register nor the city's announcement gives a girth for any of the four, so none is published here. The register entry was formalised on 9 June 2023, three weeks after the vote.

trees.name: The Stecki Plane
trees.access: Free, on the open public square at all hours
trees.transport: Fredry tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk
trees.story: This tree carries a professor's name because a district council asked for it. In May 2023 the Stare Miasto district put in a request, and the city council designated four London planes on Plac Wolnosci as natural monuments, attaching to each the name of a botanist or plant sociologist who had worked in Poznan. This one is Konstanty Stecki's. It stands at the north-west corner of the group, about thirty metres west of the Hejnowicz Plane and roughly the same distance north of the close pair on the southern side. The square around it is one of the more consequential rectangles in Polish history. The Bazar hotel at its northern end is where Ignacy Jan Paderewski spoke from a window on 26 December 1918, the evening the Greater Poland Uprising began, and the colonnade of the Raczynski Library has faced the same square since 1829. Whether this plane was already standing for Paderewski's speech is not something anyone has written down: the city dates the four only to the start of the twentieth century, which straddles the year. What is recorded is its health, checked by acoustic tomography before designation and found good to very good.

trees.name: The Paczoski Plane
trees.access: Free, on the open public square at all hours
trees.transport: Fredry tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk
trees.story: One of the four protected planes on Plac Wolnosci is named after the man who coined the word phytosociology. Jozef Paczoski, born 1864, argued that plants should be studied as societies rather than as individual specimens, gave that idea its name in the 1890s, and spent his later career teaching in Poznan. The city attached his name to this tree on 16 May 2023, when the council designated all four planes on the square as natural monuments at the district council's request. It is the eastern of the two that stand six metres apart on the southern side of the square, which is close enough that a visitor needs to know which is which. The four went in at the start of the twentieth century and stand between twenty and twenty-three and a half metres tall. Before protecting them the city had them surveyed with acoustic tomography, which reads the density of wood inside a living trunk without opening it, and all four came back sound with a low risk of failure. Poland's national register records the designation, the species and the position, and carries no field for girth or age, so neither is published here.

trees.name: The Kulesza Plane
trees.access: Free, on the open public square at all hours
trees.transport: Fredry tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk
trees.story: Plac Wolnosci has four legally protected trees and all four are the same species. They are London planes, the tree European cities reach for when the ground is paved, the air is exhaust and the roots have nowhere generous to go. Rather than number them, Poznan gave each a name: this is the Kulesza Plane, for Professor Witold Kulesza, designated with the other three on 16 May 2023 and entered in the national register three weeks later. It is the western of the pair that stand six metres apart along the southern side, the closest two of the group. The square it stands on runs as a long open rectangle between the Bazar hotel and the neoclassical front of the Raczynski Library, and it has been the city's ceremonial ground under two states and three names. The trees arrived at the start of the twentieth century, when the paving and the traffic around them were both lighter. Their condition is documented rather than assumed: the city commissioned a dendrological survey with acoustic tomography before the vote, and the four were found in good to very good health with a low risk of breakage.

trees.name: The Abakanowicz Plane
trees.neighbourhood: Centrum Kultury Zamek grounds, central Poznan
trees.access: Free; the Zamek cultural centre's halls, corridors and courtyards are open daily 9:00-22:00, though the Rose Courtyard's exact availability can depend on the centre's own programming
trees.transport: Zamek tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk
trees.story: This plane was already about seventy years old when the Kaiser's builders turned up next door. Poznan puts its age at roughly 190 years and its trunk at 411 centimetres round, the figures published when the council made it a natural monument on 16 April 2024. Wilhelm II's residence, the vast castle now running as the Zamek cultural centre, went up between 1905 and 1910, on ground where this tree was already mature. It stands in the Dziedziniec Rozany, the Rose Courtyard, tucked between the castle and the Arsenal building, which is not where anyone expects to find the oldest and thickest tree on a city's list. The name it carries is Magdalena Abakanowicz's, the sculptor who was for decades a professor in Poznan and whose crowd of headless iron figures stands in the park across the river. The courtyard is part of a building open daily from nine in the morning until ten at night, though the Zamek's own programme occasionally takes the space, so this is the one tree here you might have to come back for. Poland's national register confirms the species and the spot; the age and the girth are the city's own.

trees.name: The Zakrzewski Silver Maple
trees.access: Free, on the open public square at all hours
trees.transport: Central Poznan, short walk from Plac Wolnosci / the Old Market Square
trees.story: This is not a Polish tree. Acer saccharinum grows wild in the river bottoms of eastern North America, where it takes the spring floods that kill other species, and it reached European parks as an ornamental fast-grower with a habit of shedding limbs in storms. Poznan's finest example holds 271 centimetres of girth at about 105 years old, which is quick work, and the city made it a natural monument on 16 April 2024, naming it for Professor Zbigniew Zakrzewski. It stands on the Skwer Zielone Ogrodki, the strip of small green squares laid out where Zielona meets Strzelecka, a few minutes from the Old Market Square and free at any hour. The species gives itself away in wind: the leaves are cut into deep, narrow lobes and the undersides are almost white, so a gust turns the whole crown pale for a second and then back again. The press covering the designation called it an exceptionally fine specimen of its kind, which for a silver maple in a Polish city centre is a real compliment: most of them are planted, admired for a few decades and then quietly removed after the first bad storm.

trees.name: The Citadel Defenders' Oak
trees.access: Free, inside Cytadela Park, a large public park open during daylight hours; no gate or permission needed
trees.transport: Winogrady tram stop (lines 3, 4, 10), at the western edge of the park

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Cytadela Park sits on the ruins of a Prussian fortress that became, in February 1945, one of the last and bloodiest German strongholds of the war on this front. Soviet and Polish forces spent nearly a month reducing Fort Winiary before its garrison surrendered, and the city named this oak for the civilians who fought alongside the soldiers: the Citadel Defenders. The council made it a natural monument on 1 April 2021.

The tree itself is unremarkable in the way that matters most: quietly sound. A 2020 tomographic scan, sound pushed through the trunk to map density and rot, found the interior clean, no decay behind 325 centimetres of bark. It stands 30 metres tall with a regular crown, in the park's western section near ul. Za Cytadela.

It is one of only two natural-monument oaks inside Cytadela Park. The other, the Chuikov Oak, stands about 800 metres away, named for the Soviet general who commanded the assault this tree's own name commemorates from the other side. Age here is an estimate, put at 130 to 155 years by the arborists who examined it before designation, old enough to have stood through both the battle and the decades of silence that followed it.

trees.name: The Chuikov Oak
trees.access: Free, inside Cytadela Park, a large public park open during daylight hours, near the park's Garrison Cemetery
trees.transport: Winogrady tram stop (lines 3, 4, 10)

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
This oak split itself into a small crowd. At 170 centimetres up, the trunk divides into two parallel stems, and one of those splits again higher still, a rare growth habit that leaves three separate crowns rising from a single 421-centimetre base. It has stood near the Citadel's Garrison Cemetery since around 1840, by the register's estimate, making it the oldest protected tree inside the park by a wide margin.

Poznan named it for Vasily Chuikov, the Soviet general who commanded the 8th Guards Army during the brutal February 1945 battle for the fortress, an unusual honour to find growing in a Polish city park. The oak predates the battle by more than a century and the general's own role in it by longer still; it was already mature when the fort it now shades was an active Prussian stronghold.

Designated a natural monument on 10 June 1979, this is the oldest protection of any tree on this page, decades before Poland's newer wave of monumental-tree designations. Arborists describe it in good health, with only minor dead branches. It stands about 800 metres from the Citadel Defenders' Oak, named for the men who fought against the army this tree's own name honours, close enough to walk both on one visit to the park.

trees.name: The Chrzanowski Plane
trees.access: Free, inside Park Wilsona, a large public park with the Palmiarnia Poznanska palm house, open at all hours
trees.transport: Park Wilsona tram stop (lines 5, 8, 14), directly opposite the park's main gate
trees.story:
Four hundred and eighty four centimetres of trunk for a tree the city puts at only about a hundred years old is a startling ratio, thick enough to raise a real question about whether the age is right. Poznan's own estimate is the only one on record, so the figure stands here flagged rather than treated as settled.

The plane grows in Park Wilsona, home to the Palmiarnia, one of Europe's larger palm houses, and carries the name of Bernard Chrzanowski, a lawyer, independence activist and pioneer of Poland's hiking and tourist-trail movement who died in 1944. The council designated it a natural monument in spring 2025, alongside a ginkgo named for a different Poznan botanist elsewhere in the same park.

Whatever explains the girth, the tree needs no defending on its own terms: a London plane this size, in a park built around a landmark greenhouse, is a destination in its own right. It stands free to reach at any hour, directly opposite the Park Wilsona tram stop, no gate between the street and the trunk.

trees.name: Krzysztof the Oak
trees.access: Free. Stands on a fenced municipal playground run by Poznan's Municipal Greenery Authority, open during normal playground hours; the fence is a standard child-safety fence around a public, city-managed playground, not a locked or ticketed site, and it borders but is not part of a neighbouring Alzheimer's association building
trees.transport: Wilda district, corner of ul. Pradzynskiego and ul. Garczynskiego; nearest tram/bus stop not confirmed

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Poznan's oldest protected tree on this page stands inside a playground fence, which is not where you would expect to find a tree the city dates to as much as three centuries old. The oak took its name, Krzysztof, from Anna Siwczyk, a local artist who helped restore the square around it before her death in 2010, and the name has stuck deeply enough that in 2023 the city's greenery authority grew a batch of seedlings from its acorns and nicknamed them the Krzysztofy.

Trunk circumference runs to 375 centimetres, and an arborist's report at designation put its age between 250 and 300 years and assessed it in very good health with full mechanical resistance, a formal way of saying the wood inside is sound. The council made it a natural monument in late 2017 or early 2018, depending on whether the date used is the register's or the city's own announcement of the vote.

The fence around it belongs to the playground it stands in, run by Poznan's Municipal Greenery Authority and open during ordinary hours, not a barrier put up to keep visitors out. It borders a building used by a local Alzheimer's association, but the ground itself is public, in the Wilda district, a genuine enclave of old growth in one of the city's more built-up corners.

trees.name: The Beethoven Plane
trees.access: Free; the tree towers above the public Grand Priory Garden wall on Velkoprevorske namesti and is visible from the square by the Lennon Wall at all times. The garden itself, used by the Artiseme design gallery, may keep separate hours to enter directly.
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Malostranska tram and metro stop, via the Lennon Wall on Velkoprevorske namesti
trees.story: The thickest protected tree in Prague has a trunk seven and a half metres around, and its most famous story is almost certainly false. Local guides say Ludwig van Beethoven rested beneath this plane during his 1796 visit to Prague, dreaming of a 19 year old countess while lodging at the nearby Golden Unicorn inn. He was in the city in February. Prague historians point out that picturing a composer dreamily sitting under a bare tree in midwinter is more charming than credible. What is verified is the trunk itself: 752 centimetres around as of 2013, up from 670 in 1996. It grows in the garden of the Grand Priory Palace on Velkoprevorske namesti, towering over the wall that has carried John Lennon graffiti since the 1980s, tall enough that most people photographing the Lennon Wall never look up to notice the tree that shades it. Its exact age is disputed: the Order of Malta's own legend claims the 12th century, which is botanically impossible since this hybrid plane did not exist before 1700, while official records put the planting between 1725 and around 1810. Either way it is very likely the oldest plane tree, and the most massive protected tree of any species, in Prague.

trees.name: The Plane of Karlovo namesti
trees.access: Free, public park (Park na Karlove namesti), open at all times
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Karlovo namesti metro station (Line B)
trees.story: Prague's most photographed memorial tree earned an unprintable nickname for the shape of one branch. The plane at Karlovo namesti sends a limb down toward the ground before it curls back upward, a silhouette locals have joked about for decades. Planted before the square was landscaped into a public park in 1876, the tree is Prague's most recognisable protected tree, with a trunk measured at nearly eight metres around in 2004 and a crown that spreads across the western half of the park. It has not had an easy two centuries. Restorers opened and cleaned a large cavity in its trunk in 1985, propped up the low branch responsible for its nickname, and in 2013 ringed the whole tree in a fence after years of visitors climbing on the very limb they came to look at. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 7 October 1998 for its growth, age and value as a specimen. Estimates for its exact age disagree, ranging from about 160 to 190 years depending on the source, which would put its planting somewhere between the early 1800s and the 1860s. Nobody has found a planting record to settle it.

trees.name: The Plane of Kinsky Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden (Kinskeho zahrada), open daily
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Svandovo divadlo tram stop, entrance from Kinskeho namesti
trees.story: The largest tree on all of Petrin hill also lost its own sculpture to theft. In 1928 the sculptor Karel Dvorak placed a statue called The Fourteen Year Old at the foot of this plane in Kinsky Garden, and at some point in the following decades it disappeared. It now sits in a Prague City Museum storeroom, with a replacement reportedly still planned. The tree itself needed no help to become a landmark: at 28 metres tall with a trunk 546 centimetres around, it is visibly larger than anything else growing across the whole of Petrin, a hill covered in parks. It was planted during the first phase of the garden's construction, which ran until 1836, under a design by the Viennese architect Heinrich Koch for the Kinsky family, and Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 30 July 1998 for its growth, age and dendrological value. In 2004 it was one of thirteen Prague trees chosen for a genetic preservation programme that collects material from the city's oldest specimens before disease or storms can take them. For now it still shades the lower, flatter part of the garden nearest the entrance from Kinskeho namesti, exactly where it has stood for close to two centuries.

trees.name: The Plane of Kampa
trees.access: Free, public park (Kampa Park), open at all times
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Malostranska tram and metro stop, via the steps down to Kampa near Charles Bridge
trees.story: A countess planted this tree in 1813 to dress up her family's riverside garden with something exotic, and it has outgrown every other reason anyone remembers her. Barbora Kolowratova Krakovska had the grounds beside the Vltava planted with foreign flowers and trees that year, and this plane is the clearest survivor of her garden, now absorbed into Kampa Park. It reaches 35 metres, taller than most buildings on the island, with a trunk 504 centimetres around, and it anchors the northern end of the park right where visitors enter from beside the Liechtenstein Palace. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 8 October 1998. Its exact planting date is one of the more solid facts on this list. Most of Prague's old plane trees carry an estimated age with a decade or two of margin either side; this one has a year, because someone wrote it down at the time. Kampa itself was still gardens and orchards when the tree went in, well over a century before the 1947 to 1948 landscaping that turned the island into the public park it is today, which means the tree predates the park built around it by more than a hundred years.

trees.name: The Twin Beech of Hvezda
trees.access: Free, public nature reserve (Obora Hvezda)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Obora Hvezda or Vypich tram and bus stops

best_time.label: late October, when the canopy of Central Europe's tallest tree on this list turns copper

trees.story: One of the two tallest trees on this page stands on a 17th century battlefield and splits into two trunks a few feet off the ground, which is why it is simply named Twin Beech. At 45 metres it beats every other tree here for height by a wide margin, in the Star Game Reserve on Prague's western edge, where the armies of the Bohemian Revolt collided with the Habsburgs in 1620. The beech itself came generations later, planted sometime after 1763, when the reserve was restored and replanted with beeches, oaks and hornbeams following decades of neglect. Its trunk, 508 centimetres around where it forks, now carries a binding to keep the two main stems from splitting apart under their own weight, and a wooden fence around its base, installed after years of visitors carving initials and hearts into the bark. Prague declared it a protected natural monument on 22 August 2001. It stands about 170 metres from the reserve's Brevnov Gate, in sight of the star shaped Renaissance hunting lodge the whole park is named for, a building that has watched over this beech's entire two and a half centuries of growth without ageing anywhere near as gracefully itself.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Stromovka
trees.access: Free, public park (Stromovka / Kralovska obora)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Vystaviste tram stop, within Stromovka park near the Governor's Summer House

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold and drop within days

trees.story: Two very different ages have been written down for this tree, 80 years apart, and nobody has reconciled them. One record dates its planting to around 1804, from the earliest landscaping of the royal nursery here under the gardener Fuchs. A separate 2016 assessment put its age at only around 130 years. Both figures come from people who study this specific tree, and the gap between them is wide enough that this page states the honest range rather than pick a side: somewhere between 140 and 220 years old. What is not in dispute is the tree itself, a male ginkgo with a trunk 362 centimetres around and a crown 16 metres wide, growing near the old Mistodrzitelsky letohradek, the former Governor's Summer House, in a corner of Stromovka that used to be a nursery bed. Ginkgos are sometimes called living fossils because the species has barely changed in over 200 million years, and this one is among the oldest specimens in the Czech Republic regardless of which age estimate is correct. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree in 2004. Every November its fan shaped leaves turn a single uniform gold and drop within days, the trick every ginkgo performs.

trees.name: The Oak of Cisarsky ostrov
trees.access: Free, public riverside path on Cisarsky ostrov
trees.transport: Bus 112 to the Kovarna stop, then a short walk along the island embankment; or cross the footbridge from Stromovka

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Prague's very first legally protected oak grows on an island that used to flood every spring until imperial engineers tamed it. Cisarsky ostrov, Emperor's Island, took its name from Habsburg era work to control the Vltava, and this pedunculate oak has stood on its embankment road since sometime in the early 1800s, watching barges pass on the navigation canal beside it rather than the river itself. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 26 October 1994, the first oak in the city to receive that status, ahead of every other oak now on this list. Its trunk splits into branches unusually low, at just a metre and a half up, and the crown that results spreads wider than the tree is tall, a shape typical of an oak that grew alone in open ground rather than crowded by a forest. A 2013 measurement put the girth at 457 centimetres, and the tree is estimated at around 190 to 200 years old, above average for its age and size according to the city's own survey. It stands about 200 metres from the footbridge that connects the island to Stromovka, on a quiet embankment road most visitors to the park next door never think to cross.

trees.name: The Ash of Strahov Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden (Velka strahovska zahrada), the only part of the Strahov Monastery grounds open to visitors
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Pohorelec tram stop (lines 22, 23)
trees.story: The tallest single trunk on this page grows in the one corner of Strahov Monastery the monks decided to share. This ash reaches 37 metres in the Great Strahov Garden, the only part of the monastery complex left open to the public; the rest remains cloistered grounds. It began as an orchard tree in a working fruit garden, planted around the turn of the 19th century, long before anyone thought to protect it. Its trunk splits into three thick limbs about two metres above the ground and keeps climbing, measuring 513 centimetres around at the split as of a 2013 survey, a girth that puts it among the most massive ash trees recorded anywhere in the Czech Republic. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 13 October 2007. From the garden beneath it, visitors get one of the better free views in the city, Prague Castle and the rooftops of Mala Strana laid out below the hill, a vista the tree has been growing tall enough to share in for two centuries. At an estimated 210 to 230 years old, it was already well established when the garden's monastic orchard still supplied the friars with fruit rather than a footpath for tourists.

trees.name: The Field Maple of the Seminary Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden (Seminarska zahrada)
trees.transport: 3 min walk from the Nebozizek funicular stop
trees.story: Field maples are usually shrubs. Left alone, most stay a scrubby hedge tree, rarely climbing past a few metres. This one, in the Seminary Garden on Petrin's eastern slope, ignored the script and grew into a proper 24 metre tree, the only field maple in Prague to earn individual legal protection because of it. Its trunk measured 285 centimetres around in a 2013 survey, thick for a species whose Czech name, babyka, is usually attached to something closer to a bush. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 19 June 2009, and it stands above a small pond just below the Petrinske Terasy restaurant, roughly 250 metres north of the Nebozizek cable car stop, a stretch of the garden slightly off the paths most visitors to Petrin actually walk. At an estimated 160 to 170 years old, it has had more than enough time to prove it is the exception rather than the rule for its species. People who study field maples cite examples like this one as evidence the plant's usual shrub form is a matter of circumstance, not biology. Give it room, apparently, and a field maple will eventually decide to become a tree instead.

trees.name: Neruda's Pear Tree
trees.access: Free, public garden (Seminarska zahrada), open since 1930
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Hellichova tram stop (lines 12, 20, 22), via the Seminary Garden entrance

best_time.label: April, when it fills with white blossom before the leaves are fully out

trees.story: This pear tree remembers a poet's birthplace that no longer exists. Jan Neruda, the 19th century writer whose name now marks Prague's most photographed street on the other side of the hill, was born in an army barracks that once stood near this spot on the eastern slope of Petrin; the barracks are long demolished, but the pear tree that stood nearby when he was a boy is still bearing fruit. Prague's tree survey estimates its age at around 190 years, measured a trunk 292 centimetres around in 2015, and calls it exceptionally old for its species, since wild pears rarely reach anywhere close to two centuries. Unlike most trees on this list, it carries no formal legal protection; the city added it to its inventory of significant trees only in 2013, one tier below the memorial tree status that comes with fines for damaging a tree. It grows at a quiet path crossing in the Seminary Garden, in the lower orchard section between the Petrinske Terasy restaurant and Hellichova street, a former monastery garden open to the public since 1930. Most visitors climbing Petrin for the views pass within a few metres of it without knowing an old pear tree, let alone one tied to Neruda, is there at all.

trees.name: The Oak of Dienzenhofer Gardens
trees.access: Free, public park (Dienzenhoferovy sady), open at all times
trees.transport: 2 min walk from the Zborovska tram stop (lines 4, 5, 12, 15, 20), at the Jirasek Bridge end of the gardens

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: The street on the far side of this oak is called V Botanice, In the Botanical Garden, and there is no botanical garden. Prague's tree register calls the oak the only living reminder of the one that used to be here, which makes a 160 year old tree the last exhibit of a collection nobody can visit. It stands at the northeastern corner of Dienzenhoferovy sady, a riverside strip of grass named after Kilian Ignac Dientzenhofer, the Baroque architect who put a pavilion on this ground in 1735. Traffic now runs on three sides of it, feeding the Jirasek Bridge, and the tree has answered the way open grown oaks do, by pushing its lowest limbs sideways instead of up until the crown measured 23 metres across in 2009 against a height of only 20. Its trunk has thickened from 350 centimetres in 2004 to 393 in 2017, which is a tree still laying on wood rather than holding station. Prague protected it on 17 February 2005. Surveyors keep recording its condition as very good, which for an oak marooned on a traffic island in a European capital is a small piece of luck.

trees.name: The Red Oak of Shooters' Island
trees.access: Free, public park on the island, reached by the staircase and lift from Most Legii or the ramp from the Smichov bank
trees.transport: 3 min from the Narodni divadlo tram stop (lines 2, 9, 17, 18, 22), then the stairs down from Most Legii

best_time.label: late October, when it goes scarlet weeks after the embankment limes have finished

trees.story: An American tree turns the best colour in central Prague, on an island where Bohemian archers used to practise. Strelecky ostrov, Shooters' Island, is named for the crossbow and longbow ranges that operated on it from the reign of Charles IV, and its northern half is now a lawn under big trees with the Vltava running past on both sides. The red oak in the middle of that half arrived from North America by way of the European nursery trade, and at 352 centimetres around it is the largest oak on the island and, by the city's own reckoning, the largest red oak in the centre of Prague. It was added to the register of significant trees in 2013 at an estimated 125 years, which places its planting close to the landscaping that converted a shooting ground into a public park. Red oaks do one thing better than any native Czech tree and they do it late: the leaves go scarlet and then deep rust through the second half of October, long after the limes on the embankment have given up. Thousands of people cross Most Legii directly above this tree every day. The staircase down to it is on the bridge itself.

trees.name: The Bonsai Ginkgo of Na Slupi
trees.access: Free, the outdoor garden of the university botanical garden is open daily with seasonal closing times; the greenhouses beside the tree are ticketed, the tree itself is not
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Botanicka zahrada tram stop (lines 6, 18, 24), or 10 min south from Karlovo namesti metro (Line B)

best_time.label: mid-November, when the low spreading crown goes yellow and lays a circle of leaves on the grass

trees.story: A tree five metres tall with the trunk of one twice that height has been interfered with. The ginkgo by the greenhouse door in the Charles University botanical garden measures about 343 centimetres around at chest height and goes almost nowhere upward, spreading and drooping instead, and the accepted explanation is that somebody grew it in a barrel and pruned it like a bonsai for years before it was ever put in the ground. It carries its own cultivar name, 'Praga', probably descended from the weeping 'Pendula'. It went in around 1860 to 1870, which means it was standing here before the garden was laid out around it. Czech readers may know its outline without knowing the tree, because a ginkgo leaf is the emblem of Jaroslav Foglar's 1965 novel Stinadla se bouri and this specimen is the one usually credited with the idea, though the older ginkgo in Riegrovy sady has a claim too and Foglar never settled it. Prague listed it as a significant tree in 2013. In November the whole low crown turns one flat yellow and lets go inside a week, which on a tree this wide leaves a ring of leaves on the grass rather than a drift.

trees.name: Masaryk's Lime
trees.access: Free, but only when the Upper Deer Moat is open, usually April to October, roughly 10:00 to 18:00. The viewpoint itself sits inside the castle security perimeter and has been closed for stretches under different presidents; since 2021 it is reachable only from the Upper Deer Moat and not from Klarov. Check the castle's opening notices before making the walk for this tree alone.
trees.transport: 8 min walk from the Brusnice tram stop (lines 22, 23), entering the Upper Deer Moat and climbing Plecnik's double staircase
trees.story: A president picked a tree, and an architect built a terrace around it. Tomas Garrigue Masaryk, installed at Prague Castle from 1918, took to sitting on a bare rise above the Deer Moat under a lime already more than a century old, so he set Josip Plecnik, the Slovene architect he had put in charge of remaking the castle, to make the spot worth sitting in. Between 1922 and 1924 Plecnik terraced the slope in stone, planted it with vines and left the lime standing at the centre of a three quarter circle platform. Masaryk's own bench did not survive. Two stone ones now flank the tree, which the castle's own account puts at over 200 years old. Then the place disappeared: from 1948 the entire moat was a guarded military zone, shut for four decades, and it was Vaclav Havel who had it opened again, with the viewpoint restored in 1996. The trunk is the one thing the sources will not agree on, 249 centimetres in one survey and 349 in another, a gap too wide to split. The view is not in dispute. The Archbishop's Palace and the cathedral line up below you, from a bench under a tree, which is what the whole thing was built for.

trees.name: The Elm of Ruzova Street
trees.access: Free, visible and approachable from the public pavement on Ruzova; the small garden the tree stands in belongs to the building and is fenced, so this is a tree you look up at from the street rather than walk around
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Hlavni nadrazi metro (Line C) or the Jindrisska tram stop (lines 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, 24)
trees.story: Most of Europe's big elms are dead, and this one is standing on a side street between Wenceslas Square and the main station. Dutch elm disease, a fungus carried between trees by bark beetles, went through the continent in two waves last century and removed elms so thoroughly that a mature one is now a curiosity rather than an ordinary sight. The elm at Ruzova 941/2 has lived through both waves and shows no sign of either. It is a European white elm, the species with lopsided leaves and papery seed discs that ripen in May, 23 metres tall with a trunk 335 centimetres around, growing on a scrap of ground that was a front garden before the block turned into offices and hotels. The crown fills the courtyard behind the railings and leans out over the pavement, which is where you stand to look at it. Prague gave it legal protection only on 15 April 2022, roughly 190 years into its life, having put a fence around its base the year before. Elms that shrug off the fungus are studied as possible parents for resistant stock, so this one may yet turn out to be useful as well as old.

trees.name: The Old Town's Only Oak
trees.access: Free, small public square open at all times
trees.transport: 4 min walk from the Dlouha trida tram stop (lines 6, 8, 15, 26), or 8 min from Namesti Republiky metro (Line B)

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: The Old Town has exactly one legally protected oak and it grows on a corner nobody photographs. Rasnovka is a scrap of a square in the north of the Old Town behind the Convent of Saint Agnes, with the early Gothic church of the Holy Saviour on one side and the functionalist offices of the city's road authority on the other. The oak stands between them, planted around 1850, when this quarter was still mills, timber yards and river trade rather than a conservation area. It is a pedunculate oak, the ordinary Czech oak of field boundaries and village greens, doing the unusual thing of reaching 19 metres in the middle of a city block, and its trunk has gone from 299 centimetres in 2010 to 321 in 2017. Prague protected it on 24 March 2001, and the last survey found no damage worth recording. It is about six centuries younger than the church beside it and eighty years older than the office block, which is a fair summary of what it is doing there: the one living thing on the square that watched both of its neighbours turn up.

trees.name: The Plane of Nove Mlyny
trees.access: Free, on a public street corner
trees.transport: Petrska ctvrt, Nove Mesto; tram 3, 8 or 24 to Prazska trznice or Revolucni, short walk
trees.story:
The London plane is an accident. It did not exist before the seventeenth century, when an oriental plane and an American one crossed somewhere in a European garden and produced a tree that turned out to be almost impossible to kill in a city.

That accident is why planes line so many European streets, and why one of them stands on the corner of Nové Mlýny and Klimentská, opposite the church of St Clement, in the quiet Petrská quarter a couple of streets back from the Vltava. Prague's register of protected trees measured its trunk at 342 centimetres in 2017, and it has been adding to that figure ever since, because planes grow quickly. The register's note claims nothing grander than what it is: a locally dominant tree, above the average of its kind in size and age, protected on that basis. No planting date has been published, and that single entry is the whole of the evidence.

Plane bark is why the species won the nineteenth century. It sheds in plates instead of thickening, carrying off a year of soot and grime with it, which kept planes alive in industrial cities that killed nearly everything else. The shedding leaves the familiar camouflage of cream, olive and grey, and it shows best in winter, when there is nothing on the branches to distract from it.

trees.name: The Great Plane of Palazzo Ducale
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north of Parma railway station
trees.story:
At 47 metres this plane is the tallest tree recorded anywhere in Emilia-Romagna, taller than any specimen in a region with no shortage of old parks and avenues. Its trunk measures 6.55 metres round, thick enough that it would take four adults linking arms to circle it.

It grows a short walk from Palazzo Ducale, the summer residence Duke Ottavio Farnese began building in 1561 at the head of a park he laid out the same year. Neither the palace nor its grounds had an easy eighteenth century: during the War of the Austrian Succession in 1745, occupying troops under Prince Lobkowicz felled and burned every mature tree in the park, including those on the ornamental island at its centre, to fuel their camp fires. Duke Filippo di Borbone had the grounds replanted from 1749 under the French architect Ennemond Alexandre Petitot, and further plane trees went in around 1830 under Duchess Maria Luigia, Napoleon's second wife, who governed Parma as her own duchy after his fall.

This plane's exact planting date is not recorded, but its size puts it among the park's oldest survivors. The park holds more than 1,500 catalogued trees today and opened to the public after Italian unification, when the ducal walls came down.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Piazza della Pace
trees.access: Free, open public square, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: About a 10 minute walk north-west of Parma railway station

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story:
Piazzale della Pace did not exist as a square until after the Second World War, laid out over ground reshaped by the bombing that damaged much of central Parma. What it holds today is an English-style lawn framed by remnants of a much older avenue: four large plane trees, survivors of a row that once counted 65, and this cedar of Lebanon, the piazza's one conifer.

Protected by the city since the 1950s, the cedar was formally added to Italy's National List of Monumental Trees and the regional list only recently, alongside the square's plane trees. Its girth of over four metres marks it as a substantial, century-old specimen even before the paperwork caught up with what Parma's gardeners already knew. Tree climbers and arborists check it regularly now, work that has included tomography scans of the trunk and root aeration to keep both the tree and the pedestrians beneath it safe.

Cedrus libani is native to the mountains of Lebanon, Syria and Turkey and was one of the first conifers European gardeners collected purely for its shape and scale rather than for timber. In a square defined by its open lawn, this is the one thing in it with a genuinely different silhouette.

trees.name: The Field Elm of Parco Ducale
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north of Parma railway station
trees.story:
Dutch elm disease reached Italy in the 1930s and took most of the country's mature field elms with it over the following two decades, the same epidemic that emptied European streets and parks of the species almost everywhere else. This elm, growing near the Palazzetto Sanvitale inside Parco Ducale, is one of the few in the area that made it through.

At 3.82 metres round and 37.5 metres tall it has grown taller than the horse chestnuts and planes usually associated with the park's grand avenues, a field elm doing what the species can do when disease does not cut it short first. Ulmus minor naturally reaches a broad, high canopy on a single strong trunk, and this one has had the decades to prove it, in a park that lost every mature tree it had once already, burned for firewood by occupying troops in 1745.

The elm is deliberately not the story's dramatic tree here. It survived nothing spectacular in the way a fire or a storm is spectacular; it simply kept growing while a fungus carried by bark beetles worked through nearly everything nearby that shared its genus.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Parco Ducale
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north of Parma railway station

best_time.label: May, when the white flower spikes stand up across the crown

trees.story:
Horse chestnuts are, by the park's own count, one of its three most common old species alongside plane and lime, and this one earned an individual place on Italy's monumental register on its own measurements: 3.70 metres round the trunk. It is a broad, low-crowned tree rather than a tall one, 16 metres against the 47 of the park's tallest plane, which is exactly the shape Aesculus hippocastanum tends toward once it has had a century to fill out.

Parco Ducale's chestnuts are old enough that the park's own literature describes bicentenary specimens among them, planted in the waves of restoration that followed the destruction of 1745 and the redesign under Duke Filippo di Borbone from 1749. Spring here means candle-shaped white flower spikes across the park's oldest chestnuts, and by autumn the same trees are dropping conkers onto the paths beneath them, a seasonal cycle Parma's gardeners have watched repeat for two centuries.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Palazzo Ducale
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: About a 15 minute walk north of Parma railway station

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
This oak, 4.20 metres round and 25 metres tall, stands at the western edge of the grounds around Palazzo Ducale, the summer palace Duke Ottavio Farnese began in 1561 and the building that gives the whole park its name. Farnea, the local name the register uses for Quercus robur, is not one of the species most associated with this park; horse chestnuts, planes and limes dominate the planting record, which makes an oak this size a genuine outlier rather than one of a matching set.

Whatever stood on this ground before 1745 is not recorded individually, because the whole park lost its mature trees that year: troops occupying Parma during the War of the Austrian Succession cut and burned every one of them, including those on the park's central ornamental island, to feed their fires. Everything growing in Parco Ducale today, this oak included, is therefore at most a product of the 1749 restoration under Duke Filippo di Borbone and the French architect Petitot, or of the further planting waves that followed through the nineteenth century.

Pedunculate oaks live for centuries when left alone, far longer than this one has yet had, which makes it one of the park's trees with the most growing still ahead of it.

trees.name: The Watson Beech
trees.access: Free, always open. Stands on the open lawn at the main entrance to PSU's Millar Library, a public university campus walkway.
trees.transport: Downtown Portland, on the PSU campus; MAX Blue/Red/Green Line and Portland Streetcar both stop within a couple of minutes' walk (Transit Mall / Kings Hill-SW Salmon station area).

best_time.label: April and May, before the new leaves darken, when the whole crown is closer to red than purple

trees.story:
Portland State University knocked down a Victorian mansion to build its library, then laid out the front lawn around the tree that had stood beside it. The beech is still there. The house is not.

Frank Watson made his money in ironworks and shipbuilding, and around 1890 he and his wife Mary Whalley Watson planted this copper beech beside their new home on the corner of Hall and Park. Sources credit the planting to one or the other of them and do not agree on which. The house came down between 1965 and 1968 to make room for the Millar Library, designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. No record explains why the beech was spared when everything around it was cleared. It simply was, and it ended up the centrepiece of the lawn rather than a casualty of it.

It now stands about 25.6 metres tall with a trunk 5.71 metres around, and went onto Portland's register as Heritage Tree #54 in 1995. A photograph from 1975 shows students packed shoulder to shoulder on the grass underneath it, which is more or less what the lawn is still for on a warm day.

What it has watched is a residential corner turning into a university: Victorian houses giving way to concrete, and then fifty years of students using its shade as somewhere to meet.

trees.name: The Farrell Planetree
trees.access: Free, always open. Standing in the street planting strip at a downtown corner, fully public.
trees.transport: Downtown Portland; MAX Blue/Red/Green Line and Portland Streetcar both stop within a few minutes' walk of the Park Blocks.
trees.story:
The house this tree was planted to shade is now a parking lot. The plane tree has outlived it by more than a century.

An 1880 photograph shows it as a thin sapling beside the home of Sylvester Farrell, a feed-and-grocery merchant who moved into salmon canning and later sat on Portland's City Council. The tree was reportedly a gift from US Senator J.N. Dolph. Farrell's house is long gone, the corner it stood on has been given over to parked cars, and the plane tree carries on in the planting strip beside them.

Portland made it a Historic Landmark in 1973 and entered it on the new Heritage Tree register the same year as number 2, which makes it one of the first trees the city ever formally protected. It is about 19.2 metres tall with a trunk 4.36 metres around. Locally it gets called a sycamore, which it is not.

Portland's old nickname was Stumptown, earned honestly: the city cleared its native forest fast and left the stumps standing in the streets. This tree belongs to the second chapter, planted on purpose by people who had watched the first forest go. It has now outlasted the man who planted it, the house he planted it for, and the neighbourhood they were both part of.

trees.name: The Eliot Hawthorns
trees.access: Free, always open. Standing in the sidewalk planting strip in front of the church, fully public.
trees.transport: Downtown Portland; MAX Blue/Red/Green Line and Portland Streetcar both stop within a few minutes' walk.

best_time.label: October and November, when all four trees hang with dark red haws

trees.story:
Four trees, four separate heritage numbers. Portland registered these hawthorns individually as Heritage Trees #109 through #112, which is a lot of paperwork for a row most people walk past as a single hedge.

They stand in the planting strip along SW 12th Ave in front of the First Unitarian Church, all four planted in 1966 and all four added to the register in 1996. Lavalle hawthorns are small trees and these are no exception: 11 to 13.4 metres tall, with trunks between 1.8 and 2.26 metres around. They are also, by a wide margin, the youngest entries in this city.

They earn their place through the congregation rather than through age. Rev. Thomas Lamb Eliot led this church from 1867 to 1893 and became one of Portland's more consequential citizens, founding social and library associations and lending his name to the Eliot Glacier on Mount Hood. The members he drew in did a good deal of the civic building of early Portland, and the row went in as a tribute to that.

Come in autumn and all four hang with dense clusters of dark red haws while the leaves go bronze. That is the point in the year when the row stops reading as a hedge and starts reading as four trees.

trees.name: The Kamm Walnut
trees.access: Visible and reachable from the public sidewalk at the SW Salmon/SW 14th corner (register ownership: Portland Public Schools, standing at the edge of the Lincoln High School grounds). Stand at the street corner rather than crossing onto school property, especially during school hours.
trees.transport: Goose Hollow, a short walk west of downtown; Portland Streetcar and MAX both have stops within about 10 minutes' walk (Goose Hollow/SW Jefferson MAX station is closest).
trees.story:
A fourteen-acre estate has been reduced to a single walnut on a school lawn. This is it.

Jacob Kamm was a Swiss immigrant who engineered steamships and made a fortune moving freight on the Columbia River with the Oregon Steam and Navigation Company. He built a French Second Empire mansion out here when this was the edge of Portland. His wife Caroline Agusta Gray had grown up among the first missionary families living with the Nez Perce in Idaho.

The planting date is genuinely unsettled. The tree's own plaque says the 1880s. The city's field guide, in its narrative, dates it to around 1871 and the building of the Kamm house. Nobody has reconciled the two, so the honest answer is somewhere inside that fifteen-year window.

The Kamms sold up in 1910 and Lincoln High School took the site. When the current school building went up in 1952, architect Hollis Johnston drew his plan around the walnut rather than through it. It stands about 29 metres tall with a trunk 4.24 metres around, close enough to Interstate 405 to hear it. Ask anyone who went to Lincoln and you will usually get a story.

The tree sits at the edge of school grounds. Look at it from the corner of SW Salmon and SW 14th rather than walking onto the property, particularly on a school day.

trees.name: The Miller Pine
trees.access: Free, always open. Standing in a built-out street planter at a Goose Hollow intersection (register ownership: Right Of Way / TriMet), fully public.
trees.transport: Goose Hollow; the MAX Blue/Red Line Goose Hollow/SW Jefferson St station is a short walk away.
trees.story:
This 31-metre pine is growing out of a street planter because a florist put it in the ground before there was a street.

Through the 1870s and 1880s this stretch of Goose Hollow lay outside the city limits and belonged to Henry Miller, one of Portland's first florists, who ran a plant nursery, a seed farm and a floral supply business on the slope. The Austrian pine and a large Cedar of Lebanon a short way off both appear to be imports he planted on his own nursery ground. They were stock and demonstration rather than landscaping, which is why they sit where no landscape architect would have put them.

The register dates the planting to the late 19th century and added the tree to the Heritage list in 1993. It is roughly 31.1 metres tall with a trunk 3.23 metres around, rising out of a built-out planter at an intersection that did not exist when it was young.

There is photographic proof of its head start. A 1959 photograph of the Jacob Kamm House, a few blocks east, catches this pine and its cedar neighbour already full grown in the background.

What it has watched is a semi-rural nursery district becoming one of the densest neighbourhoods in Portland, with an interstate cut through beside it.

trees.name: The Rockey Elm
trees.access: Free, always open. Standing in the sidewalk planting strip on NW Flanders St, fully public.
trees.transport: Northwest District (Nob Hill area); Portland Streetcar NS Line stops a few blocks south on NW Northrup/Lovejoy; roughly a 10-15 minute walk from the NW 21st/23rd Ave shopping streets.
trees.story:
A Portland architect once parked his car against this elm so the removal crew could not reach it. It worked.

The city council had condemned the tree in 1963. The owner of the building in front of it wanted it gone, worried that its roots were working into his foundations, and applied for a removal permit. Lewis Crucher's car bought enough time for Mayor Terry Schrunk to place a moratorium on that permit while the city forester and the city engineer went and looked at the tree themselves.

What followed ran in the Oregonian for months: a vigil at the trunk, a poem printed in the paper, and a letter from Dr Eugene W. Rockey recalling that his father had planted the elm in 1900 in front of their newly built house, and had fitted it with a wooden slat guard to stop the family's buggy horse nipping the top off the sapling. The foresters found the tree healthy and safe. The permit was refused.

It is about 24.4 metres tall with a trunk 4.60 metres around, Heritage Tree #46 since 1995. It had already come through the Columbus Day Storm the year before the council came for it, which means it survived the worst windstorm in the region's recorded history and then very nearly lost to a building permit.

Its opposite number, the Storm Elm, stands directly across Flanders Street.

trees.name: The Storm Elm
trees.access: Free, always open. Standing in the sidewalk planting strip on NW Flanders St, fully public.
trees.transport: Northwest District (Nob Hill area); Portland Streetcar NS Line stops a few blocks south on NW Northrup/Lovejoy; roughly a 10-15 minute walk from the NW 21st/23rd Ave shopping streets.
trees.story:
The Columbus Day Storm of 1962 flattened roughly 15 billion board feet of Pacific Northwest timber and gusted to 116mph over Portland. On the north side of this block, one elm was left standing.

That is this tree, planted in 1902 or 1903 in the planting strip on NW Flanders St. It is around 24.4 metres tall with a trunk 4.30 metres around, and it went onto the Heritage Tree register as number 36 in 1994. The city's own field guide is blunt about the odds: getting through that night at all was no small thing for a mature elm on an exposed street.

The storm was not the end of the threat. Dutch elm disease arrived later, carried by a bark beetle that reached North America from Asia by way of Europe, and a smaller elm on the same block was lost to it. The elms still standing here, this one included, are now inoculated against the fungus by the city and by volunteers.

Look across the street while you are here. The Rockey Elm came through the same night and then had to be defended from a removal permit the following year. Two trees, one block, and one decade that tried twice to take them.

trees.name: The Patton Road Sequoia
trees.access: Free, always open. Register ownership is Right Of Way, meaning the tree stands in the public street verge; the register's own note ('at the entrance to the residence driveway') describes its position next to a private driveway, not that it is on private land. Stand on the street verge/sidewalk rather than the driveway apron itself.
trees.transport: Southwest Hills; no MAX or streetcar nearby, TriMet bus line 51 (Vista) serves the general neighbourhood. Best reached by car or a considerable uphill walk from downtown (roughly 3km, mostly climbing).
trees.story:
Forty-five metres of Californian giant sequoia is growing out of a street verge in the Southwest Hills, and nobody has written down when it was planted.

Sequoiadendron giganteum belongs in the western Sierra Nevada, several hundred miles south of here, where it grows in scattered groves at altitude. Victorian and Edwardian planters shipped it all over the world, and this one took to Portland's rain well enough to reach 45.1 metres on a residential road. The register carries no planting date and none has surfaced anywhere else, so the age is simply unknown. The trunk says a great many decades. No source says more than that.

The girth is unsettled too. The city register puts the circumference at 7.07 metres. An independent measurement, taken at a different height on the trunk, gives 6.74 metres. Some of that gap is probably just where the tape went round, but the two figures have never been reconciled, so treat it as somewhere close to seven metres and leave it there.

The tree stands in the public verge at the entrance to a residence driveway. There is room to stand and look from the road, and that is where to do it: the verge is public, the driveway is not.

trees.name: The Balch Creek Fir
trees.access: Free, always open. Standing on Portland Parks & Recreation land inside Forest Park/Macleay Park, on the Lower Macleay spur trail about 100 yards from the stone house ('Witch's Castle') ruin along Balch Creek. Reached on foot via a public park trail, not roadside.
trees.transport: Access via the Lower Macleay trailhead, 2960 NW Upshur St; TriMet bus lines 15, 26 and 77 stop within a few blocks (NW Thurman/27th-29th or NW Vaughn/27th), then it is roughly a 15-20 minute walk up the Lower Macleay/Wildwood Trail along Balch Creek to reach the tree.
trees.story:
This Douglas fir is 74 metres tall. Nothing else in Portland comes close.

The city register measures it at 243 feet, or 74.1 metres, with a trunk 5.58 metres around and 1.78 metres through. A student piece in the PSU Vanguard, working independently, arrived at exactly the same height and girth, which is reassuring for a measurement that is genuinely hard to take on a tree this size standing in a steep ravine.
