It grows at the bottom of the Balch Creek canyon in Forest Park, one of the largest urban forest reserves in the United States, on the Lower Macleay spur trail about a hundred yards past the stone house ruin that everyone here calls the Witch's Castle. A large stone beside the path marks it. Look up rather than around: at this height the top of the tree is well outside anything you can take in from the trail.

No age is recorded anywhere, and that is not an oversight. This is not a planted landscape tree with a date attached to it but a survivor in a patch of regrown native forest, and nobody has cored it. The ravine explains the height. Steep, shaded, wet, sheltered from the wind, and never quite worth the trouble of logging.

trees.name: The Hoyt Dawn Redwood
trees.access: Free, always open, no admission charge. Hoyt Arboretum is a public Portland Parks & Recreation arboretum within Washington Park.
trees.transport: MAX Blue/Red Line Washington Park station (the deepest transit station in North America) is about a half-mile walk along the Overlook Trail to the Arboretum Visitor Center, or take the seasonal free Washington Park shuttle from the station to the Hoyt Arboretum stop.

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns copper and then bare, which is not what a conifer is supposed to do

trees.story:
Until 1944 the dawn redwood was a fossil. Botanists knew Metasequoia only from imprints in stone and assumed it had been extinct for millions of years, until a living stand turned up in a remote Chinese valley. In 1952 this tree, grown from that discovery, produced cones: the first any dawn redwood had produced in the Western Hemisphere since the species vanished from it.

How long an absence that was depends who you ask. Portland's register says 8 million years. Travel Oregon and Hoyt Arboretum itself both say about 6 million. Neither number is the tree's age. They describe the gap in the fossil record, not the thing in front of you, which went into the ground in 1948 and is about 78 years old.

The route here was fast by the standards of botany. Harvard's Arnold Arboretum organised an international seed-collecting expedition to the Chinese stand in 1947, Hoyt Arboretum was among the institutions sent seed, and the seedlings were planted the following year. Four years after that, cones.

It is now 31.4 metres tall with a trunk 3.29 metres around, and it is an Oregon Heritage Tree. Late in the year it does the thing that makes dawn redwoods worth the walk up: a conifer that turns copper and then goes completely bare.

trees.name: The Mount Tabor Sequoia
trees.access: Free. Portland Parks and Recreation, open park.
trees.transport: Mount Tabor Park, about 6 km east of downtown. Bus 15 to SE Belmont and Tabor, then uphill.
trees.story:
Forty two metres, on a trunk 7.8 metres round, standing beside a reservoir on the side of an extinct volcano. Mount Tabor is one of the few cinder cones inside an American city, and the water bureau built open reservoirs into its slope in the 1890s with the kind of civic architecture usually reserved for banks: balustrades, gatehouses, iron railings.

Somebody planted a giant sequoia next to one of them. It is a Sierra Nevada tree, six hundred kilometres south and two thousand metres up, and it has done better here than most things do at home, because Portland gives it what California increasingly cannot, which is water.

The city added it to the heritage register in 1997. What it does not record, because the register has no such field, is when it went in. The reservoir dates the site rather than the tree, and joining those two facts would be a guess dressed as a date.

Go to the west side of the park and look for the rectangular reservoir. The tree is on its east bank and there is no mistaking which one it is.

trees.name: The Powell Butte Poplar
trees.access: Free. Public park trail, open daylight hours.
trees.transport: About 17 km southeast of downtown, off SE Powell Boulevard. Drive or bus 9.
trees.story:
Lombardy poplars are the disposable tree of the temperate world. They are planted as fast screens, they grow like weeds, they are usually rotten by fifty and gone by seventy, and nobody protects one.

Portland protects this one. The city measured the trunk at 122 inches across, which works out at 9.75 metres around, on a tree thirty five metres tall and only twelve across the crown, which is the columnar habit doing exactly what it is famous for. That girth would be remarkable on an oak. On a Lombardy poplar it is close to absurd, and it is the largest circumference on Portland's entire heritage register.

The city added it in 2019, one of the most recent designations on a list that started in 1993, which suggests somebody walked past it and thought the same thing you will.

The measurement comes from the register and we have not found a second one, so treat the number as the city's rather than as gospel. It is on the Mountain View Trail in Pleasant Valley, out on the eastern edge of the city.

trees.name: The Parkrose Beech
trees.access: Free. Public right of way at the street end.
trees.transport: About 13 km northeast of downtown. MAX Red Line to Parkrose, then a short walk.
trees.story:
Seven metres round and twenty six metres tall, at the end of a residential street in Parkrose Heights, on a strip of unimproved public right of way that never became road.

That detail is the whole story. A beech of this size in a European park would have a fence around it and a plaque. This one survives because the city ran out of street before it ran out of block, so the tree kept the ground it was standing on and the tarmac stopped short.

European beech holds its dead leaves through winter when young and drops them cleanly once mature, and at this size the trunk is the thing worth looking at: smooth grey bark stretched tight, with the surface rippling where the buttress roots begin. Beech bark does not crack with age the way oak does, so an old one looks like something poured rather than grown.

Portland designated it in 1994, the first year of the register. It has no recorded age, because the register does not have that field.

trees.name: The Knott Street Wingnuts
trees.access: Free. Street trees on the public right of way.
trees.transport: NE Knott Street at 15th Avenue, Irvington, about 3 km northeast of downtown. Bus 8 to NE 15th and Knott.

best_time.label: July, when the seed chains hang at full length

trees.story:
Nine Caucasian wingnuts line two blocks of NE Knott Street, five in front of the church and four across the road from it, and the city numbered every one of them when it designated the lot in 1996.

Caucasian wingnut is not a street tree anywhere. It comes from the forests between the Black Sea and the Caspian, it suckers freely, it wants wet feet, and no municipal planting manual recommends it. Somebody in Irvington planted nine.

What you get for that is the catkins. Wingnut hangs green chains of winged seeds up to half a metre long through summer, so the whole line drips at once, which is a thing worth timing a walk for. The leaves are pinnate and ash-like, up to twenty leaflets, and the crowns are far wider than the trunks suggest: the biggest here is 2.3 metres round and throws a crown twenty three metres across.

They are the reason to start an Irvington walk at this corner. Everything else on this page in this neighbourhood is within six hundred metres of them.

trees.name: The Eighteenth Avenue Planes
trees.access: Free. Street trees on the public right of way.
trees.transport: NE 18th Avenue at Brazee, Irvington. Bus 8 to NE 15th and Knott, then four blocks east.
trees.story:
Two London planes stand one behind the other outside the same address, and the city registered them as a pair in 2005, recording one as the north tree and one as the south. The north is 4.8 metres round, the south 4.6, and between them they throw crowns twenty six and twenty seven metres across over a street that is twelve metres wide.

That is the London plane's entire case for existing. It was a chance hybrid, probably raised in seventeenth century Europe from an American sycamore and an oriental plane, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, road salt, drought and filthy air better than anything native to any of those places. Every industrial city in the northern hemisphere planted it. Portland planted these.

The bark is the giveaway: plane sheds it in plates, so the trunk is a camouflage of cream, olive and grey, and the shed pieces lie around the base like broken crockery.

Stand between them and look up. The two crowns have grown into each other and the street disappears.

trees.name: The Irvington Elm
trees.access: Free. Street tree on the public right of way.
trees.transport: NE 18th Avenue at Stanton, Irvington. Bus 8, then a short walk east.
trees.story:
Thirty five metres tall on a trunk 4.5 metres round, which makes this the tallest street tree in Irvington and one of the tallest elms anywhere on this site.

That it is standing at all is the point. Dutch elm disease reached North America in 1930 and took an estimated hundred million trees, and it rewrote what American streets look like: the elm arch that shaded half the country's residential blocks is largely a photograph now. Portland was luckier than most, partly through geography and partly through an aggressive city programme of inspection and removal, and elms like this one are what luck plus effort left behind.

Field elm is the European native, no more resistant than any other, so this tree has simply not been found by the beetle that carries the fungus. Every year it goes unfound is another year.

The city registered it in 2003. Two blocks south stand the pair of heritage planes; the wingnut line is four blocks west.

trees.name: The Thompson Street Horsechestnut
trees.access: Free. Street tree on the public right of way.
trees.transport: NE Thompson Street at 15th Avenue, Irvington. Bus 8 to NE 15th and Knott.

best_time.label: late September, when the conkers drop

trees.story:
Twenty nine metres is tall for a horse chestnut. The species usually gives up somewhere around twenty five and spends the difference on width instead, so this one, at 4.4 metres round and twenty across the crown, is a horse chestnut behaving like a forest tree.

It is also a tree with a job. Horse chestnut is the conker tree, and its entire modern distribution outside the Balkans is down to people wanting the fruit: the species is close to endangered in its native Pindus mountains and planted by the million everywhere else. The nuts are inedible, mildly poisonous, and were carried across Europe for centuries anyway because children want them.

So the two weeks to come are the last of September, when the spiny cases split on the pavement. Before that, in early May, the whole crown goes up in white candles with yellow throats that turn red once each flower has been pollinated, which is a signal to bees and a nice thing to know while standing underneath.

Portland registered it in 2004.

trees.name: The Twenty-Fourth Avenue Catalpas
trees.access: Free. Street trees on the public right of way.
trees.transport: NE 24th Avenue at Thompson, Irvington. Bus 8, then five blocks east.

best_time.label: the second half of June, when the white bells open

trees.story:
A pair, registered together in 1994, the year Portland's heritage list opened. One is 4.1 metres round and twenty six tall, the other 3.8 and twenty three.

Northern catalpa is a tree that does everything conspicuously. The leaves are heart shaped and up to thirty centimetres long, so the crown reads as coarse from a distance. In June it flowers in upright trusses of white bells freckled with purple and yellow inside, thousands at once, and the fallen petals cover the pavement. Then it hangs seed pods like bean pods, forty centimetres or more, which stay on through winter and rattle, and which give the tree its American nickname of cigar tree.

Its natural range is small, a patch of the Mississippi basin, and it got everywhere else because railway companies planted it in plantations for fence posts: catalpa wood rots slowly. The fashion collapsed, the trees stayed.

Come in the second half of June. There is not much on this site that beats a large catalpa in full flower, and there are two of them here.

trees.name: The Overlook Planes
trees.access: Free. Street trees on the public right of way.
trees.transport: N Overlook Boulevard, about 5 km north of downtown. MAX Yellow Line to Overlook Park.
trees.story:
Three planes at one address on Overlook Boulevard, 5.4, 4.8 and 3.9 metres round, and the largest throws a crown thirty one metres across on a tree only twenty one metres tall. That ratio is the whole character of the group: they are wider than they are high, which a plane only manages with room and time.

The biggest of the three carries the largest London plane girth on Portland's heritage register, and the city designated all three together in 2018, which is late. A tree does not get to 5.4 metres round in seven years, so these were large for a long while before anyone wrote them down. That is normal for street trees and worth knowing when reading any heritage list: the designation year records when a city noticed, not when a tree started.

Overlook sits on the bluff above the Willamette with the industrial river on one side and the West Hills opposite, so the walk out here comes with a view whether or not you care about planes.

trees.name: The Irvington Sycamore
trees.access: Free. Street tree on the public right of way.
trees.transport: NE 25th Avenue at Thompson, Irvington. Bus 8, then six blocks east.
trees.story:
The city's note on this tree reads, in full, "Big 13'". That is the entire official record, written by whoever measured it in 1999, and it is not wrong: thirteen feet is 3.9 metres round, under a crown twenty six metres across.

American sycamore is the parent that gave the London plane its constitution, and side by side the difference is legible. Sycamore sheds bark higher and harder, so the upper limbs go bone white, and from a distance an old one looks as though someone has painted the top half. The leaves are broader and shallower lobed than the hybrid's, and the seed balls hang singly rather than in pairs, which is the field mark worth remembering.

It is the eastern end of the Irvington heritage cluster. From here the catalpas are a block north, the elm and the planes are six blocks west, and the wingnut line closes the walk at NE 15th, which is about a kilometre and a half all told.

trees.name: The Old Oak of Rue De Laune
trees.neighbourhood: Parc des Champs-de-Bataille / Plains of Abraham, Montcalm
trees.access: Free, no gate, no permission needed. Parc des Champs-de-Bataille (Battlefields Park, incl. the Plains of Abraham) is a National Historic Site managed by the Commission des champs de bataille nationaux, open daily dawn to dusk, one of the most visited public parks in Canada.
trees.transport: RTC bus route 11 runs along Grande Allee a few minutes' walk north; roughly 20-25 minutes on foot from Vieux-Quebec (Old Town).

best_time.label: October, when the red oaks on the plain turn and hold their colour for weeks

trees.story: La Presse reported that the oldest tree on the Plains of Abraham is a red oak on Rue De Laune, reigning there for more than 250 years. It did not say which one. Five red oaks are registered along that short stretch of the anneau, the ring road that loops the plain, and this is the largest of them by a wide margin: the city's inventory of potentially remarkable trees gives it 132 centimetres of diameter at breast height against 89 to 110 for the other four. Quebec measures its trees across the trunk rather than around it, so that converts to roughly 4.15 metres of girth. It is the best match for the newspaper's tree, on size rather than on a name, and the identification is an inference rather than a settled fact. If the 250 years hold, it was already standing on 13 September 1759, when Wolfe's men came up the cliff from the river and a battle that ended the French regime in North America was decided in about half an hour on this ground. The park around it is a National Historic Site, free, open dawn to dusk and one of the busiest public parks in Canada, and its trees are actively monitored rather than left alone.

trees.name: The Second Oak of Rue De Laune
trees.neighbourhood: Parc des Champs-de-Bataille / Plains of Abraham, Montcalm
trees.access: Free, no gate, no permission needed. Same public National Historic Site as, open daily dawn to dusk.
trees.transport: Same as : RTC bus route 11 on Grande Allee, about 20-25 minutes on foot from Vieux-Quebec.
trees.story: This oak stands fifteen metres from the tree the newspapers call the park's oldest, and nobody has put a number on its own years. The city's inventory gives it 110 centimetres of diameter at breast height, second largest of the five red oaks registered along this stretch of Rue De Laune; Quebec publishes the measurement across the trunk, which converts to roughly 3.46 metres round. The printed age claim for this corner of the park names a single tree, so there is no year to give for this one, and none is invented here. What it offers instead is the pair: two heavy red oaks close enough that you can stand between them, inside the ring road that circles the field of the 1759 battle. Chene rouge is a slow provider. Its acorns take two full summers to ripen rather than one, so in any given autumn the crown carries both this year's small green pins and last year's finished nuts, and a good year buries the grass beneath it. The Commission des champs de bataille nationaux keeps the whole park open from dawn to dusk with no gate and no ticket, and this stop costs about twenty seconds off the walk to its neighbour.

trees.name: The Wych Elm of the Plains of Abraham
trees.neighbourhood: Parc des Champs-de-Bataille / Plains of Abraham, Montcalm
trees.access: Free, no gate, no permission needed. Same National Historic Site as, open daily dawn to dusk, about 2km east across the park (still inside the same continuous Battlefields Park grounds).
trees.transport: RTC bus route 11 or 800/801 along Grande Allee/Rene-Levesque, then a walk into the park; roughly 15 minutes on foot from the Plains of Abraham Museum.
trees.story: Dutch elm disease took out most of the mature elms of North America. This park still has about 750 of them. La Presse's account of the arboricultural heritage of Parc des Champs-de-Bataille describes an elm population contemporary with the park itself, monitored and treated tree by tree against the fungus that emptied streets across the continent, which is an unusual thing for a public park to still be paying for a century on. The thickest trunk in the public part of Quebec City's tree inventory is one of those elms: 154 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to roughly 4.84 metres of girth, since the city measures across the trunk rather than around it. It is not an American elm. The municipal foresters record it as Ulmus glabra, the orme des montagnes, a European species, and the newspaper piece treats the park's elms as one population without separating the two, so that identification rests on the city's own survey. No source gives it an age, and at this size it hardly matters: it is a mature tree of a species that mostly did not get to be one. It stands near Avenue Ontario, free, dawn to dusk.

trees.name: The American Elm of Grande Allee
trees.access: Free, a public street tree on one of Quebec City's best-known avenues, no restriction of any kind.
trees.transport: RTC bus route 11 runs the length of Grande Allee; the tree is roughly 15-20 minutes' walk from Vieux-Quebec (Old Town) along the same avenue.
trees.story: The City of Quebec's own heritage record is precise about how Grande Allee got its trees: the municipal authorities widened the avenue at the end of the 1880s and lined it with ormes d'Amerique, American elms. Whether this particular elm descends from that planting is not written down anywhere. It measures 94 centimetres of diameter at breast height in the city's inventory, roughly 2.95 metres round once converted from the diameter Quebec publishes, which is a solid street tree rather than a survivor of unusual size, and the avenue has been replanted more than once in the intervening century. So it stands among the elms of Grande Allee rather than as one of the originals. The avenue itself runs from the old walled town out past the parliament to the Plains of Abraham and is known locally as the Champs-Elysees of Quebec; the city carried out its first heritage-tree inventory of the Grande Allee and Chemin Saint-Louis axis in 2011, which is how a street tree comes to be on a register at all. American elm is the tree that gave North American streets their shape, a trunk that divides low and arches out like a wine glass. Then the fungus arrived.

trees.name: The Red Oak of Grande Allee
trees.access: Free, a public street tree on Grande Allee, no restriction.
trees.transport: RTC bus route 11 along Grande Allee; about 15-20 minutes' walk from Vieux-Quebec.
trees.story: Grande Allee was planted with elms, and one of the largest trees on it is an oak. The city's inventory records this one as Quercus rubra, northern red oak, with 120 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which converts to roughly 3.77 metres of girth; Quebec publishes the measurement across the trunk rather than around it. That is a genuinely large oak for a street, and larger than either of the two elms on this avenue. Where it came from is another matter. The city's heritage page on Grande Allee names the American elm as the avenue's historic planting and does not mention oaks at all, so this tree's species and existence rest on the municipal forestry survey rather than on the heritage record, and no source anywhere gives it an age. What the heritage page does confirm is that this stretch was formally inventoried for heritage trees in 2011, so somebody with a tape measure has been here. It stands on the public pavement of one of the most-walked avenues in the city, on the route between the walled old town and the battlefield park, free and unrestricted at any hour.

trees.name: The Wych Elm of Grande Allee Ouest
trees.access: Free, a public street tree on Grande Allee, no restriction.
trees.transport: RTC bus route 11 along Grande Allee; about 20 minutes' walk from Vieux-Quebec, close to where Grande Allee meets the Plains of Abraham.
trees.story: The second European elm on this page stands at the western end of Grande Allee, close to where the avenue runs out into the Plains of Abraham, which makes it the link between the street trees and the park trees on a single walk. The city's inventory records it as Ulmus glabra, the orme des montagnes, at 109 centimetres of diameter at breast height, roughly 3.42 metres round once converted from the diameter Quebec publishes rather than a girth. As with the red oak further east, the city's heritage account of Grande Allee documents the avenue's late-1880s widening and its American elm planting, and its 2011 heritage-tree inventory, without naming this species, so the identification comes from the municipal foresters. No age is recorded for it. Wych elm is the odd one out among elms in that it spreads by seed rather than by suckering from its own roots, which is why it turns up as a planted tree in cities far from where it grows wild, and why a European elm on a Quebec avenue is less strange than it first sounds. Public pavement, no restriction, about twenty minutes on foot from Vieux-Quebec.

trees.name: The Whitebeam of Víkurgarður
trees.access: Free, public park, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Downtown Reykjavik, Aðalstræti; a 3 minute walk from the old harbour area
trees.story: Reykjavik's oldest tree stands on ground that was the city's main burial ground for roughly six centuries, from a church first recorded around 1200 until the last graves stopped in 1839. In 1883 the Danish health director Georg Schierbeck took over the disused churchyard for horticultural experiments, planting vegetables, grain, shrubs and trees to test what could actually grow in Iceland's climate, and the following summer he put a Swedish whitebeam in the ground at the corner of Aðalstræti and Kirkjustræti. It survived when almost everything else in his experimental garden did not, and at around 142 years old it now holds the title of the oldest planted tree in the country, not just the city, a distinction that says as much about Iceland's near-total historical deforestation as it does about the tree itself. Schierbeck left for Denmark a decade later, and the site passed to a local magistrate's family who kept tending it, which is most of why anything from his original planting survived at all. The whitebeam has outlasted the churchyard's headstones, the garden's original purpose, and a 1972 redesign that turned the space into more of a square than a garden, one of only a few of Schierbeck's original trees still standing.

trees.name: The Larch of Hólavallagarður
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open daily during daylight hours
trees.transport: Vesturbær district, Suðurgata; a 15 minute walk from downtown Reykjavik
trees.story: European larch does not grow wild anywhere near Iceland, and conifers in general struggle against the country's wind and thin soil more than almost any other kind of tree, which is part of why Iceland's forestry society singled one out in 2011 growing inside Hólavallagarður, Reykjavik's oldest surviving cemetery. Consecrated in 1838 and still the resting place of many of the country's most significant historical figures, the cemetery has become, almost by accident, one of the most heavily wooded plots of ground in the capital, its narrow gravel paths winding between headstones and trees rather than through open lawn the way most cemeteries are laid out. The larch was already about 80 years old when it won its designation, putting its planting around the early 1930s, decades into Iceland's first serious attempts at organized forestry after centuries in which the country had almost none. Larches lose their needles every winter, unusual for a conifer, so for several months a year this one stands bare among the cemetery's evergreens, a reminder that even the country's championed trees keep behaving like nothing else planted around them.

trees.name: The City Hall Maple
trees.access: Free, public street corner, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Downtown Reykjavik, beside Reykjavik City Hall and Tjörnin pond

best_time.label: October to November: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

trees.story: In 1918, the year the Act of Union made Iceland a sovereign state in union with Denmark, a sycamore maple went into the ground at the corner of Suðurgata and Vonarstræti, on a small patch of grass squeezed against what would later become a parking area. It grew alongside the birth of modern Icelandic statehood, was named the country's Tree of the Year in 1994, and by every recent assessment is still, in the Icelandic forestry society's own phrase, healthy as a horse, crown maintained, foliage vigorous, standing its ground on a corner most passers by would assume was chosen for parking rather than for a tree planted before the country existed in its current form. Sycamore maple is not native to Iceland any more than most of the species on this list, and a specimen this size at this age, over a century into a climate its ancestors never evolved for, represents one of the country's oldest continuous experiments in whether an imported tree can actually thrive here. It stands close enough to Reykjavik's City Hall and the Tjörnin pond that most visitors to either landmark walk directly past it without knowing it predates both the current city hall building and, in an informal sense, the country's independence itself.

trees.name: The Spruce of Elliðaárhólmi
trees.access: Free, public nature reserve, open daily
trees.transport: Elliðaárdalur valley, eastern Reykjavik; accessible via walking and cycling paths from Árbær or Breiðholt
trees.story: The Norway spruce named Iceland's Tree of the Year in 2019 is not old by the standards of almost anywhere else on this site, an estimated 50 to 60 years at the time of its selection, but it stands on ground that had no trees at all a human lifetime earlier. Elliðaárhólmi, an island within the Elliðaárdalur river valley on Reykjavik's eastern edge, only began receiving planted forest around 1950, when staff from the city's hydroelectric power company started work later taken over by the Reykjavik Forestry Society in 1972. Norway spruce imported from northern Norway went in heavily through the 1950s, 60s and 70s, part of a national effort to prove that organized forestry could work at all in a country that had lost nearly all its original woodland centuries earlier to settlement-era clearing and grazing. This particular tree, twelve metres tall by the time it won its designation, has become something like a mascot for that project, not ancient, not native, but proof that a spruce planted with real effort in the right spot can grow into something worth naming, in a country where almost no tree could make that claim a century ago.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Villa Sciarra
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Trastevere, or bus routes to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli

best_time.label: November, when it turns uniformly gold within days

trees.story: Rome's most famous old trees are cedars and planes, planted by cardinals and popes on grand estates. This ginkgo belongs to a very different Roman: George Washington Wurts, an American diplomat who bought this hillside property in 1902 and spent the rest of his life filling it with plants gathered from wherever caught his interest. He had the ginkgo planted in the early 1900s, one of the first established in the city, a species Europe had only known for about two centuries at that point, brought over from temple gardens in China where it had grown essentially unchanged since before the dinosaurs went extinct. Rome's own environment department now lists it among the city's roughly twenty official monumental trees, qualifying on three separate grounds at once: age and size, landscape value, and simple botanical rarity, since ginkgos remain genuinely uncommon in Roman parks even a century after Wurts planted his. The trunk has thickened to just over three metres around and the crown now reaches 25 metres, taller than most of the villa's own follies and fake ruins built around the same period. Wurts died in 1928 without seeing what came next: his widow, the American heiress Henrietta Tower Wurts, gave the whole seven and a half hectare estate to the Italian state in the early 1930s, on condition it stay a public park. Every November the tree does what ginkgos do everywhere, turning uniformly gold within days rather than fading gradually like its neighbours.

trees.name: Adonis
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Borghese
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Metro A Spagna, entering via Via Pinciana
trees.story: Nine trees are what remain of the eleven Cardinal Scipione Borghese planted here four centuries ago. Adonis is the largest survivor: a vast, hollow-trunked oriental plane at the entrance to what is now called the Valley of the Plane Trees, planted in the early 1600s by the cardinal's gardener, Domenico Savini da Montepulciano. At around 425 years old, it and its siblings are described by Italian foresters as the only urban stand of ancient oriental planes left in the West, and the oldest living trees in Rome. In 2021 the garden cloned it, growing a sapling from a single leaf found sprouting on the fragile trunk. The clone, planted nearby as Adonis Junior, is genetically identical to a four-hundred-year-old tree despite being six years old at planting. It was a hedge against the inevitable: Adonis is hollow and propped, and a nearby oak from the same era, nicknamed the Quercia del Lupo for a wolf-shaped burl on its trunk and already documented in a memoir of the villa's gardens by the 1650s, collapsed in a storm in 2018 after three to five hundred years standing, accounts differ. Adonis is still leafing out every spring in the hunting park a cardinal built long before anyone thought to call it a public garden.

trees.name: The Twin Planes of the Eleven Fountains
trees.neighbourhood: Trastevere, at the foot of the Gianicolo
trees.access: Paid entry, Orto Botanico di Roma
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Trastevere (Piazza Trilussa), or tram 8 to Piazza Sonnino
trees.story: Two oriental planes here are older than the university that now owns them. Rome's Botanical Garden became a state institution in 1883, but the ground itself was a private garden of the Corsini family from 1660 onward, and these two trees, flanking Ferdinando Fuga's 1742 cascade of eleven fountains, were already mature when the last Corsini cardinals walked past them. Foresters place their age at over 300 years, among the oldest confirmed trees in Rome after Villa Borghese's plane grove. The staircase they frame, the Scalinata delle Undici Fontane, sends water down five stone basins toward eleven separate jets, an 18th-century flourish built as a backdrop for planting that already existed. The garden today holds 345 centuries-old specimens across 130 species, cork oaks, Himalayan cedars and Turkish oaks among them, but the two planes at the fountains remain the postcard image, framing water and stone the way they have for three centuries, regardless of which family or which state held the deed to the land around them.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of the Orangery
trees.neighbourhood: Trastevere, at the foot of the Gianicolo
trees.access: Paid entry, Orto Botanico di Roma
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Trastevere (Piazza Trilussa), or tram 8 to Piazza Sonnino
trees.story: This cork oak has been measured twice in three years, and it grew in the interval: 5.00 meters around in October 2021, 5.30 meters by January 2024, still adding girth at an age Italy's national monumental tree registry puts at 226 years. It grows near the Orangery in Rome's Botanical Garden, one of several cork oaks the university lists among its monumental specimens, alongside Turkish oaks and a pair of Himalayan cedars near the old riding school. Quercus suber is farmed across the western Mediterranean for its bark, stripped every decade or so to make wine corks and flooring without killing the tree, and this specimen's deeply fissured, spongy trunk still shows the scars of past harvests even though nobody has stripped it in living memory. It predates the garden's official 1883 founding as a state institution by nearly a century, rooted here since the grounds still belonged to the Corsini family. Visitors tend to walk straight past it toward the garden's showier Japanese section and its cascading fountains, but few trees anywhere in the city are still visibly getting bigger.

trees.name: The Cedar of the Belvedere
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Doria Pamphilj
trees.transport: Bus 870 or 791 to the Via Aurelia Antica entrance, 10 min walk

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Sources disagree by a century and a half on how old this cedar is, and the disagreement is the most honest thing anyone can say about it. One detailed study of Villa Doria Pamphilj's tree collection places its planting in the 1600s, when the Pamphilj family first laid out the estate, which would make it over 300 years old. The tree's own entry in Italy's national monumental tree registry gives a calculated age closer to 150 years, with a trunk 4.6 meters around and a height of 30 meters. Both figures describe the same cedar, shading the belvedere terrace above the Lago del Giglio in Rome's largest public park. What is not disputed is the setting: Villa Doria Pamphilj was a private hunting and pleasure ground until the Italian state expropriated it in 1965, and this cedar, whichever planting it dates to, has shaded cardinals, princes and now Sunday joggers from the same terrace above the same ornamental lake. It is listed as the only individually registered monumental tree in a park that otherwise counts its history in family names rather than tree ages.

trees.name: The Leccio of the Lake
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Borghese
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Metro A Spagna, via the Giardino del Lago
trees.story: Marcantonio IV Borghese tore out six hundred holm oaks in 1784 to build an English-style garden around Villa Borghese's lake, and one tree, by luck or design, was left standing. This is that leccio, growing at the water's edge in what locals once called the Piano dei Licini, the holm oak plain, before the prince's landscapers decided a lake and a temple suited fashionable taste better than a forest. Italy's national tree registry measures its trunk at 4.3 meters around and calculates an age of 176 years from growth data, a figure that would place its planting after Borghese's makeover rather than before it. Older estimates, based on the site's documented history rather than direct measurement, put it closer to 300, arguing it is one of the few survivors of the original grove. Both cannot be right. This page gives both rather than pick a side. What both agree on is the tree's stature: 19 meters tall, its dense evergreen crown reflected in the artificial lake that replaced six hundred of its relatives two and a half centuries ago.

trees.name: The Cedar of the Garibaldi Mausoleum
trees.access: Free, open access, Gianicolo
trees.transport: Bus 115 or 870 to Gianicolo, short walk

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: This cedar shares its hillside with the dead of a revolution. It grows between the Fontana dell'Acqua Paola and the Mausoleo Ossario Garibaldino, the 1941 monument holding the remains of those killed defending Rome's short-lived Republic in 1849 and fighting to make the city Italy's capital between 1860 and 1870. Officially measured for the national monumental tree registry, it stands about 20 meters tall with a trunk 5.74 meters around, and its documented age of roughly 146 years puts its planting in the 1870s, soon after Rome became the capital of a unified Italy in 1871 and this hillside turned from battlefield into a place of civic memory. Cedars of Lebanon are not native anywhere near the Gianicolo; Roman nobility, and later the new Italian state, planted them across the city's hilltop gardens as a shorthand for permanence and old-world grandeur, the same reasoning that put cedars in half the noble villas on this list. This one has outlasted the reasoning: nobody plants status symbols on a war memorial today, but the tree stayed, and it is now the memorial's oldest living feature.

trees.name: The Cedar of Celimontana
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Celimontana
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Metro B Colosseo, via Piazza della Navicella

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: A few meters from Villa Celimontana's Aleppo pine grows its opposite in almost every way: straight where the pine leans, dense and dark where the pine is sparse, native to a mountain range a thousand kilometers further east. This cedar of Lebanon is one of two of Rome's officially monumental trees inside the villa, both standing along Viale Cardinale Francesco Spellman near the main entrance at Piazza della Navicella. Ciriaco Mattei began turning the site's vineyards into an ornamental garden in 1572, and cedars of Lebanon, prized in noble Roman gardens for their biblical associations with endurance, show up across the city's hilltop villas from the 1600s onward. No record fixes the year this particular tree went into the ground, only its registry status as a monumental specimen for its age, dimensions and form, so this account treats its age as undocumented rather than claim a number it cannot back. The villa passed to the Italian Geographical Society in 1926 and became public parkland in 1928, and the cedar, whatever its exact age, has outlasted every institution that has owned the ground beneath it.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of Celimontana
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Celimontana
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Metro B Colosseo, via Piazza della Navicella
trees.story: Villa Celimontana keeps two of Rome's officially monumental trees within a few meters of each other, and this Aleppo pine is the more unusual of the pair. Pinus halepensis is a Mediterranean coastal species, more at home on the cliffs above Aleppo or along the Ligurian shore than on the Caelian Hill, and its presence here fits the exotic-planting habit of the Mattei family, who turned a vineyard into this garden starting in 1572. The tree stands along Viale Cardinale Francesco Spellman near the villa's main entrance at Piazza della Navicella, its twisting, wind-shaped canopy a contrast to the straighter cedar growing almost beside it. No source gives the pine a precise planting date, only the national registry's designation as monumental for its age, dimensions and form, so this account states it as undocumented rather than invent a number. What is certain is the company it has kept: Renaissance nobles, then the Italian Geographical Society, which held the villa from 1926, and now Sunday footballers on the grounds nearby, all under the same slanted pine.

trees.name: The Fitolacca of the Capitoline
trees.access: Free, public steps, always accessible
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Piazza Venezia
trees.story: Rome's most improbable street tree is originally from the Argentine pampas, and it owes its spot on the Capitoline Hill to a 50th birthday party. Prince Baldassarre Ladislao Odescalchi planted it in 1911, the year Italy marked half a century since unification, at the foot of Michelangelo's Cordonata staircase beside the church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli. It is a Phytolacca dioica, called ombu in its native South America, a fast-growing evergreen with a swollen, buttressed trunk that looks more sculpted than grown. At roughly 115 years old it is the youngest tree on this list by a wide margin, but nothing else on the Capitoline canopy touches its scale: its crown now shades a stretch of the climb toward Piazza del Campidoglio, competing for attention with the ancient temple platform the hill was named for. Tourists photograph the she-wolf statue and the Michelangelo-designed piazza above; the tree that actually shades their walk up rarely gets a caption. It is one of Rome's officially registered monumental trees despite being, in local terms, barely out of its youth.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the German Institute
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Trastevere, or bus to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli
trees.story: Two official registers disagree about this trunk by nearly two metres. Italy's national list gives it as five metres around; the Lazio regional list, which is where the national one gets its Roman entries in the first place, says 3.3. Both are describing the same deodar standing beside the villa's main house, and neither has ever put a date on it. What the regional list does say is unusual: of the 65 monumental trees inside the comune of Roma, this is one of only three designated partly for architettura vegetale, vegetal architecture, the surveyor's term for a tree whose shape is itself the built object. Not its age. Not its girth. Its form. Cedrus deodara grows wild at 1,500 to 3,000 metres in the western Himalaya, where its Sanskrit name means timber of the gods and its wood built temples. This one arrived by way of a rich American's shopping habit. George Washington Wurts bought the hillside in 1902 and spent 26 years filling it with plants from wherever caught his attention, the ginkgo 130 metres downhill among them. The house behind the cedar became the Italian Institute of German Studies in 1931, three years after Wurts died, and the tree has been institutional property ever since.

trees.name: The Podocarp of Villa Sciarra
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Trastevere, or bus to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli
trees.story: Most trees earn a place on Italy's monumental register for being old or enormous. This one is on it for being strange. The Lazio survey gives its reason as a single letter, d, botanical rarity, and lists no other qualifying criterion at all: not age, not size, not landscape value. At two metres around and 18 metres tall it is a decent tree in a city full of far bigger ones, and the state protects it anyway, because there is essentially nothing else like it growing in Rome. Podocarps are a mostly southern conifer family that split off long before pines existed and never adopted the cone. Instead the seed sits on a swollen fleshy stalk that turns purple and gets eaten by birds, which is why Podocarpus neriifolius spread from the Himalayan foothills to New Guinea and why Buddhist communities planted it around temples across that whole range. Rome's own city government calls this specimen splendid and enormous. It stands on Viale Adolfo Leducq roughly 20 metres from the ginkgo, both of them bought by the same American collector in the same decade, which makes this stretch of path the most botanically improbable 50 metres in the city.

trees.name: The Plane of Piazza San Cosimato
trees.access: Free, public square, always accessible
trees.transport: Tram 8 to Piazza Sonnino, then 5 min walk; 10 min walk from Piazza Trilussa
trees.story: The neighbourhood had this tree scanned. Volunteers in Trastevere paid forest agronomists to run a tomography on the trunk, reading the internal soundness of the wood the way a hospital reads a body, because the tree stands directly over the square's children's play area and nobody wanted to guess. At 5.65 metres around it holds the thickest plane trunk on Rome's monumental register, thicker than the celebrated planes of Villa Borghese, and it grows not in a cardinal's garden but in a working piazza with a morning market, a football pitch's worth of parked scooters and a tenth-century church. The square was open pasture until the 1880s, the Prati di San Cosimato, grazing land outside the tight medieval lanes. When Rome became the capital and Trastevere was rebuilt, the fields became a triangular market square, and the plane either survived that or was planted into it; no document says which, and its 2013 addition to the register recorded size without age. Platanus x acerifolia is itself an accident, an eighteenth-century hybrid of the eastern and American planes that turned out to tolerate city air better than either parent. Rome planted thousands. This is the one the neighbours look after.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Cordonata
trees.access: Free, public street, always accessible
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Piazza Venezia, up Via delle Tre Pile

best_time.label: late September, when the conkers start dropping onto the ramp

trees.story: A Balkan mountain tree has no business being this large on a Roman hill. Aesculus hippocastanum grows wild in a handful of ravines in the mountains of northern Greece, Albania and North Macedonia, where the summers are cool and the soil stays damp; western Europe only met it in the 1500s, through Constantinople, and planted it everywhere as an avenue tree. Rome is close to the edge of what it tolerates, which is why the city has exactly one on its monumental register and why a trunk 3.45 metres around here counts for more than the same figure would in Vienna. It stands on Via delle Tre Pile, the ramp cars take up the Capitoline, on the right-hand side of Michelangelo's Cordonata as you climb. Roma Capitale registered it for size and for landscape value, meaning the view it belongs to rather than the tree alone. Almost everyone who photographs the staircase stands in its shade to do it. Fifty metres away on the other flank of the same climb grows the ombu from Argentina, so the two flanks of Rome's most famous stair are held by a Balkan mountain tree and a South American pampas tree, and neither is Roman at all.

trees.name: The Cedar Above the Lake
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Borghese
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Metro A Spagna, via the Giardino del Lago

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: Rome's own list of monumental trees does not describe this cedar on its own. It describes it as accompanied by a monumental holm oak, and the two really do stand 70 metres apart at the same water. That phrasing is the giveaway: this tree was never meant to be looked at as a specimen. When Marcantonio IV Borghese remade the grounds in the 1780s he was buying a painting, not a collection. His architects Antonio and Mario Asprucci dug an artificial lake, put an island in it, built a small Ionic temple to Aesculapius on the island in 1786, and planted around all of it to make the view from the bank look like a landscape that had always been there. The cedar is scenery, and it is doing the job two and a half centuries later: 4.1 metres around, 22 metres tall, a flat candelabra crown leaning out over the rowing boats. Cedrus libani was the prestige tree of that generation of Roman gardens, planted in half the noble villas on this list, but most of those sit on lawns and terraces. This one has water under it, which is why it is the one people photograph.

trees.name: The Redwood of the Pincio
trees.access: Free, open access, Pincio gardens
trees.transport: 10 min walk up the ramps from Piazza del Popolo, or Metro A Flaminio
trees.story: Thirty metres is a good height for a tree in Rome and a failure for this species. Sequoia sempervirens is the tallest living thing on earth, passing 110 metres in the fog belt of northern California, and it gets there by drinking the fog directly through its leaves during a rainless summer. Rome offers it a rainless summer without the fog. So the redwood on the Pincio has grown thick instead of tall, 4.2 metres around, and still ends up among the five tallest trees on the city's entire monumental register, which says more about Rome's trees than about this one. It grows on Giuseppe Valadier's terrace, laid out between 1809 and 1814 during the French occupation as a public promenade above Piazza del Popolo, at a moment when Roman gardening was swinging from clipped geometry to imported curiosities. Nobody has published when it was planted or by whom. It reached the national register late, in the batch of Roman trees added after the well-documented ones, and that entry is the only document about it that exists: species, girth, height, a coordinate. Everything else anyone tells you about this tree is a guess, including the ones that sound confident.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Via Corsini
trees.access: Free, public street (Via Corsini), RAMI records it as Accessibile. Resolves the access question the leads file left open: it stands on the street at Via Corsini 1, not inside the ticketed Orto Botanico or the private Corsini gardens.
trees.transport: Same walk as (Twin Planes of the Eleven Fountains), 109m away; 10 min walk from Trastevere

best_time.label: May and June, when the cream-white flowers open and you smell it before you see it

trees.story:
Rome's oldest magnolia does not stand in a garden. It stands on the pavement of Via Corsini, outside the wall of the palace whose garden it was planted for, around the middle of the eighteenth century and roughly 275 years ago. The Orto Botanico next door, the obvious home for a tree like this, only became a public institution long after it was already in the ground.

Southern magnolias had reached Europe from the American southeast only a few decades earlier, which made this one a collector's purchase rather than a street tree. It grew accordingly. The trunk measures 290 centimetres around and the crown reaches 18 metres, closer to a forest tree than to the clipped courtyard shrub the species usually settles for in Italy. Italy's monumental register lists it for age and for size, and for a magnolia that pairing is rare.

What it has watched is mostly the boundary in front of it changing hands: a cardinal's private grounds turning into a state botanical collection, and Trastevere turning from the edge of the city into the middle of it. Surveyors looked it over in late 2025 and recorded its health as good.

In May and June it does the thing the species was imported for, opening cream-white flowers the size of a spread hand, high up and out of reach, and heavy enough with scent that most people smell it before they look up.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Villa Torlonia
trees.access: Free, public park, Villa Torlonia. RAMI records it as Accessibile.
trees.transport: Bus to Via Nomentana / Villa Torlonia entrance, or 10 min walk from Bologna metro (Line B); 3.5km from the city centre

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story:
No cedar on Rome's monumental register is thicker than this one. Six metres around the trunk, 28 metres up, standing beside the staircase Giuseppe Valadier designed for the Casino Nobile. The surveyor who wrote its entry reached for the word guardiano.

Nobody knows when it was planted, and that is worth saying plainly, because the register carries a girth for it and no birth year at all. What exists instead is the estate's history. The Torlonia family bought the grounds in 1797, and the English-style landscaping that brought ornamental conifers into Roman villas came later in the nineteenth century. That puts the cedar somewhere between 150 and 220 years old, which is an inference from the garden rather than a date from a document.

Its neighbours have been unusual. The park holds a pink granite obelisk the cedar now rivals for height, a mock-medieval house covered in owls, and from 1925 to 1943 Mussolini, who rented the whole estate as his private residence for a token sum. The villa was occupied, then left to fall apart for decades, then repaired and opened as a public park. The cedar came through all of it standing where it stands now. Roma Capitale's own description of the villa calls it colossal, which for once is not municipal enthusiasm. It was measured again in March 2026 and found in good health.

trees.name: The Podocarp of Piazza Vittorio
trees.access: Free, public garden inside Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II (Giardino Nicola Calipari). RAMI records it as Accessibile.
trees.transport: Vittorio Emanuele metro (Line A), on the square; 1.7km from the Capitoline cluster
trees.story:
Italy put this tree on its national monumental register in October 2025 for one reason: it should not be here. Podocarpus neriifolius grows wild in the forests of the Himalayan foothills and southeast Asia, and Rome holds very few of any size. This is one of the largest, 230 centimetres around and 20 metres tall, in the public garden inside Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II.

Its age is not known. No planting record survives and neither register that lists it carries a date, so a century, give or take, is as precise as anyone can honestly be. The square around it was laid out in the 1880s for the new capital's civil servants, in an arcaded Turinese style that still makes this corner of Rome look imported from somewhere else, and a garden of exotic trees was exactly what that decade planted.

It has stood through the more restless version of Rome. The square's ruined fountain, the Trofei di Mario, sits a few steps away and predates it by seventeen centuries. The food market that filled the arcades for a hundred years packed up and moved around the corner in 2001. The neighbourhood became the most polyglot in the city. The podocarp, evergreen and unbothered, looks much the same in February as in August. Its health was recorded as good in November 2025.

trees.name: The Chir Pine of Colle Oppio
trees.age: 90+ years, likely planted around the garden's 1936 opening
trees.access: Free, public park, Parco di Colle Oppio. RAMI records it as Accessibile.
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Colosseo metro (Line B); joins a future Celio/Colosseum walk, 1km from Villa Celimontana
trees.story:
The roots of this pine have grown into Nero's palace. It stands on Colle Oppio directly above the Domus Aurea, and somewhere below it in the dark they have worked into the nymphaeum of Ulysses and Polyphemus.

It is not a Roman tree in any sense. The Chir Pine belongs to the Himalayan foothills, and this one was carried back from there by Giuseppe Tucci, the Tibetologist and Mussolini-era envoy who spent the 1930s travelling in Tibet and Nepal. It was already standing when the Colle Oppio garden was inaugurated in 1936, which makes it at least ninety years old and one of the very few of its species in the city. Italy's monumental register added it in October 2025 on the grounds of botanical rarity alone: 290 centimetres around, 20 metres tall.

The caveat is real and belongs in the same breath. Those roots are a genuine problem for the ruin underneath, and plans to redesign the garden above the Domus Aurea have been reported as intending to take out the tall trees over the excavation for exactly that reason. The press had already written this tree off as dying once. The register's most recent check, in late 2025, found it alive and in good health. Both things hold: it is doing well, and it is standing on ground where the archaeology has the stronger claim.

trees.name: The Cypress of Piazza di Siena
trees.access: Free, public park, walkway around the Piazza di Siena arena
trees.transport: Roughly 10-15 min walk from Spagna or Flaminio metro (Line A), inside Villa Borghese
trees.story: Eighteen cypresses once ringed Piazza di Siena when the arena was laid out in 1789, part of the original hedge and tree enclosure designed by architect Antonio Asprucci for what is now Rome's international horse show. Seventeen of those eighteen are gone. This one, according to the conservation group Amici di Villa Borghese, is the sole survivor, still standing along the same oval perimeter the arena has kept since the eighteenth century. Rome's own municipal history of the piazza confirms the original planting scheme, a boxwood hedge, eighteen cypresses and two pine groves, without naming which tree is the last of the batch, so the survivor claim rests on the advocacy group's word rather than a dendrologist's ring count. What isn't in dispute is the arena itself: it has hosted the Concorso Ippico Internazionale, Rome's showjumping event, every year since 1922, riders and horses circling the same green oval a two centuries old cypress has watched from the sidelines the whole time. The letter naming this tree was written in 2024 because Villa Borghese was losing historic specimens faster than anyone wanted, including a well loved pine on the nearby Pincio that was felled around the same period. This cypress is what the campaign wanted people to notice before it went the same way.

trees.name: The Hackberries of the Aranciera
trees.age: locally described as dating from the 1600s, no dendrological confirmation
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Roughly 10-15 min walk from Spagna or Flaminio metro (Line A), inside Villa Borghese
trees.story: A hackberry in the holm oak wood behind the Museo Carlo Bilotti carries a nickname rather than a certificate: locals call it il bagolaro del Seicento, the hackberry of the 1600s, though nobody has run the rings to prove it. What is measured is its girth, about four metres around, matched almost exactly by a second trunk growing beside it, close enough that Italy's citizen tree registry logs them as a twinned pair rather than argue over which is which. Both stand in the Lecceta, a stretch of holm oak forest between the old citrus house, now a museum holding a de Chirico and Warhol collection, and the Muro Torto, the Aurelian era wall that has marked this edge of Rome since the third century. Villa Borghese holds roughly 350 trees and only a fraction have any official monumental status; a 2024 letter from the conservation group Amici di Villa Borghese named this hackberry as one of about 30 still waiting on the paperwork that would protect it. No source gives it exact coordinates, only a location inside the wood, so finding it means wandering the Lecceta rather than following a pin. That is true of most of Villa Borghese's older trees: the park has outlived several rounds of formal cataloguing without ever finishing one.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Piazza Perin del Vaga
trees.neighbourhood: Della Vittoria (RAMI's own field note says quartiere Flaminio; the piazza sits on the boundary, so give both if the writer wants to hedge)
trees.access: Free, public piazza, no restrictions
trees.transport: In the residential Della Vittoria/Flaminio district, roughly 15-20 minutes' walk from Piazzale Flaminio or Lepanto (Metro A)
trees.story:
The children who climbed this holm oak gave it its name. From the top they would shout "Anvedi da quassù se vede tutta Roma", Roman dialect for look, from up here you can see the whole of Rome, and the tree has been Tutta Roma ever since. They were doing it around 1919, so the oak was already climbable then; the register's own reckoning puts its planting at about 1900.

That shout is now on file. When Italy added the tree to its national list of monumental trees in 2025, the criteria included historical and cultural value alongside form and bearing, which is unusual in Rome, where most entries are listed for size alone. And this is not a giant: 2.80 metres around the trunk, 18 metres tall, measured in November 2025 and found in good health.

It stands in Piazza Perin del Vaga, a residential square in Della Vittoria on the edge of Flaminio, north of the centre near the Tiber and a fair way from anything a visitor would otherwise be walking to. Which is more or less the point of it. Nobody built a monument here. A tree went into the ground around the turn of the last century, a generation of local children went up it, one of them said something worth repeating, and a hundred years later the Italian state wrote it down.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Parco degli Scipioni
trees.neighbourhood: Via Appia / Porta Latina, near the Aurelian Walls
trees.access: Free, public park within the Parco Regionale dell'Appia Antica, standard park hours (roughly 7am to sunset)
trees.transport: Entrance at Via di Porta Latina 16, near Porta Latina in the Aurelian Walls; roughly 20-25 minutes' walk from Circo Massimo (Metro B), or reachable by bus along Via Appia Antica
trees.story:
Two official surveys measured this hackberry and agreed on its waist to within a centimetre: four metres around. They do not agree on its height. Italy's national monumental tree register records 20 metres. The Appia Antica park authority, in its own catalogue of notable trees, says 15. Both figures are current, neither has been withdrawn, and there is no way from here to tell which tape was right, so take the tree as somewhere between the two.

It is about a hundred years old, which makes it younger than nearly everything around it. The Parco degli Scipioni is laid out over the tomb of the Scipios, burial vault of the family that produced the general who beat Hannibal, with the columbarium of Pomponius Hylas a few steps away and the Aurelian Walls along the edge. The park in its present form is the work of Raffaele de Vico, who designed it around 1929, and this hackberry went in as part of that design: a piece of 20th century landscaping now the largest living thing in a park built on third century BC ground.

The park authority calls it one of its most important specimens, for its size, its bearing and the balance of its crown, and rates its health as good.

A second hackberry, slightly stouter, stands about a hundred metres off against the Aurelian wall itself. It is on the register too. So far nobody else has written it down.

trees.name: The Plane of Viale Jonio
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: Montesacro, north Rome; Metro B1 Conca d'Oro, then a short walk, or bus along Via Nomentana
trees.story:
Rome's second-thickest registered plane does not grow in a villa garden. It stands on Viale Jonio in Montesacro, six kilometres north of the centre, on a road with traffic lights and a bus lane, and it measures five metres fifty-three around with thirty-two metres above it. Only the plane on Piazza San Cosimato in Trastevere beats it, and that one has the advantage of a famous square.

Montesacro was farmland until the 1920s, when Rome laid out the Citta Giardino Aniene on the far side of the river Aniene: low houses, gardens, planted avenues, a whole quarter designed at once for people pushed out of the centre. The avenues came with trees. This is what one of them looks like after a century in which the houses around it were steadily replaced by apartment blocks and the tree was not.

Two sources record it, the national monumental register through the Lazio list and a notice from the Comune di Roma itself. Neither gives an age. The suburb's own dates suggest a tree that went in with the streets, but no document says so, so it stays a suggestion.

Metro B1 to Conca d'Oro leaves a short walk. It is a long way from anything else a visitor to Rome is doing that day, and it is a genuinely enormous tree.

trees.name: The Chir Pine of Villa Fiorelli
trees.access: Free, public park, open 07:00 to sunset
trees.transport: Metro A to Ponte Lungo, then a few minutes on foot to Piazza Villa Fiorelli
trees.story:
Rome's monumental register lists exactly two Himalayan pines in the whole city. One stands on the Colle Oppio above the Colosseum. This is the other, a couple of kilometres east in a neighbourhood park of nine thousand square metres, with a trunk 2.97 metres round and eighteen metres above it.

Pinus roxburghii grows wild on the dry outer ranges of the Himalaya, from Kashmir across to Bhutan, where it is tapped for resin the way other trees are tapped for rubber. The needles come in threes and run to thirty centimetres, long enough that the crown hangs rather than bristles, and the cones are woody, hand sized things.

The ground under it stopped being farmland in July 1930, when Rome's Governorate bought the last of the Fiorelli family's land on the exclusive condition that it be used as a public park. The old manor house came down that September. Raffaele De Vico laid out the garden that replaced it in 1931, and the Tuscolano quarter's blocks of flats went up around the edge.

Two gaps worth stating. Italy's register has no age field, so nobody has dated this pine. And the city's own account of what grows in the park names walnuts, carobs, plums, a ginkgo and silk trees, without mentioning a pine at all.

trees.name: The Black Poplar of Via Conca d'Oro
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: Metro B1 to Conca d'Oro, then a short walk along Via Conca d'Oro; the Plane of Viale Jonio is about a kilometre further north
trees.story:
Making a monument of a black poplar is a bet against the species. Populus nigra grows fast on soft wood, hollows early and starts shedding limbs while an oak of the same age is still filling out, which is why few of them get old anywhere and fewer still on a city street. This one is 4.05 metres round with twenty metres above it, at the junction of Via Conca d'Oro and Via Val d'Ala.

Rome's register carries three black poplars. The other two sit 14 and 25 kilometres out, one towards the coast at the Risaro and one in Ostia, which leaves this the only one a visitor is likely to reach.

Montesacro was farmland until the 1920s, when the city laid out a garden suburb across the Aniene and planted its avenues. Nothing records when this poplar went in, and the Italian register has no age field to put it in even if something did.

One caution. The Lazio regional list still carried the tree in its November 2025 edition, and that list keeps a separate sheet for trees struck off it, with the reason each was removed, which is the closest thing this country has to a public check that a monumental tree is still standing. Nine months is a long time in the life of a poplar.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Mura Latine
trees.neighbourhood: Appio Latino, along the Aurelian Walls
trees.access: Free, on a public street beside the Aurelian Walls
trees.transport: By Porta Latina, about 100 metres from the Parco degli Scipioni entrance at Via di Porta Latina 16; roughly 20 to 25 minutes' walk from Circo Massimo (Metro B)
trees.story:
Rome's register carries two Mediterranean hackberries and they stand a hundred and twenty metres apart. The one inside the Parco degli Scipioni has a park authority's catalogue entry, a health rating and an age estimate. This one, thirteen centimetres thicker at 4.14 metres round, has a line in a spreadsheet.

It grows at the corner of Viale delle Mura Latine and Via Latina, along the Aurelian Walls. Italians call the species bagolaro, and also spaccasassi, stone splitter, after its habit of rooting into walls and rock and refusing to be shifted. The wall beside it went up between 271 and 275, nineteen kilometres of brick faced concrete thrown around the city in four years by an emperor who had stopped assuming Rome was safe. The Porta Latina is a few steps south.

The register puts the tree at twenty metres and records what earned it the designation: its size, and its form and bearing. It gives no age, and hackberries thicken quickly on good ground, so four metres round here does not mean the two centuries the same measurement would suggest in an oak.

One source only, the national register through the Lazio list. The Appia Antica park's own catalogue of notable trees describes its neighbour in detail and does not mention this one.

trees.name: The Mexican Blue Palm of Villa Sciarra
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk uphill from Trastevere, or bus routes to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli
trees.story:
A palm from the canyons of Baja California sits on Rome's monumental register, and the register is blunt about why: botanical rarity. No age, no history, no famous planter. Just a Brahea armata standing twenty metres up on the Janiculum, which the state counts as reason enough on its own.

It is a desert plant. In Mexico it grows in dry rocky ravines behind the Pacific coast, and its fronds are the colour the name promises, a stiff waxy blue grey that reads as metal rather than leaf from any distance. Once a year it sends out flower spikes that arch clear of the crown and hang several metres below it, longer than the fronds they came from.

Villa Sciarra reached the public through an American. George Washington Wurts bought this hillside in 1902 and spent the rest of his life filling it with whatever caught his eye, and his widow Henrietta Tower Wurts gave the whole estate to the Italian state in the early 1930s on the condition that it stay a park. Whether this palm was one of his, no document says.

The register gives 2.94 metres round and twenty metres tall. Palms lay down no growth rings, so the age here is not merely undocumented, it is unknowable.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of De Kring
trees.age: roughly 180 years, from a registered planting date around 1850
trees.access: Free, on the public square.
trees.story:
This Oriental plane stands by De Kring, a public square in Roosendaal, banded by the national register to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. It shares the square with a horse chestnut the register also lists, the two trees framing the same small public space from different corners.

Oriental plane is the older, wilder-growing parent of the hybrid London plane that lines so many European streets, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, and it is planted less often in the Netherlands than its more tolerant offspring. Left to grow on an open square rather than pruned to a street profile, an Oriental plane develops the same flaking, camouflage-patterned bark as its hybrid relative but with a more irregular, spreading crown, often leaning and forking low rather than rising in a single clean trunk.

The register records the species and the decade but nothing of who planted it or why, which is typical for a tree whose interest is simply having survived on the same square for nearly two centuries while whatever stood around it changed. If you know more of De Kring's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of De Kring
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, on the public square.

best_time.label: May, when the white candle-shaped flower spikes cover the crown

trees.story:
This horse chestnut shares De Kring square with the Oriental plane the register also lists nearby, banded to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old and a decade older than its neighbour. Two trees of very different origins, one from the eastern Mediterranean and one from the mountains of the Balkans, ended up planted within a stone's throw of each other on an ordinary Dutch town square, which is itself a small piece of nineteenth century planting fashion: whatever looked handsome and grew reliably got planted, regardless of where it came from.

At close to two centuries a horse chestnut has usually developed the full domed crown and heavy lower limbs the species is known for, wide enough that a tree this age can shade most of a small square by itself. Every May it produces the upright white candle-shaped flower spikes chestnuts are grown for everywhere, and by autumn the ground beneath is scattered with the spiny green cases and glossy conkers that generations of Dutch children have collected from trees exactly like this one.

The register gives no history beyond species and decade. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Catalpa of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: July, when the orchid-like flowers open in loose clusters across the crown

trees.story:
This catalpa stands southwest of a building on Burgerhoutsestraat, banded by the national register to a planting around 1900, roughly 130 years old. A London plane the register also lists grows at the front of the same building, so the property carries two registered trees framing it from different sides, one native to the eastern United States and one a hybrid bred in seventeenth century Europe.

Southern catalpa is grown for its broad, heart-shaped leaves and, through midsummer, loose clusters of white flowers marked with purple and yellow spots inside each throat, followed by long, bean-like seed pods that can hang on the bare branches well into winter, giving the species its other common name, Indian bean tree, despite having no connection to India.

A catalpa at 130 years is well into a mature specimen's proportions, wide-crowned and often leaning or multi-stemmed if it was ever cut back hard when young. The register records nothing of who planted it or why, only the species and the decade. If you know more about this tree or the building it stands beside, tell us.

trees.name: The Beech of Vrouwenhof
trees.age: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
This beech stands behind Restaurant Vrouwenhof, banded by the national register to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old. Left alone behind a building rather than beside a road, a beech this age has usually had the easiest kind of life the species can have: no pruning against traffic, no root compaction from foot or vehicle traffic, room enough to build the wide, low, dome-shaped crown that beeches produce when nothing crowds them.

A beech's bark stays smooth and grey its entire life, never cracking into plates the way an oak's does, which is part of why old beeches are the trees most often carved with initials that never grow over. At nearly two centuries this one has likely accumulated its share, along with the deep leaf litter underneath that beech woodland is known for, since almost nothing grows in the permanent shade a mature beech casts.

The register describes nothing of the tree's own history beyond species and decade, which is typical for a tree valued for standing rather than for any single event attached to it. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Poplar of the Bloemenmarkt
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, on the public square.
trees.story:
This Canadian poplar grows on a car park at the Bloemenmarkt, Roosendaal's flower market square, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. Canadian poplar is itself a hybrid, crossed from American and European black poplars sometime in the eighteenth century and planted across Europe ever since for how fast it grows: a young tree can add a metre or more of height a year, reaching a size in a few decades that other species take a century to match.

That speed comes at a cost in longevity and structural soundness, so a Canadian poplar surviving to 160 years, on a car park rather than in a sheltered park setting, is a genuinely long run for the species. Poplars of this age often carry visible deadwood and cavities, part of what makes a veteran specimen valuable as habitat even as it becomes more likely to lose limbs in storms.

The register records nothing about this tree beyond its species and decade. Growing up on a car park rather than a green space is an unusual setting for the list; if you know how it came to be there, tell us.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Pond
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: May, when the white flower spikes cover the crown and reflect in the pond

trees.story:
This horse chestnut stands behind the pond in Emile van Loonpark, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. The park's own lime, registered elsewhere on this list's original candidates, was declared dead as far back as 1998, which makes this chestnut the park's surviving veteran rather than one of a matched pair.

A horse chestnut planted beside water has usually had reliable growing conditions its whole life, and at 160 years this one should show the full domed crown and heavy branch structure the species develops when left largely alone. Every May it produces the upright white flower spikes chestnuts are planted for across Europe, and reflected in the pond behind it, the display reads differently than a chestnut standing on hard pavement elsewhere in this list.

The register gives no further history for this tree, only species and decade. Emile van Loonpark is public and open daily, and this chestnut is the reason to walk to the far side of the pond rather than stopping at the park's edge. If you know more about it, tell us.

trees.name: The Plane of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
