This London plane stands at the front of the same Burgerhoutsestraat building whose southwest corner holds a registered catalpa, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old and a generation younger than its catalpa neighbour on the other side of the same property.

London plane is the hybrid that resulted from crossing an American and an Oriental species in seventeenth century Europe, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, air pollution and hard pruning better than almost any other large tree available, which is why it became the default choice for European streets and squares from the eighteenth century onward. Its bark flakes away in patches rather than splitting, leaving a mottled grey, green and cream pattern across the trunk that keeps changing as old plates drop and new bark shows through underneath.

At the front of a building rather than tucked behind it, this plane has likely had more pruning against passing traffic than its catalpa neighbour, which a plane tolerates without much complaint. The register records only species and decade. If you know the building's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Park Plane
trees.access: Free, open park at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, near the Euromast, roughly 15 minutes
trees.story: This plane tree was already standing when father-and-son landscape architects Jan David and Louis Paul Zocher began designing het Park around it in 1852, which means the tree came first and the celebrated English-style landscape grew up around a specimen nobody planted specifically for the design. It has since survived two disasters that reshaped Rotterdam far more than any garden ever could. The German bombing of May 1940 destroyed most of the city's historic centre a short walk away; the tree stood close enough to feel it and far enough to survive. Thirteen years later the North Sea flood of 1953 put het Park itself underwater for an extended stretch, one of the worst natural disasters in modern Dutch history, and the tree came through that too, roots submerged in salt water that killed less established trees outright. Today its trunk measures 185 centimetres across, thick enough that the city's own tree inspectors check it on a regular safety schedule reserved for its most significant specimens. Het Park itself is a national monument, 21 hectares running along the Maas river beside the Euromast, and this plane is the one tree in it old enough to have watched the whole modern city rebuild itself twice.

trees.name: The Breitenbach Plane
trees.access: Free, public street at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, roughly 10 minutes
trees.story: This plane tree has been standing since 1860, older than the Westersingel canal that now runs beside it, and it survived the one event that erased almost everything else nearby: the German bombing of Rotterdam's city centre on 14 May 1940, which burned through this exact stretch of the city and somehow left the tree unscathed. Decades of care since have earned it an unofficial title, the most expensive tree in Rotterdam, for the sustained municipal maintenance a tree this old and this large now requires. It nearly lost a different fight in the 1960s, when a major redesign of the Westersingel waterway put the tree directly in the way of new plans; the city's own head of landscaping at the time, Andre Raad, pushed back hard enough that engineers rerouted the water instead of felling the tree, an unusual case of a canal moving to accommodate a plant rather than the other way round. Its more recent name comes from South African poet Breyten Breytenbach, who recited poetry beneath it in the 1970s and declared it the grave of the unknown poet, a line that stuck well enough that Rotterdam's own Poetry International later gave the spot a permanent place in the city's poetry trail. It still stands at the corner of Mauritsweg and Westersingel, doing the same job it has done since before the Netherlands had a railway.

trees.name: The Westersingel Plane
trees.access: Free, public street at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, roughly 10 minutes
trees.story: Moving a mature tree across a street sounds like a euphemism for felling it and planting a new one, but Rotterdam actually did it: sometime in the 1960s, engineers transplanted this plane tree bodily from the west side of the Westersingel canal to the east side, roots and all, rather than lose it to whatever roadworks or redesign prompted the move. It survived the operation and kept growing, now roughly 130 years old and widely considered one of Rotterdam's most impressive individual trees, a status confirmed in 2021 when it placed second in the Netherlands' national Tree of the Year competition, a public vote that draws entries from across the country. The achievement is not really about beauty or age alone. Rotterdam has fewer monumental trees than almost any comparable Dutch city, a direct consequence of the 1940 bombing that flattened its historic centre and the soft, subsiding soil across much of the region that shortens most trees' working lives regardless of what happens above ground. A plane tree that not only reached this size but survived being dug up and relocated says something about the species' famous toughness along waterways, and about a city that has had unusually good reason to fight for the few old trees it has left.

trees.name: The Wilhelmina Linden
trees.access: Free, public street at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, roughly 10-15 minutes
trees.story: An 18-year-old queen's coronation once triggered a small nationwide planting spree, and this linden on the Parklaan is Rotterdam's surviving entry in it. When Wilhelmina was crowned Queen of the Netherlands on 6 September 1898, a metalworks foundry in Doetinchem sent a brochure to every Dutch municipality suggesting they mark the occasion with a commemorative tree, offering to supply the decorative iron fencing to go around it. Towns across the country took up the idea, and Rotterdam planted this Crimean linden on the Parklaan, in what was then a fashionable new residential quarter for the city's shipping merchants. The tree's iron fence has outlasted plenty of the era's other civic gestures: it holds its own listing on the Dutch national heritage register, a decorative object protected separately from the tree it surrounds, which is either a bureaucratic curiosity or a sign of how seriously the country still takes its handful of surviving coronation trees. At roughly 128 years old, the linden has outlived the queen it honours by more than seven decades and stands a quiet, well-tended reminder that Rotterdam's grandest 19th-century street was, for one afternoon in 1898, briefly about a young monarch rather than shipping money.

trees.name: The Koningin Emmaplein Beech
trees.access: Free, public square at any time
trees.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, roughly 10-15 minutes
trees.story: Fifteen grand townhouses built between 1888 and 1891 once earned this small square a joking nickname, Rijkeluishofje, the rich people's almshouse, a dig at how sheltered and comfortable its wealthy residents had it compared with the actual almshouses the word usually described. The copper beech at its centre went into the ground around the same years the houses went up, planted alongside a decorative 1890 urn designed by Hendrik Berlage, the architect who would later define much of Amsterdam's own cityscape. The neo-renaissance townhouses around the square housed Rotterdam's shipping elite, close enough to the harbour to manage their businesses and far enough from it to avoid the noise and smell, and the beech has stood at the centre of that arrangement for roughly 135 years, its trunk now 325 centimetres around. Copper beeches are planted for their colour, deep purple-red leaves that shift with the season and light rather than staying a uniform green, and this one has had over a century to fill out into the kind of specimen that makes an otherwise ordinary residential square worth a detour. It remains free and open, a short walk from the Westersingel and Parklaan trees on the same side of the city centre.

trees.name: The Lijnbaan Plane
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Rotterdam; about a 10 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.story:
This plane was likely planted in 1851 in the garden of the Coolsingel hospital, and it was still there in May 1940 when German bombing destroyed most of Rotterdam's city centre in a single night, the hospital included. Only the tree and the building's entrance gate came through. The gate stands beside the plane today, the two of them forming what Rotterdammers now treat as an accidental monument neither was designed to be.

The tree nearly lost a different fight two decades later. When the Lijnbaan, one of Europe's first purpose-built pedestrian shopping streets, was extended and renovated in the 1960s, the plan called for a dead straight line the tree and gate stood directly in the way of. Shopkeepers fought the compromise that saved them and lost; the street bent anyway, a small square was built around the tree instead, and the shops went up around that. A Rotterdam poet, Pascale Duin, later wrote it an ode calling it a silent witness. In 2019 it was nominated to represent the whole province of Zuid-Holland in the national Tree of the Year contest. It stands free, in the open, one of two Rotterdam planes known to have survived the exact night that erased almost everything around them.

trees.name: The Memorial Yew of Eendrachtsplein
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Rotterdam; about a 12 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.story:
Rotterdam spent its first postwar years rebuilding rather than remembering, and it took one person to insist on a place to do both: Willem Ganter, first violinist of the Rotterdam Philharmonic Orchestra, who raised money for a memorial tree at the garden of the police station on Eendrachtsplein, a spot the city had trusted people to gather at even during the occupation. A 20-year-old European yew was ordered from England and planted in 1947, already a substantial tree rather than a sapling, because a memorial planted small would have taken decades to look like one.

The yew has had a harder life since than the plan intended. A new tram line cut through the area, then a metro line in 1983, and the police eventually moved out of the building entirely, which is now a cafe. The tree itself once grew on two trunks and now stands on one, having lost the other somewhere along the way, and simply outlasted every change around it regardless. Had Ganter chosen a less tenacious species, none of this would have survived to be told. It stands free, in the open, beside the entrance of the building it has outlived every use of.

trees.name: The Planes of Delftseplein
trees.species: London Plane and Oriental Plane (Platanus x acerifolia and Platanus orientalis)
trees.access: Free, public square, open at any time
trees.transport: Immediately east of Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.story:
Four planes, three London and one Oriental, went into the ground together around 1860 as planting around a pond that once sat in front of Rotterdam's original Centraal Station entrance. The pond and that entrance are both gone, replaced by later station buildings, but the trees stayed on Delftseplein through every rebuild the station itself went through, including the one that flattened most of the surrounding neighbourhood in May 1940.

Mixing Oriental plane in with the more common London plane hybrid in one planting was not unusual for 19th-century Dutch civic gardening, a hedge against uncertainty about which would thrive better on reclaimed, disturbed ground next to a working rail yard. Whichever species won that test is no longer the point; all four have made it past a century and a half. They stand together, free, immediately east of the current station building, close enough that anyone stepping off a train into Rotterdam is likely to walk past the oldest trees on the whole route without knowing it.

trees.name: The Plane of Westersingel
trees.access: Free, public street, open at any time
trees.transport: Centrum, central Rotterdam; about a 12 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal station
trees.story:
This London plane stands at a junction most people pass through rather than stop at, where the Westersingel canal crosses the Mauritsweg and Witte de Withstraat, planted sometime around 1900 to 1910 as the streets around it took their current shape. It is younger than the two more storied planes elsewhere on the same Westersingel, the one that survived the 1940 bombing and the one a South African poet once read verse beneath, and it carries no comparable story of its own beyond simply having grown steadily at a crossing for over a century.

That plainness is not nothing. Most street trees this old in a heavily bombed, heavily rebuilt city do not make it, and this one has, standing through whatever traffic patterns and canal-side redevelopment the junction has seen since the Edwardian era. It grows in the open, free, on the same short stretch of canal that carries two of Rotterdam's more famous trees, worth a stop on the same walk rather than a destination by itself.

trees.name: S'Ozzastru
trees.access: Paid entry, 5 EUR, guided visit only. Open 1 April to 2 November, visits from 10:30. Managed tourist site with ticket office, picnic area and Lake Liscia boat trips.
trees.transport: No public transport; a car is the realistic way, roughly 20 minutes from Luras or Tempio Pausania. On-site parking at the visitor centre.
trees.story:
Italy's oldest living tree has an age nobody can pin down within fifteen centuries. S'Ozzastru is a wild olive at Santu Baltolu di Carana, outside Luras in the granite hills of Gallura, and Sardinians call it su babbu mannu, the great father, or the patriarch of all wild olives. The University of Sassari puts it between 2,500 and 4,000 years old. The site that manages it says 3,000 to 4,000. The Piedmontese botanist Bruno Peyronel once suggested more than 5,000, a figure that comes with no scientific data behind it and which he applied to other trees just as freely. All of them are estimates, because an ancient olive hollows out and loses the heartwood any ring count would need, and this trunk is hollow.

The measurements are firmer, and they are what makes the visit. The trunk runs 11.5 metres around, the tree stands 14 metres tall and the crown spreads about 21 metres, which is a wild olive behaving like an oak. Sardinia declared it a national natural monument in 1991.

It is not a tree you stumble on. The grove is a managed site now, with a ticket office, a path and a guide, open from April to early November, and a second ancient olivastro stands a few metres along the same walk.

trees.name: The Second Olivastro of Santu Baltolu
trees.access: Same paid site as S'Ozzastru: 5 EUR guided visit, open 1 April to 2 November from 10:30.
trees.transport: Same as S'Ozzastru, on the same visitor path a few metres from the main tree. A car is the realistic way, roughly 20 minutes from Luras or Tempio Pausania.
trees.story:
This tree has no name of its own, which is the clearest measure of what standing next to S'Ozzastru costs a tree. Almost anywhere else on Sardinia it would be the reason people came. Here it is the one they photograph on the way back to the car. The second olivastro of Santu Baltolu is a wild olive with a trunk 5.4 metres around, less than half its neighbour's 11.5, and that ratio is the only thing that makes it read as small. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists it separately, on its own sheet, and it shares the 1991 natural monument designation that protects the grove.

Its age is the loosest figure on this page. Sardinian sources put it at around 2,000 years and none of them shows any working at all, so read that as a guess in roughly the right neighbourhood rather than a measurement. Nobody has taken a proper dating to it. If you have seen one published, tell us.

What is not in doubt is the species and the setting. Wild olives are what the Mediterranean grew before anyone cultivated anything, and two of them at this size, in the same thin Gallurese soil, on the same short guided walk, is the genuinely rare part.

trees.name: The Olivastro of Santa Maria Navarrese
trees.access: Free, standing in a public square beside the church, open at all times.
trees.transport: In the village of Santa Maria Navarrese, a coastal frazione of Baunei; walkable from the harbour and beach. A car is the realistic way to reach the village itself, about 150 km south of the Luras trees.
trees.story:
Somebody tried to burn this tree down in the early 1960s and the fire scars are still on the trunk. The olivastro of Santa Maria Navarrese survived the arson and is still rated in good condition by the region's own foresters, despite a trunk that is partly hollow, which is the usual state of an olive this old.

It stands in the village square beside the church of Santa Maria di Navarra, built in 1502 and, on every estimate anyone has offered, many centuries younger than the tree next to it. Sardinia's forestry agency measures the trunk at 8.40 metres around at 1.3 metres up, with a crown of 9 to 10 metres. The national register gives a slightly larger figure, 9.05 metres, probably taken at a different point on the trunk; nobody has reconciled the two.

The age is stated loosely on purpose. The regional agency calls it millenario, at least a thousand years, and gives no number. Local press quotes botanists at about 2,000. Neither figure comes with any working attached, and no one has published a dating.

The Region declared it a natural monument in January 1994, along with the other old olives, carobs and hackberries in the same square. It is free, in the open, and a short walk up from the harbour.

trees.name: The Ancient Trees of San Pietro in Golgo
trees.species: Wild Olive and Mediterranean Hackberry (Olea europaea var. sylvestris and Celtis australis)
trees.access: Free, a working rural church on open plateau land reached by the paved road up from Baunei (about 13km); also a stop on the Selvaggio Blu and other hiking routes. No gate, no fee found in any source checked.
trees.transport: No public transport; a car is the realistic way, roughly 20 to 25 minutes up the plateau road from Baunei. Frequently visited alongside the Su Sterru sinkhole nearby.
trees.story:
Nobody has ever put an age to these trees, and up on the Golgo plateau that feels about right. A small rural church, San Pietro, sits 13 kilometres above Baunei on a lava tableland, and it is flanked by aged wild olives and hackberries. Two of them are registered individually in Italy's national inventory of monumental trees: a wild olive with a trunk 5.68 metres around and a hackberry at 5.25 metres, standing effectively on the same spot. Sardinia's own forestry service describes the church in exactly those words, fiancheggiata da annosi olivastri e bagolari, flanked by aged wild olives and hackberries.

There is no age field anywhere for either of them and no source ventures a guess, so this page does not either. If somebody has measured them, send it to us.

The setting does most of the work. Shepherds' stone huts, the cumbessias, stand alongside the church and still fill for the annual festival, and the Su Sterru sinkhole opens in the ground nearby, which is what brings most people up the road in the first place. The long-distance Selvaggio Blu route passes through. There is no gate and no fee, and the church itself is the place to stand.

trees.name: The Cedar of Parco Aymerich
trees.age: roughly 190 years, if the 1835 planting date is accurate
trees.access: Free, open daily roughly 8:00-20:00 depending on season, managed by SardegnaForeste, the state forestry agency. Public urban park, no restriction.
trees.transport: Short walk from Laconi town centre (Piazza Marconi / Palazzo Aymerich) to the main entrance at Su Acili. Laconi is inland in the Sarcidano hills, so a car is the realistic way to reach the town.

best_time.label: autumn, when the upright cones stand along the branches

trees.story:
A Sardinian marquis with a botany habit is said to have planted this cedar in 1835, when it was already six years old, as one of the first Cedars of Lebanon brought into Europe. That account runs consistently through Sardinian sources, but the page citing it most directly is now dead, so treat the date as reported rather than proved. What two official bodies do confirm is the setting. Ignazio Aymerich began laying out this park from 1830 and filled it with rare exotic species, and the regional forestry agency that runs the park today calls the cedar imponente and the oldest of its kind on the island.

Take the 1835 date at face value and the tree is about 190 years old, which by cedar standards is early middle age; the species routinely runs past a thousand in its native Lebanon. The national register measures it at 4.4 metres round and 29 metres tall.

One detail nobody mentions: an oriental plane a few metres away is actually the thicker tree, at 4.5 metres round. The cedar is simply the one everybody comes for. The park is free and open daily under the state forestry agency, a short walk from Laconi's Piazza Marconi and the Palazzo Aymerich down to the Su Acili entrance.

trees.name: Seward Park's Big Tree
trees.access: Free, city park, open trails during park hours
trees.transport: King County Metro Route 50 stops at Seward Park Ave S and S Orcas St, at the park entrance; the old-growth interior is a further walk into the peninsula
trees.story:
Seattle's oldest known tree still carries the burn marks of two fires, one in 1508 and one in 1701, when the Puget lowlands went up and this Douglas fir did not. The scarred bark is on the trunk, which is about seven feet across. The tree is around 150 feet tall.

How old is a matter of who you ask. Friends of Seward Park, the group that looks after the forest, says 500 years. Seattle Magazine says over 400. Somewhere in that band is the honest answer, and either end of it means this tree was a mature fir before any European saw Puget Sound. Bald eagles have nested in it.

It used to carry a Heritage Tree plaque. The plaque was taken down because the number of people walking in to see it was wearing the ground away over the roots, which tells you both how good the tree is and how to behave around it.

No source publishes where it stands inside the 120 acres of old growth on the Bailey Peninsula, so the pin marks the park rather than the trunk and finding it is part of the afternoon. One warning: the young fir the park's printed tree walk starts with, near the Audubon building, is a different tree and a couple of centuries younger.

trees.name: The Volunteer Park Giant Sequoia
trees.access: Free, city park, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Metro routes 10 and 12 stop within a few blocks on 15th Ave E / E Galer St; about a 5 minute walk
trees.story:
The only measurements ever published about this sequoia are not measurements of this sequoia. The city's own tree walk, which lists it as stop 9 on the north east loop of Volunteer Park, describes it growing to 280 feet with a trunk 26 feet through. Those are the figures for the species, the largest tree on earth by volume, and nobody has put a tape around this particular trunk.

What the leaflet does confirm is the tree: a good giant sequoia standing near East Highland Drive, with the thick spongy bark that is the easiest way to identify one, and the only way to identify one without looking up.

Its age is unrecorded. Volunteer Park was landscaped by the Olmsted Brothers between 1904 and 1912, and it is tempting to date the sequoia from that work, but no source connects this tree to it, so it stays undated here rather than dated by association.

Which means there is a question on this page that somebody in Capitol Hill can answer. If you have a planting record, a nursery receipt, an old photograph of this corner of the park or simply a tape measure and a free afternoon, tell us and we will fill the gap in.

The pin marks the north east corner of the park rather than the tree.

trees.name: The Grand Fir of Kubota Garden
trees.access: Free, city park (Seattle Parks), open daylight hours
trees.transport: Metro Route 106 stops on Renton Ave S near the garden entrance; about a 5-10 minute walk
trees.story:
When Fujitaro Kubota bought this land in 1927 it had been logged, and this grand fir was one of the few trees the loggers had left. Everything else you walk past in Kubota Garden was planted afterwards, around it. The garden is the newcomer.

It now stands 139 feet tall at the base of the Spring Pond, below the Terrace Overlook, and the tree walk that covers the garden estimates it at 200 years old. That figure comes from a single document, the walk produced jointly by the city's Trees for Seattle programme and the Kubota Garden Foundation, and no second source has confirmed it, so read it as a good estimate rather than a settled number. Grand firs live comfortably beyond 250 years, so the estimate sits well within what the species does.

The interest here is the contrast. Kubota spent decades building a Japanese garden out of Pacific Northwest plants, and this fir is the piece of the actual Pacific Northwest forest that was already on the site when he started, a survivor of the original woodland standing over ponds and stone that were arranged much later.

The garden is free and open in daylight hours. The pin marks the entrance rather than the tree, so walk in and head for the Spring Pond below the Terrace Overlook.

trees.name: The Bigcone Douglas Fir of Washington Park Arboretum
trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Metro Route 11 stops on Madison St near the Arboretum entrances; several trailheads within a 5-10 minute walk of stops
trees.story:
This fir is about a thousand miles from where its species grows wild. Pseudotsuga macrocarpa is native only to the mountains of southern California, and the largest one known in Washington State is standing in a public arboretum in Seattle.

It was recorded as a state champion in Robert Van Pelt's 2003 survey of Washington's biggest trees, and the University of Washington Botanic Gardens, who run the Arboretum, list it as one of their champions and have been re-measuring it. Both of those threads run back to the same 2003 survey, so the title rests on one original piece of fieldwork rather than two.

The reason to walk out and see it is in the name. Bigcone Douglas fir carries by far the largest cones in its genus, several times the size of the ones that litter every pavement in this part of the world, and a tree that size drops them where you can pick one up. It is a curiosity rather than a giant, and it is the sort of thing an arboretum exists for.

No age or girth has been published for it. It stands on the Upper Trail just south of the Pacific Connections New Zealand Forest Garden, at the south end of the Arboretum; the pin marks the Arboretum itself.

trees.name: The AYPE Lombardy Poplar
trees.access: Free, open university campus grounds
trees.transport: Link light rail U District or UW Station; multiple Metro routes serve the campus; short walk to Stevens Way

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns yellow

trees.story:
This poplar is a leftover from a world's fair. The Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition of 1909 was held on this part of the University of Washington campus, and the university's own campus tree tour dates this burly trunk to that event, which makes it about 115 to 120 years old and one of the few living things on the grounds that saw the fair.

The building across the street backs the date up. Architecture Hall was built as the Fine Arts Palace for the same exposition, and it and the poplar have stood facing each other on the corner of Stevens Way ever since, one of them looking rather more temporary than the other.

A Lombardy poplar is a narrow upright form of black poplar, grown from cuttings rather than seed, which is why they all look identical and why they turn up in rows along drives and boundaries. This one is not a record holder and does not claim to be: bigger Lombardy poplars have been claimed elsewhere in Seattle. Its distinction is that somebody wrote down where it came from.

Campus grounds are open and free. The pin uses the campus centre, so navigate to the corner of Stevens Way and Grant Lane, opposite Architecture Hall, and look up.

trees.name: The Munmyo Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, within the Sungkyunkwan / Munmyo Confucian Shrine grounds, open daily during visiting hours.
trees.transport: Hyehwa Station (Line 4), Exit 4, about a 10 minute walk.

best_time.label: mid-to-late November, when the canopy turns gold

trees.story:
In 1519, Sungkyunkwan's head instructor Yun Tak planted this ginkgo for a very specific reason: shade for the students memorizing Confucian classics in the courtyard below, and, tradition says, because ginkgos rarely catch fire, a reassuring quality beside wooden lecture halls. Five centuries on, the tree the scholars studied under is now one of the largest ginkgos in Korea, its trunk swollen to over seven metres around and its crown spreading twenty two metres, roughly the width of a basketball court laid sideways.

Look closely at the trunk and you will see it is not one shoot but several, fused: the original stem died back at some point in its long life and seven new trunks grew from the base, knitting themselves into the single giant standing today. Three club shaped aerial roots, called yuju, hang from its lower branches, a feature that only appears on ginkgos of serious age. Rare for such an old specimen, this is a male tree, so it never drops the notoriously pungent fruit that carpets ginkgo lined streets across Seoul every autumn.

It stands in the Munmyo shrine courtyard, part of Sungkyunkwan, Korea's Confucian royal academy founded in 1398, meaning students have been examined within sight of this tree for as long as most countries have had a fixed capital city.

photo.attribution: Cultural Heritage Administration of Korea, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Changdeokgung Chinese Juniper
trees.access: Paid entry, general Changdeokgung Palace admission (around KRW 3,000); included on the standard palace route.
trees.transport: Anguk Station (Line 3), Exit 3, about a 5 minute walk to the palace entrance.
trees.story:
Look up and this Chinese juniper does not read as a tree so much as a gesture: a trunk that twists and climbs, missing one whole limb, shaped by more history than Changdeokgung Palace itself has stood. Court records describe its form as a dragon ascending to heaven, and once you see the comparison it is hard to unsee. The surviving eastern branch spirals upward in a genuine coil, while the southern branch was cut long ago and the northern one died on its own.

Planted an estimated seven and a half centuries ago, before Changdeokgung existed, the juniper predates every building around it and has outlived the Joseon dynasty that built them. It has needed help to keep going: a 2010 typhoon tore into its already reduced crown, and conservators have since propped and cabled what remains. What is left is still remarkable, a living fragment that Joseon kings would have walked past on their way to court business, its aromatic wood once prized for temple incense.

Reaching it means walking the same courtyards the royal family used for five centuries, past halls now designated national treasures. The juniper needs no separate ticket. It is simply there, along the path, doing what it has done since before Korea had a Joseon king to rule it.

trees.name: The Banghak-dong Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, viewable from the roadside; a low fence protects the root area so visitors view it from just outside rather than at the trunk.
trees.transport: Ssangmun Station (Line 4), then bus 130 to the Yeonsangun-myo stop, 6 minute walk.

best_time.label: November, when its huge crown turns bright yellow

trees.story:
When Seoul designated its very first protected tree in 1968, officials wrote down its age as 830 years. In 2013, the National Institute of Forest Science ran an actual scientific survey and came back with a very different number: closer to 550. Whichever figure is right, and this treats both as honest possibilities rather than picking a winner, it remains one of the oldest ginkgos anyone in the city can point to.

Locals call it the patriotic tree, because legend says a mysterious fire appeared on its trunk ahead of major national crises, most notably in 1910, the year Japan annexed Korea. Villagers pitched tents around its base in 1991 to stop an apartment development from bulldozing it, and won. The tree also carries yuju, drooping growths shaped like a woman's breast, which folk belief once treated as a sign of fertility and made the tree an object of local prayer.

Its neighbor is Korea's most reviled monarch. Yeonsangun, the tyrant king deposed in 1506, is buried on the hillside directly across from it, exiled even in death to the edge of the old capital. The ginkgo has stood watch over that grave for longer than anyone can precisely say, which is, in the end, the most honest thing you can say about it.

trees.name: The Jaedong Lacebark Pine
trees.access: Free, visible from the street and the Constitutional Court's public front garden.
trees.transport: Anguk Station (Line 3), Exit 1, about a 5 minute walk.
trees.story:
This pine is not native to Korea. It is Pinus bungeana, a lacebark pine from China, and the story goes that a Ming dynasty envoy brought it here as a gift some six centuries ago, though nobody can prove that part and it may well be a flattering exaggeration attached after the fact. What is certain is the tree itself: bark that flakes away in pale patches until entire sections of trunk look bone white, which is why Koreans call it baeksong, white pine.

A single trunk splits near the ground into what looks like two separate pines standing side by side, an accident of growth that makes it read as a pair rather than one seventeen metre specimen. Political legend has attached itself here too. The 19th century regent Heungseon Daewongun is said to have plotted the downfall of the powerful Andong Kim clan from a pavilion that once stood beside this very tree, watching it as he worked out how to break their grip on the throne.

The pine has outlasted the girls' high school that used to occupy this land and now stands on the grounds of South Korea's Constitutional Court, a small irony given its own role, real or invented, in a much older struggle for power.

trees.name: The Siheung-dong Ginkgos
trees.access: Free, standing at a public road intersection.
trees.transport: Geumcheon-gu Office Station (Line 1), then village bus Geumcheon-01 to the Ginkgo Tree stop, 2 minute walk.

best_time.label: November, when all the ginkgos on the intersection turn gold together

trees.story:
Five roads meet at a point in Geumcheon-gu named, quite literally, Ginkgo Tree Intersection, and the trees that gave it the name are still standing at the center of it. Local accounts count either two or three ginkgos here, depending on which one you read, all reputed to be pushing 880 years old, though that figure comes from oral tradition and district registration rather than a scientific tree ring survey, so it is treated here as a well worn estimate rather than a proven fact.

What is documented is the history underneath them. This was the site of Siheung Haenggung, a royal way station where King Jeongjo stopped overnight in the late 18th century on his repeated processions south to visit the tomb of his father, Crown Prince Sado, who had been executed by being sealed inside a rice chest on his grandfather's orders. Jeongjo's journeys here were recorded in exhaustive court detail, down to the meals served, and the ginkgos would already have been centuries old when his procession passed beneath them.

The palace itself is gone, absorbed long ago into the ordinary streets of southern Seoul. The ginkgos are what is left of it, roots planted in what was once a royal courtyard and is now a traffic circle, still marking the spot where five roads meet.

trees.name: The Hwayang-dong Zelkova
trees.access: Free, in a small public green space in Hwayang-dong.
trees.transport: Konkuk University Station (Lines 2 and 7), about a 20 minute walk or a short ride on bus 102.

best_time.label: November, when the crown turns a deep orange-brown

trees.story:
A queen once caught her breath under this tree while fleeing a mutiny. In 1882, soldiers enraged over unpaid wages and foreign favoritism stormed the palace in what became known as the Imo Incident, and Queen Min, who would later be assassinated by Japanese agents in 1895, escaped the capital in disguise. Her route south took her past Hwayangjeong, a royal pavilion built here during King Sejong's reign in the early 15th century, where she is recorded to have rested.

The pavilion is long gone, but the zelkova that stood beside it has not moved in roughly seven centuries. It has grown into a proper giant, twenty eight metres tall with a trunk seven and a half metres around, splitting into four massive limbs a couple of metres above the ground. Age and weight have not been kind to it: sections of the trunk have been treated for rot, and metal supports now brace the upper branches so they do not tear away from their own bulk.

Six younger zelkovas have grown up around the original tree over the centuries, forming an informal grove, but this is the one the Cultural Heritage Administration singled out, the one that was already ancient when a fleeing queen needed somewhere to stop.

photo.attribution: Cultural Heritage Administration of Korea, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Sillim-dong Cork Oak
trees.access: Free, inside the grounds of Geonyoung Apartment Complex 2; a marked path leads to the tree, though it sits on residential grounds so visit considerately.
trees.transport: Sillim Station (Line 2), about a 15 to 20 minute walk, or a short bus or taxi ride.
trees.story:
Legend says this oak grew from a walking stick. General Gang Gam-chan, the Goryeo dynasty commander who crushed a Khitan invasion in 1019, is supposed to have planted his cane here near his birthplace a thousand years ago, and the story is charming enough that it still gets repeated in tourist brochures today. It is also almost certainly not true as stated: when the Cultural Heritage Administration surveyed the tree before designating it a Natural Monument in 1982, its estimated age came out to roughly 250 years, not a thousand. The honest reading is that this is very likely a successor tree grown near a site the legend had already attached itself to, not the original.

Set that aside and there is still a genuinely old, sizeable cork oak worth seeing, its bark thick and deeply corked in the way that gives the species its name, standing barely ten metres from the wall of an apartment block that eventually grew up around it rather than the other way round. Its branches reach nearly ten metres east and west, a wide spread for a tree squeezed into residential grounds.

It shares its neighborhood with Nakseongdae, the park built around Gang Gam-chan's actual birthplace, so the legend, even if botanically shaky, at least has the right zip code.

photo.attribution: Cultural Heritage Administration of Korea, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Jogyesa Pagoda Tree
trees.access: Free, in the main courtyard of Jogyesa Temple, open daily.
trees.transport: Jonggak Station (Line 1), Exit 2, about a 5 minute walk.

best_time.label: July and August, when it drapes the courtyard in cream-colored flower clusters

trees.story:
Every year on Buddha's Birthday, thousands of paper lanterns get strung through this tree's canopy until the entire crown disappears under a ceiling of color, and it is large enough to make that possible: its branches spread wide enough to shade the whole courtyard in front of Jogyesa's main hall. What most visitors do not realize is that the tree is far older than the temple around it. Jogyesa's current Daeungjeon hall was only built in 1938, relocated log by log from a temple in Jeongju, while this pagoda tree had already been growing on this spot in central Seoul for roughly four centuries.

The species, Styphnolobium japonicum, was traditionally planted at Confucian academies and scholars' homes across East Asia in the belief that it brought good fortune and produced distinguished sons, which explains why old specimens turn up so often at former noble residences around Seoul rather than only at temples. In July and August it produces long, drooping clusters of small cream flowers that dust the courtyard stones below.

Jogyesa sits in the middle of downtown Seoul, a five minute walk from either Jonggak or Anguk subway stations, so the tree gets more foot traffic than almost anything else on this list, most of it people who came for the temple and only noticed the tree once they were standing under it.

trees.name: The Ginkgo Grove of the Real Alcázar
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds

best_time.label: December into January, when every leaf turns uniform gold within days

trees.story: Ten of these ginkgos are Seville survivors from a delivery of twenty-five. The trees arrived at the Real Alcázar in the autumn and winter of 1910, part of a shipment from the Royal Site of La Granja de San Ildefonso near Segovia, sent south to plant the palace's new English Garden, a cooler, shadier counterpoint to the clipped Andalusi courtyards elsewhere in the grounds. Fifteen didn't survive more than a century of Seville's dry heat, a climate ginkgos tolerate poorly compared to the temperate gardens they came from. The ten that did are now among the oldest ginkgos in Andalusia, and every December and January they do something nothing else in the garden does: every leaf turns the same intense yellow within days of each other, a uniform gold that stands out hard against the evergreen palms, cypresses and citrus around it. The species survived in the wild only in a few restricted pockets of China, kept alive for centuries as a sacred tree in Chinese and Japanese temple gardens before European botanists began exporting it in the 18th century. Its old Chinese name means duck's foot, a reference to the fan-shaped leaf that later inspired Goethe to write an entire poem about the tree's paired, seemingly single lobes. The Alcázar's ginkgos arrived almost a century after Goethe wrote it, foreign transplants in a garden that was already centuries old by the time they showed up.

photo.attribution: Juan carlos boza, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Ombú of La Cartuja
trees.access: Paid entry (CAAC museum ticket, 3.01 euros; free Tuesday-Friday 19:00-21:00 and Saturday 11:00-21:00)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Cartuja tram stop (T1), or bus C1/C2
trees.story: This ombú, a soft-wooded relative of spinach that grows to the size of an oak, is said to have come from seeds Hernando Colón, son of Christopher Columbus, brought back from South America and planted in his own private arboretum around 1529. After his death the seeds, or the seedling itself, passed to the Carthusian monks next door, and the tree has stood at the Monasterio de la Cartuja ever since, possibly the first ombú ever grown in Europe. It nearly didn't survive the twentieth century. In the early 1990s, restorers tried to seal cavities in its soft trunk with polyurethane foam, a technique meant for harder wood that instead trapped moisture and fed the fungus already eating the tree from inside. Expo '92 technicians removed the foam before it could finish the job, but the extraction itself caused more damage, and the tree has been left deliberately untouched since. Its wood is famously soft, closer to a swollen vegetable than timber, which is why arborists now recommend a fence and a no-walking perimeter rather than any further intervention. The monastery today houses Andalusia's contemporary art museum, so a tree that may have crossed the Atlantic in a conquistador's son's luggage now shares its courtyard with rotating exhibitions of modern sculpture.

trees.name: The Figs of Plaza del Cristo de Burgos
trees.access: Free, public plaza
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Plaza de la Encarnación or Alameda de Hércules
trees.story: Four of Seville's biggest fig trees didn't start out on this plaza at all. City gardeners moved these Moreton Bay figs here from Parque de María Luisa around 1925, an unusually bold transplant for trees of this size, and they took root well enough that the biggest now measures 7.2 metres around and 28 metres tall. The species, native to the coastal forests of eastern Australia, is known for the buttressed, almost architectural roots it grows to stabilize such a heavy crown, and for aerial roots that descend from its branches and thicken into secondary trunks over time. Every one of the four gets pruned back hard each spring, not for the trees' health but for Easter: Semana Santa's processions route directly through this plaza, and the candle-bearing floats need branches out of the way. The square itself has changed names more often than the trees have changed address, known at various points as Plaza de Argüelles, Plaza Virgen del Pilar and Plaza de San Pedro before settling on its current name, and locals called it the Plaza de las Magnolias for years even though the ficus, not the magnolias, dominate the space today. All four are individually protected on Seville's own register of singular trees, a rare case of a whole relocated group qualifying together rather than one specimen alone.

trees.name: The Cypress of the Glorieta de Bécquer
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa

best_time.label: November, when its needles turn rust-orange before dropping

trees.story: Seville built a monument to its most famous Romantic poet around a tree that had nothing to do with him. The bald cypress at the centre of the Glorieta de Bécquer was already standing, planted sometime between 1850 and 1870, when the city commissioned sculptor Lorenzo Coullaut Valera to surround it with white marble and bronze figures representing three stages of love, a monument inaugurated in 1911, decades before Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer's poetry made this corner of Parque de María Luisa a literary pilgrimage site. The tree itself, native to the swamps of the Mississippi basin, is a curious choice for a Mediterranean city: it needs no flooding to thrive, but it does drop its needles every winter like a broadleaf tree, a trait most conifers don't share. At around 150 to 175 years old, with a trunk 5.82 metres round and a crown reaching 33 metres, it now frames whichever restoration the poet's monument currently needs, which has been more than once. Photographers queue for the same shot from the same bench angle nearly every day of the year. Almost none of them come for the tree.

trees.name: El Gran Capitán
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1)
trees.story: Seville's tallest tree is also one of its least visited, despite standing in the middle of the historic centre. This river red gum, known locally as El Gran Capitán, rises more than 50 metres above the Paseo de Catalina de Ribera at the edge of Jardines de Murillo, a five minute walk from the Real Alcázar's own walls, yet it rarely appears in a single guidebook or walking tour. Its trunk has grown close to five metres around, and in 2025 the city carried out a precision pruning operation specifically to reduce the risk of falling limbs, treating a tree this size with the same caution as a structural repair. Eucalyptus camaldulensis is native to Australian riverbanks, not Andalusian gardens, and it owes its presence here to the same wave of botanical experimentation that filled Parque de María Luisa nearby with Australian figs: gardeners in the early twentieth century testing which imports would thrive in Seville's dry heat. This one thrived almost too well, outgrowing every other tree in the city by a wide margin while somehow staying anonymous. Locals who live nearby walk past it daily without a second look. Visitors headed for the more famous gardens on either side, the Alcázar and the cathedral, pass directly underneath it and rarely notice they've done so.

trees.name: The Centennial Hackberries of María Luisa
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story: Not every tree on this list needed royal patronage or a foreign pedigree to earn its place. The Mediterranean hackberries scattered through Parque de María Luisa, clustered most densely near the Glorieta Rafael de León, the Choza de los Carneros and the Paseo de los Rosales, are a native Iberian species that grew in this soil for generations before any garden was landscaped around it. Several specimens here are recognized as centennial by the city's own singular-trees inventory, prized less for any single record than for the deep, textured shade their slow canopies provide across the park's oldest paths. The species is tough and long-lived, tolerant of drought, poor soil and hard pruning, which is exactly why Seville's gardeners let so many of them stand while faster, showier imports like the park's Australian figs and eucalyptus got the attention. Parque de María Luisa itself was the private garden of the Palacio de San Telmo before Princess María Luisa Fernanda donated part of it to the city in 1893, decades before landscape architect Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier redesigned it for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. These hackberries predate that transformation. They were already old when the glorietas, fountains and pavilions went up around them, quiet holdovers from what the land looked like before it became a park at all.

trees.name: The Trees of the Alameda de Hércules
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Feria or Alameda de Hércules bus stops; 10 min walk from Plaza de la Encarnación
trees.story: Seville's oldest public promenade was built on a swamp, and it takes its name from the trees planted to drain it. The Alameda de Hércules, laid out in 1574 on marshy ground just north of the old city walls, is named for the white poplars, álamos in Spanish, planted to help dry and stabilize the reclaimed land, trees used as infrastructure rather than ornament. Poplars still line the central walkway today, though the ones standing now trace only to a major 1764 replanting that added more than 1,600 trees, not to the original 16th-century planting. At both ends of the promenade stand dense stands of London planes, nearly a century old themselves, that have survived every renovation the square has undergone since, including a long twentieth-century decline and its more recent revival as one of Seville's most popular nightlife streets. Two Roman columns, salvaged from a demolished temple, still stand at the promenade's southern entrance, predating every tree here by more than a millennium and giving the Alameda its Hercules name through a 17th-century statue once mounted on top of one of them. Bars and terraces now crowd the same ground the poplars were planted to drain, four and a half centuries after the swamp they replaced.

trees.name: The Orange Trees of the Patio de los Naranjos
trees.access: Paid entry (Seville Cathedral admission ticket required since 1992)
trees.transport: Inside Seville Cathedral, adjoining the Giralda tower

best_time.label: late February into March, azahar season, when the blossom scents the whole courtyard

trees.story: The orange trees that give Seville Cathedral's most famous courtyard its name aren't nearly as old as the courtyard itself. The Patio de los Naranjos, a rectangular yard 43 by 81 metres, was built between 1172 and 1186 as the ablutions courtyard of the Almohad mosque that once stood on this site, the place worshippers washed before prayer. The mosque came down after the 1248 Christian conquest and the Gothic cathedral rose around the same footprint, but the orange trees visitors photograph today only date to a 20th-century restoration led by architect Félix Hernández, replacing whatever grew here before rather than surviving from it. What has survived intact is more remarkable than any tree: the mosque's minaret, spared demolition entirely, still stands beside the patio as the cathedral's bell tower, known today as the Giralda, and a fountain basin at the courtyard's centre, possibly Roman or Visigothic in origin, still occupies the same spot where the ablutions fountain once stood. For most of its eight centuries this courtyard cost nothing to enter. That changed in 1992, when the cathedral folded it into its paid tourist route, ending a run of open public access longer than most European countries have existed. The orange trees are new. The habit of walking through them for free is the part that's actually gone.

photo.attribution: Roberto Chamoso G, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Fig of the Glorieta de Goya
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Plaza de España, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story: Two marble columns are the only physical trace left of the pavilion this fig tree now grows inside. The Glorieta de Goya, a circular clearing in Parque de María Luisa near Plaza de España, once held a full-scale replica of the Quinta del Sordo, Francisco de Goya's house outside Madrid, built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition and dismantled once the fair closed. Only two four-metre Doric columns from that pavilion's entrance survived the teardown, and they now frame a Moreton Bay fig planted in the same period, introduced to Seville in the early 20th century and naturalized well enough in the local climate that Ficus macrophylla now shows up across the city's parks and plazas. The tree has grown into the columns' role as much as around them, its crown now the dominant feature of a clearing designed to showcase a painter's house rather than a fig tree. Later redesigns in the second half of the twentieth century reshaped the glorieta's paths and plantings more than once, but the columns and the fig both survived every version. Visitors walking the park's central axis between Plaza de España and the fountain gardens pass directly beneath it, often without registering that the shade they're standing in used to be somebody's front garden reconstruction.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of the Glorieta de Doña Sol
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story: As far as one dedicated local record can tell, this camphor tree has no rivals anywhere in Seville. It stands in the Glorieta de Doña Sol, a quiet clearing in Parque de María Luisa, described as the only confirmed Cinnamomum camphora growing in the city, a species more commonly associated with temple courtyards in Japan and southern China, where individual specimens are known to live well past a thousand years. No planting record has surfaced for this particular tree, and no formal age estimate exists yet, since it was only proposed for Seville's singular-trees catalogue in 2016. What sets it apart is entirely botanical rather than historical: camphor trees produce an aromatic oil in their bark and leaves, once distilled commercially for the same compound used in mothballs and topical liniments, and crushing a leaf releases a sharp, medicinal scent unlike anything else growing nearby. The glorieta gained a small dedicated corner in 2023, the Rincón de Pepe Elías, named for a local garden historian, close enough to the camphor tree that visitors reading the memorial plaque stand in its shade without necessarily knowing which tree is the rare one. Being the only example of something is a modest kind of fame, and this tree has held it for years without anyone making a fuss about it.

trees.name: The Ficus of the Pila del Pato
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 12 min walk east from the Plaza Nueva tram stop (T1); buses on Calle Recaredo
trees.story: A residents' association liked this tree enough to put it on their letterhead. The Indian laurel fig on the Plaza de San Leandro, known by the duck fountain it stands beside, was probably planted around 1945, going by photographs from the period. It survived the plaza's 1966 rebuild, when the bare earth square was paved over with cobbles and river stone, and the paving nearly finished it: the roots stopped getting air, branches died back from the tips, and the tree went into visible decline. The parks service drilled a ring of shafts around the root crown to let oxygen and nutrients back down, and it recovered fast. A bench built too close was later removed for the same reason. In 2019 the Asociación de Vecinos Casco Antiguo, working with the city, widened the planting pit and put new planting around it, and the association took the tree as its logo. It now measures 4.77 metres round with a crown 21 metres wide, and it has quietly reduced its own canopy over the years in response to the root damage, a tree editing itself down to what it can support. The city was still working on its soil in October 2025.

trees.name: The Magnolia of the Cathedral
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Archivo de Indias tram stop (T1) is 100 m away; Puerta de Jerez metro 5 min walk

best_time.label: May and June, when the cream flowers open the size of a spread hand

trees.story: The best evidence for this tree's age is photographs it does not appear in. Shots taken from the Teatro Coliseo in 1931 and from the corner of the cathedral in 1934 show the spot empty, which puts the planting in the early 1940s and makes this magnolia much younger than the Gothic wall it stands against, begun in 1401. By 1965 it was well grown. Then the city nearly killed it by tidying up. The pedestrianisation of the Avenida de la Constitución in 2007 and the tram works that followed shrank its planting bed and laid slabs over the roots that were still doing the work, and it was one of only three notable trees on the avenue to come through those works at all. It declined so visibly that both the parks service and ordinary passers-by were alarmed. In June 2021 the city spent 18,500 euros lifting the paving again, widening the bed, draining it, treating soil that had gone too limey, and putting in irrigation and a low pomegranate hedge to keep feet off the roots. Seville's own inventory now rates it stressed but recovering. The assessment is blunt about the cause: this was not weather or disease, it was the pavement.

trees.name: The Pineapple Guava of the Plaza de Santa Cruz
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 6 min walk east from Seville Cathedral, through the Santa Cruz quarter; Archivo de Indias tram stop (T1) 8 min

best_time.label: October into November, when the fruit ripens and drops

trees.story: Children in this square have known for a century that the green fruit on it tastes of pineapple. The pineapple guava normally stops at a shrub of four or five metres. This one reached six, and it did so because it has been left alone since about 1921, when the architect Juan Talavera laid out the Plaza de Santa Cruz on ground cleared by the demolition of a church and planted the garden that still frames it. At the centre he set the Cruz de la Cerrajería, a wrought-iron cross forged in 1692 by Sebastián Conde, a blacksmith from Almonte, which had already been moved twice, from the corner of Calles Sierpes and Rioja to the Museo de Bellas Artes and finally here. The guava went in with the rest of the planting and has outlasted most of it. Its flowers are the show nobody expects from a fruit bush: white petals curled back around a crown of red stamens tipped with bright yellow pollen, held on the branch for weeks. The fruit needs a second tree's pollen to set, comes in a little larger than a medlar, and is what the neighbourhood remembers it for.

trees.name: The Pecan of the Real Alcázar
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
trees.story: The tallest tree in the Alcázar gardens is a nut tree from the Mississippi valley, and almost nobody looks up at it. The pecan stands 37 metres in the Jardín del Marqués de la Vega Inclán, the garden José Gómez Millán laid out between 1913 and 1917 over what had been the Huerta del Retiro, the palace's working orchard. It was planted with the garden, alongside the other fruit trees Gómez Millán scattered through his design, so it is roughly as old as the layout around it. An older pecan grew near the Pabellón de Carlos V and was taken down when it became decrepit, which leaves this one carrying the species almost alone in the city. It is in unusually good order. Of the fifty-six individual trees in Seville's singular-tree inventory, this is one of a handful rated optimal on all three counts the city measures: physiological state, phytosanitary state and biomechanical structure. The inventory credits careful pruning across its whole life, and a planted border that keeps visitors off the ground under its canopy. Its trunk is 2.8 metres round, its crown 24 metres across, and it fruits into autumn, though the nuts are not yours to gather.

trees.name: The Fig of the University Moat
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Puerta de Jerez metro and tram stop (T1); Prado de San Sebastián 8 min
trees.story: A man in Seville asked the parks department in 1970 whether he could plant a tree to mark his son's birth. They said yes, brought a Moreton Bay fig to a bed on the Calle Palos de la Frontera, and let him throw the first spadefuls of earth in himself. That son turns fifty-six this year. So does the tree, and it has done rather better out of the arrangement: its trunk is now 6.12 metres round, thicker than any of the far older figs elsewhere in the city's inventory, and its crown spreads 28 metres, reaching sideways over the dry moat of the old Royal Tobacco Factory, the eighteenth-century building that has housed the University of Seville since the 1950s. In November 2025 the city brought in an Air Spade, a tool that blasts compacted soil apart with compressed air without tearing roots, and cut radial trenches around it to get the ground breathing again. The delegate who ordered the work called figs like this one part of the identity of Seville. Fifty-six years is nothing for a tree. This one has not read the memo.

trees.name: The Ficus of the Altozano
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Plaza Nueva tram stop (T1) across the Puente de Isabel II; buses to Plaza del Altozano
trees.story: Triana's landmark tree began as a pot plant. The city kept large containerised specimens for dressing streets and squares during civic celebrations, and in 1972, when the monument to the bullfighter Juan Belmonte was inaugurated on the Plaza del Altozano, one of those container plants was put into the ground and left there. It is a rubber fig, and specifically the variety that was fashionable as a houseplant in the same decade, the kind that sat in a corner of a thousand Spanish living rooms. Seville's run of mild winters let this one keep going outdoors. Fifty-four years on it has a trunk 5.86 metres round and a crown 31 metres across, and it is the only shade on the square, covering both halves of it at once: the approach to the Puente de Isabel II, successor to the old bridge of boats, and the mouth of the Calle Betis running downriver. The city's inventory is candid that the tree is not especially old and says its value here is symbolic. It has paid for that status. Every year the Velá de Triana sets its stalls up around the trunk, and in some years cooks put stoves underneath, badly enough to burn the bark.

trees.name: The Magnolia of the Real Alcázar
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds

best_time.label: April to May, when it flowers

trees.story:
Four metres seventy round is a great deal of magnolia. This is a species most people meet as a well behaved garden tree with glossy leaves, and this one has a trunk six metres ten around at the base, tapering to 4.70 at chest height, carrying twenty metres of crown over the Baños de Doña María de Padilla, the vaulted rainwater tank beneath the Alcázar's Patio del Crucero.

It is not a local. Magnolia grandiflora comes from the wet forests of the American southeast and arrived in European gardens in the eighteenth century as a slow, expensive novelty for people who could afford to wait. Seville turned out to suit it better than most places did.

The city's 2022 survey of its singular trees records the tree's physiology as normal, its structure as normal and its overall condition as good, and then, in the box for biological agents, names Agrocybe aegerita, a wood decay fungus that fruits in tight clusters on living hardwoods. That is why its plant health reads as regular rather than clean. A tree this size carrying a decay fungus is neither unusual nor a death sentence, but it is the kind of thing a city writes down and comes back to.

The flowers open in May and June, cream coloured and the size of a spread hand, and you smell them before you find them.

trees.name: The Judas Tree of the Real Alcázar
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds

best_time.label: March, when magenta flowers open straight out of the bare bark

trees.story:
A Judas tree that has reached sixteen metres has done something the species does not normally bother with. Cercis siliquastrum is a small tree, usually topping out around eight or ten metres in a courtyard, and this one in the Alcázar's English Garden is twice the height of the ones people plant on purpose, with a trunk 2.20 metres round and a crown twelve metres across.

Its trick is the flowering. In March, before a single leaf shows, magenta pea flowers open straight out of the bark, on the old wood and the bare limbs as well as the twigs, so the whole frame of the tree turns pink for a fortnight. Botanists call it cauliflory, and almost nothing else in a European garden does it.

The Spanish call the species the árbol del amor, the love tree. English took the other tradition, that Judas hanged himself from one. Same tree, worse story.

The garden around it was planted from 1910, when the Alcázar laid out a cooler, shadier English counterpoint to its Andalusi courtyards. Nothing dates this particular tree. What the city's surveyors did record, when they measured it in July 2022, is a tree in optimal physiological condition with no plant health anomalies at all, which is not something they wrote about many of its neighbours.

trees.name: The Orange Tree of Pedro the Cruel
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
trees.story:
The measurements on this one tell a different story from the name. Two metres round at the base, thirty six centimetres at chest height, three metres tall: a broad old stool with a thin young trunk coming out of it, which is what a citrus looks like after it has been cut back, frozen back or died back and grown again more than once.

Seville's catalogue of singular trees lists it as El Naranjo de Pedro el Cruel, after Pedro I of Castile, called both the Cruel and the Just, who built the mudéjar palace still standing a short walk from here between 1364 and 1366. The catalogue does not say why the tree carries his name and does not date it. A bitter orange living six centuries would be remarkable, and nothing here shows that this one has. If you know when it was planted, or where the name came from, tell us and it goes on the page.

Bitter oranges have been planted in this city since Almohad rule for the scent of the blossom rather than the fruit, which is far too sour to eat straight and ends up in British marmalade instead. This one stands between the Pabellón de Carlos V and the Cenador del León, and the 2022 survey records it as physiologically stressed but in good overall condition.

trees.name: The Plane of the Macarena Wall
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: Beside the Puerta de la Macarena and the basilica, roughly 20 minutes' walk north from Plaza de la Encarnación
trees.story:
The longest surviving stretch of Seville's twelfth century wall has a plane tree growing against it. Twenty seven metres tall, 4.20 metres round at chest height and 5.90 at the base, with a crown eighteen and a half metres across, on Calle Muñoz León where the Almohad wall runs from the Puerta de la Macarena towards the basilica.

The London plane is a hybrid nobody set out to make. An oriental plane and an American plane crossed in a European garden in the seventeenth century and produced something tougher than either parent, which then went on to line half the avenues in Europe: it puts up with compacted soil, drought and dirty air, and sheds its bark in plates that carry the grime off with them. The Spanish name is plátano de sombra, the shade plane, which is an honest description of the job.

There is an administrative curiosity in the record. The city's 2022 survey lists the ground as municipal but marks it sin recepcionar, not yet formally taken over, so a monumental plane is growing in the gap between two departments. Its physiology, structure and plant health were all recorded as normal or clean at the time.

The wall behind it went up when Seville was the capital of an empire that reached Marrakesh.

trees.name: The Norfolk Island Pine of the Torre Norte
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story:
At 44 metres this is the second tallest tree in Seville's own survey of its singular trees, a conifer from a single small island in the Pacific standing taller than almost anything else the city has measured. Norfolk Island itself sits between Australia and New Zealand, and the species left it for European and Mediterranean gardens in the eighteenth century, prized for a symmetrical, tiered crown that looks almost architectural, branches whorled in even rings up a perfectly straight trunk.

The city's 2022 survey found this one in clean health throughout: normal physiology, no plant health anomalies, a sound structure, girth of 3.10 metres at chest height widening to 3.70 at the base. It stands by the Torre Norte, one of the twin towers Aníbal González built to frame the Plaza de España a few hundred metres away, so a tree from the far side of the world grows in the shadow of Seville's own 1920s monument to itself.

The pin here follows the catalogue's own coordinate rather than an independently confirmed position, in a park where more than one tree stands close together.

trees.name: The Plane of Juanita Reina
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story:
This plane's girth runs to 4.42 metres at chest height and 5.02 at the base, wider than the more famous plane this site already lists on the Macarena wall, though shorter at 25 metres than that one's 27. Seville's 2022 survey found it structurally and physiologically normal, with no disease, but flagged two biological agents living on it: Kalotermes flavicollis, a drywood termite that colonises dead and weakened wood inside an otherwise healthy trunk, and Synanthedon codeti, a clearwing moth whose larvae bore into plane bark. Neither pushed its overall condition below good.

It stands at the Glorieta de Juanita Reina, one of the many named circular clearings that structure Parque de María Luisa, a garden the city built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition out of what had been the private grounds of the Palacio de San Telmo. The plane itself is a hybrid nobody set out to make, crossed from an Oriental and an American species in a seventeenth century European garden and then planted everywhere for how well it tolerates exactly the conditions a public park subjects it to.

The coordinate here is the catalogue's own, unverified against an independent source.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Monte Gurugú
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story:
The city's 2022 survey rates this stone pine's condition as optimal across every measure it takes: physiology, structure and plant health all clean, no biological agent recorded. Its crown spreads 21.5 metres, among the widest of any tree in the catalogue, the flat, umbrella-shaped canopy the species is named for in Spanish, pino piñonero, the pine that gives pine nuts.

It stands on the Monte Gurugú, an artificial hill inside Parque de María Luisa named, like several features of the park, after a real place, in this case a mountain near Melilla in Spanish North Africa, part of the layered, faintly exotic geography the park's nineteenth century designers built into its follies and mounds. Stone pine is native across the Mediterranean and has been cultivated for its edible seeds since Roman times, one of the oldest continuously harvested nut crops in Europe.

The coordinate is the catalogue's own. Two more stone pines already published on this site, at the Jardines de Cristina and elsewhere in the city, share the species; this one is distinguished by its position on the Gurugú and its unusually wide crown.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of the Isla de los Patos
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa

best_time.label: November, when it drops its needles like a deciduous tree, the habit that confuses visitors expecting a conifer to stay green

trees.story:
This bald cypress runs 35.7 metres tall, the tallest deciduous conifer in Seville's own survey of its singular trees, with a crown spreading 23.3 metres over the Isla de los Patos, the duck island inside one of Parque de María Luisa's ponds. Bald cypress is a wetland tree from the American South, and unlike almost every other conifer it drops its needles every autumn, going fully bare through winter before releasing fresh growth in spring, a habit that regularly confuses visitors expecting a conifer to stay green.

The survey recorded it in clean health across every measure: normal physiology, structure and plant health, no biological agent noted, a girth of 5.40 metres at chest height widening to 6.70 at the base. Growing beside water suits the species particularly well; in its native range a bald cypress standing in a swamp develops knobbly root growths called knees that rise above the waterline, though the catalogue records nothing about whether this one shows them.

A second Taxodium distichum already stands on this site's Seville list; this one, larger and on an island rather than open ground, is a different tree with its own story.

trees.name: The Plane of the Avenida de Bécquer
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange, inside Parque de María Luisa
trees.story:
At 4.70 metres round, this is the widest plane in Seville's survey of its singular trees, wider than either the Macarena wall plane or the Glorieta de Juanita Reina plane already published on this site, though at 23 metres it is not the tallest. Its estimated base girth runs to about 6 metres, and the same two insects recorded on its Juanita Reina neighbour turn up here too, Kalotermes flavicollis and Synanthedon codeti, without dragging the tree's overall condition below good; the survey did flag its structure as compromised, worth a look if you visit.

It stands on the Avenida de Bécquer, a walk through Parque de María Luisa named for Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer, the Sevillian Romantic poet whose monument sits nearby in the park. Named avenues of plane trees are one of the standard structural devices Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier used when he redesigned the park's grounds for the 1929 exposition, and this is one specimen out of what was originally a planted row.

The coordinate is the catalogue's own; not independently re-verified.

trees.name: The Windmill Palm of the Inner Wall
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
trees.story:
Fifteen metres is tall for a windmill palm, a species that usually tops out well under that in cultivation. This one grows at a corner of the Alcázar's inner wall, its trunk wrapped in the dense fibrous mat the species never sheds, which gave it enough cold tolerance to become one of the few palms that survives outdoors as far north as the British Isles.

The city's 2022 survey rated it optimal on every measure it records: physiology, structure and plant health all clean, no biological agent noted. Trachycarpus fortunei comes from mountain forests in central China, considerably cooler and wetter than Seville, and it reached European gardens in the nineteenth century as one of the first palms hardy enough for a temperate climate rather than a Mediterranean one, which makes its presence inside a mudéjar palace garden built centuries before its arrival a small piece of that later horticultural history folded into an old wall.

The coordinate is the catalogue's own; inside the Alcázar's walled, ticketed grounds the named corner does more of the work than the pin.

trees.name: The Bougainvillea of the Puerta de Marchena
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
trees.story:
Bougainvillea is a vine everywhere else, sold in garden centres to climb a trellis or spill over a wall. Trained and left long enough, it can do something closer to what this one has done at the Alcázar's Puerta de Marchena: build two woody trunks, 91 and 54 centimetres round at the base, and rise 13 metres, tall enough that Seville's own survey of singular trees counted it among them rather than dismissing it as a climber.

The city's 2022 assessment found it in optimal condition throughout, physiology, structure and plant health all clean. The species is South American, and what looks like a single spectacular magenta flower is actually three tiny true flowers wrapped in three papery bracts, the bracts carrying the colour while the real flowers stay small and pale at the centre.
