The Puerta de Marchena is one of several gates through the Alcázar's inner walls, and a plant usually grown for a single summer's colour has been given more than a century's worth of wall to work with here.

trees.name: The Fan Palm of the Cenador del León
trees.species: European Fan Palm / Saint Peter's Palm (Chamaerops humilis)
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
trees.story:
Europe's only native palm usually grows as a low, multi-stemmed clump under two or three metres, more shrub than tree. This one, in the garden around the Alcázar's Cenador del León pavilion, has reached 7.2 metres, tall enough and old enough that Seville's survey of singular trees gave it a place on the list, an unusual honour for a species that spends most of its life as scrub on Mediterranean hillsides.

The city's 2022 assessment recorded it in optimal condition throughout, physiology, structure and plant health all clean. Chamaerops humilis is genuinely wild across southern Spain, Portugal and North Africa, tolerant of drought and poor soil in a way most ornamental palms are not, which is likely part of why a specimen given a long undisturbed run in a palace garden has grown so much larger than its usual roadside or scrubland relatives.

The Cenador del León, a domed viewing pavilion, gives its name to the garden around it, where this palm and a second catalogued tree both grow within the same walled space.

trees.name: The Sago Palm of the Jardín de las Damas
trees.access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
trees.story:
This is not a palm at all, whatever its common name says. Cycas revoluta is a cycad, a member of a plant lineage that predates flowering plants and even most conifers, effectively unchanged since before the dinosaurs, and a 5.5 metre specimen represents a very long, very slow accumulation of growth: cycads add height at a fraction of the rate of almost any tree, sometimes only a centimetre or two a year.

Seville's 2022 survey rated it optimal throughout, physiology, structure and plant health all clean. It grows in the Jardín de las Damas, the Ladies' Garden, one of the Alcázar's formal Renaissance-era enclosures, where its stiff crown of dark, feather-like fronds reads as almost prehistoric against the clipped hedges and fountains around it.

The species is native to southern Japan, and every part of it is toxic if eaten, a fact that has not stopped it becoming one of the most widely planted ornamental cycads in warm gardens worldwide, valued for exactly the slow, architectural permanence a specimen this size demonstrates.

trees.name: The Cypress of San Fernando Cemetery
trees.access: Free, public cemetery grounds, open in daylight.
trees.transport: On Avenida Doctor Fedriani, reachable by city bus north of the historic centre.
trees.story:
A cemetery cypress is the least surprising tree on this list and one of the healthiest: Seville's 2022 survey recorded this one's physiology, structure and plant health all as normal or clean, standing 23 metres tall with a trunk 2.79 metres round. Mediterranean cypress has marked graveyards, from Persian gardens to Italian hillsides to Spanish cemeteries, for so many centuries that its narrow, flame-shaped silhouette reads almost automatically as a marker of the dead, a association old enough that Roman writers already described the practice.

Cementerio de San Fernando, opened in 1852 outside what was then the city's edge, holds Seville's own dead across more than a century and a half, bullfighters and flamenco singers and ordinary Sevillanos beside each other, and its older sections carry exactly the kind of mature planting a working cemetery this old accumulates without anyone setting out to build a garden.

The coordinate is the catalogue's own; the cemetery is large, and this cypress is one specimen among its older plantings.

trees.name: The River Red Gum of Pedro Salinas
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: In the Nervión district, reachable by tram or city bus.
trees.story:
At 42 metres this street tree is the third tallest in Seville's own survey of its singular trees, an Australian eucalypt growing over an ordinary residential street named for the poet Pedro Salinas. Its girth runs 5.30 metres at chest height, widening to 7.70 at the base, big enough that the tree reads as out of scale with the buildings around it.

The city's 2022 assessment found no structural or physiological problems, but recorded mild plant health anomalies and named two biological agents at work on it: Glycaspis brimblecombei, a sap-sucking psyllid that arrived in Europe from Australia in the early 2000s and has spread through eucalyptus plantings ever since, and Laetiporus sulphureus, the sulfur polypore, a fungus that feeds on heartwood in mature trees. Neither has pulled its overall condition below good, but both are worth knowing before you stand under it expecting a flawless specimen.

River red gum lines watercourses across the Australian interior, and it was planted worldwide through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries for how fast it grows, which is most of how a street tree gets to 42 metres in the span of a human lifetime.

trees.name: The Fig of the Jardines de Chapina
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: In Triana, a short walk from the Puente de Chapina.
trees.story:
This fig grows two trunks from one root system, 2.10 and 1.97 metres round, and Seville's 2022 survey rated its condition optimal on every measure it took: physiology, structure and plant health all clean, the best possible mark a tree on this list can earn. It stands in the Jardines de Chapina, a strip of garden along the historic course of the Guadalquivir canal on the Triana side of the river, about 500 metres from a second Ficus microcarpa this site already publishes at El Altozano.

Indian laurel fig is native across a wide arc from India to northern Australia, and it is one of the most widely planted street and park trees in warm cities worldwide precisely because it tolerates pruning, pollution and root competition better than almost anything else, developing the dense, glossy-leaved crown and pale aerial roots that make old specimens look far larger than a single trunk would suggest.

Two Ficus microcarpa within an easy walk of each other, on opposite ends of the same riverside district, make a small Triana walk worth doing back to back if you visit one.

trees.name: The Mulberry of the Alamillo Cortijo
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: In the Parque del Alamillo, reachable by bus or bicycle from the city centre across the Puente del Alamillo.

best_time.label: June, when the mulberries ripen and drop

trees.story:
This mulberry's trunk runs 4 metres round, unusually thick for a species more often kept small and heavily pruned for its leaves than left to grow into a full tree. Seville's 2022 survey found it physiologically stressed with a compromised structure, though still supported and standing, and rated its overall condition good despite both flags.

It grows by the Cortijo, an old farmstead building preserved inside the Parque del Alamillo, the large public park built on the Isla de la Cartuja for Expo '92 around what had been the Duke of Alba's private hunting estate. White mulberry was planted across Spain for centuries to feed silkworms, an industry Seville itself once had a stake in, and a farmstead like the Cortijo would very plausibly have kept mulberries exactly like this one as a working crop tree rather than an ornamental.

Every June the tree drops pale, sweet fruit that stains whatever pavement or grass sits beneath it, the same fruit that made the species worth planting in the first place, long before anyone valued it for shade.

trees.name: The Senegal Date Palm of the Jardines de las Delicias
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián bus/tram interchange.
trees.story:
Most palms grow one trunk from one root. Phoenix reclinata grows several, suckering from its base into a clump of curved, leaning stems that can eventually spread wider than they are tall, a habit that gives the species its name and its very different silhouette from the single straight trunks of most cultivated palms. This specimen's base runs 9.70 metres round, and Seville's 2022 survey rated it optimal on every measure: physiology, structure and plant health all clean.

It grows in the Jardines de las Delicias, a garden along the old Paseo de las Delicias that predates Parque de María Luisa next door, laid out in the nineteenth century as one of the city's first fashionable promenades. Senegal date palm is native across tropical and subtropical Africa, and it reached Spanish gardens as part of the same nineteenth and early twentieth century enthusiasm for exotic planting that filled Seville's parks with trees from every warm climate on earth.

The coordinate is the catalogue's own, not independently re-verified.

trees.name: The Canary Pine of the Engineering School
trees.access: Free, on the university campus, grounds open to visitors.
trees.transport: In the Reina Mercedes university district, reachable by city bus.
trees.story:
Seville's 2022 survey rated this pine optimal across every measure it records, physiology, structure and plant health all clean, standing 26 metres tall on the campus of the university's engineering informatics school. Canary pine is endemic to the Canary Islands, an archipelago whose isolation has made it one of the most botanically distinct places in Spain, and the species is remarkably fire-adapted even by pine standards: a mature Pinus canariensis can resprout new needles directly from a badly scorched trunk, a trait almost no other pine in the world shares.

A university campus is an unusual but not unheard of setting for a catalogued singular tree, the same pattern this site has already documented at Cork's University College campus arboretum; a public university's open grounds put a tree like this within reach of any visitor walking through rather than only its students and staff.

The coordinate is the catalogue's own. If you know more about when this pine was planted or why, tell us.

trees.name: The Tipu Tree of the Parque de los Príncipes
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: In Los Remedios, on the west bank of the Guadalquivir, reachable by bus or a walk across the Puente de San Telmo.

best_time.label: June, when sprays of yellow-orange flowers cover the crown and then carpet the ground beneath it

trees.story:
At 32 metres this tipu tree is taller than almost anything else planted for its flowers in Seville, a South American species from Bolivia and Argentina that has become one of the most widely planted ornamental trees across southern Spain for the show it puts on in early summer: loose sprays of yellow-orange pea flowers covering the whole crown, followed by a carpet of fallen petals thick enough to colour the pavement underneath.

Seville's 2022 survey found it in optimal physiological condition with normal structure and no plant health problems, girth 3.24 metres at chest height widening to 4.80 at the base. It grows in the Parque de los Príncipes, a park in the Los Remedios district on the west bank of the Guadalquivir, standing without another catalogued singular tree nearby, an isolated specimen rather than part of a cluster.

Tipuana tipu was introduced to Spain in the nineteenth century and took to the country's hot, dry summers well enough that it now self-seeds in some regions, an immigrant tree that has made itself entirely at home.

trees.name: The Viscote of the Paseo de Colón
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: On the Paseo de Colón riverside promenade, opposite the Real Maestranza bullring.
trees.story:
Most people walking the Paseo de Colón toward the Maestranza bullring have never heard of this tree's species, and that is most of the reason it made Seville's list of singular trees. Parasenegalia visco, still filed by its older name Acacia visco in some sources, is South American, native to the dry forests of Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay, and it is rarely planted anywhere in Europe outside a handful of specimen collections.

The city's 2022 survey found it physiologically and biologically clean, with a structure it rated compromised but still standing, overall condition good, girth 1.75 metres at chest height and a crown 13.4 metres across, wide for a tree only 12.3 metres tall. The species carries fine, feathery bipinnate leaves and clusters of small pale flowers, closer in appearance to its more familiar acacia relatives than its unfamiliar name suggests.

It stands on the riverside promenade directly across from the Real Maestranza, one of Spain's most famous bullrings, a rare tree in plain view of one of the city's best known buildings.

trees.name: The Fig Tree of the Huerto del Rey Moro
trees.access: Free, open daily as a self-managed community garden; entrance on Calle Enladrillada 36.
trees.transport: In the Casco Antiguo near the Macarena walls, about a 10 minute walk from Puerta de la Macarena, served by TUSSAM bus lines including C4.
trees.story:
The garden around this fig was taken by the people who live on the street. In 2004 neighbours in San Julián occupied the walled plot on Calle Enladrillada rather than watch it be built over, and they have run it themselves ever since. Their own account of the place calls the fig more than 300 years old, and that is as sharp as the figure gets, because nobody has dated it any further than that.

The city's 2022 survey of singular trees measured what can be measured. The tree stands 9.4 metres tall with a crown of roughly the same span, and the trunk runs 1.47 metres around at chest height, swelling to three metres where it enters the ground. The same survey marks it stressed and structurally compromised, its overall conservation only fair.

The ground under it has been worked for a long while. The plot was the domestic orchard of the Casa del Rey Moro, a house of the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century, and it is now the largest public open space in Seville's old centre with nothing to buy in it.

The entrance is a gate at number 36, open daily, free. What you find behind it is a working neighbourhood garden with an old fig in the middle of it, held up by residents rather than by a parks department.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of the Jardines de Cristina
trees.access: Free, open public city garden at all hours; between Puerta de Jerez and the river.
trees.transport: At Puerta de Jerez, about 2 minutes' walk from the Puerta de Jerez Metrocentro tram stop (line T1).
trees.story:
Queen María Cristina had a garden opened in her name on 24 July 1830, and a local gardens association names this pine, in bed 15, as a tree of that founding period. That is a source pointing at this specimen rather than at the garden's date, which puts it somewhere around 180 to 210 years old. Nobody has counted its rings, so the band stays broad.

It has grown into the size that goes with those years. Twenty five metres tall, a trunk 2.80 metres around at chest height and 3.11 at the base, with the flat umbrella crown of a stone pine spreading 12.5 metres over the path. The city's 2022 survey finds its physiology and plant health clean and its structure compromised, which is common in a tree carrying that much canopy on one long bare stem.

The Jardines de Cristina are 8,100 square metres of public ground wedged between the Puerta de Jerez and the Guadalquivir, and this pine has stood through the whole of their public life, including the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition that rebuilt this end of Seville around it and the tram line that now runs past the gate.

Stone pine has been grown around the Mediterranean for its edible seeds since Roman times. This one is a city tree, two minutes from a tram stop, and it is free to walk under at any hour.

trees.name: The Multi-Stemmed Palm of the Conde de Colombi
trees.neighbourhood: El Prado-Parque de María Luisa, Sur
trees.access: Free, inside the public Parque de María Luisa, open daily.
trees.transport: Inside Parque de María Luisa near Plaza de España, about a 10 minute walk from the Prado de San Sebastián bus and tram interchange.
trees.story:
A date palm is meant to be one trunk and a crown. This one is a cluster of them, and that is the entire reason the city put it in its 2022 survey of singular trees: it lists the palm as multi-stemmed, which is not how the species usually presents itself.

The measurement sheet shows the consequence. There is no chest-height girth for this tree, because the standard measurement at 1.30 metres has nothing single to be taken around; the surveyors recorded 8.75 metres at the base instead, a figure that covers the whole bundle of stems rather than any one trunk. The palm reaches 15.8 metres, with a crown averaging 11.5 metres across. Physiology, plant health and structure are all rated normal, which for a tree of this shape is worth noting on its own.

It stands on the Avenida del Conde de Colombi inside Parque de María Luisa, the park Seville laid out from the Montpensier estate and filled with exotics for the 1929 exhibition, and it shares that ground with nine other trees on this map. It is a ten minute walk from the Prado de San Sebastián interchange, past the Plaza de España, and it costs nothing to stand under.

Nobody has put an age on it, and the survey does not try. If you know when it went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Harp Eucalyptus of the Guadalquivir
trees.access: Free, on the public riverside path and cycle route of the Anillo Verde (Green Ring), open at all times.
trees.transport: On the Guadalquivir riverside path in Tablada; nearest useful stop is around Avda. Maestranza Aerea, roughly a 15 to 20 minute walk to the riverbank, or reach it by bike via the segregated riverside cycle path that runs the length of the Guadalquivir.
trees.story:
Two organisms are working on Seville's big river gums at once, and this one on the Guadalquivir bank carries both. Glycaspis brimblecombei is a sap-sucking psyllid that followed eucalyptus out of Australia and reached Europe in the early 2000s. Laetiporus sulphureus is the sulphur polypore, the bracket fungus sold elsewhere as chicken of the woods, which feeds on heartwood. The same pair is recorded on El Gran Capitán in the Jardines de Murillo and on the river red gum of Calle Pedro Salinas, so this is pest pressure on a species across the city rather than one unlucky tree.

Neither has finished it. The city's 2022 survey rates its physiology and plant health clean and its structure compromised, and puts it at 18 metres tall. The trunk measures three metres around, but read that figure carefully: the surveyors took it three metres up rather than at the standard chest height, so it does not compare like for like with the other girths in the catalogue.

It stands out in Tablada, on the west bank south of the centre, on the Anillo Verde path that runs along the river. This is a bike ride or a long walk rather than a stroll from the cathedral, and the reward is a very large tree on open riverside ground with a gate nowhere in it.

No age is recorded anywhere. If you know it, tell us.

trees.name: The Grapefruit of the Cartuja Monastery
trees.access: Paid entry: inside the Monasterio de la Cartuja, now the Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporaneo (CAAC), a public museum. A monument ticket and a combined monument-plus-exhibitions ticket are both sold at a few euros each; free entry runs Tuesday to Friday 19:00-21:00 and on Saturdays. Open Tuesday to Saturday 11:00-21:00, Sunday and holidays 10:00-15:30, closed Mondays. The self-guided route through the monastery ends at the old orchards, Huerta Vieja and Huerta Grande, so any visitor who buys a ticket during opening hours reaches the tree.
trees.transport: On Isla de la Cartuja; TUSSAM bus lines C1 and C2 stop close by (Lopez Pintado/Caixa Forum, about 2 minutes' walk, or Americo Vespucio/Monasterio de la Cartuja, about 4 minutes' walk). Also reachable on foot from Triana over the Pasarela de la Cartuja footbridge.
trees.story:
Grapefruit is a young fruit. The hybrid was first recorded in Barbados in the eighteenth century, which means no grapefruit tree anywhere can be truly ancient, however large it grows. This one grows large. It stands 14 metres with a crown of 13, and its trunk runs 2.20 metres around, measured at 0.85 metres rather than the usual chest height, widening to 2.50 at the base. For a citrus, that is close to absurd.

It lives in the Huerta Grande, one of the two old orchards of the Cartuja monastery. Carthusian monks farmed this ground from the fifteenth century, and the orchards outlasted them, the English china factory that took the buildings over in the nineteenth century, and the Expo of 1992 that rebuilt the island around the walls. The monastery is now the Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporáneo, and the visitor route through it finishes in those orchards, so the tree is on the standard path rather than behind a staff door.

There is an entry fee of a few euros, waived all day on Saturdays and from seven in the evening Tuesday to Friday, and the site closes on Mondays. The city's 2022 survey rates the tree normal on physiology, plant health and structure, and gives it no age at all. Nobody appears to have recorded when it was planted. If a monastery or factory record says otherwise, tell us and we will add it.

trees.name: The Lagunaria of the Jardines de la Madrina
trees.access: Free, in the Jardines de la Madrina, a small city-run garden beside the Casino de la Exposicion. This is a separate, publicly accessible strip of the old San Telmo estate, not the same ground as the adjoining Palacio de San Telmo, whose own main gardens remain closed to the public and visitable only by appointment.
trees.transport: Near Plaza de Espana and the Prado de San Sebastian bus and tram interchange, about a 10 minute walk.

best_time.label: June and July, when the pink hibiscus flowers open

trees.story:
In Australia this species is called the itchy bomb tree, because its seed capsules split to release fibrous hairs that irritate any skin that handles them. Look, do not collect. The Norfolk Island hibiscus is otherwise a generous tree, opening pale pink flowers of obvious hibiscus shape through the first half of summer, and this is a large one: 22 metres tall, a trunk 2.75 metres around at chest height widening to 4.33 at the base, and a crown averaging 10.3 metres. The city's 2022 survey rates it optimal on physiology and good on conservation, clean on every measure it takes.

Where it stands takes a sentence of care. The Jardines de la Madrina are a small city-run garden beside the Casino de la Exposición, a surviving piece of the old San Telmo estate that the council recovered and reopened as public ground between 2013 and 2015. They are not the gardens of the Palacio de San Telmo next door, which houses the Andalusian presidency and can only be visited by appointment. This one you walk into, free, off the street.

Its age is an open question and we are leaving it open. The city's catalogue treats it as a notable old specimen, while a Seville gardens association puts the city's oldest lagunarias at the Jardines de Cristina and the Real Alcázar instead. Nobody has published a date for this trunk. If someone has one, we would like it.

trees.name: The Tembusu of Lawn E
trees.access: Free, public section of Singapore Botanic Gardens, open 5am-12am daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Botanic Gardens MRT station (Circle/Downtown Line), Tanglin Gate entrance
trees.story: This tree was already old when the Singapore Botanic Gardens opened around it in 1859. NParks estimates it at more than 200 years, based on growth patterns compared with other tembusu of known age, which makes it a survivor of whatever forest stood on this ground before the Gardens were laid out. Its most distinctive feature is a single low branch that grows out almost parallel to the ground before curling upward, a shape unusual enough that illustrator Eng Siak Loy chose this exact tree, and this exact limb, to draw on the reverse of Singapore's five-dollar note. It is the only tree ever to appear on a Singapore banknote. Tembusu wood is prized separately from the tree's fame: dense and highly resistant to termites, it has long been used in Malay boat-building and furniture, and the timber's hardness even became a figure of speech in Malay for a person with an unyielding heart. The tree's creamy-white flowers open in clusters and turn yellow with age, most fragrant in the late evening, when they once would have drawn Malayan flying foxes to feed on the fruit that follows. It stands in the free section of the Gardens, an easy walk from the Tanglin Gate, on open lawn rather than behind any barrier, close enough to Swan Lake that most visitors photograph the water first and only notice the tree, and the branch on their banknote, on the way back.

trees.name: The Fort Canning Rain Tree
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 5 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line), via the Hill Street steps
trees.story: This rain tree spreads its umbrella-shaped canopy directly over a public stairway that carries walkers out of Fort Canning Park onto Hill Street, so almost everyone who takes those steps passes under it whether they notice or not. Rain trees only arrived in Singapore in 1876, imported from tropical America and planted heavily through the colonial coffee and nutmeg plantations that once covered much of the island, and this specimen's own planting date was never recorded, though its 4.93 metre girth points to a tree well over a century old. Its most reliable feature is not size but timing: every evening, roughly ninety minutes before sunset, its paired leaflets fold shut, and they do the same on overcast days, a light-sensitive reflex that gave the species both its English name and its Malay one, Pukul Lima, five o'clock. Fort Canning Hill itself was the seat of the ancient Kingdom of Singapura before it became a British fort and then a public park, so a tree standing sentinel over one of its main entrances is, in a small way, guarding ground with a longer history than the tree itself. Clusters of pink-and-white flowers appear through the year without a single dramatic peak, and the pods that follow ripen dark and fleshy, adding to the tree's already broad, low silhouette.

trees.name: The Fort Canning Madras Thorn
trees.age: age undocumented, girth grew from 7.4m to 8.5m since 2001
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 8 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.story: NParks records this as the largest Madras thorn on Singapore's heritage register, an 8.5 metre girth today, up from 7.4 metres when it was first measured for the scheme in 2001. The species arrived in the region centuries ago with Portuguese and Spanish traders from tropical America, and by the mid-1900s it lined roadsides and housing estates across Singapore as a shade tree, until a caterpillar infestation through the 1970s got it stripped from most public planting. This one, tucked beside Fort Canning's old Service Reservoir rather than out on a street, survived that cull. Its crown is low, spreading and unusually bushy for a tree this size, shaggy with bird's nest ferns and other epiphytes that have colonized its branches over the decades, giving it a wilder look than its more manicured heritage-tree neighbours. Short, sharp thorns guard the base of each leaf, the source of both its common name and part of the Greek genus name, which references the fruit's resemblance to a monkey's earring. Those fruits split into coiled, rose-red pods each spring, exposing a sweet white pulp around glossy black seeds that draws yellow-vented bulbuls and Oriental magpie robins to disperse them, and the same pulp is eaten by people elsewhere in its native range as a sour-sweet snack or juice.

trees.name: The Fort Canning Tamalan
trees.age: likely 100+ years (planting era documented, exact date not)
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.story: This tamalan is one of the last survivors of an ornamental planting scheme that once covered much of Fort Canning Hill in the early 1900s, when the old fort grounds were being turned into a colonial pleasure garden. NParks' own register notes that few of the tamalan planted here in that era still line the hill's paths, which makes this specimen, standing at Fort Green, a rare direct witness to that specific phase of the park's history rather than a later replacement. The species is native to Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam, where it can reach 20 to 30 metres, and it was brought to Singapore purely for its looks: a crown of delicate, feathery foliage carried on branches that spread wide and low, with flower buds that open lilac, shift to pink, and fade to white as they age. Its wood connects it to a more famous family. Dalbergia is the genus behind Brazilian rosewood and African blackwood, both prized and now heavily restricted timbers, and while this tree has never been harvested, its relatives explain why the genus carries the weight it does among furniture makers and luthiers. At 5.48 metres in girth and just under 15 metres tall, it is modest next to some of Fort Canning's other heritage trees, but it is one of the few left standing from a planting era the park's own records otherwise struggle to document.

trees.name: The Terap Nasi of the 14th Century Walk
trees.age: age undocumented, girth grew from 4.1m to 5.68m since 2001
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 8 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.story: This terap grows beside Fort Canning's 14th Century Walk of History, a path named for the hill's role as the seat of the ancient Kingdom of Singapura, and it carries plank buttresses at its base broad enough to make the connection to old ground feel physical rather than just historical. Its girth has grown from 4.1 metres, when NParks first endorsed it as a heritage tree in 2001, to 5.68 metres today, real if unspectacular proof of two and a half decades of recorded growth, though nothing in the register dates its planting itself. Botanist John Henry Corner, assistant director of the Botanic Gardens through the 1930s and 40s, documented Fort Canning's terap specimens in his standard reference Wayside Trees of Malaya, giving this small grove a paper trail most street trees never get. In the wild the species can reach 45 to 65 metres; Singapore's cultivated specimens stay far smaller, but the fruit does not: each one grows to roughly 18 centimetres, ripening from cream to brown and smelling notoriously strong when cut open, guarding a sweet white pulp locals have described as tasting like tangy marshmallow. The tree's tough, fibrous inner bark was historically stripped and worked into cordage, coarse cloth and basket lining across the region, a practical use that outlived the kingdom the walking path beside it is named for.

trees.name: The Kapok Tree of Seah Im Road
trees.access: Free, public car park
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from HarbourFront MRT station (Circle/North East Line), near the Mount Faber cable car base station
trees.story: At 11.55 metres in girth, this is one of the largest-trunked trees on Singapore's entire heritage register, rising 34.6 metres from the edge of an ordinary public car park at the foot of Mount Faber. Kapok is deciduous, unusual for a tropical tree, dropping its leaves entirely before flowering, and its cream-coloured blooms open at night with a milky scent that draws bats to pollinate them, an entirely different visiting crowd than the tree gets by day. The seed pods that follow split to release a fine, water-resistant white fiber once used to stuff life jackets and mattresses worldwide, the reason the tree ended up as Puerto Rico's national tree despite originating, like this one's ancestors, in tropical America. What makes this particular specimen worth the detour is what stands twenty metres behind it in the undergrowth: a brick-entranced wartime bunker, its tunnel about 2.5 metres tall inside with small ventilation holes along the walls, largely forgotten until vegetation was cleared enough to rediscover it. Local historians believe it was built shortly before the Second World War, though its exact use, whether to hold prisoners of war or simply to store equipment and ammunition, has never been confirmed. The kapok tree is the only obvious marker for anyone trying to find it.

trees.name: The Mangrove Apples of Chek Jawa
trees.access: Free, public boardwalk (Chek Jawa Wetlands, 7am-7pm daily), reached via a paid bumboat to Pulau Ubin
trees.transport: Bumboat from Changi Point Ferry Terminal to Pulau Ubin, then a 20-25 minute walk or bike ride to the Chek Jawa boardwalk
trees.story: These two mangrove apples are, according to NParks' own register, the only mangrove trees among Singapore's 251 heritage trees, standing together beside the old House No. 1 at Chek Jawa, on the far side of Pulau Ubin from the mainland. Getting there already takes effort: a bumboat from Changi Point to Ubin, then a walk or bike ride to the free boardwalk that lets visitors cross the wetland without touching the mud beneath it. The trees themselves spend part of every day partly submerged, rising and falling with the tide in a stretch of shoreline built almost entirely on salt tolerance. Around their bases, pneumatophores, root structures that poke straight up through the mud like a field of woody snorkels, let the trees pull in oxygen from air rather than the waterlogged, anoxic soil their main roots sit in. To manage the salt that soil carries, they concentrate it in their oldest leaves and simply shed them, a slow-motion filtering system with no equivalent among ordinary garden trees. Chek Jawa itself very nearly does not exist as a public reserve at all. It was slated for land reclamation in 2001 until a citizen-led biodiversity survey and public campaign got the plan shelved, meaning this pair of trees, unremarkable in age but singular in the register, sits inside a wetland Singapore almost paved over entirely.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree of Pearl's Hill
trees.access: Free, public park (Pearl's Hill City Park), no gates or opening hours found
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 5-10 minutes, uphill) from Outram Park MRT station (East-West/North-East/Thomson-East Coast lines)
trees.story: Singapore's first prison stood on this hill, and so did its first hospital for the poor. The Bodhi tree at the top of Pearl's Hill City Park carries 6.34 metres of girth and 16.9 metres of height on NParks' heritage register, and it grows over ground that held both, which is a fair trade. The hill takes its name from Captain James Pearl, who commanded the Indiana, the ship that brought Raffles to Singapore in 1819. He liked the view enough to buy the hill and plant it with pepper. Tan Tock Seng's hospital for destitute Chinese labourers opened on its slope in the 1840s and the colonial gaol followed, both long since buried under the reservoir and the police blocks that took their place. Ficus religiosa is the species the Buddha is traditionally said to have sat beneath, and it is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus alike. The leaves are the giveaway: heart-shaped, drawn out into a long tail that sheds monsoon rain and sets the whole crown trembling in almost no wind. This is not the Bodhi tree most people in Singapore mean. That one grows at the Jin Long Si Temple and has had its own long public fight over the land around it. This is a different individual on a different hill, and it draws no crowd at all. NParks records no planting date, so its age is unknown.

trees.name: The Banyan of Tiong Bahru Park
trees.age: under 60 years (planted after the park opened in 1967)
trees.access: Free, public park, no gates or opening hours found
trees.transport: Roughly 10-15 minute walk from Tiong Bahru or Redhill MRT station
trees.story: A girth of 22.8 metres usually takes a tree several centuries. This one managed it in under sixty years. Tiong Bahru Park was developed in 1967 and NParks' own register states plainly that the banyan was planted after that, which makes it younger than the flats around it and still one of the widest trees on Singapore's heritage list. The trick is in how a banyan is put together. Ficus benghalensis drops aerial roots from its branches; they reach the ground, thicken into trunks of their own, then fuse with each other and with the original stem into a single braided mass that a tape measure reads as one enormous trunk. A banyan does not so much grow fat as recruit. Measured at the standard 1.3 metres above the ground, those 22.8 metres are really a committee. So the thing to go and look at here is not age. It is speed, and the odd architecture that produces it: a tree 18.4 metres tall occupying its patch of park like something with four times its lifespan behind it, props still coming down through the canopy in various stages of becoming trunks. In Hindu tradition the species carries its own weight, the roots read as Brahma's, the trunk as Vishnu's, the branches as Shankar's. Older banyans elsewhere in the Tiong Bahru area have been called a hundred years and more. This one, by its own record, is not among them.

trees.name: The Earpod Tree of Fort Canning
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 8-10 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.story: The seed pods explain the name: dark, flat, coiled into a near-perfect circle and close enough to a human ear that the tree is called after one in both Spanish and English. In Costa Rica, where the same species is the national tree, those pods are a roadside fixture. The earpod at Fort Canning has been on Singapore's heritage register since 2001, with 5.94 metres of girth and 17.9 metres of height, standing on the path behind the Fort Wall. It came from the tropical dry forests running from Mexico down to Venezuela, where it is one of the largest trees of that habitat, reaching 40 metres with a trunk three metres through, and where old specimens push surface roots out far enough to lift nearby paving. It arrived here as an ornamental and is now the first stop on NParks' own walking trail of the hill's heritage trees, which puts four more within a few hundred metres of it. One thing is unresolved and worth knowing before you go. Both the register and NParks' current Fort Canning trail guide describe this tree standing. A 2025 travel account describes an earpod tree somewhere in the same park that came down in a 2014 storm and kept growing on its side, its trunk now carrying orchids and ferns. Nobody has confirmed whether that is this tree or another one. If you find it lying down, it is alive, and it is still worth the walk.

trees.name: The Sausage Tree of the Sundial Garden
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10 minute walk
trees.story: A ripe fruit on this tree is a grey-brown cylinder up to a metre long, hanging from a cord of a stalk, heavy enough that nobody sensible stands under one for long. That is the whole species in one glance, and it is where the name comes from. The Gardens kept the paperwork for this particular tree. It arrived from Honolulu on 13 May 1931 and went into the ground on 19 October the same year, one of the tropical species being trialled here for economic and medicinal value, in an era when whether a plant was useful decided whether it earned a place. It has held its patch of lawn beside the Sundial Garden ever since. In its native Africa the fruit is both useful and dangerous. Raw it is poisonous. Processed it goes into herbal remedies and fermented drinks, and in several communities a fruit is buried in place of a body when there is no body to bury. The flowers that come before it are deep maroon, smell of nothing anyone would choose, and open at night for bats rather than bees. Ninety-five years in, though, the sausages are the point. Once set they hang for months, which makes this one of the few trees on this list with something to show whichever week you turn up.

trees.name: The Baobab of Melati Gate
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to the Bukit Timah Core / Cluny Park Road side
trees.story: There is a baobab in Singapore, and it is only about forty years old. Everything worth knowing about it follows from those two facts. The species belongs to dry African savannah, where it survives months without rain by storing water in a swollen trunk; Singapore delivers rain most weeks and grows very few baobabs from seed. This is thought to be one of the handful that were. NParks put it at close to thirty years old when it was endorsed as a heritage tree in 2016, which makes it around forty now. For a species that can pass a thousand years, that is a child, and it already carries five metres of girth. Baobab trunks swell out of all proportion to their height as they age, so a young one looks like a fat grey bottle with twigs on top. This is exactly that. It has moved once. In June 1996 it was lifted from elsewhere in the Gardens and replanted here beside Melati Gate on the Cluny Park Road side, a long way from the busier lawns, which is why most visitors never meet it. Its flowers are worth knowing about even if you will not see them: large, white, hanging upside down, opening after dark for bats to pollinate, and finished inside a day.

trees.name: The Cannon Ball Tree of the Ginger Garden
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10-15 minute walk to the Ginger Garden
trees.story: This tree flowers and fruits straight out of its own trunk. Ropes of waxy pink and cream flowers erupt from the bark, and behind them hang the fruit it is named for, brown spheres the size of cannon balls that crack open on the ground and smell appalling for days afterwards. It grew from seed collected in a hurry. In 1931 E.J.H. Corner, then an assistant director of the Botanic Gardens, was sailing back from home leave in England when his ship called at Colombo. He had eight hours before it left again, spent them getting up to the botanic garden at Peradeniya near Kandy, and came back aboard with cannon ball seed. This tree was planted from it that year, behind the waterfall at the edge of the Ginger Garden. The flowers make no nectar, and the pollen in the ring at their centre is sterile. Carpenter bees come for that sterile pollen anyway and collect the fertile kind on their backs on the way in, which is the arrangement the entire species runs on. Two degrees off the equator there is no season to wait for; it flowers and fruits more or less continuously. Half a dozen more heritage trees stand within about five hundred metres, which makes this the one stretch of this list you can walk rather than travel between.

trees.name: The Nutmegs of the Economic Garden
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to the Central Core
trees.story: Orchard Road is named after orchards, and the crop in them was nutmeg. Singapore grew it hard through the 1840s until disease went through the plantations in the 1860s and took the industry with it. These two trees are not survivors of that boom. They are the closest thing to it still growing in the city. They stand a few metres apart in the Central Core, on the ground of the Gardens' Economic Garden, laid out in 1879 to work out which tropical crops could be made to pay here. Nutmeg was already the answer that had failed, kept on as a specimen, and this pair are among the last of those crop plants left standing. The register lists them separately. A visitor sees one thing: two trunks a little over a metre round each, neither the sort of bulk that stops anyone in their tracks. What they do have is fruit. Nutmeg trees are either male or female, and both of these are female. The fruit is a yellow, apricot-shaped thing that splits to show a scarlet lace cage wrapped around a single dark seed. The cage is mace. The seed is nutmeg. One tree, two spices, priced separately for centuries. Nobody recorded when either of them went in. If you know, tell us.

trees.name: The Burmese Banyan of Swan Lake
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10 minute walk to Swan Lake
trees.story: Fifteen metres of girth, and almost none of it is a trunk in the ordinary sense. This is a strangler fig, and what a tape measure reads at chest height is a fused colonnade of pillar roots dropped from the branches over a century and more, thickened where they hit the ground and grown together since. It carries that mass 22 metres up, on the edge of Swan Lake. NParks will not date it. The register says only that it is thought to be as old as the Gardens themselves, which opened in 1859, and that is a tradition rather than a record. What is firmer than the tradition: the tree turns up in old paintings of the Gardens, and Herbarium staff have recalled playing around it as children in the 1930s, so it was already a landmark before the war. Even its name is unsettled. It is registered as Ficus kurzii, the Burmese banyan, but a fig specialist writing in 2024 points out that true wild kurzii does not grow this far south down the Malay Peninsula, and argues this tree is more likely a hybrid with Ficus benjamina, propagated here from cuttings for more than 150 years. So: one of the largest things growing in the Gardens, and still an open question as to what it actually is.

trees.name: The Saga Tree of the Tanglin Entrance
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 5-10 minute walk from the Tanglin Gate
trees.story: The saga was brought to Singapore to fight a grass. Between 1883 and 1885 the Gardens' superintendent Nathaniel Cantley planted it as an experiment in smothering lalang, the coarse weed grass that takes any cleared ground here within weeks. It worked well enough that the director Henry Ridley later used saga to shade the Gardens' nutmeg, and by the 1970s and 80s it had become a standard Singapore roadside tree. This one grows a few minutes inside the Tanglin entrance, near the Frangipani Garden. Its age comes out of a filing cabinet rather than off a tape. The earliest herbarium specimen cut from this individual tree is dated 1900, which is why the register says it must be well over a century old, putting it past 126 years now. Its measurements are less settled. NParks records a girth of 5.32 metres and a height of 13.1 metres; the National Heritage Board's own entry gives 4.8 metres and 24 metres. The height gap is far too wide to split, so treat both as claims and neither as final. What nobody disputes is the seeds, hard scarlet discs that children pocket and collectors hunt; one collector has mapped 57 saga trees across the island. This tree also sits in a national art collection, photographed by Robert Zhao Renhui for his 2013 work mapping exactly those trees.

trees.name: The Jelutong of Lawn S
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15 minute walk to the rainforest section
trees.story: You can see this tree from the Bandstand, which is odd for a tree standing inside a forest. The jelutong is an emergent: it does not stop at the canopy but pushes its crown out above it, and at 29 metres this one clears everything around it. What is around it matters as much as the tree. It grows on Lawn S, inside the Gardens' patch of primary rainforest, one of only two fragments of Singapore's original forest left anywhere on the island. The species is native here, so this is a tree standing in something close to the vegetation it evolved in, in the middle of a city that has built over almost all of it. Its sap made chewing gum. Gutta jelutong was tapped across Malaya as a base for the stuff, and the pale, soft timber went into pencils, which is a strange double career for a tree in a country that banned the sale of chewing gum in 1992. Nobody has dated it. The register offers no estimate at all, only four metres of girth and that height, and for once the height is the more interesting number: a native tree, in native forest, tall enough to be picked out from a lawn several hundred metres away. If anyone has measured or dated this one, we would like to hear it.

trees.name: The Mandela Tree of Orchid Plaza
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to Orchid Plaza near the National Orchid Garden
trees.story: When Nelson Mandela came to the Singapore Botanic Gardens in 1997, the Gardens dedicated a tree to him, and they picked an unlikely one. The giant cola is West African, unlike anything else growing around Orchid Plaza, and it has stood there with his name attached ever since. An orchid was named for the same visit, which is the more Singaporean gesture. The tree is the one you can walk up to. Cola gigantea belongs to the genus behind the original cola drinks. Its nuts are bitter and loaded with caffeine, chewed across West Africa as a stimulant and offered to guests as a matter of courtesy, and almost every part of the tree has a use in traditional medicine: bark for swellings and pain, other parts against fever, asthma and whooping cough. Laboratory work on its leaf extracts has since taken an interest in the anti-inflammatory half of that reputation. It is not a giant here. Three and a half metres of girth and fifteen metres of height is respectable rather than startling, and it only joined the heritage register in 2014, seventeen years after the dedication. Nobody recorded when it was planted. A dedication is not a planting, so its age is genuinely unknown, and no record of one has turned up.

trees.name: The Walking Tree of Pena
trees.access: Paid entry (Parque da Pena ticket, part of the Sintra hills palace circuit)
trees.transport: Bus 434 (Pena Circuit) from Sintra train station, about 15 min
trees.story: This tree has spent a century and a half slowly relocating itself. Planted not long after King Ferdinand II began building his Romantic fantasy palace on the ruins of a monastery above Sintra, this western red cedar grows a peculiar habit into every low branch: instead of staying airborne, they arc down under their own weight, touch the ground, take root, and thicken into new trunks entirely separate from the original. Repeat that for a century and a half and the result is a small forest walking, metre by metre, toward the nearby lake, each generation of trunks a few steps closer than the last. Forestry students have used it as a teaching example since at least 1916, and it was still notable enough in 2019 to be shortlisted for Portugal's national Árvore do Ano contest. Its perimeter now measures nearly 17 metres, though that number describes a cluster of connected trunks rather than one column the way most tree measurements do. Parque da Pena's own guides call it simply the tree that walks, and once you have seen one root touch down mid-arc, the name stops sounding like a metaphor. It stands a short walk from the Fonte dos Passarinhos, inside the park surrounding Pena Palace, one of the most visited sites in Portugal.

trees.name: The Fern Cork Oak of Quinta do Relógio
trees.age: more than 300 years, Portugal's own register puts it at 350
trees.access: Free, viewable from the public road; please don't touch or remove bark, the tree is under active pressure from souvenir stripping
trees.transport: 20 min walk from Sintra train station, on the road toward Seteais Palace
trees.story: Ferns grow straight out of this oak's bark, which is where its name comes from: Sobreira dos Fetos, the Fern Cork Oak. Portugal's forestry service classified it as a tree of public interest in 1996, by which point it had already stood beside the road to Seteais for roughly three centuries, older than the palace hotel that road now leads to. The English Romantic poet Robert Southey is said to have written that a painter should cross the Channel for no other reason than to see it, a claim that has outlived any record of when he supposedly made it. What has not faded is a more recent, less flattering kind of attention: tour guides have taken to walking groups up to the trunk to peel off pieces of bark as souvenirs, and the environmental association GAAS has publicly said the fencing the state put up around it does nothing to stop them. The tree stands on private land, but right at the roadside, visible and reachable from the public street rather than behind any gate, which is exactly why the damage keeps happening. It is Sintra's oldest documented tree, and the thing most likely to shorten that record is not age. It's whoever walks up next with a knife.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Parque da Liberdade
trees.access: Free, public municipal park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Sintra train station
trees.story: Sintra's park changed its name overnight and this tree didn't notice. Portuguese record keepers classified it as a tree of public interest in 1951, decades before 25 April 1974, when thousands of Sintra's own residents flooded this same municipal garden to celebrate the end of the dictatorship and the park was renamed Parque da Liberdade, Liberty Park, that same year. The tree itself, a London plane with a trunk measuring nearly ten metres around at its base, had already been growing for a century by then, planted sometime in the early to mid-1800s depending on which record you trust: the official government register puts it at roughly 200 years old, while a local history blog's own measurements suggest closer to 150. Either figure makes it one of the thickest plane trees documented anywhere in Portugal, rivalled mainly by a single private specimen near Figueira da Foz. Locals just call it the Platano Gigante, the giant plane, and treat the ground beneath it as one more park bench, shaded regardless of the hour by a canopy that has had a century and a half, at minimum, to fill in.

trees.name: The Araucaria of Monserrate
trees.access: Paid entry (Parque e Palacio de Monserrate ticket)
trees.transport: Bus 435 (Monserrate Circuit) from Sintra train station, about 15 min
trees.story: The tallest tree in one of Portugal's most exotic gardens came from an island most of its visitors couldn't place on a map. Francis Cook, the English textile magnate who bought the crumbling Monserrate estate in 1856, spent the following decades turning its grounds into a private arboretum stitched together from wherever his money could reach: Mexico, the Himalayas, Australia, and this Araucaria heterophylla, native only to a single island in the Tasman Sea, Norfolk Island, some 1,600 kilometres from the Australian mainland it is usually filed under. Planted in Monserrate's mid-19th century expansion, it now stands over 50 metres tall with a crown spreading 22 metres across, by most measurements the tallest tree in the entire garden and a strong candidate for the tallest on mainland Portugal. It grows at the low point of the grounds, beside the ornamental lake, so that visitors coming down through Cook's Himalayan and Mexican plantings see it rising above everything else before they reach the water. Cook never lived to see the tree reach anything like its current size. What he built instead was a garden designed to keep growing into something stranger than he planted, and this conifer, alone among everything else at Monserrate, decided to do that by going straight up.

trees.name: The Pohutukawa of Monserrate
trees.age: genuinely uncertain, estimated between 175 and 275 years
trees.access: Paid entry (Parque e Palacio de Monserrate ticket)
trees.transport: Bus 435 (Monserrate Circuit) from Sintra train station, about 15 min

best_time.label: late May and June, when it blooms scarlet, six months off the New Zealand summer it evolved for

trees.story: New Zealand's Christmas tree blooms scarlet in Portugal in early summer instead, six months off its native schedule and a hemisphere away from the only place it grows wild. This Metrosideros excelsa, a pohutukawa, is one of a pair planted in the grounds Francis Cook built around Monserrate Palace in the second half of the 19th century, though no record pins the planting to a specific year; estimates for this specimen, known locally only as New Zealand Two, range across a full century, sometime between 1750 and 1850, wide enough that even Monserrate's own material describes it simply as older than Cook's own tenure rather than assigning it a date. What is measured rather than estimated is its girth, just over 9 metres around a trunk that has grown the tangled aerial roots the species uses in the wild to grip volcanic coastal cliffs, here gripping nothing but Portuguese hillside soil a mountain away from any coastline. In New Zealand the tree is a national symbol, its flowering timed so precisely to the southern hemisphere summer that it marks the calendar the way certain trees elsewhere mark autumn. Cook's Monserrate collects that kind of geographic joke throughout its grounds, a garden built to prove a 19th century Englishman could grow almost anything on a hillside above Lisbon, if he imported the whole world to do it.

trees.name: The Red Oak of Geleen-Oost Station
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.

best_time.label: October, when the crown turns deep brick red

trees.story:
This Northern red oak grows by Geleen-Oost railway station, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. Northern red oak is an American import, brought to Europe from the eastern United States in the seventeenth century for its faster growth and brilliant autumn colour compared with the native pedunculate oak, and it was planted widely across Dutch railway corridors and parks through the nineteenth century.

A station planting from this era usually marked the railway's own arrival in a place, and Geleen-Oost's station has stood on this line since the industrial growth that turned the wider Sittard-Geleen area from farmland into one of Limburg's coal and chemical centres. The oak has outlasted whatever version of the station building stood here when it was planted.

Red oak's leaves are more deeply cut and pointed than the native oak's rounder lobes, and in October the crown turns a deep brick red rather than the duller brown most European oaks manage, one of the more reliable ways to tell it apart from a distance. The register records only species and decade. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Jardin d'Isabelle
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
This copper beech grows in the Jardin d'Isabelle, a historic town garden in Sittard, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. The register attaches an actual story to the site rather than leaving it blank: the poet Charles Beltjens is said to have met his beloved here, in what was already, by the tree's own lifetime, an established city garden rather than a new planting.

Copper beech is a colour variant of the ordinary European beech, its leaves running dark purple-red through summer instead of green, a mutation first found wild and then propagated by grafting and cutting ever since it was noticed. Left to grow in a sheltered garden setting for a century and a half, this one has had about as easy a life as a beech can have: little pruning, no root compaction, room to build the wide, low crown the species produces when nothing crowds it.

A European ash the register also lists stands a few steps away in the same garden, so this beech is one half of a small cluster rather than a lone specimen. If you know more of the garden's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Ash of Jardin d'Isabelle
trees.age: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.story:
This European ash shares the Jardin d'Isabelle with the copper beech the register also lists nearby, banded to the same decade, a planting around 1870 and roughly 160 years old. Ash dieback, the fungal disease that has killed a large share of the Netherlands' ash population since around 2010, makes every surviving ash this age worth noting: a tree that has stood for a century and a half in a garden setting and made it through more than a decade of a disease that has taken down ash trees far younger.

Ash is among the last trees in a Dutch garden to come into leaf each spring and among the first to drop in autumn, leaving it bare for more than half the year, and its matt black, hoof-shaped buds are one of the easiest ways to identify it through the winter months when nothing else here carries them.

The register gives no history of the tree itself beyond species and decade, unlike its beech neighbour a few steps away, which carries an actual anecdote attached to the garden. If you know whether this ash shows any sign of dieback, or more of its history, tell us.

trees.name: The Sycamore of Janskamperstraat
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.story:
This sycamore maple grows on Janskamperstraat in Geleen, banded by the national register to a planting around 1910, roughly 120 years old. Sycamore is one of the faster-growing large maples planted across the Netherlands through the early twentieth century, valued for tolerating wind, salt and poor soil better than most other broadleaf trees, which made it a common choice for streets and windbreaks in industrial and mining towns like Geleen was becoming through this period.

At 120 years a sycamore has usually reached close to its mature size, with the broad, five-lobed leaves and winged seed pairs, the helicopters children collect every autumn, that the species produces in quantity. Its bark develops a distinctive scaly, plated pattern with age, flaking in irregular patches that can make an old sycamore look almost as textured as a plane tree from a distance.

The register records nothing about this specific tree's history beyond species and decade, which is ordinary for a street tree whose interest is simply having outlasted whatever else stood on the street around it. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Oak of Middengebied Noord
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, on public municipal land.
trees.story:
This oak on the Rijksweg Noord in Geleen carries the register's most detailed physical description on this list: a trunk running four and a half metres around, grown wide and open since it has stood in unenclosed ground since it was planted, roughly around 1910, making it about 120 years old. The register calls the result a strikingly broad crown, the shape a pedunculate oak builds when nothing crowds it from any side.

What makes the register's note worth reading in full is the concern it raises about the tree's future: land immediately east of it is under development, a district plan called Middengebied Noord, and the register's surveyor notes it looks likely the oak will be spared, then adds that keeping this monumental oak a good place to stand matters for whatever comes next. That is an unusually direct piece of advocacy for a database that otherwise sticks to measurements and dates.

It stands visible from Rijksweg Noord, opposite a hospital, free to see at any hour. If the development around it has moved forward, or if you know how the oak has fared, tell us.

trees.name: The Pin Oak of Sittard's Stadspark
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: October, when the finely cut leaves turn bronze-red and hold through winter

trees.story:
This pin oak grows in Sittard's Stadspark, banded by the national register to a planting around 1910, roughly 120 years old. Pin oak is another North American import, native to wet bottomland from the Great Lakes down through the Mississippi valley, and it was planted across Dutch parks through the early twentieth century for a growth habit unlike almost any native oak: a straight central trunk holding a distinctly layered crown, upper branches reaching up, middle branches running level, and lower branches sweeping down toward the ground, sometimes low enough to brush a visitor's head.

Its leaves are the most deeply cut of any oak commonly planted in Europe, with narrow, bristle-tipped lobes that give the crown a fine, almost feathery texture from a distance, and in autumn they turn a rich bronze-red that holds on the branches, often through much of the winter, longer than most other oaks manage.

A tulip tree the register also lists grows a short walk away in the same park, so this pin oak is one stop on what could be a short walk through Stadspark's older plantings. The register records nothing further about this tree specifically. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Tulip Tree of Sittard's Stadspark
trees.age: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1920
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.

best_time.label: October, when the whole crown turns a clean, even butter yellow

trees.story:
This tulip tree grows in Sittard's Stadspark, a short walk from the pin oak the register also lists nearby, banded to a planting around 1920, roughly 110 years old. Liriodendron tulipifera comes from the eastern United States, where it grows as one of the tallest broadleaf trees in North America, and the name undersells what it actually produces: cup-shaped flowers, greenish yellow with an orange band inside, closer to a magnolia in shape than a tulip, opening from late spring high in the crown where they are easy to miss from directly underneath.

The leaves are the more reliable identifying feature, four-lobed with a flat or slightly notched tip as if squared off with scissors, unlike any native European tree, and in autumn they turn a clean, even butter yellow across the whole crown rather than the patchy colour many species manage.

A municipal park stocked with North American specimens like this one and the pin oak nearby reflects an early twentieth century fashion for filling Dutch parks with trees that had no local precedent, chosen for how unlike anything native they looked. The register records only species and decade for this one. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Mulberry of Vasil Levski
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Central Sofia, near the Regional History Museum (former Central Bath); a 5 minute walk from Serdika metro station

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: According to a story that has passed down through Sofia for generations, Vasil Levski, the revolutionary Bulgarians call the Apostle of Freedom, used to tie his horse to a mulberry tree on what is now Iskar Street whenever he stayed at Hadji Mano's inn nearby, a stop confirmed by Levski's own surviving notes referencing a stay at Manoviya han. He was executed by the Ottomans in 1873, and the tree he supposedly used is still standing, about a hundred paces east of the old Central Sofia Bath, now generally called the oldest tree in the capital. How old exactly is genuinely unresolved: estimates from different experts range from roughly 220 years to more than 600, a gap wide enough to place its planting anywhere from the Bulgarian National Revival period back to before the fall of Constantinople, and even its species is described inconsistently across sources, some calling it a white mulberry, others simply a mulberry without specifying which. What survives every version of the story is the tree's role as a fixed point through Sofia's growth from Ottoman provincial town to national capital, still rooted in the same spot while the city grew up entirely around it, and its formal status today as an officially protected specimen.

trees.name: Ivan Vazov's Spruce
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Borisova Garden, central Sofia; a 10 minute walk from Vasil Levski metro station
trees.story: Ivan Vazov, the author routinely called the Patriarch of Bulgarian Literature, planted a spruce in Borisova Garden in 1885, decades before Sofia's own cultural establishment got around to building him a monument. That marble bust went up in 1920, sculpted by Zheko Spiridonov and funded by the city's Art and Industrial School, and it now stands near a tree that has since grown to roughly 30 metres, taller than most buildings in the surrounding park. Picea abies grows naturally in Bulgaria's mountain forests rather than in lowland Sofia, so a spruce this size and age inside a city park represents decades of deliberate cultivation rather than a wild survivor, tended carefully enough to outlast the writer who planted it by more than a century. Vazov himself lived until 1921, long enough to see his own tree well established, and Borisova Garden, opened as the city's grand municipal park in the 1880s, has grown up around both the tree and the bust as one of Sofia's most visited green spaces. Few visitors walking past either object today realize the taller of the two is also the older.

trees.name: The Oak of Pencho Slaveykov
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Lozenets district, Ulitsa Sveta Gora; about a 20 minute walk from Vasil Levski Stadium

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: When the Slaveykov family moved from Plovdiv to Sofia after Bulgaria's 1878 liberation and bought a garden in what is now the Lozenets district, they got more than a plot of land. The garden held a surviving fragment of Kurubaglar, an old oak grove that had once covered a wide stretch of the area later swallowed by the city, and one of its oaks, later named for the poet Pencho Slaveykov, is reckoned by some accounts at more than 500 years old, old enough to have been standing through the entire span of Ottoman rule the 1878 liberation ended. A more conservative count of the garden's roughly 28 other trees puts their age nearer 300 years, itself old enough to make the plot one of Sofia's oldest continuously wooded pieces of ground. Pencho Slaveykov wrote some of his best known work in this garden, and it became a regular meeting place for the literary circle around the journal Misal, Bulgaria's most influential turn of the century intellectual gathering, whose members included the poet Peyo Yavorov and the critic Dr. Krastev. The site was declared a national cultural monument in 2005, though the park around the oak has since fallen into visible disrepair, its benches broken and its fountain dry, a contrast the tree itself seems entirely unbothered by.

trees.name: The Gray Poplar of Doctors' Garden
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: Central Sofia, near Alexandrovska Hospital; a 10 minute walk from Sofia University metro station
trees.story: Doctors' Garden started life in 1896 as one of Sofia's first botanical gardens, a role it kept for roughly four decades before the collection was absorbed elsewhere and the grounds became an ordinary public park. Its oldest tree predates even that botanical mission: a grey poplar planted in 1892, four years before the garden's formal opening, making it the first tree in the ground on a site that would later fill with imported rarities like ginkgo, bald cypress and thorny honey locust brought over from North America. Populus canescens is a wild-type species, unlike the ornamental poplar cultivars usually chosen for city planting, and its survival as a deliberately kept specimen among later collections of showier imports is itself part of what earned it protected status. The garden takes its name from the doctors of the nearby Alexandrovska Hospital, who used the grounds for open air recovery and, informally, still do, so this poplar has spent more than a century sheltering patients on the same soil where it was one of the first things anyone thought to plant.

trees.name: The Hajdukova Murva (Hajduk's Mulberry)
trees.access: Restricted; stands within the grounds now used by RK Nada rugby club at the former Stari plac stadium, visible from Zrinsko-Frankopanska and Plinarska streets
trees.transport: Lučac-Manuš district; about a 20 minute walk from the Riva

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: In 2015 a team from Zagreb's Faculty of Science took a DNA sample from an ailing mulberry tree in Split and cloned it 105 times, once for every year of HNK Hajduk Split's existence. The tree had stood in the courtyard of the club's first home, Stari plac, since before Hajduk itself existed, and every player who wore the checkerboard shirt between the club's founding in 1911 and its move to Poljud in 1979 walked past it on the way to training. Supporters kept coming back long after the club left: candles still turn up at its roots on the anniversaries of dead club legends, an unofficial shrine nobody organized and everybody understands. By 2014 the tree was ailing badly enough that the city's mayor stepped in personally to back a rescue, and the arborists who examined it put its age at around 120, close to two decades before the club it would outlive by a century was even founded. The clone count of 105 was symbolic, tied to the club's anniversary, but the genetics were real: each seedling carries the original's exact DNA, distributed around Split with the first planted ceremonially at the university campus in 2016. As far as anyone has documented, Hajduk remains the only football club anywhere with its own cloned tree.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Đardin
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: At the Golden Gate, a 5 minute walk from Diocletian's Palace's Peristil

best_time.label: November: the whole crown turns butter gold, then drops in a day or two

trees.story: Split's own park authority has only ever given one tree its highest rarity grade, and it stands a few steps from the busiest gate of Diocletian's Palace. The ginkgo in Đardin, the compact 19th-century garden wedged between two old Venetian bastions just north of the Golden Gate, was singled out in a municipal botanical survey as a Category I rarity, officially the single most valuable tree in the park and, by the same assessment, in the city. Ginkgo biloba is itself a botanical anomaly wherever it grows, a conifer relative with fan-shaped leaves and no living close cousins, a lineage old enough to have shared the planet with dinosaurs and simply outlasted them. No record gives this particular specimen's planting date, only its rank, so its age here is an estimate rather than a documented figure. What is documented is the garden around it: cleared as parkland in 1808, when the wall between two Venetian bastions came down under French rule, and made the city's main public garden in 1859. The tree has outgrown both the empire that freed its ground and the kingdom that gave the park its purpose, and neither gets a plaque nearly as pointed as the one the city's own botanists gave the tree itself.

trees.name: The Cypress of Kolombatović
trees.access: Free, public promenade on Marjan hill, open daily
trees.transport: Marjan hill, via Šetalište Ivana Meštrović; about a 20-25 minute walk from the Riva
trees.story: The cypress on Marjan's Kolombatović walkway went into the ground in 1908, the same year the man it honors died. Juraj Kolombatović was a Split zoologist who spent much of his career naming fish nobody else had described, and in 1903 he became founding president of the Marjan Society, the group that turned decades of scattered tree planting on the barren hill above the city into an organized, permanent effort. Aleppo pines had gone in as early as 1852, but Marjan stayed a patchy, half wild slope until Kolombatović's generation gave its reforestation an institution to answer to. When he died, the society planted a Mediterranean cypress in his memory, and the promenade running past it now carries his name, Kolombatovićevo šetalište, the same path that leads to Split's zoo and natural history museum today. More than a century on, the cypress stands taller than most of the pines planted decades before it, on a hill that is now one continuous forest instead of the bare outcrop Kolombatović's own contemporaries described. It is the one tree on Marjan with a name attached to a specific act of memory rather than a species list.

trees.name: The Black Walnut of Đardin
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily
trees.transport: At the Golden Gate, a 5 minute walk from Diocletian's Palace's Peristil

best_time.label: late September into October, when the walnuts ripen and drop

trees.story: The black walnut growing in Đardin, Split's 19th-century public garden by the Golden Gate, is not a Mediterranean tree at all. Juglans nigra is native to eastern North America, and Split's own botanical survey lists it as a Category II rarity precisely because it is almost never seen this far south on the Adriatic, a temperate forest species making an unlikely living among the palms, planes and pines the city's actual climate can support. Nobody has recorded when it went in or who planted it, only that it survived long enough, and improbably enough, to earn a rarity grade alongside the garden's more famous ginkgo. Đardin itself dates to 1859, when the ground between two former Venetian bastions became the city's main public garden, decades after French forces first cleared the fortification wall in 1808, so the walnut has had, at most, a century and a half to establish itself as one of only a handful of its kind on this stretch of coast. It stands without a plaque, its rarity administrative rather than advertised, recorded in a municipal botanical assessment rather than on any sign a visitor would actually see walking past it.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Villa Fondi
trees.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)
trees.access: Free, public municipal park (Villa Fondi De Sangro, owned by the Comune di Piano di Sorrento, houses the Georges Vallet archaeological museum). Open as a public park; no permission needed to walk the grounds.
trees.transport: Circumvesuviana train from Sorrento station to Piano di Sorrento station (one stop, a few minutes), then about 10 minutes on foot via Via Ripa di Cassano.
trees.story:
