Three metres and eighteen centimetres round, and it stops at eleven metres tall. This holm oak spent its life spreading instead of climbing, on a terrace above Piano di Sorrento with the Bay of Naples in front of it and Vesuvius across the water.

The ground belonged to Giovanni Andrea De Sangro, Prince of Fondi, who built the villa in 1840. The garden around it was laid out in 1875. Italy's national monumental-tree register and the Regione Campania's own card for this oak agree on its measurements to the centimetre and put its age at roughly 150 years, which would make it a planting of that first garden or something a little later. Nobody has counted the rings, so the date stays an approximation, exactly as the register leaves it.

The villa passed to the comune, was restored in the 1990s and now holds the Georges Vallet archaeological museum, so the oak keeps company with Roman finds dug out of the peninsula. The park is free to walk.

One thing to expect: the two official records place this tree about 60 metres apart, both inside the same small park, so the pin gets you to the terrace rather than to the trunk. It is a short look around.

The tree is in Piano di Sorrento, not in Sorrento itself: one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station, then ten minutes on foot.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Villa Fondi
trees.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)
trees.access: Free, public municipal park (Villa Fondi De Sangro, owned by the Comune di Piano di Sorrento, houses the Georges Vallet archaeological museum). Open as a public park; no permission needed to walk the grounds.
trees.transport: Circumvesuviana train from Sorrento station to Piano di Sorrento station (one stop, a few minutes), then about 10 minutes on foot via Via Ripa di Cassano.
trees.story:
In 2014 the WWF called the pines of Villa Fondi the last of their kind left standing in the built-up area on the tufa slope of Piano di Sorrento, and objected to a plan to cut them back hard. The Soprintendenza confirmed the villa and its park trees were protected. The pruning did not happen.

This is the largest of them. It measures 4.18 metres round and twenty metres tall, carrying the flat spreading head that stone pines grow into once they have the room. The national register and the Regione Campania card give those figures identically and put the tree at around 150 years, presumably a planting of the garden laid out in 1875 around the De Sangro family's villa of 1840.

Its health has been a local subject. A 2020 description of the garden mentions a big pine on the sea-facing western side, put at roughly 200 years old, attacked by bark beetles and saved by dendrosurgery. Whether that account is about this exact pine is not clear: it names a different pine species than the register does, and the garden may hold more than one old specimen. Nothing on record says the registered tree has gone.

It stands in the same free public park as the holm oak, beside the Georges Vallet archaeological museum, in Piano di Sorrento. From Sorrento it is one Circumvesuviana stop and a ten-minute walk.

trees.name: The Cemetery Cypress of Piano di Sorrento
trees.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)
trees.access: Free, public municipal cemetery, open daily during standard daylight hours set by the Comune di Piano di Sorrento (exact hours vary seasonally and around 1/6 January; check locally). No permission needed to enter.
trees.transport: Circumvesuviana train from Sorrento station to Piano di Sorrento station, then about 15 minutes on foot uphill via Via Gennaro Maresca.
trees.story:
The cemetery opened in 1876, and by the account the register recorded this cypress went into the ground the same year. It has stood over every burial the place has ever had.

That dating comes from local testimony rather than a document, which the Regione Campania card says openly; it calls the tree over 130 years old at its last update, which puts it near 150 now. Measured rather than remembered: 2.66 metres round and ten metres tall, figures the national register and the regional card give identically.

At that girth an Italian cypress reads as a column rather than the thin dark spire the species is usually planted as. Two more cypresses in this same cemetery are on the national register, at 2.70 and 3.25 metres round, so the thickest trunk you see here is not this one. Go by the coordinates instead, and give yourself a minute: the two official records for this tree sit about 90 metres apart inside the grounds.

Piano di Sorrento's municipal cemetery is a free, everyday public place, open through the daylight hours the comune sets, which shift with the season. It is a working cemetery, so the usual quiet applies.

The walk is in Piano di Sorrento rather than Sorrento: one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station, then about fifteen minutes uphill on Via Gennaro Maresca.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Via Maresca
trees.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)
trees.access: Free, standing on a public street corner. Visible and reachable at any time.
trees.transport: Circumvesuviana train from Sorrento station to Piano di Sorrento station, then about 12 minutes on foot via Via Gennaro Maresca (on the way up to the cemetery).
trees.story:
The register lists this plane as a landmark rather than a specimen: it is how you know you have reached the second-to-last bend on the climb to the cemetery. A century of shade on a steep road earns a tree that job.

Local testimony recorded by the Regione Campania puts the planting at around 1920, so roughly 105 years, and nobody holds a document proving it. What is measured rather than remembered: 2.95 metres round and ten metres tall, identical in the national register and the regional card, whose coordinates land within five metres of each other. You will not have to hunt for this one.

A second plane stands beside it with a slimmer trunk, and the registered tree is the more imposing of the pair. At the last survey in 2020 its crown carried no dead stubs, which for a tree working a hot roadside on the Sorrentine peninsula is a better report than it sounds.

Via Gennaro Maresca is a public street in Piano di Sorrento, the comune next door to Sorrento, not Sorrento itself: one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station, then about twelve minutes on foot uphill. Keep going for a few more minutes and you reach the cemetery cypress, which makes the two of them one short climb rather than two errands.

trees.name: The Six Araucarias of Largo Jose Afonso
trees.access: Free, open public square
trees.transport: In the centre of Setubal, a few minutes on foot from the station
trees.story: Six trees stand in a ring around one old circular stone tank with a fountain at its middle, and at twenty-six metres they are the tallest classified trees in the city. They were planted around 1919, which means they have watched the square change names three times and change purpose twice. It began as the Passeio do Lago, named for a garden with a lake at its centre. In January 1911 it became the Parque das Escolas, after two primary schools opened on it, one for boys and one for girls, so the young trees spent their first decades in a schoolyard. Through the 1930s the square held two open-air cinemas, one of them run by the volunteer fire brigade and the other called the Cine Parque, and films were projected under these branches on summer evenings. The name it carries now arrived in 1988, for Jose Afonso, whose song Grandola, Vila Morena was the radio signal that launched the revolution of 1974, and Grandola is in this district. The trees are evergreen, so they look the same in January as in July.

trees.name: The Plane of Largo Doutor Francisco Soveral
trees.access: Free, open public square
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot
trees.story: This tree is not a specimen you look at, it is the ceiling of a small square in the old town. Twenty-six metres tall with a crown twenty-seven metres across, it covers the whole of Largo Doutor Francisco Soveral, so the shade underneath is not a patch but a room. That is what the plane was bred for. It is a hybrid, a cross between the American sycamore and the Oriental plane that turned up in Europe in the seventeenth century and proved almost impossible to kill in a dirty city: it shrugs off exhaust, tolerates brutal pruning and sheds its bark in patches to throw off the grime, which is why half the capitals of Europe are lined with them. In a port city with a canning industry those were useful qualities. At around seventy years it is one of the younger classified trees here and it earns its place on presence rather than age, which is worth being honest about. Come in summer and you will understand why the state bothered to protect a seventy-year-old street tree.

trees.name: The Silky Oaks of Largo Marques de Pombal
trees.access: Free, open public square
trees.transport: In the centre, about 200 m from Largo Jose Afonso

best_time.label: April and May, when the whole crown turns orange

trees.story: For eleven months of the year this is a tall Australian tree that most people walk past. For a few weeks in spring it covers itself in orange, in dense one-sided combs of flower that look more like a bottlebrush than anything a European tree does, and the whole square changes colour. The parish, which knows its own trees, describes them as rare in Portugal, and there are two of them here, standing metres apart on what used to be the Praca de Sao Pedro. Silky oak is not an oak at all. It belongs to the protea family, its nearest relatives are the banksias and grevilleas of Australia, and it was carried around the world in the nineteenth century for exactly the display it puts on here. In its native Queensland it grows to forty metres in rainforest; on a Portuguese square it settles for nineteen. The two trees are near twins and the register separates them only by trunk girth, so stand between them and you are looking at both.

trees.name: The Melaleuca That Grows Sideways
trees.access: Free, public waterfront garden
trees.transport: On the Sado waterfront, about 10 min walk from the centre
trees.story: Two metres round the trunk, three and a half metres tall, and a crown eleven metres wide. Those numbers describe a tree that decided early on to spend its life going outwards rather than up, and the result in this waterfront garden is a low sprawling dome of long branches running almost horizontally from the base, which you walk under rather than look up at. The parish calls it a living monument, and it is the strangest thing on this page. Melaleuca armillaris comes from the coast of New South Wales, gets its name from the bracelet-like rings its cream flowers form along the stems, and has papery bark that peels in soft sheets. It is planted along the Sado waterfront because it tolerates salt wind, which is the same reason it grows low and wide: this is what the species does when it spends a century in the path of weather off the water. The register puts it at 150 years, which is high for its kind and which no other source confirms, so treat the number lightly and the tree seriously.

trees.name: The Stone Pines of Rua Henri Perron
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: North of the centre, about 20 min walk or a short bus ride
trees.story: These two were here before the street was. The parish describes the stone pines on this road as survivors of the woodland that covered the ground before the city expanded northwards over it, which makes them older than the neighbourhood rather than planted into it, and it explains why they stand where they do rather than in any pattern. The larger has a trunk four and fifteen metres around, the thickest of any tree in central Setubal. Stone pine is the umbrella pine of every Portuguese and Italian horizon, the one with a bare trunk and a flat spreading head, and it is a working tree as much as an ornamental one: its cones hold pine nuts, which take three years to ripen and are still harvested commercially across this part of Portugal. The shape is not decorative either. A stone pine sheds its lower branches as it grows so that the crown sits above browsing height and above the reach of ground fire, which is a design for surviving exactly the landscape this city was built on.

trees.name: The Box Elder of the Jardim do Bonfim
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from the centre
trees.story: The ground this tree stands on was called the Campo da Barbuda in the sixteenth century, long before anyone thought to make a garden of it, and the box elder is now the oldest thing in what became Setubal's main park. It is a maple that does not look like one. Where every other maple carries a single lobed leaf, Acer negundo splits its into three, five or seven separate leaflets, so people routinely mistake it for an ash and it is sometimes called the ash-leaved maple for that reason. It is North American, it grows fast, it is short-lived by maple standards, and at nearly four metres round and a hundred and seventeen years old this one has outlasted what the species usually manages. That is the reason it is classified. It comes into leaf late and drops early, and in the weeks between it does what a park tree is for: it holds up a large amount of shade over the benches underneath.

trees.name: The Norfolk Island Hibiscus of Montalvao
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from the centre, in the Montalvao district
trees.story: This tree comes from an island of thirty-five square kilometres in the Pacific, thirteen thousand kilometres away, and there are not many of them in Portugal. Lagunaria patersonii is native to Norfolk Island and Lord Howe, grows into a neat dense pyramid, and flowers in summer in pale pink cups that look like a small hibiscus, which is where the common name comes from. It also has a famous defence: the seed capsules are packed with fine stiff hairs that irritate skin badly enough that Australians call it the itchy bomb tree, so admire the fruit and do not open it. Setubal planted it for the same reason coastal cities everywhere did, because it stands up to salt wind and poor soil without complaint. At sixty-two it is the youngest tree on this page, and it is classified not for its age but because the species is genuinely uncommon here. The parish route lists it among the trees worth walking to, which is a fair verdict on a tree most people would pass without a glance.

trees.name: The Poplars by Bocage's School
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: North of the centre, about 18 min walk
trees.story: Two black poplars of twenty-five metres stand beside the Escola Secundaria du Bocage, which is named for Manuel Maria Barbosa du Bocage, the poet born in this city in 1765. Bocage is the reason Setubal has a literary reputation at all. He ran away to sea, deserted, wrote satirical verse sharp enough to get himself arrested by the Inquisition in 1797, and produced sonnets that Portuguese schoolchildren still learn; the school that carries his name has stood here since the trees were young. Black poplar is a riverside species and it behaves like one: fast, tall, thirsty, and among the first trees to break bud in spring and among the last to hold its leaves in autumn. It also moves. The leaves are set on flattened stalks that twist in the smallest breeze, so a poplar makes noise where other trees are silent, which is why they were planted along roads and rivers across Europe. Stand under these two on a windy afternoon and the sound is the point.

trees.name: The Pepper Tree That Mended Nets
trees.access: Free, public street
trees.transport: East of the centre, about 15 min walk

best_time.label: late autumn, when the clusters of pink peppercorns turn red

trees.story: In a city built on sardines, this street tree used to work for the fleet. The parish records that the resin of the Brazilian pepper was used on fishing nets, a treatment that stiffened and waterproofed the fibres and slowed the rot that salt water works on anything organic. Setubal canned fish on an industrial scale from the nineteenth century onwards and the port is still the reason the city exists, so an ornamental avenue tree quietly feeding the tackle shed is a better fact than most trees on this page can offer. The species is Brazilian, related to the cashew and the mango, and it is the source of the pink peppercorns sold in supermarket grinders, which are not true pepper at all. It fruits heavily in autumn and winter, hanging clusters of small bright red drupes on a tree that is otherwise unremarkable, and that is the moment to see it. It is about eighty-three years old and thirteen metres tall, which is respectable rather than impressive; the story is the reason it is here.

trees.name: The Peruvian Pepper of the Jardim de Palhais
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: East of the centre, about 12 min walk

best_time.label: October and November, when the pink drupes hang in strings

trees.story: The Peruvian pepper is the weeping cousin of the tree on the avenue nearby, and the two together make a small lesson in how the same idea arrived in Europe twice. This one is Andean, it was carried back by the Spanish in the sixteenth century, and the Inca used its fruit for a fermented drink and its resin for embalming. What it looks like is a willow that took a wrong turn: long drooping compound leaves on branches that hang almost to the ground, so from underneath it forms a green tent. Crush a leaf and it smells sharply of pepper, which is the family trait, and in autumn it carries loose pink drupes on strings. At around a hundred and two years it is among the older trees in Setubal, and it stands alone in a small garden in Sao Sebastiao, off the line of the main walk. One honest caveat: this is the only tree on this page that the parish route does not cover, because the garden sits in a different parish, so it rests on the national register alone.

trees.name: The Ginkgos of Place de la République
trees.age: over a century, planted late 1800s to early 1900s
trees.access: Free, public square (Place de la République, central Strasbourg)
trees.transport: Tram B, C, E or F, Republique stop, right at the square

best_time.label: November, when both crowns turn butter gold and drop within days of each other

trees.story: Two ginkgos face each other across Place de la Republique, each more than 470 centimetres around, and Strasbourg tells a story about how they arrived: a gift from the emperor of Japan to the German Kaiser. Local reporting cannot say which Kaiser, Wilhelm I or Wilhelm II, and no document has ever been produced, so the gift belongs to the city's oral tradition rather than to its archives. The setting is not in doubt. The square was built as Kaiserplatz and finished in 1887, the ceremonial heart of the Neustadt, the new German quarter laid out after the annexation of Alsace in 1871. The trees went in between then and the early 1900s. They have stood through the return to France in 1918, the German annexation of 1940, the liberation of 1944, and the raising of the war memorial at the square's centre, a mother holding two dying sons, one in French uniform and one in German. In 2021 one of the pair reached the final of France's Arbre de l'Annee and did not win, which is also the most recent dated confirmation that both are alive and healthy. Nobody has counted their rings, so their age is inferred from the square around them. Ginkgo has a reputation for surviving whatever is thrown at it. It suits this square better than whoever planted them can have known.

trees.name: The Spy's Gate Planes of the Meinau
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc Schulmeister, the current 7-hectare park created in 1971 on the former estate)
trees.transport: Tram A, Schluthfeld or Rome stop, short walk; several bus lines also serve the Meinau district
trees.story: Napoleon's spymaster bought a meadow here in 1806 and called it Meine Aue, my meadow. The name stuck to the whole district, which is why a Strasbourg suburb is called the Meinau. Charles-Louis Schulmeister, who had talked his way into the Austrian high command and fed it false information before Austerlitz, built a chateau on the ground in 1807 and 1808. Two plane trees stood at its gate. Everything else went. Schulmeister lost the estate in 1836, ruined. The chateau became a sugar refinery and was pulled down in 1873 after the city bought the land. The grounds opened as a public park in 1934 and were rebuilt into the seven hectares of Parc Schulmeister in 1971. The two planes are what is left of the entrance, still standing as a pair on the same spot. Whether they were Schulmeister's own planting or arrived with one of the later landscapings, no source says, so the pair carries no date. What is documented is the site: the city's register lists the trees, and the chateau's story is told the same way by local historians and by the park's own record. This one is a trip rather than a stop, 3.7 kilometres south of the old town and a tram ride out. Go for the story as much as for the trunks, then walk the park, which is one of the quieter big green spaces in Strasbourg.

trees.name: The Great Plane of Parc du Contades
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc du Contades, Strasbourg's oldest public park, laid out from 1764)
trees.transport: Tram B or E, Faubourg-de-Pierre or Broglie stop, short walk; also served by several bus lines
trees.story: Alsace's regional register dates this plane to the 1730s, which would make it older than the park it stands in. The Parc du Contades was laid out from 1764 as a promenade for the Marshal de Contades, then military governor of Alsace, and it is Strasbourg's oldest public park. If the register is right, the tree was already thirty years old when the first paths were drawn around it. That date comes from the Collectivite europeenne d'Alsace, a body entirely separate from the city's own remarkable-tree list, which is what gives it weight. Its page could not be read directly, only through a search extract, so treat the 1730s as a strong claim rather than a settled one. The height is disputed in the ordinary way. The city says 40 metres. Other listings say 43, and one says nearly 45. Take 40 and upwards, and accept that nobody has recently gone up it with a tape. On the register's dating, this tree stood through the creation of the park around it, the Revolution that turned a marshal's promenade into public ground, the German annexation of 1871 that built the Neustadt right up against it, and two wars in which the city changed hands. It sits at the centre of the park and cannot be walked past without noticing.

trees.name: The Plane of the Fish Market Square
trees.access: Free, public square in Strasbourg's Grande Ile old town (UNESCO World Heritage historic centre)
trees.transport: Tram A, B, C, D, E or F, Homme de Fer or Langstross-Grand'Rue stop, short walk through the old town
trees.story: A trunk five metres around is a park tree's measurement. This one is standing on paving in the middle of a medieval city, in a corner of the Place du marche aux poissons, where fish were sold beside the Ill for centuries before the trade moved indoors. The Grande Ile is Strasbourg's original island city and has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988, the first entire city centre to be listed. Almost nothing grows large here because almost nothing has room to. Paving, cellars and the foundations of the surrounding houses leave very little soil, which is what makes a girth of over 500 centimetres the fact worth reporting about this tree. Somebody made room for it, and successive administrations have left it alone. The city's own register is the only source that describes it. No newspaper has profiled it and no association has labelled it, so a municipal listing and a measurement are what is on record, and no more than that. It works as a five-minute stop rather than a destination. The cathedral is three minutes east, the Petite France quarter about ten minutes west along the water, and the square itself has the Historical Museum on one side and the river on the other, which makes this the rare old-town tree you can photograph with something other than a wall behind it.

trees.name: The Old Plane of Quai de la Bruche
trees.access: Free, public quayside in the Petite France quarter, shading a well-known cafe terrace
trees.transport: Tram A, B, C, D, E or F, Homme de Fer or Faubourg-National stop, short walk into Petite France
trees.story: Postcards and travel listings will tell you this plane tree was planted in 1667. It was not, and the reason is botanical rather than archival: the London plane is a hybrid of the oriental and American planes that only appeared in Europe during the 18th century. In 1667 the tree did not exist as a kind of tree anywhere on the continent. Something old did stand here, though. The quay was called the Wasserzoll until the Revolution, after the water toll charged on goods entering Strasbourg by river, and that toll was collected, in the register's own phrasing, in the shade of the ancient tree still standing on the spot. A local history of the quay identifies the older tree as an enormous walnut that failed to survive the hard winter of 1704 and had to be felled. The plane, it says, is its authentic successor. So the honest version: an ancient tree marked this corner of the Petite France by the 1660s, and today's plane, roughly 450 centimetres in girth and one of the oldest street trees in Strasbourg, is very probably the replacement rather than the survivor. Even the city's register hedges, saying only that this is perhaps that tree. It now shades a cafe terrace on the quay, which is a demotion from tax collection and a considerable improvement.

trees.name: The Great Beech of Parc de l'Orangerie
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc de l'Orangerie, Strasbourg's oldest and grandest public park, laid out in 1692)
trees.transport: Tram E, Droits de l'Homme stop, short walk into the park

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.story: Strasbourg's oldest park is full of beeches and the register singles out one of them: more than four metres around the trunk, with a crown the city calls exceptionally well developed. In a beech that combination is unusual. A forest beech grows tall and narrow, and only spreads like this when it has had open ground and no competition for a very long time. The Parc de l'Orangerie gave it exactly that. The park was laid out in 1692 for the governor of Alsace, which makes it older than almost every French public garden that was not royal, and it was rebuilt as an English landscape park in the 1800s, the moment when planting fashion changed from avenues to single specimen trees standing alone. The pavilion at its centre carries the Empress Josephine's name. The same grounds now hold a zoo, a lake, a stork colony and the grandest green space in the city. No age has been published for this beech and no journalist has written about it, so its dimensions are all anyone has recorded. European beech has thin, smooth bark that carves easily and scars permanently, which is why the old ones in busy parks end up covered in initials. Look down as well. On a beech this size the roots run over the surface like cables.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Place de l'Université
trees.access: Free, public square in front of the University of Strasbourg's Palais Universitaire
trees.transport: Tram B or E, Universite stop, right at the square
trees.story: Purple-leaved beeches are a mutation that gardeners decided to keep. Copper beech is the same species as the green European beech, one that occasionally throws a seedling whose leaves carry so much red pigment that the green underneath barely shows, and the European ones descend from a handful of such accidents found in German and Swiss forests from the 1600s onward. Nurseries have propagated them ever since for exactly this job: one dark tree in a formal civic square. This one is 26 metres tall with a trunk over 330 centimetres around, among the largest specimens on the city's list. It stands on Place de l'Universite in front of the Palais Universitaire, the enormous neo-Renaissance block the German administration put up in the 1880s when it rebuilt Strasbourg's university as a showpiece of imperial science. The tree belongs to that project, in a square designed as its forecourt. Since then the university has been German, French, German again and French again, evacuated wholesale to Clermont-Ferrand during the Second World War, and put back together. The beech stayed. No age is on record, and the city's register is the only source describing it. In late spring the new leaves are almost translucent red before they darken. By high summer the crown is dense enough to leave the ground beneath it nearly bare.

trees.name: The Rabin Memorial Cedar
trees.access: Free, outdoor grounds of a public municipal building (Centre administratif de l'Eurometropole), open during the building's public hours; a real destination rather than a park, so check the centre is open (Mon-Fri 8am-5:30pm, Sat 8am-12:30pm) before visiting
trees.transport: Tram B or F, or bus, toward the Centre administratif / Etoile area
trees.story: This tree has a birthday: 25 May 1996. Strasbourg planted a blue Atlas cedar that day in memory of Yitzhak Rabin, the Israeli prime minister shot dead six months earlier by an opponent of the Oslo accords, at the end of a peace rally in Tel Aviv. Ancient trees are almost always dated by estimate. This one carries a date, which makes it both the easiest age in the city to state and the youngest entry here: thirty years, planted by a municipality that wanted a living object rather than a plaque. Cedrus atlantica comes from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, where it reaches 40 metres. The Glauca cultivar planted here is selected for needles so grey-blue they read as metallic in flat light, and it holds them all year, so there is no season when this tree is not doing its one visual trick. The city's own register is the only source recording the memorial, which is thin for a fact this specific, though a dated planting is the kind of thing a municipality keeps rather than invents. It grows in the grounds of the Eurometropole's administrative centre rather than in a park, an unglamorous address for a memorial, and that makes one practical detail matter: the grounds follow the building's hours, weekdays and Saturday mornings. Go on a working day. The cedar is outdoors and free to walk up to.

trees.name: The Layering Thuja of Parc de l'Orangerie
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc de l'Orangerie)
trees.transport: Tram E, Droits de l'Homme stop, short walk into the park
trees.story: This tree is quietly making copies of itself. Its lowest branches have bent to the ground, rooted where they touch it and sent up new stems, a process called layering that turns one trunk into a small colony over a few decades. It is the same trick that keeps some ancient yews going indefinitely, and it is rare to see in a public park, because ground-level branches are usually the first thing a maintenance crew takes off. Thuja plicata comes from the Pacific Northwest, the rainforest strip running from northern California to Alaska, where it reaches 60 metres and where the coastal peoples built canoes, longhouses and woven bark clothing out of it. Almost every one in Europe was planted, most of them as hedging, which makes a full-sized specimen doing what the species does in the wild worth the few extra minutes inside the Parc de l'Orangerie. Crush a leaf spray between your fingers as you pass. Western red cedar smells strongly of pineapple, and unlike most conifer scents it stays on your hands. No age is recorded and the city's register is the only source describing it, so the layering and the dimensions are what there is. The great beech of the same park stands a few minutes away, which makes the pair a short walk rather than two separate trips.

trees.name: The Parasol Pine of Parc de l'Orangerie
trees.access: Free, public park (Parc de l'Orangerie, Strasbourg's oldest public park, laid out in 1692)
trees.transport: Tram E, Droits de l'Homme stop, short walk into the park
trees.story: Strasbourg's register singles this pine out for three things, and one of them is the ivy on its trunk. The other two are shape: a crown flattened into a parasol, and a bole the register calls tortuous, notably tall and notably thick. That is broadly what a Scots pine becomes with time, shedding its lower branches and spreading what is left across the top, until a twisting bare trunk is holding up a flat green ceiling. The ivy is not the problem people assume. It is a climber rather than a parasite, rooted in the ground and using the trunk only to get up to the light. Pinus sylvestris has the widest natural range of any pine on earth, from Spain to eastern Siberia, and the city's own species note says it reaches thirty metres and can live five or six centuries. It says nothing about what this particular tree has managed, and neither does anything else we could find: the register is the only source describing it, as it is for the great beech and the layering thuja in the same park. Those two stand a few minutes away, which turns this into three listed trees on one short walk. Parc de l'Orangerie has been a garden since 1692, which is the reason trees this size are standing near the middle of a city at all.

trees.name: Birger Jarl's Oak
trees.access: Visible year-round from nearby Kungsholmen streets and the Kristineberg motorway interchange; the tree stands on a traffic island and is not meant to be approached on foot
trees.transport: Stadshagen or Thorildsplan metro station, then a short walk toward the Kristineberg interchange

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Stockholm's founding date is usually given as 1252, when the regent Birger Jarl is credited with establishing the city, and this oak has been growing on Kungsholmen for almost exactly as long, roughly 800 years, according to trunk measurements the city has taken over the decades. Nobody claims Birger Jarl planted it himself; the name is a nod to its age matching the city's own rather than a documented act. What makes it remarkable today has less to do with the tree and more to do with what grew up around it: when engineers built Essingeleden, one of Stockholm's busiest motorways, they routed the Kristineberg interchange so that this single oak now stands on a traffic island roughly ten metres from six lanes of moving cars. City surveys rate its trunk, over two metres across, among the nine thickest oaks in Stockholm and give the surrounding habitat the same protection status as a nature reserve, despite being wedged into asphalt rather than parkland. It is not a tree to picnic under. It is visible from the road and from nearby streets on Kungsholmen, a genuinely ancient survivor that the city built a motorway interchange around rather than through, when it could easily have gone the other way.

trees.name: Lyell's Oak
trees.access: Free, open access, Royal National City Park (Djurgarden), open at all times
trees.transport: Bus toward Norra Djurgarden or a walk/cycle from Ostermalm via Djurgardsbrunnsviken

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: In 1835, the Scottish geologist Charles Lyell was in Stockholm gathering evidence for one of the founding ideas of modern geology, that Scandinavia's land was slowly rising out of the sea, a process now called postglacial rebound. To measure how much the land had lifted, Lyell needed a fixed reference point old enough to have been growing when earlier surveyors recorded the water line, and he found one in this oak on Norra Djurgarden, alongside a second oak, Fiskartorpseken, by a nearby royal fishing cottage. He measured the oak's girth and height above the water of Husarviken bay and used its estimated age to help calculate how much the shoreline had shifted, fieldwork now considered a small but real contribution to a theory Charles Darwin would later draw on directly. The oak has kept growing steadily in the two centuries since serving as scientific apparatus: 4.04 metres around in Lyell's own 1835 measurement, 5.20 metres when the Swedish botanist Rutger Sernander surveyed Djurgarden's oaks in 1926, and 6.30 metres by a 2011 measurement, a slow, legible record of exactly the kind of long, undisturbed growth that made it useful to Lyell in the first place.

trees.name: The Elms of Kungstradgarden
trees.access: Free, open access, Kungstradgarden (public square and park, open at all times)
trees.transport: Kungstradgarden metro station, adjacent
trees.story: On the night of 12 May 1971, a small crowd of Stockholmers climbed into these elms and refused to come down, stopping city workers who had arrived with chainsaws to fell them for a new metro station entrance. Four of the trees took saw damage before officials called off the operation for safety reasons, and none came down that night or afterward: the plan for the metro entrance was scrapped, and the elms stayed exactly where 19th-century planters had put them, already old growth by the time Stockholm considered removing them. What Swedes call Almstriden, the Elm Conflict, became one of the country's defining environmental protests, credited with a lasting shift in Stockholm's own planning culture toward fewer demolitions, fewer new roads through old neighbourhoods, and more parks left alone. Several of the surviving elms still carry visible chainsaw scars from that night, kept rather than smoothed over. The trees now face a slower threat than any road planner: Dutch elm disease, against which the city vaccinates them every year, though the precaution did not save one elm lost to the fungus in September 2025, felled before it could infect its neighbours. The rest keep standing in one of Stockholm's most visited parks, a protest still legible in living wood.

trees.name: Prince Eugen's Oak
trees.access: Free, open access, Royal National City Park (Djurgarden), open at all times
trees.transport: Tram 7 (Djurgardslinjen) to Waldemarsudde, short walk

best_time.label: October to November: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Sweden once made cutting down an oak a capital offense, because the navy needed every mature oak trunk for warship hulls and the crown claimed ownership of the species outright, a protection that stayed in force in some form until the 1830s. This oak, growing today just north of the painter Prince Eugen's old home at Waldemarsudde, is one of the direct beneficiaries: at 300 to 400 years old, it predates that legal protection's repeal by a comfortable margin and is Stockholm's largest tree by volume, 45 cubic metres of wood by a 2006 measurement, with a trunk 9.2 metres around and a canopy 21 metres tall. It originally grew as three separate trunks fused near the base, the kind of multi-stemmed form old oaks take when a young tree loses its main leader and several side branches compete to replace it. Prince Eugen, the so-called Painter Prince, bought Waldemarsudde in 1899 and would have known this oak as an already-ancient fixture of the grounds decades before his own paintings made the estate famous; the tree outranks his tenure there by centuries in one direction and, since his death in 1947, has outlasted him by generations in the other. It remains the benchmark against which Djurgarden's roughly 3,000 other protected oaks are measured, the single largest specimen in a park that holds more ancient oaks than almost anywhere else in Northern Europe.

trees.name: The Bidwill Kauri Pine
trees.access: Free; Royal Botanic Garden Sydney, open daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Martin Place or St James stations
trees.story:
The seed was picked on New Year's Day, 1849, at Maryborough in Queensland, by John Carne Bidwill, the first director of the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney. It went into the Palm Grove in 1853 and the tree that came up is still standing there, more than 170 years later, pushing well clear of the palm canopy around it as one of the tallest things in the garden.

It is the Garden's type specimen of Queensland kauri, the first of the species planted here, and other kauris in Sydney get measured against it. A 2015 heritage survey of the Domain does exactly that: a companion kauri on Central Avenue, 31 metres tall with a canopy 16 metres across, is described as approaching the size of the 1853 tree in the Palm Grove. It has not caught up.

Kauris are slow and can run past 300 years, so at 170 this one is barely middle-aged. What it has instead is priority.

Nobody has published a trunk measurement for it, so if you get a tape around it we would like the figure. And our pin marks a point in the Palm Grove rather than the trunk itself, so allow a minute of standing among the palms and looking up. You are looking for the one that overtops the palms.

trees.name: The Quad Jacaranda
trees.age: not documented; the current tree is a 2017 clone, the site has carried a jacaranda since 1928
trees.access: Free; university campus grounds, the Quadrangle is generally open to visitors during daylight/campus hours
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Redfern station, or bus along City Road/Parramatta Road

best_time.label: late October and November, when the Quadrangle turns purple

trees.story:
The jacaranda in the Quadrangle is about nine years old. Say that first, because everything written about this tree is really about a different one: the jacaranda planted in the south-eastern corner in 1928 by Associate Professor Eben Gowrie Waterhouse, which toppled on 28 October 2016 after a root fungus ended 88 years of it. The BBC reported the death.

What stands there now was planted on 20 July 2017 and is a genetic clone of the tree that fell, propagated so the replacement would be the same jacaranda rather than merely another one. That is worth being clear about. You are not looking at a tree from 1928. You are looking at its cutting, growing into the same corner of the same sandstone quadrangle, with a flame tree put in beside it as a companion the same year.

The folklore transferred intact. Generations of Sydney students have held that if you have not started studying by the time the jacaranda flowers, you will fail your exams, which is a superstition that survives because the timing is genuinely cruel. The purple arrives in late October, just as the semester runs out.

The Quadrangle is open to visitors through daylight hours and the tree is easy to find. In flower it draws a crowd with phones. Out of flower it is a young tree with a great deal expected of it.

trees.name: The Port Jackson Fig of Vaucluse House
trees.access: Free; the pleasure garden at Vaucluse House is open to the public Wednesday to Sunday, 10am-4pm, no charge (only the house interior is ticketed)
trees.transport: Bus 325 from Town Hall Station (Stand A, York Street) stops outside the gates; or T4 train to Edgecliff Station then transfer to the 325
trees.story:
Two records date this fig and they land a few years apart. Museums of History NSW puts the giant Port Jackson fig at the eastern corner of Vaucluse House in the mid-1850s. The State Heritage Register listing for the property calls it a Port Jackson fig of about 1859. Neither is a planting receipt, so the honest answer is that it went in somewhere inside that window, roughly 170 years ago, and nobody has narrowed it since.

It was planted as part of a fashion. Sydney's villa gardens were being laid out in the Thomas Shepherd manner, with specimen trees placed for effect on lawns meant to be walked across, and this fig is one of the survivors of that generation of planting. The Port Jackson fig is the local species rather than the imported showpiece, and it grows into exactly the wide, dark, low-branching shape those gardens were designed around. A century and a half on, it is doing what it was placed there to do.

Be careful which fig you are told about. A separate Moreton Bay fig stood between the house and the tea rooms until 1996, when it was removed and replaced by a cutting. Different tree, other side of the house.

The pleasure garden is free and open Wednesday to Sunday, ten until four, with only the house interior ticketed. Our pin is good to the eastern side of the house rather than to the trunk.

trees.name: The Vailele Moreton Bay Fig
trees.access: Free; public street tree on the road verge, viewable and reachable at any time from the public footpath (no permission or ticket needed, this is council land not the private garden of Vailele next door)
trees.transport: Sydney Ferries F3 route from Circular Quay to Woolwich Wharf, about 23 minutes, then a short walk along the foreshore to Gale Street
trees.story:
This fig was dated by photograph. Hunter's Hill Council's tree register found what appears to be a small fig near this spot in pictures from about 1913, then a full-grown specimen in 1943 aerial survey imagery, and concluded that it would support a planting date of around 1900. That is one council reading two photographs, and it is the only source we have found on this tree at all, so treat the age as a reasonable inference rather than a record. If somebody has a better one, we want it.

The rest of the assessment is easier to check by standing in front of it. Seventeen metres tall, a canopy eighteen metres across, and a health rating that calls it an excellent example of the species. It grows on the Gale Street verge in Woolwich, on council land beside the side entrance of Vailele, a sandstone Federation house of about 1892; the register describes the tree as an important remnant planting associated with the house. The verge is public, so this one can be reached from the footpath at any hour.

Most people will see it from the water first. The register notes how visible it is from the Lane Cove River, and the best way here is the F3 ferry from Circular Quay to Woolwich Wharf, twenty-three minutes, then a walk up from the foreshore.

Do not confuse it with the two forest red gums further along the same street.

trees.name: The Camperdown Cemetery Fig
trees.access: Free; Camperdown Cemetery is a public heritage cemetery and park, gates generally open daylight hours
trees.transport: About 15-20 minutes on foot from Newtown or Stanmore stations, or a short bus ride from the Sydney CBD (roughly 4km away)
trees.story:
The canopy spans more than thirty metres, in a walled cemetery of four acres. It shades a good share of the dead.

The tree went in in 1848, the same year the cemetery itself opened, and the date is carried by a 1962 local history of Camperdown, a 1997 landscape management plan and the cemetery's own tree survey, with a 2010 account written from a site visit giving the same year independently. The reason given for the planting is softer. It is believed to have marked the roofing of the Cemetery Lodge, which the sources report as tradition rather than record, so take the ceremony loosely and the date firmly.

With the oaks put in the same year, it is the oldest tree in the Marrickville district. Camperdown is the oldest surviving cemetery in Sydney, the walled remnant of a much larger burial ground that Newtown grew around, and the fig stands near the Lodge by the Church Street entrance, so it is the first thing you meet coming through the gate.

Nobody has published a trunk measurement, which for a fig of 178 years is a gap worth closing. If you tape it, send us the number.

The cemetery is free and open through daylight hours, fifteen to twenty minutes on foot from Newtown or Stanmore stations. Our pin sits on the cemetery rather than the tree, though at that size it will not cost you long.

trees.name: The Wishing Tree
trees.access: Free; Royal Botanic Garden Sydney, open daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Martin Place or St James stations, same cluster as the Bidwill Kauri Pine
trees.story:
A plaque on the trunk explains that this tree will never reach the grandeur of the one it replaced, because a storm damaged its crown soon after it was planted. It is an unusually honest thing for a label to say, and it is accurate.

The original Wishing Tree was a Norfolk Island pine set out from a tub around 1816, under Elizabeth Macquarie's eye. By 1905 it was over thirty metres and the most popular tree in the Royal Botanic Garden, with a custom attached: three times around it forwards, three times backwards, and then make your wish. In the 1930s it was found to be dying of old age, and a replacement was bought with money raised by the Farmer's Children's Radio Birthday Club and planted nearby. The original came down in 1945 and its timber was turned into souvenirs, sold to raise funds for returned servicemen.

So the tree you will stand in front of, on the harbour side of the garden, is that 1930s replacement. Roughly ninety years old, shortened by one storm early in its life, and still being walked around: visitors were doing their six laps in 2018.

Two notes. The spot where the original stood now holds a Wollemi pine, a different tree with a different story. And our pin follows a map node named for the Wishing Tree rather than a surveyed position, so leave room for a short hunt.

trees.name: El Drago Milenario
trees.age: disputed: a modern study puts it near 700 years, popular tradition says 1,000 years or more
trees.access: Paid entry to Parque del Drago, the 3-hectare botanical park laid out around the tree in 1996. The tree is partly visible from outside the park; the full view of the crown and base is from inside.
trees.transport: Central Icod de los Vinos, a few minutes on foot from the town's main square. A car is the realistic way to reach the town, roughly 20 km west of Puerto de la Cruz.
trees.story: Nobody can date this tree, and nobody is going to. Dracaena draco lays down no annual growth rings, so the standard method of reading a trunk fails on it completely, and the estimates fill the vacuum accordingly: current scientific work puts El Drago Milenario near 700 years with a margin of a century or more either way, while tradition, the tourist literature and the tree's own name insist on a thousand or more. The name is a claim, not a measurement. What can actually be measured is everything else. The base is about 20 metres around, the tree stands 18 to 21 metres tall depending on who did the measuring, and the crown spreads roughly 20 metres across on more than 300 primary branches, which together make it the largest and oldest known living specimen of its species anywhere. Spain declared it a national monument in 1917. It has needed help since: conservators opened it up in 1985 to install internal ventilation against fungal rot, and in 1993 the road that ran past it was moved to spare it exhaust fumes and passing hands. The sap runs red when the bark is cut, the dragon's blood that Europe once bottled as dye and medicine. It stands in Icod de los Vinos, in a park built around it in 1996, partly visible from the street and properly visible only from inside.

trees.name: Pino Gordo
trees.access: Free. A marked trail of roughly 150 to 200 metres from a signed parking and viewpoint area just off the TF-21 mountain road toward the Parador; benches and information panels on site.
trees.transport: By car via the TF-21 a few kilometres above Vilaflor village. No public transport reaches the viewpoint directly, so a car is the realistic way.
trees.story: Vilaflor de Chasna put this tree on the town's coat of arms, which is a fair indication of how the place rates it against everything else it owns. Pino Gordo is a Canary pine with a trunk 9.36 metres around, the thickest native tree in Spain and widely called the most voluminous pine in Europe. It is also over 45 metres tall, which almost anywhere else would be the headline and here is not even the record at this viewpoint: the tree 150 metres up the trail is eleven metres taller. Estimates put it at roughly 700 to 800 years, meaning it was already a substantial pine when Castile finished taking the island in 1496, and a seedling several centuries before that. The bark carries fire scars. Canary pine is one of the few pines able to resprout straight from a scorched trunk, which is how a tree can spend seven centuries on a dry volcanic slope that burns and keep its crown. It grows at over 1,400 metres in the Corona Forestal, the pine belt that rings Teide, and reaching it costs nothing: a signed parking area off the TF-21 toward the Parador, then a marked trail of 150 to 200 metres, with benches and information panels at the tree.

trees.name: Pino de las Dos Pernadas
trees.access: Free. On a small rise by the same signed viewpoint and parking area as Pino Gordo, with benches for viewing.
trees.transport: By car via the TF-21 above Vilaflor village, the same stop as Pino Gordo. No public transport reaches the viewpoint directly.
trees.story: At 56 metres this is the tallest native tree in Spain, and it stands 150 metres from the thickest one. Pino de las Dos Pernadas is the taller and slimmer half of the pair above Vilaflor de Chasna: about eight metres around against Pino Gordo's 9.36, and roughly 500 to 600 years old against its neighbour's 700 to 800. The name is a description rather than a story. At around ten metres up, the trunk divides into two limbs of near-identical thickness that carry on skyward side by side, two legs, dos pernadas, and the split is the first thing you notice from the bench below. On the age estimates it germinated somewhere around the Castilian conquest of the island in the 1490s, and it has spent the centuries since on a slope that burns periodically; like every Canary pine here its bark is thick enough to survive fire that would kill most conifers outright. The setting is the Corona Forestal at over 1,400 metres, looking out over the pine belt below Teide. It is free, on the same short marked trail from the same parking area on the TF-21, which is what makes these two a genuine pair rather than two entries that happen to share a road.

trees.name: El Gran Ficus
trees.neighbourhood: El Botanico, Puerto de la Cruz
trees.access: Paid entry to the botanical garden (around 3 euros), open daily 09:00-18:00, closed 1 January, Good Friday and 25 December.
trees.transport: Central Puerto de la Cruz, walkable from the town centre, with a local bus stop 'Jardin Botanico' right outside. Between the island's three stops, a car is the realistic way.
trees.story: This tree keeps adding trunks. El Gran Ficus drops aerial roots from its branches, and the ones that reach the ground thicken, stiffen and set as columns, so what began as a single Moreton Bay fig is now a colonnade about 30 metres high that visitors walk into rather than around. It is the youngest tree on this list by centuries. The garden's Swiss head gardener Hermann Wildpret, in post from 1860 to 1893, planted it in the 1870s, which makes it roughly 150 years old; one guide puts it at about 200 without naming a planting date, and the documented planting is the better bet. The garden itself is far older, founded by royal order of Carlos III in 1788 and inaugurated in 1792 to acclimatise tropical plants to a European climate, so the fig is a latecomer to its own address by a century. Sources disagree on the fine print of what it is, some naming the Lord Howe Island form of the species rather than the mainland Australian one; nobody has settled it, and if you know, tell us. The garden is compact, about two hectares, and charges a few euros, but this is not a specimen you have to hunt for once you are through the gate.

trees.name: The Kastro Plane
trees.access: Free, public street corner, viewable anytime
trees.transport: Kastra, Ano Poli district; about a 25 minute uphill walk from Aristotelous Square, or a short bus ride into the old town
trees.story: At the corner of two narrow streets below Thessaloniki's Byzantine walls stands a tree old enough to have watched the Ottomans arrive. Core-sampled in 2019 as part of a university study, the Kastro plane came back at approximately 828 years, more than double the age of the next oldest tree the same study found in the city, and its size in photographs over a century old is barely different from its size today, the signature of a tree that stopped growing quickly long ago rather than one still filling out. Part of its trunk is dead, hollowed and split, but enough living tissue remains around it to keep the crown alive, a common shape for a tree this age rather than a sign of imminent failure. For most of its life it grew beside a public fountain, fed by an aqueduct running down from the nearby Vlatades Monastery, at the exact spot where an Ottoman Turkish neighbourhood met a Greek one. The fountain was demolished around 1940 when the street was widened, and researchers who study the tree today note its vigour has declined somewhat since, water it no longer gets. It still stands at the corner of Acropoleos and Eptapyrgiou streets, a short climb up from the modern city into the old one.

trees.name: The Navarino Square Plane
trees.access: Free, public square, open anytime
trees.transport: City centre, beside the Galerius Palace archaeological site; short walk from Aristotelous Square or Egnatia Street
trees.story: This plane tree has spent three centuries next to one of the more improbable ruins in central Thessaloniki: the palace the Roman emperor Galerius built for himself around 300 AD, excavated directly beside the square where the tree now stands. Core-sampled at around 310 years old, it grew up during the Ottoman period beside a public fountain that made this corner the social centre of the old Lefko Temenos neighbourhood, a meeting point for the district's merchant class long before the square took its current name from a 19th-century naval battle. Its most quietly remarkable feat is what it did not do: on 18 August 1917, a fire that started in a kitchen a few streets away spread through the wind-dried Ottoman-era city centre and destroyed roughly a third of Thessaloniki in a single day, and flames reportedly reached this tree's position without taking it down. Three other plane trees the city has since identified as comparably old all stood, by chance or design, outside that fire's path too. Today the tree shares its square with a fountain sculpture of a whistling boy and the low Roman walls it has outlived by seventeen centuries.

trees.name: The White Tower Plane
trees.access: Free, public square, open anytime
trees.transport: Waterfront, directly across from the White Tower; about a 10 minute walk along the seafront from Aristotelous Square
trees.story: Standing across the square from the White Tower, Thessaloniki's best-known monument, this plane tree is younger than its two counterparts in Kastra and Navarino Square, core-sampled at around 235 years old, yet it is the largest of the four by a clear margin: 26.4 metres tall with a trunk 140 centimetres through at chest height, taller and thicker than the 828-year-old tree in the old town above it. The gap says less about the tree's own vigour than about its ground: a wide-open waterfront square, full sun and no competing canopy, will grow a plane tree faster than a narrow street between old stone walls, whatever extra centuries the older tree has had to work with. Both were included in the same 2019 university study that first proposed protecting Thessaloniki's oldest trees as natural monuments, dated by core sample rather than the rougher girth-based estimates most cities settle for. The White Tower itself, an Ottoman-era fortification turned museum, has stood on the waterfront since the 15th century, more than seven times longer than this tree, and yet the two are usually photographed together, the tower for what it has witnessed and the tree for simply being enormous.

trees.name: The Apostolou Pavlou Plane
trees.access: Free, Atatürk Museum grounds, Tuesday to Sunday 10:00-17:00
trees.transport: Ano Poli district; about a 20 minute walk uphill from the city centre
trees.story: The youngest of Thessaloniki's four core-sampled ancient planes, at around 205 years old, grows at the entrance to a house built in the final years of the Ottoman era and preserved today as the Atatürk Museum, the birthplace, by tradition, of the Turkish republic's founder, and now free to enter for anyone who visits. The tree is close to 21 metres tall, younger and slighter than its counterpart across town by the White Tower, but old enough to have stood over the building through the last Ottoman decades, the Greek annexation of the city in 1912, and everything since, including the handover of the building itself to the Turkish state as a museum. It was identified alongside the other three trees on this list in the same 2019 university study that dated all four by core sample rather than estimate, part of a proposal to give Thessaloniki's oldest trees formal protection as natural monuments, the kind of status usually reserved for buildings rather than the plants growing next to them.

trees.name: The Oldest Elm of Tilburg
trees.age: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot.
trees.story:
The register says two things about this tree and both are worth having. It is the oldest elm in Tilburg, and it was already standing before the park was laid out around it.

That second fact is the interesting one. A park built around an existing tree is a different object from a park planted from nothing: somebody stood on this ground, looked at what was here, and drew the paths to keep it. The elm was the reason for a decision rather than the result of one.

Being the oldest elm anywhere in the Netherlands is a harder thing than it sounds. Dutch elm disease arrived here in the 1920s and the second, far more aggressive strain in the 1970s, and between them they killed most of the mature elms in the country. Whole avenues went. An elm that reached a century and a half through both waves did so partly by luck of position, standing alone in a park corner rather than in a line where the beetles could work along it.

It is in the south corner. Elms leaf late and hold on late, so in November it is often still green when the rest of the park has turned.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Frater Paullussehof
trees.age: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.access: Free. Public planting in a residential courtyard, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km northwest of Tilburg station, on foot.

best_time.label: July, when the whole tree smells of honey from a street away

trees.story:
The oldest tree standing in Tilburg is a lime, which in a town that may be named after a lime is a decent piece of luck, and it is not on the square where anyone would look for it.

Silver lime is worth learning to recognise, because the trick is easy and it works from thirty metres. The underside of every leaf is coated in fine white felt, so on a windy day the whole crown flickers between deep green and pale silver as the leaves turn over. No other large lime does this.

It has a second habit that is less charming. Silver lime flowers late, in July, and its nectar is famously hard on bumblebees; you sometimes find them stunned or dead under a big one in high summer. The mechanism has been argued over for decades and the current reading is that it is less about toxicity than about a starving late-season insect finding a huge, tempting, low-yield food source at the wrong moment.

So: go in July for the scent, which is heavy and carries a long way down a street, and look at the ground while you are there.

trees.name: The Canadian Poplar of the Wilhelminapark
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot.
trees.story:
Poplars are not supposed to get this old, which is the entire reason to go and look at this one.

Canadian poplar is a hybrid of the European black poplar and the American eastern cottonwood, first raised in France in the eighteenth century and then planted across Europe by the million for the same reason people plant it now: it grows faster than almost anything else, throwing up several feet a year on wet ground. The trade-off is that it is soft-timbered, brittle in storms and generally treated as a crop rather than a monument. A hundred years is a good run. Most are taken out well before that because a limb has come down.

This one is somewhere past a century and a half and still standing in the northeast corner of the park, which means it has been through every serious storm since the 1860s without losing enough to condemn it.

The sound is the other thing. Poplar leaves are held on flattened stalks that let the blade pivot, so the whole crown rattles in wind that barely moves the trees beside it. On a breezy day you hear this one before you see it.

trees.name: The Sessile Oak of the Korvelplein
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Public square, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Tilburg station, on foot or a short bus ride to Korvel.
trees.story:
In 1923 they took the church off this square.

The old Korvel church stood in the middle of the Korvelplein. It was removed and replaced by a new one built at the edge, which left a large empty space in a busy district, and the response was to plant it properly with trees. This oak is one of those, and the register bands it slightly earlier, 1900 to 1910, so it may have been standing before the clearance and been kept.

It is a sessile oak rather than the pedunculate oak that turns up everywhere else in the Netherlands, and the difference is easy once you know it. Pedunculate oak hangs its acorns on long stalks and has almost no stalk on the leaf. Sessile oak does the reverse: acorns sitting tight against the twig, leaves on a clear stalk of a centimetre or more. Sessile is the upland species, the one that prefers drier and poorer ground.

A square is a hard place to be a tree. Paving over the roots, salt in winter, cars, and a hundred and twenty years of it. This one has managed, and the Korvelplein is one of the more pleasant squares in the city because of trees like it.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Leijpark
trees.age: roughly 85 to 95 years, from the register's planting band of 1930 to 1940
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.

best_time.label: March, when it flowers on bare twigs before anything else moves

trees.story:
This park was dug by unemployed men.

Leonard Springer, the most sought-after garden architect in the Netherlands, drew the Leijpark in 1919 as his last large design. Then nothing happened for fifteen years: the land could not be bought and there was a farm sitting in the middle of it. It was finally laid out between 1934 and 1939 as a work relief project, in the depths of the depression, thirty hectares in the English landscape manner along the little river Leij that gives it its name.

So this silver maple was planted by men who were there because there was no other work. Springer designed the picture and never saw it finished.

Silver maple is another American import chosen for speed, and it has the finest-cut leaf of any maple you will meet here, deeply divided into five narrow lobes with silvery-white undersides. It flowers absurdly early, in March, before any leaf, small red and yellow tufts straight on the bare twigs. It is one of the first trees in the park to do anything at all after winter.

Stand in the middle of the park and it is the one with the pale flickering crown.

trees.name: The Oak of the Leijpark
trees.age: roughly 85 to 95 years, from the register's planting band of 1930 to 1940
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns are down

trees.story:
The youngest tree on this page and the one that will outlast every other by centuries.

It went in with the rest of the Leijpark planting between 1934 and 1939, part of the work relief scheme that finally built Springer's 1919 design. At under a century it is barely started. Pedunculate oak routinely reaches four hundred years in the Netherlands and the veterans on sandy ground in Brabant go beyond that, which means the silver maple beside it, the poplar in the Wilhelminapark and the elm in the south corner will all be gone while this one is still filling out.

That is a genuinely strange thing to stand in front of. A park laid out in a depression by men who needed the wages, planted with trees on wildly different clocks, and the plainest one in it is the one making the long bet.

It is on the northwest side, in Springer's English landscape arrangement of grass opening into stands of trees. Come in October: an oak this age is producing serious quantities of acorns, and the ground under it is worth looking at.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Villa Garden
trees.age: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Tilburg station, on foot.

best_time.label: July, when the scent fills the whole garden

trees.story:
This small park was somebody's garden, designed by Leonard Springer.

That is all the register says about it, and it is enough to change how the place reads. Springer laid out estates, cemeteries, arboreta and the Leijpark on the other side of town, and he also took private commissions from people building villas. A garden of that kind was made to be walked in by one family. This one ended up as public ground, which is the usual fate of a nineteenth century villa garden in a city that grew past it.

The lime is from that planting, banded 1880 to 1890. Silver lime was a favourite of designers in exactly this period, because it does something no other large tree does: the white-felted undersides of the leaves make the whole crown pale and unsettled whenever there is wind, so a single one placed against darker trees lifts a composition without any need for flowers.

So look at it as a piece of design rather than as a specimen. It is standing where a professional put it, for a reason he could have explained, in a garden whose owner is long gone and whose gate is now open to everyone.

trees.name: Kelch's Linden (Kelchi pärn)
trees.access: Free, stands in public space near Niguliste Church in the Old Town
trees.transport: Central Tallinn Old Town, short walk from Vabaduse väljak (Freedom Square) tram/bus stops

best_time.label: July to August, when it flowers

trees.story:
A chronicler is said to lie under this lime. Christian Kelch, the Baltic-German pastor who wrote a chronicle of Livonia and died in 1710, gave the tree the name it still carries, and the tradition in Tallinn is that he is buried at its foot. Nobody has dug to check.

The numbers are firmer than the legend, if older than anyone would like. In 1999 the trunk measured 462 centimetres round at chest height, the tree stood 16 metres tall, and a ring assessment put it at 340 to 350 years. Carry that forward and it lands near 370 now, which sits comfortably with the other date attached to it: a 1938 newspaper gave its planting as 1680. It is generally called the oldest tree in Tallinn.

It looks its age. Two main branches are what remains of the crown, the base is hollow and has been sealed against further rot, and it has been pruned to keep weight off what is still holding. When Tallinn was named European Tree City in 2015, this tree was part of the argument.

It stands beside Niguliste, the church that burned in the air raid of March 1944 and took decades to rebuild. The lime, by then already close to three centuries old, needed no rebuilding.

trees.name: The Süda Street Ginkgo (Süda tänava hõlmikpuu)
trees.access: Free, stands at a public street corner
trees.transport: Central Tallinn, Tatari neighbourhood, walkable from the city centre

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns gold and drops the lot within days

trees.story:
This tree gave the Estonian language a phrase. In the late 1980s a new Soviet parade grandstand and an annex for the Estonia Theatre would have taken out the ginkgo on the corner of Peeter Süda street. Public opposition stopped the project, and hõlmikpuu sündroom, ginkgo syndrome, has meant a building plan blocked by a protected tree ever since.

It was not born on this corner. Heinrich Kühnert brought ginkgo seed home from Germany in the late 1800s and raised it in the family's private park a few hundred metres away. When the street was widened in 1913 his son Ernst moved the tree here, and it has been measured on and off ever since: six metres tall in 1928, 8.2 metres in 1955, 13 metres with a trunk 164 centimetres round by the 2017 survey, which put its age at over 110 years. It is the largest ginkgo in Estonia and has been protected since 30 April 1966.

Its health is not perfect. In 2017 the Estonian Dendrology Society reported that the crown had gone lopsided in the shade of a neighbouring maple and needed dead wood taken out. Forty years after it beat the grandstand, planning arguments still happen around it rather than through it.

Come in late October. Ginkgos turn a hard clean yellow and then drop the lot within days.

trees.name: The Windecki Red Oak (Windecki punane tamm)
trees.access: Free; stands in Windecki park, a former manor summer estate park now open ground in the Maarjamäe area
trees.transport: Pirita/Maarjamäe district, Tallinn; reachable by bus along Pirita tee, roughly 15-20 minutes from the centre
trees.story:
The house burned down in 1995. The oak the owner planted is still standing.

Robert Weisse built Windecki as a summer estate on the terrace below the Lasnamäe cliff and laid out its park before his death in 1886. The timber main house went up in flames a century later and was never rebuilt. What survived is the planting: 32 trees where there were 42 in 1995, a row of seventeen old European larches, and this red oak.

The dendrologist Olev Abner surveyed the ground in 2017 and made the case that it is probably the oldest red oak in Estonia, thicker in the trunk and taller than either of the two others the country protects individually. He recorded it at 24 metres high and 83 centimetres through. The age comes from the park rather than from a ring count: if the oak went in with Weisse's original planting, it is roughly 140 to 150 years old now, and that "if" is the whole basis for the number.

There is a second wrinkle. A 2007 survey of the same park recorded its largest red oak at the same 24 metres but only 61 centimetres through, which is either a different tree or a different tape measure. Estonia gave this one formal protection in 2020.

Maarjamäe is twenty minutes out from the centre, and the park is small enough to find it in.

trees.name: The Huecki Lindens (Huecki pärnad)
trees.access: Free, street trees standing in public space in front of the historic Huecki house
trees.transport: Central Tallinn Old Town, short walk from the Old Town's northern gate area

best_time.label: July to August, when it flowers

trees.story:
Two limes, planted in 1883 to mark two hundred years of one family at one address. The Huecks acquired Lai 29 in 1683 and the trees went in for the bicentenary, which is a grand way to note a property anniversary and has outlived everyone involved. Sirp, the Estonian culture weekly that records the year, hedges it with "apparently", so take 1883 as the best account anyone has rather than a documented planting.

They belong together and are protected together, listed as a single natural monument since 2009: two common limes in front of one house, each around 25 metres tall. There is one obvious place to stand, on the far pavement, where both fit in the frame at once.

The interesting part is underneath. Lai is a paved Old Town street with almost nothing beneath it for a root to work with, and Sirp describes the pair as growing in the middle of a stone desert. Whatever the family thought it was planting, the result has spent 143 years making a living out of the gaps between cobbles and cellar walls, at a size that would be respectable in a park with proper soil.

The house behind them still carries the family's name.

trees.name: The Signposted Oak of Jardin des Plantes
trees.access: Free, public botanical garden (Jardin des Plantes, 7 hectares, open daily)
trees.transport: Central Toulouse; Toulouse metro Line B, Palais de Justice or Carmes station, then a short walk (exact stop not independently verified )

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Two entirely separate sets of people decided this oak was worth pointing at. Toulouse's urban tree inventory carries it under the city's own remarkable label, and volunteer mapmakers have independently marked the same spot in the Jardin des Plantes as a named, signposted specimen: chene pedoncule, pedunculate oak. Neither of them recorded how old it is, and no other source names it, so the honest answer on age is that nobody has published one. What the two records do between them is confirm that the tree exists, where it stands and what it is, which is more than most entries on a municipal list can claim. It grows in a seven hectare botanical garden on the Allee Jules-Guesde, the middle link in a chain of three public gardens that run into one another along the eastern edge of the city centre. Pedunculate oak is the great long-lived oak of northern Europe, routinely passing five hundred years where nothing interferes with it, and it is not a Mediterranean tree by temperament. This far south it is planted rather than wild. In autumn it drops acorns on long stalks, the peduncles the species is named for, which is the detail that separates it from the sessile oaks it otherwise resembles. Free, open daily, and central.

trees.name: The Wych Elm by the Grand Rond
trees.access: Free, public garden area (Boulingrin / Jardin du Grand Rond)
trees.transport: Central Toulouse; Toulouse metro Line B, Palais de Justice or Carmes station, then a short walk (exact stop not independently verified )
trees.story: A big elm in western Europe is unusual enough to be the story. Dutch elm disease, a fungus carried between trees by bark beetles, killed most of the continent's large elms across the twentieth century in two waves, the second and far worse one from the 1960s onward, and a mature wych elm still standing in a city centre has survived something that removed its species almost everywhere else. This one is on Toulouse's own list of remarkable trees, at the Boulingrin, the local name for the Jardin du Grand Rond, a circular garden about two hundred metres across that the city's main avenues run into. The Boulingrin holds a dozen elms nearby; the register marks only this one as remarkable, so trust the pin over the nearest elm. The register is also all there is.
