It gives the species and the position and then stops: no age, no measurements, no description, and no other source names this tree at all. So take the species as the reason to go and treat any claim about its size as unmeasured. Wych elm is the elm that does not sucker, which means every one of them grew from a seed rather than from a parent's roots, and the seeds are the thing to look for. They come out in spring before the leaves, flat papery discs in dense clusters, green and then pale, hanging thickly enough to pass for foliage from a distance.

trees.name: The Osage Orange of the Grand Rond
trees.access: Free, public garden area (Boulingrin / Jardin du Grand Rond)
trees.transport: Central Toulouse; Toulouse metro Line B, Palais de Justice or Carmes station, then a short walk (exact stop not independently verified )
trees.story: This tree drops fruit that nothing alive is meant to eat. The Osage orange produces heavy green spheres the size of a grapefruit, wrinkled like a brain and full of sticky latex, and no native North American animal disperses them. The standing explanation is that the animals which did, mammoths and giant ground sloths among them, went extinct around thirteen thousand years ago, and the tree has been dropping its fruit into an empty niche ever since. It got a second career from people instead. Osage orange wood is dense, springy and almost rot-proof, the timber the Osage nation made bows from, and American farmers planted it by the million in the nineteenth century as living fence, until barbed wire arrived and made it redundant in about a decade. Toulouse has one on its remarkable tree list near the Boulingrin, at the edge of the Grand Rond. The register gives the species and the position and nothing else, no age and no measurements, and no independent source names this specific tree, so what is documented is that the city looked at it and marked it out. Standing in front of one, that is easy enough to believe. The bark alone is worth the detour, deep orange-brown and fissured into long twisting ridges.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Place Saint-Georges
trees.access: Free, public square (Place Saint-Georges, central Toulouse)
trees.transport: Toulouse metro Line A, Capitole or Esquirol station, then a short walk
trees.story: The small dark berries on this tree are edible, and they taste faintly of dates. Mediterranean hackberry has been the standard tree of squares across southern France and Spain for centuries, partly for the fruit and mostly for the shade: deep-rooted, drought-hardy, indifferent to paving and heat, carrying a dense rounded crown on a trunk that stays smooth and grey for decades, closer to a beech than to an oak. This one holds Place Saint-Georges, a few minutes' walk from the Capitole, and it is on Toulouse's own list of remarkable trees. Be clear about what that list says. It records the species and the position, gives no age and no measurements, and files the tree at the adult development stage rather than the oldest category it uses, so this is a mature specimen and not an ancient one, listed for what it does to the square rather than for its years. That is a reasonable case to make in a city built almost entirely of brick, which takes in the day's heat and hands it back all evening. Toulouse's squares live or die on their canopies, and the species that copes best in them is the one that came from a hotter climate to begin with. The berries ripen dark in autumn and the birds usually get there first.

trees.name: The Grieving Hackberry of Terre-Cabade
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open daily 8h-18h
trees.transport: Guilhemery / Cote Pavee district, north-east of the centre; nearest metro/tram stop not verified
trees.story: This tree came up between two gravestones and neither of them has moved. The hackberry in Terre-Cabade cemetery has grown to over four metres around the trunk and twenty-six metres tall out of a gap barely wide enough to start in, and the association Arbres et Paysages d'Autan has classified it an arbre exceptionnel for Haute-Garonne. It is the best documented tree on this page by a distance: the city's remarkable tree register and an independent regional survey both name it, which none of the others manage. Nobody has published an age. Four metres of girth on a Celtis australis means a long-established tree rather than a young one, and that is as far as the evidence goes. The association's description adds something worth watching for on a hot afternoon. It says the leaves change their shape through the day to cope with the heat, which in a walled cemetery with very little shade reads as a working adaptation rather than a curiosity. Terre-Cabade opened in the nineteenth century on the hill east of the centre, brick walls and cypresses and a climb to get up to it, and the tree stands in the middle of the graves rather than at the edge of them. Free, open daily from eight until six.

trees.name: The Plane of Place Anatole France
trees.access: Free, public square (Place Anatole France, Saint-Cyprien)
trees.transport: Saint-Cyprien district, left bank of the Garonne; nearest metro/tram stop not verified
trees.story: Toulouse's register calls this tree Platanus x hispanica and this page calls it Platanus x acerifolia, and both are right. The London plane is a hybrid of an American and an Oriental plane that appeared in seventeenth century Europe without anyone writing down where, and the argument over whether to name it after Spain or after London has never been settled. Botanists still use both, for the same tree. This one stands on Place Anatole France, on the city's own remarkable tree list and nowhere else. That list is the whole file: no age, no measurements, no independent source, and a record of the adult development stage rather than the register's oldest category, so this is a substantial mature plane and not a veteran. One thing worth stating plainly, because a search will turn it up. Toulouse has a well known plane with an enormous burl growing out of its trunk in the Jardin Royal, and this is not that tree. No source connects the two, and this page does not either. What this one offers is the ordinary excellence of the species: a wide clean crown thrown over a busy square, and bark that sheds in plates all summer instead of letting a century of city grime build up on it.

trees.name: The Judas Tree of Fer a Cheval
trees.access: Free, appears to be a public sports-ground/park area (Fer a Cheval, Saint-Cyprien); not independently confirmed
trees.transport: Saint-Cyprien district, left bank of the Garonne; nearest metro/tram stop not verified
trees.story: The flowers on this tree come straight out of the bark. Judas trees are cauliflorous, meaning the blossom breaks directly from the trunk and the oldest branches rather than from new shoots, and for two or three weeks in early spring a mature one is covered in hard magenta pea flowers before a single leaf has opened. The name is probably a mistranslation. Cercis siliquastrum is the arbre de Judee, the tree of Judea, where it grows wild; somewhere along the way that turned into the tree Judas hanged himself from, with the flowers reddening in shame, which is the better story and almost certainly not the origin. Toulouse has one on its remarkable tree list in the Fer a Cheval part of Saint-Cyprien, on the left bank of the Garonne. Two honest caveats come with it. The register gives the species and the position and nothing else, no age, no size, no description, and no other source names it. And the setting needs checking on the day: the ground here maps as sports fields, which normally means you can walk through it, but this page has not confirmed the exact site or its hours. Go expecting a public sports ground rather than a garden. The flowering is the reason to come, and it is short.

trees.name: The Second Plane of Fer a Cheval
trees.access: Free, appears to be a public sports-ground/park area (Fer a Cheval, Saint-Cyprien); not independently confirmed
trees.transport: Saint-Cyprien district, left bank of the Garonne; nearest metro/tram stop not verified
trees.story: The plane avenues of the Canal du Midi are being cut down. A fungal canker with no treatment reached them in the early 2000s and tens of thousands of trees have been felled and replaced with other species along a waterway that begins in Toulouse, which is the largest thing to have happened to plane trees in this region in two centuries. City planes like this one are not part of that avenue and not part of that programme, worth knowing before you assume every plane in Toulouse is under sentence. This one stands on the Fer a Cheval sports ground in Saint-Cyprien, on the city's remarkable tree list, about a hundred and seventy metres from the Judas tree, which makes those two the closest thing the list offers to a short walk. The rest are scattered across the city as separate errands. The register records the species and the position and adds nothing: no age, no girth, no independent source, and the adult development stage rather than its oldest. The species became the standard tree of industrial-era boulevards for practical reasons, chief among them that it shrugs off hard pollarding year after year. Same access note as its neighbour: this is a sports ground, not a garden, so expect a running track.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Eglise Saint-Sylve
trees.access: Free, public. Stands at the Eglise Saint-Sylve on Rue Calvet; register coordinate sits at the edge of the church building itself, consistent with the church forecourt/approach rather than an enclosed courtyard. Same churchyard-default pattern as other Toulouse church-ground trees on this site.
trees.transport: La Colonne / Faubourg Bonnefoy district, north-east of the centre; nearest metro/tram stop not verified
trees.story: Toulouse's tree inventory files this one as libre, free grown, and that word is worth more than it looks. A municipal inventory is mostly trees cut to fit something: a pavement width, a facade line, a run of overhead cable. This hackberry has been left alone, so it carries the shape the species makes on its own, a broad rounded dome of dense leaf on a smooth grey trunk that stays smooth for decades. The register also puts it at the mature stage, a step further along than the hackberry on Place Saint-Georges, though still not the oldest category the city uses. That is the entire biography. Toulouse's remarkable tree list is the only source that names it, and the list carries no age, no girth and no measurement of any kind, which is true of nearly every tree on this page. Nobody local appears to have written the tree up at all. It stands at Eglise Saint-Sylve on Rue Calvet, out in the Faubourg Bonnefoy northeast of the centre, on the open ground in front of the church rather than inside an enclosed yard, which is the usual reason a tree in a dense city gets to keep its years: the soil around it was never wanted for anything else. Free, open, and a separate errand rather than a stop on the Jardin des Plantes walk.

trees.name: The Lime of Rue de la Solidarite
trees.access: Free, public street tree on Rue de la Solidarite, Soupetard. Register coordinate reverse-geocodes to a street-furniture point (waste basket) directly on the road, about 70 metres from the nearest school entrance (Ecole elementaire publique Soupetard, 37 Rue de la Solidarite) rather than on the school's own grounds, so this is ordinary public street frontage, not a school-access case.
trees.transport: Soupetard district, about 2.8km north-east of the centre; nearest metro/tram stop not verified

best_time.label: June, when it flowers and the pavement under it smells of lime

trees.story: For about a fortnight in June this lime does something no other tree on the street can: it fills the air. Tilia platyphyllos carries small yellow green flowers among the most heavily scented in the European flora, loud with bees for the whole of that fortnight, and those same flowers are picked and dried into tilleul, the infusion in every French pharmacy cupboard. The rest of the year it is a large tree on a quiet road. This one holds a stretch of Soupetard, a residential district about 2.8 kilometres northeast of the Capitole, and it is on Toulouse's own list of remarkable trees. That list is also the only source for it. No age, no girth, no measurement, nothing published anywhere else, which is the standard state of affairs for the trees on this page. What the register does add is that the tree sits at its adult stage and is semi free in form, meaning somebody pruned it at some point and then let it be, which is the ordinary life of anything growing at the kerb of a working street. It stands on the roadway itself, roughly seventy metres from the primary school at number 37, on public pavement you can walk up to at any hour. Go in June. Out of season this is a good tree on a plain street, a long way from everything else on the list.

trees.name: The Zenpukuji Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, temple grounds open daily
trees.transport: 7 min walk from Azabu-Juban Station (Namboku/Oedo lines)

best_time.label: late November, when the ginkgo turns deep gold

trees.story: The upside-down tree Tokyo never quite got over. In 1229 the Buddhist monk Shinran planted his walking staff in the ground here before leaving Zenpukuji, or so the story goes, and the staff took root and grew into this ginkgo. Whatever the truth of the legend, tree-ring estimates put the trunk at roughly 750 years old, which makes it the oldest living thing in Tokyo and a rare tree that has outlasted the city around it more than once. Its aerial roots hang from the lower branches like stalactites, thick and pendulous enough that locals nicknamed it Sakasa Icho, the Upside-Down Ginkgo. The tree was declared a National Natural Monument in 1926, one of the first in Tokyo. Then came March 1945: American incendiary bombs burned most of the temple to the ground and scorched the ginkgo's trunk black. Ginkgos are famously fire-resistant, sappy and slow to catch, and this one kept living. New growth eventually covered the char. Every autumn it turns a shade of gold that draws photographers who have never heard of Shinran.

trees.name: The Sensoji War Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, temple grounds open daily
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Asakusa Station (Ginza/Asakusa/Tobu lines)

best_time.label: late November, when the leaves turn gold

trees.story: This ginkgo used to be a national treasure and technically is not one anymore, and the reason why says everything about it. Legend holds that a branch stuck in the ground here by the shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo, visiting around 1189, took root and grew into this tree, which would make it roughly 800 years old. The Japanese government designated it a Natural Monument in 1930. Then, on the night of March 10, 1945, American firebombs burned nearly all of Asakusa to the ground, including Sensoji's main hall and its five-story pagoda, both later rebuilt from scratch. The ginkgo was hit directly. Its trunk is still hollow and blackened five or six meters up, a permanent scorch mark from a night that killed roughly 100,000 people in Tokyo. The fire damage was severe enough that the monument designation was revoked after the war. The tree itself was not deterred: it kept growing, and it is the one part of Sensoji that watched the temple burn and rebuild around it rather than the other way around.

trees.name: The Ueno Toshogu Camphor
trees.access: Free to view; a 500 yen fee applies only if you also want to enter the shrine's inner hall precinct by the karamon gate
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Ueno Station (JR/Ginza/Hibiya lines)
trees.story: Ueno Park's biggest tree predates the shrine built around it by more than two centuries. This camphor was already an old tree in 1627 when Ueno Toshogu was founded to enshrine Tokugawa Ieyasu, and it has stood on this rise since before Ueno was Ueno at all, which is why the shrine's own literature calls it Ueno's ancestral tree. Its trunk runs more than eight meters around, the widest in the park by a comfortable margin. The shrine itself survived the 1657 Meireki fire, the 1868 Battle of Ueno between shogunate loyalists and the new imperial army, the 1923 earthquake, and the 1945 air raids that destroyed most of Ueno's other historic buildings, largely because an Edo-era engineer built its main hall with unusually deep foundations. The camphor watched all four disasters from a few meters away and came through each one with nothing worse than scorched leaves. Its canopy now shades the approach to the shrine's gold-leafed karamon gate, a combination that has made this corner of the park a minor pilgrimage for anyone who likes their history literally rooted in place.

trees.name: The Head-Betting Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Hibiya Station (Hibiya/Chiyoda/Mita lines)

best_time.label: late November, at the peak of its golden colour

trees.story: An engineer once bet his own head on this tree's survival, and won. In 1901, city planners preparing to build Hibiya Park, Japan's first Western-style public park, needed the road at its edge widened, and this 400-year-old ginkgo stood directly in the way. Honda Seiroku, the park's designer, refused to let it be felled and reportedly told his superiors he would offer his own head if the transplant failed. Over 25 days in 1902, laborers moved the tree roughly 450 meters to its current spot, an operation that reportedly needed 20,000 kan, close to 75 tons, of root ball and trunk. It worked, and the tree kept the nickname Kubikake Icho, the Head-Betting Ginkgo, ever since. It survived a second scare in 1971, when a firebomb thrown by a radical group during a protest burned down the neighboring Matsumotoro restaurant and scorched the ginkgo black; it leafed out again the following spring. Honda kept his head. The tree, seven meters around and still growing, kept its park.

trees.name: The Shiba Toshogu Ginkgo
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Shibakoen Station (Toei Mita line)

best_time.label: late November, when the ginkgo turns gold

trees.story: A shogun planted this tree with his own hands, or so Shiba Toshogu has claimed for almost four centuries. In 1641, Tokugawa Iemitsu, the third Tokugawa shogun, is said to have planted this ginkgo himself at the shrine built to deify his grandfather Ieyasu. It has been designated a Tokyo Natural Monument ever since records began keeping track, one of the city's officially protected trees. The shrine originally sat inside the vast precinct of Zojoji temple next door, the Tokugawa family's own funerary temple, until the Meiji government's forced separation of Buddhist and Shinto sites in the 1870s split them into two addresses. Zojoji's main hall was destroyed in the 1945 air raids that leveled most of Shiba; the shrine's smaller buildings burned too. The ginkgo, planted by the man whose family the whole complex was built to honor, came through the fires that took the buildings around it. Today it stands about 21 meters tall in front of the shrine's gate, with Tokyo Tower rising directly behind it, so most cameras pointed this way are aimed at the 1958 steel lattice rather than at the tree in front of it.

trees.name: The Three Hundred Year Pine
trees.access: Paid entry, 300 yen
trees.transport: 7 min walk from Shiodome Station (Oedo/Yurikamome lines)
trees.story: The biggest black pine in Tokyo grows in a garden that floods on purpose. Hamarikyu was built on reclaimed tidal land as a shogunal duck-hunting villa, and its ponds still rise and fall with Tokyo Bay through a working seawater gate, the only tide-powered garden pond left in the city. This pine was planted around 1709, when the sixth shogun Tokugawa Ienobu rebuilt the estate into something closer to its current form, and it has spent three centuries spreading rather than climbing: its lowest branches now sprawl low and wide across log supports, some running more than 20 meters from the trunk. Locals simply call it Sanbyakunen no Matsu, the Three Hundred Year Pine. The garden survived two disasters that erased most of its original structures, the 1923 earthquake and the 1945 firebombing, and the tree's low, horizontal shape likely helped it through both: black pines built close to the ground catch less wind and radiant heat than tall ones. What is left today is one tree and one tea house rebuilt from photographs, inside a garden that Tokyo Bay still floods twice a day.

photo.attribution: Kimon Berlin and Gribeco, Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Sperm Discovery
trees.access: Paid entry, 500 yen (University of Tokyo botanical garden)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Hakusan Station (Toei Mita line)

best_time.label: late November, when the leaves turn gold

trees.story: In 1896, a botanist working under this tree changed what science understood about how plants reproduce. Hirase Sakugoro, an artist-turned-researcher with no university degree, spent years examining ginkgo ovules from this specimen at what was then Tokyo Imperial University's botanical garden. He discovered that ginkgo trees produce swimming sperm cells, motile and flagellated like something out of animal biology, a reproductive method no other seed plant on Earth was known to use. It overturned assumptions about the evolutionary line between ferns and flowering plants and made the ginkgo, already ancient as a genus, into a living fossil in the most literal sense: a plant still reproducing the way its ancestors did 200 million years ago. The discovery is commemorated with a stone marker at the tree's base, placed for its sixtieth anniversary in 1956. The tree itself, one of the female specimens whose ovules made the discovery possible, is estimated by ring count at around 300 years old, and it still drops a heavy carpet of ginkgo nuts every autumn, oblivious to its own scientific importance.

trees.name: The Kameido Tenjin Wisteria
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Kameido Station (JR Sobu line), or 10 min from Higashi-Ojima Station (Toei Shinjuku line)

best_time.label: late April into May, when the wisteria hangs in flower

trees.story: Claude Monet may owe part of his water lily garden to this shrine, according to art historians who trace a line from Hiroshige's woodblock prints to Giverny. Utagawa Hiroshige painted Kameido Tenjin's wisteria and its arched drum bridge in his 1856 series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, and that print reportedly reached and influenced French Impressionists including Monet, who filled his own garden with wisteria decades later. The shrine was founded in 1663 on marshy ground, and its first head priest planted wisteria because the vines tolerate wet soil; the fifth and eighth shoguns, Tsunayoshi and Yoshimune, are both recorded visiting specifically to see it bloom. Today around 50 wisteria plants across 15 trellises still frame the bridge every late April, trained and pruned continuously since the Edo period even if individual vines have been replaced along the way, the way a shrine's sacred rope gets rewoven without anyone calling it a different rope. Exactly how old any single living vine is remains unclear. What is certain is that people have been coming here to see wisteria bloom for more than 360 years.

trees.name: The Meiji Jingu Gaien Ginkgo Avenue
trees.access: Free, public avenue
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Aoyama-itchome Station (Ginza/Hanzomon/Oedo lines)

best_time.label: late November, when the whole avenue turns gold

trees.story: Every one of these 146 ginkgo trees was already a young adult when it was planted. In 1908, gardeners collected seeds from ginkgos at Shinjuku Gyoen and grew 1,600 seedlings in a nursery; only the straightest, best-shaped survivors, already six meters tall, were selected fifteen years later to line this avenue when Meiji Jingu Gaien opened in 1923 as a memorial to Emperor Meiji. The landscape architect who laid it out planted them nine meters apart along a 300-meter stretch running straight toward the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery, engineering the perspective so the trees appear to funnel toward the building's dome from any angle on the street. A century on, the tallest reaches 28 meters, and every November the avenue turns the same uniform gold that has made it one of the most photographed streets in Japan, filled with tour groups and engagement shoots in equal number. A 2023 redevelopment plan for the neighboring stadium district reignited public debate over whether construction work threatens the ginkgos' roots, a reminder that even Tokyo's most photographed trees remain, legally, just trees.

trees.name: The Meoto Kusu
trees.access: Free, shrine grounds open daily
trees.transport: 1 min walk from Meiji-Jingumae Station (Chiyoda/Fukutoshin lines)
trees.story: This is the youngest tree on this list by roughly six centuries, and also the one most people specifically travel here to touch. Two camphor trees were donated to Meiji Jingu when the shrine was built in 1920 to deify Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, planted side by side just in front of the outer worship hall and bound together with a sacred straw rope, a shimenawa, that marks them as one connected being rather than two separate trees. They are called Meoto Kusu, the Married Couple Camphors, and generations of visitors have prayed here for good marriages and family harmony, a tradition now widened into a general wish for good relationships of any kind. Camphor trees can live over a thousand years, so at just over a century old these two are barely past childhood by the standards of their own species, let alone the 750-year ginkgo across town in Motoazabu. What they lack in age they make up in company: Meiji Jingu draws close to three million visitors in the first three days of January alone, more than any other shrine in Japan, and a large share detour past these two camphors on the way to the main hall.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of the Giardino Sambuy
trees.age: 100 to 200 years, by the regional register's age band
trees.access: Free, public garden in Piazza Carlo Felice, open at all hours
trees.transport: Directly opposite Porta Nuova station, 1 min walk. Metro Porta Nuova

best_time.label: July and August, when it hangs half-metre chains of winged seeds

trees.story: The first monumental tree on this walk is sixty seconds from the platform you arrive on. Giardino Sambuy fills the middle of Piazza Carlo Felice, directly opposite Porta Nuova station, and the heavy fluted trunk near its centre belongs to a Caucasian wingnut six metres round. The species comes from the forests of the Caucasus and northern Iran and reached European gardens in the 1780s, which is why it turns up in exactly the sort of nineteenth century civic planting this garden is. The garden carries the name of Ernesto Balbo Bertone di Sambuy, who ran Turin's public gardens before becoming its mayor, and who laid out the Giardini Cavour at the next stop. The first two stops on this walk are in that sense the same man's work. Come in July or August. A wingnut in fruit hangs its seeds in chains up to half a metre long, green ropes of small winged nutlets that dangle straight down through the canopy and make the tree unmistakable from across the square. The register measures it at twenty-seven metres and puts it between one hundred and two hundred years old. It is the widest trunk the register records anywhere near the city centre.

trees.name: The Plane of the Giardini Cavour
trees.age: about 150 years, from the garden's laying out in the 1870s
trees.access: Free, public garden, open at all hours
trees.transport: About 10 min walk north from Porta Nuova station along Via Lagrange
trees.story: This garden is built on the rubble of Turin's defences, and the humps you walk over are the evidence. When the seventeenth century fortifications came down the ground was left uneven, and between 1872 and 1875 Ernesto Balbo Bertone di Sambuy turned that awkward topography into an English style garden of irregular mounds and curved beds, planting large trees straight into it: planes, limes, oaks, horse chestnuts, magnolias. This plane is the one that did best. It stands thirty-four metres tall with a crown thirty metres across, so it covers most of the garden on its own, and it is five and a half metres round the trunk. Platanus x acerifolia is a hybrid of the oriental and the American plane that turned up in seventeenth century Europe by accident and then became the standard city tree everywhere, because it puts up with compacted soil, drought and filthy air, and sheds its bark in plates to shed the dirt along with it. Turin took to it harder than most Italian cities: half the trees on the regional monumental register for the comune are planes. Look for the flaking camouflage bark and the fruit balls that hang on stalks all winter.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Giardini Cavour
trees.age: about 150 years, from the garden's laying out in the 1870s
trees.access: Free, public garden, open at all hours
trees.transport: About 10 min walk north from Porta Nuova station along Via Lagrange

best_time.label: November, when it turns hard yellow and drops the lot in a day or two

trees.story: Sixty metres from the plane stands a tree with no living relatives. Ginkgo biloba is the only surviving species of an entire order of plants, closer to the conifers than to anything else with a broad leaf, and near identical leaves come out of rock two hundred million years old. This one is twenty-seven metres tall and three metres seventy round, planted with the rest of the garden in the 1870s. The register lists it for its particular vegetative architecture rather than its size, and standing under it shows why: the trunk goes up hard and straight, the limbs come off it in tiers, and the fan shaped leaves sit in flat sprays instead of a dome. Go in November. Ginkgo autumn is one of the few reliable spectacles in the plant world, because the leaves turn from green to a hard uniform yellow and then let go, very often most of them within a day or two, leaving a gold floor under a bare tree. Nobody records whether this one is male or female, so no promises about the fruit. Cities usually plant males, because the female drops a fleshy seed coat that smells strongly of rancid butter.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Valentino
trees.age: 100 to 200 years, by the regional register's age band
trees.access: Free, public park, no gates
trees.transport: About 15 min walk south from Porta Nuova, or tram 9 and 16 along Corso Massimo d'Azeglio
trees.story: This one stands by itself on open grass, which is why it looks the way it does. A Mediterranean hackberry with room on every side builds a wide even dome, and this one carries twenty-three metres of height over a trunk four metres seventy-five round, at the northern end of Parco del Valentino near Corso Massimo d'Azeglio. Celtis australis is southern European, tough, and largely ignored, which is a shame, because the wood used to be the reason anyone cared about it. It is flexible enough that whip handles, walking sticks and pitchfork shafts were made from nothing else, and the trade lasted into the twentieth century. The leaves are lopsided at the base, long pointed, and rough on the upper side like fine sandpaper. In autumn the tree carries small dark fruits on long stalks that taste faintly of dates and that birds strip fast. It is the only hackberry on Turin's monumental register. The park it stands in opened in 1856 as the city's first public park, laid out in the French manner by the gardener Jean-Pierre Barillet-Deschamps, and everything else on this walk from here south is inside it.

trees.name: The Oak behind the Castello del Valentino
trees.age: over 200 years, by the regional register's age band
trees.access: Free, public park, no gates
trees.transport: Tram 9 or 16 along Corso Massimo d'Azeglio, then into the park behind the Castello del Valentino

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Every other tree in Turin that the register dates past two hundred years is a plane. This oak is the exception, and it is the only reason the city's oldest age band contains a second species at all. It stands behind the Castello del Valentino near the rock garden the park calls the Rocaille, four metres round and twenty-eight metres tall. Quercus robur is the oak of northern European woodland and it is near its southern limit here on the Po plain, growing where the water table sits close enough to the surface to carry it through an Italian August. The castle it stands behind was rebuilt in the seventeenth century as the residence of Christine of France, and it has housed the city's engineering and architecture school since 1859, so the oak has spent most of its life being walked past by students who were not looking. The Rocaille is much newer than the tree: the artificial cliffs, streams and grottoes were built in 1961 for Italia 61, the exhibition marking a century of Italian unity. Look for a short heavy trunk and limbs coming off it almost horizontally, which is what an oak does when it grows with space around it.

trees.name: The Plane by the Eridano
trees.age: over 200 years, by the regional register's age band
trees.access: Free, public park, no gates
trees.transport: Tram 9 or 16 along Corso Massimo d'Azeglio, then to the riverside path at Viale Virgilio
trees.story: Six metres round, and it is the widest trunk in the park. This plane stands on the river side of Viale Virgilio opposite the Eridano, and the regional register puts it in the oldest band it uses, over two hundred years, which would make it older than the park around it. That is entirely possible. Parco del Valentino opened to the public in 1856, but the grounds of the Castello del Valentino had been Savoy property with planted avenues for two centuries before that, so a handful of trees here predate the park by a long way. It is not the tallest plane in Turin. At twenty-six metres it is fourteen short of the one waiting at the end of this walk, and the whole difference sits in the trunk: this tree put its growth sideways instead of up. That usually means light and space on every side rather than a place in a row. The Po running just behind it is the other half of the explanation, because a plane with its roots in a river's water table grows fat with very little effort. Stand at the base and the bark reads as a jigsaw of grey, olive and cream.

trees.name: The Plane at the Borgo Medievale
trees.age: 100 to 200 years, by the regional register's age band
trees.access: Free, public park. The Borgo Medievale courtyard is free; its museum house charges
trees.transport: Tram 9 or 16 along Corso Massimo d'Azeglio, then 5 min into the park to the Borgo Medievale
trees.story: The medieval village beside this tree was built in 1884 and there is nothing dishonest about it. Alfredo d'Andrade put up the Borgo Medievale for the Esposizione Generale Italiana as a full scale working model of a fifteenth century Piedmontese village, copying real buildings from real valleys, and it came out so well that the city kept it instead of pulling it down. The plane standing near it is thirty-six metres tall and five metres ten round, the second tallest tree on Turin's monumental register, and it is genuinely old in a way the village is not. The register bands it between one hundred and two hundred years, so it may well have been a young tree already standing when the exhibition opened. Three monumental oaks grow beside it, registered as a group rather than as individuals, which is why they get no entries of their own here. What makes this stretch worth slowing down for is the scale of the contrast: a row of low timber and stone houses with the roofline of a small mountain village, and then one tree going up more than twice their height directly behind them. The village courtyard is free to walk into.

trees.name: The Plane of the Fontana dei Dodici Mesi
trees.age: over 200 years, by the regional register's age band
trees.access: Free, public park, no gates
trees.transport: Tram 9 or 16 to Corso Massimo d'Azeglio near Ponte Isabella, then 3 min into the park
trees.story: Forty metres, and nothing in Turin is taller. This plane stands beside the Fontana dei Dodici Mesi at the southern end of Parco del Valentino, and it clears the second tallest tree on the city's monumental register by four full metres. The fountain would be worth the walk on its own. Carlo Ceppi built it in 1898 for the Esposizione Generale Italiana, a great oval basin ringed by twelve statues, one for each month, with four more for the rivers of the Turin plain. The tree is older than the fountain. The register puts it past two hundred years, five and a half metres round, with a crown thirty-two metres across, the widest canopy it records anywhere in the city. Forty metres is a serious height for a plane growing outside a forest, and it happens here for the same reason the fountain does: the Po is a couple of hundred metres away and the water table under this end of the park never really drops. Come late in the afternoon, when the light comes up the river from the west and the statues are lit from behind. It is the last stop, and the tram back to Porta Nuova runs from Corso Massimo d'Azeglio.

trees.name: The Grandfather Plane of Parco della Tesoriera
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Corso Francia, Pozzo Strada; tram 3 or 9, short walk into the park
trees.story:
Turin calls it il nonno, the grandfather, and at six metres sixty-five around it holds the widest trunk on the city's monumental tree register. The crown spreads twenty-five metres against a height of twenty-eight, which in a park this size means the tree is most of the view.

The park was a private estate before it was a park. Aymo Ferrero di Cocconato, treasurer general to the Duke of Savoy, had the villa at its centre built in 1715, and the name Tesoriera comes from that office rather than from any family. The villa now holds the city's music library, so on a summer afternoon there is usually something being practised behind the windows while the plane does the shading outside.

The register gives the age as over two hundred years, which is a band rather than a date. This is also the tree most often named when anyone in Turin is asked which is the oldest in the city. That claim is not settled anywhere and this page will not settle it either. What is documented is the girth, and nothing else in Turin comes close to it.

It is three and a half kilometres west of the trees in the centre, out along Corso Francia, so it is a trip of its own rather than an extension of the walk through the Giardini Cavour and the Valentino. Tram 3 or 9 puts you at the gate.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of the Giardini Reali
trees.access: Free, public gardens
trees.transport: Piazza Castello, central Torino; multiple tram and bus lines to Piazza Castello, short walk

best_time.label: late October into November, when the whole crown turns orange-brown

trees.story:
This tree is protected for being unusual rather than for being large. Zelkova carpinifolia grows wild in a narrow band of forest in the Caucasus and northern Iran, it is uncommon in Italian gardens, and Piedmont's register lists it on exactly that ground: botanical rarity. The trunk is three metres fifty around and short, and out of it comes the shape the species is known for, dozens of near-vertical stems rising together, so the whole tree reads as a vase rather than a dome.

Its height is an open question. The regional register measures twenty-four metres. A published walking route through Turin's monumental trees says twenty-seven. Nobody has reconciled the two, and that gap is what happens when one figure is taken with an instrument and the other by eye. The register's age band is equally wide, a hundred to two hundred years.

It grows in the Giardini Reali Inferiori, the lower royal gardens beside the Palazzo Reale, ground that belonged to the House of Savoy until the monarchy ended in 1946. The gardens were laid out for a court that wanted rarities, which is a large part of why a Caucasian tree is standing in the middle of Turin at all.

In late autumn the whole crown turns orange-brown, and after the shape that is the moment the species is known for.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Via Santa Croce
trees.access: Free, public garden (Comune di Trento)
trees.transport: roughly 10 min on foot from Trento station, in the historic centre
trees.story: Trento's oldest tree went into the ground in 1835, and the city only made it official in 2024. That year the comune finalised a list of eighteen monumental trees and entered thirteen of them on the national register, and the local press led on this one. ANSA, il Dolomiti and the Trentino all reported the same planting date and the same framing: a plane that has watched nearly two centuries of Trentine history from a small garden off Via Santa Croce. The history it watched was not gentle. In 1835 Trento was an Austrian city and had been since the prince-bishops lost their power in the Napoleonic settlement. The tree was mature when the railway came up the valley in the 1850s, standing when Cesare Battisti was hanged in the castle in 1916, and about eighty years old when Italy took the city in 1918. It has spent more of its life under Vienna than under Rome. It stands in the Giardino Martino Martini, a small public garden named for the Trento-born Jesuit who mapped China for European readers in the 1650s. Free, open, and about ten minutes on foot from the station. As monumental trees go this is an easy one. No cable car, no opening hours, no gate, and the rest of the centre cluster is within a few hundred metres.

trees.name: The Black Poplar of Largo Pigarelli
trees.access: Free, public garden (Comune di Trento, listed in its official park/garden directory)
trees.transport: roughly 10 min on foot from Trento station
trees.story: A black poplar with a trunk of 570 centimetres is a rarer thing than it sounds. Populus nigra is one of Europe's most threatened native trees, not because anyone cuts them down but because nearly every poplar planted along a European road or river for two centuries has been a hybrid with an American species, and the native form has been bred out of its own landscape. It is also fast, soft and short-lived by the standards of this map. Most do not last long enough to be measured at nearly six metres round. This one made Trento's list of eighteen monumental trees in 2024, named in the national coverage as the black poplar of Largo Pigarelli. What that coverage does not give is an age, and neither does anything else we found. The register's girth is the only measurement on record, with no second reading to check it against, so the number stands uncorroborated and the tree is flagged for it. The garden is small and municipal, listed in the comune's own directory of parks, a few minutes on foot from the station in a stretch of the centre where several monumental trees stand within a short walk of one another. Free, no gate, no hours. Poplars move in wind more than any tree of their size, which is the thing to stand under it for.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Via Vannetti
trees.neighbourhood: Piazza Dante / city centre, next to the station
trees.access: Public street frontage next to the Piazza Dante garden; free
trees.transport: roughly 5 min on foot from Trento station
trees.story: This plane belongs to a garden it no longer stands in. The comune's page for the Giardino di Piazza Dante describes monumental planes and walnuts surviving from the garden's original nineteenth century planting, and this tree stands at the edge of that garden with a street address on Via Vannetti, a few steps outside the railings. The comune does not name it individually, so the link is inference rather than record, and we have flagged it on that basis. What is on record is the national monumental register entry that put it on this list. No age has been published for it. The garden it came from was laid out in 1879 on ground that only existed because of the railway. The Adige used to run where Piazza Dante is now. The river was diverted in the late 1850s to clear space for the line, and the city planted its first public garden on the reclaimed strip. The trees left from that first planting are products of the railway as much as of any gardener. Practically, this is the easiest tree in Trento to reach. Five minutes from the platforms, on an open public street, at any hour, with no gate and nothing to pay, and the Piazza Dante elm is thirty seconds further on.

trees.name: The Elm of Piazza Dante
trees.neighbourhood: Piazza Dante / city centre, next to the station
trees.access: Free, public garden; comune.trento.it describes it as 'il primo giardino pubblico di Trento' (Trento's first public garden)
trees.transport: immediately next to Trento's main railway station
trees.story: Step off a train at Trento and the walk to a centuries-old elm takes under two minutes. The Giardino di Piazza Dante faces the station, and the comune's own description of it puts an elm and a group of yews along the north side, all of them called secolari, of the centuries. The elm is on the national monumental register. Nobody has published a precise age, so a hundred years is the floor rather than the estimate. The garden was designed in 1879 by the engineer Annibale Apollonio and was the first public garden Trento had. It has been restored in stages since 2007, and the Art Nouveau pavilion inside it now holds a children's library, which means that on a weekday afternoon the oldest tree in the square has small children reading underneath it. That is a better use of a monument than most of them get. Stand between the elm and the yews for a minute, because the pairing is instructive. The elm is a fast hardwood that can put on a metre of shoot in a good year and hollows from the inside once it stops. The yews beside it grow so slowly that they outlive almost everything planted with them. Ten metres apart, two entirely different bets on how to last. Free, open, no gate and no hours.

trees.name: The Elm of Maso Ginocchio
trees.access: Free, public garden (Comune di Trento), with entrances from Via Veneto, Via G. Giusti and Via Monte Baldo
trees.transport: roughly 15-20 min on foot south of the centre
trees.story: Europe lost most of its mature elms inside a single lifetime, and this one is still standing. Dutch elm disease is a fungus carried by bark beetles that blocks a tree's water vessels from the inside. It swept the continent from the 1930s and killed elms by the tens of millions, which is why an elm of any size is now worth going to see. The Italian tree register notes exactly that about this one, that it came through while others nearby did not. Its trunk measures 393 centimetres around, past the threshold that gets a tree onto the national monumental register on girth alone. No age has been recorded for it, and no height either. The register's description is honest about the setting: the tree sits in a corner of the garden and takes some finding, then stops being easy to overlook once you are in front of it. The Giardino di Maso Ginocchio is an ordinary municipal park, about 3.6 hectares in the San Giuseppe and Santa Chiara district south of the centre, with a playground, a small animal enclosure and entrances on Via Veneto, Via Giusti and Via Monte Baldo. Local reporting in 2016 grumbled about its upkeep. It is free and it is open, and the elm is the reason to walk the fifteen minutes out.

trees.name: The Cedar of Parco Gocciadoro
trees.access: Free, public park (Comune di Trento)
trees.transport: roughly 25-30 min on foot east of the centre, or local bus to the Gocciadoro area
trees.story: This cedar was planted around the year Italy was founded, in a city that would not join it for another fifty seven years. Local reporting in 2024 dates it to roughly 1861, the year of Unification, and ranks it the second oldest of Trento's eighteen monumental trees after the 1835 plane in Via Santa Croce. Trento was Austrian in 1861 and stayed Austrian until 1918. A Himalayan cedar going into the ground here was a Habsburg garden fashion, not an Italian one. That reporting stops short of a girth, so there is nothing to check the register's 525 centimetres against, and it names the cedar only by park rather than by position. The flag on this entry is for the missing measurement. The park is also not a one-tree park: the same article credits Gocciadoro with a tulip tree of thirty five metres, the tallest of the city's monumental trees. Cedrus deodara is the easiest cedar to name once you know it. The needles are longer than any other cedar's, the tips of the branches droop instead of reaching, and a mature tree carries a slightly mournful posture that the Lebanese and Atlas cedars do not. The park is public and free, roughly twenty five minutes on foot east of the centre or a short bus ride.

trees.name: The Chestnut of Sardagna
trees.neighbourhood: Sardagna (across the Adige, reached by cable car)
trees.access: Free, public hillside area on the Sentiero dei Castagni (Chestnut Trail), reached via the Funivia Trento-Sardagna cable car or by road
trees.transport: Funivia Trento-Sardagna cable car (about 4 minutes, 200m to 600m elevation) from the city centre, then a walk on the marked Sentiero dei Castagni

best_time.label: October, when the burs split open and the chestnuts are there to gather

trees.story: Somewhere in this chestnut grove above Trento stands a tree that stopped a runaway bus in January 1949. Local accounts name it, along with the Castegnar della Lasta and one or two others, and none of them says whether either is the tree the national register mapped here. This entry is the register's, and its pin is approximate: we know the locality, called Castagnara, and not the trunk. Come expecting a grove rather than an appointment. The grove earns the trip on its own terms. Sardagna sits on the mountainside across the Adige from the city, and the way up is a cable car that climbs from 200 to 600 metres in about four minutes. In 2025 the chestnuts here won a De.Co. mark, the municipal designation Italian towns give a food that belongs to one specific place, and the district and the forestry service waymarked the Sentiero dei Castagni through the trees the same year. The village held a festival when the mark came through. Go in October. Sweet chestnut is one of the few trees on this map whose best moment is edible: the spiny burs split open on the ground and the nuts are there to gather. Free, public, and on this one the walk is at least half the point.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Cortesano
trees.access: Free, on a public street (Salita ai Spiazzi) near the church of Sant'Antonio in the Cortesano hamlet
trees.transport: Trentino Trasporti bus line 3 from central Trento to Cortesano, about 24 minutes, then a short walk
trees.story:
Most hackberries with a trunk this thick are twice as tall. This one measures 410 centimetres around and stops at ten metres, an odd shape for Celtis australis, a species that normally runs to twenty-odd metres of straight grey trunk under a high rounded dome. Cortesano sits 570 metres up, nearly four hundred metres above the centre of Trento, and what grows well on that hillside is not what grows well down in the Adige valley.

It stands on the Salita ai Spiazzi, the lane climbing through the hamlet, near the church of Sant'Antonio. It is one of the eighteen trees Trento formally recognised as monumental in 2024, when the comune finished its list and entered thirteen of them on the national register, and it is the only one of the eighteen this far out of town.

Nobody has published an age for it. Italy's register carries girth, height and altitude and no age column at all, and the press coverage that named this tree named a place rather than a date, so the field is left blank instead of guessed at. Only one report puts it precisely, at the church, which is why the entry is flagged.

Getting there is a bus rather than a walk: line 3 out of the centre, about twenty-five minutes up the hillside, then a short climb. What you get for it is a hamlet, a church, and a tree built like a barrel.

trees.name: The Beech of Malga Brigolina
trees.access: Free, open pasture below Malga Brigolina on Monte Bondone; the malga itself is a working agritur, open from early June to late September
trees.transport: Trentino Trasporti bus B202 (Trento to Sardagna, Candriai, Vaneze, Vason and Viote) to Candriai, then about 15 minutes on foot on the waymarked Giro della Selva path, which starts near the village football pitch. By car, the gravel forest road signposted for the malga turns off on the way up from Sopramonte, just before Candriai.

best_time.label: October, when the beech turns copper and the pasture around it goes brown

trees.story:
Four and a half metres of trunk, and nothing else growing within reach of its branches. Fagus sylvatica is Europe's great crowding tree: in a wood it goes up straight and clean and throws a shade so heavy that almost nothing lives beneath it. This one was left standing on its own in an alpine pasture at around 940 metres on Monte Bondone, and it grew the other way, low and broad, until Italy's national register recorded its girth at 465 centimetres on sheet 08/L378/TN/22.

The meadow belongs to Malga Brigolina, a working mountain dairy at 990 metres that feeds walkers from early June to late September. The beech stands out in the grass below it with nothing around it, which is why it reads as architecture rather than as forestry.

Nobody has published an age. Italy's register carries girth, height and altitude and has no age column at all, and local accounts get no further than secolare, centuries old, so the field here is left empty rather than guessed at. If you know the number, or know who measured it, tell us.

The bus up the Monte Bondone road stops at Candriai, and a waymarked path called the Giro della Selva leaves the village near the football pitch and reaches the malga in about fifteen minutes, level and shaded most of the way. The pin is the register's, so expect the meadow rather than an exact spot.

trees.name: The Wild Cherry of Passo del Cimirlo
trees.access: Free, in public forest managed by Trento's forestry agency (Azienda Forestale Trentino Sviluppo); an unpaved provincial road and walking trails cross the pass, no gate or fee
trees.transport: Trentino Trasporti bus line 5 from the city centre (Piazza Dante / S. Francesco) to Povo, then about 45 to 60 minutes on foot up the unpaved provincial road toward the pass, climbing from about 600m to 790m

best_time.label: April, when the wild cherry flowers white before its leaves come in

trees.story:
One of Trento's 18 monumental trees stands well outside the city, at a mountain pass most residents know for hiking and old war ruins rather than for a tree. The Comune di Trento's own open register puts this wild cherry at 3.59 metres round and 26.5 metres tall, at 790 metres above sea level on public forest land managed by the province's forestry agency.

Passo del Cimirlo sits between Monte Celva and the Marzola massif, linking Povo to the villages of Oltrecastello and Roncogno on an unpaved road that has carried foot and cart traffic for longer than anyone living remembers. During the First World War the Austro-Hungarian army dug trenches and built gun batteries across this ground as part of the ring of forts defending Trento; the nearby Forte Roncogno and the Batteria Cimirlo are still standing.

A wild cherry this size is unusual on its own terms. Prunus avium is a fast grower and rarely a long liver by forest-tree standards, which makes a trunk over three and a half metres round a genuine rarity rather than simply an old specimen of a long-lived species. Trento added it to its monumental tree list in 2021 alongside 17 others, from a Himalayan cedar in a city park to a beech on a Monte Bondone pasture; this is the one that asks for the longest walk to see.

trees.name: The Redwood of Miramare
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story: The man who planted this tree was shot by a firing squad in Mexico eleven years later. Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg began the Miramare park in the spring of 1856 on a limestone headland with almost no soil on it, and he treated the whole thing as an experiment: he wanted to find out which foreign species would hold on to bare Adriatic rock. Soil was carted in. Within ten years the garden had cedars from Lebanon, North Africa and the Himalaya, firs from Spain, cypresses from California and Mexico, and this coast redwood from the fog belt of northern California. Maximilian kept ordering plants for it after he sailed for Mexico to be crowned emperor, and he never came back. The redwood took. It is now 4.25 metres round the trunk and thirty metres tall, the largest of the two redwoods here and one of twelve protected trees standing within three hundred metres of each other. Put a hand on it. The bark is soft, dry and fibrous rather than hard, and on old trees it goes thirty centimetres deep, which is what lets a redwood walk out of a fire that kills everything around it. This one is a child by the standards of its species, which passes 115 metres at home.

trees.name: The Monterey Cypress of Miramare
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story: In the wild this species survives in two groves on the California coast, together covering less than a square kilometre, and it is listed as threatened. Planted anywhere else with sea air, it grows into one of the fastest and heaviest conifers a garden can hold. That is the paradox of the Monterey cypress, and this is what it looks like when it goes well: 4.1 metres round the trunk, eighteen metres tall, and far wider than it is high, because an old Monterey cypress stops climbing and starts spreading until the crown flattens out like a table. Maximilian's gardeners put it in after 1856 among the cypresses ordered from California and Mexico, and on a headland that gets the bora full in the face it has done the thing the archduke was testing for. The wind has pushed the whole crown away from the sea, so the tree leans its weight inland and reads as a permanent record of the direction the worst weather comes from. Crush a leaf between your fingers and it smells of lemon. The Italian sources describing the park call this simply the cypress, and one of them names the wrong species for it, so trust the trunk rather than the label.

trees.name: The Ghost Pine of Miramare
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story: Trieste calls this one il pino fantasma, the ghost pine, and the name is a description rather than a flourish. Its needles are long, grey and set so thinly on the branch that you can see straight through the crown to the sky behind it, which no other pine in the park lets you do. Stand under it on a bright day and the tree casts almost no shadow. It comes from the dry foothills that ring California's Central Valley, where it grows on serpentine and rubble that defeats everything else, and it was one of the more eccentric things Maximilian's gardeners were given to try. Italy's register protects it on grounds of botanical rarity, a category only two trees in the whole Trieste list are given. The cones are the other reason to come. A ghost pine cone is the size of a human head, weighs up to a kilogram, and hangs on hooked scales that will draw blood if you grab one wrongly; the people who lived in its native range ate the seeds, which are large and oily and worth the trouble. At 2.5 metres round and twenty metres tall it is not the biggest tree here, and it is the strangest.

trees.name: The Greek Strawberry Tree of Miramare
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story: This is a shrub that forgot to stop. Arbutus andrachne normally tops out as a thick bush on a Greek or Turkish hillside, and the Italian register lists this one at 2.04 metres round the trunk and twelve metres tall, which for the species is close to absurd. It is the reason the tree is protected on botanical rarity as well as on size. The bark is the thing to look at. Each summer the outer layer peels away in thin sheets like sunburn, and what is left underneath is a bare trunk the colour of cinnamon, cool and slightly waxy to touch, with no fissures anywhere on it. Run a hand along it and the surface feels closer to skin than to timber. Maximilian's gardeners planted it after 1856 among the Mediterranean species that were meant to prove the headland could hold a garden, and unlike the common strawberry tree it was never a safe bet this far north. Fifty-nine of its common cousins, Arbutus unedo, grow a couple of hundred metres away as a registered stand, and none of them has done what this one did. Its flowers come as small white bells in spring, its fruit as round orange berries.

trees.name: The Great Plane of the Giardino Pubblico
trees.access: Free, public park open daily
trees.transport: About 15 min walk east from Piazza Unita, or any bus along Via Giulia
trees.story: The city dug up the pavement around this tree and threw it away. The Giardino Pubblico's biggest plane is 542 centimetres round the trunk and thirty-four metres tall, the largest tree in Trieste by measurement, and the paving laid over its root plate was slowly suffocating it, so the municipality broke the surface out and replaced it with draining material. That is what caring for a 180 year old tree in a city actually looks like. The garden around it was begun in 1854 by Muzio de Tommasini, a serious botanist who happened also to be the podesta of Trieste, on ground bought from Benedictine nuns after a plan to build a church and housing there was dropped. He planted the planes himself. Three hectares now hold roughly 320 large trees from five continents, arranged along paths lined with the bronze heads of Triestine writers, and Italo Svevo walked here often enough that the garden turns up in what he wrote. Nine planes in this garden are on Italy's monumental register and this is the heaviest of them. Stand back far enough to take in the whole trunk: the bark flakes off in plates and leaves the pale patchwork that is the only thing about a London plane you can identify from a hundred metres.

trees.name: The Twin Horse Chestnuts of the Giardino Pubblico
trees.age: about 170 years, planted with the garden from 1854
trees.access: Free, public park open daily
trees.transport: About 15 min walk east from Piazza Unita, or any bus along Via Giulia

best_time.label: May, when it puts up hundreds of white candles at once

trees.story: Two horse chestnuts stand thirty metres apart in this garden and the register measured both at exactly 335 centimetres of girth and exactly twenty-three metres of height. Identical to the centimetre, listed as two separate protected trees, and there is no way to tell from the paper which is which. They were almost certainly planted together when Muzio de Tommasini laid the garden out from 1854, and they have grown at the same rate for 170 years because nothing has happened to one that did not happen to the other. A third, slightly smaller at 317 centimetres, stands further north. Come in May. The horse chestnut is one of the few big trees that flowers in a way you notice from the other end of a park, holding hundreds of white candles upright on the ends of the branches, each one flecked with yellow that turns pink once the flower has been visited and no longer wants bees. The species itself is not from anywhere near here. It was unknown to western Europe until the sixteenth century and comes from a handful of mountain valleys in Albania and Greece, where it is now endangered in the wild.

trees.name: The Valonia Oak of the Giardino Pubblico
trees.age: about 170 years, planted with the garden from 1854
trees.access: Free, public park open daily
trees.transport: About 15 min walk east from Piazza Unita, or any bus along Via Giulia

best_time.label: September and October, when the shaggy acorn cups are on the tree

trees.story: This is the only valonia oak in Friuli Venezia Giulia, and it is the only tree on Trieste's entire monumental register protected for botanical rarity and nothing else. Every other entry earns its place on size, age or the look of the thing. This one is here because there is no second example within a region of 1.2 million people. At 179 centimetres round it is also one of the smallest trees on the list, which tells you how little the measurement matters in this case. The acorns are the reason the species was ever worth anything. A valonia acorn sits in a cup covered in thick shaggy scales that curl outward like a sea anemone, and those cups are extraordinarily rich in tannin. For centuries the eastern Mediterranean shipped them west by the boatload to tan leather, and the trade was large enough that the Greek and Turkish groves were managed for it. The species is semi-evergreen, holding tired leaves through mild winters and dropping them late. It grows wild in Greece, western Turkey and one wood in Puglia. Muzio de Tommasini, a botanist before he was a mayor, would have known exactly how unusual it was to put one in the ground here.

trees.name: The Plane of the Boschetto Roundabout
trees.access: Free, on a public street at the entrance to the Boschetto
trees.transport: About 20 min walk uphill from the Giardino Pubblico along Via Giulia, or bus to Boschetto
trees.story: Trieste's oldest tree stands on a traffic roundabout. The municipality's survey of its 48 monumental trees puts this London plane above 200 years, which makes it older than every park in the city: older than the Giardino Pubblico begun in 1854 a kilometre downhill, older than the Miramare park begun in 1856, older than the Ferdinandeo villa on the slope above it. It was in the ground when Trieste was still Austria's only real seaport and the road it stands on was a country lane. It is five metres and ten centimetres round the trunk and twenty-five metres tall. The London plane was the tree of choice for the avenues and gardens Trieste built in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, which is why nearly a fifth of the city's protected trees are planes, and this is the survivor from the first of those plantings. A second registered plane stands twenty-five metres away, 440 centimetres round, and the two of them frame the entrance to the Boschetto del Ferdinandeo, the wooded hill that Triestini have walked up on Sunday afternoons for as long as the trees have been there. Take Via Giulia out of the public garden and keep climbing.

trees.name: The Bagolaro of Piazza Hortis
trees.access: Free, on the open public square, no gate or opening hours
trees.transport: About a 10 minute walk south-west of Piazza Unita d'Italia
trees.story:
For over 180 years this hackberry has stood in what is now Piazza Hortis, and for most of that time nobody thought about what people were doing to its roots. In 2025 the city fenced it off: pedestrians had been crossing the square for generations without knowing they were walking on top of nearly two centuries of root plate, compacting the soil the tree breathes through. The comune spent about 17,000 euros on the fence and on new drainage-friendly planting around the base, part of a wider programme that has already stripped suffocating pavement away from monumental trees elsewhere in the city.

Trieste has identified 48 monumental trees within its borders, the highest concentration the comune has recorded of any Italian city, and this bagolaro is one of them. In September 2024 it was fitted with a TreeTag, a small ID marker placed as part of a European citizen-science campaign that measures a tree's condition and records the data for researchers to track over time.

Celtis australis is native across the Mediterranean and famously slow to give up: its wood was used for cart axles and ploughshares because it resists splitting even when green. This one has outlived the square's own name twice over, and the piazza, library and street around it are all named for Attilio Hortis, the Trieste historian and librarian who died a century ago.

trees.name: The Siberian Elm of Piazzale Rosmini
trees.access: Free, public garden with children's play areas, open daily
trees.transport: About a 12 minute walk south of Piazza Unita d'Italia, adjoining Piazza Hortis
trees.story:
The garden at Piazzale Rosmini climbs the San Vito hill above the church of Madonna del Mare, nine and a half thousand square metres of slope and lawn that the city's own parks department singles out for two things: its valuable trees and its play areas for children of different ages. The Siberian elm growing there, 3.58 metres round and 24 metres tall, is one of Trieste's registered monumental specimens and the garden's standout tree.

Ulmus pumila earned its place in European gardens for the same reason it earns a mention here: it shrugs off Dutch elm disease far better than the native field and wych elms the fungus devastated across the continent from the 1970s onward. A healthy elm of real size in a European city is worth noticing partly for that reason alone, a survivor by constitution rather than by luck.

Like the bagolaro at Piazza Hortis, this elm was fitted with a TreeTag in September 2024, part of the same citywide EU citizen-science campaign that is slowly building a public record of condition and growth for Trieste's 48 monumental trees. No individual age has been published for it, so none is claimed here.

trees.name: The Kew Gardens Red Oak
trees.access: Free, public park, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Streetcar (504 King or 501 Queen) to Kew Beach; Woodbine subway station + 15 min walk
trees.story:
Toronto has an official tree, and this is it. The city gave the title in 2022 to a northern red oak in Kew Gardens, a trunk 5.3 metres round under a crown reaching about 36 metres, with one long limb that sags all the way down to the grass.

Arborists read its start off a diameter of 169 centimetres and put it at roughly 220 years, with a band running from about 200 to 260. Nobody has cored it, so that band is the honest answer: it may or may not predate the founding of the town that became Toronto.

Everything else on this corner arrived afterwards. Joseph Williams farmed the land from the 1850s and ran amusement grounds beneath these branches; the city bought the 8.4 hectares in 1907. The creeks that once ran down to the lake here were culverted while the oak stood over them. Forests Ontario designated it a heritage tree in 2021, and a Heritage Toronto plaque went up in May 2023, which is late recognition for something that was already large when the first houses in the Beaches were built.

A native plant garden now grows under the low limb. Stand beside it and the limb is at shoulder height, which is not how most people expect to meet a 36 metre tree.

trees.name: The King's Oak
trees.access: Free, public waterfront park, open at all hours
trees.transport: Streetcar 509/511 to Exhibition Loop, then 10 min walk; or Exhibition GO station

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
On 12 May 1937, while George VI was being crowned in London, Toronto put an oak in the ground on the lakeshore and planted about 150 more trees around it before the day was out.

The oak is the centre of the arrangement. Around it run concentric rings of silver maples, the Empire Circle, one ring for each dominion and colony of an empire that has since stopped existing. The rings are still there. So is the oak, 89 years on, an ordinary pedunculate oak carrying a considerable amount of ceremony: a stone and plaque beside it, dedicated by Justice John A. Hope and unveiled by Sir William Mulock in August 1938.

Then it happened again. On 6 May 2023, for the coronation of Charles III, the city planted a companion oak next to the first one and added a second plaque. Eighty-six years apart, the same gesture, the same species, the same patch of grass. The second planting is also the reason we know the first tree is still standing.

This is the youngest tree on this page and the only one whose birthday is known to the day; every other age here comes off a tape measure around a trunk. Coronation Park has since been restored in phases, and the first phase went to this oak and its circle of maples.

trees.name: Big Red
trees.access: Free, public memorial park beside the Long Branch Cenotaph, open at all hours
trees.transport: Long Branch GO station or 501 Long Branch streetcar loop, 10 min walk

best_time.label: late October, when the crown turns the deep red it is named for

trees.story:
The Long Branch Hotel burned down in 1958. The oak beside it did not, and it is still on the corner.

Big Red is a northern red oak at Long Branch Avenue and Park Boulevard, named by the neighbourhood for what it does in October. Diameter measurements put its start in the late 1810s; Forests Canada rounds that to about 200 years and the early 1800s, which is close enough agreement to work with. Its height is less settled. Forests Canada records 24 metres, a 2024 local report says 33, and neither explains how it was measured, so both figures are on the record and neither has won.

In the late 1800s it stood near a fountain in the grounds of the Long Branch Grove and Resort, a lakeside destination Torontonians came out to by train. The resort went. The hotel went. The streets arrived. In 1933 the cenotaph went up beside the oak, and the tree has stood next to the names of three wars ever since, which is the reason to come in November rather than the reason to come in October.

Forests Ontario made it Long Branch's first heritage tree in April 2018, listed at 200 years. It is by some distance the oldest thing on that corner.

trees.name: Corsan's Turkish Hazel
trees.access: Free, public park (Etobicoke Parks System since 1959), multiple entrances off Kipling Avenue and Wingrove Hill
trees.transport: Islington subway station, then bus along Kipling/Burnhamthorpe, roughly 15-20 min total
trees.story:
George Hebden Corsan was an internationally known swimmer and a health food evangelist, and he spent forty years proving that nut trees would grow in Ontario. This is one of the trees that proved it.

Corsan bought twelve acres here across 1911 and 1912 and turned them into a nut farm, eventually cultivating more than 400 varieties and collecting the name the Nut Man of Islington. Metropolitan Toronto bought the land in 1959 and made it Echo Valley Park, which is the only reason a private obsession is now something anyone can walk through.

The Turkish hazel is one of five of his nut trees on the heritage register, alongside a hican, a black walnut and two more walnuts. The register recorded this one at 100 years old in 2017 and dates the planting loosely to the 1900s, without tying it to Corsan's own arrival, so early last century is as close as the evidence gets. A 1971 survey by the University of Toronto's Shade Tree Research Laboratory listed Turkish hazel among the nut species still growing on the site, which is the second account standing behind the register entry.

Two honest gaps. All five trees share a single map pin, so the last part of the walk is a short hunt. And nobody has published a sighting since the 2017 nomination. If you find it, or work out which of the five is which, tell us.

trees.name: The Uithof Linden
trees.access: Viewable from the public street at any time; the farmhouse grounds themselves are institutional, not open parkland
trees.transport: Bus or tram to Utrecht Science Park, then a short walk, roughly 20-25 minutes from Utrecht Centraal

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: This linden has outlived the entire farming landscape it was planted into. It went into the ground around 1750 on the south side of a farmhouse called de Uithof, following a Dutch custom of the time: plant a linden on a farmhouse's sunniest side and it will shade the house all summer while dropping its leaves in time to let winter light back in. That practical 18th-century logic is most of why lindens are the tree most often found beside old Dutch farms, more common there than any species chosen for beauty alone. The land around this particular farmhouse, once part of a monastery estate called Oostbroek, gave its name centuries later to something nobody planting the tree could have predicted: De Uithof, now Utrecht Science Park, one of the largest university campuses in the Netherlands, built up around the old farm over the second half of the 20th century. The farmhouse itself survives as a listed national monument, a low 17th-century building now surrounded by university faculties and student housing rather than fields. At roughly 275 years old, the linden is one of the oldest Dutch lindens still standing anywhere, having watched a working farm turn into a research campus without ever leaving the spot it was planted for shade.

trees.name: The Oude Hortus Ginkgo
trees.access: Paid entry, Universiteitsmuseum ticket or separate Oude Hortus ticket
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station

best_time.label: November: the whole crown turns butter gold, then drops in a day or two

trees.story: A ginkgo is either male or female for its entire life, except this one, which has been both since sometime in the 19th century, when a gardener grafted a female branch onto the male trunk so the tree could finally produce the seeds its species is famous for. The graft still shows on the bark today, a visible seam between two sexes on one plant, and it worked: this ginkgo, planted around 1770 in what was then Utrecht University's working medicinal garden, is now old enough that the University Museum's own researchers call it possibly one of the oldest ginkgos growing anywhere outside Japan. The species itself had only just reached Europe when this seedling went into the ground, imported from a country most Dutch botanists of the time had never visited, decades before Charles Darwin was born. The garden around it operated as a teaching collection for medicinal and useful plants from 1723 until 1920, when the university's plant science moved elsewhere and left this walled plot as what it is today, a quiet historic garden behind the University Museum rather than a working laboratory. The tree has outlived that entire purpose. A visit requires a museum ticket, the price of admission for standing next to something that predates the country's current constitution by decades.

trees.name: The Handkerchief Tree of the Oude Hortus
trees.access: Paid entry, Universiteitsmuseum ticket or separate Oude Hortus ticket
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station

best_time.label: mid-May, when the white bracts hang like handkerchiefs
