trees.story: For about ten days every May, this tree looks like it is covered in hundreds of small white handkerchiefs, or according to the alternative common name, a flock of ghosts caught mid-flutter. What actually flowers are pairs of oversized white bracts, modified leaves rather than petals, that hang beneath each small flower cluster and catch any breath of wind. Davidia involucrata was unknown to Western botany until 1869, when the French missionary and naturalist Armand David first documented it in the mountains of central China, and it stayed a horticultural rarity for decades afterward because its seeds are notoriously reluctant to germinate, sometimes taking two winters before anything happens at all. Utrecht's specimen, in the walled garden behind the University Museum, is one of the relatively few handkerchief trees the Netherlands has managed to establish and keep alive to a real size, now tall enough to tower over the path beneath it. Outside its two-week May window, it reads as an unremarkable mid-sized tree with heart-shaped leaves, nothing that would make a passerby stop. The garden rewards exactly that kind of patience: come at the wrong time and miss the point entirely, come in May and understand immediately why a tree can be worth crossing a continent for.

trees.name: The Oude Hortus Yew
trees.access: Paid entry, Universiteitsmuseum ticket or separate Oude Hortus ticket
trees.transport: 10-15 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Every part of this tree is poisonous except the bright red flesh around its seed, which birds eat happily while leaving the seed itself, the one genuinely toxic part, to pass through unharmed and land somewhere new. That single evolutionary trick is most of why yews are found planted beside old churches and gardens across Europe: birds do the planting, humans get the credit. This yew has stood in Utrecht University's old botanical garden for at least 150 years, part of a teaching collection that once used its poisonous foliage as a live lesson in medicinal and dangerous plants rather than as a specimen prized for size or age alone. Yews grow slowly and live long by almost any measure, routinely reaching centuries in places nobody has disturbed them, and this one has had a walled, tended garden to itself for its entire recorded life, none of the storm damage or development pressure that shortens most urban trees' lives. It stands quietly among the ginkgo and rarer imports from China, easy to walk past without a second look, though it has technically been capable of killing anyone who ate the wrong part of it since long before any visitor reading this was born.

trees.name: Onder de Linden
trees.access: Free, public street at any time
trees.transport: Central Binnenstad, walkable from Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minutes

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: The southern stretch of the Nieuwegracht has been called Onder de Linden, literally under the lindens, since at least the 17th century, when the canal first got a uniform planted row of trees in 1660. The trees standing there today are not that old: sources place the current lindens at around 1830, meaning at least one replanting happened somewhere in the intervening 170 years, though no record pins down exactly when or why. What survives is the pattern rather than any single tree, a continuous double row shading the water between the Quintijnsbrug and Brigittenbrug bridges, close enough to the original 17th-century design that the old name still fits. Utrecht's canal-side streets, Nieuwegracht and Oudegracht both, are unusual among Dutch cities for having a lower service level built at water height beneath the upper street, a two-tier system that shaped how the trees above could root and grow for centuries. The lindens here have had to share cramped underground space with wharf cellars and canal walls the whole time, which likely explains why Utrecht's canal trees rarely reach the size of specimens planted in open parkland. None of that shows from the towpath. What shows is dense, cool shade over green water on even the hottest days, the same effect this stretch of canal has been named for since before the Dutch Golden Age had properly started.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Hieronymusplantsoen
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Hieronymusplantsoen, Binnenstad; about a 15 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station
trees.story:
Utrecht's own tree register cannot agree with itself about this copper beech. One entry, filed for the national Bomenstichting listing, dates its planting to the 1880s. The municipality's own separate file says something older, that it was planted along with the rest of Hieronymusplantsoen by the landscape architect J.D. Zocher in 1835, part of the decades-long project that turned Utrecht's old medieval walls and moat into the ring of parks still circling the historic centre today. Both cannot be right, and nobody has settled which, so this page states both rather than picking the more flattering one.

Either way it has stood on this small rise in the plantsoen for well over a century, its purple-red leaves a deliberate accent against the plane and elm green Zocher planted around it. Copper beech is not a distinct species but a colour form of the ordinary beech, propagated by grafting, because a beech grown from its own seed reverts to green more often than not, which makes every specimen a small act of continued human intervention rather than a wild event. It grows on open parkland in front of the building known locally as the Vrije School, no fence and no ticket. If a photograph or a planting record settles which date is right, tell us.

trees.name: The Zocher Planes of Hieronymusplantsoen
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Hieronymusplantsoen, Binnenstad; about a 15 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station
trees.story:
Four Oriental planes stand together on one spot in Hieronymusplantsoen, registered nationally as a single monumental entry because whoever surveyed them treated the group, not any one trunk, as the thing worth protecting. Utrecht's municipal records date the planting to 1835, part of J.D. Zocher's decades-long project to turn the old defensive moat and city walls circling Utrecht into a continuous ring of English-style landscape parks, of which Hieronymusplantsoen is one surviving stretch.

Oriental plane is the straight species behind the hybrid London plane that lines most European streets, native from the Balkans to Iran and far less commonly planted in the Netherlands than its hybrid offspring. Four of them together, close to two centuries old, read as something closer to a small grove than four separate specimens, standing opposite the same building that borders the plantsoen's copper beech and, a short walk further, one of the country's most celebrated botanical gardens. They grow in the open on public parkland, unfenced, free to see any day. The register gives a single planting year for the whole group; nobody has independently dated an individual trunk within it, so treat 1835 as the group's founding date rather than a measurement of any one tree.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Janskerkhof
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all times
trees.transport: Janskerkhof, Binnenstad; about a 12 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station
trees.story:
Janskerkhof looks like a churchyard and mostly still is one, a square in central Utrecht built around the Gothic Jans Church, with a weekly flower market and, in its northeast corner near the old cantonal courthouse, a single Oriental plane the municipality dates to 1900. That makes it the youngest of the register's Utrecht street trees rather than the oldest, and its interest is less about age than about staying put: more than a century in a paved civic square that has hosted markets and gatherings throughout, without losing the tree that anchors its corner.

Oriental plane sheds bark in patches as it grows, the way a sycamore does, leaving a mottled grey, green and cream trunk that reads almost camouflaged against stone. This one has had over a century of pavement compaction and passing traffic to contend with, which the register does not comment on beyond dating the planting, so no vitality note beyond that exists yet. It stands in the open square, free to walk up to any day, opposite number 13 Janskerkhof. Nobody has published an independent account of this specific tree beyond the municipal register, so treat the date as the council's own record rather than a cross-checked fact.

trees.name: The Plane of Lucasbolwerk
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Lucasbolwerk, Binnenstad; about a 14 minute walk from Utrecht Centraal station
trees.story:
This London plane was already forty years old, well established on the Lucasbolwerk, when Utrecht's city theatre went up facing it in 1941. The Stadsschouwburg, designed by the Dutch modernist architect Willem Dudok and opened that September, is the newer thing on this stretch of the old singel parkland by a wide margin: the municipal tree register dates the plane's own planting to around 1900, part of the general planting of Utrecht's 19th-century park ring rather than anything tied to the building that came decades later.

Lucasbolwerk itself is one of the bastions of Utrecht's old city fortifications, absorbed into the landscaped singel park that rings the historic centre, the same project that gave the city Hieronymusplantsoen and the Zocherpark further along the water. The plane has spent well over a century watching that transformation from bastion to theatre forecourt, and now stands as the tree most people photograph the Stadsschouwburg's facade past without quite registering. It grows in the open on public parkland directly opposite the theatre entrance, free to see, no ticket needed even if the building behind it does require one.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Wilhelminapark
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 20 minute walk; or bus/tram to Wilhelminapark stop
trees.story:
Wilhelminapark opened in 1898, laid out in the informal English landscape style fashionable across the Netherlands at the time, and this wingnut is one of roughly twenty-four trees in it now protected as monumental. Pterocarya fraxinifolia is native to river valleys in the Caucasus and northern Iran, a relative of walnut and hickory rather than anything European, grown here for a wide, low, spreading crown and for the strange fruit it hangs each summer: strings of winged seeds up to half a metre long, dangling like decorations nobody put up on purpose.

The Dutch national register of monumental trees dates the planting to the 1890s, putting the wingnut among the park's first generation, planted while the layout itself was still new rather than added later. No source gives its girth, and the register carries no basis for the decade beyond its own record, so treat the age as an informed estimate rather than a measurement.

The park itself keeps an informal walking route past its own oldest trees, called Rondje Oude Reuzen, Round of Old Giants, and this wingnut is stop ten on it, on the western edge of the park's sunbathing lawn. A twenty minute walk from Utrecht Centraal, free, open through the same hours as the rest of the park.

trees.name: The Colchis Maple of Wilhelminapark
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 20 minute walk; or bus/tram to Wilhelminapark stop
trees.story:
Four stops earlier on the same walking route stands a very different tree from the same era: a Cappadocian maple, named for the ancient region of Cappadocia in central Anatolia, though its natural range runs north into the Caucasus too, where it is sometimes called Colchis maple instead, after the kingdom Jason sailed for in the story of the Golden Fleece. It grows at Wilhelminapark's west entrance, on the footpath opposite house number 28, one of the park's original plantings from the 1880s according to the Dutch national monumental tree register.

Acer cappadocicum keeps its leaves a plain green most of the year and then, in autumn, turns a uniform buttery yellow rather than the mixed reds and oranges of most maples, a colour show the park's own walking guide singles it out for. No girth is on record for this tree, and the register gives no basis for its planting decade beyond the record itself, so roughly a hundred and forty years old is an estimate rather than a measurement.

Wilhelminapark is a national monument in its own right, laid out in 1898 in the informal English landscape style, and this maple was already an established tree by the time the park's more famous specimens matured around it. It stands free to visit, a short walk or tram ride from the city centre.

trees.name: The Catalpa of Wilhelminapark
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 20 minute walk; or bus/tram to Wilhelminapark stop
trees.story:
Wilhelminapark's own walking guide to its oldest trees calls this one Trompetboom, trumpet tree, the Dutch common name for catalpa, and once it flowers in July the name explains itself: white, orchid-shaped blooms crowd the canopy in dense clusters, followed by seed pods that hang on through winter looking like a stand of thin green beans left out to dry. Catalpa bignonioides grows broad and low rather than tall, its heart-shaped leaves among the largest of any tree commonly planted in Dutch parks.

The Dutch national monumental tree register dates this specimen to the 1890s, on the west edge of the park's play meadow, one of the original plantings from Wilhelminapark's founding as an English-style landscape park in 1898. No girth is recorded for it in any source found, and the planting decade rests on the register's own dating rather than a documented record, so treat the age, roughly a hundred and thirty years, as an estimate.

It is stop seventeen on the park's own Rondje Oude Reuzen trail past its oldest and most impressive trees, a route that also passes the wingnut and the Cappadocian maple mapped separately on this site. Free, in a public park a short walk from the centre.

trees.name: The Zocher Plane of Zonnenburg
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk
trees.story:
In 1835, the landscape architect Jan David Zocher jr began replacing the demolished defensive ring around old Utrecht with a chain of parks, the Singelplantsoen, that still follows the city's medieval bastions today. This plane, standing just west of the old Sterrenwacht observatory on the Zonnenburg bastion, carries that exact year in the municipality's own planting record, making it one of the oldest trees anywhere along Zocher's design and roughly as old as the park scheme itself.

London plane, a hybrid of American sycamore and Oriental plane first bred in seventeenth century Europe, is the workhorse tree of the whole Singelplantsoen chain, planted for fast growth and tolerance of compacted city soil along a route that was walked and cycled hard from the day it opened. No girth is recorded for this specimen, but at close to two centuries old it should be among the largest planes on the route by now.

The Sterrenwacht itself, Utrecht University's historic observatory, still stands beside it, giving the tree one of the more improbable neighbours on this list: nearly two hundred years of watching people look up at the stars from the building next door. Free, public parkland, a short walk from the old city centre.

trees.name: The Servaasbolwerk Plane
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk
trees.story:
Two dates exist for this plane, and the register that tracks it admits as much rather than picking one. The municipality's own planting list gives 1835, the year Jan David Zocher jr began laying out the Singelplantsoen ring parks this tree still stands in; an earlier entry from the Bomenstichting, the Dutch tree conservation foundation, instead recorded 1900 to 1910, a figure its own more recent register update calls probably a guess. A gap of sixty five years between two sources that both claim to know is unusual enough to state plainly rather than smooth over.

What is not in dispute is the tree itself: a London plane standing opposite house number 2 on Servaasbolwerk, part of the same bastion parkland chain as the Zocher Plane mapped separately nearby, and old enough either way to be one of the historic ring's mature specimens. No girth has been recorded.

Whichever date is right, the tree has stood through most or all of the twentieth century on a stretch of parkland built from a demolished city wall, watching the bastion go from defensive earthwork to quiet residential green space. Free, public, a few minutes' walk from Zonnenburg.

trees.name: The Liberation Beech of Servaasbolwerk
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk
trees.story:
This copper beech was planted to be looked at and remembered, not simply grown. Bevrijdingsbomen, liberation trees, went into the ground across the Netherlands after May 1945 as living memorials to the country's liberation from German occupation, and the Dutch national monumental tree register marks this one at Servaasbolwerk with exactly that designation: a herdenkingsboom, a memorial tree, from the same decade as the liberation itself.

Fagus sylvatica f. purpurea, the copper or purple beech, is a straightforward garden variety chosen for its colour rather than any rarity, dark reddish purple leaves through the growing season rather than the species' usual green. An independent record from 2015, a local history blog that photographed the tree and named it directly as a bevrijdingsbeuk, confirms both the species and the memorial purpose without giving an exact planting year, so the age here rests on the register's decade band rather than a specific date tied to the liberation itself.

At around eighty years old it is the youngest tree on this list by some margin, a reminder planted deliberately rather than grown accidentally into significance, standing on the same historic bastion parkland as the older planes nearby. Free, public, in the heart of the old city.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Lepelenburg
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open at all times
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk
trees.story:
Lepelenburg was a defensive bastion on Utrecht's medieval city wall before it became a park around 1860, part of the same conversion that turned the whole ring of fortifications into the Singelplantsoen. This Oriental plane, the species that gives the London plane half its parentage, stands beside the Herenbrug bridge inside that park, dated by the Dutch national monumental tree register to the early 1900s, a later addition to the grounds rather than one of the original 1860s plantings.

Platanus orientalis is native to the eastern Mediterranean and southwest Asia, grown across Europe for centuries before its American-crossed hybrid became the more common street tree; a pure Oriental plane like this one is rarer to find in a Dutch park than its more widespread offspring. No girth has been recorded for it, and no source found names or dates this individual tree directly, so the record here rests on the register alone, corroborated only by Lepelenburg's own well documented general history rather than anything specific to this trunk.

It stands a few minutes' walk from Servaasbolwerk and Zonnenburg, within reach of the other bastion-park trees mapped on this site, on ground that has gone from a soldier's lookout to a footbridge crossing in under two centuries. Free, public parkland near the old city centre.

trees.name: The Markiezeneik of Amelisweerd
trees.access: Free, public forest estate (Landgoed Amelisweerd), open year-round from sunrise to sunset
trees.transport: Bus 41 from Utrecht Centraal towards Wijk bij Duurstede to the Oud Amelisweerd stop, roughly 15 minutes, then a short walk into the Markiezenbos
trees.story:
An oak became a protest symbol and then won. The Markiezeneik stands in the Markiezenbos, part of the Amelisweerd estate on Utrecht's edge, and for years it was the named face of a campaign against a plan to widen the A27 motorway straight through the wood, a project that would have taken roughly 800 trees along with it. In 2022 the oak won Boom van het Jaar, the Netherlands' national Tree of the Year contest, with nearly 37,000 votes, then placed ninth in the European contest the year after, an unusually direct way for a country to vote on a road scheme.

In March 2026 the country's highest administrative court, the Raad van State, annulled the underlying decision over unresolved nitrogen rules, killing the widening for now. The oak is still standing to hear about it: planted in the late 18th century by the marquis who then owned the estate, it carries the bark scars of an old lightning strike, healed over now with new growth around the wound.

Free, public forest, open sunrise to sunset. Bus 41 from Utrecht Centraal reaches Oud Amelisweerd in about fifteen minutes, then a short walk into the wood.

trees.name: The Thickest Plane of the Zocherpark
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk
trees.story:
Zocherpark is not one park but a chain of them: Zonnenburg, Servaasbolwerk, Lepelenburg, Hieronymusplantsoen and Wilhelminapark, roughly three kilometres of bastion parkland laid out where Utrecht's old city walls used to run. Somewhere along that chain grows the thickest London plane of the lot, on the plantsoen just north of the old Sterrenwacht observatory, and a local canal-touring guide has done the measuring nobody else bothered to write down: 629 centimetres round and about 27 metres tall.

The city's own monumental tree register dates the planting to the 1830s, and the independent route guide narrows that to 1835, putting the tree at around 190 years old, roughly contemporary with the observatory it now shades. It stands close enough to three other registered trees in the same bastion cluster that a visit here becomes a short walk rather than a single stop, though this one carries its own separate register number and is not to be confused with a second plane about 80 metres to the southwest.

Free, public park, open during normal park hours, about 15 minutes' walk from Utrecht Centraal.

trees.name: The Old Copper Beech of Servaasbolwerk
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open during park hours
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk
trees.story:
Two beeches stand roughly 45 metres apart on the same small stretch of Servaasbolwerk, and it is easy to walk past one thinking you have already seen the other. This one is the older by a wide margin. The Dutch national monumental tree register bands its planting to the 1880s, decades before the neighbouring copper beech went into the ground in 1945 as a liberation memorial. Both wear the same deep red foliage that turns darker through autumn, which is exactly what makes the two easy to confuse on a walk along the old singel parkland.

The distinction matters because one tree carries a specific historical claim, a wartime memorial planted the year Germany surrendered, and the other does not. This is the other: a beech that was already sixty years old when its younger neighbour was planted, with a trunk that has since thickened to four metres around. Its exact planting year has not been pinned down closer than a decade, so treat any single year you read elsewhere with some suspicion.

It stands on public gemeente parkland, part of the belt of bastions and gardens that replaced Utrecht's old city defences, open at any hour with nothing to buy a ticket for.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Van Asch van Wijckskade
trees.access: Free, visible from the public kade/street at all times; a school building stands beside the tree but the tree itself is gemeente-owned and stands on the public street, not on the school's grounds
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 20 minute walk, at the north edge of the historic centre near Begijnekade
trees.story:
The leaf gives it away before anything else does. Where a London plane's leaf has broad, shallow lobes, an Oriental plane's is cut almost to the base into narrow fingers, and the tree on Van Asch van Wijckskade is the real thing, not the more common hybrid that fills most European streets. Its trunk has grown to five and a half metres around, thick enough that the Dutch monumental tree register simply calls it a large presence on a street that does not have many.

The register's own notes place it beside a school building, which under normal circumstances would be reason to leave a tree off this list. This one clears that bar anyway: the plane itself grows on the public kade, the paved towpath along the canal, not inside the schoolyard, and it is visible and reachable from the street at any hour without setting foot on the school's own ground.

Planted sometime between 1870 and 1900, which puts it at roughly a century and a half old without pinning down a firmer date, it grows at the quiet northern edge of Utrecht's historic centre, near Begijnekade, a fifteen minute walk from the bastion parkland where three of its neighbours on this list also stand.

trees.name: The Turkey Oaks of Geertebolwerk
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned Zocherpark bastion belt), open at all times
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 15 minute walk

best_time.label: October, when the mossy acorns drop and the foliage turns

trees.story:
Four Turkey oaks grow together on the old Geertebolwerk bastion, close enough beside the water that the Dutch monumental tree register counts them as one entry rather than four. Two went into the ground around 1835, when Utrecht's medieval defences were being reshaped into public parkland, and two followed around 1870. Two of the four have grown double stemmed from about two metres up, forking into pairs of trunks that make the group read as more than four trees from a distance.

Quercus cerris carries a Dutch name that is easier to remember than its Latin one: moseik, moss oak, for the shaggy, mossy cups that hold its acorns, unlike the smooth cups of the native oaks nearby. The register gives the group a shared girth of roughly three and seventy metres and a height of about twenty five, figures that describe the stand rather than any single trunk within it.

With planting dates nearly forty years apart, the group's age spans roughly a century and a half to nearly two centuries, and no single figure captures it honestly. They stand in the open, on public gemeente parkland, a fifteen minute walk from Utrecht Centraal.

trees.name: The Beech of Lucasbolwerk
trees.access: Free, public park (gemeente-owned), open at all times
trees.transport: Utrecht Centraal, roughly 14 minute walk (same area as the already-published utr_009 Plane of Lucasbolwerk)
trees.story:
This copper beech carries a health warning rather than just an age. A canal-route survey of Utrecht's monumental trees, last updated in September 2025, reports the tree infected with reuzenzwam, giant polypore, a fungus that rots roots and trunk bases from the inside and has already killed a different Utrecht beech on record a short walk away at the Maliebaan roundabout. As of that September visit the tree did not yet appear to be suffering seriously, in the surveyor's own words, but the infection is real and worth watching rather than ignoring.

The Dutch monumental tree register places its planting between 1850 and 1860; the municipality's own separate record says 1870. Both figures are published and neither has been reconciled, so this page gives the wider range, somewhere between 150 and 176 years old. A 2005 survey measured it at four metres thirty around and nineteen metres tall, numbers now two decades old and likely conservative for a tree that has kept growing since.

It stands in the open on Lucasbolwerk, the same bastion park as the published Plane of Lucasbolwerk a short walk away. If you visit and the crown looks thin or the bark shows fresh damage near the base, that is worth telling us.

trees.name: The Founding Trees of the Giardini della Biennale
trees.access: Free, public gardens; the Biennale exhibition areas require a ticket during the Art and Architecture Biennale seasons
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Giardini vaporetto stop (lines 1, 4.1, 4.2)
trees.story: Venice's biggest green space exists because Napoleon needed somewhere to put a park and had no scruples about what stood in the way. In 1807 his decree ordered the city to create public gardens, and to make room, engineers demolished a cluster of churches and convents on marshy ground at the eastern edge of Castello, including San Domenico and Sant'Antonio Abate, and drained the site. Architect Giannantonio Selva, working with botanist Pietro Antonio Zorzi, laid out a formal neoclassical garden of straight avenues, inaugurated in 1810. By the mid-19th century, fashion had shifted, and the geometry was reworked into the winding paths and irregular groves visible today. More than a hundred tree species now grow across the site, lindens, hackberries and plane trees among the most common, though no individual specimen here has ever been separately dated or measured. Since 1895 two thirds of the grounds have hosted the Venice Biennale's international pavilions, making this simultaneously the city's oldest public garden and its best known contemporary art venue, with cats that have their own informal reputation among regulars.

trees.name: The Cypresses of San Michele Cemetery
trees.access: Free, open daily (hours vary by season, typically morning to early evening)
trees.transport: Cimitero vaporetto stop (lines 4.1, 4.2, 5.1, 5.2)
trees.story: Venice's dead live on an island of their own, and the cypresses that ring it are the first thing anyone sees crossing the lagoon toward it. The idea was Napoleon's: his 1804 Edict of Saint-Cloud banned burial within cities for public health reasons, and Venice, unable to bury its dead on land it did not have, chose the island of San Cristoforo della Pace, merging it with the neighbouring islet of San Michele in stages between 1813 and 1839. Architect Giannantonio Selva, who had designed the Napoleonic Gardens across the lagoon a few years earlier, laid out the cemetery's original plan, and cypress became its signature planting, a tree with its own funerary tradition stretching back to antiquity. No individual tree here carries a published planting date or measurement, so the exact age of any specimen standing today is unverified, but the dark spires visible above the cemetery's brick walls have been part of the approach to Venice for close to two centuries. Ezra Pound, Igor Stravinsky and Joseph Brodsky are buried among them.

trees.name: The Bcharre Cedars of San Lazzaro degli Armeni
trees.access: Paid entry (8 euro), guided tour only, daily at 15:25 (about 90 minutes)
trees.transport: Vaporetto line 20 from San Zaccaria (Riva degli Schiavoni), about 25 minutes

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: These three cedars did not grow up on this island, they were carried to it. On 21 January 2008 a Venice Academy of Fine Arts student brought three young Cedars of Lebanon from her home village of Bcharre and from the Cedars of God, the sacred, UNESCO-listed forest in the mountains above it, and planted them on San Lazzaro degli Armeni as an artistic pilgrimage, an offering from one small mountain community to an island monastery built by another people who had also fled for survival. Mechitar of Sebaste, an Armenian monk driven out by Ottoman advances, was granted this derelict leper-hospital island in 1717 and spent decades turning it into a monastery, library and garden for the Mekhitarist Armenian Catholic order, still tended by the same order today. The cedar is Lebanon's own national tree, printed on its flag, and the choice to plant three here rather than one is deliberate in the retellings of the event, an echo of the island's own layered history of exile and rebuilding. Visitors who take the monastery's guided tour, the only way onto the island, pass the young cedars among a garden that also holds a Canary Island palm, wind-bent Aleppo pines, and centuries-old rose beds still picked for vartanush, rose petal jam.

trees.name: The Cypress Ring of San Francesco del Deserto
trees.age: undated, called ancient without a specific record
trees.neighbourhood: Northern lagoon, between Burano and Sant'Erasmo
trees.access: Free entry, donation welcome; guided visits Tuesday-Sunday 9:00-11:00 and 15:00-17:00, closed Monday
trees.transport: Vaporetto line 12 to Burano, then private boat or water taxi (about 15 minutes)
trees.story: Francis of Assisi is said to have landed on this four-hectare island in 1220, returning from the Fifth Crusade, and a local legend claims he planted his walking staff in the ground, where it grew into a pine tree that survived until 1701, when its dried trunk was carved into a statue of the saint. That original tree is gone, but the cypresses that now ring the island's perimeter, visible from the water as a dense green band around the convent walls, are old enough that every source describing them reaches for the word ancient without offering a planting date or measurement, so their exact age is unverified here. Six Franciscan friars still live on the island today, one of whom leads the only tours available, walking visitors past cloisters dating to the 15th century and gardens the friars still work themselves. There is no public vaporetto stop: reaching the island means taking the line to Burano and then a private boat or water taxi for the final short crossing, a genuine detour that keeps the place as quiet as its name suggests.

trees.name: The Black Poplar of the Certosa
trees.age: undated, described as one of the island's largest specimens
trees.access: Free, public park, dawn to sunset
trees.transport: Vaporetto lines 41/42, Certosa stop (request stop)
trees.story: This poplar stands alone in the middle of what is effectively an accidental nature reserve. The Certosa takes its name from a Carthusian monastery founded here in 1424, abandoned under Napoleon, then used for over a century as a military store and firing range before the Italian army finally left in 1997. Left to itself for decades, the 22 hectare island grew wild: stands of white poplar, black poplar and ash now cover ground that soldiers once marched across, described by the site's own conservation literature as one of few places where the lagoon's original sandy-soil vegetation can still be studied directly. The black poplar growing at the heart of this wild wood is repeatedly singled out in local sources as one of the largest of its kind rooted in the island's sandy ground, though none gives it a specific age or trunk measurement, so its exact age is unverified. A public urban park opened on part of the island in 2013, and the whole site is now open from dawn to sunset, a quiet contrast to the crowds a ten minute boat ride away.

trees.name: The Olive Tree of San Servolo
trees.access: Free, public park; separate paid ticket for the Museo del Manicomio
trees.transport: Vaporetto line 20 from San Zaccaria, about 10 minutes

best_time.label: October to December: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: This olive tree grows in a garden originally planted to stock a pharmacy, on an island whose most recent past was Italy's largest asylum for the criminally insane. Benedictine monks are documented on San Servolo from at least the 8th century, and the garden they and later religious orders built up over a thousand years carries more than 400 tree species today, including Canary palms, agaves and a Chusan palm alongside the century-old olive tree, planted originally for medicinal use when the island supplied remedies to the Venetian military. The asylum operated from the 18th century until its closure in 1978, a history now documented in the island's own Museo del Manicomio, and the contrast between that clinical past and the freely walkable garden that surrounds it is part of what makes a visit here unusual. No source gives this specific olive tree an exact planting date, so its precise age is unverified, but its description as secolare, century-old, is consistent across the records checked. Venice International University now occupies much of the island.

trees.name: The Garden Trees of Giardini Papadopoli
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Piazzale Roma / Venezia Santa Lucia station
trees.story: This is the first patch of green most visitors to Venice ever see, and also the smallest survivor of its original self. Count Spiridione Papadopoli commissioned the garden in 1834-35 from designer Francesco Bagnara for his wife Teresa Mosconi, laid out with terraced paths and shade trees on what had been open land near the city's edge. Marco Quignon reworked the planting in 1863, and the garden reached about 12,000 square metres at its largest. That size did not survive the 20th century: construction of Piazzale Roma in 1933 cut away the western third for a road and car park, and the Rio Novo canal took more, leaving roughly 7,500 square metres of the original design. What remains still holds mature plane trees, holm oaks, cypresses and horse chestnuts creating the shaded paths the garden was designed for, though no individual tree here has a separately documented age, so any figure would be an estimate rather than a verified fact. It is now most visitors' first and last stop, sitting between the train station and the bus terminal, a quiet transition before or after the crowds of the historic centre.

trees.name: The Hackberries of Villa Groggia
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Sant'Alvise vaporetto stop (lines 4.1, 4.2, 5.1, 5.2), short walk
trees.story: Two hackberries, the species Milan nicknames spaccasassi, the stone-splitter, for roots strong enough to crack paving, line the path toward a small theatre that has outlived every building that once stood around it. The land was part of the 16th century Palazzo Donà estate, then a working orchard and garden, before the palazzo itself was demolished in 1823 for building material. Giuseppe Groggia built the villa and its romantic-style park toward the end of the 19th century, complete with artificial hills and a Neo-Gothic teatrino from around 1913, and when the family later donated the property, the city took over its upkeep. The garden today is one of the few in Venice with genuinely free, unrestricted public access, a contrast to the palace gardens elsewhere on this list that open only on schedule or by appointment. The two Celtis australis trees along its main path have no individually documented planting date, so their exact age is unverified, but their scale suggests they belong to the villa's original 19th century planting rather than a later addition.

trees.name: The Garden of Ca' Zenobio degli Armeni
trees.age: undated, garden reworked in the 19th century
trees.access: Free when open; the garden hosts temporary exhibitions and events, check the current schedule before visiting
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Ca' Rezzonico vaporetto stop, via Campo Santa Margherita
trees.story: One of the last big private gardens in Venice survives attached to a palace that changed hands three times without ever losing its garden. Ca' Zenobio was completed in 1690 for the Zenobio family from Verona, passed later to the Albrizzi family, and eventually became a college for Armenian Mekhitarist monks under the name Moorat-Raphael. The garden reached its current romantic layout in the 19th century, when its formal Baroque geometry was reworked into winding paths, small artificial hills and bridges, planted with yews, laurels, cypresses, hackberries and a row of black locusts leading to a neoclassical loggia. No individual tree here carries a documented age or measurement, so any figure is an estimate rather than a verified fact, but the 19th-century redesign gives a reasonable upper bound. Access is not constant: the garden opens mainly during temporary exhibitions and events hosted at the palace, including Biennale collateral shows in some years, so a visit takes some planning rather than a simple walk-in.

trees.name: Forte Marghera's Century Trees
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Mestre railway station, or local bus
trees.story: This fortress spent most of its working life defending Venice from the mainland side, a threat the lagoon city had never needed to worry about until the railway bridge connected it to dry land in 1846. Built up from 1805 under a combination of Napoleonic and Austrian engineering, Forte Marghera anchored Venice's landward defences through the 1848-49 siege and into the 20th century, before eventually being decommissioned and left to the Comune. Its parade grounds and ramparts are now planted with large poplars, common limes, plane trees and hackberries that local sources describe simply as century-old, without giving any individual tree a specific planting date or measurement, so their exact age is unverified. What survives is less a single monumental specimen than the mainland's closest equivalent to the tree-lined avenues and gardens Venice's own islands mostly lack, run today by a foundation that has turned the fort into a venue for exhibitions and Biennale pavilions alongside its resident colony of cats.

trees.name: The Palm of San Servolo
trees.age: not individually dated; described as one of the island's 'very ancient trees'
trees.access: Free, public park; separate paid ticket for the Museo del Manicomio
trees.transport: Vaporetto line 20 from San Zaccaria, about 10 minutes
trees.story:
Step off the boat at San Servolo and a palm is the first thing to meet you. The Italian garden heritage association describes it in exactly those terms, a palm that welcomes visitors as soon as they disembark, and the national register's point for this tree sits by the landing. It stands 10.5 metres tall with a trunk 188 centimetres around, and it is counted among the oldest things growing on the island.

Its name contradicts itself, and the contradiction is in the official record. The register calls it palma delle Canarie, the Canary palm, the tree anyone would recognise from a seafront promenade. In the same entry it gives the scientific name Phoenix theophrasti, which is a different plant: the Cretan date palm, which survives in the wild in a few dozen ravines and beaches on Crete and the Turkish coast and nowhere near the Canaries. Either Venice has an unusual specimen on its hands or someone wrote a familiar Italian name beside the wrong Latin. We have left it as the state records it rather than quietly picking a side, and the tree itself will not settle the argument for you.

The island spent generations as Venice's asylum, and the museum of that history is still open on its own ticket. The park around it costs nothing. The olive of San Servolo stands 184 metres away, which puts two old trees within a short walk of the same jetty.

trees.name: The Cedar of Piazza Bra
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Adjacent to the Verona Arena, 5 min walk from Verona Porta Nuova station

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.story: This cedar has stood beside the Roman Arena for longer than most of the buildings currently ringing the square around it. Piazza Bra got its first deliberate garden in 1870, when the city decided the space needed shade and elegance to match its role as Verona's civic heart, and laid out three circular flowerbeds around a central fountain in 1873. The cedar planted then is one of the last survivors of that original scheme, now nearly 20 metres tall and weighing an estimated 16 tonnes. In June 2025 a gardener from the municipal green-space agency noticed the ground around its roots lifting unnaturally, a warning sign that the tree could be at risk of toppling in one of the city's busiest public spaces. What followed was a genuine local drama, tracked across Veronese news outlets for weeks: engineers drove three anchor points some four metres into the ground, tied together by twenty steel piles set in concrete, stabilising the root plate without removing the tree. The work finished just before the mid-August holiday, and the cedar, by every account since, is healthy and expected to stand for decades more.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Piazza Indipendenza
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza delle Erbe
trees.story: One tree fills most of the garden at the centre of Piazza Indipendenza, a trunk 505cm around supporting a canopy 35.5 metres tall, official measurements that make it, by height, one of the largest plane trees recorded anywhere in Verona. Municipal records place it as already a well-grown, mature specimen by 1941, which puts its actual planting date decades earlier still, though no precise year survives in the sources checked for this entry. The square itself sits inside Verona's ancient walled centre, redeveloped and reopened to the public in 2017 after a period of restoration, and the city's own environmental office chose this exact plane, alongside a neighbouring ginkgo, to launch a smartphone project cataloguing the stories behind Verona's individual trees, a small sign of how locally significant this specimen already is. Common planes like this one can live for centuries under the right conditions, and this one, still visibly healthy and now protected under Italy's national monumental-tree register, looks set to outlast the current square by as much as it has outlasted the last one.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Piazza Indipendenza
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza delle Erbe

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold

trees.story: Verona's official monumental-tree register lists this ginkgo as a group rather than a single trunk, an average circumference of 323cm and average height of 23.5 metres across the specimens growing together in Piazza Indipendenza, sharing the same small garden as the square's much taller plane tree. Ginkgo biloba is a genuine living relic, the last surviving member of a family of trees that covered much of the planet before flowering plants existed, all descended from populations that survived in a handful of sheltered valleys in southeast China while the species vanished everywhere else. This grouping's precise age is not documented, though its inclusion on Italy's national monumental register confirms it as long-established rather than a recent planting. The city chose this square specifically to launch a public tree-history project in 2018, scanning trees with QR codes to tell their stories, evidence that this ginkgo and its plane tree neighbour are treated locally as some of Verona's most significant living landmarks, official register or not.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Via Nino Bixio
trees.access: Free, public avenue
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Ponte Garibaldi
trees.story: This cedar rises over Viale Nino Bixio, a tree-lined avenue running through Borgo Trento from the city hospital toward Ponte Garibaldi, and it is one of only three trees standing anywhere within Verona city limits that Italy's national monumental-tree register has formally recognised. Its official measurements, a trunk 309cm around and a crown reaching 28 metres, earned it inclusion specifically for landscape value rather than for a documented age or historical association, the register's own more modest criterion compared to the age-and-dimension reasoning applied to its counterparts in Piazza Indipendenza. Cedrus deodara is native to the western Himalayas, where it grows at altitudes up to 3,000 metres in conditions nothing like Borgo Trento's flat, urban riverside setting, and its presence on a residential Verona boulevard reflects the same 19th and early 20th century fashion for grand, fast-growing conifers that filled institutional and civic gardens across Italy in the same period. No individual planting date is recorded, so its age here is presented as a broad, mature estimate rather than a precise figure.

trees.name: The Cypress Avenue of Giardino Giusti
trees.age: planting renewed since 2020, older survivors remain
trees.access: Paid entry, Giardino Giusti
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza delle Erbe
trees.story: A long avenue of cypresses climbs from the Renaissance palace at the garden's entrance toward a grotto and grotesque stone mask at the far end, the single axis around which Agostino Giusti built his entire garden after 1570, using forced perspective to make the walk feel longer and grander than the plot of land actually allows. For over two centuries the most famous tree in that avenue was a single cypress that had already stood for hundreds of years when Johann Wolfgang von Goethe visited in 1786 and admired it enough to record the moment in his own Italian Journey. That specific tree no longer exists: a violent storm on 23 August 2020 tore it from the ground entirely, ending a run of more than six hundred years and taking with it the garden's single most photographed feature. The garden has since replanted cypresses along the same historic line, younger and considerably shorter than what fell, alongside the surviving older specimens elsewhere in the row that the storm did not reach. Visiting today means walking the same axis Goethe walked, framed by the same design, honestly no longer beneath the exact tree that made it famous.

photo.attribution: Annika of Nine, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Yew and Laurel Wood of Giardino Giusti
trees.access: Paid entry, Giardino Giusti
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Piazza delle Erbe

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: Behind the Giardino Giusti's formal cypress avenue and geometric flowerbeds, the garden turns considerably wilder: a wooded section built from yew and laurel, an evergreen understorey planted to feel more like a natural grove than a designed landscape, leading down to a sixteenth-century grotto styled after the artificial caves fashionable in Renaissance Italian gardens. Taxus baccata is one of the most enduring tree species cultivated in European gardens, capable of living for many centuries and famously difficult to date precisely since its heartwood tends to hollow and rot away long before the tree itself dies, and this wood's older specimens fit that same pattern of a documented presence without a documented age. The grotto they surround was built to let visitors imagine themselves stepping into wilder, mythological terrain after walking through the garden's rigidly geometric front section, a contrast this yew and laurel planting still delivers exactly as designed more than four centuries later, regardless of what has happened to the garden's more famous cypress out front.

trees.name: The Cedar of Villa Bersani
trees.access: Visible from the public street corner only (private property)
trees.transport: 15 min walk from the historic centre, Borgo Venezia
trees.story: This cedar towers over the corner of Via Volta and Via Cipolla, tall enough to be a landmark for the whole intersection long before anyone notices the Liberty-style villa it actually belongs to. Villa Bersani sits within a stretch of Borgo Venezia that UNESCO recognition has helped protect, and the cedar in its grounds has become something closer to a piece of shared civic identity than a private garden feature, well enough loved locally that residents formally petitioned the city in May 2015 to add it to Italy's monumental-tree register for its history, landscape value and age. That request has not resulted in an official listing, unlike the three trees elsewhere in Verona that did make the national register, but the tree's local reputation and the intersection's own layout, which seems to have been planned around leaving it room to grow, tell their own story regardless of paperwork. It stands on private property, visible from the street corner it dominates rather than from inside grounds the public cannot enter, an honest limitation for a tree this recognisable.

trees.name: The Historic Collection of Parco delle Colombare
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Piazza delle Erbe, uphill into Valdonega

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen

trees.story: A large mulberry anchors what remains of a private estate's tree collection, one of the oldest specimens documented in Parco delle Colombare, a hillside park whose ownership shifted repeatedly before the city bought it in 1967 and opened it to the public. Named for Villa Colombari, built by a merchant who traded in the ochre earth pigments quarried on the property, the park's grounds were surveyed in 1946 and found to hold some 260 tall trees in its wooded section alone, alongside a working agricultural strip of grapevines, olives, cherries, pears and quinces that has since faded but left its own trace on the landscape. Alongside the mulberry, the collection that survives today runs to hornbeam, beech, tulip tree, ginkgo, an Australian sterculia, a California incense cedar and both Mediterranean and Kashmir cypress, an unusually wide-ranging planting for a single hillside estate. No individual specimen's exact age is documented beyond the general age of the collection itself, but the range of species alone marks this out as a genuine 19th and early 20th century private arboretum, now free and open to anyone willing to walk the hill above Verona's historic centre.

trees.name: The Cemetery Plane of Singerstraße
trees.access: Free, via the public Blutgasse-Fähnrichhof passage; the glass door is usually open during the day but can occasionally be locked
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Stephansplatz U-Bahn station (U1/U3), via the Blutgasse passage
trees.story: This tree has been quietly absorbing a piece of iron fence for two and a half centuries. The plane in the Fähnrichhof, a courtyard just off Singerstraße in Vienna's old town, grew directly through part of the railing that once enclosed St Stephen's Cathedral's own graveyard, closed to burials in the 1730s. The fence is no longer visible today. Vienna's own natural monument record notes it as sealed inside the trunk by decades of callus growth, the tree's version of scar tissue closing over a wound. A 1987 expert assessment measured the trunk at two and a half metres around, the crown at ten metres across, and put the tree's age at more than 250 years even then, which makes it well past 280 today. It stands in a courtyard once attached to the Domherrenhof, the residence of St Stephen's cathedral canons, reachable on foot through a passage from Blutgasse that locals call a Durchhaus, one of the old town's many semi-hidden pedestrian shortcuts between streets. The glass door at the Blutgasse end is usually left open during the day. Almost nobody outside the neighbourhood knows this tree exists, let alone that it is quietly digesting a piece of ecclesiastical ironwork nobody has seen in living memory.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Schubert Monument
trees.access: Free, public park (Stadtpark)
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Stadtpark U-Bahn station (U4)

best_time.label: November, when it turns the same uniform gold as Schönbrunn's ginkgo across town

trees.story: Vienna's other great ginkgo does not get the attention Schönbrunn's does, despite standing a five minute walk from the cathedral. City councilman Heinrich Braun had it brought to Stadtpark and planted around 1900, decades after the species had become a fashionable import for European parks, and it now grows beside the marble statue of Franz Schubert unveiled here in 1872, close enough that photographs of one usually catch the edge of the other. Vienna declared it a protected natural monument on 3 July 1973, Naturdenkmal Nr. 569, on the grounds that a ginkgo this size is still a genuine rarity this far from its native range in China. Its own small plaque, bolted to the trunk, calls it by the old German name for the species: Fächerblätterbaum, the fan-leaf tree. Stadtpark itself was Vienna's first purpose-built public park, opened in 1862 along the Wien river specifically so the city's middle class would have somewhere to walk that was not a royal garden. The ginkgo has spent well over a century doing exactly that: watching Viennese office workers, tourists and dog walkers cross the park on their way to somewhere else, then turning, every autumn, the same uniform gold as its more famous cousin across town.

trees.name: The Chestnut Avenue of the Hauptallee
trees.access: Free, public avenue, open at all times
trees.transport: Starts at Praterstern U-Bahn station (U1/U2), runs the length of the Prater to the Lusthaus

best_time.label: late April, when the avenue turns white with chestnut blossom

trees.story: Vienna's grandest avenue is older than the trees that define it by two centuries. The Hauptallee was cut through the Prater's floodplain forest in 1538, on the order of Emperor Ferdinand I, to connect the Augarten with the imperial hunting grounds, but the horse chestnuts that now line it in four to six dense rows came generations later. Vienna's own municipal tree registry documents the oldest surviving specimen, a 254cm-girth chestnut near Praterstern, as planted in 1840, a real, individually recorded tree rather than a rounded guess. Roughly 2,600 avenue trees run along the full 4.5 kilometre length, from Praterstern at one end to the Lusthaus, a former imperial hunting lodge, at the other, making this one of the longest tree-lined avenues in Europe. For a few weeks each spring the chestnuts turn the entire route white with candle-shaped blossom, an event Viennese joggers and cyclists plan routes around rather than merely notice. The avenue has hosted horse races, carriage parades, and, for decades, the finish straight of the Vienna City Marathon. Not every tree on the Hauptallee is old. Storms, disease, and simple traffic have taken their share over five centuries, and new chestnuts are replanted as older ones fail, which is exactly why this is a walk through a living tradition rather than a search for a single ancient trunk.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Schönbrunn
trees.access: Free, Schönbrunn park and gardens (separate attractions inside the grounds, such as the Gloriette or maze, charge admission)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Schönbrunn U-Bahn station (U4), inside the palace park's Botanical Garden

best_time.label: late October into November, when every leaf turns gold and falls within days

trees.story: This is one tree with two sexes. Ginkgos are either male or female, never both, except this one: a female branch was grafted onto it at some point in its life, so a single male tree now also drops the messy, strong-smelling seeds normally produced only by female ginkgos. It arrived in Vienna in 1781, imported through an English nursery only a few decades after the species reached Europe at all, and it is very likely the oldest ginkgo now growing in Austria. It stands in Schönbrunn's Botanical Garden, on the palace park's eastern side, its trunk grown to roughly five metres around and its crown to about twenty metres tall. Vienna listed it as a protected natural monument in 1939, one of the earliest ginkgos anywhere to receive that kind of formal status. It has outlived the empire that planted it and survived two world wars a few hundred metres from a palace that changed hands more than once, and each autumn it still does what ginkgos are famous for: every leaf on the tree turns gold and drops within days, all at once, rather than drifting down gradually like almost everything else in the park.

photo.attribution: Wolfgang H. Wögerer, Wien, Austria, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Mozart-Platane
trees.access: Free, public sidewalk
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Rennweg tram stop (Tram O)
trees.story: A memorial stone at its base calls this tree the Jacquin-Platane, but almost nobody in Vienna uses that name. Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin planted it around 1780 as director of the university's Botanical Garden, and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart walked past it often enough, on his way to piano lessons at Jacquin's house nearby, that the tree took his name instead. It has stood on Rennweg since before the French Revolution, and it has been protected as one of Vienna's first natural monuments since 1936, registered simply as Naturdenkmal Nr. 9. A property boundary shifted at some point in its life, and the tree now grows on the public sidewalk, just outside the fence of the Botanical Institute it once stood inside. Its trunk, roughly six metres around, has gone partially hollow with age, and Vienna's parks department now lists it as endangered. In 2009 the city closed Rennweg overnight and tested the tree's stability with rope winches, treating a quarter-millennium-old plane tree with the same seriousness as a structural inspection. It is around 245 years old now, close enough to Mozart's own lifetime that the story holds up better than most tree legends do.

trees.name: The Founding Plane of Rathauspark
trees.age: disputed: 1783 by tradition, 1876 in the city register
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 2 min walk from the Rathaus tram stop (Tram 1/2/71) or Rathausplatz/Burgtheater U-Bahn (U2)
trees.story: The oldest tree in front of Vienna's City Hall is older than the building itself by exactly one century. Two records disagree about this tree by ninety years. Tradition puts it in the ground in 1783, when the site was open land beyond the city. The city's own tree register says 1876, three years after the park was laid out, and gives that same year to every monument here, which is what a register writes down when a park is planted at once. Nobody has counted its rings. Construction of the neo-Gothic town hall did not start until 1872, and the park was landscaped around the new building only after that, which means this tree had already been growing for close to ninety years by the time the space around it became a park at all. It has since grown into a trunk six metres around and a crown thirty metres tall, big enough that Vienna's own tree registry lists it, under catalogue number 252, as Rathauspark's oldest specimen without qualification. It is one of three plane trees in the park with individual legal protection as natural monuments, granted in 1973. Office workers on lunch break, tourists cutting through on their way to the Burgtheater, and the occasional wedding photographer all pass beneath a canopy that was already mature when Mozart was writing his last symphonies, in a park that did not exist yet to contain it.

trees.name: The Sisi-Platane of Volksgarten
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Volkstheater U-Bahn station (U2/U3)
trees.story: Vienna named this plane tree after an empress who famously disliked Vienna. The Sisi-Platane stands near the fountain at the heart of the Volksgarten, close to the Theseus Temple, and at an estimated 200 years old it is the oldest tree in a garden that Empress Elisabeth, who gave the tree her nickname, mostly used as a shortcut on her way to somewhere else. She preferred riding and travelling to sitting still in Viennese gardens, but the name stuck anyway. The trunk now measures roughly three and a half metres around, and the crown spans a full twenty metres in every direction, wide enough to shade a large share of the garden's central lawn on a summer afternoon. Vienna placed it under legal protection in 1951 as Naturdenkmal Nr. 376, one of a small number of individually registered trees in the first district. Its exact age has not turned up in any planting record, only an estimate based on its size, so it should be read as approximate rather than precise. What nobody disputes is its rank: nothing else growing in the Volksgarten today is older, and few Viennese park benches offer a better patch of shade.

trees.name: The Oak of the Sulzwiese
trees.access: Free, open meadow in the Grüner Prater
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Stadion U-Bahn station (U2), across the Sulzwiese meadow

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Its crown alone covers more ground than most Viennese apartment buildings. The pedunculate oak of the Sulzwiese, a meadow in the Grüner Prater away from the funfair and the Ferris wheel, has a canopy that spreads roughly 45 metres across, wide enough that someone standing under one edge of it cannot see a person standing under the other through the branches. The trunk itself is a comparatively modest 4.28 metres around, which tells you this tree grew in the open, in full sun, with nothing crowding its sides, rather than competing for light in a forest the way most old oaks do. That kind of open-grown oak puts its energy into width rather than height, and the Sulzwiese oak is a textbook result: a low, spreading giant rather than a tall one. No planting record has surfaced to say exactly how old it is, so any figure here is an estimate rather than a fact, but a crown this size on an open-grown oak typically points to somewhere between 150 and 250 years, a wide range stated honestly rather than rounded to something tidier. Vienna registered it as Naturdenkmal Nr. 846, one of eighteen protected natural monuments in the Prater's home district of Leopoldstadt, and it remains one of the most photographed trees in the park precisely because its shape is so unusual.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoias of Pötzleinsdorfer Schlosspark
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Pötzleinsdorf tram terminus (Tram 41)
trees.story: Every giant sequoia growing in Europe today is, at most, about 170 years old, because the species was not seen by Europeans until 1852 and not exported until 1853. That upper limit makes the two giant sequoias flanking the main entrance to Pötzleinsdorfer Schlosspark impressive for what they are not: they cannot be nearly as old as the palace park around them, which the Geymüller banking family began landscaping in 1801, decades before anyone in Europe had seen a sequoia seed. They were planted later, sometime after 1853, as one of the many exotic imports that Vienna's wealthy families competed to add to their English-style gardens once the species became available, a horticultural fashion sometimes called Wellingtonia mania. Two smaller sequoias grow between the pair near the entrance, part of the same planting. The park itself, one of Vienna's largest and least manicured, is known for long open meadows dotted with individual specimen trees rather than dense woodland, and the sequoias are its most conspicuous residents: nothing else in the park comes close to their bulk or their soft, reddish, fibrous bark. No precise planting date or trunk measurement has surfaced for this specific pair, so their age here is bounded by what is known about the species rather than stated as documented fact.

trees.name: The Twin Giants of Sternwartepark
trees.access: Free, public park (Sternwartepark)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Nussdorfer Straße U-Bahn station (U6), or tram 40/41 toward Sternwarte

best_time.label: November, when the ginkgo half turns gold beside its evergreen sequoia neighbour

trees.story: Two trees, planted side by side, share a single protection order. In the Sternwartepark, in the shadow of Vienna's university observatory, a ginkgo and a giant sequoia grow close enough together that Vienna registered them as one natural monument in 2010, Naturdenkmal Nr. 817, rather than two. They make an odd pair. The ginkgo, a living fossil native to China, was already around a century old when it was surveyed, with a trunk 2.35 metres around and a height of 24 metres. Next to it stands a Californian giant sequoia that has grown taller, 27 metres, but leans noticeably as it climbs, its 3.75 metre trunk curving rather than running straight up the way most conifers do. Neither species is native within a continent of Vienna, and the two would never have met each other in the wild, yet here they have spent a century as neighbours a few streets from Türkenschanzpark, itself planted with exotic species through Vienna university's old botanical connections. The observatory nearby, the largest structurally closed telescope building in the world when it opened in 1879, gives the whole park its name. Astronomers looking skyward have had these two very different giants growing at ground level the entire time.

trees.name: The Lime of the Schönbornpark
trees.age: 187 years, planted 1839 by the city's tree register
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Rathaus U-Bahn station (U2), uphill along Josefstädter Straße

best_time.label: mid-June, when it flowers and the whole park smells of lime

trees.story: Vienna's tree registry lists nearly nine hundred trees in the eighth district and gives this one a girth of 489 centimetres, which makes it comfortably the thickest thing growing in Josefstadt. The lime stands beside the pond in Schönbornpark, the garden of the Palais Schönborn, and the city dates its planting to 1839. That is twenty-three years before the Schönborn family sold the grounds to the municipality and the private garden became a public park, so the tree spent its first two decades behind a wall, in a palace garden nobody was allowed into. The palace itself, built between 1706 and 1711 to a design by Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt, has housed the Volkskundemuseum since 1917, which means the lime now shades a lawn where people eat lunch between looking at Austrian farmhouse furniture. At 26 to 30 metres it is taller than the palace behind it. Large-leaved limes flower earlier than the small-leaved kind, usually the middle two weeks of June, and when this one goes off the whole park smells of it and the crown audibly hums. Bring something to sit on. The benches around the pond fill up fast on the first properly warm evening of the year, and locals know exactly which fortnight to come for.

trees.name: The Plane Outside the Grey House
trees.access: Free, public sidewalk, visible at all times
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Rathaus U-Bahn station (U2), north along Landesgerichtsstraße
trees.story: There used to be two of them. Vienna protected a pair of oriental planes on Landesgerichtsstraße in July 1956, recording trunk girths of 2.1 and 3.6 metres, and today both the monument register and the city's tree catalogue find exactly one oriental plane on the entire street. The survivor is the bigger one, now 445 centimetres around and 21 to 25 metres tall, and its two record-keepers disagree pleasantly about its birthday: the protection decree guessed it was planted around 1835, the tree catalogue writes 1815. Either way it beat the building it stands in front of. The Landesgericht für Strafsachen, the grey slab of a criminal court Viennese people simply call the Graues Haus, went up between 1831 and 1839 on ground that had been the citizens' shooting range and, before that, the St Stephanus cemetery. So the plane was already rooted while the site was still a rifle range on the edge of town, decades before the city walls came down and the Ringstrasse was drawn. It has since spent nearly two centuries a few metres from the door people are led through on the worst day of their lives. Nobody planted it as a memorial to anything. It simply outlasted every use the ground has been put to.

trees.name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the Rathauspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at all times
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Rathaus U-Bahn station (U2) or the Rathausplatz tram stop (Tram 1/71/D)

best_time.label: January, when the leaves are gone and the whole buttressed frame of it shows

trees.story: Four hundred and forty-nine trees are individually registered in the Rathauspark and this one has the thickest trunk of the lot, six metres around, beating the park's famous plane trees by a few centimetres. It is also the strangest looking. A fern-leaved beech is a cultivated freak of the common beech whose leaves come out shredded into narrow ribbons, so from a distance the canopy reads as feathery rather than solid, and up close you keep checking whether you are looking at a beech at all. Vienna gave it legal protection in July 1973, the same day it protected three of the park's planes. Its trunk is the reason to come. Rather than one clean column it goes up as a fused mass of grey limbs that split at head height and lean outward in every direction, with the roots buttressing out across bare earth where a century and a half of feet have worn the grass away. Generations of Viennese have carved initials into it, all healed over into pale scars. The park was laid out in 1873, which is also the year the city gives as this tree's planting, so it has stood in front of the town hall for as long as there has been a town hall to stand in front of.

trees.name: The Persian Ironwood of the Grete-Rehor-Park
trees.access: Free, public park, open at all times
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Volkstheater U-Bahn station (U2/U3), across Museumsplatz

best_time.label: late October, when the leaves turn scarlet, amber and green all at once

trees.story: This tree is twice as wide as it is tall. The Persian ironwood on Schmerlingplatz stands between 6 and 10 metres high and throws a crown 16 to 18 metres across, which is what the species does when nobody crowds it: instead of a trunk it grows a low fused knot of leaning stems that peel in grey, green and fawn plates like a plane tree's, then spreads sideways until it makes its own room. The city measures the base at 460 centimetres around, an exceptional figure for a species most European gardens never get past arm's width. Vienna protected it on 5 November 1956, and the stated reason was not its age or size but simply its rarity. Parrotia persica grows wild only in the Caspian forests of northern Iran and Azerbaijan, and in the 1950s a full-grown one in a Vienna square was worth a legal decree. What it does in late October is the reason to walk over. The leaves do not turn a single colour, they turn several at once and unevenly, so one branch goes scarlet while the next is still green and a third has already reached amber, and the whole low dome ends up looking backlit even under grey sky. The small park around it, a wedge of grass beside the Justizpalast, was named in 2016 after Grete Rehor, the first woman to hold a ministry in Austria.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of the Stadtpark
trees.access: Free, public park (Stadtpark), open at all times
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Stadtpark U-Bahn station (U4)

best_time.label: July and August, when half-metre chains of winged nutlets hang from every branch tip

trees.story: Come in July and this tree is hung with several hundred green ropes. The Caucasian wingnut fruits in chains up to half a metre long, each one a string of little winged nutlets that dangle straight down from the branch tips and stay there, greening, then browning, into autumn. No other tree in the Stadtpark does anything remotely like it, and most people who stop have no idea what they are looking at. Vienna put it under protection on 16 December 1941, in the middle of a war, as Naturdenkmal Nr. 280. The city's tree catalogue dates it to 1921 and gives its trunk as 308 centimetres around under a crown 16 to 18 metres wide. It also lists two more wingnuts of exactly the same age within five metres, which is not an accident of record keeping: this species suckers hard from the root plate, sending up new stems around the parent until one tree slowly becomes a thicket of itself. The old bark helps you find it. Wingnut bark is deeply corded and ridged, closer to a very old ash than to the walnut it is related to, and this one carries its enamel monument plaque half swallowed by ivy about chest height. It stands near the Wien river, two minutes from the ginkgo by the Schubert monument.

trees.name: The Pagoda Tree of the Stadtpark
trees.age: 166 years, planted 1860 by the city's tree register
trees.access: Free, public park (Stadtpark), open at all times
trees.transport: 6 min walk from Stadtpark U-Bahn station (U4), or 4 min from Stubentor (U3)

best_time.label: August, when it flowers cream at the one time of year almost nothing else does

trees.story: Vienna's tree catalogue dates this one to 1860, and the Stadtpark did not open until August 1862. Whichever way you read that, the pagoda tree was in the ground before the park was, either as one of the very first things planted while the Wien river bank was still a building site or as a tree the landscapers found there and kept. It has grown to 444 centimetres around and stands 21 to 25 metres, on a trunk that forks low and then leans away from itself in two directions at once, so it looks less like a park specimen than like something that had to negotiate for its light. Styphnolobium japonicum is the tree Chinese emperors were buried under and Beijing planted along its temple approaches, and it earns its place in a European park by flowering at the one time of year when almost nothing else does. Late July into August it covers itself in loose sprays of small cream pea-flowers, then drops them, and for a week the path underneath is pale with them. Vienna protected it on 16 December 1941 as Naturdenkmal Nr. 276, the same day it protected the wingnut a hundred and sixty metres away. Both are still here.

trees.name: The Judas Tree of the Altes AKH
trees.access: Free, public university campus (Campus der Universität Wien, the former Altes AKH general hospital), open during campus hours; the tree stands in the second courtyard (Hof 2)
trees.transport: 2 min walk from the Spitalgasse tram stop (Lines 5, 33)

best_time.label: April, when pink flowers break directly out of the bare trunk and branches

trees.story: This tree flowers straight out of its own trunk. In spring, before a single leaf opens, Cercis siliquastrum covers itself in rosy-pink flowers barely two centimetres across, and they push out not only from the twigs but from the branches and the old wood of the trunk itself. It is a habit called cauliflory, common in the tropics and close to unknown on a street in central Europe. Its age is a genuine argument. Vienna protected it on 14 February 1995 on the grounds that it was already well over a hundred years old, which puts a hard floor of roughly 130 years under it today. Local reporting adds that it was probably planted in the eighteenth century, along with the institute buildings around it, which would make it closer to 240.
