Nothing settles that, so the range stays wide. Even its monument number is disputed: most sources call it Nr. 762, while the city's own 2025 press release calls it Nr. 769. The courtyard was part of one of the most modern hospitals in the world when Joseph II opened the Allgemeines Krankenhaus in 1784, on ground that had held a poorhouse since 1693. The hospital moved out and the University of Vienna took the buildings in 1998, so the second courtyard now has cafe tables around it. The tree grows as ten old stems with young shoots between them, renewing itself indefinitely as long as nobody tidies it up.

trees.name: The Field Elm of Burggasse
trees.access: Free, public street tree on a traffic median, visible and reachable at all times
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Kirchengasse tram stop (Line 49, recently renamed from Siebensterngasse), or 8 min from Burggasse-Stadthalle U-Bahn station (U6)
trees.story: Europe lost most of its large elms in the second half of the twentieth century, which is reason enough to look at a field elm planted in 1915 and still standing. Ulmus minor was the species Dutch elm disease hit hardest: a fungus carried tree to tree by bark beetles that killed the great majority of Europe's mature elms from the 1960s onward. No record says this particular tree survived a particular outbreak. It simply kept going while the species around it did not. It grows on the narrow green strip down the middle of Burggasse, between the roadway and a service lane, which is an odd address for a protected natural monument and is precisely why it earned the status. Vienna's tree catalogue gives the planting year as 1915, a trunk 290 centimetres around, a height of 16 to 20 metres and a crown almost as wide as the tree is tall. The city protected it on 8 August 2006 as Naturdenkmal Nr. 794, and the decree's stated reason is plain: its size, and what it does for the character of the street. Two city departments record it at two different addresses, one calling it Burggasse 26 and the other Burggasse 39. Only one field elm appears in the whole Neubau district list, so this is one tree with two addresses. Its crown is cut back regularly for the power lines and the traffic, so expect a working street tree rather than a park specimen.

trees.name: The Turkish Hazels of Resselpark
trees.access: Free, public city park (Resselpark), open at all times
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Karlsplatz U-Bahn station (U1/U2/U4)
trees.story: Vienna protected these two trees for looking alike. Naturdenkmal Nr. 545, granted on 25 April 1972, covers a pair of Turkish hazels standing opposite the main entrance of the Technical University, and the reason recorded for the designation is their uniform growth and their appearance as a pair, not anything about either tree on its own. They are not twins. The city tree catalogue dates one to 1900 and the other to 1917, seventeen years apart, with trunks of 281 and 237 centimetres, and they stand about thirty metres from each other in the same sightline. That they grew into a matched pair regardless says something about the species. Corylus colurna is the tree-sized hazel of the Balkans, Anatolia and the Caucasus, and it builds a stubbornly regular cone on one straight trunk, which is why cities plant it along streets and why these two arrived at the same silhouette from different decades. It is also why they are the oldest trees in this small park and still look like street furniture rather than veterans. Resselpark is named for Josef Ressel, who patented a screw propeller in 1827 and watched other people make it work. It lies between the Karlsplatz and the Karlskirche, so the hazels look straight at Fischer von Erlach's dome and its two carved columns, and the Secession building is five minutes west. Both trees stand on open public ground at any hour.

trees.name: The Twin Planes of Am Platz
trees.access: Free, public square in front of Hietzing's parish church, open at all times
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Hietzing U-Bahn station (U4)
trees.story:
Two Oriental planes stand in front of the Hietzing parish church, and the district tells their story as a thank-offering for surviving the plague. By that account, published by the district office, Countess Scalquiogni, a lady-in-waiting at the Habsburg court, gave Hietzing three plane trees in 1732 in gratitude for coming through an epidemic. Two of the three are still here. In April 2020 the district called them 288 years old, which fits that date to the year.

Vienna's own tree cadastre disagrees, and not by a little. It records the same two trunks as planted in 1810 and 1860, which would make the younger of the pair a nineteenth century street tree rather than a Baroque gift. Both readings are on the record. The 1732 account is the more specific and comes with a name attached; the cadastre is the city's working inventory. Expect the truth to sit somewhere in that gap.

They measure about 4.2 metres around each and stand 13 metres apart, on a square that has been Hietzing's Sunday gathering place since the Middle Ages. Vienna protected the pair as a single natural monument, number 122, in March 1939.

In late February 2020 the storm named Yulia tore into both crowns. The district had them pruned back for safety and cabled, which is what the steel running through the canopy is holding together.

trees.name: The Oak of Schönbrunn's Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, Schönbrunn park and gardens (separate attractions inside the grounds, such as the Palm House or the Gloriette, charge admission; the Botanical Garden itself is free and open daily)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Hietzing U-Bahn station (U4), inside the palace park via the Hietzinger Tor

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
In September 1941 three trees in one corner of Schönbrunn's botanical garden were put under protection. A survey of Vienna's natural monuments printed in 1949 went back through the list and marked one of them destroyed by war events, a Japanese pagoda tree that stood about thirty metres from here. This oak is one of the two that came through. The yew twelve metres away is the other.

No source will give it an age. The register recorded none in 1941 and has recorded none since, so what there is to go on is the trunk: 6.21 metres around, measured a metre off the ground. A tree that thick has been growing for centuries, but girth alone will not say how many and nobody has counted, so any single figure you see for this oak is somebody's estimate.

The ground explains the tree. This was the Habsburgs' own botanical garden, begun in the 1750s and stocked from imperial collecting expeditions, and Schönbrunn is federal property rather than municipal, which is why Vienna's city tree inventory has no record of this oak at all. The pedunculate oak was there as the native, the plainest thing in a garden full of imports.

Come in through the Hietzinger Tor. The botanical garden is free and open daily; the Palm House and the Gloriette a short walk away are separate tickets and a different afternoon.

trees.name: The Yew of Schönbrunn's Botanical Garden
trees.access: Free, Schönbrunn park and gardens (separate attractions inside the grounds, such as the Palm House or the Gloriette, charge admission; the Botanical Garden itself is free and open daily)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Hietzing U-Bahn station (U4), inside the palace park via the Hietzinger Tor

best_time.label: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story:
Nobody has measured this tree. There is no girth on file, no height, no age and no photograph in the usual archives. What exists is a line in Vienna's register of natural monuments, number 181, protected on 4 September 1941, and a printed survey from 1949 that lists it again with nothing written beside it.

That blank is the point. The same 1949 survey marks the tree that stood about thirty metres away, a Japanese pagoda tree carrying number 179, as destroyed by war events. This yew and the oak twelve metres from it carry no such note, which is the nearest thing to a wartime health certificate a tree can hold.

Yews reward exactly this kind of neglect. Taxus baccata grows slowly, tolerates deep shade and hard cutting, and can carry on for centuries without ever getting spectacular enough to attract a tape measure, which is roughly how a protected tree spends eighty-five years on a government list without acquiring a single number.

So this one comes with an honest hole in it. It stands in the corner of Schönbrunn's botanical garden near the Hietzinger Tor, it has been there since before the bombing, and it looks the same in February as it does in July, which is what a yew is for. The garden itself is free and open daily. If you get a tape around it, tell us what it says.

trees.name: The Plane of Dr. Karl Lueger-Platz
trees.access: Free, on a public square
trees.transport: On the Ring, between Stubentor and Stadtpark; U3 Stubentor or U4 Stadtpark, both a short walk
trees.story:
Planted in 1928, and already four metres thirty-four around the trunk. That is what a London plane does with a century and enough root room, and it is why people looking at a tree like this guess two or three hundred years. Vienna's tree cadastre has the planting year written down, which ends the guessing before it starts.

The city protects it as a Naturdenkmal, a natural monument, which for a street tree means it is not going to be removed for roadworks or sightlines. It stands on the Ring between Stubentor and the Stadtpark, on a stretch that otherwise runs the better part of a kilometre without a protected tree, so it fills a real gap for anyone walking the Ring for its trees rather than its buildings.

The square carries the name of Karl Lueger, mayor of Vienna from 1897 to 1910, whose antisemitic politics have kept that name under public argument in the city for decades and keep it there now. The tree went into the ground eighteen years after he left office. It is the address you will be looking for.

Both records of this tree, the monument register and the cadastre, are Vienna's own. They agree with each other, which is not the same as two independent sources, and the trunk figure is a measurement rather than an estimate.

trees.name: The Oak of Grimmelshausengasse
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: Grimmelshausengasse, Landstraße; tram O or bus 74A, short walk; roughly midway between the Stadtpark and Rennweg

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
Vienna protects this oak as a natural monument and has published almost nothing else about it. No planting year, no trunk measurement, no entry in the city's tree cadastre, which lists Vienna's street and park trees by the hundred thousand. There is a register line saying the tree is protected, and there is the tree.

Better to say that plainly than to fill it in. A pedunculate oak in the third district is unusual on its own account: Vienna's streets were planted with planes, limes and maples, species that tolerate a pavement, while Quercus robur is a tree of heavy field soil and river meadow and rarely gets a city street to itself. This one stands on Grimmelshausengasse, a short residential road in Landstrasse, roughly midway between the Stadtpark and Rennweg, and somebody with the authority to do it decided it was worth protecting.

The street is named after Hans Jakob Christoffel von Grimmelshausen, who published Simplicissimus in 1668, drawing on his own childhood in the Thirty Years War, and produced one of the first great novels in German and still one of the bleakest. The oak is nowhere near that old. Nothing at all says how old it is, which is why the age here is empty rather than approximate. Go for the tree, not for the paperwork.

trees.name: The Second Plane of Rathauspark
trees.access: Free, in the public Rathauspark next to Vienna's city hall, open during daylight hours year-round.
trees.transport: U2 Rathaus, about 3 minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Vienna's tree register says this plane was planted in 1873. It gives that same year to every protected tree in the Rathauspark, and 1873 is when the park itself was laid out around the new town hall. That is what a register writes down when a whole park goes in at once, so the date says more about the city's paperwork than about this tree. Several of the park's trees arrived as mature stock, already grown on the day they were planted. The honest answer on age is a band rather than a year, somewhere between a century and 160 years, and nobody has counted the rings.

The trunk has been measured, and it comes to 5.97 metres around, within a few centimetres of the thickest in the park. Vienna gave it individual legal protection as a natural monument in 1973, one of three planes here to get it.

Even at the low end of that range it has stood through the annexation of 1938, the war, and the ten years of four-power occupation that followed, all of it playing out around the building it faces. The famous plane is at the front of the park with a legend and a disputed 1783 date attached to it. This one is at the north end doing the same work with none of the attention, a mottled grey column splitting into heavy limbs under a crown wide enough to shade that corner on its own.

trees.name: The Plane of Hügelgasse
trees.access: Free, a street tree standing in front of Hügelgasse 7, visible and reachable from the public footpath at any time.
trees.transport: U4 Unter St. Veit, about 6 minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Most of the protected trees in this corner of Vienna stand in private courtyards. This one stands on the pavement. Hietzing's list of natural monuments reads largely as addresses with "im Hof" after them, in the courtyard, behind a gate somebody else controls. The entry for this plane says "Hügelgasse, vor Nr. 7", in front of house number 7, which is the difference between a tree you can read about and a tree you can put your hand on.

It is not the biggest plane in Vienna and does not pretend to be. The trunk measures 2.2 metres around. What it has is a crown 16 metres across on an 18 metre frame, which on a narrow residential street means it covers the road, both pavements and the fronts of the houses on either side. In summer the whole block sits under it.

Vienna entered it on the register of natural monuments on 17 January 1955, four months before the State Treaty ended the four-power occupation of the country. It has held the same patch of pavement in Unter St. Veit, the villa quarter west of Schönbrunn, ever since.

Nobody has put an age on it. The register carries its height, its girth and the day it was protected, and nothing at all about when it went into the ground. If you know, tell us.

trees.name: The Plane of Alser Straße
trees.access: Free, a street tree on Alser Straße, visible and reachable from the public footpath at any time.
trees.transport: U6 Alser Straße, a short walk.
trees.story:
A protected plane on Alser Strasse has stood for about a century and a half without ever making it into the walk Vienna's other planes did. The city's tree register puts its planting at 1894 and its trunk at 3.15 metres around, modest next to the giants of the Rathauspark a few stops away but enough on its own to earn the tree individual legal protection.

Alsergrund is the district built around Vienna's old General Hospital, and this stretch of Alser Strasse runs past the hospital's former grounds, now the University of Vienna's main campus. Most of the city's protected trees cluster inside the Ringstrasse parks a kilometre south. This one stands alone on an ordinary street, marked out only by being larger than a street tree here is expected to get.

It grows on the public footpath, a short walk from the U6 station that shares the street's name. The register gives no reason beyond its own measurements: no legend, no named planter, just a plane that outgrew its neighbours and got a law written around it.

trees.name: The Third Plane of Rathauspark
trees.access: Free, public park, open at all times
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Rathaus U-Bahn station (U2) or the Rathausplatz tram stop (Tram 1/71/D)
trees.story:
Rathauspark's plane trees carry three separate protection orders, all granted the same day in 1973, and this is the last of the set to make it onto this page. The first two already here, one with a six-metre trunk and a rumoured planting year of 1783, the other just under six metres round, get the story so far. This one is smaller, 526 centimetres, but belongs to exactly the same legal designation and stands only 55 metres from the second, close enough that a single stop in the park now takes in all three.

Vienna's own tree register gives every protected tree in Rathauspark the same planting year, 1873, the year the park itself was laid out around the new town hall. That is a blanket date rather than a measurement, the kind a register writes when a whole park goes in at once, so read the resulting age, around a century and a half, as an estimate rather than a count of rings.

It stands a three-minute walk from the Rathaus U-Bahn stop, free and open at any time, on the same lawn as its two sibling planes and the park's fern-leaved beech, which between them make Rathauspark one of the densest single stops on this whole page.

trees.name: The Black Pine of Ebner-Eschenbach-Park
trees.age: not documented; protected as a natural monument since 1942
trees.access: Free, public city park (Ebner-Eschenbach-Park, 6,200 sqm, run by the city of Vienna, playgrounds and open lawns), open at all times
trees.transport: Tram 9 or 41/42 to Gersthofer Strasse / Sternwartestrasse area, then a short walk; roughly 10 min walk from Waehring-Geblergasse or Gersthof stations
trees.story:
Ebner-Eschenbach-Park takes its name from Marie von Ebner-Eschenbach, the Austrian writer whose village stories and epigrams made her one of the most important German-language writers of her era, and this Austrian pine has stood on the park's lawn for longer than the park has carried her name. Vienna protected the tree as a natural monument in 1942, citing its size and its role in the park's landscape, but nobody has published a girth, a height or a planting year for it since, an unusually thin record for a tree the city thought worth protecting outright.

Austrian pine, Pinus nigra, is native to the mountains ringing the Mediterranean and was planted across Vienna's parks through the nineteenth century for its tolerance of poor, dry soil, exactly the conditions of ground that had recently been fields rather than forest. This one has had eight decades of legal protection and, going by the timing of that 1942 order, considerably longer than that actually growing.

The park itself is small, about 6,200 square metres, bordered by Klostergasse and three other streets in the Cottage district of Wahring, open at all times with playgrounds and lawns around it. It sits roughly 850 metres from the ginkgo and giant sequoia already published at Sternwartepark, close enough to walk between the two on the same outing.

trees.name: The Sessile Oak of Belvedereallee
trees.access: Free, in the Prater (Vienna's largest public park), open at all times
trees.transport: Bus 77A to 'Freudenau' or 'Lusthaus', then a short walk; a longer alternative is the Hauptallee on foot from Praterstern (U1/U2), roughly 45 minutes
trees.story:
This sessile oak stands on Belvedereallee, a quieter stretch of the Prater than the chestnut-lined Hauptallee that gets all the postcards, in what is left of the floodplain forest that covered this ground before Emperor Ferdinand I ordered the first avenue cut through it in 1538. Vienna protected the tree as a natural monument in 2009, recording a trunk 4.5 metres round at chest height and a crown spreading close to 29 metres, big enough that Naturdenkmal Nr. 818 reads more like a description of a small wood than a single specimen.

Nobody has published an age for it, and this pass has not guessed one: sessile oaks growing wild in a remnant floodplain forest do not follow the growth-rate tables a planted park tree does, so a girth-based estimate here would be a guess dressed as a number rather than the honest gap it actually is.

It stands roughly 1.8 kilometres from the Hauptallee chestnuts, deep enough into the Prater that reaching it means committing to the park rather than passing through it: a 45-minute walk from Praterstern, or a shorter bus ride to the Freudenau or Lusthaus stops nearby. Free, open at all times, no ticket and no gate.

trees.name: El Titan, the Ficus of the Parterre
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Xativa / Estacio del Nord (metro/train)
trees.story: Gardeners planted this fig by accident in 1852, confusing the young sapling for one of the 47 magnolias also going into the newly laid-out Parterre garden that year, the same year Valencia's first railway line opened. The mistake became the city's most celebrated tree. Its trunk now measures nearly 13 metres around, its canopy reaches almost 23 metres high with a spread beyond 35 metres, and the shade it casts covers something close to 1,000 square metres of ground, the widest canopy of any tree in Valencia. It has outlasted a windstorm in 1926 and the catastrophic flood of 1957 that reshaped the whole city's relationship with the Turia river, and in 1915 it became a study subject for Madrid's School of Agricultural Engineers, evidence of how early its scale was recognised as remarkable. For decades it also hosted Sunday sardana dancing and other Valencian cultural gatherings in its shade. A nearby petrol station, whose underground tanks threatened its root system, was finally dismantled in 2020 after years of pressure to protect the tree, valued by the city at some 380,000 euros.

trees.name: The Olive Tree of La Rambleta
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Bus lines 8, 89 to Parque de la Rambleta

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story: This olive has stood through more than a dozen generations of Valencians without ever needing to move, unlike almost every other tree on this list, which the city has planted, transplanted or rescued from demolition at some point in its life. It grows in Parque de la Rambleta, a 14 hectare green space wedged between the San Marcelino neighbourhood and the General Cemetery in the south of the city, among a Mediterranean garden of date palms, Greek olives, cypresses, carob trees and a cedar of Lebanon. City sources place its age at roughly 400 years, without an individually documented planting record, which is typical for old olives generally: the species hollows and re-grows from its own base over centuries, making ring counts unreliable even where felling would be permitted. It is named directly, on the city's own monumental trees route, as the oldest single tree among all five of its mapped trails, a title that puts it ahead of trees standing in far more visited parts of the city.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Jardín de Monforte
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Alameda metro station

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold and drop within days

trees.story: This ginkgo has survived every conflict Valencia has been through since the mid-19th century simply by belonging to a species built to survive almost anything. Ginkgo biloba is often described as a living fossil, its lineage traceable back some 250 million years, largely unchanged, and famous for its ability to resist fire, disease and pollution better than almost any other large tree. This particular specimen grows in the Jardín de Monforte, a roughly 12,000 square metre neoclassical garden the Marquis of San Juan built from an orchard he bought in 1849, filling it with marble statues, fountains and specimen trees over the following decades. Declared a National Artistic Garden in 1941, it remains the last 19th century historical-artistic garden intact in Valencia, and this ginkgo, planted not long after the garden's founding, is described by the city as the best known of its kind in Valencia. A second, younger female ginkgo grows nearby in the same garden.

trees.name: The Ficus of the Countess of Ripalda
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station
trees.story: A garden fashion imported from the French Riviera is the reason this tree exists at all. In 1891, the widowed Countess of Ripalda hired Valencia's head gardener, Fernando Llopis, to lay out the grounds of her new palace, and Llopis suggested a Moreton Bay fig after seeing the species become fashionable among wealthy families on the Cote d'Azur, a garden idea Valencian gardeners of the period regularly borrowed from that stretch of coast given its similar climate. The palace itself did not survive the 20th century, demolished in 1968, and when the demolition crew asked how to remove the tree along with it, head gardener Vicente Peris told them that severe pruning alone would be enough to kill it. He was wrong in the way that mattered: rather than dying, the fig grew stronger, and it now stands alone at the entrance to Plaza Legion Espanola, the sole surviving trace of a palace and garden otherwise erased from the site entirely.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Avenida de Aragon
trees.access: Free, public traffic island / street planting
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Aragon metro station
trees.story: This oak is the last physical trace of an orchard that vanished under the city growing around it. It once stood on the medieval Camino del Cabanyal, irrigated by the historic Mestalla and Algiros channels that watered Valencia's huerta, the market-garden belt that surrounded the walled city for centuries. Urbanisation swallowed the area from 1902, when the arrival of the railway brought streets and buildings to what had been open orchard, and the tree found itself progressively boxed in: it stood within the grounds of the old Aragon Central railway station until that structure disappeared in 1974, then inside Public Works Ministry land until 1982, when the area around it was finally redeveloped into the landscaped avenue setting it keeps today. It now grows on a traffic island between Avenida de Aragon and Avenida Blasco Ibanez, next to the Mestalla stadium's parking area, a centuries-old survivor of a landscape that otherwise no longer exists anywhere nearby.

trees.name: Los Tres Amigos
trees.access: Free, public street planting
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station
trees.story: Three palms standing together at the entrance to a single street have become a landmark specific enough to have lent their nickname to nearby shops and a bar. Los Tres Amigos are believed to be the last visible trace of a private estate garden that once stood in this part of Valencia, before the neighbourhood around Plaza de Espana was fully urbanised in the early 20th century, leaving the three Phoenix canariensis specimens standing where a garden wall or gate might once have framed them. Palms of this species can live well over a century, and these are estimated at around a hundred years old, though no individual planting record survives to confirm an exact date. In January 2015 the local Abastos-Finca Roja neighbourhood association formally adopted the trio as a protected ensemble, a grassroots gesture of the kind more often given to a single monumental specimen than to a street corner planting. They remain, in the association's own words, a gateway to the street they mark.

trees.name: La Mas Delgada del Paseo
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Alameda metro station
trees.story: A gardener's mistake left this palm standing taller and thinner than every other one around it. When Jardines del Real, also known as Viveros, was planted with rows of Washingtonia filifera palms in the early 20th century, young Washingtonia robusta saplings, a related but distinct Mexican species that grows noticeably taller and more slender, were mixed in by error, the two species being difficult to tell apart while young. By the time gardeners realised the mix-up, this particular tree had already grown tall enough that removing it would have left an obvious gap, so it was left to keep growing rather than corrected. Decades later, it now rises well above its shorter filifera neighbours along the path dedicated to the Peris family of head gardeners, a slender, singular silhouette visible from some distance across the park, and locally nicknamed simply the thinnest one on the promenade. Jardines del Real itself began as royal grounds attached to a palace demolished in the early 19th century, later reopened as one of the city's main public parks, which is why its formal rows of palms still read as a planned avenue rather than an accidental grove, this one slender exception included.

trees.name: The Palm of Vicente Peris
trees.access: Free, public promenade
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Alameda metro station
trees.story: This palm survived being in the way twice, first of traffic and then of a demolition crew, thanks to one head gardener's refusal to let it simply be cut down. It originally grew in the courtyard of a Marist Brothers school at Plaza Mirasol, until the early 1960s, when that building and others nearby were demolished to widen what had been the narrow street of Les Granotes into today's Calle Poeta Querol. Rather than lose the tree, head gardener Vicente Peris asked mayor Adolfo Rincon de Arellano to close the surrounding streets to traffic for a single night, and the palm was loaded onto two trucks and moved under cover of darkness to a new home at the start of Avenida de Aragon, beside La Alameda, where it still stands today. The relocation is documented specifically enough, down to the mayor's name and the two-truck detail, that it reads as verified local history rather than embellished legend, a rare case on this list of a tree's survival being an entirely deliberate human choice rather than an accident of neglect.

trees.name: The Eucalyptus of Benimamet
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Adjacent to Les Carolines metro station (Line 4)
trees.story: At just over 41 metres tall, this eucalyptus is the tallest tree in the province of Valencia and the fourth tallest recorded anywhere in the wider region, a scale confirmed by the city's own maintenance crews, who need aerial platforms and, for its highest branches, help from the fire service just to prune it safely. It grows in the Parc Lineal in Benimamet, on the northwestern edge of the city, next to the tram line that was later routed underground past it, and is formally listed both by the Valencia city council and in the Comunitat Valenciana's own Catálogo de Árboles Monumentales y Singulares, the regional register that protects it by law. Eucalyptus camaldulensis, native to Australia, was planted widely across Mediterranean Spain from the early 20th century onward for its fast growth and tolerance of poor, dry soil, but few specimens anywhere in the region have been left to grow as large as this one. Its trunk runs some 6.1 metres around at the base, with a crown spreading 30 metres wide, dimensions that make it visible well beyond the park it stands in.

trees.name: The Kashmir Cypress of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Paid entry to the Jardí Botanic (small fee)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station
trees.story: This tree belongs to a species that survives today largely because it has been useful to Buddhist ceremony as much as to botany. Cupressus cashmeriana is the national tree of Bhutan, found wild only in the eastern Himalayas between roughly 1,500 and 2,800 metres of altitude, and it has long been deliberately preserved around Buddhist temples and monasteries even as habitat loss elsewhere pushed it onto international conservation watch lists. Western science only formally described it in 1848, when British botanist William Griffith encountered it in Kashmir and initially misnamed it, before John Forbes Royle corrected the naming to reflect the region where it was first documented. Valencia's specimen grows in the university's Jardí Botanic, one of the oldest botanical gardens in Spain, on Calle Quart near the city's old medieval walls, its foliage a distinctive bright blue-green among the garden's wider conifer collection. No individual age or planting date is documented for this specimen, so any figure given is a broad estimate rather than a verified record, but the species' own rarity, not its size or age, is what makes it worth including here.

trees.name: The Ficus of Plaza Centenar de la Ploma
trees.age: roughly 150 to 190 years, undocumented individual planting date
trees.access: Free, public plaza. The trunk area is fenced to protect the root plate, but the tree is fully visible and approachable from the plaza.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station, in the Barrio del Carmen
trees.story:
There are two giant figs here, their canopies touching so closely they read as one crown, and only one of them lets you walk up to it. The one in the plaza is this one, and it is not the modest half. It stands 27.8 metres tall with a canopy 28 metres across and a base circumference of 15.6 metres, where aerial roots have come down and fused into secondary trunks. Ficus macrophylla in its columnar form does this, building extra legs for itself until the line between trunk and root stops being obvious.

The measurements do not fully agree. Valencia's municipal tree observatory records 7.68 metres around at chest height; the regional monumental-tree register lists 13.7 metres, almost certainly taken lower on the same fused mass. Both figures are real and neither is wrong.

Its twin stands thirty metres away, inside the walled courtyard of the former Palacio de Raga, now a Generalitat residence for the elderly. Local memory holds that one to be the older of the pair, supposedly a gift from the botanist Cavanilles to Francisco Martinez de la Raga, which would put it well past two hundred years. No planting date is documented for either. Both belong to the wave of Australian figs Valencia planted from the 1850s, the same fashion that produced El Titan across town.

The plaza tree is fenced at the base to keep feet off the root plate. Everything above that is open to anyone crossing the square.

trees.name: The Ficus of the Corts Valencianes
trees.age: sources disagree: called both 'century-old' and dated to the second half of the 19th century
trees.access: RESTRICTED: this is the working seat of the Valencian regional parliament (Corts Valencianes), inside the Palau de Benicarlo / Palau dels Borja. The garden and ficus are visible only on a free guided tour, offered Mondays and Fridays mornings at 10:00/11:00/12:00/13:00, must be booked in advance by phone or the Corts Valencianes website, and NOT offered in August. This is not a walk-up, casual-visit tree.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station
trees.story:
One of the largest fig trees in Valencia grows in a garden you can enter twice a week, by appointment, and not at all in August. It stands in the courtyard of the Palau de Benicarlo, also known as the Palau dels Borja, which is the working seat of the Corts Valencianes, the Valencian regional parliament. The only way to stand under it is the free guided tour of the building, offered on Monday and Friday mornings and booked in advance through the parliament itself. The tour runs about an hour and spends most of it on the debating chamber rather than the garden, which is worth knowing before you go.

The tree is in the same weight class as the city's famous ones. The regional register measures its trunk at 13.6 metres around, within centimetres of El Titan in the Parterre. Its age is disputed. One account calls it simply a century old, 22 metres tall with a crown spreading more than 12 metres. Another dates its origins to the second half of the nineteenth century, which would make it something between 127 and 176. Both figures are in circulation and neither has a planting record behind it.

So this is the least casual visit on the list, and the only tree here that requires a phone call. It also spends its life inside a security perimeter, tended by a government that lists it as one of the region's monumental trees.

trees.name: The Ficus of the Alameditas de Serranos
trees.age: undated; garden itself dates to 1830 but no individual planting record for this tree survives
trees.access: Free, public riverside garden promenade beside the old Turia riverbed, at the foot of the Torres de Serranos gate
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Alameda metro station, or any bus serving the Torres de Serranos / Puente de Serranos stop
trees.story:
This promenade was a leather-tanning ground before it was a garden. In 1830 the Baron de Herves laid out the Alameditas de Serranos as two tree-lined walks flanking the Serranos gate, on ground previously used for curing hides, and the staircases either side of the gate followed in 1837. The fig that grows there now is the smallest of Valencia's registered monumental figs, and not by a little: 6.2 metres around, against the 9.3 to 13.8 metres of the giants in the Parterre, the Glorieta and the Palacio de Raga. It is still large enough that the city had to send crews in 2022 to cut it back where its branches had grown into the traffic.

Nobody knows when it went in. The garden dates from 1830, which is the only firm ceiling anyone has, and no individual record for this tree survives, which is why the age range given here is as wide as it is.

There is also a contradiction worth stating rather than smoothing over. At least one survey of the Alameditas says the promenade holds nothing of particular age or botanical interest beyond an Acacia farnesiana. The regional catalogue, meanwhile, lists this fig as a protected singular tree, a legal designation under the Valencian tree law of 2006 that requires meeting specific criteria. The register is the stronger evidence. The disagreement is real all the same.

It stands at the foot of the Torres de Serranos, the old city gate.

trees.name: The First Ficus of the Glorieta
trees.age: undated for this specific specimen; the Glorieta's ficus were planted across the 1850s-60s and sources say each has a different estimated age
trees.access: Free, public garden bordering the Palace of Justice
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Xativa / Estacio del Nord (metro/train), same stop as El Titan
trees.story:
In 1957 the Turia flood came close to putting this tree's crown under water. The Glorieta sits low beside the Palace of Justice, and the flood that permanently changed Valencia's relationship with its river ran deep enough here that the garden's giant figs were nearly submerged. All three of them came through it.

Three is the number that matters. The Glorieta holds three Ficus macrophylla, catalogued individually, and this is the first of the set, with a trunk 9.7 metres around. They are not triplets: sources on the group state plainly that each of the three carries a different estimated age, and none of them assigns a figure to this one. What is agreed is the era. The planting belongs to the 1850s and 1860s, when Valencia was filling its new public gardens with Australian figs, sometimes on purpose and sometimes not.

Fifty-five metres away, across the street in the Parterre, stands El Titan, which went into the ground in 1852 because a gardener took a fig sapling for one of the 47 magnolias he was supposed to be planting. The same error is recorded on this side of the road, in the same batch of work, by the same hands.

So do not treat this as a lesser copy of the more famous tree. It is the other half of a walk that takes about a minute: two separately named gardens, one origin story, and four enormous figs between them.

trees.name: The Caucasian Elm of the Botanic Garden
trees.access: Paid entry to the Jardi Botanic (small fee), the same garden as the Kashmir Cypress.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station

best_time.label: September to October: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story:
At roughly 33 metres, this is one of the tallest things growing in Valencia's botanic garden, and it belongs to a species most visitors have never heard of. Zelkova carpinifolia comes from the forests of the southern Caucasus and northern Iran. It is an elm relative that grows a short trunk and then breaks into a dense sheaf of near-vertical branches, so the crown reads more like a bundle held upright than a spreading canopy.

Its trunk measures 5.3 metres around at chest height. That is the figure in the regional register, and an independent field measurement taken in April 2014 put it at 5.27 metres, which is about as close as two separate people with tape measures ever get.

Its age is not recorded anywhere. The garden moved to this site, the old Huerto de Tramoieres outside the medieval wall, in 1802, which sets a ceiling and nothing more. Beyond the register entry and that one measurement, this tree has almost no paper trail: no newspaper feature, no garden monograph, no planting note. For a tree this size that is unusual, and it is better said out loud than filled in with a plausible number.

It shares the garden with the Kashmir Cypress, and one modest entrance fee covers both. In autumn the whole crown turns orange-brown, which is the species' best-known feature after its shape.

trees.name: The Palm of the Palacio de Pineda
trees.age: undated; palace itself built 1728-1731 but no record found of when the palm was planted
trees.access: Free entry to the courtyard, which now operates as a public cafe terrace (Palau Pineda Cafe i Menjars) inside the building that houses the UIMP (Universidad Internacional Menendez Pelayo) Valencia campus. Publicly walk-in accessible during cafe hours, not a ticketed monument visit.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Angel Guimera metro station
trees.story:
You can order a coffee under this one. The Palacio de Pineda was built between 1728 and 1731 for Francisco Salvador Pineda, and its walled rear courtyard, laid out as a private garden, now works as the terrace of a cafe inside a public university campus. A single Canary Island Date Palm stands at the centre of it, listed in the regional catalogue of monumental and singular trees, with tables arranged around its base.

How old it is, nobody knows. The palace has a construction date to the year and the palm has nothing at all. No planting record turned up in any source, and the catalogue entry confirms only that it is large enough and notable enough to be protected. Palms are difficult to age in any case: there are no growth rings to count, and the trunk reaches close to its final thickness early and then mostly just gets taller. Anything from eighty years to two and a half centuries is defensible here, which is a long way of saying the number is unknown.

The building has housed the Valencia seat of the UIMP, a Spanish public university, since the early 1990s, and that is the only reason the courtyard is open at all. For the two and a half centuries before that it was somebody's private garden, and this palm was standing in it while the door stayed shut.

trees.name: The Oldest Oak of Vilnius
trees.access: Free, inside Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), open daily
trees.transport: Short walk (10-15 min) from Cathedral Square / Vilnius Old Town centre

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
This oak lost roughly eighty percent of its root system and is still alive. The damage was done slowly and out of sight, by construction and transformer works beside it, and only became clear when Bernardinai Garden was overhauled in 2012. The rescue was blunt. Arborists took some twenty tonnes of weight out of the crown so the roots still working could carry what was left, then cleaned and treated the cavities in the trunk. Fourteen years later it is still the tree the city points people towards.

Its official entry does not bother with a name. It is listed simply as Seniausias ąžuolas, the oldest oak, protected as a municipal heritage object since 29 May 1996, with a trunk about five metres round. The sources put it at over four hundred years and none of them says how that figure was arrived at, so read it as the received number rather than a measurement.

It stands at the southern end of the garden, close to the footbridge over the Vilnia, which puts it a few minutes from Cathedral Square and a few steps from Užupis. Three more protected trees stand within a few hundred metres of it, so this is a stop on a walk rather than a destination on its own.

trees.name: The Daukantas Memorial Oak
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story:
The tree commemorates a walk. Simonas Daukantas, the 19th-century historian, came to Vilnius University on foot from Žemaitija, and the oak that carries his name in the courtyard named after him was grown from an acorn brought back from that same corner of the country.

It is not an old tree, and it is not here for that. Nobody has published a planting date. Lithuanian Wikipedia says it went in for the university's 400th anniversary, and since the university was founded in 1579 that points at 1979 and an age of about forty-seven. The year is arithmetic on the anniversary, not something any source states.

The planting did not go smoothly either. Two earlier saplings failed and were replaced, and some of those survivors are now said to stand next door in the Sirvydas Courtyard, which is why accounts of which oak is which do not entirely line up. The tree Vilnius protects under this name, listed as a heritage object since 29 May 1996, is the one at this pin.

Daukantas walked from Žemaitija to study here, which in the 1810s was a serious undertaking rather than a gesture. The tree is the university's way of keeping the walk in the ground. If you know which oak is which, or when this one actually went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Linden of Daukša Courtyard
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story:
Somebody has carved a chapel into this tree. It is a small niche cut into the trunk with a two-pitched roof above it, and inside stands a wooden figure of an old warrior holding a sword. No source names the carver. Lithuania has a long tradition of little roofed wooden shrines by roads and in yards, but putting one inside a living lime in a university courtyard is not the usual practice.

The tree holds the M. Daukša Courtyard of Vilnius University's central buildings together. History Faculty students meet under it, alumni come back to it at reunions, and the student corporation Korp! Tilia is said to have taken its name from it. Tilia is the linden's own genus, which makes the name either a good joke or a flat description.

Vilnius has protected it as a municipal heritage object since 29 May 1996. What nobody has written down is how old it is. There is no year in the register, none in the literature, and no published girth to reason back from. If you have measured it, or know when it went in, tell us and it goes on the page.

trees.name: The Ash of Mickiewicz's Courtyard
trees.access: Free, inside a Vilnius University courtyard open to the public during the day
trees.transport: Short walk (5-10 min) from Cathedral Square
trees.story:
Vilnius has protected this ash since 1996 and nobody has recorded a single measurement of it. No height, no girth, no age. The register gives the name and the coordinates and stops there, which is unusual for a tree a city considers worth protecting.

It stands in the Adomas Mickevičius Courtyard of the university's central buildings, named for the Romantic poet who studied here. The courtyard's name is not evidence about the tree: no source connects Mickiewicz to this particular ash, and it would be easy and wrong to imply he ever stood under it.

What is worth knowing is the species. European ash has had a hard thirty years across the continent as dieback thinned it out of woodland from Poland to Ireland, which makes a mature, protected ash in a city courtyard a better thing to stand under than it was a generation ago. This one has old university walls on four sides and a slot of sky above it, and it has grown up through the slot.

How much of the university's history it has actually stood through, nobody can say, because nobody has dated it. If anyone has put a tape around this trunk, we would like the number.

trees.name: The Nine-Trunked Willow of Sereikiškės
trees.access: Free, inside Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), open daily
trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from Cathedral Square, same park as the oldest oak
trees.story:
Nine trunks, one tree. The count sits in the tree's official name rather than in a description someone added later: it is registered as the devynkamienis gluosnis, the nine-trunked willow, and the encyclopedia entry for the garden calls it exactly the same thing.

Multi-stemmed trees are the running theme of Bernardinai Garden. Within a few hundred metres of this willow stand a four-trunked large-leaved lime and an ash whose own sources cannot agree whether it has three trunks or four. Whether that is old coppicing grown out, storm damage, or simply what a wet riverside park does to its trees, nobody has written down.

Nor has anyone dated this one, and no source commits to which willow it is. White willow and crack willow are both ordinary in Lithuanian parks and the register stops at the genus. Both of those gaps are the kind a person standing in front of the tree could close in a minute, so if you get close enough to look, tell us what you see.

It has been protected as a municipal heritage object since 1996, stands beside the main path through the garden about ten minutes from Cathedral Square, and shares a short walk with the oldest oak in the city.

trees.name: The Four-Trunked Linden of Bernardinai Garden
trees.access: Free, inside Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), open daily
trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from Cathedral Square, same park as the oldest oak
trees.story:
Four trunks leave the ground here as one tree, and Vilnius has protected the result since 1996 without ever writing down how old it is.

It is a large-leaved lime, didžialapė liepa, and the two sources that list it cannot even agree on the adjective: keturkamienė in the municipal register, keturliemenė in the garden's own inventory. Both mean four-stemmed. Neither carries an age, a height or a girth, which for a designated heritage object is a striking amount of blank paper.

Large-leaved lime flowers ahead of the small-leaved kind, in June, when the bees find it before you do. The rest of the year it is a shape: four heavy stems rising together, which is not how a lime looks in a textbook and is exactly how they often look in old gardens that have been cut back and left to recover more than once.

The garden around it has been rebuilt repeatedly, most recently in a full restoration finished in 2012, so the ground at its feet is a good deal newer than the tree standing in it. If you know when it was planted, or have a tape measure and five minutes, we would like the numbers.

trees.name: The Three-Trunked Ash of Bernardinai Garden
trees.access: Free, inside Bernardinai Garden (Sereikiškių Park), open daily
trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from Cathedral Square, same park as the oldest oak
trees.story:
Two official sources have counted this tree's trunks and come to different numbers. The municipal register, which supplies the coordinates on this page, calls it Trikamienis paprastasis uosis, the three-trunked common ash. The encyclopedia entry for Bernardinai Garden lists a four-trunked ash among the same 1996 protected inventory, plus a second, plainer Sereikiškės Park ash besides.

It gets muddier. The register itself carries another ash about thirty metres away with no trunk count at all, which might be that second entry or might be this same tree written down twice under another name.

This page goes with the register's count and the register's pin. If you count four when you get there, tell us, because a reader with working eyes settles it faster than any amount of desk research.

No age has ever been recorded for it, and neither source gives a height or a girth. What it does have is position. It stands in the lower part of Bernardinai Garden, a short walk from the pedestrian bridge over the Vilnia and about ten minutes from Cathedral Square, on the same loop as the nine-trunked willow, the four-trunked lime and the four-hundred-year-old oak at the southern end.

trees.name: The Sapiegos Park Linden
trees.access: Free, in the public Sapiegos Park (Sapiegos rumu parkas), open to visitors
trees.transport: Antakalnis district, about 2.2 km from the Old Town cluster; reachable by city bus

best_time.label: midwinter, when the leaves are off and the break and the bare trunks are fully in view

trees.story:
On 18 July 2023 a storm took the top off the oldest lime in Vilnius. The arborist who examined the wreck found the trunk completely rotten inside, and a crown that earlier bad pruning had left top-heavy, which in a gale works as a lever. The tree had stood 28 metres. Roughly 11 to 12 metres of it are left.

It survived. Enough of the lower trunk is sound that dormant buds were expected to break and rebuild something of a crown, and the arborist's own verdict was that it will not live another 300 years, but that our grandchildren might see new growth. Weeks after the break it was entered as a candidate in Lithuania's Tree of the Year competition, damage and all.

Two trunks, 4.40 metres round measured before the storm, and an age the register puts at 300 to 350 years. Vilnius has protected it as a botanical heritage object since 29 May 1996, listed as Seniausia liepa, the oldest lime. It stands in Sapiegos parkas in Antakalnis, by the gates of the palace.

This is a single stop rather than part of a walk, 2.2 km from the trees in the Old Town. The most recent detailed report on its condition is from 2023, so you may find it further gone or well on the way back. Tell us which.

trees.name: The Pine of Kalnai Park
trees.access: Free, in the public Kalnai Park (the Song Valley amphitheatre park), open at all times
trees.transport: About 1.3 km from the Old Town cluster (Bernardinai Garden); walkable, views over the Old Town
trees.story:
Vilnius protects this pine by name and has written down almost nothing else about it. The register carries Kalnų parko pušis, the pine of Kalnai Park, a designation and a coordinate, and then stops: no age, no girth, no height.

Scots pine is the commonest tree in Lithuania and grows on every sandy hill in the country, which is what makes one singled out for protection worth the climb. It stands on the southwestern slope of Dainų slėnis, the Song Valley, behind the spectator stands of the amphitheatre, on a wooded hillside in Kalnų parkas that gives back a view over the Old Town on the way up.

The pin is honest rather than exact. The register rounds its coordinates, and no survey position or photograph exists to sharpen them, so expect to walk the slope and look rather than arrive at a trunk. The park is small enough that this costs a few minutes.

Nobody has dated it. No core, no published girth, no planting record, and nothing to reason back from. If you know the age, or have put a tape around this trunk, tell us and it goes on the page.

Kalnų parkas is free and open at all hours, about 1.3 km from Bernardinų sodas, which makes this the tree that extends the Old Town walk rather than sitting inside it.

trees.name: The Amur Cork Trees and Crimean Linden of Bernardinai Garden
trees.species: Amur Cork Tree (Phellodendron amurense) and Crimean Linden (Tilia x euchlora)
trees.access: Free, in the public Bernardinai Garden, the same park as the city's other four shipped trees
trees.transport: Old Town, inside the existing 0.7 km Bernardinai Garden walk
trees.story:
You can press a thumb into the bark of an Amur cork tree. It is thick, spongy and cut with deep fissures, closer to a layer of insulation than to a skin, and it is the reason to come and put a hand on it. Two of them stand in Bernardinų sodas beside a Crimean linden, and Vilnius designated the three together in 1996 as one heritage object, a group rather than three trees.

Phellodendron amurense comes from the Amur river basin, Manchuria and Korea, where the winters are harder than anything Vilnius produces, which is why it is comfortable in a Baltic park. It carries clusters of small black fruit in autumn. The Crimean linden beside them, Tilia x euchlora, is a hybrid lime with glossy dark leaves that European cities have planted along streets for well over a century.

The group sits inside the same short loop as the rest of the garden's protected trees: the nine-trunked willow, the four-trunked lime, the multi-stemmed ash, and the oldest oak in the city at the southern end.

The documentation is thin, and worth saying plainly. No age, girth or height has ever been published for any of the three, and the only real record is the city's own designation, which is what the later listings repeat. The pin puts you in the right part of the garden rather than at a particular trunk, so use the bark: nothing else growing here feels like it.

trees.name: The Chestnut of the Gasthuishof
trees.age: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820
trees.access: Farmyard on the Ulingshofweg, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 6 km south of Venlo station, at Tegelen near the German border.

best_time.label: October, when the spiny husks split open on the ground

trees.story:
The farm is nearly four centuries old and the tree is only two, which is the correct order for once.

The Gasthuishof stands close to what was the border between the duchy of Gelre and the duchy of Gulik, two of the patchwork states that made up this part of Europe before anyone drew a Netherlands or a Germany. That line is now the boundary between Venlo and Kaldenkirchen. The original farm here was timber; it was replaced by a stone building in 1654, which is when the place stopped being provisional.

The chestnut went in around 1810 to 1820, on the yard.

Sweet chestnut is a Roman import to northern Europe, brought for the nuts, and it is a farmyard tree for practical reasons rather than decorative ones. It produces heavily, the nuts store, and a mature tree will feed a household through a winter. Old ones develop a spiral in the bark, the ridges twisting slowly round the trunk as it grows, which is the easiest way to spot one at distance.

October is the month. The spiny husks split on the ground and you can pick them out with your boot.

trees.name: The Chestnut of the Vrijbroekweg
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years by the register, and possibly more: a passer-by's account puts it before 1870
trees.access: Recorded as visitable in the national register; the tree stands at Vrijbroekweg 20.
trees.transport: About 3 km southwest of Venlo station, on the Vrijbroekweg.

best_time.label: October, when the nuts drop

trees.story:
The national register of monumental trees contains, for this tree, the testimony of an old man who walked past.

It is written down as exactly that: according to an elderly passer-by, the tree is older than 1870, and in that year it was damaged on one side by a fire, from which it recovered quickly enough. No document, no source, no name. Somebody stopped, told the surveyor a story, and the surveyor thought it worth recording rather than discarding.

That is the right call and it is worth defending, because oral memory is often the only evidence a tree has. A fire that scorched one flank in 1870 is the kind of thing a family repeats for a century and no archive ever notices. It also happens to be checkable in principle: fire damage on a chestnut leaves a permanent scar down one side where the cambium died, with the bark rolling in over the edges of the wound for decades afterwards.

So look at the trunk all the way round. If one side carries an old healed scar, an anonymous man was right and the register is better than its sources.

October for the nuts.

trees.name: The Sequoia of the Toernooiveld
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Grounds of Kasteel Arcen, recorded as visitable in the national register. The castle gardens charge admission, so check before setting out.
trees.transport: About 12 km north of Venlo, at Arcen on the Lingsforterweg.
trees.story:
Planted on a field named after jousting, which is a collision of two ideas about display separated by five centuries.

The Toernooiveld belongs to Kasteel Arcen, north of Venlo on the Maas. The sequoia went in between 1860 and 1870, which puts it within about fifteen years of the species arriving in Europe at all. Seed reached Britain in 1853 and the tree was an immediate sensation: enormous, foreign, from a part of California nobody had seen, and expensive. Owners of country places across Europe bought them the way they bought anything else that announced reach.

This is one of the earliest in the Netherlands, and it is now more than a century and a half into a lifespan that runs to three thousand years.

The bark is the reason to go rather than the height. It is thick, soft and fibrous, and you can push a fist into it. That is fire adaptation: in a Sierra Nevada forest the outer layer chars and insulates while the living tissue survives, which is how these trees outlast dozens of fires.

The castle gardens charge admission, so check before making the trip.

trees.name: The Catalpa of the Waterloo Monastery Park
trees.age: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.access: Free. Monastery park at Steyl, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 5 km south of Venlo station, in Steyl on the Waterloostraat.

best_time.label: early July, when it hangs with white bells

trees.story:
It stands directly beside a giant sequoia, and the pairing tells you what the monastery gardeners were doing.

Steyl is a village on the Maas that became a centre of Catholic missionary orders from 1875, and the communities that settled here laid out grounds on a scale a village would never otherwise see. What they planted was not native. It was a collection: species from the Americas and Asia, arranged so that a walk through the park was also an argument about the size of the world.

A catalpa and a sequoia side by side is that idea in two trees. One from the southeastern United States, one from the Sierra Nevada, planted within a decade or so of each other by people whose whole purpose was to send members abroad.

The catalpa is the more surprising of the two. It comes into leaf later than anything else, holds enormous heart-shaped leaves, then flowers in late June and early July in upright spikes of white bells marked yellow and purple in the throat. After that it hangs slender beans up to forty centimetres long, which stay on all winter.

Go in the first week of July.

trees.name: The Sequoia of the Waterloo Monastery Park
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Monastery park at Steyl, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 5 km south of Venlo station, in Steyl on the Waterloostraat.
trees.story:
The second of the three sequoias at Steyl, and the one standing in the monastery park itself.

By the time this one was planted, between 1900 and 1910, the species had been in Europe for half a century and the novelty had worn off, which makes the choice more interesting rather than less. Somebody here wanted another one specifically, next to the catalpa, in a park that a religious community was still actively building.

What a hundred and twenty years produces is a tree that has finished being a curiosity and started being infrastructure. A sequoia at this age is a fixed vertical in the landscape, visible from outside the grounds, and the sort of thing local people give directions by.

It is also, in the strictest sense, only just beginning. Giant sequoias run past three thousand years and the largest ones alive were already old when Rome was founded. This tree is at about four percent of that.

The cones are worth looking for on the ground. They are surprisingly small for the tree, about the size of a hen's egg, and they can stay closed and viable on the branch for twenty years, waiting for fire.

trees.name: The Sequoia of the Sequoiahof
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Street tree on a residential street, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 4 km south of Venlo station, on the Sequoiahof at Steyl.
trees.story:
The street is named after the tree. That is rare enough to be the whole reason to come.

Streets get named after landowners, saints, battles, queens and, in the twentieth century, after whatever the developer's theme was. Getting a street named after a species because a specimen of it is standing there requires the tree to have been the most notable thing on the site at the moment somebody had to fill in a form, and it means the tree was there first.

So the Sequoiahof at Steyl is a piece of evidence. Whoever laid out this housing worked around a giant sequoia planted between 1900 and 1910 by the religious communities that shaped this village, decided it was the defining feature, and wrote that down permanently.

That also makes it the least protected of the three sequoias here. The other two are in institutional grounds. This one is in front of a house, on a residential street, with everything that implies about roots under paving and branches near gutters.

Stand back on the far pavement to see the shape. Then go and push the bark, which is the same soft fibrous stuff as on the others and never stops being surprising.

trees.name: The Red Oak of the Hagerhof
trees.age: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. Public children's farm, open in daylight.
trees.transport: About 2 km southwest of Venlo station, at the Hagerhof on the Hagerlei.

best_time.label: late October, when it goes scarlet

trees.story:
It is behind the animal paddock at a children's farm, which is the least dignified address of any tree on this page and probably the best one.

The Hagerhof was an estate before it was a kinderboerderij, and this oak is from that earlier life, planted somewhere between 1900 and 1910. Red oak was the standard choice for a country place at that date: American, fast, and reliably the reddest thing in the grounds for two weeks in late October, which native oaks never manage.

The leaves are the easy way to tell it apart. Big, with pointed lobes ending in tiny bristles, nothing like the small soft rounded lobes of a Dutch oak. The acorns are squat and broad in a shallow saucer, and they take two years to ripen rather than one.

What makes this worth including is the traffic. Most of the trees on this site are visited by adults who came deliberately. This one has small children running past it all day, none of whom are there for the tree, some of whom will remember it anyway.

Late October, when it turns.

trees.name: Dab Mieszko I (King Mieszko I's Oak)
trees.access: Free, public street/forest edge, open at any time
trees.transport: Bus or metro to Ursynow, then a short walk, roughly 30-40 minutes from the centre

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Warsaw's oldest tree survived six centuries of Polish history only to be set on fire by a person, not a storm, in June 2019. The oak, named for Poland's first recorded ruler though it began growing roughly two and a half centuries after his death around 992, stands at the edge of Natolin Forest on the city's southern edge, one of the last fragments of the wild Mazovian woodland that once covered this ground before Warsaw existed at all. Most of its crown has died back over the decades; steel cables and supports now hold the one thick surviving branch upright, and a cavity in the trunk has been filled with brick and cement, an old-fashioned repair meant to keep vandals and rot out rather than to look convincing. The arson attack in 2019 might have finished a lesser tree; this one produced leaves again the following spring. Its exact age has shifted across different surveys and plaques over the decades, estimates ranging from roughly 600 to 640 years depending on which measurement is cited, and an older on-site plaque is now known to have understated it. Whatever the precise figure, it remains the region's oldest documented oak and the clearest living link this city has to the forest it was built on top of.

trees.name: The Poplar of the Defenders
trees.access: Free, public street, open at any time
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Ochota, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from the centre
trees.story: A mass grave was reportedly dug beneath this tree in August 1944, according to testimony from survivors of the transit camp that once stood around it. The poplar was already mature by then, planted in the mid-1920s in what was still open ground on Warsaw's western edge, and stood inside the barricaded defense line that Polish forces held here during the September 1939 siege of the city, growing up alongside genuine combat rather than merely outliving it at a distance. Five years later the same patch of ground became Zieleniak, a market square the Germans converted into a transit camp for tens of thousands of Ochota residents rounded up during the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, a place survivors would later describe as a site of mass killing before deportation. Remains were exhumed from beneath the poplar after the war ended. None of that history shows on the tree itself today: at roughly 25 metres tall with a 453-centimetre trunk, it was named Warsaw's Tree of the Year in 2025 and reached the national final the following year, recognised now for its size and condition rather than for what the ground beneath it once held. The Barykada Wrzesnia monument stands beside it, the closest thing the site has to an explanation.

trees.name: Dr Korczak's Oak
trees.access: Free, public street corner, open at any time
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Wola, then a short walk, roughly 15 minutes from the centre
trees.story: Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage from this corner for 29 years, until German soldiers marched him and roughly 200 children from the building to a train bound for Treblinka in August 1942, where all were murdered. He was offered a chance to walk away alone, by then already a well-known pediatrician and radio personality; he refused, choosing to stay with the children rather than abandon them, and that refusal is most of why his name is still known today far beyond Poland. The orphanage building itself, designed in 1911 for the Jewish charity Pomoc dla Sierot and completed the following year, is the only structure on this stretch of what was then Krochmalna Street to survive the district's wartime destruction; everything burned around it, then everything else standing was cleared after the war, leaving Korczak's building alone on ground later renamed Jaktorowska Street in 1970. The Hungarian oak growing at its corner, protected as one of Warsaw's natural monuments and formally named for Korczak, stands roughly 22 metres tall with a trunk 440 centimetres around. No record fixes exactly when it was planted, so it may or may not have already stood here while the orphanage still operated, but it has grown up beside the one building in the neighbourhood old enough to remember.

trees.name: Ciechomski's Pear
trees.age: disputed, possibly younger than the 1870 legend claims
trees.access: Free, public street corner, open at any time
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Stary Mokotow, then a short walk, roughly 15-20 minutes from the centre
trees.story: A pear tree is a strange choice for a memorial, which is exactly why this one has stayed interesting long after the man it supposedly honours. Walenty Ciechomski was the last soltys, the village administrator, of Mokotow before the settlement was absorbed into Warsaw, and a veteran of the failed 1863 uprising against Russian rule; his gravestone at Sluzew cemetery still identifies him by that title alone. Local tradition holds that the pear was planted in 1870 to mark his settling on this corner, and the story has been repeated long enough to earn the tree informal protected status under his name. Historians examining the claim more recently have pushed back on most of it: a pear is an unusual and impractical species to plant as a personal memorial, the tree's apparent age does not obviously match an 1870 planting, and the likelier explanation is that it simply seeded itself on the corner sometime later, with Ciechomski's name attached to it afterward rather than at the root. Nobody disputes that Ciechomski himself was real, or that he fought in an uprising that cost Poland dearly and gained it nothing immediate. What is genuinely uncertain is whether this particular tree has anything to do with him at all, and this entry says so rather than repeating the tidier version of the story.

trees.name: The Royal Oaks of Lazienki
trees.access: Free, the park gardens are open daily to the public at no charge (only some buildings/museum interiors are ticketed)
trees.transport: Bus or tram to Lazienki Krolewskie, short walk within the park to the New Orangery area

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: For almost two centuries, two pedunculate oaks have grown side by side in the Romantic Garden of Lazienki Krolewskie, the park Poland's last king built for himself in the 18th century. The palace museum's own page on the park's oldest trees states it plainly: both oaks measure 450 centimetres round and 28 metres tall, and both hold protected natural-monument status. That girth on a pedunculate oak points to real age, roughly two hundred years, old enough that the pair were already substantial trees when Poland was partitioned off the map of Europe entirely, decades before the country existed again to protect them. Lazienki is the most visited royal park in the country, its lake, palace and open-air theatre drawing crowds who mostly walk past two more oaks without a glance. These stand near the New Orangery, on the western side of the path called Chinska Droga, close enough together that a visitor can take in both in one stop. The garden itself is free every day, no ticket needed beyond the museum buildings and the odd ticketed pavilion, making this the easiest stop on the whole Warsaw list to fold into an ordinary afternoon in the park.

trees.name: King Jan's Linden
trees.access: Paid entry to the Wilanow palace park grounds
trees.transport: Bus to Wilanow, short walk into the palace park grounds

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: Local and museum tradition names this lime for King Jan III Sobieski, who built Wilanow Palace in the late 17th century and is documented, in general accounts of the gardens, as having planted lindens on the grounds himself. No source ties this specific tree to that planting, so its age stays undocumented here rather than borrowed from a king's biography, but the name has stuck regardless, one linden singled out among the palace's roughly two dozen protected monument trees. Wilanow's own inventory of its monument trees records 27 of 28 as living in good condition, with only a single dead specimen elsewhere in the gardens, its crown already removed, nothing like the healthy tree this one is described as. It grows on the south side of the main avenue leading up to the palace, close enough to the approach that anyone walking in sees it before they see the building. Wilanow is Warsaw's grandest surviving baroque residence, spared the destruction that levelled most of the city in 1944, and its gardens charge an entry fee, a rare exception among the free public parks the rest of this page favours.

trees.name: Niemcewicz's Walnut
trees.access: Free. The palace's terraced garden, where the tree stands, has been open to the public daily April-October, 8am-6pm, since 2025
trees.transport: Metro or bus to Ursynow (SGGW campus, Nowoursynowska 166), short walk to the Krasinski Palace
trees.story: A black walnut, a species more at home on the eastern seaboard of North America, grows by a Polish palace named for a man who spent time in exile there. Julian Ursyn Niemcewicz, writer, playwright and a companion of Tadeusz Kosciuszko through Poland's failed 18th century uprisings, owned this estate from 1822 and built a library on it; the poet Juliusz Slowacki visited in 1830 and admired what he found. Polish Wikipedia's own article on the palace, citing Warsaw city hall's register of natural monuments, confirms the walnut by name as a protected specimen, and a 2023 photograph on Wikimedia Commons shows it still standing that year. No source dates its planting to Niemcewicz's own tenure, so this page states the naming rather than inventing a birth year to match it. The building passed through several owners after him and has belonged to Warsaw's agricultural university since 1956, its grounds closed to outsiders for decades until the terraced garden behind the palace reopened to the public in 2025, free, after nine years of local campaigning. The tree that outlasted every one of those owners is now something almost nobody who planted it could have counted on: visible again.

trees.name: The Szustra Oaks
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily to the public at no charge
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Dolna/Pulawska, short walk into the park

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Five pedunculate oaks stand together near Palac Szustra, the neoclassical villa at the heart of Park Morskie Oko, registered as one natural monument in 1978. Princess Izabela Lubomirska commissioned the palace and its grounds in the 1770s, designed by the architects Szymon Boguslaw Zug and Efraim Szreger; the estate passed to Anna Potocka in 1820, and in 1845 the banker Franciszek Szuster bought it and opened the lower part of the grounds to the public as a promenade, which is where the district gets its name. The palace burned during the 1944 Warsaw Uprising and was rebuilt after the war. Warsaw's own environmental department lists a pedunculate oak next to the palace among the park's protected natural monuments, though the register gives no age or measurements for any of the five, only their 1978 designation date.
