Park Morskie Oko, also called Park Promenada-Morskie Oko, is one of Mokotow's most visited green spaces, its ponds and paths busy on any warm weekend, and the oaks stand a short walk from the palace steps, easy to overlook next to a building with so much of its own history on display. Nobody has measured them yet: if you know how old they are, this is the page to tell us on.

trees.name: The SGGW Oak
trees.access: Free, stands on a public avenue with open pavement access
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Aleja Niepodleglosci / Rakowiecka, Mokotow

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: An oak stands on Aleja Niepodleglosci, on the edge of what was once the main campus of SGGW, the Warsaw University of Life Sciences. The school received this land in 1923, carved from the old Pola Mokotowskie exercise fields, and spent the interwar years raising pavilions, a library and student housing on the site. In 1956 Warsaw swapped that land for territory further south in Ursynow, and SGGW has been based there ever since; nothing agricultural remains in Mokotow except this avenue and its name. The oak was declared a protected natural monument in 1974, by which point the university it once fronted had already left the neighbourhood behind. No source beyond the city's own register of protected trees has produced an age or a girth for it, so both stay open questions, exactly the kind a passer-by with a tape measure could close in a minute. Aleja Niepodleglosci is a wide public avenue, walked and cycled every day, with no gate anywhere near the tree and nothing to buy a ticket for. It is easy to find and, once you know which side of the street to look on, impossible to miss.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Botanical Garden
trees.access: Paid entry to the Botanical Garden. Open March to October; in winter only the greenhouses open, so the outdoor grounds where this tree stands are seasonal.
trees.transport: Tram or bus to Plac Na Rozdrozu, right by the garden gate on Aleje Ujazdowskie; also walkable from Metro Politechnika (M1 line)
trees.story:
The Warsaw University Botanical Garden protects twenty three trees as natural monuments under one legal designation from 1974, and this ginkgo is one of them, planted in 1824 in a garden that had already existed for six years by then. Ginkgo biloba had barely reached European gardens a generation earlier, brought from China as a curiosity that turned out to outlive nearly everything planted around it, and this tree has now stood through two centuries of a garden that itself survived the war that flattened most of the city around it.

It shares its 1974 designation with two common beeches elsewhere in the garden, and one of those beeches was blown down by wind in 2020, according to a news report at the time. That loss does not touch this ginkgo, a separate tree under the same paperwork, but it is a reminder that a shared designation protects individuals, not a group's survival as a whole.

No girth or height has been recorded for it in what is available so far, unusual for a tree this documented. It stands a few hundred metres from the Royal Oaks of Lazienki, close enough to fold into the same walk through central Warsaw's parks. The garden charges admission and closes its outdoor grounds over winter, opening again each March.

trees.name: The Grant Memorial Bur Oak
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stands on open U.S. Capitol Grounds parkland (Union Square), no restriction, viewable and approachable year-round.
trees.transport: On the National Mall side of the Capitol grounds; roughly 10-15 min walk from Capitol South or Union Station Metro (both serve multiple lines).
trees.story: In the 1930s Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. cleared about 250 trees out of Union Square and transplanted 41 more. This bur oak he left exactly where it was. It has grown on this spot since at least 1850, when the United States Botanic Garden moved its greenhouse collections onto this ground, which makes it one of the very few trees on the Capitol campus that predates the twentieth century redesign of everything around it. The Architect of the Capitol puts it at 150 to 175 years. The National Park Service witness tree survey is more careful and says the true age is simply unknown, noting only that aerial photographs taken at the Grant Memorial's dedication in April 1922 already show a large, well developed tree. Read 175 years as a floor rather than a figure. What it has outlived: the demolition of the old Botanic Garden buildings in 1930, Olmsted's redesign of the square, and the 1971 installation of the Capitol Reflecting Pool, which took out most of the trees that were still standing. When surveyed in November 2006 it measured 125 feet tall, with an 85 foot crown and a trunk 165 inches around, the largest bur oak recorded in Washington. Bur oaks can approach a thousand years and are not considered mature until 200 or 300. By the standards of its own species, this giant is still young.

trees.name: The First Cherry Trees of the Tidal Basin
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stand on open NPS parkland along the Tidal Basin path, walkable any time.
trees.transport: About a 15-20 min walk from Smithsonian Metro (Blue/Orange/Silver) via the Mall, or shorter from a Tidal Basin paddleboat-dock parking area; no direct Metro stop.

best_time.label: early April, when the whole basin comes into bloom for about a week

trees.story: Two trees started everything the Tidal Basin is now known for. On 27 March 1912 First Lady Helen Herron Taft and Viscountess Chinda, wife of the Japanese ambassador, each planted a Yoshino cherry on the north bank, the first two of a gift of more than 3,000 from Tokyo. Around a hundred of that original planting are thought to survive. These two are the ones you can actually pick out, marked by a bronze plaque at their base. They are old for what they are. Yoshino cherries in cultivation usually manage 50 to 100 years, and these are past 114, which is why the Park Service treats their survival as a story rather than a footnote. They were rooted here before the Lincoln Memorial was finished, before the Jefferson Memorial went up across the water, and before the festival that now walks well over a million people past them every spring. One honest note on the pin. The coordinates come from the surveyed position of the commemorative marker rather than from the trunks, and the marker itself has since been replaced by another one nearby, so expect to hunt for the plaque along a short stretch of path roughly 125 feet south of Independence Avenue. The trees are within a stone's throw of it.

trees.name: The Battery Kemble Chestnut Oak
trees.age: over 165 years, likely pre-dating the Civil War
trees.access: Free, fully public NPS park (part of the Civil War Defenses of Washington / Rock Creek Park system), open trails and lawn, no restriction on viewing.
trees.transport: No direct Metro; roughly 20-25 min from Foggy Bottom or Tenleytown Metro by bus/car. A neighbourhood park in the Palisades, not a downtown walk-up.
trees.story: The largest tree in Washington may owe its size to having been cut down. In 1861 the Union Army built Battery Kemble on this hill to defend the capital from the west, and the standard practice at the city's earthworks was to clear the ground for a field of fire, felling trees about five feet above the soil. Chestnut oak, unusually among oaks, resprouts readily from a cut stump. This tree's low, wide, multi stemmed form is exactly what that produces, which is why every account says it was around before the Civil War instead of giving it a planting date. The measurements do the rest of the talking. Casey Trees' volunteer big tree survey crowned it the city's largest known tree in 2023, at 24 feet 3 inches around, and American Forests lists it as a national co-champion, meaning no bigger chestnut oak has been recorded anywhere in the United States. Take the 165 years as a floor: the root system under those stems could be considerably older than the trunks standing on it. It grows in a quiet neighbourhood park in the Palisades rather than downtown, and no source publishes coordinates for the tree itself. The pin is the park, so the last stretch is done on foot and by eye. At that circumference, you will know it when you reach it.

trees.name: The National Mall Jefferson Elm
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stands in the open lawn of the National Mall, one of the most visited public spaces in the US, no restriction.
trees.transport: On the National Mall; about 10 min walk from Smithsonian Metro station (Blue/Orange/Silver).
trees.story: Every 'Jefferson' elm planted in the United States is a cutting taken from this tree. It went into the ground around 1935, one of roughly 600 American elms set in four rows to frame the Mall's central green, and by rights it should have died with the rest. Dutch elm disease reached the Mall in 1950 and had killed more than 200 of that planting by 1994. In the early 1990s the Park Service pathologist Horace Wester noticed that tree number 3-487 leafed out earlier than its neighbours and held its leaves longer. A decade of testing by the Park Service, the National Arboretum and Michigan State confirmed genuine resistance to the disease. DNA work then found something stranger: the tree is triploid, carrying 42 chromosomes where an American elm carries 56, which appears to explain both the resistance and the strong U shaped branch unions that keep it from splitting in storms. In February 2005 cuttings went out to commercial nurseries as the 'Jefferson' cultivar, named for the drive it stands beside. It is neither the oldest nor the biggest tree in this city, and it may be the most consequential, because American elms are going back into streets across the country on the strength of its genetics. The survey that recorded it placed it across Jefferson Drive from the Freer Gallery without giving a coordinate, so this pin is close rather than exact.

trees.name: The Washington Monument Witness Mulberry
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stands on open NPS parkland on the Washington Monument grounds, directly on a paved circular path, unrestricted viewing.
trees.transport: About 10-12 min walk from Smithsonian Metro station (Blue/Orange/Silver).

best_time.label: May to June: pale sweet fruit, the leaves that fed the silk trade

trees.story: This tree fell over in May 2019 and the Park Service refused to remove it. Days of rain had saturated the ground on the Washington Monument lawn, the main buttress root snapped, and the larger of two old white mulberries here went down. Instead of cutting it up, arborists raised the trunk back by about ten degrees, enough to encourage new feeder roots without tearing what was left of the root plate, and built it a steel crutch. It has been standing nearly horizontal on that prop ever since, living on roughly 60 percent of its roots. Its neighbour, the shorter of the pair, leans hard and is crutched too, and is in better condition. Both are recorded by the Park Service witness tree programme as part of the landscape planted after the monument was completed in 1885, probably in the 1890s, which puts them somewhere around 130 to 140 years old. Be clear about what this is. It is not a grand tree and it is not a pretty one. It is a public agency visibly refusing to give up on something that history happened around, propped in plain sight at roughly seven o'clock on the circular path. And it is fragile: the most recent confirmation of its condition we have found dates from December 2023, so that is the last time anyone we can cite looked at it.

trees.name: The Botanic Garden Elm
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stands on open U.S. Capitol Grounds parkland (Union Square), unrestricted viewing, about 350m from the Grant Memorial Bur Oak in the same square.
trees.transport: Same as the Grant Memorial Bur Oak: roughly 10-15 min walk from Capitol South or Union Station Metro.

best_time.label: September to October: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.story: When Union Square was rebuilt in the 1930s, five Caucasian elms survived the clearance. Four were dug up and transplanted. This one was left exactly where it grew, which is why it matters more than the other four. It has stood on this spot since around 1850, when the United States Botanic Garden moved its greenhouse collections here, some of them gathered on the Wilkes Expedition of 1838 to 1842. Zelkova carpinifolia comes from the mountains of the Caucasus and northern Iran and is still an uncommon tree in American planting. This one is almost certainly among the largest in the country, though it will never appear in the national register of champion trees, which tracks native species only. The Park Service survey calls it the most historically significant tree remaining in Union Square, because it is the one that combines all three things: planted in the Botanic Garden's own period, never moved, and genuinely rare. Its position saved it twice. Sitting at the far southwest edge, well outside the central vista Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. was carving, it escaped the 1930s clearance that took 250 trees, then escaped again in 1971 when the Capitol Reflecting Pool went in and destroyed most of what remained. The Architect of the Capitol puts it at 150 to 175 years. The Grant Memorial bur oak, from the same original planting, stands about 350 metres away across the same square.

trees.name: The Arboretum Willow Oak
trees.age: rumoured to date to the Civil War era, confirmed fully grown by the 1940s
trees.access: Free. U.S. National Arboretum, open to the public daily (check usna.usda.gov for current hours), no admission fee.
trees.transport: No Metro station on site. Roughly 16 min by WMATA bus from downtown (checked by an earlier pass: Massachusetts Ave NE + 1st St NE to 21st Pl NE + Maryland Ave NE) or DC Streetcar from Union Station plus a short walk/bus leg.
trees.story:
The second largest tree in Washington is dying, and the people who measured it said so out loud. When Casey Trees brought its 2023 big tree survey to the National Arboretum, this willow oak came in at 287 inches around, beaten by a matter of inches only by the chestnut oak at Battery Kemble. Standing under it, the Arboretum's own arborist put the other half of the story just as plainly: this tree is near the end of its life. The 2012 derecho tore into it, carpenter worms were treated in 2015, and it has been decaying and taking storm damage ever since. Staff are not removing it. They trim the rotting limbs to keep visitors safe and go on buying it time, which is a decision about what an old tree is worth rather than a horticultural one.

Its age is folklore. Casey Trees repeats a local story tracing it to the Civil War, but the earliest hard evidence anyone cites is a 1940s photograph showing it already grown and visibly smaller than it is now. Ninety years is the floor, 160 the hopeful ceiling.

Two honest notes before you go. Nobody publishes where inside the grounds it stands, so the pin is the Arboretum and the last stretch is a question for staff. And the most recent confirmation of its condition we can cite is August 2023, before the storms of the summers since. If you find it changed, or gone, tell us.

trees.name: The Survey Lodge Catalpas
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stand in the open on NPS parkland right by the Survey Lodge Ranger Station building (itself closed to the public, used as an NPS office), on the walking paths southwest of the Washington Monument.
trees.transport: About 10-12 min walk from Smithsonian Metro station (Blue/Orange/Silver), same approach as the nearby Washington Monument Witness Mulberry, roughly 250m away.

best_time.label: late May into June, when the catalpas open white orchid-shaped flowers by the thousand

trees.story:
The small stone building these catalpas flank was made out of the Washington Monument's leftovers. Survey Lodge went up in 1889 from marble and granite spare from the monument itself, and housed the boiler that drove the first elevator to the top. The trees came about thirteen years later, part of an oval carriage road lined with fir, pine, crape myrtle and catalpa that was in place by 1902. They stand where a visitor walks straight into them, between the lodge's front door and the road, which is why the Park Service lists them among the trees on this ground worth protecting rather than treating them as ordinary shade.

The date is not perfectly settled, and the two accounts of it do not pretend otherwise. The National Park Trust says flatly that they were planted in 1902. The Park Service is more careful and says only that they could date from the turn of the century planting. Either reading puts them here through the 1930s, when the monument beside them shut for its first major restoration and the ground was dug over around their roots.

Nobody has settled the species either. Northern and southern catalpa both grow in Washington and neither source says which these are, so you can work on it yourself in June: the northern carries fewer, larger flowers, the southern more of them and smaller. Both hang the same long seed pods afterwards.

The lodge is a ranger office and closed. The trees are not.

trees.name: The Willow Oak Circle
trees.age: at least 45 years, possibly around a century
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stands in the open on NPS parkland (Constitution Gardens / West Potomac Park) just south of the Vietnam Women's Memorial, no restriction.
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro (Blue/Orange/Silver) or a similar walk from the Lincoln Memorial end of the Mall.
trees.story:
Nobody can say whether these trees are a century old or fifty, and both answers come from the same two sources. Cross the grass south of the Vietnam Women's Memorial to the next path and you end up standing inside a tight ring of willow oaks without having meant to. That is the whole experience of the place, and both the Park Service and the National Park Trust describe visitors arriving in it by accident.

The two theories run like this. One says the circle was planted in the 1920s to ring a picnic clearing, which would make the trees about a hundred. The other says they went in during the 1970s rebuilding of Constitution Gardens, done for the Bicentennial in 1976, which would make them about fifty. Neither source picks a side, and neither will we, so the age here is a range wide enough to hold two entirely different stories.

What the circle has watched is not in doubt. It was already standing when the Vietnam Veterans Memorial was dedicated just south of it in 1982, and when the Women's Memorial was added in 1993. Willow oaks are the workhorse of the National Mall, planted here by the thousand along avenues and lawns. These are the ones somebody arranged into a shape on purpose.

Neither source counts them, incidentally. Go and count them.

trees.name: The Cork Trees of the FDR Memorial
trees.age: at least 80 years as of the original 2006 HALS survey, so roughly 100 years now
trees.neighbourhood: Tidal Basin / West Potomac Park (FDR Memorial)
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stand in the open on NPS parkland within the FDR Memorial (no admission fee, open 24 hours, staffed during the day), directly on the waterfront path.
trees.transport: About 10-15 min walk from Smithsonian Metro station (Blue/Orange/Silver) along the Tidal Basin path, close to the two 1912 cherry trees.
trees.story:
In 1962 the National Park Service went looking for a record of who planted these trees and found that nobody had written it down. The letter noting the gap survives. Rather than treat an unrecorded planting as an accident to be tidied away, the Service kept them on the grounds that they were, in its own words, very attractive old trees. That is the entire provenance of a small stand of Amur cork trees growing on ground where almost everything else has a paper trail.

They were here long before the memorial they now sit inside. The Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial was dedicated in 1997 and its landscape was laid out around plantings left from an older scenic drive along the Tidal Basin. A sign beside the trees calls them eighty years old, which would put the planting somewhere around the 1930s, but the sign's own date is not known, so read eighty as a minimum and roughly a century as the working figure.

You will recognise them by their manners rather than their height. Amur cork trees throw heavy, low, sprawling limbs, and these have let theirs down onto the ground, which is why the Park Service has put up two signs asking people not to climb them. The bark is thick and deeply corky, which is where the species gets its name.

Walk past the visitor centre restrooms and follow the waterfront path between Room Three and the water.

trees.name: The Montrose Park Tulip Poplar
trees.age: not documented; among DC's largest tulip poplars
trees.access: Free, public NPS-adjacent city park, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Georgetown; no Metro station in the neighbourhood, roughly 20-25 min walk from Dupont Circle or Rosslyn Metro, or DC Circulator bus to Wisconsin Ave/M St then a 15 min walk uphill

best_time.label: October, when a hundred feet of crown turns clear yellow over Lovers Lane

trees.story:
Two websites call this the second largest tree in Washington. Casey Trees, whose volunteers did the measuring, ranks it fifth. Their survey put it at 235 inches around and roughly 110 feet tall with a crown spreading about a hundred feet, behind two willow oaks and the chestnut oak out at Battery Kemble that holds a national co-championship. What both readings agree on is narrower and still worth the hill: no bigger tulip poplar has turned up in the District's surveys.

Nobody has dated it. The Historic American Landscape Survey recorded it under its witness tree program, which is a heritage listing rather than a birth certificate, and neither that record nor Casey Trees puts a year on the tree. Tulip poplars rarely pass 250 years and a trunk this thick is not the work of a few decades, but any age you see attached to this tree, here or anywhere, is arithmetic from its girth rather than a measurement.

It grows on the slope in the northwest corner of Montrose Park, where Lovers Lane starts dropping toward Dumbarton Oaks Park, so the beech grove walk begins more or less at its feet. No tree level coordinate is published anywhere, so the pin is the corner of the park and the last stretch is done by eye. At 235 inches around, that is not a hard search.

trees.name: Frederick Douglass's Magnolias at Cedar Hill
trees.access: Free grounds access; the house tour that passes closest to the trees needs a free timed ticket (recreation.gov, small booking fee) or first-come at the visitor centre
trees.transport: Anacostia; roughly 15-20 min walk from Anacostia Metro (Green line), or a short ride on the B2 bus to the site

best_time.label: May and June, when the cream flowers open outside the study window

trees.story:
Frederick Douglass planted these two magnolias for his wife, or so his household always said. The window the tradition gives runs from 1877, when he bought Cedar Hill and moved his family up onto the Anacostia ridge, to 1882, when Anna Murray Douglass died. There is no receipt, no diary entry and no nursery record. The story comes down through the family and the site rather than on paper, which is how most of what is known about any house's garden survives. Casey Trees, on the grounds in February 2026, found both trees still standing outside the window of his study.

That study is the reason to come. Douglass worked here for the last eighteen years of his life, through his term as US Marshal for the District and his appointment as minister to Haiti, and the view out of it was these two trees. Southern magnolias hold their leaves all year, so they were green outside that window in every season he wrote at it.

The Cultural Landscape Foundation records two magnolias east of the residence dating to the late nineteenth century, which puts the pair itself beyond dispute even where the planting story rests on memory.

The grounds are free to walk. The house tour that brings you closest runs on timed tickets, booked in advance or picked up at the visitor centre.

trees.name: The Olmsted Tuliptree, Capitol Grounds
trees.access: Free, always-open public federal grounds (Capitol Square)
trees.transport: Capitol Hill; roughly 8-10 min walk from Union Station or Capitol South Metro

best_time.label: September to October: clear yellow, one of the most reliable autumn trees

trees.story:
Frederick Law Olmsted planted more than 1,050 trees on the Capitol grounds and about 45 of them are still alive. This is the largest of the three tulip trees among the survivors. His General Plan for the grounds dates from 1874 and the planting ran on into the 1890s, so the tree is somewhere between about 130 and 150 years old, dated by the works rather than by the wood.

It stands in Capitol Square along Northeast Drive, across from the Russell Senate Office Building, which is worth noticing because the building is the younger of the two. Russell opened in 1909, decades after the tree went into ground Olmsted had already landscaped. He was not decorating: his argument was that the Capitol looked smaller than it deserved on its bare hill, and the terraces and plantings were his answer to that, an architectural case made in trees.

A tuliptree of this age is an unlikely thing to find on ground worked over as often as this. Terraces, a subway, an underground visitor centre, security lines and a century and a half of ceremonies have gone in around it, and it is among the few living things on the 274 acre campus that predate almost all of them.

No tree level coordinate is published. The Architect of the Capitol names the drive and the building it faces, which is enough to find it on foot in a few minutes.

trees.name: The Dumbarton Oaks Beech Grove
trees.age: not documented; predates the park's 1920s-30s design
trees.access: Free, always-open NPS-administered public park (Dumbarton Oaks Park, distinct from the adjacent paid-entry Dumbarton Oaks Garden/museum, same estate's former grounds)
trees.transport: Georgetown; roughly 20-25 min walk from Dupont Circle or Rosslyn Metro; enter via the Lovers' Lane gate off R Street, a few minutes downhill from the Montrose Park Tulip Poplar

best_time.label: late October into November, when two acres of beech turn copper at once

trees.story:
Beatrix Farrand did not plant these beeches. When she laid out the park below Dumbarton Oaks around 1930, the American beech grove at the Lovers' Lane gate was already standing and already old enough to be worth keeping, so she designed around it and made it the way in. Two acres of smooth grey trunks is what you walk through before the park proper starts.

Nobody has dated them. American beech is slow, and a grove substantial enough for a landscape architect to build an entrance around in 1930 had to have been there well before her, but there is no ring count and no planting record, so anything more precise than that would be invented.

The grove carries a survey number, HALS DC-13, filed at the Library of Congress under the same witness tree program that recorded the tulip poplar up the hill in Montrose Park. It has also had a hard century. When the Dumbarton Oaks Park Conservancy started work in 2012, this grove was the first thing it took on, clearing invasive growth and rebuilding the way water moves down the slope, and that work is still running.

One thing to sort out before you go: this park is free, open and run by the Park Service. The formal gardens next door, on the same estate's old ground, charge admission and are a different visit entirely.

trees.name: The Jan Dzierzon Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Szczytniki, on the riverside path between the Zwierzyniecki and Szczytnicki bridges
trees.access: Free, on the public riverside boulevard/embankment along the Oder canal, open at all times
trees.transport: Tram stops serving Most Zwierzyniecki, about 10 minutes' walk along the river path

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: In 1865 the mayor of Breslau bought a piece of riverbank so that this oak would not be cut down. Artur Hobrecht made the purchase on the city's behalf and the tree carried his name for the next eighty years, the Hobrecht-Eiche, until Breslau became Wroclaw in 1945 and the new Polish city renamed it for Jan Dzierzon, the Silesian priest and beekeeper who worked out that drones hatch from unfertilised eggs. It has been a protected natural monument since 16 February 1953, decision 5/53, one of three on this page designated on the same day. A dedicated survey of the monument trees of Wielka Wyspa puts it at 652 centimetres round and 22 metres tall, which is within half a centimetre of the girth recorded for Dziadek, a kilometre away. Poland's national register has no column for either figure, so the measurements come from that survey rather than from the state. The same survey is blunt about its condition: the interior is substantially decayed, the trunk is hollow and the structure is poor. The tree is alive and comes into leaf, standing on the open boulevard along the Oder canal between the Zwierzyniecki and Szczytnicki bridges, where anyone can walk up to it at any hour.

trees.name: The Dziadek Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Dabie, on the edge of Park Szczytnicki
trees.access: Free; the tree stands on the public street/pavement in front of the training centre building, not inside its grounds
trees.transport: Tram/bus stops on ul. Kopernika, a few minutes' walk from Park Szczytnicki

best_time.label: midwinter, when the leaves are gone and you can see how much of this trunk is still holding on

trees.story: Wroclaw's oldest tree is called Grandpa and it is held together with steel. Dziadek is reported at somewhere between 440 and 460 years old, which puts its start in the era when this was Habsburg Breslau, and its trunk now carries damage serious enough that the branches are reinforced with elastic bindings and clamps. The measurements tell the same story from another angle: 652.5 centimetres round in 2019, up from 629 in 2015, against a height of only 17 metres, the shortest and thickest of the four oaks on this page. A trunk that wide under a crown that low is what a very old tree looks like once it has begun losing its upper limbs. It has been a protected monument since 16 February 1953, decision 2/53. What it has stood through includes the Prussian takeover of Silesia, two centuries of German Breslau and the eighty-day siege of 1945 that left most of the city in ruins and changed both its country and its language. It stands on the public pavement of ul. Kopernika, in front of a training centre but not inside its grounds, on the edge of Park Szczytnicki. Poland's register records the protection and nothing about the tree's size; those numbers come from a survey of the island's monument trees.

trees.name: The Piotr Wlast Oak
trees.neighbourhood: Dabie, near Park Szczytnicki and the Wroclaw Zoo
trees.access: Free, standing on public ground
trees.transport: Bus/tram stops near the Wroclaw Zoo entrance on ul. Wroblewskiego, a few minutes' walk

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: This is the one in the group that is not falling apart. Its three companions on Wielka Wyspa are variously hollow, lightning-struck and clamped together; this oak was recorded in good health at the last survey, with a large, well-formed crown and no bracing, standing 25 metres tall on 510 centimetres of girth. It has been a protected natural monument since 16 February 1953, decision 3/53, the same morning's work as two of the others. The name is a dedication rather than a date. Piotr Wlostowic, Piotr Wlast, was a twelfth-century Silesian magnate and founder of monasteries whose reputation is tied to this region, and nobody is claiming the tree goes back to him: no independent age estimate for this oak has been found at all, and Poland's national register carries no age field to consult. So it ships here with its girth, its height and its designation date, and without a number for its years. It stands on public ground on ul. Wroblewskiego, a few minutes from the entrance to Wroclaw's zoo, which opened in 1865 and is the oldest in Poland. Free, open, and the healthiest tree of this walk.

trees.name: The Jan Stanko Oak
trees.access: Free, inside the public Park Szczytnicki, open at all times
trees.transport: Tram stops around Hala Stulecia (Centennial Hall) / Park Szczytnicki, a short walk

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.story: Lightning found this oak and it is still in leaf. The strike left it in poor structural condition, which is the surveyors' phrase and not a euphemism, and it went on growing: 554 centimetres round and 26 metres tall, the tallest of the four oaks on this page. It stands inside Park Szczytnicki near the narrowing of the park pond, a few minutes from the Hala Stulecia, Max Berg's concrete dome of 1913 that went on the UNESCO list in 2006 and drew the world's architects to this corner of the city. Unlike the other three, this tree was not protected in the 1953 batch. Its designation came on 2 April 1976, decision 26/76, twenty-three years later. It carries the name of Jan Stanko, the fifteenth-century physician and naturalist who compiled one of the earliest catalogues of Central European plants and animals, which is a fair patron for a tree in a park built as a botanical showpiece. No age estimate for it exists in any source found: the register that protects it records a species, a position and a date, and has no column for age or girth anywhere in it, so the girth and height here come from a dedicated survey of the island's monument trees.

trees.name: The Willow-Leaved Ash
trees.access: Free, open access, York Museum Gardens (daily, 9am-6pm)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from York railway station
trees.story: At twenty-four metres, the Willow-Leaved Ash is the tallest of six trees in York Museum Gardens officially recognised as Yorkshire county champions, the largest recorded example of its kind anywhere in the county. The Tree Register keeps that list, and this ash earned its place with a trunk that measures three and a half metres round and leaves noticeably narrower than an ordinary ash's, more like a willow's, which is where the name comes from. It was planted sometime in the gardens' first century, when the Yorkshire Philosophical Society was still filling the grounds it had laid out around the ruins of St Mary's Abbey with specimens gathered from across the world. The Tree Register puts its age at the top of the 80 to 150 year range shared by the garden's six champions, and its own crown agrees: the upper branches have started to die back, the way an ash tree typically signals it is entering its final decades. It still stands as one of the most noticeable trees in the garden, tall enough to be seen from most of the surrounding lawns. Visit while the crown holds. A champion tree's title from the Tree Register is a record of what was measured and when, never a promise of permanence.

trees.name: The Cut-Leaved Hornbeam
trees.access: Free, open access, York Museum Gardens (daily, 9am-6pm)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from York railway station
trees.story: The Cut-Leaved Hornbeam's trunk is hollow, its canopy hangs low enough to brush the grass, and the whole tree curls into itself rather than growing straight up, more contorted shrub than the neat street tree hornbeams usually become. That shape earned it a place on the Tree Register's list of Yorkshire county champions, the largest recorded example of its cultivar in the county. Ordinary hornbeam wood is famously hard, historically turned into butchers' blocks and mallets because almost nothing else in an English wood could take that kind of daily battering, and this specimen's finely cut, deeply serrated leaves are the whole reason a gardener chose this cultivar over the plain species when the Yorkshire Philosophical Society was planting out its new grounds around the ruins of St Mary's Abbey in the nineteenth century. In autumn its leaves turn a rich golden brown, and the hollow trunk, rather than weakening the tree, has become one of its most photographed features, a reminder that hollowing out is something old trees do to survive, not a sign they are dying. It stands among the garden's roughly 80 to 150 year old champions, part of a small cluster of record-holding trees inside a single city garden.

trees.name: The Pear-Barked Beech
trees.access: Free, open access, York Museum Gardens (daily, 9am-6pm)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from York railway station

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.story: Halfway up the trunk of this beech, at almost exactly two metres, the bark changes: rough and fissured like a pear tree's below the line, smooth and grey like an ordinary beech's above it. That is because it is not one tree but two, grafted together when the Yorkshire Philosophical Society was filling York Museum Gardens with botanical curiosities, and the join has held long enough that the tree now stands nineteen metres tall with a trunk almost three metres round, one of Yorkshire's six Tree Register champions inside these ten acres. Pear bark grafted onto beech rootstock, or the other way round (records from the planting era do not say which), was the kind of horticultural party trick Victorian garden designers liked to show off, proof that a garden could out-engineer nature as easily as display it. Two centuries on, most visitors walk past the graft line without noticing it is there at all, distracted by the ruins of St Mary's Abbey behind it or the river beyond the lawn. Look for the seam in the bark at head height and the whole two-tree history becomes obvious in a way no plaque could improve on.

trees.name: The Cut-Leaved Alder
trees.access: Free, open access, York Museum Gardens (daily, 9am-6pm)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from York railway station

best_time.label: February and March, when its reddish-purple catkins hang before the leaves appear

trees.story: On the lawn closest to the River Ouse, the Cut-Leaved Alder produces small woody cones through the whole of winter and reddish-purple catkins every spring, and its leaves are cut so finely they read as feathery rather than solid, moving differently in the wind than every ordinary alder nearby. That difference is why the Tree Register lists it as a Yorkshire county champion, one of six inside York Museum Gardens. Alders are river trees by nature, at home in the wet ground the Ouse leaves behind after York's regular floods, and this one has grown to ten metres with a trunk over a metre and a half round without ever leaving the damp lawn it was planted on. Decay has started at its base, the kind of slow hollowing that in most trees signals age rather than danger, and the Yorkshire Philosophical Society's original nineteenth century planting scheme is the likeliest source for a cultivar this particular. Standing at the garden's low point by the water, it is easy to see why this spot was chosen for it: alders do not just tolerate wet feet, they need them, and the Ouse has kept this one fed for the better part of a century and a half.

trees.name: The Elaeagnus-Leaved Pear
trees.access: Free, open access, York Museum Gardens (daily, 9am-6pm)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from York railway station
trees.story: Pyrus elaeagrifolia, the Elaeagnus-Leaved Pear, only reached Britain around 1844, imported from the eastern Mediterranean and Anatolia as a garden curiosity rather than a fruit tree, and York Museum Gardens planted one of the country's earliest examples not long after. It grows at a visibly unusual angle, leaning rather than standing straight, and its narrow, silvery-grey leaves look more like an olive's than a pear's, the resemblance the species name refers to. The Tree Register has measured its girth at over two metres and named it a Yorkshire county champion, the largest recorded example of the species in the county, one of six such champions inside these ten acres beside the ruins of St Mary's Abbey. Its lean has become pronounced enough that York Museums Trust has already taken cuttings, a quiet insurance policy against the day this specific tree eventually comes down, propagating its replacement before the original is gone rather than after. For now it is very much alive and still leaning, one of the garden's 80 to 150 year old champions, an unfamiliar Mediterranean pear still settled at whatever angle its roots have chosen.

trees.name: The Small-Leaved Lime
trees.access: Free, open access, York Museum Gardens (daily, 9am-6pm)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from York railway station

best_time.label: October, when its small heart-shaped leaves turn a clean yellow

trees.story: Tilia cordata, the Small-Leaved Lime, is Britain's only native lime, and in the wild it all but disappears once you travel north of the Midlands, which makes the twenty-five metre example growing in York Museum Gardens an outlier by geography alone before it even earned its Tree Register title. Its trunk measures nearly three metres round, tall and arrow-straight in a garden of stranger, more contorted specimens, and that unusually columnar shape, rather than any historical event, is what put it among the ten-acre garden's six Yorkshire county champions. Small-leaved limes can live for centuries in the wild, some of England's oldest documented trees among them, but the Tree Register's estimate for this specimen sits within the 80 to 150 year range shared by the garden's whole set of champions, planted out after the Yorkshire Philosophical Society began filling the grounds around the ruined St Mary's Abbey in the nineteenth century. Its bright green leaves, heart-shaped and small enough to look almost dainty against its height, turn a clean yellow every autumn. A native tree standing this far outside where its wild relatives usually grow is itself the whole story.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Zuiddijk Cemetery
trees.age: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free, public cemetery grounds, open in daylight.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves come out translucent copper-red

trees.story:
This tree's own file cannot agree with itself about its age. The register's planting band puts it in the 1880s, while the note underneath says the cemetery dates from the early twentieth century and that the copper beech was planted when the cemetery was. Nobody has reconciled the two, so the age here is a range rather than a date, and the later reading would make it younger still.

What is not in doubt is that it was planted as one of a set. The register reckons there were once several copper beeches along the avenues of this burial ground, and five of them still stand further east, listed under a number of their own. This one has the middle of the ground to itself.

A copper beech is a colour mutation of the ordinary green beech. The purple pigment masks the chlorophyll underneath, so the dark form grows a shade less vigorously than a green one and rarely wins a fight in a wood. Nurseries propagate the good ones by grafting, because seedlings are a lottery. Which is to say that almost every large copper beech you meet is somewhere a person decided to put one, and a cemetery avenue was exactly that kind of decision.

You will find it in the middle of the burial ground off the Zuiddijk in Zaandam, open in daylight. Only the national register describes this tree.

trees.name: The Plane of the Westzijde
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, on the public square.
trees.story:
A plane tree handles dirty air by taking its skin off. The bark comes away in irregular plates, carrying the year's soot and grime with it, which leaves the trunk mottled in olive, cream and grey and is the reason this species ended up lining the streets of every industrial city in Europe.

Zaandam was a good place to need that trick. The Zaan district ran first on wind and then on coal: hundreds of mills sawing timber, crushing seed for oil and grinding pigment for paint, and after them the cocoa and biscuit works whose smell still carries across the town on the right wind. The register puts this plane's planting between 1900 and 1910, which sets it down in the middle of all that.

Everything around it has since changed. The register's note on the tree is really a note about its neighbours: the Zaan bank is under heavy development, and this early twentieth-century plane has outlasted those developments for well over a century now. The mills, the wharves and most of what it was planted beside have gone.

Planes are hybrids, oriental plane crossed with American sycamore, and in city terms they are close to indestructible. Cut back to stumps they come again, which is precisely why councils keep planting them. This one stands on the public square at the Westzijde; the pin marks the square rather than the trunk itself.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Kerkbuurt
trees.age: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
trees.access: Free, public planting, always open.
trees.story:
A fungus at the foot of a tree is the last thing to appear, not the first. By the time brackets are showing at the base, the organism has usually been working through the roots and the butt of the trunk for years, and what you can see is only its fruit.

That is roughly the story the register tells here. After a century of standing quietly in the green strip of the Kerkbuurt, this horse chestnut has gone downhill sharply in the last few years, and the inspectors think the heavy fungal growth at its base is the likely reason. They are careful about it: possibly, they write, not certainly.

They put the planting at around 1925, which makes the timing tidy to the point of being irritating. It is faltering at almost exactly a hundred. A horse chestnut does not read as an ancient tree at that age, but a hundred years is a long working life for one standing in a village verge.

Westzaan is a ribbon village strung along a single old road, and the Kerkbuurt is its church quarter. Nothing in the register says this tree is coming down, but one in that condition is worth going to see sooner rather than later. It still flowers white in May and it still drops conkers in autumn.

The national register is the only source that describes it, so if you know its history, tell us.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Dorpsstraat
trees.age: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.access: Free, a small public municipal garden.
trees.story:
One of the most planted trees in Europe is a threatened species in the wild. Aesculus hippocastanum survives naturally in a handful of mountain ravines in Greece, Albania and North Macedonia and nowhere else on earth, which is why the conservation lists rate it vulnerable while millions of them stand along streets from Dublin to Kyiv. It arrived in the west in the sixteenth century by way of Constantinople and Vienna, as a curiosity for rich gardens.

This one grows beside Dorpsstraat 507 in Assendelft, and the house number rewards a second look: the Dorpsstraat runs the whole length of a village that is essentially one very long road laid across the polder. The register puts the tree's planting between 1900 and 1910, so about 120 years, in a strip of municipal garden it has had to itself ever since.

The name is a puzzle you can work on while standing there. Look at the twigs in winter, at the scar where last year's leaf came away: a horseshoe outline with a row of small dots where the nails would sit. Whether that is where the horse in horse chestnut comes from, or whether it comes from the Ottoman habit of dosing broken-winded horses with the seeds, has never been settled.

Nobody recorded who planted this one. The register's history field is blank and no second source mentions the tree at all.

trees.name: The Almez of Parque Bruil
trees.age: Centennial, no exact figure recorded, probably around 150 years
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: About 10 minutes on foot east from Plaza del Pilar, or 5 minutes from Plaza San Miguel. The park entrance is on Calle Asalto.
trees.story: In December 2025 this tree came third in Spain, with 1,799 votes, in a national poll for tree of the year. It was put forward not by the city but by the neighbourhood associations of San Agustin, Tenerias, La Madalena, Las Fuentes and San Miguel, which is a fair description of who actually uses the park. It is a hackberry, called almez or litonero here, fifteen metres tall and just over four metres round at chest height. What it grew up in is the interesting part. Juan Bruil, a Zaragoza banker who was briefly finance minister in 1854, bought the old Augustinian estate here in 1842 and had French gardeners lay out grounds around it. He stocked them with deer, pheasants, swans and monkeys, built an auditorium and commissioned a roller coaster, and let the public in on Sundays. The city did not own the land until 1959, and the park as it stands opened in 1965. The tree has had a harder recent decade than that history suggests: in 2015 residents asked the council to look at it because feet had compacted the soil over its roots, and in 2017 it was fenced. It now looks the better for it.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Parque Bruil
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: About 10 minutes on foot east from Plaza del Pilar. The park entrance is on Calle Asalto.
trees.story: This is the tree the neighbourhood meets at. In February 2012 a public gathering was called with the instruction to meet at the holm oak of Parque Bruil, and the reason was not affection but alarm: work remodelling the park had cut into its root plate and the tree had no protection plan of any kind. Holm oak is the native oak of this dry country, evergreen, small dark leaves furred pale underneath, and it was one of the species Juan Bruil's French gardeners put in when they laid out these grounds after 1842, alongside mulberries and plums and a great deal of imported novelty. The city measured it at two metres forty round at chest height and fourteen metres tall in 2004, which for a species that grows slowly on thin Aragonese soil is a considerable tree. What it has watched is a long argument about who the ground belongs to. It stood in a private garden that opened to the public one day a week, then in an estate the city spent years expropriating, and since 1965 in a public park that has been dug up and rebuilt around it more than once. It is still here.

trees.name: The London Plane of Calle Asalto
trees.access: Free, on the public pavement
trees.transport: On Calle Asalto between Parque Bruil and the Museo de Historia de Zaragoza, about 8 minutes on foot from Plaza San Miguel.
trees.story: The street is named after the thing that happened to it. In February 1809 French troops finally broke into Zaragoza through the medieval wall along this line, ending a second siege that had cost the city tens of thousands of lives and had been conducted, by the end, house by house. A stretch of that wall still stands opposite this tree. The plane itself is two metres eighty round at chest height and seventeen metres tall, growing out of a pavement beside a busy road, and the city's catalogue lists its single reason for protection as size. It carries large pruning stubs where structural branches were taken off, which is what happens to a big tree on a narrow street. London plane is a hybrid that has never been found growing wild, and it became the standard European street tree for one reason: it sheds its bark in plates, and with the bark goes the soot, which mattered enormously in a nineteenth century city and still matters here. Stand with your back to the wall the French came through, and the tree is the older-looking of the two things in front of you.

trees.name: The Yew of the Paraninfo
trees.access: In the grounds of a working university building. Depends on the Paraninfo being open, and needs checking on the ground.
trees.transport: Plaza Basilio Paraiso, at the top of Paseo Independencia, on the tram line through Gran Via.

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.story: There is one yew in Zaragoza's register of singular trees, and this is it. The catalogue gives its reason for protection as the species being very uncommon in the city, which is a polite way of saying that a tree of cool wet northern churchyards has no business in a place that spends August above thirty five degrees. It is thirteen metres tall and one metre twenty round, and it is one of a pair, both male, so neither will ever carry the red berries that yews are known for. What they stand in front of is Ricardo Magdalena's Faculty of Medicine and Sciences, projected in 1886 and inaugurated on 18 October 1893, a building of brick and ceramic in a deliberately Aragonese key that now serves as the university's ceremonial hall, its general library and its natural sciences museum. Local tradition holds that these two yews are survivors of an older botanical garden on this ground, and that would make them older than everything around them. It is a good story and the evidence for it is thin, so treat it as a story. Yews are slow, dense and long lived, and this one is doing something its species is not built for.

trees.name: The Olive of the Facultad de Medicina
trees.access: Free, on the public university campus
trees.transport: Campus San Francisco; tram or bus to Plaza San Francisco, short walk

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.story:
Four metres ninety around at the ground and two metres fifty at chest height, on a tree only five metres tall. That is an olive doing what olives do: pouring everything into a fluted, folded, half-hollow base while the crown stays low enough to pick from a short ladder.

It grows on the University of Zaragoza's San Francisco campus, behind the Facultad de Medicina and the Colegio Mayor Pedro Cerbuna, on ground the city's own ordinance lists as university property rather than municipal. Zaragoza's catalogue of singular trees rated its condition very good when it was surveyed in 2005, and that catalogue is the only source that describes it.

Nobody has dated it, and with an olive nobody easily could. The heartwood rots out of the middle of an old olive and what survives is a ring of living wood that splits into separate strands, so there are no rings left to count and the tree can renew itself from the base more or less indefinitely. Estimates for olives of this shape run from two hundred years to well over a thousand, and a number picked out of that range would be a guess wearing a decimal point.

What the girth does say is that the tree is almost certainly older than the campus around it. This edge of Zaragoza was farmland before the faculties arrived, and an olive that wide was somebody's crop long before it was a specimen.

trees.name: The Honey Locust of Calle Aznar Molina
trees.access: Free, on a public street
trees.transport: Casco Historico, near Parque Bruil; a short walk from the already-published Parque Bruil trees
trees.story:
Somebody took three main branches out of this tree and it became a parasol. The honey locust on Calle Aznar Molina now carries a flat, wide, almost horizontal crown on a short trunk, a shape no honey locust arrives at by itself, and it makes this one of the strangest-looking protected trees in Zaragoza. The city's catalogue records the pruning as plain fact and rated the tree's condition good when it was surveyed in 2005.

Gleditsia triacanthos is North American, from the Mississippi basin, and in its wild form it is armed: branched thorns up to fifteen centimetres long growing straight out of the trunk and the older wood, generally read as a defence against browsing animals that no longer exist on that continent. Street plantings are usually the thornless kind, chosen for the fine doubled leaves that cast a light, moving shade and fall small enough that nobody has to rake them.

It stands in Tenerias, the old tanners' quarter on the edge of the historic centre, three hundred metres from the trees of Parque Bruil, so it joins that walk without a detour. The catalogue is the only source that names it, and it records no age for it.

Stand directly underneath and look up. The flat crown against the sky is the entire point of this tree.

trees.name: The Tree of Heaven of the Jardin Botanico
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Parque Grande; tram to Parque Grande stop, short walk to the botanical garden entrance
trees.story:
Zaragoza protects, as a singular tree, a specimen of the species European cities spend the most money trying to get rid of. Ailanthus altissima was sent to Europe from Beijing by a Jesuit missionary in 1751 and planted as a fast curiosity and a possible host for silkworms. It escaped. It now takes over railway sidings, demolition plots and riverbanks across southern Europe, resprouts from any cut root, releases a compound that suppresses the plants around it, and sits on the European Union's list of invasive species of concern.

This one earned its place by being the best of its kind here. Of the four tree of heaven specimens on the city's register, this is the one rated in very good condition at the 2004 survey: two metres fifty-seven around, fifteen metres seventy tall, standing at the entrance to the botanical garden inside the Parque Grande.

It is a handsome tree when something keeps it in order. The leaves are pinnate and can reach a metre in length, very large for anything hardy in Europe, and in a good summer the female trees hang thick with papery winged seeds that turn from green to a dull red before they go brown.

The catalogue is the only source describing this tree, and it gives no age. What it gives instead is a judgement, and the judgement is that of four candidates this was the one worth keeping.

trees.name: The 1780 Planes of Platzspitz
trees.access: Free, open access, Platzspitz (public park, open at all times)
trees.transport: Zurich Hauptbahnhof (central station), short walk
trees.story: Platzspitz is Zurich's second-oldest public park, laid out on the wedge of land where the Sihl and Limmat rivers meet, and its own conservation survey has tagged its plane trees by planting year with a simple system of coloured markers: brown for 1780, blue for 1806, green for 1836, red for 1960, violet for 2005. The brown-tagged cohort, planted in 1780, includes at least one specimen the city's own gardeners describe as priceless, a tree already a generation old when Napoleon's armies crossed the Rhine, and the park itself has been rebuilt and replanted around it for two centuries since. Platzspitz's own documented history as a public space runs back roughly 450 years, documented in plans and drawings, though little from the earliest layouts survives above ground; the 1780 planes are themselves already part of that long rebuilding rather than an original feature. The tagging system means a visitor with sharp eyes and no guidebook can date individual trees just by checking the colour of the marker at the base, a small piece of park bureaucracy that turns Platzspitz's plane trees into a walkable timeline of Zurich civic gardening since the late 18th century.

trees.name: Alfred Escher's Giant Sequoia
trees.access: Free, open access, Belvoirpark (public park, open at all times)
trees.transport: Tram to Bahnhof Enge or Brunaustrasse, short walk
trees.story: Alfred Escher built modern Switzerland's railway network, founded the bank that became Credit Suisse and the institution now known as ETH Zurich, and by most accounts had almost no time left over for anything else. In 1858, he apparently made an exception: he planted this giant sequoia at Belvoirpark, his family's lakeside estate, to mark the birth of his only daughter, Lydia. The tree has since grown into the oldest confirmed giant sequoia in Zurich, well over 160 years old, a California native that tolerates Central European frost far better than its coastal redwood relatives and can, in its native range, live past 3,000 years, which makes even this Escher-era specimen a relative sapling by the standards of its own species. Belvoirpark itself began as Escher's grandfather's vineyard hillside, purchased in 1826 and planted with what were then exotic North American species around a new villa; the city of Zurich has owned the grounds since 1901, and what was once a private garden for one of the country's most powerful families is now a public park anyone can walk into and stand beneath a tree Escher planted for a child who would have been barely taller than it herself.

trees.name: The Lindens of Lindenhof
trees.access: Free, open access, Lindenhof (public square, open at all times)
trees.transport: Zurich Hauptbahnhof (central station) or Rennweg tram stop, short walk uphill

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.story: Zurich's history is often said to begin on this hilltop, a Roman customs post and later a Carolingian imperial palace, and lindens have been planted here continuously since at least 1474, when a chronicle records 52 trees going into the ground at once. None of those original trees survive; a severe storm in 1861 destroyed much of the historic stand, and an attempt to replace the lindens with other species was rejected by Zurich's own residents so firmly that the substitutes were dug up and replaced with lindens again within 15 years. Most of what grows on Lindenhof today dates from that 1860s-1870s replanting, making the oldest individual trees a little over 150 years old rather than the 500-plus years the site's own name and reputation imply. One tree breaks that pattern in a different direction: in 1971, the year Swiss women finally won the right to vote at the federal level, a new linden was planted here specifically to mark it. Lindenhof's real age is the age of the tradition of replanting it, not any single trunk standing today.

trees.name: The Mammutbaum of Hohlstrasse
trees.access: Visible from Hohlstrasse; stands on private bank premises but directly beside the public street and sidewalk
trees.transport: Zurich Altstetten railway station, short walk
trees.story: This giant sequoia predates the seven-storey bank building that now looms over it by decades, and it nearly lost that seniority battle anyway. Around 2012, plans for the Limmattalbahn, a new tram line through Zurich's Altstetten district, threatened to require felling the roughly 120-year-old tree to make room for the widened road. Julius Baer, the private bank whose Altstetten offices had been built around the sequoia rather than the other way round, spent years in negotiation with the tram line's operators rather than accept the loss, eventually reaching a settlement in which the route was adjusted and the tree kept its ground. It stands today nearly 15 metres tall, still growing on a stretch of Hohlstrasse that has since gone through a full redevelopment masterplan, approved by Zurich's city council in 2026, which explicitly names the sequoia as a feature to preserve rather than remove. A bank saving a tree from a tram line is not the story anyone would predict for one of Zurich's oldest giant sequoias, and it is not the kind of protection any nature reserve or heritage listing arranged. It happened because the people who owned the ground next to it decided the tree was worth the years of negotiation, which is its own kind of durability.

trees.name: The Plane of the Potgietersingel
trees.age: roughly 175 to 225 years, from the register's planting band of 1800 to 1850
trees.access: Free. Public park along the singel, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km northwest of Zwolle station, on the Potgietersingel.
trees.story:
Thirty three point six metres tall, and a trunk seven point one nine metres round. Those are measured numbers, not estimates, which makes this tree the most precisely known thing on this page and one of the largest planes in the Netherlands.

Seven metres of girth means roughly two and a quarter metres of diameter. Four adults with their arms out would not close a circle round it.

It is standing on a defensive earthwork. Zwolle's seventeenth century fortifications were demolished in the nineteenth, as they were in almost every Dutch town, and the earth was reshaped into a ring of singels and parks. So the ground here is made ground, thrown up to stop artillery and then handed to a garden designer, and this plane has had close to two centuries of deep, loose, undisturbed soil that no city street could offer it.

That is most of the explanation for the size. The other part is the species: planes tolerate everything a city can do to them, and given room they simply keep going.

Bark in flaking cream and olive plates, big maple-shaped leaves, and hard bristly seed balls hanging on their stalks all winter.

trees.name: The Beech of the Boschwijk Avenue
trees.age: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.access: Free. Open grounds east of the city.
trees.transport: About 4 km east of Zwolle station, at Park Boschwijk.

best_time.label: early May, when the new leaves make the avenue glow

trees.story:
In 1799 the mayor of Zwolle published a 34 verse poem about this garden.

Rhijnvis Feith owned Boschwijk, a small country house not far outside the city, and he was one of the best known Dutch poets of his generation as well as a magistrate and mayor. He came out here in his free time specifically to write. 'Ode aan Boschwijk' is the result, and it is about this ground.

The beech is banded 1750 to 1800, which means it was somewhere between a sapling and a young tree while he was writing. It stands on the west side of the beukenloofgang, the beech avenue, which is the feature of the place: two rows planted close so the crowns meet overhead and make a green tunnel.

A beech avenue is a designed effect that takes a century to work and then works forever. It is also a slow-motion contest, because beeches planted that close spend their lives shading each other out, so the ones that survive are the ones that got up fastest.

Go in early May, when the new leaves are still translucent green and the tunnel glows rather than darkens.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Park Eekhout
trees.age: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.access: Free. Public park, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 900 m northwest of Zwolle station, in the Park Eekhout.

best_time.label: early May, when the white candles are up and the throats are still yellow

trees.story:
A horse chestnut that has reached a hundred and seventy years is doing better than most of its kind manage now.

The species has had a bad half century in Europe. Bleeding canker, a bacterial infection that leaves rusty weeping patches on the bark, has killed a large share of mature trees since the 1990s. The horse chestnut leaf miner, a moth whose larvae tunnel between the leaf surfaces, arrived in the Netherlands around 2002 and now browns the foliage of nearly every tree in the country from July onward. The moth does not kill, but a tree that loses its leaves two months early every year for twenty years is a weakened tree.

So an old, big, still standing chestnut is worth registering as the survivor it is.

It stands in the southeast part of the Park Eekhout, on the ring of the old fortifications, banded 1850 to 1860.

Come in the first half of May, before the miner gets going. That is when the tree does the thing it was planted for: hundreds of upright white flower spikes over the whole crown, each one with a yellow throat that turns red once the flower has been pollinated and no longer wants visitors.

trees.name: The Red Oak of Boschwijk
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Open grounds east of the city.
trees.transport: About 4 km east of Zwolle station, at Park Boschwijk.

best_time.label: late October, when it goes scarlet

trees.story:
It was planted for one week a year and it delivers.

Red oak is North American, it reached Europe in the seventeenth century, and it was planted across Dutch estates in the nineteenth for a single reason: nothing native here turns that colour. In late October a mature one goes deep scarlet and then rust, and it holds it for a fortnight while the beeches around it are doing their more restrained copper.

The leaves are the easy way to tell it from a native oak. They are much larger, with pointed lobes ending in tiny bristles, where a pedunculate oak has small soft rounded lobes and no bristles anywhere.

This one stands by the drive to number 7 on the west side of Boschwijk, banded 1860 to 1870, so it is a generation younger than the beech in the avenue and belongs to a later phase of planting on the same ground.

The acorns are worth a look too: squat and broad with a shallow saucer of a cup, quite unlike the neat long acorn of a native oak, and they take two years to ripen rather than one.

trees.name: The Gate Beech of the Park Eekhout
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Public park, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 900 m northwest of Zwolle station, at the Park Eekhout.
trees.story:
The register calls these the poortbomen, the gate trees, which is a job description rather than a species.

Planting a pair of matched trees where a path enters a park is one of the oldest moves in the trade. It makes an entrance out of a gap, and it does it without a gate, a wall or a sign. You know you have arrived somewhere because two large trees have agreed to stand opposite each other. On the way out they frame the street.

This beech is one of that pair, banded 1860 to 1870, planted into the park that was made on the city's demolished fortifications.

Beech was the right choice for the role and a slightly cruel one. The species casts denser shade than any other large tree here, so a gate flanked by two of them is genuinely darker than the ground on either side, and stepping through is a change in light as well as in place. That is the effect, and it took a century and a half to mature.

The bark stays smooth and thin all its life, which is why a beech at a park entrance is always the one covered in carved initials.

trees.name: The Copper Beech by the Fountain
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Public square, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 700 m north of Zwolle station, at the Van Nahuysplein.

best_time.label: late October, when it turns burnt copper

trees.story:
A dark tree next to moving water was somebody's decision.

This is a designed pairing and it still works: a copper beech placed to the left of a fountain on a square at the end of the Wilhelminasingel, planted between 1860 and 1870, when the ring of parks on the old fortifications was being finished and the city was arranging its new edges to be looked at.

Purple foliage was a strong colour to have available. Copper beech is a mutation of the common beech, propagated by grafting rather than seed, and in a nineteenth century planting scheme it functioned as the darkest tone on the palette, the thing you put where the composition needed something heavy. Against pale water and spray it does exactly what was intended.

A hundred and sixty years later it is also just a very large tree in the middle of a city, which is worth going to stand under. The canopy on a mature one is dense enough that the ground beneath stays dry in light rain.

In the last week of October it turns from purple to a deep burnt copper and the square changes colour with it.

trees.name: The Oak of the Kranenburg Cemetery
trees.age: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.access: Free. Public cemetery, open in daylight. Visit quietly.
trees.transport: About 4 km northeast of Zwolle station, on the Kranenburgweg.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns cover the ground

trees.story:
It is in the new section, and it is a century and a half old, which tells you something about the scale a cemetery is planned on.

Burial grounds are the best places in a Dutch city to find big trees, and the reason is mechanical rather than sentimental. The ground is never redeveloped, never dug for services, never paved, never parked on, and nobody is in a hurry. A tree planted at the edge of a cemetery in the 1860s has had the single most stable century and a half available anywhere inside a growing city.

Oaks in particular are a standard choice for the setting, for the obvious reason that they outlast everybody in it several times over. Pedunculate oak routinely reaches four hundred years here, so this one is at roughly a third of its life.

It is easy to identify: acorns on long stalks, and leaves that sit almost directly on the twig with two small lobes clasping back around it.

Go in October. An oak this age in a good mast year covers the ground beneath it, and a quiet cemetery is one of the few places nobody sweeps them up.
